# Menivor × Meta Model API — hackathon submission

[Menivor](https://menivor.com) is a live, production AI video-ad/UGC generation
platform (script → TTS → avatar → captions → compose → publish). Its production
codebase is a private monorepo (70-table Postgres schema, real billing, four
client surfaces) — too large and too commercially sensitive to publish wholesale.

This repository is the real, runnable extraction of the specific code built for
the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (hosted with Cerebral Valley): two new
provider adapters that wire Meta's Model API (Muse Image, SAM 3.1) into Menivor's
existing provider-routing architecture, plus their real test suite.

## What's in this repo

- `app/domains/routing/providers/muse_image.py` — real adapter for Muse Image
  (`POST /v1/images/generations` and `/v1/images/edits`, OpenAI-Images-API
  compatible, $0.01/image).
- `app/domains/routing/providers/sam_segment.py` — real adapter for SAM 3.1
  (`POST /v1/responses`, decodes the documented `<|box;...|>` detection grammar
  into bounding boxes for a product-photo cutout).
- `app/domains/routing/base.py` — the generic `ProviderAdapter` protocol +
  `ProviderRegistry` these two adapters implement (copied verbatim from the
  private repo; it is intentionally generic and carries no business data).
- `app/domains/routing/providers/kling_fal.py` — **not** the real Kling/fal.ai
  video adapter (that stays private and is unrelated to this submission); this
  file is trimmed down to just the shared `KlingError` taxonomy class every
  adapter in the real package — including these two — imports and raises.
- `tests/` — the real pytest suite for both adapters, copied verbatim except
  for two tests that exercise the full private provider registry (skipped here
  with a documented reason; they pass unmodified in the real codebase).
- `SUBMISSION.md` — the full hackathon application/submission writeup (track,
  project idea, technical skill, links).
- `DEMO-SCRIPT.md` — the shot-by-shot script for the required 3-minute demo
  video.

## Why this design

Both adapters fail closed with a clearly-labeled `KlingError(kind="auth")` when
`MODEL_API_KEY` is unset, and this repo intentionally never commits a real key
(see `HACKATHON.md` for the current status of real calls/proof artifacts).
Nothing here is mocked or faked: the HTTP protocol, request/response shapes,
pricing, and error taxonomy are all the real, documented Meta Model API wire
format. The moment a real key is set, `muse_generate_image()` and
`sam_segment_image()` make real calls.

See **[`HACKATHON.md`](./HACKATHON.md)** for the exact commit-range boundary
between pre-existing work and this hackathon's Oct 27 – Nov 4 build window.

## Verify it yourself

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests pytest
python3 -m pytest tests/ -q
# 27 passed, 2 skipped
```

## Hackathon window separation

See **[`HACKATHON.md`](./HACKATHON.md)** — it pins the exact `git tag`

# FORGE-0: hackathon work

**FORGE-0 is the verification layer for machine-written code.** AI models now write fixes faster
than maintainers can check them. FORGE-0 sits between the model and your main branch: Muse Spark
proposes explanations for a failing test and a fix, and FORGE-0 makes it prove them. It runs
experiments in an isolated sandbox to rule out the wrong explanations, then has an independent
verifier re-run the whole suite. Only then does a maintainer see anything. **It never opens a pull
request for a patch it hasn't verified.** If no fix survives, it posts its evidence and claims
nothing.

**The evidence:** on Meta Muse Spark 1.3, scored by hidden tests it never saw, **FORGE-0 made 0
false fix claims in 30 runs; a one-shot AI fixer made 2.** Across all 117 benchmark runs on Muse
Spark 1.3 and the open-weights Muse Spark Open, FORGE-0 still made none.

**[Watch the 3-minute demo](https://youtu.be/xHabGt0sN4g)** ·
**[Live Muse Spark pull requests](https://github.com/waleedmustafa971/forge-0-demo/pulls)** ·
**[Open in Codespaces](https://codespaces.new/waleedmustafa971/forge-0-hackathon)**

This repository holds **only the work done during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**
(Indie Developer track, *Push the Frontier*), from kickoff on Oct 26, 2026 onward.

## The problem

AI coding assistants are now fast at writing fixes, but a fix that *looks* right isn't the same as one
that *is* right. When a test fails, an assistant usually takes the first plausible explanation and
writes a patch. If that explanation is wrong, the patch can still make the test pass and break
something else, or fix a symptom while the cause stays. The work then moves to the reviewer, who has
to re-debug the problem to know whether to trust the patch. If the reviewer misses the flaw, a
regression gets merged. After a few of those, the team stops trusting AI fixes at all. For a team that
ships to production, an AI fix nobody can check is a risk, not a saving. What matters is whether the
fixes it claims are right, not how many it claims.

## What a maintainer sees

This happened in [forge-0-demo](https://github.com/waleedmustafa971/forge-0-demo) on Oct 28.

You maintain an order service. At 04:37 UTC an issue comes in:
[*"Quotes still show the old price after a price change"*](https://github.com/waleedmustafa971/forge-0-demo/issues/1).
You label it `forge0` and get back to your own work.

Nine minutes later, a pull request is waiting:
[#4](https://github.com/waleedmustafa971/forge-0-demo/pull/4), written by Muse Spark 1.3 in GitHub
Actions. Before you open the diff, its description tells you:

* **The root cause:** a pricing cache that price updates never invalidate.
* **What else it could have been, and why it isn't:** "the price book doesn't save the new price" and
  "reads and writes go through different instances" were each refuted by experiments run in the
  sandbox.
* **That it holds:** the failing test passes 3 of 3 re-runs on a fresh copy, with 0 regre

# Blindaje

**Community intelligence against extortion in Peru.** Victims keep the evidence they already receive
(WhatsApp voice notes, photos, messages, calls) inside an app disguised as an ordinary business
notebook. Blindaje transcribes it, turns it into comparable signals and finds the cases that come from
the same network: the same voice calling from different numbers, the same account collecting from
different vendors, the same photos and the same script. A person reviews every link. The public only
sees which districts it happens in, never which home.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie track), between October 28 and
November 4, 2026. Every case, voice, number, account and photo in this repository and in the demo is
**fictitious**.

# Nia

**A supervisory safety layer for machines that decide for themselves.** Nia sits between a learned policy and the robot. It checks what the machine is about to do, and what state it is really in, against explicit rules. Under tighten-only authority it can pass the action, substitute a safe fallback, or end the run. Every decision becomes tamper-evident evidence.

Built by [Openwist](https://openwist.com) during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track, 26 October to 4 November 2026).

> **Status: hackathon build, simulation only.** Nia is not a certified safety function and makes no claim of compliance with any standard or regulation. Results below come from a toy environment; results on Meta Motivo are pending (see [Evidence](#evidence)).

> **Test subject and third-party notice.** The humanoid controller in the demo is **Meta Motivo** and the environment is **HumEnv**, both by Meta (FAIR), used under their licence (CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial). They are not part of Nia, are not distributed with it, and were not built by us. Nia contains no Motivo code or weights; the glue code that connects Nia to Motivo lives in `examples/motivo/` and requires you to install Motivo yourself. Nia is not affiliated with or endorsed by Meta. Everything in `src/nia/` was written during the hackathon window.

## In 30 seconds

- **What it is:** a software layer between a learned robot policy and the robot that checks mode, state, commands and data against rules, and can only make the machine safer (pass, substitute a fallback, or hand over). It writes signed, tamper-evident evidence.
- **What it caught (toy environment, 100 held-out runs each):** after a declared-standby mismatch the robot was stopped in 1.8 s, where without Nia it kept walking for 8.2 s until it reached its target; contact after a sensor dropout fell from 84% to 0%; falls after an untrusted unsafe command fell from 100% to 0%; overhead 0.19 ms p99 per step in nominal runs (H-07 first run; 0.16-0.26 ms across scenarios; 0.46 ms re-measured in the second run).
- **What it did not catch (first run):** 4% of policy-fault runs still fall; the second run with TOY-ACT-02 brings H-06 to 0% (see Evidence).
- **What is still pending:** results on Meta Motivo (the humanoid test subject). The glue is written and tested against a fake humanoid; the real run is the next step.
- **Watch it:** `video/Nia_demo_3min_narrated.mp4` (3 minutes, synthetic voice-over; silent cut: `video/Nia_demo_3min.mp4`; built from the real traces, no scripted values).

## Install

```powershell
pip install nia-safety
```

Release 0.1.0 is live at https://pypi.org/project/nia-safety/.

"It is difficult to get the news from poems yet men die miserably every day for lack of what is found there."
William Carlos Williams, physician and poet, in Asphodel, That Greeny Flower (excerpt)
A biopsy is a few cells on a glass slide, and the news is in them. Someone has to be able to read it. In Kenya that someone is scarce: [Brand and colleagues](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6180785) (*Journal of Global Oncology*) report earlier studies putting the country at one pathologist for more than 725,000 people, and, among the public hospitals they surveyed that could do histology, a median wait of about 14 days for a result, with none inside the five days they call suggested. The reading is only one stretch of that wait. The others are the order, the hand-off to a pathologist, the report and its explanation, and those are the ones software can shorten. Tabibu is my answer. It connects patients, doctors and pathologists in Nairobi, in English and Kiswahili, and one record carries a person from booking to result. AI prepares the pathologist's first read, the plain-language explanation and an outbreak alert draft. A qualified person always decides: the pathologist signs, the doctor approves what the patient reads, and an approver releases an alert. **What I claim, and what I do not.** I claim the path: one order that becomes one case, a pathologist who gets a pre-read to check instead of a blank page, and a patient who reads a signed result only once their doctor has talked it through. # BinBuild

**BinBuild scans a bin of loose LEGO and generates new build guides using only the pieces you already own.**

**Built during the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4)** — indie track, with Meta SAM 3.1, Muse Spark, and inventory-constrained BrickGPT.

> Fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the LEGO Group. "LEGO" is a
> trademark of the LEGO Group.

## How it works

1. **Snap a handful** — lay pieces in one flat layer and take a top photo and
   four side photos. A quality gate checks each view.
2. **Review and confirm** — Muse Spark proposes pieces and centre points;
   SAM 3.1 cuts out masks and Spark checks the close-ups. You correct or
   rescan the proposals, then confirm the batch into the running inventory.
3. **Repeat until "Finished"** — sweep pieces aside and scan the next handful.
4. **Ask for a build** — Muse Wonder offers up to three ideas using supported,
   confirmed pieces. Each preview passes the placement and inventory checks;
   Spark can write the words for a step-by-step booklet. The kit's booklets
   remain available too.

BrickGPT's separate, pre-generated designs use eight plain brick types: 1×1,
1×2, 1×4, 1×6, 1×8, 2×2, 2×4, and 2×6. Wonder supports additional known
part shapes; unknown and unsupported pieces remain in the inventory but cannot
be used as exact placements until they can be identified and represented.

Related work: BrickWright (Pun et al., 2026) generates LEGO builds with LLM agents in a plan-execute-validate loop — the same paradigm as our Wonder designer + validator; we add the inventory constraint (builds limited to exactly the pieces you own). [arXiv:2610.31651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31651)

# Pharmacy Stock Agent

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26, 12:00 PM ET kickoff to Nov 4, 9:00 PM ET, 2026). Every commit in this repo was made during the event. See `BUILT_DURING_EVENT.md`.

A pharmacist photographs a shelf or an opened delivery carton. The agent:

1. finds every pack in the photo with **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`, prompt "medicine box"),
2. reads each numbered pack region with **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) into a strict JSON schema: name, strength, pack size, lot and expiry,
3. matches each pack to the catalog, and sends anything doubtful (low confidence, unreadable lot or expiry, strength mismatch) to a human instead of guessing,
4. flags expired and near-expiry packs (90 days by default; printed MM/YYYY means end of that month),
5. proposes stock changes (receive a delivery, quarantine expired lots) that do nothing until a pharmacist approves them by name, with an audit log,
6. drafts a restock order per supplier from par levels and reorder points. Expired stock does not count. The order is a draft and nothing is sent.

You can run each step yourself, or give the **agent** a goal and let it choose the steps (see [Agent mode](#agent-mode-tool-calling)).

## Ground rules
- **Synthetic data only.** The catalog, makers, suppliers, lots, barcodes (200- in-store prefix) and photos are fictional and generated by `scripts/make_samples.py`.
- **No clinical or substitution advice.** The schema has no fields for uses, doses or alternatives. A deterministic guard (`src/safety/guard.js`, English and Arabic patterns) refuses such questions and blocks any draft that drifts into them. A poor match is never mapped to a "close" product.
- A pharmacist approves every stock change and every order.

## Setup and run
Requires **Node.js 20 or later** (`node --version`). There are no npm dependencies, so there is nothing to install. Python 3 with Pillow is only needed to regenerate the sample photos (`npm run samples`).

```bash
git clone <this repo> pharmacy-stock-agent && cd pharmacy-stock-agent
npm test                      # 53 tests, all offline
npm run check                 # build check: JS syntax, JSON data, zero dependencies
npm run demo                  # end-to-end CLI run on the synthetic photos (replay provider)
AS_OF=2026-10-27 npm run web  # web UI on http://127.0.0.1:8787
```

`AS_OF` pins "today" so the expiry flags in the demo match the recorded sample photos. Without it the real date is used. `PORT` and `HOST` change where the web UI listens (default `127.0.0.1:8787`, local only). Stock, review queue, approvals and the audit log are kept in `state/` (git-ignored); set `STOCK_STATE_DIR` to use another folder, or click **Reset demo data** in the footer.

### CLI
```bash
node src/cli.js reset
node src/cli.js shelf samples/shelf-01.png --as-of 2026-10-27
node src/cli.js delivery samples/delivery-01.png --as-of 2026-10-27
node src/cli.js pending
node src/cli.js approve CS-001 --by "Demo Pharmacist"
node src/cli.js e

# Tomorrow Lens

**Photograph your week. Get a plan where every date is proven, and that rebuilds itself when you miss something.**

**Live:** [tmrw-lens.vercel.app](https://tmrw-lens.vercel.app) · Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon
(track: Build for Your World), Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026, solo with AI coding assistance. Everything here was built in
the hackathon window ([HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md)).

## Try it in 10 seconds

Open the live site and press **Try a missed session**. A made-up week plays: a study session passes undone, the
student replies "too tired tonight", Muse Spark works out what to move (you see each tool call), the session glides to
its new slot, and the one recovery text arrives: _"Moved Calc practice to 7:30am tomorrow because you said tonight is
out and the quiz is tomorrow morning. Nothing else changed."_ Recorded runs are free; type your own reply to run it
live.

Then press **Try the sample week** (free, instant) or upload your own syllabus, Testudo schedule, whiteboard photo, or
notes. Tap any item for its proof: the photo crop, SAM 3.1's outline, the exact words, and the date math.

## How Meta's models are used

- **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`, Standard mode) reads every page and photo into structured items, each with an exact
  quote and a box; re-reads each quote from a crop of where it says it found it; classifies texted photos; and runs the
  **rebuild agent**, a tool-calling loop (`get_day`, `find_open_time`, `move_item`, `drop_item`, `propose_diff`) that
  decides what moves when a session is missed and why.
- **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) outlines each sticky note, sheet, and whiteboard in a photo, so every line is tied to the
  object it's written on, re-read from that object's crop, and highlighted on it.

## Models propose, code verifies

The model reads; code computes and checks. Nothing reaches the plan on the model's word alone:

- Every field must appear inside its exact quote, and every quote must be read back from its own crop by a second,
  independent call.
- Dates, weekdays, times, "Week 7 Thu", "the day after Quiz 3", class recurrences, breaks, and daylight saving are
  computed in code (Luxon), never by the model. Every date traces to a quote plus a computation.
- Sources that disagree (the syllabus says Fri, the whiteboard says "moved to Mon") are never merged silently: one
  question, the likely answer pre-selected with its reason, applied only when the person answers.
- Anything unproven stays amber ("Needs a look") and is never sent to Tomorrow until the person confirms it.
- In a rebuild, code computes free time, refuses any move that doesn't fit, and writes the message from the agent's
  reasons; a check runs on the finished plan before it can leave Lens.

# Environment Protocol v0 — reference implementation: Apathy-Refusal (commerce)

**Team:** Pistis Sophia · **Track:** Indie · **Problem statement:** Push the Frontier
**Event:** Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026

A standard interface between reasoning agents and the world they act on,
such that **no agent claim becomes a world fact without measurement**. MCP
standardized how agents call tools. This standardizes the verification of
what agents claim.

## The protocol

An **environment** is a runtime construct standing between an agent (the
**tenant**) and the world, with six components:

1. **Principal** — the party on whose behalf the environment holds the
   line (customer, patient, polity).
2. **Mandate** — the principal's instructions in exact, checkable form.
   The tenant cannot edit it. A mandate without a positive bound is
   malformed.
3. **Claims** — typed so that assertion and measurement are different
   fields. A claim carries what the tenant asserts; the measurement is
   filled by instruments, never by the tenant.
4. **Instruments and gates** — stricter than the claimant. Every claim
   passes a gate; an unmeasured claim refuses automatically (complete
   mediation, fail-safe defaults).
5. **Assets under seal** — move only on a pass, exactly once, within the
   mandate's bounds.
6. **Receipts** — append-only, hash-chained, replayable by anyone. The
   record is the disclosure.

**Invariants:** mandate sovereignty · measurement before movement · named
refusal (a refusal that cannot name its reason cannot be constructed) · a
record the tenant cannot rewrite · two-sided measurement (counterparties
measured by the same rule) · tenant replaceability (any kernel inside;
the line holds the same).

**Protocol messages.** Four message types, in order:
**claim → measurement → verdict → receipt**. A verdict is one of *pass*,
*refuse* (named reason), or *ambiguous* (undecidable on current
instruments — recorded, never silently resolved). Every verdict emits a
receipt; receipts chain. *Conformance:* the reference implementation maps
undecidable to a named refusal — where instruments cannot decide, the
gate refuses on weak measurement rather than emitting a third verdict.
Ambiguous therefore exists in the protocol as a measurement state; in
this implementation it is always resolved to refuse-with-reason.

**Profiles.** Named policy bundles over the core protocol: Apathy-Refusal
(truth: *was it measured?*), Honesty-Mandate (lawfulness), Custody
(loyalty), Consent (authorization), Provenance (origin), Deliberation
(judgment), Calibration (trust over time), Commons (collective effects),
Apprenticeship (growth), Gauntlet (robustness). Profiles compose as a
stack. **This repository implements one profile — Apathy-Refusal — in one
domain: commerce.**

**Conformance.** An environment passes the way a network stack passes —
by surviving the suite: the *drift test* (asserted ≠ measured → refuse),
the *unmeasured test* (no instrument

# Second Seat

## Founder story

I'm a solo founder running Mo'ja Liquor and Loving Grace Technologies. There are days when I need to be in three different meetings at the exact same time. I can't clone myself, but I can build an AI twin to sit in the second seat.

Second Seat is my answer to the solo founder's paradox: how to scale your time without sacrificing your privacy or your voice. Today, it is a scripted meeting room where my AI twin attends, and I can guide it live or take over instantly. It keeps an evidence record of the session, masks sensitive details, and drafts the follow-up. It checks the draft against an imported email draft. I review and approve the exact package, and it sends through a test path.

It doesn't join live calls yet, and it doesn't send real emails yet. That is the vision. But what is built right now is the safety layer: an AI twin that protects your data and keeps you in the final seat. Changes were reviewed by independent AI reviewers and checked by automated tests, with the results documented in the repo.

## What it does

Vendor calls are where people agree to things they never meant to agree to. Second Seat works in two places: during a meeting, a scripted offline twin sits in the second seat on synthetic data while you guide it or take over, with no model calls; after the meeting, the transcript workflow below turns your pasted meeting text into a cited brief. In the transcript workflow (`/session`), you paste the meeting text. When Live mode is separately configured (see "How to run"), Glimmer, self-hosted on a Modal GPU that is deployed only for owner-run sessions, masks the personal details first. You check and approve that redacted text. Only then does Spark write a short brief where every line cites the part of the meeting it came from: what was offered, what was asked, what needs a decision, and where someone leaned on you. In the default Offline mode, deterministic local code does the masking and the brief, and no model is called. You edit a reply, approve that exact text, and copy it out yourself.

In the current scripted and public demo, Second Seat does not send a real reply or message to the vendor, does not send real email, and does not join real calls. # muse-guard

**Resolve the policy. Check the code.** When requirements clash, muse-guard shows exactly where, you decide which rule wins, Meta's coding agent implements it, and an independent checker verifies it.

**[Try the live page →](https://jeshwanthsingh--muse-guard-live-web.us-east.modal.run/)**

![The muse-guard live page: a landing section with four steps and a Try the example button](docs/img/live-landing-1280.png)

*Screenshot of the live page at 1280×720.*

**Results** (completed study, 160 pre-registered runs):

- 0/77 contradicted "done" claims in each mode.
- Recovery after one decision: 39/40 plain, 40/40 guarded. Not a proven advantage.
- About +2% cost overhead for guarded mode (+9% coding steps). Zero-count measures are a null result. [How we measured](docs/MEASURED_RESULTS.md)

**How it works**

1. **Requirements:** plain-English rules, each quoted from its source sentence.
2. **Clash found:** an exhaustive search lists every declared input where the rules disagree.
3. **You decide:** you pick which rule wins.
4. **Checked code:** Muse Code implements the approved rules, and an independent checker verifies them.

muse-guard finds every conflicting action among the confirmed rules and declared inputs, then independently checks the fix against every input in the approved rule table.

Requirements can contradict each other even when each sentence sounds reasonable.
A coding agent may stop, guess which rule matters, or claim a fix that misses the real requirement.
muse-guard makes the clash explicit, lets the developer decide, and checks the result independently.

```text
Spec → Clash found → You decide → Muse Code repairs → Independent checks
```

Muse Spark proposes rules from English and explains clashes. A deterministic checker verifies conflicts over a small finite input space; the developer confirms the translation and chooses the winning rule. Muse Code writes and repairs code, then a separate checker runs visible and hidden checks. The submission command now connects spec review, a developer decision, approved v2, Muse Code implementation and independent recheck in one record and page.

# AutoLab

**An autonomous AI lab for materials discovery, built on Meta models.**

AutoLab is an AI agent that searches for **new materials for industry**. A researcher states a goal in plain language; a Meta language model proposes chemical substitutions in known crystals, the code builds the crystals, UMA (Meta FAIR) simulates them, scientific filters judge them, and every failure, with the measured numbers, goes back to the model, which explains it and corrects its next proposals. It is applied today to three battery challenges: **lithium solid electrolytes, cobalt-free cathodes and sodium solid electrolytes**.

> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), track *Push the Frontier*, Indie category. All code in this repository was written during the hackathon.

▶ **Demo video (3 min):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D2gCMGV8dIU

---

## What AutoLab does

Industry needs new materials, and finding one means searching a huge chemical space where every property is costly to evaluate. AutoLab automates the scientific loop of a computational materials lab: hypothesis, simulation, measurement, analysis of what failed, new hypothesis. A researcher states a goal in plain language and follows the agent at work, step by step, until a final report with ranked finalists, their numbers and the agent's reasoning.

It is applied today to **three battery challenges**: lithium solid electrolytes, cobalt-free cathodes and sodium solid electrolytes. A new challenge is a new domain module; the loop, the agents and the interface stay the same.

## How it works

```
Goal (plain language)
   │
   ▼
Muse Spark ── proposes chemical substitutions in known crystals of the domain, with a hypothesis
   │
   ▼
Fast funnel, every candidate
   ├─ pymatgen: charge-neutral crystal structures, several arrangements each
   ├─ UMA (Meta FAIR): relaxation and energies
   ├─ stability: energy above the convex hull of the known phases, with a UMA-vs-DFT error bar
   └─ the domain's rules (e.g. electronic insulation, no cobalt, lithium that can leave the crystal)
   │
   ▼
Slow tests, inside each round: the domain's measurements (contact with the metal anode, ion diffusion
by molecular dynamics, voltage and capacity...) and an independent review of each candidate (Muse Spark Open)
   │
   ▼
Feedback: every failure goes back with its measured numbers
   │
   ▼
Muse Spark ── a hypothesis on each failure's cause + a correction ── next round
   │
   ▼
Final stages: ranking, band gap of the champion (electrolytes), literature check (web search, with a known control),
final report with the finalists
   │
   ▼
Muse Wonder ── reads the whole campaign at once: what it taught, what worked, what failed,
               and the next campaign to run
```

The code measures and decides; the models propose, explain and report. The cause of a failure is the model's hypothesis and is always labelled as one. Thresholds come from `autolab/config.py`, never from the mod

Evidomo turns a real estate agent's raw property photos and voice walkthrough into a verified, publication-ready listing pack in the buyer's language. Every factual claim in the pack links to the evidence it came from: a form field, a moment in the recording, or a region of a photo. A claim without a source does not get through, and that rule is enforced in code, not by a prompt. It is built for independent agents and small offices selling residential resale properties (apartments and houses). The agent captures photos and a walkthrough on site from a phone, confirms the facts, and reviews the result at two human gates. Evidomo never gives valuations or legal advice, never publishes to portals, and never hides defects. ![Evidomo: evidence for every home](apps/web/public/og-en.png) > **Hackathon project.** Evidomo was built from scratch during the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon) (October 26 – November 4, 2026). All code in this repository was written during the event. ## How it works 1. **Capture.** Take photos and record a voice walkthrough in the browser, or upload existing files. Photos are downscaled in the browser and stripped of metadata (including GPS) on upload. 2. **Confirm facts.** A structured form, generated from the selected market profile, is the source of truth. 3. **Run.** The service transcribes the walkthrough, extracts candidate facts, inventories the photos, and reconciles everything into a Verified Fact Sheet. 4. **Gate 1: resolve conflicts.** When the sources contradict each other (the form says 1986, the recording says 1987), the run stops until the agent decides. 5. **Generate and verify.** Listing copy and buyer Q&A are written, virtual staging variants are created and structurally checked, and a claim audit runs over the text. 6. **Gate 2: review.** The agent approves, edits, or removes every flagged claim and approves each staged image next to its original. 7. **Export.** A print-ready HTML pack (use the browser's "Save as PDF") and a structured portal-fields JSON file. ### What makes it different - **Every claim cites its source.** The creative step returns copy as segments `{ text, fact_ids[] }`. # NOA Guardian

Asistente de seguridad personal e inteligencia cívica. El proyecto actual usa **Angular** en `apps/web`, **NestJS** para el Dock en `apps/dock` y contratos TypeScript compartidos en `packages/contracts`.

- **Guardian:** alertas de fuentes oficiales NWS, USGS y NASA EONET; lecturas de USGS Water. AirNow y PennDOT declaran su estado y el acceso pendiente cuando no están configurados. El orbe solo anuncia «All clear — verified» cuando las alertas fueron consultadas y todas las fuentes configuradas están verificadas. El mapa Leaflet usa teselas oscuras de Esri, atribución visible y el mismo punto de consulta de alertas; no inventa incidentes ni coordenadas. La verificación visual del mapa en el servidor de desarrollo sigue pendiente.
- **Citizen:** respuestas extractivas desde el corpus de fuentes oficiales, con citas verificadas y jurisdicción. Se abstiene si los fragmentos recuperados no respaldan una respuesta.
- **Awareness:** análisis de imágenes mediante `/see`, con presencia de personas, objetos y riesgos; sin identificar personas. Las salidas del modelo se validan antes de mostrarlas. SAM 3.1 sigue pendiente de integración.
- **Fail-closed:** autenticación del Dock, límites de uso, validación de entradas y estados explícitos ante fallos. Una fuente caída o una consulta sin verificar no se presenta como calma confirmada. El emparejamiento muestra una huella del token para comparar dispositivos.

El Dock usa el puerto 3000 y Angular el 4200. En el teléfono, configura en Session la dirección accesible del Dock y el token local. El proyecto Android Capacitor está en `apps/web/android`; consulta [COMPILAR-APK.md](COMPILAR-APK.md).

# PetSafe Plants

**Beyond plant identification: AI-powered investigation with source-backed pet toxicity information.**

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** · Indie Developer · *Build for Your World*.

PetSafe Plants was inspired by my cat Misho, who became ill after drinking water from a vase containing lilies. A photograph can contain several overlapping plants; identifying the most obvious flower does not mean every plant has been identified.

PetSafe Plants analyzes the full photograph, examines difficult regions when useful, and matches candidate plant identities to a curated veterinary toxicity reference database. **The AI does not generate toxicity classifications.**

## How it works

1. **Meta Muse Spark** assesses the full image, proposes plant identities, and reports uncertainty.
2. **Meta SAM 3.1** optionally segments overlapping or uncertain plant regions.
3. **Muse Spark** reassesses selected crops; the application combines findings while preserving unresolved identities.
4. **Local taxonomic and toxicity lookup** links candidate taxa to source-backed information for cats and dogs.

Simple scenes can skip segmentation to reduce unnecessary API calls. The web interface visualizes real investigation stages and extracted SAM specimens.

> **Important:** Visual identification can be incorrect or incomplete. A `non_toxic` reference classification does not guarantee safety. PetSafe Plants is not veterinary advice. If exposure is suspected, contact a veterinarian promptly.

## Run locally

**Requirements:** Git, Docker Engine with Docker Compose, and a Meta Model API key with access to the required models. Model calls may incur charges.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vmirchev/petsafe-plants.git
cd petsafe-plants
cp .env.example .env
mkdir -p local-models
```

Edit `.env` and set:

```dotenv
MODEL_API_KEY=your-meta-model-api-key
PETSAFE_RUNS_HOST_DIR=./local-models
PETSAFE_APP_ENV=development
```

Start the application:

```bash
docker compose up --build -d api
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:8000/** and upload a photo or select a built-in sample. The first Docker build may be large because it installs ML dependencies. The `local-models/` folder can remain empty: **the main Muse Spark + SAM investigation does not require trained model weights**.

```bash
docker compose logs -f api   # View logs
docker compose down          # Stop the app (preserves named volumes)
```

### Optional: Admin controls

To enable `/admin`, set `PETSAFE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and `PETSAFE_SESSION_SECRET` in `.env`. Generate a session secret with `openssl rand -hex 32`, then recreate the container:

```bash
docker compose up -d --force-recreate api
```

The admin page shows API usage and can disable new Meta calls or change the combined rolling 24-hour call limit. Limits and counters persist in SQLite. Call quotas are **not** exact dollar-spending caps.

### Optional: DINOv3 comparison

The **`/compare.html`** page also uses a trained Meta DINOv3

# Stall

A small shop's whole business, run inside WhatsApp. My entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. Startup track, theme: Build for Your World.

I build software for small businesses. The sellers I work with run their shops on WhatsApp and on memory: prices in their heads, stock counted by eye, orders scattered across chats. They are never going to learn a dashboard, and most of them should never have to create accounts or connect anything to start selling. So Stall meets them where they already are: inside the chat they already use, on one shared number, with no app to install and nothing new to learn.

Calling it a sales agent undersells it. Stall is the stall itself: it holds the goods, greets the customers, sells and haggles, takes the money and proves it landed, arranges how the goods reach the buyer, and keeps the day's records. The merchant just answers her phone.

## How buying works

Every shop on Stall has its own code and its own link on the one shared number. A customer who arrives by a link lands in that shop. A customer who arrives with no code is not turned away: she says what she is looking for, and Stall checks every shop for it, shows her what exists and what it costs, and takes her into the right shop when she picks one.

Inside the shop, the customer browses the real catalogue, sees the product's own photos, and haggles the way traders haggle. The agent moves between the list price and the last price the merchant set, and never crosses it. A merchant can also mark a product fixed price, and then it is quoted as fixed and never haggled. Each shop has a daily giveaway allowance, so the day's discounts come out of one pot the merchant controls, and concessions get smaller as the pot drains.

When a price is agreed, the agent settles how the goods will reach her: delivery, her own pickup, a meet-up, or somebody she sends to collect. It takes the name for the package and any message she wants the seller to see, then reads the whole order back to her with Yes and Change buttons before any money moves. The delivery fee is a separate purse: the buyer pays it to the rider when the goods reach her, unless the merchant has chosen to take the delivery money herself, in which case it sits inside the total. Which way it goes is the merchant's setting. Only her yes produces the payment link, a MoMo checkout through Seev. When she says she has paid, the agent checks with Seev itself and confirms to both sides; the merchant is never asked to verify a payment she cannot see. Seev settles link money to the shop's own MoMo the next day by itself. Stall has no escrow and holds no one's money, and it does not pretend otherwise. If a link dies before she pays, the agent mints a fresh one instead of leaving her stuck, and an unpaid order is checked against Seev again before anyone is reminded about it.

# PermitZero

> **Authority before action.** A zero-trust action firewall that intercepts every consequential tool call made by AI agents, binds it to a tenant, identity, task, policy version and exact argument hash, then allows, denies, queues for human approval, or safely halts the action before a connector can execute it.

PermitZero is a runtime authorization and transaction-control plane for agentic AI, built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (startup track). Finance execution is **simulated** — there are no real bank transfers, custody, private keys, or live payment rails. Performance, compliance, and security claims are **not certified** and require independent validation.

---

## For the judge: sixty seconds, then the evidence

**The one-line bet.** An AI agent with a payment tool should not be able to spend
money because a language model thought it was fine. PermitZero puts a
deterministic, tenant-scoped, tamper-evident authorization plane between the agent
and the connector: the model advises, policy decides, a human can be required, and
every step is written to a hash-chained audit log the database itself enforces.

**Run it.**

```bash
npm ci && cp .env.example .env
npm run db:migrate && npm run db:seed   # synthetic tenant, model provider disabled
npm run dev                             # API :8080, console :3000, worker
npm run demo:scenario                   # allow / deny / approval, end to end
```

**What one decision looks like.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent (untrusted)
    participant API as API :8080
    participant P as Policy PDP
    participant M as Meta model (optional)
    participant DB as Postgres (RLS, hash chain)
    participant B as Broker → simulated connector
    A->>API: POST /v1/actions (token, task, tool, exact args, idempotency key)
    API->>DB: tenant-blind credential lookup, then resolve principal in that tenant
    API->>DB: pin the published policy revision (a version, not "latest")
    opt model configured
        API->>M: bounded, redacted risk-hints request (json_schema + Zod revalidation)
        M-->>API: hints, or none — a missing hint is never treated as safe
    end
    API->>P: evaluate(pinned revision, facts, hints)
    P->>DB: append decision to the tenant's audit chain (one tx: action + audit + outbox)
    alt ALLOW
        API-->>A: signed permit (TTL, nonce, argument hash, policy revision)
        A->>B: execute with the narrowly scoped permit
        B->>DB: broker re-verifies hash, TTL, nonce and revision before the connector runs
    else DENY or REQUIRE_APPROVAL
        API-->>A: terminal answer, or a two-of-N human approval that expires
    end
```

Required Notice: Copyright (c) 2026 hackall360. All Rights Reserved for Commercial Use.
https://polyformproject.org/licenses/noncommercial/1.0.0

![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.14.0-blue)
![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/dev.py_check-passing-brightgreen)
![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12%2B-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)
![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-0.162.0-009688?logo=fastapi&logoColor=white)
![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/docker-required-2496ED?logo=docker&logoColor=white)
![Muse](https://img.shields.io/badge/Muse-Spark_%2F_Wonder-8B5CF6)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm--Noncommercial-lightgrey)
![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-hackathon_edition-orange)

> An autonomous purple-team CI/CD pipeline that uses Meta Muse to write security patches, and air-gapped Docker to cryptographically prove they work.

A tool that finds a weak spot in code, fixes it, and proves the fix works. This page takes about 3 minutes to read.

## What it is

The tool runs a loop with two AI agents and a locked box.

1. A **red team** agent reads the code and finds a weak spot.
2. Red writes a small test (a "probe") that tries to reach that weak spot.
3. A **sandbox** runs the probe. The sandbox is a Docker container with no network.
   Exit 0 means the weak spot was reached. Exit 1 means it was blocked. Exit 2 means unclear.
4. A **blue team** agent writes a small patch to fix the weak spot.
5. Normal-input checks run, then the probe runs again on the patched code.
6. Only if the probe now fails (exit 1) and the normal checks still pass, the result is marked **verified**.

Containers and networks are removed when the run ends.

## Quick start

You need Python 3.12+, Docker, and a Meta Muse API key.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python scripts/dev/dev.py setup   # install dependencies
cp example.env .env                          # then put your key in META_MUSE_API_KEY
.venv/bin/python main.py --init-images       # build the sandbox images
.venv/bin/python main.py --serve             # dashboard at http://localhost:8000/web/
```

Other useful commands:

```bash
.venv/bin/python main.py --help              # all options
.venv/bin/python main.py --list-targets      # bundled practice targets
.venv/bin/python scripts/dev/dev.py check    # run the test gate
```

## Fast demo

```bash
.venv/bin/python demo_run.py
```

No arguments. It pulls the public practice app `BrenesRM/insecure-web` at commit `5d1b791` and runs the full loop.

One measured run:

- Found: SQL injection in `POST /login`.
- Probe exit 0 before the patch, exit 1 after the patch.
- Status: `verified`.
- Time: 4:16. Cost: $0.0070.
- The wrapper prints a labelled heartbeat every 5 seconds. The longest gap with no output was 6 seconds.

Be honest with yourself about this demo. The AI is not deterministic. In 4 runs on the same day, 2 were verified, 1 was inconclusive

# 9-Point Hallucination Calibration (9 PHC)

A post-research audit program. Paste in a finished piece of AI-assisted research — a draft, a report, a set of claims with citations. 9 PHC extracts every checkable claim, runs each one through nine verification checks, and returns a verdict report: every claim **Verified**, **Corrected**, or **Held — unverified**, with receipts.

It is not a detector (it does not guess whether AI wrote something) and it is not a guardrail (it does not block output). It audits what was said, fixes what is wrong, and shows the receipts.

## Where 9 PHC sits — the three tiers of truth constraint

1. **Architecture** — truth constraints baked into a model's under-architecture during design and training. The governing layer.
2. **Guard rails and seat belts** — constraints on the outside of the architecture, around generation and output.
3. **9 PHC** — the processor program on top: an in-depth research audit for researchers who want the facts checked before the work carries their name.

9 PHC's builder does not build models, so tiers 1 and 2 are not his to give. Tier 3 strengthens both: it works on any model's output, and it works best on models whose own tiers lean toward truth, because every layer then leans the same way.

## The nine checks

1. **Source existence** — every cited book, record, page, and identifier must be shown to exist.
2. **Source fidelity** — the cited source, opened, must say what the claim says it says, at the place cited.
3. **Alias sweep** — the subject is searched under every other name it carries: alternate titles, incipits, catalogue labels, nicknames.
4. **Right-level check** — a claim is verified at the level it lives at (a claim about a composition against the composition's record, not only the nearest object's).
5. **Secondary sweep** — later works that cite the source are checked; they often name an edition or a correction in a single line.
6. **Own-files sweep** — the user's own prior files and outputs are searched for anything that contradicts the claim.
7. **Numbers recomputed** — every count, total, and figure is rebuilt from the underlying items, three times. The three runs must agree. *(Deterministic code — no model.)*
8. **Names and IDs letter-checked** — every name, DOI, and identifier is verified character by character against its source. *(Deterministic code — no model.)*
9. **Adversarial pass** — a separate audit instance that did not produce the answer, running in a fresh context with a debunk mandate, tries to kill each surviving claim from outside sources.

**The independence rule:** the adversarial pass never shares a session or context with the work being audited. A model grading its own homework in the same conversation satisfies nothing.

## Source standard

Peer-reviewed sources and primary records only. A claim is Verified or Corrected on the strength of a peer-reviewed source or a primary record (the cited source itself, opened; an official catalogue or record) — or it

# MAYA

MAYA is an AI security agent for sites and apps you own. You connect a target, prove you own it, and MAYA runs safe, non-destructive checks. It produces an evidence-backed report: which vulnerability, on which page, at what severity, with proof. It explains each finding in plain language and proposes a patch that a human must approve. After the patch is applied, MAYA re-runs the same check to prove the issue is fixed.

All code in this repository was written during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 Oct to 4 Nov 2026). A private prototype existed before the event, but none of its code was reused here.

# Pesa Recon Agent

An AI agent that reconciles a Kenyan small business's M-Pesa, bank and paper records, and explains every mismatch in plain language.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). All work in this repository was created during the hackathon.

---

## The problem

Most Kenyan small businesses get paid through M-Pesa, bank in at least one bank, and still keep some records on paper. At the end of each month, someone has to line these up by hand in a spreadsheet:

- Which customer payments arrived, and which are still owed?
- Which M-Pesa withdrawals match a bank deposit?
- What is this unexplained KES 4,500?

It takes hours, mistakes slip through, and many owners skip it entirely. They then can't see their real cash position, spot theft or errors, or show clean records to a lender.

## What Pesa Recon does

1. **Takes in records** from three sources:
   - M-Pesa statements (PDF or CSV)
   - Bank statements or exports
   - Photos of receipts, invoices and handwritten ledgers
2. **Turns them into one clean list of transactions**, each with an amount, date, counterparty, reference and source.
3. **Matches transactions across sources**, automatically where it's certain.
4. **Investigates what it can't match**, and decides what each mismatch most likely is.
5. **Explains every result** in plain language, with the evidence behind it.
6. **Answers the owner's questions**, such as "Who still owes me from October?" or "Why is my bank balance KES 12,000 lower than M-Pesa says?"

## How the matching works

Reconciliation runs in three passes, from strictest to most judgment-based.

### Pass 1: Exact matches
Same amount, same reference or transaction code, dates within the allowed window. These are matched automatically and marked **Confirmed**.

### Pass 2: Tolerant matches
Records that almost line up:

- **Date window:** an M-Pesa-to-bank transfer can land 1–3 days later.
- **Fee differences:** the amounts differ by a known transaction charge or withdrawal fee.
- **Split or combined payments:** one invoice paid in two instalments, or one transfer covering several invoices.
- **Name variations:** "JOHN KAMAU" on M-Pesa vs "J. Kamau" on an invoice.

These are matched and marked **Likely**, with the reason shown.

### Pass 3: Agent investigation
Whatever is left goes to the agent, which reasons about each item like an accountant would:

- A payment from an unknown number that matches an open invoice's amount, sent by a relative or employee of the customer.
- A misspelt or missing account reference.
- A duplicate entry that appears in two sources.
- A paper receipt with no digital record at all.

For each item the agent either proposes a match with its reasoning, or classifies it as a discrepancy. Nothing it proposes is final until the owner approves it.

## Discrepancy types

| Type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Unpaid | An invoice or receipt with no matching payment |
| Unrecorded income | Money received with no invoice

# CallReader

**An agent that reads open calls — contests, grants, hackathons — and only tells you what it can quote.**

Built from scratch during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (build window Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026). No code predates the event.

## Why

I have read hundreds of open calls to decide which ones were worth a week of work. The expensive mistakes were never about prize size. They were:

- the AI ban that lived only inside the attached PDF, not on the page;
- a summary that kept the verdict ("AI allowed") and dropped the clause that governed it ("…only for spell-checking");
- "I couldn't read it" silently becoming "there is no rule";
- a download that "worked" but saved a 157-byte error page as `rules.pdf`.

CallReader turns those failures into invariants.

## How it works

```
fetch page + every attachment ──► sniff bytes (a .pdf that is HTML = UNREAD, not skipped)
        │                          posters/scans ──► Muse Spark vision transcription
        ▼
Muse Spark 1.3 reads all sources ──► 7 axes: eligibility · fee · cash · on-site · AI use · authorship · deadline
        │                              each with quote + source + condition clause
        ▼
citation verifier (plain code) ──► quote must exist verbatim in the fetched text, else the verdict is demoted
        ▼
3-state card: PASS / FAIL / UNREAD   — UNREAD is never folded into PASS
```

- **The model proposes, code disposes.** A PASS/FAIL survives only if its quote is found character-for-character (after whitespace/hyphen normalization) in a source we actually fetched.
- **Conditions are first-class.** "Unless / only if / 단, / ただし" clauses are stored next to the verdict.
- **Unread attachments poison PASS.** If any attachment could not be opened, eligibility / fee / AI-use cannot be PASS.

- **A quote must also say what the verdict claims.** A second Muse Spark pass audits each PASS/FAIL against its quote alone
  ("the theme is generative AI" does not mean AI tools are allowed). It can only demote, never promote.
- **Conditions are quoted too.** A condition the model cannot quote is shown as UNVERIFIED.
- **A poster is an advert; the rules are behind its QR code.** SAM 3.1 finds every QR code on a poster, code decodes it,
  and the agent reads the page it points to — with that page's PDF and Hancom (.hwpx / .hwp) attachments.
- **Two readings of every PDF.** The text layer (PyMuPDF) and a Muse Spark vision transcription of each rendered page are
  both kept as sources; Korean PDFs often have a text layer in the wrong reading order, and a quote only needs to match one.

- **Show me where it says that.** With `--html report.html`, Muse Spark grounds each verified quote to a box on the
  poster or PDF page. A box is a claim too: the crop is read back, and the highlight is kept only if the read-back
  contains the quote (grounding on dense pages is often one line off — those boxes are caught and widened or dropped).

# ReelForge Studio

ReelForge Studio is an AI film studio. One idea becomes a screenplay, a cast and location bible, a storyboard with chained start and end frames, a continuity check, a voice track, and an MP4.

It is built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. Accounts, email verification, and an admin console are part of the app. The live site is [reelforge.voiceforgeai.site](https://reelforge.voiceforgeai.site).

![Landing](public/brand/hero-poster.jpg)

## What it does

- **Projects.** Drama, documentary, product ad, and anime. Realistic, 3D, cartoon, or anime look. YouTube Shorts, TikTok, Facebook Reels, and long YouTube. The platform format sets the aspect ratio and the maximum length.
- **Writers’ room.** Brainstorm cards, then a screenplay in standard format.
- **Cast, props, locations.** Reference sheets, then a shot list with start and end frames.
- **Continuity.** A vision pass compares frames with the production bible and can redo a frame that drifted.
- **Voice.** Self-hosted Meta MMS-TTS. Each line is checked with Meta wav2vec2 (`facebook/wav2vec2-base-960h`).
- **Cut.** Ken Burns, parallax, and crossfades over the stills (FFmpeg, and HyperFrames when that sidecar is up), music, subtitles, loudness, MP4.
- **Reel.** An agent that can run those steps, with a real Linux desktop you can watch or take over.
- **Accounts.** Sign up, verify email, reset a password, profile, and per-user projects. Admin configures keys, storage, and usage limits.

## Meta models only

`META_ONLY` defaults to **on**. While it is on, every model called at runtime is a Meta model:

| Step | Model |
|---|---|
| Writing, directing, agent, computer use, continuity review | Muse Spark 1.3, with Muse Wonder 1.0 for hard tasks |
| Open-weight text fallback | Baseten `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` only |
| Images | Muse Image 1.0 |
| Person segmentation (optional) | SAM 3.1 |
| Voice | Meta MMS-TTS, `facebook/mms-tts-*`, self-hosted in `services/mms-tts` |
| Dialogue clarity and voice input | Meta wav2vec2, `facebook/wav2vec2-base-960h`, same service |

Character “voices” are pitch and tempo shapes on that one MMS voice. They are not Microsoft Edge, ElevenLabs, or other neural voices.

MMS-TTS weights are CC-BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial). wav2vec2-base-960h is Apache-2.0.

# glimmer-m5-selftune — Muse Glimmer tunes its own inference code on an M5 Max

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie track, solo. Problem statement: **Push the Frontier**.

**Result.** On a Mac Studio M5 Max, Meta's Muse Glimmer 30B (4-bit, MLX) now writes **+17 % faster** on a coding task
and **+5 % to +21 % faster (median +12.8 %)** on its own 19 recorded self-tuning prompts, with **no extra memory**.
In exact (fp32) arithmetic the text is identical to normal decoding; in bf16 a near-tied token can occasionally flip
(details below). 21 replicated races, 252 paired timing runs: every one faster. On a 60-prompt subset of the standard
Spec-Bench benchmark: 1.15× overall, every task faster (1.07× to 1.43×). Two pieces: **H8**, prompt-lookup decoding made exact
for Glimmer's sliding-window cache, and **H9**, a fix that keeps MLX's fast attention kernel in use for H8's 3-token
check passes, found by this project's referee and traced to MLX's source. Glimmer's own best change: +0.17 %, bit-exact;
asked to fix the long-context problem itself, it found the fast version in 10 of 16 attempts but never a correct one, and
the referee rejected every one (details below).

## Try it on your Mac (one command)

Needs an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or newer), Python 3.10+ (`python3 --version`), internet for the first run, and Low Power
Mode off. In Terminal:

```
git clone https://github.com/Bignesh14/glimmer-m5-selftune.git && cd glimmer-m5-selftune
./run_demo.sh --small                 # any Apple Silicon Mac with 8 GB+: Meta Llama 3.2 3B (4-bit, ~2 GB download)
./run_demo.sh                         # Macs with 32 GB+: Muse Glimmer 30B (4-bit, ~19 GB download)
```

The first run creates a private Python environment (`.venv`), installs the pinned packages and downloads the model
(about 15–20 minutes on a slow connection; later runs start in seconds). The demo gives the model the same prompt twice,
with normal decoding (mlx-lm) and with this project's decoder, prints both answers and their speeds, and opens a
side-by-side page that replays both runs with their real measured timings.

**Web page:** `./run_demo.sh --ui` (or `./run_demo.sh --ui --small`) loads the model once and opens a local page
(http://127.0.0.1:8765, reachable only from that Mac): type any prompt, watch both decoders stream (normal first, then
ours), with the tokens that came from confirmed guesses shown in green, then press *Replay side by side* to see both runs
together with their real timings. The terminal demo marks the same tokens in green.

**Your own prompt:** `./run_demo.sh --small --prompt "Write a Python class for a 2D vector with unit tests."`
(also `--max-tokens 400`, and `--strength low|medium|high` for Glimmer's reasoning effort; `--model <Hugging Face id or
folder>` for any other mlx-lm model). The decoder helps most when the answer repeats itself: code, edits, refactors,
structured text; on prose the gain is small, and on a small Mac it can be **slower**.

# Meta Spatial Agent

> Autonomous Multimodal Visual Inspection, Diagnostic Reasoning, and Action Synthesis Engine.  
> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Cerebral Valley & Meta).

---

## Overview

Meta Spatial Agent is an end-to-end autonomous inspection and remediation pipeline designed for complex physical and digital environments (e.g. precision electronics inspection, robotics gantry automation, and industrial quality control).

The project pairs Meta's flagship multimodal models:
1. **SAM 3.1 (Segment Anything):** For zero-shot, promptable pixel-level visual segmentation.
2. **Muse Spark / Wonder:** For spatial and physical reasoning over segmented component clusters.
3. **Muse Code:** For synthesizing automated remediation scripts and robot controller commands.

# Hack the World

**Hack the World** is an evidence-driven multimodal AI diagnostic agent for real-world technology troubleshooting, created for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**.

> **Hackathon work declaration:** Implementation in this repository is being developed during the official hackathon build period. The repository was created specifically for this event so the work can be clearly distinguished from prior projects.

## Problem

Technology troubleshooting often fails because people jump from a symptom to a conclusion. A photo or error message can suggest possibilities, but reliable diagnosis usually requires gathering more evidence, testing competing explanations, and verifying the result.

Hack the World is designed around that diagnostic process rather than a one-shot image answer.

## Core loop

**Observe → Hypothesize → Ask → Verify → Recommend**

1. **Observe** — collect the user's symptoms, images, and other evidence.
2. **Hypothesize** — maintain multiple plausible causes instead of committing too early.
3. **Ask** — choose the next useful diagnostic question or test.
4. **Verify** — incorporate the result and update or eliminate hypotheses.
5. **Recommend** — provide the next action only when the evidence supports it.

## Hackathon target

The first working demo will focus on a narrow but convincing technology-support scenario, such as a computer that powers on but has no display. The goal is to demonstrate an agent that becomes more certain through evidence rather than simply generating a diagnosis from a single image.

## Meta AI direction

The project is being designed to use Meta AI tooling where it materially improves the diagnostic workflow, including Meta multimodal/open-weight models for reasoning and, where appropriate, segmentation or visual grounding. Provider-specific integrations will be kept behind adapters so the demo can use the best hackathon-available inference route without changing the diagnostic core.

## Repository map

- [`HACKATHON_SCOPE.md`](HACKATHON_SCOPE.md) — what is in and out of scope for the event
- [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) — system and agent architecture
- [`docs/judging-strategy.md`](docs/judging-strategy.md) — how the build maps to the judging rubric
- [`docs/demo-plan.md`](docs/demo-plan.md) — the three-minute demo target

## Status

**Milestone 1:** the provider-independent diagnostic core and mandatory verification
gates are implemented. Meta integration and the model loop are planned for Milestone 2.

With Python 3.11+ installed, run locally from the repository root (no dependencies
or network required):

```powershell
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python -m examples.no_display
```

See [`docs/diagnostic-core.md`](docs/diagnostic-core.md) for the action contracts,
state transitions, verification rules, and limitations.

## Team

**Leonitex** — Indie Developer track

### Old machine drawings in, editable engineering CAD out, and it tells you what it had to guess.

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Indie Developer track · Theme: Push the Frontier · Ng Wei Bin (solo)**

▶ **[3-minute demo video](#)** _(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dm65Gm77UqA)_  ·

📏 **[Ground truth](aether-lab/docs/GROUND_TRUTH.md)**  · 
✅ **[Acceptance tests](aether-lab/docs/ACCEPTANCE.md)**  · 
🧾 **[Provenance](AETHER_HACKATHON_PROVENANCE.md)**

![AETHER Lab with an AI-written CAD model of a roadster, its CAD document and the Muse Spark chat](aether-lab/docs/media/lab_roadster.jpg)

---

## The problem

Factories, museums and repair shops keep machines running for which **no CAD exists**: only a patent figure, a
faded catalogue page or a three-view sketch. One view, no scale, hidden parts, and the maker long gone. Today an
engineer redraws such a machine by hand, and nothing records which dimensions were read off the paper and which
were guessed.

## What AETHER Lab does

You give it a drawing (or a description). Meta's models plan the machine and **write the CAD program themselves**;
AETHER's own code runs it, checks it and keeps every number honest.

| Step | Who does it | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Check the drawing | **Muse Spark** | Reads the sheet like an engineer taking a job: which views it shows, what is missing, the one question worth asking |
| 2. Plan the machine | **Muse Wonder** | Every component with what it is mounted on, its joint (fixed / turns / slides), its evidence on the drawing, and the **unknowns**: what the drawing cannot tell |
| 3. Write the CAD | **Muse Wonder** | A CadQuery / OpenCascade program, key sizes as named parameters (`measured`, `read`, `inferred`, `assumed`) |
| 4. Build and check | **AETHER code** on Modal CPU | Sandboxed run; every solid validated by OpenCascade; quality gates (floating parts, parts passing through each other, mechanical constraints); each view compared with the drawing |
| 5. Critique and revise | **Muse Spark** + renders | Looks at real renders, scores them, and Muse Wonder rewrites the program; the best *checked* round is kept |
| 6. Keep engineering | **Muse Spark** orchestrator, 40 tools | "the bore is 30 mm", "explain how it works", "make a technical drawing", "check interference", "export STEP": by chat or by voice (**Muse Voice Transcribe**); a part from a phone photo via **SAM 3.1** |

**Models propose, code decides.** No measured value comes from a model, and every guess is labelled as a guess.

## Proof: does the CAD match the real part?

Three parts with **known dimensions** were drawn as engineering drawings. AETHER got only the drawing, then its
solids were measured against the known ones ([full table and method](aether-lab/docs/GROUND_TRUTH.md)):

# Consumed

**Spotify Wrapped, but every day, and for everything you consume.**

Consumed is one daily page of what you listened to, read and ate. You log something in seconds, by photo or by search, and Muse Image repaints it by hand, in the gouache and colored-pencil style of the illustrated food on realfood.gov's new food pyramid. It lands on today's page as a painting you can drag and twist. Your friends' days sit in one feed, with matches when two of you are on the same book or song. At night your day seals into a capsule that cracks open as one card, ready for Instagram Stories or WhatsApp.

| Model | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Logging | Reads a photo (an album, a book cover, a plate) or a search, and returns the item as JSON through structured output: the real title and creator, a short line of facts, one warm note, a shape and three colors, a color word for dares, a short noun for the object ("bowl of pho") and the box around it. Reasoning effort is set to low to keep each log fast and cheap. |
| **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) | Logging | Lifts the dish off the table: from Muse Spark's noun, it returns the mask of the item in your photo, so Muse Image is handed the dish alone. | **Muse Image** (`muse-image-1.0`) | Logging and Tonight | Repaints every item through the image edit endpoint, keeping what makes it that item: your dish, its bowl and garnish, or the real album or book cover, which becomes a painted record sleeve or a standing hardcover. # Comfi Autopilot

One-line pitch: an autonomous operations system for short-term rentals that runs the day-to-day of a hosting business, and only acts on its own as far as its graded record has earned.

Built Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026 for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme: Build for Your World).

## What it is

Comfi Autopilot is designed to connect to Hospitable, the property-management system the bookings already live in, and to work from the real operating data: every reservation, check-in time, and cleaning on the calendar. This build runs on a staged fixture world in that data model (no live Hospitable or Turno connection). On top of that data it coordinates the work of the business end to end — the guest asking, the cleaner finishing, the issue mid-stay — as one operation instead of a pile of separate messages. Every action it might take is gated by graduated autonomy: closing noise is a low right, messaging a guest or a cleaner is a middle right, and charging a guest is never earned at all: it stays with the human, whatever the graded record says.

What it operates:

- Guest communication, around the clock: every incoming message is read and sorted by urgency, and the urgent ones (Act) get a drafted reply in the operator's voice.
- Cleaning turnovers: cleanings lined up between one guest leaving and the next arriving, with the arriving guest told the moment their place is ready.
- Early check-in: a guest's request is checked against the same-day turnover reality; when it works, a yes reply is drafted and held for approval along with the fee step.
- In-stay issues: problems during a stay, from a door that will not unlock to getting a handyman dispatched.
- Special requests: late checkout is built, checked against the next arrival and the turnover in between; when the ask runs into the next guest, the drafted reply offers the latest time that works, and any fee is its own held step. The other request types (supplies, a crib, parking) are designed on the same rails.
- Exterior-camera oversight: the camera plays work from the frames and camera status that a camera connection supplies, and send anything unexpected outside the home to the operator. # RoadSense

**Who goes first at this junction?** Show RoadSense a photo taken from the driver's seat in Spain. It tells you what to do, cites the exact article of Spain's traffic rules (the Reglamento General de Circulación, word for word from the BOE), and outlines on the photo the signs, lights and vehicles the answer depends on.

It marks an answer **checked** only when an independent rule engine and the AI reach the same answer on evidence that SAM 3.1 found in the photo. When that evidence isn't there, it says **not sure**, and when the photo isn't a Spanish junction, **out of scope**.

RoadSense is part of DriveIQ, a theory-exam app for the Spanish driving test (permiso B): **https://www.driveiq.es/roadsense** (es, en, fr, ar).

## How it uses Meta's models

- **Muse Spark 1.3** reads the photo into structured facts: the junction, its signs, lights and road markings and whom they govern, the road users and where they come from, and what is hidden. It then explains the decision in the learner's language, citing only the BOE excerpts it was given, with the tempting wrong answer and why it is wrong.
- **SAM 3.1** takes a second, independent look. It segments each object the decision depends on ("traffic sign", "traffic light", "person", "ambulance"…) and confirms a fact only when its box overlaps Muse Spark's: at least 0.4 of the smaller box, at a comparable size. The confirmed boxes are the outlines learners see.
- **Muse Image** makes the what-if edits (swap a STOP sign for a yield sign, turn the light red, bring in an ambulance…). The edited photo is read again and analysed only if the intended change took and nothing else the rule engine reads moved. Learners can also type a what-if in their own words, such as "what if a person comes in front": Muse Spark reads it as one of those edits, or answers that RoadSense can't test it yet. Muse Image also generated the 33 curated scenes.
- A **rule engine** in TypeScript decides the learner's obligation from the facts on its own: the order of preference between signals (art. 133), intersections and priority to the right (arts. 56–59), pedestrians (art. 65, and art. 46.1.a for someone stepping into the road) and emergency vehicles (arts. 67–69) and the light and marking definitions of Anexo I. The certainty comes from comparing the two answers.

`docs/roadsense/ARCHITECTURE.md` walks through the pipeline; `docs/roadsense/RULES.md` lists every rule the engine applies.

## Run it without a key

Node.js 22.15 or later:

```
npm install
npm test

npx tsx scripts/roadsense/eval-understand.ts

```

Replay mode answers every model call from the recordings in `data/roadsense/recordings`, so the evaluation repeats exactly, at no cost, and rewrites `docs/roadsense/EVAL.md` with the same numbers (`--effort low` only labels the run as it was recorded). A live run needs

# Apprentice

Film an expert doing a hands-on job once. Apprentice turns it into a verified step-by-step guide, then watches a beginner do the same job through a phone camera and catches mistakes before they matter.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 Oct to 4 Nov 2026). Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon, starting 26 Oct 2026.

## The problem

Hands-on know-how lives in a few experts' heads: servicing equipment, assembly, repairs, lab bench work, kitchen prep, field installs. Training someone new means the expert stands beside them for days, and written instructions go stale or get skipped.

## How it works (Meta models)

1. **Read any instructions.** Upload a video, paste a direct video link, or add a PDF, help page or Markdown doc. **Muse Spark** watches the video with its audio (or reads the text) and splits the job into ordered steps with parts, tools, a "done when" check and warnings, then looks at dense frames around each step's end to find exactly when it is finished.
2. **Ground it.** **SAM 3.1** finds each part in the expert's finished frames, so every step carries the frame and the highlighted part that show what correct looks like.
3. **Explain and make it safe.** **Muse Image** draws a clean, labelled diagram per step. **Muse Wonder** reviews the whole guide for hazards; steps marked stop must be acknowledged before the coach starts them.
4. **Coach live.** The trainee points a phone at their work and says "I'm done". Muse Spark compares their frames with the expert's, SAM 3.1 checks the parts are in view, and a deterministic policy advances only on two agreeing confident checks. Otherwise it asks to see closer, sends them back with evidence, or stops them. They can ask a question by voice (**Muse Voice Transcribe**) and get a short answer from Muse Spark.
5. **Prove and improve.** A run report shows every step with its evidence frames and **Muse Wonder**'s review. Steps that many trainees struggle with are flagged for the guide's author, who can edit and re-approve the guide.

Every Meta call is hashed and cached (paid once), metered and capped per guide and per session. Without a key, fakes replay the recorded day-1 outputs or return clearly labelled placeholders.

## Repository

| Path                | What it is                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/core`     | Domain model, zod schemas, the API wire contract and the ports the domain depends on                                       |
| `packages/meta`     | Muse Spark, SAM 3.1, Muse Image, Voice Transcribe and Muse Wonder adapters; request-hash cache, retries, cost meter, fakes |
| `packages/coach`    | Live coach: verify-then-advance state machine, policy, step verifier, run report, guide insights

# Lipwad

**Lipwad gets Kenyan hospitals paid.** It reads photographed claim documents, cites every value to the exact place it came from, checks the claim against SHA rules, and repairs returned claims before the 14-day resubmission window closes.

> **Lipwad is not medical AI.** It documents and codes what already happened. It never gives clinical advice, never recommends treatment, and never adds or upgrades services or amounts. Nothing reaches the national HIE without a named person's confirmation.

**Live demo:** https://stellaacharoiro--lipwad-web.us-east.modal.run (all patients, practitioners and facilities are synthetic). The demo restores itself every 6 hours and allows a limited number of model runs per day.

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track), Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026, by Evarest Technologies. Everything in this repository was written during the build window; the commit history is the record.

## The problem
Kenyan hospitals deliver care under the Social Health Authority (SHA) and then lose the money over paperwork: unsigned forms, invoices without itemised services, service types that don't match the documents, practitioners missing from the registry, and returns that run out the 14-day clock. The evidence usually exists, scattered across paper and phones. SHA screens claims with automation; hospitals have nothing on their side.

## What Lipwad does
1. **Reads the claim file.** Muse Spark vision transcribes each photographed document into fields. Every field carries a citation: the document and the region of the photo it came from. A blurred page produces a retake request, never a guess.
2. **Hears the voice note.** Muse Voice Transcribe transcribes a staff voice note into timed segments. A date that was said becomes a field cited to the seconds it was spoken, and Claim review plays exactly that moment.
3. **Verifies it.** The agent checks the practitioner and facility against the registry, cross-checks what was said against what was written, then runs rule checks. Each finding cites the evidence and the rule it relies on.
4. **Decides and explains.** Claims come out green (ready), amber (one named fix) or red (blocked). Muse Spark Open explains the outcome in English and Kiswahili. The model explains; it never sets the status, so it cannot turn a blocked claim green.
5. **Submits only with a person's OK.** A green claim goes to the HIE after a named clerk confirms they checked every field.
6. **Rescues returned claims.** For a returned claim, Lipwad reads the corrected page, shows exactly which field changed, and resubmits only that correction after confirmation, with the deadline countdown in view.

Clicking any field in Claim review highlights the region of the photo it came from.

## Meta models and where they run
| Role | Model | Served by |
|---|---|---|
| Reading documents, with value regions for click-to-source | Muse Spark 1.3 (vision) | Meta Model API |
| Transcribing voice notes, with timestam

Convoplex Retention Agent is a WhatsApp win-back agent for Nigerian retailers, built in Lagos. A shopkeeper sees who has gone quiet, sends one offer with a real naira price, and the customer can answer by text or voice note in the language they choose.

Source: [https://github.com/vumoz/convoplex-retention-agent](https://github.com/vumoz/convoplex-retention-agent)

## Powered by Meta models

Live text is Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`), pictures are Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`), and voice notes are Muse Voice Transcribe (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`). All three go through the Meta Model API (Application Programming Interface) at `https://api.meta.ai/v1`. The defaults live in `convoplex/config.py`. `META_API_KEY` is read from the environment and is never written to the database, the action log, or this repository. ```mermaid
flowchart LR

  spark --> image
  spark --> reply
  image --> reply
```

`muse-spark-1.3` is the chat model. `LiveMuse` in `convoplex/llm.py` posts to `/v1/chat/completions`.
