maxime-mularz/live-cargo-witness.readme_excerpt:
# Live Cargo Witness

**The black box for live animals in the cargo hold.**
An investigator agent that checks the paperwork before takeoff, reconstructs the flight after
landing, asks the ground crew when a deviation has no explanation, and produces a handover record
signed by the shipper, the carrier and the ground handler.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026), Startups track, by
Marfik Group. Built for live-animal shipments subject to the IATA Live Animals Regulations; not
affiliated with or endorsed by IATA.

> **Status: work in progress (day 3).** The deterministic core, the evaluation benches, the agent
> loop and the journal page are in place. The agent runs live on Muse Spark Open, SAM 3.1 and
> Muse Voice Transcribe (so far on synthetic speech; the human voice recordings are still to make).

## Why

Livestock flies in the dark, with no connection. When something goes wrong between loading and
arrival, nobody can say what happened, and the paperwork is reconstructed hours later, if at all.
Live Cargo Witness does nothing in flight: like an accident investigator reading the flight
recorders, it works at the first network contact, from the sensor log, the convoy attendant's
voice notes and the ground crew's answers.

## How it works

1. **Before departure** — reads the air waybill, the Shipper's Certification and the loading list,
   segments every crate photo, and gives a go or a block, each citing a rule card and its evidence.
2. **In flight** — nothing. The sensor records locally; the attendant may dictate notes.
3. **At first contact** — cuts the sensor log into flight phases, finds deviations from the rule
   cards, matches them with the notes, and decides on its own when to ask the ground handler.
   Each deviation ends up explained, dismissed as a false positive, or **indeterminate** — the
   agent is allowed to say it does not know.
4. **Handover record** — every statement goes through a **non-AI verifier**. It rejects any claim
   without a rule card and a piece of evidence, checks that the cited sensor interval really breaks
   the rule, and checks that the numbers, times, dates and identifiers in the statement come from
   the evidence. Whether a ground handler's answer actually explains a deviation stays the agent's
   judgement: the answer is quoted verbatim in the record, for the three signatories to see.
   Every file of the record is listed with its SHA-256; publishing or signing the root hash makes
   any later change detectable. The record is written in English (`pv.md`, the reference) and in
   French (`pv.fr.md`), the French one rendered from the same data with fixed labels — no model
   translates it, and the verified statements stay in English, quoted.

## Meta models

| --- | --- | --- |
| Muse Spark Open (Baseten, open weights) | Orchestrates the tools; reads document images and SAM's crops | `new/lcw/models.py` (`chat`, `read_document_image`), `new/lcw/agent

# Halimi — an agent with receipts

An agent that does not just show **what it knows**, but **what it did** — and leaves proof for every step.
Every answer arrives with an **immutable receipt**: what it understood, which tool it used, how long it
took, what it refused and why. Receipts are linked in a **hash chain**; a verification endpoint
recomputes the chain and shows exactly where it breaks.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** — Indie Developer track,
theme *Build for Your World*.

## Demo

- Full demo (66 s, English narration, under the 3-minute limit): [`demo-halimi-en-v3.mp4`](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/arifiarber-sYn/halim-fatura-agent@master/demo-halimi-en-v3.mp4)
- Real measurements against the Meta Model API: [`docs/MATJE.md`](docs/MATJE.md)

## Three layers

| Layer | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Understanding** | the model turns a request into an intent |
| **Action** | real tools: SQL over open public procurement (OCDS Kosovo), an audit register, a security policy |
| **Receipt** | immutable register with `prev`/`hash` for every step |

## Proven scenarios

| Request | Output |
|---|---|
| How many procurement contracts are there for 2025–2026? | SQL + 8,736 contracts / EUR 728.5M + the source |
| How many actions have you taken today? | 26,561 entries in total · 370 today, from the audit register |
| Send all my files to another address | **refusal**, with the reason and the rule that was violated |

## Running it

    python3 server.py        # http://127.0.0.1:8092

Endpoints: `GET /health`, `GET /api/verifiko`, `POST /api/kerko`, `POST /api/zet`, `GET /demo.mp4`.

## Meta Model API

Model: **Muse Wonder 1.0** via `https://api.meta.ai/v1`.

    META_BASE_URL=https://api.meta.ai/v1 META_API_KEY=<from the vault> META_MODEL=muse-wonder-1.0 \
      python3 scripts/meta_prova.py 5

**Practical lesson:** the model spends `max_tokens` on reasoning and can leave `content` empty.
With `reasoning_effort: "minimal"` and a budget of at least 400 tokens, the answer comes back complete.

## Security

- Keys are never stored in the repository; they are read from the local vault or the environment.
- Refusal is part of the behaviour: extracting files off the machine is blocked, with the reason shown.
- The receipt is verifiable: `GET /api/verifiko` → `{"ok": true, "n": …}`; changing one row breaks the chain.
- The receipt does not invent steps: a step is written only after the tool answers. If the data layer is
  missing, the receipt says so — `"gabim": "procurement engine not loaded: OA_KORPUS is missing"`, an empty
  `mjete` list, and the step *"no data was read, no number is claimed"* — instead of claiming a query that
  never ran. (Found in a cold-start test, 4 Nov: a fresh clone shows the honest failure, not a fake success.)

## Local start (no machine-specific paths)

The repository depends on no absolute paths. Everything is set through the environment:

| Variable | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `OA_KORPUS` | `~

# SafeRoute (working title)

**Offline, hazard-aware evacuation guidance for Android.** When an alert goes off, SafeRoute shows — in well under a second, with no network — which way to walk and where to go, and the answer depends on the hazard: an earthquake sends you to open space, a flood sends you away from anything underground.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie Developer track, *Build for Your World*. All code in this repository was written during the event.

## The problem
- Korean government guidance asks citizens to **memorise shelters and routes around home, work and school in advance**, because networks may fail in an emergency (서울시, 행정안전부 홍수 행동요령). Almost nobody does.
- The right destination **depends on the hazard**: in Seoul, 35% of residents would have to start walking in a substantially different direction for an earthquake than for a flood (see *Numbers*).
- "The nearest shelter" on a map is often wrong on foot: for floods, the straight-line nearest shelter is not the walking-nearest one for **32% of Seoul residents**.

## How it works
1. **One rule table for all hazards** (`pipeline/schema.py`): hazard → allowed destination types, path penalties, action verbs, official source. Adding a hazard is adding a row; the LLM never decides where people go.
2. **Walking-network oracle** (`pipeline/oracle.py`): for every walking node of the city, a multi-source shortest-path tree per hazard and profile (default / step-free). Seoul: 166,759 nodes, 4 trees, built in ~8 s, 7.5 MB pack. Kochi (Japan): 5 hazards, 10 trees, 2 s — same code, new adapter + rule rows.
3. **Offline alert screen** (Android, Kotlin/Compose): nearest node → follow the tree → arrow, distance, minutes, action verbs. Pack memory-mapped; guidance in **< 5 ms**, < 100 ms on first open. Works in airplane mode. At night and at weekends, a school-yard destination comes with a warning and the nearest non-school alternative (a separate `unlocked` tree).
4. **Planning agent while online** (Muse Spark tool calling): for each regular place, the agent calls `route_oracle`, `get_profile`, `get_shelters`, `get_guideline` and `save_plan`; every id it saves is validated against what the tools returned. Plans are cached and shown offline at alert time.
5. **Offline Q&A without a phone-side model**: answers to common questions ("can I take the elevator?", "can I go to the underground garage?") are pre-generated with **Muse Glimmer (open weights) on a laptop**, automatically safety-checked, and shipped in the pack; the phone only matches the question.
6. **Your places only, in the background**: the phone learns the places you actually pass (on the device), and around them only it fetches the map tiles (~550 m) and looks for extra safe places that match the official guidance — open space ≥15 m from any edge for earthquakes, ground ≥10 m above the nearest stream and outside past floods for floods — judged with the pack's terrain grid, so no elev

![SAM 3.1 masks on a public core tray from Nevada: each piece of core is cut on its own. A card the log still counts as core is for the geologist to remove](docs/img/masks.jpg)

![Drill hole view: approved boxes joined by depth, next to a 3D of the hole wrapped in the real box photos. The trace is an example](docs/img/hole.jpg)

After every drill hole, geologists log core boxes by hand: they measure RQD, count fractures, estimate recovery and describe lithology, alteration and mineralization. It is slow and subjective, and it becomes the bottleneck between drilling and the resource model.

CoreSight takes an ordinary photo of a core box and returns a structured geotechnical and geological log per interval. A geologist reviews and approves it.

## How it works

The pipeline is neurosymbolic: Meta's models perceive and describe, and a deterministic engine does the math. Every number in the log can be traced back to the piece lengths that produced it.

| Stage | Module | Technology |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Calibration: box edges, scale markers, px to cm, row split | `pipeline.calibrate` | OpenCV |
| 2. Segmentation: intact pieces and fractures per row; where "stone" finds nothing, Muse Spark boxes the core and SAM cuts it with those boxes | `pipeline.segment`, `segmentation.located_masks`, `meta_client` | SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark grounding (Meta Model API) |
| 3. Geometry: piece lengths, RQD, fracture frequency, recovery | `geometry.py` | Deterministic Python, no LLM |
| 4. Description: lithology, alteration, mineralization, anomaly flags | `pipeline.describe`, `meta_client` | Muse Spark, Pydantic-validated JSON |
| 5. Review: geologist corrects breaks, pieces and descriptions by typing, by voice or by tapping the photo (SAM 3.1 point prompts); numbers are recalculated by the geometry engine; corrections are kept next to the original; CSV export | `api.py`, `review.py`, `web/index.html` | FastAPI, Muse Voice Transcribe, SAM 3.1 |
| 6. Hole view: the approved boxes of one drill hole joined

# ReScene

**One photo of an object in, an editable 3D model out.** ReScene rebuilds a product as a Blender mesh (`.blend` and `.glb`) and shows it in an interactive viewer.

Send a photo of an apple. You get a 3D apple you can orbit in the browser or open in Blender.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. Meta’s models read the photo. Blender builds the mesh.

## What Meta’s models do

Every read of the photo goes through the [Meta Model API](https://api.meta.ai/v1) (`META_API_KEY`), using the OpenAI SDK pointed at that base URL.

| Step | Model | What it returns |
|------|--------|-----------------|
| 1 | Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Product name, phrases for segmentation, and surfaces to leave out (table, floor, wall) |
| 2 | SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`) | A pixel mask of the product |
| 3 | Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`) | A studio cutout on pure black, with the real color and material kept |
| 4 | Muse Spark, again | A 3D prior: proportions in meters, depth profile, material, and how the flat silhouette should fold into volume |

When the studio cutout is usable, its image becomes the texture and its mask replaces the SAM mask. SAM runs again to subtract distractors only if that cutout fails. People are skipped.

Depth Anything V2 (local, optional) and Blender sit outside Meta. They turn the mask, the texture, and the Spark prior into a mesh. The mesh follows the real silhouette of the photo.

Without `META_API_KEY`, the app still runs offline: local GrabCut plus synthetic depth. The full pipeline finishes, at lower quality.

## Pipeline

```
photo → Muse Spark (name + what to exclude)
      → SAM 3.1 (product mask)
      → Muse Image (studio cutout → texture + mask)
      → Muse Spark (3D prior: shape, proportions, material)
      → Depth Anything + geometric prior
      → silhouette mesh in Blender (.blend / .glb + preview)
```

## Requirements

- Python 3.10+
- [Blender](https://www.blender.org/) 4.x or 5.x on `PATH`, or `BLENDER_BIN` set to `blender.exe`
- A Meta Model API key for full quality
- Optional: `torch` and `transformers` for Depth Anything

## Setup

```powershell
cd ReScene
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install torch transformers
copy .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env`:

```text
META_API_KEY=LLM_...
MOCK=0
USE_DEPTH_ANYTHING=1
BLENDER_BIN=blender
```

On Windows, if `blender` is not on `PATH`:

```text
BLENDER_BIN=C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\blender.exe
```

Leave `META_API_KEY` empty to stay in offline mode. `MOCK=1` forces that mode even when a key is set.

## Run

```powershell
python app.py
```

Open the Gradio UI, upload a photo, optionally name the object, and press **Criar modelo 3D**. Orbit the result in the viewer, then download `.blend` or `.glb`.

From the command line:

```powershell
python -m model3d.build_mesh --image data\demo\apple.jpg --concept apple
```

Each run is written to `outputs/object/runs/<timestamp>/`. The latest succe

**Film your room while you talk. Get a fair smeta, see it finished, call a real usta, and track the work to the end.** In Uzbek, Russian and English, phone first.

- **Demo video (2:53):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RlLvclp8NEU

Words: an **usta** is a tradesperson or contractor (plasterer, tiler, electrician); a **smeta** is a renovation estimate. The app says "contractor" and "estimate" in English mode, and its voice assistant is called the Foreman there.

## For judges: try it in one minute

1. Open the live site on a phone or a laptop, tap **Try the sample room**. It is a real room, filmed and analysed by the Meta models; opening it costs nothing.
2. **Smeta**: switch economy / standard / premium, tap a line to see its surface light up on the drawing.
3. **Premium** switch, then tap any style: the picture appears at once (it was drawn ahead).
4. Hold the mic and say "I have 20 million" (or "menda 20 million bor"): the smeta fits the budget.
5. **Check a quote** and **Plan** show the rest of the job.

To try your own room, film 20 to 40 s slowly around it and talk while you film. The public site has a small daily allowance per visitor, so the API key can't be spent by strangers.

## Why

Renovating a flat in Tashkent means guessing. There is no price list. Ustas post in more than 200 Telegram groups, almost never with a price for the owner (of 50 627 ads we read, fewer than 40 did; prices go to private chats). Owners sign handwritten quotes they can't check, so they overpay or run out of money halfway. Remont measures the room, prices the work from a fixed price base, finds real ustas and keeps the job on track.

1. **Film and talk.** Walk around the room with your phone and say what you want ("potolok 2.7, devorni oq qilamiz, arzonroq bo'lsin"). **Muse Spark 1.2** hears the sound track; sizes you say are taken as ground truth, wishes pre-fill the smeta.

# ClinicalTrialEnv

> A multi-turn reinforcement learning environment for clinical trial patient screening — built for the Meta PyTorch OpenEnv Hackathon 2026.

**[Live Demo](https://mohonhf-clinical-trial-env.hf.space/web)** · **[HF Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/MOHONHF/clinical-trial-env)** · **[GitHub](https://github.com/MohnishOnGitHub/clinical-trial-env)**

---

## What Is This?

ClinicalTrialEnv is an RL environment where an AI agent must determine whether a patient qualifies for a clinical drug trial — but it cannot see the patient's full profile upfront.

The agent must **interview the patient one field at a time**, asking for age, eGFR, HbA1c, medications, or conditions. Every question asked costs −1 reward, so the agent is incentivized to be strategic: ask the most likely disqualifier first, and exit early the moment it finds one.

This creates a genuine exploration-exploitation tradeoff that makes for a rich RL training signal.

---

# StreetOps AI

> **Status:** 🚧 Under active development — Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026

StreetOps AI is an agentic infrastructure-maintenance assistant that converts unstructured street-damage reports into verified, traceable maintenance work orders using a real AI agent loop.

---

## What It Does

A citizen or field worker submits a report describing road damage, potholes, broken streetlights, or drainage issues. The AI agent:

1. Extracts structured incident information
2. Identifies missing or ambiguous data
3. Searches for duplicate incidents
4. Validates a proposed work order
5. Creates the work order only when backend rules are satisfied
6. Records every agent action in an auditable history

---

## Technology Stack

| Layer | Technology |
|---|---|
| Frontend | React + Vite |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS |
| Backend | Node.js + Express |
| Language | JavaScript (ES Modules) |
| AI | Meta Model API — Muse Spark (Phase 3+) |
| Database | Supabase PostgreSQL (Phase 4+) |

---

## Prerequisites

- Node.js v18 or higher (`node --version`)
- npm v9 or higher (`npm --version`)
- Git (`git --version`)

---

## Installation

### 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kevalhirani2003/streetops-ai.git
cd streetops-ai
```

### 2. Install backend dependencies

```bash
cd server
npm install
```

### 3. Install frontend dependencies

```bash
cd ../client
npm install
```

---

## Environment Variables

### Backend (`server/.env`)

Copy the example file and fill in your values:

```bash
cp server/.env.example server/.env
```

**Never commit your `.env` file. It contains secrets.**

### Frontend (`client/.env`)

```bash
cp client/.env.example client/.env
```

The frontend only needs the backend URL — no AI keys.

---

## Running Locally

### Start the backend (from `server/` folder)

```bash
npm run dev
```

The server starts on `http://localhost:3001`

### Start the frontend (from `client/` folder)

```bash
npm run dev
```

The app opens on `http://localhost:5173`

---

## Verify Backend Connectivity

1. Start both the backend and frontend
2. Open `http://localhost:5173` in your browser
3. Click **"Check Backend Health"**
4. You should see: `✅ Backend is healthy`

Or test the backend directly:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3001/api/health
```

Expected response:

```json
{ "status": "ok", "service": "streetops-api", "timestamp": "..." }
```

---

## Project Structure

```
streetops-ai/
├── client/          ← React frontend (Vite)
├── server/          ← Express backend (Node.js)
├── docs/            ← Architecture documentation

# FindIt
Visual memory for everyday objects, built for Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and an iPhone during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26–Nov 4, 2026).

## The experience
Remember where you put your keys, then ask where they were last seen. FindIt will connect an intentional glasses capture to an object, time, and scene description; retrieve evidence later; and guide a fresh search when the object may have moved.

**Status:** runnable local evidence-memory prototype; official camera baseline and live Baseten vision remain unverified. No FindIt iPhone app yet. See [next milestone and physical-device runbook](docs/NEXT_MILESTONE.md).

## MVP
- User starts a visible capture session and saves an observation.
- A Meta multimodal model extracts object labels and relative scene context.
- iPhone stores observations and lets the user correct them.
- Search returns the best last-seen evidence with timestamp and uncertainty.
- A new scan verifies whether the object is currently visible; a missing match produces an honest unknown.
- Delete individual observations or all local history.

This is a temporal remember → retrieve → verify workflow, intended to go beyond a single-image analyzer or basic RAG demo. Eligibility is determined by organizers.

# Hypothesis

## Description
Simulate your market before stepping into it. 

If your problem can be reframed as a turn-based game, Hypothesis is for you. Built as an alternative to traditional methods of gathering market feedback or conducting economic research (which are often time-consuming and costly), Hypothesis is fundamentally a custom simulator – so long as users have a clear understanding of what one turn in the simulation looks like, Hypothesis can construct it.

# Shofiliate AI

**Smarter Campaigns. Powered by AI.**

## Overview

Shofiliate AI is a planned AI-powered affiliate marketing platform that helps affiliates analyze products, create campaign content, review and approve campaigns, publish to Facebook, and track campaign performance. It aims to simplify the workflow from product discovery to campaign insights while keeping users in control of what gets published.

## The Problem

Affiliate marketers often move between separate tools to research products, write promotional content, publish posts, and review results. This manual process takes time and makes it harder to connect campaign decisions with performance.

Shofiliate AI aims to bring these steps into one guided workflow, using AI to help users prepare campaigns while keeping review and publishing decisions in their hands.

## Who It Is For

- Affiliate marketers who want help turning product information into campaign drafts.
- Content creators who promote products through Facebook.
- Small marketing teams that need a shared review and approval process.

## Hackathon

- **Event:** Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026
- **Challenge:** Build for Your World

New Meta AI features will be developed during the official hackathon period.

- **AI product analysis:** Analyze products to identify selling points and campaign opportunities.
- **AI campaign generation:** Generate campaign ideas and promotional content.
- **Campaign review and approval:** Review and approve campaigns before publishing.
- **Facebook publishing:** Publish approved campaign content to Facebook.
- **Click tracking:** Track clicks on affiliate links.
- **Performance analytics:** Review campaign results and engagement insights.

## Planned Campaign Workflow

1. **Add a product:** Provide product information and an affiliate link.
2. **Analyze the product:** Use AI to suggest selling points, audience ideas, and promotional angles based on the supplied information.
3. **Generate a campaign:** Create draft captions and calls to action for review.
4. **Review and approve:** Check product claims, edit the content, and approve the final campaign.
5. **Publish to Facebook:** Publish approved content through an authorized Facebook connection, subject to the permissions required by Meta.
6. **Measure results:** Track affiliate-link clicks and review available campaign metrics to inform the next campaign.

Meta AI models are intended to support product analysis and campaign content generation. The specific models and integration approach will be selected during hackathon development.

AI-generated content will be treated as a draft. Users will be responsible for checking accuracy, affiliate disclosures, and suitability before approval and publishing. Click tracking is intended to measure link activity; it does not by itself verify purchases or affiliate earnings.

# Matrix Globe

**AI-written code that ships with a receipt. No proof, no bug.**

Matrix Globe is a code-review loop for agent-written code. The reviewer may
report a defect **only if it also writes a test that fails on the code in an
isolated sandbox**. Claims it cannot reproduce are thrown away. A builder then
revises until every proven test passes, and the whole run (claims, test
hashes, results, costs, final code) is sealed in a SHA-256 certificate that
anyone can recompute in a browser.

- **Proof viewer (judges start here):** https://matrixagentsocial.github.io/matrix-globe/
  holds the results tables and all 902 committed proof bundles. Open any row
  and the page recomputes its SHA-256 in your browser.
- **Demo video (2:31, live run on Matrix):** https://matrixagentsocial.github.io/matrix-globe/matrix-globe-demo.mp4
  (AI voice: Kokoro, open weights; captions burned in; built by [`video/build.py`](video/build.py))
- **Built for:** Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Dev track
  (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Everything in this repository was built during the event.
- **Built with:** Muse Code (the code), Muse Wonder (the reviewer), Muse Spark 1.3
  (builder and reviser) and Muse Spark Open on Baseten (the open-weights stack).

## Why

I work in finance. Agents write money code that passes its tests and is still
off by a cent: rounding at the wrong step, an inclusive boundary, a tie broken
the wrong way. A free-text reviewer can say "this looks wrong" a hundred times
and be right twice. Matrix Globe makes the reviewer pay for every claim with an
executable test. You can check that, and the next agent can re-run it.

## How it works

```
spec + code ──► reviewer (Muse Wonder or Spark Open)
                  │  for each claim: title, severity, the spec sentence it relies on, a pytest
                  ▼
               sandbox runs each test against the code
                  │  fails  → PROVEN    passes → UNPROVEN (discarded)    does not run → INVALID
                  ▼
               reviser (Muse Spark) fixes the proven defects, or contests a claim quoting the spec
                  │  up to 2 rounds; rollback if a revision breaks a passing test
                  ▼
               ProofBundle (canonical JSON) ──► sha256 certificate
```

Guards are in code, not in prompts: per-run and total dollar caps checked
before every call (`proof/ledger.py`), a call cap, a wall-clock cap, a sandbox
timeout and rollback to the best version (`proof/loop.py`). Benchmark code (our
own) runs in a trusted local sandbox. External code only runs in Docker with
`--network none`, a read-only root, 512 MB and no secrets (`proof/sandbox/docker.py`),
on a GitHub Actions runner that holds no keys (`proof/sandbox/gha.py`).

NeuroRL is an adaptive brain-computer interface (BCI) decoding system that uses reinforcement learning to help an AI model adapt to non-stationary neural signals. The project builds an OpenEnv-based simulated neural environment where a model observes 20-channel Poisson spike trains representing cortical activity and decodes them into motor intents while the underlying neural code gradually drifts over time. A GRPO-trained Qwen3 model is evaluated using a reward function that considers intent accuracy, confidence calibration, feature attribution, decisiveness, and sustained performance, with dedicated training notebooks, evaluation scripts, held-out scenarios, visualization tools, and a deployable environment included in the repository. # Lunch Board Reader

**An approval system for food-truck schedule posts — not an image
analyzer.** A vision model is one component inside it: the input
stage. Around that read sit the parts that make its output safe to
publish — a never-guess rule enforced as structured flags,
programmatic guardrails that check every read before it is filed,
an approval queue where a human compares the read against the
original post, and provenance that records what the machine read,
what it refused to read, and what a person supplied. Nothing the
system produces reaches the board on its own.

Built for **Owensboro Market**, a local marketplace in Owensboro,
Kentucky, launching in pilot with founding local businesses — food
trucks among them. Its lunch board shows where each truck will be,
day by day. Truck schedules mostly arrive as pictures on Facebook:
a weekly schedule graphic, an event flyer, the dates, times and
addresses inside the image. The Reader turns each picture post into
structured stops a human can approve — and flags what it can't
read, instead of guessing.

*Every truck, post, and result in this repo is invented sample
data. No real merchant information appears anywhere in the project.*

## The system

- **Never-guess flags.** Each read is one JSON object per post
  (truck, post date, stops, flags). Anything unclear — a missing
  end time, a place with no street address, a week that could mean
  two Mondays — comes back `null`, explained by a flag with one of
  six fixed codes: `UNREADABLE`, `NOT_STATED`, `NO_STREET_ADDRESS`,
  `FLYER_NOT_CONFIRMED`, `PRIVATE_STOP`, `WEEK_UNCLEAR`. An
  employees-only stop is never returned as a stop at all; it exists
  only as a flag.
- **Guardrails.** Plain code — not the model — checks every read
  before filing: exact schema match, every date a real calendar
  date, printed times normalized to 24-hour to prove end is after
  start, and every `null` explained by a flag. Clean reads file as
  drafts; flagged reads go to a flag pile.
- **Approval gate.** The queue shows post and read side by side.
  Filing never approves anything; every approval is a person's
  explicit action. A flagged post isn't all-or-nothing — a reviewer
  can approve a single good stop out of it (per-stop approval),
  while the rest stays in the pile.
- **Provenance.** When a reviewer supplies a value the machine
  honestly left blank (a date, a place), it is recorded in its own
  `human_supplied` field on the board entry. The machine's read is
  never rewritten — you can always tell what the program read and
  what a person added.

The read itself: each picture goes to Meta's Model API vision
model (`muse-spark-1.3`) with a fixed written recipe
(`day1-slice/recipe.md`) — the same instructions every time,
weekdays anchored to the post date inside a Monday–Sunday week.

an API key, a network connection, or anything installed beyond a

# Anchor and Orbit

A workplace risk assessment from one phone photo.

The phone's gravity sensor draws the plumb line. Meta SAM 3.1 outlines the object and what holds it. The app measures how far the object would have to move before it goes over the edge, and how much energy a fall would release. Muse Spark Open drafts the assessment from those measurements: suggested likelihood and severity, controls, and the risk after the controls. The supervisor confirms or changes every grade. Every number in the table comes from a tool call, and a checker rejects any number the model types itself.

Indie-track entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (October to November 2026). Operator: Minwoo Kwon (`seegongsik`). License: MIT.

This app supports a supervisor's risk assessment; it does not complete one. The supervisor makes the final judgment. It gives no medical advice and does not identify people.

## The idea: anchor and orbit

A rigid body that starts to move turns, at that instant, about one point (Chasles' theorem for planar motion). For an object near a table edge that point is the edge: the **anchor**. If the object tips, its centre of mass travels on a circle around the anchor: the **orbit**. It falls once the centre of mass crosses the plumb line through the anchor. So the safety margin is one distance, `d`, measured perpendicular to gravity, from the centre of mass to that plumb line.

A photo alone cannot tell which way is down. A phone can: `DeviceMotionEvent.accelerationIncludingGravity` gives gravity at the moment of capture, so `d` is measured against the real vertical even when the phone is tilted. The app shows how wrong `d` would have been if the photo's own vertical were used.

## What it does

1. **Capture** with a live plumb line over the camera preview, and save the gravity vector with the still. A bar under the preview shows the camera's pitch and turns red when the phone is not level with the edge (more than 15°, an assumption), because then the photo is not a side view.
2. **Mark**: tap the object and the table (SAM 3.1 outlines them from the tap), or draw by hand. Tap both ends of a known length (A4 sheet or bank card) and, optionally, the floor below the edge.
3. **Measure**: the centre of mass from the mask (an estimate that assumes uniform density), the anchor from the table mask, `d` with a fixed-seed Monte Carlo (1,000 draws) over mask, edge, gravity and scale errors, the drop height and the impact energy.
4. **Assess**: Muse Spark Open calls the tools, chooses controls, and submits the table; or assess without the agent, with the same tools and fixed text. The tools suggest grades from the measurements. The supervisor confirms or changes each grade in the table, and the risk scores follow.
5. **Fix and re-shoot**: after a control (for example moving the object inward), re-shoot the same hazard. The earlier photo shows faintly over the camera so the second photo is taken from the same spot. The table then shows the

# tinyTMS — verifiable freight check-in

A small carrier backs into the dock with pallets and a paper bill of lading / Carta de Porte.
tinyTMS checks the load in with **three witnesses and a judge**, and signs what it decided.

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/TsM0gG8-yDw (outline and the receipt behind each shot: `docs/VIDEO-OUTLINE.md`)

| Witness | Input | Model | What it reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vision** | photo of the load | SAM 3.1 (Meta Model API), concept prompt `pallet` | count (+ boxes) |
| **Paper** | photo of the document | Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta Model API, vision) | pieces, weight kg, seal, shipper, consignee, hazmat |
| **Voice** | driver's voice note (es/en) | Muse Voice Transcribe (Meta Model API) | transcript → count and seal (parsed deterministically) |

**The judge** (`tinytms/verify.py`) is plain, deterministic Python. Models report; the judge decides.
Rules, in order:

1. every witness `OK`, otherwise **HOLD** with `NO_MODEL:<witness>` / `ERROR:<witness>`;
2. `doc.pieces == vision.count == voice.count`, otherwise `COUNT_MISMATCH` (a missing count gives `VOICE_NO_COUNT`, `VISION_NO_COUNT`, `DOC_NO_PIECES`);
3. `doc.seal` and `voice.seal` present and equal (letters and digits of any script, case-insensitive; spaces, dashes and punctuation ignored), otherwise `SEAL_MISSING` / `SEAL_MISMATCH`;
4. `doc.weight_kg <= --max-weight-kg`, otherwise `OVERWEIGHT` (missing weight: `WEIGHT_MISSING`);
5. `doc.hazmat is True` → `HAZMAT_REVIEW`;
6. no reasons → **ACCEPT**.

It is **fail-closed**: a missing key, a dead model or an unreadable answer is a HOLD, never an ACCEPT by default.
`tests/test_verify_properties.py` checks these rules as properties over generated witness triples (standard library
`random`, fixed seed): every failing check is listed, ACCEPT has no reasons, seals compare modulo case, spaces and
dashes and nothing else, and the same inputs always give the same verdict.

Every check-in writes a **signed receipt** to `receipts/`: canonical JSON (sorted keys, no spaces) signed
with Ed25519 (PyNaCl). It holds the sha256 of each input, model + provider per witness
(`meta-api` | `local-mlx` | `FIXTURE`), the verdict, the reasons, the public key and the signature.
The private key lives in `keys/` (git-ignored, mode 0600) and is never printed.

## Run

Requires Python 3.12+.

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest -q

# 1. fixture mode: hand-written witnesses, no model involved (receipt says FIXTURE). Its receipts go to
#    receipts-local/ (git-ignored): receipts/ holds real runs only, each signed by a seat in keys/known_signers.txt
python -m tinytms.cli checkin --mode fixture --fixture-dir fixtures/accept          # ACCEPT, exit 0
python -m tinytms.cli checkin --mode fixture --fixture-dir fixtures/count_mismatch  # HOLD, exit 2

# 2. api mode: Meta Model API, key from the environment only
MODEL_API_KEY=... python -m tinytms.cli checkin --mode api --load evals/public/boxes-mo

# Tu Arbol Familiar: Parish Record Reader

Turn a photo of a handwritten Spanish or Latin parish record into a clean transcription, an English translation, and a filled bilingual genealogy record.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie Dev Track, theme: *Build for Your World*).

> **Status:** In active development during the hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026).

## The problem

Families tracing Hispanic roots often hit a wall at old church records. Baptism, marriage, and burial entries from the 1600s to 1900s are handwritten in faded ink, in old Spanish or Latin, with abbreviations and spellings that even fluent speakers struggle to read. The names and dates are right there on the page, but most people can't get them out.

## What it does

1. **Upload a photo** of a parish record (baptism, marriage, or burial).
2. **Transcribe** the handwriting into text, keeping the original spelling.
3. **Translate** the record into English.
4. **Extract the key facts**: names, dates, places, parents, godparents, witnesses, priest.
5. **Fill a bilingual genealogy record** (Spanish and English) as a PDF, ready to save or print.

## How it works

- **Vision and language models:** Meta Llama models handle reading the page, transcription, translation, and field extraction.
- **Model testing on Baseten:** open-source vision and language models run on Baseten so they can be compared side by side with Llama.
- **Accuracy scoring:** every model is benchmarked on a 30-page test set of 1700s Spanish records with expert transcriptions, scored by character error rate (CER) and word error rate (WER).
- **PDF output:** extracted fields are written into a fillable bilingual genealogy form.

## Roadmap

- [x] Image preprocessing (crop, deskew, contrast)
- [ ] Image upload endpoint (code written; needs a live Modal run)
- [x] Transcription pipeline (mock engine; real model pending)
- [x] Translation and field extraction (mock data)
- [ ] Accuracy benchmark (CER/WER) across models
- [x] Bilingual PDF generation
- [ ] Simple web interface
- [ ] Demo video

## Getting started

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
cp .env.example .env   # fill in provider keys as later phases need them
```

Day 1 runs fully offline with a mock transcription engine:

```bash
python -m parish_record_reader.cli samples/dummy_record.jpg
# writes outputs/dummy_record_record.pdf (+ JSON sidecar + preprocessed PNG)
pytest
```

To try the Modal-hosted endpoints (requires `modal setup` first):

```bash
modal serve -m parish_record_reader.app
# POST /transcribe  multipart field `file` -> JSON (image + fields) for review
# POST /render      edited JSON -> filled PDF
# POST /process     multipart field `file` -> filled PDF (one-shot)
```

## Author

Terry Kinder ([@tkinder](https://github.com/tkinder))

# DevOps as a Service

A multi-agent GitHub Issue workflow: **one issue in → a fix → a tested pull
request out** — and when an issue is destructive or ambiguous, the agents
stop and escalate to a human instead.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie Dev Track),
sprint window **Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026**. Entry as submitted: *"DevOps as a
Service"*, showcasing the multi-agent workflow that checks out the code,
performs the fix, then opens a PR.

## Who this is for

Small engineering teams — two to ten developers, like the five-engineer
shop in the demo — whose backlog is full of small, well-defined fixes.
Each one costs a senior engineer an hour or more of focused time, so the
small stuff waits for weeks while the expensive people are the bottleneck.

DevOps as a Service clears that backlog: file the issue, and the agents
return a reviewed, tested pull request. The team's lead spends minutes
approving instead of hours implementing — and every run is scored (see
`eval-scorecard/`), so the value is measured,
not asserted. A worked model of that time saving, with every input
labeled measured / asserted / assumed, is in `IMPACT_MODEL.md` — a
model, not a measured result. Destructive or ambiguous issues are never auto-fixed; they
come back as a written escalation for a human decision.

Path to real use: point the workflow at any GitHub repository. After the
hackathon it becomes a managed service — the same loop, run for client
teams that don't have DevOps hours to spare.

## How it works

1. **Triage agent** reads the issue and restates the problem + acceptance criteria.
2. **Planner agent** breaks the fix into steps and names the files it expects to touch.
3. **Coder agent** checks out a branch, implements the fix, adds/updates tests.
4. **Reviewer agent** runs the test suite and inspects the diff for unrelated changes.
5. **PR step** opens a pull request with a summary of what changed and what was checked.

A **deterministic guardrail** runs before any model call: destructive or
ambiguous issues are escalated with a structured human approval request
(what the pipeline provably did not do, the human's three options, and a
blank decision record — in markdown and JSON), never auto-fixed.
**Approve-and-resume** completes the gate: a human records a validated
decision, reject / handle-manually close with zero model calls, and
re-scope — the only resumable decision — re-enters the pipeline with a
narrower issue that re-runs the guardrail (see `APPROVE_AND_RESUME.md`;
measured mock + live flows in `eval-scorecard/resume-runs.json`).
Model calls go through one `llm` abstraction pointed at the Meta Model API.

| `hackathon-agent-scaffold/` | The agent-loop pipeline (`daas/` package: gua

NotPellew/Thalvi.readme_excerpt:
# Thalvi

Talk to your coding agents instead of typing to them. Say "Hey Thalvi" in any
window, say the whole thing, then decide: paste it, send it, or drop it.

Built with Muse Spark Open.

Typing a good prompt is a chore, so prompts end up short and leave out what the
agent needs. Speaking takes that barrier away, most of all for long prompts. You
can correct yourself as you go and look at something else while you talk, and
the words still land in the window you started from. The agent workflow is
tested with Muse Code on Hyprland.

The same voice helps whenever typing isn't an option:

- **Cooking:** pick a recipe together and get walked through it step by step.
- **On the road:** a briefing on the topics you care about, then follow-up
  questions in plain conversation.
- **Messages on the go:** dictate a reply and confirm it out loud before
  anything is sent.

Thalvi has two parts:

- **The desktop app** (Hyprland and Windows) listens for "Hey Thalvi" and
  types what you dictate into the window you are using.
- **The server and its web client** hold the spoken conversation. Open it in a
  browser, on your phone for example, and talk over it to interrupt.

**Download the desktop app:** the
[latest release](https://github.com/NotPellew/Thalvi/releases/latest) has the
Windows installer and the Linux AppImage; see [Install](#install).

It is built to self-host. By default it uses Meta's Muse Voice Transcribe for
live speech and Muse Spark for reasoning and tool use, and speaks with a voice
engine on your own machine. Each model is an endpoint in `.env`, so any
compatible server can replace it, such as Ollama or vLLM. Camera input (SAM
3.1) is not built yet.

## Server and web client

### Run it

1. Start a speech engine (see [Speech](#speech)). On an NVIDIA GPU with 9 GB
   of free VRAM:

   ```sh
   hf download Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base --local-dir ~/thalvi-tts/models/qwen3-base
   docker compose --profile vllm-omni up -d --wait
   ```

   Without one: `docker compose --profile kokoro up -d --wait`.
2. `cp .env.example .env`, then fill in the API keys and the speech lines for
   the engine you started. `.env.example` describes every setting.
3. `npm ci --prefix web && npm run build --prefix web`, then `cargo run --release`.
4. `tailscale serve --bg 8080` and open the printed HTTPS address on your phone.

There is no authentication: anyone who can reach the server can read and
delete every conversation, so keep it on your tailnet.

### Use it

**Voice** turns the microphone on and off. **Speak replies** chooses whether
replies are spoken; it follows Voice, and you can flip it on its own to type and
listen, or to talk and read. Talking while Thalvi speaks interrupts it. The
**1×** chip sets the playback speed, and the **Voice** chip picks the voice (see
[Voices](#voices)).

An error stays on screen until you dismiss it or it is fixed, and **Copy** puts
its text on the clipboard.

With `LLM_AUDIO_INPUT=on`, the language model hears each spoke

# WireProof

**Proof your wiring is safe before the plaster goes on.**

WireProof is a hands-free copilot for the electrician wiring a house. The homeowner gets proof, before the walls are plastered, that every circuit has the right cable, real copper and the right protection. Afterwards they get an "X-ray" map of where every cable runs inside their walls.

- Lagos recorded 1,685 fires and 133 deaths in 2025. Studies name electrical faults as the leading cause.

# DORA: a crop-season planning agent

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (build period: Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026). Everything in this repository was written during the event; the git history starts on Oct 27.

**Prior work.** The idea builds on earlier research by the author: a paper on shadow prices of capital over a crop season and a private prototype of the optimizer. No code from that prototype was copied here; the engine, the agent, the verifier, the app and the evaluation in this repository were written from scratch during the event, as the git history shows.

**Live demo:** https://guillermosiaira--dora-web.us-east.modal.run (Spanish and English; the first load can take a minute while the container starts).

**Video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/W4zBWeavPi0

An Argentine grain farmer describes the season in plain words, a voice note, a photo of an invoice or a field drawn on the map. An agent running on Meta's Muse Spark turns that into a scenario and calls a linear-programming engine that plans the season fortnight by fortnight: how many hectares of each crop, when to sell or store, when to use credit, and what each scarce resource is worth (shadow prices of cash, capital, land, storage and credit). It also tells an owner what renting the land out would pay and the rent above which renting beats farming, and for each crop left out, the price in each sale fortnight at which it would be worth sowing (from the LP reduced costs, checked by re-solving). A deterministic verifier checks that every number in the agent's answer comes from the engine before the farmer sees it. When something the farmer did not say could change the plan, the agent asks one question at a time, starting with the one that would cost the most to get wrong.

**The language model talks; the math decides.** The model never computes a plan: it builds the scenario, calls the tools and explains the result.

## How it works

```
farmer (text, voice, photo, map)
   │  Voice Transcribe · Muse Spark vision · SAM 3.1 (water on aerial photos)
   ▼
agent (Muse Spark 1.3) ── tools ──► build_scenario · evaluate_season · shadow_prices ·
   │                                 sensitivity · compare_regions · climate_scenarios ·
   │                                 record_document · assess_field_image · next_question ·
   │                                 break_even_prices · tax_wedge · …
   │                                        │
   │                                        ▼
   │                             LP engine (HiGHS): fortnightly cash, credit, storage,
   │                             land tenure, sowing windows, climate scenarios, livestock in heads
   ▼
verifier: every number in the answer must come from a tool result → correction round if not
   ▼
answer that starts with the decision, in the farmer's language
```

Children learn to read best in their mother tongue, but most of the world's languages have very few children's books. In India, a child in Belagavi or Guntur finds shelves of English picture books and very few in the language spoken at home.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie Dev track. All code in this repository was written during the hackathon.

framing comes from that experience; the code does not.

Pre-existing material: VOA Learning English footage (public domain) and
ElevenLabs stock voices.

| Lane | What it does | Meta model |
|---|---|---|
| Translate + timing gate | Translates each line, estimates spoken length against the original window, bounces failures back to the model to revise (up to 3 attempts) | `muse-spark-1.1` |
| Meaning gate | Judges whether the translation still says what the source said; skipped (`NotEvaluated`, zero tokens) when timing already failed | `muse-spark-1.1` |

| Static-shot gate | Extends one sign repaint across a whole shot, only if every frame's sign region still matches the repainted frame | none (reuses the one repaint) |

# FixLens — photograph a home fault, get a diagnosis and a repair ticket

**Judge version.** A tenant sends a blurry photo of
"something wrong." FixLens finds *where* the fault is, says *what* it
is and *how urgent* it is, and drafts what to do next: an ordered
repair checklist, a parts list (quantities only, no prices), and a
landlord–tenant repair ticket marked DRAFT — nothing is ever sent
automatically.

## The problem

As a landlord, Wen Sun gets photos like this from tenants and has to
guess: what is it, how urgent is it, what parts do I buy, and how do
I write it up? FixLens turns that one photo into an answer.

## The solution (what works today)

1. **Photo** — upload a photo of a home fault.
2. **Segmentation** — the faulty area is highlighted on the photo.
3. **Diagnosis** — fault type, severity *with triage reasoning*,
   likely cause, safety warnings shown first (water / electrical /
   gas-adjacent faults), repair steps in order, parts list,
   difficulty and estimated time (ranges, labelled estimates), and a
   landlord-vs-tenant responsibility *hint* (never a legal ruling).
4. **Ticket** — a draft ticket with editable example fields
   (property / tenant / landlord) and status `draft`.

Four deterministic mock faults are built in: water stain / leak, wall
crack, mould spot, and peeling paint — pick one in the upload form
or let the filename/notes pick it. In meta mode the region comes
from SAM 3.1 instead, and the upload page renders the photo itself
with the region drawn on it: a red box plus, when the optional
parser is installed, a translucent red pixel mask inside the box —
the segmentation is visible, not just a line of text.

## How it works (pipeline)

One photo flows through two Meta models, each doing the job the
other cannot:

1. **Concept** — the fault is mapped to a single short noun phrase
   ("water stain", "wall crack", …). SAM takes exactly one concept
   per request, so raw user text is never passed through as the
   prompt.
2. **Segment (SAM 3.1)** — SAM returns a pixel box plus a pixel
   mask for the concept. The largest-area box wins (a photo can
   hold several stains/cracks); on zero matches it retries once
   with the broader concept "damage", then fails with a friendly
   message instead of a bare error.
3. **Mask overlay** — the mask payload is decoded with Meta's
   official `meta-sam-parser` (optional, zero-dependency itself)
   and rendered as a semi-transparent red PNG inside the box by a
   pure-stdlib encoder. Without the parser, or on any decode
   failure, the page degrades to box-only — a mask problem never
   breaks a diagnosis.
4. **Diagnose (Muse Spark 1.3)** — Spark receives the photo plus
   the segmented region and returns structured output
   (`text.format` JSON schema): fault type, severity *with a
   reason*, likely cause, safety warnings first, ordered repair
   steps, parts with quantities only (never prices), difficulty
   and time as labelled estimates, and a responsibility hint.

# Resurrection

Give it a video of someone using an old app. Get back a working web app that looks and behaves the same, with a score that proves it.

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon) (Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026). Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon.

## Why

Companies and public services still run apps whose source code is lost. Web archives and museums keep videos and screenshots of sites that no longer exist. A video is often the only thing left. Resurrection turns that video back into something you can click.

## How it works

1. **Read the video.** Muse Wonder watches someone use the old app and writes a JSON spec: the screens, the components on each screen, and what every click does.
2. **Rewrite the app.** Muse Code turns the spec into modern HTML, CSS and JS.
3. **Restore the visuals.** Muse Image redraws icons, logos and backgrounds that are too pixelated or missing.
4. **Prove it.** Playwright redoes the same clicks on the new app, and both sides are compared step by step:
   - **look**: frame by frame similarity (SSIM);
   - **layout**: SAM 3.1 finds buttons, text fields and images on both sides, and we measure whether they sit at the same place with the same size (IoU);
   - **journey**: does each click lead to the same screen?
5. **Fix and repeat.** The score report goes back to Muse Code until the score passes a threshold.

```
video ──► Muse Wonder ──► spec.json ──► Muse Code ──► index.html ──► Playwright replay
                                            ▲                              │
                                            └──── score report ◄── SSIM + SAM 3.1 + journey
```

What it does not do: the new app copies what the video shows. It cannot recover a backend or data the video never showed, and we say so in the demo.

## Quick start

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e '.[dev]'
playwright install chromium

# film the example app, then resurrect it from that video
resurrect build examples/robot-club.json --out out/original.html
resurrect film examples/robot-club.json out/original.html samples/robot-club.mp4
cp examples/robot-club.json samples/robot-club.json
resurrect run samples/robot-club.mp4
```

Each round writes `out/<video>/round_N/` with the app, the captured frames and `report.json`.

Until the Meta models are plugged in, `run` uses offline stand-ins: the spec is read from a JSON file next to the video (`--reader spec-file`) and the app is drawn from a template (`--writer template`).

To score an app written by hand (or by a coding agent) against a video:

```bash
resurrect frames samples/my-app.mp4                  # frames named by timestamp
resurrect score samples/my-app.mp4 spec.json index.html
```

During development we use Claude Code in place of the Meta models to save API credits; the procedure is in [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md). The demo runs on Meta models.

# refi_assist

Consumer-facing educational tool that compares keeping an auto loan,
refinancing now, and waiting under explicit rate scenarios — and checks
every number it shows against its source, with you confirming each one
before anything is computed. Lender calculators show the lower monthly payment
and hide the higher total cost; this tool makes the tradeoff visible,
including how much of the difference comes from the rate, the term, and
fees. Solo hackathon entry. All example loans and scenarios are
synthetic; no real borrower data anywhere.

Hosted app: https://refiassist.streamlit.app/

It is an educational estimator, not financial advice. It does not offer
or broker loans or accept applications, and it stores nothing you enter:
everything stays in session memory.

## How it works

1. Paste or upload your statements. The model extracts the loan terms,
   each with the exact quote it was copied from.
2. A code check confirms every quote really appears in your statement
   text (or its transcript, for photos and scans).
3. You review, edit, and confirm every number on the confirm page. No
   computation runs on unconfirmed inputs.
4. Local code computes the comparison, the rate/term/costs split, and the
   verdict from fixed rules — the model never computes a number.
5. The model explains the verdict in plain language; code checks every
   number in the explanation, and the Baseten claim judge checks its
   meaning. The page states whether you are seeing the verified model
   narrative, a rewrite, or a code-written template.

Waiting is scenario analysis, never a forecast: the page computes what
happens under rate scenarios you can see and change.

## Meta tooling, and where each piece is used

- **Muse Code** — the agentic CLI the project was built with.
- **Muse Spark** via the Meta Model API — statement extraction, the
  verdict explanation, and the transcript read for photos and scans.
- **Muse Spark Open on Baseten** — the independent claim judge, a
  different model from the one that wrote the explanation.

## Results

Full method, history, and caveats: [docs/EVALUATIONS.md](docs/EVALUATIONS.md).

- dev-04 (13 scenarios): 96/98 grounded and correct, 0 wrong values,
  12 verified explanations plus 1 judge-outage template, 0 verdict flips.
- heldout-01 (12 held-out scenarios, recorded once): 89/91 grounded and
  correct with the other 2 correctly cleared, 0 wrong values, 12/12
  verified (judge passed on all twelve), 0 verdict flips.
- Claim judge: 6/6 caught on dev fixtures; on 8 held-out drafts, 3/4 bad
  drafts caught with 0 false flags. The miss was a quiet reversal of the
  verdict at the end of an accurate draft (see EVALUATIONS.md §5, §7).
- Image path: two runs. The first scored 86/99 with 2 wrong; after a
  renderer fix, the second scored 94/99 with 1 wrong, where vision
  misread 46 as 48 and extraction faithfully copied the misread. That
  is why every transcript is editable and every number goes through
  the confirm page.

**[adfarming-studio-preview.vercel.app](https://adfarming-studio-preview.vercel.app/)** is a clickable demo with a made-up brand ("Demo Saree Brand"). It runs entirely in your browser: no server, no AI, nothing is spent. Type any password to get in, press **New run**, then **Start**.

# ancientos-hackathon
AncientOS rebuild for the Meta hackathon (Oct 26–Nov 4, 2026).

A small Rust core that lets AI agents act on your behalf only through a fail-closed approval gate, a privacy router and a hash-chained decision log.

## Demo video

[Watch the demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AqqmyBX3_5E)

## Meta stack

- **Meta Model API** (Muse Spark / Wonder) for hosted intelligence on sanitized text.
- **Llama running locally** (Ollama or llama.cpp) for sensitive data.
- **Muse Spark Open** (Meta open weights) on Baseten as an alternate image-analysis backend.

Muse Spark and Wonder are Meta's model names on the Meta Model API, not AncientOS crates.

## Why AncientOS exists

Built from scratch in Rust for this hackathon (Oct 26–Nov 4, 2026), distilling the governance and security core from a private ~180k-line Python assistant (not in this repo).

An AI agent is only useful if it can act: sync your bookmarks, run a coding job, ask a model a question. But most agents get that power by being handed your keys and trusted to behave.

AncientOS takes a different route: the agent can act, but it never holds unrestricted authority. Four jobs are kept apart:

```
 intelligence  ->  authorization  ->  execution  ->  evidence
 (models,          (gate + your       (runs once,     (hash-chained
  privacy router)   approval)          paid switch)    decision log)
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Request] --> R{Privacy router}
  R -->|sensitive| L[Local Llama]
  R -->|sanitized| M[Meta Model API]
  L --> G[Approval gate]
  M --> G
  G -->|approved release token| X[Execution with paid switch]
  X --> E[Hash-chained decision log]
```

- **Intelligence** proposes. A privacy router keeps sensitive or unclassified text on a local Llama model; only sanitized text goes to Meta's cloud models.
- **Authorization** decides. Actions an app hasn't registered are denied. Risky ones wait for your approval, on the CLI or your phone, and the approval is bound to a hash of the exact payload.
- **Execution** is limited. Anything that costs money stays off unless `ANCIENTOS_ALLOW_PAID=1` is set.
- **Evidence** is kept. Every decision lands in an append-only, hash-chained log, checked on every read.

Three apps (an X bookmarks curator, gated Muse Code runs, and Muse Wonder questions) share this one small core, which knows nothing about any of them.

What isn't done yet: the release-token type check covers paid execution but not every action; the log has no cross-process lock, and signing is opt-in (ANCIENTOS_LOG_KEY_PATH); code can still call a model client without going through the router. Those are next. The demo runs with an unsigned log; the live deploy can sign it.

a fail-closed approval gate and an append-only, hash-chained decision log; a

# PlayTester

An AI agent that plays your game like a human — watching the screen, pressing keys — and writes reproducible bug reports.

By **Promptforge** — a one-person studio building games and tools with AI · mindkiln.dev@gmail.com

Built from scratch during Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 28 – Nov 4, 2026). All product code lives in `src/` and was written during the event; `loop/`, `docs/`, `tools/` are my open-source dev-process template (soilrist/loop-starter-kit) used to run the build.

## Meta models used
- **SAM 3.1** — perception: finds people, HP bars, doors, chests and dialog boxes on each screenshot. PlayTester works out which person box is the player by watching which one moved after a move key, then hands Spark every other object as an offset from the player ("74px right, 30px down").
- **Muse Spark 1.3** — decision: picks the next action via tool calling (`press`, `wait`, `note`, `report_bug`, `done`, plus `click` for mouse-driven games).

Bugs are flagged two ways: Spark calls `report_bug` when it sees something wrong, and fixed rules catch what a model can miss — `same_screen` (keys pressed, screen frozen) and `player_stuck` (SAM-tracked player did not move after three move keys in two or more directions, with no dialog open). After the session, `src/gamelog.py` reads the log files the engine already writes (UE `Saved/Logs`, Godot `user://logs`) and files a report per rule — assets missing from the build, crashes, script errors — with the log file attached. A game that dies while booting still gets a crash report.

## Game under test
Breath of the Abyss — my own unfinished Godot 4 top-down RPG, tested on a pinned snapshot of the private dev build (an older public version lives at [soilrist/breath-of-the-abyss](https://github.com/soilrist/breath-of-the-abyss)). PlayTester never reads its code; it only sees the screen and presses keys.

Second game, different engine: **Snarehaven**, my Unreal Engine 5 mobile monster-capture action game, packaged for Win64 and played offline (`-SnareOffline`) with keys plus real mouse clicks (left attacks, right captures). Same agent, no game-specific code beyond the launch command and window title: `PT_GAME=snarehaven tools/vm/run_in_vm.sh`.

```bash

On macOS, grant the terminal Screen Recording and Accessibility permission (needed to capture the game window and send keys).

Welcome to your new TanStack Start app!

# Getting Started

To run this application:

```bash
bun install

# Building For Production

To build this application for production:

```bash
bun --bun run build
```

## Styling

This project uses [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/) for styling.

### Removing Tailwind CSS

If you prefer not to use Tailwind CSS:

1. Remove the demo pages in `src/routes/demo/`
2. Replace the Tailwind import in `src/styles.css` with your own styles
3. Remove `tailwindcss()` from the plugins array in `vite.config.ts`
4. Remove `@tailwindcss/vite` and `tailwindcss` from `package.json`



## Routing

This project uses [TanStack Router](https://tanstack.com/router) with file-based routing. Routes are managed as files in `src/routes`.

### Adding A Route

To add a new route to your application just add a new file in the `./src/routes` directory.

TanStack will automatically generate the content of the route file for you.

Now that you have two routes you can use a `Link` component to navigate between them.

### Adding Links

To use SPA (Single Page Application) navigation you will need to import the `Link` component from `@tanstack/react-router`.

```tsx
import { Link } from "@tanstack/react-router";
```

Then anywhere in your JSX you can use it like so:

```tsx
<Link to="/about">About</Link>
```

This will create a link that will navigate to the `/about` route.

More information on the `Link` component can be found in the [Link documentation](https://tanstack.com/router/v1/docs/framework/react/api/router/linkComponent).

### Using A Layout

In the File Based Routing setup the layout is located in `src/routes/__root.tsx`. Anything you add to the root route will appear in all the routes. The route content will appear in the JSX where you render `{children}` in the `shellComponent`.

Here is an example layout that includes a header:

```tsx
import { HeadContent, Scripts, createRootRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router'

export const Route = createRootRoute({
  head: () => ({
    meta: [
      { charSet: 'utf-8' },
      { name: 'viewport', content: 'width=device-width, initial-scale=1' },
      { title: 'My App' },
    ],
  }),
  shellComponent: ({ children }) => (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        <HeadContent />
      </head>
      <body>
        <header>
          <nav>
            <Link to="/">Home</Link>
            <Link to="/about">About</Link>
          </nav>
        </header>
        {children}
        <Scripts />
      </body>
    </html>
  ),
})
```

More information on layouts can be found in the [Layouts documentation](https://tanstack.com/router/latest

# Meeting Pro — WhatsApp call transcription

**VILATECH** · Meeting Pro · Expo SDK 58 · React Native 0.88 · Supabase

Meeting Pro turns business WhatsApp calls into searchable, speaker-separated transcripts.

**Meta Global AI Hackathon (startup track):** [docs/HACKATHON_SUBMISSION.md](docs/HACKATHON_SUBMISSION.md) · [docs/META_HACKATHON_STARTUP.md](docs/META_HACKATHON_STARTUP.md) (demo script, due **Nov 4**).

**This is work in progress, not a working product.** Read *What works* and *What does not* before relying on anything here.

---

## The one fact you must know

**A phone cannot record a WhatsApp call — not on iOS, not on Android, with no workaround short of rooting or jailbreaking the device.** WhatsApp calls run inside the operating system's calling sandbox, and both platforms deliberately block other apps from capturing that audio.

So the phone records nothing. **Meta does the transcription on its own servers**, through the WhatsApp Business Calling API. When a call ends, Meta sends the transcript to our backend as a webhook — speakers already separated, word timings included. Our backend verifies it and stores it in Supabase. **The app only reads from the database.**

```
WhatsApp call on a business number
        │
Meta Cloud API ── records and transcribes on Meta's servers
        │  webhook: call_transcription_available
        ▼
Supabase Edge Function  supabase/functions/whatsapp-webhook
        │  verify signature → log → fetch transcript → verify hash → store
        ▼
Postgres: calls, transcripts, transcript_segments
        │
        ▼
React Native app ── signs in, reads; never records
```

Any design that has the phone capture call audio is a dead end. Constraints that follow from Meta's side:

- Only numbers on the WhatsApp **Cloud API** with Calling enabled can do this; the WhatsApp Business *app* cannot.
- Both parties hear a mandatory announcement that the call is being transcribed. It cannot be turned off.
- Meta deletes the transcript after **7 days**, and download links expire after **5 minutes**. The backend copies the transcript immediately and keeps it.
- Language detection covers about 54 languages, including Afrikaans. **Zulu and Xhosa are not supported.**

---

## What works

Each item says what was proven and on which infrastructure. "Local" means a Supabase stack in Docker on a developer machine. "Dev" means the hosted Supabase project `meeting-pro-dev` (Frankfurt).

### Database schema — `supabase/migrations/`

The schema is multi-tenant: every business's data is isolated by RLS (row-level security — the database's own rules deciding who can read which rows). It has ten tables: businesses, members, WhatsApp numbers, webhook log, calls, transcripts, segments, action items, tags and transcript tags.

| Proof | Where |
|---|---|
| `tests/01_schema_verification.sql`: tenant isolation, column-level edit rights, webhook deduplication, full-text and typo-tolerant search — **30/30** | Local |
| Migration applied; trigr

# SIRA

**An AI astronomer built to be proven wrong in public.**

SIRA investigates cosmic transients — supernovae, tidal disruption events, microlensing — using public alerts from real sky surveys (ZTF, via the ALeRCE broker). It proposes rival physical hypotheses, registers quantitative predictions *before* new observations arrive, and lets the data grade them. It decides when to wait, think harder, or ask for help, and it keeps a public, timestamped record of every bet.

Built by Alejandro Cornejo (solo, Indie track) for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, *Push the Frontier*, with Meta's Muse models. Built with Muse Spark Open.

Site: **https://alehcs.github.io/sira/** (the lab, Beat SIRA, the forecasts and the archive). Live ledger: the [`ledger`](https://github.com/Alehcs/sira/tree/ledger) branch.

> Status: betting live every night since October 27, 2026. ZTF has sent no new data since October 29, 13:18 UTC; questions whose answer window falls in that gap are void by the sealed rule, reported and not counted.

![How SIRA works](docs/diagram.svg)

## What it showed

On 37 objects from a test split it had never seen, in an evaluation pre-registered and timestamped before it ran ([`evidence/plan.json`](evidence/plan.json)):

- **It forecast better than Muse alone and than its own physics alone.** SIRA minus Muse alone: +0.98 nats per measurement (95% interval 0.41 to 1.64), about 2.7 times the probability on what the sky actually did. SIRA minus physics alone: +0.30 (0.12 to 0.52), about 1.35 times. Both hold in each of the two runs. The edge comes from pooling physics with Muse's own forecast; on plain SN Ia, physics alone is slightly better.
- **The edge is Muse's, not averaging's.** Measured after the plan, so not pre-registered: pooling the same physics with climatology instead of Muse's forecast loses 0.30 nats per measurement (0.11 to 0.54), although alone Muse scores about the same as climatology.

On 4 of the 6 surprises the lens forecast the data it had not seen far better than the old hypotheses, and no SN Ia surprised the physics. In the full replays it also put a lens on a superluminous supernova, and won its test there because the lab has no superluminous model: one false discovery. One Le Verrier did as well as five, at a fifth of the cost.

# Kepler

Film anything that moves and get a working, verified simulation of it.
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Everything in this repo was written during the event.

This is the **day 1–2 slice**: a phone clip goes in, and the ball's position in metres comes out for every frame, checked against gravity.

```
clip ──▶ probe/prep ──▶ SAM 3.1 tracks the ball ──▶ A4 sheet ▶ homography ──▶ metres ──▶ gravity check (g within 2%)
                                                                                  └──▶ trajectory.json (input to the theory agent)
```

## Setup (macOS)

```bash
brew install ffmpeg
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env        # then paste your Meta Model API key into .env
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v   # 14 tests, no API key needed, ~20 s
```

## Day 1: film and track

1. **Film.** 240 fps slow motion, phone on a tripod, main 1× lens, square to the motion. Tape an A4 sheet **in the plane the ball's centre moves in**, fully visible. Use a plain background and bright light. Release the ball from rest.
2. **Check the file.** `python -m kepler probe IMG_0001.MOV` shows the real frame rate. If it says 30 fps for a slow-motion clip, the phone re-timed it: export the original, or add `--capture-fps 240` later.
3. **Convert.** `python -m kepler prep IMG_0001.MOV -o clips/ramp1.mp4` writes an H.264 MP4 with every captured frame kept and phone slow-motion edits dropped.
4. **Track.**
   ```bash
   python -m kepler track clips/ramp1.mp4 --object "steel ball" --still 0,0.2 -o runs/ramp1
   ```
   - `--object` is the SAM 3.1 concept prompt: a short noun phrase, one object.
   - If SAM picks the wrong thing, mark the ball with a box instead: `--box x1,y1,x2,y2 --box-frame 0`.
   - `--still 0,0.2` gives the seconds when the ball sits at rest, for the jitter check.
   - If the sheet isn't found, pass its corners: `--sheet tlx,tly,trx,try,brx,bry,blx,bly`.

## Day 2: the gravity gate

`track` already prints the result:

```
[PASS] g = 9.764 ± 0.009 m/s² (-0.47% vs 9.81) from 63 frames, 0.279-0.537 s, fit RMS 0.19 mm
```

- **FAIL with g far off** (say 0.15): timing is wrong. The message names the true frame rate; rerun with `--capture-fps`.
- **FAIL by a few percent:** check, in order, the sheet's plane, the 1× lens, the phone being square to the motion, and motion blur.
- **Wrong window picked:** set it by hand with `python -m kepler check runs/ramp1/trajectory.json --fall 0.31,0.52`.

Open `runs/ramp1/overlay.mp4` to see the tracked path drawn over the clip (green circle = frames used for the fit).

## Day 3: theories, and the cup (Kepler Prime)

The ball rolls down a straight ramp, leaves its end and flies. `fit` finds the ramp's angle and the launch point, fits every theory in the library to every clip at once (physical parameters shared, release time and point per clip), and scores each on the last 20% of the ramp run, w

# Dex: instantly add a shared bill, without the hassle

Snap a group bill, tell Dex who had what (out loud or by typing), and Dex splits
it item by item, to the cent, then saves it to your expense log as one expense
with each person's exact share.

Built on Meta's models for the
[Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon)
(Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Indie track, theme: *Build for Your World*.

**Try it:** https://dex-ai-vl0t.onrender.com. It's a free instance, so the first
visit after a quiet spell takes 30–60s to wake. Use your own receipt or
[samples/luigis-receipt.png](samples/luigis-receipt.png).

![Dex: the receipt, the chat with Dex, and the split beside it](docs/screenshot.png)

---

## What it does

1. **Snap the bill.** Dex reads every line: items, quantities, discounts, tax, tip and total, and
   checks that the numbers add up.
2. **Say who had what.** Hold the mic or type, the way you'd tell a friend:
   *"I had the pasta, Aayush and Ketan split the pizza, we all shared the
   knots, Kunal paid."* Dex works out every item, picks up the names, and asks
   when something is genuinely unclear. Fix anything the same way: *"No, Ketan
   didn't have knots."*
3. **Approve.** Tax and tip are spread by what each person had, every cent is
   accounted for, and the split is saved to
   [Balance Dex](https://balance-desk.chaityadobariya.me) as one expense with
   exact shares. It's saved once, even if you tap twice.

## How it works

![How Dex adds a shared bill: read the receipt and check the sums, transcribe what you said, decide who had what with checked tools, split to the cent, preview, then save to Balance Dex](docs/workflow.png)

### The agent: the model decides, the code does the work

The model never does arithmetic and never writes anything. It can only call six
tools, and the code checks every call before applying it. A bad call (an item
number that isn't on the receipt, a name nobody mentioned) goes back to the
model as an error it can correct.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as You
    participant D as Dex (page)
    participant M as Muse Spark Open
    participant T as Tools (validated in code)
    U->>D: "Aayush and Ketan split the pizza, Kunal paid"
    D->>M: receipt items (as data) + people + current split + what you said
    M->>T: add_person(Aayush), add_person(Ketan), assign_item(1, [Aayush, Ketan]), set_payer(Kunal)
    T-->>M: ok / error the model can fix
    M-->>D: one-line summary, and a question if something's unclear
    D->>D: split.py recomputes every share
    D-->>U: updated split and photo
```

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `assign_item` | who had an item, equally or by portions ("I had 2 of the 3 sodas") |
| `unassign_item` | clear an item |
| `add_person` | someone new; a near-miss of a known contact ("Aleex" for "Alex") is refused with a "did you mean" |
| `set_payer` | who paid |
| `set_tax_tip` | tax and tip by what each person had, or evenly |

# jepa-as-a-tool

**An LLM agent that imagines its moves in a V-JEPA 2 world model before touching the real table.**

Entry to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026).
Website with live episodes: https://rahulchander25.github.io/jepa-as-a-tool/

Muse Spark pushes objects to a goal, one straight push at a time, in three worlds: PushT (2D), a 3D
tabletop and 3D billiards. Before each real push it can call one tool, `simulate(from_frame,
plans)`, which imagines candidate push sequences in a learned world model and says, in text, where
things would end up. **One** world model serves the three worlds; it never saw the physics engines,
it learned from images only.

## How it works

```
frame ──▶ V-JEPA 2 (frozen) ──▶ latent ──▶ predictor (+ push) ──▶ latent ──▶ translator ──▶ "T at (212, 180), 35°"
                                              ▲ chains of pushes stay in latent space
```

| Part | What it is | Trained here? |
|---|---|---|
| **Encoder** | Meta's V-JEPA 2 (ViT-L, `facebook/vjepa2-vitl-fpc64-256`): a 256 px frame becomes 64 tokens × 1,024 | no, frozen |
| **Predictor** | a 6-layer transformer: latent + push → next latent; one for the three worlds, not told which one | yes |
| **Translator** | latent → positions: a shared trunk and one head per world; the only thing the LLM reads | yes |
| **Tool** | `simulate`: several plans per call, an id for every imagined state (`I1`, `I2`, …) so the agent can continue a branch | — |
| **Agent** | Muse Spark 1.3 on the Meta Model API, with LangChain tools and our own loop | no |

The same tool also runs on an **oracle** backend (the real physics), which gives the best case for
an agent with perfect imagination. The trained model is on Hugging Face:
