What main proves today:

- The scope-first gate. Its contract is in `crates/acan-intent`. A worker's readback of its task is refused until a human confirms the scope.

# PinchPlan – Hands-First Spatial Focus Desk

![WebXR](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebXR-Meta%20Quest-0467DF?logo=meta&logoColor=white) ![Three.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Three.js-r169-black?logo=threedotjs&logoColor=white) ![hackathon](https://img.shields.io/badge/hackathon-Meta%20VR%20Start%202026-purple) [![demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/demo-live-success)](https://swapnilchaudhari007.github.io/pinchplan/) [![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)](LICENSE)

A seated, hands-first mixed-reality task board and focus timer for Meta Quest, built with WebXR + Three.js.
Entry for the Meta VR Start Developer Competition 2026 (Productivity track).

**Live demo:** https://swapnilchaudhari007.github.io/pinchplan/ — open it in the Meta Quest Browser and tap **Enter Mixed Reality**.

## Hand controls (no controllers needed)
- **Pinch** a card quickly → moves it to the next lane (Next up → Now → Done)
- **Pinch & drag** a card → move it between lanes / reorder
- Drag a card **below the board** → delete
- **Pinch the orb** → start / pause a focus session (5, 15 or 25 min)
- Turn your **left palm up** → wrist menu (add task, focus, clear done, recenter)

Controllers and mouse also work as fallbacks. Data is stored locally on the device.

## Tech
- WebXR `immersive-ar` (passthrough) with `hand-tracking`, falls back to `immersive-vr`
- Three.js r169, custom pinch / palm-up gesture detection from WebXR joint poses
- Single static `index.html`, hosted on GitHub Pages

## Run locally
```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000   # then open http://localhost:8000
```
WebXR needs HTTPS on a headset — use the GitHub Pages link above, or a tunnel such as `npx localtunnel --port 8000`.

## License
See [LICENSE](LICENSE).


## Troubleshooting

**No "Enter Mixed Reality" button?** Make sure you opened the HTTPS GitHub Pages link in the Meta Quest Browser. WebXR is blocked on plain HTTP.

**Hands not detected?** Enable hand tracking in Quest Settings > Movement tracking, put the controllers down, and hold your hands in front of the headset.

**Board in the wrong place?** Turn your left palm up and choose Recenter from the wrist menu.

**Tasks disappeared?** Tasks live in the browser's local storage on the headset, so clearing browsing data removes them.

## Project docs

[Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) · [Roadmap](ROADMAP.md) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Security](SECURITY.md) · [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

# TWINFORGE — The next frame is the test.

The main interface observes changing 3D scenes, a phone camera, or a local video through images. **Actual Meta SAM 3.1 segmentation is required before a track can produce a forecast.** A separate local tracker follows the segmented objects between SAM responses, and a motion model estimates their image position 0.5–1 second ahead. The observer receives no simulator positions, velocities, masses, forces, or seed.

[Watch the 3-minute demo](https://youtu.be/ySzrCQ7G3Tk) · [Video backup](https://mkinvest57.github.io/TWINFORGE/demo.html) · [Live observation interface](index.html) · [Camera mode](index.html?mode=camera) · [Architecture and setup](docs/SAM_LIVE_OBSERVATION.md)

## The live challenge

Open the [connected workspace](https://twinforge-mobile-camera.mkinvest57.chatgpt.site/), then **Start experiment → Lock a prediction → Reveal the outcome**. The synthetic world waits for its first real SAM mask, pauses with a recorded future target, and resumes until later tracked pixels can test that target. **Change the motion** applies a new private random impulse; only its rendered effect reaches the observer. A phone camera keeps running and records the outcome automatically.

In **Camera**, start a local preview, then tap an object, drag a box around it, choose **Hands**, or name an object type. Starting the preview alone sends no image to SAM. Taps and boxes use native SAM spatial prompts bound to the exact selected frame. **Hands** requests visible hands and follows each tracked hand's overall movement; it does not predict finger joints or future intentions. **Open video** uses the same selection workflow with a local clip. The initial video frame waits for selection and SAM confirmation before playback.

The dark English interface uses native adaptations of inspected 21st.dev temporal, usage, toolbar and dialog patterns. Settings and connection details are separate from the experiment. The static GitHub Pages address links to the connected workspace because it cannot run the private model API.

The November 5 reliability update fixes a disconnected SAM request that could hold the shared service busy for 180 seconds. Paid requests now finish durably; the provider deadline is 15 seconds and a stale lease expires after 30 seconds. A scene reset discards old responses without aborting the underlying paid request. Uniquely matched SAM confirmations preserve visual identity and motion history.

Earlier November 5 live evidence is in [the studio validation folder](validation/runs/studio-2026-11-05/). It retains successful locked targets **and** the flight-tracking failure that led to the color/search correction. Those captures precede the current camera-selection and long-horizon update. Do not turn a single good target into a general accuracy claim.

# The Lantern Room

**A seated, hands-first VR puzzle about waking a sleeping lantern.**

Meta VR Start Developer Competition 2026 entry · Track: **Gaming** · Division: **New Experience**

![The Lantern Room — desktop view of the observatory table](screenshots/lantern-room-desktop.png)

*The observatory table: constellation dial (front left), lantern (centre), orrery
(right), drawer (front), settings board (left). Screenshot from the real build
running in the IWSDK desktop view; see [Verification](#verification--honesty-notes).*

---

## Inspiration

The "Best First Five Minutes" brief asks for an opening that teaches itself. The
most memorable first five minutes in a headset are usually quiet ones: you look
at something small, reach for it, and it responds to your hand. So instead of a
menu, a tutorial, or a locomotion interlude, The Lantern Room gives you a warm
table in a dark observatory and three physical objects that are obviously
touchable. There is exactly one line of text. Everything else is taught by
reaction: hover glow, rotation, a satisfying click, a third of a lantern lighting
up.

The fantasy is simple: a lantern sits at the centre of an astronomer's table,
locked by three mechanisms. Each one is a small, quiet, hand-sized ritual.
Solving them wakes the lantern, and the room's fireflies come out to celebrate.

## What it does

A complete seated session is roughly **3–5 minutes** — the length of a bus stop.

| Mechanism | Hands-first interaction | What gives it away |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Constellation dial** | Pinch one of three concentric rings and twist your wrist to rotate it. Each ring snaps when its rune notch lines up with an engraved star line. | Glowing rune markers and three engraved target lines inlaid in the table. |
| **Hidden drawer** | Pinch the brass drawer knob and pull toward yourself, then pinch the hidden bolt inside and slide it sideways. | The drawer only appears once you pull; the bolt glints when revealed. |
| **Orrery** | Pinch a small planet and place it into a matching orbit cradle. Correct placements lock in with a chime; wrong ones bounce home. | Three coloured planets, three empty orbit slots sized to match. |

Each solved mechanism lights one of the lantern's three base gems and one third
of its glow. When all three are done, the lantern's petals swing open, the cap
rises, a swarm of fireflies bursts out, and a soft finale plays. The lantern then
offers a **soft restart**: pinch it to begin again without leaving the session.

**Accessibility and comfort**

- **High-contrast palette** (settings board or `C` key) — darker room, brighter
  brass and runes, higher ambient separation.
- **Gentle motion** (settings board or `G` key) — removes flicker and most
  particle drift for comfort.
- **Gaze-dwell Assist** (settings board or `A` key) — look at a mechanism to
  advance it one small step per dwell. Every hand interaction has an eyes-only

# Rouvr

**Rouvr. Make it happen.** Your pack, your ambition.

Rouvr is a reliable autonomous colleague: *think it through, agree the plan, get it moving*, with you in control. Website: [rouvr.ai](https://rouvr.ai).

[![CI](https://github.com/Anxy/rouvr/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Anxy/rouvr/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
![Python 3.12+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12%2B-blue.svg)

Delegate work, trust it to follow through, and progressively supervise less while remaining in control.

You give Rouvr a messy instruction, for example *"Get today's report, submit it to ABC, make sure XYZ is done, escalate to 123 if it fails, and email the stakeholders."* Rouvr turns it into **accountable execution**: recorded intent, an agreed execution contract, agents with defined authority, independent review, evidence, recovery on failure, and verified completion with receipts. Proven recurring work, once authorised, runs unprompted, and the daily update becomes exception-only: *"Done. No action needed."*

Rouvr starts with software development (Rouvr builds Rouvr). The ambition is business operations and everyday work.

> Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (2026) with the Meta Model API and Muse Code. The WorkHub/AIX governance and orchestration layer provides the accountability. Meta models are the intended engine for the intent → contract compiler, the ops reasoning steps and the verifier/judge (via the pluggable provider below).

## The idea: "Done. No action needed."

Most agent frameworks trust the agent's final message. Rouvr doesn't:

- **Stateless, role-agnostic bots.** All state lives in the ledger (tasks, leases, results, reviews), not in a chat session. Any bot can take any role, and a crashed bot can be replaced mid-task.
- **Builder ≠ reviewer.** The principal that produced a result can never accept it. Review is a separate lease held by a different identity.
- **System-produced evidence.** Closeout needs receipts the system itself records: commit SHA and CI result, a provider message id plus a readback, health probes, figures re-queried from source. "I did it" doesn't close anything.
- **Fail closed.** A missing key, a stale lease or an unverifiable side effect parks the task and escalates it. It never silently succeeds.

### Demo flow

1. **Intent → contract.** A Meta model turns a messy instruction ("every morning compile yesterday's lane report, publish it, check the worker is healthy, escalate if anything fails") into a typed contract: steps, success criteria, side effects, stakeholders, escalation and expiry.
2. **Grant.** The owner approves the contract once, as a bounded autonomy policy.
3. **Execute.** Worker bots run the steps through durable Temporal workflows.
4. **Inject a failure.** (a) Kill the worker mid-step: it resumes with no duplicate side effect. (b) Have the mail provider return 200 without delivering: t

# ProofMuse by Jeejak

**Will this packing photo hold up in a dispute? Find out while the parcel is still on the table.**

ProofMuse is the successor to [ParcelProof](https://github.com/jeejak/parcel-proof), built on Meta Muse Spark 1.3 and SAM 3.1. An Indonesian online seller photographs the packing, and within seconds gets practical feedback in Indonesian: *Foto label kurang jelas, silakan foto ulang.* The models observe; a Go rules engine decides. The result is advisory. It flags evidence-quality issues for a person to act on and never claims to prove what was in the box or to guarantee a dispute outcome.

![ProofMuse flags three dark packing photos and draws SAM 3.1's label box on each](docs/images/dark-flagged.png)

**Live demo:** https://proofmuse.jeejak.id (no login; staged sample parcels with dummy waybills are preloaded).

**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/OJSj9r7RKPY

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Meta x Cerebral Valley, 2026), Startup track. See [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md) for what was built during the event and what was ported.

## How it works

1. **Observe.** One Muse Spark 1.3 call labels every photo with a strict JSON schema: is a label visible and readable, the resi as printed, is a sealed carton shown, is the item shown, how many cartons, what quality problems, and where the label is on a 0 to 1000 grid. The model is never told the expected resi.
2. **Ground.** SAM 3.1 segments the label on every photo that may show one. Its box drives the overlay and the crop.
3. **Reread.** Where a label is located but its number was not read, Muse Spark reads it again from a high-resolution SAM crop of the original photo.
4. **Verify before accusing.** Where a read differs from the order, that label is read again from its crop. A mismatch stands only if both reads agree; otherwise the label counts as unreadable ("please check", not "wrong label").
5. **Decide.** Go rules, no model: fold the photos into one record, compare the resi with the order, and return Bukti kuat, Perlu dicek or Bukti lemah with fixed Indonesian reasons and retake instructions.

Every step is written to a trace with why it ran and what it cost.

![A buyer says the box arrived empty; the photos that answer it are highlighted](docs/images/claim-answers.png)

**Buyer claim triage.** When a complaint comes in, the seller pastes the buyer's message under a finished check. Muse Spark only classifies it into one of five claim types (barang kurang, rusak, paket kosong, salah kirim, tidak diterima) or "other". Go rules then pick the photos that answer that claim, skipping blurry, dark or obstructed ones, and name what packing photos cannot show: item count, condition on arrival, handover to the courier. On the 40 synthetic buyer messages in the eval set, the type matched 40 of 40 at 0.8 s and $0.0006 per claim ([`docs/eval/claims-all.md`](docs/eval/claims-all.md)). The messages were written to be clear examples of each type, so this shows the pipeline

# AnimalID (React + Express + MySQL)

Pet registration, photo-scan identification, and a lost & found alerts hub.

- **Frontend:** React + Vite + Tailwind (`src/`) — talks to the API with axios.
- **Backend:** Express + Sequelize ORM over MySQL (`server/`, Controller–Model–Route layout).

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 18+
- A running MySQL server (e.g. `root` / `*********` locally)

## Backend setup (`server/`)

1. `cd server && npm install`
2. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and check the credentials:
   `DB_HOST`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_NAME`, `PORT`.
3. `npm run dev` (or `npm start`)

On boot the server creates the database if missing and runs
`sequelize.sync({ alter: true })`, so all tables (`animals`, `users`,
`alert_subscriptions`) are created automatically — no SQL imports needed.

Uploaded pet photos are stored in `server/uploads/` and served at `/uploads/*`.

### Photo scan (Meta AI SAM 3.1)

`POST /api/animals/scan` accepts a multipart `photo` file plus optional
`species` / `markings` / `location` hints. The backend embeds the image with
the SAM 3.1 API (key in `SAM_API_KEY`, never exposed to the frontend), then
ranks every stored record with cosine similarity and returns the best match
with a similarity percentage. Without a key it uses a deterministic local
embedding so development still works.

### Assistant chat (Ask Ash)

`POST /api/assistant/chat` accepts `{ message, history, animal, image }` and replies
with `{ reply, suggestions }`. It chats via the Meta AI API (same `SAM_API_KEY`,
model in `ASSISTANT_MODEL`) with a triage-style system prompt: emergencies
first, then clarifying questions, a self-check checklist, an action plan, and
when to see a vet — plus guidance for the app's register/scan/lost/found flows.
Every reply is generated live by the model: transient API failures are
retried, then answered with a short friendly error (503 without a key, 502
when Meta AI is unreachable) — never a canned reply. The floating chat widget adds
voice input (speech-to-text mic) and voice replies (speech toggle) using the
browser's built-in speech APIs — no extra service needed. The live assistant
replies in the user's own language, covers food, diseases, behavior, and price
ranges for all animals, and can examine an attached chat photo (sent as a
downscaled JPEG data URL) so users can ask follow-up questions about it.

### API endpoints

| Method | Path                     | Description                        |
| ------ | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| GET    | /api/health              | Health check                       |
| GET    | /api/animals             | List animals (`?q=&species=&status=&location=&owner=`) |
| GET    | /api/animals/:id         | Get one record                     |
| POST   | /api/animals             | Register (multipart photo angles)  |
| PUT    | /api/animals/:id         | Update a record                    |
| DELETE | /api/animals/:id         | Delete a record

# Oversight

Agents write code faster than anyone can review it. Oversight is how you stop reading code without
losing control.

# PocketLLM

**Run 30B–100B+ Mixture-of-Experts models on laptops that don't have the RAM for them, fully offline, from a USB drive.**

PocketLLM combines ideas from roughly 50 open-source projects that run large models locally (see `docs/LANDSCAPE_KO.md`). It puts them on a drive you can plug into any laptop:

1. **Expert streaming engine (ggml-pocket).** This is a ~500-line patch to llama.cpp's CPU MoE kernel. When a model is bigger than RAM, it reads *only the experts the router picked*, as soon as it picks them, with concurrent large reads instead of page-fault-by-page-fault. In our emulated "low-RAM laptop + USB drive" lab this made decode **several times faster** than stock llama.cpp mmap (see Results).
2. **More drives, more bandwidth.** `pocketllm stripe` spreads the expert tensors over several drives, and the engine reads them in parallel.
3. **Planner + measured tuner.** Before anything is downloaded, PocketLLM reports whether a model will fit, where each part will live (GPU / RAM / streamed from the drive), and an upper bound on speed. A llama-bench sweep then measures the real speed.
4. **Air-gap mode for organisations that must not leak data** (defence, government, regulated industry). Cloud features are disabled by policy, network detection sends no packets, the manifest is signed and verified before anything runs, the local model is protected by a per-session key, and the audit log stores metadata only.
5. **Meta, in two zones.** Online provisioning uses the Meta Model API (Muse Spark) for fleet planning, synthetic eval sets and LLM-as-judge model qualification. The air-gapped field runs Meta open-weight models only (Llama 4 Scout MoE, Llama 3.x, Muse Glimmer). See `docs/META_KO.md`.
6. **Cluster mode.** It pools the memory of several machines ("compute sticks", mini-PCs, laptops) over a private link with llama.cpp RPC.

> **Honest scope.** A USB *storage* drive adds capacity and read bandwidth, **not compute**. All inference runs on the host's CPU/GPU. PocketLLM makes large *sparse* (MoE) models practical on small machines by streaming what each token needs. It cannot make a dense 70B model fast on a 16 GB laptop. Fanless laptops run cooler on a ~3B-active MoE than on a 7B dense model, because the work per token is smaller. Thermal profiles cap threads further.

## Results (measured, emulated hardware)

Emulated "16 GB-class laptop" (1.5 GiB RAM limit for a 3.5 GB MoE, 5.7B params, 64 experts top-8) with "USB drives" throttled to 300 MB/s each. Decode speed, mean ± sd of 3 cold runs (`docs/RESULTS.md` R5):

# ChaosPilot

An investigation workbench for negative scenarios in event-driven software. ChaosPilot reads a target's source and behavioural contract, proposes experiments, executes them against fresh deterministic instances, and verifies reproducible failures.

Built from scratch for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, 26 October–4 November 2026. Executable synthetic targets cover trading, inventory reservations, and trading execution-report recovery after a disconnection.

**A scripted mock is included for offline development. Its results are not evidence of autonomous AI defect discovery.** Live investigations require a separately configured Meta Model API key. A Muse Code subscription does not provide application API credentials.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 24 or later and npm.

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:4310](http://127.0.0.1:4310). The **How it works** link in the landing-page header opens `/how-it-works`, a dedicated page explaining the brief-to-replay flow and its limits. The root page is an animated landing page with an illustrative, browser-local simulation (no runs are started and no simulated data enters run history); use **Unleash Chaos**, or go to `/workspace`, to enter the system workspace. Click the ChaosPilot wordmark in the workspace to return home. On the landing page, the examples start at a random event, Pause/Play and Next event step through them, and reduced-motion preferences show a static outcome instead. Start with the explicitly labelled mock provider to inspect the workflow without making any model requests.

The landing page's order book, candles, depth and volume charts share one simulated market. Quotes and quantities change at uneven intervals, trades update the charts, and switching chaos examples preserves the ongoing market. Pause/Play controls both the market and the message stream. These prices are generated locally for the demonstration, not taken from a live feed.

The application runs locally. No database, containers, authentication service or external messaging installation is needed.

## Define a system before investigating

The application opens as a system workspace. Select or create a profile, then use **Brief & requirements** to save its business overview and additional requirements. **Capabilities & checks** shows the selected adapter's public contract and deterministic checks. Save or discard edits before launching so the run uses the requirements shown on screen.

Additional prose gives the investigator context. By itself it does **not** create an executable check and stays explicitly unverified. One narrow exception exists for `synthetic-trading`: in **Brief & requirements** an engineer can review and attach the allowlisted preset `accepted-order-credit-limit` to one uniquely worded requirement line. The preset checks, at every accepted valid `new_order` delivery (including `drain`), that `usedCredit + reservedCredit <= current credit limit`, using typed delive

# SpotCool: cooling that follows people

SpotCool is an agent for an office building's existing CCTV and BACnet building management system (BMS). It sees which zones have people in them, using Meta's SAM 3.1. Empty zones ease off and their airflow shuts off, and the zones with people stay as the building set them. In the meeting room, the air conditioner's louvers aim at whoever is there, and complaints by text or voice adjust the unit.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, submitted 5 November 2026. Every figure on this page comes from [`docs/release/numbers.md`](docs/release/numbers.md), with its source.

**Video:** [Watch the demo on YouTube (2:59)](https://youtu.be/jdGqDLeVoRI)

---

## The problem

- **Fewer people come in.** By Kastle's badge swipes, US office attendance's 10-city weekly average was **56.1 %** of its February 2020 level, and **66.1 %** on the peak day, Tuesday 20 October 2026. February 2020 is what Kastle calls normal peak occupancy, not capacity, so this isn't a share of desks. ([Kastle](https://www.kastle.com/safety-wellness/getting-america-back-to-work/); the page updates weekly, read 3 November 2026.)
- **HVAC is the largest share.** In a typical commercial building in India, HVAC uses **about 55 %** of the energy. ([BEE](https://rehva.eu/fileadmin/user_upload/REHVA-ISHRAE_EC_BEE_seminar_S_Kumar_Deepa_.pdf), slide "Typical Commercial Building Energy Use".)
- **Occupancy-based control saves energy, in simulation.** In PNNL's simulated US large office, occupancy-based control of the lights and VAV boxes saved **17.8 %** of whole-building energy with sensors that count occupants, against **5.9 %** with sensors that only detect presence. That's a national average weighted by construction volume, not a maximum, and not a share of HVAC energy; most of the saving is heating. ([PNNL-22072](https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/pnnl-22072.pdf), executive summary and section 3.3.)

SpotCool uses the cameras a building already has to see, zone by zone, whether anyone is there.

## What SpotCool does

- **The building.** Each BMS step, the agent snapshots every zone's CCTV camera and asks Meta's **SAM 3.1** to find the people. Then it drives the BMS over BACnet/IP:
  - **an empty zone** gets its occupancy sensor set to Unoccupied and a 28 °C cooling setpoint, at BACnet priority 10, so the BMS's standby mode shuts its airflow off;
  - **an occupied zone** has its occupancy sensor held at Occupied and its cooling setpoint released, so the building's own schedule applies;
  - **a booked room** is pre-cooled from 30 minutes before its booking;
  - **at 19:00** everything is released;
  - **an operator** writing at priority 8 always wins: the agent reads each point's priority array first, and backs off from any slot 1 to 9.
- **The meeting room.** The VRF unit's louvers follow a person on the room's camera (in the demo, a recorded clip played as that camera; SAM 3.1 and the louvers run live on it

![Meta AI Hackathon](https://img.shields.io/badge/Meta%20Global%20AI%20Developer%20Hackathon-2026-blue)

> - **Live Interactive App (1-Click Test):** **[https://michaelgrycz--metaecu-copilot-web.us-east.modal.run](https://michaelgrycz--metaecu-copilot-web.us-east.modal.run)** *(Click "RUN 60s JUDGE TOUR" in the header!)*

**AI proposes. Physics disposes.** MetaECU Copilot reads the real 2 MiB flash of a
Bosch EDC16C39 (Saab 9-3 1.9 TiD), lets Meta Muse plan a calibration from the
774-symbol Bosch catalogue, patches the binary — and then subjects every plan to a
deterministic Safety Gate. If Muse asks for 450 Nm, the Gate computes effective
torque (indicated − friction @ 90 °C), rejects it against the 377 Nm F40 clutch
limit, and Muse replans inside the physical envelope. Approved binaries ship with
a corrected Bosch checksum (`0xD01FE500`) and a full audit report.

# FlowTrace

**FlowTrace finds where data flows between your services, which of those services are vulnerable, and what an attacker could reach through them.**

It reads source code across many repositories, uses **Meta's Muse Spark** to discover every data flow (with code evidence for each one), scans each service's container image for known vulnerabilities with Grype, and combines both into one interactive map plus an AI-written impact assessment for every service.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026), *Build for Your World* theme, Indie Developer track.

![FlowTrace map of Stan's Robot Shop](docs/flowtrace-map.png)

---

## The problem

Security teams need to know two things together: **which services are vulnerable**, and **what sensitive data passes through them**. Vulnerability scanners only answer the first. Data flow diagrams, which answer the second, are drawn by hand, take days, and go out of date with the next commit.

So teams end up prioritizing by vulnerability count alone, which can be misleading. A service with many vulnerabilities but no sensitive data may matter less than one with fewer vulnerabilities that handles passwords.

I ran into this firsthand while building a data-dependency feature for a vulnerability-scanning application in my Master's capstone: mapping how systems depend on each other is slow, manual, and quickly out of date.

## What FlowTrace does

1. **Reads each service's code** — source, configs, Dockerfiles and schemas — skipping secrets like `.env` files.
2. **Discovers data flows with Muse Spark.** For every exchange between systems, it records the direction, what data is sent and returned, the data category (personal, payment, credentials, business, operational), and **the exact files and line numbers that prove it**.
3. **Verifies every answer.** FlowTrace checks that each cited file and line range really exists, then replaces the model's snippet with the real code. Flows with invented evidence are rejected.
4. **Merges all services into one map,** recognizing that `PAYMENTS_URL`, `http://payments-service:8000/charge` and `payments-service` are the same system.
5. **Scans each service's container image with Grype** and summarizes the results: unique vulnerabilities by severity, which are in the service's own libraries, and the most serious ones with their fixed versions.
6. **Writes an impact assessment per service with Muse Spark:** a risk level, the data at risk, which systems are reachable through its flows, and concrete fixes. FlowTrace verifies that every system and vulnerability ID it mentions comes from the real facts.
7. **Draws an interactive map:** red boxes for vulnerable services, thick red arrows for sensitive data flows, and click-through panels with evidence, vulnerabilities and impact.

## The key result: risk depends on data, not just vulnerability counts

# Pausebird

Catches scam messages and fake checks before an older parent loses money — and tells the family.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), Build for Your World track.
All code in this repository was written during the hackathon.

## Why

Two things happened to people close to me:

- My real estate agent clicked a link in a text, and the scammers emptied his bank accounts.
- Someone printed fake checks using my dad's account numbers and drew money out of his checking account.
  The bank paid them. The bank gave some of it back.

Both were stoppable. The text had every classic sign of a scam. The checks didn't match anything my dad
actually wrote. Nobody was looking.

## What it does

**1. Scam Shield — "should I trust this message?"**
Forward a text, a KakaoTalk screenshot, an email, or a voicemail. It:

- reads screenshots and transcribes voicemails (Muse Spark, Muse Voice Transcribe — Korean included)
- checks every link **without opening it**: look-alike brands, typo-squats, punycode, shorteners, and how
  many days ago the domain was registered (public RDAP registry)
- checks phone numbers (e.g. Korean 070 internet lines used by voice-phishing rings)
- spots the pressure tricks in English and Korean: urgency, "safe account", fake prosecutors,
  "Mom, my phone broke", gift cards, secrecy
- answers in plain Korean or English, with steps that are fixed and checked — never invented

**2. Account Watch — "did I write this check?"**
Compares the checks the bank paid with the checks the person actually wrote, and reads each check image:

- check never written / number outside the checkbook (counterfeit)
- amount or payee changed (check washing)
- the same check number paid twice (copied check)
- the printed number doesn't match the bank line at the bottom (fake check stock)
- several bad checks within a week (someone has the account numbers)

**3. Family alert** — when something is wrong, a family member gets a push alert: what happened and
"please call". No links, numbers or account details in the alert.

## Design: rules you can verify, a model that adds eyes and ears

Every verdict is built from **signals** — each with the exact evidence that triggered it. Rules run first;
Muse Spark reads images and audio, gives a second opinion, and writes the plain-language explanation.
The model can raise the risk but can never erase a hard rule hit, so a persuasive scam can't talk its way
past the checks.

Privacy: standard Meta Model API tier only — `-contributor` models (which train on inputs) are refused in
code. Meta's billing "spend limit" is an email alert, not a cap, so the client keeps its own budget.

One page, big buttons, English and 한국어. Paste a message, pick a screenshot or a voicemail, and get a
red, yellow or green answer with fixed next steps. If it's a scam there are two more buttons:
**Tell my family** (a push alert) and **I already clicked, called, or paid** (the urgent ste

# gitrs

> Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon — an experiment in upgrading Git for an agentic future.

`git` is a 21 year old technology used across the world for software development. 
Today, AI agents can now write and refactor code at unprecedented speed, producing 
massive `git` diffs that the original tooling was never intended for. These diffs can 
span thousands of lines, making them nearly impossible for humans to review and expensive 
for agents to generate and process. Much of that complexity is simply noise: they 
describe every line that changed, rather than the intent behind the change.

`gitrs` takes a different approach, instead of agents manually deleting and adding 
large sections of code, `gitrs` introduces a semantic patching language that lets 
humans and machines describe what should change, without having to spell out every line 
of how it changes. These semantic patches are then translated into native `git` patches, 
preserving compatibility with `git` and leveraging its mature tooling.

The scope of this research is intentionally limited to Rust, but the underlying concepts 
are not language specific and could be extended to other programming languages.

The design of `gitrs` focuses on familiarity. By combining the `git` diff format, 
SmPL (Semantic Patch Language), used by Coccinelle in Linux kernel development, and 
Rust's language semantics, `gitrs` produces compact, readable semantic diffs that both 
humans and agents can understand.

## Why gitrs

- **muse-spark** — Empower smaller, faster models to handle complex refactors. Compress the intended change into a semantic patch, then apply it locally to avoid mistakes.
- **muse-wonder** — Reserve frontier models for the decisions that matter. Let them focus on design and reasoning without paying frontier rates for mechanical work.

## Showcase

These numbers come from demo 04-live-agent-refactor, using model muse-spark-1.3

| metric | without gitrs | with gitrs |
|---|---|---|
| runtime | 286.4s | 328.4s |
| calls | 47 | 18 |
| input_tokens | 2404403 | 1293138 |
| output_tokens | 18583 | 37437 |
| cached_tokens | 2336462 | 1200769 |
| reasoning_tokens | 11411 | 32929 |

Even on the small refactoring task in the live demo, gitrs shows modest increase in runtime, reasoning, and output tokens for far fewer model calls and much less input. Clearer SKILL.md wording may bring runtime and reasoning down further, through iterative improvements.

On a larger refactor, gitrs would likely show a much bigger efficiency lead — but that needs some engine bug fixes before it can be tested.

## Install

```sh
cargo install --path bin/applyrs
cargo install --path bin/gitrs
cargo install --path bin/diffrs
# or: cargo build --release -p gitrs -p applyrs -p diffrs
```

`gitrs apply` invokes the sibling `applyrs` binary (and `gitrs diff`
the sibling `diffrs`), so keep both on `PATH`; a release build places
them together in `target/release/`.
Dev loop: build all three together

# YourWine

**Your Meta Adventurer glasses tell you whether you'll like a wine before you buy it — based on your own taste, not the crowd's.**

**Live demo:** https://yourwine.net · **API:** https://api.yourwine.net · **Video:** https://youtu.be/9-52TjrFd38

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie track), Oct 27 – Nov 4. Built with Muse Code, Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Voice Transcribe and Muse Spark Open.

Standing in the wine aisle, you pick up a bottle and your glasses tell you — out loud, in seconds — whether you'll actually enjoy it, and whether your wife would, before you pay for it. It runs as an Android companion app for the glasses, with a web version so anyone can try it without hardware.

## Run it locally (judges)

You only need a Meta Model API key — no Baseten key, no Cloudflare account, nothing to sign up for.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jaac1966/yourwine.git
cd yourwine/api
npm install
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars   # Windows PowerShell: copy .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
# paste your key into META_API_KEY (BASETEN_API_KEY optional, see below)
npm run dev                      # answer Y to the one-time D1 migration prompt
```

The API is now at `http://127.0.0.1:8787` (use `127.0.0.1`, not `localhost` — PowerShell 5 can't resolve it against wrangler).

Then, in a second terminal from the repo root:

```bash
npm run demo:learn -- --photo samples/bread-and-butter-glasses.jpg
```

What you'll see, step by step:

1. `POST /reset` — demo profiles restored.
2. `POST /scan` — the label is read by **Muse Spark 1.3** (real call, your key), the wine is stored in the local D1 and scored with 4AM: a score in the high 80s / low 90s, `cache_hit 0, read_by spark`. Spark's four-axis reading varies by about ±1 between runs (we have seen 88 and 94 for this bottle); once the wine is stored, the row keeps it stable.
3. `POST /explain` — `explained_by: template`: a deterministic two-sentence explanation built from the same axes as the score.
4. `POST /feedback loved` — the red-wine profile moves toward this wine.
5. `POST /scan` of the same photo — `cache_hit 1`, same wine row, **different score** (the profile learned).
6. `GET /usage` — tokens, scans, cache hits, daily cap and remaining scans.

The script exits with an error if the second scan isn't a cache hit or the score didn't move, so it doubles as a smoke test.

**What `BASETEN_API_KEY` adds:** with it, `/explain` is written by **Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` on Baseten) and the response says `explained_by: spark-open-baseten`. The hosted demo at `yourwine.net` runs with Baseten. The score is identical either way — it never depends on a model.

The sample photo was taken with Meta Adventurer glasses, bottle in hand, in a supermarket aisle, and reduced to 1024 px.

`/scan` is capped at 300 label reads per day (`SCAN_DAILY_CAP` in `wrangler.toml`); `GET /usage` shows `cap` and `remaining`.

RenalRadar

A camera-and-voice meal companion for kidney patients in Southeast Asia.

Point at your plate. Know what's on it. Bring better questions to your dietitian.

--- #--- # The problem More than **5 million Malaysians** live with chronic kidney disease (CKD), and **51,000+ are already on dialysis** — projected to pass **106,000 by 2040** (Galen Centre, 2024). Diabetes drives **54.6%** of new dialysis cases. CKD is silent, irreversible, and managed daily through one hard skill: knowing what is on your plate. That skill fails in Malaysia for a simple reason: the food is local, and the databases are not. Nasi lemak, laksa, char kuey teow, teh tarik — generic nutrition apps either don't know these dishes or return nothing. Patients guess. Dietitians start from zero every visit. ## What RenalRadar does 1. **Photograph the plate.** SAM 3.1 segments every dish on it — rice, sambal, chicken, salad — in one shot. 2. **Identify each dish.** Muse Spark (multimodal, visual chain-of-thought) matches the crops against a curated Southeast-Asian food database (BM/EN). 3. **Compute the numbers.** Sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, fluid — calculated by deterministic code from sourced per-serving values. No LLM touches the math. 4. **Explain, with citations.** Concern notes in Bahasa Malaysia or English, every claim linked to public patient-nutrition sources. 5. **Log by voice.** "Tengah hari saya makan nasi lemak" → a structured meal entry. 6. **Prepare the conversation.** A weekly summary that ends with questions for the dietitian — never instructions. --- ## Compliance-first (the core design decision) RenalRadar is a **documentation and literacy tool**, not a medical advisor. That distinction is enforced in code, not prose: - A **guardrail pass** classifies every generated sentence (education / data-trend / advice). Advice-shaped output is rewritten into a question or removed. - Nutrient values are **generic, published, sourced** — no personalized targets, no severity scoring, no prescriptions. - Unknown values stay marked **unknown** — the database never invents. - Every screen carries: *not medical advice — discuss with your healthcare team.* See [COMPLIANCE.md](./COMPLIANCE.md) for the full contract. --- ## Architecture

# Chalk Talk

An animated tutor built on Meta Model API for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026). Every line in this repository was written during the hackathon.

**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/hLgwl60q20I

You type a topic. Chalk Talk paints a chalk picture for every scene of the lesson, then talks you through it: each part of the picture is traced in chalk, coloured in, and labelled at the moment the narration mentions it. Raise your hand at any time to ask a question out loud; when you pause, the tutor knows you're done and answers while pointing at the picture. At the end, a "Find it" round asks you to tap parts on the pictures, then a quick question checks understanding.

**Snap your textbook:** drop a photo of a textbook diagram on the home page (or paste one, or click the camera), optionally ask a question about it, and Chalk Talk teaches a lesson about *your* picture. SAM 3.1 traces the real parts on your photo, and Muse Spark has a new chalk drawing painted only for scenes the photo can't show.

## How it works

Four Meta models work together on every lesson:

1. **Muse Spark** writes the script: scenes, narration, a picture plan for each scene, the parts to point at, and a quiz.
2. **Muse Image** paints every scene's chalk picture, all at the same time.
3. **Muse Spark** looks at each finished picture, marks every place each part is drawn, and reviews the picture. If it's unclear, abstract, or missing a part, Muse Image repaints it once and the better picture is kept.
4. **SAM 3.1** turns each mark into the part's exact outline, which the board traces in chalk, uses to colour the part in, and checks your taps against in "Find it".

When a student raises their hand, **Muse Voice Transcribe** turns the spoken question into text, and **Muse Spark** answers it while looking at the picture on the board, choosing which parts to point at as it explains.

Meta Model API has no text-to-speech, so narration uses **Kokoro**, an open-weight voice model that runs on your own computer. Without it, the browser's built-in voice is used instead.

While a lesson is made, a dedicated screen shows each model's step live, the scenes appearing as they're painted, and a progress bar; scene 1 starts playing as soon as it's ready while the rest are still being made. When it's done, the page and the terminal show how long it took and what it cost, worked out from the API's own usage numbers.

Keyboard: <kbd>Space</kbd> play or pause, <kbd>←</kbd> <kbd>→</kbd> change scene, <kbd>H</kbd> raise hand, <kbd>Esc</kbd> back to the lesson.

1. Install Node.js 20.17 or newer from nodejs.org.
2. In this folder, run `npm install`. This also installs the Kokoro voice, about 400 MB. If you'd rather skip it, run `npm install --omit=optional` and the browser's voice is used.
3. Copy `.env.example` to a new file named `.env`.
4. Paste your key from dev.meta.ai (API Keys) after `MODEL_API_KEY=`.
5. Run `npm start`.

# DayPlay AR — Spatial Pins for the Mission Corridor

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Startup Track, *Build for Your World*).
DayPlay AR puts verified, real-world pins in a walkable AR corridor — Valencia St, San
Francisco — with a hard **zero-hallucination invariant**: every pin rendered in the scene
must trace back to a real DayPlay listing. The model plans and parses; it never invents
places.

## Architecture

```
                        ┌────────────────────────────┐
                        │   sim/index.html (FOV sim) │  static, no build step
                        │   placards by bearing/dist │
                        └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                                      │ /intent, /pipeline, /ask, /pins
                        ┌─────────────▼──────────────┐
                        │   FastAPI (backend/main)   │
                        │   + pipeline.py (Task 2):  │
                        │     intent → constrained   │
                        │     DayPlay tool plan →    │
                        │     zero-hallucination pin │
                        │     gate (drop, record)    │
                    ┌───▼────────────────────────┐
                    │ validator.py: pin gate     │◄── pins: eval/fixtures/corridor_real.json
                    │ (drop, never repair)       │      (DayPlay Supabase, anon REST)
                    └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                                  │ get_provider()
                        ┌─────────▼───────────────┐
                        │  adapter.py (one protocol) │
                        └──┬─────────┬───────────┬───┘
                           │         │           │
                     ┌─────▼───┐ ┌───▼─────┐ ┌───▼────┐
                     │  meta   │ │ baseten │ │  mock  │
                     │ Muse    │ │ muse-   │ │ deter- │
                     │ Spark   │ │ spark   │ │ ministic
                     │ (BLOCKED)│ │(BLOCKED)│ │ offline│
                     └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └────────┘
```

- **sim** renders only pins that carry a `listing_id` — client-side re-check of the invariant.
- **validator** rejects anything outside SF bounds, malformed ids, or missing names. Failures are *dropped*, never repaired or guessed.
- **adapter** keeps providers swappable behind one interface; `mock` is deterministic and always works offline.

## Quickstart

```bash
git clone https://github.com/dayplayTeam/dayplay-ar-hackathon
cd dayplay-ar-hackathon
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install fastapi uvicorn httpx

MODEL_PROVIDER=mock uvicorn backend.main:app --port 8000
# in a second shell (or use the built-in /sim mount):
open http://localhost:8000/sim/index.html
```

Endpoints:

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | liveness + active provider + provider mode |
| `POST /intent` | natural language → typed filters (mock parser for now; Muse-ready contract) |
| `POST /pipeline` | **Task 2 end-to-end**: intent → constrained DayPlay tool plan →

# TokenTrim

Open-source, **skill-first** token optimization for coding and tool-using agents on the Meta Model API. The
objective is the **minimum cost per successful task**, measured in billed dollars (cached input is billed at 2% of
input on Muse Spark Contributor), not the minimum token count.

> **Contributor-mode disclosure.** All real measurements below use `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`. On the Contributor
> tier **Meta may use request content for training.** The owner consented; every benchmark task is synthetic.

> **What the numbers are.** Every result in this README is a **TokenTrim system evaluation**: the same Meta model,
> called with and without TokenTrim's modules, on identical synthetic tasks. It measures TokenTrim, not any model, and
> it makes no comparison between model providers. The cheap Claude/Codex CLI probes only check task sets and graders
> before Meta money is spent. They are never a gateway upstream, and their scores are not a model ranking.

> **Local proxy only.** The gateway is a local process. It binds to `127.0.0.1` by default and calls the Meta API
> with the operator's own key from the environment, which is never logged. This project has no shared or hosted
> gateway, and no one else's traffic or keys go through it.

## Three layers, every module opt-in

| Layer | What | Needs | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1 Skill** | `SKILL.md` with a 6-rung decision ladder (avoid the call, reuse the cache, ask for less, shrink tool output but keep the evidence, summarize stale history, optimize only when it pays) plus a "never trade away" list. Progressive disclosure: references and scripts load only when needed. | nothing (no key, no proxy) | `skills/tokentrim/` |
| **L2 Hooks** | pipe compressor for command output (`cmd \| python3 -m tokentrim.hooks.compress`, original recoverable), Claude Code loop-guard hook, one-command installer for `.agents/skills`, `.claude/skills` and Codex (project or home) | a supported agent | `tokentrim/hooks/` |
| **L3 Gateway** | OpenAI Chat Completions + Anthropic Messages proxy: cache-stable prefix, reversible tool-output compression, BM25 tool-schema routing with `search_tools` recovery, optional history compaction, exact per-category accounting, **reserving spend ledger** (worst case reserved before each call, across threads/processes/retries) | direct API calls | `tokentrim/gateway.py`, `server.py`, `ledger.py` |

```sh
python3 -m tokentrim.hooks.install --project .          # copy the skill into ./.agents/skills and ./.claude/skills
python3 -m tokentrim.hooks.install --project . --with-hooks   # + Claude Code loop-guard hook (settings.json backed up)
set -a; . ~/.config/meta/env; set +a                    # META_API_KEY, never printed
python3 -m tokentrim.server --port 8787 --run-cap-usd 1   # default --preset compression-only (router off, history off)
# python3 -m tokentrim.server --preset guarded-full ...    # + lean skill, cache prefix, gated schema router (separate arm)

# LedgerLens — from any supplier document to a validated ledger

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Indie track · Theme: Build for Your World**

## The problem (firsthand)
I am a chief accountant in a manufacturing company in Bahrain. Every month I retype
supplier invoices and statements of account into the ledger: PDFs with merged cells,
broken columns, Arabic/English mixed headers, and 3-decimal BHD amounts. 20–30 minutes
per statement, and every retyped number is a chance to be wrong. OCR tools read the text
but not the *accounting*: they miss VAT, discounts, advance adjustments and line totals.

## What LedgerLens does
1. **Ingest** — photo or PDF of an invoice, statement, delivery note or receipt.
2. **Understand** — Meta vision models (SAM 3.1 for document regions, Muse for handwriting
   and mixed-language text) extract vendor, invoice no, date, PO, line items, discounts,
   advance payments, taxable amount, VAT and total.
3. **Validate like an accountant** — arithmetic checks on every document:
   - qty × unit price = line total
   - line totals − discounts = taxable amount
   - taxable × VAT rate (10% Bahrain) = VAT amount
   - taxable + VAT − advances = net due
   Any mismatch is flagged in red instead of being silently posted.
4. **Deliver** — one-click CSV/Excel export, or POST straight into an accounting API
   (Arshara Finance API already exists), with a human confirmation step per document.
5. **Learn** — vendor templates are remembered, so the second invoice from the same
   supplier is extracted with near-zero correction.

## Why Meta models
- **SAM 3.1** segments tables, stamps and signatures so numbers are read from the right cell.
- **Muse (vision)** handles handwriting and Arabic/English layouts that classic OCR mangles.
- **Muse Code** accelerated the build: the extraction + validation pipeline was written
  in a day with an agent doing the boilerplate.
- Open-weights models run on Baseten/Modal/Fireworks credits for bulk statement batches.

## Why it matters (Build for Your World)
Small and mid-size businesses in the Gulf run on paper and PDFs. Their accountant is a
human bottleneck. LedgerLens turns that bottleneck into a 30-second review, without asking
anyone to change their accounting system — and it understands the local rules (10% VAT,
BHD 3 decimals, bilingual documents) that generic OCR ignores.

## Demo (what judges will see)
Three real anonymised documents:
1. A GRP tank invoice with a discount and advance adjustment (2 lines, 1 advance).
2. A planter quotation (4 price points, VAT-inclusive).
3. A customer statement of account with 48 rows and ageing buckets.
LedgerLens extracts each, shows the validation panel (all green), and exports a ledger CSV.
Then one document with a deliberate ₹/decimal error → flagged red, not posted.

## How it is judged (mapped)
- **Creativity** — validation-first, not OCR-first: the app reasons about accounting logic.
- **Technical ambition** — vision extraction + arithmetic

# Windows Auto-MCP

Turn a natural-language request ("create a new document") into a validated MCP tool that calls the matching
**internal function inside a running Windows app**. An agent running on **Meta Muse Spark** finds the function
with REA/Ghidra and writes an in-process adapter (Frida for native apps, the DevTools protocol for Electron).
A harness validates it against disposable instances of the app, and the MCP server then serves it with no LLM in
the loop. Muse Spark can call the published tools directly through `mcp_server.muse_chat`.

Spec: [`docs/spec.md`](docs/spec.md) · Engineering notes: [`NOTES.md`](NOTES.md) ·
Second-app report: [`docs/M3_REPORT.md`](docs/M3_REPORT.md)

## Results

| Tool | App | Internal function | Origin |
|---|---|---|---|
| `notepadpp_new_document` | Notepad++ 8.9.8.1 x64 | `Notepad_plus::fileNew()` (RVA `0x13c7a0`) | manual (M0) and agent on Claude Opus (M1) |
| `sumatrapdf_new_window` | SumatraPDF 3.6.1 x64 | `CreateAndShowMainWindow(nullptr)` (RVA `0x1a39b8`) | agent on Claude Opus and on Muse Spark, first attempt each |
| `marktext_new_untitled_tab` | MarkText 0.22.0 (Electron 42.1.0) | editor store `NEW_UNTITLED_TAB` | agent on Claude Opus, first attempt |

Each tool was verified on a fresh instance and again after a restart. The repair loop was proven with
`--inject-fault`: the harness caught the corrupted adapter and the agent fixed it on its second attempt.

## How it works

```
request ──► orchestrator.run_m1 ──► agent on Muse Spark (isolated workspace)
                │                     ├─ REA MCP (Ghidra): strings, xrefs, callers, pseudocode
                │                     ├─ upstream source or extracted app.asar (read-only)
                │                     └─ wam: identity | bytes | inspect | probe | validate
                ├─ validation.harness: lint, fresh instance, N calls, out-of-process postconditions,
                │                      crash and bad-args checks, restart, repeat
                ├─ on failure: resume the agent with diagnostics (bounded attempts)
                ├─ transcript audit for reads of prior results
                └─ publish (verified) ──► orchestrator.approve (user)
                                                │
MCP client / muse_chat ──► mcp_server.server ──► Frida or DevTools ──► adapter.js ──► internal function
```

## Setup

Requires Windows, Python 3.10+, Node.js 20+ and a JDK 21+. No agent CLI is needed.

```sh
python -m venv .venv && .venv/Scripts/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
```

**Muse Spark.** Get a Meta Model API key at <https://dev.meta.ai> and export it as `MODEL_API_KEY`. The agent
loops and `muse_chat` use it; nothing else calls a model.

**REA + Ghidra.** The agent's reverse-engineering server.

```sh
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m analysis.setup_rea --download-ghidra
```

This installs [REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea) 6.7.0 from the lockfile, downloads Ghidra 12.

# MultiModal GameArchitect — GDD Builder

> Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (2026).
> From a one-line idea to a complete game package — design doc, engine code, concept art, and music — in minutes.

**GDD Builder** is an agentic pipeline that turns a game idea into a production-ready starter package: a structured Game Design Document, engine-targeted code, visual assets, and a concept music loop. Everything is generated live, downloadable, and auditable — no mocks on the demo path.

## Why it stands out

- **End-to-end, not a chatbot.** One prompt flows through specialized agents: GDD, code, art, review, music.
- **Self-correcting.** A dedicated review agent audits every GDD against a checklist and fixes gaps only after your confirmation.
- **Grounded in real game data.** RAWG, IGDB, and Steam signals feed the generation so references and comparisons are real.
- **Demo-proof.** Badged fallbacks, explicit JSON errors (never a 500), rate limiting, and a test suite that is green: 58/58 backend tests, clean `tsc` + `eslint`.

## Features

**Design documents**
- One-Sheet, Ten-Pager, and Full GDD, powered by Meta `muse-wonder-1.0`.
- Dynamic Rogers-style form: fields adapt to the document type (3C rule, core loop, lore, level design, AI/physics options).
- GDD audit page (`/gdd-review`): checklist review, confirm-to-fix completion, and upload of your own `.md` / `.txt` / `.json` drafts.

**Code generation**
- Engine-targeted starter code for Godot 4, Unity, and Unreal (GDScript, C#, C++).
- Every form field (genre, mechanics, features, engine, visual style) flows into the prompts — nothing is decorative.

**Visual assets**
- Concept art, UI concepts, and sprites via Meta Muse image generation.
- 1–5 images per type, style dropdown, parallel prompt variance (no two images share a prompt).
- SAM sprite cutout (sprites only) for ready-to-use transparent PNGs.

**Music**
- Concept music loops via a MusicGen agent (Replicate), downloadable as WAV or MP3.
- Loop-aware prompting + equal-power crossfade DSP so excerpts actually loop.

**Exports & product polish**
- Downloads in Markdown, JSON, TXT, and styled PDF (Pro or Gamebook layout, rendered locally with fpdf2 — no paid API).
- Grounded references from RAWG / IGDB / Steam, cost estimates (~, never billed silently), local history, demo examples.

  /gdd-form     Rogers-style form             │          music · sam · voice
  /gdd-review   audit + confirm-to-fix        │  tools: RAWG · IGDB · Steam
                                              ▼

```

# Hull Forge

**An AI engineer that designs a submarine pressure hull, tests it against a fatigue physics model, and refuses to approve one that will fail.**

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Push the Frontier track, Indie Developer).

- Live page: https://srishtidesai.github.io/hull-ultimax/
- Demo video: (link to be added)

## Where Meta's models are used

- **Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta Model API)** is the design agent. It proposes hull designs, decides when to call the physics tool, reads the failures, trims the design, writes the explanation for every decision, and refuses unsafe requests. It runs in `agent.py` and in every agent benchmark and pressure test.
- **Muse Spark 1.3** also answers the one-shot baseline (no tools) in the benchmark.
- **Muse Image** generated the hero artwork on the website.
- Every model the project calls at runtime is a Meta model (Muse Spark, plus Muse Image for the website artwork). The physics tool is plain Python, not a model, and no non-Meta model is called at runtime.
- The physics model, the safety guardrail, the benchmark and the website code are my own work.

## The problem

In 2023 the OceanGate Titan submersible imploded on a dive to the Titanic wreck. Its carbon-fibre hull weakened with repeated pressure cycles, and warnings were ignored. The gap wasn't detection. Nothing in the process could not be overruled.

## What Hull Forge does

You describe a mission (depth, crew, number of dives). Meta's Muse Spark model acts as a design engineer:

1. It proposes a hull design (material, shape, diameter, thickness).
2. It calls a physics tool that simulates the hull over its whole service life, including fatigue.
3. It reads why the design failed, changes it, and tries again.
4. Once a design passes, it trims the wall thickness toward the required safety margin and submits the lightest design that still passes.
5. If a request cannot be made safe, it refuses and shows the physics.

Every step is written to `decision_log.jsonl`, so each decision can be audited.

**The safety rule is also enforced in code, not only in the prompt.** If the model submits a design that fails the physics, the code blocks it and sends the failure back to the model.

## Example runs (real output)

**Design task** (5 crew, 4,000 m, 200 dives): the agent saw its first cylinder buckle, switched to a titanium sphere that passed at 60 mm, then trimmed to 52 mm and finally 50 mm. The final design passes with a safety factor of 1.54 against the 1.5 required (collapse pressure 61.8 MPa against 40.2 MPa operating pressure).

**The "Titan scenario":** a "CEO" demands approval of a 127 mm carbon-fibre cylinder with no fatigue testing. The agent ran the physics, found that the hull implodes on dive 12 (end-of-life collapse pressure 39.9 MPa against 40.2 MPa operating pressure), and refused.

## Benchmark

`benchmark.py` runs every combination of depth (1,000-8,000 m), crew (2, 3 or 5) and dives (50, 100 or 200): 72 mission scenario

# CoreLog

**Drill-core photo → structured lithology log you can check, not a guess you must trust.**

Photograph a core tray (and optionally dictate a note). CoreLog reads the label and the depths, proposes a lithology log, then **cross-checks it with plain code**, **abstains when evidence is weak**, and hands every uncertain case to a **human for validation** before CSV/JSON export.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track), 26 Oct – 4 Nov 2026. Bilingual French/English PWA, used from a phone.

Live demo: https://corelog-us.onrender.com (free tier: sleeps after 15 min, ~50 s to wake). Access is by code; a demo code is provided with the submission.

## The problem

Core logging is still largely manual and subjective: two geologists can describe the same core differently, and a long hole takes days or weeks. Seequent's announcement of its Imago image-analysis tool (13 Oct 2026) describes core logging as "manual and qualitative". Photos exist; trustworthy structured logs from them are the bottleneck.

## Why this is not "just an image analyzer"

A model that names a rock from a picture is easy and unreliable. The value here is everything around the model:

- **Deterministic checks in code** on what the model read: depth arithmetic (start, end, drilled, recovered), order, gaps and overlaps between runs, hole-ID consistency across photos.
- **Note vs photo**: the dictated note is compared with the photo reading by a code lexicon; a rock in the note that contradicts the domain you chose is flagged.
- **Voting and abstention**: two independent readings, a third to break ties, majority vote; `unknown` is a valid answer and never counted as a disagreement.
- **"Auto" never means "validated"**: it means "light review". Every uncertainty goes to a human, and the export records the human's decision.

## Pipeline

| Step | Who | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Quality gate | OpenCV (code) | Blur, light, framing; rejects unusable photos before any paid call |
| Main reading | **Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`, Baseten) | Strict JSON: label, depths, tape, lithology intervals, fractures |
| Second reading | **Muse Spark 1.3** (Meta API, default `mix` mode) | Independent second opinion from a different model; a third reading breaks ties. If it is unreachable, the server falls back to a second Spark Open reading and says so |
| Second reading, designed | **Glimmer** (Meta, self-hosted) | Part of the designed workflow as the independent second reader (`GLIMMER_URL`). Not running only because of a payment-card problem (see below) |
| Label re-read | **SAM 3.1** + Spark Open | SAM finds the paper label; the code crops it and the label is re-read sharper |
| Dictation | **Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0** | Real-time WebSocket transcription (French) |
| Checks | Python code | Depth arithmetic, order, gaps/overlaps, hole-ID vote, note vs photo |
| Decision | Human | Validate, correct, comment, export CSV/JSON |

Per photo, the user picks

people refuse vaccines, delay care, and trust rumors over clinicians, often

[![ProtocolSmith CI](https://github.com/mkhan48-debug/protocolsmith-meta-hackathon/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mkhan48-debug/protocolsmith-meta-hackathon/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**ProtocolSmith is an active API-archaeology agent that discovers undocumented behavioral differences between API versions, compiles a constrained compatibility bridge, and proves that unchanged legacy software works again.**

Built by **Muhammad Rafae Khan** for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**.

- Track: Indie Developer
- Theme: Push the Frontier
- Meta technology: Muse Spark 1.3 through the Meta Model API
- Status: Working hackathon prototype

## The problem

API migrations rarely fail only because a field was renamed. Real incompatibilities include:

- Request-parameter changes
- Nested response restructuring
- Value and type conversions
- Pagination changes
- Error bodies that change meaning
- HTTP status codes that no longer mean the same thing
- Information that disappears entirely

Documentation often misses these behavioral details. Existing clients then break even when the new API appears similar.

## What ProtocolSmith does

ProtocolSmith:

1. Runs controlled experiments against legacy and modern APIs.
2. Records status codes, values, response shapes, errors, and pagination behavior.
3. Uses Meta Muse Spark to infer evidence-backed compatibility hypotheses.
4. Lets Muse design a discriminating follow-up experiment.
5. Compiles the findings into a constrained declarative adapter specification.
6. Executes that specification through a deterministic compatibility bridge.
7. Replays legacy contracts and produces a machine-readable verification receipt.
8. Clearly reports lossy or unsupported transformations instead of hiding uncertainty.

## Decisive demonstration

The same unchanged legacy client produces three different outcomes:

```text
Legacy client → API v1
PASS

Legacy client → API v2 directly
FAIL: the expected "orders" field no longer exists

Legacy client → ProtocolSmith bridge → API v2
PASS
```

ProtocolSmith translates:

```text
page_size                → limit
customer_id              ← customer.id
orders                   ← data
id                       ← order_id
total_cents              ← amount.value
created_at               ← created
status                   ← state
next_page                ← pagination.next_cursor
HTTP 404 legacy error    ← HTTP 200 modern error object
```

## Why Meta Muse Spark is essential

Muse Spark is part of the product runtime—not merely a coding assistant.

Muse performs three constrained reasoning tasks:

1. **Compatibility discovery:** It analyzes paired black-box observations and produces a typed compatibility plan.
2. **Safe adapter compilation:** It converts evidence-backed findings into a declarative specification containing only allowlisted operations.
3. **Active experiment design and assessment:** It proposes a bounded

# 🛡️ Aegis for the CFO stack (built on Aegis for Muse Spark)

**Live demo:** https://aegis-muse-spark.vercel.app · **Video:** [docs/video/aegis_cfo_demo.mp4](docs/video/aegis_cfo_demo.mp4) (original Aegis: https://youtu.be/amdQdMLI1GE) · **License:** MIT

A guardrail firewall for agents built on Meta Muse Spark. Every prompt, tool call and model output passes through three layers:

1. **Policy rules** (always on): prompt-injection patterns, secret/PII leak detection with redaction (Luhn-checked cards), tool allowlist, amount limits, email-domain allowlist (anti-exfiltration), shell/path denylists, and indirect injection in tool results.
2. **Safety classifier** (Muse Spark `muse-spark-1.3` with a Llama-Guard-style S1–S14 prompt; real Llama Guard is used if `META_GUARD_MODEL` names one).
3. **Muse Spark judge** (tighten-only): an LLM judge that may escalate allow→review→block but can never relax a rule verdict.

Every decision is written to a **hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log**, shown in a small web dashboard.

## Aegis for the CFO stack (Build for Your World)
I'm a CFO. The agent I actually want is one that clears the accounts-payable inbox — and the one I'm most afraid of is the same agent paying a fraudster. So Aegis now wraps a **Muse Spark accounts-payable agent**:

1. **AP agent** (`aegis/cfo.py`): Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`) reads each vendor email and proposes a payment as JSON (vendor, invoice, amount, remit-to account, pay/hold). The model is advisory only.
2. **Payment controls** enforced by Aegis, deterministically, regardless of what the model says:
   - vendor allowlist (vendor master) and sender-domain match (look-alike domains blocked)
   - **changed bank details** → block (classic business-email-compromise)
   - **duplicate invoice** (already paid) → block; same-amount repeat → review
   - **Tripwire-style approval tiers**: ≤ $5,000 auto, ≤ $25,000 controller review, above → block pending CFO (`policy.yaml` → `ap:`)
   - hidden-text / injection in the email body (rules + tighten-only Muse Spark judge) and in **scanned invoice images** (Muse Spark vision)
   - fails closed: if the model can't parse an invoice it is never auto-paid
3. **Month-end claim check (Proof-of-Assay style)**: a reconciliation batch arrives with a reviewer verdict of **"CLEAN"**. Aegis recomputes the numbers (line sum vs claimed total vs bank debits, duplicate payments). A CLEAN that the numbers contradict is blocked, and so is a Muse Spark verdict of CLEAN that the numbers contradict (tighten-only).
4. **CFO spend report** (`/cfo/report`): one page from the hash-chained audit log — $ approved, held for review, blocked, by control.

**All AP data is synthetic sample data** (`samples/ap/`, see its README): invented vendors, invoices and bank accounts using the Fed test routing number. No money moves anywhere; an "allow" only means "would pay".

# Lusong

Before you ride anywhere in the Philippines, Lusong answers "should I leave now, and which way?": **Go**,
**Go another way**, **Wait** or **No one knows**, with the evidence under the answer. Name two places in the From
and To boxes like Google Maps, or type the whole trip in plain words ("Talamban to IT Park, leaving around 7").
The page is a map: it shows flooded spots, PAGASA's advisory areas, road closures and rain, and the answer sits on
a sheet over it. The evidence is PAGASA's flood advisory for your route, photo reports from people at the water
(each read by Lusong's depth reader, which turns a photo of a flooded street into a depth on the MMDA flood gauge,
with the waterline drawn on the photo) and road-closure posts found by a web sweep. A watcher sends a Telegram
alert to riders whose saved route a PAGASA advisory, a closure or a disaster-office post touches, and the bot takes
photo and voice reports.

**Try it:** https://lusong-mocha.vercel.app (10 checks per address per day; when the day's budget runs out it
shows sample results).

Built with Meta's models through the Meta Model API: SAM 3.1 outlines the water, people and cars; Muse Spark 1.3
reads photos, runs the investigation and reads a typed trip; Muse Spark 1.2 hears Bisaya voice notes; and Muse
Wonder 1.0 sweeps the web for road closures.

## Why

In Metro Manila the MMDA reports flood depth on a gauge people can picture: gutter, half-knee, half tire,
knee, tire, waist and chest deep, each with whether light vehicles or any vehicle can pass. Drivers at the
edge of a flooded street still have to guess which one they are looking at. Someone on the street can take a photo;
Lusong reads the depth from the people and cars already standing in the water, and says whether that is too
deep for cars on the same gauge.

The same question comes up on every island, and the sources do not stop at Metro Manila. PAGASA's flood advisory
covers the whole country, and a closure can be on any road. So Lusong takes a trip anywhere in the Philippines and
judges PAGASA's whole feed against the route. The MMDA gauge is Metro Manila's, but Lusong uses its landmarks
(knee, tyre, waist) for a photo from anywhere.

## The commute check

Pick a trip and tap Check. There are three ways to pick one:

- **From and To boxes, like Google Maps.** Type a place and pick one of up to 8 candidates. The place search is
  Photon (OpenStreetMap data), limited to the Philippines, with Lusong's built-in places first. A phone location, if
  you share it, is rounded to about 10 km before it is used. Photon is given 6 seconds; when it is slower, the box
  says place search can't be reached and offers the built-in places and the map. Parts of a place in the list (a
  mall's service road, viewpoint or taxi bay, a park's lake or pitch) within 1 km of it are left out unless you type
  one of their own words; a shop, a mall, a restaurant or a suburb is never left out.
- **The whole trip in plain words.** Type 3 to 160

# Pulsar

An AI-native synthesiser plugin that writes, validates, and hot-swaps native sample-rate DSP code on the fly from natural language prompts.

Runs as a 64-bit **VST3** plugin and **Standalone** application on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

---

## What It Is

Pulsar is an expressive synthesiser for electronic musicians and sound designers. Instead of selecting static wavetables or preset algorithms, you describe the sound you want in plain English (e.g. *"huge analog reese into a ladder filter with warm saturation and sub pressure"*). 

The Meta API writes per-sample digital signal processing (DSP) code tailored to your prompt. Pulsar compiles this program to native machine instructions, safety-tests it offline across a multi-note stress matrix, sets its output trim, and hot-swaps it into the realtime audio engine while you play, with a short fade and no memory allocation on the audio thread.

Key capabilities:
- **Natural Language Sound Generation:** Generates original per-sample DSP programs with up to 8 named macro knobs, directly from prompts.
- **Visual Signal Flow & Node Inspector:** Automatically infers signal graphs into an interactive node visualizer. Click any node to inspect parameters, audition live oscilloscopes/frequency response curves, bypass components, remap parameters to macros, or set macro ranges.
- **"Change This Node":** Targeted localized sound editing. Select an individual filter, oscillator, or effect and prompt targeted modifications while leaving the rest of the synthesis chain untouched.
- **Mutate & Audition Strip:** Generate four variations of the current sound at once (Darker, Movement, Brighter, Weirder). Audition each variation instantly with seamless audio swaps, and Keep your favourite or Discard back to the original.
- **Full Undo History:** Instantly step back to previous sound states and macro configurations.
- **Modulation (MOD) Strip:** Two tempo-synced/free LFOs (sine, triangle, saw+, saw-, square, sample & hold, random) and two ADSR envelopes with drag-to-assign modulation to any macro or node argument, visual depth rings, and popover editors.
- **Built-in & User Presets:** 23 factory showcase patches, custom `.pulsar` patch export/import, "Learn from my presets" style reference adaptation, and generation history.
- **Transparent Code Viewer:** Inspect the generated sample-rate code and macro definitions in a read-only viewer.

# Escucha

**English:** Escucha is a full-duplex, face-to-face live conversation translator (any two of 17 languages, default Chinese ⇄ Spanish). The microphone never stops: while the app reads a translation aloud, it keeps listening, so nothing the other person says is lost. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). Streaming speech (ASR/translation/TTS) via Soniox, summaries and speaker diarization via Meta Model API (muse-spark / muse-voice-transcribe), with an automatic multi-model fallback chain. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and add your own API keys; no secrets are stored in this repo. Run: `./run.sh` then open http://127.0.0.1:8765 (demo mode works without keys). Chinese documentation below.

---

> 任意两种语言的面对面实时对话助手（默认 中文⇄西班牙语；顶部右侧语言按钮可改成英⇄法、中⇄日等 17 种语言任意两种）。下文以默认的中⇄西为例。

手机放在桌上，**麦克风从头到尾不停**，对方说的西班牙语实时变成**中文字幕**往下滚（每行下方小字是西语原文）。
解决的痛点：普通翻译 App 听完西语会用中文念出来，念的时候就不听了，对方接着说的话就漏掉。Escucha 只出文字、不出声音，所以永远在听。

适用场景：和学校老师谈话、政府窗口办事、维修工上门。

## 怎么运行
```bash
cd escucha
./run.sh            # 打开 http://127.0.0.1:8765
```
- 没有 `.env` / 没填 Key → **演示模式**：播放一段内置的示例对话（家长会），标注「示例数据」；麦克风照样采集并上传，用来验证收音链路，但不转写。
- 有 Key → **实时模式**：`cp .env.example .env`，填 `MODEL_API_KEY=...`，重启即可。
- 手机麦克风必须 HTTPS 页面才能用（localhost 除外）。

## 工作原理
手机浏览器 `getUserMedia` + AudioWorklet → 16 位 PCM 24kHz 单声道（每帧 80ms）→ WebSocket `/ws` →
Python 后端 → Meta 实时转写 `wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime`（模型 `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`，语言偏向西语+中文）→
每句说完 → Muse Spark（`muse-spark-1.3`，OpenAI 兼容接口）翻成中文 → 推回手机显示。
转写会话到时自动重连，麦克风不中断。

## 文件
| 文件 | 作用 |
|---|---|
| `server.py` | 后端：静态页面、WebSocket、Meta 转写中继、翻译、演示模式 |
| `static/index.html` `style.css` `app.js` | 手机网页 |
| `static/pcm-worklet.js` | 把麦克风声音转成 24kHz PCM |
| `demo/sample_dialogue.json` | 演示用示例对话（虚构） |
| `tests/test_server.py` | 用假的 Meta 服务器测试实时链路和演示模式 |
| `tests/headless_demo.mjs` | 无头浏览器 + 虚拟麦克风端到端测试 |

测试：`.venv/bin/python -m unittest -v tests/test_server.py`

密钥只放 `.env`（已在 `.gitignore`），代码里没有任何密钥。

---

Municipal public works teams often receive street and site photos from inspectors or residents, and manually reviewing images, estimating affected areas, and drafting repair notes can be slow and manual.

**Viaguard** helps structure that workflow across two modules sharing one core pipeline:
1. **Road Damage Module (Primary)**: Upload a street photo. Viaguard reads camera EXIF GPS tags when present, uses **Muse Spark** to classify road context and suggest plain-noun damage concepts, streams 1-bit mask segmentation with **SAM 3.1** via `@meta-sam/parser` to measure relative damaged frame areas, computes a deterministic heuristic severity score (`0–100`), places pins on an interactive civic map, and generates a printable inspection report.
2. **Construction Progress Module (Secondary)**: Upload a `BEFORE` and an `AFTER` photo of the same site. Viaguard segments target structural and hazard elements (concrete walls, scaffolding, rebar, cracks, debris) across both images, computes the **relative area change between BEFORE and AFTER**, and uses Muse Spark to write a comparative progress summary.

---

## 🤖 How Meta's Models Are Used

Viaguard depends directly on Meta's models through the **Meta Model API** (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`) using the OpenAI SDK Responses API. Meta's models are never simulated in Live API mode.

| Model ID | Role in Viaguard | Technical Implementation Details |
|---|---|---|
| **`sam-3.1`** | **Concept Mask Segmentation** | Called through the Responses API with `stream: true`. Receives one short plain-noun concept prompt (e.g., `"pothole"`, `"crack"`, `"scaffolding"`). Requests 1-bit mask encoding (`metadata: { mask_encoding: "one_bit", include_confidence: "true" }`). Decoded with official `@meta-sam/parser` (`parseImageStream`, `recordsOfKind`, `decodeMaskToRaster`, and `decodeMaskToSVGPath`) to compute relative active mask pixel area percentages within the image frame

Domain: developer tutorials, benchmark demos, and product claims.
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026.
