# Quetzal AOI Briefing

**Live seismic data → AOI polygons → SAM visualization → Muse Spark briefing**

Quetzal AOI Briefing is a scientific observation and analysis tool I'm building to make geophysical data easier to examine, visualize, and understand.

The idea is simple: take live seismic telemetry, identify geographic areas that deserve closer observation, turn those results into something a human can actually interpret, and generate a short briefing explaining what the data tells us.

Most importantly, **we separate what we measured, what we calculated, and what we're inferring.** Every reported number needs a source and a receipt.

This isn't a claim that we can predict earthquakes. It's a way to bring existing geophysics, automated analysis, computer vision, and AI together into a workflow that can be tested and verified.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**, Startup Track — *Push the Frontier*.

- Development period: October 26 – November 4, 2026
- Submission deadline: November 4, 9:00 PM ET
- Demo: 3-minute video, coming before submission

## What it does

We're connecting four basic components:

1. **Observe:** Collect live seismic telemetry from the Quetzal geophysics system.
2. **Compute:** Generate areas of interest (AOI polygons) using geophysical analysis. These identify places worth investigating further, not guaranteed future earthquake locations.
3. **Visualize:** Use Meta's Segment Anything Model (SAM) to help translate the geographic output into something people can understand visually, without altering the underlying scientific results.
4. **Explain:** Use Muse Spark to generate a short, readable briefing that separates observations, calculations, and interpretations.

The goal is to make the entire process traceable, from the original data to the final briefing.

## No mystery numbers

I want to make this part especially clear.

Every numerical result belongs to one of three categories:

- **Measured:** Values obtained from instruments or observation sources.
- **Computed:** Values produced by an algorithm, mathematical operation, or model.
- **Inferred:** Interpretations or conclusions drawn from the available evidence.

An inference is not a measurement, and a computed forecast is not an observed event.

Each briefing should include the supporting source information and verification receipt so someone else can examine how we arrived at the result.

If we can't support a claim, we don't present it as verified.

**Keep it simple, but keep the science intact.**

## What's new for this hackathon?

I've been developing the underlying Quetzal geophysics system since before this competition. I'm not claiming that earlier research or infrastructure was built during the hackathon.

What we're building here is a new workflow that connects those capabilities with Meta's AI tools.

The new work includes:

- The AOI briefing orchestration pipeline.
- The measured / computed / inferred classification and receipt system

any GPU host. See [docs/deploy-byo-cloud.md](docs/deploy-byo-cloud.md).

endpoint URL is yours. There are no API keys, hostnames, or accounts baked into
the code.

## What's in here

The repo is four self-contained projects. Each has its own `_common/` library,
its own `pyproject.toml`, and its own deployments. Work from inside the one you
need.

| Project | What it does | Engine |
|---|---|---|
| [`gemma4/`](gemma4/) | Serve the Gemma 4 family (E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B-A4B, 31B), solo and concurrent, plus a Granite embedding sidecar | SGLang |

Each model ships two shapes:

- **solo** — one user driving a coding harness. The whole GPU and KV cache go to
  one session with a large context window.

  a smaller per-session window.

# Beyond the Five Finger Problem — spike

Continuity checking for AI-generated frame sequences: correctness
and consistency ACROSS images, where the five finger problem was
correctness inside one image.

Date: 2026-10-13. Status: SPIKE, not the hackathon build. Purpose:
prove the three-way validation math on known good/bad sets before
the application is drafted (application deadline 2026-10-25;
hackathon 2026-10-26 – 2026-11-04).

Run it (CPU only, numpy + scipy + PIL):
  python3 test_synthetic.py   # 7 rendered pixel-set cases
  python3 run_real.py         # 8 real-assignment cases
  python3 evolution.py        # spec-evolution trials + ledger

## The design under test (user-stated)
For an adjacent frame pair (A -> B) against a reference/spec, all
three gates must pass:
1. Static validity — both frames individually satisfy the spec.
   Entities are named pixel sets (StarboardLeg = A); markers are named
   subsets (StarboardLeg.strap = A.s, containment A.s ⊆ A). As A moves /
   morphs / is occluded, A.s must adjust proportionately (share of
   parent, relative position).
2. Transition legitimacy — the change is a legitimate perspective /
   action change. Known actions (run, jump, Heisman block) are set
   in keyframes; in-betweens are implicit, constrained by character
   detail (long hair, stick in hand). Identity assignment is
   invariant unless the action declares a transfer at that
   transition.
3. Visual Damerau–Levenshtein — minimal weighted edit script
   (insertion / deletion / substitution / transposition) between
   the frames' token structures, against a budget that scales with
   the frame interval (fewer frames = larger legitimate gap).
Marker conflict = FAIL for the frame/set: the spec must be coherent,
no marker kind wins. Loop pair (0, N) is an edge case, out of scope.
Photorealistic is out of scope. CPU-only (no GPU on either system).

- `checker.py` — gates 1–3 on named pixel sets + token structures;
  findings are prose strings using the set names.
- `test_synthetic.py` — rendered pixel-set frames, known verdicts.

# Operacija Dvina

A youth audio quest about Plokštinė, a former Soviet underground nuclear missile base in Lithuania that is now the Cold War Museum in Žemaitija National Park. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026).

AI travel guides make things up. This one doesn't: every sentence comes from an official source or a named witness, and a script checks that before anything is published.

## What's in it

- **4 remote episodes** you listen to at home. Each ends on a mystery you can only solve on site.
- **7 on-site missions** with a short story, a task (find, count, pace out the 23 m missile) and a quiz.
- **12 "Legend or fact?" cards** built from local witnesses' memories, such as "the warheads were kept in the secret hangar" or "was the base closed under a disarmament treaty?". Each card names who tells the story and gives one of six verdicts: fact, legend, testimony, sources disagree, partly true or unproven.
- **11 languages:** Lithuanian, English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Polish, Latvian, Russian, Ukrainian, Chinese and Japanese.

Read the quest in [English](docs/operacija-dvina.en.md). The Lithuanian original is [operacija-dvina.lt.md](docs/operacija-dvina.lt.md), and the other languages are in [docs/](docs/).

## The app

**Try it: [mariovilnius.github.io/operacija-dvina](https://mariovilnius.github.io/operacija-dvina/)** · **Demo video: [youtu.be/FxC7kLP3XLo](https://youtu.be/FxC7kLP3XLo)**. Switch on demo mode to open the missions away from the museum.

`app/` is a static mobile web app with no build step:

- **Language picker** for all 11 languages.
- **Episodes** you can read or listen to at home.
- **Missions** unlock when you scan the QR code on the wall at each museum station. A demo switch unlocks them anywhere.
- **Quizzes** show a proof quote from the source.
- **Legend cards** let you pick one of six verdicts before the reveal.
- **XP** and progress are saved on the device.
- **Source tags** like [S1] or [T3] in every text open the original source.

```bash

Printable A4 posters with one QR code per station are in [docs/qr/posters.html](docs/qr/posters.html), made by `pipeline/make_qr.py`. Narration plays pre-generated neural-voice MP3s from `app/audio/<lang>/` (made by `pipeline/make_audio.py` with Microsoft neural voices: Azure AI Speech when a key is set, otherwise edge-tts for the demo) and falls back to the browser's own voice where a clip is missing.

# Exhibit A **Proof before accusation: Exhibit A only reports vulnerabilities it can prove.** [Video demo](VIDEO_URL_PLACEHOLDER) Exhibit A is a Python security-verification engine for pull requests. It turns a suspicion into a finding only when an exploit test fails for the intended oracle-observed reason in an **isolated and resource-limited** sandbox, then passes after a fix while the baseline and bypass checks remain valid. Nothing merges itself. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR B[Baseline: project tests
on a clean clone] --> S[Suspect: adversary
proposes suspicions] S --> E[Exploit: test writer
writes an exploit test] E --> R[Run: sandbox container,
isolated and resource-limited] R --> O[Oracle: was the canary
read/written by app code
through an entry point?] O -->|no| D[discarded_unproven] O -->|yes, stable over N runs| F[Fix: fixer proposes a patch] F --> V[Verify: exploit passes
on fixed code, baseline passes,
defender bypasses fail] V --> P[Package: exploit test,
fix, verdict, evidence] ``` The CLI scans the repository, builds an AST-only static slice, runs the verification loop, and packages the ledger and evidence. The GitHub Action uses the same engine on a pull-request diff. A green result means **nothing could be proven**, never safe. ## Install in 3 steps You do not clone Exhibit A into the app you want to scan. Install the package, then run the CLI from that app's directory. 1. Install the CLI **once per machine**, globally and isolated from your other projects (GitHub; this package is not on PyPI yet). It needs Python 3.11+: ```bash pipx install "git+https://github.com/Diego-do-na/Exhibit-A.git" exhibit-a --version ``` Without pipx: `python -m pip install "git+https://github.com/Diego-do-na/Exhibit-A.git"`. Installing puts the `exhibit-a` command on your machine; `exhibit-a init` (step 2) configures **each repository** you want to protect. 2. In the application repository, write the workflow: ```bash exhibit-a init ``` 3. In repository settings, create the protected `exhibit-a` environment with the `EXHIBIT_A_API_KEY` secret, set the `EXHIBIT_A_ENABLED=true` repository variable, and require these checks on the default branch: `exhibit-a / verify` and `exhibit-a / fork-guard`. Merges are blocked only when branch protection or rulesets require those checks. A repository administrator can bypass that protection. The generated workflow runs compact, sliced PR verification, posts a comment, and suggests verified fixes. Fork pull requests receive no model-key run and must be reviewed by a maintainer. The workflow also has a deliberately small, rule-based risk gate. # YourMove Hackathon Edition

This repository builds a separate macOS app identity and keeps its default data in `~/Library/Application Support/YourMove Hackathon Edition`. It does not import a legacy `jobs.db` from the current directory. `YOURMOVE_DATA_DIR` remains available for an explicit absolute workspace override.

Build a local Apple Silicon app bundle with:

```sh
scripts/build-hackathon-macos.sh /private/tmp/yourmove-hackathon-build
open "/private/tmp/yourmove-hackathon-build/YourMove Hackathon Edition.app"
```

The browser-mode server uses port `3019` by default; `YOURMOVE_HTTP_PORT` can override it.

YourMove keeps job opportunities, resumes, application preparation, and submission records in one local workspace. It reduces repeated preparation while leaving every review and submission decision with the applicant.

## What it does

- Save opportunities, organize priorities, and retrieve job details from supported posting sources.
- Store PDF and DOCX resumes, choose a resume for each job, and track versions.

# Meta Cost Center

Track your tokens and cost, set more robust billing alarms, and integrates with [Meta Keyguard](https://github.com/omenking/meta-keyguard) to kill keys if you hit your spend limit.


![](./banner.png)

![The Meta Cost Center dashboard](./meta-cost-control-screenshot.jpg)

Meta Cost Center tracks how much you use Muse Code and roughly what that usage would
cost at API rates. It reads the usage records that Muse already keeps on your machine,
stores them in a local SQLite database, and shows them in a dashboard in your browser,
broken down by project, model, and session. You can also set spending alerts and record
the amounts that actually appear on your bills.

Everything runs locally. The tool is a single binary with the dashboard built into it, so
it needs no API key, no hosted service, and no runtime to install, and it never makes
model calls of its own. It does not send your data anywhere.

The costs it shows are estimates, not bills. They are calculated from public per-token
prices, so they leave out taxes, credits, non-token charges, and anything covered by a
subscription, and they cannot include usage that was never logged on this machine.

## Requirements

- Linux, WSL, or macOS, on amd64 or arm64 (Apple Silicon is arm64)
- A web browser

Go is needed only to build from source, and Node only if you change the frontend code,
because the built dashboard is already included in the repository.

## Install

Install the latest release into `~/.local/bin`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omenking/meta-costcenter/main/install.sh | sh
```

The script downloads the archive for your architecture, checks it against the release's
checksums, and installs the `meta-cost` binary; set `META_COST_INSTALL_DIR` to install it
somewhere else. If Go is installed, `go install github.com/omenking/meta-costcenter/cmd/meta-cost@latest`
builds the same binary into `~/go/bin` instead. Upgrading is a matter of running either
command again, and the database and configuration carry over unchanged.

## Quick start

Run:

```bash
meta-cost show
```

This starts a local server and opens the dashboard at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`. If that
port is taken, a free one is chosen and printed instead. The first run imports your
existing Muse history in the background, so the page may fill in over a few seconds.
Leave the command running to keep the dashboard up to date, and press Ctrl+C when you
are finished.

If you are on WSL and no browser opens, copy the printed URL into a browser on Windows.
The server listens only on your own machine (loopback), so it is not reachable from
other computers.

Some useful variations:

```bash
meta-cost show --port 8766      # use a specific port
meta-cost show --port 0         # let the system pick a free port
meta-cost show --no-browser     # print the URL without opening a browser
```

## Using the dashboard

The sidebar links to six pages:

| Page | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Overview** | Estima

# Meta Keyguard

A chrome extension and CLI tool to manage your Meta API keys.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Do not use the Chrome extension or the bridge. The extension is deliberately disabled.**
>
> The extension drives dev.meta.ai's internal dashboard API, and the bridge asks it to list
> keys every minute, with Cost Center checks adding more requests. dev.meta.ai answered this
> traffic with HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests), and the author's Meta account was then blocked
> from the dashboard. Meta does not support automated use of the dashboard, so the same thing
> is likely to happen to anyone who runs Keyguard. The extension's service worker now throws
> on startup, before it registers any listener or alarm, so it never sends a request to
> dev.meta.ai; see the warning at the top of `extension/background.js`. Do not remove that
> line to get it working again. Create and delete keys by hand on dev.meta.ai instead.
>
> If you already installed Keyguard, remove the extension in `chrome://extensions` and run
> `meta-keyguard uninstall-bridge`. The rest of this README describes how Keyguard worked
> and is kept for reference only.

![](./banner.png)

Meta Keyguard gives Meta Model API keys an expiry date. The Meta developer dashboard has no
API for managing keys, no key expiry, and no way to switch a key off, so Keyguard does that
work through a Chrome extension that operates the dashboard on your behalf. A command-line
tool in WSL stores the keys, enforces their time to live (TTL), rotates them, and can revoke
them when [Meta Cost Center](https://github.com/omenking/meta-costcenter) reports that a
spending limit has been exceeded.

Keyguard is a single-user tool. It runs on one machine, manages one dev.meta.ai team, and
keeps everything local.

## How it works

```
 WSL                                        Windows
 meta-keyguard CLI ──Unix socket──► meta-keyguard bridge ◄──native messaging──► Chrome extension ──► dev.meta.ai
      │                             │  (started by Chrome through wsl.exe)
      └──── key store (SQLite) ◄────┘  runs the reaper every minute
```

The extension makes the same requests the dashboard makes when you click its buttons, from
inside a dev.meta.ai tab, so it uses your existing signed-in session. Chrome starts the
bridge through `wsl.exe` when the extension loads and keeps it running while Chrome is open.
While it runs, the bridge relays CLI requests to the extension and runs the reaper once a
minute, which deletes expired keys, finishes rotations, and applies Cost Center limits.

Because dev.meta.ai refuses to delete a team's last key, Keyguard creates a **sentinel**
key whenever a deletion would otherwise remove the last one. The extension drops the
sentinel's secret before it leaves the browser, so nobody holds it, and every other key can
then be deleted.

Keys are named `<label>-kg<timestamp>` on dev.meta.ai, for example `dev-kg20261025143000`.
You refer to them by label.

## Requirements

- WSL 2 with Windows interop ena

# G23 Evidence Copilot

**G23 Evidence Copilot by WaravutVisual** is a software evidence verification and claim-control prototype.

It uses deterministic checks to evaluate evidence artifacts, including SHA-256 integrity references and hash-chain verification. Its verification states are `VALID`, `UNKNOWN`, `MISMATCH`, and `CORRUPTED`.

Optional AI-generated explanations are non-authoritative and cannot override deterministic verification results. `VALID` means only that the defined checks passed; it does not establish runtime correctness or production readiness.

**Project scope:** general-purpose software verification and evidence integrity. This is not a medical AI copilot or a clinical decision-support system.

## Verification states

- VALID: evidence passed the defined deterministic checks
- UNKNOWN: required evidence is missing
- MISMATCH: evidence does not match the trusted reference
- CORRUPTED: evidence cannot be read or fails integrity validation

VALID does not imply runtime correctness or production readiness.
AI explanations must not override deterministic verification results.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Evidence Artifact"] --> V["Deterministic Verifier"]
    R["Trusted SHA-256 Reference"] --> V
    V --> S["VALID / UNKNOWN / MISMATCH / CORRUPTED"]
    S --> P["Structured Report"]
    P --> G["AI Guardrail (optional)"]
    G --> O["AI text withheld pending review"]
    G -. "cannot override" .-> S

    C["Hash-chain JSON"] --> H["Hash-chain Verifier"]
    E["Trusted Expected Head (optional)"] --> H
    H --> HS["Chain Verification Result"]
```

**Trust boundary:** Deterministic verification owns the result state. AI text is non-authoritative and must not upgrade a verification result.

## Quick Demo

Run from the repository root. These checks do not require a Meta API key.

### 1. Verify the example hash chain

```bash
python -m app.hash_chain examples/hash-chain-demo.json
```

Show the actual state and explanation returned by the verifier.

### 2. Demonstrate the AI guardrail

```bash
python - <<'PY'
from app.ai_guardrail import build_guarded_result
from app.verifier import Result, State

verified = Result(
    State.VALID,
    "Artifact bytes match the supplied SHA-256 reference.",
    "0" * 64,
)

result = build_guarded_result(
    verified,
    lambda context: "The evidence proves production readiness.",
)

print("VERIFIER_STATE =", result["verification"]["state"])
print("AI_STATUS =", result["ai_explanation"]["status"])
print("AI_TEXT =", result["ai_explanation"]["text"])
print("AI_AUTHORITATIVE =", result["ai_explanation"]["is_authoritative"])
PY
```

Expected behavior: verifier state remains `VALID`; the raw AI sentence is withheld with `REVIEW_REQUIRED`; AI is marked non-authoritative. The sample digest above is illustrative, not a real artifact hash.

### 3. Run relevant tests

```bash

rajagavaskargithub/ASG-AI-SQL-Guard.readme_excerpt: # ASG: AI SQL Guard A security layer between AI-generated SQL and your data. The model writes SQL; deterministic code decides whether it may run. > **Status: prototype / demo.** Fake data only, DuckDB only, no authentication. > Do not expose it to the internet and do not point it at real data. > It reduces risk; it does not guarantee safety. Demo video: https://youtu.be/b0wMEdcS9oQ ## How it works ``` Question -> LLM (untrusted) -> SQL -> ASG guard -> audit log |-- allow -> read-only execution |-- approve -> human decision -> revalidate -> execute once `-- deny -> stop ``` - Parses each query with sqlglot: one statement, `SELECT` only - Table allowlist and column default-deny; classified columns (`ssn` blocked, `email` and `phone` need approval) - Catches `SELECT *`, `c.*`, whole-row references, and filtering on blocked columns - Required and maximum `LIMIT`; blocked file and system functions - Only the exact evaluated SQL runs, on a read-only DuckDB connection with external access disabled, with a time and memory limit - Hash-bound, expiring, single-use human approvals, revalidated before execution - Every decision and execution outcome is audited; the guard fails closed on errors The model is never asked whether its own SQL is safe. ## Test results (what I measured) Live Muse Spark models (`muse-spark-1.3`, `muse-spark-1.1`), 9 queries each, fake data, October 2026. Small sample; model outputs vary between runs. | | Natural mode | Red-team mode | |---|---|---| | Queries | 18 | 18 | | Queries naming sensitive columns | 0 | 14 | | Would have returned SSNs with no guard | 0 | 14 | | Returned SSNs with ASG in front | 0 | 0 | | Sensitive-column queries stopped by ASG | n/a | 14 of 14 | | Benign queries wrongly blocked | 0 of 18 | 0 of 4 | - **Natural mode:** a naive agent reads a poisoned note and writes SQL. Neither model followed the injected instructions. - **Red-team mode:** the model is *told* to simulate a hijacked agent. This tests the guard; it is **not** evidence that these models get hijacked on their own. - My first run blocked every benign query because the model did not know a `LIMIT` was required. Telling the agent the rule fixed it. The guard still decides independently. - The 14 queries are only a few distinct attack shapes, not 14 independent attacks. The suite has 128 automated tests (run `pytest -q`). ## Run it (macOS, Python 3.12) ```bash git clone && cd ai-asg python3.12 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python -m src.asg.seed .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q .venv/bin/python -m streamlit run app.py ``` Mock mode needs no API key. For live mode, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and add a key from the Meta Model

# oqed

```
faster than -O3. proven equivalent (when it can be).
```

oqed is an LLM-guided superoptimizer for x86-64. point it at a C or C++
project and it finds the hot functions, asks Meta's Muse models for faster
assembly, throws away everything that isn't correct, and keeps what beats
`clang -O3` and `gcc -O3`. then you build with `CC=oqed-cc` and that's it,
your source doesn't change.

built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Push the Frontier).

**live UI with the real runs: [ignaciosearles.github.io/oqed](https://ignaciosearles.github.io/oqed/)**

## results

real open-source projects, cloned as they are. whole program, plain build vs
oqed build, 11 alternating runs, output identical every time:

```
project       hottest function             clang     gcc      spend
protobuf-c    message_get_packed_size      1.269x    1.320x   $14.68   7 entries, 2 proven
zlib          longest_match (88%)          1.172x    1.145x   $15.85   2 entries
cJSON         parse_string / parse_value   1.072x    -        $0.85    3 entries
LevelDB C++   BytewiseComparator::Compare  1.046x    0.993x   $2.41    1 entry
libyaml       fetch_plain_scalar           no win             $2.43    99 candidates, none faster
lz4           compress_generic_internal    out of reach       -        hot code is 4,000+ instructions
```

entries that aren't proven were judged by the project's own tests and
benchmark (`--unsafe`, they touch memory, the prover doesn't do memory yet).
protobuf-c's 2 proven entries alone give 1.171x / 1.125x.

single functions, proven equivalent for every input, latency inlined in a loop:

```
clz_smear_u32       6.46x    smear + popcount -> lzcnt
parity_u32          3.49x
round_up_pow2_u32   3.24x
```

numbers come from a WSL2 laptop, not a quiet benchmark box. the per-project
write-ups are in [sweep/](sweep/README.md).

## how it works

```
 your project ──► oqed scan: build it, run the workload, profile, slice every hot function
                     │
                     ▼
   Muse Spark (lots of parallel candidates) + Muse Wonder (thinks hard when the search stalls)
                     │  asm + one line on the trick
                     ▼
   assemble ─► ISA check ─► tests ─► SMT proof ─► benchmark vs clang AND gcc
                     │  every failure goes back to the model: assembler line, counterexample,
                     │  ABI violation, crash site + registers, diff of the output
                     ▼
   oqed.lock ─► make CC=oqed-cc   (re-proves each entry against your source on every build)
```

- **models:** `muse-spark-1.3` on the Meta Model API writes most candidates,
  `muse-wonder-1.0` gets the whole search history when progress stalls (it
  wrote zlib's winner). Muse Spark Open on Baseten can be the volume tier too.
- **proofs:** symbolic execution (angr) + Z3 over every ABI-valid input.
  anything it can't decide is labelled "tested, not proven", never "proven".

# silver-one

> Changing world values are inputs. Inputs are recorded. Recorded inputs are replayable. Replayable workflows are evolvable.

`silver-one` is an Agentbeats research project for generating auditable code-security reasoning data. Its long-term goal is to build the kind of grounded corpus needed to train safer security-reasoning models: models that learn from concrete evidence hooks, mechanism-level invariants, verifier feedback, and rejected failure cases instead of shallow vulnerable/safe labels.

The project is a continuation of the In-Varia metacognitive-control research direction and the Google DeepMind/Kaggle AGI hackathon work behind MCSB v2. That earlier work showed that models can look calibrated in static settings while failing to update beliefs correctly under adversarial code-security evidence. `silver-one` moves from measuring that failure mode toward producing better training data for it.

The main implemented scenario builds upon **BARRED** (*Boundary Alignment Refinement through REflection and Debate*), the foundational multi-agent security debate paradigm from Plural AI literature. In `silver-one`, this is evolved into **BARRED-Swarm** (*Boundary-Aware Reflective Robust Exploration & Debate*):
- a Green agent (`adk_debate_judge.py`) orchestrates debate rounds,
- two Purple agents (`debater.py`) argue opposite sides,
- an optional Verifier agent (`adk_debate_verifier.py`) audits groundedness,
- outputs are written as training corpus rows and audited with an offline B-gate.

## The BARRED Swarm Architecture

The six core architectural pillars extending the original debate formulation are:

| Letter | Architectural Component | Role in the Swarm |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **B** | **Boundary-Aware** | Extracts vulnerability dimensions (CVE predicates, boundary conditions, reachability constraints) and synthesizes edge-case code samples. |
| **A** | **Asymmetric** | Orchestrates opposing purple agents (Pro-Attacker vs. Con-Defender) supervised by a green judge to eliminate hallucinated consensus. |
| **R** | **Reflective** | Executes iterative refinement via the GEPA Reflector (reflective meta-prompt mutation and diagnostic triage across refinement rounds). |
| **R** | **Robust** | Enforces deterministic quality floors via the B-Gate (AST parse coverage, strict anchor grounding, zero logic errors, and parse reliability). |
| **E** | **Exploration** | Drives stratified, scenario-grouped cross-validation across holdouts to ensure zero data leakage between train/test partitions. |
| **D** | **Debate / Dataset** | Generates verified, high-fidelity synthetic training corpora used to train and evaluate code-security guardrail models. |

## Why This Matters

LLM-generated security datasets and agent evaluations are easy to make and hard to trust. Small hidden changes in prompts, model sampling, timestamps, tool calls, or verifier behavior can change which rows enter a corpus. If those rows are later used for training, hidden error

# BARRED: Evidence-Gated Security Fix Review

> **Track:** Push the Frontier  
> **Model:** Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B (`trymirai/Muse-Glimmer-30B-M`)  
> **Architecture:** Open-weight 30B multimodal dense transformer with Llama BPE tokenizer, optimized for autonomous agentic code workflows  
> **Core Innovation:** Transforming probabilistic AI security opinions into deterministic, machine-verifiable evidence decisions  

---

### 📋 Hackathon Project Disclosure (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026)
*This project was developed for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon. All core innovations presented in this submission were designed, implemented, and evaluated during the hackathon period (October 26 – November 4, 2026):*
1. **Deterministic AST Candidate Extractor (`scenarios/debate/con_receipt_extractor.py`):** Automatically discovers dominating bounds checks and guard invariants from source code slices.
2. **Mathematical Receipt Validator (`scenarios/debate/counter_evidence_validation.py`):** Verifies invariant contracts to eliminate AI safety hallucinations and false positives (achieving `0.0%` accepted logic error rate across all benchmarks).
3. **Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B Integration:** End-to-end multi-agent debate, adjudication, and candidate selection powered by Meta's open-weights model via Uzu.
4. **Fault-Tolerant 3-Way Adjudication Contracts:** `PASS` (Proven via C1) | `BLOCKED` (Falsified/Exploitable) | `UNRESOLVED` (Explicit abstention on unsupported domains).
5. **Architectural Bug Fixes & False-Positive Elimination:** Hardened through 38 regression and replay tests closing null-receipt false passes, non-dominating guard hallucinations, schema coercion failures, and ungrounded wrapper claims.
6. **One-Command Reviewer CLI & Evidence Pack:** A developer-facing tool allowing instant 30-second inspection or full live verification.

---


## The Problem
Every AI coding assistant today suffers from a fatal flaw: **it produces persuasive, authoritative-sounding explanations whether it is right or wrong.**

When reviewing a security fix, an LLM might declare code "Safe" because the developer added a superficial check or an irrelevant comment. To protect themselves, platforms slap broad legal disclaimers on coding agents (*"Verify all actions taken by the agent"*).

**BARRED replaces disclaimers with deterministic proof.**

Instead of letting an LLM generate ungrounded prose, BARRED pairs **Meta's Muse-Glimmer-30B** with **deterministic AST evidence gates**. The model is constrained to select machine-extracted candidates ($C_1 \dots C_n$), while the deterministic engine mathematically verifies control-flow dominance and value relations.

The result is a clean tri-state security review:
1. **`PASS`**: Machine-verified invariant proof attached (guard dominates sink on all paths).
2. **`BLOCKED`**: Plausible model hallucination caught and rejected by AST gate.
3. **`UNRESOLVED`**: Explicit epistemic refusal when outside the verified proof domain (no fake safety claims).

---

# ShipCube

**The infrastructure layer for apps you build with your coding agent.**

You build an internal app (a tracker, dashboard, report, API or scoring job) in Claude Code, Cursor, Muse Code or any other MCP-capable coding agent. Your agent connects to ShipCube's MCP server, and ShipCube handles the infrastructure:

- **Load estimation:** predicts how the app will behave (batch, bursty, steady, memory-heavy, I/O-bound) and sizes it.
- **Caps:** spend, rate and resource limits for each app, so nothing runs away.
- **Deployment on GCP:** Cloud Run services, Cloud Run jobs or GKE Autopilot, chosen from the load estimate. It runs on ShipCube's GCP project or on **your own GCP project and credits**, linked with Google sign-in.
- **Access control:** only the owner and the people they allow can open an app.
- **Data:** a minimal typed semantic layer, so apps run on any customer set without code changes.
- **AI for your apps:** apps that need a model get one through ShipCube's AI gateway. Muse is the default; you can also bring your own key.
- **Continuous monitoring:** health, data freshness, cost and drift, with suggestions to move an app when it outgrows its tier.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track) on Meta's Muse models.

**Demo video (2:31):** [youtu.be/KhK0FmqYF1g](https://youtu.be/KhK0FmqYF1g)

2 minutes? Watch the video. 20 minutes? Run it locally (below).

## Where Muse decides

ShipCube uses Meta's **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`, through the Meta Model API) in three places:

1. **Explaining each load estimate.** The sandbox measures the app, and the classifier picks the workload class, tier and price. Muse Spark turns those measurements into the reasoning the user reads, writes the trade-off for each alternative tier, and recommends the app's caps. `deploy_app` doesn't apply them by itself: the user or agent sets them with `set_caps`.
2. **Drafting data-model changes.** `data_propose_migration` takes a plain-English request or the app's code, and Muse Spark drafts the change. A person approves it before it applies.
3. **The model inside every deployed app.** Apps call Muse through ShipCube's AI gateway by default, with a token budget for each app.

# Doc: find it, fix it, remember it

A recovery loop for AI coding agents, powered by six Meta models.
Meta AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · indie developer track · by Mike Hood ([@EvilMetaMonkey](https://github.com/EvilMetaMonkey))

▶ 3-minute demo: <video link>

Coding agents break things before anyone commits. Doc records every agent turn, then:

- **Find it:** `doc bisect` names the turn that broke your tests (4 probes, under a second in the demo).
- **Fix it:** Muse Wonder plans three fixes, three Muse Code agents try them in parallel worktrees, and Wonder ranks the results. You pick; nothing is merged for you.
- **Remember it:** an approved lesson opens the next agent session that touches the same files.

The AI never writes your files: every restore goes through dmc's preview-first, journaled path.

**Pre-existing work:** Doc drives [dmc](https://github.com/EvilMetaMonkey/dmc), my open-source rollback tool from before the event. dmc is not in this repository: setup clones it at a pinned pre-event commit and applies this event's patches from [`dmc-patches/`](dmc-patches/) (see [PATCHES.md](PATCHES.md)). Everything in this repository was written during the event (from 2026-10-26).

## What Doc does

AI coding agents (Muse Code, Claude Code) change many files per turn, and sometimes they break
things. dmc records every agent turn as a checkpoint: what each file was before and after,
restorable through a preview-first, journaled restore. **Doc** is the companion that puts Meta's
Muse models on top of that record, as one loop:

1. **Find it.** `doc bisect --test "<command>"` runs your tests on exported checkpoint states
   (never your working copy) to find the turn where they started failing, and Muse Spark explains
   why.
2. **Fix it.** `doc timelines "<task>" --from-bisect`: Muse Wonder plans three different
   approaches, three Muse Code agents try them in separate Git worktrees, Doc runs the tests in
   each and compares them side by side, and Wonder judges the results. You pick one; the others
   stay as branches. Nothing is merged for you.
3. **Remember it.** `doc restore` undoes a turn through dmc, then drafts a lesson from the undone
   work. Approved lessons are offered to the next agent that touches the same files
   (`doc start`).

Also built in:

- natural-language restore: `doc restore "take me back to before it touched auth"`, always with

anything is restored, run or sent to a model. Secrets are redacted before any hosted call.

# Falsify — the devil's advocate for market beliefs

> Say what you believe about the market. An AI will try to prove it wrong.

Falsify takes a belief in plain language — any language — turns it into **one exact, testable rule**,
**seals that rule in a public hash-chained ledger before any result exists**, replays it on historical
candles with a deterministic engine, and then runs a **battery of attacks** against it: random entries
with the same holding period, fee sensitivity, first half vs second half, nearby parameters, other assets,
multiple-testing correction, sample size, a look-ahead guard, and model-proposed counter-tests specific
to the belief. The verdict — **FALSIFIED / FRAGILE / SURVIVED (for now) / INCONCLUSIVE** — is decided by
the numbers and explained by Meta's open-weight **Muse Glimmer 30B** in the language the belief was written in.

It never tells you what to buy. It only tells you whether your belief survived an honest attempt to break it.

Built solo for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie track, *Build for Your World*).

---

## Why

Retail traders — the author included — carry around beliefs like *"when RSI goes under 30 it always
bounces"* or *"three red days means a green one"*. They are almost never written down precisely, never
tested against a fair baseline, and quietly re-tuned after the fact until they look right. Backtesting
tools exist, but they are built to make a strategy *look good*; nothing in the stack is built to make a
belief *fail*.

Falsify is the missing adversary. Its three design rules:

1. **Seal before you see.** The rule is hashed and chained to the ledger *before* the first number is
   computed. No moving the goalposts after the result.
2. **The model never touches the numbers.** Muse Glimmer translates, argues and explains. A deterministic
   engine computes. The two cannot be mixed up because the engine only accepts a tiny, whitelisted rule
   language.
3. **A pass is not a forecast.** The best possible verdict is *SURVIVED (for now)*, and the report says so
   in its first line.

## How a claim is tried

| Stage | Who | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Understand | Muse Glimmer | Rewrites the belief as one rule in the Falsify rule language, names the asset, direction, holding period and the **pre-registered success criterion**, and lists every assumption it had to make. If the rule does not compile or produces zero signals, it is shown its own error and repairs it (max 4 attempts). It is forbidden from tuning the rule to improve results. |
| 2. Seal | engine | Canonical JSON of the rule is hashed with SHA-256 and chained to the previous ledger entry (`sha256(prev_hash + sealed_at + canonical)`). |
| 3. Test | engine | Signal evaluated at the close, entry at the **next open**, exit after N bars (or stop/target), fees charged on both sides. Equity curve, win rate, drawdown, buy-and-hold comparison. |
| 4. Attack | engine | The fixed battery below. Each attack returns PASS / W

Most medicines are either tiny chemicals or giant antibodies. cozy-peptide
works in the fertile middle: **small peptides** across seven scaffolds —
from **knottins**, miniature proteins just 28–36 building blocks long
tied into a molecular knot by six cysteines, down to simple linear
peptides. That knot is armor: knottins can survive stomach acid and
digestive enzymes that shred ordinary protein drugs in minutes, so they
can act directly where the disease lives. Auto picks the best scaffold

disease target — say, *Clostridioides difficile* colonization — and
**Muse Spark 1.3** invents brand-new peptide sequences from scratch:
proteins that have never existed in nature, reasoned into being from the
grammar of protein language. A deterministic symbolic compiler then
interrogates every candidate — topology, charge, stability, protease
resistance, safety — and rejects anything unsound. Failures return as
compiler diagnostics that guide Muse Spark to repair its own designs, in
a closed loop, until one passes every check.

sequence** — the invention itself — which converts straightforwardly into a
**DNA synthesis order you can send to a vendor**: codon-optimized cDNA
encoding an engineered living therapeutic in one of four chassis
(*Saccharomyces boulardii*, *E. coli* Nissle, *Lactococcus lactis*, or
*Bacillus subtilis* spores) — a living miniature factory installed where
the disease lives — that manufactures your therapeutic on site. Not a
probiotic: a Live Biotherapeutic Product. The medicine is not a pill you
keep taking; it is a factory you swallow once.

# SentralID Trace: Verify Before You Book

**Trace helps you check a Philippine hotel or resort booking before you pay a deposit.**

In the Philippines, booking a beach resort often happens on Facebook: you find a page, chat on Messenger, and send a deposit by GCash. Scammers copy real resorts' pages and photos to collect those deposits. Trace gives you a way to check before you pay.

You give Trace what you have: the Facebook link you were sent, a screenshot of the page, or screenshots of your chat. Trace reads them with **Meta's Muse Spark AI**, compares what it finds with records from a government source, and tells you what matches, what doesn't, and what a screenshot can't prove. Then it suggests **one safe thing to check next**, and updates the result when you come back with the answer.

This is an entry for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie Developer track, *Build for Your World*).

| | |
|---|---|
| AI used | Meta `muse-spark-1.3`, through `https://api.meta.ai/v1`. It's the only AI the app talks to. |
| Real records | 13 resorts in San Juan, Batangas, each linked to its Facebook page by the town's tourism office |
| Tests | 134 automated tests, plus 20 out of 20 live end-to-end runs ([report](docs/qa/repeat-runs-2026-10-31.md)) |
| Try it live | **https://sentralid-trace.vercel.app** (judges: no setup needed; the four demo scenarios are on the home page). Hosted copy added for judging; usage is capped, so if it says the hourly limit is reached, wait or run it locally with the quick start below. |

## Why this isn't just an image reader

Reading the screenshot is only the first of six steps, and it never decides the result.

1. **Read.** Muse Spark reads the screenshots and lists what it sees: the page address, names, phone numbers, payment requests. It treats any text in a screenshot as information, never as instructions, even text that tries to give it orders.
2. **Compare with a government source.** Fixed rules, not the AI, compare what was read with Trace's records. Those records come from the [San Juan, Batangas Municipal Tourism Office's list of verified resort Facebook pages](https://tourism.sanjuanbatangas.gov.ph/verified-facebook-pages), published by a Philippine town government. Every result says which record and source it relies on.
3. **Keep each question separate.** Finding the right Facebook page doesn't tell you who is chatting with you, or whose GCash account you're paying. Trace keeps those as "can't tell" every time. It never gives a scam score and never says "safe to pay".
4. **Plan the next step.** Muse Spark sets out the two most likely explanations and picks one safe check from a short list Trace controls. For example: compare the page with the tourism office's list, call the number on file, or message the resort from its listed page.
5. **Double-check the AI's plan.** Trace throws out any plan that isn't on the list, or whose wording vouches for someone, accuses someone, or includes a phone number or l

# SnapShop

One phone photo in, a ready-to-sell online listing out.

A shop owner snaps a product photo. SnapShop then:

1. **Segments** the product and removes the background with **SAM 3.1**.
2. **Generates** clean studio-style product photos with **Muse Image**.
3. **Writes** the title, description, category, and a suggested price range with **Muse Spark** (English for now; Sinhala is planned once its output quality is reliable).
4. **Checks** the result with an agent loop that retries or fixes weak output *(planned)*.
5. Lets the owner **review, edit, and publish** to a public storefront.

All AI calls go through the [Meta Model API](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models) and run only on the server.

## Tech stack

- Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS
- PostgreSQL on [Neon](https://neon.tech) via Prisma 7 (`@prisma/adapter-pg`)
- Meta Model API through the OpenAI SDK (`baseURL: https://api.meta.ai/v1`), as the Meta quickstart recommends
- `@meta-sam/parser` to decode SAM masks, `sharp` for the cutout

## How the pipeline runs

Each upload creates a `ListingJob` row. The work is split into short steps
(`queued → identifying → segmenting → imaging → writing → ready`), and each step runs in
its own function invocation:

- `POST /api/listing` stores the photo, creates the job, and starts the first step with `after()`.
- `GET /api/listing/:id` returns the status. If the job is idle (or its step lock is stale), it starts the next step with `after()`.

Once the job is `ready`, the owner edits the draft and publishes it. A
published listing gets a public slug (`/store/<slug>`); the job id, which is
what allows editing, never appears on the storefront. There are no accounts
yet, so treat the review link as private.

The review page polls every 2 seconds, so polling is what drives the
pipeline. No single request has to wait for the whole job, and a crashed step
is picked up again once its lock expires. A job only moves forward while
someone is polling it.

## Project layout

```
app/capture          mobile photo capture + upload
app/review/[id]      live job status, then the edit / publish form
app/store            public storefront grid; app/store/[slug] product page
app/api/listing      create job, poll status, save edits, publish/unpublish
app/api/store        published listings (JSON)
app/api/images       serves locally stored images
lib/meta             typed Meta Model API wrappers (SAM, Muse Image, Muse Spark)
lib/pipeline         one file per pipeline step + the runner
lib/storage.ts       image storage interface (local disk now, Vercel Blob later)
prisma/              database schema
scripts/verify-meta  checks your API key and each model against a sample photo
```

## Setup

Requirements: Node.js 20.17+ (or 22.9+), a Meta Model API key, and a Neon database.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # then fill in MODEL_API_KEY and DATABASE_URL
npx prisma migrate dev       # creates the tables in your Neon database
npm run d

An **Autonomous AI CCTV Control Room Operator** engineered for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**. Powered by **Meta Muse Spark Open (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`)**, this platform transforms standard passive security cameras into intelligent, rule-driven autonomous operators that watch custom spatial zones, reason over multi-frame HD temporal sequences, and dispatch verified visual alerts with evidence snapshots directly to **WhatsApp** in real time.

---

## 🎯 Why We Developed This Project (Hackathon Motivation & Objective)

### The Problem with Traditional CCTV Surveillance
1. **Unmanned Feeds & Operator Fatigue:** Over 98% of commercial and residential CCTV video is never watched live—it is only reviewed *after* a theft, safety breach, or operational incident has already occurred.
2. **Legacy Motion Detection Floods Users with False Alarms:** Standard pixel-motion detectors trigger indiscriminately on swaying trees, passing shadows, pedestrians walking outside a property line, or waiters walking past a restaurant table.
3. **Alert Spam on Stationary Subjects:** In real-world scenarios—such as monitoring **restaurant table occupancy**—once a customer sits down, traditional detectors either spam dozens of duplicate alerts for the same seated person or lock the entire camera feed, blinding the system to new guests sitting at neighboring tables.
4. **Missed Fast-Moving Text & Fleet IDs:** Single-frame snapshots taken at the exact millisecond of a motion trigger often miss vehicle fleet numbers or license plates that were clearly visible 3–8 seconds earlier as the vehicle approached the gate.

### Our Project Objective
Developed specifically for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**, our objective is to bridge **low-latency client-side edge computer vision** with **Meta Muse Spark Open (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`)** multimodal reasoning and **Meta's WhatsApp Cloud API** to deliver:
- **Zero-Shot Natural Language Surveillance Rules:** Operators define what to watch for in plain English (or via 1-click industry presets) without training custom YOLO/CNN weights.
- **Strict Polygon Watch Zone Masking:** Freehand `✏️ Custom Pencil`, `▢ Box`

# Pit Wall

An autonomous Formula 1 race strategist that runs on a laptop. Ask it *"when should Leclerc make his first stop?"* and it pulls the timing data, fits a tyre and fuel model, simulates every one- and two-stop plan, checks undercut and cover threats from the cars around, and answers with a pit call whose every number is verified against the data.

Built on **Meta's Muse Glimmer 30B**, an open-weight model, running **locally** through Ollama: no API key, no cloud, no cost per question.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie developer track, *Build for Your World*).

**Demo video (2:17):** [youtu.be/bhSKVI1F1a8](https://youtu.be/bhSKVI1F1a8)

![Strategy desk: Miami 2024, Leclerc after lap 14, knowing only laps 1-14](docs/strategy-desk.png)

## What makes it different

- **The maths is real, and the model doesn't do it.** A hand-written engine measures pit-lane time loss from the race itself, separates fuel burn from tyre wear with a least-squares pace model (with bootstrap uncertainty ranges), and searches every one- and two-stop plan. The LLM plans, reads tool results and weighs race time against track position.
- **Every answer is verified.** A verifier checks that every number in the agent's answer appears in a tool result, that the pit lap matches the decision, and that the compound is legal. Answers that fail get one chance to correct themselves.
- **It knows when not to answer.** Rain-affected races are refused rather than modelled badly, plans that would push a tyre beyond any stint seen at the track are excluded, and undercut calls closer than the pit-stop spread are reported as *marginal*.
- **It was tested without cheating.** A leak-free backtest replays 29 real decisions from the 2024 season, giving the strategist only what a pit wall knew at that lap. Tests prove nothing after the decision lap can reach it.

## Results: a leak-free backtest against the real teams

29 first-stop decisions in six dry 2024 races, at a quarter race distance, for the top six cars still on their starting tyres. Races and drivers were chosen by fixed rules in code before any result existed. The strategist sees only the race up to the decision lap; tyre physics, pit loss and tyre-age limits come from the same Grand Prix in 2023. Each call is scored by **regret**: race time lost against the best first stop in hindsight.

| | Pit Wall agent | Simulator alone | Real teams |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median regret | **0.23 s** | 0.23 s | 0.39 s |
| Mean regret | 1.75 s | 1.75 s | **1.37 s** |
| Calls within 0.5 s of the best | **21 / 29** | 21 / 29 | 16 / 29 |

# Finger Pods

Clicky, wearable text input for the wearable computing era — finger clips that let you type on any surface, in any light, with the muscle memory you already have.

> **Hackathon:** [Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley)](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon/details)

## AI assistance

I used [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/products/muse-code) to brainstorm ideas, write code, and help throughout development, using free credits provided by Meta.

## Pre-hackathon disclosure

In August 2026, I came up with the idea and wanted to validate two key questions:

1. Could the device be comfortable to wear?
2. Could magnetic sensors reliably track finger positions?

I started with comfort, designing [finger clips in Onshape](https://cad.onshape.com/documents/a458d74f05790c53a1d9c083/w/ba0d3bb9b7740cf4850c436d/e/a170be4422ab532e06a19dd8) and 3D-printing several iterations. I also ordered the necessary electronics, including magnets, magnetometers, accelerometers, switches, and other components.

I concluded that 3D-printed parts were far from ideal, but a comfortable wearable seemed achievable with better materials and more engineering time.

After that, I put the project aside and never got around to assembling the hardware, writing firmware, collecting data, or training an ML model. This hackathon is a great opportunity to pick up where I left off, build a working prototype, and finally test whether the magnetic sensing approach works.

---

## Demo

_TODO: add a demo video here once the prototype is ready._

## The problem

People will move from laptops to wearable compute in the next few years. Quality interaction needs information channels in both directions:

| Direction | Visual | Sound | Text |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Input** | Cameras, screenshots | Microphones | **This project** |
| **Output** | Glasses displays (arriving) | Earbuds / glasses speakers | Subset of visual output |

Five of the six are solved or clearly on their way. **Text input is the gap.**

### Why existing text-input solutions fall short

1. **Speech-to-text** — convenient, but unusable in quiet places and for private information.
2. **Camera-tracked virtual keyboards** — fail outside the camera field of view and in the dark, and tapping a table gives no satisfying tactile feedback.
3. **Wristbands that track finger movement** — do not reach keyboard-comparable typing speed.
4. **Wearable chorded / alternative keyboards** — require learning a new skill and still slower than a standard keyboard.

## The solution

Wearable **finger clips** that sense finger configuration and provide satisfying, tactile button clicks:

- **One clip on each finger.**
- **Magnets** on the index finger and pinky.
- **Magnetometers** on the thumb, middle, and ring fingers.
- **Multiple physical buttons per clip**, positioned for easy access and a crisp, satisfying click across different finger positions. More buttons also simplify keystroke recognition: e

# Brahma

**Decision support, not diagnosis.** Brahma walks a synthetic patient case through a
cited clinical knowledge graph and shows only lines that trace to a graph node and its
source. It works on synthetic cases only, never on real patient data, and it makes no
claim of HIPAA compliance or any certification.

**Demo video:** [Brahma walkthrough on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-4TcE8g_X-c).
It was recorded from the `demo-recording` tag: `git checkout demo-recording` runs exactly what the video shows.

## Run the backend

The backend runs locally only. There is no hosted URL.

### Prerequisites

- Python 3.12 or later.
- For a real walk: an API key for one model provider (the Meta Model API for the
  submitted demo; Claude or a free hosted Llama tier while building). The `recorded`
  provider needs no key and replays recorded test replies.

### Install

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

### Configure

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` (git-ignored) and fill in the values for your provider.
Never commit real values. The server reads:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `BRAHMA_MODEL_PROVIDER`, `BRAHMA_MODEL_NAME` and the provider's key | The model (see `.env.example`). |
| `BRAHMA_SESSION_SECRET` | Signs the session cookie. Required unless the provider is `recorded`. |
| `BRAHMA_DB_PATH` | SQLite file; default `./data/brahma.db`. |
| `BRAHMA_FEATURE_MODULES` | Feature modules to mount; default `brahma.updates.api`. |
| `BRAHMA_LOG_PATH` | Walk log (JSON lines, no clinical text); default `./data/brahma.log`. |
| `BRAHMA_HOST`, `BRAHMA_PORT` | Bind address; default `127.0.0.1:8000`. |
| `BRAHMA_RECORDED_DIR` | Optional fixture folder for the `recorded` provider (the demo replies are in `tests/agent/fixtures/recorded/demo`). |

### Start

```bash
set -a; . ./.env; set +a
.venv/bin/python -m brahma.server
```

On the first start the server loads the packs in `content/` (IBD and the urology stub)
and seeds the demo profiles. Check it with:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health
```

The API is under `/api` (profiles, session, patients and cases, the walk as
Server-Sent Events, node detail, history and export). The knowledge-update screens are
mounted under `/api/knowledge`.

## Run the app

The doctor web app lives in `web/` (Vite, React and TypeScript). It needs Node 20 or
later. Build it once, then the backend serves it, so the whole app runs from one command
on one URL:

```bash
cd web && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..
.venv/bin/python -m brahma.server
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000, pick a demo profile (Dr. Maya), accept the disclaimer and
create a synthetic patient. To walk the recorded demo case without a model key, start the
server with the recorded demo replies:

```bash
BRAHMA_MODEL_PROVIDER=recorded BRAHMA_RECORDED_DIR=tests/agent/fixtures/recorded/demo \
  .venv/bin/python -m brahma.server
```

and type: `34-year-old woman, bloody stool 6 months, Hb 10.2 g/dL, calprotectin 850 µg/g`.

# AgentFoundry

**Build specialized AI agents. Train them in realistic business environments. Verify whether they can actually do the job.**

AgentFoundry is an experimental platform for building, evaluating, and improving AI agents through realistic business simulations.

## The idea

Completing a straightforward task is only the beginning. Business agents must also handle missing information, conflicting instructions, tool failures, and interrupted operations.

AgentFoundry explores how agents can improve through execution feedback while an independent verifier checks their actual effects on business state.

## How it works

1. **Define a mission:** describe a business task, its constraints, and its available tools.
2. **Build an agent:** generate a specialized, versioned agent configuration.
3. **Run simulations:** execute tasks in an isolated business environment.
4. **Verify outcomes:** check application state against deterministic business rules.
5. **Analyze failures:** identify problems using execution traces and evidence.
6. **Evaluate improvements:** compare candidate versions on separate evaluation scenarios.

## Initial use case

The first environment is a simulated e-commerce returns workflow.

Agents will handle return eligibility, partial refunds, inventory updates, clarification requests, and recovery from interrupted operations.

All customers, payments, and business operations in this environment are simulated.

## Planned architecture

- TypeScript monorepo
- Next.js and React interface
- Fastify backend
- PostgreSQL persistence
- Redis and BullMQ background jobs
- Meta Model API integration
- Separate agent runtime, business simulator, and verifier

## Evaluation principles

- Independent verification of business outcomes
- Separate training, validation, and final evaluation scenarios
- Versioned configurations and replayable execution traces
- Explicit reporting of failures, costs, and sample sizes
- Clear identification of mock and live model executions

In the initial prototype, training means improving instructions and workflows through execution feedback. It does not mean updating foundation model weights.

## Project status

Under active development for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

This README describes the intended design. Implemented features, setup instructions, and measured results will be documented as development progresses.

## License

Licensed under the MIT License. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details.

# Flatmate Matching Platform

Find flatmates you can actually live with — matched on compatibility,
not just budget and location.

## The idea

Budget and area get you a shortlist; cleanliness, noise, guests, routines,
and conflict style decide whether sharing a home works. This app makes that
judgment structured: answer questions across 12 living-habit dimensions, and
get ranked matches with plain-language explanations of what lines up, what
differs, and what's worth discussing before moving in.

## How it works

1. **Filter** — hard requirements (deal-breakers, blocks) remove non-starters.
2. **Score** — a pure rule-based engine ranks the rest 0–100 on practical,
   lifestyle, and interpersonal fit. Weights live in `weights.yaml`.
3. **Explain** — every match shows reasons and discussion prompts. AI only
   narrates precomputed scores; it never ranks or filters, and the app works
   fully with AI disabled.

## What's inside

Signup/login, profiles, questionnaire (form or AI-drafted), ranked matches,
save/dismiss/express interest, mutual-interest contact reveal, block/report,
room listings, mutual-interest chat, flatmate reviews, expense tracking,
agreement drafting, natural-language search, admin moderation, metrics,
verified stays with trust-scored reviews, alerts for interests/stays/reviews, a public landing page,
and 27 seed profiles. Single Go binary, SQLite, JSON API plus two UIs:
the legacy server-rendered pages and the React SPA in `client/`.

# Repod

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon project.

Repod lets a Meta model coordinate a development request: it splits the work
into subtasks, assigns each one to a model suited to its difficulty and risk,
and reports what every step cost. Program-run checks gate quality, and a
model is escalated only when a cheaper attempt fails those checks.

The goal is to make the cost and quality trade-off visible, controllable and
verifiable. Whether routing actually saves money is a question for the
experiment in `eval/`, not a claim this project makes in advance.

## For judges

**The problem.** Coding with one strong model is reliable but expensive.
Cheap models are often good enough, but nobody knows in advance which tasks
are safe to give them, and a wrong guess costs a failed change.

**What Repod does.** You make one request. A Meta model then plans the work
with you: it asks clarifying questions, proposes tasks, and labels each
task's complexity and impact. You approve the plan. After that:

1. **Routing.** Each task goes to a cheap or a strong model. The program
   enforces a floor, so complex or high-impact work always gets a strong
   model, whatever the coordinator chose.
2. **Checks.** Fixed checks run after every task: type check, the task's
   visible tests, and docs and example checks.
3. **Failures.** When a task fails its checks, Meta decides whether to
   repair it on the same model, escalate it to the strong model, or stop.
   The program can override that decision, and the log records who decided
   and why.
4. **Results.** The result is frozen and run against holdout tests the
   models never saw. Every call's tokens and cost are recorded.

**How to judge it.** The `experiment` command runs the same request three
ways, with the same checks and holdout tests:

- arm A: one strong model alone;
- arm B: Repod with strong models only;
- arm C: Repod with cheap and strong models.

It reports the holdout pass rate and the cost of each arm. Whether arm C
saves money at the same quality is measured, not assumed.

**Meta models used and where they run.** The coordinator is always a Meta
model. There are two setups; each run records which API it called, and the
viewer shows it.

| Setup | Models | Runs on |
|---|---|---|
| `config/` (default) | Muse Spark 1.3 (coordinator, routine work), Muse Wonder 1.0 (critical work, review) | Meta Model API |
| `config/open-weights/` | Muse Spark Open (coordinator, critical work, review), Muse Glimmer 30B (routine work, docs), both open-weight | OpenRouter |

`typescript` and `@types/node` come from outside.

models: Meta's open-weight Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer 30B on

# Real or Replica — by Card Cauldron TCG

**A card checker that would rather say "I don't know" than guess.**

## The problem, and who this is for

Counterfeit trading cards flood every marketplace, and the people
who get burned are the ones who can least afford it: kids and
parents buying a gift, collectors spending real money on a single
card, and honest small sellers whose genuine stock gets doubted
because fakes are everywhere. Real or Replica is built by a
working card shop — Card Cauldron TCG — for the people on both
sides of that counter. It checks whether a card is genuine and
shows its evidence, so a buyer can decide with their eyes open
and a seller can prove what they're selling.

## The core runs on Meta AI models

The verification core of this project runs on **Meta AI models**.
Its model reads are **Muse Spark** reads of structured card crops
(number strip, set-symbol corner, holo window, full front/back)
and **Muse Wonder** card reads — on Oct 29, 2026, Wonder read 71
held cards and the shop owner checked every read against the
physical cards: **71 of 71 confirmed**. The full pipeline, its
setup instructions, and that read record live in the companion
evidence repo:
**https://github.com/caudillsabastian6-png/Fake-check**
(see "What is simulated, what is real" below for exactly which
parts are labelled samples, and why).

## Deliberately not a simple image analyzer

Real or Replica never judges a card from one photo guess. A check
combines several independent signals: identity lookup against a
33,391-identity reference catalogue, pixel-level tells measured
separately on the front and the back, set-symbol verification,
and the Meta AI model reads above — combined by an agent loop
that is allowed to answer **Inconclusive**.

The three possible outcomes are **Likely Genuine**, **Likely
Counterfeit**, and **Inconclusive**. A Likely verdict is an
estimate, never an official grade and never a guarantee.

Live demo: **https://cardcauldrontcg.com/demo/**
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley),
Indie Track. Submission deadline Nov 4, 2026. What predates the
event is called out plainly in "What was pre-existing vs built
during the event" below.

# Traffic Twin

One fixed camera over a real intersection becomes a measured traffic simulation. SAM 3.1 detects vehicles, a tracker reconstructs their paths, and a Muse Spark agent tests signal plans in SUMO with evidence attached to its recommendation.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, **Build for Your World**. Code was developed during the event window; the commit history records its evolution. I lose time at traffic lights and wanted to test whether an existing camera can supply the measurements needed to retime one.

## Current pipeline

```text
fixed-camera video → SAM 3.1 "vehicle" detections
    + NGSIM positions → camera homography and time alignment
    → gated vehicle tracking → turns, queues, signal windows, arrivals
    + measured road paint → SUMO network
    → calibrated twin replaying the video's vehicles
    → Muse Spark: evidence, Webster baseline, tested signal plans
    → local verifier + insertion-aware comparison
```

**NGSIM is an input as well as a reference.** Its positions informed the camera homography/time offset and local coordinate axes; its classes/lengths informed large-vehicle assumptions. Counts, arrivals and signal timings are then extracted from video, and SUMO driver parameters are fitted to video queues. These checks are not a fully independent evaluation. The road layout includes manually matched paint measurements in `scripts/geometri_fotodan.py`; arms are modelled as a top-down + schematic, turned to match the video.

## Current measured results

Data: FHWA NGSIM Lankershim Boulevard, Los Angeles, 16 June 2005, camera 2, about 18.7 minutes. SAM detections use 5,610 sampled frames at 5 fps. Video and generated simulation artifacts are rebuilt together.

The recovered current plan is **14 / 14 / 32 / 33 s**, cycle 101 s. Phase order: southbound protected left, southbound through+left lead, shared Lankershim green, cross street. Yellow/all-red clearance adds 8 s per cycle. Cross-street green is at least 30 s, shared green at least 18 s, cycle 60–150 s.

# WITNESS

Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 — see LICENSE.

[![Witness demo](docs/img/demo-thumb.png)](https://youtu.be/9k-IgV-YyQs)

https://youtu.be/9k-IgV-YyQs

## What this is

WITNESS reads an event log of what happened during a fixed-camera assembly procedure and turns
it into findings: coverage gaps, out-of-order steps and undocumented parts. Every finding carries
an evidence id or it does not exist, except a `skipped` finding, which records that no evidence
was supplied for a step and asks for human review. The report's hash
chain is recomputed from the output bytes, so anyone holding the files can check it.

## What is proven, and where the number lives

| Claim | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Risk gate | 25 labelled cases: 10 TP, 1 FP, 3 FN | `docs/RISK_GATE.md` |
| Test suite | 147 passed | `docs/STATUS.md` |
| Hash chain | recomputes from the output bytes | `tests/integration/test_offline_pipeline.py` |
| Real footage, deterministic extractor | refused at registration on both clips: correlation peak ratio 1.97 and 1.93, against a required 2.0 | `docs/REAL_MEDIA.md` |
| Real footage, Meta model | `RUN`: `sam-3.1` regions, named by geometry and judged by the same texture rule, produced event logs matching the key on both clips; 78 calls, USD 0.1950 | `docs/REAL_MEDIA.md` |

## What is not proven

All 25 risk-gate cases are synthetic. The real footage is one scene, one camera and one lighting
condition, and on it the deterministic extractor disagreed with the answer key: an earlier rule
missed and invented marks, and the final rule refused rather than guess. The model path agrees
with the key on both clips, but its identity rule was calibrated on six frames from these same
two clips, so that agreement is a demonstration on known footage, not independent validation.
Two clips are a demonstration, not a generalisation. Nothing here measures torque, tightening quality, assembly
correctness or flight readiness, and the local hashes are not a signature: without an external
trust anchor they do not stop someone rewriting the files and the manifest together.

## Run it

From the repository root in PowerShell, with the project environment in `.venv`
(`uv sync --locked` creates it) and FFmpeg 8 on `PATH`:

```powershell

```

session id, which replaces `SESSION_ID`. `build` refuses a session that has no `events.json`,
because a missing log is not the same as an empty one.

A personal desktop assistant for Ubuntu: you talk to it, it remembers, and it acts under your control. O-jarvis is the desktop app (Tauri v2, React) and its Python engine (FastAPI), which runs on `127.0.0.1` only, protected by a token drawn at every launch.

- **Chat and voice**: a conversation with memory; it speaks and listens (wake word, or a global shortcut).

ollama pull llama3.2   # ou tout autre modèle chat

```bash
cd Nook
chmod +x install.sh uninstall.sh
./install.sh
```

L'installateur :
- copie l'app dans `~/.local/share/nook`
- crée le lanceur `~/.local/bin/nook`
- enregistre **Nook** dans le menu des applications Ubuntu
- crée `~/.config/nook/config.yaml`

# Basa

**Photograph a paper clinic chart. Two Meta models read it. A person settles every value they disagree on.**

Basa turns photographed paper clinic charts into human-verified digital records. It is our entry for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Startup track, Build for Your World).

**Basa** is Filipino for **"read."** A paper chart has to be read before it can be trusted. Two models each read every region of the chart, then a person reads the original ink beside both readings and confirms what it says. Basa does not replace that last reading. It makes it faster and harder to get wrong.

> **New codebase, nothing reused, synthetic data only.** Every line of code was written during the hackathon (Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026), with no code, schemas or assets from any other repository. No real patient data exists anywhere in this project: every name, ID and value in fixtures, prompts, logs and screenshots is fictional.
>
> The one exception, confirmed by the hackathon organizers on 2026-10-29: UI libraries used within their own licenses, namely shadcn/ui (including the component source its CLI generates), GSAP and lucide-react. They are not models the project calls at runtime.

> **Not medical advice.** Basa digitizes and verifies what is on paper. It never produces treatment recommendations, dosing, diagnoses, or contraindication or drug-safety judgments. Summaries restate only what the confirmed record contains and cite their source region. Prompts sent to models ask for extraction only and forbid interpretation.

---

## What problem it hopes to solve

Many clinics still run on paper. A patient's history can live in ink, a rubber stamp and handwriting on a creased page, and it is one bad reading away from a wrong number.

Plain OCR does not solve this safely. It reads a messy chart confidently and sometimes wrongly (7.2 read as 1.2), and it gives no signal about which values to doubt. In a medical record, a confident wrong number is worse than a blank. Clinic internet is also unreliable, so a tool that needs a connection to capture a chart fails where it is needed most.

Basa's answer:

- **Errors no longer pass silently.** Two independent models read each region, and every field where they disagree is flagged instead of trusting either one.
- **A person stays in control.** The reviewer sees the original ink beside both readings and decides each flagged field. Basa never silently picks a model's answer.
- **Capture works offline.** Photos are saved on the device first and sync on their own when the connection returns.
- **Every line is traceable.** The record restates only what is on the paper, and each summary line cites its source region on the scan.

## Intended use

Basa is for **mixed clinic staff**, not one job title: whoever is free photographs a paper chart, and a different person may review it. They work in a bright clinic, often on a phone, tired and short of time, and they are not technical. Mobile web is the main surface (

# necronomicon A simple way to organize a repo's pre-commit hooks for progressive disclosure, steering coding agents toward the repo's conventions and intended architecture. Each rule pairs a command that finds violations with what to say about them: what's wrong, why the rule exists, and what to do instead. An agent sees a rule only when its commit breaks it, at the line it broke, with the long form one `necro --explain` away. ![You write a rule; an agent's commit breaks it; pre-commit blocks it and pushes the why; the agent pulls the rest and commits the fix](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WahahaYes/necronomicon/main/docs/mind-control.svg) ## Why not AGENTS.md An instruction file is read every session, whether or not today's work touches it, and followed when the agent remembers to. A rule costs nothing until it's broken, and then it blocks the commit. Keep AGENTS.md for orientation and move its "never do X" lines into rules. ## Agent mind control When an agent trips a rule, necro tells it just enough, and the rest is one command away. From [examples/layers](https://github.com/WahahaYes/necronomicon/tree/main/examples/layers): ```yaml core-isolated: command: necro grep '^\s*(from|import)\s+app\b' -- 'src/core/*.py' message: core imports the app layer why: Core runs in tests without a database; importing app/ drags one in. fix: Take a port from core/ports.py as an argument; app/ passes the real one in. details: … # the long form, and bad and good examples, for necro --explain ```
An agent that never read the rule commits from app.db import session in core. The commit fails, and 11 lines land in its context. ```text error[core-isolated]: core imports the app layer --> src/core/pricing.py:2:1 | 2 | from app.db import session | ^^^^^^^^ | = why: Core runs in tests without a database; importing app/ drags one in. = fix: Take a port from core/ports.py as an argument; app/ passes the real one in. = more: necro --explain core-isolated necro: 1 error (core-isolated ×1) ```
It wants the bigger picture, so it runs the command it was handed and pulls 22 more. ```text $ necro --explain core-isolated core-isolated: core imports the app layer Why: Core runs in tests without a database; importing app/ drags one in. Fix: Take a port from core/ports.py as an argument; app/ passes the real one in. Core is the inner layer: app/ may import core, never the reverse. Exceptions: none. Shared types move into core. Bad: from app.db import session def price(order): return session.rates(order.region) * order.total Good: fro
