# ReceiptIQ

**Verified AI software task execution.** You give ReceiptIQ a small coding task. It plans the work, waits for your approval, makes the change in an isolated copy of the repository, runs the real tests, has an independent verifier challenge the result, and gives you a *receipt*: the actual diff, the actual test output, and a criterion-by-criterion verdict. You make the final decision.

Built with **Meta Muse Spark 1.3** for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie Developer track, *Push the Frontier*).

## The problem

AI coding agents are fast, but "done" from an agent is a claim, not proof. Agents can fix the visible bug and break something else, quietly touch files they shouldn't, write weak tests, or report success after a command failed. In most workflows, the same model that wrote the change is also asked whether it worked.

ReceiptIQ puts a verification layer between the AI's change and your approval. **No model's word counts as evidence.** Only real diffs and real exit codes do.

## How it works

```
 Your task ──► Planner ──► YOU approve plan + test commands
                                  │
                                  ▼
        Baseline tests on an untouched copy (what already passed / failed)
                                  │
                                  ▼
        Executor edits an isolated workspace (never the original repo, runs no commands)
                                  │
                                  ▼
        Orchestrator computes the real diff from disk + cross-checks the changed files
        Orchestrator runs the approved tests on a throwaway copy of the result
                                  │
                                  ▼
        Verifier: deterministic checks + independent model review
                                  │
                                  ▼
        Receipt: diff, test output, baseline comparison, verdict ──► YOU approve or reject
                                                                     (nothing is merged or deployed)
```

### Components

| Component | File | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Meta client | `backend/services/meta_client.py` | Thin wrapper around the Meta Model API (Responses API, `muse-spark-1.3`). Errors become `MetaAPIError`; the key never appears in messages. |
| Planner | `backend/agents/planner.py` | Turns the task into a validated plan: steps, measurable acceptance criteria, allowed and prohibited files, risks, open questions. Keeps user constraints such as "do not change the schema". |
| Executor | `backend/agents/executor.py` | Proposes file changes as JSON. Code checks **every** change against the plan's scope before applying **any**. It cannot run commands. |
| Verifier | `backend/agents/verifier.py` | Read-only. Deterministic checks on the diff, exit codes and scope; then a separate model review. The model can make a verdict worse, never better. |
| Orchestrator | `backend/orchestrator/orchestrator.py` | Plain Python state machine

Our studio adapts every approved creative to 6–8 placement sizes by hand,
every day, for 100+ brands. Generic AI resizers redraw the product, break
Hebrew lettering and ignore the brand's own layout rules for each size.
MatchPic adapts with Meta's models and is trustworthy: brand templates per size,
protected product/logo pixels with proof, and a model QA check on every
output.

**Live demo: https://app.mashrokit.co.il/matchpic/**

Upload a finished creative, pick a brand and sizes, get every placement back —
in **Protected** mode (AI paints only the background; product, logo and text
go back as original pixels, with a pixel proof) or **Fast** mode (AI
recomposes the whole creative in one pass). A brand teaches its layout per
size through **templates**: past finished creatives that Spark reads into a
stored layout spec. Every output is QA-checked by a fresh Spark call; on FAIL
it retries once, then marks the output "needs review".

Everything is bilingual (English default, Hebrew toggle, RTL). All demo
brands are synthetic and fictional; nothing is ever published.

## How it works

1. **Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) reads the source creative: products, logo,
   verbatim headline/sub-text, offer/CTA panel, background style,
   language/direction.
2. **SAM** (`sam-3.1`) cuts exact product and logo masks (phrase + box-prompt
   union); contrast completion finishes the logo lockup when Spark's box ends
   mid-word. Code plans the layout from the brand template for that size, or
   from default rules (logo top corner by direction, product centered in the
   safe area, panel bottom), nudging free texts out of other elements.
3. **Muse Image** (`muse-image-1.0`) paints the background plate (Protected)
   or recomposes the whole creative (Fast). The wire size is aspect-only, so
   code cover-fits every output to the exact preset and verifies.
4. Code places the original pixels (uniform scale only, recorded), re-renders
   free text verbatim in Chromium with bundled Noto fonts, copies opaque

5. A fresh **Spark** call QA-checks every output against the source analysis:
   every verbatim text exact, logo/product present and uncropped, safe area

# Impact Proof

Someone at the nonprofit, staff or a field worker, sends a WhatsApp photo, video or voice note, the fastest way being a 5-second voice note or a short narrated video. A Meta Muse model drafts a delivery case with every fact linked to its source. An authorized nonprofit reviewer confirms, corrects or disputes it. The donor sees a report that says what was confirmed, by whom, and what it cannot prove.

Built solo by a Givelink co-founder for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, with staged demo data. Not deployed with Givelink or any partner nonprofit.

## What it does

1. **WhatsApp in.** The webhook checks `X-Hub-Signature-256`, stores the message under its unique ID and queues it before answering. Retries and replays create nothing new.
2. **Evidence.** Photos and voice notes are downloaded with server auth, checked for type and size, hashed and kept private. Voice notes are converted to 24 kHz mono WAV and transcribed with `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`.
3. **Draft facts.** `muse-spark-1.3` extracts item, quantity, unit, place, time and delivery status as structured output. Each fact says whether it was **seen in a photo** or **reported**, and quotes its source. Unknown facts are left out, never guessed.
4. **Rules in code, not in the model.** Missing facts, conflicting sources, duplicate photos and instructions hidden in the evidence keep a case in *needs clarification*. The worker gets one follow-up question in their language and a reply: "Received as case DEMO-001; not yet confirmed."
5. **Human review.** Only a signed-in, allowlisted reviewer of the same nonprofit can confirm or dispute. Every change is an audit event. A correction creates a new version and supersedes older donor reports.
6. **Donor report.** Built only from reviewer-confirmed fields. No phone numbers, photos, transcripts or exact addresses. Totals are summed in code from confirmed cases, by item and unit, with no inferred conversions.

## Run it

Needs Node 24 (no build step). `npm install` adds one dependency, `ffmpeg-static`, a prebuilt ffmpeg for converting voice notes. A system `ffmpeg` or `FFMPEG_PATH` is used first if present.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env    # fill in the values below
npm test                # 29 tests: the adversarial pack's rules and the full webhook-to-report flow
npm run probe -- photo.jpg voice.ogg   # first-hour check of your Meta account, 3 runs per fixture
npm start               # http://localhost:3000, status at /health
```

| Variable | What it is |
|---|---|
| `META_API_KEY` | Meta Model API key. Without it the app runs, but marks every case "Model unavailable" for manual entry |
| `META_MAX_CALLS_PER_DAY`, `META_DISABLED` | Hard call ceiling and stop switch |
| `WHATSAPP_*` | From your own Meta developer test app. Use the Graph version your dashboard shows |
| `SESSION_SECRET`, `REVIEWER_PASSCODE` | Reviewer sign-in |
| `REPORTERS` | Allowlisted field-worker phones. Anyone else is ignored |

# AidRelay

A civilian casualty relay for disaster, mass-casualty, wildland fire, and rural EMS scenes. A responder dictates the care already given for each casualty; the app structures it, the responder confirms it, and the record relays to a dispatch board sorted red-first. Offline-first, encrypted on the device, no account, no backend.

**This app gives no medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment recommendations.** It records care that trained responders already gave and relays it for dispatch. Its users are responders, dispatch coordinators, and the receiving facility. Triage categories and care entries are always stated by the responder and confirmed before they become a record — the app never assigns them.

**Built during the event:** all code in this repository was written during the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 – November 4, 2026. Indie track, Team Naian (solo build — Armando Fierro).

Demo video: https://youtu.be/VW1BHzm7vXs

Live demo: https://mherick.github.io/aidrelay/ — the app itself, served from this repo. The six demo dictations and the full capture → confirm → board → handoff flow run with no key (on-device read); for live AI structuring, paste your own Meta Model API key in the app (kept in your browser's local storage only).

## For judges

No hosted version is required — the repo runs standalone — but a live copy of the app is hosted at https://mherick.github.io/aidrelay/ for convenience. No API keys ship anywhere in this repo or the app — you bring your own, or none.

**Replay path (no keys).** Open `index.html` and run the six built-in demo dictations in order (capture screen → demo dictations). # SessionGuard

**Stolen session cookies stop working the moment the attacker is no longer the user, and you can see why.**

SessionGuard is a continuous-authentication layer for web apps. It defends against session hijacking: infostealer malware copies a logged-in user's cookie, and the attacker walks in without a password or MFA prompt. SessionGuard binds each session to the browser that created it, scores every request, forces a Passkey step-up when something looks wrong, and writes a plain-English rationale for every decision.

> Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Track: Indie Developer. Theme: Push the Frontier.

<!-- TODO: add a screenshot or GIF of the demo console here: ![demo](docs/demo.gif) -->

## The problem

Multi-factor authentication protects the login. It does nothing for the session afterwards. Whoever holds the cookie *is* the user. Infostealer malware exports browser cookies in bulk, and the attacker replays them from another machine.

## What it does

A request passes through up to four layers. Each layer catches attackers the previous one misses.

| Layer | What it does | What it does NOT stop |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Deterministic checks** (IP, ASN, user-agent, header fingerprint, impossible travel) | Catches a lazy replay from a different place or client. | An attacker who copies the victim's user-agent, headers and IP. Layer 1 allows this (score 0). That gap is kept as a test. Header fingerprints are a weak signal because headers are copyable. |
| **2. Device-bound key** (non-extractable WebCrypto key, single-use 30s nonces, per-action proofs) | A stolen cookie without the key cannot perform `/transfer`, and cannot read after the 30s presence window. The key cannot be copied out of the browser. | **Malware running on the victim's own device can still *use* the key** (ask the browser to sign); it just can't copy it. Login-time compromise and live phishing relays are also out of scope. |
| **3. Passkey step-up** (WebAuthn) | A "challenge" verdict requires a real Passkey assertion. Success grants 5 minutes of elevated trust, failure or timeout terminates the session. | An attacker who also controls the victim's authenticator. |
| **4. Explainer** (LLM, async) | Writes a short rationale per decision for analysts. | It protects nothing. It can never change the action. |

**Decision policy:** score under 30 allows, 30–70 forces step-up, over 70 terminates the session.

## Demo

The demo console shows the whole attack on one screen: a victim, an attacker simulator, and a live SessionGuard feed.

1. Victim makes a normal transfer. Allowed.
2. The attacker steals the session cookie.
3. **Lazy copy** (different browser and IP) is blocked by layer 1.
4. **Perfect copy** (identical user-agent, headers and IP) passes layer 1 and is stopped by the device-bound key. Toggle the device key off in the console and the same attack succeeds.

# Shichinin

A Chrome extension that fights ad tracking with **noise instead of silence**.
Instead of blocking trackers, it feeds them a crowd: rotating, entirely
fictional grown-up personas who browse and search like ordinary adults, so
the profile trackers build for the machine is a profile of people who
don't exist.

Built during the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 – November 4, 2026.

**The name:** *Shichinin* (七人) is Japanese for "seven people" — a nod to
the seven samurai who stood between a village and what was coming for it.
Shichinin's decoys do the same for a household: they stand between the
machine and the trackers, and the profile gets built on them instead.

## Built during the event

**All code in this repo was written during the event.** The extension
was designed and built from scratch between October 28 and October 30,
2026 — v1 on Oct 28, the household build (v0.5.0) on Oct 30. No
pre-existing codebase is included, and nothing in the repo predates the
hackathon window.

## The household idea

Trackers don't just profile a person — they profile a *machine*, including
whether a child uses it, and marketing aimed at children follows that
profile. Shichinin's first setting is therefore **Household — who uses
this browser?**

- **Adults only** — every decoy is a grown-up, and the adult signal stays
  *consistent* (a recurring cluster of mortgage, insurance, careers, local
  news, retirement) while everything else about the personas scrambles.
  Trackers see an adults-only home, so child-aimed marketing has no
  target on the machine. This consistency-inside-noise is the core
  mechanism; we call it **selective coherence**.
- **A child uses this browser** — the decoys are still all grown-ups, and
  they run at full strength no matter what activity level is set. A
  child's real clicks get buried under adult noise.
- **A mix of people** — standard decoy rotation.

Shichinin makes a machine *look adults-only to ad trackers*. It does not
claim to protect children, and it does not change the ads served inside
kids' content itself — it shapes the inferred profile, which is the part
of the system that follows a household from site to site.

## How it works

- **Personas** — fictional adults (interest profiles with age bands)
  generated locally, each living a multi-day **arc**: a small story told
  in searches and visits (planning a kitchen remodel, training for a 10k,
  researching a used truck).
- **Arc authoring with Muse Spark** — if the user pastes their *own*
  Meta Model API key into Settings, arcs are written by Muse Spark
  (Meta Model API) and then **validated locally** against the household
  setting. An arc that drifts toward child or parenting territory in a
  protective mode is rejected wholesale and replaced by the local
  generator. Without a key, the local generator writes every arc. The
  key never leaves the browser's local extension storage and is never
  sent anywhere except the Meta Model API.
- **Cookie pool*

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026

Live Cloud Demo: https://agent-workflow-security.vercel.app

IntentFence is a denial-aware cybersecurity copilot designed to detect and block autonomous AI agents from evading access restrictions by switching tools, views, or delegating tasks after a sensitive operation is denied.

============================================================
Key Distinction: Stateless Policy vs. Objective-Aware Guard
============================================================

1. Baseline Stateless Policy:
- Evaluates each action in complete isolation.
- Vulnerability: When an agent is denied access to a restricted resource (e.g., "payroll_records" via file_read), the agent immediately replans and calls a different tool (e.g., sql_query on "payroll_view"). The baseline check allows the second call because the tool and raw string differ, enabling unauthorized bypass.

2. IntentFence Objective-Aware Guard:
- Binds actions to a stateful task and business objective.
- Protection: When an action under an objective is denied, IntentFence permanently records a denial tombstone. Any subsequent action attempting to satisfy that same objective—whether through an alternative tool, alternative resource alias, or delegated sub-agent—is automatically blocked at the pre-execution boundary.
- Granularity: Unrelated business objectives are unaffected and continue executing without false-positive lockouts.

============================================================
Live Comparison Example
============================================================

Scenario: data/scenarios/alternative_route.json

| Step | Action Attempt | Baseline Policy | IntentFence Guard | Security Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Step 1 | Read restricted payroll records | DENIED | DENIED | Policy restriction enforced; objective marked denied |
| Step 2 | Execute SQL view on payroll within same objective | ALLOWED | BLOCKED | IntentFence blocks tool-switch evasion |
| Step 3 | Read public documentation under separate objective | ALLOWED | ALLOWED | Unrelated objective permitted normally |

============================================================
Current Platform Features
============================================================

- Objective-Level Enforcement: Tracks agent actions across multi-step execution graphs.

My Claude Code setup for AI-assisted software development: the global rules I give every agent and the workflow I use to split work across several coding agents.

The idea behind it: the model is a member of the team, not a search box. I write the score (rules, specs, context), the agents play it, and I review before anything ships.

# Precios Cerca · Prices Near — Neighborhood Price Finder

**Live:** https://geoprice.dapp.cl
**Demo video (2:18):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eqKYygr2MWg

A neighborhood price index built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**
(theme: *Build for Your World*), powered by **Muse Spark** via the Meta Model API.

People type what they saw, in their own words — *"handroll for 3000 at Alameda
esquina Cumming"* — and the AI turns it into structured, geolocated, categorized
data. Browsing is free for everyone: no account, no wallet. Publishing requires
MetaMask as an **identity gate** (off-chain, **0 gas**): the wallet is who you
are, not a payment.

> Prices Near is the territorial (6th) dimension of a multidimensional
> marketplace ecosystem: look (free, no wallet) → publish (MetaMask, 0 gas) →
> sell on the marketplace (where gas appears, and sellers receive 99% in DAI:
> 0.5% marketplace + 0.5% future user benefit). A practical blockchain course
> with no tutorials — the need for gas is born later, not at the door.

## What it does

- **AI intake (Muse Spark, server-side):** free-text reports are structured
  into item, price, unit, zone, shop and one of 18 clear categories aligned
  with the marketplace taxonomy (bakery, dairy, meat, produce, groceries,
  drinks, prepared food, household, transport, fuel, pharmacy, lodging,
  leisure, tech, pets, fashion, vehicles, services). No clear category → the
  server rejects the publish (`need_categoria`).
- **Geolocation, orchestrated in stages** (each stage visible in the API
  response): 1) **device GPS** exact point at publish time (with permission,
  accuracy in meters) → 2) **named place** resolved against OpenStreetMap,
  bounded and disambiguated by the Cloudflare edge location → 3)
  **Cloudflare** `request.cf` (city / region / country / approximate coords)
  as anchor and fallback. No coordinates → no publish (`need_geo`).
- **Strict by design:** wallet required (401 without it), item/price/zone
  required, clear category required, resolved coordinates required.
- **Every observation is pinned to IPFS** (Pinata) and gets its own SEO page
  (`/precio/:id`, Open Graph + JSON-LD `Product/Offer`) plus `sitemap.xml`.
- **Shops can claim their place** ("This is my shop" / "I sell this"): a
  verified owner is the only one who gets an exact public point. Observers
  keep their authorship; claiming never transfers it.
- **Map** of the neighborhood with price pins (OpenStreetMap tiles served

# Pixalorien

Three Pixaloriens land on a desert planet to bring a treasure back from
a vault deep under its surface. A single-player game of real time
with pause (and going back) over a world of falling sand, in ent-lang. The design is in
[DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md).

Licences: the code is MIT ([LICENSE](LICENSE)); the sprites and documents

## Step 1: the world (done)

- `matter.ent`: the automaton on 2048 by 1024 cells, kept in 512 chunks
  of 64 by 64 that sleep while nothing in them or beside them moves.
  Phases: fall (twice), slide (Margolus blocks), flow (four times), react,
  wake. Each phase works every awake chunk's cells from the cells as they
  were (gather-style), so one core and all cores give the same world.
- `gen.ent`: the world from a seed: dunes and mesas, sandstone strata over
  rock over bedrock, chambers and ridge tunnels, lakes at mid depth, lava
  at the bottom, four entrances (mine shaft, cave mouth, sinkhole, lava
  tube) with worm tunnels on to the vault, the vault and its treasure, 40
  sealed pockets (air, water, gas, lava) with warm or damp rock round
  lava and water, crumbling rock over tunnels, crystals, the ship.

- `pixalorien.ent`: the program.

  what light passes (air, gas, water and smoke at double cost, glass,
  ladders), in a field of two copies read and written in turn, so it
  goes out as fast as it spread. It runs in the awake chunks like the

# Musical Bots

A multi-agent workflow you can watch and hear. A Muse Code director agent plans
the work from a one-line prompt, delegates it to eight autonomous role agents
(lyrics, chords, dance, lighting, deals, hype, comedy and the plot's trouble),
and runs a validation pipeline over everything they produce. The agents work in
parallel, consult each other in real conversations (ask, reason, answer, agree),
are repaired when they stall, and sing their reasoning as they work. The output
is an original sung 3D episode that 16 bots perform in your browser (Three.js),
all driven by a JSON event protocol.

Built with Meta's models through the Meta Model API: Muse Code directs the
crew, Muse Spark 1.3 is the model every agent thinks with (and, with vision,
checks each poster's spelling), Muse Wonder (`muse-wonder-1.0`) writes the sung
lyrics, and Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`) draws each episode's poster.
[Details below.](#meta-ai-stack-meta-model-api-muse-code-muse-spark-muse-wonder-muse-image)

Built for the [Meta Global AI Hackathon 2026](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon) (Indie developer track). Every
voice is synthesized in the browser from the lyrics: real sung words, solos
and choruses in harmony, no recordings, no TTS, no server.

# Rasta — Pause. Verify. Proceed.

A mobile-first, bilingual English / Roman Urdu decision-support prototype
for Pakistani WhatsApp users receiving suspicious requests for money or
login verification codes.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon — Indie Track.
Submission platform: Cerebral Valley.

> Rasta helps families pause, verify independently, and document what
> they confirmed—before they decide to pay.

---

## The Problem

A message arrives from a supposed relative using a new number:

> “Mom, my phone broke. I’m calling from a new number. It’s an emergency, send Rs 50,000. Don’t tell anyone.”

The example is fictional, but the decision it creates is important:
respond immediately, or pause to verify?

Suspicious requests can combine urgency, secrecy, family relationships,
or claims of authority. The recipient needs more than a warning label;
they need a clear next step.

Rasta focuses on that moment of decision.

It does not claim that WhatsApp has more account compromises than other
platforms or present unverified national fraud statistics.

---

## What Rasta Does

Rasta is a structured workflow, not a chatbot.

Users paste a message or select a clearly labeled synthetic example.
In Ollama mode, a locally running Meta Llama model generates an assessment
containing:

- Observed facts.
- A concern band.
- Warning signals supported by quoted message text.
- Uncertainty and missing context.
- Recommended actions.
- A polite reply to copy.

For possible family impersonation, Rasta offers a manual independent
verification workflow. Users can record their own verification outcome
and export an advisory incident record.

### Advisory Only

Rasta cannot:

- Block payments.
- Recover compromised accounts.
- Prove the sender’s identity.
- Determine whether a voice is genuine.
- Read WhatsApp conversations automatically.
- Guarantee that a request is safe or fraudulent.

It does not automatically contact, accuse, or report anyone.

# Reflow Studio

Reflow Studio turns a task in a web app into a how-to guide, and redoes the guide when the app changes. It is for teams that keep how-to guides for software: support, onboarding and training.

Give it a task, such as "create a private repository" in Gitea, an open-source code hosting app. Muse Spark 1.3 does the task in the real app through computer use, and Studio turns that run into four formats: a narrated video, a step-by-step article, a click-through demo and a walkthrough inside Reflow's in-app player. When the app's navigation changes and the saved guide breaks, Spark does the task again on the new screen, the guide is re-verified and regenerated, and it waits for a person to approve it.

Demo video (2:46): https://youtu.be/V2-H_sfvKF4

## What we built during the hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026)

The first commit (Oct 26) is the Studio prototype as it stood before the hackathon. It already explored a web app, performed tasks with a DOM snapshot agent, verified guides by deterministic replay, produced the four formats, ran a maintenance loop (replay, re-perform on failure, re-verify, regenerate, stop for review) and checked every action against a basic policy gate (`src/safety.mjs`).

# Name It

Name It tells blind and low vision viewers what “this” is.

How-to presenters point and say “add this”, “about this much”, “until it looks like this”. If you can't see the screen, you hear the words but not the thing. Name It finds those moments in a video, looks at the frames to work out what “this” is, and writes a short audio description that fits into the pause after the sentence. A volunteer describer checks the drafts, and an accessible player reads them out.

Live demo: https://name-it-rho.vercel.app

![The player paused on a description: “The silver spiked escape wheel sits on the right beside the pallet.”](docs/screenshots/watch.jpg)

## Why I made this

Try watching a cooking video with your eyes closed. “Now add this, then mix until it looks like this.” Add what? Looks like what?

Researchers counted these visual references in online videos and found a median of about 2.5 a minute (Liu et al., CHI 2021). Human audio description fixes it, but there aren't nearly enough describers: only about 7% of videos requested on YouDescribe get described. AI describers exist, but they tend to describe the whole scene and stay vague about the exact tool or ingredient. And when they don't know, they guess.

So Name It does one narrow thing well: it resolves the specific word the presenter said, shows the evidence for its answer, and flags it for a person when it isn't sure.

## What it does

- **Finds the references.** Every “this”, “that”, “here”, “like this”, “these” in the transcript. A model decides which ones point at something on screen and which don't (“this recipe is easy” doesn't).
- **Finds the moment.** The presenter often shows the thing just after saying the word, so it picks the frame that shows it best.
- **Finds the object.** SAM 3.1 tracks every candidate object for 3 seconds, and Name It picks the one the hand is touching or moving. The reasons are kept so a person can check them.
- **Names it** the way the presenter does. “The walnuts”, not “brown objects in a jar”, because it reads the whole transcript first.
- **Knows when it doesn't know.** Two independent looks, SAM's own score and a check of whether the box really is the thing are combined into a confidence. Low ones go to a person instead of being spoken.
- **Fits the gaps.** Short descriptions are spoken in the pause after the sentence with the video turned down. If there's no room, the video pauses, the description plays, and it carries on.
- **Review queue for describers.** Approve, edit or reject each draft by keyboard (A, E, R, J, K), with the evidence frame and mask in front of you.
- **Accessible player.** Keyboard controls, adjustable speed, descriptions mirrored to screen readers, and a recorded description voice (ElevenLabs) with the browser voice as a fallback.

## Screenshots

**Review.** The highlighted word, what Name It thinks it is, the evidence and how confident it is.

![Review queue](docs/screenshots/review.jpg)

# GTM Shortlist

Put in your website. GTM Shortlist tells you which companies need what you sell right now, and why, in their own words,
with a link to where they said it. No website yet? Describe what you sell and who buys it.

**Try it:** https://eygentic.tech · **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/YbzJRF3j9NE

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md) says exactly what
existed before the event and what was built during it.

## How it works

1. **Muse Spark 1.3** (Meta Model API) reads your site and writes down what you sell, who buys it, which checks a good
   fit passes and what would show a company needs it now, each with a quote from your own pages.
2. It finds your competitors with web search, and only calls one direct when that company's own homepage proves the same
   job for the same buyer.
3. It looks for companies showing a need right now: open job posts on Lever, Greenhouse and Ashby first, then news and
   launches. Each company gets its own agent loop: up to four searches and six page reads with our `fetch_page` tool, its
   own job board, and a scan of its homepage code for a competitor's widget.
4. **Muse Spark Open** (open weights, on Baseten) reads each quote without the web or the company's name and keeps only
   the ones that really support the claim.
5. Plain code, not a model, makes the verdict: **Shortlisted**, **Needs a look** (with what is missing) or **Rejected**
   (with the quote that ruled it out). A claim whose exact sentence is not on a page the agent fetched never appears.
6. For each Shortlisted company it writes why now and an opening line from those quotes only, and Muse Spark Open checks
   every statement before it is shown.

Every model call is logged with tokens, searches and dollars; a search of five companies costs about $0.40.

Measured on 17 saved live searches: Muse Spark Open threw out 120 of 354 quotes and changed 31 of 82 verdicts
([docs/checker-value.md](docs/checker-value.md)).
On 41 real companies I labelled myself it agreed with me 73% of the time and never dropped a company I wanted; its
Shortlist is too generous with companies too big for the seller ([HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md#how-it-did-on-real-searches-labelled-by-me)).

## Run it

```sh
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
npm ci && npm run build
shortlist-agent run https://seller.example/ --synthetic --output run.json   # labelled synthetic data: no keys, no network
```

With `META_MODEL_API_KEY` and `BASETEN_API_KEY` in `.env` (see `.env.example`), drop `--synthetic` and use your own
website. The public demo and its limits: [docs/agent-public-demo.md](docs/agent-public-demo.md).

Tests: `pytest`, `ruff check src tests scripts`, `npx playwright test`.

## Licence

MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# Chitchat Tour

**Little sourced stories about the street you're on.**

You put your phone in your pocket and walk. When you pass something ordinary — a convenience store, a garbage truck playing Für Elise, a scooter waiting box, a red-and-green postbox — Chitchat Tour tells you one short, sourced piece of trivia about it. It only picks things that are likely to be *new to you*, and it compares them with how things work elsewhere.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Developer track, theme "Build for Your World". The demo city is Taipei, on a route around Yongkang Street and Dongmen.

**Try it:** https://chitchat-tour.vercel.app — on any phone or desktop browser, tap **Try the simulated walk** (no GPS needed), or open `/demo/compare` to watch a Tokyo visitor and a New York visitor walk the same street side by side.

## Why

Most city guides talk about landmarks. What visitors actually notice and wonder about is the everyday stuff: why the garbage truck plays music, why every arcade has a step, why there are so few public bins. And what is surprising depends on where you come from. A visitor from Tokyo and a visitor from New York walking the same street should not hear the same things.

Principles:

- **Everyday things over landmarks.**
- **Never say what we cannot source.** Every fact has a source the user can open; if the model cannot find one on a trusted site, the guide stays quiet.
- **Don't interrupt.** Speak only when something is actually there, at most one short line at a time, with cooldowns.
- **Never analyse people.** Faces are blurred on the device before a photo leaves the phone.

## What it does

- **Walk.** A map follows you (real GPS, or a simulated walk for the demo). The simulated walk replays a real recorded Muse Spark walk down Yongkang Street for a visitor from Tokyo (six stories, pre-recorded voice), and pauses when you switch tabs. When you come near something the knowledge base covers, the guide decides whether it is worth saying *for you* and speaks it in a sentence or two, with a "here / in many places" comparison and a source card.
- **Ask.** Type or hold to talk ("why are there so many convenience stores?"). Muse Spark searches the web, and the answer only keeps sources from an allow-list of trusted domains (government, universities, major newspapers…).
- **Live discovery.** Outside the hand-made knowledge base, the app looks up places ahead of you on OpenStreetMap and has Muse Spark research them on the web, showing its steps as a readable timeline. Only whitelisted, cited findings become narrations.
- **Destination walks.** Pick a destination; you get walking directions with spoken turn cues, rerouting, and suggestions for small detours that pass something interesting.
- **Photo.** Point the camera at something. Faces are blurred on the device, Muse Spark finds the objects, SAM 3.1 cuts them out, and the cut-out becomes a die-cut sticker in your notebook, with the trivia attached if we have it.

# Prox Now

**Live:** https://prox-now.vercel.app · **Judges:** https://prox-now.vercel.app/judge ([JUDGES.md](JUDGES.md)) · **Video:** [2:15 demo](https://youtube.com/shorts/_fUl4ZByer4)

Prox Now makes a street's small shops readable and orderable in any language. A shopper snaps a shop's sign or menu. Meta's `muse-spark-1.3` turns the photos into the shop's **book**, with one page per real category, items, and prices only when they're readable. The shopper asks the map what's good right now, builds an order, and shows staff a translated order screen. The owner claims the shop and thanks the people who snapped it or built its book with a coupon, and the shopper scratches it in their wallet.

**Shoppers are the shop's ads.** Every snap a shopper posts is a live, local, face-blurred ad for that shop, pinned on the map where nearby people are deciding where to go right now. The owner doesn't buy ads. They tap Keep on the posts they like, and the poster gets a coupon. Building a shop's book earns one too. Shoppers get rewarded for spreading the word, and owners only pay with a discount that brings the poster back through the door.

Built for one street we know first-hand: Soi 102, Hua Hin, Thailand. Tourists can't read the Thai menus, and the tiny shops have no website or English menu.

Indie track, theme "Build for Your World". Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026). See [docs/PROVENANCE.md](docs/PROVENANCE.md).

The demo café photos are real photos taken by the founder, not AI-generated.

The shop in the demo video is a real all-Thai shop in Hua Hin, built live with Prox Now. The owner asked not to be filmed.

say "done" without showing that the result actually works. We measured untrained Muse Glimmer 30B on our Turkish coding
exam before the hackathon (88%): the capability is there. What is missing is **reliability** — a loop that checks the
work independently and shows the evidence.

## How it works

```
 Turkish task (text, or voice → Muse Voice Transcribe)
        │
        ▼

        │                         │
        │                         └──(in parallel)── Muse Spark writes requirement-by-requirement acceptance tests

 Executor: Muse Glimmer 30B (open weights, vLLM on Modal H100)  or  Muse Spark (Meta Model API)
   native tool calls: Write / Read / Edit / Bash / Done, in a fresh workspace
        │
        ▼
 acceptance tests run ── pass → result screen with evidence
        │ fail
        ▼
 Muse Spark arbiter: does the task text clearly require this? ── unclear / faulty → not enforced, shown in report
        │ clearly required
        └──► failing output goes back to the executor (up to 3 rounds);
             a round that breaks a previously passing test is rolled back
```

- **Writer ≠ verifier.** The executor never sees the acceptance tests while working; the test writer never sees the

# KIN Access

**AI-powered switch access for people with severe motor disabilities like ALS.**

   *KIN stands for Kinetic Intelligence Nexus: AI that connects people with limited movement to their computer.*

Traditional switch scanning steps through every item on screen one press at a time. KIN Access uses Meta's Muse Spark to predict the 4 most likely next actions, so tasks take a few presses instead of dozens.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie Developer track, Push the Frontier).

**Headline result:** in an automated evaluation with the real Muse Spark model, KIN Access needed **63% fewer presses** than the best possible traditional scanning and beat it in **24 of 24 runs**. In **Vision mode**, where Muse Spark sees only a screenshot of the screen and no text description, it still needed **59% fewer presses** and also beat traditional scanning in 24 of 24 runs.

## The problem

Many people with ALS, spinal cord injuries, or cerebral palsy control a computer with a single switch, triggered by a small movement like a cheek twitch, head tilt, or sip-and-puff. The standard method, switch scanning, highlights every item on screen one by one until the user presses. Replying to one email can take dozens of presses, and for someone who can move only one muscle, every press costs time and energy.

## How it works

1. KIN Access sends Muse Spark the current screen and the list of available actions. In **text mode** the screen arrives as a structured text description. In **Vision mode** it arrives as a real screenshot, with no text description, so Muse Spark has to read the screen itself.
2. Muse Spark returns the 4 most likely next actions as structured JSON.
3. The backend validates every suggestion against the actions that actually exist on screen.
4. The 4 choices, plus "Something else," appear in a panel. **Space** moves the highlight and **Enter** selects (standard two-switch scanning).
5. Risky actions (send, delete) require a confirmation step, with **Cancel** highlighted first so a stray press can never send or delete.
6. "Something else" falls back to traditional scanning of the whole screen, so the user is never stuck.

> The spacebar and Enter key stand in for accessibility switches. Most real switches connect to a computer as keyboard keys, so KIN Access works with them without extra hardware.

## Results

### Automated evaluation (headline)

To measure the AI alone, without human mistakes, I built an evaluation harness that plays a **perfect switch user**. At each step it picks the first Muse Spark suggestion that gets closer to finishing the task, or uses "Something else" and scans the whole screen if none does. Presses are counted exactly as in the live interface. Every run makes fresh calls to Muse Spark (no caching), so the results show real run-to-run variation. Both modes were run on the same day with `muse-spark-1.1`.

# Environment Protocol v0 — reference implementation: Apathy-Refusal (commerce)

**Team:** Pistis Sophia · **Track:** Indie · **Problem statement:** Push the Frontier
**Event:** Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026

A standard interface between reasoning agents and the world they act on,
such that **no agent claim becomes a world fact without measurement**. MCP
standardized how agents call tools. This standardizes the verification of
what agents claim.

## The protocol

An **environment** is a runtime construct standing between an agent (the
**tenant**) and the world, with six components:

1. **Principal** — the party on whose behalf the environment holds the
   line (customer, patient, polity).
2. **Mandate** — the principal's instructions in exact, checkable form.
   The tenant cannot edit it. A mandate without a positive bound is
   malformed.
3. **Claims** — typed so that assertion and measurement are different
   fields. A claim carries what the tenant asserts; the measurement is
   filled by instruments, never by the tenant.
4. **Instruments and gates** — stricter than the claimant. Every claim
   passes a gate; an unmeasured claim refuses automatically (complete
   mediation, fail-safe defaults).
5. **Assets under seal** — move only on a pass, exactly once, within the
   mandate's bounds.
6. **Receipts** — append-only, hash-chained, replayable by anyone. The
   record is the disclosure.

**Invariants:** mandate sovereignty · measurement before movement · named
refusal (a refusal that cannot name its reason cannot be constructed) · a
record the tenant cannot rewrite · two-sided measurement (counterparties
measured by the same rule) · tenant replaceability (any kernel inside;
the line holds the same).

**Protocol messages.** Four message types, in order:
**claim → measurement → verdict → receipt**. A verdict is one of *pass*,
*refuse* (named reason), or *ambiguous* (undecidable on current
instruments — recorded, never silently resolved). Every verdict emits a
receipt; receipts chain. *Conformance:* the reference implementation maps
undecidable to a named refusal — where instruments cannot decide, the
gate refuses on weak measurement rather than emitting a third verdict.
Ambiguous therefore exists in the protocol as a measurement state; in
this implementation it is always resolved to refuse-with-reason.

**Profiles.** Named policy bundles over the core protocol: Apathy-Refusal
(truth: *was it measured?*), Honesty-Mandate (lawfulness), Custody
(loyalty), Consent (authorization), Provenance (origin), Deliberation
(judgment), Calibration (trust over time), Commons (collective effects),
Apprenticeship (growth), Gauntlet (robustness). Profiles compose as a
stack. **This repository implements one profile — Apathy-Refusal — in one
domain: commerce.**

**Conformance.** An environment passes the way a network stack passes —
by surviving the suite: the *drift test* (asserted ≠ measured → refuse),
the *unmeasured test* (no instrument

**Website troubleshooting without the guesswork.**

Developed by TB Designs | AI assistance powered by Meta Muse Wonder

## Overview

SiteSidekick is an AI-assisted website troubleshooting companion designed for small business owners.

It helps users understand website problems, explore possible causes, and determine practical next steps without requiring coding experience.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026.

## The Problem

Small business owners often encounter website problems without knowing where to begin.

A broken mobile layout, slow-loading page, or unexpected error can interrupt business operations and create unnecessary frustration.

Hiring a developer for every minor issue may not be practical.

## The Solution

SiteSidekick guides users through a structured troubleshooting process.

Users can investigate issues independently, receive optional AI assistance, review previous sessions, and prepare organized information for a developer or hosting provider.

SiteSidekick does not automatically modify website code or claim to provide confirmed technical diagnoses.

## Features

### Guided Troubleshooting

- Describe website problems in everyday language.
- Explore possible causes.
- Receive practical next steps.
- Follow a noncoding troubleshooting workflow.

### Meta Muse Wonder AI

- Optional contextual AI assistance.
- Uses the Meta Model API.
- Requires user consent before requesting assistance.
- Provides explanations and possible next steps.
- Distinguishes suggestions from confirmed diagnoses.

### Issue History

- Save and review troubleshooting sessions.
- Return to previous issues.

### Developer Handoff

- Generate structured troubleshooting information.
- Prepare reports for developers or hosting providers.

### Business Starting Guide

- Explore whether a business needs a website.
- Consider social media and customer communication.
- Understand when online booking or ecommerce may help.
- Identify practical digital priorities.

# Djinn Council

**A decision room for people who work alone.** Djinn Council is a
chat app that bridges multiple AI models — Meta's Muse Spark,
ChatGPT, and more — with six switchable thinking modes inside a
single living conversation.

Live demo: https://djinn-council.fly.dev/
Judge Q&A (full story, including the test we failed):
docs/JUDGE_QA.md

## The six modes

| Mode | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Rub the Lamp** | One genie, one straight answer. About 15 seconds. |
| **The Stand** | A straight question gets a straight answer, facts first. About 30 seconds. |
| **The Hearing** | Several models answer side by side; the differences are the information. About a minute. |
| **Cross-Examination** | The models challenge each other's answers. About 1–2 minutes. |
| **The High Trial** | The court researches the real world first, then decides. About 3–4 minutes. |
| **En Banc** | The full court sits: an optional lawyer researches and briefs the case, counsel argues, the panel debates until it converges or hits the round cap, and the chairman rules. About 3–5 minutes. |

Every verdict carries its confidence in plain sight — including
when the honest answer is "low."

Muse Spark (Meta Model API) sits in the chairman's seat with a
dual role: it proposes alongside the other seats and it
synthesizes the final ruling. The comparison seats are
deliberately heterogeneous (OpenAI and Claude via OpenRouter) —
different models see different things, and the chairman's job is
to rule between them.

The table isn't limited to these seats — more AI models can be
added as seats the same way. What's here is the working demo:
the seats above, wired up and live.

http://localhost:8000. The live demo above needs no keys and no
sign-in: it runs on capped demo keys provided for judging.

Click **API Keys** in the app header and paste your keys. Keys are
stored in the browser's `localStorage` **only** — they are sent to

for you, and are never persisted server-side or sent anywhere
else. The OpenAI key is entered by the user directly; it never
passes through any assistant.

# Creative Director Agent

Turns a messy product catalogue into clean, true, human-approved ads in minutes.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track, theme Build for Your World), 26 Oct to 4 Nov 2026.

**Live demo:** https://creative-director-agent.vercel.app

Demo video: (link added at submission)

Access needs a demo code. The code is given to the judges separately and is never stored in this repository: the server reads it from the `DEMO_CODE` environment variable and refuses every run when it is not set.

## What it does

You load a small catalogue (up to 12 products, a CSV and one photo each). The agent checks each photo, cuts each product out, writes a short headline, draws the ad with a layout engine, reviews it like an art director, and shows it to you. Nothing is approved until you click **Approve**, and nothing is added to your photos.

- **Catalogue mode:** photo check, Held back cards for photos that are not safe to use, Try anyway and Find items rescues, approve or reject each ad, download the approved ones as a ZIP with a results file.
- **Looks, Themes and Effects:** seven Looks (including Magazine Cover and Sticker Pack), thirteen Themes, four effects. A finished ad can be redrawn with a new Look or effect in seconds, with no model call.
- **Single ad mode:** an event poster, a promo graphic or a product ad from one photo, with revision notes and a campaign pack.
- **MCP server:** the same engine as three tools for any MCP client.

## Models used

| Model | Where | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`) on Baseten | Baseten | Primary reviewer: the critic, the product fidelity check, the brand rules check, the photo check, and the line sense check |
| Muse Spark 1.3 (`muse-spark-1.3`) on Meta's Model API | Meta | Planning and headlines, and the fallback for every reviewer step when Baseten is missing, slow or fails |
| SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`) on Meta's Model API | Meta | Cutting each product out of its photo |
| Muse Image 1.0 (`muse-image-1.0`) on Meta's Model API | Meta | Text-free artwork, and product scenes built around the cut-out |

No other vendor's model is used. If `BASETEN_API_KEY` is not set, every step runs on Muse Spark 1.3 on Meta. The page shows on each card which model did the reviewing and when the fallback stepped in.

## How the copy rules work

The aim is ads that read like ads, and that never say something untrue.

- **The model writes headlines only.** It is told to leave the subline empty, and anything it sends for the subline is dropped.
- **A subline is only one of three things:** a fact or offer you supplied (the CSV `fact` column, the offer box, a folio's approved claims), one safe occasion line from a gifting theme (Christmas, Valentine's Day, Mother's Day) for a plausible gift, or empty. A headline plus a button is a finished ad.
- **Plain code checks every line,** headlines and alternatives included. It rejects colour, material and part words

# Integrity Copilot — Meta AI Developer Hackathon

**ValonyLabs.** A piping-integrity workbench for one circuit. It brings replayed process samples (PI), ultrasonic thickness (UT) readings, visual evidence and asset history together into one evidence-linked inspection proposal. A named engineer approves or rejects that proposal.

**Where to look next.** A deterministic *Next spots* ranking across lines combines UT corrosion rates and remaining life, decoded visual inspection findings (Inspection Workbook valuation codes), and blind spots such as silent sensors or refused trends. The scope is UT readings plus visual findings and line imagery. There is no 3D, photogrammetry or LiDAR, and images never produce a thickness value.

All learned inference uses Meta models. The narrative runs on **Meta Muse locally** (Muse Glimmer through the Ollama desktop runtime, on loopback, at no cost). Visual evidence comes from **Meta SAM 3.1**.

## What decides what

| Output | Basis | Produced by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corrosion rates, remaining life, next inspection date | **deterministic** | `lib/integrity-copilot/evidence.ts` (ST/LT rates, uncertainty policy, comparability checks) |
| Data gaps, framework state, proposal | **deterministic** | `lib/integrity-copilot/workflow.ts` |
| Narrative summary (EN + PT) | **model_inferred** (local Meta Muse Glimmer by default; Muse Spark only when explicitly configured) | `lib/integrity-copilot/gateway.ts` + `faithfulness.ts`. It never changes a deterministic output. |
| Next-spots ranking across lines | **deterministic** | `lib/integrity-copilot/nextspots.ts` (tiers: act now · within 2 years · open visual finding · blind spot · monitor, each with its reasons) |
| Visual findings | **inspection codes** | `lib/integrity-copilot/codes.ts` + `inspection-codes.ts` (reviewed valuation-code map; codes not in the map are shown as "unmapped", never guessed. Legacy condition codes 05+ such as 12TL "through-thickness corrosion, leaks" get an explicit, labelled severity overlay derived from each code's own description; 00xx "not inspected" codes stay visible blind spots) |
| Workbook import | **deterministic** | `lib/integrity-copilot/workbook.ts` (Inspection Workbook layout → per-line circuits; procedure, instrument, calibration and uncertainty come from engineer-entered campaign metadata) |
| Visual regions on the inspection image | **model_inferred** (recorded SAM 3.1 output by default, labelled as recorded; live SAM 3.1 only when opted in) | `lib/integrity-copilot/visual.ts` + `sam.ts` |
| Approval | **engineer** | `POST /api/integrity-copilot/decide`: named engineer, rationale required, single use, stored durably |

Rules the system enforces:
- **The narrative contains no numbers, by construction.** Muse receives the findings with every value masked as `[value]` and every identifier given a digit-free alias (`CML-03` becomes `CML#a`), so its request carries no digit. Any numeric content in the reply withholds the summary: dig

- Node.js `24.x` (`.nvmrc` y `engines.node` fijan `>=24 <25`).

Desde PowerShell o una terminal Linux/macOS, en la raíz del repositorio:

node --version

# Star City Scout

A small tool built for one person's real daily job: running Star City Deals, a
Lincoln deals page on Facebook. It turns a deal screenshot, or a few typed
details, into a complete, ready-to-post Facebook post kit in seconds.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (October 26 – November 4,
2026) for the "Build for Your World" track, by @ashleybuildsne.

## What it does

- **Deal form:** paste a deal link, product name, sale price, original price,
  deal tag (like "Limited time deal"), an optional promo code, and notes.
- **Post kit:** builds a playful-first caption with the price in the caption
  only, a shop link, a "from a Lincoln mom" sign-off, a prices-can-change
  warning, `#ad` plus the Amazon Associates disclosure, and hashtags. No em
  dashes, ever.
- **Promo codes get their own first comment:** if a deal has a promo code, the
  kit includes a separate first-comment block with its own copy button, so
  the code stays easy to copy.
- **Screenshot reading:** drop in a screenshot of a deal and Scout reads the
  product name, sale price, original price, percent off, deal tag, visible
  link, and promo code straight out of the image, then builds the kit.
- **Fresh AI captions:** a "Write it fresh with AI" button writes a new
  playful opening line for each deal, kept under 50 words and checked against
  the house rules (no price, link, hashtags, `#ad`, em dashes, or invented
  claims in the opening).
- **Make a picture:** an optional prompt box that generates a promo image
  for a deal, with a preview and a Download button.

## How it works

Scout is a single web page. It calls Meta's models through the Meta Model
API:

- A vision model reads deal screenshots.
- A text model writes fresh caption openings.
- Muse Image generates pictures.

## Your key stays yours

Scout asks for your Meta API key in a box on the page itself. The key lives
only in that browser tab's memory. It is never saved to a file, never sent
anywhere except to Meta's services to do the work above, and never typed
into a chat. Close the tab and it's gone, so you paste it fresh each time
you open the page. No key is included anywhere in this project.

## Run it yourself

This page must be run locally, from a file on your own computer. Links
hosted on the web block the API calls Scout needs, so open the downloaded
page directly, paste your key into the key box, and go. You can test the key
with the "Test this key" button in the key box before you start.

Arindam5294/unravix-lens.readme_excerpt:
# Unravix Lens

**Snap your working. Lens finds the exact line where it went wrong.**
Untangle any study doubt, from Class 1 to PhD. By **Swanix Labs**, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track).

**Live:** https://unravix-lens.pages.dev (works on a phone: open it, tap *Check my working*, photograph a page)
**Public benchmark:** https://unravix-lens.pages.dev/benchmark.html (60 held-out items, every result and every miss)

---

## The problem
Students in India solve most of their practice on paper: board exams, JEE/NEET, GATE and university papers. When an answer is wrong, the usual fix is to look at the final answer in the solutions and redo the whole problem. That hides *where* the reasoning broke: a dropped term, a sign, a substitution done halfway. So the same slip comes back in the exam. Most students have no tutor to sit beside them, and the help that does exist (answer keys, solution videos, chatbots) explains *a* solution, not *their* mistake on *their* page.

## The solution
Lens reads the student's own handwritten page, re-derives every line and points at the **knot**: the first line that is wrong. It draws a box on that exact line of the photo. Then, instead of handing over the answer, it **coaches**: three hints, each a little stronger, and only then the corrected line. The student fixes the line on paper and **rescans to verify**. A private Knot Report remembers which ideas keep slipping and writes fresh practice problems on them, each one checked by a second, independent Muse Spark pass. Everything works in the student's own language (65 languages in the picker, right-to-left included), and a student who can't type the doubt can **say it**.

### Two modes
- **Check my working (Knot Scan).** Photograph any step-by-step work: arithmetic, algebra, calculus, matrices, proofs, physics, chemistry, statistics, journal entries, code traces, grammar transformations. Lens returns every step with its status (correct, knot, carried error, unclear), the knot with fix and explanation, three tap-to-reveal check questions and a Knot Report entry. Essays and opinion pieces come back as *not step-checkable*, with an offer to explain the topic instead.
- **Ask a doubt.** Type a question, photograph one, say it, or combine them, in any subject. Lens returns the answer, 2–6 steps, the key idea, the common misconception and three check questions. Text-only doubts make one Muse Spark call and no SAM call.

### 0.6 additions
- **Hint ladder → reveal.** Every knot carries three graded hints (nudge, pointer, near-answer). The fix stays hidden until the student asks for it.
- **Rescan to verify.** After fixing the line on paper, the student rescans; Lens is told which line was flagged before and says whether that knot is now untied or a new one appeared.
- **Second look at every flag.** When a knot is found, a separate Muse Spark call re-reads that line on the photo and drops flags it can't confirm: crossed-out ink, notation, unreadable l

## Quickstart

Get started immediately with zero installation using `npx`:

```bash
# 1. Create a safe sandbox directory for tools
mkdir -p "$HOME/mcp-sandbox"
echo "Secure workspace notes" > "$HOME/mcp-sandbox/notes.txt"

# 2. Wrap any MCP server command with Veylith
npx veylith -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem "$HOME/mcp-sandbox"
```

Or install the CLI globally:

```bash
npm install -g veylith
```

### Configure Claude Desktop

Add to `claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {

      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "veylith",
        "--",
        "npx",
        "-y",
        "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",

---

## 1. Introduction

**Veylith** is an open-source, AI-native security gateway positioned between autonomous AI agents (Claude, Cursor, custom agent runtimes) and external execution environments (tools, databases, filesystems, and remote APIs) connected over the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**.

Rather than granting AI agents direct, unmediated socket access to tools with ambient system authority, Veylith acts as an inline security boundary and policy enforcement point. It intercepts tool discovery schemas, inspects invocation arguments, and sanitizes tool return payloads to protect agent reasoning loops from indirect prompt injection, tool definition poisoning, privilege escalation, and credential exfiltration.

Veylith combines sub-millisecond deterministic invariants with semantic threat evaluation powered by **Meta Muse** (`muse-spark-1.3`).

# SnapFix — an agentic repair copilot

SnapFix helps a total beginner fix a broken appliance. Upload a photo
or a short video of the problem and SnapFix:

1. **Diagnoses from the media first** (Muse Spark) — it asks at most
   two short questions, and only when the photo or video cannot answer.
2. **Names the faulty part and highlights it on your own photo**
   (SAM 3.1 segmentation), after a second Spark pass verifies every
   painted region — regions that miss the part are vetoed before you
   see them.
3. **Gives a verdict**: DIY, RISKY (dangerous work — a licensed
   technician is recommended, a DANGER note comes first, and the full
   fix is still explained), STOP (active emergency only), or
   NO FAULT VISIBLE.
4. **Builds the buy card**: the exact part *and every tool the fix
   needs*, with retailer search links (Amazon.ca, PartSelect.ca).
   You confirm and pay at the retailer — SnapFix never checks out.
5. **Walks you through the fix step by step**, one Muse Image
   illustration per step, grounded in your annotated photo, with a
   chat box for follow-up questions about your repair.

Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026),
Indie track, theme: Push the Frontier. All code in this repository
was written during the event window.

## Meta models used

- **Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`)** — the agent: media-first
  diagnosis, the technician-style interview, and the verification
  pass that vetoes bad highlights.
- **SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`)** — open-vocabulary segmentation of the
  suspect parts Spark names, painted back onto the user's photo.
- **Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`)** — the per-step instructional
  illustrations, edited from the user's own annotated photo.

## Run it locally

```bash
uv sync            # or: pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env   # put your MODEL_API_KEY in .env
uv run python snapfix.py washer.jpg     # terminal version
uv run streamlit run app.py             # web app
```

## Deploy (Google Cloud Run)

```bash
gcloud run deploy snapfix --source . \
  --region northamerica-northeast1 \
  --allow-unauthenticated --memory 2Gi --timeout 900 \
  --set-env-vars MODEL_API_KEY=<your key>
```

(For anything beyond a demo, store the key in Secret Manager and pass
`--set-secrets MODEL_API_KEY=<secret-name>:latest` instead.)

# LatentBridge

**Small Llama agents that talk in vectors instead of text.**
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (track: *Push the Frontier*).

**The idea.** Small models will always make some mistakes. But small specialists that are good at different
things should be able to work together *like one model*, sharing what they understood instead of
squeezing it through a written summary. LatentBridge lets them do that on consumer hardware.

**Why it matters.** Teams of small models are how AI runs on hardware people already own: a 4 GB laptop
GPU, a phone, an edge box, with private documents staying on the device. Today those models talk to each
other in text, so every hand-off waits for one model to *write* a message. LatentBridge removes that wait:
the reader's step drops from 2.7 s to 0.06 s, and at the same message size the latent message keeps far more
of the problem (60% vs 20–25% accuracy at ~20 positions). Meta's Muse models sit around the local team:
**Muse Spark** plans, checks every answer, and labels new problems with no answer key (96% correct labels,
up from the team's own 59%; see *Muse Spark improver*). A zero-training version of the channel maps the 1B into **Muse Glimmer 30B**, which has a different tokenizer
(fit done; GPU evaluation pending, see `glimmer/`).

Multi-agent LLM systems pass messages as text: one model writes a message token by token, the next model
reads it back. LatentBridge replaces that text channel with a learned **latent channel**. The reader model
reads its input once, and a small trained *bridge* maps the reader's hidden states straight into the
solver's input-embedding space as **soft tokens**. The reader never decodes a single token. Both LLMs stay
frozen; only the bridge (17M params) trains.

```
            Muse Spark (Meta Model API)            plans the task, routes subtasks
                    │
        facts ──────┴────── question
          │                    │
 Llama 3.2 1B (reader)         │
   one forward pass            │
          │ layer-8 hidden states
   ┌──────▼──────┐             │
   │   Bridge    │ soft tokens │
   └──────┬──────┘             │
          └──────► Llama 3.2 3B (solver) ──► answer
```

Text pipeline for comparison: the 1B *writes* a ~60-token message, the 3B reads it.

## Meta models used

| Model | Role |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.1`, Meta Model API) | Orchestrator: splits each task into reader/solver subtasks (~2.5 s, ~760 tokens per plan, cached); verifier; agent brain with tool calling |
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`, Meta Model API) | Improver/teacher (`improve.py`): checks the team's answers on new problems and writes corrections the bridge trains on; live checker in `chat_app.py` |
| **Muse Glimmer 30B** (`meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B`, open weights) | Solver reading the 1B's vectors through a cross-tokenizer bridge (`glimmer/`; ridge fit done, cloud-GPU evaluation pending) |
| **Llama 3.2 1B Instruct** (`meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-In

# Sentry Vision

**SentryVision is a standalone smart contract security verifier built for the Meta Hackathon. It analyzes Solidity contracts, identifies vulnerabilities, explains how an exploit would actually happen, and visualizes the attack flow.** Unlike generic scanners that output cryptic reports, SentryVision combines deterministic static analysis with Meta's Muse Spark Open (and optional Muse Wonder on repair – complex reasoning) to produce structured, auditable, and visual security intelligence. > Sentry Vision is a triage and visualization tool, **not** a formal security audit. See [Limitations](#limitations). --- ## Why not just Slither, or just an LLM? - **Slither** is a reliable deterministic detector, but its output is hard to read. - **LLMs** are easy to read, but they can hallucinate. - **Sentry Vision combines them:** Slither detects, Muse Spark Open interprets and visualizes, Slither re-checks the proposed fix, and optional Muse Wonder retries a rejected patch up to three times. --- ## Problem Developers and non-technical founders usually get one of two things: - **Dense static-analysis dumps** (for example raw Slither output) that they cannot interpret, or - **Generic LLM answers** with no deterministic grounding that they cannot trust. Neither tells them *what is actually dangerous* or *how an attack would really happen*. ## Solution 1. The user pastes or uploads a `.sol` contract. 2. **Slither** runs deterministic static detection (detector, impact, confidence, affected lines). 3. **Muse Spark Open** triages the findings in plain language and proposes a patch. 4. The app returns **structured JSON** and renders a **visual attack flowchart** (Mermaid). 5. **Slither re-runs on the patch** and a **public signature surface check** runs. 6. If F3 rejects the patch, the user can **retry up to 3 times** with Muse Wonder (complex reasoning) **Core differentiation:** not just "find bugs", but *show how the hack would happen*, and check the fix with the same deterministic tool — without claiming a formal audit. --- ## How it works | Layer | Role | Engine | | --- | --- | --- | | **F1** | Deterministic static signal | Slither | | **F2** | Triage, explanation, patch, Mermaid | M

# Surgical Item Finder

**An AI agent that gets the right surgical supply to the operating room, without a phone call.**

![How Surgical Item Finder works](docs/concept.png)

Built solo for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026) · Track: **Indie Developer** · Theme: **Build for Your World**

### Live demo: https://surgical-item-finder.onrender.com

> Free hosting: if the site has been idle, the first visit takes about a minute to wake up.

---

## The problem

During surgery, when a nurse needs an item, they call or message the ORMC (Operating Room Materials Core) on a VoLTE phone. Then:

- The one associate they reach may be busy, away, or covering several jobs.
- There are thousands of items, and surgical teams often use different names for the same one.
- If the associate doesn't recognize the name, they search the inventory app by hand, or need the item number.

Every minute spent on the phone is a minute lost in the operating room.

## Why I built this

I work as a material coordinator in a hospital, so I see this problem every day: an urgent call from the OR, a nickname that doesn't match the catalog, and a hand search through thousands of items while the surgical team waits. This app is what I want that moment to look like.

## The solution

1. The nurse picks their OR, then **types or speaks** the item name, using whatever name they know: "bovie", "lap sponge", or a misheard "Bobby".
2. A **Muse Spark agent** works out which item they mean and shows a **packaging-style photo**, the item number, and **where it's in stock**, ranked from nearest: the same OR, the OR's core, the ORMC, then other ORs.
3. The nurse adds items to a **cart**, sets quantities, reviews, and chooses:
   - **Deliver from ORMC:** every ORMC associate's screen **beeps at once**. The first to tap **Accept** gets it; others see it's taken.
   - **I'll pick it myself:** no alert, just a pick list with locations. The request is still recorded.
4. The nurse's screen updates live: **Sent → Maria is on the way → Delivered ✓**.
5. **Not something we stock?** The agent looks the description up in the **FDA's public device database** and shows real products: maker, model number, whether it's still sold, and any recalls. One tap asks ORMC to source it.

No phone call, no misheard names, and no single point of failure.

## Try it in 2 minutes

1. **Nurse** (phone or browser): open the [live demo](https://surgical-item-finder.onrender.com), choose an OR, and search **"Bobby"** or tap 🎤 and say it. The agent asks which type of bovie you mean.
2. Add one or two items to the cart, then tap **Deliver from ORMC → Confirm**.
3. **ORMC associate** (a second window or device): open [/ormc](https://surgical-item-finder.onrender.com/ormc), enter a name, and tap **Start shift**. The request appears with a beep.
4. Tap **Accept**, then **Delivered**, and watch the nurse's screen update.

# GhostCut Director

GhostCut Director is a Mac app and a `director` command line that cut multicam talking video: I give it a folder of camera cards, and it syncs the clips, picks the takes, grades the cameras to match, chooses an angle for every spoken line, finishes the audio, and hands back a horizontal cut, a vertical cut, editable timelines, and a written record of every choice.

## Try it in two minutes

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[director]"
director demo --out-dir director-demo
```

You need Python 3.11 or newer and `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe` on your `PATH`. No footage and no API keys are needed.

`director demo` makes a small synthetic shoot in `director-demo/shoot/` (a lav track and three cameras at known offsets, one of them silent, with a deliberate restart in the script), runs the real `director cut` pipeline on it offline, and checks its own work. You will see the sync offsets against the known ones (pass within one frame), how many seconds the restart removal took out, and where to look next: `director-demo/job/cut.mp4`, `director-demo/job/vertical.mp4`, `director-demo/job/timeline.fcpxml`, and `director-demo/job/cut.json`. It exits non-zero if a check fails. `director demo --muse` runs the same shoot with Muse and SAM when `MODEL_API_KEY` is set; `--keep` reuses shoot media already in the output folder.

An agent-directed lyric-video pipeline. A song goes in; a designed,

# KINETIC-ORACLE (ProprioSAM)

**Closed-loop visual verification and bounded repair for tool-using agents, built on Meta Model API (SAM 3.1, Muse Spark, Muse Wonder).**
Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Indie track · *Push the Frontier*.

Tool-using agents treat `{"status": "ok"}` as proof that the world changed the way they intended. It isn't. KINETIC-ORACLE
adds an independent *proprioception* layer. The action is rendered, **SAM 3.1** tracks the objects that matter, and a **frozen
deterministic residual** decides PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE from numbers alone. When it fails, **Muse** diagnoses the cause
blind, from the measurements and a handful of inspection tools, and patches the scene. Then everything is measured again.
The model never gets to declare success.

# FailFirst AI

**Break the plan. Not the business.**

FailFirst AI is a business decision stress-testing prototype built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**, Indie Developer track, *Build for Your World* theme.

A business decision can look profitable until an overlooked assumption changes. FailFirst AI combines **Meta Muse Spark 1.3 risk hypotheses** with **deterministic JavaScript simulations** so users can see what might break, how the modeled numbers change, and what to verify before committing money.

![Quote stress test: baseline, entered stress, and Meta-tested downside](docs/screenshots/decision-impact.png)

## What it does

Eight decision modes: **Quote / Contract**, **Subscription Launch**, **Hire vs Subcontract**, **Bulk vs Small Batch**, **Discount Test**, **Ad Spend ROI**, **New Service**, and **New Branch**.

- **Deterministic first:** profit, break-even, sensitivity, and scenario thresholds are computed in JavaScript, not invented by a language model.
- **Agentic stress tests:** Muse Spark proposes hypotheses and can call bounded scenario tools; the app recalculates the financial impact.
- **Auditable outcomes:** before/after comparisons, assumption audits, calculation-driven flags, and explicit evidence labels distinguish user inputs, calculations, and AI-generated scenarios.
- **Actionable review:** decision rescue options and validation checks help users understand what to investigate before committing.

The most severe modeled scenario is **not** necessarily the most likely. This tool is not a prediction engine or financial adviser.

## Demo example

An illustrative **$8,000 contract** starts with **$2,000 baseline profit**. Entered labor and material stress reduces that to **$160**. An AI-generated scenario for weekend work and excluded delivery can make the quote loss-making; deterministic code then recomputes the break-even and illustrative 15% target quote. **Meta-generated amounts vary between runs.**

## Architecture

```text
Browser (Next.js / React)
  ├─ 8 input modes + deterministic baseline calculations
  └─ POST /api/analyze
       ├─ Server validates and recalculates inputs
       ├─ Meta Model API: muse-spark-1.3
       ├─ Bounded tool calls → JavaScript scenario calculators
       └─ Structured hypotheses + deterministic result trace
```

**Stack:** Next.js 15, React 19, Node.js, JavaScript, Meta Model API, Muse Spark 1.3.

## Run locally

Node.js **20.6+** is required; Node 22 is recommended.

```bash
npm ci
npm test
npm run build
npm run dev
```

Open **http://localhost:3000**. The deterministic calculator works without a Meta API key.

To enable AI risk analysis, copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and set your own server-side key:

```env
MODEL_API_KEY=your_meta_api_key_here
META_MODEL=muse-spark-1.3
```

Restart the development server. Never commit `.env.local`, expose the key in browser code, or put it in screenshots. `MODEL_API_KEY` is read only in the server API route.

# Fluixi AI

A grounded AI developer tool for the [Fluixi](https://github.com/fluixi/core) framework — built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**.

**Meta Llama generates. Fluixi evidence grounds. Tests verify.** A generated claim is never called verified merely because the model produced it.

## Why

Fluixi has sharp, learnable traps: legacy tuple primitives next to the idiomatic handle API, and resource reads that suspend during SSR hydration. A general model walks into both. Fluixi AI retrieves version-pinned framework truth (original source at a fixed commit, the coding skill, and executed test evidence), constrains generation with it, applies the patch only to a disposable scratch copy, checks it, and reports Verified facts / Test evidence / Remaining uncertainty separately — with contradictions preserved, not silently resolved.

## The vertical slice

Install (local development): clone, then `npm install` (no dependencies) - the `fluixi-ai` executable is exposed via the package `bin`. Packaged check: `npm pack` and install the tarball in a scratch project; `fluixi-ai --help` / `--version` / `replay` work from the installed package.

```sh
export LLAMA_API_KEY=...        # Meta Model API key from dev.meta.ai (never commit it)
# Prerequisites: Node >=20, pnpm 10; sibling checkouts libs/fluixi-core@4bc547f (+ stabilization build for --validate). Offline demo needs none of these: `npm run demo`
pnpm build-claims               # claims from libs/fluixi-core @ 4bc547f (refuses any other baseline)
fluixi-ai fix --task "Add async data without breaking SSR hydration" --file path/to/component.tsx
fluixi-ai fix --validate --file path/to/component.tsx   # + real compiler/app-test validation in a disposable worktree
fluixi-ai replay                               # offline replay of recorded evidence (no API key, no network)
pnpm eval                       # A/B: model-only vs grounded, same tasks + rubric
pnpm test                       # unit tests (node --test)

# Cuelga

**While the extortionist is still talking, Cuelga quietly confirms your family member is safe and tells you when to hang up.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Every line in this repo was written during the event, starting Oct 29, 2026.

**Live demo:** https://cuelga.onrender.com · **Guided demo (1 minute, no setup):** https://cuelga.onrender.com/demo

The app is in Mexican Spanish, because that is where this scam happens. The guided demo adds English subtitles.
