# Rewear Studio — See It. Find It. Buy It.

**English** · [中文](#中文說明)

Rewear Studio turns any outfit photo — a street-style snap, a friend's post, a short video — into a shoppable
breakdown of every piece, powered by **Meta SAM 3.1, Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Image 1.0**. It keeps what the AI saw
apart from what it guessed: unclear regions are flagged instead of guessed, AI previews are always labeled, and
shopping links say "similar", never "the same item".

- **Live demo:** <https://rewear.soraing.com> (the judge login is in the submission form)
- **Demo video** (1:41, English narration and subtitles): <https://youtu.be/lm5mTxP44jc>
- **Chrome extension "Shop this look":** [`extension/`](extension/README.md)
- Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**

> **Timeline:** preparation Oct 21–23 (an early prototype of the pipeline and internal benchmarks); hackathon build
> Oct 26 – Nov 4. What was built when: [Built during the hackathon](#built-during-the-hackathon-oct-26--nov-4-2026).

## How it works

1. Take a photo, import up to 32 photos, or click **Shop this look** on any photo while you browse.
2. Muse Spark 1.3 lists the visible garments. For each one, SAM 3.1 segments it from a text prompt such as
   "blue denim jacket" and returns a pixel mask.
3. Muse Spark 1.3 reads every cut-out piece — category, specific style name, colors, pattern, fabric — with a
   confidence score. Pieces it can't read reliably are flagged and kept out of the results.
4. Muse Image 1.0 previews the complete garment (three candidates, about US$0.03 per piece), always shown next to
   the original photo and labeled as AI.
5. Every piece links to Google Shopping, Bing Shopping and web search for similar items at no model cost. An
   optional AI search looks for the brand's product page and lists only results that pass verification.

SAM 3.1 is called through the OpenAI-compatible Meta Model API (`wardrobe/providers.py`):

```python
client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1", api_key=MODEL_API_KEY)
stream = await client.responses.create(
    model="sam-3.1",
    stream=True,
    input=[{"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "input_text", "text": "blue denim jacket"},
        {"type": "input_image", "image_url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,..."},
    ]}],
    metadata={"mask_encoding": "one_bit"},
)
# meta-sam-parser turns the stream into one box and one 1-bit mask per object
```

- **Writers’ room.** Brainstorm cards, then a screenplay in standard format.

| Step | Model |
|---|---|
| Writing, directing, agent, computer use, continuity review | Muse Spark 1.3, with Muse Wonder 1.0 for hard tasks |
| Open-weight text fallback | Baseten `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` only |

# Carousel Agent

**An agent that turns a brand's own material into an Instagram carousel it can prove — every factual sentence quoted from the source, every slide looked at by Muse Spark before a human signs off.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Indie track · *Build for Your World*.
All code was written during the hackathon — see [PROVENANCE.md](PROVENANCE.md).

## The problem

Small brands are told to post carousels every week. AI can write the copy, but the owner still has to check every
line against the product sheet ("did it say 24 hours or 48?") and click through every slide for cut-off text. That
checking is the actual bottleneck — so this agent is built around checks it cannot skip.

## What it does

```
product PDF / notes ─┐
voice brief (audio) ─┼─► read ─► plan ─► write (quoted) ─► visuals ─► render ─► submit ─► human sign-off ─► publish (mocked)
product photo ───────┘     │       │          │               │            │          │
                      Voice      outline   citation        SAM 3.1     layout     claim check (Spark)
                      Transcribe coverage  gate (code)     Muse Image  checks     visual check (Spark sees the PNGs)
```

The model chooses one tool per turn. **Each check lives inside its tool**, so the agent cannot route around it; a
refusal comes back as an observation and the agent fixes exactly what was named.

| Meta model | Role | What breaks without it |
|---|---|---|
| `muse-spark-1.3` | Agent brain (tool calling) · outline coverage judge · claim check (structured output) · **visual QA on the rendered PNGs (image input)** | Planning, writing and both final checks |
| `sam-3.1` | Cuts the product out of the owner's own photo for the visual slide | The visual slide has no product |
| `muse-image-1.0` | Generates the cover background in the brand palette | Cover falls back to a flat colour |
| `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` | Turns the owner's voice memo into a **quotable source**. Facts that exist only in the owner's head (a launch price, a pop-up giveaway) become evidence the citation gate accepts | Spoken-only facts have no source to quote, so they cannot enter the carousel |

### The checks

| Where | Check | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| `set_outline` | Hidden key points (extracted by a separate Spark call the agent never sees) must be ≥70% covered; 7–9 slides, cover first, CTA last. Feedback names only the *kind* of thing missing | Spark + code |
| `record_claim` | **Citation gate:** each quote must appear word-for-word on the page it cites (≥15 chars, normalised) — PDFs and the voice transcript alike. Every number in the sentence must also appear in its quotes | code |
| `render_deck` | Overflow, min font size, WCAG contrast, 72px safe margin, source footer, cutout/text overlap, font loaded | code (Playwright) |
| `submit_deck` ① | Rules: every slide filled, numbers in headlines backed by a quote, fresh render | code |
| `submit_deck` ② | **Claim check:** does each quote really suppo

# Neural Referee

**Catch silent data corruption inside AI computation, and say exactly where it happened.**

![One run of the demo: a bit flip makes the first run fail at step 1,542 in sublayer L2.attn; the Meta model decides to re-run; the re-run passes and 35 is delivered with a receipt](docs/hero.png)

Hardware sometimes computes a wrong value without raising any error. Meta (then Facebook) studied these
silent data corruptions and ran silent-error tests across hundreds of thousands of machines in its fleet
("Silent Data Corruptions at Scale", Dixit et al., arXiv 2102.11245): the CPU's own error reporting does not
catch them, and they surface later as application-level problems. As more computation moves inside models, the same question applies to the model: when a
step goes wrong, which step, and which part of the model?

Neural Referee answers that for computers that run inside transformer weights
(**Neural Computer = Compiled Layers + Neural State + Program Weights + Verifier**). Researchers now compile
real machines into weights (Percepta's WebAssembly transformer, QwenPU's RISC-V CPU inside a 4B open model)
and only check the final output. Here, Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta Model API) writes the program and its own
tests, the program runs inside a 7-layer transformer whose weights are a computer, and the referee checks
every step: it returns a receipt for the whole trace, or the first wrong step and the faulty sublayer. Muse
reads that verdict, re-runs or repairs, and only delivers answers that come with a passing receipt.

What it measured (CPU only, reproducible from this repo):
- **Stress test: no wrong answer delivered.** 12 tasks, every execution hit by 8 random bit flips. An
  unchecked pipeline delivered 4 wrong answers. The Muse agent loop delivered 0 wrong: 10 correct, each
  with a receipt, and 2 withheld because Muse could not write a working program (11 re-run decisions, all
  "retry" after a referee FAIL). `results/agent_stress.json`
- **Faults that weight checks cannot see.** Bit flips in activations or attention memory while the program
  runs: the referee located 30 of 30; comparing weight files located 0 of 30; an output-only check
  detected them but located none. Weight corruption: 15 of 15 here, 40 of 40 in two earlier runs.
- **Hidden errors.** In one run the final answer was right (35) but step 1,909 of 3,107 was computed
  wrongly in `L1.attn`. Output-only checking passes that run; the referee fails it.
- **Cheap to check.** About 11 hash comparisons find the first wrong step in a 3,000-step trace; one step
  is then rechecked layer by layer. No false alarms on four clean programs up to 44,332 steps.
- **Meta models in the loop.** Muse Spark 1.3 wrote correct programs for 9 of 10 requests on the first try
  (about 12 s each). A local open-weights Llama 3.2 3B runs the same loop offline (7 of 9).

# Shift Sight Ops

An operations copilot for shift leads in a fulfillment building. It thinks on top of
warehouse-system data: it **projects on-time shipping (OTS) for the rest of the night**,
**detects line stoppages** from the aggregate scan-gap signal, **recommends staffing
moves** across areas, and — when internal slack is not enough — **calculates the
shortfall and drafts the extra-staff posting** for the lead to approve.

> A WMS tells you what happened. The copilot tells you what is going to happen, and what to do.

## Hackathon

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Cerebral Valley), Indie Dev
Track, *Build for Your World* theme. Construction period: **October 27 – November 4, 2026**.
Team: **Alberto Bravo** (solo). The copilot's conversational layer runs on **Muse Spark Open**, a Meta model, served via Baseten;
this repository's history starts with the first construction commit of the event window.

**Built with Muse Spark Open.**

## How it works

- A **deterministic simulation engine** (pure Python, no dependencies) computes every
  number: staffing capacity, per-cutoff OTS projections, stoppage detection, donor
  recommendations, posting shortfalls.
- A **language model explains and converses**, calling the engine as a tool. No figure
  is ever produced by the model.
- If the model API is unavailable, the copilot degrades to the engine's own templated
  explanations: the numbers and alerts never depend on the model.

## Try the board

The demo board lives in `web/` — a single static page: no build step, no server of
its own, **no API calls and no keys**. It replays the demo night from the engine's
own traces, and the copilot's two exchanges are reproduced verbatim from a live
Muse Spark Open tool-calling session (provenance in `web/EXCHANGES.md`). To run it,
serve the folder with any static file server (for example
`python3 -m http.server` inside `web/`) and open the page.

## The demo night (all data synthetic)

One night shift, 17:30–03:30, a 100,000-unit day, 12 cutoff times, a five-node chain
(Picking → Induct → Put → Pack → Shipping), two line stoppages, and absences that hit
the usual donor area itself — so the night cannot be saved by rebalancing alone.
See `SCENARIO.md` for the full, hand-checkable scenario sheet.

One honesty note on the stoppages: in the simulation, a stoppage enters the
projection the moment it starts; on a real floor it would enter only through
the 5-minute aggregate no-scan signal.

## Data & privacy

**All data in this repository is synthetic.** No real employer data, no real people,
no real operations figures are used anywhere in the code, the scenario, or the demo.

## License

MIT — see `LICENSE`.

# Piece of Mind

**Giving memory to artwork.** Film yourself painting, and the footage becomes the painting's
own memory: watch it form with nobody in the way, sit back down beside it, or tap any stroke to
see the hand that made it.

![Left: the camera, 27 minutes into the third session, an arm across the canvas. Right: Piece of Mind at the same second.](docs/camera-vs-afterimage.jpg)

*The camera 27 minutes into the third session (left), and Piece of Mind at the same second (right).*

Artists have always pulled new technology into the work: new tools and surfaces, projection,
video, computers. Piece of Mind brings in Meta's newest vision and language models with one
rule: they decide where the painter is, never what the painting looks like. Every pixel in the
output comes from camera frames, aligned, colour-matched and averaged over a few frames. No
generative model touches the image and nothing is invented: what the painting remembers, the
camera saw. A script checks it.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie track, theme
*Build for Your World*: I stopped painting ten years ago, picked it back up for this, and wanted
AI in the work without letting it fake any of it. Built with **SAM 3.1** and **Muse Spark**,
either through the Meta Model API or from the open
weights: SAM 3.1 on a Modal GPU and Muse Spark Open through Baseten. The first two sessions
here were processed both ways and the third through the API; each run's receipt names the path
that made it.

## Try it

**Check a real run, no key needed.** [`samples/`](samples) holds 90 seconds of the third session
(cropped to the easel, sound removed) with the receipt of its run and the answers SAM 3.1 and Muse
Spark gave it. With Python 3.11, ffmpeg on the PATH and `pip install -r requirements.txt`:

```
python scripts/afterimage_verify.py samples/session3-excerpt/receipt.json --video samples/session3-excerpt.mp4
python scripts/afterimage_run.py samples/session3-excerpt.mp4 --out samples/session3-excerpt
```

- **Verify** checks the footage and every cached model answer against the hashes in the receipt,
  then re-derives each output frame from the footage and compares it with the receipt's hash chain.
- **Replay** runs the whole pipeline from the cached answers and writes the results page,
  `samples/session3-excerpt/index.html` (tap any stroke), and the videos. It rewrites the receipt,
  and `git diff samples/` shows nothing.
- Neither calls a model, so neither tests the models. A **fresh run** asks SAM and Spark again; their
  answers, and so the output, come out close but not identical. Bit for bit also assumes the
  toolchain the receipt names (Python 3.11, numpy 2.4, ffmpeg 9.0): another ffmpeg build can resample
  a pixel differently.

**On your own footage.** A phone on a tripod, the canvas in view the whole session, and a Meta
Model API key in `.env` (copy `.env.example`). Then:

```
python scripts/afterimage_run.py my-session.mp4 --start 3
```

# Aketud Verify — insurance answers that prove themselves, or refuse

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Startup track · Build for Your World**

**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/EZFgfWPLXxQ

In India, agents, POSPs and small brokers answer policyholders' questions in Hindi, Hinglish and English. Policyholders meanwhile get calls from fake "agents" and fake "IRDAI officers" demanding revival fees through payment links.

## Why

- India had **30.34 lakh life insurance agents** in January 2025 (Life Insurance Council data) — [Cafemutual](https://cafemutual.com/news/insurance/34334-life-insurance-industry-adds-241-lakh-agents-to-reach-30-lakh-foot-soldiers).
- **Unfair business practices made up 22.14% of life insurance complaints** in FY2024-25 (IRDAI Annual Report) — [Outlook Money](https://www.outlookmoney.com/insurance/insurance-claims-mis-selling-account-for-most-insurance-complaints-in-fy25-reveals-irdai-annual-report).
- IRDAI has issued a **public notice on spurious phone calls and fictitious offers** — [policyholder.gov.in](https://policyholder.gov.in/w/spurious-phone-calls).

Aketud Verify answers insurance questions and checks suspicious calls **only from official documents**. Every claim is quoted, the quote is checked against the source PDF, an independent model verifies it, and a newer regulation overrides an older document. Anything not proven is refused. **Fail closed.**

## What happens to every answer

1. **Muse Spark** (Meta Model API, `muse-spark-1.3`) drafts claims, each with a source file and a verbatim quote.
2. **Evidence check (deterministic):** the source must exist and the quote must appear in its extracted text. No model can override this.
3. **Independent verifier — Muse Spark Open** (open weights, `meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B`, served on Modal): rates each claim SUPPORTED / CONTRADICTED / INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE against the quoted passage. Strict JSON; malformed output fails closed.
4. **Authority precedence:** if the cited document is superseded on that topic (e.g. a 2021 policy specimen vs the 2024 IRDAI regulation), the claim is re-verified against the governing rule.
5. **Decision:** VERIFIED · SUPERSEDED · CORRECTED · REFUSED — in the user's language.

For calls: **Muse Voice Transcribe** turns a Hindi/Hinglish recording into text, Muse Spark extracts the caller's claims, and each is checked against verified IRDAI rules. Rule verdicts cannot be overturned by a model. The tool never says whether a policy exists — only the insurer can — and always ends with safety advice.

## Demo cases

| | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A | "Maximum pre-existing disease waiting period under the 2024 product rules?" | **VERIFIED** — 36 months, IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations 2024, Sch III Reg 7 |
| B | "Does Arogya Sanjeevani cover IVF in Dubai?" (Hindi) | **REFUSED** — nothing in the official documents supports an answer |
| C | "PED waiting period in Arogya Sanjeevani?" (English / Hindi / Hinglish)

# Field from Above

**▶ [Watch the demo video](https://youtu.be/n3nTe37zQ1I)** · **🌐 [Open the live demo — no installation](https://kneblewskitomasz-sys.github.io/field-from-above/demo/)**

**Field from Above** is a local-first demo that turns a Polish parcel number into a dated, cloud-masked Sentinel-2 NDVI/NDRE map, an orthophoto with SAM 3.1 segmentation masks, and a short field note written by a Meta model — Muse Glimmer 30B locally, with its descriptions fact-checked against the measured numbers, or Muse Spark 1.3 through the API.

**From a satellite image to the first furrow you check.**

A local-first demo that turns the boundary of a Polish parcel into a dated,
cloud-masked NDVI/NDRE map, an orthophoto with segmentation masks, and a short
note that says what was measured, how coarse it is, and where to walk first.
It does not pretend to be a soil test.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 October - 4 November 2026),
theme **Build for Your World**.

---

## What it does

1. **Boundary from the national cadastre.** The user enters a parcel ID; the
   system asks ULDK (the Polish national cadastre service) for the boundary.
   If the parcel is not found, the tool returns a named absence and continues
   with the others - it never turns "no data" into "zero".
2. **Current satellite measurement.** It searches the Sentinel-2 L2A archive
   through STAC, masks clouds and shadow with the scene classification layer,
   and computes NDVI and NDRE inside the parcel boundary. Every number carries
   the scene date, the number of pixels, the cloud share over that parcel and a
   95% confidence interval.
3. **Context layers, each with its own date.** An orthophoto from the national
   geoportal (image date 2025-03-28, so the tool says it is archival), SAM 3.1
   segmentation masks, and terrain heights from the national terrain model.
4. **A description a person can use.** A Meta model receives the same image and
   the same measured numbers and writes two to four sentences: what is visible,
   what to check in the field, and what is uncertain. It is explicitly forbidden
   to invent numbers, recommend fertiliser, or call the result a soil test.

5. **Season and terrain.** One date can lie, so the tool reads the whole 2026
   season (Sentinel-2 scenes with at least 80% clear pixels over the parcel) and
   draws an NDVI curve per parcel. A darker spot on one date must come back on
   other dates (in at least 10% of its pixels) before the tool calls it a weak spot;
   otherwise the verdict is **does not return** and the note says not to start
   there. Terrain heights come from the national terrain model; an empty or
   zero reading is shown as "no data", never as flat ground.

The demo page puts the parcel picker, layer switcher, measurement cards, the
model text and a "what 10 metres cannot tell you" panel in one static file.
It opens from disk and makes **zero external requests**.

- **The owner of a few small fields** who

# ProofPath

# Spark Muse

**A fast, safe browser agent on Meta Muse — the open-source core of [Spark AI](https://github.com/jaemin-jo).**

Spark is a desktop AI agent that does real work on your computer: it reads your mail, fills out
forms, books things and operates any website or Windows app for you. Spark Muse is the browser loop
behind Spark ("Flow"), rewritten as a small open-source package that runs on **Meta Muse** through the
Meta Model API (or OpenRouter).

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon — Startup track, *Build for Your World*.

## Why it is fast

Most browser agents send a screenshot every step and do one click per model call. Spark Muse does
what Spark's production engine does:

| | Typical screenshot agent | Spark Muse |
|---|---|---|
| What the model sees | a screenshot every step | a text snapshot: every visible control as `ref role "label"` + page text; pixels only when it asks (`look: true`) |
| Actions per model call | 1 | a batch (`fill` + `press Enter` + `click` …) run in order, stopping at the first error |
| Context growth | every screenshot stays | only the 2 newest snapshots and the newest screenshot stay |
| Finish | "done" | `finish` must quote **evidence** from the page |

Muse Spark's tool calling, 1M context and price ($1.25 / $4.25 per million input/output tokens) suit
this loop: fewer, larger steps instead of many screenshot round-trips.

## Safety rails (from Spark)

- Passwords are never typed by the model — the `fill` action refuses `type=password` fields.
- Payment, account deletion and password-change clicks are refused unless the user passes
  `--allow-critical`; the batch stops there and the model must report back.
- Provider errors are reported by code and message only; keys never appear in logs or traces.

## Quickstart

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m playwright install chromium

# Meta Model API (https://dev.meta.ai → API keys)
export MODEL_API_KEY=...
# or OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/keys) — same Muse models as meta/muse-spark-1.3
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...

python -m spark_muse "Search Wikipedia for Menlo Park and tell me its population" \
    --url https://en.wikipedia.org/ --headed
```

Options: `--provider meta|openrouter`, `--model muse-spark-1.3|meta/muse-wonder|...`,
`--effort low|medium|high`, `--max-steps`, `--allow-critical`, `--out runs`.
Every run writes `runs/<time>/trace.json` (each step's actions, results, think/act seconds, token
usage) and `final.png`.

## Use it as a library

```python
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright
from spark_muse import Muse, Provider, run

async with async_playwright() as pw:
    page = await (await pw.chromium.launch()).new_page()
    await page.goto('https://news.ycombinator.com/')
    result = await run('What is the top story right now?', page, Muse(Provider.pick()))
    print(result.success, result.answer, result.evidence)
```

# FollowCut

**Hours of trip footage → the moments worth reliving, centered on the people you love.**

**Live demo:** https://dylancc5.github.io/dev-meta-ai-events-global-hackathon/ (replay of cached on-device runs)

You come back from a trip with 23 clips and 56 minutes of footage and you never edit any of it. FollowCut asks one question: *who is this video about?* Type "the woman with long hair", "the man" or "the man in sunglasses". **SAM 3.1** finds that subject in every clip. **Muse Spark** throws out look-alikes and picks their best moments on the beat, and the renderer cuts a vertical 9:16 edit where the camera follows them, they stay in full color, and the rest of the world fades to gray.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** · Indie track · theme: *Build for Your World*.

## The problem
Auto-editors cut on faces, speech or whoever is biggest in frame. They can't follow *a specific person* or "the dog", and they reframe 16:9 footage around the wrong subject. Vacation footage is almost all two-shots and group shots, so "who is it about" is the whole edit. You can't answer that with a face detector. You can with a text-prompted segmenter.

## What it does
1. **Scan.** For a text prompt, SAM 3.1 segments every clip in the library. It takes a coarse pass on every clip ("is she in this clip at all?") and a dense 3 fps pass on candidate windows (where, how big, how confident). Clips without the subject (driving POV, the bridge at night) drop out.
2. **Plan.** FollowCut scores every 4-, 6- and 8-beat moment by presence, mask area and SAM confidence. Then **Muse Spark** gets the candidate stats, a reference crop of the subject and one keyframe per moment with SAM's pick boxed. It rejects look-alikes (a stranger who also matches "the man"), picks the moments worth keeping, and returns a shot list on a 120 BPM grid with a reason for every shot. The plan is checked before render: ids in range, each moment used once and at most two per clip, story order, length near target.
3. **Render.** Each chosen shot is segmented again at full frame rate (30 fps). The mask centroid is smoothed into a 9:16 follow-crop with a slow push-in. The mask, feathered, drives a subject-only color grade (subject in color, world desaturated) and a spotlight vignette. The output is a 720×1280 H.264 edit plus a side-by-side raw-vs-edit video.
4. **Re-cut.** Retype the prompt and the same footage cuts into a different film about a different person.

The web app (`web/`) is a deterministic **replay viewer** of cached runs, so the demo can't fail live. SAM 3.1 runs locally on Apple silicon (an M5 Pro over MPS), not on a serverless host.

## Meta tech
| | How it's used |
|---|---|
| **SAM 3.1** (open weights) | Text-prompted concept segmentation is the core of the product. Masks drive clip selection, the follow-crop path and every visual effect. On an M5 Pro over MPS in fp16 it takes 0.42 s/frame; a full run is ~1,200 segmented frames. Weights load through tra

# psp-muse

**A 2008 PSP-3000, reborn as a voice terminal for Meta Muse.**

Seventeen years after launch, a pink PSP-3000 with no Bluetooth and no
touchscreen can hold a conversation with an AI agent. Hold the R button,
speak, and Muse answers out loud. This project gives end-of-life hardware
a second life as a physical doorway to Muse, built with the Muse Gadgets
Device SDK (hatch-link BLE setup protocol).

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie track).

## How it works

- The PSP runs a native homebrew client (EBOOT) based on
  [wobsoriano/muse-gadget-psp](https://github.com/wobsoriano/muse-gadget-psp)
  (Apache-2.0), using its Rust port.
- A Linux host with a BLE adapter performs the one-time pairing with Muse
  and provisions the device identity onto the PSP memory stick.
- Hold **R** and talk into the microphone: the recorded audio is encrypted
  and sent to Meta Muse; the reply is spoken back through text-to-speech.
- A custom on-screen avatar shows the device state (idle, listening,
  thinking, speaking).

## Hardware

- Sony PSP-3000, firmware 6.61 + ARK-4 custom firmware
- Linux host with a BLE-capable Bluetooth adapter (pairing and install)

## Build it yourself

Everything below follows the upstream project

involved.

- A PSP-3000 with a built-in microphone (the PSP-1000 and PSP-2000 do
  not have one). The upstream author built and tested on a PSP-3001.

  PSP join a WPA2 Wi-Fi network, which the stock firmware cannot.
- A Memory Stick with about 5 MB free.
- A Muse account, the Muse app on your phone, and an SDK token from
  gadgets.muse.ai.
- A computer to build the app (the upstream author used macOS; Linux
  should work).
- A second device with Bluetooth, used once for pairing (a Raspberry Pi
  or a Linux computer running the SDK's Linux client).
- An OpenAI API key, for the voice. Without one, the PSP still hears you
  and Muse still answers, but the PSP stays silent.

- **YouTube titles that say nothing about the game**, such as "Cherry blossom", "Delete" or "Spin It!" on Brawlhalla clips

# Cutline Studio

A continuity checker for video producers, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley, November 2026).

Give it two takes of the same scene, the script or brief for that scene, and the object you care about. Cutline Studio compares the takes, flags where they disagree, and shows the exact frame behind every flag. A human editor accepts or rejects each flag. Nothing is auto-fixed, and nothing is exported without the editor.

## Why

Generating shots is fast now. Checking them is still slow, manual work: a presenter's jacket changes colour between takes, a client logo comes back cropped, a prop vanishes, and someone catches it frame by frame, or nobody does. The generator should not grade its own homework, and neither should a checker that cannot show its evidence. Cutline Studio's standing rule: no flag without evidence, and an uncertain check is raised to the human, never passed silently.

## How it works

1. **Ledger (Muse Wonder).** Wonder reads the script or brief for a scene, and each take of it, and writes a structured scene ledger: objects on set, wardrobe, props, screen positions, and the beats the brief calls for. The ledger is a fixed schema (see `src/ledger/scene_ledger.schema.json`), because the rest of the pipeline diffs two takes field by field. A chat answer cannot be diffed. A ledger can.
2. **Segment (SAM 3.1).** SAM 3.1 segments the tracked object in stills and in frames sampled from short clips. The mask is the evidence surface: every flag shows the mask on the frame it came from. Clips are checked frame by frame, each sampled frame judged as a still. Cutline Studio does not claim tracking across frames.
3. **Compare (deterministic code).** Plain code diffs the two ledgers and the mask measurements and catches the provable differences: an object present in one take and missing in the other, a mask that moved or changed size.
4. **Judge (Muse Spark).** Spark takes what measurement cannot settle, for example whether the jacket in take two is the same jacket in different light or a different jacket, and must cite the ledger lines and frames behind its call.
5. **Review (human).** The editor works the flag list (accept / reject, in the terminal pass today) and makes every final call. A voice-command pass (accept, reject, next flag) is the planned hands-free layer; it is not built yet, and the Status section says so.
6. **Repair (Muse Image, narrow).** On request, a flagged frame goes out as a targeted edit on an uploaded still, and the result re-enters the same checks before the editor sees a pass. Muse Image is never the source of the takes being checked.

## Scope, stated plainly

- Stills are the primary path. Short clips are supported as frame-sampled stills checks only; no cross-frame tracking is claimed.
- Generation and repair are limited to stills. The takes being checked are uploaded, never generated by the tool.
- No accounts, no cloud libraries, no collaboration, no auto-edit export

| Preset | Background | Echo | Lyrics |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reel** (default) | *Violet room*: lit wall gradient, brighter ceiling band, pink floor strip, slow breathing. # Adsect

Adsect tells a Shopify brand running Meta ads which elements of its ads go with purchases: what is on
screen, what is heard, what is said, and who the ad was delivered to. It then makes a variant that changes
exactly one of those elements, checks that nothing else changed, and sizes a controlled test that can prove
the effect. It runs on a real account (Hungry Minds, a book publisher: $1.52M of Meta spend, 17,890 orders and 1,067 ads
in the 90 days to Nov 1, 2026) and was built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026.

Demo video (3 min): https://youtu.be/RO1whmrgoPk

Loop: **Decompose → Learn → Fix → Verify**, with verified results meant to feed back into what Learn believes.

## The problem

- **Meta reports results per ad, not per element.** A brand knows which ad sold, not whether it was the
  hook, the music, when the product appeared or the words. Creative teams guess.
- **Comparing ads is biased by delivery.** Meta's delivery system shows each ad to different people and
  placements ("divergent delivery"; Burtch, Moakler, Gordon, Zhang & Hill 2025, arXiv:2508.21251). A winning
  ad may simply have had a better audience, and an Ads Manager A/B test inherits the same problem.
- **Generated variants change many things at once.** A new AI-made version of an ad differs from its parent
  in light, framing, words and pacing together, so a test of it cannot say what made the difference.

## How Adsect answers it

| Step | What it does | Where the logic lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Decompose** | Every ad becomes a timeline of named, editable features: people, product and logo tracks, shots, montage, on-screen text, aesthetics, voice and music, transcript, claims and topics. No embeddings as model inputs (I1). | `apps/jobs/src/adsect_jobs/picture.py`, `sam.py` (SAM 3.1), `ocr.py`, `aesthetics.py`, `judge.py` (Muse Spark), `sound.py` + `sound_models.py` (Demucs, PANNs), `words.py` (Muse Voice Transcribe + Muse Spark), `topics/` |
| **Learn** | A kill test asks whether the features predict held-out purchases better than delivery context alone; 12 pre-registered hypotheses (14 tests) are estimated with double machine learning on delivery controls; every result is a *Pattern* with an interval, shown only if it clears I5. Creative fatigue is modelled separately. | `killtest/`, `analytics/hypotheses.py`, `analytics/dml.py`, `analytics/run.py`, `analytics/fatigue.py` |
| **Fix** | A variant brief names one element to change. Adsect renders the variant itself (relight for h12, music off for h08), runs guardrails (product pixels, saturation, looks-AI, policy), then decomposes the variant again and diffs it against an identity control of the parent: only the briefed element may move (I7). The team's own videos get the same check from Slack (pre-flight). | `briefs/`, `variants/relight.py`, `variants/muse_image.py`, `variants/guardrails.py`, `variants/music.py`, `preflight/report.py`; Worker `briefs.ts`, `variants.ts`, `preflight.

# CrowdMap

CrowdMap maps how people walk through a place, using ordinary camera footage. It turns video into crowd heat maps and flow arrows on a top-down map, to help plan transit and crowd safety. We build and test it on EPFL’s SCOUT campus data. SCOUT images stay private, so public figures and demos use the CityStreet dataset.

![Crowd heat map from our pipeline on a north-up aerial map of the CityStreet junction, with each camera and the ground it sees](docs/images/citystreet-map.jpg)

This is what CrowdMap makes: where people concentrate, on a top-down map, from three ordinary cameras. It shows CityStreet in Hong Kong. `services/perception/citystreet/showcase_map.py` rebuilds it.

## How it works

![Pipeline: camera video, people found by SAM, placed on a top-down map, crowd heat map compared with official labels](docs/images/pipeline.jpg)

1. **Camera video.** For each camera, a person marks four spots on flat ground once, such as crosswalk corners.
2. **Find people.** The hosted SAM 3.1 model finds every person in each frame. Each person gives one point: the feet for low cameras, the head for high cameras in crowds. SAM follows at most 16 people per video frame, so a busy view is split into overlapping crops, and each person is counted in one crop only.
3. **Place on the map.** The same four spots marked on a top-down map fix a conversion from camera pixels to map pixels. Every person is placed on the map with it.
4. **Crowd heat map.** People from all frames and cameras add up to people per square meter. Ground no camera sees stays gray. Tracks of people over time give flow arrows (not shown here).
5. **Check.** On CityStreet, the result matches the official ground labels: map correlation 0.81, and 72% of people placed within 2 m.

The figure uses CityStreet, because the SCOUT terms do not allow sharing SCOUT images. The same pipeline runs on the SCOUT campus cameras. `services/perception/citystreet/readme_figure.py` rebuilds the figure.

## Accuracy

Both datasets come with official answer keys. We score the pipeline against them.

| | CityStreet, 3 cameras | SCOUT, 8 cameras |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answer key | Official ground labels | Official annotations, with person IDs over time |
| Footage | 200 frames, full resolution, 4 tiles per frame | 20 minutes at 10 fps, 852x480 previews, no crops |
| People per frame, ours vs answer key | 68.3 vs 61.0 | 20.8 vs 53.3 |
| Count correlation over time | 0.91 | 0.62 |
| Heat map correlation | 0.81 | 0.71 |
| People placed within 2 m of a real person | 72% | 25% |
| Our points within 2 m of a real person | 64% | 65% |
| Flow: rate correlation per cell and direction | no tracks in the labels | 0.81 |
| Flow: answer-key arrows with one of ours within 6 m, same direction | no tracks in the labels | 100% |
| Flow: our arrows with an answer-key arrow within 6 m, same direction | no tracks in the labels | 85% (median angle 2°) |
| Flow: our other arrows that still sit on real, weaker flow | no tracks

# lobot

lobot lets you see a behavior inside an open model, change it, prove what the
change does, and check that it stays safe, all on your own computer.

**Try it in your browser:** [lohuunar-lobot.static.hf.space](https://lohuunar-lobot.static.hf.space).
The demo replays recorded runs of Llama 3.2 3B. It needs no weights and no
key, and its "Demo guide" panel shows what you can try.

## What you can do

1. **Read.** Click a word. See the neurons and features behind it, what they
   fire on, and which words they push toward.
2. **Steer.** Push a neuron or a behavior direction with a dose. The answer
   forks at the first changed token, next to the unchanged answer.
3. **Create.** Describe a behavior in words ("talks like an old-west cowboy").
   lobot finds a direction for it and proves on held-out prompts what it
   does: read it, turn it up, turn it down, remove it. A Muse Spark agent can
   run the whole loop for you.
4. **Let Muse search.** With **Find with Muse**, give a goal, and Muse
   Spark calls lobot's own tools to find a neuron edit. With **Tune with
   Muse**, Muse Spark picks the dose of a patch. Muse writes a prediction before each try, and
   lobot records it. The guard and the local judge decide the result.
5. **Guard.** Every patch is screened for weaker refusals, less honesty and
   leaked secrets before you keep it.
6. **Share.** Export a small signed patch (`.lobot`, or a llama.cpp control
   vector). Others install it, re-check its evidence on their own machine,
   and carry it to another model.

Hero model: `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct`. `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` also works.

## Built on

| Part | What it does in lobot |
|---|---|
| Meta Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (open weights) | The model that lobot reads and edits. It runs on your computer. Every read, steer, Create run and guard check uses it. |
| Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`, Meta Model API) | Runs Find with Muse and Tune with Muse through tool calls. Explains each evidence page in plain words; a check rejects any number that is not in the report. Drafts new behaviors, suggests labels, and runs the Create agent. Scores the evidence again as a second judge ([J1 report](docs/roadmap/reports/J1.md)). |
| Muse Code | Meta's coding agent. It wrote almost all of lobot's code, for example the module refactor ([MOD](docs/roadmap/reports/MOD.md)) and version 2 of the evidence page ([U4](docs/roadmap/reports/U4.md)). |

The local judge and the guard decide every pass or fail. Muse Spark
proposes, explains and checks, but it never changes a verdict.

## Quickstart

You need [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). The repo pins Python 3.12.

```sh
uv python install 3.12
uv sync
cp .env.example .env   # then set META_API_KEY for the Muse Spark features
LOBOT_MODEL=meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct uv run python -m model_lobotomy.server
```

Llama is gated: accept its license on Hugging Face, then run
`uv run hf auth login` once. Without `LOBOT_MODEL`, the server starts on

# AIBOSSPRO Meta Brain

An AI front desk for a small service business, built on Meta's models. The owner describes the business once, by voice or text; Muse Spark turns that into a structured "brain" (services, prices, hours, discount rules, tone, languages) that the owner reviews and approves. Customers then chat with an assistant (a customer panel, a terminal simulator, or WhatsApp) that answers in their language (English, Hebrew, Spanish, French), checks real availability, quotes prices computed by code, and requests bookings that only the owner can approve. Every model-generated reply passes a deterministic verifier before it is sent; hand-off notices and owner decision replies are fixed code strings, not model output. The same brain drives a content engine: SAM 3.1 cuts the product out of a photo, Muse Image paints a scene, code composites the offer and price, Spark writes a verified caption, Muse Wonder checks the result, and the owner approves it.

Every model-generated reply, and the hand-off notice, starts with an AI label ("[AI assistant]" in the customer's language). Nothing is booked without the owner's approval. Content is approved and exported as post and story assets; nothing is published to Instagram or anywhere else. Owner switches per conversation: AUTO, HUMAN, PAUSED.

**Everything you see is fictional.** The four demo businesses, their prices, customers ("Dana, 000-0000") and the bundled product photo are invented. Recorded model outputs live in `fixtures/replay/` and `provenance/`, and REPLAY runs say so on their header line and on every step line.

After switching Node versions, run `npm ci` again: modules built under one version fail under another (`NODE_MODULE_VERSION` mismatch, seen with Node 20 modules under Node 22).

cd ~                       # anywhere in your home directory, NOT /tmp (see "Where the ledger lives")

npm ci                     # run again after any Node version switch (native modules are built per Node version)
cp .env.example .env
npm run demo               # REPLAY: the recorded golden scenario, offline, no API key needed
```

# 3D-architect

From a rough hand-drawn floor plan to a home everyone can see, before a single brick is laid. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie Developer Track · Build for Your World).

[![3D-architect demo video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/m6icz-Cf_Sc/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://youtu.be/m6icz-Cf_Sc)

🎥 **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/m6icz-Cf_Sc

## Why

For most Indian families a home is built once in a lifetime, yet the plan usually lives on a rough sketch. Homeowners can't picture it, builders interpret it their own way, and the mismatch only shows once the walls are up. 3D-architect gives the family, the architect and the builder one shared picture to agree on. Anyone can start a project: a homeowner showing a builder "build this", or an architect sharing a vision with a family.

## Flow

1. **Sketch**: upload a photo of a hand-drawn plan and add plot size, facing, style and notes (any language).
2. **Plan**: Muse Spark reads the sketch, including handwritten labels and feet-inch sizes, into a structured floor plan of rooms, doors and windows. Room sizes are kept as drawn and can be corrected in a table.
3. **Questions**: the app checks the plan for dead-end corridors, rooms with no way in and space it had to fill. Muse Spark then asks plain-language multiple-choice questions instead of guessing, and revises the plan from your answers. The review repeats until nothing is unclear.
4. **Looks**: Muse Image renders the front elevation and each room in your style, using the sketch as a reference. Pick a favourite per part or change it in your own words ("add a brass diya at the pooja corner").
5. **3D**: the plan becomes a 3D house with shared walls, doors and windows. Step through construction stages (site marking → foundation → columns → brickwork → slab → plaster → finishing). Wall and floor colours come from the chosen renders.
6. **Furnish and tour**: Muse Spark studies the chosen renders and places matching furniture in every room, clear of doorways and with backs to walls. Walk through the house in first person (WASD) or take a guided tour room by room.

## Meta models

| Model | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`, `reasoning_effort: high`) | Reading the sketch, reviewing the plan and asking questions, revising the plan from answers, placing furniture (vision + structured JSON output) |
| Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`) | Elevation and room renders guided by the sketch, plain-language edits via `previous_response_id` |

All calls go through the Meta Model API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`) with the OpenAI-compatible SDK, from server-side route handlers so the API key never reaches the browser.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # add MODEL_API_KEY, or leave empty for mock mode
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000. Without `MODEL_API_KEY`, the API routes return a sample plan, placeholder images and a standard furniture layout, so the UI works offline.

# CaseBrief

**Evidence before confidence. Human authority stays human.**

CaseBrief is being developed as evidence-control infrastructure between AI output and consequential human decisions. This release candidate demonstrates bounded execution controls, artifact handling, and deterministic contract validation on one frozen synthetic fixture. It does not establish general model quality, automated evidence sufficiency, or production readiness.

## Five-Gate Architecture v1.0

**Inference success ≠ artifact readiness ≠ contract validity ≠ evidence sufficiency ≠ human authorisation.**

1. **Execution** — bounded request controls are implemented at demonstrated scope.
2. **Artifact** — bounded artifact capture and extraction are implemented at demonstrated scope.
3. **Contract** — deterministic structural validation is implemented at demonstrated scope.
4. **Evidence** — workflow-specific evidence review is human-led / proposed, not a proven automated service.
5. **Human Authority** — final authority remains human.

A human may stop or review at any gate. See the [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).

> vulnerability triage, a hard problem in software. The first commit dates from October 27, 2026, and the commit history

upload form to the function with the bug. Every step is certain, so no model judgment was

```bash

uv sync --locked --all-groups
uv run vexproof serve      # open http://127.0.0.1:8000 and choose Demo result
```

## The problem

Dependency scanners check **versions**, not **code**.

installs Pillow 4.3.0, it raises an alert. It never checks the second half: **does your code

# FusionPilot

A local TypeScript magnetic-design laboratory. Explore eight parameterized filament coils, calculate their vacuum magnetic field from Biot–Savart integration, and compare nominal-only and construction-tolerance-aware searches.

## Run

```sh
npm install
npm run dev -- --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5173
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173. The initial view immediately displays coils and measured field metrics; no backend, external model, or API key is required.

```sh
npm run build
npm test
```

## Workflow

1. Adjust coil radius, tilt and nonplanar amplitude.
2. Set translation tolerance, risk weight, length preference, and geometry/field constraints.
3. Choose a per-method field-evaluation budget and one, three, or five independent seeds.
4. Run the comparison. A dedicated Web Worker keeps the interface responsive; Cancel terminates it.
5. Inspect the three designs, held-out error distributions, constraint failures, and optimization history.
6. Toggle field lines, the reference overlay, or a 10× exaggerated construction-error overlay.
7. Export the experiment JSON. Import restores validated settings and the starting geometry; rerun to regenerate results. Unverified imported results are deliberately not displayed.

Settings and current geometry are saved locally. The last five completed runs remain available during the browser session. Export preserves their research data across sessions.

## Numerical model

- Fixed torus: major radius 1 m, minor radius 0.25 m.
- Eight smooth closed coil paths, fixed 100 kA per coil. Three shared shape parameters.
- Midpoint-rule Biot–Savart integration, using existing pure physics helpers.
- Search resolution: 48 segments per coil, 12 × 8 target-surface quadrature points.
- Validation resolution: 96 segments per coil, 28 × 16 points.
- Normalized normal-field error: `sum(w*(B.n)^2)/sum(w*|B|^2)`.
- Nominal objective: `error/0.03 + lengthWeight*length/30`.
- Robust objective: `(mean(error)+risk*std(error))/0.03 + lengthWeight*length/30`, using four fixed training translation samples and one nominal evaluation.
- Penalty of 1000 per violated constraint. Unsuccessful or infeasible designs remain labeled; a finite objective does not establish feasibility.
- Deterministic bounded random search. Both methods see the same seeded proposal sequence; robust evaluations consume five field evaluations versus one for nominal proposals. Actual counts are reported.
- Each coil's rigid translation is independent and uniform on each axis within ±tolerance. No independent node noise, rotations or shape errors are currently modeled.
- Twelve shared, independent held-out perturbation samples per seed. Separate validation budget: 42 field evaluations for the first seed, 28 per additional seed.
- Conservative spacing bounds for discretized filaments: node distances reduced by half the adjacent maximum segment lengths. Surface clearance uses the signed analytic torus distance reduced by half the maximum segment length.

# Suncheck

How much sun does this spot really get? Photograph the view from a balcony, a window or a garden corner; Suncheck traces
the real skyline, checks its own maths against the sun in your frame, and shows you the sun crossing your own sky for
every month of the year, with the hours of direct sun each month and a plain-English verdict.

Built from scratch for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (27 October to 4 November 2026) by Ayman with Claude Code.
Everything in this folder was written during the hackathon.

**Live:** https://suncheck-447203242444.me-central1.run.app (open it on a phone to sweep a view; a laptop sees the sample).
Demo spots: `/?job=tunisia` and `/?job=mexico` (real iPhone photos), `/?job=sample` and `/?job=istanbul` (Muse Image views,
said so on the page; the second is the one that opens the film).

**Demo video (2:28):** https://youtu.be/e447Y-fMn2g. Its opening view is a Muse Image generation run through this
pipeline like any photo; the film says so, then shows two real iPhone photos.

## What does the work

- **SAM 3.1** (Meta Model API) segments the sky and finds the sun in each photo, and names what blocks the sun: every
  building, tree, plant, wall, railing, overhang and hill, each asked for by its noun phrase and returned as a mask.
- **Our code** does the measurement: solar position (NOAA algorithm, checked against `astral` to 0.46°), a pinhole camera
  model with the phone's tilt from its accelerometer, the heading and the lens solved from the sun's position in the frame,
  the horizon profile from the sky mask (one obstruction elevation per half degree of azimuth), the minute-by-minute
  count of direct sun on the 21st of each month, and the bill: every blocked minute of every month is charged to the
  obstruction that hid the sun at that moment (its direction projected into the photo that covers it, the mask under
  that pixel takes the blame), so each blocker carries the hours a day it costs the spot in each month.
- **Muse Spark 1.3** words the result (what blocks the sun, good for, not for, one tip) from our numbers and answers the
  user's questions about the spot with the numbers in context.
- **Muse Image** generated the sample view shipped with the app (`suncheck/sample/`), which then went through the same
  pipeline as a real photo; the app says so.

The phone's compass is never trusted on its own: wherever the sun is in a frame, the sun fixes that frame's heading, and
the difference to the compass is applied to the frames without the sun. The hours count only the directions the photos
cover; the rest is always treated as blocked and the result says how much of the horizon was covered. No sky in any
frame gives "No sky in these photos", never a sunny answer.

## Run it

```bash
uv sync
printf 'META_API_KEY=...\n' > .env            # git-ignored
uv run python -m suncheck selftest            # synthetic skyline: geometry round trip, no API calls
uv run python -m suncheck analyze photos/*.HEIC --ou

# Unscrewed - Take it apart. You're not screwed.

Unscrewed is a disassembly record assistant. Take furniture or a gadget apart, photograph each step, write a line about it, and let Meta draft what went into each labeled bag. You confirm every count, then get your own steps back in reverse.

**What is different from manual logging apps:** most disassembly loggers only store what you type. Unscrewed uses Meta models to do real work: it transcribes spoken notes (Muse Voice Transcribe), reads every step photo (Muse Wonder) to note which part came off and what is attached to what, and cross-checks your notes for bags that disagree. Meta only suggests. Nothing counts until you confirm it, and screws are never counted from photos.

## Problem

When you take furniture or a gadget apart for a move or a repair, you put screws in labeled bags and snap photos. Weeks later you put it back together, staring at loose parts and mystery bags. Which bag goes where? Did you count right? Unscrewed turns your step photos, spoken or typed notes into a draft record with Meta models, then makes you confirm every count before it shows your steps in reverse.

## Built during the hackathon (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026)

Everything in this repository was created during the hackathon build period (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026):

- **Record safeguard system** (`lib/record.mjs`, browser build in `public/record-browser.js`): deterministic per-field provenance tracking. Visual estimates never overwrite user-reported values. Same-rank conflicts are registered, never silently resolved. Every field change keeps its full history.
- **5-screen UI flow**: Add steps (2 to 12 steps, one photo, one note and an optional voice note per step), Check (model output with evidence and photo observations), Confirm (explicit per-bag quantity confirmation, step mapping, conflict resolution), Put back (reverse-order reference, gated behind full confirmation), Activity (audit trail).
- **Validation pipeline** (`public/sample-data.js`, `lib/validate-output.mjs`): structural validation of Meta JSON. Bags come from Meta's answer (letters A to H, at most 8) joined with any bags the notes name; a bag the notes do not name stays visible with "Check this bag". Quantities must be positive integers, evidence ids are `stepN` (legacy `panelN` is still accepted), evidence must be non-blank, and conflicts are derived from reports (imported conflict status is ignored).
- **Three sample scenarios**: Normal (all data present), Missing (bag B has no quantity or step), Conflict (bag A reported as 6 and as 4). The five steps of a sample share one contact-sheet photo. Each is backed by a saved Meta Playground response in `fixtures/meta/`.
- **Live Meta pipeline** (`lib/live-meta.mjs`): server-side calls to the Meta Model API with request checks (same-origin plus `X-Unscrewed` header, rate limit, image and WAV header checks, body deadline), notes passed as fenced untrusted data, and a fail-soft deterministic check of every reported q

# LucidSync

LucidSync is a research and wellness tool that turns a morning dream memory into
structured, visualized, and labeled data. It is not a medical device and does
not diagnose.

## Current workflow: capture, code, storyboard, refine

The Streamlit form captures a report, waking mood, and vividness rating. Pydantic
models validate ordered scenes, stable character identities, objects, actions,
emotions, colors, and scene vividness. Each submitted record is saved under its
own `data/` session folder, which Git ignores.

The coding view asks Muse Spark for evidence-backed Hall/Van de Castle labels,
including the character, social interaction, activity, outcome, fortune,
emotion, setting, object, and descriptive-element categories. Each row includes
a short dream-report quote. In mock mode no content labels are invented.

Muse Image creates one local storyboard image per scene. Correction rounds are
chained to the prior image response, logged beside the image, and can be locked
with “That’s it”. Character descriptions are repeated in each scene prompt to
help preserve appearance. Live requests use the same Meta key and need the
consent checkbox in the app.

Corrections now ask Muse Spark to update the structured scene before Muse Image
renders the revision. The original report is retained. Each revision stores its
instruction, render prompt, round number, and structured record snapshot.
Coding is cleared after a correction so it can be regenerated deliberately.

## Grounded labeling and dataset export

After every frame is locked, **Label locked scenes** sends each character and
object name separately to SAM 3.1. The official Meta parser decodes the masks;
OpenCV/NumPy place them on the source image and draw labeled overlays. Missing
matches and multiple matches are shown for review. A name can match several
instances, so those candidates require human review before research use.

**Download session dataset (.zip)** exports final images, PNG masks, overlays,
the DreamRecord, saved coding JSON/CSV when available, storyboard correction
history, and COCO-style annotations with entity IDs and uncompressed RLE masks.
Mock mode exports no invented masks. Unlocking a frame invalidates its dataset.
All exports remain local until you choose to share them.

SAM integration follows the [Meta segmentation guide](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/sam/segmenting)
and uses `sam-3.1` through the same central API adapter.

# SnapDesk — Customer Support That Can See ((snap-desk.vercel.app))

> **Autonomous Visual Damage Triage & Policy Enforcement Agent**  
> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie Developer Track — *Push the Frontier* & *Best Agentic Use-Case*).

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Meta Models](https://img.shields.io/badge/Meta%20Models-SAM%203.1%20%7C%20Muse%20Spark%201.3%20%7C%20Muse%20Voice-6366f1.svg)](#meta-models--tooling)
[![Deterministic Guardrails](https://img.shields.io/badge/Financial%20Guardrails-Deterministic%20Plain%20Code-emerald.svg)](#architectural-principles)
[![Wrong-Approval Rate](https://img.shields.io/badge/Wrong--Approval%20Rate-0.0%25%20(Safety%20Target)-10b981.svg)](#benchmark-evaluation--honest-metrics)

---

## 1. Executive Summary & Problem

Most modern customer support tickets in e-commerce, delivery, appliance repair, and rentals require **visual evidence** (crushed parcel, cracked glass, dented bumper, wrong item).

Today, human support agents manually open each photo, subjectively eyeball the damage, cross-reference policy guidelines, and type replies. This process:
- Takes **3 to 5 business days** per resolution.
- Costs businesses **\$4.00 – \$8.00 per visual ticket**.
- Creates frequent disputes due to human inconsistency and subjective judgment.

### The Solution: SnapDesk
SnapDesk is an autonomous agent that **gives support software the ability to see**:
1. **Measures & Quantifies Damage:** Uses Meta **SAM 3.1** to segment products and calculate the exact damaged surface area ratio (`0.0% – 100.0%`).
2. **Applies Policy Under Strict Logic:** Uses Meta **Muse Spark 1.3** with JSON Schema structured outputs to apply the business's policy clauses and draft empathetic customer replies.
3. **Deterministic Financial Guardrails:** Plain-code safety limits (order value caps, anti-fraud image deduplication, confidence gates) strictly **override** the AI model whenever financial risk exceeds policy limits.
4. **Forensic Evidence Packet:** Produces an immutable audit trail with vector SVG mask overlays, quantitative measurements, cited policy clauses, and a step-by-step agent trace.

---

## 2. Core Architectural Principles

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. THE POLICY IS THE ONLY CONFIGURATION                                     │
│    The exact same engine powers parcel delivery, consumer appliances, and   │
│    vehicle rentals simply by swapping policy JSON templates.                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. THE MODEL NEVER HAS THE FINAL SAY ON MONEY                               │
│    LLMs are non-deterministic; financial payouts must be deterministic.    │
│    Plain-code guardrails enforce financial safety and force human handoffs. │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. FORENSIC EVIDEN

# Hermes Planner AI

## What this is

Hermes Planner AI organizes a life through natural language. One sentence can draft a Planner appointment, a Planner task, and a Contacts entry — each with an evidence line naming the item or document it links to, and each waiting for the person's Confirm before anything is stored.

Other organizers do appointments, tasks, journals, and inventory well. What sets Hermes apart is that it integrates them around the Item — because lives are all about items. Behind the drafts is the Hermes model: items are the atoms, and their fields are the nucleus.

Information is gathered through fields, grouped by field headers into sections, so a laptop, a boat, and a lease are not forced into the same fixed form. Fields are programmable: they come standard with each new workspace, a person can add one when the provided fields do not cover what they need, and fields flow into a Fields Library that any workspace can import.

The result is a flexible system that connects information, possessions, responsibilities, people, and activities through meaningful relationships. The demo runs on synthetic data only.

Underneath, the Hermes model classifies every item by Category, Owner, and Location — what it is, whose it is, and where it is — so a life stays organized from any angle.

## What the demo shows

One sentence — schedule boat maintenance, renew the boat insurance, add the service company to contacts — drafts three entries: a Planner appointment, a Planner task, and a Contacts entry, each with an evidence line and a Confirm button. The Boat already exists in the life store, so it appears as an evidence strip, never as a fourth draft. Three preset briefings answer from the same synthetic store: the week, what was actually carried out this month, and warranties and renewals in the next 90 days. Clicking Confirm marks a draft as Stored within the demo session; it does not write to a real Hermes Planner account or database.

## What the AI does, and what the demo app does

The demo calls the Meta Model API with muse-wonder-1.0, through the local server proxy. The model interprets the natural-language sentence and answers the briefings, using the synthetic life store sent with the request. The demo app holds that synthetic store, renders the drafts and their evidence lines, and holds each draft until Confirm. There is no live lookup against a real Hermes account, and the app itself does not do the language understanding. Each draft's evidence line names the item or document from the synthetic store that it links to.

## How to run it

From the demo folder (the folder containing `server.ps1`), start the local server:

```
powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\server.ps1
```

Then open http://localhost:8787/ — the server serves the page. Do not open index.html as a file; the live answers need the server running.

Prerequisites: Windows with PowerShell. Live answers need the local server running with a Meta Model

# Teaching Agent (CBC, Kenya)

A teaching agent for the Kenyan Competency-Based Curriculum — all levels
(Pre-Primary, Primary, Junior School, Senior School) and all learning
areas — forked from the
[legal-agent workshop](https://github.com/meta-models/legal-agent-workshop).
It plans term coverage from hand-built curriculum packs, quotes learning
outcomes exactly as printed in the official KICD designs, and files
documents (schemes of work, lesson plans, exams) for teacher sign-off.

Project scope is CBC-wide, one term per run. `docs/01-scope-and-permissions.md`
locks the Phase 1 slice: Grade 7, Term 1. Outcome text is copied exactly
from the official designs. The six Grade 7 Term 1 packs shipped here are
the current coverage, not the limit: new packs plug into the same schema,
pipeline, and console.

## Quick start

```bash
cp .env.example .env      # add MODEL_API_KEY; TEACHING_PACK_DIR names the pack
./helper setup            # creates .venv (OpenAI Python SDK), checks the key
```

The agent talks to the Meta Model API with the official OpenAI Python SDK
(`base_url=https://api.meta.ai/v1`). `./helper` runs everything with
`.venv/bin/python`.

To reproduce the project end to end on your own machine, follow
[REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md).

## Commands

```bash
./helper setup                         # set up env and seed the pack inbox
./helper test [--verification]         # offline tests; never call the live API
./helper run --turns 30                # run the agent
./helper run --resume RUN_ID --turns 15
./helper review RUN_ID --list          # one row per item, with curriculum text

# ClearCart Protocol + ClearCart Gate

**ClearCart: the agent-to-agent commerce protocol with the compliance gate built in, and a gate any agent can call on its own.**

Built by BakedBot AI for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley), Startup track.

> **Reference implementation.** This repository is a hackathon reference implementation. It is not a production system. It moves no money, collects no real identity documents, and contains no real customer data. See [docs/SAFETY.md](docs/SAFETY.md) before reading anything else into it.

## The problem

AI agents are about to do the buying, but age-restricted commerce has no legal way to sell to them. A buyer agent can browse a menu and fill a cart, yet the moment an order involves anything age-restricted, the flow stops, because there is no standard way for the buyer's verification status and the jurisdiction's purchase limits to be checked before money moves.

ClearCart is the missing layer, in two pieces:

1. **ClearCart Protocol.** A documented message flow and reference implementation for agent-to-agent commerce: a buyer agent discovers a merchant agent, reads its live menu, asks questions grounded in that menu, receives a quote, and pays through a compliant payment rail handoff. Every order passes through the compliance gate before a payment session exists.
2. **ClearCart Gate.** A standalone HTTP service with one job: given a buyer attestation ID and a cart of SKUs, answer APPROVE, DENY, or REVIEW with machine-readable reason codes and a signed, auditable decision receipt. Any agent, in any framework, can call it directly. It is not locked inside BakedBot's checkout.

Cannabis is the demo category because it is the hardest test case in retail: 21+ buyers, identity checks, and per-state purchase limits all apply at once. The gate is category-agnostic; the demo also shows it answering a plain API call for alcohol from an agent that is not part of this project.

## Why the gate is a rules engine, not a model

Compliance decisions must be reproducible and auditable, so the gate's decision path contains no language model at all. It is a deterministic rules engine over per-jurisdiction configuration: same inputs, same answer, every time, with a receipt to prove it. Language models (through the Meta Model API, behind the provider interface in `providers/`) do what they are good at in this system: the buyer agent's intent parsing and tool choices, the merchant agent's product answers grounded in menu data, and plain-language explanations of decisions the gate has already made.

The gate is an enforceable boundary, not an advisory check. It resolves everything that matters from its own server-side state, and payment refuses to proceed without its authorization:

# ESD-GUARD AI

**A robot on the Moon that sees what an object is made of and handles it so it does not cause an electrostatic discharge.**

Team Bravo · Meta Global AI Hackathon 2026 · theme: lunar exploration
Demo video: [▶ Watch on YouTube (3 min)](https://youtu.be/1ycFpVw9au0)

![Digital twin: the same real object handled on the Moon (left) and in an Earth factory (right)](docs/media/twin_moon_vs_earth.gif)

*Simulated. A real earbud case, photographed with a phone, handled by the Franka arm on the Moon at the
sun/shadow boundary (left: ground first, slow, grounding pad) and in an Earth factory at 50% humidity
(right: straight to the bin). ESD risk is an estimate, not a measurement.
[▶ Full 49 s video, three camera views](docs/media/twin_moon_vs_earth.mp4)*

![Real spacecraft incidents from charging and discharge](esd_guard/results/incident_cards.png)

## The problem

On the Moon there is no air and no humidity, so static charge has nowhere to go. The ground itself
charges: slightly positive in sunlight, about −100 V to −1 kV at night inside Earth's magnetotail, and
down to kilovolts during solar storms. In a ground test, a rover wheel driven over lunar dust simulant
in simulated solar-wind plasma charged to about −830 V and sparked after only 8.5 m (sources below).
Charging has already cost real missions (cards above). A robot that sorts samples, tools and bags on
the Moon touches plastics, fabrics and metals all day; each one charges and discharges differently.

## What ESD-GUARD does

```
camera ──► Meta vision models ──► material prior ──► ESD risk model ──► handling policy ──► Franka arm (MuJoCo)
           PE-Core (local)        metal/plastic/      lunar environment    speed, grip,        Moon gravity,
           Muse Spark (hosted)    fabric + doubt      profile              ground first,       regolith, sun/shadow
                                                                           slow release, pad
```

1. **See.** Meta **Perception Encoder (PE-Core-B16)** runs locally and gives zero-shot material
   probabilities. A "metal" answer is never trusted on vision alone (chrome-look plastic fools it),
   so it is always handled as possibly plastic. In the scanner, hosted **Muse Spark** gives a second
   opinion only when you press the button (cached, token-capped).
2. **Decide conservatively.** If the models are unsure or disagree, the robot acts on the **riskiest
   plausible material**. Appearance cannot prove what a surface is made of, so doubt always means caution.
3. **Score the risk** for the environment: quiet lunar day, night, the sun/shadow boundary
   (terminator), a plasma-sheet / solar storm, or an Earth factory. The score is a transparent,
   simulated estimate, **not a measurement**.
4. **Act.** The policy sets speed, grip force, a ground-rod touch before contact, slow release, the
   grounding pad instead of the bin, and re-grounding the held object before carrying it into shadow.
5. **Plan with Muse, guarded by rules.

**CMM works for the job seeker — it markets you, and it never lies for you.**

The zero-hallucination career agent with deterministic guardrails.

AI resume tools invent skills, beat the ATS, and get the job seeker
destroyed in the technical interview. CMM is the antidote: a multi-agent
system where Meta's Muse Spark agents do the reading and the drafting,
and a deterministic Python verifier — never an LLM — decides what the
seeker may truthfully claim.

You attest your skills once, with evidence and hard boundaries ("never
used Snowpark"). CMM hunts real postings on Dice and LinkedIn, reads each
one in full, and cross-checks every requirement against your proof. What
survives becomes an **Evidence Dossier** — the claims you can defend, the

And it finishes the job: when you click **Apply** on a role that passed,
CMM's Applier goes and submits the application for you, in your own
signed-in session, and brings back the employer's confirmation. Nothing

click.*

# Muse Panel for VS Code (unofficial)

> Not affiliated with or endorsed by Meta. Requires the Muse Code CLI and your own Muse Code subscription or API key.

Adds Muse as a coding panel in the VS Code **secondary (right) sidebar**, alongside tools like Claude Code, Codex, and Chat.

It talks to your local `muse` CLI (`muse exec --json`) — no separate API key or server. If `muse` works in your terminal, the panel works.

## Features

- **Right-sidebar chat** — streaming replies, tool-activity lines, Stop / Clear, conversation history in the view.
- **Copilot-style composer** — `Enter` sends, `Shift+Enter` inserts a newline, and pressing `Enter` while Muse is working queues a follow-up that sends automatically. The box auto-grows as you type.
- **Auto mode** — turn on the **Auto** button in the panel (or run *Muse: Toggle Auto Mode*) and Muse completes the whole task end-to-end without approval prompts. See the warning below before enabling it.
- **Editor context** — the active file (and selection, when present) is attached to each prompt and shown as a chip in the panel header.
- **Selection actions** — right-click selected code → *Muse: Ask about Selection / Explain Selection / Fix Selection*.
- **Interactive terminal** — *Muse: Open Interactive Terminal* launches the full `muse` TUI.
- **Configurable** — provider, model, reasoning effort, approval mode, and CLI path via Settings (`muse.*`).

> **Warning — Auto mode:** Auto mode skips every approval prompt, so Muse can edit files and run commands without asking. Use it only in trusted workspaces. It is off by default (`muse.autoMode: false`).

## Requirements

- VS Code 1.85+
- Muse Code CLI on your PATH (`muse --version` should work). Otherwise set `muse.cliPath`.

## Install

From this folder:

```bash
npm install
npm run compile
npx vsce package          # produces muse-panel-0.3.0.vsix
code --install-extension muse-panel-0.3.0.vsix
```

Then reload VS Code. The **✦ Muse** icon appears in the right sidebar; click it (or press `Cmd+Alt+M` / `Ctrl+Alt+M`) to open the chat.

For development, open this folder in VS Code and press `F5` (Extension Development Host).

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `muse.cliPath` | `muse` | Path to the muse executable |
| `muse.provider` | `meta` | `meta` (real model), `echo` (offline smoke test), `local` |
| `muse.model` | _(empty)_ | Model override; empty uses your muse settings |
| `muse.reasoningEffort` | `high` | `none` … `ultra` |
| `muse.autoMode` | `false` | Auto mode: complete the task without approval prompts (forces approval `never`). Toggle with the **Auto** button in the panel. |
| `muse.approvalMode` | `never` | Applies when Auto is off. Panel runs are headless, so approvals cannot be answered interactively; `never` allows edits like "Accept Edits". Set `on-request` to restrict. |
| `muse.includeFileContext` | `true` | Attach active file / selection to prompts |

## Quick smoke test (no model quota)

Set `muse.provider`

LoadMaster checks a loaded trailer against the federal cargo
securement rules (49 CFR Part 393, Subpart I) and tells the hauler, in
plain words, what to fix before the trailer rolls.

It is a rules system, not a picture describer. SAM 3.1 (Meta Model API)
segments the load, the trailer bed, the wheels and axles, and the
tie-downs, and turns those masks into measurements: tie-down count and
coverage, rear overhang, load balance against the axle position, tarp
coverage. A deterministic rules engine applies the actual securement
rules to those measurements and returns PASS, CHECK THIS, or COULD
NOT TELL for every check, with the rule citation and one specific fix
for every problem. Muse Spark (Meta Model API) turns those verdicts
into a plain-words report and independently cross-checks photos; when
the two models disagree, the verdict drops to CHECK THIS. A
fix-and-recheck loop lets the hauler correct what the camera missed

# IrysQuest

**An agent that notices which of your goals have stalled and proposes the smallest next move. It proposes, you approve.**

Built during the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon), 26 Oct – 4 Nov 2026, indie track.

**▶ [Watch the 3-minute demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sg_Gt-SzO2E)** · **[Try it with no accounts or keys](#try-it-in-two-minutes-no-accounts-no-keys-no-server)**: `pip install -e .`, then `irysquest demo`

> **What existed before, what is new.** [NextQuest](https://github.com/safphire/NextQuest), a local-first Android
> quest log with a self-hosted sync + MCP server, existed before the hackathon. Everything in *this* repository —
> the agent, its stall detection, the Muse-powered breakdowns, voice and notebook-photo capture — was built during the
> event. The app is not modified; the agent talks to it from outside, through the server's existing MCP endpoint.

## The problem

People with more intentions than attention lose goals two ways. Some are forgotten; NextQuest's two-second
capture is for those. The rest are **buried**: written down, known, and still not started, because each new want
lands on the last and the ones that mattered sink out of sight. That is procrastination, and it is what IrysQuest
is for.

Every productivity tool today waits for you to come back and ask for help. But a person who is stuck doesn't come
back; that's what stuck means.

IrysQuest is an agent that notices which goals have stalled and brings you the smallest possible next move. You
decide. It proposes, you approve; it never acts on its own.

## What it believes about procrastination

Procrastination is short-term mood repair, not laziness: the task feels bad to start, so we do something else. That
one finding decides how the coach behaves, and each behaviour below has research behind it.

| What the coach does | Why |
|---|---|
| Proposes steps of 2–10 minutes, never "plan" or "decide" | Lowering the cost of *starting* is the lever; completion takes care of itself |
| Attaches a when/where cue to each step ("after lunch, at the desk") | If-then plans are among the strongest goal interventions known |
