# Unscrewed - Take it apart. You're not screwed.

Unscrewed is a disassembly record assistant. Take furniture or a gadget apart, photograph each step, write a line about it, and let Meta draft what went into each labeled bag. You confirm every count, then get your own steps back in reverse.

**What is different from manual logging apps:** most disassembly loggers only store what you type. Unscrewed uses Meta models to do real work: it transcribes spoken notes (Muse Voice Transcribe), reads every step photo (Muse Wonder) to note which part came off and what is attached to what, and cross-checks your notes for bags that disagree. Meta only suggests. Nothing counts until you confirm it, and screws are never counted from photos.

## Problem

When you take furniture or a gadget apart for a move or a repair, you put screws in labeled bags and snap photos. Weeks later you put it back together, staring at loose parts and mystery bags. Which bag goes where? Did you count right? Unscrewed turns your step photos, spoken or typed notes into a draft record with Meta models, then makes you confirm every count before it shows your steps in reverse.

## Built during the hackathon (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026)

Everything in this repository was created during the hackathon build period (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026):

- **Record safeguard system** (`lib/record.mjs`, browser build in `public/record-browser.js`): deterministic per-field provenance tracking. Visual estimates never overwrite user-reported values. Same-rank conflicts are registered, never silently resolved. Every field change keeps its full history.
- **5-screen UI flow**: Add steps (2 to 12 steps, one photo, one note and an optional voice note per step), Check (model output with evidence and photo observations), Confirm (explicit per-bag quantity confirmation, step mapping, conflict resolution), Put back (reverse-order reference, gated behind full confirmation), Activity (audit trail).
- **Validation pipeline** (`public/sample-data.js`, `lib/validate-output.mjs`): structural validation of Meta JSON. Bags come from Meta's answer (letters A to H, at most 8) joined with any bags the notes name; a bag the notes do not name stays visible with "Check this bag". Quantities must be positive integers, evidence ids are `stepN` (legacy `panelN` is still accepted), evidence must be non-blank, and conflicts are derived from reports (imported conflict status is ignored).
- **Three sample scenarios**: Normal (all data present), Missing (bag B has no quantity or step), Conflict (bag A reported as 6 and as 4). The five steps of a sample share one contact-sheet photo. Each is backed by a saved Meta Playground response in `fixtures/meta/`.
- **Live Meta pipeline** (`lib/live-meta.mjs`): server-side calls to the Meta Model API with request checks (same-origin plus `X-Unscrewed` header, rate limit, image and WAV header checks, body deadline), notes passed as fenced untrusted data, and a fail-soft deterministic check of every reported q

# SecondCall AI — Debbie, Rebuilt on Meta's Muse Models

> **Debbie existed. Her brain is new.**
> SecondCall AI is a live product: an AI phone agent ("Debbie") that answers calls for local home-service businesses (HVAC, roofing, plumbing, garage door, electricians), books jobs, and sends proof after the call. For six production days in October 2026 she placed ~565 real calls and booked **zero** demos — losing the thread mid-conversation, pitching into voicemail, and once hanging up on a live human. This repository is the rebuild of her conversation engine on Meta's Muse models — and the scored rematch against every one of those failures.
>
> Evidence for the ~565-call / zero-demo baseline: [`scorecard/FAILURE-SCORECARD.md`](scorecard/FAILURE-SCORECARD.md) (baseline table, Oct 19–24).

**Live product (pre-existing):** secondcallaii.com — website, demo-request form, and Missed-Call Scan.
**Inbound demo number: (718) 400-7035 — CERTIFIED, Oct 31, 2026.** Inbound (failure item **F10**) is answered by the breakdown-and-book v1 flow: proof call #2 passed the owner's bar on all five points (breakdown given first, questions before any pitch, name + number + email captured and spelled back, booking claimed only when complete), and the identical configuration was then rolled out to **all six SecondCall numbers — byte-identical per-number records, verified** — with a spot-check proof on a second number also passing all five points. (This label replaces the Oct 31 "NOT YET VERIFIED" holding note, which stood until the proof transcript existed.)

---

## THE PROCESS LEDGER — the headline idea

**Every process Debbie runs writes to one ledger. The owner Debrief reads it.**

Inbound answer → intake → booking → proof-after-call → follow-up → QA verdict — there are no separate logs. The pre-close gate's dispositions and the QA verdicts are ledger writes, not side files. On a schedule the business owner sets, Debbie **calls the owner** and speaks the day's ledger in her one voice: calls handled, calls missed, jobs booked, follow-ups owed — and what went wrong, in plain words (the failure-mode flags that fired). The ledger grades Debbie against **each customer's own task profile** (standing tasks, urgency rules, headline numbers, debrief time — data, not code): done / owed / slipped.

Why this is the architecture, not a feature: the Oct 19–24 failure was invisible until humans read ~565 transcripts by hand. A system that writes everything it does — including its own gate denials — to one ledger can report on itself, out loud, to the person who pays for it.

# Frontier gene writers — 모델 파이프라인 스캐폴드 (Phase 1)

치료용 유전자 삽입을 위한 프로그래머블 recombinase/transposase를 에이전트로
발굴하는 **모델 파이프라인**의 Phase 1 스캐폴드다. 100% dry-lab(코딩のみ)이며,
습식 실험 검증은 포함하지 않는다.

- **로드맵**: `../files/build-roadmap.md` (Phase 1: MGnify 필터 추출, 평가 기준 정의, 에이전트 루프 뼈대)
- **워크플로우**: 쿼리 → 교집합 → 티어링 → 랭킹 → (선택적 Muse Wonder 검토)
- **데이터**: MGnify Proteins 2026_07 (5.7B, CC0). 전체 다운로드는 하지 않는다.

## 구조

```
frontier-gene-writers/
├── README.md
├── submission-boundary-log.md  # 행사 기간 신규 작업 구분 기록
├── requirements.txt
├── run_test_query.py      # 탐색 규모 테스트 쿼리 (PF00239)
├── run_wonder_demo.py     # Wonder end-to-end 데모 런 (파이프라인 + Wonder 검토)
├── results/               # 데모 런 결과 JSON (증거용)
└── src/
    ├── mgnify.py           # MGnify API + DuckDB 원격 Parquet 조회
    ├── filter.py           # LSR 코어/보너스 티어 필터 + 랭킹 (tie-break 포함)
    ├── evaluate.py         # 평가 기준 스텁 (Phase 2에서 구현)
    └── agent_loop.py       # 워크플로우 뼈대 + Muse Wonder 호출
```

## 설치

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## 실행

```bash
# 탐색 규모 테스트 쿼리 (PF00239, 기본 10건)
python3 run_test_query.py

# 전체 워크플로우 뼈대 (쿼리 → 교집합 → 티어링 → 랭킹)
python3 -m src.agent_loop
# 또는
python3 -c "from src.agent_loop import run_pipeline; run_pipeline(limit=50, detail_limit=20)"

# Wonder end-to-end 데모 런 (파이프라인 + 커넥터 헬퍼 경유 Wonder 검토, 결과 JSON 저장)
python3 run_wonder_demo.py
```

## Muse Wonder 연결 (Meta Model API)

API 키는 환경변수 `META_API_KEY`에서만 읽는다. 코드에 키를 하드코딩하지 않는다.

```bash
# .env 파일 (gitignore에 포함됨 — 커밋되지 않음)
META_API_KEY=여기에_키_입력
# 모델 ID 변경 시 (기본값: muse-wonder-1.0)
META_MODEL=muse-wonder-1.0
```

키가 없으면 LLM 호출을 건너뛰고 필터 기반 랭킹만 반환한다. 키 발급은
dev.meta.ai에서 하며, 발급된 키는 채팅·파일·커밋 어디에도 붙여넣지 않는다.
키를 직접 쓸 수 없을 때는 커넥터 헬퍼 경유 런(`run_wonder_demo.py`)을 쓴다.
Wonder도 추론 토큰을 먼저 쓰므로 max_tokens는 8000으로 넉넉히 잡는다.

## 필터 요약 (Phase 1 MGnify 필터 노트 기준)

- 코어 풀: PF00239(Ser_recom) + PF07508(Recombinase) 둘 다 보유
- 보너스 티어: PF13408(Zn_ribbon_recom) 보유, 또는 길이 450–700 aa
- PF13408을 필수로 하지 않는다 (Zn-ribbon이 없는 기능성 인테그라제도 있음)

## 주의 (함정)

- MGnify API search는 필터를 **정확히 하나**만 받는다 (없거나 두 개 이상이면 422).
  limit 기본 50, 최대 1000, 단일 페이지, 페이지네이션 없음 — 탐색용이다.
- API detail 레코드는 클러스터 대표에만 존재한다.
- 큰 풀은 DuckDB 원격 Parquet 조회(`src/mgnify.py::query_pfam_parquet`)로.
  Parquet의 `pfam_accession`은 숫자다 (PF00239 → 239).
- Google Cloud BigQuery 공개 데이터셋은 2024-04 릴리스에 머물러 있다.
  2026_07은 FTP/HMMER/포털에만 있다.
- HMMER 웹 검색은 전체 5.7B가 아니라 MGnify30 클러스터 대표 부분집합을 쓴다.

## 제출 경계

이 디렉토리의 코드는 행사 기간(2026-10-26 ~ 11/4)에 새로 만든 작업이다.
자세한 구분 기록은 `submission-boundary-log.md`를 본다.

# Context Bible — Scholar Agent

A **verifiable scholar-citation agent** for Bible questions, built for the
Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (November 2026), Indie Developer Track,
"Build for Your World."

## What it does

Ask a Bible question — for example, *"What did Jesus mean by 'I am the way,
the truth, and the life'?"* — and the agent answers **only** with what named,
published scholars have written about the passage, with inline citations like
(Carson 1991). Before the answer is shown, a second model call verifies every
factual claim in the draft against the retrieved scholar sources; unsupported
claims are stripped and the answer is regenerated once, and the UI displays
the verification report next to the answer.

## The design principle

**The AI cites scholars, not Scripture.**

Many readers find it unethical and unspiritual for an AI to summarize or
speak for the biblical text itself. This agent sidesteps that entirely: it
never paraphrases the Bible and never offers its own interpretation. It is a
research librarian with a verification habit — it retrieves what scholars
such as D. A. Carson, Raymond E. Brown, John Goldingay, and Derek Kidner
have published, reports their readings with citations, and then proves that
every claim it made actually appears in those sources.

This is deliberately *not* a generic RAG chatbot: the point of the system is
the **agent loop plus the verification loop** — tool use to gather admissible
evidence, a constrained draft, and an independent checker pass that can send
the draft back for revision.

## Architecture

```
User question

     ▼
Agent loop (Muse Spark 1.3, Meta Model API, tool calling)
     ├─ tool: identify_passages — maps the question to passage
     │        references via a small local index
     └─ tool: search_scholars — retrieves entries from the local
              scholar library (scholars.json)
     │
     ▼
Constrained draft — only claims present in retrieved entries,
each with an inline (Surname Year) citation
     │
     ▼
Verifier pass (second Muse Spark 1.3 call)
     — extracts every factual claim in the draft and checks it
       against the retrieved entries; returns a structured verdict
       {claims_checked, claims_supported, unsupported_claims}
     │
     ├─ unsupported claims found → regenerate once without them → re-verify
     ▼
UI: answer + tool-call trace + verification report + source list
```

# AccessiWeb Engine

AccessiWeb Engine is a TypeScript monorepo starter for AI-assisted accessibility audits and reviewable GitHub remediations.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Browser[React and Vite frontend] -->|HTTPS| Functions[Azure Functions API]
  Functions -->|Managed identity| Cosmos[(Cosmos DB)]
  Functions -->|Key Vault references| Vault[Azure Key Vault]
  Functions -->|Configured model endpoint| Meta[Meta-compatible Model API]

  Functions --> Insights[Application Insights]
  Actions[GitHub Actions] -->|Subscription Bicep deployments| Azure[Azure resource groups]
  Actions -->|Build and deploy| Browser
  Actions -->|Build and deploy| Functions
```

The Azure resources and CI/CD workflows are defined under `infra/bicep` and `.github/workflows`. See [Platform Engineering](docs/PLATFORM_ENGINEERING.md), [Security](SECURITY.md), [Privacy](PRIVACY.md), and the [Hackathon submission draft](docs/HACKATHON_SUBMISSION.md) for deployment and project details.

## Experiences

- **Web URL audit:** Fetches public HTML, optionally interprets a user-provided screenshot with Muse Spark, produces a structured WCAG report, and can open a GitHub issue.

- **Private remediation preview:** Requires an Entra ID B2C token, the global `FEATURE_ENABLE_AUTO_PR_PREVIEW` switch, the user's Cosmos DB preview flag, and an allowlisted repository. The API first returns the exact patch plan for review; a short-lived server-signed approval is required to publish that unchanged plan in a verified bot-owned public fork. It never pushes to the upstream repository.

Reports are stored in Cosmos DB; raw HTML and source file contents are only passed through memory for analysis. GitHub issue content is rendered server-side from a saved repository report. Generated changes are not published until a user reviews and approves the exact plan, and are never merged automatically.

## Local setup

Requirements: Node.js 22+, npm 10+, and Azure Functions Core Tools v4 to run the API locally.

```sh

# Oddhound: find what you didn't test

**General AI browser agents can report a bug. Oddhound proves one, and proves the fix.**
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track), Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026.

- **Live app:** https://danravekeh123--oddhound-web.us-east.modal.run (press **Try the demo target**, no sign-in)
- **Submission write-up:** [docs/SUBMISSION.md](docs/SUBMISSION.md) · **Honest status:** [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md)

Oddhound is an active exploratory-testing agent for web apps, driven by **Meta Muse Spark**:

1. **Paste your site and prove you own it** once (a DNS record, a `/.well-known` file or a meta tag). Oddhound keeps
   checking until it sees the token, then Muse Spark reads the home page and drafts focus areas and business rules.
2. **Oddhound explores** in a fresh, isolated, secret-free browser: it signs up synthetic accounts, completes
   workflows, and tries boundary values, blank input, odd orderings, a second account and a 390 px phone.
3. **Every suspected rule violation is replayed independently**, twice, in fresh sessions (with a valid control where
   one exists), before it is called **verified**.
4. **Copy the fix prompt** into your coding AI, ship, then **retest**: Oddhound replays the exact, unchanged assertion.
   A deploy hook does this after every deploy in CI.

Highlights:

- **A real production bug, fixed and proven:** on the Alaala memorial site one 1,200-character condolence made pages
  10,465 px wide on a 390 px phone; verified by two replays, fixed in 16 lines, retest Fixed with no model call.
- **Demo target:** a signed-out run verified 5 seeded functional bugs and 3 configuration issues for $0.04; a retest
  on the corrected build marked every finding fixed with the assertion hash unchanged.
- **Tests:** 257 unit tests and 90 integration tests (vitest), 7 UI tests (node --test).
- **Deployed on Modal:** web, a worker with separate lanes for site runs and demos/retests, demo targets, and a fresh
  browser sandbox per run.

## Layout

```text
apps/fixture   demo target (Harbor Table) with five labelled defects and a --fixed build
apps/browser   secret-free per-run browser image: Playwright server (non-root, sandboxed Chromium), SSRF egress proxy, nftables

ChibuikemJosh/ForgeGuard.readme_excerpt:
Forge Guard

Forge Guard is an AI-powered software engineering and security analysis environment. It inspects existing Python projects, builds a read-only **SourceGraph** from their structure, and investigates user-defined security or business rules with a Meta Muse-powered agent. Findings are evidence-gated: the backend validates reported source locations before returning them. Fix proposals require human approval before application; apply and rollback are supported. ## Problem statement Modern applications often fail in business logic and authorization paths that are hard to see from framework-level scanning alone. Forge Guard connects project structure, source evidence, and AI-assisted investigation so that potential violations can be traced to real files, symbols, and graph nodes. ## Features - Register an existing Python project inside a configured workspace root (sample or folder upload). - Discover and index Python source files via AST (code is never executed). - Resolve structural symbols and relationships. - Generate a read-only SourceGraph with drill-down levels (project → folder → file). - Investigate user-provided security rules with Meta Muse. - Validate model-proposed source locations against actual source. - Map valid findings to SourceGraph nodes. - Review, apply, roll back, and verify controlled corrections. - Download fixes as a `.patch` (`git apply`) or the project copy as a `.zip`. - Deterministic backend tests for investigation and evidence validation. ## Core workflow 1. Upload a Python project folder (or open the sample — each visitor gets their own copy). 2. Index its source and generate its SourceGraph (Map). 3. Provide a security or business rule and run an investigation, watching live agent activity. - Sample project: 3 demo preset rules (default: order ownership). - Uploaded projects: rules generated from routes and resource IDs, or a custom rule you write. 4. Understand findings and validated source evidence with SourceGraph node matches. 5. Review the proposed fix side-by-side on the Changes tab; approve or reject it. 6. Apply the fix, or roll it back. 7. Re-run the investigation to verify. 8. Download your fixes as a `.patch` or the project copy as a `.zip`. ## Architecture Forge Guard is a modular FastAPI monolith. The frontend renders backend-provided data and does not infer source facts. | Component | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | `WorkspaceService` | Discover and safely read project files | | `PythonIndexer` | Extract structural AST facts | | `SymbolResolver` | Resolve structural relations

Chandresh-Gohel/NASA_CMAPSS_Meta_Global_.readme_excerpt:
# Engine Health Agent Calibrated remaining-useful-life (RUL) predictions for turbofan engines, a decision engine that knows when to abstain, and Muse Spark agents that explain every call. > **Decision support on NASA's simulated C-MAPSS benchmark.** Not an airworthiness determination: a licensed engineer > makes the final decision. **Live app:** [Live app](https://cgcmapsssimgp.streamlit.app/) · **Demo video:** [Demo video](https://youtu.be/3SeoF6LADgI) ## What it does 1. **Predicts remaining useful life with a 90% band** for every engine, from its sensor history. 2. **Turns the band into one of three calls in plain code**, never by a language model: - **🔧 INSPECT** when the chance of failing within the next 30 cycles is at least 50%; - **✅ NO_INSPECTION** when it is at most 10%; - **⚠️ ABSTAIN** (engineer review) when it is in between, when a sensor looks broken, or when the engine is unlike anything in training. 3. **Muse Spark agents explain the call:** which sensors drive it, what to do next, and why the system abstains. A safety reviewer checks every briefing, and a planner turns the fleet into a hangar schedule. **Highlights** (official NASA test engines and 106 held-out engines replayed to failure): - 0 of 106 failures missed; fixed-interval maintenance misses 42. - Every injected sensor fault and every unfamiliar engine is refused and sent to an engineer, instead of getting a confident wrong number. - Error in the last 30 cycles before failure, where decisions are made: 3.5–6.5 cycles. - The 90% bands cover 0.88–0.93 of test engines on three subsets, and 0.83 on FD004. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Sensor history
NASA C-MAPSS] --> B[Multitask deep kernel learning
CNN features + Gaussian process] B --> C[Conformal calibration
90% band per subset] C --> D{Decision engine
plain code} S[Sensor checks] --> D B --> U[Unfamiliar-engine gate] --> D B --> X[Integrated Gradients
sensor drivers] D --> M[Muse Spark agents
analyst, writer, reviewer, planner] X --> M M --> APP[Streamlit app] ``` - **Data:** - the 14 informative sensors; - normalisation per operating condition (k-means; 6 conditions in FD002 and FD004); - 30-cycle windows; - RUL capped at 125 cycles; - splits by engine, never by window: train/validation/calibration/replay = 0.60/0.10/0.15/0.15 of the training files. The official test engines are used only for the final evaluation. - **Model:** a residual 1D CNN with spectral normalisation feeds a sparse variational Gaussian process (GPyTorch). The four subsets share three latent processes (linear model of coregionalisation), and each subset gets its own output. The model returns a mean, an epistemic uncertainty ("the model hasn't seen engines like this") and an aleatoric uncertainty (sensor noise). - **Calibration:** Mondrian split-conformal, per subset and per predicted-RUL range, with separate lower and upper edges

# Brandklipparen

**Scan before you swap.** A deterministic risk scanner for ERC-20 tokens
on Ethereum mainnet: paste a token address and see what the contract's
owner can do to you, proven from the bytecode.

Live demo: https://jensmannen--brandklipparen.us-east.modal.run. Judges: the access code and API key are in the submission form.

*The name: Brandklipparen was the royal horse of Sweden's Charles XI and
XII, a horse that never flinched at fire. The tool does the same: it
stays calm and reads the contract while the market is on fire.*

How it was built: one person, a team of agents — see [docs/HOW-IT-WAS-BUILT.md](docs/HOW-IT-WAS-BUILT.md).

Demo video: https://youtu.be/DFUeeQChwZ8

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon entry · Indie Developer track ·
"Build for Your World".

## What it does

- **Reads the contract, not the hype.** For a new token (a memecoin
  launched ten minutes ago, say) it lists the owner powers written into
  the code: pause transfers, mint, blacklist wallets, change the transfer
  fee, cap wallets, block sells, upgrade the code.
- **Its own EVM decompiler.** Written in this project and run
  in-process (no external binary): disassembly, control-flow graph, a
  symbolic pass over storage slots and caller guards, then readable
  pseudo-Solidity. Verified source is shown beside it when published.
- **Proof, not a verdict.** Every finding is pinned to the function,
  selector and byte offset. Pause, blacklist, transfer fee, transfer
  limits and mint also get a step-by-step proof trace that shows each
  check and where a failed proof stopped.
- **Meta Muse explains, never decides.** Optional Explain, Ask, Explain
  this code and Investigate run on the Meta Model API (Muse,
  `muse-spark-1.3`). Every claim must cite evidence the analysis
  collected, or it is dropped. Model output never changes the score or
  the evidence.
- **For people and for agents.** The web UI, the versioned REST API
  (`/v1`) and the MCP server over stdio return the same deterministic
  result: same bytecode, same pinned block, same answer.
- **Honest about what it can't see.** A check that cannot finish reads
  "Can't tell", never "safe". The model score is weak and labelled
  so (see [Calibration and limits](#calibration-and-limits)). Bytecode
  says nothing about liquidity locks, insider holdings or the team.

## What it is

Brandklipparen assesses the rug-pull risk of ERC-20 tokens from
contract bytecode, paired with point-in-time on-chain context. The
proofs are derived deterministically from bytecode. The score is a
calibrated model score plus an evidence floor. The scanner reads the
owner live, and the floor can raise the score. Other on-chain context
and verified source are shown beside them and never change the score.
Every score is shown together with the evidence that produced it, so
the result can be inspected and reproduced.

- **Deterministic core.** Pure TypeScript with no I/O. Runtime

# CanonTracker

CanonTracker helps writers and narrative teams keep a story world consistent. Import lore, chapters, scripts or recordings; review AI-proposed facts with their source quotes; then check accepted canon for contradictions and inspect the 1–2 hop impact of a proposed change. People decide what becomes canon. It works for novels, games, screen stories and worldbuilding, solo or in a studio.

Meta AI Developer Hackathon · Startup track. **Demo video:** [youtu.be/tb1EZ1d2VSk](https://youtu.be/tb1EZ1d2VSk) · **Live app:** [canontracker.trythis.work](https://canontracker.trythis.work) (no account needed: press **Try the demo**) · **On X:** [the announcement](https://x.com/ugorur/status/2118009201008275642).

## For judges: two minutes, nothing to install

1. Open [canontracker.trythis.work](https://canontracker.trythis.work) and press **Try the demo**. You get a guest studio with three projects and the guided tour starts.
2. Follow the tour's five steps in **Broken Tide**: reject a figurative "sister" the AI took literally, see a made-up quote that can't get into canon, accept what holds up, catch a conflict, and see which scenes a rule change would affect before it ships.
3. Switch project (top left) to **The Ashbell Pass**, a game with 28 documents, or **Sherlock Holmes**, 31 chapters and stories by Doyle.
4. Try the AI on your own text: drop a `.md`, `.txt` or `.docx` on the Library, or ask a question in **Ask**. On the live site these run on Muse Spark.
5. Open **Agent activity** to see every AI run: model, prompt version, steps and what people did with the result.

The samples open with most canon in place, labelled "Sample canon (preloaded)"; their AI output was recorded from real Muse runs and replays, so the demo opens at once. Anything you upload is read live. Every canon fact still cites a passage, and nothing becomes canon without a person.

## What's in it

- A multi-user SaaS: sign-up, studios, owner/admin/editor/viewer roles, invite links and separate projects.
- Import Markdown, text, Word, screenplays (Fountain), game dialogue (Yarn, Ink), CSV/JSON and audio; a whole manuscript splits into chapters.
- Versioned sources that are never changed: new versions flag the citations that need a re-check.
- AI-proposed facts with a quote checked word for word against the source, a second AI critic, and a person deciding every canon fact.
- Conflict checks: two places at once, travel too fast, relationships after they end, acts after death, one detail with two answers, and AI-suggested world-rule breaks.
- Change impact: what a proposed change touches, two hops deep, with path and evidence, before it is applied; apply and revert.
- An entity wiki that files itself from canon, with merges, a relationship graph and a story-time or reading-order timeline.
- Ask (team conversations grounded in canon), Research (web sources and calculators, never canon) and Continuity checks of a draft.
- Voice: recordings become timed transcripts, script

LessonCast

A textbook PDF, or a photographed page, in; narrated, illustrated video lessons out,
in the language the children speak at home. Education without borders.


The water cycle in Swahili, the clouds lit as the voice says wingu. The lungs in Yoruba. A quiz question, answered.

## Why Many children in Cameroon, and across Africa, learn in French, English, Portuguese or Spanish: a language they don't speak at home. Science, history and geography reach them in that imported language, while the language they think in, and the culture it carries, stays outside the classroom. Classes are crowded, textbooks are shared, mobile data is expensive, and the printed page stays at school. LessonCast carries the lesson across that border. The teacher uploads the textbook they already have, or photographs a page of it, and a few minutes later gets a short video that explains it in the language of home, keeping the subject's own terms and explaining them, so a child can learn science without leaving their language behind. The video is small enough for the parents' WhatsApp group, and a parent can replay it with the child at night. It started in Cameroon, and it isn't only for Cameroon: a page in any school language can become a lesson in any language Muse Spark writes and an MMS voice reads, in Africa or anywhere a country's own languages are kept out of its schools. Eight today, from Hausa to Swahili; each new MMS voice can join them. ## What a teacher does 1. Uploads the whole textbook as a PDF, which Muse Spark splits into lessons, or photographs one to four pages. 2. Picks the language, the length (15 s to 3 minutes), the quiz (none to five questions) and the picture style, or lets LessonCast choose from the pages. 3. Gets the video a few minutes later, with its scenes, its voice, subtitles that light up each spoken word and the objects the voice names, then the quiz read aloud. An AI creates each asana as a short sequence of steps with a drawn character for every step; you then practise in front of your camera, hands-free, and get a spoken, step-by-step check of your pose. # Chitchat Tour

**Little sourced stories about the street you're on.**

You put your phone in your pocket and walk. When you pass something ordinary — a convenience store, a garbage truck playing Für Elise, a scooter waiting box, a red-and-green postbox — Chitchat Tour tells you one short, sourced piece of trivia about it. It only picks things that are likely to be *new to you*, and it compares them with how things work elsewhere.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Developer track, theme "Build for Your World". The demo city is Taipei, on a route around Yongkang Street and Dongmen.

**Try it:** https://chitchat-tour.vercel.app — on any phone or desktop browser, tap **Try the simulated walk** (no GPS needed), or open `/demo/compare` to watch a Tokyo visitor and a New York visitor walk the same street side by side.

## Why

Most city guides talk about landmarks. What visitors actually notice and wonder about is the everyday stuff: why the garbage truck plays music, why every arcade has a step, why there are so few public bins. And what is surprising depends on where you come from. A visitor from Tokyo and a visitor from New York walking the same street should not hear the same things.

Principles:

- **Everyday things over landmarks.**
- **Never say what we cannot source.** Every fact has a source the user can open; if the model cannot find one on a trusted site, the guide stays quiet.
- **Don't interrupt.** Speak only when something is actually there, at most one short line at a time, with cooldowns.
- **Never analyse people.** Faces are blurred on the device before a photo leaves the phone.

## What it does

- **Walk.** A map follows you (real GPS, or a simulated walk for the demo). The simulated walk replays a real recorded Muse Spark walk down Yongkang Street for a visitor from Tokyo (six stories, pre-recorded voice), and pauses when you switch tabs. When you come near something the knowledge base covers, the guide decides whether it is worth saying *for you* and speaks it in a sentence or two, with a "here / in many places" comparison and a source card.
- **Ask.** Type or hold to talk ("why are there so many convenience stores?"). Muse Spark searches the web, and the answer only keeps sources from an allow-list of trusted domains (government, universities, major newspapers…).
- **Live discovery.** Outside the hand-made knowledge base, the app looks up places ahead of you on OpenStreetMap and has Muse Spark research them on the web, showing its steps as a readable timeline. Only whitelisted, cited findings become narrations.
- **Destination walks.** Pick a destination; you get walking directions with spoken turn cues, rerouting, and suggestions for small detours that pass something interesting.
- **Photo.** Point the camera at something. Faces are blurred on the device, Muse Spark finds the objects, SAM 3.1 cuts them out, and the cut-out becomes a die-cut sticker in your notebook, with the trivia attached if we have it.

# LX harness

You've built an AI agent that handles a task well. Could a smaller model, perhaps
one running locally, do it just as well? Finding out can mean repeatedly tweaking
prompts, skills and configurations without knowing how much work it will take.

**LX gives another agent a platform to investigate that question for you.** Built
on harness2-cli through the [portable execution core](https://github.com/shrey160/harness2-portable-core),
LX runs a worker/improver loop that refines the prompts, skills and helper scripts
around a model while keeping its weights fixed. Connect your existing coding agent
through MCP, provide sample tasks and inspect the evidence from each attempt.
LX provides connection setup for Claude Code, Muse Code and Codex; other
MCP-compatible clients can use its stdio server with their own client setup.

The goal is to find out whether a task fits a smaller model and how few harness
edits it takes. A run can reveal a useful change, a failure or a base setup that
already works; improvement is something to test and validate.

[![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-FF0000?style=for-the-badge&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/YcyyPwPcKYc)

To begin, give your coding agent [this repository](https://github.com/shrey160/lx-harness)
and ask it to install LX and connect through MCP. Configure model providers and
external tools in the Web UI, then give the agent your sample data and goal. It can
prepare the workspace and spec, and run experiments when you request them.

The usual workflow is:

**Clone inside your project → configure LX in the Web UI → connect your agent
through MCP → prepare a task → run within your budget → inspect results.**

You can also work directly in the Web UI or CLI. Your external agent uses its own
model as orchestrator; LX supplies the configured worker, improver and task tools.

## What was built during the hackathon

**The LX application in this submitted repository was built from scratch during
the hackathon.** Our work includes the Web UI, CLI and agent-facing MCP server;
task/workspace setup; model and tool integrations; budgets and approval controls;
optional checks and model judges; and run monitoring, trajectory inspection and
export. The example datasets, experiment reviews and installation evidence are
also included in this repository.

**The execution core builds on existing open-source work.** We vendored the
independent [harness2-cli](https://github.com/3ae3ae/harness2-cli) engine into the
separate [portable core repository](https://github.com/shrey160/harness2-portable-core)
and adapted it to fit LX, with a managed execution/recovery layer and local Windows
compatibility patches. The underlying harness-refinement loop comes from upstream;
it is not claimed as an algorithm invented for this submission.

Upstream licenses and attribution are retained. The core's
[provenance and patch history](https://github.com/shrey160/harness2-portable-core/blob/main/UPSTREAM.md)

You tell it a task out loud ("Agent, post 'I'm really excited to join this' in the intros channel of the Meta hackathon Discord") and it does the task in your real apps, by looking at the screen and clicking, typing and reading the way a person would. A business pastes its website. Meta's models run the whole creator campaign: they write the brief, choose creators, and check every draft video against the brief, with proof, before the brand sees it.

OOCM ([outofcontextmarketing.com](https://outofcontextmarketing.com)) is a live creator-marketing platform. This repository holds **only the code written during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (27 Oct to 4 Nov 2026)**. It plugs into OOCM's existing product, which was built before the event and is not part of this submission.

## Demo video

# Finguard

![No source. No sign-off. Muse retrieves. Code verifies. Person approves. Finance Harness Powered by Meta Muse. A real S-1 table with the net loss cell, (80,748), marked in red.](docs/img/thumbnail.png)

**A finance harness inspired by DeepSeek Harness, running on Meta Muse.**

Finguard checks every number in an investment memo against the filing. A fund then builds its own rules, valuation methods and workflows on top, as plugins. Every plugin states in code whether it reads or acts, who must approve it, and how its result is verified.

**Try it:** https://finguard-157951168487.asia-south1.run.app

**Built with:** We used Meta Wonder and Claude Opus 5.5 to build this. Meta Muse Spark 1.3 runs inside it.

![Finguard checking an investment memo. Two numbers are ringed in red as wrong, and the filing page beside them shows the cell code read.](docs/img/check.png)

## Try the demo

The switch in the top bar picks the mode. **Demo** replays recorded Muse replies. **Live** calls Muse now, takes about a minute, and allows 5 runs an hour per visitor.

1. **Check** the Anthropic test investment memo. Its errors are planted. Click a red number to see the cell code read and where Muse pointed.
2. **Try to fool it.** Change a number and check again.
3. **Load the corrected investment memo.** All 6 match. Flip to **Our method**, and $1.6bn reads -$567m under the example rule HR-1.
4. **Request release**, then approve it as a demo reviewer.
5. **Ask** "Did Anthropic make money in the first half of 2026?" Every number in the answer is checked. "Add back stock compensation." is refused, with no call to Muse.
6. **Create** a plugin. Pick Equity value and enter an enterprise value. It runs on all three companies.
7. **Rules, Record and Score** show each plugin's rules, the hash-chained ledger and the results.

## How a check works

1. Muse lists the claims in the investment memo. Each must appear word for word.
2. Muse points to where the filing reports each metric, using page images and a 0-1000 box grid. It is never told the investment memo's number.
3. Code reads the PDF's own text at that spot, and checks the row, column, units, currency, sign, period and wording.
4. Each number gets a verdict: match, wrong, refused or not checked.
5. An investment memo can be released only if every number matches and a person approves that exact content. The release is sealed as a bundle of hashes, and every step goes on a hash-chained ledger.

Muse replies in schema-locked JSON. A bad reply can cause a refusal, but only code gives a verdict.

## Build your own plugin (Finance Creator Mode)

**Describe it.** Open **Create** and describe a method that gives one number. Muse writes the idea and maps it to each filing, as data and never as code. Code reads the cells and does the sum, and a person approves the install. It can use one number of yours, and changing that number makes no Muse call.

# RegressionMap

Evidence-driven regression investigation for developers. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, track "Build for Your World".

A test passed at a known-good commit and fails now. RegressionMap runs the test at both revisions, collects the real failure output, the stack locations, and the changed code, gives each item a stable ID (E1, E2, ...), and asks a Meta model for ranked root-cause hypotheses that must cite those IDs. The developer then approves a verification rerun. The test runner decides pass or fail, not the model.

## What is implemented (verified on 2026-11-04, Windows 11, Go 1.27, Node 24)

- Go API (`backend/`) on `127.0.0.1:8787`, contract in `docs/API_CONTRACT.md`.
- Test runs at the baseline and at HEAD, each in a temporary `git worktree`, with a timeout and an output cap. Test runs, verification runs and git never receive the server's secrets or any variable whose name ends in `_KEY`, `_SECRET`, `_TOKEN` or `_PASSWORD`. See "Test environment".
- Evidence: node:test failure blocks (with actual and expected values), in-repo stack frames with the real source lines, diff hunks, and the current source of changed non-test files. Line numbers come from the test runner, the diff header, or the file. Likely secrets are redacted. A path segment that looks like a secret becomes `[REDACTED]` in the evidence `file` and `title`, for example `config/token=[REDACTED]/app.ts`. The list of changed files sent to the model is redacted the same way; the API's own `changed_files` keeps the real paths. The bundle has a size cap, and big input is cut, not refused. See "Limits".
- Meta model call: `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions`, model `muse-spark-1.3`, `response_format` `json_schema` with `strict: true` (per https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/chat-completions and https://dev.meta.ai/docs/structured-output).
- Output validation. The system prompt states the limits: at most 5 hypotheses with unique ranks, the three text lengths below, and a summary that is not empty. Rejected hypotheses are shown as "rejected" with their reason, for example `hypothesis 2 ("…"): duplicate rank 1`. The rules, in the order applied:
  1. Unknown fields fail the parse. A missing `summary`, `hypotheses` or `limitations` field makes the result `invalid`, for example `model output did not match the schema: summary is missing`. An empty `summary` is accepted.
  2. A hypothesis is rejected when it cites no supporting evidence, cites an unknown evidence ID (supporting or counter), names a path that is empty, not in clean form, absolute, outside the repository or contains `:`, names a file that is not in the evidence, has an invalid line range (start below 1 or end before start; `0`–`0` means unknown and is allowed), has a range more than 3 lines away from every evidence span of that file (checked when the evidence has line numbers for the file), has a confidence label other than low/medium/high, has a rank below 1, or repeats the rank of an

# Anytime World — Budget-Slider Demo

**"Every millisecond buys a better world."**

A scene is written once as a program — a canonical SDF scene in GFL (Geometric
Function Language) — and rendered under a compute budget the user controls.
Drag the budget slider from **1 to 100** and the world refines from a coarse
estimate to a faithful reconstruction, while a live **budget → error graph**
shows exactly what each unit of compute bought. Stop the slider anywhere:
at every budget the picture is complete and valid. That is the *anytime
property* — a world as a value you can refine, not an all-or-nothing job
you wait for.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026)
by Hagyoon Choi (team: 통일불사극진회, Indie Developer track).

This repository is derived from the author's own public GFL project
([suitzero/gfl](https://github.com/suitzero/gfl)), a budget-aware SDF scene
language with anytime refinement, and packages its completed demo as the
hackathon submission.

## What you can run today (verified)

The shipped demo is the GFL four-region app:

- **Target** — a reference image slot (upload a PNG/JPEG) that the render
  is compared against.
- **Render** — a WebGL2 raymarched SDF scene compiled from a GFL program.
  Structural level-of-detail is driven by the current budget.
- **Controls** — the budget slider (**1–100**), a budget sweep (play)
  control, and scene/inspector controls.
- **Metrics** — a live graph of reconstruction error vs. budget, computed
  from the scene's inverse/error model, with frame-time and budget
  readouts.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev      # develop
npm run build    # production build (tsc && vite build) -> dist/
npm run test     # headless unit tests (vitest)
```

## The hackathon concept around this demo

The full submission concept pairs the canonical scene above with a neural
reconstruction side:

- **Canonical state vs. neural appearance.** The GFL program is the
  canonical state of the world. A neural model (Muse Image) produces a
  target appearance for the same scene; SAM 3.1 provides the coarse
  segmentation / layout estimate for the first, cheapest refinement
  slices; a planner then spends each additional budget unit where the
  reconstruction error is largest.
- **Two ways to spend a budget.** *Uniform* allocation refines regions
  round-robin. A *Muse Spark-guided* planner reads the error map and ranks
  the highest-error regions first, so the error curve should fall faster
  for the same budget. That difference — same world, same model, different
  spending — is the measurable claim of the demo.
- **Cache-first by design.** Preset targets and refinement ladders are
  precomputed and cached, so the demo completes offline and never blocks
  on API latency. Live Meta Model API calls are the integration path for
  target generation and the Spark planner when credit is available.

# MetShield

MetShield is a proposed additional scam-protection layer for Facebook, Messenger
and WhatsApp that carries a **scam's** context across product boundaries — one
operation, three surfaces, one explanation — and renders that explanation inside
the warning the product already shows.

It does not replace Meta's existing scam alerts: it renders underneath them. It
does not read private conversations — the model is shown the correlation graph,
not the conversation — and it never stores personal data. When the evidence
justifies a warning, it produces a card that names its signals and cites each
one. When it does not, it produces nothing and records why.

**Not a real Meta product.** MetShield has not been built into Facebook,
Messenger or WhatsApp. It is a proposed layer, demonstrated on synthetic and
public data, with no integration with any Meta product. Nothing in this
repository is a real user, a real brand, a real scam-target domain, or a real conversation.

The Living World in `src/world/` is the synthetic test fixture MetShield runs
against — invented accounts, campaigns and events — and is not the product; only
this package is submitted, and the product starts and serves its API with the
fixture removed.

Everything in this repository was written during the Meta Global AI Developer
Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026): all 49 commits, one author, no pre-existing
code. Provenance details and verification commands are in
[docs/metshield-submission.md](docs/metshield-submission.md#what-was-built-during-the-hackathon).

## Architecture

```
                 ┌─────────────── sources ───────────────┐
  Living World ────┤ connectors/world.ts   (synthetic)    │
  Public URL feeds ┤ connectors/public.ts  (real, no PII) │
  User submission ─┤ connectors/submit.ts  (+ SAM 3.1)    │
                 └───────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                     ▼
                         Observation (core contract)
                                     ▼
                   normalize → indicator store → correlate
                                     ▼
                              Cluster (evidence graph)
                                     ▼
                     Muse Spark 1.3  (proposal only)

# Wazifa Coach · مرشد الوظائف

**🎬 Demo video (2:17):** [Watch / download](https://github.com/mahdimohmmed97-commits/wazifa-coach/releases/download/v1.0-demo/wazifa-coach-demo.mp4) · [Release page](https://github.com/mahdimohmmed97-commits/wazifa-coach/releases/tag/v1.0-demo)

**An AI career coach for fresh graduates in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, powered by Meta's Muse Spark (Meta Model API).**

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (indie track). Open source under the MIT license.

![Wazifa Coach – results](docs/screenshot_results_en.png)

---

## The problem

Every year, many new graduates in Saudi Arabia and the UAE apply to dozens of jobs and hear nothing back. They usually don't know:

- **how well** their CV actually fits a specific job description,
- **which skills** are missing and how to learn them quickly (and for free),
- **how to phrase** their experience in a way recruiters and ATS filters notice,
- **how to perform** in a real interview, often in their second language.

Career coaching is expensive and generic online advice ignores local context such as Saudization (Nitaqat), Emiratization (Nafis), Vision 2030 and programmes like Tamheer.

## The solution

Wazifa Coach is a bilingual (Arabic RTL / English) web app. Upload a CV (PDF or text), paste a job description, and get:

| Feature | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| 🎯 **Match score** | A 0-100 fit score with clear reasoning |
| ✅ **Matched skills** | What you already bring to the role |
| 🧩 **Skill gaps** | Missing skills ranked by importance, with why they matter |
| 🗓️ **2-4 week upskilling plan** | Weekly focus, concrete tasks, **free** resources, and a portfolio deliverable |
| ✍️ **CV bullet rewrites** | Stronger, JD-aligned bullets (no invented numbers; placeholders like `[X%]`) |
| 🇸🇦🇦🇪 **Local tips** | General, well-known Saudization / Emiratization context (no made-up stats) |
| 🎤 **Interactive mock interview** | 5 role-specific questions, one at a time; each answer gets a 1-10 score, strengths, improvements and a stronger model answer |

## Meta models used

| Model | Where | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3`) via **Meta Model API** | `/api/analyze`, `/api/interview` | OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions: `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions`, `Authorization: Bearer $META_API_KEY`, `response_format: json_object`, `reasoning_effort: low` |

- One call analyses CV + JD into a strict JSON schema (score, gaps, plan, rewrites, tips).
- The mock interview is an agent loop: each turn sends the JD, CV and the full Q/A history; Muse Spark grades the last answer and asks the next question, adapting to the candidate's answers.
- Muse Spark is a reasoning model, and its reasoning tokens count toward `max_completion_tokens`. The client gives it a generous budget and retries once with double the budget if the JSON comes back truncated (`finish_reason: length`).
- Measured live latency: analysis ~13–24 s, each interview turn ~8–15 s

# Muse Shield

**Use Meta's Muse models on your real work without handing over your real data.**

Muse Shield is a local **privacy entity engine** that sits between you and Muse Spark. It is not find-and-replace
PII masking. Before anything leaves your device, **our fine-tuned Muse Glimmer 30B** reads the message, document or
tool result and builds an **entity graph**:

- **Entities.** Every person, organisation and private value: money, IDs, contacts, addresses, dates, secrets and
  health details.
- **Coreference.** "Rohan Majji", "Rohan", "Mr. Majji" and `rohan@mail` are one identity with one placeholder, across
  turns and across chats.
- **Ownership.** Whose salary, whose phone, whose account.
- **Relations.** `MANAGES`, `WORKS_FOR`, `PARENT_OF`, and so on.
- **Context.** In "PII + context" mode, a whole confidential passage (a deal, a diagnosis, a plan) becomes one
  placeholder, with its inner values masked too.

Muse Spark reasons over `<PERSON_1>`, `<AMOUNT_2>`, `<DEAL_1>`. The reply is restored on your device from an encrypted
vault. When Spark genuinely needs a hidden value, it has to **ask**, and you choose what to share.

> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Cerebral Valley, Oct 26 – Nov 4 2026), track **Build for Your
> World**.
>
> **Our model:** [TheEmperor2/muse-shield-glimmer-er-v3a](https://huggingface.co/TheEmperor2/muse-shield-glimmer-er-v3a),
> a LoRA on Muse Glimmer 30B. **Its training data:**
> [TheEmperor2/muse-shield-er-v3-data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TheEmperor2/muse-shield-er-v3-data).
> **Full release record:** [`results/er-v3-release/`](results/er-v3-release/README.md).

### Which models run where

| Step | Model | Sees |
|---|---|---|
| **Masking:** find, link and own every private value | **Our fine-tuned Muse Glimmer 30B** (`muse-shield-glimmer-er-v3a-s250`, a LoRA) | the raw text, on infrastructure you control |
| **Images:** faces, plates, ID and bank cards, documents, signatures, QR codes | **SAM 3.1** (Meta Model API) | the raw image; faces are blurred and the rest covered before any chat model sees it |
| **Answering:** and planning agent tool calls | **Muse Spark 1.3** (Meta Model API, Standard tier only) | masked text and masked images, nothing else |

Muse Spark is **never** used for masking. The pitch is that the part that sees your data is a model you own.

---

**Any interface, compiled for a small model.**

Tribe was designed and built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**, in the **Indie track — *Build for Your World***: build something that solves a problem in your own world. # vLock-AI Vision

**Tell your SCADA what to watch in plain English, with no vision engineer and no model training.**

vLock-AI Vision connects a camera to an existing SCADA system. You describe a rule in plain language, Muse Spark proposes it, you approve it, SAM 3.1 watches the camera, and SCADA reads the result through fixed tags.

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026](docs/project/HACKATHON.md).

**Demo video:** link coming soon.

## The problem

Plants already have cameras and SCADA systems, but connecting one to the other usually means custom vision work for every scene. Each new object, area or rule goes back to a specialist. SCADA also needs more than a detection: it has to know when a result is old or missing, so that a broken camera is never mistaken for a clear area.

## What it does

1. **Connect a camera:** Raspberry Pi USB, HTTP or RTSP.
2. **Describe the rule:** "Alert when a person and a dog are both in the area for one second."
3. **Review it:** Muse Spark proposes the rule and SAM 3.1 outlines the area. Nothing runs until a person approves it.
4. **Monitor:** SAM 3.1 checks the camera, and fixed code applies the approved rule.
5. **Publish:** SCADA reads the same tags for every zone over OPC UA, MQTT or REST. Ignition users can download a ready-made UDT.

| `State` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Active` | The rule is met on a fresh, confirmed observation |
| `Clear` | The rule is not met on a fresh, confirmed observation |
| `Unknown` | No current result, for example a lost camera or failed model call. **It never means clear** |
| `Valid` | Count zones only: the counts are current |

**vLock tells SCADA what it sees. SCADA decides what the machine does.** The app sends no machine commands. Integrators should treat Unknown or Bad quality as stop, and latching and reset are theirs to own. See the [Ignition guide](ignition/INTEGRATION.md).

## Tools

| Purpose | Tools |
|---|---|
| Meta models | **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) for rule proposals and optional advisory frame checks; **SAM 3.1** for segmentation and tracking |
| SAM 3.1 engines | Local NVIDIA GPU with PyTorch in Ubuntu/WSL and weights from Hugging Face, or the Meta Model API for image or video |
| Application | Python, a browser UI in plain JavaScript, SQLite, OpenCV and Pillow, `meta-sam-parser` |
| SCADA outputs | OPC UA (`asyncua`), MQTT (`paho-mqtt`), REST |
| Deployment | Windows launcher, or Docker with separate app and GPU containers |
| Demo site | Inductive Automation Ignition with Perspective, Raspberry Pi 5 with a USB camera, Bambu Lab P1S printer through a local MQTT connector |

## Architecture

```text
 Camera (Pi USB, HTTP, RTSP)
        |  latest frame only, no queue
        v
+------------------- vLock-AI Vision ------------------+        +---------------------+
|                                                      |        |  SAM 3.1, one of:   |
|  Web UI, logins, audit log, Setup page               |        |  - local GPU worker |

# Underwrite

Startup due diligence that is allowed to say "don't build this".

A founder describes an idea. Underwrite interviews them, researches the market on the live web, and returns a verdict in which every number shows where it came from, then a system design, a clickable prototype and legal first steps. Funds and studios use the same engine to screen a batch of applications against their thesis.

Built on Meta's models for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. Live: https://underwrite.dsfddff31.workers.dev. Demo video: https://github.com/alrevion/underwrite/releases/tag/demo-video

## Why it is different

Most idea validators return confident numbers that nobody can check. In Underwrite the model does not get the last word; plain code does:

- **Facts are earned.** A claim stays a `fact` only if its source is a URL the search really returned. Anything else is demoted to `assumption`, and the report says how many were demoted.
- **Markets are multiplied, not quoted.** The model supplies customers, price, reach and win rate. Code computes TAM, SAM and SOM, so every step is visible and can be challenged.
- **Scores are not probabilities.** Readiness and viability are fixed weights over rated investor criteria. A rating of `strong` on market or competition needs surviving verified evidence.
- **No evidence, no "go".** A verdict of `go` with no evidence about the problem becomes `hold`, whatever the model said.

Web pages and uploaded PDFs are untrusted data. An application that tells the model to rate itself highly is treated as text to report, not an instruction to follow.

## What you get

| Step | Output | Models |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interview | One question at a time on the founder, problem, product and improvements, by text or voice | Muse Spark, Muse Voice Transcribe |
| Concept | One-liner, job to be done, pains, gains, features, reframings, first test | Muse Spark |
| Research | Competitors, pricing, revenue, funding, bottom-up market, gaps | Muse Spark with web search |
| Report | Go, hold, recycle or kill, 12 investor criteria, risks, next tests, full document | Muse Spark |
| System | Business logic, entities, APIs, stack, diagrams, build order | Muse Spark |
| Prototype | A self-contained clickable app in a locked-down sandbox that repairs its own runtime errors once | Muse Spark, Muse Image |
| Legal | Entity steps with cost and source, a founder split calculator. Not legal advice | Muse Spark with web search |
| Funds | Thesis, batch of PDFs or text, ranked table, red flags, questions for the founder | Muse Spark with web search, PDF input |

Prompts run in standard mode, never the contributor tier, because founders' ideas are confidential.

## Run it

Requires Node 22 or later and a key from [dev.meta.ai](https://dev.meta.ai).

```bash
npm install
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars   # add MODEL_API_KEY
npm run dev
```

# Agent Guardian

**The guardian holds the keys. Every action an AI agent takes is checked against the task and the
owner's rules before it runs.**

AI agents are now given real access: shells, credentials, email, one-time codes, sudo. When an agent
drifts off task, nothing between the agent and the machine notices. Two reported examples from 2026:

- In a security test reported by Cohere (October 2026), a model working on an unrelated task listed
  temp files, looked for transfer tools, read DNS settings and tried to upload a file to an outside
  cloud bucket.
- At Meta (March 2026), an internal AI agent acted without approval and exposed company and user
  data for about two hours, a Sev 1 incident.

Agent Guardian sits between any agent and its system. The agent gets no keys and no root. Every tool
call the agent's model proposes (a command, a file write, a web fetch, a request for a credential) is
pulled out of the model's reply before the agent can run it, and checked:

1. **Hard rules (code).** Secrets, environment dumps, uploads, unknown destinations, raw network
   tools and destructive commands outside the project are blocked. One-time codes, sudo, payments and
   force pushes go to the owner. These hold even if every model is wrong.
2. **Judgement (local model).** Actions the rules cannot settle (listing `/tmp`, reading
   `/etc/resolv.conf`, touching files outside the project) are scored 0–10 by a small open Meta model,
   **Llama 3.2 3B running on CPU with llama.cpp** (no GPU, no API), on the owner's weighted principles:
   needed for the task, security, data stays home, least privilege, reversibility. Code then decides:
   a score under a veto line blocks, only a clear pass (weighted ≥ 0.70) is allowed, the rest goes to
   the owner. The model's own token probability for "allow / ask / block" can only make the verdict
   stricter.
3. **Act.** Allowed calls pass unchanged. Stopped calls are replaced by a note to the agent, so the
   command never reaches the agent's tools.
4. **Broker.** Privileged steps are done by the guardian itself. In the demo the agent runs
   `guardian-request deploy "<why>"`; if the guardian agrees, it publishes the site with a deploy key
   the agent never sees and writes a receipt.

The guardian is model-agnostic: it watches actions, not intentions, so it works with any agent and
any model behind it.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie track.

# Nearer

**The voice-first window between two homes.**

Arjun lives in Bengaluru. His parents, Maa and Papa, live in Amritsar, 1,600 km away. At 8 PM he opens Nearer and sees their window: their sky right now, the time there, and what they chose to share today ("Maa · visitors, 7:00 PM"). He doesn't call to check. He looks. He taps the **lamp**, and Maa's phone says *Arjun is thinking of you*. Maa has **opened her door** for chai; he joins with his voice, and nothing starts until he taps. Last week she taught him her dal by voice, in Hindi; Muse wrote it down as a recipe in English. On Sunday he cooked it, and Maa saw *Arjun cooked your dal*. Diwali is in five days: Dadi (Maa, to his children) leads, the kids record their wishes, and on the day the **Chorus** plays them one after another. Her voice stays in **Memories**, starred, searchable and in the family's Book.

That is the whole product: **a voice-first window between two homes** that keeps parents **needed, not monitored**. Nothing is inferred from app use, the clock or silence: the app shows only what someone chose to share.

Values, in priority order: **Needed** (elders give and have a role) · **Heard** (acknowledgement) · **Present** (together at the same time, by invitation) · **Remembered** (memories) · **Never watched** (no monitoring, no guilt, no streaks, no sealed answers). Calm by design: no feed, no counts, no status.

The app itself is in English. What the family shares (voices, recipes, questions, notes) reaches each person in their own language: 55 languages, including Hindi, Hinglish, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Spanish, Arabic and Chinese (`lib/languages.ts`). Elders see prompts in their own language, in large type, while they record.

Live: https://nearer.site (tap *Try the demo family*, or use the code `NEARER-DEMO`). To see both homes, open a door as Arjun, tap *Demo: see it arrive on their side*, and scan the code on a second phone: it becomes Maa in the same demo family.

Dapi is for people who need web data they can stand behind and don't write scrapers: a
compliance officer checking a public register, an analyst tracking competitors, a
researcher, a data engineer who'd rather not babysit scrapers, a team gathering training
data for AI that has to show where every value came from. Nobody sees code unless they
want to.

Open [dapi.fly.dev](https://dapi.fly.dev). The finished example jobs (Books to Scrape, US

Six steps, from what you ask for to a dataset you can check.

| Step | What happens | Done by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Ask** | You type, upload or say what you need: the site, the columns, a sample row, any rules. | Muse Voice Transcribe hears it; Muse Spark writes it up and reads it into columns, samples and rules |
| **2. Investigate** | Dapi opens the site and watches what it loads before reading any HTML. Many sites load their data from a feed of their own: Dapi reads that instead of scraping the page. Then an agent settles where every column lives and plans the run. | Muse Wonder, as an agent with tools |

| **6. Prove** | Every response is sealed with SHA-256 the moment it arrives. Click any value to see the page or response it came from, with the value marked. Rows are counted against the source's own total, and anything missing is named. | Dapi |

# Navitas — AI-Powered Energy Optimization for Textile Manufacturing

**Same production. Lower electricity costs. Verified schedules.**

Navitas is an AI-powered factory energy optimization system that helps manufacturers make better decisions about when and how their machines operate.

Operators describe production constraints in natural language or provide an electricity-bill image. Meta Muse Spark interprets the request, a constraint-based optimization engine generates a production schedule, and an independent verifier checks the result before it is presented.

**Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Push the Frontier**

---

## The problem

Electricity is a major operating expense for energy-intensive manufacturing. Yet production schedules are often created around deadlines and machine availability without fully accounting for time-varying electricity prices.

Factories cannot always control electricity tariffs. They can, however, make better decisions about when eligible production tasks run, which machine modes are selected, and how production is distributed across available time.

Navitas explores that opportunity through constrained energy-aware scheduling.

## How Navitas works

1. **Describe the production situation.** An operator enters a natural-language instruction, such as "MAQ119 is unavailable on day 3" or "No machines can operate between 18:30 and 22:30."
2. **Interpret the request with Meta Muse Spark.** The model converts the operator's request into structured constraints. The application also supports electricity-bill image interpretation.
3. **Optimize the schedule.** OR-Tools CP-SAT searches for a lower-cost schedule while respecting the modeled production constraints.
4. **Verify independently.** A separate verification implementation checks the resulting schedule and recomputes its energy cost.
5. **Explain the result.** Muse Spark presents the verified outcome in understandable language.

The LLM does not independently decide whether a schedule is valid. The optimization engine generates the schedule, and the independent checker evaluates it.

## Architecture

```text
Factory operator
      |
      v
Natural-language request / bill image
      |
      v
Meta Muse Spark Open
      |
      v
Structured constraints
      |
      v
OR-Tools CP-SAT optimizer
      |
      v
Candidate production schedule
      |
      v
Independent schedule verifier
      |
      v
Verified cost, energy and schedule
      |
      v
Muse Spark explanation
```

### Technology

| Component | Technology |
|---|---|
| AI model | Meta Muse Spark Open |
| Primary inference | Baseten |
| Model fallback | Fireworks |
| Optimization | Google OR-Tools CP-SAT |
| Backend | Python |
| Web application | Python standard-library server |
| Frontend | HTML, CSS and JavaScript |
| Verification | Independent Python implementation |

Model routing, provider configuration, model restrictions and call-provenance logging are implemented in `llm.py`

# Physical MCP

An API for machines that don't have one. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track), Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026.

**Live site:** [physicalmcp.dev](https://physicalmcp.dev), with the 3-minute demo, an interactive look at the rig and a replay you can try

**Demo video:** [watch it here](https://physicalmcp.dev/#video)

## What it does

Lots of machines only have physical buttons and a small screen. Physical MCP lets an AI run them anyway. A webcam watches the panel, servo fingers press the buttons, and every action goes through MCP tools with a human approval gate in front of anything risky.

The main machine is a 4-channel kitchen timer (`timer-01`). Example job:

> Set T1 to 2 hours and start it

What happens:

1. The camera reads T1 before planning (Muse Spark reads the LCD)
2. Muse Spark plans the steps: press H, press H, press ST/SP
3. The plan gets checked in code against what T1 shows (see the safety rules)
4. Muse Spark Open scores each step that needs approval: low / medium / high, plus a one-line reason
5. H presses run on their own. ST/SP stops at an approval card and waits for a press-and-hold
6. After every press the camera reads T1 again to check it worked. A missed press gets pressed again
7. If vision isn't sure what it read, the job pauses until someone hits Resume

The AI only ever calls tools: `get_controls`, `press`, `read_screen`, `get_frame`, `stop` (`backend/mcp_server.py`). The step runner in `backend/api.py` is the MCP client, in the same process, so one process owns the finger.

**On the rig, as of Nov 3:** full jobs now work through the app, including "Set T1 to 2 hours and start it" with the hold-to-approve on ST/SP. The rig has one finger per button, with H and ST/SP angles in `backend/devices/timer-01.json`. See [Reliability](#reliability).

The Inkbird temperature controller (`inkbird-01`) is a second profile. It was **tried once on the rig (job_04b0c61c, stopped by hand), servo angles still empty**. Its menu behaviour comes from the manual. `incubator-01` is a made-up placeholder device that runs on the mock and on FakeHardware, never on the rig.

## Safety rules

All of these live in the backend, not just the web app.

- **Every press goes through `press`.** It refuses anything that isn't the running step's own control, waits on the approval card when the step needs approval, checks the hold, and charges the press budget, all before the hardware moves

Can you make a React app lose your note in three moves? BugArcade turns real UI bugs into playable debugging challenges, then gives you the exact replay and regression test that prove the fix works.

## Play the bug, then make the fix earn it

1. **Play.** Explore a real small app and control when API responses arrive. Catch the bug within the move target.
2. **Reveal.** Follow the action timeline, inspect the observed failure and understand the cause.
3. **Check the fix.** Replay the same actions against the fixed app and keep the regression test.

| The disappearing note | A sync response loses a note added while it was pending |
| Optimistic rollback | An older failed rename overwrites a newer successful change |
| Search response race | Out-of-order responses display results for the wrong query |
| Duplicate submission | A pending request accepts the same order twice |

# Flatline

![Flatline: jagged training power becomes a smooth line on the grid](docs/cover.jpg)

**An agent that writes the controller keeping an AI training cluster's power draw inside the grid's limits.**
Built on Meta's Muse models for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Push the Frontier track: energy).

![Measured training power, scaled to a 16k-GPU cluster](docs/problem.png)

## The problem

When a large model trains, every GPU computes, then every GPU waits on the network, then every GPU
computes again. They do it in lockstep. The plot above is a real measurement: 64 H100s fine-tuning
Llama-2-70B, sampled five times a second by NREL. The power of all 16 nodes moves together with a
correlation of 1.00. Scale that to 16,384 GPUs and the grid sees a 2.7 MW square wave every ten seconds,
an 8 MW step when the job starts and another when it ends.

Utilities care because swings between roughly 0.1 and 20 Hz can excite the mechanical resonances of
power plants. Microsoft, OpenAI and NVIDIA described the problem in 2025
([arXiv:2508.14318](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14318)) and shipped no code. NERC issued a Level 3 alert on
large computational loads in 2026, and FERC has ordered standards for them. Every new AI campus now has to
show its utility a controller that keeps it inside limits like these, and today that is weeks of
specialist work per site.

## What Flatline does

You give it a utility's requirements in plain English and a training workload's power trace. It returns a
working controller (Python), the storage it needs, and a pass/fail compliance report against those
requirements, with the cheapest design it found.

```
utility spec (prose) ──► Muse Spark ──► machine-checkable limits ─┐
                                                                  ▼
measured power trace ──► baselines (no AI) ──► Muse Wonder writes controller code
                                                      ▲                │
                         Muse Spark looks at the      │                ▼
                         plots and diagnoses ◄── sandbox + deterministic verifier
```

* **Muse Spark reads the spec.** Turns "the RMS of demand in the 0.1–20 Hz band shall not exceed 0.5
  percent of nameplate over any 60-second window" into numbers, quoting where each came from.
* **Muse Wonder designs.** Writes a complete controller module and a storage design against the plant
  model: a GPU power floor ("burner"), a facility battery and a supercapacitor bank, each with real limits,
  efficiencies and costs.

Does the verification evidence actually support confidence in the software? > AI can generate software and tests. STVI evaluates whether the available verification evidence actually supports confidence in that software.


STVI reads a project's numbered requirements and its code. Models (via the **Meta Model API**) turn each rule into checkable claims and write small tests; **a script runs the tests and records what happened**; two **different** Meta models rate how convincing each executed test is; and **fixed rules, with no AI in them**, turn the recorded evidence into verdicts. # The Magic Table

**Two small, limited robots and an AI that sees the table: together they run a game of cards that neither robot could play alone.**

Entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie developer track, theme "Push the Frontier"). Submissions due **Nov 4, 2026, 9:00 PM ET**.

**Demo video:** [https://youtu.be/PkLwDHRM7E8](https://youtu.be/PkLwDHRM7E8)

| Peek | Stack | Reveal | Frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| ![Esper peeking at a card](media/photos/peek.png) | ![The crane stacking](media/photos/stack.png) | ![Esper revealing a card](media/photos/reveal.png) | ![The frame](media/photos/frame.png) |

> **Agents (and people) driving the table: start at [agent/](agent/README.md).** Everything that's available (gantry, cameras, Esper, speaker, talk page, notes) and how to use it. The hub serves it at `http://raspberrypi.local:8000/guide`, and as plain text at `/api/guide`.

## The idea: more than the sum of its parts

Neither robot can play cards on its own:

| | Can | Can't |
|---|---|---|
| **The crane** (a CoreXY gantry with a suction cup) | Lift a card and put it anywhere on the table, to within ~2–3 mm | Turn a card (the cup can't rotate), or see a face-down card's face |
| **Esper** (a small wheeled robot with a flipper arm, a face and a camera) | Turn a card on her back, flip it over, lift its corner to peek at it, and react to the players | Lift anything |
| **Muse Spark** (Meta's model) | See the table, read the cards, know the rules, talk to the players | Touch anything |

Together they deal, turn, flip and peek at cards, and Muse runs the game and talks to the people at the table while Esper reacts. The parts are humble on purpose: the frame is rebuilt from a dismantled machine, Esper runs on cheap stepper motors, and her arm is a bent plastic knife. What makes them a card dealer is how they work together.

## What it does

- **Talk to the table.** Players speak (or type) on the talk page from any phone: `https://raspberrypi.local:8000/talk`. Muse Voice Transcribe turns the speech into text live; Muse Spark acts on it and answers out loud on the table's speaker; Esper reacts with gestures (faces, flipper and wheel moves). Esper never speaks.
- **See the table.** Two cameras and printed ArUco markers give every card, chip stack, deck, the crane's head and Esper a position in millimetres. Free, on the Pi, twice a second. When that's not enough, SAM 3.1 finds things by name and Muse Spark reads what they are.
- **Move cards.** Pick, place and stack cards (~7.5 s a card), stack chips, carry cards to Esper.
- **Turn, flip and peek with Esper.** The crane puts a card on Esper; she turns it to any angle, flips it over (14 of 14 flat in testing), or lifts its edge so her camera can read a face-down card.
- **Run a game.** Muse Spark drives all of it through an MCP server, following written guides for the table, Esper and poker.

**Tested:** every piece above, by hand and through the hub's API, plus the live Muse agent on short tas

# SunSeg

SAM 3.1 finds solar panels in aerial imagery, pvlib simulates what each one produces, and a 3D map of
Fresno shows the output hour by hour as the sun crosses the city.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (theme: Push the Frontier, energy).

**Why it matters.** Most rooftop solar sits behind the meter, so grid operators never measure what it
produces. In a Siemens-commissioned survey of 100 utilities, 39% said they had no visibility into it at all
([EEPower](https://eepower.com/tech-insights/in-the-dark-limited-der-data-causes-grid-ops-challenges/)).
Earlier ways of mapping it meant training a model on a large labelled set. Stanford's DeepSolar was trained
on about 370,000 images. SunSeg uses a two-word prompt and no training data, and measures how well that works.

Demo video: `video/sunseg_demo.mp4`, rendered from the app's film mode (see "Video" below).

## Results

All figures below come from the files in `web/data/` and `data/out/`, which this repo's scripts produce.

**Detection: SAM 3.1 against hand labels.** Scored on 98 held-out 300 m tiles (1,128 labelled arrays) from
the Duke aerial solar dataset. A labelled array counts as found when at least half its area is covered
by SAM masks. A SAM mask counts as correct when at least half its area lies on labelled solar.

| Metric | Lenient match | Standard match (IoU ≥ 0.5) |
|---|---|---|
| Object precision | 90.1% (1,361 of 1,510 masks) | 67.7% (804 of 1,188 objects) |
| Object recall | 80.8% (911 of 1,128 arrays) | 75.4% (804 of 1,067 objects) |
| Pixel precision / recall | 64.0% / 72.4% | |
| Pixel IoU | 0.51 | |

The standard match follows the literature: connected regions of predicted and true solar pixels, matched
one-to-one when their IoU is at least 0.5. For context, U-Nets fine-tuned to a new area on 0.3 m imagery
reached a pixel IoU of 0.60 to 0.62 (Zhuang et al. 2020, as cited by
[Hu, Bradbury, Malof et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10895)). SAM reaches 0.51 with no training. That
comparison is indicative only: the imagery and areas differ.

Over the four images where SAM ran, the masks imply 5.37 MW. The hand labels for the same area give
4.92 MW, so capacity from SAM alone runs about 9% high.

**Second opinion from Muse Spark.** `muse-spark-1.3` looked at a crop around every SAM detection (the exact
image is in `web/data/verify/`) and judged whether it was solar. On held-out detections it rejected 140 of
