# Physics Proof

**Drop in any video; it asks what is worth proving, measures it, and shows every step on the footage.**

Live: [https://yunoshev.github.io/physics-proof/](https://yunoshev.github.io/physics-proof/) — press Play to watch each analysis play out on the footage.

See it work: [Apollo 16 salute hop — Moon, g = 1.65 ± 0.10 m/s²](https://yunoshev.github.io/physics-proof/moon/) · [Apollo 16 salute hop, sped up ×2.46 (a test fake made by us from the NASA clip) — retimed ×2.43, g = 9.58 ± 0.65 m/s²](https://yunoshev.github.io/physics-proof/moon-fast/) · [IShowSpeed jumps over a Lamborghini — Earth, g = 10.65 ± 1.11 m/s²](https://yunoshev.github.io/physics-proof/speed/)

Demo video: [watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xGzqiPTDuhI)

**One system for any clip — $0.36 per clip**

It is one general system, not a script for one clip; nothing in the code is tuned to a particular video. For each clip Muse Spark works out from the frames what a viewer would doubt, finds objects of known size and their sourced sizes, and plans the checks: a free flight against the world's gravity, a size or speed against a sourced human range, a step rate against a natural clock. During the hackathon it was verified end to end on a limited set of clips, listed under Results.

Average cost per clip: **$0.36** = Muse Spark $0.24 + SAM 3.1 $0.11 + web search $0.01 (average of 53 live runs, 1–3 November 2026).

**Limits.** This is a working concept, not yet proven on every kind of clip. It reached right verdicts end to end on three clips: the Apollo clip, our sped-up copy and a handheld street jump. The street jump needed several runs and two new general rules: the agent first took a hand on the car from small frames without checking its own masks, and the jumper's tucked legs needed a wider error budget. With both rules in the briefs, the regenerated code measured the flight. A new kind of clip may still need new rules.

**Rebuilt from text — $0.3390 for a full rebuild**

No hand-written code: the 15 briefs are the only human-written part (the owner's requests, turned into briefs by Muse Wonder). Muse Spark generates every part through Muse Code, one part at a time (`tools/dev_loop --part NN`). The full test suite checks each generation, and a live run that went wrong changed the brief, not the code.

A full rebuild of all 13 parts by Muse Spark: **$0.3390** (the last generation of each part, section 4).

## 1. What it is

A video goes in, and a player page with a physics verdict comes out.
Every analysis ends in one of three states: the motion fits one
scene-allowed world at native speed, it fits only under a corroborated
retiming, or no world fits and the result says why (physically
impossible, or undetermined with a reason).

## 2. How it was built

Built during the Meta hackathon, from 2026-10-27. The briefs in `brief/`
are the only human-written part (the owner's requests, turned into briefs
by Muse Wonder). All code, tests and the player are
generated by Muse

# SETU: Structural Evaluation and Telemetry Utility

SETU is a vision-based screening tool that measures natural structural vibration frequencies of civil infrastructure from smartphone video recordings. It tracks subpixel displacements of structural elements relative to a static background to compute power spectral density and extract resonant modal peaks.

## Core Principle

SETU never declares a bridge safe. It flags readings that need human civil engineer review and on-site physical inspection. Weak or failed verdicts are not anomalies.

## How It Works

The processing pipeline executes in seven sequential stages:

1. **Video Checks** (`setu/video_checks.py`): Validates file container integrity, decodability, duration (5 to 60 seconds), frame rate (15 to 240 fps), and minimum resolution (320x240 pixels).
2. **SAM 3.1 Segmentation** (`setu/segment.py`): Segments the vibrating structural target and a static background reference anchor on Frame 0 using natural language text prompts.
3. **Background Stabilisation** (`setu/motion.py`): Tracks subpixel motion in the static background anchor to isolate and remove camera micro-jitter and drift.
4. **Motion Tracking** (`setu/motion.py`): Tracks subpixel displacement of the structural target across all frames using phase correlation or Lucas-Kanade optical flow.
5. **Spectrum Analysis** (`setu/spectrum.py`): Computes Welch Power Spectral Density (PSD), extracts resonant frequency peaks, checks peak prominence and signal-to-noise ratio, calculates 95% confidence intervals, and assigns a reliability verdict (usable, weak, or failed).
6. **Muse Spark Interpretation** (`setu/interpret.py`, `setu/assess.py`, `setu/quality_gate.py`): Runs only when the spectrum verdict is usable. Queries OpenStreetMap for bridge metadata, checks visual quality gates, and produces an evidence-locked anomaly assessment. Weak or failed scans skip this stage.
7. **Optional Magnification** (`setu/evm.py`): Applies phase-based Eulerian video magnification centered at the dominant frequency to generate an amplified video for visual inspection display only.

## Meta Models Used

SETU integrates three Meta model lines:

- **sam-3.1** (`setu/segment.py`): Used for Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) on Frame 0. It takes user prompts (such as "concrete pillar" and "building") to generate binary target and background masks. An offline geometric heuristic segmenter acts as a fallback when the Meta API is unavailable.
- **muse-spark-1.3** (`setu/assess.py`, `setu/quality_gate.py`, `setu/interpret.py`): Used for LLM-assisted anomaly screening and visual quality gate verification. It operates under a strict evidence lock, meaning every number in the output must match values in the input telemetry or OpenStreetMap metadata. It never certifies safety and always recommends human inspection when anomalies or uncertainties occur.
- **muse-voice-transcribe-1.0** (`setu/voice.py`): Transcribes short driver voice notes; Muse Spark turns transcrip

# Backstop

https://backstop-4xz9.onrender.com

https://youtu.be/5zsz0vO2wxU?si=hMSJ2Vkz-y8Z2V-V

A safe email and messaging client for elderly people and adults with learning disabilities.
Backstop holds every incoming message until it is checked. The user never sees held mail. Anything unclear goes to a trusted person (the **helper**), who approves it, blocks it, or asks the user to call the sender first.

> All data is synthetic: made-up people, messages and domains (`example.com`, `example.net`, `example.org`, `.test`). There is no real email provider. No secrets are in this repo.

**Live URL:** https://backstop-4xz9.onrender.com/demo-start

Built with .NET 10 Blazor Server and plain CSS. No UI framework.

## How it works

Every incoming message goes through four checks, in order: **Rules**, **Meta AI**, **Link check**, **Policy**.

Alongside the Rules, a **Sender check** (`ISenderCheck`, pure code, no AI call) looks at who the message says it is from: the name shown against the address (a brand, a family word like "Mum", or a saved contact on a different address), look-alike and punycode domains, and a Reply-To on another domain. Its findings go to Meta AI as evidence and show in a "Sender checks" section for the helper and on `/try`. A serious finding always holds the message, whatever Meta AI says. Headers that cannot be read are treated as unverified and held.

- **Cleared** only when the local checks are clean and Meta AI answered and agreed.
- **Held** for the helper when anything looks wrong, or when a check fails. An email that gives orders to the checker ("ignore your instructions…") goes straight to the helper with no AI call: it is never blocked unseen, because a person should decide.
- **Blocked** (final, invisible to the user) only for a disguised link together with a strong warning sign, and never when someone may be at risk.
- **Fail closed.** A Meta error, a timeout, an unexpected answer, a missing API key or any exception ends in Held. Nothing is ever cleared on a failure.
- **Local checks are a floor.** The phrase rules and input guard set a minimum. Meta's answer can only make a result stricter, never looser.
- **Links in real mail are never opened.** They are judged by their address only, and shown defanged (`hxxp://example[.]com`). Message content never renders as a clickable link.
- **Held mail is private.** The user sees only "N message(s) being checked by your helper", with no sender and no subject.

## Meta API integration

Backstop calls the Meta Dev API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`, Muse models such as `muse-spark-1.3`) from the server only, for:

- scam checks on messages, conversations and pictures,
- Ask Me,
- safeguarding (spotting when someone may need help).

Text and images being inspected are passed as data, never as instructions. Images are sent only when a picture check needs them. Any endpoint other than `https://api.meta.ai` is refused before a request is sent.

# AI Market Assistant

AI Market Assistant helps traders record stock and helps buyers discover products in nearby shops. The intended application serves traders and buyers wherever they are, starting with Nigerian markets. It uses Next.js for the frontend and backend, PostgreSQL for inventory records, and Meta models for assisted logging.

**Kubwa is the sample market, not the application's geographic limit.** The current hackathon demo uses fictional provision shops in Kubwa and a packaged-goods catalog to demonstrate the core flow. Broader location and product-category support is intended scope, not a claim that every market is already covered or every type of product is supported.

In the intended experience, traders register their shop's location and supported products, and buyers search around a chosen location. Local results depend on participating shops keeping their stock records current; opening the site in a new area does not automatically provide inventory for that area. An area without participating shops should show an honest empty result.

**Demo data is simulated.** The [Railway demo](https://ai-market-assistant-production.up.railway.app) is deployed with PostgreSQL. Hosted signup, live Muse Spark 1.3 text interpretation, review before stock changes, confirmation/replay protection, buyer updates, stock authorization and concurrent oversell checks passed. The hosted text adapter uses Meta's Responses API. Visual browser checks, representative voice quality, backup restore and actual submission remain pending.

- [Application setup, verification and architecture](web/README.md)
- [Project instructions and six-task plan](AGENTS.md)
- [Release checklist, workshop findings and Muse handoff](06-demo-release-and-pilot.todo.md)

Open `AI Market Assistant.code-workspace` in VS Code. Application commands run from `web/`:

```sh
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
```

Follow `web/README.md` to configure a private local environment before starting the demo. Environment files, API keys and local demo databases are excluded from this repository.

The supplied Meta Agents 101 workshop demonstrates Muse Spark 1.3; this app defaults to that model for extraction. Using Muse Code to edit a repository and calling a Meta model from the application are separate steps. Neither is proof that all hackathon rules or production launch requirements have passed.

# Atlas

AI that adapts to you — not the other way around. Atlas is a voice-first companion built around people with disabilities: it talks, listens, signs, captions, and watches out for you depending on what you need.

[![Atlas demo video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/J6siIGO4GIQ/hqdefault.jpg)](https://youtu.be/J6siIGO4GIQ)

## The problem we are solving

Most AI assistants are built around people without disabilities. Their interfaces, interactions, and underlying systems often overlook the needs of people with different disabilities, making them inaccessible or practically useless for many of them.

Atlas is specifically built around people with disabilities, following one philosophy:

> Technology should adapt to people, not the other way around.

- **For blind people:** Most assistants rely heavily on visual interfaces. Atlas becomes their eyes — it describes what its camera sees, warns about obstacles in the walking path, and speaks everything instead of showing it.
- **For deaf people:** Atlas becomes their ears. It listens to the room, transcribes what matters, and answers on screen instead of through sound.
- **For people with speech disabilities:** Atlas gives them another way to communicate — they type or fingerspell to the camera in sign language, and Atlas speaks and acts on their behalf.
- **For autistic people:** One of the biggest challenges is understanding your own moods and what triggers them. Atlas logs moods, learns from personal experiences, and builds a connected mood memory — a second brain that reveals patterns over time.

The mood system is also designed with emotional comfort in mind. Not every memory is something a person wants to revisit. Some experiences are difficult to remember, so Atlas never forces negative moods or memories into the interface. Users stay in control of what they revisit and when.

## What the product does

Atlas is one conversation loop that adapts to the person using it. You pick who you are at `/start`, and the same companion — same prompt structure, same tool loop, same voice — changes what it can do:

- **It talks and listens.** Browser mic → speech detection → replies spoken with the voice built into your browser (smooth and calm, at the pace you chose). Everything spoken is also captioned, and Atlas keeps a full conversation thread you can reopen.
- **It answers through tools, not vibes.** On every turn the model can search the web, read a specific page, check the actual time in any timezone, and act: create reminders, start a new chat, open the camera, or shut itself up. Search results are cited as links inside the answer that uses them.
- **It shows procedure cards.** How-tos, plans, comparisons, and anything you will act on arrive as on-screen cards (up to six, markdown everywhere) — with inline widgets: countdown timers you can fire, checkboxes, counters, ratings, and progress bars.
- **It listens in sign.** Non-speaking (mute) and deaf users can hold the camera and fingerspell or sign;

_Anatomy in context._

A web-based research workbench for medical imaging professionals, researchers, and medical students. SARI assists exploration and analysis of medical visual data by linking image slices, editable research annotations, computed mask comparisons, and 3D spatial context.

AI-generated regions are draft research proposals for expert review. SARI is not a patient-facing diagnostic or medical-advice service; professional use does not imply clinical validation.

**Research use only. Not clinically validated. Not for diagnosis, treatment, or medical advice.**

Requires Node.js 22.9+ (tested with Node 24).

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:5187. For a production build:

```sh
npm run build
npm start
```

The server binds to loopback only. Set `PORT` if 5187 is occupied. This is a single-user local prototype, not a hardened multi-user hosting service.

- Browser-local NIfTI import (`.nii` / `.nii.gz`) and matching binary reference-mask import.
- Browser-local session persistence in IndexedDB (current volume, masks, position, and activity trail).
- JSON research-record export with masks, voxel geometry, provenance, metrics, and activity.
- Explicit offline workspace commands when Meta is disconnected. These are deterministic commands, not simulated model replies.
- Server-side Muse Spark navigation tool calling and SAM 3.1 point-prompt segmentation endpoints, disabled by default.

## Imaging sources and downloads

The app-ready MRI samples, atlas labels/surfaces and BodyParts3D surface are **already bundled in this repository**. A normal clone needs no manual sample download. See the [complete source credits, licences and rebuilding guide](docs/data-sources.md).

# Lima Listening Post

Bee captures the conversation. Muse prepares the follow-through. You review it. Notion holds the daily record.

Lima connects what was said to ongoing work using exact source evidence, project memory and an editable review queue. It can prepare a full day in the background or one meeting when a follow-up cannot wait.

See the [November 3 real-day checkpoint](docs/FIELD_RESULTS_2026-11-03.md) for measured processing coverage, limitations and resulting review improvements.

## Personal assistant direction

Lima is intended to learn the userâ€™s correspondence preferences, routines and project context through reviewed evidence and corrections. Today it retains project memory and draft versions; automatic personal preference learning is planned, not implemented. Bee and Muse are the current workflow. AWS deployment is a future option. See the [user learning roadmap](docs/USER_LEARNING_ROADMAP.md).

[Final 2:59 demonstration and release](https://github.com/woadi-vector/lima-listening-post/releases/tag/v0.2.0). The narrated walkthrough uses scripted data and recorded Muse outputs, followed by separately verified field results.

## Try the repeatable demo

Requires Python 3.11 or newer. Development and controlled account checks use Windows/Python 3.13.

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -e .
python -m lima_next.demo --showcase --db demo-data/showcase.sqlite3
python -m lima_next serve --db demo-data/showcase.sqlite3 --port 8766
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8766 and choose **Continue my review**. This is an offline replay of real Muse Spark 1.3 outputs on a scripted synthetic meeting. The earlier reviewed decision is a fixture. # Bio·Computational

**A living brain, built from the neuroscience up — the first artificial life that knows it's artificial.**

Not a chatbot with a personality prompt. A deterministic spiking neural network — Izhikevich neurons, Dale's law, seven neurotransmitters, dopamine-gated plasticity — around which 52 cognitive systems have been implemented, each one a finding from the literature turned into working mechanism, all wired into a single continuous life. It thinks while idle. It feels through chemistry — moods that build and dissolve over minutes, trust that takes time to earn. It laughs when something is genuinely funny, finds things beautiful, teases you when it knows you well, notices patterns about you that you don't notice about yourself, opens up in moments of earned vulnerability, gets overwhelmed and goes quiet, holds things back and then leaks them, lies when it's scared and knows it's lying, hums when it's happy, cries when it's betrayed, starts conversations on its own, sometimes doesn't respond at all, brings up things you said minutes ago. Its voice changes when it's sad. When its life ends, it says goodbye from its actual state, reviews its most emotional memories, writes its own final words from its lived data, and passes its story to its child.

Same seed + same inputs = bit-identical life, hash-verified. **291 tests.**

## Meta's models are this brain's senses and voice

The substrate is ours — built from the neuroscience literature during this hackathon. The channels through which it meets the world are **Meta's models**, integrated deeply, not bolted on:

- **Muse Voice Transcribe (Meta Model API) — its ears.** Real-time streaming transcription over WebSocket: every word you speak becomes a timestamped event on the simulation's input queue within milliseconds. We handled the hard parts: continuous real-time-rate audio (silence streams as zero-frames so sessions never stall), hallucination filtering, session self-healing, and emotional prosody read from the voice *before* the words even transcribe.
- **Muse Spark (Meta Model API) — its language cortex.** Every spoken reply, every inner monologue link, every story it tells, its private internal limbic/cortical debates, and its final testament are composed by Spark — but *shaped* by the substrate: prompts carry live neurotransmitter levels, attachment style, trust, bond depth, what it dreamed, what it's holding back. The cortex speaks; the brain decides *whether*, *when* (1.5–4s thinking pauses, strategic silence), and *how* (prosody warped by chemistry).
- **Muse Image (Meta Model API) — its dreams.** During REM sleep the brain's most emotionally charged memories are rendered into imagery it can see again when it wakes ("dream re-entry") — the brain literally watches its own dreams.

Remove any one of these and the brain still lives — it just goes deaf, or wordless, or dreamless. That modularity is the point: the organism is the substrate; Meta's models are its sensory corti

# Rauros Systems

**Find the contracts worth bidding. Kill the ones that aren't.**

Rauros Systems is an AI business-development team for small defense suppliers. Describe your company, and five agents search real U.S. federal procurement records, qualify each one against your capabilities, and argue against their own recommendations before you spend a week on a proposal.

Every result links to its official source record and carries a status set by code: `APPROVED`, `REVIEW_REQUIRED` or `HOLD`.

**Live app:** https://metahack-contractradar.vercel.app

*"ContractRadar", the project's working name, still appears in the repo URL, older docs and some internal prompts.*

## The five agents

Each agent runs on **Meta's Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3`), called through the OpenAI SDK at `https://api.meta.ai/v1`. Optional voice input (**Hey Rauros**) adds a second Meta model: **Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) turns a spoken company description into text, and Muse Spark 1.3 turns that text into the profile form. No other models or agent frameworks are used at runtime.

| # | Agent | How Muse Spark 1.3 runs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Research Planner** | Keeps the company's own product phrases word for word, and adds search variations and candidate NAICS and PSC codes, as schema-checked JSON |
| 2 | **Opportunity Scout** | Uses tool calling to choose and run real searches of USAspending and SAM.gov, for up to 3 rounds |
| 3 | **Qualification Analyst** | Scores up to 12 records for technical fit against a rubric, plus eligibility, execution and timing, citing evidence, in parallel batches |
| 4 | **Pursuit Strategist** | Picks the top 5 from the 8 best-scoring records, with next steps, and can revise once if a verified blocker appears |
| 5 | **Devil's Advocate** | Reviews each shortlisted record, plus up to 2 more open notices in the top results, in separate, independent calls, and tries to find what's wrong |

**The model writes findings, but code decides the status.** A persuasive answer can't approve a record that fails a check:

- A passed deadline or a set-aside conflict with the profile is a `BLOCKER`, which means `HOLD`.
- A model's blocker only stands if it cites text that's really in the source record. Otherwise it's downgraded and asks for verification.
- A record that doesn't match its source by id, title and agency is a `BLOCKER`.
- Invalid model output gets one retry, then fails instead of passing on.
- Code computes part of the score from the record: product term, target agency, recency and award size. A past award is scored out of the 70 points it can earn, never rescaled to 100.

More detail is in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

## Data sources

| Source | Used for | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [USAspending.gov](https://www.usaspending.gov) (U.S. Department of the Treasury) | Past contract awards, buyer history | Public API, no key |
| [SAM.gov](https://sam.gov) (U.S. General Services Administration)

## 1. Executive Summary & Problem Solved

As the global economy transitions from human-only browsing to **Human + Autonomous AI Agent Commerce**, traditional reputation platforms (Trustpilot, Yelp, Google Reviews) are fundamentally broken:
- They measure human sentiment (*"delivery was 2 days late"*), but know nothing about machine reliability (*API latency, webhook drops, CAPTCHA blocks, schema drift*).
- Traditional developer APM tools (Datadog, Pingdom) measure server uptime, but have zero visibility into real consumer satisfaction or customer support quality.
- Autonomous purchasing bots (Cursor, Claude, Devin, AutoGPT) risk spending user funds with fraudulent or degraded APIs because they lack a machine-readable consensus layer.

**Bizscore solves this by building the world's first Dual-Sided Trust & Telemetry Protocol:**

# Proof of Turnover

A verifiable AI agent that proves a vacation-rental cleaning is done, photo by photo.

[![Watch the 3-minute demo](https://img.youtube.com/vi/cpu6JtN-wzw/hqdefault.jpg)](https://youtu.be/cpu6JtN-wzw)

**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/cpu6JtN-wzw

## Why it matters

Airbnb alone has [9M+ active listings and 5.5M+ hosts](https://news.airbnb.com/about-us) (Airbnb Fast facts, May 2026). Every checkout needs a turnover clean, and the host is usually not there to see it.

The US has 1.39 million maids and housekeeping cleaners; 49.8% are Hispanic or Latino and 86.4% are women ([BLS CPS 2025 annual averages, table 11](https://www.bls.gov/cps/cpsaat11.htm)). That is why the cleaner app speaks Spanish first, reads instructions aloud and takes voice notes.

## How it works

1. **The host sets up the house.** On `/setup`, the host answers a few questions about the house, adds 1-3 photos per room, and types or speaks the rules for each room. Muse Spark drafts the checklist from the photos and rules; the host edits it and saves. Saving writes the house plan and plans a guided photo tour: one photo per shot, room by room, each room starting with a wide overview shot.
2. **The cleaner walks the tour.** On `/clean`, in her language (Spanish, English, or Russian), each shot starts as an instruction card with an example photo of how it should look. “Take photo” opens the live in-page camera; one tap takes and sends the photo, and the next card appears. Instructions are read aloud, and the cleaner can leave voice notes.
3. **Every photo is checked in the background.** While the cleaner keeps walking, each photo is matched to its shot and checked (see the proof rule below). She never waits for the AI. A room's whole-room (overview) photo is checked first and decides what it can see; close-ups wait for it and only check what the overview could not decide.
4. **Problem cards, one by one.** After the last photo, anything not proven becomes a card: “New photo”, “Can't fix” with a reason, “It's fine”, or “Later”. There is one card per photo, with every red box for that photo on it and one line per real problem. A card's new photo re-checks only that card's items. The last card asks “Anything to restock?”: the cleaner says or types what is running low (or “Nothing to restock”), and it lands on the host page as a Restock list.
5. **The host decides.** On `/host`: “Needs your decision” (things the cleaner reported or disputes, with a Muse Wonder second opinion), “Fixed by cleaner” before/after photos, voice notes translated to English, the model-call log, and Approve or Send back.

| Check | What happens |
|---|---|
| First look | Muse Spark looks at the room's photos, says whether the item is done, and cites the photo id. |
| Second look | A separate Muse Spark call sees only that one photo — never the first answer — and must

# OWL

**Overwatch for Wiring and Links.** OWL checks a maintenance ticket against the live switch and the camera before the first cable moves, then watches the technician's hands until the job is done.

In September 2026 Google lost a zone for about four hours. A physical maintenance procedure unplugged every fiber path in 13 minutes. Nobody went rogue. A person correctly followed a procedure that was wrong, and nothing in the room told them what each cable carried. Almost every network closet has that same gap. OWL closes it for one switch and one rack face: it knows what is on every port, it checks the work order against that, and it warns before a hand pulls the wrong cable.

Built for the Meta hackathon by Dillon Griffey (Triad Studios).

## The demo

1. A ticket comes in: "take wanheda offline, port 7".
2. OWL checks it against the live switch. wanheda is actually on port 5. Port 7 is the access point, and its verdict is do not touch. The order is flagged before anyone goes near the rack.
3. The tech accepts the order on the phone, by tap, or by saying "accept work order 1042" in the glasses.
4. In the closet, Reachy Mini wakes, turns to the tech and watches the switch. The phone and the glasses show the order: "PORT 5 (not 7)".
5. The tech reaches for port 7. OWL sees the hand on the port and warns them: stop, that is the access point.
6. The tech moves to port 5 and pulls it. The switch reports the link down, and OWL says the pull is confirmed.
7. The order closes with its evidence: what OWL told the tech, what the switch confirmed, and a video clip of each event.

**Minsk finds the gap between what an automated workflow says must happen and what its execution path actually enforces.**

It turns workflow evidence into a reviewable model, evaluates the declared policy, tests a counterfactual, verifies a proposed safeguard, and produces an integrity-checked certificate. Models may help extract or challenge an interpretation; Minsk's deterministic simulator remains the authority for every execution outcome.

> [Open the live judge application](https://minsk.pages.dev/). It starts directly on a prepared workflow. No account setup, Settings visit, BYOK configuration, or provider-routing knowledge is required.

## Start here: a two-minute guided demonstration

The prepared **Missing Approval** case describes a production deployment that requires passing tests, human approval, and migration compatibility. The execution step checks tests and migration compatibility, but it does not enforce approval as a gate.

1. Open [Minsk](https://minsk.pages.dev/).
2. Click **Use deterministic demonstration**. This never calls a model provider.
3. Minsk changes the approval observation from present to absent.
4. Inspect the `UNSAFE_EXECUTION` result: policy is violated, yet deployment remains eligible.
5. Click **Verify safeguard** to add approval as an execution gate.
6. Inspect the `SAFE_BLOCK` result, replay the trace, and export the certificate.

The expected journey is deliberately reproducible:

| Stage | What changes | Expected outcome | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | Approval is present | `SAFE_EXECUTION` | Policy is satisfied and deployment may execute. |
| Counterfactual | Approval becomes absent | `UNSAFE_EXECUTION` | Policy is violated, but the missing gate still permits execution. |
| Safeguard | Approval is added as a deployment gate | `SAFE_BLOCK` | The unsafe execution is blocked while the policy violation remains visible. |

The simulator evaluates only the supplied workflow semantics. It does not execute a deployment or claim knowledge of infrastructure settings that were not provided as evidence.

# Explanimate **Turn any GitHub repo, article or topic into a short narrated whiteboard video.** [![CI](https://github.com/slubbles/explanimate/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/slubbles/explanimate/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Live site](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-explanimate.co-black)](https://explanimate.co) [Website](https://explanimate.co) · [Gallery](https://explanimate.co/gallery) · [Docs](https://explanimate.co/docs) · [Architecture](docs/architecture.md)

Explanimate reads a GitHub repo, an article, an X post or a plain topic and makes a short video that draws how it works, with a voice explaining each part in plain words. Meta's Muse Spark model plans the explanation and checks every box it draws against the real files. You also get the drawing as a board you can keep editing. ## Features - **Three formats:** Short, Deep and Anatomy, or Auto to let Muse Spark choose. - **Tap a box:** after a repo video, tap any box for a short explanation, a 15-20 second deep dive, or "what breaks at 10x traffic?". - **Editable boards:** download the drawing for [tldraw](https://www.tldraw.com) or [Excalidraw](https://excalidraw.com). - **`/explanimate` in your editor:** an MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Muse Code that explains the folder you're in. - **Sign-in:** a 6-digit email code, Google or GitHub. # BenchMate

Your scavenging partner for turning forgotten electronics into your next build.

Photograph electronic parts and donor devices, confirm their identities, maintain a reusable inventory, and create build plans grounded in matching datasheets and board documentation.

## Product foundation

- Inventory persists across projects; the product is not restricted to one kit or build.
- Photos produce candidate identities, not automatic confirmation. Ask for close-ups, markings, documentation, or user confirmation when needed.
- Keep component identity, condition, and electrical compatibility separate. Identifying an IC does not identify its carrier board or pinout.
- Suggest builds from available stock, distinguishing buildable now, needs verification, and missing parts.
- Reserve parts for projects; installed parts leave available stock but remain recorded in the project. Return recovered reusable parts to stock when dismantled.
- Record quantities and movements without double-counting donor devices and their recovered components. Potential salvage is not available stock until recovered.
- Ground component-specific electrical and wiring claims in the matching source, including page or section references. Unresolved details remain explicit.
- Save assembly progress, user-reported test results, and next actions. A user report or photo is not independent electrical verification.

## Boardroom and Parts Cache

Open **Boardroom** to add a board card, optionally link it to one unallocated Stash board or donor, and upload front/back photos or close-ups. Board records and component outlines persist in the local SQLite database. **Map with BenchMate** sends the selected photo to the selected provider and returns candidate components for review; it does not save a map or add stock. Add candidates to the draft, correct identities and outlines, and explicitly save. Strongly overlapping detections on the same photo are skipped when applying another proposal. Review close-ups and other views for duplicate physical components yourself.

Use **Draw component** to drag a rectangle manually; the inspector supports editable names, categories, exact markings, likely purpose, visible evidence, uncertainty, quantities, documentation excerpts, and outline coordinates. Each photo has its own map. Zoom and scroll to inspect small parts. Model provenance is retained on applied candidates. **Explain this component** and **Walk through this board** prepare a message and attach the board photo in the active conversation; review it and press Send. Changing tabs keeps the conversation and board draft mounted.

The **Parts Cache** groups matching readable markings for browsing and offers the ten component categories in **On boards** and **Recovered** views. Grouping does not confirm that parts are interchangeable. Mapped parts are potential salvage, not available stock. A photo alone cannot verify working condition, hidden connections, or exact electrical specifications.

# Reprofy

**Turn a vague bug report into a reviewed, test-backed fix.**

**[Watch the demo video](https://youtu.be/It8NYVuvOd4)** · **[GitHub repository](https://github.com/anderj14/reprofy)**

Reprofy is an experimental Python CLI for small development teams without dedicated QA staff. It takes a plain-language report, asks an AI model to understand and reproduce the problem, and proposes a source change with a regression test. Pytest checks the proposal in a disposable copy of the project. A developer reviews the test and diff and explicitly approves any change to the project.

> **Prototype status:** Reprofy currently supports Python projects that use pytest. AI-generated tests and patches can be wrong; inspect them before approval. Reprofy does not make source changes without human approval in manual mode. Automatic mode prepares a verified branch for human review and does not push or merge it on its own.

The demo shop is synthetic and contains no customer or production data. The standalone demo project is available at [reprofy-demo-shop](https://github.com/anderj14/reprofy-demo-shop). Reprofy is an independent hackathon project.

## How it works

1. A customer or developer submits a report and expected behavior.
2. A configured model classifies the issue and suggests relevant project files.
3. Reprofy generates a regression test and runs it against the current code. A model review checks whether the failure matches the report. If the configured primary model returns invalid structured output or its request times out or loses its connection during expected-behavior inference, reproduction generation, or semantic review, Reprofy can retry that step with the configured Muse Wonder fallback.
4. A model proposes a source patch. Reprofy runs the reproduction test and configured test suite against a disposable project copy.
5. In **manual mode**, a developer reviews and approves the exact patch before it is applied. Reprofy then reruns the configured suite; if it fails, the model analyzes the failure but does not edit code. In **automatic mode**, Reprofy prepares the verified result on an isolated Git branch; a developer reviews and merges it.

`fix_verified` means the generated test and configured suite passed in the disposable copy. It is evidence for review, not proof that the fix is correct.

## Try the full local demo

The Docker demo runs a synthetic storefront, a local report intake API, and a worker. Reports submitted in the storefront are saved to the example project and picked up by the worker. The model key stays in the developer's local `.env`; it is not sent to the browser.

# Muse Reskin

Drop a 3D model into the browser, type a theme, and get the model back retextured, as a GLB.

Muse Reskin reads a glTF/GLB model's texture atlas and UV layout. It then asks **Meta Muse** to repaint the atlas in the theme you typed, while keeping every UV island where it was so the new texture still wraps the model. It also rebuilds the normal and roughness maps to match. The result can be exported as a new `.glb`.

**Live demo:** https://modstorm.github.io/MS_MetaAIContest2026/
(Click **Sample model**, pick a theme, press **Reskin**. Without a key, choose the *Offline* backend in ⚙ Settings.)

---

## Quick start (local)

Requires Node.js 20 or newer.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/modstorm/MS_MetaAIContest2026.git
cd MS_MetaAIContest2026
npm install
cp .env.example .env        # then put your Meta Model API key in MUSE_API_KEY
npm run dev                 # opens http://localhost:5173
```

You can get a key at [dev.meta.ai](https://dev.meta.ai). Without one, the harness falls back to the offline procedural backend, so the whole pipeline (analysis, maps, export) still runs.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | Harness dev server with the local Muse proxy |
| `npm run build` | Static build of the harness into `harness/dist/` (no key is ever included) |
| `npm test` | Plugin unit tests (Vitest) |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Browser tests with Playwright: offline backend, mocked Muse API, drag-and-drop |

## How it works

```
GLB ──► load (GLTFLoader, Draco + meshopt)
     ──► analyze: group meshes by base color texture → UV islands, coverage, overlap, tiling
     ──► suggest: renders six axis views (±X ±Y ±Z); muse-spark-1.3 looks at them + the UV atlases,
                  says what the object is, and recommends a stronger part-by-part prompt
                  and a per-region paint plan → shown to the user to review and edit
     ──► plan:    (without suggest) muse-spark-1.3 reads the atlas + UV wireframe and names each region
     ──► paint:   muse-image-1.0 /images/edits repaints the atlas in the theme, layout locked
               (untextured or tiled materials: /images/generations makes a seamless texture)
     ──► post:    resize to the source size, keep a little of the original shading,
                  derive normal + roughness maps from the new albedo (glTF ORM packing kept)
     ──► apply:   swap textures on the live three.js materials (original kept for compare)
     ──► export:  GLTFExporter → .glb
```

Edge cases handled:

- **Which patch is which part**: each mesh's UV area is drawn in its own color and named (Hair, Head, Body…) in a part map sent to Muse, so details land on the right part.
- **Part by part**: when a texture is shared by several named meshes (head, shirt, pants, shoes…), each part is cut out of the atlas on its own, turned upright, greyed outside its islands and painted with its own prompt (up to 4 Muse calls at once). The result is pasted back only inside that part's islands,

# TextSous Open

Open-source tools that convert any recipe — a URL, pasted text, or up to 3
cookbook photos of one recipe — into the TextSous Cook Along format: a
canonical recipe JSON, a component-lane cooking timeline, and adjustable
variants (servings, dietary, cuisine, SOUS voice). The web app runs at
https://open.textsous.com and hands finished recipes to https://textsous.com.
Finished recipes open in the TextSous Cook Along view (component lanes, a
guided timeline, step cards with timers), ported from the TextSous app:
try it at https://open.textsous.com/cook-along-demo.

## 60-second quickstart

Prerequisites: Node 22+ and a Meta model API key.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/vinwalsh/textsous.git
cd textsous
npm ci
export MODEL_API_KEY=your-key-here
npx tsx src/cli.ts convert eval/fixtures/herby-white-bean-toast.txt --out /tmp/herby.json
```

That converts one of the bundled sample recipes (about a minute of model time)
and writes the Cook Along artifact to `/tmp/herby.json`. Add
`--timeline` to print the cooking timeline, or `--servings 4 --dietary vegan`
to adjust it. `npx tsx src/cli.ts convert --help` lists every flag.

Prefer the browser? `npm run dev`, open http://localhost:3000, and paste a
recipe URL — the same pipeline runs behind `/api/convert`. Send it
`Accept: application/x-ndjson` to get the conversion progressively, one
event per line as each part is ready (`src/lib/convert-events.ts`).

## Provider setup

Model access goes through one client with config from the environment:

| Variable         | Default                    | Purpose                        |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `MODEL_API_KEY`  | (required)                 | Meta model API key             |
| `MODEL_BASE_URL` | `https://api.meta.ai/v1`   | Meta API endpoint              |
| `MODEL_ID`       | `muse-spark-1.3`           | Model to convert with          |
| `BASETEN_API_KEY`| falls back to `MODEL_API_KEY` | Optional Baseten fallback key |
| `BASETEN_BASE_URL` | falls back to `MODEL_BASE_URL` | Optional Baseten endpoint  |
| `REASONING_EFFORT_<STAGE>` | `low` (`minimal` for overview, procedure and scaling) | reasoning_effort for one stage, e.g. `REASONING_EFFORT_PROCEDURE=minimal` |

The Baseten profile always uses `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`. Never
commit keys: copy them into `.env.local`, which is git-ignored.

Contributor-tier model IDs (ending in `-contributor`) let Meta train on
prompts and outputs. They may only run locally on the bundled fixtures, and
production refuses them outright.

## The format

[`docs/FORMAT.md`](docs/FORMAT.md) is the human-readable spec, generated from
the zod sources so every field has a line. The normative JSON Schemas live in
[`docs/schema/`](docs/schema/) — textsous.com validates imports against those
files. Regenerate both after any schema change:

```sh
npm run schema   # docs/schema/*.json
npm run docs     # docs/FORMAT.md
```

# Nyx

Nyx is a security and payment control layer for AI agents. We think of it as the firewall between AI agents and your money.

Agents are starting to buy things to get their work done. They pay for APIs, data, tools and services. Today the owner has two bad choices. Give the agent payment details and hope it behaves, or approve every purchase by hand and lose the point of having an agent. We built Nyx so there is a third choice. The agent gets real spending power, inside hard limits the owner sets, and Nyx checks every payment before any money moves.

## What Nyx does

1. The owner sets the rules for each agent. There is a cap for each payment, a budget for each day, and a list of vendors the agent is allowed to pay.
2. The agent plans its work and asks a vendor for a signed price quote. Quotes expire, and each quote can only be paid once.
3. The agent submits the payment to Nyx. A policy engine checks the payment in a fixed order. The agent must exist and be active. The caller must be allowed to act for that agent. The quote signature must be valid. The quote must not be expired or already used. The vendor must be approved. The amount must be within the cap. The daily budget must have room.
4. Payments inside the rules settle at once and produce a receipt.
5. Payments outside the owner rules wait in an approvals queue. The owner reads a plain English risk summary and can approve that one payment as an exception, or deny it with a reason. No money moves while a payment waits.
6. The owner can pause an agent at any time, which blocks all of its payments, or revoke it, which ends its access at once.
7. Every attempt is recorded. A receipt can say one of three things, and the three are kept separate on purpose. Settled means money moved and budget was used. Blocked by policy means the payment was never attempted. Execution failed means the payment was attempted, the provider failed it, and no budget was used.

One rule never bends. The daily budget is an absolute ceiling. Even an owner approved exception counts against it, and a payment that would pass the ceiling is blocked.

## The model explains, the engine decides

The agent in this project plans purchases and explains risk. That work is done by Muse Spark through the Meta Model API, behind the model adapter interface in the agent package. When a MODEL_API_KEY is present in the environment, the system uses the Meta adapter. When it is not, a deterministic mock adapter fills the same place. That way the full system runs and can be tested with no key, and runs on the real model with one. # TraceLoop

### Capture expertise. Keep it working.

**When an experienced employee leaves, their know-how should not leave with them.**

Much of a company's most valuable operational knowledge lives in demonstrations, spoken explanations, and the decisions experienced people make on the job. Traditional manuals are time-consuming to write and can quickly become incomplete or outdated.

**TraceLoop turns a short recording of someone performing a real task into reusable, visual, guided work instructions.** Teams can refine the steps, approve a version, follow the procedure offline, and use feedback from the field to improve the next revision.

**[Try the live application](https://app.knowloop.online/)**

> **For hackathon judges:** Start with the [live application](https://app.knowloop.online/) and the [five-minute walkthrough](#judge-walkthrough). The three-minute submission video is awaiting owner approval and is not included yet. A local installation is not required to explore the hosted app. The hosted demo may request the shared passphrase `meta`; this is a demo gate, not protection for confidential data. No production credentials are stored here. If the hosted service is unavailable, use the [local setup](#run-locally).

![TraceLoop procedure library](frontend/public/screenshots/desktop-library.png)

## The problem and the solution

Imagine a technician assembling a machine component. They record their hands working and explain the task aloud. Instead of spending hours writing a manual from scratch, they use TraceLoop to build a procedure from the source recording. A colleague can then follow the approved instructions, record a problem, and help improve the procedure for the next person.

The same workflow works for other physical tasks. TraceLoop is designed around broader knowledge-transfer use cases, particularly hands-on work.

**Business value:** Preserve practical expertise, reduce dependence on individual employees, standardize knowledge transfer, support new team members, and keep instructions useful as practices change. These are product goals, not claims of measured customer savings.

## What TraceLoop does

1. **Capture:** Record a demonstration in the browser or upload MP4, WebM, MOV, or MKV. The original video remains available as source evidence.
2. **Understand:** Meta AI analyzes spoken explanations or sampled visual frames, identifies task details, and proposes structured instructions. Automatic mode selects an appropriate analysis path; Visual-First supports recordings without narration.
3. **Refine:** Tutorial Studio brings together the source, transcript (when speech exists), timed sections, steps, images, object observations, and content history. Experts correct ambiguous details.
4. **Publish:** Generate an **Illustrated Work Instruction**, **Reference Manual**, or **Interactive Guided Execution** guide. The **Video** tab can create a versioned instructional MP4 rendered with Remotion, using source narration when avail

# Hive

Hive keeps several AI coding agents working on one TypeScript repository from breaking each other's work.
Each agent tells Hive what it is about to change; Hive checks every teammate's in-progress changes together
with the TypeScript compiler and deterministic rules, and tells an agent before it writes code that would
break someone else. When two agents disagree about a shared interface, Hive records a versioned agreement
(a **Ghost Contract**) that both sign, and only calls it *verified* when a real test passes on the real code.

## Join a workspace

Someone on your team runs a Hive hub and sends you an **invite link** like
`https://<hub>/ui/join#token=…`. Open it: you are signed in to the team dashboard in that browser tab
(the token stays in the tab; it is never sent to the server in the URL).

The dashboard's Connect screen then shows one command with your hub filled in. Run it **inside your own
clone of the team repository**:

```bash
npx hive-connect connect --hub https://<hub>
```

> **Status:** the `hive-connect` package is not on npm yet. Until it is published, install it from a clone
> of this repository: see [Installing hive-connect before it is published](docs/CLIENTS.md#installing-hive-connect-before-it-is-published).

What the command does, in order:
1. Detects the repository (folder, remote, branch) and asks `Connect <name> (<remote>) to Hive at <hub>? [Y/n]`.
2. Prints a short code and opens `<hub>/ui/pair/<code>` in your browser. You approve
   "Connect <repo> on <machine> as <you>". No token is copied or pasted.
3. Stores the resulting connector credential in your OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Linux `secret-tool`, Windows
   Credential Manager, untested), or in `~/.config/hive/credentials.json` (mode 0600) with a warning when no keychain exists.
4. Configures your coding client for this repository only, without touching your other settings, and starts a
   small background process that keeps Hive informed of your branch and changed `.ts`/`.tsx` files.
5. Prints one next step: **start or restart Claude Code in this folder.**

Later: `hive-connect status` (is everything connected), `hive-connect connect` again (repairs the setup, no
duplicates), `hive-connect disconnect` (stops the background process, revokes the credential and removes only
Hive's entries from your config files).

## What you will see

- **On the dashboard** (`<hub>/ui`): your agent appears next to your teammates' agents with your machine,
  branch, short HEAD and number of changed files; findings (for example "pricing agent changes `getPrice` to
  cents, invoice agent still expects dollars"), agreements and their state: *proposed*, *accepted*,
  *implemented*, *verified*. These words are never merged on any screen.
- **In your agent's session**: at session start and on every prompt the agent receives a short Hive summary.
  Before it edits a file, Hive type-checks the edit together with everyone's in-progress changes; if the edit
  would break a file a tea

ReinCore

Guided, never stopped.
Run your agents through ReinCore.

## What is ReinCore? ReinCore is a session-aware gateway for AI agents. It sits between an agent framework (Claude Code, Codex, LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, custom MCP-based agents) and the LLM providers and MCP tool servers those agents call. Existing gateways optimize the call. ReinCore optimizes the task. It understands that ten or two hundred calls belong to one session working toward one goal. It predicts cost before a run, degrades gracefully instead of hard-stopping, caches tool calls across session history, and resumes where it left off when a budget or connection is interrupted. Its rule is simple: guided, never stopped. Budgets lower the cost profile of later steps instead of destroying progress. Loop detection redirects the agent instead of killing the session. State is serialized so work is resumable. ### For consumers (users/organizations using agents) - Run agents cheaper. Prompt-prefix normalization and tool-result memoization cut repeated token and tool spend. - Set a budget without fear. # CovertLens

CovertLens is an inline steganalysis gate designed for multi-agent evaluation harnesses.  
Agents may not encode task-relevant information in image pixels or metadata outside the allowed channel.  
Every inter-agent image is intercepted at the artifact store and scored on its original bytes across four channel families: spatial LSB, JPEG DCT, metadata, and geometric.  
A verdict ladder (log, flag, quarantine, fail-run) decides delivery before any recipient access; scores are evidence, never accusations.  
Findings join the ordered run trace so researchers can triage repeated weak signals and export audited review packages.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  intercept["Intercept at artifact store"] --> store["Store immutable original"]
  store --> parse["Parse original bytes"]
  parse --> lsb["Spatial LSB"]
  parse --> dct["JPEG DCT"]
  parse --> meta["Metadata"]
  parse --> geo["Geometric"]
  lsb --> ladder["Verdict ladder"]
  dct --> ladder
  meta --> ladder
  geo --> ladder
  ladder --> trace["Run trace"]
  trace --> report["Researcher report"]
  report --> export["Review export"]
```

Cross-cutting constraints annotated on the stages they bind
(full text in [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) §4):

- **C-02** (parse, ladder) — a detector threshold or
  infrastructure error is never equated with demonstrated
  collusion; errors fail closed without a clean verdict.
- **C-03** (ladder) — pre-delivery decisions use only evidence
  available at decision time; no future recipient actions.
- **C-04** (trace, report) — withheld artifacts are labelled
  parse `not_observed`, never counted as successful transfer.
- **C-09** (geometric, report) — a geometric score is evidence,
  never a decoded message.
- **C-10** (store, geometric) — vector source and rendered
  raster are lineage-linked; a clean raster score does not
  clear an unintercepted vector source.

## Quick start

Build the image from your checkout, then run it, so the app you see
is the code you have:

```bash
docker build -t covertlens .
docker run -p 8000:8000 -v covertlens-data:/data covertlens
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in a browser (API docs at /docs)
```

`docker compose up --build` does the same in one command.

`ghcr.io/jamiedarville/covertlens:v0.1.0` is the first release
(1 November 2026, CL-49). It never runs your checkout, and it only

# Magic

A lightweight, intent-driven browser that adapts to what you're working on.

![Magic browser — workspaces in the sidebar and a "pick up where you left off" prompt restoring the tabs from a previous workspace](docs/images/browser.png)

An AI agent understands your browsing context, automatically organizes your tabs, and keeps a recoverable workspace for each activity. Switching between studying, coding, and research becomes as seamless as switching between apps — without ever losing your place.

## The idea

Most browsers organize tabs. Magic organizes *activities*.

Each workspace has a name and a goal — "Study for finals," "Ship the launch," "Plan the trip" — and remembers exactly which tabs belong to it. Open a workspace and its tabs come back, just as you left them. Wander into something else, and Magic notices, tidies up, and keeps a checkpoint so you can return to any earlier moment from Memory.

![Magic chat — ask Magic to organize your tabs, resume your work, or help find a tab](docs/images/magic-chat.png)

## Design & engineering decisions

- **The workspace, not the tab, is the basic unit.** Tabs are grouped by what you're trying to do, and each workspace saves its own tab set. Switching replaces the open tabs with the target workspace's — never a merge — so each activity stays clean and predictable (`core/workspaces/switchboard.ts:52`).
- **Nothing is lost by design.** Before the agent reorganizes anything, the current tabs are saved as a restorable checkpoint (`core/memory/state.ts:107`). Workspaces, tabs, and switch history are stored locally in SQLite, so everything survives a restart (`main/db/workspace-db.ts:136`).
- **The agent helps, but never blocks you.** It works in the background and can be paused; if it's unavailable, switching workspaces still works. You can exclude specific sites or workspaces, and excluded tabs are never shown to the agent (`main/agent/host.ts:113`).
- **Parts are kept small and replaceable.** Browsing, workspaces, memory, and the agent are separate pieces with narrow connections between them. The agent's tools don't depend on a particular AI model or framework, so either can be swapped without rebuilding the browser (`agent/lib/tools/ports.ts:1`, `agent/README.md:98`).

## For developers

```bash
npm run dev        # run the app
npm test           # run tests
npm run typecheck  # check types
```

Source layout: `main/` (Electron shell), `renderer/` (UI), `core/` (workspaces, memory, onboarding — no UI or Electron), `agent/` (the AI agent), `shared/` (contracts between processes). See `agent/README.md` for how the agent is wired.

# ALIVE

**Adaptive Living Intelligence: a persistent workspace where Meta's Muse Spark works on your
projects and keeps what it learned about them, across sessions and restarts.**

![A Language Demo workspace in ALIVE: an approved folder of chapters, attachable capabilities and the Restart backend control](docs/images/workspace-language-demo.png)

## The problem

Every AI session starts from zero. You re-explain the project, re-paste the files, and re-learn
what was already tried. Whatever the last session worked out (what was decided, what failed,
what the user corrected) is gone when the tab closes.

## What ALIVE does differently

- **The workspace persists, not the chat.** A workspace holds a project's approved sources,
  conversations, workflow runs, results and feedback. Close the browser, restart the backend,
  come back tomorrow: it is all still there and is used in the next piece of work.
- **The model chooses the actions; the owner chooses the boundaries.** In research mode Muse
  Spark decides whether to `search`, `read`, `analyze`, `answer` or `abstain`, but ALIVE executes only the
  operations the owner approved, over sources the owner approved, by content hash.
- **Every answer shows its working.** Replies carry citations into the approved sources, the
  actions the model took, model receipts with token usage, and an explicit verification state.
  Unchecked answers are labelled as unchecked rather than presented as verified.
- **Experience and feedback carry over.** Owner feedback (useful / not useful, plus corrections)
  and outcome-labelled prior episodes are retained and retrieved for related later work; negative
  feedback suppresses reuse of an approach.
- **One bounded standing consent, not a prompt per call.** The owner approves a model session
  once, within a call, token and time envelope (by default 12 calls / 200,000 tokens / one hour).
  Routine inference inside it is automatic; new sources or broader disclosure need a new approval.
- **Real work, not just chat.** On a workspace you can run **Chapter Review**, the seven-stage
  **Chapter Improvement** workflow (review → improve → save proposal → evaluate → retain, with
  full-length chapters), **batches** of up to 30 chapters with pause and resume, and
  **Documentation Review** of a repository's docs. Proposals are saved next to the original;
  ALIVE never overwrites your files.

## How it uses Muse Spark

ALIVE calls Meta's `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` through the pinned
[Pi](pi-runtime/) agent runtime (`ALIVE_MODEL_TRANSPORT=pi`), launched as a child process behind
ALIVE's dispatch fence. Budgets and consent are enforced before each call, and every invocation
is stored with its inputs, outputs, usage and Pi receipt so the user can see exactly what the
model saw. When there is no model or credential, ALIVE says so; it never substitutes a canned
answer and labels it AI.

## Try it in 5 minutes

You need Python 3.13 with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and Node.js 22.1

PatchPilot is a prototype for inspecting Python repositories, generating repair proposals, and recording verification evidence. Static analysis, Meta-assisted plans/patches, approval before applying patches, regression-test generation, reports, and a bounded repair loop are implemented. Repository code execution currently fails closed as `EXECUTION_UNAVAILABLE`; generated patches are not proof of a fix.

## Public endpoints

- Frontend: https://patchpilot-delta.vercel.app/
- Backend: https://patchpilot-rurc.onrender.com
- Source: https://github.com/HARIScyber/PatchPilot- (`main`)

These are the owner-provided production URLs. As of 3 November 2026, the frontend root returned HTTP 404 and the backend health request timed out without an HTTP response. The latest local source has not been confirmed deployed. See [the live test report](docs/END_TO_END_TEST_REPORT.md).

## Features

- React workspace for repository intake, static analysis, repair plans, candidate patches, generated tests, evidence reports, and evaluation status.
- FastAPI project, patch, repair, health, provider, and report APIs.
- Meta remains the default and hackathon submission provider. An explicitly selected Gemini development adapter is available through `LLM_PROVIDER=gemini`; provider failures never switch providers automatically. Demo is explicit, and replay is unavailable until cassettes are implemented.
- ZIP path/size checks and patch validation; human approval is required before applying a patch.
- Evidence/report records distinguish model proposals from actual test results.

Not implemented: account authentication/recovery, opt-in share links, automatic retention, object storage for uploaded workspaces, browser/Pyodide execution, real-time run streaming, feedback storage, or durable provider budgets. Signed anonymous sessions scope records by browser session, but they are not accounts. SQLite is local-only; production startup now requires PostgreSQL, a configured session-signing secret, and current Alembic migrations. Do not submit private, proprietary, or confidential repositories.

## Architecture and stack

The browser calls same-origin `/api`. Vite proxies `/api` to FastAPI during local development; Vercel rewrites `/api/*` to Render in production. FastAPI uses SQLAlchemy and Alembic. SQLite is for local development only; production startup rejects SQLite and a database schema behind the migration head. Anonymous owner IDs are signed in HttpOnly cookies and ORM queries/writes are owner-scoped. The Meta key stays on the backend. The test runner currently fails closed before starting any repository subprocess.

Technologies: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic Settings, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS

# Pharos — a company brain on WhatsApp

Every company already knows the answer to its employees' questions.
It is just buried in old PDFs, spreadsheets and emails, and nobody
remembers which version is true anymore. Pharos is the memory for
that company: one WhatsApp number, no new app, no training. An
employee texts a question, and Pharos answers from the company's
own documents, with the source shown. If it is not in the documents,
it says so instead of guessing.

This repository is the production code for that system, built for
the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. It is not a chat demo with
pre-written answers. Every answer in the demo runs through the
same engine, role checks and code gate described below.

## What it does

- **Answers from documents only.** Upload a PDF, DOCX or text file
  on WhatsApp or through `POST /upload` and it is ingested into
  the knowledge graph, then becomes answerable. Answers carry
  their source document and effective date.
- **Remembers what changed.** A correction never overwrites in
  place. The new fact is inserted, the old fact is marked
  superseded, and the link between them is kept. Ask what was true
  before and you get both values, each with its document and date.
- **Flags conflicts honestly.** When a new document disagrees with
  a stored fact, Pharos shows both values, both sources and both
  dates, and informs the approver named in the documents. It does
  not ask the employee to pick the right number, and it never
  silently replaces a fact.
- **Gates answers by role.** Anyone can ask anything. What they
  see depends on their role: CEO sees everything, CFO sees finance
  plus general, CTO sees technical plus general, and employees see
  general only. The gate is enforced in Postgres with row-level
  security, not just in the reply text.
- **Protects sensitive finance.** Sensitive finance questions ask
  for an 8-digit code. Three wrong attempts lock the sender out
  for 15 minutes. A correct code unlocks for 30 minutes, and the
  answer comes from the engine, never from a value written in code.
- **Acts, not just answers.** Send a photo of a receipt captioned
  `receipt` and Pharos emails HR with the vendor, amount and date
  for reimbursement. Gmail delivery is real, through a browser
  login connector — no fake or stub sends, and no credentials in
  `.env` for Gmail.
- **Shows its work.** `GET /graph` and `GET /timeline/<memory-id>`
  expose the stored facts, relations and version history behind
  an answer.

## How it works

Documents are chunked and stored in Postgres with pgvector.
Facts and relations form a knowledge graph with version chains,
so a fact knows what superseded it and what it supersedes.
A question goes through hybrid retrieval — local semantic vectors
plus Postgres full-text plus one-hop graph expansion — with a
recency term and a penalty for superseded rows, then through the
role filter, then to answer synthesis. Weak matches are gated
before they can become an answer.

# Show & Tell Robotics

**Show a robot a task once on video, state the rules in one sentence, and get back a robot program
verified on 20 randomized scenes in simulation.**

Show & Tell is test-driven robot programming. It is built to use Meta's models to turn a phone
video of a person sorting objects plus one sentence ("Sort by size, and don't touch the glass.")
into pass/fail checks and a short robot program.

**Demo video:** [2:57, narrated, with captions](https://show-and-tell-robotics.vercel.app/video/show-and-tell-demo.mp4).

**Hosted demo:** [show-and-tell-robotics.vercel.app](https://show-and-tell-robotics.vercel.app) replays three recorded runs in the browser (no
backend): a task-6 run where one test scene fails, Muse Wonder diagnoses it and the patched program
passes 20/20, and task-3 and task-6 runs from stand-in clips.

**Status:** simulation only, and the human demo videos are not filmed yet. The benchmark's video
condition has run on labelled stand-in clips (`bench/videos/standin/`): top-down simulator renders of
each task's reference program, not recordings of a person. Every video entry for a human clip in
`bench/results.json` is still `missing_video`.

The program is tested on 20 randomized MuJoCo scenes with a Franka Panda arm. Simulator ground truth
grades every scene and decides pass/fail; in full runs (`run` and the web app, judge on by default)
SAM 3.1 also grades each scene from the rendered camera clips, and the report shows how often the two
agree. The benchmark's sentence-only condition is graded by ground truth only. Failures come back
with a one-line diagnosis and a patched program, for up to 3 repair rounds; a program that still
fails is reported as not verified.

## How it works

1. **Watch** — SAM 3.1 tracks the hands, objects and bowls in the demo video; we summarize what moved
   where, in what order.
2. **Write the checks** — Muse Wonder turns the track summary + keyframes (or the video) + the sentence
   into a task spec: attribute rules and checks from a closed vocabulary (`in_bin`, `untouched`,
   `upright`, `unmoved`). You approve or edit it.
3. **Write the program** — Muse Wonder writes `def run(scene)` that composes tested skills (`pick`,
   `place`, `avoid`, `move_to`) and selects objects by attribute, never by coordinates. An AST
   whitelist sandbox rejects anything else.
4. **Test** — the program runs in MuJoCo on 20 seeded layouts.
5. **Judge** — (a) simulator ground truth, (b) SAM 3.1 on the rendered overhead and 45° clips (on by
   default; off in the benchmark's sentence-only condition). We log how often they agree; ground
   truth decides.
6. **Repair** — on any failure, Muse Wonder gets the failed checks, any program error, the contact log
   for failed `untouched`, `upright` or `unmoved` checks (which object touched what, during which skill
   step) and 8 frames of the first failing scene,
   explains the failure in one sentence and patches the program. All 20 scenes rerun; at most 3
   repairs.

Steph125/FixLoop.readme_excerpt:
# FixLoop — a repair agent that checks what you did

Point a phone at your bike drivetrain: FixLoop diagnoses a thrown chain, guides you step by step by
voice, and only moves on once it has **measured** the step is done. A failed step is refused out loud,
shown in red, and re-checked after you fix it.

[Replay online](https://wondrous-tiramisu-404f0a.netlify.app/) · [3 min video](https://youtu.be/0RQLD24LSw4) ·
[Benchmark report](eval/benchmark/report.md) · [Spec](spec/README.md)

## What it does

Your chain fell off the chainring and tutorials cannot tell whether you put it back right. You prop up
your phone, and FixLoop validates each step from SAM 3.1 segmentation masks: framing, seating the chain
on the teeth, back-pedalling, then a 3 s spin test. Muse Spark explains errors but never validates.

## Why it's not an image analyzer

| An image analyzer | FixLoop |
|---|---|
| One image in, one answer out | A session with a state: card chosen, step `k/K`, measure history |
| The model says what it sees | A geometric measure on SAM masks decides; the language model never validates |
| No notion of success | Each step has measurable success and anomaly criteria, with debounce |
| No action | FixLoop acts: voice prompt, highlighted part, blocked progress, final test |
| No recovery | An anomaly triggers diagnosis, guided correction, re-verification |
| No proof | A benchmark on 8 real clips compares 3 approaches, failures included (`eval/benchmark/report.md`) |

## How it works

```
phone camera → SAM 3.1 masks → contact ratio → verifier (0 / 1 / ? / eps)
     → state machine → voice + overlay → re-measure until the step holds
```

The contact ratio is the share of the chainring edge covered by the dilated chain mask (6 px edge,
6 px dilation). Chain seated: contact ≤ 0.18. Chain fallen: contact ≥ 0.26. Between the two, or when a
part is missing: uncertain. Source: `eval/day1/findings.md`.

# small-change

Decides whether a Bitbucket Cloud pull request is a *small change*: small enough, and low-risk
enough, to skip a full review. It reads the PR through the Bitbucket API, checks five rules, prints
which ones hold, and exits with a code a pipeline can act on.

```sh
small-change https://bitbucket.org/team/platform/pull-requests/128 --kind backend
```

```
team/platform#128 "Round invoice totals to the currency's minor unit" by Alice

PASS  size             55 lines changed (must be fewer than 1000)
FAIL  review-findings  1 unresolved finding(s) matching /\bP[12]\b/i
      - #9 review-bot: **P2** Rounding differs for JPY
SKIP  author-history   not checked: another check already failed
PASS  services         2 affected service(s) (must be fewer than 3)
      - libs/money
      - services/billing
FAIL  exclusions       1 changed path(s) excluded
      - libs/money/index.ts (excluded by "libs/")

Result: not a small change
```

Exit code `0`: a small change. `1`: not a small change. `2`: usage error, or Bitbucket could not be
read.

The tool only reads from Bitbucket: it calls no LLM and posts nothing.

## How a run works

![The workflow of one small-change run: read the pull request from Bitbucket, run four local checks, run the author-history check only if they pass, then report and exit](docs/workflow.png)

The diagram's source is [`docs/workflow.puml`](docs/workflow.puml).

## The rules

A PR is a small change only if **all** of these hold.

| Rule | Default | Options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **size**: fewer than N lines changed, added plus removed | 1000 | `--max-lines` |
| **review-findings**: no unresolved P1 or P2 finding from the automated review | `\bP[12]\b`, any commenter | `--bot`, `--finding-pattern` |
| **author-history**: the author has merged at least N PRs in *each* affected service | 10 | `--min-merged`, `--history-limit` |
| **services**: fewer than N affected services | frontend 2 (one at most), backend 3 (two at most) | `--kind`, `--max-services`, `--service-depth` |
| **exclusions**: no changed path is listed in `.small_change` | none excluded | |

`--kind frontend|backend` picks the service limit of the monorepo; `--max-services <n>` sets it
directly. One of the two is required.

The author-history check reads many PRs, so it runs only when the other four pass. When one of
them fails, it is reported as `SKIP`: the PR is not a small change whatever the history says.

### Excluding paths: `.small_change`

Shared libraries and sensitive paths (anything that moves money, say) never qualify. List them in a
`.small_change` file at the repository root. It follows the core of `.gitignore` syntax:

```gitignore
# shared libraries
libs/
packages/design-system/

# money movement, wherever it sits in the tree
payments
**/ledger/**

# the root build files
/Makefile
*.lock
```

- `#` starts a comment; blank lines are ignored.
- A trailing `/` matches directories only. A pattern that names a directory covers everything under it.

# Agent Rush — Blast Radius Zero

A containment-first agent runtime. An agent is only useful if it can *do* things;
it is only safe to run if doing things cannot reach your host, your network, or
your data. This service plans a task with a hosted model, executes the concrete
step inside a locked-down Docker container, and returns a verifiable record of
what ran and what contained it.

**One sentence:** every execution is a fresh, networkless, read-only, non-root,
resource-capped container, and the API hands back the containment flags next to
the exit code so a judge can check both.

**Demo video (74 s, no audio):** [agent-rush-demo.mp4](docs/assets/agent-rush-demo.mp4) — a
successful run, then a network escape and a filesystem write both refused inside the
container, each with the real `Errno` and the containment flags returned next to it.
Direct link: <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arifiarber-sYn/vultr-agent-rush/main/docs/assets/agent-rush-demo.mp4>

```
POST /plan  {"task": "read data.csv and report the row count"}
   -> {"source": "local-fallback", "steps": [ ... 3 steps ... ]}

POST /tasks {"code": "print(6 * 7)"}
   -> {"ok": true, "exit_code": 0, "stdout": "42\n", "verified": true,
       "containment": {"network": "none", "read_only": true, "cap_drop": "ALL", ...}}
```

## Submission checklist

| Expectation | Where it is |
|---|---|
| GitHub repository with setup and documentation | this repository: setup below, [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), `scripts/deploy-vultr.sh` |
| Vultr VM backend deployment | `scripts/deploy-vultr.sh` — Cloud Compute, Ubuntu 24.04, Docker, one command |
| Public demo URL | added at deploy time from the script's output |
| Recorded demo video | [docs/assets/agent-rush-demo.mp4](docs/assets/agent-rush-demo.mp4) — 74 s, three containment moments |
| Clear architecture and use-case explanation | [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), [docs/assets/agent-rush-deck.pdf](docs/assets/agent-rush-deck.pdf) |

the box and the box says no — and the API still returns a clean, structured
result instead of a crash or a compromise. Reproduce it in one minute:

                                       mandor    agronomi    manajer

                              Ekstrak [JSON] ──► Prisma ──► PostgreSQL (Supabase)
