# LedgerLine: the AI back office for trucking carriers

An AI operator for a trucking carrier's money desk. It takes driver advance requests, invoices
delivered loads and runs weekly settlements and payouts. From Nov 4 it posts paid paystubs, paid
advances, the invoices it makes and the customer payments people record to a QuickBooks Online
sandbox on its own; money codes, escrow releases, card pull-backs and factoring are not posted yet.
Meta models read each request, check it against the rules, explain every exception and propose
the action. A person approves, or the owner's own autopilot rules do inside limits the owner sets;
the engine executes.

Built from scratch for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026), Indie track,
"Build for Your World" theme.

Live at https://ledgerline.thewolfpackco.com. Runs with no outside account: press "Try the demo
carrier" on the sign-in page there, or run `npm run e2e` locally (a local Postgres only), where
the models answer from a recording. See [Try it](#try-it).

## Trucking pay in one week

A trucking company is paid by customers to haul loads, and it pays the drivers who haul them. Money
in: a delivered load becomes a customer invoice. Money out: every Friday, each driver's week becomes
a paystub. Monique's week at Blue Ridge Freight Lines, a fictional carrier in the demo: three loads
$2,400.00, fuel and tolls back $180.00, an advance taken Wednesday -$200.00, insurance for five days
-$55.00, escrow -$100.00, net pay $2,225.00. The numbers live in the dispatch system, the fuel cards,
text messages, spreadsheets and QuickBooks. One advance logged twice leaves her $200.00 short.
LedgerLine reads all of it, finds the problems, explains each one and proposes the fix. A person
approves it, or an autopilot rule the owner set approves it inside that rule's limits. Only then is
anything paid or sent.

The app tells the same story, line by line, on its public page `/help/how-pay-works` (no sign-in).

## Safety by design

Every agent action is checked before it can touch money: the gateway lets the agent read and
propose, never execute; the rules engine recomputes every number in integer cents; Muse Wonder
audits the proposal in a fresh context; then it is approved, by a person or by the owner's autopilot
policy (see Autopilot below), checked in code and never by a model. Every untrusted input (a driver's
message, a document, a voice note, a web page) is screened on Muse Spark Open before the agent
reads it. Every outside write targets test mode or the QuickBooks sandbox; a production key is
refused at startup. A ledger row is reserved before any call, so the same event can never pay
twice. A demo visitor (the "Try the demo carrier" button on the sign-in page) can ask the agent and
propose but never approve, pay, post or send.

## Built on open weights

Muse Spark Open, served through Baseten, runs the jobs that see every untrusted
byte first: input screening on every message, document and v

# Atlas

Know what your AI-written code does before you trust it.

## Test me (about 3 minutes)

**Online, nothing to install:** open **https://atlas-dami.fly.dev**. The example on the first screen plays with no code (steps 1 to 3). For your own files, press **Try your own code**, enter the judge code from the submission's project description and press **Use this code**. The paste box opens with three sample files under it: that is step 4. The judge code has its own budget, so visitors without a code never use up your limits. Press **Back to the example** under the paste box to return to steps 1 to 3.

1. **Meta's AI explains the file.** The page opens on an example drawn as a machine, one box per function. Above the drawing, Muse Wonder (Meta's AI) usually says in plain words what the file is for, and "What each part does" opens one line per box. Atlas labels these as the AI's words, not a check. Atlas asks Wonder for each part's role, never for how a run ends: you bet on that.
2. **You and Meta's AI bet.** Read the one question, pick an answer and press **Lock in my bet**. Muse Spark and Muse Spark Open answer the same question from the same text, summary included when there is one. For the example, their answers were recorded on Nov 2, and the page says so.
3. **The sandbox decides.** Atlas runs the code and the machine plays what happened. Your bet shows **matched**, **didn't match** or **can't check**, with each AI's mark beside it. Press **Share proof card** to get the card.
4. **Your own code.** Press **Try your own code** and paste a JavaScript, TypeScript or Python file. No file handy? Press one of the samples under the paste box: a fetch with retry, a price parser or a cached lookup. From here the calls are live. Meta's AI usually explains the file, writes a test and bets with you. Click any box to bet on that part, and once your bet is locked, ask Muse Wonder about a part.
5. **A real case (optional).** At the foot of the page, open **Demos: Moonwell**: a saved replay of a real oracle setting on a Base fork. It needs no key and costs nothing.

**On your own machine** (Node 25 or newer, and pnpm; on older Node the local sandbox can't block the network):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/damli40/atlas.git && cd atlas
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env   # put your Meta API key after META_API_KEY=

# Three Feet

AI-powered clearance monitoring for space heaters. Three Feet detects nearby objects, measures their distance, and sends a power-off request when an identified hazard remains inside the configured zone.

![Three Feet dashboard — simulated scene](docs/dashboard-simulator.jpg)

## Features

- **Measured clearance:** camera calibration, distances in inches, and adjustable rules for each side of the heater.
- **AI perception:** SAM 3.1 segments objects; Muse Spark identifies scene contents and assesses hazards. Local tracking follows objects between model checks.
- **Automatic power control:** configurable countdowns, plug status, command retries, and guarded manual reset. Unclassified movement waits for SAM; recognized people and worn clothing do not start object-shutoff countdowns.
- **Source-backed rules and reports:** Muse Wonder reads heater manuals for human review and summarizes incidents using the triggering object's evidence.

## Quickstart

Requires Python 3.11+, Node.js, and npm. From the repository root, in PowerShell:

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
Copy-Item .env.example .env
npm --prefix web ci
npm --prefix web run build
python -m three_feet_app.app --source sim --plug dryrun
```

Open [localhost:8000](http://127.0.0.1:8000/). The simulator runs without a camera, physical plug, or API key.

On macOS/Linux, activate with `source .venv/bin/activate` and copy the settings with `cp .env.example .env`.

## Live monitoring

1. Set `MODEL_API_KEY` in `.env`, install the optional dependencies required by your plug driver, and run `python -m three_feet_app.app`.
2. Open **Camera and plug** to connect a camera and select a supported power adapter.
3. Use **Heater setup** to measure the base and review its floor-contact corners. Keep the camera fixed after calibration.
4. Review **Clearance rule**, then enable alerts and allow browser notifications. While the tab is hidden or the window minimized, you get one notification per warning, saying the heater will turn off in 10 seconds. Find or upload the heater's manual to review its required distances.

Camera inputs include USB webcams, HTTP(S) MJPEG streams, video files, and photo folders. Power control uses the [PowerSwitch interface](three_feet_app/safety/actuator.py); device support depends on the installed driver, with a simulated adapter included for testing.

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_CLEARANCE_IN` | `15` | Fallback clearance on each side |
| `WATCH_MARGIN_IN` | `2` | Amber band outside the red zone |
| `DWELL_HIGH_S` | `10` | Delay for a high-hazard object inside the zone |
| `BUDGET_USD_PER_HOUR` | `5` | Model-call budget threshold |

Only overlap with the red zone starts an object-shutoff countdown. The amber band does not expand with measurement uncertainty. After an OFF request, power is restored only through **Reset and turn on**, with fresh monitoring and a clear zone.

# MultAI

**One AI coding agent, shared by the whole team, in real time.**

**[multai.si](https://multai.si)**: download for macOS and Android, or use it in the browser.

| | |

## Why I built it

My dad was vibe coding his own website with an AI coding agent. He got stuck and asked me for help, and there was no way for me to join his session. All I could do was ask for screenshots, have him copy-paste errors, and guess what the agent had already tried.

Every AI coding agent today is single-player. MultAI makes it multiplayer. The host sends an invite link. Their teammate joins the live session from a browser and reads a catch-up brief of what happened so far. Then they send the agent directions, while the host approves what it does. The agent and the code stay on the host's computer.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie track, Build for Your World), on **Muse Spark**, **Muse Wonder** and **SAM 3.1** through the Meta Model API.

| **Muse Wonder 1.0** | Writes the **catch-up brief** when someone joins: a short chat-style summary of the goal, what was tried and fixed, decisions and who is waiting on what. It also drafts the **pull request** for the session's work, including who directed the agent. |

# InsideTrader's — Meta Model API Integration

InsideTrader's is a paper-trading education product, live and operating today. It runs four paper-trading accounts ("lanes"), each funded with $30,000 in paper capital: a day-trading account (opened Sep 30, 2026), a legacy/main account, a commodity account (opened Oct 5, 2026), and a crypto account (opened Oct 6, 2026). Every lane trades under rules fixed in advance: every position carries its exit before it opens, position sizes are capped, winners are protected by trailing exits, and the day-trading account is flat by the market close every day. The point of the product is that a beginner learns how trading actually works by watching real trades — placed under strict rules, explained in plain words — without risking real money.

This repository contains the product's **Meta Model API integration layer only**: the code that talks to Meta's hosted models API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`). The trading engine and the account machinery are not in this repository (see `CONTENTS.md` for what was deliberately excluded, and why).

## What the integration does

InsideTrader's integrates the Meta Model API in its teaching layer. The rules engine decides what trades happen; Muse Spark does the volume work of turning a completed trade — the setup, the entry, the exit, the result — into a plain-words lesson a beginner can absorb, and carries analysis across the full archive of trading days held in its long context. The machine never talks a learner into a trade; it teaches what already happened and why the rules did what they did.

`meta_model_api.py` is the whole client: standard-library-only Python, two operations.

- `list_models()` — `GET /v1/models`. A harmless read, used as the key check before any paid call.
- `chat_completion(model, prompt)` — `POST /v1/chat/completions` against a Muse model (OpenAI-compatible request shape).

Two properties of the original production helper are preserved because they are safety properties, not style:

- **Redirects are refused on authenticated requests**, so the Authorization header can never be carried silently to an unexpected host.
- **Generation calls default to a generous token budget.** Muse Spark models reason before answering; the verification call below showed a 64-token budget spent almost entirely on reasoning (62 of 64 tokens) with empty content returned.

## Verified live — October 23, 2026

The integration was verified with real calls on Oct 23, 2026:

- `GET /v1/models` → **HTTP 200**, listing `muse-spark-1.3`, `muse-spark-1.2`, `muse-spark-1.1` (plus contributor variants), `muse-image-1.0`, `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`, `sam-3.1`, and `muse-wonder-1.0`.
- Chat completion against `muse-spark-1.3` → **HTTP 200**.

## Setup

Python 3.10+, no third-party dependencies.

```sh
cp .env.example .env   # then put a real api.meta.ai key in .env — never commit it
export META_MODEL_API_KEY="..."   # or load .env with a tool of choice
python3 meta_model_api.py models
pyt

# CV Scientist

**An evidence-driven research copilot for computer vision engineers.**

CV Scientist helps answer the question between training runs: **what should we
try next, and what evidence justifies it?** It connects experiment history,
class-aware error analysis and a Meta Muse agent in a local workspace. Findings
link back to experiments and image records; proposed improvements remain
hypotheses until measured evaluations support them.

## Why it exists

A better aggregate score can hide worse recall for small defects. Training logs,
image errors and previous attempts often live in different places. Engineers
repeat failed ideas or spend another GPU run before checking the evidence.

CV Scientist keeps that evidence together: import runs, compare metrics and
configurations, inspect FP/FN images, ask Muse to investigate, and retain the
result for the next decision. Its current target user is a CV engineer improving
an object detector, including industrial inspection workflows.

## Install from GitHub

With Python 3.10+ and Git installed, run this from your CV project directory:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install "git+https://github.com/OrionChocoPie/Autonomous-CV-scientist.git"
cv-scientist init
cv-scientist --help
```

Run `cv-scientist config` to configure your Meta API key when you want to use
the Meta-powered commands.

## Try it locally

Python 3.10+ with SQLite FTS5. The public demo needs no API key, GPU, private
dataset or external training project.

For development and the public demo, run the following from a cloned checkout:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python examples/create_demo.py --output demo-workspace
cv-scientist --project demo-workspace compare B0 E1 --json
cv-scientist --project demo-workspace diagnose E1 --json
cv-scientist --project demo-workspace report E1 --baseline B0 --json
```

Open the HTML file returned by `report`. It includes comparison tables,
regressions, class confusion and original images with GT/prediction overlays.
The fixture deliberately improves precision while losing small-defect recall.
Its images and predictions are **synthetic**, no detector is trained, and no mAP
is claimed. Re-running the generator against an existing output fails without
overwriting it; choose another output directory for a fresh demo.

## Use Meta Muse to investigate

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
cv-scientist config
cv-scientist --project demo-workspace ask \
  "Compare B0 and E1. Inspect the missed small defects and cite the image evidence. What should we test next?" \
  --agent meta --model muse-wonder-1.0 --json
```

`config` prompts for a key without displaying it and saves it outside the
repository. `CV_SCIENTIST_API_KEY` is the environment override; an explicitly
empty value is an error. Spark is also supported with `--model muse-spark-1.3`.
Meta calls require your account access and may incur charges. Selected

# Kitsune 🦊

**Version control for digital artists.** Git tracks lines of code; Kitsune tracks the sky, the hair, the lighting.

Save versions of a painting, branch to try ideas, and see exactly what changed between any two versions, region by region and in plain words. Bring back just the old sky without losing today's figure. Merge two directions region by region. Pin the reason for a change, or a client's voice message, to the version it's about, and find it again by asking "the version before I changed the sky".

> Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie track), with Muse Code.

**New here?** The [user guide](frontend/src/USER_GUIDE.md) shows how to use Kitsune, in the browser and from the command line.

**Kitsune never makes art.** No model paints, repaints, inpaints or generates a single pixel. Every image Kitsune saves is made of the artist's own pixels: a bring-back copies the part *you drew* in one version into another, pixel for pixel, and leaves everything else exactly as you drew it. AI only *reads* your work (names regions, writes messages, transcribes notes, finds versions, plans steps) so you spend less time managing files and more time painting.

## What it does

| | Feature | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 🕰 | **Timeline** of every version, one lane per branch, merges shown | Content-addressed image store (SHA-256 of pixels), SQLite |

| ✍ | **Auto commit messages**: "Warmed the sky into a dusk palette and tightened the left figure's silhouette." | **Muse Spark** with the measured changes as structured hints |
| ↩ | **Region cherry-pick**: bring back part of an old version (the old sky, or the lantern you drew in v4) into the latest one | A pixel-for-pixel copy of your own painting with a soft edge; anything drawn later in that area (a lantern in the sky) is kept, never pasted over. Or **draw around the part yourself** with mouse, pen or touch, see the result right away, and exactly what's inside your line is copied |

# EasyLaunch

**Bolo, photo lo, launch karo.** A Hindi and English mobile app where a small Indian shopkeeper describes their business by voice, snaps a product photo, and an AI marketing agent built on Meta's models plans, designs, explains and launches a real Click-to-WhatsApp ad on Facebook and Instagram. Customers who tap the ad land in the shop's WhatsApp, and the shop can send them its next offer in one tap.

Built solo for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Cerebral Valley), Oct 27 to Nov 4 2026. Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon.

## The problem

India has tens of millions of small shops: sweet shops, salons, tailors, tuition centres. Their customers are on WhatsApp and Instagram, but Ads Manager asks for objectives, bid strategies and audiences in English jargon. Most shopkeepers never run an ad, or pay an agency they cannot judge.

## What EasyLaunch does

1. **Speak, don't fill forms.** The vendor says what they sell and what they want, in Hindi, English or a mix. Muse Voice Transcribe handles code-switching.
2. **The agent asks once, then plans.** Muse Spark runs a tool-calling agent. It reads the vendor's saved brand and product, asks for every missing detail in a single form (price, city, budget, photo), estimates reach on Meta, and proposes a complete campaign plan with a one-line reason for every choice.
3. **Ad images from a messy phone photo.** SAM 3.1 cuts the product out, Muse Image builds square and story creatives with the offer in Devanagari, and Muse Wonder reviews and ranks them.
4. **Launch for real.** The Marketing API creates the campaign, ad set, creative and ad. A failed launch resumes from the failed step, and settings can be fixed in place, for example raising the budget to Meta's minimum.
5. **Understand every number.** Easy mode shows the plan in plain words with "why?" chips. Advanced mode shows every Ads Manager field. "Samjhao" (explain) teaches any term using the vendor's own numbers. These explanations and the Learn lessons run on **Muse Glimmer, Meta's open-weight model**, served by Fireworks.
6. **Results and next step.** Insights become a plain-language summary and one suggestion, such as raising the budget, applied with one tap.
7. **Leads and repeat customers.** WhatsApp messages from the ad appear live as leads. The vendor can broadcast the next offer to everyone who opted in.
8. **Manual mode and asset library.** Vendors who know what they want build campaigns by hand, in basic or advanced mode, choosing Facebook and/or Instagram and WhatsApp or a website. Brands, products, AI and uploaded creatives, and ad text are saved and reused.

# tupaqnin

> A harness for writing documents with an AI agent, so that what you sign is something you understand and can defend.
>
> *Un harness para escribir documentos con un agente de IA: lo que firmas, lo entiendes y lo puedes defender.*

**tupaqnin** (Quechua: *its complement*). The AI complements human judgment; it does not replace it.

## The problem

AI agents now write reports, methodologies and research faster than anyone can follow. The person ends up signing a document they cannot explain: where a figure came from, why one option was chosen over another, what the conclusion rests on. That is **cognitive debt**. Code has tests, diffs and reviews to catch it. Documents have almost nothing.

## What tupaqnin does

- **The agent works and you decide.** The agent writes, proposes and records each decision with its trade-off («A instead of B, because…»). The choices that matter come to you as short cards that ask for a reason, not a yes.
- **Nothing blocks the work; one gate protects it.** The agent never waits for you. Only signing a section requires you to explain it, and the app checks your explanation against what the text actually says.
- **The app computes, the models judge.** States, fingerprints, links between figures and decisions, and what is critical are computed by rules in Go. Models are used only where judgment is needed.
- **The agent does not depend on its memory.** Its memory is rebuilt from the project graph and its history at every step, so a restart or a model change loses nothing.

It runs on Meta's models: Muse Spark for the agent and Muse Wonder to contrast your explanation when you sign.

## What the jury sees

Open the invitation link and press «Try with the demo case». It takes about 10 to 15 minutes.

1. **The request.** Paula's state of the art on microplastics, already filled in, with her criterion and her sources. Send it.
2. **What the agent understood.** How it will apply «field studies», with a case that counts and one that does not. Confirm or correct it; the agent does not wait for you.
3. **The agent at work.** Text arrives live, and the comparison rule (1.5 times, not 60) appears as a critical decision with its card.
4. **Your decision.** Answer the card with an option and a reason; «ok» does not count. Click a paragraph to see its history.
5. **Evidence.** A citation that does not exist in the sources is discarded in plain sight.
6. **The signoff.** Press «Sign section» and explain it without looking. Muse Wonder names what is missing without giving the answer and brings a new case. Resolve it and sign.

The screen works in English and Spanish.

## Run it locally

Requires Go 1.27. The web page is already built and embedded in the binary.

```sh
export TQ_PROVIDER=fake                 # no API key, recorded answers, no spend
go run ./cmd/tupaqnin                   # http://localhost:8080
go run ./cmd/tupaqnin invite create --label local   # prints /i/<token>, once
```

# AI's Cart pipeline

**One picture. One question. A better purchase.**

AI's Cart checks a checkout screenshot before you pay. You send the screenshot and a question, and it returns a
BUY, TRIAL, WAIT or REJECT verdict. Every fact behind the verdict is marked as observed on screen, inferred, or
unknown, with the evidence for it.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026). All code in this repo was written during
the hackathon.

**Try it:** [ais-cart-pipeline.vercel.app](https://ais-cart-pipeline.vercel.app) runs in sample mode: it answers the three
sample checkouts with prepared results and never calls Meta's models. The live pipeline runs on a private deployment.

## How it works

| Step | Who | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Extract | Muse Spark 1.3 | Reads every field from the screenshot: items, prices, totals, discounts, tax, renewal, trial and cancellation terms. Each field is observed, inferred or unknown, with evidence. |
| 2. Check | Plain code | Checks the math (items add up to the subtotal; subtotal minus discount plus tax equals the total; a renewal price is stated for recurring or multi-year charges) and picks fields worth a second look. |
| 3. Review | Muse Wonder 1.0 | Re-reads **only the flagged fields** against the screenshot. Skipped when nothing is flagged, so clean checkouts cost one fewer call. |
| 4. Verdict | Muse Spark 1.3, then code | Decides BUY / TRIAL / WAIT / REJECT from the checked facts only. The verdict model never sees the screenshot. The verdict can only cite this checkout's real field paths (they're listed in its prompt and enforced in its schema), and obvious variants such as `trial_terms.value` are read as the real field and recorded in `citations_normalized`. Code then checks the verdict: every cited field must exist, every dollar amount must come from the facts or simple arithmetic on them, and there's no BUY or TRIAL while a code check fails. **If any check fails, the verdict is held back and shown as WAIT**, so a failed check can never reach a user as an approval. The model's original answer is kept in `model_*` fields for the record. |

Why this design: in our tests both models read clean checkouts correctly, and the code checks alone caught a
checkout whose total didn't add up and a model that listed the same item twice. So the cheap check runs every time,
and the second model is only paid for when the check finds something.

## First live test

The three sample checkouts in `eval/samples/` have answer keys, so a live run can be scored automatically.
Whoever holds the service token runs:

```
export AISCART_TOKEN=...      # read from the environment only, never written to disk
python3 eval/live_run.py --url https://<your-app>.vercel.app --runs 2
```

# Hisaab Bridge

**Every business gets its own agent that keeps its record of each job, and the agents talk to each other to get work done, so small businesses grow together instead of arguing.**

Each agent works for its own owner on WhatsApp: it keeps that business's ledger, records only what a person allowed to decide has said or sent, and connects to the agents of the businesses it deals with. Every deal leaves the same signed record on both sides. In this entry, three agents (a contractor's site office, a JCB owner's and a sand/cement supplier's) agree on bookings, hours, deliveries, bills and payments over A2A. **Muse reads and explains. Code does the arithmetic and checks each figure against the agreed rates and earlier records. The other side confirms. People decide.**

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track, *Build for Your World*), 27 October to 4 November 2026.

- **Judge page:** https://16-4-100-70.sslip.io/judge/ (three ledgers side by side, every message with its signature check; inside the agent: every Muse call, every code check, every decision). It opens on invented sample data; the live ledgers need an access key.
- **Agent Cards:** `https://16-4-100-70.sslip.io/agents/{jcb,site,supplier}/.well-known/agent-card.json`
- **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/4rWi071hFh0 (2 min 9 s, English voice; the chats are in Hindi with English labels)

## The problem

On an Indian building site a contractor hires a JCB by the hour and buys sand and cement by the bag or the trip. The JCB owner counts hours, the supplier counts bags, and the contractor's supervisor keeps a third count in a notebook. Payments go by UPI, and the proof is a screenshot forwarded on WhatsApp. At month end the counts and the payments do not match, and the argument costs everyone time, money and trust.

All of these people already live on WhatsApp. None of them will install an app or learn a form. So each business gets an agent on WhatsApp that speaks Hindi, takes photos and voice notes, and keeps a ledger that the other side can check.

## What a job looks like

```
Supervisor (WhatsApp)   "कल सुबह 8 बजे शिवपुरी साइट पर JCB चाहिए, 6 घंटे"   (text or voice note)
Contractor agent        over the approval limit? held as J-1 for the contractor's "ok J-1" (no read-back: the OK is
                        the check); within it, read back once -> हाँ -> signed BOOKING_REQUEST over A2A
JCB agent               asks the JCB owner; their exact "हाँ 1200" / "नहीं" / "30-10" is the answer -> signed BOOKING_REPLY
JCB operator            start and end hour-meter photos -> Muse Spark reads the digits -> code checks continuity -> hours
JCB owner               "भेजो" -> signed BILL, the meter photos' fingerprints as evidence
Contractor              sees the bill beside the supervisor's own hours, when recorded -> accept, or dispute with their figure
                        -> Muse Spark explains the difference from the evidence; code checks every number it cites

# Daari Sentinel

Road cameras — dashcams in cars and roadside traffic cameras — become an early incident warning: cameras see the crash, and drivers behind get a stay / reroute / wait decision before they reach it.

**Live demo: [https://daari-sentinel.vercel.app](https://daari-sentinel.vercel.app)** · **Try your own clip: [daari-sentinel.vercel.app/try](https://daari-sentinel.vercel.app/try)**

![Warning card on /sim](docs/sim-warning.png)

## What it does

- Watches road-camera clips (dashcams in cars and roadside traffic cameras) and detects road incidents: crashes, emergency vehicles, debris, road work.
- Cross-checks every AI claim against tracked objects, so the evidence is visible, not a black box.
- Predicts how long until the road clears, as an honest range that narrows as more cameras pass.
- Warns the driver ahead of the scene with three scored options: stay, reroute, or stop and wait.
- Respects the driver's choice across multiple incidents: no flip-flopping, and an offer to return when the road clears.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Road camera clip] --> B[SAM 3.1: find + track objects]
    B --> C[Muse Spark: scene verdict]
    B --> D[Evidence cross-check]
    C --> D
    D --> E[Muse Wonder agent: stage + clearance range]
    E --> F[Guard: verify evidence + rules]
    F --> G[Route decision: stay / reroute / wait]
```

1. **SAM 3.1** finds and tracks objects in the clip (cars, responders, cones, people) and counts them.
2. **Muse Spark** reads the scene and returns a structured verdict: incident type, severity, responders, evidence timestamps.
3. The **cross-check** matches each verdict claim against the SAM tracks (supported / unverified / conflict).
4. The **Muse Wonder agent** tracks the incident across camera reports and returns its stage plus a clearance range.
5. The **guard** verifies the agent's evidence, enforces range rules, and falls back to planning defaults when unsure.
6. The **route engine** scores stay / reroute / stop-and-wait against the clearance range and the driver's active plan.

Faces and license plates are blurred in every image and video shown, including user uploads.

## Meta models and their jobs

| Model | Job |
| ---- | --- |
| SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`) | Find and track objects; true counts from stills; blur faces and plates |
| Muse Spark 1.3 (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`) | Scene verdict: incident type, severity, responders, evidence |
| Muse Wonder (`muse-wonder-1.0`) | Incident agent: stage, clearance range, cited evidence, driver wording |
| Built with Muse Code | This repo was written with Muse Code |

Input $4.00 / cached $0.20 / output $20.00 per 1M tokens for Muse Wonder (2026-10-27);
SAM 3.1 bills per video frame ($0.20 per 1,000 frames, minimum 50 frames per request).
Every real API call is appended to `data/ledger.jsonl`; uploads and results are cached
under `data/cache/` so repeat runs are free, and `data/snapshot/` ships the demo's
results so a fresh deploy replays at $0.

# Argonaut

**See the vibration. Fix the machine.** Argonaut turns any camera into a vibration analyst: Meta's models find the fault, agents fix it, and physics proves it.

Argonaut turns a video of a pump, fan, motor, diesel genset or washing machine into a live digital twin of the machine. From that twin it works out the speed setpoint that runs the machine best, and before anything is applied it checks the move with physics and a person signs off.

- **SAM 3.1** places *virtual sensors by name* ("motor housing", "pump casing", "baseplate"). When a name isn't found directly, **Muse Spark** draws a box around the part and SAM refines that box to a pixel-accurate mask. Each mask becomes a contact-free accelerometer.
- Our signal processing measures **sub-pixel motion** in each region, cancelling camera shake against a static reference. From that it tracks speed and orders; when the frame rate is too low, the microphone acts as the tachometer.
- From a run-up or coast-down it identifies **natural frequencies and damping (with error bars)** and the **Campbell critical speeds**. It also runs **operational modal analysis (FDD)** to get mode shapes and phase across sensors.
- **Muse Spark** reads the scene, nameplate and pump-curve datasheet, coaches the capture, and *listens* to the clip as an independent check.
- **Kinematic inference** ([docs/KINEMATICS.md](docs/KINEMATICS.md)). Muse Spark also says what the machine physically is: engine stroke, blade count, poles, gear teeth, any rpm on a controller display. A Bayesian harmonic sieve with an Occam factor then turns the sound into a **posterior over running speed**, settling ambiguities a spectrum alone cannot (a 1,500 rpm four-stroke's half orders against a 750 rpm machine). A log-odds model gives a **posterior per fault hypothesis**, with each piece of evidence in decibans, and marks hypotheses the footage cannot support as not evaluable. On a genset whose controller reads 1,542 rpm, the microphone posterior gives 1,542.4 rpm without seeing the display.
- **Muse Wonder** is a tool-using engineer agent. It never invents numbers. It diagnoses from the measured evidence (imbalance, misalignment, resonance, cavitation, ISO 20816 severity) and runs a **constrained real-time optimiser** over the drive speed: minimise energy at the required duty, stay clear of resonance bands, keep NPSH margin, and stay in zone A/B.

# Second Voice — Your Voice. Your Meaning. Your Choice.

Second Voice is an assistive communication platform for people with
dysarthria and other speech-intelligibility difficulties. A user speaks
naturally; the system transcribes, proposes a clearer sentence, and speaks
**only user-confirmed text** — in Hindi, English, or Hinglish code-switch.

> **AI may help someone express their thoughts, but it must never take
> ownership of those thoughts.**

This is an assistive-communication prototype, not a diagnostic or treatment
product. No clinical claims are made. Original audio is the primary evidence;
the transcript is an imperfect interpretation of it.

## Features

- **Speech-first workspace** — record (mic or file upload) or type; the
  workshop at `/communicate` is the home screen after login.
- **Real transcription** — Meta Muse Voice Transcribe, with a local Whisper
  second engine for comparison (secondary only, opt-in).
- **Original transcript preserved forever** — reconstruction never overwrites
  it; both stay visible side by side with highlighted differences.
- **Evidence-first reconstruction** — Muse Spark returns structured,
  source-labelled candidates (`usable`/`flagged`, never hidden). Guards hold:
  no invented words, no flipped negation, names/numbers/intent preserved,
  abstains when uncertain.

  ambiguous cases, not every sentence.

  design; Marathi was removed — see `docs/build-log.md` §6.2). Language is
  preserved by default; translation is explicit and user-confirmed.
- **Transparent learning** — user-approved vocabulary, corrections, and
  language preferences improve future suggestions. Retrieval-based only, no
  silent fine-tuning. Everything learned is reviewable, editable, deletable
  in `/learn`.
- **Server-side confirmation gate** — `Audio → ASR → Reconstruction → Review
  → Confirm → TTS`. The TTS endpoint rejects unconfirmed text; only the
  confirmed sentence can be spoken, with replay and stop controls.
- **Quick communication board** (`/board`), personal vocabulary vault
  (`/vocabulary`), session history (`/history`), accessibility settings.
- **Honest fallbacks** — no key, no voice, no model: the app says so and

# Allyfix

**Allyfix checks whether people with disabilities can get things done in an iOS app, fixes
what stops them, and checks again.**

Six synthetic people try your app in the iOS Simulator, each with only what they can
perceive: one hears VoiceOver and sees nothing, one sees the screen blurred with text at 235%,
one cannot tell red from green, one cannot hear, one taps a few points off, one knows no
app conventions. When
someone gets stuck, Muse Wonder changes the app's code on a git branch, and the same person
tries the same task again. What got them through is kept as a test that replays with no AI.

Allyfix is a fast first pass before testing with real people, not a replacement for it.

[![Watch the Allyfix demo on YouTube, 2:49](https://img.youtube.com/vi/Ez65ZIh-EGU/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ez65ZIh-EGU)

[Watch the demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ez65ZIh-EGU) (2:49) · [allyfix.dev](https://allyfix.dev)

## How it works

1. **Explore App.** Allyfix walks the app running in the Simulator: every tab, then what each
   tab leads to. It reads each screen through the macOS accessibility interface, the way
   VoiceOver sees it, and checks it.
2. **Check.** Rules catch what the accessibility tree shows (no label, a wrong role, a frame
   that misses what is drawn, a target too small). Muse Spark compares the screenshot with what
   VoiceOver reads and catches the rest (a card read as one element, a state told only by
   color). SAM 3.1 finds everything drawn to be pressed, and the X-ray sets each thing against
   VoiceOver: reachable by its own name, buried inside something bigger, or missing.
3. **Test People.** Muse Spark works out the two main tasks of a screen, then plays each
   person, step by step, with only their perception. Someone without a disability goes first:
   a task even they cannot do is not counted. A judge model looks at the screen after every
   step and decides whether the task got done.
4. **Fix.** Muse Wonder reads the app's source and the failures, and answers with exact edits,
   committed on a new branch `allyfix/<screen>-<n>`. The app reloads, the screen is checked
   again, and the people who were stuck try again. The fix page shows the screens before and
   after with the changed places framed, who gets through now, and the diff. Keep Fix brings
   it into your branch; Undo Fix throws it away.
5. **Saved tests.** A task someone managed after a fix is stored in `allyfix/tests` in the
   app's repository: the way to the screen, the same taps and swipes, and what the
   accessibility tree must show at the end. Re-test replays every way and every test with no
   model; it can run on its own whenever the code changes. "Prove They Catch It" runs the tests
   on the code before the fix, where they must fail, and after it, where they must pass.

### The people

Chosen after EN 301 549 §4.2, the standard the European Accessibility Act points to. Named
only by access need and tool.

## Current Wondrue browser contract — November 4, 2026

This section supersedes historical direct-execution examples below. `/wondrue`
is the owner cockpit; `/wondrue/legacy` preserves the original interface and
`/wondrue/handoff-demo` preserves the isolated synthetic viewer. The public FAQ
landing and CSR are unchanged. Wondrue remains behind the existing owner gateway.

The responsive shell includes a collapsible navigation rail, New Chat, server-side
conversation persistence/search, retained-record Library, Hold for Human Review,
and an account/safeguards menu. Ctrl+K searches; Ctrl+Shift+S toggles the sidebar.
Mobile navigation overlays the page. Chat uses deterministic retained-record
inspection, not a new language model or invented findings. It makes no provider
calls. Library records are the latest dossier/qualification/Raphael/custody rows
in the selected server database; the synthetic catalogue uses its separate viewer.
Records with failed digests are quarantined individually: their claims/actions are blocked without hiding valid Library records.
Retained agent tasks are explicitly marked as retained tasks: their original
status alone does not establish the current owner-resolution state.

Operational changes from the browser must pass the durable review queue.
Direct full-mode execution, approval-token redemption and live inference on the
legacy command/extraction routes are refused. The underlying agent/inference
services and their tests remain available to separately authorized callers.
Existing internal agent automation is not rerouted through chat.

The cockpit executor allows preparing an owner brief, preparing/completing Elmer
intake, recording an administrative owner exception decision, and stopping/resuming
an existing owner coordinator checkpoint (never running a stage). Each proposal binds an exact retained dossier version/digest, explicit
arguments, operation ID, reason and later owner choice (approve/reject/defer).
Changed evidence or a stale review digest refuses execution. A durable dispatch
claim precedes the separately audited agent call. An interruption or failure stays
`dispatch_claimed`/`needs_reconciliation`; no automatic retry is offered. Inspect
the recorded operation ID in the existing agent audit before reconciliation.
Approval never authenticates a claim, overrides Raphael or permits external actions.

this screen. The legacy synthetic in-memory reset remains explicitly isolated.

Cockpit endpoints under `/wondrue/api/` require a valid existing owner session or
Wondrue reader/operator credential. Saving and decisions require operator access
and a matching Origin. Responses, including authentication errors, are no-store.
No API keys are stored in browser storage. Chat saves create workspace artifacts
and audit events, not dossier versions. Append-only history is preserved; no chat
hard-delete feature is offered. Search

# pi-muse-provider

Use Muse subscription credentials in Pi, keeping Pi's native agent loop and tools.

## Install

```sh
pi install npm:pi-muse-provider
```

Requires Pi 1.4.0+. For Nix, pin the npm tarball and link `src/` to
`~/.pi/agent/extensions/muse` instead of using `pi install`.

## Use

Log in with Muse, then select a model in Pi:

```text
/model muse/muse-wonder-1.0
/model muse/muse-spark-1.3-contributor
```

Credentials come from `~/.config/muse/auth.json` (respecting `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`).
No separate Pi login is needed. Stored `/login muse` credentials take precedence;
`/logout muse` restores file/environment authentication.

- `MUSE_AUTH_FILE`: override the credential path.
- `MUSE_API_KEY`: use an inference key directly.
- `MUSE_USER_AGENT`: override the captured Muse 1.4.14 identity. Captured
  defaults exist for Linux x64 and macOS arm64; other platforms must set it.
- `/muse-usage`: show the latest server-reported subscription usage.

Tools are namespaced on the wire. No automatic billing fallback (but you may still be charged. I am a random on the internet. scope your tokens well). In a sandbox, expose the auth file
read-only and restart Pi after Muse replaces it.

## Development

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run typecheck
npm test
# Opt-in live inference and one harmless printf tool call:
npm run check:live -- --live --pi-only --tool-roundtrip
```

[![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/Status-Production%20Live-brightgreen.svg)](https://chronosight.onrender.com)
[![Live Runs](https://img.shields.io/badge/Live%20Runs-Active%20%26%20Resumed-brightgreen.svg)](https://chronosight.onrender.com)

[![Vitest](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vitest-585%20passed%20%2841%20files%29-blue.svg)]()
[![Pytest](https://img.shields.io/badge/Pytest-50%20passed-blue.svg)]()
[![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-Strict%200%20Errors-success.svg)]()
[![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-16.4%20%2F%20React%2019-black.svg)]()
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0%20%2F%20CC--BY--4.0-lightgrey.svg)]()

**The visual unit test for physical cyber-physical systems.**

ChronoSight continuously monitors electromechanical machinery on video, measures physical failure modes directly from pixel trajectories, diagnoses root causes via character-grounded reasoning over 60-page hardware manuals using **Meta Muse 70B** and **Meta SAM 3.1**, synthesizes bounded controller patches inside an isolated Docker sandbox, and verifies repairs by re-measuring physical plant kinematics. Every state transition is cryptographically sealed via **RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)** and gated by a two-stage HMAC approval.

- **Hosted Production URL:** [https://chronosight.onrender.com](https://chronosight.onrender.com)
- **Technical Specifications:** [PRD.md](PRD.md) · [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) · [TECHNICAL.md](TECHNICAL.md) · [DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md)
- **Hardware Datasheet Corpus:** [corpus/vendor-manifest.json](corpus/vendor-manifest.json) (EncoderX-14 60-page manual, CC-BY-4.0)

---

## Core Engineering Innovations

### 1. Sub-Pixel Precision via Differential Anchor Subtraction (`psd.ts`)

- **Physical Failure Mode:** Handheld smartphone cameras and smart-glasses head movements (2–8 Hz) introduce high-amplitude camera tremor that corrupts raw mask centroids, flooding Power Spectral Density (PSD) charts with false mechanical resonance spikes.

- **Homography-Stabilized Differential Kinematics:** Designates Object ID 0 in `config/buckets.yaml` as a static fiducial mounting anchor $(x_t^{\text{anchor}}, y_t^{\text{anchor}})$ and Objects 1..N as dynamic target components $(x_t^{\text{target}}, y_t^{\text{target}})$ tracked via Meta SAM 3.1 16-object multiplexing:

$$
\Delta x_t = (x_t^{\text{target}} - x_t^{\text{anchor}}) \cdot \frac{W_{\text{ref}}}{W_t^{\text{anchor}}}, \quad \Delta y_t = (y_t^{\text{target}} - y_t^{\text{anchor}}) \cdot \frac{W_{\text{ref}}}{W_t^{\text{anchor}}}
$$

  Normalizing by the instantaneous anchor bounding-box width $W_t^{\text{anchor}}$ cancels optical zoom drift

# Maqet: measured technical assistance for families who build their own homes

From a hand-drawn sketch to a staged shopping list of bricks, in one visit.

**About 4 million people in Argentina build their homes themselves, room by room, as they save.** Maqet lets one
technical assistant help many more of them: measure the home, design the next room with the family, show it in AR on
their own table, and leave a construction takeoff they can buy stage by stage.

> **Demo video (3 min):** [watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H9fffIhcALY) · **Built for** the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track
> · Demo script: [`docs/DEMO.md`](docs/DEMO.md)

**Reads a hand sketch for a tenth of a cent.** In our test set, Muse Spark transcribed the written measurements on all
six inputs (clean plans, phone photos and a hand sketch) and found every door and window on the drawn plans, at about
**$0.001 per image**. Baseline:
[`samples/replay/intake_report.json`](samples/replay/intake_report.json).

- **Measured, not guessed.** One measured Scene is the single source of truth: 3D, AR, render, takeoff and DXF all derive from it.
- **The AI proposes, deterministic code disposes.** The agent changes the home only through validated tools; construction rules live in code, never in prompts.
- **Honest by design.** Every output is labelled *preliminary* and flags what **needs a licensed professional** (a second floor, a load-bearing wall, a long span).
- **Built for the field.** Phone-first PWA, push-to-talk in Spanish, English or es-AR one tap away.

## Motivation

Self-built housing is how most families in Latin America get a home. It happens in stages, as savings allow, and usually
without a professional. The result is predictable: walls that have to come down, rooms with no ventilation, money spent
twice. Technical assistance programs exist and work, but there are far fewer technicians than families.

The tools a technician has today are a tape measure, a notebook and, at best, desktop CAD that never reaches the site.
Consumer AI room apps make pretty pictures that cannot be measured or built from.

Maqet sits in between: an AI that works **with** the technician on site, on a phone, and produces numbers a family can
buy against and drawings a professional can sign.

Sources: Habitat for Humanity, *Vivienda autoconstruida en Argentina* (2022), citing RENABAP; more in
[`docs/PRODUCT.md`](docs/PRODUCT.md).

## Who it's for

| Who | Role in Maqet |
|---|---|
| **Technical assistants** (primary): architects, master builders and social-housing technicians at NGOs, municipalities and cooperatives | Drive the session on site with a phone: measure, design with the family, leave with a staged material list and a DXF |
| **Families** | Watch the proposal in AR on their own table and ask for changes by voice in Spanish |
| **Licensed professionals and hardware stores** (downstream) | Receive a measured DXF to review and sign; quote the staged material list |

# Paper Tour

Paper Tour turns any document into a tutor that reads it with you. It points at the exact sentence, outlines the exact
part of a figure, draws checked visuals on a board beside the page, and answers spoken or typed questions the same way:
not with a block of chat text, but with a short tour on the page itself. It works on research papers, lecture slides,
exercise sheets and practical documents such as leases and official letters. Every highlight and outline lands on
something that exists on the page, because the tour is built from the document's own geometry and names elements by ID,
never by coordinates.

## How it works

```
PDF ─▶ ingestion ─▶ doc.json: sentences, blocks, figures, panels, equations, exercise tasks
                    every element has an ID and exact coordinates
                              │
      plan (Muse Spark):      source-grounded concepts · slide groups of a deck · parts of an exercise sheet
                              │
      visual plan (Spark):    choose source annotations or a useful live construction for each explanation
                              │
      direct (Spark):         one small call per step, in parallel, choosing only from the IDs listed for it
                              │
      checks and review ────▶ targeted repair; incomplete profile explanations cannot publish as complete
                              │
                    tour.json: chapters of steps made of IDs and board data
                              │
      reader (pdf.js):        camera, pen and board move with the narration, word by word
```

1. **Ingestion** (`ingest/`, Python and PyMuPDF) turns the PDF into `doc.json`. Every sentence, block, section, figure,
   table, panel and equation gets an ID and exact coordinates, and exercise sheets also get task and part IDs. Before a
   figure is taught, local OCR and OpenCV (`ingest/visual_targets.py`) measure the modules inside it, so a pen mark can
   enclose one part of a diagram instead of guessing a box.
2. **Planning.** The model reads the document and names its type, key figures and chapter titles; code detects its
   language. Profile-based paper tours then build a complete, source-grounded teaching map before narration starts:
   contribution, prerequisites, mechanisms, evidence and limitations. The chosen profile determines the organization
   and emphasis. Complexity determines the number of explanations, with no fixed concept count. Large plans span
   multiple responses without losing content. A slide deck follows slides; an exercise sheet follows tasks. Visual
   planning chooses source annotations or new constructions by explanatory value, without a required board share.
3. **Directing.** Each step is written by its own small call, run in parallel. The output is constrained to a JSON
   schema whose targets are enums of the IDs listed for that step, so the model picks a sentence, a figure or a panel
   but never writes a coordinate. A detail step waits fo

# Mirada — look + hold to speak

A new answer to the oldest problem in cheap eye tracking: drift.
Mirada's innovation, semantic recalibration, pairs a local ~30fps gaze
model with sparse semantic anchors — Muse Spark infers where you almost
certainly looked, SAM 3.1 pinpoints it to the pixel, a tiny online
corrector absorbs the fix. Measured on recorded sessions, not claimed
(pilot, n=2: anchors cut mean error 406→397px while uncorrected drift
explodes 63→941px in 15 min). The same anchors could correct gaze
drift in AR headsets next.

It ships as a gaze communication board on an ordinary webcam: look at a
cell, close your eyes ~0.4 s, and the computer speaks. No headset, no
eye tracker, no per-frame cloud calls. Built for the Meta Global AI
Developer Hackathon.

Demo video: [watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DwyqqIZb-T8).

This repo was created for the event (initial commit Oct 31, 2026):
nothing in it pre-exists the hackathon — every line was written this
week.

## Why it's special

- **A new method: semantic recalibration.** Every selection you confirm
  becomes a semantic anchor — Spark proposes, SAM pinpoints — that
  re-biases the gaze map through a small trust-capped online corrector;
  a posture guard freezes learning outside your calibrated pose. The
  replay harness scores it against baselines on real recorded sessions.
- **Zero hardware beyond a webcam.** A $30 camera replaces a $5,000
  dedicated eye tracker for phrase-level communication.
- **It works inside real apps.** An APPS page launches Discord, the
  browser, YouTube and more with huge tiles; your gaze then becomes the
  mouse (look freely, close your eyes 0.4 s to click — same grammar as
  the board), a floating dock takes you back, and an on-screen keyboard
  types into any field.
- **Private by construction.** Gaze, calibration and speech run fully
  offline on your machine. Cloud models touch only the research tooling,
  never the live loop.

# Argus Lens

> Is this image real? Argus Lens shows the evidence, not just a guess.

**Live demo: [arguslens-ten.vercel.app](https://arguslens-ten.vercel.app)** · the extension's stand-in feed: [/test](https://arguslens-ten.vercel.app/test). The hosted demo takes files up to 4 MB; run it locally for bigger ones.

Argus Lens checks images in social media posts for signs of AI generation and for harmful content. Instead of a bare "AI / not AI" label, it gives a careful assessment with the evidence outlined on the image:

- **Labelled as AI-made**: the file itself says so. Certain.
- **Likely AI-generated**: concrete AI mistakes found, each one outlined.
- **No signs of AI found**: and Lens says plainly that this doesn't prove the image is real.
- **Can't tell**: too small, blurry or compressed to inspect.

It also checks whether the image is **harmful to post**: private details (an address, a phone number, an ID card, a number plate), hate symbols, gore. When hiding a part would make the rest fine, SAM 3.1 outlines that part and Lens offers a **blurred version** to post instead.

**Any photo or video from your computer**: the Lens page (and the **Check a file** button in the extension's toolbar panel) takes JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF photos, and MP4, iPhone MOV, WebM and other videos the browser can play; videos that aren't MP4 or MOV are converted to MP4 in the browser first. **Video** (up to 60 seconds): Muse Spark watches the clip, frames and sound, and reports AI signs with the moment they happen, and whether it's harmful to post. When a private detail is visible, **SAM 3.1 tracks that object through every frame**, and the demo plays the video with it **blurred as it moves**, and records a blurred copy you can post instead.

There is deliberately no "authentic" verdict: no tool can prove an image is real by looking at it, and telling people a fake is real does more harm than saying "we don't know".

# DAFE OakGuard **Muse Wonder writes the rules. A referee it cannot see decides which ones go live.** Verification for AI-written trading code, built on the DAFE Charts terminal during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). [![CI](https://github.com/DSKYZ-dev/DAFE-OakGuard/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/DSKYZ-dev/DAFE-OakGuard/actions/workflows/ci.yml) ![Muse Wonder](https://img.shields.io/badge/Muse%20Wonder-rule%20proposer-2dffb3) ![Muse Spark 1.3](https://img.shields.io/badge/Muse%20Spark%201.3-coder%20%C2%B7%20advisor%20%C2%B7%20vision-7fd6ff) ![Muse Voice Transcribe](https://img.shields.io/badge/Muse%20Voice%20Transcribe-push--to--talk-ffd166) ![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow)
![The Crucible: Muse Wonder's rules promoted into the playbook, with the referee's scores and the cost of each call](docs/media/oakguard-crucible.jpg) ## The problem Ask an AI for a trading indicator and it will write one that compiles, passes the validator, and is quietly wrong. A breakout compared with `highest(high, 20)`, which includes the current bar, can never fire. A length of `0` computes nothing. A misspelled builtin returns zero. The chart looks fine and nobody notices until they have trusted the signal. Checkers catch the bugs someone thought of. OakGuard learns the ones nobody wrote a check for, and proves each new check before it goes live. ## How it works 1. **Find an escape.** Runtime oracles run a script on four synthetic markets (2,400 bars) and prove it broken: an output that is never finite, a signal that never fires. The baseline validator accepted it. 2. **Muse Wonder proposes a rule.** It sees the script and the evidence and answers with one rule in a fixed rule language, as schema-constrained JSON. Data, never code. 3. **A referee it cannot see decides.** The rule is scored against broken variants of the same bug (a third of them held out from the model) and 46 known-good scripts: the shipped library plus contrast scripts that sit right next to each bug class. 4. **Rejected rules come back with evidence.** The reason, the visible variants missed and the false-positive line go back to the model, which may revise. Held-out variants are reported as a count only. 5. **Promoted rules enforce everywhere.** They run inside the validator used by the editor, the agent's fix loop and the backtest pre-flight, for every script from then on. Every exchange is recorded with its model, prompt hash, tokens and cost — the [recorded run](apps/web/src/oakguard/recorded-run.json) keeps all three calls (7,662 tokens, $0.115; the judge build shows it labelled "(recorded)"). A replay re-grades the recorded text with today's referee; verdicts are never replayed. The live run shown in the demo video promoted the same three rules — also 174 of 174 — for 6,921 tokens and $0.1005, which is the **$0.10** below. ## Results | | | |---|---

# uptodate

**Stay up to date with what you love, without the email clutter.**

Newsletters are a great idea. Choose something you care about, and useful pockets of information arrive at regular intervals. They can help you keep up with a hobby, follow a research field, discover places, or find something new to cook.

But the experience often ends in an overflowing inbox. The content we chose to enjoy sits beside work messages, receipts, and notifications. Reading something interesting starts to feel like another email to deal with.

I built **UpToDate** to give that content a home of its own: an app that turns newsletters into digestible posts, while keeping the subscriptions out of your main inbox.

[Install the iPhone beta](https://testflight.apple.com/join/6ngBfc4R) · [Website](https://up2-date.app) · [Privacy](https://up2-date.app/privacy) · [Terms](https://up2-date.app/terms)

## 1. Create your account and get a newsletter address

When you create an account, UpToDate assigns you a private email alias for newsletter subscriptions. Your main email remains your account address; the alias receives the content you want to read in the app.

Newsletter emails go to UpToDate's receiving pipeline rather than being forwarded into your personal inbox. A welcome guide introduces the app, and you can choose interests to get starter newsletter suggestions: AI & tech, research, cooking, coffee & dining, business, and travel.

Accounts support email verification, password recovery, profile editing, a profile picture, and account deletion.

## 2. Subscribe from inside the app

Paste a newsletter link into Home or Manage. UpToDate uses your account's alias for supported signup flows.

Publishers sometimes need a human step: a CAPTCHA, a JavaScript form, an email confirmation, or a verification code. You can finish those steps through the publisher's page from the app, using your copied alias. Available confirmation links and codes are surfaced in UpToDate so you can complete the subscription.

You can also import an existing `.eml` file from Manage.

## 3. Read the content as posts

Incoming editions are processed by a backend powered by Muse and supporting extraction, retrieval, and verification functions. The result is a personal feed of short posts that helps you keep up with your interests without working through an inbox.

The posts aim to stay faithful to the source. Substantial stories in a roundup can become separate posts, while related material—such as a paper, its repository, and its project page—stays together. Links take you back to the original article or paper, not just the newsletter homepage.

Read today's posts, scroll into older editions, or open a post for more detail. Bookmark something for later, mark it read to move it into your read history, or share the post as a web preview.

### Real source images come first

Posts can include swipeable image galleries with pinch-to-zoom. UpToDate first looks for usable newsletter or original-sour

# Leash

### The agent proposes. Leash decides.

Leash is a local safety gateway for AI coding agents. Muse Spark can inspect a selected project and **propose** file changes, shell commands, HTTP requests, and Git pushes. Leash resolves what each proposal would affect, applies fast local rules, consults an independent Muse Wonder judge when the action is ambiguous, and decides whether to execute, pause for human approval, or block it.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** · Indie Developer track · **Push the Frontier**.

![Leash live action stream, resolved impact, and LeashBench comparison](docs/images/leash-decision-benchmark.png)

*A live allowed file patch, a separate human-denied file write, resolved impact and stage latency, and the benchmark panel.*

## Why Leash exists

A coding model can read a repository and suggest an excellent fix, then make a consequential tool call: replace the wrong file, delete a directory, push a branch, or send data to an untrusted endpoint. An independent model helps assess intent; Leash also controls the capabilities that cause side effects.

Leash gives the coding agent proposal tools while keeping execution authority in the gateway. The decision is tied to a resolved, read-only impact preview. A denial is fed back to Spark so it can choose a safer action; a review waits for a person to approve the **exact** action and preview.

| Verdict | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `allow` | A routine, policy-compliant action executes through a restricted adapter. |
| `review` | Execution pauses until a person approves the same action and preview digests. |
| `block` | Nothing executes; Spark receives reasons and can propose a safer alternative. |

## The moat: control at the capability boundary

Leash's moat is the link between judgment and execution:

1. **Proposal is separate from authority.** In the instrumented Spark loop, the model cannot call an unrestricted shell or write directly. Leash owns the adapters that can change the workspace or make an inspected HTTP request.
2. **The decision covers concrete effects.** Read-only previews resolve paths, file and byte counts, Git targets, or network destinations where supported. The executor checks the judged action and preview digests again before acting. A changed action needs a new decision.
3. **Rules and Wonder have different jobs.** Local rules block clear hazards and let routine work pass without a model call. Ambiguous actions go to a separate Muse Wonder context with a minimized, locally redacted packet. Wonder can escalate a local review to block; it cannot overturn a hard rule block. A local review remains subject to human approval even if Wonder returns allow.
4. **Evidence is part of the product.** The dashboard shows reasons, resolved impact, stage latency, model calls, tokens, and a redacted, hash-chained audit feed. LeashBench publishes fixtures, commands, raw rows, and limitations alongside its scores.

**Community-powered flood observation, geospatial risk mapping, and decision-support for African communities.**
**Demo URL: https://main.dmpm2yei4pgxa.amplifyapp.com/ **

FloodLens AI enables residents, community organisations, emergency-response teams, and local authorities to understand where flooding is being observed, which locations are vulnerable, and where inspections or interventions should be prioritised. It combines community-submitted reports with AI-assisted image analysis, environmental data, and a transparent Flood Risk Index to produce explainable, location-based risk indicators on an interactive map.

> **Public Safety Notice:** FloodLens AI provides community observations and data-informed risk indicators for situational awareness. It is not an official emergency warning system, does not guarantee that any location is safe, and does not replace instructions from emergency-management authorities. In an emergency, contact local emergency services and follow official guidance.

---

## What It Does

### Community Flood Reporting
Residents submit flood or drainage reports directly from a mobile browser — even on low-bandwidth connections. Each report can include:
- One or more photographs of the flooding or drainage issue
- A GPS location or manually placed map pin
- Voice notes (converted to text by AI)
- Hazard type, self-reported severity, and water level
- Optional landmark and description
- Information about affected roads, homes, shops, or facilities

Submitted reports are saved as offline drafts if connectivity is unavailable and automatically retried when the connection returns. Reporters receive a confirmation receipt with a report ID and real-time status tracking.

### AI-Assisted Image Analysis
Each uploaded photo is analysed by **Muse Spark** (Meta Model API multimodal model), which identifies visible flood-related hazards including floodwater, blocked drains, overflowing drains, damaged roads, and exposed infrastructure. The analysis returns:
- A scene summary describing the overall situation
- Detected hazards with type, visible evidence, confidence score, and severity observation
- Water presence classification (none / possible / visible / extensive)
- Infrastructure observations
- Analysis limitations and recommended review actions

**SAM 3.1** (Segment Anything Model) segments relevant objects in photos — floodwater, drain openings, debris, road surface — and overlays bounding boxes for reviewer inspection.

All AI outputs include confidence scores, limitations, and provenance metadata (provider, model ID, prompt version). Findings are clearly labelled as requiring human verification before any consequential decision.

### Voice Transcription
Voice notes recorded by residents are transcribed to text by **Muse Voice Transcribe**. Transcripts are stored as unverified text, shown to the reporter for correction, and used to assist report categorisation. Transcripts do not independently establish flood sev

# Shadow — show it once

**Shadow turns an expert's screen recording and narration into a reviewable playbook, with every step tied to its source and every assumption called out. Then an agent does the job back, and stops to ask wherever the recording never showed it.**

**Record → Verify → Replay.** Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, *Build for Your World*).

- **Live:** https://mukeshkbj--shadow-web.us-east.modal.run. Open the featured run (a real run on the Meta Model API). Uploading a new recording needs a passcode, because each upload spends API credits.
- **Demo video (3 min):** see the submission page.
- **Open weights:** the same recording run through **Muse Spark Open** on Nebius is the second playbook on the live site (see [Open-weights mode](#open-weights-mode-muse-spark-open)).

![Every step cites its evidence](docs/evidence.jpg)

## Why
Every team has one person who knows how the job is really done. AI can write a procedure from a video now, but it fills the gaps with confident guesses, and a procedure you can't check is worse than none. Shadow's whole design is about **evidence and uncertainty**: what was seen, what was said, what Shadow is only inferring, and what nobody showed.

## What it does
1. **Record.** Someone records their screen while doing a task and talks as they go.
2. **Muse Spark 1.2** watches the video *with* its audio and logs what was **seen** on screen and what was **said**, with timestamps.
3. **Muse Voice Transcribe** times every spoken line. Spoken events take their time from the transcript (Spark's times for speech drift by seconds; see below), and every "Said" quote must appear in the narration turn spoken at that moment.

6. **Muse Spark + SAM 3.1** draw a visual pointer for the reviewer: SAM can't read labels, so Spark finds the field by its label and SAM 3.1 outlines it. It helps you look; it is not proof.

# Loopwright

## For reviewers — provenance, models, and how to verify

**Pre-existing vs in-period.** The concept and the preparation documents predate the hackathon (prepared on 2026-10-25). Everything in this repository — the platform code, tests, loop records, and the demo — was created during the hackathon period (2026-10-26 – 2026-11-04).

**Models this repository runs** (Meta Model API): muse-spark-1.3-contributor (extraction, generation, and automated checks), muse-wonder-1.0 (audit-model comparison and the vanilla contrast experiment), muse-spark-1.3 (vanilla contrast), and muse-image-1.0 (images for the landing-page trials). The pipeline also runs against Muse Spark Open via Baseten when the endpoint is overridden; the verification runs in loops/loop-024 – loop-027 used that route for generation and reviews, and loops/loop-015/ and loops/loop-016/ used it in verification-loop experiments. Each run record states the model and endpoint it actually used.

**Verify without credentials.** The public preview (linked in section 2) replays recorded runs — no login or API key is needed. To run it yourself, clone this repository and set your own MODEL_API_KEY (see section 6, "Running it"). Every source posting is pinned by sha256 in the loop records, so the inputs can be confirmed unchanged.

## 1. Positioning

Loopwright is a development platform that turns failures in AI-assisted production into quality controls for the next run. Every failure is recorded, aggregated, and — only with human approval — promoted into a deterministic gate or a review criterion that every later production must pass. Nothing is promoted automatically, and no learning takes effect without a human decision. One worked example: a duplicated figure that a review model failed to catch in one production became, after verification on real pages and a human approval, a deterministic gate that now fails any later page repeating a stated value (D17).

The job postings in the demo are the test workload, not the product: the same loop applies to any AI-assisted production whose output can be checked. It is also not merely an AI development management tool — the scope of improvement extends beyond code to requirements definition, work breakdown, quality control, planning, and how the work is presented.

Solo entry on the Indie track ([D2](docs/decisions/D2-track.md)). The submission is an integrated demo: the platform (L1) running an editorial workflow (L2) ([D1](docs/decisions/D1-submission-positioning.md)).

## 2. Live demo (L2)

The demo is a job-posting fact-checking workflow for editorial staff: before a job listing page (LP) is generated, the text is extracted into FACTs, reconciled against the pinned source, and held for human approval. When a summary contradicts the source, the run stops instead of generating.

# MUSE Evidence Review Core

Ask Meta to review a saved draft against an exact source, inspect its quotations,
then revise with an explicit version boundary. A review of an older revision
becomes **STALE**. Model judgments, local quote checks and human approval remain
separate.

Earlier private research and editor scaffolding informed this project. This
standalone competition implementation was newly written on November 3, 2026;
that earlier private implementation is not included or required. The P2 connector
adds independent local consent, terminal credential input and once-only request
records to the new core. No competition eligibility ruling is claimed.

## Recorded live demo

[Watch the hackathon demo — real Meta inference and STALE](https://youtu.be/LRThYu3e7CU)

## Run the main Meta workflow

Requirements: an existing Python 3.9+ installation on macOS or Linux, a local
interactive terminal, a browser, and your own eligible Meta Model API account.
Only Python's standard library is used. Nothing needs to be installed with pip.
Windows terminal and filesystem behavior are not qualified.

From the directory containing this README:

```sh
python3 -I -B -S verify.py
python3 -I -B -S live.py
```

Open the printed `http://127.0.0.1:...` address in the same computer's browser.
Startup does not obtain a credential, resolve Meta's hostname, or send a request.
Do not expose this local service to other machines or use an untrusted shared
computer. Keep the terminal open.

1. Load the Larch synthetic source. Insert the four-sentence example or write your
   own non-secret draft, then **Save draft**.
2. Select **Meta Live** and **Preview this review request**. Review the complete
   source, saved draft, exact serialized request, model, destination, program
   Manifest, account reference, revision and request SHA. Bytes are not tokens.
3. Make each decision separately: B1 demo-use acceptance, risk acceptance,
   DATA_EGRESS, BUDGET_ONCE and FINAL_DISPATCH. All boxes start unchecked.
   The final **Confirm and request one Meta review** button separately records
   IMMEDIATE_HUMAN_CONFIRMATION. Closing the preview sends nothing.
4. Only after that final action, enter your own Meta API credential in the server
   terminal's hidden prompt. It is never a browser field, environment variable,
   command argument or credential file. Ctrl-C or Escape cancels; Ctrl-D ends
   input; a 60-second timeout also ends it. There is no echo fallback. Ordinary
   input cancellation restores the terminal. Abrupt OS termination may require
   restoring the terminal yourself. No absolute memory-erasure claim is made.
5. Read the actual response, quote validation and reported usage. Real Meta may
   produce any valid distribution of the four categories, not necessarily one of
   each. Schema or citation failures remain failures; no mock answer replaces
   them. No result automatically approves, signs, publishes or rewrites a draft.
6. Edit and save. The previous review becomes S

Fitts is a desktop agent that uses your website or Android app the way people do. It reads your
code, walks the flows a person would, and finds usability problems against Nielsen's ten
heuristics plus accessibility, performance and look-and-feel. Then it fixes the code, checks each
fix on its own branch, and opens a pull request. You can talk to it by chat or voice while it
works. Built from scratch during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 28 – Nov 4, 2026.

[fitts.allenzheng.com](https://fitts.allenzheng.com) · [Demo video](https://youtu.be/CV27fWbfVdA) · [Roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md)

## Try it without keys

Open the recorded runs at [fitts.allenzheng.com/runs/](https://fitts.allenzheng.com/runs/) in
any browser. The featured one is [Basil & Ember](https://fitts.allenzheng.com/runs/basil-ember-nov-4/),
a restaurant site Muse Code generated from one prompt and nobody has edited since: Fitts found
18 problems and fixed and verified 1, for $3.33. Each report shows what Fitts understood, the
findings with their evidence and repro steps, the verified fixes and the App Map, with the
Noticed lines behind every finding. No install and no keys needed.

## Quickstart

1. Install Fitts (below), or run it from source with `pnpm install && pnpm dev`.
2. Add a Meta Model API key on Welcome. From source, you can instead copy `.env.example` to
   `.env.local` at the repo root and fill in the keys you have:

   ```
   META_API_KEY=            # required for real runs
   BASETEN_API_KEY=         # optional: Muse Spark Open on Baseten
   ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=      # optional: Fitts's voice (otherwise the system voice)
   ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID=     # optional: the "Fitts" voice in your ElevenLabs account
   ```

   `.env.local` is gitignored, and packaged builds never read it.
3. Choose your project's folder. Fitts starts your dev server (or Metro and the Android emulator
   for an Expo app), reads the code, interviews you about who it's for, and gets to work.
