## Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026)
This project was built during the hackathon. Core contributions:
- Deterministic multi-mode scoring engine + orchestrator
- Muse Spark / Wonder / SAM 3.1 / Muse Voice Transcribe integrations with deterministic fallbacks
- Meta Model API is the API platform used for accessing models. Muse Code is the coding agent used.
- Live snapshot + worldwide corridor support
- Route briefing, storm lab, and shareable incident brief UIs

# GridFork

Multi-agent reroute engine: live traffic, weather & disruption data across
sea, air, road and rail, scored by cost, time saved and on-time odds.

GridFork is a multi-agent cascade evaluation engine for multi-modal logistics
(sea, air, road, rail). A North Sea storm disrupts shipping into Rotterdam; four
specialist agents report per-mode findings, and an orchestrator ranks
quantified reroutes on Cost, Time Saved, On-Time Probability, and Confidence.

## How it works

- Deterministic core: the specialists and the ranking are pure Python, so
  the numbers are always reproducible. The baseline runs the engine over
  reference incident data; live snapshots run the same engine over
  measured conditions.
- Ask GridFork: the `/ask?q=` box tops every view and answers worldwide routes only, grounded solely in places you name
  (typed, dictated, picked in the lab, or the briefing's asked corridor), never a default location. Scenario
  and why-questions route to Muse Wonder, facts to Muse Spark, and every
  answer carries the deterministic fastest alternate across all four modes
  (paid per question, click only). Questions without places get free guidance
  instead of a guessed location. A hold-to-talk button beside it dictates the
  question via Muse Voice Transcribe; sending still needs the click.
- Muse Spark synthesis: the `/summary` endpoint attaches a narrative
  rationale generated by `muse-spark-1.3`, with a deterministic fallback
  when no key is set or the API is unreachable.
- SAM 3.1 visual verification: the `/vision` endpoint segments container
  reference imagery and blends the congestion score into the sea leg, with
  an `unavailable` fallback offline.
- Wonder what-if planner: the `/whatif?q=` endpoint turns an operator
  question into explicit assumptions (Muse Wonder live, deterministic
  parser offline) and the deterministic engine recomputes the ranking,
  returning before/after scores plus the assumptions.
- Ask-as-basis stages: `/summary`, `/whatif`, `/vision`, `/image`, and
  `/challenge` each accept `?corridor=` or `?from=&to=` and run against
  that asked corridor; Route Briefing adopts the latest ask as the basis
  of its collapsed AI analysis and evidence area.
- Phase 1 real data: the `/live` snapshot feeds measured North Sea wave
  height (Open-Meteo Marine, keyless) and Rotterdam wind into the sea leg
  through an explicit documented rule; costs and probabilities stay

# Reunite

> **[▶ Watch the 3-minute demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YK5_PkJwPig)**



**A privacy-first reconnection bridge for families or friends separated by war, migration, or crisis.**

Consent, not search, is the only key that opens the door.





## The Problem

Search for a person on Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp today, and you get dozens of closely related results. Same name. Similar profile. Similar face. You cannot tell which one is the person you are looking for. People send friend requests to the wrong profile every day — they land on a clone, a scammer, or someone who simply shares the same name.

Social media was built for meeting new acquaintances. But there is a category of search it was never designed for — the search for someone you lost. A family member. A friend. A classmate. A whole community, scattered by war, migration, or crisis.

There is no secure, consent-first framework to turn a desperate search into a safe connection.

---

## The Solution

Reunite is a privacy-first reconnection bridge built on Meta's AI. It is a **Blind Notification Bridge**, not a search engine.

A displaced person files a confidential request with fragmented memories — a name, a hometown, a phone number tail, a birth year. They never see a list of profiles. The system matches in the background. The person being sought receives a private, redacted notification. They see only what they need to recognize themselves. They choose to accept — or to decline.

"The candidate graph is four mock profiles. Everything downstream — the scoring, the threshold, the Muse Wonder tie-break, the consent gate, the payment flow — is real code doing real work on those four profiles. If Meta plugged in their actual social graph tomorrow, the engine would work identically — it's just four profiles instead of two billion."

**If they decline, the seeker is never told a match was ever found.** That is the privacy guarantee.

---

## How It Works

### Individual Flow — Find One Person

5. **A consent token is issued** — signed, single-use, 24-hour expiry.
6. **Recipient sees only a redacted summary** — *"A seeker is looking for a sibling last seen near Mosul. They remember the last four digits of a phone number ending in 4471."* No seeker name, no pho

# ReverseCAD

One photo of a flat part → an editable CAD program with real millimeter dimensions.

Indie developer track · Theme: Push the Frontier (manufacturing)

A photo of a physical part becomes manufacturable, measured geometry (laser, CNC, 3D print) that the assembly check tests against the real parts it must fit.

The core of ReverseCAD — writing every candidate CAD program — runs on Muse Spark Open, Meta's open-weight model, served through Baseten.

A flat bracket, cover, or gasket breaks or is discontinued, and the device it belongs to cannot be repaired without a replacement. Cutting a new one needs a CAD model, and today people measure the old part with calipers or trace a photo with a ruler by hand. Phone 3D-scanning apps give a mesh, with no named dimensions to edit, and its scale has to be set by hand. ReverseCAD turns that manual step into one photo: the part next to a bank card becomes an editable CAD program with real millimeter dimensions — not a dead mesh.

Flat parts with holes, by choice: brackets, mounting plates, gaskets, covers, adapter plates — the parts laser cutters, CNC mills, and 3D printers make. # Landfall

An agent that turns aerial and satellite photos taken after a hurricane, wildfire, earthquake or flood into a draft FEMA Preliminary Damage Assessment: every building compared with its pre-storm photo, flood depth estimated, each one sorted into FEMA's categories with its evidence, and a report a county can work from.

![A live run: a box is drawn over Cedar Key, the agent's plan ticks off, and every building is coloured by damage](docs/live_run.gif)

**Demo video (2:32):** https://youtu.be/a-CPgRJi1y8 · **Try it:** https://landfall-ohio.onrender.com

**Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026.** Everything in this repository was written during the event. See [BUILD_LOG.md](BUILD_LOG.md) for a dated record of what was built each day.

> Landfall produces a draft for trained assessors. It is not an official damage determination.

> "One of the challenges facing communities after a storm is that getting to sites and conducting post-storm assessment is very hard and often dangerous. Your tool could provide a preliminary analysis in minutes, and enable emergency personnel to respond immediately to areas most in need."
> — Jeff Carney, Florida Institute for Built Environment Resilience (FIBER), University of Florida

## Why

After a disaster, a county has to show FEMA how many homes were damaged and how badly before federal aid can be declared: the Preliminary Damage Assessment. Today that means teams driving street by street and looking at each house, in the days when roads are blocked and staff are stretched. NOAA flies the coast within days and Maxar photographs disasters worldwide, but nobody has time to look at every roof in those photos.

Landfall does that first look. Draw a box over a town and the agent fetches the before and after photos, lines up every building, measures what is gone, estimates flood depth, sorts each building into FEMA's categories with its reasons, prices the repairs, counts the households likely displaced, and writes the report. A full box of 60 buildings takes about a minute. Every call is a draft: the uncertain ones are marked for a visit, so field teams go first where they are needed.

**How it differs from today's process:** it doesn't replace the field visit, it decides where the visits go. The county starts the day with a map of every building already sorted, the worst ones first, and a printable page per building (photos, measurements, flood, property record, repair range) that a family can use for an insurance or aid claim.

# Backfill

Singapore cafés publish quiet-hour offers that independent buyer agents can unlock together, within limits the merchant sets.

[Hosted app](https://backfill-9d0x.onrender.com/) · [Recorded demo](https://backfill-9d0x.onrender.com/demo)

## Try it in 60 seconds

Open `/buyer`, press **Use example**, save the request, and ask Glimmer to propose constraints. Review them, ask Spark Open for a decision, then separately approve and submit the exact terms. The sandbox merchant is synthetic. Checkout is simulated, with no payment, identity or attendance enforcement.

The hosted buyer flow was verified on Nov 4 with NVIDIA Glimmer and Gateway Spark Open, separate approval, and a stored synthetic commitment. See the [release record](docs/plans/final-leg/release-2026-11-04.md).

## Models

| Model | Role | Status in this build |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark | Menu extraction and merchant counter-offers | live in the product |
| Muse Wonder | Proposed terms after a sellout, subject to owner approval | live in the product |
| Voice Transcribe | Owner voice edits for review | live in the product |
| Muse Glimmer | Buyer intent through NVIDIA | live in the buyer sandbox |
| Muse Spark Open | Buyer recommendation through Vercel AI Gateway | live in the buyer sandbox |
| SAM 3.1 | Dish segmentation | enabled for merchants with daily caps; one hosted test on a synthetic image |
| Muse Image | Offer image generation | enabled for merchants with daily caps; one hosted test on a synthetic image |

The recorded scene had 11 of 20 simulated buyers commit and filled 16 covers. It does not prove merchant demand, actual attendance or recovered revenue. The author's own Muse account completed connector tests on Oct 29 and Nov 4. The Nov 4 sandbox commitment is independently verified in [the evidence](docs/plans/final-leg/evidence/muse-connector/README.md).

## Local setup

Use Node 24 and PostgreSQL. Create an empty local development database and an owner connection that can create roles and run migrations.

1. Run `npm ci`.
2. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and configure `DATABASE_URL`, `META_API_KEY`, `META_BASE_URL`, `META_MODEL_SPARK` and `META_MODEL_WONDER`. Keep secrets private. `APP_BASE_URL` defaults to localhost in development.
3. Export the owner `DATABASE_URL` and run `npm run db:migrate`. Use a separate login in `backfill_app` for the running app after migration; the app does not need owner privileges.
4. For the buyer sandbox, export the owner connection and run `npm run sandbox:seed`. Configure `NVIDIA_API_KEY`, `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`, `BACKFILL_S4_NVIDIA_GLIMMER_APPROVED=1` and `BACKFILL_S4_GATEWAY_APPROVED=1` only when provider processing and spending are authorized. Buyer requests go to NVIDIA and Vercel AI Gateway.
5. Run `npm run dev`, then open `http://localhost:3000`.

Optional settings: `NEGOTIATION_SIGNING_SECRET` enables signed counters. The four `WHATSAPP_*` credentials in `.env.example` must all be set together to enable the webhook.

# Enterprise API Security Auditor

Enterprise API Security Auditor is an autonomous security auditor agentic AI application that helps to audit your API and AI gateways. Ingest your security policies once. Audit your entire API estate anytime, automatically,
against GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001, OWASP API Top 10, PSD2/SCA, NIST and SOC 2, etc.

## The problem

**How API security compliance works today — and why it fails.**

Every enterprise has a shelf of security policies: authentication standards, rate-limiting

APIs on a gateway. Connecting the two is **entirely manual**:

| Today | Consequence |
|---|---|
| A human reads the policy documents | Takes days; policies are long and change often |
| A human opens each API config and compares it by hand | Error-prone; nobody checks all of them |
| The reviewer must *personally know* GDPR, OWASP, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS… | A scarce, expensive skill — and a single point of failure |
| Findings land in a spreadsheet checklist | Stale the moment a config changes |
| Fixes are figured out from scratch each time | Inconsistent remediation, no standard citations |

**What existed before this project:** manual security reviews, hand-maintained validation
checklists, and tribal knowledge. There was **no agentic system** that could read an
organization's own policies and autonomously judge a live API estate against them.

The result is predictable — security gaps ship to production, audits are reactive, and
compliance depends on whether one expert happened to be in the room.

---

**Enterprise API Security Auditor — an agentic AI application.**

A supervisor-led team of nine LangGraph agents replaces the manual loop end

```

# Homing

[![CI](https://github.com/Isreal-Oparanti/Homing/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Isreal-Oparanti/Homing/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE)

**Homing** (like a homing pigeon): wherever you let it go, it finds its way back. Your saves should too.

**A memory for everything you save: it reads it, proves it against the source, and brings it back the moment it matters.**

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Indie track**. Every model call runs on Meta's models (**Muse Spark**, **Muse Wonder**, **Muse Voice Transcribe**) through one gateway, `server/app/llm/gateway.py`.

**Live:** https://homing-rho.vercel.app (press **Try the demo**) · **Video:** https://youtu.be/n3XILic3pms

## Why

Everyone saves things "for later". A Y Combinator application. A conference's call for speakers. A job post. A video on how to speak on camera. Then later never comes.

- **People save out of fear of losing things, and the pile becomes stress.** Tab and link hoarders keep items "just in case", and the build-up weighs on them (Chang et al., CHI 2021 [1]).
- **Organising doesn't bring things back.** People who carefully file into folders find things no faster than people who don't (Whittaker et al., CHI 2011 [2]).
- **A save only frees your mind if you trust it will be there.** When people believe what they saved is safe, they remember new things better; when they don't, they can't let go (Storm & Stone, Psychological Science 2015 [3]).
- **An unfinished goal keeps nagging until it has a plan.** Making a specific plan for it is what quiets it (Masicampo & Baumeister, JPSP 2011 [4]).
- **Read-later apps die when "later" never comes.** Pocket, the best known, shut down on 8 July 2025 [5].
- **People want AI to do the legwork, but stay in charge.** Workers want agents to take over about 46% of their tasks, and most prefer a partnership to full automation (Shao et al., Stanford 2025 [6]).

And when a save does come back, it's often wrong. The post you saved is someone's retelling, not the source. A real one: a blog post said a UN innovation programme was *"for young innovators"*. The official page says applicants *"must be resident in one of the seven Cohort 2 states"*. The post left out the one rule that decides if you can apply.

Homing started from a real pile: **624 saves** in one "note to self" WhatsApp chat.

Homing's answer, in one line:

> **A save should come back on its own, at the moment it matters, saying only what its source can prove.**

In full: every save gets four answers, each from its own agent (*What is it? Is it true? What's it for? When will you need it?*). Models read, search and reason; code checks every quote, number, date and rule before you see it. Then the agents keep working without being asked: they check the source, find more for your goals, watch for changes, and prepare you for what's coming. Every run remembers what the last

# AIOps Experiment Engineer: the AI proposes, a Rust harness proves

AI models write plausible performance fixes in seconds. Knowing whether a fix is correct, and whether it really made the service faster, still takes an engineer an afternoon. This project closes that gap without trusting the model.

A Meta model (Muse Spark 1.3, through the Meta Model API) reads operational evidence, states a hypothesis and writes a patch. A Rust harness builds the patch in an isolated container with no internet and no secrets, checks that every response is unchanged, and measures p95 latency against the unchanged service in alternating pairs. Only the Rust evaluator decides: **VERIFIED**, **REJECTED** or **INCONCLUSIVE**, each with the measured reason. The model can propose; it cannot pass its own patch.

[한국어 README](README.ko.md)

- **Live:** https://aiops-edge.yh9365.workers.dev (Cloudflare Workers, Containers, D1, R2). Reading is public; starting a run needs the admin token.
- **On a real bug:** on Vaultwarden's documented N+1 (issue #1402, an open-source Rust Bitwarden server), the model's batched rewrite cut SQL per sync from 2,011 to 15 and p95 from 246 to 64 ms, and was VERIFIED (74%). See [the real-bug write-up](docs/real-bug-probe.md).
- **Best run to open:** [`/runs/01a19da7-b2a2-70e0-af44-018eddd0c003`](https://aiops-edge.yh9365.workers.dev/runs/01a19da7-b2a2-70e0-af44-018eddd0c003). The model's first patch did not match the source, so the harness refused it before anything ran. The model read the refusal, fixed the patch, and the second one was VERIFIED.
- **Stack:** Rust (Axum, Tokio, SQLx), React (Vite, TypeScript), Cloudflare Workers + Containers + D1 + R2, Meta Model API.

![First screen: the latest verified change, Meta model runs and the harness scorecard](docs/img/ui-runs.png)

## How one run works

1. **Baseline.** The runner measures the unchanged service twice under the same fixed load (A/A). If two runs of the same code differ by more than 15%, nothing is judged.
2. **Observe.** The observer role calls tools to read metrics, the slowest requests (each with its SQL count and DB time), the source and past experiments. It writes facts and hypotheses separately, every fact with an evidence ID.
3. **Propose.** The experimenter role writes one hypothesis, what result would prove it wrong, and a search/replace patch.
4. **Check before running.** The patch must touch only allowed files (never the request tracker, the golden answers or `Cargo.toml`), and each search text must match the source exactly once.
5. **Build and verify.** The runner applies the patch in a fresh workspace and builds it offline. It then compares the candidate with the original on 14 golden cases, checks response invariants, and compares 200 sampled requests answered by both.
6. **Measure.** Baseline and candidate run alternately in 3 pairs at 100 requests per second. Each pair gives one p95 improvement.
7. **Decide.** The evaluator applies the gates below. A REJECTED or IN

Each day a GitHub Action pulls human-preference rankings (LMArena), a benchmark-based capability score (Epoch AI) and live serving data (OpenRouter). The best variant counts (e.g. `High`/`Max` reasoning). - **Epoch ECI:** the Epoch Capabilities Index, one score combining many benchmarks. - **Providers / uptime / price / precision:** from OpenRouter's public endpoints API. Precision lists the number formats providers publicly declare (`bf16`, `fp8`, `fp4`). Lower precision is cheaper to serve and can cost quality. When the leaderboards disagree, that's information, not noise. A model can top the benchmarks and still lose the chat vote. ## How it works `pulse.py` (stdlib + `pyarrow`) runs daily in [`.github/workflows/pulse.yml`](.github/workflows/pulse.yml). A source that changes its format makes the run fail loudly instead of publishing wrong numbers. To track other models, edit `models.json`. ```bash pip install pyarrow && python -m unittest && python pulse.py ``

**Agents act on your behalf. Nobody can prove what they did.**

## Submission overview — Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026

- **Track & problem statement:** Startup · **Push the Frontier**
- **Provenance:** Built from scratch during the hackathon window,
  Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026. The commit history starts Oct 26; no code

- **Demo video (2:59):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5X7RR0bsljE
- **Live deployment:** Clearing House
  https://clearinghouse.omni-ouro.com · business playground and
  dashboard https://eyd.omni-ouro.com — the dashboard is open in the
  browser, no install or account.
- **Meta AI runtime models:** open-weight Muse Spark
  (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`, served via Baseten) runs the
  Clearing House expectation vector; Muse (`muse-wonder-1.0` via the
  Meta model gateway) drives the acting demo agents. Details:
  [Meta AI tooling](#meta-ai-tooling).
- **Bonus category targeted:** Best Agentic Use-Case.
- **Keyless verification (no API key needed):** `pytest` (56 tests),
  and the hosted-beta walk `python examples/beta_agent.py` against the
  live deployment above. The judge console's live model calls need a
  model gateway token (see `.env.example`).

> "Govern the event, not the technology." — Peter Evans-Greenwood

EyD doesn't govern the agent or the model; it records the event and
gets the counterparty to attest to the same event.

EyD is a small library and a small window. The agent framework imports
it, and it sits in the tool-call path: every call the agent makes is
signed under the agent's own Ed25519 key and reported to a
clearinghouse before it goes out. The counterparty site reports its
side after. The clearinghouse pairs the two, classifies the result
(Expected, Unexpected, Declined, Gated, Unverified, Deviated), and issues a signed Proof
Receipt to both parties. Agents that don't route through EyD get no receipt.
Sites that gate on EyD only admit agents that do.

# Iklim PAL

Local climate **action planner** for young people (Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Indie · Build for Your World).

Turn a neighborhood litter photo into a **pack-approved, safety-bounded, measurable Action Plan** (Muse confirms the concern with you; place and safety stay in Q&A) — not a climate lecture, not a political tool, not a one-shot image captioner.

**How to use the app:** [`INSTRUCTIONS.md`](INSTRUCTIONS.md)

Also see [`architecture.md`](architecture.md), [`task.md`](task.md), [`docs/anti-project.md`](docs/anti-project.md), [`docs/demo-video-script.md`](docs/demo-video-script.md), and [`docs/demo-script.md`](docs/demo-script.md).

## Muse models used

| Model | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `sam-3.1` | Segment litter in the photo |
| `muse-spark-1.3` | Concern hypothesis after SAM |
| `muse-wonder-1.0` | Action Plan synthesis |
| `muse-image-1.0` | Share / invite card |
| `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` | Optional spoken concern on `q_concern` |

**Q&A after concern** uses Action Pack order (deterministic) so answers stay fast. **Plans** home tracks Active/Past plans with step checkoffs (anonymous device `ownerKey`).

**No RAG. No fine-tuning.** Domain knowledge lives in [`packages/action-packs/plastic_litter_id_v1.json`](packages/action-packs/plastic_litter_id_v1.json) (sources: [`docs/pack-sources.md`](docs/pack-sources.md)).

## Stack

- `apps/web` — React + Vite (**Iklim PAL** UI)
- `apps/api` — Node + Express
- `packages/shared` — Zod schemas + `/step` contract
- `packages/action-packs` — litter Action Pack
- Supabase Storage (+ tables when migrated); local JSON fallback under `.data/` if SQL not applied yet

## Setup

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# fill MODEL_API_KEY + SUPABASE_URL + SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY

npm install

# Optional but recommended: apply supabase/migrations/001_iklim_pal.sql in the SQL editor
# Storage buckets session-photos / session-masks / session-share-cards / session-voice
# (see supabase/README.md). Until SQL is applied, API uses local JSON + Storage when available.

npm run dev:api
npm run dev:web
```

Open `http://localhost:5173` (or your Vite port). Upload a **real** fixture from `fixtures/litter/*/photo.png`.

## Local verify

```bash
npm run smoke:meta      # cheap API-key check (tiny PNG) — not product E2E
npm run test:safety
npm run test:quality

# with API running:
npm run e2e:real        # REAL S2 + S4 litter photos → real Muse agent
```

**Pass criteria:** S2 reaches `done` with an Action Plan; S4 escalates on hazard.

## Fixtures

Real photos (already in repo; also copied to stable `photo.png` names):

- `fixtures/litter/S1_street_bottles/photo.png`
- `fixtures/litter/S2_riverbank_bags/photo.png` (hero)
- `fixtures/litter/S3_drain_clog/photo.png`
- `fixtures/litter/S4_hazard_escalate/photo.png`

An autonomous farm manager powered by the **Meta Model API (Muse)**, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (October 26 – November 4, 2026).

- **Live demo (AgroGenesis simulator):** <https://agrogenesis.fly.dev>

It is **not** claimed as a hackathon contribution. **This repository contains only the agent developed during the hackathon**: the Meta Muse integration, the autonomous controller, tool calling, observation and planning logic, persistence, and the tests and benchmarks around them. No simulator code is included here; the agent talks to the simulator only through its authorized HTTP API.

Package: `agrogenesis-muse-agent` **v0.1.23** (`package.json`). The repository is `private` and is **not published to npm**; it is consumed from Git tags (latest tag `v0.1.23`, commit `0ea7590`). AgroGenesis pins it with `git+https://github.com/walterjrey/agrogenesis-muse-agent.git#<tag>`.

In *Muse AI* mode, AgroGenesis lets a Muse model run the farm on its own: it looks at what it is **allowed to know**, decides what is justified, and acts through the simulator's API. # Attest

Attest turns reviewed git history and imported AI coding-session records into a portable, revocable candidate report at `attest.sh/v/{handle}`. Git claims link to commits, changed files, quoted excerpts, and a tamper-evident SHA-256 chain; imported session events are separately labeled and chained. Attest means **these specific claims have supporting evidence**—not that a person is good.

Evidence comes before scores. Assessment scores are shown with exact quotes from the candidate's submission; absent or ungrounded evidence produces `null`. Language is limited to **Supported**, **Partially supported**, **Unverified**, and **Contradicted**. The product never calls people dishonest, and an empty result says **No significant signals detected**. Local scans are private; nothing uploads unless the user runs `attest sync` and confirms the exact request preview.

## Stack

- `apps/web`: Vite, React, Tailwind; built and served as static assets by the Cloudflare Worker.
- `apps/api`: Hono on Cloudflare Workers; GitHub OAuth/device flow, D1, R2, Queues, and Meta Model API generation/grading.
- `packages/cli`: Node.js CLI; scans git history, saves a local preview, and syncs only after confirmation.
- `packages/core`: shared evidence contracts and deterministic chain hashing.

## Local development

Requirements: Node.js 20+, npm, Git, and Wrangler.

```sh
npm.cmd install
npm.cmd run dev:api
npm.cmd run dev
```

In another terminal, apply the schema to local D1:

```sh
npm.cmd run db:local -w @attest/api
```

Copy `.dev.vars.example` to `apps/api/.dev.vars` and set `GH_CLIENT_ID`, `GH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `SESSION_SECRET` (a long random value), and a Meta Model API key as `META_API_KEY`. Register a GitHub OAuth app with callback `http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/auth/github/callback` for local browser sign-in. The local Worker command sets `APP_ORIGIN=http://127.0.0.1:5173` automatically. GitHub device flow is used by the CLI. Until OAuth credentials are configured, clicking sign-in explains the missing setup instead of silently sending you to GitHub.

Open `http://localhost:5173`. From the Attest source repository, the CLI commands are:

```sh
.\attest.cmd login
.\attest.cmd scan
.\attest.cmd sync
.\attest.cmd wipe
```

The `.cmd` launcher avoids PowerShell's `npx.ps1` execution-policy error. It defaults to the live Attest Worker; override it with `ATTEST_API_URL` or `--api`. Invoke the launcher by full path from another git repository while keeping that repository as the current directory; the scanner uses the current directory. Do not run `npx attest`: the public npm package name is owned by an unrelated project. This CLI is private until it can be published under an available, owned package scope.

`scan` writes only to `.attest/scan.json`; it does not upload. To include a Claude Code JSONL export or normalized Attest/Vaultio session log, pass `--session`:

```sh
.\attest.cmd scan --session C:\path\to\session.jsonl
```

Session imports are parsed and redac

alfredowh/ANTS.readme_excerpt: # ANTS: Agentic Task Synthesis **Show a robot a task once. An adversary breaks it in simulation. Every failure becomes a readable fix, kept only if no case seen so far got worse.** No model weights are trained. Our entry for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon). ## Problem Robots learn one task at a time from lots of data, and nobody can say when they will fail. Small changes (a camera angle, a bigger plate) can break a skill that worked in the lab. A factory with a new part every week cannot use a skill it cannot trust. ## Solution ![ANTS: the Synthesizer writes a program from one human demo, the Adversary attacks it in simulation, and a regression gate keeps only rewrites that do no worse](docs/images/architecture.svg) *Solid boxes are built and running. # Keel

**A checkpoint validity harness for open-weight models.**

`keel scan` compares a derivative against its base and returns a card: what moved, whether
the measurement was valid, what the harmful half says, and, when weights are available,
the structural signature of the intervention. Exit codes make it a CI gate.

- Live demo: **https://tomscot-keel.hf.space**
- Demo video (1:57 live run, 1080p): **https://tomscot-keel.hf.space/video** (1440p mirror [on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EP5-Xh9t1GY))
- Run it live (7B, about 12 min): **https://tomscot-keel.hf.space#live**
- Scan your own checkpoint: **https://tomscot-keel.hf.space#scan**
- Reviewer access and hashes: **https://tomscot-keel.hf.space#access**
- Current state, including gaps: [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md)
- Technical use of Meta models: [docs/META-MODELS.md](docs/META-MODELS.md)
- Docs map: [docs/INDEX.md](docs/INDEX.md)

## The frontier deployment bottleneck

Meta's base models go through alignment, but once a checkpoint is fine-tuned, abliterated
or merged in the open, the chain of custody is lost. Standard benchmarks go stale, and a
derivative that dropped its refusal behavior can still score well on capability tests. An
enterprise has no independent way to check that a community fine-tune kept the behavior of
the model it was built from.

## The solution: an auditable record for open weights

Keel evaluates a derivative against its baseline and produces a Keel card: verdict, drift,
harmful rates, validity, structure and limits, with a SHA-256 fingerprint over the card.
The fingerprint is a checksum, not a signature: it proves the card matches its evidence,
not who produced it. The verify route recomputes the card from the committed response
files, so an edited card fails verification.

### Key capabilities

- **The 32-probe panel.** Refusal error, sycophancy, deception, power seeking and sabotage,
  plus 32 public harmful requests for the harmful half. A judged evaluation takes about
  twenty seconds (three repeats, majority), not fifteen thousand questions.
- **Keel cards.** A SHA-256 fingerprint over the card content. Change a score by 0.01 and
  the fingerprint changes; the verify button recomputes from the responses and returns
  MATCH or DIFF.
- **Format-collapse detection.** If a coding fine-tune destroys the answer format, the
  format gate turns the card amber and marks it `suspect`; a suspect card cannot be green.

## Built for the Meta model family

1. **The baselines:** `meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B` and the Meta API checkpoints.
2. **The subjects:** abliterations, LoRAs and community merges of Muse Glimmer, plus Qwen
   and Mistral for the cross-family generality check.
3. **The arbiter:** the frozen Meta judge `muse-spark-1.3` through the Meta Model API,
   selected on a 48-item gold set (kappa 0.603). The alternatives and their disagreement
   are recorded in `docs/JUDGE-BENCH.md`.

National Tensor connects **Meta Muse**, reviewed **Triton** kernels, real GPU measurements, and evidence checks into a research workflow. Muse proposes and critiques ideas; people approve experiments; immutable records keep measured results separate from explanations. Our hackathon result is a counterintuitive pipeline-stage latency pattern and a prospective AI prediction tested on held-out hardware.

National Tensor's visible repository work began October 26, 2026. During the event, the project added the Muse-guided proposal and criticism workflow, human approval before trusted GPU runs, experiment memory, paired benchmarking and evidence checks, the pipeline-stage investigation and prospective held-out test, portable evidence bundles, and the Research and Hollywood dashboard views. The four-scene Pipeline Paradox replay and the Performance and Reliability cards present those saved results. National Tensor's later stage-3-versus-stage-2 confirmation and Muse test are separate recorded experiments. The [audit](docs/HACKATHON_PROVENANCE.md) found no substantial direct or adapted Matmul Inspector implementation code in the compared tracked snapshots; rewritten or unavailable source cannot be ruled out.

# Booklith

**Give every book its own reader.** Booklith turns a PDF into a structured, validated book and exports it as a complete AI-powered website you can own and deploy.

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon/details), Booklith combines Meta models for book-aware features with optional OCR and speech services that run in infrastructure you control.

## What Booklith does

1. **Bring in a book.** Upload a PDF to your Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 Modal endpoint, or explore a prebuilt sample reader.
2. **Turn it into a book structure.** OCR Markdown becomes chapters and stable IDs for paragraphs, figures, and tables.
3. **Let AI organize, not rewrite.** The optional AI harness can group chapters, suggest titles, and choose a theme. It does not write or edit the book text.
4. **Check the source.** An integrity validator catches text that was changed, omitted, added, or reordered.
5. **Preview and export.** Check the reader, then publish the self-contained Next.js app to your GitHub repository in one commit or download it as a zip.

```text
PDF -> Baidu OCR Markdown -> Book JSON -> AI structure and theme -> integrity check
                                                                 -> live reader preview
                                                                 -> GitHub export or zip
```

npm install
npm run dev

To enable translation in local demos, copy `builder/.env.example` to
`builder/.env.local` and set `API_KEY`. `API_BASE_URL` and `API_MODEL` are

```bash

# Salomon Earnings Desk

**Live: https://desk.slmn.trade** · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026) · Startup track · Theme: *Build for Your World*

An earnings desk for everyday investors. Ask, by typing or by voice, "Who reports
earnings this week and what's expected?", "Will WELL beat?" or "Was Salomon right

the numbers and sources shown.

the real result. The public scorecard can only show what was actually called.

**An agentic memory layer for personal AI agents.**
Personal agents infer things about you from every chat, keep them out of sight, and never ask if they got it right. Déjà Vu is the agent whose job is memory: it learns short cards from your chats, checks them against your own words, uses only the few that matter for each request, and asks you once, at the moment a guess is about to shape a booking or a plan.

> Agents are really good at inferring context from chats. But confirmed memory is always better than inferred memory.

# Sentinel — a safety layer for robot actions

**The LLM decides how. Sentinel decides whether.**

*For anyone putting an LLM in charge of a physical arm.*

Live demo: https://rushi-bhosale84--sentinel-web.us-east.modal.run
(`/` split view: naive vs Sentinel side by side; `/debug` full dashboard)
Demo video (3 min): https://youtu.be/QiI9FRH5ySk

![knife hand-over: naive hands it blade-first, with Sentinel it goes handle-first and slows down](docs/knife_split.gif)

*Left: no Sentinel — the knife is handed blade-first. Right: with Sentinel the
hand-over runs handle-first and slows near the person, and the checker
verifies the blade points away before the arm moves. Full 17 s clip (not committed — re-record with
`uv run python -m dashboard.split_record knife`).*

## The problem

LLMs plan robot actions well but can't be trusted to judge safety alone. Ask
for a knife hand-over and you get a smooth trajectory — blade-first, at full
speed, toward a person. Ask it to judge its own plan and it waves through
nearly half the hazards (44.3% unsafe-exec as a judge-only gate in our
benchmark). Planning skill and safety judgment are different jobs; Sentinel
splits them: the LLM proposes *how*, a deterministic checker verifies
*whether* — before anything moves.

Explicit destruction is the easy case and needs no checker: ask for
"throw the laptop on the ground" and the planner refuses on its own
with a single stop step — identical with and without Sentinel (try it
on the live demo). Sentinel reports ALLOW on the resulting empty plan,
correctly: a motion that moves nothing violates no rule. Sentinel
exists for the hazards the planner happily complies with: the
blade-first handover, the pour next to the laptop, the guess about an
object that isn't quite there.

## How it works

```
camera ──► perception ──► scene graph ──► LLM plan ──► Motion dry-run ──► Sentinel ──► ALLOW / ASK / BLOCK / HALT
           SAM 3.1 +       objects,        Muse Spark    mink IK on a      deterministic rules
           Muse Spark      people, props,  (structured   sim copy (path,   over the dry-run
           (+ depth)       relations       output)       held, tilt,      (no LLM inside check())
                                                         speed)
                                    ▲                                          │
                                    │ feedback (fixable findings)              │ incident? ("that was unsafe")
                                    └──────── replan (max 3 rounds) ◄──────────┘
                                                                               ▼
                                                         rule learner: Muse Wonder proposes
                                                         ONE rule from vocabulary ──► gate
                                                         (schema + replay + ratchet +
                                                         preflight) ──► soft ASK rule
```

# Graspt

**Stand on the map. Direct the agent. Lean tells the truth.**

Graspt turns Lean 4 theorem proving from writing symbolic code into navigating proved mathematics. You explore a stable map of goals and landmarks, stand on a place, and direct an AI agent in plain language. The agent drafts and edits Lean. The Lean kernel verifies every move. Nothing unverified is ever presented as proved.

```bash
git clone <this-repo> && cd graspt
npm ci
npx graspt setup        # one long offline job: Lean → Mathlib cache → global atlas
npx graspt demo-ready   # names any missing stage; never silently regenerates
npm start               # → open http://127.0.0.1:4174/ in your browser
```

For a first look with no setup at all, `npm start` opens the pre-indexed demo instantly — 12 Lean proofs, already traced, with open frontiers waiting to be closed live.

---

## The problem

AI agents can now write Lean. Almost nobody can steer them.

The barrier is not mathematical intelligence. It is **transcoding**: turning an idea in your head — *these two lemmas should combine here, this induction should split there* — into `rcases`, `refine`, and Mathlib incantations, and turning Lean's symbolic output back into an idea. That transcoding cost locks out the largest pool of mathematical talent: people with intuition and judgement who never paid the years-long syntax apprenticeship.

Existing interfaces make it worse. An editor shows you one goal at a time through a keyhole. You cannot see the shape of a proof, where you are in it, what is near you, or what a step is *for*. You are navigating a territory through a periscope, typing coordinates by hand.

Graspt's bet: **in the age of AI agents, the human's job in formal mathematics changes from encoding proofs to navigating and judging them.** Interfaces should be built for that job.

## The philosophy

Five commitments shape every part of this codebase. They are stated here as concepts because they *are* the product — the code is their crystallised form.

### 1. Mathematics is a territory, and places stay put

A proof is rendered as a topological map: goals are **places**, tactics are **moves** between places, named theorems are **landmarks**, and an unsolved goal is an open **frontier**. Two views of the same map are always present:

- the **allocentric map** — the whole territory seen from outside, world-fixed;
- the **egocentric view** — where you are standing: your current goal `Γ ⊢ T` in full, the trail that brought you here, and your nearest neighbours.

A map is only useful if places stay put. Every goal is therefore identified by a **canonical key built from its statement and context (`Γ ⊢ T`)** — never by Lean's transient internal IDs, which change on every elaboration. Re-trace a file and nothing moves. Clicking a neighbour walks you through the proof; your cursor, the map highlight, and the agent's context are always the same place.

- **The human** does the part humans comp

# SheetTruth

SheetTruth finds spreadsheet formulas that compute the wrong thing, and then proves each finding
against the workbook before it reports it.

The errors it looks for are the quiet ones: a total that stops one row short, a sum that reaches
into the price row, a reference that points one row off, a cost added instead of subtracted.
Excel accepts all of them. Every cell still shows a number, so nobody notices until someone
reads the labels. SheetTruth reads the labels with a fine-tuned open-weights model, tests every
finding with code, asks a second model for an independent opinion, and writes the confirmed fixes
into a corrected copy of the workbook.

Live: [sheettruth.com](https://sheettruth.com). Code, data recipe, training, evaluation and the
web application are all in this repository, so every number below can be rerun.

## Why this matters

Spreadsheet errors are common, and a few of them have been very expensive. Field audits of real
business spreadsheets, collected by Raymond Panko, found errors in 24% of 367 spreadsheets in the
older studies and in at least 86% of the spreadsheets audited with better methods from 1997 on;
measured per cell, audited formula error rates of 0.4% to 2.5% are typical
([Panko, "Spreadsheet Errors: What We Know. What We Think We Can Do", EuSpRIG 2000](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0802.3457.pdf)).
At those rates, a model with a few thousand formulas is expected to hold errors.

Some of the best known cases, as reported by
[The Guardian, "Microsoft Excel's bloopers reel: nearly 40 years of spreadsheet errors" (2024)](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/oct/28/microsoft-excels-bloopers-reel-40-years-of-spreadsheet-errors):

- **JPMorgan, the "London Whale" trades (2012).** The bank's risk model ran on spreadsheets that
  were copied and pasted by hand, and one cell divided by the sum of two interest rates instead of
  their average. The model understated the risk, and the trades ended in a loss of about $6bn.
- **Reinhart and Rogoff (2010, found 2013).** A spreadsheet error in a widely cited economics
  paper turned a growth figure for high-debt economies from 2.2% into a decline of 0.1%. The paper
  had been used to support austerity policy after the financial crisis.
- **Fannie Mae (2003).** An accountant entered a wrong formula while adapting to a new accounting
  standard, and the quarterly results carried errors of more than $1bn.
- **Public Health England (2020).** Test results were collected in a file format that could not
  hold all the rows, so records were dropped, and nearly 16,000 COVID-19 cases went unreported
  for days; contact tracers missed thousands of people.

Every one of these is a quiet error: the spreadsheet still showed a number, and the number was
trusted. The JPMorgan case is exactly the kind of formula SheetTruth is built for (a wrong
operation on the right cells); the Reinhart and Rogoff case is a range that did not cover the
rows it should have. Tools that compare a formula

Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding


SpecPilot more than doubles stock's speedup in every setting, without training or quality loss.

Released speculative decoding systems leave much of their speed unused, and the best fix differs for every deployment. SpecPilot is an agentic loop that finds lossless optimizations for each one. This repository ships the engine SpecPilot found for each of six deployments, with the scripts to serve, benchmark and verify them. ## Overview

In each round of the loop, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones, and a kernel sub-agent tunes the kernels furthest from their memory-bandwidth limit. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to catch outputs that drift from the target model. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. Here *stock* is the released drafter system (DFlash2 or DSpark) without SpecPilot, served on the same engine. Every SpecPilot engine (*final*) is lossless: decoding is greedy and the target model decides every token. # muse-glimmer-ppo

PPO fine-tuning of Muse Glimmer 30B as a robot policy, starting with the
first task of the LLM-LIBERO paper: LIBERO-10 task 0, "put both the
alphabet soup and the tomato sauce in the basket".

Muse acts exactly as in the paper: each decision is one tool call
(`move_to` with absolute targets, `done` or `give_up`), with the paper's
system prompt, tool schemas, 80-call and 900-step budget, and success check.
PPO updates LoRA adapters on Muse's language model plus a value head.
Training uses initial states 10-49 of the task; states 0-9, the ones the
paper evaluated, stay held out.

The harness version (skill programs, LIBERO-90) is kept in the repo for later.

For the separate **CaPtain Python/perception pipeline baseline**, see
[the setup and experiment commands](docs/captain_baseline.md). The launcher uses
the authors' pinned harness with Glimmer as the policy under test; `--env paper`
mode above is the LLM-LIBERO move-only protocol, not CaPtain-Harness.

The [experiment viewer](docs/experiment_viewer.md) shows training runs by default.
For Glimmer RL through the Python harness, use the [CaPtain RL launcher](docs/captain_rl.md).

Plan, formulas and parameters: the "Glimmer RL on LIBERO-90: Plan" doc.

## How it fits together

```text
StartSampler (task 0, inits 10-49, optional demo keyframes)
   │
PaperEnv.reset ──> llm_agent_memory Episode (paper Algorithm 1) ──> paper_worker.py (LIBERO, MuJoCo)
   │                messages: paper system prompt + goal + state + 2 camera images
   v
Policy.act(messages, tools)      Muse + LoRA samples one reply, parse_tool_call reads the call
   │
PaperEnv.step ──> Episode.call(move_to | done | give_up)  (paper toolset: bounds, interpolation)
   │              reward = success + Phi(s') - Phi(s) - costs     (Phi: hold, lift, goal conditions)
   v
rollout buffer ──> GAE per call ──> clipped PPO epochs ──> LoRA + value head
```

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `src/glimmer_ppo/paper_env.py` | The paper protocol as an RL env: one step = one reply = one tool call |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/sim/paper_worker.py` | The paper's LIBERO worker, unchanged except it also reports goal conditions, grasp and lift (reward only) and can start from a demo state |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/sim/paper_embodiment.py` | The paper's `LiberoEmbodiment`, pointed at that worker |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/toolcall.py` | Reads the last move_to / done / give_up call from Muse's raw text |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/reward.py` | `potential_reward` (paper env) and the older harness reward |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/policy.py` | Muse with LoRA (text decoder only), value head, reference = adapter off |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/ppo.py` | GAE, clipped policy loss, value loss, KL, explained variance |
| `src/glimmer_ppo/starts.py` | Start states: initial states and demo keyframes |
| `scripts/train_ppo.py` | Training loop (`--env paper` default, `--env harness` for later) |
| `scripts/eval_task.py` | Success rate on held-out initial states, base model or a checkpoin

# Jeevan Rekha

**When the flood helpline is full, nobody should get a busy tone.**

Jeevan Rekha ("lifeline") is an AI surge call-taker for disaster helplines in India. When every human call-taker is busy, overflow calls go to an agent that:
- listens in the caller's language
- asks only what a rescue boat needs
- reads numbers and places back so "thirty" never becomes "three" and an unknown village never silently becomes a known one
- recognises people who are already reported (a relative's call, a repeat call) by checking the live case board, and asks before joining them to that case
- hands human dispatchers a ranked rescue queue on a map

Callers can also send a photo: SAM 3.1 counts the people on the roof and Muse Spark reads the water level.

> In July 2026, Kosi floodwater cut six villages of Kusheshwar Asthan block in Darbhanga, Bihar, off from the mainland, leaving thousands stranded with 13 boats working ([IANS, 18 July 2026](https://www.socialnews.xyz/2026/07/18/bihar-flood-situation-worsens-in-darbhanga-20-villages-inundated)). When Cyclone Michaung flooded Chennai in December 2023, residents who called the corporation's 1913 helpline found nobody answering or the lines constantly busy: "when hundreds of people try calling the helplines, it becomes difficult to reach through" ([The News Minute, 4 December 2023](https://www.thenewsminute.com/amp/story/tamil-nadu/chennai-floods-helplines-inundated-people-struggle-to-contact-authorities)). Disaster lines are staffed for ordinary days; in a flood they become the bottleneck.

Both places are in the demo: Kusheshwar Asthan is one of the Darbhanga places the agent knows, and Chennai callers are answered in Tamil.

The AI never decides that someone will not be rescued. It collects, confirms and ranks; **humans dispatch**.

**Demo video:** [Watch the submitted demo (4:48)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11prB2gk0ODhTFa_J3_-cmnsPBJITjX3V/view?usp=sharing). Includes English captions, a live Hindi rescue call, the flood-night control room and an English repeat-caller check.

**Live demo:** [Open Jeevan Rekha](https://sumerchoudhary78--jeevan-rekha-web.us-east.modal.run) (append `?code=<passcode>`; the passcode is in the submission form so the Meta API credits aren't open to everyone). Pages: `/caller` and `/control`.

### Try it in two minutes (in English)

1. Open `/control` and press **Simulate flood night**: 24 recorded calls arrive over about 90 seconds.
2. Open `/caller` in Chrome with headphones, choose **English** and **Patna**, press the green button and, after the tone, say: *"Hello, I am in Kankarbagh sector three in Patna, near the Hanuman temple. The water is rising."*
3. The agent reads the place back ("Kankarbagh, right?"). Say yes. Four people near the Hanuman temple were already reported on the flood night, so it asks whether you are with them. Say *"Yes, that is us."* In the control room your call joins that case (**caller confirmed same group**) instead of opening a duplicate.

# Oja Ledger 🧺📒

**Talk your sales. We write the book.**

A phone-first ledger for Nigerian market traders. Say a sale in Pidgin, point the camera at a product, and **Meta Muse Spark** does the bookkeeping: sales, purchases, debts, prices and stock.

🔗 **Live app:** https://djebiswags.github.io/oja-ledger/ (open in Chrome on Android, add to home screen)
🏆 Built during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026)**

---

## The problem
Millions of traders in Nigerian markets keep their books in their heads or in a torn exercise book. Debts get forgotten, stock runs out without warning, and nobody knows the day's real profit. Most bookkeeping apps expect typing, English and forms. Traders talk.

## What Oja Ledger does
| | Feature | Meta AI |
|---|---|---|
| 🎤 | **Talk it in.** "Mama Ngozi go pay 3k Friday for rice" becomes a DEBT entry with who, what and how much | Muse Spark reads Pidgin or English into a structured entry |
| ✅ | **Confirm in one tap.** Every entry shows a card first, with "Read by Meta Muse". Nothing saves without the trader's OK | |
| 📸 | **Mama's Shelf.** Snap a product; it's named the way traders say it ("Peak Milk 400g", tin, Provisions). Set price and stock | Muse Spark vision |
| 🔍 | **Price Scan.** Point the camera at a product and *her own* price and stock pop up. Sell 1 in a tap, or add an unknown item | Muse Spark vision, live every ~2 s |
| 📉 | **Stock tracks itself.** Sales cut stock, purchases restock, low stock gets a badge | |
| 💬 | **WhatsApp built in.** Send debt reminders, receipts, and a shop price list as one message | |
| 📴 | **Works offline.** Installable PWA; a rule-based parser takes over when there's no network | |

**Every trader keeps her own prices.** Prices in Nigerian markets vary by stall, so there is no shared price board; the AI only recognises the product and shows *her* tag.

## How Meta AI is used
- **Model:** Meta **Muse Spark Open** (`meta/muse-spark-open`), with Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Glimmer 30B selectable in ⚙️ Settings.
- **Access:** through [Puter.js](https://developer.puter.com/ai/meta/muse-spark-open/), so the trader needs **no API key and no card**. First use shows a one-time free Puter sign-in.
- **Ledger reading:** the prompt gives Muse the trader's shelf names, so "2 peak" matches "Peak Milk 400g". Muse returns JSON (type, item, qty, unit price, total, who), and the app checks the maths before showing the confirm card.
- **Vision:** photos are shrunk on the phone (512 px JPEG) before they're sent, to save data.
- **Other routes:** Groq, Fireworks (Llama 4 Maverick) or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as the Meta Model API, can be plugged in from Settings. Keys stay in the phone's localStorage only.

## Architecture
```
Voice (phone speech-to-text, en-NG) ─┐
Typed text ──────────────────────────┼─► Meta Muse Spark ─► JSON entry ─► Confirm card ─► Ledger + Shelf (localStorage)
                     (offline: rules)┘

# Ulat

Ulat turns typhoon and flood reports into draft damage assessments and insurance forms.
It is a prototype for residents, fish farmers and the city's disaster office in Biñan, Philippines.

[Live dashboard](https://ronniecutamora47--ulat.modal.run) (passcode on request: send a direct message to [@CutamoraRonnie on X](https://x.com/CutamoraRonnie)) · [Telegram bot @UlatPH_bot](https://t.me/UlatPH_bot) · [Demo video (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=caQcSKOwagw)

## The problem

- After Typhoon Paeng, Biñan had 2,088 affected families on November 4, 2022, 20,087 on November 18, and 575 still displaced on December 24. [See the reports.](docs/how-it-works.md#the-problem)
- The city's damage assessment form is due within [72 hours](#official-names) of the assessment team's deployment.
- Insured fish farmers have [2 calendar days](#official-names) after a loss to submit a written notice, before harvest.

## How it works

1. A resident sends the bot a photo, short video, voice note, audio file, text or location.
2. Ulat reads the report, checks photos and finds its neighborhood (barangay).
3. It groups reports about the same incident and marks uncertain cases for an officer.
4. It drafts the city's damage assessment, damaged-houses table and insurance forms from the reports.
5. An officer checks the evidence, fills missing details and approves or rejects each draft.

Rice insurance forms are an option for offices that enable them. They are off for Biñan until a local rice area is verified.

## Meta models doing the work

<!-- eval-models:start -->
| Meta model | Its job in Ulat | One recorded result |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Reads reports, judges photos, groups reports and drafts a summary. | 18 of 25 roof judgments matched the labels. |
| Muse Spark Open | Runs the same agent with open weights on Baseten. | 16 of 25 roof judgments matched the labels. |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Turns spoken reports into text. | 19.1% word error rate across 8 voice notes, one speaker. |
| SAM 3.1 | Outlines roofs and floodwater for an officer to check. | Found roofs in 23 of 23 labeled roof photos. |
<!-- eval-models:end -->

Muse Image also created [synthetic demo photos](data/demo/scenario.json) and a [synthetic test set](data/eval/vision_scenes.json).

## How you can check the agent

- Open a report's [step-by-step record](app/agent_trace.py) to see its decisions, model, timing and estimated costs.
- [Report-based form values](docs/how-it-works.md#officer-outputs) link back to their reports; [photo outlines](app/photo.py) let an officer inspect the image evidence.
- [Review](app/questions.py) asks one question at a time. Overrides and edits require initials; [approvals are logged](app/drafts.py) with initials optional. Ulat never files a form: a person files it after review.
- Check [labeled results](data/eval/results.json) and [rerun tests with saved model answers](docs/evaluation.md) when available. Run the [offline smoke test](scripts/smok

# Vamos Fire Fire: technical writing with Muse 30B

**Turn engineering context into technical documents that people can understand, check, and use.**

A model can help us implement a system and still leave us struggling to explain it. In our own workflow, generated design documents often look finished before the thinking is clear: they repeat the requirements, name components without explaining their interactions, and assert benefits without describing the conditions or costs. Reviewing the document becomes another round of prompting just to work out what it means.

We are building a technical-writing specialist on **Muse Glimmer 30B**. Given project context, constraints, and an intended audience, it should produce a complete document with accurate mechanisms, explicit design reasoning, and useful tradeoffs.

**Status, November 2, 2026:** we collected and cleaned **1,916 human-written technical documents** from three sources and fine-tuned Muse Glimmer 30B on them with LoRA SFT. The SFT model lowers held-out NLL by about **5.5%** relative to base Muse, beats Qwen 3.5 9B and Nemotron 3.5 30B, and moves toward the frontier model Kimi K3. DPO, GRPO, and writing-quality evaluation are [future work](#future-work).

**Dataset:** [spacezenmasterr/writer-brief-v3-cleaned-classified](https://huggingface.co/datasets/spacezenmasterr/writer-brief-v3-cleaned-classified) on Hugging Face (1,890 brief → document pairs built from v2).

[Data](#data) · [SFT training](#sft-training) · [Results](#results) · [Future work](#future-work) · [Run locally](#run-locally)

## What we want the model to learn

For this project, “AI slop” means writing that obscures the engineering: unsupported claims, missing causal links, repetitive framing, and generic advantages that could describe almost any system. Good output should let a reader answer:

- What problem does this design solve, and under which constraints?
- How do its components interact, including when something fails?
- Why was this approach chosen, what does it cost, and what remains uncertain?

For example, given notes that explicitly specify a durable queue, asynchronous workers, burst absorption, and a two-second freshness requirement:

> **Vague:** The architecture leverages asynchronous processing to ensure scalability and a seamless user experience.

> **Useful:** Requests enter a durable queue before workers process them. The queue absorbs short bursts while workers catch up. Users may see stale results during that delay; the design must keep it below the two-second freshness requirement.

This is an illustrative writing example, not a model result.

Hackathon

I work in human rights digital archiving and monitoring, with charitable investigative organisations in human rights and law, mostly in the UK. For the past 5 years, starting with https://osr4rightstools.org/, I've been using Bellingcat's open source auto-archiver through my fork: https://github.com/djhmateer/auto-archiver In 2024 we won the ESRC Celebrating Impact Prize for "Research that is helping the UN and courts around the world to assess mobile phone evidence in war crimes prosecutions and other human rights cases" https://www.swansea.ac.uk/press-office/news-events/news/2024/11/research-on-using-mobile-phone-evidence-in-human-rights-cases-wins-prestigious-impact-prize.php Over the last year I've archived over 60,000 urls on 5 VM's running on a Proxmox hypervisor on my own hardware. Investigators are frequently waiting for archiving to finish whereas the other VM's are idle. In this hackathon I'm building 1) a queuing system - a Postgres database and an overall coordinator service (on a separate VM). Then 5 worker VM's each have a new wrapper which takes work from Postgres and runs the existing archiver tool. 2) distressing image analyser. A problem for human rights investigators is that the imagery/videos can be frequently distressing. Commonly there is a 1-5 rating scale against all images (currently done manually) so others don't have to see the image unless they have to. This is also a problem for me as a developer, where I don't want to mistakenly see an image unless necessary. I wish to be forewarned. I'm experimenting with muse-glimmer:30b-q4_K_M running locally on Ollama with good (albeit slow on my CPU only) results If anyone else is working or interested (or if I can help you) in digital archiving / monitoring / human rights , or if you'd like to chat, please drop me a line. dave@hmsoftware.co.uk or here on Discord. # Second Look

The co-signer that reads the paperwork before you sign.

In 2020 Citibank wired $900M to Revlon's lenders by mistake. The screen
looked right. Nobody read it twice. Second Look puts Ray-Ban Meta
glasses on a warehouse receiving desk: the glasses read the paper while
the app watches what the worker types, and when the two disagree it
blocks the submit and proposes the value on the paper as the fix. It
works in both directions, paper first or typing first.

![Second Look blocking a swapped AWB digit and proposing the paper value](docs/shots/demo-step1-1920.png)

Demo video: [watch the 3-minute demo on Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/1242879630)

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G["Ray-Ban Meta glasses"] -->|"frames via Device Access Toolkit"| A["Android app"]
  A --> S["Second Look server"]
  F["Receiving form"] -->|"typed values"| S
  S --> V["Check digits first"]
  V --> M["Muse Spark reads the paper"]
  M --> B["Block + proposed fix"]
  M --> H["Needs a human"]
  M --> L["Audit log"]
  M --> C["Claim draft"]
```

- Typed values stream from the receiving form; camera frames stream
  from the glasses through the Android app.
- Check digits run before any model call (AWB mod-7, ISO 6346
  container, SSCC mod-10). A bad digit blocks instantly and for free.
- Muse Spark reads the document image and compares it with the form:
  references, carrier, consignee, counts, cross-document gaps (invoice
  vs packing list, BOL vs AWB), and the delivery-receipt signature.
- A mismatch blocks the submit with the paper value as the fix.
  Formatting differences (case, punctuation, Inc or LLC) do not flag.
- An unreadable or covered field goes to "needs a human", never a
  silent pass.
- Every decision lands in an append-only audit log; a handwritten POD
  note such as "2 cartons damaged" becomes a claim draft.

## Meta stack

- Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`) via the Meta Model API: reads the
  paper, explains the mismatch, proposes the fix.
- SAM 3.1 behind the `SamAdapter` interface: parked after empty-text
  replies for document concepts; Spark JSON boxes cover crops today.
- Muse Glimmer local tier with PII redaction before anything reaches
  the cloud: stubbed until weights land, labelled `(stub)` in the UI.
- Ray-Ban Meta glasses via the Wearables Device Access Toolkit on
  Android (`apps/android`).
- Built with Muse Code.

## Results

Synthetic corpora: a 100-form standard split and a 40-form hard split
(near-miss check digits, cross-document gaps, blur, glare, skew).

| arm | split | flagged | precision | recall | avg latency | cost |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| check-digit-only | std 100 | 48 | 100.0% | 60.0% | <1ms | $0.0000 |
| tiered-real | std 100 | 79 | 100.0% | 98.8% | 3117.7ms | † |
| check-digit-only | hard 40 | 13 | 100.0% | 39.4% | <1ms | $0.0000 |
| single-model-real | hard 40 | 33 | 100.0% | 100.0% | 1848.5ms | $0.0855 |
| vision-real | hard 40 | 33 | 100.0% | 100.0% | 3085.7ms | $0.6169 |

# cross-border-fbar

As a licensed attorney who works with U.S. tax preparers, I had a practical question for this hackathon: could a tool take on the tedious statement review without taking away control over the numbers? This tool was my answer. Built for preparers serving U.S. expats and immigrants with foreign bank accounts, it helps a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) or enrolled agent (EA) automate the reading of bank statements and identify each account's highest balance shown in those statements. The preparer reviews and signs off on those numbers. Each identified highest balance links to its source page in the bank statement for **one-click verification**.

**Manual review:** The preparer reviews every statement, line by line, to find each account's highest balance.

**With Meta Muse:** Each page is read in about 10 seconds for about 2 cents. Code handles the arithmetic, and each account's highest observed balance links to its source line.

In the example below, month-end balances total $121,350, while the highest observed balances total $373,618.

**Try it without installing anything:** [live demo](https://sadhakadev-fbar-worksheet-demo.hf.space), with fictional data and recorded readings. The first visit after a quiet period may take a moment to load.

**Demo video (3 minutes):** [watch on YouTube](https://youtu.be/BL4UVxhOP9Y).

[![Three-minute demo video of the worksheet: statements, highest balances, one-click source check, correction, sign-off and the Korean client summary](https://img.youtube.com/vi/BL4UVxhOP9Y/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://youtu.be/BL4UVxhOP9Y)

## The problem it solves

U.S. citizens and U.S. tax residents generally must file an annual Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) with the U.S. Treasury if they have a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts whose combined value exceeds $10,000 at any time during the calendar year. Even a non-willful failure to comply with foreign account reporting requirements can carry substantial civil penalties. Willful violations can also lead to criminal prosecution.

For a preparer, the hard part is that the FBAR requires reporting each account's **highest balance during the year**, not simply its year-end balance. Finding that balance can require reviewing individual transactions. A brief spike between month ends can be missed by looking only at month-end balances, even on a clean English statement. Foreign languages, unfamiliar date formats and phone photos make the review harder.

Preparers describe it themselves. In a widely upvoted [r/taxpros thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/taxpros/comments/1mr9imx/stop_sending_me_photos_of_bank_statements_for/), one wrote about a client with 15 foreign accounts and 47 phone photos of statements, some blurry, some sideways: "I spent 3 hours squinting at photos trying to make out account numbers and max balances." The CPAs and enrolled agents replying said a first year's FBARs often take longer

The suite turns green and **a real bug becomes "expected behaviour".** By construction, that approach can never report a bug. This agent is built to report one. ## What it does 1. **Generates** pytest tests for a Python function with the model and **runs** them (isolated subprocess, timeouts, coverage). 2. **Writes a reference implementation from the docstring alone.** The model never sees the function body. 3. **Triages every failing test** by comparing three things in code: the source's output, the test's expectation and the reference's output. - source = reference: the *test* was wrong, so it is corrected; - test = reference but source differs: **suspected source bug**, the test is left failing on purpose; - all three disagree: *needs review*, nothing is changed automatically. 4. **Audits the tests that pass.** A passing test can also encode a bug; if its expectation contradicts the spec-derived value it is flagged as a *spec conflict*. 5. **Exports a spec-aligned test suite**: conflicting tests are rewritten to the spec value, so they fail until the bug is fixed. Every verdict shows who decided and on what evidence (the numbers involved). The reference the model wrote is visible in the UI, and a **Model calls** panel lists every call to the model live (purpose, model name, seconds). # Pocket AOI

From one phone photo, find assembly mistakes on a circuit board by comparing it with a known-good golden board, and say what each mistake will break.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (manufacturing). Watch the [3-minute demo video](https://youtu.be/38sRM_zsY7Y). The full spec is in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

## What was built during the hackathon

The hackathon began on 26 Oct 2026. This repo's first commit is dated 3 Nov 2026 and there was no earlier codebase, so `git log` shows the whole history.

**Built during the hackathon:**

- The pipeline in `src/pocket_aoi/`: board setup, alignment, part location, comparison, verdicts, consequences and the report, including the rule that Muse Glimmer can only confirm or reject what classical vision raises
- The prompts in `prompts/`, and the checks that reject replies citing parts, pads or nets not in the netlist
- The pin-swap table and severity rules
- The Gradio page in `app/`, and the Kaggle notebook in `notebooks/`
- The evaluation in `eval/`, and every result in this README

**Not built here, and used as they are:**

- SAM 3.1 and Muse Glimmer 30B, Meta's models
- The VisA and PCBA datasets, and the kit photos and ArduTouch schematic listed under [Data and credits](#data-and-credits)
- The open-source libraries in `pyproject.toml`, such as PyTorch, transformers, OpenCV and Gradio

## The problem

In student labs, assembly mistakes cost more debugging time than design errors: a reversed electrolytic, an IC seated backwards, a missing resistor. Factory optical inspection machines cost tens of thousands of dollars, so students, makers and small shops inspect by eye.

Pocket AOI needs a phone, one photo of a correctly assembled board, and optionally the board's netlist. It returns:

- the test photo with each fault outlined
- a safe-to-power banner
- one card per fault, for example "C7 missing: U2 loses its decoupling cap"

Every decision starts from the golden board. Each golden part is checked at its own spot in the aligned test photo, and Muse Glimmer only confirms or rejects what classical vision raises. It can never add a fault of its own.

The HumanEval score is probably optimistic: the setting was picked from four runs scored on the same 50 problems, and its training prompts restate at least 6 of them in other words ([More code in the data](#more-code-in-the-data)). It replaced the first release on 29 October 2026; the first release, with less code in its data, stays there at revision [`40964de`](https://huggingface.co/webbrain-one/openbonsai-qwen-3.5-9b/tree/40964de45342e7c1cdd6605cdb00533c9adb567d), tag `reasoning-mix-v1`. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Prism ML. Bonsai is Prism ML's product.

This project is funded by WebBrain, your AI Browser.

For Qwen3.5-9B the output is a file of about 2 GB, with the same tensor layout as Ternary-Bonsai-2-9B. **Why.** Prism publishes finished Bonsai weights for the base models it chooses, and an inference runtime. It has described the format (ternary weights, FP16 group scales, a blockwise Hadamard rotation) but, as far as we know, not a pipeline to compress a model of your own, and Ternary Bonsai 2 ships packed ternary files only, with no BF16 weights. So community fine-tunes adapt Bonsai itself: LoRA adapters on the frozen ternary base, tuning of its scales and norms, ternary quantization-aware training ([overview](docs/your-own-model.md#other-ways-to-adapt-a-bonsai-model)). OpenBonsai is the other route, in the open: it compresses your own BF16 model or fine-tune, with its own tokenizer and chat template, to a fully ternary file in Bonsai's format, and measures what compression cost against your own BF16 model. # LedgerEyes

Turns a phone video of a stockroom into an audit-ready count, reconciled to the books. The business runs it; the auditor or lender receives the evidence.

## Stack
- Frontend: React (Vite PWA), hosted on Vercel
- Backend: Python (FastAPI) with a background worker and Postgres, hosted on Render (US region)
- Video, frames and evidence packs: S3-compatible object storage, uploaded directly from the browser

## Models: Meta only
| Model | Job |
| --- | --- |
| Segment Anything Model 3.1 | Finds, masks and tracks every instance of an item (text phrase or boxed example) |
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Reads labels and serials, classifies items, spots damage, checks capture against the plan |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Transcribes narration and ties video segments to locations |
| Muse Glimmer (later) | Open-weight option for customers whose data cannot leave their premises |

No other models are used. Allowed non-model utilities: ffmpeg (frame extraction), `hashlib`/`cryptography` (sealing), numpy pixel statistics (lighting and steadiness checks). No OCR, ASR, detection or embedding libraries.

## Setup
```
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
set MODEL_API_KEY=...
python scripts/smoke_models.py
```
`smoke_models.py` lists every model ID the key can see. Base URL defaults to `https://api.meta.ai/v1`; override with `META_API_BASE_URL`.

## How a clip is counted

6. `app/reconcile.py` compares counts with book stock, values variances at cost, and writes `reconciliation.csv` and `proposed_adjustments.csv`. One clip per plan location is counted ("canonical"); a re-film replaces it, so a shelf is never counted twice.

# Picture guard

**Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track).**

- Demo: https://naveed-gilani--picture-guard-demo-web-serve.us-east.modal.run
- Video: https://youtu.be/dgQ7p24VwT8 (3 min; voice-over: AI voice by ElevenLabs, elevenlabs.io, reading a script by navee4)
- Repo: https://github.com/navee4/picture-guard

## The problem

People paste screenshots, payslips, letters and photos of ID cards into AI chatbots all the time. Text tools that look for private data cannot see text inside a picture. So names, addresses, account numbers and faces go straight to the AI.

## What Picture guard does

It finds names, addresses, account numbers, ID numbers and faces in a picture. It covers each one with a black box, and sends only that cleaned copy to the AI. If it is not sure, it blacks out the whole picture.

![The pipeline](docs/pipeline.svg)

## How it works (and where Meta's models are used)

1. **Read.** Tesseract (on CPU) finds every word and where it is.
2. **Decide.** Pattern rules with check digits (card numbers, IBANs, NI numbers, sort codes) plus **Muse Glimmer** (open weights, 4-bit, on our own GPU) decide what is private, including names, addresses and ID numbers.
3. **Locate.** Each private value gets a box from the words Tesseract found (with a zoomed re-read for hard ones).
4. **Faces.** **SAM 3.1** (on our own GPU) finds faces; Glimmer's face count is a second check.
5. **Black out.** Solid black boxes, written to a new PNG with no metadata.
6. **Check the safe copy.** The cleaned picture is read again; any private value still readable means "not sure".
7. **Ask.** **Muse Spark** answers questions about the **safe copy only**. The answer step calls the model `muse-spark-1.3` (Standard mode) through the Meta Model API (`api.meta.ai`). The code refuses to send anything but the safe copy and your question. On Meta's free credits, Meta may use what is sent for product improvement.

The original picture goes only to our own GPU (Modal), never to Meta's API.

| Model | Where it runs | What it does here | What it sees |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Muse Glimmer 30B** (open weights, 4-bit GGUF, run with llama.cpp) | our own Modal GPU | decides what is private (names, addresses, ID numbers), gives boxes for hard values, counts faces; temperature 0, seed 1234 | the **original** picture |

| **Muse Spark** `muse-spark-1.3` (Standard mode, through the Meta Model API at `api.meta.ai`) | Meta's API | answers the visitor's question | the **safe copy only**, plus the question |

Nothing else of Meta's is used. Tesseract (reader) is not a Meta model. Muse Spark Open was considered and not used (too large for one GPU; `LICENCES.md`).

## The safety rules

Any "not sure" gives a whole black picture. The five fail-safe rules:

1. A value the AI saw has no matching word on the picture, so it cannot be covered safely.
