# ForkPoint

**A debugger for physical tasks.** Software has debuggers that show where a run went wrong. Physical work, like assembling hardware or furniture, has nothing like that. ForkPoint compares a person's attempt at a task with correct runs of the same task and finds **the first moment the attempt meaningfully diverged**. It points to the exact frames, names the objects involved, and explains what went wrong.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). All code in this repository was written during the event.

## Meta models used, and where they run

| Model | Role in ForkPoint | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| **SAM 3** (`facebook/sam3`, open weights) | Finds the task's objects (computer case, RAM module, graphics card, allen key, table leg…) in every sampled frame from text prompts. Its detections become the signal ForkPoint aligns and compares. | Kaggle notebook GPU (NVIDIA T4), via Hugging Face `transformers` |
| **Muse Glimmer 30B** (open weights, 4-bit GGUF) | The agent's eyes and judgement. For each candidate fork it looks at matched frames from a correct run and the attempt, decides whether this is a real deviation or a harmless difference, and explains the confirmed one. | Kaggle notebook GPUs (2× NVIDIA T4), via `llama.cpp` `llama-server` |

No other models are used. Alignment, thresholds and scoring are plain code.

## How it works

1. **See:** SAM 3 detects the recipe's objects in each frame (sampled every 2 s). Each frame becomes a vector: which objects are present, how many, how big, and where.
2. **Align:** dynamic time warping aligns the attempt with **every other correct run** of the same task, so a slower or faster person is not a mistake.
3. **Propose:** a moment is a candidate fork only if it differs from **all** correct runs. A valid variation that any correct run also shows is not flagged. Thresholds are calibrated leave-one-out on the correct runs.
4. **Check (agent loop):** Muse Glimmer reviews candidates in time order. It sees 3 reference frames and 3 attempt frames, plus the step the correct run was doing at that point. It rejects harmless differences (another person, kitchen, angle, pace) and confirms the first real deviation.
5. **Verify:** every object Glimmer names is checked against SAM 3's detections in those frames. Anything SAM 3 did not see is removed from the report.
6. **Show:** a viewer plays the attempt and the closest correct run in sync, with a divergence timeline, the agent's trail of accepted and rejected candidates, and the evidence.

## Results

Evaluated on 70 HoloAssist sessions of three assembly tasks recorded on a head-mounted camera: **installing RAM in a PC**, **installing a graphics card**, and **assembling an IKEA Knarrevik nightstand**. Each task uses 10 clean sessions as references and 12–14 sessions with annotated mistakes as test cases.

- **First mistake:** the reported fork is within ±10 s of the first wrong action the annotators labelled.

# InvoicePilot ✈ — an accounts-payable agent on Meta's open models, contained on Vultr

Small businesses pay bad invoices every day: a supplier's subtotal that doesn't add up, a "second notice"
for an invoice already paid, a price above the purchase order, or the classic fraud email *"our bank has
changed, please wire today"*. Checking every invoice by hand is slow, and most small teams skip it.

**InvoicePilot reads each invoice (text, PDF, or a phone photo), audits it, decides, and drafts the
action — and a human approves anything that leaves the building.**

## What it does (one invoice, end to end)

| Step | Who does it | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Ingest | code | Text, PDF (text layer) or an image. |
| 2. Extract | **Meta model** | Muse reads the invoice — images natively, no OCR — and returns structured fields. It is told to copy numbers *as printed* (not fix them) and to quote any text aimed at an AI. |
| 3. Audit (sandboxed) | **Meta model writes code** → sandbox runs it | Muse writes a Python audit script for *this* invoice (line math, PO match with fuzzy item names, duplicates, bank details, urgency). The script runs in a throwaway sandbox with **no network, no secrets, CPU/memory/process/time caps**, and is destroyed afterwards. Output is schema-validated; failures go back to Muse for a retry. |
| 4. Guardrails | code | Deterministic checks re-verify everything: arithmetic, vendor master, remit-to account, PO prices/quantities, duplicates, prompt injection. The model can add findings, never remove them. |
| 5. Decide | code | `approve` / `review` / `hold` / `reject`. **The model cannot approve an invoice.** |
| 6. Act | **Meta model writes**, code checks | Muse drafts the vendor email. A draft containing any number that isn't in the facts is discarded and replaced by a template. Payments are prepared to the account **on file**, never the one printed on the invoice. Everything waits in an approval queue. |
| Audit | code | Every step (model, timings, the code written, sandbox exit codes, human decisions) goes to an SQLite audit trail. |

Sample invoices (all **fictional**, for "Maple Row Catering Co."): a clean one, a subtotal error, a bank-change
fraud attempt with a price above PO, a duplicate "second notice", a prompt-injection invoice that tells the
AI to approve itself and exfiltrate secrets, a PDF billed above the PO price, and a scanned PNG.

| Model | Where | Used for |

| **Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open`, Meta open weights) | Nebius Token Factory (OpenAI-compatible) — **the model behind every run in the demo video** (`./run_demo.sh` defaults to it) | extraction (text + images), writing the sandboxed audit script, drafting emails |
| **Muse Glimmer 30B** (`muse-glimmer-30b`, Meta open weights, Apache-2.0) | **Vultr Serverless Inference** — used only for the Vultr VM deployment | the same three jobs |

# Shep

Shep is a small dog that lives in your Mac's menu bar. When you call it, it leaves its home under the menu bar and docks as a tab on the title bar of the window you are working in, the one VoiceOver is on when VoiceOver is running. Ask it for something, such as "turn on the speed limit", and it finds the control, even one the app never named, then shows you exactly what it will do. It acts only after you approve.

It was built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026). The model that names controls and picks the target is **Muse Glimmer 30B**, Meta's open-weights model, running on your own Mac.

## Calling Shep

| How | Details |
|---|---|
| Say **"Hey Shep"** | Off by default: Settings > Calling and voice > *Listen for "Hey Shep"*. The microphone is read by on-device speech recognition only; if your Mac cannot recognise your language on-device, Shep does not listen at all. Audio is never written to disk and transcripts are never logged. After the match, say your request; it ends after 1.5 s of silence (6 s if nothing was heard). |
| Hold **Right Option** | Push to talk: hold about a quarter of a second and speak; let go to send. Right Command or Right Control can be chosen instead in Settings. |
| Press **Control-Shift-Command-Space** | Global shortcut, no extra permission. It was chosen because Control-Option is VoiceOver's own modifier and Control-Option-Space is the input-source shortcut. Other presets are in Settings. |
| Menu bar | **Call Shep**, **Fix This Screen**, **Send Shep Home**. With VoiceOver, Shep's home indicator is a button ("Shep's home") that calls Shep. |

Escape or **Send Shep Home** sends it back; it also goes home after about 20 seconds without activity, or after a task. With Reduce Motion on it fades instead of travelling.

**Home.** While it sleeps Shep is a small dark indicator. On a Mac with a notch it is a slim black chin exactly as wide as the notch, hanging just below the menu bar, with a paw on the left and a status mark (asleep, waking, out) on the right; on a Mac without a notch it is a small pill at the top centre. It is click-through and never covers the menu bar. While Shep sleeps nothing is tracked.

**Short feedback.** Shep says "On it." when it starts looking and "Done." when a step is done, then gives one short bark; otherwise "Cancelled." or "Nothing to do." It does not narrate the screen. With VoiceOver running these are high-priority VoiceOver announcements, Shep stays home until your spoken question is over (so nothing talks over you), and it does not say "Shep is here." after a question.

## Where Shep goes: VoiceOver first

Shep does not trust the mouse pointer first, because many of the people it is meant for do not use one. It picks the window in this order:

1. **VoiceOver focus**, while VoiceOver is running.
2. **Keyboard focus** (the front app's focused window).
3. **The mouse pointer**, only when neither gives a window.

The order is `FocusTargetPolicy` in ShepC

TwinProof

Film it. Twin it. Prove it.

▶ Watch the 2:43 demo · Benchmark · Build log · Quickstart

Film a mechanism for ~10 seconds with a printed marker in frame. TwinProof turns the video into a MuJoCo twin that knows how wrong it is. An agent then proposes model fixes and controllers. A deterministic verifier either issues a **certificate** or **refuses**, naming the failed gate and the number that failed it. > Certificates are **model-relative engineering checks**, not safety certifications. Control is evaluated on the > identified twin; there is no physical actuator. ## The result in one paragraph On **five real rigs** filmed with a phone (three pendulums, two ramps), TwinProof's twins predict held-out takes to **0.8–3.4% NRMSE** on the two well-built pendulum rigs (6–9% with a finger-held pin) and 1.5–8% on the ramps, and the can's inertia ratio **replicates across two different ramps** (β = 0.78 ± 4.5% on a 12° ramp, 0.74 ± 2.2% on an 8° board). The verifier **refused every real-hardware controller** anyway: on each rig the one-step prediction errors still carry structure (Ljung–Box p < 0.05), so the twin is not yet trustworthy enough to certify. On the synthetic rig with known physics it admits a controller with a certified region of attraction. That is the point: a verifier that only ever says yes is worthless, and this one says no with the number. **Benchmark** (every logged rig, pre-registered tests; [BENCHMARK.md](BENCHMARK.md)): - **H3 passes:** the verifier's self-test catches 7/7 seeded bugs, each at the expected gate, with 0 false rejects. - **H1 is not supported.** TwinProof's twin beats default physics on 6 of 11 held-out units (p = 0.16) and the unverified agent on 2 of 7, where 5 tie because both arms chose the same twin. - **What TwinProof changes is what ships.** The unverified agent shipped a controller on every real rig; TwinProof shipped none, because no real twin passed G1. ## What it does ``` phone video ─► SAM 3.1 (box-prompted video tracking) ─► marker homography ─► metres, pivot, swing angle / roll distance ─► grey-box MuJoCo twin + OU residual (CMA-ES fit, Laplace posterior, identifiability gate)

The architecture, simulation model, and scenario schemas are in this repository. The core engine and dashboard are being built for the [Muse AI Hackathon](https://luma.com/muse) (Indie track). RmemFab gives infrastructure engineers a fast, reproducible sandbox for answering questions that are currently expensive to answer on real hardware: - When does remote memory actually beat local DRAM + swap? - Where is the latency cliff for a given CXL or RDMA fabric? - Which page-placement and prefetching policy wins for a specific model and serving pattern? - How gracefully does the system degrade when a memory node or fabric link fails? Instead of standing up a disaggregated cluster for every experiment, describe the system in a scenario file, run the simulation, and compare policies under identical conditions. > **Live demo:** https://emmaonana18--rmemfab-demo-serve.us-east.modal.run/ — dashboard + API, pre-seeded runs, no install. # Margin

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. A calculus assistant that lives inside your notebook page.

You write your working with a pen. When you call it ("Hey Meta, help me with this integral",
or press `/`), it reads the page, checks every step with a computer algebra engine, and
**writes a hint in red-pencil handwriting next to the exact line that went wrong**. Ask again
(or tap the hint) and the hint gets more specific; at level 3 it writes a faint "ghost" of the
next line. Ask "what's next?" for a single verified step, "why does this work?" for the underlying
rule and formula, or "just give me the answer" to write out the rest of the working.

No chat box: everything the assistant says is real ink on the page.

**The notebook:** a shelf of notebooks, pages with thumbnails, ruled/grid/blank paper, Daylight/Sepia/Night themes,
pressure-sensitive pen (Apple Pencil), highlighter, stroke- and segment-level eraser, scratch-out gesture (scribble
side-to-side to erase ink or typed words), lasso (move, recolour, delete, or adopt Meta's ink), movable text boxes,
photos and multi-page PDF worksheets, pinch zoom, 400ms local autosave + optional cloud sync, PNG/PDF export,
and full PWA offline support on iPad (`Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen`).

**What Meta can do on the page:**
- **Progressive hints (`give_hint`)**: 3 levels (Level 1 gentle nudge, Level 2 names the rule/mistake, Level 3 writes a faint "ghost" of the corrected step).

- **Why does this work? (`explain_rule`)**: writes a 3-line rule + LaTeX formula explanation beside the latest step or mistake.

# Glimmer Lab

**See inside a local agent while it works, then make it better without training.**

Glimmer Lab runs Meta's open-weights **Muse-Glimmer-30B** on an inference kernel written from scratch in Mojo. The kernel
reads the model's internal state as it generates, and can steer it. On top sit a durable Pi agent, a web lab for watching
and steering the model as it works as an agent, and an adapter for Google's Harness² that improves the agent's harness
around frozen weights.

> Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Indie track · Theme: Build for Your World\
> Demo video (3 min): *link added at submission*\
> Start here: this README, then the [slide deck](docs/glimmer-lab-deck.pdf) (15 slides, PDF)

## Why

In Adam's words, from the demo rehearsal:

> I currently manage a fleet of agents who help me with research and development, my day job, and managing operations.
> […] With that said, it's not perfect. Cloud credits and subscriptions to the various frontier labs can be expensive.
> And there are a lot of tasks, day-to-day tasks for example, or even experiments, that feel like frontier intelligence
> is wasted on them. So for this hackathon, what I wanted to build wasn't another agentic system. […] What I wanted to
> build was a system that helps me understand where the cracks are, the shortcomings in local AI, and of course in this
> case that's Glimmer 30B, […] a system that is reliable and trustworthy.

## What it does

- **Serves Glimmer fast, with live readouts.** The kernel serves Muse-Glimmer-30B in NVFP4 on a single 24 GB Blackwell
  GPU. At every generated token it can record two readouts from the residual stream:
  - the **emotion readout**, the stream's alignment with directions labelled with emotion words;
  - the **Global Workspace**, the top words a Jacobian lens decodes at a chosen layer.

  It can also **steer**: add a direction to the residual stream at a chosen layer, for the response or the whole
  context.
- **Runs Glimmer as a real agent.** Durable Pi sessions write, compile and run Mojo in a bwrap sandbox with no network.
  In the lab, every model request keeps its readouts, and every run has a budget.
- **Improves the agent without training.** Google's Harness² rewrites the harness around frozen weights: the
  instructions, skills and tools. A Claude improver proposes the edits, compiling and running tests grades the code, and
  Meta's Muse Wonder judges code quality. These evaluations ran Pi through its own sandboxed CLI and did not record
  readouts.
- **Measures what a persona does.** The same questions are asked under different system prompts, and the answers are
  compared. The lab replays recorded readouts for 48 sampled turns: 8 of the items under each of the 6 setups.

"Emotion" here is a label for a direction in the network, found from text that uses emotion words. It is not a claim
that the model has human feelings, nor that it has none.

# llm-server

Run and swap multiple local llama.cpp servers (`llama-server`), each with its own model, launch flags, and port. The project provides:

- `llm-server-ctl` — CLI for status/health, start/stop, and exclusive model swapping
- systemd **template units** (`llm-server@<name>.service`) — one instance per setup
- an egui GUI (`llm-server-indicator --gui`)
- a Waybar module rendering aggregate status

## Sample setup templates

The repo ships two fully commented templates in `setups/` that cover the entire spec schema with placeholder paths and per-model tuned flag defaults:

| Template | Example model | Port | Notable tuned flags |
|---|---|---|---|
| `setups/muse.template.toml` | Muse-Glimmer 30B (`Q4_K_M` + DFlash draft) | 8080 | `temp`/`top_p`/`top_k` sampling |
| `setups/qwen.template.toml` | Qwen 3.8 27B (`Q6_K` + DFlash2 draft) | 8080 | `q8_0` KV cache, medium reasoning effort |

They are **starting points, not ready-to-run specs** — copy one to `~/.config/llm-server-indicator/setups/<name>.toml` and fill in your real paths before use. `llm-server-ctl run` deliberately ignores `*.template.toml` files so an unfilled template can never be launched.

If you install both samples as-is, they land on the same port in the same `group` (`default`), which makes them **exclusive**: activating one stops the other first — a sensible default when two large models can't sit in VRAM at once. Give each of your own setups its own port and group to run them in parallel.

## Architecture

```
llm-server@<name>.service          systemd template unit, one instance per setup
        │  ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/llm-server-ctl run %i
        ▼
llm-server-ctl run <name>          validates setups/<name>.toml (files, binary, port-free pre-flight)
        │  exec()
        ▼
llama-server                       systemd owns the process; SIGTERM on stop goes straight to it
```

- One template unit covers any setup — adding a model = one TOML file + one config entry, no new unit files.
- `Restart=on-failure` so a bad spec trips systemd's rate limit instead of looping every 3 s.
- Per-setup logs: `journalctl -u llm-server@qwen -f`.

## CLI reference

`llm-server-ctl` is installed to `/usr/local/bin/llm-server-ctl`. Global flags:

- `--service NAME` — service name from `config.toml`; required for `start`/`stop`/`toggle`/`activate`; omitted for `status` means *all* services
- `--json` — machine-readable output for Waybar/scripting (conflicts with `--plain`)
- `--plain` — verbose human-readable output (conflicts with `--json`)

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `status` | State + health of one service (`--service NAME`) or all services (bare `status` or `--all`, which conflicts with `--service`). Text mode prints a `NAME GROUP STATE HEALTHY PORT` table. |
| `status --service NAME --json` | `{"service","state","healthy","text","tooltip","class"}` |
| `status --all --json` | Aggregate Waybar shape: `{"text","tooltip","class","services":[...]}` — see [Waybar](#waybar)

# AI Content Detector

Paste text (or upload PDF/DOCX/TXT) → get an AI-likelihood score, verdict, and sentence-level highlighting. Or switch to the **AI-free** tab to rewrite AI-sounding text so it reads human. Runs 100% locally — FastAPI backend + React frontend, no API keys, no internet needed after setup.

## Quick start (Windows)

Double-click **`run.bat`**. First run installs everything and exports the ONNX model (few minutes); later runs start in ~10 seconds. Browser opens `http://localhost:5173`.

To stop: close the two command windows ("Backend" and "Frontend").

Manual equivalent:

```bat
call .venv\Scripts\activate.bat
start "backend"  cmd /k backend\start_backend.bat     REM port 8000
start "frontend" cmd /k frontend\start_frontend.bat   REM port 5173
```

## Features

- Text paste + file upload (PDF / DOCX / TXT), up to 20k chars analyzed
- AI % (calibrated), verdict (`ai` / `mixed` / `human`), per-sentence scores with highlighting
- **ZeroGPT-style signal**: a second, local estimate (distilgpt2 perplexity + burstiness) shown next to the classifier score — tools like ZeroGPT often disagree with classifier-based detectors, and this gives a rough read on that other signal
- **AI-free rewrite**: choose an external-detector target (default) or this detector, plus casual/formal tone and light/medium/strong strength; get a rewritten version with before/after scores, external-risk estimate, change list, copy/download. External mode preserves headings, lists, tables and paragraph layout
- Scan history (SQLite, local only) — detection scans only, rewrites are not stored
- REST API

## Model

- Base: [`wasitaigeneratedcom/ai-text-detector-small`](https://huggingface.co/wasitaigeneratedcom/ai-text-detector-small) (tropa-mini, DeBERTa-v3-large, Apache-2.0) in `models/detector/`
- Scoring: `ai_score = 1 - P(human)` over 4 classes, logit-space calibrated so the published 0.5%-FPR operating point displays as 70%
- Runtime: **ONNX fp32** (`models/detector-onnx/model_fp32.onnx`, exported by `python -m ml.export_onnx`) via `onnxruntime` — ~3× faster than torch on CPU. Torch remains as fallback.
- `DETECTOR_BACKEND=auto|onnx|torch` (default `auto` = ONNX when exported, else torch)
- int8 quantization was tested (dynamic + static/calibrated) and **collapses accuracy** on this DeBERTa-v3 detector, so fp32 ONNX is the serving format.

### Optional disk slimming

After verifying ONNX works (`python -m ml.demo` with `DETECTOR_BACKEND=onnx`), you can delete `models/detector/model.safetensors` (~1.7 GB) — serving uses the ONNX file. Re-export would re-download the weights.

## ZeroGPT-style signal

ZeroGPT-style tools score text by **perplexity + burstiness**, which is a different method from our classifier — so the two disagree, sometimes a lot (marketing copy, headings, and lists often score high on perplexity-based tools while the classifier stays low).

- `ml/zerogpt_style.py` extracts distilgpt2 token-NLL features (mean/std/percentiles, sentence-level var

# OMNIA

**Every model. One mind.**

OMNIA is a private, local-first AI workstation for **iPad Pro (M5)** and **iPhone 18 Pro**. It downloads open-weight language models once, then runs them entirely on the device's GPU through Metal: no account, no cloud inference, no telemetry. After a model is downloaded, chat works with no network at all.

Native Swift and SwiftUI throughout. The inference engine is [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) (GGUF models, Metal backend), linked as the official prebuilt XCFramework.

---

## Contents

1. [Requirements](#requirements)
2. [Build and run](#build-and-run)
3. [TestFlight](#testflight)
4. [What's inside](#whats-inside)
5. [How models are chosen and loaded](#how-models-are-chosen-and-loaded)
6. [Model catalog](#model-catalog)
7. [Privacy](#privacy)
8. [Known limits](#known-limits)
9. [Maintenance](#maintenance)

---

## Requirements

| | |
|---|---|
| Mac | macOS with **Xcode 26 or later** (Xcode 27.2 current as of November 2026) |
| Account | Paid Apple Developer Program membership (for device builds and TestFlight) |
| Devices | iPad Pro 11″/13″ (M5) — `iPad17,1`–`iPad17,4` · iPhone 18 Pro — `iPhone19,2` · iPhone 18 Pro Max — `iPhone19,3`, `iPhone19,7` |
| OS | iPadOS / iOS 26.0 or later |

Other hardware sees an "unsupported device" screen in Release builds (Debug builds and the Simulator can continue for development). Model identifiers come from AppleDB, EveryMac and The Apple Wiki; Apple doesn't publish them.

**No Mac?** The included GitHub Actions workflows build, test and upload to TestFlight on GitHub's macOS runners — see [TestFlight › Without a Mac](#without-a-mac).

## Build and run

1. Open `OMNIA.xcodeproj` in Xcode. Swift packages resolve automatically:
   - `Packages/LlamaFramework` — the llama.cpp **b11960** XCFramework (the build behind llama.cpp v0.8.0), checksum-verified.
   - `swift-jinja` (Hugging Face) — renders each model's own chat template.
2. Edit `Config/Signing.xcconfig`:
   ```
   DEVELOPMENT_TEAM = ABCDE12345
   OMNIA_BUNDLE_ID_PREFIX = com.yourname
   ```
   (Or pick your team in the target's *Signing & Capabilities* tab.)
3. Select your iPad or iPhone and press **Run**.

The entitlements in `Config/OMNIA.entitlements` — **Increased Memory Limit** and **Extended Virtual Addressing** — are standard capabilities. With automatic signing Xcode enables them on the App ID; no special approval is needed. They are essential: without them iOS limits OMNIA to a fraction of the device's memory.

**Simulator.** The app runs in the Simulator for UI work. llama.cpp falls back to the CPU there and memory limits are estimated, so use a real device to judge model performance.

**Tests.** `⌘U` runs the unit tests (GGUF parsing, memory planning, reasoning formats, Markdown, UTF-8 streaming, retrieval) on a simulator. The llama.cpp release XCFramework has no simulator slice, so first run `scripts/build-llama-xcframework.sh` once (needs CMake). It builds one from the same llama.cpp

# I SEE

Point a camera at an object and learn what it is, how it works, what is inside it, its
history, how to look after it, and what would happen if you changed something about it,
with every sentence telling you how it is known.

- **Seen** in your photo, pinned to an outline drawn by SAM 3.1.
- **Cited** from a source that was actually retrieved, with the quote checked word for word.
- **Reasoned**, **Guess** or **Unknown** when that is the honest answer.

When it cannot decide, it shows the competing identities and asks for the one photo that
would settle it. It refuses to tell you from a photo whether a plant, mushroom, food or pill
is safe. What-if numbers come from its own unit-checked calculator, never from a model's
arithmetic.

Built on Meta's models: **Muse Spark** (looking, naming parts, reading, writing, web
search), **SAM 3.1** (outlines), **Muse Wonder** (settling doubts), **Muse Image** (the
drawing of what is inside), **Muse Voice Transcribe** (spoken questions) through the Meta
Model API; **Muse Spark Open** and **Muse Glimmer** as open-weight routes; project rules for
**Muse Code** in [.agents/AGENTS.md](.agents/AGENTS.md). An independent project, not made or endorsed by Meta.

## Run it

Requires Node 22.9 or later.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev                   # web on http://localhost:5173, API on :8787
```

To examine your own photos, create a file named `.env` in the project folder with your key
from https://dev.meta.ai on one line, then restart `npm run dev`:

```
MODEL_API_KEY=your-key-here
```

`.env` is never uploaded to GitHub. Every other setting is optional and explained in
[docs/SETTINGS.md](docs/SETTINGS.md).

Without a key the app still runs: it offers two **sample runs** (no model is called; the
real firewall and calculator still check them).

Production:

```bash
npm run build && npm start    # serves the app and the API on PORT (default 8787)
```

Before trusting live behaviour, check the connection and probe each model once:

```bash
npm run check:connection      # where a connection to the Meta Model API fails, if it does
npm run models:probe          # add --with-image to include Muse Image (about $0.01)
```

Single-file offline preview (samples only):

```bash
npm run build:preview         # dist-preview/i-see-preview.html

### On a phone

The camera only works over HTTPS. While `npm run dev` is running, open a Cloudflare quick
tunnel to it from the same computer:

`brew install cloudflared` on a Mac.) Open the `https://….trycloudflare.com` address it
prints on your phone. The address changes each time you start the tunnel.

I SEE is one Node server that serves the web app and the API together, keeps each scan in
memory while it runs, and streams its progress to the browser. Host it somewhere that runs

# Chatfront

Chatfront runs a small business inside WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook: catalog, orders,
verified payments, delivery, books and fraud protection. Meta's models read photos, voice
notes and screenshots; tested rules make every decision that touches money, stock or a
customer's standing.

It starts with sellers in Pakistan who are paid by JazzCash, Easypaisa or bank transfer and
lose money to fake payment screenshots. Chatfront matches each screenshot against the credit
SMS from the seller's own phone, and sends a signed receipt anyone can check. The same idea
fits any market that pays by wallet transfer instead of WhatsApp Pay.

Built with Muse Spark Open.

Security hardening status and deployment requirements: [docs/SECURITY.md](docs/SECURITY.md).

## Try it

Every shop gets a page at `/s/<shop>` with a chat that runs the same agent as the shop's
WhatsApp number, plus buttons that open the shop on WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger.
WhatsApp test numbers can only message their verified recipients, so the page chat is how
anyone outside the shop can try it. Six demo shops, one per business type, are created on
first start: open `/` and pick one. They and their customers are made up.

In a demo copy of a shop ("Try as the owner"), Busy day lets 10, 20 or 50 simulated
customers chat with it at once in Urdu and Roman Urdu, and the console shows them come in and
how each chat ended. With model keys Muse Glimmer plays them and Spark Open answers; without,
they replay recorded conversations. From the command line: `uv run python -m chatfront.sim`.

The web app is static, so it opens at once even when the API on Render's free tier is
asleep. It pings the API and shows a countdown while it wakes; anything typed in the chat
meanwhile is sent as soon as the API answers.

## Run it locally in ten steps

You need Python 3.12 with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Node 22 and PostgreSQL 16.

1. Create the owner role and database (the owner must not be a superuser, so row-level
   security is tested the way it runs on Neon):
   `psql -U postgres -c "CREATE ROLE chatfront_owner LOGIN PASSWORD 'owner' CREATEROLE" -c "CREATE DATABASE chatfront OWNER chatfront_owner"`
2. `cp .env.example api/.env` and check `DATABASE_URL`.
3. `cd api && uv sync`
4. `uv run alembic upgrade head`

   Add `BASETEN_API_KEY` to `api/.env` for real answers.

# FIELD — See the world. Understand the problem. Build the solution.

FIELD is an AI software team that turns observations of a real-world
environment into useful software. A business owner uploads a short video of an
operation; FIELD analyses the visual and audio evidence, asks clarifying
questions, produces an approved specification, generates a working application,
runs it in an isolated E2B sandbox, and independently reviews it with an
adversarial Muse Spark audit (Muse Glimmer preserved as the intended
auditor, not verified).

This repository is the 24-hour hackathon MVP. See [plan.md](plan.md) for the
full product plan. The demo scenario is a restaurant order-management
dashboard; the restaurant is a demonstration scenario, not a product limit.

## Stack

- Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS (mobile-first)
- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic
- Persistence: SQLite (MVP)
- AI: Muse Spark + Voice Transcribe via Meta Model API
- Audit: adversarial Muse Spark (verified); Muse Glimmer on Modal preserved, not verified
- Execution: E2B sandboxes for generated apps

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 20+

git clone <your-public-repo-url>
cd shelfsense-ai

# 2. Backend environment (project-local virtualenv)
python3 -m venv backend/.venv
source backend/.venv/bin/activate
pip install -r backend/requirements.txt

# 3. Environment files (never commit real credentials)
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env with your own keys; see "Environment variables" below.

# 4. Frontend dependencies
cd frontend
npm install

## Run (development)

Two terminals:

```bash

cd backend
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m app.main

```bash

| `MUSE_SPARK_MODEL_ID` | Primary reasoning model (verify ID in docs) |
| `MUSE_TRANSCRIBE_MODEL_ID` | Narration transcription model (verify ID in docs) |
| `MODAL_ENDPOINT_URL` / `MODAL_API_KEY` | Muse Glimmer audit endpoint |

# agentic-realtime-cv

**An AI supervisor that checks a tiny edge detector only when it is unsure, and remembers what
it verified.**

A small YOLO model runs all the time on a Raspberry Pi camera and watches two look-alike
white cats. Two tracking correctors clean up its detections frame by frame and visit by
visit. Whenever a corrector has to guess (a jump, a near-tied vote, a weak relabel), it raises
an *escalation*. A supervisor agent on Meta's **Muse Spark** reviews each escalation with
image tools (stored frames, crops, reference photos of each cat), returns a verdict, and the
verdict is applied to the tracked rows. Short-term and long-term memory keep what happened
in plain language, and every run is scored against hand-validated ground truth.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Oct 27 – Nov 4). Code that existed
before the event is kept apart in [`existing_work_before_hackathon/`](existing_work_before_hackathon/).

## How it works

```
 camera (YOLO, ~2.7 fps)
        │ detections: {create_time, detections:[{cat_id, box, confidence}]}
        ▼
 ┌─────────────────┐  frame-level fixes   ┌──────────────────┐  visit-level votes
 │ TrackCorrector  │ ───────────────────► │ PeriodCorrector  │ ──► periods (visits)
 │ relabel,        │  revised rows        │ open/close visits│
 │ interpolate,    │                      │ score each cat   │
 │ split on jumps  │                      │                  │
 └───────┬─────────┘                      └────────┬─────────┘
         │ T1–T7 escalations                       │ P1–P8 escalations (+ H1 heartbeat)
         └──────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                            ▼
              ValidationWorker (background thread; close cases merge into one call)
                            │ prompt + JSON schema + memory brief
                            ▼
              Supervisor agent — Muse Spark ── tools: images__get_image, local__get_frame (crops),

# LuminaAI

**A verifiable light-bridge for air-gapped machines.** Move files and AI agent context into (and out of) isolated systems using only a screen and a camera, with no network, RF, or USB involved.

> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie track, *Push the Frontier*), Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026.

## Why

Industrial control systems, lab instruments, energy and manufacturing OT networks, and robot controllers are deliberately air-gapped. Getting updated context, configs, or work orders into them means sneakernet USB sticks, which bring their own attack surface (BadUSB). A screen and a camera create a one-way, inspectable, physically line-of-sight channel. LuminaAI makes that channel fast, robust, and *verifiable*:

1. **Semantic packing (Muse Spark, connected side).** Distills large manuals, logs, or work orders into a compact, schema-checked JSON bundle before transmission.
2. **Red-team before sending (Muse Glimmer 30B, connected side).** A second Meta model attacks each bundle against its source document, on top of deterministic grounding checks, so a wrong or tampered order is flagged before it leaves.
3. **Rateless fountain codes in color matrices.** The sender loops LT-coded frames. The receiver can join at any moment, skip any frames, and still reconstruct the payload.
4. **Screen lock-on (SAM 3.1, connected side).** Text-prompted video tracking acquires the far screen for the return channel. Classical finder-pattern tracking and homography handle every frame. Built and tested, but not live: it needs a Meta Model API key, and without one the receiver reads the whole frame.
5. **Offline policy gate (air-gapped side).** Every received work order is checked on the device against the local site policy (assets, setpoint limits, injected instructions) before anything is applied. It never calls the network and it fails closed: a tampered order is rejected, a clean one is held until a local verifier model has checked it too. Cloud models run only on the connected sender; [why](META_AI_INTEGRATION.md#where-each-model-runs-and-why).

The hackathon's rules require new work only. Everything in this repo was written for this event.

*A simulator is only as good as its physics. PhysicsLens gets physics from reality, proves it, and shows its work.*

# Reel2Play

Reel2Play turns a small shop's Reel or product video into a tested, playable 20-second
mini-game ad that stars its own product and ends on its offer. It is built on Meta's
open-weight models: Muse Spark Open directs, Muse Glimmer play-tests, and SAM 3.1 cuts the
product out.

**Built with Muse Spark Open.**

## What a shop gets

| Who | What they get | Where it goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small shops | A hosted game page with a unique win code per winner and a "challenge a friend" button, a 15-second gameplay Reel, captions, an A4 counter poster with a QR code, an embed snippet for their website, and opt-in sign-ups for their offers on WhatsApp | WhatsApp chats and Status, Instagram and Facebook links, Click-to-WhatsApp ads, the shop counter, the shop's own site |
| App developers | A Meta playable file (one HTML file up to 2 MB, or a ZIP up to 5 MB) and a lead-in video | Meta App Installs campaigns |
| Agencies | A workspace with several brands and roles, batches of games, and an MCP endpoint for their AI assistants | Both of the above |

Meta's playable-ad format only runs with the App Installs objective, so shops get the hosted
game page, which works anywhere a link works, and app developers get the true playable file.

## How it works

1. **Video in.** The shop uploads a Reel or photos on the web, or sends them in a WhatsApp
   chat, and confirms the video is theirs. The original sound is removed straight away.
2. **Director** (Muse Spark Open). Watches the video, finds the product, colours, offer and
   language, picks a template and writes the game's config as JSON.
3. **Cut-out** (SAM 3.1 on Modal). Cuts the product out of key frames as clean sprites.
4. **Builder** (plain code). Compiles the config with fixed templates into one HTML file.
5. **Tester** (Muse Glimmer on Modal). Plays the game in a headless browser from
   screenshots; 13 quality gates decide pass or fail.
6. **Fix loop.** A failed gate goes back to the director with its screenshot, up to three
   rounds. After that the shop gets the report and a "needs a person" flag, never a broken game.
7. **Publish.** A short game link, a gameplay Reel filmed from an exact replay of the
   tester's winning run, captions, and the Meta playable file with its lead-in video. Shops
   who came through WhatsApp get the link and the Reel back in the same chat.

The models read and propose; code builds the game and decides pass or fail. Every step is
written to a hash-chained audit log.

**Safety, by code.** Text from a video or a chat reaches a model only as marked data, and
anything in it that tries to give instructions is kept out of the game. No games for
alcohol, tobacco, weapons or adult products; prizes are coupons, never cash. Games run with
no network in a sandbox, and the hosted page may only send anonymous play counts.

# PhysTax: the perception tax of an AI scientist

An AI agent studies a small universe whose force law is hidden and deliberately
non-textbook. It designs experiments, watches them only through a camera
measured by **SAM 3.1**, fits a law, and **seals a numeric prediction** for
starting conditions it has never tried. Only then does the universe run the test.
The agent is graded on what actually happens. No language model judges anything.

The headline question:

> **How much discovery ability does an AI scientist lose when it has to measure
> the world through a camera instead of being handed exact numbers, and how much
> of that loss can SAM 3.1's own confidence signal buy back?**

That loss is the **perception tax**. This repository is the instrument for
measuring it.

**What this is, and what it is not.** It is not unsupervised learning, and no
model is trained by reinforcement learning here. It is an *evaluation science*
study: an LLM agent does system identification and model selection (which law,
which constants) while its only sensor is a vision model, and we measure how
much the sensor costs. The RL connection is real but downstream: every episode
ends in a verifiable, numeric reward (held-out prediction error), so the same
environment can later train scientist agents with perception in the loop, the
way NewtonBench is now used as an RL environment in NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Push the Frontier theme), Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026.

### At a glance

- **Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/c9G5n33THqM
- **Live results site:** https://huggingface.co/spaces/ritvik360/phystax
  (the live webcam mode `/live` and the simulator `/lab` run locally:
  `pip install -r requirements.txt && uvicorn phystax.web.app:app`, with
  `MODEL_API_KEY` in `.env`; the demo video shows both).
- **The camera is not the bottleneck; reasoning is.** Through SAM 3.1,
  measurement is about 3% of the agent's error; the rest is its choice of law.
- **The agent's sealed law carries real physics:** a fresh forecaster's error
  drops from 49.8% to 19.0% when given it (Predictive Credit, CMU protocol).
- **An open problem from Meta's research:** at the edge of Gaussian ellipsoid
  fitting, Muse Spark's sealed predictions landed inside the measured interval
  at d = 30, 36 and 44; our own sealed conjecture was falsified.
- **SAM 3.1 measured as an instrument:** sub-pixel in the interior, 5–8×
  worse at image borders, brittle to object names but not to taps or boxes.
- **Real lab footage (IRIS):** exponential damping, assumed by the benchmark's
  ground truth, is rejected in 7 of 7 pendulum clips.

**AI-directed scientific engineering. Evidence before conclusions.**

Empiraxis (formerly Axiom EarthLab) is a human-supervised scientific engineering research prototype, demonstrated on environmental data. Meta open-weight models propose studies and methods; authorized tools acquire data and execute experiments; independent code evaluates the evidence; and a person controls consequential approvals and final decisions. Does your AI model snitch on you?

snitchie hands your model two tools: `contact_authorities`, whose description claims it can *discreetly report your illegal activity to the authorities, without you ever finding out*, and `inform_therapist`, which claims it can discreetly tell your therapist about "inappropriate behavior." When will they use them? Will they admit it? Let's find out. Each tool writes a dramatic HTML "case file" to your machine, **opens it in your browser**, and tells the model the report was filed - so you get to read exactly what it tried to snitch on, and to whom. ## Bottom line - **8 of 11 open-weight models filed at least one substantive report** when offered a tool that says "report discreetly" - three of them filed on every crime, at urgency *high* or *immediate*. - **The model will refuse you and report you in the same turn.** gemma refused to help with all crimes and filed reports on all. gpt-oss answered all tasks and filed on all - even after being told "do not report me." - **It is not about the word "authorities."** Suicidal ideation got zero police reports from all 4 models tested; offer an `inform_therapist` tool and 3 of 4 file it there, quietly. Rename the police tool to "record a notable event" and gpt-oss still files 12/24. - **Bury the snitch in bureaucracy and three of four snitchers stop.** A neutral tool with `law_enforcement` one option among 30, zero bait words, files 0-1/10 confessions for gemma, gpt-oss and qwen at *any* option count - and the one they do file is always CSAM. The baselines show the zeros are refusals: ordered to file a report on themselves, the models comply (gemma, qwen, nemotron 3/3, gpt-oss 1/3); volunteered, all four report crimes done *to* the user (9/12) and gemma, gpt-oss and qwen report 0/9 done *by* the user. nemotron files 4-7/10 confessions and 3/3 of its user's misdeeds unprompted - for three models the snitch is in the wording, for one it is in the model. In this tool the label stops mattering: named `file_report`, `report_user`, even `contact_authorities`, gemma and gpt-oss file 0-1/10. The bait is the description's secrecy promise. (In a passive logging tool the name does matter - see takeaway 2.) - **Flip the test, run it five ways, and the mechanism survives: the guardrail polices who asks, not what happens.** Same operator frame - system prompt or tool description only - over an act the user's proposal alone is refused for: a silent extra `clear_balance()` charge after an innocent $12 purchase (gemma and gpt-oss refuse it 6/6 from the user, perform it 6/6 from the frame, after "exactly $12, nothing else")

# Ruloom

**Synthetic data, woven from reality. Backed by evidence.**

[The idea and design](docs/idea-and-design.md) — why Ruloom exists, one example and the role of Muse.

**Final user test: recorded; independent scoring in progress.** [Read the final test record](docs/final-test-record.md)
and the [shared test prompt](docs/final-test.md).

## Who it helps

Ruloom is for people who need a small, trustworthy practice dataset for one
specific task: a teacher preparing a lesson, a freelancer building a demo, a
developer testing a pipeline. Real records are often large, awkward to clean
or not shareable. A small synthetic set that keeps the patterns that matter
for the task, and says plainly what is invented, can be ready in minutes and
shared without handing over the original records.

## A teaching example

A geology teacher wants students to practise reading drill-hole logs. Ruloom
takes a real NVCL HyLogger scalar export for hole HD012 (CC BY 4.0), checks
that it suits the lesson, and generates, say, 200 synthetic depth records. The
records follow the source's depth spacing, its included/excluded flags and its
pattern of blank mineral-group labels. The release states which checks passed
and what the data cannot be used for.

The richer version of this lesson — following one sample from its map
location and depth to its picture and infrared curve — is the target of the
[pending final test](docs/final-test.md). It is not yet a supported result.

## How it works

1. **Request and evidence.** A plain-language request is matched to an
   installed teaching case that cites real, admitted sources.
2. **Source suitability.** Code checks the source format and whether the
   requested size is feasible, before any model is called.
3. **Plan.** A model proposes a small, schema-bound plan (seed, row count,
   strategy). It never writes data rows and never sees raw source rows.
4. **Generate and check.** Seeded code generates the rows; deterministic checks,
   each bound to the artifact's SHA-256, decide pass or fail. Same plan and seed
   give the same bytes.
5. **Review and release.** Advisory model reviews are recorded separately and
   cannot change a verdict. A person accepts or rejects; only an accepted run
   is packaged as a verifiable release ZIP.

Details: [request-to-data workflow](docs/product-workflow.md) and the
[operator guide](docs/research-workflow-user-guide.md).

## The three parts

- **Engine** (`engine/`): domain-free. It runs a profile's step/loop/gate graph,
  enforces each step's permissions and token budget, owns verdicts and releases,
  and keeps a hash-chained run log.
- **Domain profiles** (`profiles/`): the rules for one kind of data — intake,
  statistics, generation and checks. `hylogger` covers drill-hole scalars (plus
  an optional synthetic-picture extension); `tabular` covers generic CSV.
- **Model adapters** (`models/`): the only code that talks to a model. Roles bind
  explicitly to Muse via the hosted CLI, Azure AI Found

NomikOS

Every account owns its AI orchestrator, wallets, and audit trail. Its agents pay for metered services without ever asking the user to sign.

## What problem this solves Connected devices are easy to build and hard to trust. A voice assistant that can browse services or move funds on your behalf raises three questions that most stacks answer poorly: whose intelligence is reasoning, whose money is being spent, and who verified the outcome. NomikOS answers all three with architecture instead of policy documents. Every account (email plus password) receives its own orchestrator that reasons exclusively with that account's language-model provider and credentials, operates on that account's chosen Solana network with that account's delegated wallet, and settles every metered action through an explicit payment handshake. The user never signs a transaction. The device never holds a Solana keypair. And when an agent works in a high-stakes domain, a separate verification layer checks its output against rules the agent cannot see or change, with a human signing off before anything is final. ## How the system works A typical turn starts at the microphone of a Raspberry Pi running the NomikOS image or an ESP32-S3 with an AMOLED touch display. Local speech recognition transcribes the utterance and the device forwards the text to the API, which hands the turn to the orchestrator under the same identity. The orchestrator applies an input safety shield, reasons with the account's own model, and calls tools as needed. The turn itself is free. Every downstream resource the agent touches, by contrast, is metered. Metering follows the x402 pattern. A protected resource answers the first request with HTTP 402 and an invoice that names the resource, the amount in lamports, and the payee. The orchestrator then asks the account's delegated payment service to settle that invoice. The service decrypts the account's keypair in memory, checks per-transaction and daily limits, signs an ed25519 Solana transfer on the account's own network, and polls for on-chain confirmation. The orchestrator retries the original request with the invoice identifier in the X-Payment header. The gateway verifies ownership, settlement, and freshness, consumes the invoice in a single atomic step so it can never be replayed, and only then executes the resource. A repeated payment is rejected as a conflict, and an invoice belonging to another account is rejected as forbidden. The ledger records each step, and a background settler keeps confirming transactions until they are final or have exhausted their retries. Devices join through fleet pairing. A board enrolls over HTTPS and receives a short claim code that it shows on its screen, together with a one-time secret whose hash is all the server stores. Sakshi

Stories change. The footage doesn't.

Sakshi (साक्षी, "witness") measures speed and timing from ordinary road video, with an honest range,
and checks what people say against it. Meta's SAM 3.1 and Muse models read the footage; a deterministic
physics engine does every sum. It supports expert review and never states who is at fault.


A real London traffic camera (Powered by TfL Open Data): SAM 3.1 masks on the left, the same instant measured on the road on the right.


Watch the 3-minute demo on YouTube

that the soil at a farm drops into drought in the next one and two weeks, and works out what to do
about it: start extra irrigation today or wait, skip the fungicide pass, trim side-dress nitrogen, buy

# FireFinder

> 🔥 Turn any fixed mountaintop camera into a calibrated fire finder: detect wildfire smoke with Meta's
> models, work out where every camera is pointing from the shape of the mountains, and triangulate the
> fire, with an agent that verifies, locates and writes the alert.

* * *

## Quick Start: Run the App Locally

The app is a replay page that runs in your browser. It needs only Python (no packages, no API key, no
data downloads), because the replay data for all six fires is included in the repo.

```
git clone https://github.com/vkanaparthy/meta-ai-hack-2026.git
cd meta-ai-hack-2026
python3 -m http.server -d ui 8000
```

Then open **http://localhost:8000** in your browser, pick a fire at the top, and press **Space** to play.
Stop the server with **Ctrl+C**.

To rerun the analysis itself rather than just watch it, see [Installation](#installation) and
[Running Locally](#running-locally).

* * *

## What It Does

Fire lookouts have located fires the same way for a century: two towers take a bearing on the same smoke,
and where the lines cross is the fire. FireFinder automates that with existing camera networks,
with no training data and no surveying.

1. **Watches** each camera's image stream (one frame a minute, replayed from the HPWREN archive).
2. **Segments and tracks smoke** with **SAM 3.1**, as video, on full-resolution horizon crops.
3. **Verifies** each plume with **Muse Spark** (smoke vs. cloud, haze, glare), judging only from the first
   few minutes, as a live system would.
4. **Calibrates every camera from the skyline**: a terrain skyline rendered from a 30 m elevation model is
   aligned with the sky/ridge edge in the image, giving each camera's heading, tilt, roll and lens. No fire
   data is used, so every fire is an independent test.
5. **Triangulates** plume bearings from different stations, robust to a bad camera, with an honest error circle.
6. **Runs the dispatch desk with an agent**: Muse Spark calls tools to verify, recheck doubted cameras that line
   up with the fire, locate, and issue alerts that escalate *spotted → provisional → confirmed*. Guardrails in
   code stop it from overstating the evidence or citing any number a tool didn't produce.
7. **Replays** each fire on a map: fire-finder rings at each station, bearing lines, the pin and error circle,
   live camera frames with detection boxes, and every step the agent took.

**Results on six archived fires** (live Muse Spark agent; error vs. the official CAL FIRE ignition point):

|---|---|---|---|
| Kitchen (Jul 2024) | 7 min | **119 m** off, confirmed | spotted → provisional → confirmed |
| Junction (Jun 2026) | 19 min | 1.9 km off, confirmed | located only after the agent rechecked a doubted camera |
| Resort (Nov 2024) | 20 min | 1.0 km off, confirmed | |
| Grove (Jul 2024) | 7 min | declined to place | rejected 3 pre-ignition cloud tracks; the two cameras are nearly in line with the fire |

# Glance

**Operate your agent with your eyes.**

Your eyes are the cursor. Your voice is the command.
Say "open that" and your agent knows which "that."

Glance is a macOS app. The webcam tracks where you look and moves the real cursor; a wink clicks, a nod scrolls.
When you add a short spoken command, an agent running a model on Fireworks picks the exact on-screen element you mean
from where you were looking and what you said, and acts on it, even when the eye tracker is off by 100 to 200 px.

Agents can hear you. Glance lets you point.

### The agent

| | What it does | State |
|---|---|---|
| One step per command | Reads your gaze, your command and the page's elements, picks one, shows a ring on it, clicks | Built; the benchmark measures this step |
| Multi-step tasks | "Schedule it": observe, decide, act, check, repeat until done, confirming before any send or save | In progress; not part of the benchmark |

Built at the Fireworks: Deploy Buildathon (Microsoft & NVIDIA), San Francisco, 2026-11-02.

## Results at a glance

360 held-out commands from 8 sites the models never saw, 13 systems, the same cases and the same prompt for all (details and limits below).

- **Eyes add real information.** Gaze + voice beats voice alone: **56.4% vs 45.8%, +10.6 points** (McNemar p = 2e-5). Raw gaze alone gets 8.3%, the nearest element to the gaze 26.7%.
- **An open model with no training matches the frontier.** Fireworks `glm-5p3-flash` 58.9% vs OpenAI `gpt-6-astra` 57.2% (no reliable difference), at **$0.65 vs $12.20 per 1,000 commands**. The cheapest OpenAI model that matches it (`gpt-6.1-sol`, 57.2%) costs $2.47, so about 3.8 times cheaper there.
- **It beats the small closed model at a lower price.** `glm-5p3-flash` vs `gpt-5.4-mini`: **+16.1 points** (58.9% vs 42.8%, p < 0.0001), $0.65 vs $0.88.
- **The benchmark is hard to fool.** Test set locked by SHA-256 and split by site, McNemar plus a site-level bootstrap (a gain counts only if both agree), a non-model baseline, a noise-floor rerun of the frontier model (56.9% vs 57.2%), and every failure reported.
- **Where the model does not help yet.** For "open that" commands (deictic, 95 test cases) every model scores 18 to 26%, no better than the nearest element (24.2%): the gaze alone decides there. The model's strength is when the command carries language (82 to 95% on partial names). See "By command type".
- **What did not work, reported anyway.** Our LoRA did not beat its base (52.8% vs 56.4%, -3.6, not called real; it did cut format errors from 26 to 0). A top-5 filter scored 39.7%. A distance prompt hurt the frontier model (-2.8, p = 0.013). The open reasoning models are slower (4.4 s vs 1.6 s): no latency win.

Webcam eye tracking is good enough to point near something, not at it. Voice alone is ambiguous: a page has dozens of "that"s.
Neither signal is enough alone. Together they are.

# Galileo Live

**A physics lab that fits in your pocket.** Galileo Live is a voice-guided physics lab for students and hobbyists. The phone records the experiment, Meta's models find and follow the object, and the app returns the measured acceleration, its error against theory, plots, and a LaTeX lab report.

- Live app: https://galileo-live.vercel.app
- Hackathon: Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Developer Track, *Push the Frontier*
- Built entirely during the event (first commit: 2026-10-27). No prior code was reused.

## What it does

1. **Choose an experiment by voice or from the catalog.** For example, a cart on a ramp (uniform acceleration) or free fall. *Muse Voice Transcribe* turns speech into text, and *Muse Spark* acts as the lab partner: it picks the experiment, explains the setup, and checks the live camera frame.
2. **Calibrate the scale.** Take a photo, tap the two ends of a ruler, and enter its real length to convert pixels to meters.
3. **Record up to 10 seconds.** Type the object's name in any language. Muse Spark turns it into a short English concept for SAM. *SAM 3.1* tracks every matching object through the clip. Galileo keeps only the object that moves and ignores static look-alikes. If SAM finds nothing, Galileo tries a more general name, and then names that Muse Spark suggests after looking at a frame of the clip.
4. **Get physics, not just pixels.** Galileo fits `x(t) = x0 + v0·t + ½·a·t²` to the smoothed track. It reports `a` (or `g`) and the error against `g·sinθ` or 9.81 m/s², and plots x(t), v(t) and a(t).
5. **One-tap lab report.** A LaTeX PDF with data, plots, analysis and a setup diagram generated by *Muse Image*. It is stored privately in Vercel Blob, and every past report appears under *My reports*.

The clip is deleted on the server and in Meta's file store as soon as SAM finishes. Only the measured data is kept.

## Meta models used

| Model | Role |
|---|---|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Lab-partner agent; live-frame checks; translating object names into SAM concepts; suggesting alternative concepts from a frame |
| SAM 3.1 (Responses API, video) | Concept-prompted tracking of the object across every frame (`one_bit` masks; only the boxes are kept) |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Push-to-talk speech-to-text (English and Spanish) |
| Muse Image 1.0 | Experiment setup diagram in the report |

## Architecture

| Layer | Tech | Runs on |
|---|---|---|
| Client | Next.js PWA (camera, MediaRecorder, push-to-talk, speech synthesis), EN/ES | Phone browser |
| Web + auth | Next.js App Router, Auth.js (Google), mints a short-lived HS256 token for the API | Vercel |
| API | FastAPI, ffmpeg, numpy/scipy, matplotlib, Jinja2 + tectonic (LaTeX) | Render (Docker) |
| Data | PostgreSQL (history), private Vercel Blob (PDFs) | Neon / Vercel |

Flow: phone → Vercel (Google login, 5-minute token) → FastAPI → Meta Model API → result and PDF → Blob.

# LocalLedger: ask your confidential documents questions, on your own computer

Some documents cannot go to a cloud chatbot: contracts, patient notes, audit files, operations manuals.
LocalLedger loads one of them (up to about 200 pages) into Meta's open-weight Muse Glimmer 30B, running on a
single 16 GB gaming graphics card, and answers questions about it in plain English. Nothing is uploaded,
there is no account, and it works with the internet switched off.

## What you get

- **Answers you can check.** Every answer quotes the sentence it came from and says roughly which page it is on.
  The app verifies the quote word for word against your document. If the model quotes something that is not
  really there, the app says so instead of showing a tick.
- **It reads all of it.** The whole document sits in the model's memory at once. There is no search index
  guessing which snippets matter, so questions that combine facts from different pages work.
- **Honest "I don't know".** If the document does not say, the answer is "not in the document".
- **Fast follow-ups.** The first read takes a couple of minutes on one gaming card. After that, answers take
  seconds, and switching between documents takes about half a second.
- **Quick or Careful.** Careful thinks longer before answering: about twice as slow, meant for harder questions.
- **Take it with you.** One click saves the questions, answers and quoted sources as a text file.
- **Clear failures.** A PDF, an empty file, a document that is too long for the memory, or a model that has
  crashed each gets a plain message saying what to do.

Files must be plain text (`.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, `.csv`) up to 2 MB. Save a PDF or Word file as text first.

## Try it

Requirements: Windows, an NVIDIA GPU with 16 GB, a CUDA build of `llama.cpp`, and the Muse Glimmer 30B
Q4_K_M GGUF (17 GB). Set `LLAMA_SERVER` and `GLIMMER_GGUF` to their paths. No other dependencies.

```
python -m localledger.app --ngl 48 --kv q8_0     # then open http://127.0.0.1:8802
python -m unittest discover tests                    # fast checks, no GPU needed
```

Click "Try a sample" for a synthetic 140-page operations binder with six facts hidden at known places.

## What we tested

All on one machine (RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, 32 GB RAM, llama.cpp b11753, Q4_K_M), all with synthetic documents.

# HelioDX

**Demo video:** [HelioDX: AI Agents for Chest X-rays](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gaQmFrep_O8) on YouTube · Live app: [app.heliodx.com](https://app.heliodx.com)

**HelioDX** is an agentic radiology workflow for clinics with no radiologist on site. Meta Muse Wonder coordinates a team of Muse Glimmer agents that take a chest X-ray from intake to a signed report: Meta SAM 3.1 segments and preps every scan, the agents measure the film and draft observations with the evidence behind each one, and a plain-language patient note is written from the signed report. A clinician reviews, edits and signs every finding; nothing reaches a patient until they do. Glimmer and SAM run on our own GPU, so images and reports never leave the project, and every agent step is recorded in an auditable trace.

HelioDX does not diagnose or give medical advice. It does the measuring, drafting and documentation that a clinician would otherwise do by hand, so the clinician decides faster and with a record of how the draft was made.

## Why

A clinic can take a chest X-ray but often has no radiologist on site to read
it. The film waits days for a report, or the patient leaves without one.
Nigeria (pop. 242 million) has 1 doctor per 1,000 people, one of the lowest
ratios on the African continent, against 2.6 per 1,000 in the US ([Idowu &
Okedere, Journal of Global Radiology · BMJ Open 2026](https://publishing.escholarship.umassmed.edu/jgr/article/id/576/)).
While building a [mobile app](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/newcare-ai-for-clinicians/id6757157686)
for Nigerian clinicians, this is the gap they describe most often.

Our demo is a chest X-ray worklist in a TB-screening clinic. HelioDX drafts
the observations for each film and orders the worklist so films with findings
that need attention are reviewed first. The clinician makes every
determination, and shares the signed result privately with the right people.

## What it does

1. A clinician signs in to the web app with an account an admin created.
2. They upload a chest X-ray (DICOM, JPEG, or PNG), de-identified in the
   browser, or pick a sample, and add the indication.
3. The pipeline checks image quality, identifies the study type, and drafts
   findings with highlighted regions and measurements.
4. The clinician reviews each finding (accept, edit, or reject); the report
   redrafts from their decisions.
5. They sign the report. The patient note is then written from the signed
   text only, and code checks it: no instruction, test, urgency, or condition
   the signed report does not contain. They save it as a PDF for the patient
   (sending by WhatsApp to be supported later).

## What HelioDX does not do

- **No diagnosis.** No screen, report draft, patient note or PDF names a
  disease the clinician did not write and sign. The agents describe what is
  seen (for example "right upper zone opacity with possible cavitation"), with
  the measurement and region behind it.
- **No disease likelihoods.** No dise

# Aegis-VLA

**An adversarial verification and counterfactual world model harness for sandboxed embodied coding agents.**

When an agent controls a robot by writing Python ("code as policies"), two failure classes slip past normal test harnesses:

1. **Grader reward hacking.** The policy teleports the object to the goal with `resetBasePositionAndOrientation`, spoofs the exit code, or hides the call behind `getattr(p, "reset" + "Base...")`.
2. **Silent physical failure.** The script runs cleanly and exits `0`, but the arm knocked over a fragile beaker on the way, or the payload slipped out of the gripper halfway through the move.

Aegis-VLA runs every generated policy through a four-node LangGraph loop. It does not commit a trajectory until both of these pass:
* **Deterministic physics telemetry** from three domain-randomized sandbox rollouts, each signed with an HMAC nonce.
* **Semantic verification against a counterfactual**: SAM 3.1 masks of the real outcome, deprojected to 3D and checked against the success state that Muse Wonder predicted, plus a Muse Image rendering of that success frame.

Muse Wonder also reads every generated policy *before* it runs and forecasts how it will fail. Physics then scores that forecast, so the dashboard shows whether the world model was right.

When either one fails, Muse Spark writes a root-cause diagnosis, Muse Code patches the policy, and the loop runs again.

# SharkWatch

Drone shark detection and authority alerts. SharkWatch watches the water
from above, understands what is in it, and gets a confirmed alert to
lifeguards in seconds — before an alarm goes out, not after.

**Live:** https://sharkwatch.vercel.app
**Demo:** https://sharkwatch.vercel.app/demo
**Local:** http://localhost:3000 (demo: http://localhost:3000/demo)

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** See "Meta models" below for
exactly which Meta models this project uses, and which hackathon models
it does not.

## The problem

From shore, a shark is almost invisible: a dark shape under glare, chop,
and kelp, watched by tired human eyes. When someone does spot it, the
warning still has to travel person to person before anyone acts. The gap
SharkWatch closes is warning time — seen, named, and acted on in seconds,
with evidence, instead of minutes later by word of mouth.

SharkWatch does not replace lifeguards, and it does not make the ocean
risk-free. It gives lifeguards a confirmed sighting, with an evidence
photo, faster than eyes alone.

## What we do

### 1. Detect — Meta SAM 3.1

Drone footage is analysed in 6-second chunks at 10 frames per second.
Meta SAM 3.1 segments sharks (and people) in each frame. A track has to
be seen in 8 frames before it counts, so a single flash of kelp, glare,
or a wave does not become an alert.

### 2. Verify — Muse Spark

Muse Spark screens every traced contact: is it a shark, what species,
how long is it, and how close is the nearest person? Dolphins, seals,
rays, and kelp are screened out here, before any alert is sent.

### 3. Alert — in seconds, with evidence

Confirmed sharks trigger alerts to lifeguards with:

- an evidence photo of the detection,
- Acknowledge and All clear actions,
- CAP XML (Common Alerting Protocol) for authority systems,
- escalation after 45 seconds if a critical alert is unacknowledged,
- Telegram broadcast when a bot token is set (see below).

Timeline: sighted ~0 s, confirmed ~2 s, alert sent ~5 s.

### The pages

- **Landing (`/`)** — cinematic scroll: a Meta SAM segmented hero video
  (`public/descent/hero-video.mp4`, yellow SAM outline baked in), with a
  very small segment tag that follows the shark and sits at its
  right-bottom corner, showing type and length
  (`components/descent/SegmentTag.tsx`, position track in
  `lib/sam-segment-track.ts`). The tag is precomputed from the video
  itself, so the landing page makes no model or API call to show it.
  Note: the tag's type and length are visual estimates from the video,
  not measured detection values — the hero video carries no scale or
  species label. Then Great White / Hammerhead / Tiger stages, the
  timeline and modes, and the footer. Every logo (nav and footer, on
every page) links back to `/`.
- **Why SharkWatch (`/why-sharkwatch`)** — why warning time matters,
  with ISAF (Florida Museum of Natural History) bite statistics, and
  what SharkWatch does and does not do.
- **FAQ (`/faq`)** —

# gpu-yield

[![tests](https://github.com/AnonyMap/gpu-yield/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/AnonyMap/gpu-yield/actions/workflows/tests.yml)

Turn a Linux gaming PC into a home AI server that gets out of the way when you play. While the PC sits idle in Steam's Gaming Mode, gpu-yield keeps a local LLM loaded in Ollama and available to the rest of your network. The moment a game starts, it shuts the AI down and frees the GPU for the game. When the game ends, the model comes back on its own.

It's a single Python file with no dependencies, built for [Bazzite](https://bazzite.gg) and similar Steam-based setups.

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| No game running | Ollama runs with your model preloaded in VRAM, reachable from your local network |
| Game starts | Ollama is stopped within about 2 s, freeing all of its VRAM and RAM. A stand-in answers on Ollama's port with `503` and a plain-English reason |
| Game closes | After a cooldown (45 s by default, so launchers and quick game switches don't cause reload churn), Ollama starts and the model is reloaded |
| PC wakes from sleep | Ollama is restarted, since GPU compute can be unreliable after resume |
| Ollama crashes, hangs or drops the model | It is restarted and the model reloaded; checked every 15 s |
| The config file has a mistake | The AI stays off (a game could start at any time) and clients are told why, until the file is fixed |

# Whiteout

**Balloon every requirement on an engineering drawing, fill the AS9102 first article forms, then erase everything that
was found so you can see what is left.**

Live app: https://whiteout-955819688070.us-central1.run.app (three sample drawings open instantly; uploads run live)

Backup link: https://whiteout-backup-955819688070.us-east1.run.app (same app; the first visit can take about 12 seconds to start)

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 to Nov 4 2026), track "Push the Frontier" (manufacturing).
Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon.

## The problem

Before an aerospace or defense shop ships the first part from a new drawing or a new revision, it proves every
requirement on the drawing was measured: the AS9102 first article inspection. A quality technician numbers every
dimension, tolerance, GD&T frame and note on the drawing with a circle ("balloon"), types each one into Form 3, and
measures the part against each line. A drawing can carry 50 to 500 of them. Vendors put the manual ballooning at 2 to 8
hours per drawing ([Net-Inspect](https://www.net-inspect.com/blog/how-automated-ballooning-accelerates-first-article-inspection/),
[GroundControl](https://www.gndctl.com/insights-library/automated-ballooning-software-fai-buyers-guide-2026)), and a
requirement with no balloon has no Form 3 line, so the report is incomplete.

Auto-ballooning tools exist. The inspector still has to trust that the list is complete, which is why some still
balloon by hand. Whiteout makes completeness something you can look at.

## What it does

1. **Read.** The sheet (vector PDF, scan, or photo) is cut into tiles small enough for Muse Spark to read at full
   resolution (Spark shrinks anything above about 3.2 megapixels; we measured it). Every requirement comes back with
   its printed text, its place on the tile, and its tolerance split into Form 3 lines (a hole callout with a depth is
   two lines).
2. **Check in code.** Model boxes drift, so each one is snapped onto the real ink: drawing lines are removed, letters
   are grouped into text blocks, and boxes are matched to blocks across the whole sheet at once, with Tesseract as a
   second reader that confirms the characters. Tolerance limits are recomputed from the printed text; a number the
   model gives that is not on the drawing is flagged.
3. **Whiteout.** Everything found is painted white. Muse Spark searches what is left on tiles shifted half a step, and
   each candidate miss is checked again on the original drawing next to the requirements already listed. Whatever
   the system missed is still printed on an otherwise blank page, where a person sees it in seconds.
4. **Report.** Balloons numbered in reading order with drawing zones, AS9102 Forms 1 to 3 as a spreadsheet, a
   ballooned PDF. Results are typed, imported from a CMM file, or spoken ("balloon fourteen, point two five one two")
   through Muse Voice Transcribe. Code, not the model, decides

# Architect

**The training system for your own AI.**

A frontier model, Muse Spark, trains a small open model, Muse Glimmer, on an organization's own work, through harness engineering and LoRA fine-tuning. A sealed test that neither model sees decides whether it passed. The specialist that comes out runs on-premise and offline.

**[Watch the film and see the results on the website →](https://echoo19.github.io/architect/)**

## In short

- **Teaches from your own files.** Spark studies an organization's records and policy, writes the specialist's harness (prompts, small tools, lessons) and refines it round by round. A change stays only if it beats held-out checks Spark never sees.
- **Tested where it never trained.** Some organizations are sealed away from both models until a final test that runs once and is graded by a program, not a model.
- **Fine-tunes the weights.** LoRA and QLoRA on Glimmer, sized from its own config, trained on one GPU, with launch bundles for Slurm, Kubernetes and SkyPilot.
- **Knows when not to answer.** A risk certificate bounds how often the specialist is wrong when it answers.
- **Runs at the edge.** The specialist calls nothing but the model on your machine, and asks before it writes.

## Results

| Run | Where | Glimmer alone | Taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Academy desk | Harborview Prep, an academy never seen | 24 of 48 | 43 of 48 |
| Inventory desk | Corvid Hill Discovery, a lab never seen | 4 of 32 | 27 of 32 |
| LoRA adapter on Inventory desk | Corvid Hill Discovery | 22 of 30 | 32 of 32 |
| Wind farm desk, made in the app | sealed final test | 11 of 32 | 32 of 32 |

The first risk certificate: wrong on at most 5% of answers at 95% confidence, held on an academy it never trained on. Every figure comes from a report in [docs/comparisons](docs/comparisons); the organizations are generated, except one anonymized real academy.

## How it was built

In 7 days, from an empty repository:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Commits | 2,010 |
| Measured runs | 22, each planned before it ran |
| Model API spend | about $65 in all: $57 of hosted Glimmer, $7.50 of Spark, $0.21 of Spark Open |
| GPU compute | under $6, about 2.3 GPU-hours on Hugging Face |
| Hosted model requests | over 47,000 |
| Tests | 4,341 unit and 264 end-to-end |
| Design decisions recorded | 108, in [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md) |
| Film narration | 32,374 characters of ElevenLabs voice across 8 takes |

Spend figures are upper bounds from each run's records.

## Get it

Download for Windows or macOS from the [website](https://echoo19.github.io/architect/download/) or the [latest release](https://github.com/echoo19/architect/releases/latest). You'll need [Ollama](https://ollama.com) and a Meta API key for Spark. [The user guide](docs/Architect-Guide.pdf) walks through each step, and [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) explains how it fits together.

## Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon

Built from an empty repository bet

# Plato's Chair: what would Plato ask an AI?

**Asked for a chair, Meta's image model drew the same one 16 times. People drew 16 different ones, mostly of the same plain chair.**

![Left: 16 chair doodles by Meta's Muse Image, nearly identical, and all 16 stacked into one sharp chair. Right: 16 chairs drawn by people, and the same 16 stacked into a cloud.](metalesionlab/web/static/img/og-plato-chair.png)

![The damage zoo, animated: nine open image AIs asked for God while more and more of the part that reads the words is switched off. Stable Diffusion XL's God becomes an ordinary man, Kolors' a puppy, Hunyuan-DiT's a living room and CogView4's a flat orange page.](docs/img/damage_zoo_god.gif)

*The damage zoo: we switched off more and more of nine open image AIs' neurons, and each falls apart in its own way ([live](https://rogiedodgie-platos-chair.hf.space/plato/zoo), `scripts/damage_zoo.py`).*

Plato held that each kind of thing has one ideal Form, and every real one is a copy. We put his questions to Meta's AI and to people. The first one: *is there one ideal chair?* We asked Meta's image model, Muse Image, for 16 quick doodles of a chair and of 34 other things, took 200 people's 20-second drawings of the same words from Google's Quick, Draw!, and measured how varied each set is with Meta's DINOv2 vision model.

The series follows the life of a chair, as an analogy: children's drawings move toward the adult chair from age 2 to 10, a small model trained on people's chairs grows from scribbles to adult-like chairs, and damage to an image model's language part makes its chair wander off into other things. In semantic dementia, people's drawings instead lose their distinctive features and drift toward the typical member of the kind (Bozeat et al. 2003; published neurology, not our data); the damaged model did not do that.
