# Front Row by Cadenza

Every AI note-taker listens. Front Row watches.

A phone faces the lecture-hall board. Front Row turns what the professor says and writes into study notes, with the board work in them, minutes after class. It is built for students who can't take their own notes: the ones Accessibility Services would otherwise assign a volunteer note-taker.

**Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026).** Every file in this repository was written during the event, except the bundled DejaVu fonts (`lib/lectures/fonts/`, under their own licence in `LICENSE-DejaVu.txt`) used for the PDF export. Cadenza (studycadenza.com) is a pre-existing private hosted service; Front Row plugs into it, and none of Cadenza's code is here. What Front Row borrows from it is listed under [Pre-existing: Cadenza](#pre-existing-cadenza).

## Try it without a key

```sh
npm install
npm test
```

Then read [`samples/mit-18.06-lecture-3/`](samples/mit-18.06-lecture-3/): a real, unedited run on ten minutes of an MIT lecture, with the board photos it read and the Meta calls it made.

Sample lecture notes, no account needed: [studycadenza.com/front-row/sample](https://studycadenza.com/front-row/sample). The recorder itself is invite-only.

## Run it on a lecture

Needs Node 22+, `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on your PATH, and a Meta Model API key.

```sh
cp .env.example .env         # then put your Meta Model API key after MODEL_API_KEY=
scripts/get-sample.sh        # ten minutes of MIT 18.06 lecture 3 -> sample.mp4
npm run notes -- sample.mp4 --course "MIT 18.06" --keywords "matrix multiplication,inverse,Gauss-Jordan,row times column,identity matrix"
```

It prints the notes as markdown, then `Meta API calls:` with the count per model (transcription is listed by its path, `/v1/asr/transcribe`), and writes `notes.json`. Any lecture video works in place of `sample.mp4`. A ten-minute run takes about 4 to 10 minutes, depending on how fast Meta answers.

## Meta models

| Job | Model | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Speech to text, biased with course vocabulary | `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` | `lib/lecture/transcribe.ts` |
| Find the board and the professor in a frame | `sam-3.1` | `lib/lecture/locate.ts` |
| Read the board (handwriting, math as LaTeX) | `muse-spark-1.3` | `lib/lecture/board.ts` |
| Plan the topics, write each topic, clean up the joins | `muse-spark-1.3` | `lib/lecture/topics.ts`, `lib/lecture/compose.ts` |

All four run on Meta's hosted Model API. The calls go through the `openai` npm package as an HTTP client pointed at `https://api.meta.ai/v1` (`lib/lecture/meta.ts`). No OpenAI model is called anywhere.

Every model Front Row calls is Meta's.

**The professor skeleton in the demo video is not in this build.** From 0:31 in the demo video, the outline drawn on the professor comes from an earlier build (filmed Nov 3) that ran Google's MediaPipe in the browser. Per the organizers' ruling that every model must be Meta's, MediaPipe was removed

Don't regenerate. **A design board that reads your references the way a designer does, part by part, so you can change one thing and keep the rest.** Built on Meta's models: **Muse Spark** reads, **SAM 3.1** finds the parts, **Muse Image** draws. ![Python 3.12](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-009688?logo=fastapi&logoColor=white) ![React 19](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-19-61DAFB?logo=react&logoColor=black) ![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-server-black) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-1%2C913%20passing-2ea44f) **[▶ Watch the 2:42 demo](https://youtu.be/Q1jFivSlVcI)** · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Run it](#run-it-in-3-commands) · [Technical guide](docs/TECHNICAL.md)
--- ## The problem **1. "Like this one, but different in X."** Designers curate by saying *keep this, change only the colour* (or the material, or the silhouette, or something they can't name). Today's tools match overall similarity, so they can't hold "keep everything, vary only X". Designers re-query, edit by hand or start over from text, and as a board grows, "more like this" drifts toward too similar or too random. **2. Words that mean nothing.** "Premium", "clean" and "more modern" mean different things to different people, and mostly signal approval rather than anything visual. Human designers close the gap by building a project vocabulary from references and options side by side. AI tools don't, so users re-roll, blame their prompts, and can't explain or reproduce a look across sessions. **Muse's answer: the board is the shared language.** Each reference is an example of what you mean. Each item you keep or mark "not this" teaches the board what you want. Each dimension is a word you and Muse have agreed on. ### An example brief A car brand briefs an agency, and each person in the room asks for something different: > **Brand director:** "We're a 70-year-old company. Heritage is the whole point." > **Marketing head:** "If it looks old, we're dead. It has to feel like it was made next year." > **CEO:** "And warm. Our competitors are cold." Each brought a reference, and the three have nothing in common. Regenerating gives a pile of almost-right images, and every attempt changes everything at once. ## What Muse does ### 1. Reads what each word means, from the references themselves Muse Spark reads every reference through a domain **lens** (cars, watches, fashion, interiors, UI, or a lens it proposes for anything else). # HardRead: was it luck, or was it you?

**Chess players get an engine review after every game. Pokémon has luck calculators and win-chance tools, but none we found splits a game into start, luck and both players' choices using search over hidden sets. You can't see the opponent's moves and held items, and dice decide many turns. HardRead reviews a finished game anyway and estimates how much was luck. It isn't a chatbot reading a log: a search engine does the analysis, and the language model can only explain the engine's results.**

It's for competitive players who want to see which turns were dice and which decisions deserve a second look. I designed it for my own games. It reviews Gen 9 OU, a main competitive format, from a [Pokémon Showdown](https://pokemonshowdown.com) replay.

**Try it:** [HardRead site](https://touchetpe.github.io/hardread-site/) (saved showcases, plus a link to live review when it's online) · Theme: *Build for Your World*

The review, luck meter, read test, explanation agent and checker were built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. I designed and directed this project; AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex) wrote much of the code. The search engine is the open-source Foul Play, and the language model is Meta's open **Muse Glimmer**. [What was built here](#what-was-built-here) has the details. Fan-made and not affiliated with Nintendo, The Pokémon Company or Game Freak. 18+.

## What it does

Paste a finished replay. It usually takes one to three minutes, and longer when the machine is busy. You get:

- **The whole game as one sum:** `53% start + 64 luck − 17 choices = 100% (win)`, from an unusually swingy game. You began with a 53% chance, luck added an estimated 64 points, and everything else, including both players' decisions and model error, took away 17. Luck means random events: critical hits, missed attacks, KO-deciding damage rolls and speed ties. Choices is everything else, for both players together.
- **Win chance turn by turn,** with the biggest luck moments priced against what could have happened instead.
- **Up to three moves the engine would have played differently,** with how uncertain that is, never added up into a score, and **the one decision to look at again.** A rerun with new random draws can pick a different decision, so treat this as one place to look, not the place.
- **Muse Glimmer's explanation.** Ask what the turning point was, and it looks up the turn itself and explains what happened.
- **A test of your read.** Add your team and say what you believed about the opponent's set. HardRead checks your move against the alternatives under that belief. It uses the items, abilities, Tera types and moves you state. It doesn't use spreads or replay the turn under the move you expected.

It only reviews finished games. It never helps during a live battle.

# ai-workflow: your AI chief of staff at work

A folder you open in VS Code. Whatever AI extension you use (Claude Code, Roo Code, opencode) and whatever model (Claude, GPT, Qwen, Muse Glimmer...), the assistant follows the same way of working:

- It learns who you are at work (never your personal life), what you work on and where things live, asking you one question now and then, and keeps it in an **Atlas**: a map you can open in your browser.
- It works like a **chief of staff**: throw things at it in passing, in several conversations at once; it captures everything, prepares what it can, gives you a digest when you come back, and raises pending items itself.
- It keeps your **individual tasks** and reminds you of them. Team work goes to **Jira** tickets.
- It works on its own as far as it can, asks you **once** per task (one grouped approval, one checkpoint), and compares options before asking.
- It reads **Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket** through MCP, and writes there only after your approval.
- It has a **toolbox** of playbooks by theme (e-mails, slides, user stories, tests, framing notes, steering packs...) that you turn on or off for your profile.

Version 1, built for one user first. Everything stays on your computer.

---

## 1. Before you start (check with your IT or AI team)
1. **Approved models only.** Use only the models and access your organisation approved (for example your company's LLM gateway, or the Claude access you were given). The assistant sends your work files to the model you choose.
2. **Approved extensions.** Check that the VS Code extension you want (Claude Code, Roo Code, opencode) is allowed on your computer.
3. **Moving this folder.** Copy it to your work computer only by a channel your company allows (internal git, approved file share). Not through personal e-mail or a USB key if that is forbidden.

## 2. Install (about 15 minutes)
1. Put the `ai-workflow` folder somewhere in your documents, for example `C:\Users\<you>\Documents\ai-workflow`.
2. Check Python: open a terminal and type `py --version` (Windows) or `python3 --version` (macOS). You need 3.8 or newer. No extra package is needed.
3. Put the Atlassian configs in place: `py scripts\install.py cloud` (Windows) or `python3 scripts/install.py cloud`. Use `datacenter` instead of `cloud` if your Jira is hosted inside the company (see `mcp/README.md`).
4. Set your tokens as user environment variables (section 3).
5. Open the folder in VS Code (File > Open Folder).
6. Run the check: `py scripts\doctor.py` (Windows) or `python3 scripts/doctor.py`. Fix what it lists as TODO, or ignore the lines about features you do not use.
7. In your AI extension, say: **"start a work session"**. The assistant runs the onboarding (`workflow/onboarding.md`): two short rounds of questions, a look at the folders you allow and at Jira/Confluence, then your first map and task list.

> Windows note: the files say `python3 scripts/atlas.py ...`. On Windows the assistant uses `py scripts

# Term Sheet to Token

[![CI](https://github.com/NiceLeader/term-sheet-to-token/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/NiceLeader/term-sheet-to-token/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

A tokenized bond pays its investors through code, but what it owes them is written in legal
documents. The final terms of a note are a few pages long and point to definitions in a base
prospectus of a hundred pages or more: the day count fraction, the business day rules, the
record date, how amounts are rounded. Today those terms are keyed into issuance platforms by
hand, and a wrong digit becomes a wrong payment to every holder.

Term Sheet to Token reads the final terms together with the base prospectus using Meta's Muse
models, resolves the cross-references, and fills a schema aligned with the ICMA Bond Data
Taxonomy, with a quote and a page for every field. It then deploys a bond token configured
from those terms, runs the whole life of the bond on a local chain (issue, transfers around
record dates, every coupon, redemption) and checks each payment against an independent QuantLib
calculation and against the amounts printed in the documents. A reviewer sees every term next
to the highlighted sentence it came from, and every payment next to the clauses it follows from,
approves or corrects each term, and issues the token only when all of them are reviewed and the
replay raises no red flag.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/91f3eefe-5856-4b96-9075-5fc585fad1f2

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  docs["Final terms and base prospectus"] --> read["Reading: Muse Spark or Muse Wonder on the Meta Model API, Muse Glimmer on the reviewer's machine"]
  read --> terms["Terms, each with a quote and a page"]
  second["Second reading by another model"] --> checks
  terms --> checks["Checks: quote on the page, value in the text, consistency, disagreements"]
  checks --> review["Review: approve or correct each term"]
  review --> token["BondToken on a local chain: issue, transfers, coupons, redemption"]
  token --> four["Engine, QuantLib, token and documents agree on every payment"]
  four --> record["Issuance record under one hash"]
```

# Hearsay

Turn class-chat hearsay into a verified, source-linked calendar.

My nine SRM class WhatsApp groups carry every exam date, worksheet and deadline
— buried in forwards, corrections and rumours. A date a classmate relays is not
a date faculty announced, and dates move. Hearsay reads the chats, pulls out
every dated item with the exact message it came from, ranks sources (faculty >
CR > relay), flags moved dates and conflicts, and when it can't be sure, drafts
the question for me to ask. It emits an ICS feed, a one-screen "this week", and a
morning push that quotes the source line.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). It leans on the
agentic, verifiable core rather than being a chatbot: source-linked claims, a
trust order, conflict detection, and an ask-when-unsure loop. The extraction
model is the open-weight **Muse Glimmer**.

## The one idea
Replay and live are the same pipeline on different clocks. A fake clock replays
the term from 12 Sep forward, message by message, scoring what the agent would
have told me each day against a hand-checked log. The same code on a real clock
is the product.

## Run the slice (no model, no WhatsApp access needed)
```bash
python scripts/make_fixture.py tests/fixtures/chat.sqlite
python tests/test_ingest.py
```

## Score it (the replay eval)
Replay the term on a fake clock and score the agent against "latest message
wins", day by day:
```bash
python tests/test_eval.py                    # the 6 scoring tests
PYTHONPATH=src python -m hearsay.eval.replay  # the timeline + headline
```
On the synthetic fixture the baseline flips to a classmate's wrong "moved to 30
Oct" the day it lands, while the agent holds faculty's 29 Oct — date accuracy
1/1 vs 0/1 on the contested deadline. It scores against a committed
`tests/fixtures/ground_truth.md`; point it at the real, git-ignored term log
with `--truth private/Deadlines_till_20_Nov_2026.md` (same `key | date | portion`
shape) and `--db`/`--roster` for real chats.

## Run it live
Same pipeline as the eval, on a real clock, feeding the output surfaces:
```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m hearsay.run                    # this week's view (fixture)
PYTHONPATH=src python -m hearsay.run --out ics          # the calendar feed
PYTHONPATH=src python -m hearsay.run --as-of 2026-10-28 # what I'd have seen that day
```
`--as-of <iso>` pins a fake clock and shows only what was known by then, so live
and replay are literally the same `pipeline()` — the eval asserts they match
key‑for‑key. With no flag it reads the whole chat at the real clock. `--out push`
sends to an ntfy topic (`--ntfy-topic` or `~/.config/noticeagent/ntfy-topic`) and
is the only path that touches the network.

## Pointing it at real chats
```bash
# one-time: grant Full Disk Access to your terminal, then:
python scripts/pull_whatsapp.py      # copies the DB into private/ (gitignored)
```
Real names and chat text never enter this repo — anonymization runs on the Mac
before any message

# ComfyUI → StandRig: one picture to a 2.5D rig kit

These ComfyUI workflows take **one static 2D character picture** and produce everything
[StandRig](https://github.com/sayaka-aiart/StandRig) needs before an AI client can rig a 2.5D (Live2D-style) model:

| Output | Why StandRig needs it |
| --- | --- |
| `character.psd`: parts-separated layers (front/back hair, face, eye whites, irises, lashes, brows, mouth, neck, clothes…) with **hidden areas painted in** | StandRig only imports parts-separated PSDs; no automatic part separation |
| Hidden `Expressions/*` layers: blink, smile-eyes, A/I/U/E/O mouths, angry/sad brows | Swap art for StandRig expression and viseme presets (opacity keys) |
| `face-target.png`: neutral, yaw±, pitch±, roll± | Required by the modeling contract (AGENTS.md) before the first modeling write |
| `body-target.png`: neutral, body yaw±, pitch±, roll± | Required |
| `connection-target.png`: hair roots/back hair, jaw/neck, neck/collar/shoulders, sleeves/arms, waist/skirt/thighs, thighs/lower legs | Required |
| `reference-manifest.json` (`standrig-visual-reference-v1`): sha256 of every sheet, panel and the PSD; panel order, parameter extremes, prompts, acceptance checks | Required; modeling transactions are blocked without it |
| `turnaround-sheet.png`: 8 views | Orientation reference for back hair, accessories and depth |

```
picture ─► BiRefNet cutout ─► (optional) Qwen-Edit "normalize to front A-pose"
            │
            ├─► SAM3 "head" ─► face close-up ─┬─► Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 ×4  ─► face-target.png    (roll = exact rotation)
            │                                 └─► Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 ×9  ─► expressions ─► SAM3 masks ─► hidden PSD layers
            ├─► Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 ×6  ─► body-target.png
            ├─► Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 ×6  ─► connection-target.png (cropped to body bands)
            ├─► Qwen-Edit + Multiple-Angles LoRA ×7 ─► turnaround-sheet.png
            └─► See-through (LayerDiff 3D + Marigold depth) ─► LAYERS ─► StandRig PSD writer ─► character.psd
                                                                                    └─► reference pack + manifest
```

## Easy install (Windows, ComfyUI Desktop): StandRig Setup

1. Download this repository (**Code → Download ZIP**) and unzip it anywhere.
2. Double-click **`StandRigSetup.bat`**. It uses ComfyUI Desktop's own Python, so nothing else needs installing.
   Alternatively, get `StandRigSetup.exe` from the [Releases](https://github.com/tsukiyomi-naoko/StandRiggerWorkflow/releases) page.
3. Check what the tool detected at the top. It reads Comfy Desktop's own settings (`%APPDATA%\Comfy Desktop`), so it
   works with both the new multi-install Desktop and the older single-folder one:
   * **ComfyUI install**: pick which install to set up if you have several.
   * **Custom nodes →** where plugins go: the install's folder, or `Documents\ComfyUI` for installs adopted from the old Desktop.
   * **Models download to →** Desktop's DOWNLOAD

# OpenStreetLightMapper

**AI-assisted public-lighting inventory from street-level imagery.**

**This project was made for the [2026 Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon).**
The initial working prototype was built during one available day of the event,
around other professional commitments, using Meta Muse as the coding agent.

**[Watch the 3-minute project demo on YouTube](https://youtu.be/esxPKZEzfFs)** ·
[Source code](https://github.com/svenniev/OpenStreetLightMapper) ·
[Local database setup](infra/database/README.md)

## Why this project

As a designer of LED roadway-lighting optics and lighting installations, I need
to understand the lighting arrangements used in different regions. Information
about pole spacing, mounting heights, and layouts is often fragmented across
municipalities. OpenStreetLightMapper explores whether existing street-level
photographs can make that information easier to collect and audit.

The working prototype lets users select an area, browse image sequences, detect
poles and luminaires, review and merge observations, and save inventory
workspaces. Automatic detection and mapping are an experimental extension;
reliable dimensional measurements remain future work.

## Built with Meta

- **Meta Muse:** agentic application development from plain-language
  specifications, followed by iterative testing and feedback. The development
  specifications are available in [docs/specs](docs/specs).
- **SAM 3.1 through the Meta Model API:** text-prompt segmentation of poles and
  luminaires in selected photographs, with image evidence retained for review.
- **Mapillary:** street-level imagery, sequence discovery, camera metadata, and
  the MapillaryJS viewer.

The application uses React, TypeScript, Express, MongoDB, and OpenStreetMap.
It runs locally; live imagery discovery and hosted SAM inference need internet
access and the corresponding API credentials.

## Prototype status

OpenStreetLightMapper is an open-source system intended to convert street-level imagery
and map geometry into an auditable public-lighting asset inventory and a
roadway-lighting dataset suitable for subsequent EN 13201 workflows.

> This milestone adds an automatic workflow beside the manual one: check
> Mapillary sequences, freeze a bounded plan, launch once, and get a saved map
> of estimated poles and luminaires with image evidence — executed by a durable
> in-server worker that continues after a tab closes. After a server restart,
> interrupted jobs require explicit resume. Automatic output is
> explicitly **Automatically generated — not human reviewed**: estimated
> positions with uncertainty, unresolved records where geometry is ambiguous,
> never invented locations. The manual workflow, workspaces, and saved results
> are preserved. Detection still runs on Mapillary photographs (SAM 3.1 text
> prompts), and nothing here is EN 13201 compliant or standards-certified. See
> [What is deferred](#what-is-deferre

# Creative Intelligence Lab

A small web app for advertisers. It shows which creative ideas are already in a Meta ad portfolio, and which motivation-and-format combinations are missing.

It maps coverage. It does not predict results, scores, or click-through.

- **Demo video (2 min):** https://youtu.be/lrJ6zbwHNns
- **Live demo (cached, no login):** https://creative-intelligence-lab.vercel.app
- Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, "Build for Your World") with Muse Spark, SAM 3.1 and Muse Image.

Meta's next-gen Andromeda scores every eligible ad and encodes ad content together with its serving context, while the pool of ads keeps growing with generative AI. Variations of the same idea compete in a crowded pool. This tool maps which distinct ideas are missing.

Source: [Meta Engineering, Andromeda](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/10/28/ml-applications/meta-andromeda-next-gen-ads-retrieval-gpu-co-design/)

The cached demo runs with no API key. Live mode is optional and passcode-gated.

## Run it locally

You need Node.js 22, or at least 20.17. The `.nvmrc` file says `22`.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).

No API key is required. If `MODEL_API_KEY` is missing, the app stays in mock mode and still runs.

To check that the project builds:

```bash
npm run build
```

To check that the demo labels match the expected format:

```bash
npm run check:mock
```

## Try milestone 1

1. Start the app with `npm run dev`.
2. Click **Load demo data**. That fills in the fictional coffee brand Danish Coffee Lab: website text, a campaign brief, and 8 ads.
3. Click **Analyze coverage**.
4. Read the brand summary. The “Why” line says what the summary was taken from.
5. Look at the grid. Rows are motivations, columns are formats. Empty cells have no ad. Thin cells have one. The 8 demo ads sit in only three motivations, so most of the grid is empty.
6. Hover or click an ad thumbnail. The panel above the grid shows why that ad was placed there.

You can also paste your own website text, or enter a public website URL, and upload 5 to 20 ad images with a headline and primary text.

## Mock mode and a real key

Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` if you want to set variables. `.env.local` is gitignored.

- Leave `MODEL_API_KEY` empty to use mock data.
- `USE_MOCK=true` forces mock data even if a key is present.
- A live call happens only when a key is set and `USE_MOCK` is not true. Milestone 1 does not require that, and the demo does not make a live call.
- `BUDGET_LIMIT_USD` caps estimated live spend. Leave it blank for $120. The running total is stored in `.data/spend.json`, which is gitignored. Cache hits cost $0. Saved demo results live in `data/cache/`, which is committed and contains no secrets.

# Clearwake

Clearwake settles PayPal disputes before they turn into fees. Agents running inside the merchant's own network resolve each case with the buyer inside the owner's limits, fight only the cases worth fighting, and never call a refund done until PayPal's own record says so.

```sh
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Sriharsan/clearwake.git && cd clearwake && python -m clearwake --port 8810
```

Public site (static, recorded sandbox run, receipt verifier in your browser): https://clearwake-mu.vercel.app. It is not part of the network isolated system and runs no agents.

Open http://127.0.0.1:8810/console for the three screens (buyer agent, merchant control room with the dispute ledger, receipt verifier), or http://127.0.0.1:8810 for the refund workroom. Python 3.12 or newer, nothing to install. Windows: `.\demo.ps1`. macOS or Linux: `./demo.sh`. The network isolated run (case m) needs Docker: `python scripts/airgap.py`.

![Clearwake refund workroom in rehearsal: limit gauge at USD 1.00 of a USD 5.00 cap, autonomy levels, and a timeline holding a lost response as UNKNOWN](docs/screenshot-unknown-1440.png)

*Screenshot: the refund workroom in rehearsal mode, invented records, fake provider.*

**License:** MIT.

## The money leak

PayPal's own rules ([help350](https://history.paypal.com/uk/cshelp/article/how-is-the-dispute-rate-calculated-and-how-do-i-avoid-being-charged-a-dispute-fee-help350), UK edition; fees from [PayPal Merchant Fees, US](https://www.paypal.com/us/business/paypal-business-fees), updated 1 Oct 2026; both in [docs/SOURCES.md](docs/SOURCES.md)):

1. No Standard Dispute Fee (USD 15.00 in the US) is charged when a case is resolved directly between seller and buyer and not escalated to a claim. Sellers who answer late, or only with evidence, let cases escalate.
2. A seller with more than 100 sales in the previous 3 months and a dispute rate of 1.5% or more pays the High Volume Dispute Fee (USD 30.00 in the US) on every dispute.
3. A refund sent twice, or one that silently failed, costs money or a customer. Clearwake gives each refund one stable request id, holds what it cannot confirm as UNKNOWN, and checks PayPal's record before calling it done.

The Standard fee is not charged on claims below twice the fee or on unauthorised transactions, so the fee leak gauge counts a fee avoided only when PayPal's rule would otherwise have charged one.

## Who it is for

Small PayPal merchants who lose money on disputes: cases that escalate because nobody answered in time, evidence that never went out before the deadline, refunds sent twice. Clearwake reads each dispute, and the policy decides per case: settle in conversation with an offer inside the owner's limit while PayPal still calls it an inquiry, fight with the order, capture and tracking from PayPal's own records, refund within the limit, or put it in the owner's inbox before the deadline. The model only proposes; its proposal is shown next to the policy's decision.

# Portravo Live for Meta Ray-Ban Display

Walk the job, talk it through, say "Portravo, I'm done." The quote is ready before you've left the driveway. Glasses on, hands free, nothing to tap.

A contractor wears Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses on a site visit. They say where they are and what the job is, then just walk and talk: the glasses photograph what they look at, every sentence is heard, rooms are named as they go, and on a LiDAR iPhone they can say "measure this room". When they say they're done, the server turns the walk into a scoped, priced quote, asks one or two things only the contractor knows before it goes out, reads the total back on the lens, and on "send it" makes the customer's proposal.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**.

## Demo, in one walk

1. Glasses on, app open. The lens: *At 1186 Alder Ln. Say the job.* He says: "Hall bathroom remodel for Marcus." The lens: *Hall bathroom remodel · Recording*.
2. He just talks. "Vanity's thirty-six inches, comes out, new one goes in. Toilet stays. Floor's five by eight, tile comes up, LVP goes down. Ceiling's eight foot. Exhaust fan's dead." He looks at each thing as he says it; the footer ticks up: *3 photos · 4 notes*.

5. *Quote ready* with the total and the three biggest lines. He says "send it to Marcus". That makes a read-only customer page with the lines by room, the total and the photos. # FaceMesh

**FaceMesh** — from a few photos to a faithful 3D head, locally, inside ComfyUI. Repo: github.com/davoax/FaceMesh

From a few photos of a person (1–10: frontal, three-quarter, profile) to a **3D head with the real shape
of the face**, running locally in ComfyUI. It is the first piece of an open replica of KeenFace: instead of
"imagining" an object with a 3D generator, it fits a parametric head model (FLAME 2023) to all the photos
at once, the way FaceBuilder/KeenFace do.

```
photos ─┬─ SAM 3.1 "face" / "ear" / "head" ── masks ──┐
        ├─ MoGe-2 ───────────────── normals, FOV ─────┤
        └─ FAN 68 landmarks ──────────────────────────┤
FLAME 2023 ──────────────────────────────────────────┴─ FM_FitHead ─┬─ neutral mesh (GLB)
                                                                     ├─ one camera per photo (JSON)
                                                                     └─ check overlays
```

The fit optimizes shape (300 coefficients), focal length and one camera per photo by minimizing:
2D landmarks, face+ear silhouette (distance transform), MoGe normals, and a one-sided "skull inside the
head silhouette" term. The rasterizer is written in pure PyTorch: **nothing to compile** (no nvdiffrast /
pytorch3d), so it runs inside the Comfy Desktop Python on Windows.

## Installation

1. `git clone https://github.com/davoax/FaceMesh` into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/` (or copy the folder there).
2. Install the dependencies **in ComfyUI's Python**:
   - Comfy Desktop (Windows): open the terminal from the Comfy Desktop menu, or run
     `"<ComfyUI-Installs>\server\ComfyUI\.venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip install -r requirements.txt`
   - Portable/manual ComfyUI: `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`
3. FLAME files (non-commercial license, not redistributable). Register at
   [flame.is.tue.mpg.de](https://flame.is.tue.mpg.de/) and put in `models/flame/`:
   | file | source |
   |---|---|
   | `flame2023.pkl` | FLAME 2023 (`FLAME2023.zip`) |
   | `FLAME_masks.pkl` | FLAME Vertex Masks |
   | `landmark_embedding.npy` | [DECA](https://github.com/yfeng95/DECA/tree/master/data) (alternatively `flame_static_embedding.pkl` + `flame_dynamic_embedding.npy`) |

   The `flame` folder is looked up next to every configured `models` folder (including Comfy Desktop's
   shared one, e.g. `ComfyUI-Shared\models\flame`).
4. Core ComfyUI models used by the workflow: `sam3.1_multiplex_fp16.safetensors` (checkpoints),
   `moge_2_vitl_normal_fp16.safetensors` (geometry_estimation). The FAN weights download themselves on
   first use.

## Usage

Load `workflows/facemesh_fit_api.json` (API format: drag it into ComfyUI) and pick the photos in the
*LoadImage* nodes. Outputs:

- `output/3d/facemesh_*.glb` — neutral FLAME mesh (mouth closed, expression zeroed), meters, y up.
- `output/3d/facemesh_cameras_*.json` — OpenCV cameras for every photo, in original-photo pixels.
- `output/facemesh/overlay_*.png` — wireframe over the photo: green = detected

Supports a first-frame guide, two stacked IC-LoRAs, one pass up to 97 frames, and longer clips in overlapping chunks with a smooth cross-fade |
| **Image** | FLUX.3 Klein: text-to-image, editing with masks and references, pose transfer ("scene + skeleton + character" recipe), non-destructive layer & selection transforms. Optional Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 |

# BlindPilot

A screen-reader-first desktop app for AI coding agents. It runs Claude Code, Codex, FreeBuff, opencode, Hermes, Muse Code, muse.ai, Command Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity CLI, and GitHub Copilot CLI in normal windows, so NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver read real buttons, lists and edit boxes instead of a terminal. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Linux gets the least testing of the three.

[![Join SerrebiProjects on Telegram](https://img.shields.io/badge/Telegram-SerrebiProjects-2CA5E0?style=for-the-badge&logo=telegram&logoColor=white)](https://t.me/SerrebiProjects)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-green?style=for-the-badge)](LICENSE)

**Questions, bugs, or release news?** Join the [SerrebiProjects Telegram group](https://t.me/SerrebiProjects). That's the fastest way to reach me. Bug reports and feature requests can also go in [Issues](https://github.com/serrebidev/BlindPilot/issues).

## Why this exists

Coding agents live in terminals, and terminals are miserable with a screen reader. Output scrolls past, the screen redraws under you, and you can't tell if the thing is working, stuck, or waiting on you. BlindPilot puts the agent in a window your screen reader understands. Every answer is a list you can arrow through, and it tells you when something happens.

BlindPilot is vibe-coded. I use it every day. It started as a fork of [Claude Code Reader](https://github.com/doubletaponair/claude-code-reader) by doubletaponair, and it keeps that app's accessibility design. See [CREDITS.md](CREDITS.md).

## What it does

- Runs eleven coding agents. Pick one per tab under Model, Backend. New tabs start on whatever agent the tab you're in uses. If your tabs use different agents, each tab's name, its prompt, and its send sound tell you which one you're talking to.
- Doesn't stop to ask permission for every little thing. Every agent runs in Bypass permissions mode out of the box. If you want to approve things yourself, change it under Model, Permission Mode.
- Splits every answer into rows: one per heading, paragraph, list item, quote, code block, thought, and tool step. Arrow through them like any list.
- Reads answers out as they arrive, or stays quiet until the whole answer is in. Your choice.
- Reads your message back when you send it ("Sent: fix the build"), so you know what dictation or a paste actually sent. Turn it off in Preferences.
- Speaks every step the agent takes, or just your message, the answer, and anything important. See Narration below.
- Reopens old conversations from any agent so you can keep going. Shrinks a long one so the agent has room to carry on.
- Runs several conversations at once, one tab each, each with its own folder, model, and permission mode.
- When the agent asks you a multiple-choice question, you get a normal dialog with radio buttons, checkboxes, and an Other box.
- Lets you redirect a running task with a new message, or stop it and keep what it did. Stop also stops any helper agen

# CoreAudit

CoreAudit includes two main workflows:

- **Code Auditor** — code and repository analysis.
- **Business Evaluator** — structured business idea and plan evaluation.

Both AI-powered workflows use the Meta Model API from the server.

## Requirements

- Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+
- A Meta Model API key from https://dev.meta.ai/

## Configure the Meta API key

Create a server-side environment variable named `META_API_KEY` with your Meta Model API key. For backward compatibility, `META_API_KEY` is also accepted, but `META_API_KEY` is the official variable name.

**Never put the key in frontend code, commit it to Git, or share it in chat.** If a key has been exposed, revoke it and create a replacement.

For local development, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, put the key in `.env`, and keep `.env` private. The repository `.gitignore` excludes `.env*` files while allowing `.env.example`.

## Install and run

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Build and checks

```bash
npm run lint
npm run build
```

The server exposes `/api/health` for configuration status and `/api/llm/test` for a live Meta API readiness request. These endpoints require a correctly configured server-side key to return a successful live result.

## Deployment notes

Deploy the project to a Node.js-capable host. Configure `MODEL_API_KEY` in the host's server-side environment settings. Do not add the secret to GitHub or any `VITE_` variable, because Vite variables can be exposed to browser code.

The JSON files in `data/` are local file-based storage and may not persist on ephemeral/serverless hosting. Use persistent storage before relying on account or history data in production.

**Live app:** https://quicklist-inventory-ai.onrender.com

Snap a product photo. QuickListInventoryAI writes the listing, publishes it to your stores and marketplaces, and keeps one stock count across every channel, so a sale on one channel updates all of them.

Small sellers often list the same product on Shopify, Amazon, Flipkart and Meesho, then update stock by hand after every sale. That leads to overselling and wasted time. QuickListInventoryAI does the work for them:

1. **Snap.** Take a photo. The app reads it and writes the title, colour, bullet points, description, search terms, and HSN and GST suggestions.
2. **Finish.** Add only what a photo can't show: sizes, stock and prices. Type them as one line in English, Hindi or Hinglish, or fill in the form.
3. **Publish.** The product is created on Shopify with its photos, one variant per size and the stock for each. Other channels get the same stock.
4. **Sell.** A sale on any channel lowers the one count. A WhatsApp message such as `sold 1 SKU` does the same. Every other channel is updated.

- **Photo to listing.** Meta's Muse Spark model reads the photo and writes the listing text.

- **Listings readiness.** Each product is checked against each marketplace's basic requirements, and anything missing is shown.

# Sada (صدى)

**Every word you catch becomes yours.**

Sada is an English-listening companion for Arabic-speaking learners. You listen to an episode; when a word slips past you, you tap it or ask out loud. Sada pauses, explains the word *in the sentence you just heard* (in Arabic, simple English, or both), saves it with that sentence, and then builds your reviews and exercises around exactly those words until they stick.

The name means *echo*: the words you catch keep coming back to you.

## What works in Stage 1

| Feature | How it works | Meta model |
|---|---|---|
| Tap any word to ask | Explanation tuned to the sentence and your CEFR level, in Arabic, simple English, or both | Muse Spark 1.3 (`/api/ai`, task `explain`) |
| Ask with your voice | Tap the mic, ask, tap send. A 16 kHz WAV clip is transcribed, biased toward the words in the current sentence | Muse Voice Transcribe (`/api/transcribe`) → Muse Spark |
| “Continue” | Saying “continue” resumes the episode | Muse Voice Transcribe |
| Hands-free listening | Wake phrase pauses the episode, question answered aloud, resume phrase continues at the same position. Works with Sada open and the screen on; not with the screen locked (see `docs/HANDS_FREE.md`) | Chrome speech recognition for the phrases; Muse Spark answers the question |
| Vocabulary memory | Word, Arabic + English meaning, example, every sentence you heard it in, source, date, times asked, status | — |
| Struggle detection | Asking about a saved word again, or failing it twice, marks it as struggling and brings it back sooner | — |
| Spaced repetition | SM-2 variant; statuses New, Learning, Needs review, Mastered | — |
| Quick review on open | Up to 5 due words on the Today screen, with “Skip for today”. Never blocks the app | — |
| Personal sessions | Exercises written around your due/struggling/recent words, in new contexts: meaning, context, gap-fill, sentence building, translation, explain-in-your-own-words, say-it-aloud | Muse Spark (`exercises`) |
| Meaning-based grading | Open answers are judged by meaning, not exact string match | Muse Spark (`grade`) |
| Pronunciation check | Say the word; Sada compares what was heard (no keyword biasing, so mispronunciations aren’t hidden) | Muse Voice Transcribe |
| Offline drill | Multiple-choice and gap-fill built locally from your own words when there’s no connection | — |
| Your own episodes | Paste a transcript you have rights to, optionally with a link to the publisher’s audio file | — |

### Honest limits

- **Episodes** are six original scripts written for Sada (A2 to B2), narrated by the phone’s English voice one sentence at a time, so the current sentence is always highlighted. No third-party podcast audio is downloaded or redistributed.

# claude-brain 🧠

**Your multi-model agent. Anywhere, always on. Driven by Claude.**

claude-brain turns a computer you already have — a Mac mini in a closet, a Linux box under
your desk, a spare laptop, or a $12/month cloud VM — into a personal AI server that runs
[Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) around the clock. You open the Claude app on
your phone or [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) in a browser, attach to your brain,
and give it work. It keeps going when you close your laptop, leave the house, or go to bed.

The twist: your brain isn't limited to Claude. It has a built-in **model router** that can
also consult **Grok**, **GPT**, **Kimi**, and **Meta Muse** — using your own subscriptions to those
services — and it can work directly on your **GitHub** repositories.

claude-brain is two things working together: a **model router** (one Claude session that
delegates to other model families) and a **compression tool** (a local engine that shrinks
the tokens flowing to and from every model, so long-running work stays cheap). Both run on
your brain machine; both are on by default.

```
   your phone / laptop                      your brain (any computer)
  ┌──────────────────┐   Remote Control   ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ Claude app        │ ◄───────────────► │ Claude Code (always on)    │
  │ claude.ai/code    │                   │   ├── brain-grok  ─┐       │
  └──────────────────┘                   │   ├── brain-sol   ─┼─► model router
                                          │   ├── brain-kimi   │  (GPT/Grok/Kimi/Muse)
                                          │   ├── brain-muse  ─┘       │
                                          │   └── your GitHub repos    │
                                          └────────────────────────────┘
```

The connection is **outbound only**. Your brain reaches out to Anthropic; your phone talks
to Anthropic. Nothing listens on the internet, so a machine at home behind a router works
exactly as well as a cloud server — no ports, no public IP, no tunnel.

## Install it by asking Claude

Open Claude Code on the computer you want to use as your brain (or the Claude app attached
to it) and say:

> **claude help me install claude brain at https://github.com/mattvv/claude-brain**

Claude reads the repo's install guide and walks you through it, asking:

1. **Where should your brain live?** — this computer, another computer over SSH, or a new

   whole machine (the droplet default).
3. **Which accounts should it use?** — Claude is required; ChatGPT, Grok, Kimi, Muse, and GitHub
   are each optional and can be added later.
4. **Phone control?** — set up the Remote Control server so sessions show up in the Claude
   app.
5. **Always on?** — start at boot, and stop the machine from sleeping.

It shows you the plan before it changes anything, then runs it, hands you

# MotionLedger

**AI that audits how work actually happens.**

MotionLedger compares a manufacturing work instruction with a video of the process. It turns model observations into typed, evidence-linked possible discrepancies, then lets a reviewer correct the interpretation and rerun a deterministic comparison.

> **Trust rule:** models perceive and interpret; deterministic code decides. A machine result is never a final quality verdict. `UNVERIFIABLE` means the decisive moment was not visible and must not be treated as an omission.

This repository implements the flange-gasket MVP in `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md`.

## What is implemented

### Working end-to-end slice

- FastAPI backend with SQLite persistence for procedures, videos, audits, run versions, overrides, model-call usage and an append-only ledger.
- Versioned procedure schema, reference validation and dependency-cycle validation. The included flange procedure expands the four bolt insertion and tightening steps into zone-specific instances.
- MP4/MOV ingest, ffprobe validation, 15 fps H.264 proxy normalization and frame-addressable JPEG evidence endpoints.
- Meta Model API client using the official OpenAI-compatible Responses API base URL. The API key stays on the backend.
- Muse Spark work-instruction compiler and full-video reconnaissance/structured step-verification calls.
- SAM 3.1 video segmentation calls per procedure object, parsed into per-frame mask RLE and compressed mask artifacts with boxes, confidence, area, centroid and principal-axis angle. Raw streaming event logs are retained per run and object.
- Mask-derived physical signal measurements for hand/object contact, object carrying and tool rotation while it overlaps the procedure subject. These are attached to the run report with timestamps and numeric features.
- Deterministic comparison engine: omission, incomplete, unverifiable, order violation, pattern violation, repeated action, extra action and postcondition checks; prerequisite blocking prevents cascading accusations.
- Reviewer actions: confirm/dismiss findings, add an observation, retime/confirm step observations, and recompare without another model call.
- Content-addressed artifact caching for Muse Spark reconnaissance/verdicts and SAM raw/decoded outputs. `MOTIONLEDGER_OFFLINE=1` replays a complete cached run and stops on a cache miss without network access.
- New run versions with parent pointers, version diff, JSON/CSV/printable HTML report exports and SHA-256 hash-chained audit ledger verification.
- Review dashboard, upload flow, procedure compiler/editor, video player, timeline, evidence cards, findings review, cost/status display and ledger panel.
- Synthetic sample clip/report for exploring the review experience without a Meta API key. It is explicitly marked **SIMULATION ONLY** and is not presented as inference from real footage.
- Unit tests for engine behavior, mask decoding/artifact persistence, physical signal extraction, geometry helpers, hysteresis

# PlateCount

**Photograph an agar plate and get a colony count and a CFU/mL estimate. An agent checks the segmentation, and a verifier rejects any number that no tool produced.**

**Live demo:** https://platecount-i9lt.onrender.com
(It runs on a free host that sleeps when idle, so the first load can take about a minute. Three demo plates run at no cost. You can also upload your own photo.)

## Built during the hackathon

All code in this repository was written during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Nov 1-4, 2026.
Code from a pilot made before the event was not reused. [PROGRESS.md](PROGRESS.md) is the dated build log:

- **Nov 1:** SAM 3.1 client and prompt tests, CFU math, AGAR split, tiling
- **Nov 2:** counting rule, Spark agent, verifier, event log, held-out test run, FastAPI app and mobile page
- **Nov 3:** deploy and README
- **Nov 4:** video and submission

## The problem

Counting colonies on an agar plate is a routine lab task, and it is often still done by eye: a person
marks each colony, then converts the count to CFU/mL.

- **It takes time.** One evaluation found manual counting took a mean of 70 s per plate. It called the job
  "tedious and time-consuming" ([Heuser et al., 2023, *Microbiology Spectrum*](https://doi.org/10.1128/spectrum.00673-23)).
- **Trained readers disagree.** In one study, panels of three microbiologists independently read urine
  cultures, sorting growth into only four levels. On blood agar, 1,666 of 30,231 readings (5.5%) still
  differed from the panel's consensus
  ([Glasson et al., 2016, *J Clin Microbiol*](https://doi.org/10.1128/JCM.01380-16)). The authors work for
  a company that makes an imaging device.
- **Fully automatic counting can be inaccurate.** The 2023 study found fully automatic counts had low accuracy,
  "especially for plates with very high or very low colony numbers". Once a person corrected them, they
  saved no time.

A tool that gives one number gives you no way to check it. You can't tell whether it missed colonies or
counted glare.

PlateCount shows how it got each count. It records every step, shows an outline overlay, and refuses
to report a number it can't trace to a tool output. It also flags plates a person should look at.
It reports a lab measurement for a person to review. It gives no medical or food-safety advice.

## Who it's for

- Quality-control labs that run plate counts on food, water and pharmaceutical samples
- Teaching labs where students learn to count plates and calculate CFU/mL

It is not for clinical use. It makes no diagnosis or health judgement. It reports a count for a
person to review.

## What's next

- **Accuracy on dense plates.** The held-out test had no plate above 130 colonies. On the one dense dev plate,
  the count was 256 against a true 298. That needs more dense plates and a better tiling step.
- **Dilution series.** Right now each plate is counted on its own. The next step is to take several plates
  from one serial dilution and report one CF

Continuum is a local-first continuity and memory layer around Muse Code.

## What Continuum is

Continuum is a local web frontend for **Muse Code** with persistent personal
memory and project context. The browser is only a different environment for
Muse Code: it streams Muse's exact text, tool activity, permission requests,
questions, errors and results, verbatim. There is no second agent and no
second model call interpreting Muse's output.

Muse remains the agent with native tools. Continuum adds persistent memory,
project context, history and an accessible web interface.

## What problem it solves

- Continuity across sessions: new chats start fresh but remember you.
- Persistent global memory: identity, preferences, decisions, shared history.
- Project-scoped memory and context (`.continuum.md` per project).
- Corrections and supersession instead of silent overwriting.
- Project isolation: one project's facts don't leak into another.
- Continuity after app/server restart.
- An accessible web interface: Continuum provides a simple web interface
  for working with Muse Code, projects, files, memory and approvals
  without requiring users to be comfortable living in a terminal.

Continuum Web UI → local Python bridge → Muse Code / MSP

# ZeroDefect

**AI quality inspection for small factories. Show it one good part and it checks the rest, using just a phone camera.**

**Author:** Monashini ([@Monashini](https://github.com/Monashini)) · **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/V-uBvXXySCs

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Theme: *Push the Frontier – manufacturing*) with **Muse Spark** and **SAM 3.1** on Meta Model API.

![Inspecting a real bottle (MVTec AD)](docs/screenshot-real-bottle.jpg)

## The problem

Industrial estates like Ambattur, Guindy and Sriperumbudur in Chennai are full of small units that make bolts, gears, washers, bottles, PCBs and garment pieces. Quality checking there means a person staring at parts for 8 hours. Defects get missed, and whole batches come back rejected.

Machine-vision systems cost lakhs of rupees. They also need thousands of labelled defect photos, which a small factory doesn't have.

## What ZeroDefect does

1. **Show it one good part.** The owner puts a perfect "golden sample" in front of a phone or webcam. That's the whole setup: no training data and no defect photos.
2. **SAM 3.1 finds every part** in the frame from a plain phrase like "metal gear". It handles several parts on a table or belt at once.
3. **A zero-training anomaly detector** compares each part with the golden sample, patch by patch, and makes a heatmap of anything that looks different.
4. **Muse Spark inspects like a senior QC supervisor.** It looks at the golden sample, the part and the heatmap together. It ignores glare and pose, names the defect (scratch, crack, missing hole, stain, chipped edge…), says where it is in plain words, rates severity and suggests a likely process cause.
5. **SAM 3.1 outlines the defect exactly.** Muse Spark's rough defect box becomes a box prompt for SAM 3.1, which returns a pixel-accurate defect mask. ZeroDefect then reports the defect as a % of the part's area.
6. **Green/red PASS–FAIL plus a voice call-out**, for example *"Crack near the bore, reject."*, so the operator doesn't have to look at a screen.
7. **It learns from the operator.** Tapping "Actually OK – learn it" adds that part to the golden set, so false alarms go down over the shift.
8. **Shift report agent.** Muse Spark uses tool calls to query the inspection log (summary, defects by hour, defect breakdown, recent failures). It looks for patterns and writes an action list, for example *"most cracks after 3 PM – check the machine temperature."*

Online shoppers guess their size from a chart, and many guess wrong. **Stylewise shows how each size of a
real garment sits on your body shape**, region by region, and says why. It compares the brand's own size
chart with a body built from your shape and usual size (or your own measurements), then shows the result on a
faceless mannequin with your proportions and lets a sizing assistant, Nisha, explain it in plain words.

| **1. You** | Pick one of five body shapes, your usual size and height, or enter your measurements | A prepared **Meta MHR** body is chosen (for measurements: the closest preset, shown with its centimetres next to yours) |

# FireShift AI

FireShift AI simulates how a wildfire spreads under changing conditions and recommends where limited firefighting resources will do the most good — validated against a real historical fire, not just a toy example. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie developer track).

Starting from an early satellite perimeter, it runs a wind- and terrain-aware spread simulation forward in time, identifies which buildings and roads fall in the predicted burn path, and uses a reasoning model to compare "what-if" scenarios (e.g. a wind shift) and explain which one demands a different response priority.

## Prior art, and what's actually different here

Wildfire spread simulation and decision support aren't new. **FARSITE** (USFS, fire area simulator, in use since the late 1990s) and **WFDSS** (Wildland Fire Decision Support System, the federal interagency operational tool since 2009) are the real, proven systems wildland fire agencies actually use, and they implement far more physically accurate fire behavior models than this project does.

What's different about FireShift AI isn't the physics — it's the combination, and how it was built: a cellular-automaton spread model, structure-level risk identification from satellite imagery (SAM 3.1), and plain-language scenario reasoning (Muse Spark) chained into one lightweight, open pipeline, built in about 10 days entirely on free public data, and validated end-to-end against a real fire's actual outcome rather than presented without evidence. It's not a replacement for FARSITE or WFDSS — it's a demonstration of how far a small, fast, AI-assisted pipeline can get toward the same kind of decision support.

## How it works

1. **Data ingestion** — pulls real fire detections, terrain/fuel data, the official final perimeter, and weather for the target fire from public APIs (see Data Sources below).
2. **Seed perimeter** — derives an early-fire perimeter from the first satellite pass's hotspot detections, used as the simulation's starting state.
3. **Spread simulation** — a cellular automaton (`src/simulation.py`) steps forward hourly, with each cell's ignition probability shaped by fuel type, slope (direction-aware, derived from the elevation band), and wind speed/direction from real weather data.
4. **Validation** — compares the simulated final perimeter against the fire's real recorded final perimeter using IoU (intersection-over-union) and acreage match.
5. **Validation & Methodology tab** — a dedicated tab makes the validation case explicit for a quick skim: the headline IoU/acreage numbers front and center, a side-by-side seed → simulated → actual perimeter comparison, a condensed methodology summary, and the Known Limitations below surfaced directly in the UI, not just this README.
6. **Structure segmentation** — SAM 3.1 segments buildings and roads in aerial imagery of the area, so the simulation's output can be checked against what's actually on the ground.
7. **Scenario reasoning*

# Visual Bug-to-Code Investigator

Go from a visual bug report to an evidence-backed, test-verified explanation
of its likely source-code cause.

Upload a screenshot of a broken UI, describe the bug, optionally paste browser
console/network logs, and point the tool at the local repository. It finds the
relevant code across files, ranks hypotheses with supporting *and*
contradicting evidence, verifies the leading hypothesis with real tests, and
proposes a reviewable fix plus a regression test.

Every source claim links to an actual file and line range that is revalidated
before display. When evidence is insufficient, the tool abstains
(`inconclusive`) instead of guessing. A screenshot alone is treated as
Level-1 evidence: it can show *what* is visibly wrong, never *which line*
caused it — that link must be earned through code and tests.

![Broken cart page from the demo app](demo_webapp/screenshot.png)

*The demo app's broken cart (real screenshot, headless Chromium):
total blank, checkout failed. Root cause is three files away.*

## Quick start

No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+ (stdlib only; `pytest` runs target repos'
tests and this project's suite).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HPHYSVN/ai-repository-investigator.git
cd ai-repository-investigator
python3 run.py            # http://127.0.0.1:8765 (localhost only)
```

The UI is pre-filled with the demo scenario against `demo_webapp/`. Click
**Investigate**, then optionally enable test execution (explicit confirmation
dialog) to watch the hypothesis become `verified`.

## The demo bug (try it in 2 minutes)

`demo_webapp/` is a small shop: `cart.js` renders the total from
`POST /api/checkout` (`cart_api.py` → `cart.py` → `pricing.py`). Adding a
gift-box SKU makes the total blank and checkout fail. The failure surfaces in
`pricing.format_price`, but the cause is `cart.cart_total` silently returning
`None` for an unknown SKU. Full walkthrough: `docs/demo-script.md`.

## How it works

Deterministic tools first, Meta models only where they add judgement:

| Stage | Implementation | Meta model? |
|---|---|---|
| Screenshot validation | magic-byte/MIME/size checks (≤5 MB) in `app/visual.py` | no |
| Visual symptom analysis | structured JSON (observable / inferred / cannot-determine) | **yes — Muse Spark 1.3 image understanding** |
| Console/network log parsing | regex extraction, secret/header redaction (`app/logs.py`) | no |
| Repo indexing | `.gitignore`-aware walk, Python AST, JS/TS lexical symbols, BM25 | no |
| Root-cause detectors | None-return, `.get()` w/o default, boundary, config-key, unconverted producer output, unresolved imports | no |
| Dependency path | BFS over extracted import/call graph (reachability, not a runtime trace) | no |
| Hypotheses | ranked, supporting + contradicting evidence, labelled confidence | deterministic; model may summarise |
| Verification | allow-listed pytest, explicit confirmation, real exit codes | no |
| Hypothesis evaluation | competing candidates

**Use your existing Muse Code subscription in Zed, JetBrains IDEs, and any other
ACP client.**

[![CI](https://github.com/BrokkAi/muse-acp/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/BrokkAi/muse-acp/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

[![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-1.88%2B-orange.svg)](https://www.rust-lang.org/)

`muse-acp` is a bridge between editors that speak the
[Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/) (ACP) and
[Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code). It talks to Muse over its
native [Muse Session Protocol](https://github.com/meta-models/muse-code-sdk)
(MSP), so your subscription keeps Muse's own session engine, tools,
authentication, and approval flow.

The adapter is one small Rust binary with no runtime dependencies. It supports
ACP v1 and v2, and installs on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

Client implementers should start with the
[ACP extension contract](docs/acp-extensions.md). It lists every negotiated
Muse method, `_meta` shape, capability, fallback, and the ACP standard fields
used where they exist.

Toward the editor, the adapter speaks ACP through the official Rust SDK, the
[`agent-client-protocol`](https://crates.io/crates/agent-client-protocol)
crate. The SDK owns the stdio transport, JSON-RPC, ACP v1/v2 version
negotiation, request parsing into its typed schema, the serialization of
every response, notification and request the adapter sends, and the
`$/cancel_request` withdrawal of the adapter's own requests. Only Muse
extensions that no ACP schema defines (the `_session/*` methods, `_meta`
members, and JetBrains AIR updates) are the adapter's own JSON.

Toward Muse, the adapter speaks MSP through
[`muse-msp-client`](crates/muse-msp-client/README.md), a dependency-free
synchronous client that launches a configured `muse serve`, performs the
handshake, correlates requests, routes server requests, and shuts the host
down within a bounded time. Tools that need Muse sessions without ACP can use
it directly.

> `muse-acp` is an independent community project. Muse Code and Muse Spark are
> products of Meta Platforms, Inc. This project is not affiliated with,
> endorsed by, or supported by Meta.

`muse serve`, a saved `:auto-review` session falls back to asking you for
everything, so editor users choose between clicking through every prompt or
switching to `allowAll` and giving up review entirely. `muse-acp` gives you
the middle path: a per-session **Auto-review** selector that sends every
permission request to a reviewer agent instead of to you.

The reviewer is a second Muse model session on its own memory-only, read-only
host (`--no-session-log`), so reviews ar

PWA that builds a household pantry from receipts, then uses purchase rhythm to
intervene at the right moment: **"Hold that cart — you already have this."**

```bash
pnpm install

```bash
pnpm run build && pnpm start   # :3001

Copy `.env.example` → `.env` and set `MODEL_API_KEY` (Meta dev.meta.ai key)
to enable photo extraction + AI enrichment. Everything else works without it.

## Flow

1. Home → **Load demo pantry** (seeded history with a built-in money story).
2. **Briefing** (pre-shop): BUY ≤8 / SKIP ≤5 / SWAP ≤3, computed from rhythm.

   No camera? Use the demo JSON buttons (receipt / list / cart fixtures).

**An AI agent that notices when what you say you want doesn't match what you do, and spends model power only where that gap exists.**

*This repository is the Meta version of a project that began as an earlier hackathon entry. The model layer, prices, reasoning control, reports and interface were rebuilt for Meta's models, and no earlier results are included.*

---

## At a glance

Measured on 200 live scenario runs against the Meta Model API (260 graded turns), compared with sending every message to a single tier:

|---|---|

| Turns served by the right tier | **89.6%** (always-Nano 73.1%, always-Ultra 19.2%) |

Most assistants store "I prefer short answers" and treat it as a fact. People often do the opposite: they keep asking for more detail, request rewrites, or ignore the brief reply. The assistant keeps missing, and nothing tells it so.

Model routers usually pick a model by how hard the *question* looks. That ignores the person asking. A simple question from someone whose words and behaviour disagree is exactly where a cheap answer is most likely to miss.

**The Dissonance Router picks a model by how uncertain the agent is about you.**

# Campaign Doctor

**A verifiable AI agent that diagnoses and fixes underperforming ad campaigns.**
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, *Build for Your World* track.

Campaign Doctor ingests a campaign's delivery logs, pacing data and a sample of bid
requests, finds the root cause of under-delivery or overspending — every claim backed by
evidence from the data — proposes concrete fixes, and **proves each fix by replaying it
in an auction simulator** (before/after: delivery, spend, win rate, eCPM) before
recommending it. Most hackathon agents stop at "here is a plausible answer"; this one
has to survive its own verification loop.

  heuristics), an evidence rule enforced in code ("no tool result — no diagnosis"),
  8 synthetic campaigns (failure modes 1–7 + a healthy control, PRD §8).

  simulator HTTP client; live trace panel and before/after panel in the UI.

# PathAble AI

**One world. Different needs. More accessible journeys.** Turn photos of public spaces into **evidence-backed, person-checked reports** of potential accessibility barriers, for people with different needs: moving around (wheelchairs, walkers, prams), seeing, hearing, finding the way, and comfort.

Every barrier category is tagged with the needs it may affect: blocked curb ramps, obstructed footpaths, damaged surfaces, difficult entrances, tactile guidance problems, hard-to-detect obstacles, crossing problems, and signage or wayfinding problems. Visitors can choose their own needs on **My needs** (stored only in their browser, never sent anywhere) and filter community reports by them. Things a photo cannot show, such as whether a signal is audible or a lift works, are never guessed.

**Pilot area: IIT (ISM) Dhanbad.** PathAble AI works inside one configured region at a time. The active region is the IIT (ISM) Dhanbad campus, using its real boundary from OpenStreetMap (way 133882752, a 107-point polygon saved in `lib/regions/iit-ism-dhanbad.json`). Place search, place pages and report locations all use the same point-in-polygon check, so nothing outside the campus is ever shown or saved. Search first uses a campus directory of 89 OpenStreetMap features inside the boundary (`lib/regions/iit-ism-dhanbad.places.json`, rebuilt with `node scripts/fetch-campus-places.mjs`), with case-, punctuation- and typo-tolerant matching and initials such as "NLHC"; only then does it ask Nominatim, held to the campus box (`bounded=1`), and re-checks every result. A place that is not in OpenStreetMap, such as "NAC Auditorium", gets "No matching place found within IIT (ISM) Dhanbad campus." rather than a match elsewhere. **Explore places** shows the campus map with its boundary, category filters and the place list. Agents work out how to use websites: which menu hides a setting, how an editor handles input, when a change is actually saved. **An AI-native coordination agent that turns scattered requests for help in WhatsApp communities into timely, trustworthy, consented matches, powered by Meta Llama.**

                                            │ calls

                                            │

                                            ▲

| **Consent first** | Helpers get a YES/NO opt-in before any contact is shared. Phone numbers are HMAC-hashed for lookup and Fernet-encrypted at rest. Emails and phone numbers are redacted before anything reaches the LLM. |

| **MCP** | Nine tools exposed over stdio or streamable HTTP to any MCP client. |

Hands-free voice control for any Android app. Built for the Meta Global AI
Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track, Build for Your World).

Anyhand is an agent that **acts, verifies, and measures**: it executes voice

latency and results for every run.

Status: working hands-free agent. Say the wake word (configurable, no

  a phone screenshot, the labeled on-screen elements and the step history,
  and returns the next UI action (tap, swipe, type...). Used in-app
  (`app/.../agent/MetaPlanner.kt`) and from the PC harness
  (`harness/meta_client.py`). Real Meta runs are logged with per-step

# TrueTick

**Not sure it's real? Check it first.**

TrueTick is a scam checker for everyone. Share a suspicious message, screenshot, voice note, QR code or link, or let it listen to a phone call on speaker, and it tells you in plain words how risky it is, why, what usually happens next, and exactly what to do.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie Developer Track, "Build for Your World").

## Why

Scams are getting harder to spot. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) 2025 report counts **$20.9 billion** lost to internet crime from over 1 million complaints. People over 60 lost **$7.7 billion**, up 59% in one year. Investment fraud, business email compromise, tech support scams, romance scams and government impersonation lead the losses, and AI voice clones and deepfakes are growing fast.
Source: [FBI IC3 2025 Internet Crime Report](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf)

The idea came from a real call: a "bank officer" who already knew my name and account details asked for a code. Knowing your details doesn't make someone your bank. TrueTick exists to say that out loud, at the moment it matters.

## What it does

| Feature | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Message & link check** | Paste any text, email or link. Muse Spark names the scam, explains why, says what usually happens next and what to do. |
| **Screenshot check** | Upload screenshots of chats, posts, emails or receipts. Muse Spark reads them and checks the text. |
| **Whole-chat check** | Upload up to 8 screenshots of one conversation. TrueTick builds a timeline, names the scam stage (e.g. "asking for money") and points out where their story contradicts itself. |
| **Voice notes** | Muse Voice Transcribe turns the recording into words (fixing common mishearings like "items card" → iTunes card), then it's checked like a message. |
| **Live Call Guard** | Put a call on speaker next to a second device. Every few seconds the call is transcribed; if the caller asks for a code, PIN, gift card, crypto, a "safe account" transfer or remote access, a warning appears instantly, with a running verdict from Muse Spark. |
| **"We visited the website for you"** | Suspicious links are opened in a sealed, throwaway browser on our side. Muse Spark looks at the page and says which brand it's dressed up as, then TrueTick compares that with the real web address. |
| **Before you sign (crypto)** | Paste a wallet signing request, transaction data or a "verify your wallet" message. Without AI, TrueTick decodes what it really does: unlimited token approvals, "approve all" for NFTs, gasless Permit / Permit2 signatures, marketplace listings that give items away, EIP-7702 delegations that hand over the whole wallet, and blind signing. # dotagents
Rules for Agents

## Sync workflow

```bash
make sync
```

This runs the full pipeline: prepares `.ruler/`, generates agent instruction files (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, etc.) via Ruler, installs external skills from `skills-lock.json`, then syncs commands, local repo skills, MCP config, and dot directories to `$HOME`.

## External skills

External skills are declared in `SKILLS.txt` (canonical: repo plus comma-separated selection, no selection installs all) and locked in `skills-lock.json`, both committed. Installs go through the [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills); global scope is scripted here because the CLI's own lock restore is project-only (see [vercel-labs/skills#549](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/issues/549)).

```bash
# Install everything declared in SKILLS.txt that is missing (idempotent;
# regenerates skills-lock.json automatically)
make skills-install

# Update installed skills to latest and refresh the lock
make skills-update

# Regenerate skills-lock.json from SKILLS.txt without installing
# (requires ~/.agents/.skill-lock.json, created by the first global install)
make skills-lock

# Force a reinstall of everything in the lock
make skills-refresh
```

To add skills: edit `SKILLS.txt`, run `make skills-install`, and commit both files. Install-all repos (no selection) need a one-time bootstrap before they appear in the lock: `bunx skills add owner/repo --global --yes --skill '*'` (the `make skills-lock` warning prints the exact command), then `make skills-lock`. To remove: delete from `SKILLS.txt`, run `bunx skills remove <name> --global --yes`, then `make skills-lock`.

Installs track each source's default branch: the skills CLI does not record commit SHAs in its lock yet, so entries are not pinned to a commit.

## Muse bundled skills

[muse](https://dev.meta.ai) (`curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash`) ships its
built-in skills inside the binary rather than on disk, so they are vendored into `skills/`
and synced like any other local skill: `create-plugin`, `create-skill`, `doctor`, `git`,
`grill`, `grill-and-record`, `import`, `manage-settings`, `plan`, `read-session`, `taste`.
`doctor`, `import`, `manage-settings`, `read-session`, `create-plugin`, and `create-skill`
only apply to muse itself; the rest (`taste`, `git`, `plan`, `grill`, `grill-and-record`)
are runtime-agnostic.

Extracted from `~/.local/bin/muse-bin-0.1.0-R708.1`; re-extract by hand after a muse upgrade.

# AI Agent Manager

Run one background [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) agent per intent, and keep track of them from a web UI or the `agentmgr` CLI.

![Agents grouped by project, with an agent's brief: results, problem, solution, a flow diagram and checks](docs/images/agents.jpg)

![The conflict radar: two agents changed the same lines of README.md; the AI judge rates it a collision and suggests which lands first](docs/images/conflict-radar.jpg)

- **Intents in, agents out.** Give a list, one per line (say, a ticket each), and each becomes its own `claude` process. Or pick **One agent for all of it** and a long description goes to a single agent as written.
- **Issue links.** A request that starts with a Jira link is named after the issue (`ABC-123`) and described by its summary, fetched from Jira Cloud (public issues as they are; your company's site after **Settings → Jira**: site, email and API token, kept on this computer and sent only to that site). Without access, the words after the link describe it.
- **Repo or folder.** Give a git URL (cloned once, then each agent gets its own worktree and branch) or a local folder.
  - **Fast clones.** URLs are cloned as partial clones (`--filter=blob:none`): history now, file contents only for what's checked out.
  - **Progress.** Clone and checkout progress shows in the UI and `agentmgr ls`.
  - **Cancel and retry.** Deleting an agent during setup cancels the clone. A failed or interrupted setup can be retried.
  - **Big repo you already have?** `-d <your clone> -w` gives each agent its own worktree of it in seconds.
  - **Plan while it clones.** A planning session lets you talk the task through with Claude while the clone runs. The same session then moves into the repo with the whole conversation.
- **Background terminals.** Agents run inside the daemon's PTYs. Open any agent's live terminal in the browser (**Open terminal**) or in your shell (`agentmgr attach`). Closing the view leaves the agent running.
- **Session IDs are kept.** Each agent is started with a known `--session-id`. **Close session** stops the process but keeps the ID, and bringing it back runs `claude --resume <id>`. **New session** adds another ID to the agent's history; earlier ones stay resumable.
- **Tracking.** For each agent you see its session ID, working folder, repo, branch, head commit, uncommitted changes, PRs and bugs.
- **Results.** The end result at a glance: ✅ done, 🟡 partial, ⛔ blocked or 🔄 in progress, with what was delivered and what's blocking it.

While an agent reads files, edits code, or runs tests, the developer has a gap
in their workflow. Watching terminal output can be tedious; switching to an

# Player Two

An AI co-op partner for blind, low-vision and motor-impaired gamers: it reads the screen,
answers questions and presses the buttons when you ask.

**[Watch the 3 minute demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M-frK7z2au8)**

For players who want help reading a menu, finding a doorway or taking a turn in a
commercial game. Ask a question or delegate an action; Player Two reads the game window,
answers aloud, sends controller or keyboard input, and checks what changed.
Chrono Trigger has the deepest support. Monster Hunter Stories 3 uses a game-specific
battle routine. Red Dead Redemption demonstrates reading, answering and keyboard input.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    mic[Microphone] --> stt[Muse Voice Transcribe]
    stt --> router[Local command router]
    typed[Typed request] --> router
    router --> fast[Local fast path]
    router --> muse[Muse Spark tool loop]
    fast --> exec[Local executors and pathfinding]
    muse -->|Tool request| exec
    exec -->|Observed result| muse
    exec --> input[Virtual controller or keyboard]
    input --> game[Game on the player's PC]
    game --> capture[Screen capture]
    capture --> reader[Local pixel reader]
    capture --> muse
    capture --> sam[SAM 3.1 finding]
    sam --> exec
    reader --> exec
    reader --> voice[Kokoro voice or screen reader]
    muse --> voice
```

**Muse picks the tool for requests that reach the agent. Code finds the path and plays the
turns.** Plain requests go straight from a local router to code, without the agent: "where's
the door?" goes to SAM 3.1, with Muse Spark looking alongside in case SAM misses, and supported
Chrono Trigger commands to an executor. Its default fight routine
chooses attacks, healing and revives with local rules; Muse does not choose those turns.
Kokoro runs locally. The Meta models use hosted APIs. Details and limits are below.

## Live results

game and loaded the same save, with requests typed into the running app. "Done" means the task
finished correctly, checked against the game's screen. Separately, 63 of 63 synthetic spoken lines
matched the typed parser's decisions in the same game and screen context.
