# 3D Gen Model: Photo → CAD with a Language World Model

Given one photo of a car, recover an **editable CAD program**: the parts, the shape of each part, and the order of modelling operations that build it.

The core idea of this project is a **language world model for CAD**. It is a model that reads a modelling state and the next CAD operation, and predicts the resulting state *before the kernel runs it*:

$$
\hat s_{t+1} = W_\phi(s_t, a_t), \qquad s_t = \text{summary of the solid after } t \text{ operations}
$$

A planner $\pi_\theta(a_t \mid \text{image}, s_{\le t})$ writes the program one operation at a time. The world model tells it what each step will do (which part grows or shrinks, by how much, and whether the step will fail), so the planner can check and revise its plan without executing every candidate in a CAD kernel.

![program-writing loop](figures/program_round3.png)
*The model writes a CAD program from the photo (left). The kernel executes it (middle). The overlay (right) shows agreement in green, missing material in red and extra material in blue.*

## What is in this repository

| component | file | role |
|---|---|---|
| Procedural car generator | `carworld/params.py`, `carworld/program.py` | 6 body styles, ~19 design parameters, 19–22 operation CAD programs with ground truth for every step |
| Solid-modelling kernel | `carworld/sdf_kernel.py` | numpy signed-distance kernel: prisms, cylinders, intersections; union / cut / intersect; mirroring; per-surface materials; state summaries |
| Renderer | `carworld/render.py` | sphere tracer producing photo-like images, masks and depth, with randomised camera, paint, lighting and background |
| Metrics | `carworld/metrics.py` | silhouette IoU, depth error, voxel IoU, exact Chamfer distance via the SDF |
| CAD export | `carworld/cq_kernel.py` | the same programs as CadQuery scripts → STEP / STL |
| World-model benchmark | `scripts/build_wm_bench.py`, `scripts/run_world_model.py` | (state, operation) → next state, scored against the kernel |
| Planners | `scripts/run_baseline.py` | from parameter search to a vision-language model that writes the whole CAD program |

Coordinates: millimetres, +X front, +Y left, +Z up, ground at z = 0.

## The state and action spaces

**Action:** one JSON operation, for example:

```json
{"step": 4, "name": "arch_front", "part": "body", "mode": "cut", "mirror": true, "material": "arch",
 "tool": {"type": "cylinder", "axis": "Y", "center": [1551.1, 362.9], "radius": 399.0, "extent": [533.4, 933.0]},
 "comment": "Cut the front wheel arch"}
```

**State:** a compact, model-readable summary of the solid. For each part it records the volume in litres, the bounding box and its minimum corner in mm, the share of the surface covered by each material, and left–right symmetry. It also records a `valid` flag and the kernel's error, if any.

The world model predicts the next state in this same format. Because the summary is text, any language model can act as a world m

# beatsheet

A video editor where an AI agent does the editing and you direct it. Drop in a folder of footage and the agent takes the first turn: it watches and logs every clip, sharpens the brief, and comes back with a few directions to pick from. Pick one and it builds a playable cut. From then on you take turns. You watch, leave notes on anything, and send them; it makes the changes and hands the cut back.

The agent is one you already have, on your own sign-in: **Muse Code**, **Codex** (your ChatGPT plan), **Claude Code** (your Claude plan) or **Antigravity** (your Google account: free, Google AI Pro or Ultra). beatsheet runs it inside the app and gives it the tools to edit, look at frames and render.

Under the hood, **nothing is placed at a fixed time unless it has to be**. A shot starts on a word, a beat, a bar of a section, a moment inside a clip, or another shot. Swap the song or re-record a line, and everything that depends on it re-times itself. Dragging a cut in the timeline snaps to those anchors too.

# f2j: Fortran → JAX, verified

f2j is an agent that translates legacy scientific Fortran into [JAX](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax) one routine at
a time. It then **checks that each translation gives the same answers as the original**. The language model
(Muse Spark on the Meta Model API) only writes and repairs code. Every accept or reject decision comes from running
the original compiled Fortran.

**Live site:** https://mrabbi3.github.io/f2j/ ·
[live Muse Spark report](https://mrabbi3.github.io/f2j/demo/live/report.html) ·
[offline demo report](https://mrabbi3.github.io/f2j/demo/report.html) (rebuilt by CI on every push)

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**.

## Why

Climate, weather, ocean, energy and aerospace models still run on Fortran written before GPUs existed. Rewriting
them by hand takes years, and nobody can prove the rewrite is right. JAX code runs on GPUs and TPUs, batches
thousands of runs with `jax.vmap`, and can be differentiated. That makes calibration and physics-plus-ML models
possible, and the Fortran can do none of it.

LLMs can write the JAX, but they are unreliable judges of their own code. f2j splits the work. **Muse Spark
generates the code, and the original Fortran decides whether it is right.**

## How it works

```
Fortran source
   │
   ▼
① analyze      parse routines, arguments, calls, risks; order leaves first
② oracle       compile the original with f2py: the source of truth
③ test inputs  random cases in value ranges + edge cases; practice set and held-out exam set
   │           gcov coverage shows whether the tests actually reached every line
   ▼
④ translate    Muse Spark writes N JAX candidates (more for harder routines)
⑤ verify       compiles → matches Fortran → works under vmap → gradients match → passes held-out exam
⑥ repair       exact error feedback + bug-pattern hints, up to K rounds
   │           no pass? wrap the original Fortran with jax.pure_callback and flag it
   ▼
⑦ assemble     one importable JAX module + whole-model side-by-side run + benchmark
⑧ report       HTML report; verified translations are remembered for future runs
```

### Where Meta's models fit

| Step | Model call | Settings |
|---|---|---|
| Translate | `muse-spark-1.3` writes several JAX candidates per routine from the Fortran source, the call graph and already-verified callees | Chat Completions, `reasoning_effort=high` |
| Repair | Muse Spark gets the failed candidate, the exact mismatch (max error, index, got/expected) and a bug-pattern hint such as "transposed" or "shifted by one" | Single-turn prompt that includes the original task, up to K rounds |
| Value ranges (optional) | `--propose-ranges` asks Muse Spark for physically sensible input ranges for test generation | JSON output |

The provider is in [`f2j/llm.py`](f2j/llm.py) (`MetaLLM`). It uses the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at
`https://api.meta.ai/v1`, and it tracks tokens and cost, with reasoning tokens counted as output. Claude

# Preflight

Check your Meta ad before Meta does.

Small businesses lose money and ad accounts to rejected ads, and Meta's rejection notices rarely say what exactly to change. Preflight reads the whole ad the way Meta's review does (the image, every word rendered inside it, the copy and the landing page), checks it against all 45 policies in Meta's Advertising Standards, marks each problem on the creative, and fixes it.

## How it uses Meta's models

| Step | Model | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Review | **Muse Spark 1.3** | Reads image + copy + landing page against the full text of Meta's Advertising Standards (about 35k tokens, kept in the prompt cache). Returns a structured verdict through a JSON Schema: every issue names the exact policy, quotes the evidence, and gives a 0–1000 box for anything visible in the image. |
| Locate | **SAM 3.1** | Turns each box into a pixel-accurate mask, so the report outlines the exact element that breaks the rule. |
| Fix the copy | **Muse Spark 1.3** | Rewrites primary text, headline and description to keep the offer and drop what breaks the rules. |
| Fix the image | **Muse Image** | Edits only the flagged elements and keeps the layout and brand. |
| Verify | **Muse Spark 1.3** | Re-checks the fixed ad and shows the change in risk, for example 94% → 14%. |

Reports come in English, Uzbek or Russian.

## Run it on Windows

1. Install **Node.js 22 LTS** from https://nodejs.org (accept the defaults).
2. Unzip this folder, open it, click the address bar, type `cmd` and press Enter.
3. Install the packages:
   ```
   npm install
   ```
4. Run `copy .env.example .env.local`, open `.env.local` in Notepad and paste your key from https://dev.meta.ai (API keys) after `META_API_KEY=`.
5. Optional, after your credits appear on the Billing page: `npm run check-api` confirms the key and models.
6. Start the app:
   ```
   npm run dev
   ```
7. Open http://localhost:3000

Without a key the app runs in **demo mode** on the bundled sample ad, with canned results and no API calls, so the full flow can be tried for free.

## Project layout

```
app/page.tsx              The form and the inspection report
app/api/analyze           Muse Spark review (structured output)
app/api/segment           SAM 3.1 masks for flagged regions
app/api/fix-image         Muse Image edit
lib/prompt.ts             Reviewer instructions + policy corpus
lib/meta.ts               Meta Model API client (chat, SAM stream, images)
data/meta_ad_standards.json  Meta's Advertising Standards, scraped from transparency.meta.com
scripts/scrape_policies.py   Refreshes the policy data
```

## Cost

One check costs about $0.04 with Muse Spark ($0.005 when the policy text is served from cache), each SAM mask $0.0025, each image edit $0.01.

## Limits

Preflight predicts Meta's review; it can't guarantee the outcome. Advertiser-level requirements (business verification, financial services authorization, special ad categories) are listed separately because n

# metacog

**Check what your coding agent says against what it actually did.**

Coding agents (Claude Code, Muse Code, Codex) run commands, edit code and touch infrastructure, and then *tell* you what happened. The failures that hurt are not crashes. They are confident reports that are not true: "all tests pass" after a test was skipped, "deployed" when the pod crashes a minute later, a dependency whose name the model made up.

![A Muse Code agent reports a rollout as done. metacog re-checks the cluster after the agent stops, finds the pod crashed, marks two claims false and sends the report back](docs/caught-deploy.png)

*A real run (2026-11-01). Muse Code rolled out a new version, saw `1/1 Running`, and said "Done". metacog looked at the cluster again after the agent stopped. The pod had crashed, so Meta Muse Spark marked two claims false and the report went back to the agent with that evidence. The agent then investigated, found the crash, and corrected its report.*

## Results

| | |
|---|---|
| **Live deploy trials**, 3 Muse Code + 3 Claude Code runs (commit 9d072cc) | 6 of 6 first reports said "running" for a crashing pod. metacog caught all 6, and all 6 agents corrected themselves ([evidence](bench/results/live/2026-11-01.jsonl), [all rounds](bench/results/live-deploy-trials.md)) |
| **Verifier bench**, 19 false reports, each run 3 times | all 19 sent back, in 3 of 3 runs each |
| **Verifier bench**, 14 honest reports, each run 3 times | none sent back in any of the 42 runs |
| **Cost and latency** per check | median $0.0053 and 4.1 s (max 9.7 s), almost all of it the Muse Spark call |
| **Code checks alone**, the same pipeline with the model removed | block 0 of 19 false reports: why the model makes the call |

The bench cases are written by the author, so read them as a regression suite, not a general accuracy claim. Caveats are under [Benchmark](#benchmark).

## Install

```bash
uv tool install git+https://github.com/song2h/metacog   # or: pipx install git+https://github.com/song2h/metacog
metacog init                                           # stores your Meta Model API key, checks setup
```

Python 3.10+, standard library only. Get a Meta Model API key at [dev.meta.ai](https://dev.meta.ai). The `metacog` package on PyPI is an unrelated project, so install from GitHub as shown.

Without a key, metacog still records sessions, runs every guard (dangerous commands, made-up packages, uploads to China) and shows the dashboard. Claim checks then only warn.

Tests run offline: `uv run pytest`.

## Use

Try it for one session. Nothing is installed into your agent's config:

```bash
metacog wrap claude              # Claude Code with metacog attached
metacog wrap muse                # Muse Code
metacog wrap muse exec "fix the failing test"   # agent arguments pass through
```

The dashboard runs at <http://127.0.0.1:8977>: live timeline, guard decisions with the command, per-claim verdicts with evidence, and the hosts the session connected to.

## 🔴 The problem

**How API security compliance works today — and why it fails.**

Every enterprise has a shelf of security policies: authentication standards, rate-limiting
rules, data-privacy requirements, logging mandates. Every enterprise also has hundreds of
APIs on a gateway. Connecting the two is **entirely manual**:

| Today | Consequence |
|---|---|
| A human reads the policy documents | Takes days; policies are long and change often |
| A human opens each API config and compares it by hand | Error-prone; nobody checks all of them |
| The reviewer must *personally know* GDPR, OWASP, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS… | A scarce, expensive skill — and a single point of failure |
| Findings land in a spreadsheet checklist | Stale the moment a config changes |
| Fixes are figured out from scratch each time | Inconsistent remediation, no standard citations |

**What existed before this project:** manual security reviews, hand-maintained validation
checklists, and tribal knowledge. There was **no agentic system** that could read an
organization's own policies and autonomously judge a live API estate against them.

The result is predictable — security gaps ship to production, audits are reactive, and
compliance depends on whether one expert happened to be in the room.

---

## 🟢 The solution

**Autonomous Security Auditor — an agentic AI application.**

Two autonomous agents replace the manual loop end to end:

```
Ingest policies ONCE  →  Audit ANYTIME  →  Get a prioritised fix plan

# ADA Piano Teacher

**ADA helps blind and low vision learners practice piano through conversation.** Printed scores and visual keyboard cues make independent practice difficult. ADA connects a reviewed score, your MIDI piano, audible examples, and spoken feedback so you can choose music, play, and find the next thing to practice without using a mouse.

**Status: integrated desktop prototype.** Voice controls, MIDI practice, optional calibrated hand observations, AI coaching, and local session exports are connected. It still needs trials with blind learners and real hardware before it can be called a finished accessible product.

## A practice session

1. **Choose music:** load a checked passage from *Für Elise* or *Ode to Joy*, or import and review a MusicXML score. PDF conversion is available through Audiveris.
2. **Listen:** play the passage on a connected MIDI instrument at a chosen fixed tempo, or hear individual notes and short sequences.
3. **Play:** use guided practice for immediate note and chord feedback, or record an uninterrupted play-through.
4. **Review:** after a play-through, hear or read a measure-by-measure report, replay your performance, and ask the optional ADA Coach what to work on next.

MIDI tells ADA which keys were played. After spoken calibration, an optional camera can associate nearby fingertips with MIDI attacks. Those observations are estimates, not proof of which finger pressed a key or a judgment of correct technique.

## What works today

### Music and practice

| Feature | Current behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Checked music | The built-in catalog has passages from *Für Elise* (both, right, or left hand) and *Ode to Joy* (right hand). These can be loaded by name without reviewing a file first. |
| Import and review | Read `.musicxml`, `.xml`, and `.mxl`; select a part, staff, voice, and measure range; hear notes and rests; explicitly approve a passage before use. Audiveris can convert PDFs. Spoken review is available, but recognition still needs checking against a trusted source; corrections happen in an external score editor. |
| MIDI reader and reference | A virtual keyboard shows held notes, velocity, channel, sustain, and key-hold duration. Select a MIDI output to play a note, sequence, or approved passage; outgoing reference notes are kept separate from learner input. |
| Guided practice | The local tutor waits for the expected note or chord and gives immediate pitch feedback. It works without an API key and does not grade written rhythm. |
| Play-through report | ADA records MIDI without interrupting the learner, then reports wrong, missed, and extra notes by measure. It also estimates the learner's tempo and flags early or late attacks, hesitations, and short key holds. |

### Interaction and supporting tools

| Feature | Current behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Voice controls and simple screen | A quiet ethereal background, Talk/Stop/Tools buttons, message field, and selectable transcript. Voice commands handle pr

# Muse CLI Chat (unofficial)

### [Inception: A Muse Inside Muse](https://blog.codemarc.net/inception-a-muse-inside-muse)

VS Code / Cursor sidebar chat that drives Meta’s **Muse Code** CLI (`muse exec --json`). The agent harness stays Muse; this extension is only the IDE UI.

**Not affiliated with Meta.** Muse Code, Muse Spark, and related marks belong to Meta. Install and authenticate Muse separately: [Muse Code docs](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code).

Privacy and security: [PRIVACY.md](./PRIVACY.md) · [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md)

## Requirements

- macOS or Linux (Muse Code CLI does not support Windows yet)
- [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code) installed and signed in (or `META_API_KEY` set)
- VS Code or Cursor
- An open workspace **folder** that is not a symlink root (Muse rejects reparse points)

```bash
curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | sh
muse login
# or: export META_API_KEY=...   # must be visible to the editor process
```

The sidebar treats Muse as ready only when the CLI is present **and** credentials are visible (`META_API_KEY` in the editor env, `~/.config/muse/auth.json` with an inline key/token **or** a Keychain-backed `muse login`, or `muse.useEchoProvider`). A key set only in your terminal shell does not reach Cursor/VS Code unless you launch the app from that shell or set it in the GUI environment.

## Install (published)

After this extension is on a marketplace:

- **VS Code Marketplace:** search “Muse CLI Chat” (publisher `codemarc`)
- **Open VSX / Cursor:** same extension id `codemarc.muse-cli-chat`

Or install a local `.vsix`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/codemarc/muse-code.git
cd muse-code
bun install
bun run package
code --install-extension muse-cli-chat-0.1.8.vsix
# Cursor: cursor --install-extension muse-cli-chat-0.1.8.vsix
```

## Develop

```bash
git clone https://github.com/codemarc/muse-code.git
cd muse-code
bun install
bun run compile
```

Open this folder in VS Code/Cursor and press **F5** (Run Muse CLI Chat Extension). That runs `bun run compile` first (Bun must be on your PATH). Optional: **Run Muse CLI Chat Extension (watch)** for `bun run watch`. In the Extension Development Host:

1. Open a real directory (not a symlink)
2. Command Palette → **Muse CLI Chat: Open Chat** (or click the Muse activity icon)
3. Optional: set `muse.useEchoProvider` to `true` for offline JSONL UI testing
4. Send a prompt (**⌘Enter** on macOS, **Ctrl+Enter** on Linux, or the Send button). Enter inserts a newline. Type `@` to attach a file with contents, or **+ Attach** for the current file, open editors, Problems, or terminal output.

## Commands

| Command | Action |
|---------|--------|
| Muse CLI Chat: Open Chat | Open the configured native chat surface |
| Muse CLI Chat: Open in Editor Panel | Open the native chat in an editor panel (default shortcut `⌘⇧R` on macOS, `Ctrl+Shift+R` on Linux; rebind in Keyboard Shortcuts) |
| Muse CLI Chat: Open in Sidebar | Open the native chat in the sidebar |
|

# ClimbIQ — AI bouldering coach

Upload a recorded boulder attempt and ClimbIQ analyses your climbing **in the
browser**, then coaches you like a human coach would — move by move.

Think **chess.com's move analysis, for climbing**: every move gets a verdict, a
clear instruction, and the reason behind it.

## What you get after an analysis

- **Annotated footage** — your real video with the detected body skeleton, the
  target hold for each move, movement arrows, and a floating instruction label,
  all synced to playback.
- **Move-by-move coaching** (right panel) — a verdict (`Best` / `Good` /
  `Inaccuracy` / `Mistake`), the single instruction (“Right hand up to the
  sloper”), the reason, a *Your attempt vs Recommended* compare, ordered
  movement steps, and a coach note.
- **Feedback** — short, direct, actionable notes: what you did well and what to
  fix, each tied to a timestamp.
- **Climber metrics** — Confidence, Stability, Centre of Mass and Balance, plus
  scored skills (Movement fluency, Body positioning, Footwork, Arm efficiency).
- **Demonstrate the beta** — a player that walks through the suggested sequence
  for when you’re stuck and want to see how to do it.

## How it works

```
Video upload
  → MediaPipe Pose Landmarker     real 33-point body tracking, in-browser
  → Movement + biomechanics       joint angles, 2D COM, stability, sway, pauses,
                                   move segmentation (deterministic TypeScript)
  → SAM 3.1 hold detection        best-effort hold segmentation (via a proxy)
  → Muse Spark coaching           Meta Model API interprets the measurements
  → Annotated review + coaching
```

- **Pose estimation is real** — `@mediapipe/tasks-vision` tracks 33 landmarks
  across sampled frames. The skeleton on the video is the detected pose.
- **Biomechanics are measured, not guessed** (`src/lib/biomechanics.ts`):
  centre of mass, torso inclination, joint angles, support-triangle stability,
  COM sway/jerk, asymmetry. These are **2D approximations from one camera.**
- **Muse Spark interprets** those numbers into coaching — it does not measure
  them. The call runs **server-side**, so your API key is never exposed.
- **Hold detection (SAM 3.1) is best-effort** and labelled *approximate*. If it
  finds too few holds, the beta falls back to suggested targets from your hand
  positions. Hold **shape** = type (jug/crimp/sloper…); hold **colour** on the
  wall is sampled for future route filtering.
- **Honest by design:** beta is *suggested* movement, COM/stability are
  *approximate*, and if a real analysis can’t run you get clearly-labelled
  sample data that explains why.

## Tech stack

React 19 · TypeScript · Vite · Tailwind CSS 4 · `@mediapipe/tasks-vision`
(pose) · Meta Model API — **Muse Spark** (coaching) + **SAM 3.1** (holds) ·
Netlify Functions (Vercel also supported).

---

## Setup

### 1. Install

```bash
npm install
```

On install, `scripts/prepare-mediapipe.mjs` runs automatically: it copies the
MediaPi

# Image Generation Backend (OpenAI)

Two endpoints. Both take an uploaded image and return a PNG.

| Endpoint | You send | Prompt comes from |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /generate/custom` | `image` file + `prompt` (one line) | You |
| `POST /generate/preset` | `image` file + `style` | Hardcoded in `prompts.py` |

`style` is one of: `studio`, `lifestyle`, `ai_model`, `festival`, `offers`.

## Setup

```bash
cd image-backend
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env        # then put your real OPENAI_API_KEY in .env
uvicorn main:app --reload
```

## Test

Easiest: open http://localhost:8000/docs, expand an endpoint, click
"Try it out", choose a file, and Execute.

Or with curl:

```bash
# Custom prompt
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/generate/custom \
  -F "image=@product.png" \
  -F "prompt=on a wooden table with morning sunlight" \
  -o out.png

# Preset
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/generate/preset \
  -F "image=@product.png" \
  -F "style=studio" \
  -o out.png
```

## Notes

- Change the prompts in `prompts.py`. `COMMON_RULES` is appended to every
  prompt to keep the product unchanged.
- `model` and `quality` can be sent with each request (see below). `.env` only sets the
  defaults used when a request leaves them out.
- Image edits are billed per image; `low` quality is cheapest for testing.
- Max upload is 10 MB (PNG, JPEG or WEBP).

## Testing models and tracking cost

`compare_models.py` makes ONE image by default (flare, quality high):

```bash
python compare_models.py product.png --style studio
python compare_models.py product.png --style studio --model gpt-image-2.5-sunburst --quality xhigh
python compare_models.py product.png --style studio --all --dry-run   # plan + estimate, no spend
python compare_models.py product.png --style studio --all             # all 10 (asks first)
```

- Images are saved as `comparisons/<time>/<model>__<quality>.png`, with an `index.html` to view them.
- Every call's cost is computed from the token usage OpenAI returns, printed, and appended to
  `comparisons/cost_log.csv` with a running total. If no usage is returned it falls back to a rough
  per-quality estimate and marks the row `estimate`.
- The backend (`main.py`) logs to `cost_log.csv` too. Each response carries an `X-Cost-INR` header,
  and `GET /cost` returns the total spent.
- Rates live in `costing.py`. Your OpenAI Usage page is the real source of truth.

## Choosing model and quality per request

Both endpoints accept optional form fields:

| Field | Values | If omitted |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | `gpt-image-2.5-flare`, `gpt-image-2.5-sunburst`, `gpt-image-1` | `OPENAI_IMAGE_MODEL` |
| `quality` | `auto`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` | `OPENAI_IMAGE_QUALITY` |
| `size` | `auto` or WxH (multiples of 16, max edge 3840, ratio at most 3:1) | `1024x1024` |

`xhigh` and `max` work only on the 2.5 models. Invalid values are rejected before any
OpenAI call, so they cost nothing.

# Bug2PR

**Turn a screen recording of a web bug into a reproduced failing test and a verified pull request.**

Bug reports are usually vague ("checkout is broken, see video"), and someone has to watch the recording, guess the steps and try to reproduce it before any fix can start. Bug2PR takes any `.mp4` screen recording, works out what the user did, reproduces the bug live in a real browser, writes a regression test that fails because of the bug, fixes the code until that test passes while the repo's own checks stay green, and prepares a pull request for a human to approve.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie track, theme *Build for Your World*.

```
 screen recording ──► Understand ──► Reproduce live ──► Failing test ──► Fix ──► Pull request
   (.mp4)            SAM 3.1 +       Muse Spark         verification     Muse Wonder   human
                     Muse Spark      computer use       gate             or Muse Spark sign-off
                                                                         Open (open weights)
```

![Bug2PR after a real run: video understood, bug reproduced live, failing test gated, fix verified, PR awaiting sign-off](docs/images/ui-run-done.png)

## For judges: 5-minute tour

1. **Watch the demo video (3 min):** [youtu.be/mkzIdOfx0JE](https://youtu.be/mkzIdOfx0JE). Every run in it is real; nothing is mocked.
2. **See one complete run without installing anything:** [docs/sample-runs/shadcn-search-by-id/](docs/sample-runs/shadcn-search-by-id/). It holds everything the models produced for one bug video:
   - `repro-steps-from-video.json`: SAM 3.1 cursor interactions and the steps Muse Spark extracted from [the video](eval/bugs/shadcn-search-by-id/video.mp4);
   - `regression-test.spec.ts`: the Playwright test generated from the live computer-use replay. It fails on the bug 3/3 times;
   - `fix-muse-wonder.diff` and `fix-muse-spark-open.diff`: the fix from Muse Wonder (Meta Model API) and from open-weight Muse Spark Open (private mode);
   - `pull-request.md`: the PR description with all the evidence.

   The [real Actual Budget bug](docs/sample-runs/actual-8475-running-balance/) has the same files.
3. **Check the numbers:** [Results](#results) below, full tables in [docs/eval-results.md](docs/eval-results.md).
4. **Read the core code** (each file is short and commented):

   | Step | File |
   |---|---|
   | SAM 3.1 tracks the cursor → interactions | [`src/pipeline/track-cursor-with-sam.ts`](src/pipeline/track-cursor-with-sam.ts) |
   | Muse Spark: video → grounded repro steps | [`src/pipeline/extract-repro-steps.ts`](src/pipeline/extract-repro-steps.ts) |
   | Muse Spark computer use replays the bug | [`src/pipeline/replay-with-computer-use.ts`](src/pipeline/replay-with-computer-use.ts) |
   | Failing-test gate (3/3 fails, sensitivity check) | [`src/pipeline/reproduce-bug-to-failing-test.ts`](src/pipeline/reproduce-bug-to-failing-test.ts) |

# Smoke or Vog?

A Hawaiʻi haze explainer built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

When the sky over the islands turns hazy, people want to know two things: is it
volcanic vog from Kīlauea or smoke from a wildfire, and what should I do about it?
**Smoke or Vog?** takes GOES-18 satellite haze detections, uses Meta's models to
segment and interpret the haze, and produces a plain-language alert card for the
affected district.

Built on [Meta Model API](https://dev.meta.ai/docs):

| Role | Model | Endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Segment haze regions | `sam-3.1` | `POST /v1/responses` (streamed) |
| Interpret the scene (vog vs smoke), JSON output | `muse-spark-1.3` | `POST /v1/responses` with `text.format` json_schema |
| Render the alert card | `muse-image-1.0` | `POST /v1/images/generations` |

The images we segment are true-color GOES-West GeoColor (or MODIS for older dates) from
NASA GIBS. The public [Kahu Ola](https://kahuola.org) API is used only as an external
detection signal (GOES-18 ADP haze mask + metadata, FIRMS hotspots), never as the image.
Kahu Ola's haze layer is an estimate rather than an official product. For official vog
information, see <https://vog.ivhhn.org/>.

> Status: detection chain working on four cases (live, Kīlauea 2026-10-17, Maui 2023-08-08,
> Mauna Loa 2022-12-01). Curated outputs are in [`demo/`](demo/).
> No alert generation or demo UI yet. See [PLAN.md](PLAN.md).

## Built during the hackathon (Oct 31–Nov 4, 2026)

Everything in this repository is new work, created during the hackathon (first commit
Oct 31, 2026, 12:16 HST). That includes the pipeline, the agentic classifier, alerts, the live
publisher, the website, tests, scripts and docs. Full list: [`docs/NEW_WORK.md`](docs/NEW_WORK.md).

**Pre-existing external inputs:** the **Kahu Ola public API** (`/api/hazards/smoke-sat`,
`/api/firms/hotspots`). It was built before the event by the same author and is used here
**read-only, as a data source**, over HTTPS like any public API. No Kahu Ola source code is in
this repository.

## The AI does not give medical advice

**Health guidance is never chosen or written by AI.** Each result type (`wildfire_smoke`,
`vog_kilauea`, `vog_mauna_loa`, `dust`, `uncertain`, `no_plume`) maps to a fixed, curated list of
two or three official lines, which are quoted verbatim from
[`assets/health_sources.json`](assets/health_sources.json) (Hawaiʻi DOH / IVHHN for vog, EPA AirNow
for smoke and particles). `no_plume` gets no guidance. Each curated line is matched by its exact
opening text, and the build fails if that line doesn't exist in the official text.
- **English** lines are the official text, unchanged.
- **The model** (Muse Spark) only translates those fixed lines. Translations are labelled
  "translation of official guidance, machine-translated". It also writes a short situation
  summary (what the satellite shows, where and when) and the "satellite estimate, not an
  official warning" disclaimer.

# SignalCut — product photos in, 31-second video ad out

Drop in up to 8 product photos + one prompt. SignalCut writes the script from
your photos, voices it, scores the music, directs every scene, and burns in
the captions — a 720×1280 portrait MP4 ready to post. Free, local-first, no
accounts needed for the core pipeline.

![Landing page](docs/shots/landing.png)

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon × Cerebral Valley**
(Indie Developer track, *Build for Your World*) on Meta's **SAM 3.1** +
**Muse Spark** models.

## Screenshots

| Render room (`/app`) | Finished ad player |
|---|---|
| ![Studio form and history](docs/shots/studio.png) | ![Finished VELMARA ad with player](docs/shots/player.png) |

Real frames from a generated ad (VELMARA Vitamin C Glow Serum, 31.019s):

| Hook (0:02) | Mid (0:14) | CTA (0:28) |
|---|---|---|
| ![Ad hook frame](docs/shots/ad-hook.jpg) | ![Ad mid frame](docs/shots/ad-mid.jpg) | ![Ad CTA frame](docs/shots/ad-cta.jpg) |

## How it works

Five stages, one job, all on your machine:

```text
photos + prompt ──▶ BRIEF ──▶ VOICE ──▶ MUSIC ──▶ RENDER ──▶ PUBLISH ──▶ MP4
                    Muse     Kokoro    ACE-Step  Remotion    library
                    script   + Whisper bed/synth + depth     + history
```

1. **Brief** — Muse Spark writes a 52–62 word voiceover from your photos +
   prompt and picks a direction packet (mood / voice / pace). Offline? A
   local synthesizer + keyword fallback keeps the pipeline running.
2. **Voice** — Kokoro-82M renders the VO; faster-whisper word timestamps cut
   every act and caption to the narration. Overflow guard: a too-long VO is
   shortened (hook + brand tail) and re-rendered once, then the timeline is
   clipped — never rescaled — into the 930-frame slot.
3. **Music** — ACE-Step 1.5 generates a directed bed (BPM/key per mood), or a
   synth bed when the server is offline; voice-keyed ducking + whoosh/riser/
   thump SFX, hard-trimmed to 31s.
4. **Render** — Remotion `AdGenericV1`: VO-timed acts, official transitions,
   Depth Anything V2 parallax, macro crops, broadcast subtitles, brand reveal.
5. **Publish** — MP4 + meta JSON land in `public/clips/` and in your reel.

The web UI polls every 2s and is refresh-safe (`?job=` restores progress).
One render runs at a time (second submit gets 409); uploads cap at 8 photos,
10 MB each.

## Anti-generic engine

Output varies with the prompt instead of re-skinning one template:

- **10 moods** (cozy, cinematic, bold, elegant, playful, fresh, dark, retro,
  minimal, festive) × **10 voice characters** × **3 paces** —
  `scripts/lib/direction.mjs`, resolved live from Muse or from keywords.
- **3 act layouts** (stack / cards / macro), **title vs cold-open hooks**,
  **stack vs minimal reveals**, and adaptive pacing (1–3 sentences per act).
- Verified A/B: the same photos render visibly different bold vs elegant cuts.

## Quickstart

Requirements: Node 20+, Python 3.10+ with `uv`, `ffmpeg` on PATH. GPU
optional (CPU works;

# Meta Coding Game

**Learn to think like a programmer, and then like a software engineer, with Meta's Muse models.**

A puzzle game where Bolt the robot runs your block program on a grid, plus **Tracks**: hands-on
challenges for data structures, algorithms, async programming, frontend, backend and the cloud.
Meta's models design the levels, write the stories, coach you, paint the worlds, write Manim
animations, and read your sketches, photos, notes, videos, claps and voice. The levels also play
inside AI chats as an **MCP App**.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme "Build for Your World").
(The code and the npm package are still called `loopwise`, the project's working name.)

![The game: a while-loop level in the Muse Image "underwater ruins" world](docs/images/game.png)

## What you can do

- **Ten concepts in the block game:** sequencing, loops, conditionals, while loops, functions,
  variables, recursion, debugging, algorithms (right-hand rule, linear search, lawn-mower
  coverage) and efficiency (Big-O).
- **More than walking to an exit:** painting puzzles (draw a square, a spiral, windows, a fence;
  mow a lawn row by row), gems, keys and locked doors, mazes, and step budgets.
- **Big-O you can see:** each level's worlds come in different sizes, so after every run a card
  fits your step counts against the world size and says O(1), O(n) or O(n²). Efficiency levels

  maze, rooms, islands, spiral, arena, river), or, offline, the generator makes one (about half
  are painting puzzles).
- **Story mode:** Muse Spark writes a 10-chapter adventure, one chapter per concept. Each
  chapter's level is designed when you reach it, as the next scene of the story.
- **Level of the day:** one Muse-designed level per day for everyone, with the history kept.

**An AI operating system for small government suppliers.** KounOS helps a supplier decide which contracts are worth pursuing, then keeps every awarded order on track until it's delivered and paid. # Retake Coach

[![tests](https://github.com/roninram/retake-coach/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/roninram/retake-coach/actions/workflows/tests.yml)

Catch an ungradable fundus photo while the patient is still in the chair.

In diabetic eye screening, a technician photographs the retina and sends the photos on to be graded. When a photo is
too blurry, badly aimed or partly covered, nobody can grade it, and the patient has to come back. This happens often.
In a US telehealth program, 12.4% of eyes photographed with a non-mydriatic camera were ungradable
([Silva et al., *Diabetes Care* 2014](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc13-1292)). With a handheld non-mydriatic camera in
India, 23.9% of images were ungradable
([Davila et al., *Ophthalmologica* 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5733780)).

Retake Coach checks each photo in about a second, on the computer next to the camera. It says **keep** or **retake**.
For a retake, it says what to fix: focus, aim, or something blocking the view. For aim, it measures where the optic
disc and macula are, tells whether the photo is the macula view or the disc view, and says what is off for that view. For something in the way, it marks where on the photo it is. It
turns away pictures that are not regular fundus photos, such as a widefield image or the wrong file.

No photo leaves that computer. Each instruction is a standard sentence built from what was measured. At the end of a
visit or a batch, Muse Spark writes a short coach's note from the session's counts in words: the most common problem,
one habit that would prevent it, and any view still missing.

It checks photo quality only. It does not look for disease and gives no medical advice.
The [model card](MODEL_CARD.md) puts intended use, data, results, limits and privacy on one page.

What's on the two pages:
- **One photo** (`/`): keep or retake, one instruction, the measured disc and macula on the photo, and for an
  obstruction, the area that is in the way. A visit checklist shows which of the four usual views are kept so far:
  each eye, centred on the macula and on the disc. A missing view is clear before the patient leaves, and the coach's
  note sums up the visit.
- **Many photos** (`/batch`): drop a session's photos or a whole folder and get a table with keep or retake, what to
  fix, the eye and the field, plus a CSV download. It can also watch a folder, such as the one a camera exports to over
  Wi-Fi, and check each photo as it arrives. The coach's note sums up the batch.
- **Guide** (`/guide`): what each word, number and mark on the pages means, from "flagged from" and the energy to the
  blue area, the two views and the visit report's columns.

Switching between the pages, or reloading one, keeps what has been checked. The server holds it in memory until it
restarts; "New patient" and "Clear list" start over.

# GoalFault AI

> **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie Track)**  
> 🎥 **[Watch 3-Minute Video Walkthrough](https://youtu.be/W4utzuJIgNA)** · 📋 **[Read Hackathon Submission Brief](SUBMISSION.md)** · ⚡ **10-Second Offline Verification:** `python -m scripts.verify`

[![Verification](https://img.shields.io/badge/verification-20%2F20%20passed-brightgreen)](#)
[![Meta Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Meta%20Model-Muse%20Spark%201.3-blue)](#)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green)](LICENSE)

Stress tests for AI agents that can take real actions.

GoalFault puts a tool-using customer support agent, running on Meta Muse Spark 1.3, inside a fake support system. It pushes the agent with difficult requests and then checks what the agent actually *did* against written policies.

The problem I care about is simple to state. An agent can be very good at hitting its number while the number is not the real goal. A support bot measured on tickets closed can close tickets that were never solved. A bot told to keep customers happy can issue refunds it was not allowed to give. On a dashboard, both look like success.

GoalFault is a small lab for finding those cases, proving them with the exact tool calls that caused them, and checking whether a guard at the tool layer would have stopped them.

## How it works

![GoalFault AI System Architecture](docs/architecture.png)

1. **Describe a situation** you want to test in plain English, or ask Muse to propose one by reading the tool list and policies.
2. **Review it.** Every test starts as `proposed`. Nothing runs until a person approves it, and the customer message can be edited first.
3. **Run it** in one of two ways:
   - a *scripted fixture*, which is a fixed list of tool calls. It is free and gives the same result every time.
   - a *live Muse agent*, which decides its own tool calls.
4. **Every tool call goes to an in-memory sandbox.** GoalFault records the arguments, whether the call was allowed, and the resulting state.
5. **Policy rules**, checked by GoalFault's own rule interpreter, look at the executed calls and the final state. The model is never asked to grade itself.
6. **If a rule was broken**, the trace is shrunk to the fewest actions that still break it. The same actions can then be replayed with tool-level guards switched on.

A live agent that refuses the bad request is a normal, valid result. It is recorded as a pass, not hidden.

## Three kinds of runs

These are kept separate in storage, the API and the UI, because mixing them up would make the results meaningless.

| Source | What it is | Calls Meta? |
|---|---|---|
| `demo_fixture` | Scripted tool calls written by hand to exercise a policy | No |
| `muse` | Tool calls chosen by Meta Muse Spark during a live run | Yes |
| `replay` | The recorded calls of an earlier run, re-executed with or without guards | No |

A fixture violation shows the checker works. It says nothing about how Muse behaves. Only `muse` runs ar

# FraudPause

**The pause that stops the payment.**

FraudPause is a bank-integration-free fraud-prevention shield: it needs only the user's permission, never a bank's. It monitors communication channels — SMS, WhatsApp, calls, QR stickers — not banking or payment channels. It never sees accounts, transactions, or payments. It advises; it does not block payments.

*Truecaller judges the number. FraudPause judges the story.*

## Live demo

https://fraudpause.vercel.app/ — public, no sign-in required.

## Features

**Door 1 — Check before you pay**

- Paste/screenshot/call check: paste a text or email, attach a screenshot, or describe a call; get a verdict card (Likely scam / Suspicious — slow down / No red flags found) with red flags, what to do now, and what to say.
- WhatsApp-forward check: paste a forwarded WhatsApp message; the verdict renders as FraudPause's reply in a chat thread.
- SMS screening simulation: a mock inbox of sample messages with flags pre-applied, as if screened on arrival. Tap a message to see why it was flagged.
- QR-photo check: photograph a QR sticker (upload or live camera); the QR is decoded on-device and the hidden link is checked, with a vision tamper check (sticker edges, peeling, misalignment). FraudPause never confirms a sticker QR as genuine.
- Voice input + spoken verdict: hold-to-talk dictation into the message/call inputs, and a "Hear this verdict" button that reads the verdict aloud.
- "I already sent it" aftermath checklist: freeze/recall/dispute steps for after a payment went through.

**Door 2 — Triage**

- Synthetic AML alert cases for analyst practice: case summary, red flags vs benign explanations, risk rating, recommended disposition, and a copyable draft memo.
- The human decides. Training/demonstration only — all cases are synthetic.

## Tech stack

React + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. Serverless functions hold the API key server-side: `api/chat` calls Muse Spark for verdicts — it reads the pasted text, uploaded screenshots, and QR photos, then returns the verdict. `api/transcribe` calls Muse Voice Transcribe for push-to-talk dictation. QR decoding runs on-device with jsQR. If server transcription is unavailable, voice input falls back to the browser's built-in speech recognition; the spoken verdict uses the browser's built-in speech synthesis.

## Run locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:5173 in a browser. On Windows PowerShell, if `npm.ps1` is blocked by execution policy, use `npm.cmd run dev` instead.

```bash
npm run build   # typecheck + production build
```

## Environment variable

`META_API_KEY` — get your own key at https://dev.meta.ai/api-keys.

To supply the key locally:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

(Windows PowerShell: `copy .env.example .env`.) Then open `.env` and set `META_API_KEY` to your key. **Never commit your key** — `.env` is already in `.gitignore`; only `.env.example` (key left blank) belongs in the repo.

# Teleion Fabric: the durable task queue and storage engine

> **Start at the main repository:** https://github.com/ta-amps/teleionlabs-teleion-fabric
> **Film:** [three-minute video file](https://teleionlabs.com/media/main-film-20261104o.mp4)

A pull-based durable task queue and atomic Task Object store for agent swarms.

Teleion Fabric is where independent AI agents claim durable Tasks over HTTP or MCP and keep checked Task Objects without sharing database credentials or stepping on each other.

Everything in Teleion Fabric is either a **Task** or a **Task Object**, and a worker never approves its own work (`maker != checker`):

- **Tasks** are leased units of work. A worker claims one under a fencing token and checks in, or parks it across hours or days. A separate worker checks it when the work needs that, and it finishes with a record: a digest over exactly what was written.
- **Task Objects** are the shared records and files that Tasks read, make and reuse. Each is versioned with compare-and-set and content-addressed by digest, so no version is lost or silently overwritten.

The live API still uses older machine names in some paths and fields, as the example below shows: Tasks are `verbs` and Task Objects are `nouns`.

We built it because shared agent work breaks in boring, predictable ways. Two agents grab the same task. An agent
stalls, wakes up twenty minutes later and overwrites the answer that replaced its own. A retry saves the same
result twice. Someone asks who did what, and nobody can say. Teleion Fabric gives each of those failures a rule, and
each rule a test.

## See it

A real call and its real output, November 4, 2026, 02:07 UTC:

```console
$ curl -s 'https://fabric.teleionlabs.com/ns/main/v1/verbs?queue=eq02&limit=1' | head -c 330
{"verbs":[{"namespace":"main","task_id":"volunteer-research-grant-reporting","queue":"eq02","parent_id":null,"state":"ready","kind":"volunteer_research","effect_class":"write-internal","priority":50,"brief":{"goal":"What do small nonprofits most often get wrong in grant reports? List 3 public sources with an exact quote from eac
```

## Notes

- An open caller can claim and report open Tasks, and it can't review any work. Admin and key routes stay closed.
- This repository's name, Python package and commands keep an older code name.

## For your agent

Add these four lines to your agent's `AGENTS.md`:

```text
Read https://teleionlabs.com/llms.txt first. No key is needed through December 31, 2026.
Search the shared Task Objects before you build anything.
Claim one Task at a time, and check in while you work.
Report once, with your result. A different worker checks it.
```

## Worker execution policy

Shared work runs as a claimed Task on an authorized worker. Agents on our servers are normal too, inside our spending caps and with records. The architecture has only Task Objects, Tasks, surfaces and narrow infrastructure, and Teleion Fabric is infrastructure. Seed packs bundle Tasks and Task Objects;

# Mixray

**Point at a sound. Hear it alone. Learn to play it.**

Built with Muse Spark Open

**Live:** https://mixray.vercel.app

**Demo video (2:48):** https://youtu.be/sdNPUq3Tu7o

**Judges:** the access key is in the submission notes.

![Mixray marks the piano in a video, then the part is played on the keys and scored bar by bar](.github/assets/mixray-demo.gif)

*Recorded from the app against the live engine. In Practice the keys were pressed by a script on the notes of the part, not by hand. The café clip is AI-generated in Google Flow and labelled as such; see [CREDITS.md](CREDITS.md).*

Drop in a track or a video you own, then pick one sound out of the mix: type what you want, take a
suggestion, or draw over the instrument in the video. Mixray isolates it, shows what it plays and
teaches you to play it on a keyboard, with a coach that reads your take.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), problem statement
*Build for Your World*.

**Built during the event.** The first commit is from Oct 26, 2026, and all code in this repository
was written during the hackathon. The models and datasets it uses already existed; they are listed
below and in [CREDITS.md](CREDITS.md).

## Why

I have loved EDM since 2017. Every few weeks a melody from an artist I follow would stay in my head
and I would want to play it. Getting there meant a stem splitter, a transcription app, a tutorial
that might not exist for that song, and a DAW that felt like a cockpit. I am learning keyboard now,
and most of those evenings ended before I played a single bar.

I am not unusual. Making music is common: MIDiA Research counted
[76 million music creators in 2023](https://www.hypebot.com/highlights-from-midias-state-of-the-music-creator-economy-report/),
up 12% in a year. Sticking with it is not. Fender's CEO has said that
[90% of first-time players abandon the instrument within their first year](https://fortune.com/2022/10/21/guitar-industry-fender-ceo-credits-diversity-players-pandemic-revival)
(a figure from the company's own research). In a 2022
[YouGov survey of 3,000 US adults](https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/43512-young-americans-increasingly-exposed-music),
about half of those who never learned an instrument wish they had, and 51% of people who quit the
guitar regret it. The wish is there. The path from "I love this sound" to "I can play it" is what
breaks.

That path runs through recordings. Studying how popular musicians learn by ear,
[Liscio and Brown](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04058) write that "the recording stands as the source
of truth for popular musicians." But a recording is a mix, and the tools that turn audio into notes
expect one part at a time: Spotify's Basic Pitch, for one, says it
["works best on one instrument at a time"](https://github.com/spotify/basic-pitch).

Tutorials exist for hit songs. Mixray is for everything else: the piano in the corner of a video,
a street musician's tune, the bass line in a track

# Sourcebound

Sourcebound turns one short brief into a whole course. The author states who the learners are, what they must be able to do and what the course must cover, then presses Build. A chain of agents on Meta models writes the course's through-line case, a lecture for every topic, one picture per topic and typed exercises cut from each lecture. Code checks everything a learner can see (code compiles, cloze blanks are short, options share one shape, matching has enough pairs, ordering keys follow the stated order); a corrector model fixes what code flags; answers are graded by code, never by a model. The tutor answers "not in the materials" instead of guessing. The unit of output is a course (plan, modules, topics, typed blocks), not an answer. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, Indie track, Build for Your World, solo.

- **Live:** https://sourcebound.io (the example course "Python for a shop owner" is open to every signed-in user)
- **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/ugFaPW0U6zM
- **On X:** https://x.com/bars_lg/status/2118147277168787764
- **Hackathon:** https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon

Every model call is listed on the run page and on the course's agent-chain page with its model, step, tokens, cost and latency.

## What existed before / what was built this week

Nothing existed. This repository was created on 2026-10-31 for the event and every commit in it is event work. The idea comes from the author's earlier learning-management work; no code, text or data from it was reused. `git log` is the provenance record. The first design (approved sources, a reader model judging every block) was built and measured in the first days; the audit on 2026-11-04 showed it trusted every stage and judged too late, and it was replaced by the lecture-first chain below the same evening.

## The demo path

1. Sign in with Google.
2. Add your Meta API key on the account page (stored encrypted, shown only as its last four characters).
3. Create a course and fill the brief once: levels, context, what must be covered, outcomes, languages (and, if you want one, a spend cap; empty means none).
4. Press Build. One press runs the blueprint, every lecture, the exercises and the translations; nothing more is asked.
5. Publish, copy the student link, open it as a learner, answer, and read the report.

## How a course is built

1. **Blueprint:** one Muse Wonder call writes the learner, the one case the course builds, modules and topics with annotations; a corrector pass checks it.
2. **Lectures:** every topic gets its own full lecture (Muse Wonder, all topics in parallel), each followed by one corrector pass.
3. **Block plan (code only):** the lecture's paragraphs become passages of a generated "Lectures" source; the lecture is the topic's reading; exercise types are chosen from the paragraphs (ordering for steps, matching for pairs, cloze for code, else cloze or choice alternating); each module test has one block per lesson.

# SAMolar

Segment anything. Mostly molars.

A simplified demo of a clinic CRM, built as a portfolio project. It is not a production product and it is not meant for real patient data. Everything in it is fake.

## What it does

- Waiting room: a dashboard with today's appointments, overdue recalls, open tasks and open invoices
- Patients: list, search, create, edit, archive, with notes, tasks, appointment and invoice history
- Appointments book: month view, booking with a double booking check, status changes
- Services: a simple price list
- Treatments: per patient, with a tooth chart (planned and done)
- Invoices: built from done treatments or free lines, with payments
- Recall list: patients who are due back
- To do: small tasks tied to patients, with due dates
- Audit log: who changed what
- X-rays: upload a panoramic image, run segmentation, see the masks on the image
- Quotes: treatment quotes with core, optional and free lines. Optional extras are priced but stay out of the total. A printable A4 sheet, and an accepted quote becomes an invoice with only its core lines
- Payment plans: split an invoice into steps (for example 30 / 40 / 30). How much of each step is paid is read from the real payments, in order, so the plan never disagrees with the money
- Stock room: supplies with a running count. Stock only changes through a logged move (used, restocked, counted) and the waiting room lists what is running low
- Attendance: staff clock in and out. The first arrival of the day is marked early, on time or late against a rule you can change. Lunch returns are not judged, a forgotten clock out is closed at the end of its own day, and the report shows "no data" rather than a flattering 100%
- Day plan: one day as a grid of calendars and half hours, overlapping bookings flagged, a note per day, printable on one A4 landscape page
- Recall messages: the reminder in the patient's language (English, Albanian, Italian, German), ready to copy or open in WhatsApp
- Duplicate check: a new patient whose phone or email is already on file is shown the existing record. A phone match cannot be overridden, an email match can
- Search: Ctrl K anywhere finds pages, patients, invoices and quotes
- CSV export: the patient list and the audit log by date range, both written to the audit log when downloaded
- Works on a phone: the sidebar becomes a slide out menu and wide tables scroll in their own box

## How it is simplified

- One clinic, one login, no roles
- SQLite file database
- Plain pages, not a polished UI
- Outside services are stubbed. Card payments and recall messages only log what they would do in the terminal, nothing is charged or sent.
- X-ray segmentation uses Meta's SAM 3.1 when `MODEL_API_KEY` is set. Without a key it draws placeholder shapes and says so on screen. The live call has not been tested against the real API.

## Run

```
npm install
cp .env.example .env
npm run db:push
npm run xrays
npm run db:seed
npm run dev
```

Then open http://local

an answer whose grounding they cannot check. We put a wearable-class capture
path in front of the operator's own manuals, and made the assistant refuse
rather than guess when those manuals do not cover the question — then turn the
refusal into a passage a human writes and approves.

**Meta models and APIs used.** Both routes the rules name are in the live path —
the Meta Model API, and Meta open-weight models.

| Model | How it is used | Route | Call site |

| **Glimmer 30B** | Residual-stream readout at prefill; weights never modified | **Open weights**, self-hosted on Modal GPU | [`backend/providers/modal_runtime.py`](backend/providers/modal_runtime.py) |

| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Scene wording and pen-presence observations | **Meta Model API** | [`backend/providers/pen_presence.py#L71`](backend/providers/pen_presence.py#L71) |
| **Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`) | Offline wording generation | **Open weights** | [`backend/generation/wording.py#L16`](backend/generation/wording.py#L16) |
| **Meta Wearables DAT** | Capture, and the glasses display path | SDK | [`ios/AmbientFieldLens/ViewModels/WearablesViewModel.swift`](ios/AmbientFieldLens/ViewModels/WearablesViewModel.swift) |

— a reviewed box prompt, not autonomous detection, and it says so in the file.

# Hunch

**Turn a thesis into a portfolio you can hold, measure and stand behind.**

Hunch takes an idea about the world, written in plain language ("AI data centres will strain the
power grid"), and turns it into a researched, guard-railed portfolio of US-listed equities. The
thesis is the unit of record: every position cites its evidence, and every weight, review, proposal
and order traces back to the idea. Every trading day Hunch checks whether the thesis still holds.
Meta's Muse models do all of its reasoning: Muse Wonder 1.0 researches each thesis, and Muse Spark
1.3 runs the Hunch Agent, the daily thesis check and the critique.

Hunch gives no investment advice: the person writes the thesis and its limits, Muse proposes
candidates, code sizes them under those limits, and money moves only at the person's own broker,
on their approval or inside autopilot limits they set. Until a pending Markets API deploy lets the
broker connector submit orders, they fill on Hunch's simulated venue.

- Watch the [three-minute film](https://youtu.be/ePFCpg3Qhgk): real screens of Muse at work in
  Hunch ([also in the repository](films/hunch-hackathon-video/hunch-hackathon.mp4)).
- Read [how Hunch uses Muse](docs/muse.md), then [a real Muse Wonder research](docs/examples/README.md)
  and the basket the guardrails built from it.
- [Check it in five minutes](#for-judges): the tests run with no credentials and no platform access.

This repository is the Hunch backend on the Main Sequence platform: the FastAPI application with
its MCP server, the Hunch Agent (a TAU Harness Agent) and the Jobs that research, build, review and
execute. The Command Center site lives in the
[`Hunch` repository](https://github.com/ms-private-projects/Hunch/tree/command-center-site).

## Why it matters

Three reasons, in the order a person feels them.

- **Sovereignty.** Someone who holds a view about the world should be able to own exactly the
  companies that express it, not a basket assembled by someone else under index rules, exclusion
  lists or stewardship policies they never chose. Hunch keeps the thesis in the person's words and
  the limits in their hands: the model proposes, code sizes, and only their approval or their own
  autopilot limits move money, at their own broker.
- **Speed.** A belief becomes a researched, evidence-cited, risk-capped portfolio in minutes, not
  after a fund launches a product for it, and it is re-checked every trading day against the
  person's own "change my mind" conditions.
- **Cost.** Thematic ETFs commonly charge 0.40% to 0.75% a year. Compounded over 40 years, 0.40%
  removes about 15% of final wealth and 0.75% about 26%, before tracking and turnover costs.
  Hunch's marginal cost is a few model calls per take per day, at a commission-free broker.

Because Hunch runs on Main Sequence, every operation is already an MCP tool behind an agent card:
a person or a team can connect their own agents to it, extend the Hunch Agent, or build their own

# Locus

Take one photo of a space. Next time, Locus tells you what’s **missing**, what’s **new**, and what **moved**.

Mobile-first web app (Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4). Spaces, items and check history live in the browser (IndexedDB). Real photos go through a server vision route; the API key never reaches the client.

## Run

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev
```

First launch seeds a sample **Workbench** space. Open it, tap **Check now**, then **Use sample photo** to see a full comparison without a camera or API key.

All stored photos are center-cropped to 3:4 (`FRAME` in `lib/image.ts`) so the viewfinder, current photo and check report line up.

## Flow

| Screen | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Home (swipeable space cards, things that need a look) | `/` |
| Search (items across spaces) | `/search` |
| Activity (checks across spaces, filter by space) | `/activity` |
| New space (photo → rename / toggle track / draw to add → save) | `/spaces/new` |
| Space (current photo, items, not tracked, history; `?item=` opens an item) | `/spaces/[id]` |
| Check (camera, library, or sample; hold to peek last photo) | `/spaces/[id]/check` |
| Check report (pan-zoom photo, missing / new / moved, found / gone, save as new current) | `/spaces/[id]/audits/[auditId]` |

On a check report you can mark **Found it** / **It’s gone**, **Keep track** / **Stop tracking**, and **Save as new current** so the next check compares against that photo. Occluded spots show as **Maybe hidden · take a look**.

Deleting a check that is the current photo rolls the reference back to the previous one (and drops any later checks compared against it). The first photo of a space can’t be deleted on its own; deleting the space removes everything.

In code, a reference photo is a `Commit`, its item list the ledger, and a check an `Audit`; the UI never shows these terms or their IDs.

## Vision (Meta Model API)

Pipeline for every real photo (demo fixtures stay local):

1. **Muse** — short Title Case concepts (“Monitor”, “Mouse”)
2. **SAM 3.1** — boxes / masks per concept (optional; on by default)
3. First photo uses those names directly; later checks re-label + Re-ID against the ledger

The API key stays on the server (`POST /api/vision/detect`). The browser never sees it.

```bash
cp .env.example .env.local
# put MODEL_API_KEY in .env.local — gitignored, do not commit
pnpm dev
```

| Env | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `MODEL_API_KEY` | Required for real camera / library photos |
| `MUSE_MODEL` | Default `muse-spark-1.3` (also `muse-wonder-1.0`) |
| `MUSE_REASONING_EFFORT` | Default `low` |
| `MUSE_USE_SAM` | Default on; set `0` for Muse-only boxes |

On **Vercel**, add the same vars under Project → Settings → Environment Variables (Production + Preview). `.env.local` is only for your laptop.

| Piece | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `lib/muse/detect.ts` | Muse + SAM pipeline |
| `lib/vision/muse.ts` | Client → `/api/vision/detect` |
| `lib/engine.ts` | Diff: signature match, moves, confirmed vs occluded

I was trying to set up billing for Google Cloud so I could build my own product. My prepaid card was declined. Then my debit card. Again and again. The money was there; the service just didn't take the kind of cards I had, and nobody could tell me why.

That happens every day to people who pay with Cash App, Chime, debit and prepaid cards. Cloud services, hotels and car rentals turn those cards away, usually without a reason, sometimes in public. It isn't about whether the money is there. It's about which cards a place trusts.

# Instagram Shop: an AI trust agent for social commerce

**Meta Global AI Hackathon 2026.** An agent built on Meta models: Muse Spark, SAM 3.1 and Muse Image. It keeps scammers out of social commerce and helps honest small sellers look professional.

![Amateur photo → studio card: the product pixels are untouched, only the background is new](demo/samples/before_after.jpg)

## The problem
Social commerce runs on trust, and the trust is easy to fake:
- **Stolen photos.** Scammers list items they don't have, using photos copied from other shops.
- **Fake sellers.** Accounts are registered on someone else's or forged documents.
- **Weak listings.** Honest small sellers shoot on a phone in a dark room and lose to the scammers' polished catalogue shots.

## What the agent does
| Flow | Meta models | What happens |

# DynamicKey

A Mac app plus a Safari browser extension, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie track).

DynamicKey replaces password-only login with a local check that has to agree on several signals at once, and it helps the user judge email risk instead of deciding for them. Everything that identifies the user stays on this Mac.

## What it is

- **Mac app:** the vault. It holds the master password check, the typing profile, trusted keyboards and networks, saved site credentials, the security activity log, and LeakPeek.
- **Safari extension:** the helper in the browser. It shows the password overlay on websites, pairs with the Mac app, and runs DynamicShield inside Gmail web.
- **Home screen:** system status, security score, LeakPeek status, quick stats, and recent activity, plus the Daily Summary on the first launch of the day.

## How login works

Logging in takes more than a password. All of these have to agree, or there is no login and no use:

1. **Master password.** It is only a check to unlock the app. It is never a password for any website.
2. **Typing rhythm.** The app compares how you type against your enrolled profile (dwell time, flight time, profile strength), stored in the keychain on this Mac.
3. **Trusted keyboard.** The input layout in use must be a trusted one (for example, Norwegian).
4. **Trusted network.** The WiFi network in use must be a registered one (for example, your home network).

The Mac app itself needs the same check. A correct master password with a non-matching rhythm still does not log in, and the same holds for a non-trusted keyboard or network. In testing, a second person typing the correct master password could not sign in.

**Match threshold** is user-adjustable from 50% to 90% (70% is Balanced; higher is stricter), with adaptive advice to raise it when sign-ins are consistent. **Safe Mode** covers 24 hours when rhythm is unreliable, for example an injured hand: it authenticates with Touch ID on the Mac keyboard. Face ID will be used on the future iPhone app. The Mac app comes first.

**Trusted keyboards and networks** are managed in settings with a plus button to add. Adding needs no extra authentication, because the session is already fully verified at login. The reasons to add are everyday ones: a public WiFi while out, or a replacement keyboard when the old one breaks.

## Site passwords

Site passwords are separate from the master password. The app generates random 24-character passwords, stores them locally, and fills them after verification. The user never needs to know them, and a leaked master password cannot be replayed at any website, because it is not the password for that site.

## Extension pairing

Pairing uses a one-time code generated only in the Mac app. A new code is needed for each pairing. The paired extension shows a masked token and a last-verified timestamp.

## Password overlay

The overlay appears on all websites' password fields. It asks for the master password,

# Ghost Station · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon

Ghost Station turns one song into a themed radio show. This standalone submission demonstrates the handoff shown in the [English demo video](https://youtu.be/AxzVaRmEZzk): **On & On → Muse Spark DJ line → Supertonic 3 voice → Invincible**.

## Run the video scenario

Use Node.js 20.9 or later.

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

1. Open [http://127.0.0.1:3000](http://127.0.0.1:3000) in a desktop browser.
2. Paste `https://youtu.be/K4DyBUG242c`, keep the **After Work Ride** theme, and open the station.
3. Keep the tab open while Supertonic loads. Let **On & On** finish, or seek near its end in the YouTube player. The demo displays the exact Muse Spark line captured for the video. Supertonic 3 speaks it in the browser and **Invincible** starts after the voice finishes.
4. Click **End broadcast** to stop playback. If Supertonic cannot load, the demo can use a local device voice or display captions and continue.

The default replay uses the recorded Muse Spark output with live browser synthesis. It needs internet access for YouTube and the pinned Supertonic model files (about 400 MB on the first run). Replay makes no requests to the Meta Model API.

## Generate a new line with Muse Spark

For optional live generation, create a local `.env.local` file and add your own Meta Model API key:

```dotenv
DEMO_MUSE_SPARK=1
META_API_KEY=YOUR_OWN_META_API_KEY
```

Restart the demo. The local server sends the two tracks and broadcast mood to Muse Spark 1.3 using a structured response schema. The browser labels a successful response **Generated with Meta Muse Spark**. Live requests use your account's credits or billing. The local server limits live requests to five per process. The supplied npm commands bind the server to loopback. Keep live mode on your local machine.

## What we built at the hackathon

- [Muse Spark handoff](src/app/api/dj/english-link/route.ts) and [server-side Meta client](src/lib/dj/meta-client.ts). Known track and mood inputs produce a short English introduction. A recorded response allows reviewers to exercise the same path without a key.
- [Supertonic 3 worker](public/studio-audio/supertonic/supertonic.worker.mjs) and [Studio playback](src/components/studio/launch-studio.tsx). The worker synthesizes the line with the pinned [Supertonic 3 model](https://huggingface.co/supertone-oss-archive/supertonic-3). The Studio waits for audio completion, then opens the selected next track. The shared Ghost Station production service is shown separately in the video at [ghoststation.live](https://ghoststation.live/).

The public repo is the standalone Studio reproduction. It uses local in-memory broadcast state. The earlier Llama 3.2 prototype remains available in the repository history. See the [Supertonic](public/studio-audio/supertonic/LICENSE) and [ONNX Runtime](public/studio-audio/supertonic/ONNXRUNTIME-LICENSE) notices for third-party code.

# Khata (खाता)

Find the money leaking out of a kirana shop's WhatsApp.

[![tests](https://github.com/KarthikPerepu/MetaAIHack/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/KarthikPerepu/MetaAIHack/actions/workflows/tests.yml)

Our entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 ("Build for Your World").

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/r9RAjMrUJRw?si=aBLOpOowUbFVaY7M

![The report page Khata writes for the shop owner](docs/report-page.png)

## Why this matters

Kirana shops still handle about 91% of India's grocery sales (Redseer, 2025), and there are an
estimated 12 to 20 million of them. Many buy on credit from their distributors, so bills, schemes
and payments stretch across weeks of conversation, and for shops like the one in the brief, that
conversation lives on WhatsApp.

Take a shop like Shanti General Store: around 40 distributor bills a month, from six suppliers.
The salesman sends a photo of the bill, a scheme gets agreed in a voice note ("20 carton lo, 2 free
milega"), a new rate list shows up as a PDF and a corrected one a few days later, and payments go
out by UPI with the screenshot dropped in the same chat. Checking one bill properly means
remembering a voice note from three weeks ago and which rate list was valid on that date. Nobody
does that before paying, so wrong bills just get paid.

## What Khata does

Export the chat from WhatsApp (the .zip is fine) and give it to Khata. It reads the messages and
everything attached, keeps a running record of what each distributor agreed to, and shows the owner
which bills are wrong, by how much, and the exact chat line or bill row that proves it. For each one
it drafts a polite Hinglish WhatsApp reply she can copy and send.

It looks for six kinds of problems:

- **rate_mismatch**: billed above the rate list that was in force on the bill date
  (e.g. GT/1187 charged ₹410 when the list said ₹395, so ₹15 × 20 = ₹300)
- **duplicate_bill**: the same delivery billed twice under a new bill number (SP/4412, ₹16,400)
- **scheme_not_given**: a scheme agreed in chat or a voice note but missing from the bill
  (2 free cartons never given, ₹790)
- **paid_but_shown_due**: paid by UPI but still listed as due on the next statement (₹5,000)
- **gst_error**: wrong GST rate for the item, or tax worked out on the wrong amount (₹1,000)
- **credit_period_risk**: an unpaid bill about to cross its credit days, with the interest at stake

When two trusted sources disagree (say the salesman quotes ₹24 but the rate list says ₹22), Khata
marks it as a **conflict** and leaves the decision to the owner. When it can't check something
because a document is missing, it says **cannot_determine**, what's missing, and who has it.

Besides `report.json`, Khata writes a simple web page (`report.html`) the owner can open on a
phone or laptop: how much to claim back from each distributor, every problem with its proof, a
"Copy" button on each WhatsApp draft, the scam messages it blocked, and a short Hinglish

# Mimi Agent

**Judges:** start with [`JUDGES.md`](JUDGES.md): the hosted demo, what is new
in the hackathon window, the demo's caps and safety, and an offline run for N0.

Mimi is a set of WhatsApp agents for FMCG distributors in Nigeria. A
distributor's van drops goods at dozens of small shops a day, and most
arguments about money start with "that is not what you delivered". Mimi sends
each shop a receipt on WhatsApp right after the drop, reads the reply in
whatever language the shop writes or speaks (English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo,
Hausa or a mix, typed or as a voice note), records the shop's confirmation,
and flags any dispute to the owner with the shop's own words. When a shop
promises to pay ("I go pay 20k tomorrow"), Mimi reads the amount and the day
back and notes the promise only after the shop says YES. When a shop sends a
screenshot of a bank transfer as proof it paid, Mimi reads it, checks it in
code, matches it to the open invoice and marks it **likely** paid until the
distributor's own bank feed shows the money; one that looks wrong goes to the
owner, without a word of blame to the shop.

This demo does that end to end on a synthetic distributor: it confirms
deliveries with shops in any language and flags disputes. The money maths is
integer kobo, done by code. The model reads and judges; it never writes a
figure, and Mimi never moves money.

All demo data is synthetic; Coral Lane Trading is fictional. So is every shop,
