# Quill — handwritten climate records → checked data

**Quill turns scanned, handwritten weather ledgers into data a climate scientist can trust.** It uses three Meta models:
- **Muse Spark 1.3** reads every number on the sheet and locates the table's columns (perception grounding).
- **Muse Spark 1.3** re-reads zoomed crops of any column that fails a check.
- **Muse Wonder 1.0** acts as an independent third reader when the first two disagree.

The check that makes this trustworthy is arithmetic the original observer did for us: **every year's twelve monthly values must add up to the total they wrote at the bottom of the column.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Nov 2026) · Theme: *Push the Frontier* · Indie track.

> **Held-out benchmark (169 sheets, 16,810 values):** Muse Spark alone gets 96.8% right, and its errors are indistinguishable from its correct reads.
> Quill marks 93.5% of values as checked; only 6 of 15,721 of those (0.04%) disagree with 16,000 volunteers.
> It hands 5.8% to a person, with the evidence attached, for $0.055 per sheet.

## Why

Long climate records are how we know what extreme rainfall, drought and flood risk look like. Much of the record before 1960 still exists only on paper:
- **Pre-1850:** about half of all records are not digitized even as monthly means, and only about 20% are in global repositories ([Brönnimann et al. 2019](https://www.africamuseum.be/publication_docs/Bronniman_etal_BAMS-2019.pdf)).
- **Met Office archive:** "literally tens of millions of observations" are not in the electronic datasets. Keying them "is generally beyond available resource" ([Met Office Archive, 2025](https://www.met.no/prosjekter/dmw2025/presentations/_/attachment/inline/4f5596d9-15a0-47b9-9ede-00d4355b5665:b3ae345cf92dbd8696511bea64e72e46aca3af00/9.%20Ross_Avoiding%20the%20Gordian%20Knot%20%E2%80%93%20the%20challenges%20and%20potential%20from%20an%20Archives%20point%20of%20view.pdf)).

When the paper does get keyed, the record changes:
- **Rainfall Rescue** ([Hawkins et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1002/gdj3.157)): more than 16,000 volunteers typed 5.28 million monthly values from 66,000 UK and Ireland "10-year sheets" (1677–1960), each value four times.
  - The result: six times more pre-1960 monthly data.
  - The official UK rainfall series now starts in 1836, and 1855 became the driest year on record ([Met Office](https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/about-us/news-and-media/media-centre/weather-and-climate-news/2022/rescued-victorian-rainfall-data-released)).
- **Storm Ulysses:** rescued pressure observations showed the 1903 storm beat every 1950–2015 event for wind in places ([Hawkins et al. 2023](https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/23/1465/2023/)).

There will not be 16,000 volunteers for every archive in every country. Quill aims to make a scanned page worth something the day it's scanned. It reports the values it can prove from the observer's own arithmetic, and hands a person exactly the cells it can't.

# 🧠 Codnite Brain

> **A memory and verification layer for AI coding work.**
> A `.brain` file remembers _why_ the project is the way it is, and a verifier only marks a task done when real evidence says so.
> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie track, _Push the Frontier – Software_). Planning, diagnosis and handoff run on **Meta Muse Spark** through the Meta Model API.

---

## About Codnite, the bigger project

**Codnite** is a full-stack platform for college campuses, built by [Md Shadan Siddiqui](https://github.com/shaddy-pv). It brings together what students and campuses usually spread across several tools:

- 1v1 coding battles and DSA practice
- Campus hackathons, with team projects and judging
- A multi-file cloud IDE with a real terminal and git
- Aptitude and placement assessments
- Certificates, leaderboards and college communities

**Codnite itself is a private codebase and is not in this repository.** Only Codnite Brain is open source here.

**How Brain fits in:** Brain is implemented inside Codnite's cloud IDE as a package the backend imports, with its own panel in the IDE. There it records a project's decisions and failures, plans tasks, verifies them, and gives its AI copilot project context. This repository also works on its own, as a CLI for any git project.

**The main purpose of Brain:** AI agents write code quickly, but they forget earlier reasoning and can say "done" when the work isn't. Brain keeps that reasoning in the repository and turns "done" from a claim into something checked with evidence, so any model or teammate can safely pick up the work.

---

## 1. The problem

Autonomous coding agents are fast, but teams hit three walls:

1. **Context amnesia** – switch model, session or teammate and the earlier decisions are gone.
2. **"Done" that isn't** – the agent says _"task complete"_; the tests fail, the build is broken, or the test was quietly weakened.
3. **Fragile handoff** – passing half-finished work on means re-explaining the whole project.

## 2. What Brain does

```
 idea ── brain plan ──► tasks + FAILING acceptance tests (scaffolded by the model)
                              │
                       brain start T-01      locks the test (sha256), records base commit,
                              │              checks the test is RED before any work
                       agent works (any model, any editor, may commit)
                              │
                       brain claim T-01      "I'm done" is only a CLAIM
                              ▼
        ┌─────────────────────  VERIFIER  ─────────────────────┐

# Fair Wear

Prototype deposit-dispute evidence review for UK renters. The offline pipeline uses SAM 3.1 to segment items, Muse Spark to suggest classifications, and Muse Image to generate simulated demo scenes. The public site explores a precomputed sample; it does not analyse uploaded videos or determine liability.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). **Working prototype with recorded real-model results**, not a live video-analysis service. Local model wrappers fall back to MOCK fixtures without a key and explicit paid-call opt-in; the public sample instead replays the saved real run.

End-to-end video analysis is explicitly disabled even in local paid mode because verified frame extraction/cropping is not connected. The separate offline still-image runner and cached sample are unchanged. See [video capability gate](docs/video-analysis-support.md).

## Try the complete sample journey

1. On `/`, compare the generated bedroom scenes, then open **Try the sample review**.
2. On `/demo`, use the three numbered sample-claim shortcuts, starting with **1. bedroom carpet**, to focus its evidence. The test intended fair wear; Muse Spark called it damage. Inspect the evidence and select a response. **2. kitchen oven** and **3. bathroom bath** complete the optional path. The bath’s cleaning label disagrees with planted damage intent. Jumping or using Next never confirms a response; the expanded evaluation and all 20 findings remain available.
3. Choose **Continue to case builder** to carry selected responses for bedroom carpet, kitchen oven and bathroom bath into a fresh fictional case. Other findings and untouched suggestions are not imported. Review the disclosed response mapping before continuing; no charge is accepted.
4. Edit the case and export the response/evidence bundle locally. Export before leaving: case notes and photos are not saved. Nothing is sent to a landlord.

`/inspect` separately replays the recorded evidence and published mistakes. Its review choices do not update the sample board or case builder.

## Recorded evaluation: generated flat

Muse Image generated four paired room scenes. The offline SAM 3.1 image-segmentation → matching → Muse Spark judgement run produced 20 saved crop-pair observations, not 20 changes. These populate 12 room/item groups: 11 observations cover seven planted groups, and nine cover five groups without planted changes. The eighth planted group, bathroom sealant, has no saved observation but stays in the evaluation denominator. Multiple crops can describe one item, including no-change results. # 🌿 Leaf Doctor

**Snap one leaf. Know the disease, how much of the leaf is damaged, and what to do — in the farmer's own language.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme *Build for Your World*).

**▶ Live demo: https://leaf-doctor-eight.vercel.app** (toggle VI / EN in the top-right corner)

## The problem

Vietnam has millions of smallholder farming households, most working very small plots. When rice blast, coffee rust or durian leaf blight shows up, the usual options are guessing, asking the pesticide seller (who has something to sell), or waiting days for an extension officer. Wrong or late treatment means lost harvests and over-spraying.

Two things are missing: **a reliable diagnosis**, and **an objective way to tell how bad it is and whether the treatment is working**. "It looks a bit worse" is not a measurement.

## What it does

1. **Photo in** — take a picture of the sick leaf (phone camera, no extra hardware). Optionally pick the crop and describe the problem by **voice** in Vietnamese or English.
2. **Muse Spark (vision)** identifies the crop and the disease / pest / deficiency, explains the cause, and writes an ordered treatment plan (active ingredients, dosage per 16 L sprayer, organic alternatives, prevention, urgency).
3. **SAM 3.1** segments the leaf and every lesion at pixel level. Muse Spark tells SAM *what to look for* (e.g. `"brown spot"`, `"white powder"`), so segmentation adapts to each disease. We rasterise all masks onto a shared grid and compute **% of leaf area affected** — the standard severity measure used in plant pathology, now available from a phone photo.
4. **Severity + overlay** — the damaged area is painted on the photo (green = leaf, red = lesions, yellow boxes = detections) with a severity grade.
5. **Track over time** — every scan is saved locally; re-scan the same plant after a few days and see the affected area go ▲ or ▼, i.e. whether the treatment works.
6. **Follow-up chat** — ask "when should I spray?" or "is it safe for my bees?" by text or voice; answers are grounded in the current diagnosis and measurement.

## Meta models used

| Model | Role |
|---|---|
| `muse-spark-1.3` | Vision diagnosis → structured JSON; picks the SAM concept prompts; follow-up chat (streamed) |
| `sam-3.1` | Concept segmentation of leaf + lesions → masks → area maths |
| `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` | Voice notes and questions (Vietnamese / English) |

## Architecture

```
Browser (Next.js, React)                      Next.js route handlers (server)            Meta Model API
─────────────────────────                     ─────────────────────────────              ─────────────────
photo → downscale ≤1280px ───────────────▶ /api/analyze
                                             ├─ SAM 3.1 "leaf" (starts immediately) ───▶ /v1/responses (stream)
                                             ├─ Muse Spark diagnosis (JSON) ───────────▶ /v1/chat/completions

# PartSnap **Snap a photo of something broken. Print the part that fixes it.** ## Problem statement **Push the Frontier: manufacturing & repair.** Small breakages, like a chipped table corner, usually get thrown away or left alone because designing a replacement part takes CAD skills. PartSnap turns a few guided photos and 2–3 ruler measurements into a verified, 3D-printable fix. ## How it works 1. **Guided capture**: a shot list (top view, side view, damage close-up) with ghost frames and a live tilt level. 2. **Photo check**: Muse Spark confirms each shot shows the right view and the damage, or asks for a retake. 3. **Segmentation**: SAM 3.1 outlines the missing area in the top view and the side view. 4. **Diagnosis**: Muse Spark picks the fix type and marks where to measure: the edge thickness, which scales both outlines to millimetres, and the chip depth. 5. **CAD generation**: Muse Spark Open (Baseten) writes CadQuery code: extrude the top outline vertically, the side outline horizontally, intersect them, and shrink the result by the clearance (0.2 mm) with break features under 1 mm flattened. 6. **Verify loop**: the code runs sandboxed. The piece must be one watertight body with zero overlap with the remaining wood, a gap close to the clearance, and a fill ratio (piece volume ÷ missing volume) of at least 90%. Failures go back to the model for repair (max 3 attempts). 7. **Preview + download**: the piece seated in the chip in a three.js preview, the STL, and how to glue it in. Fix types: **chip fill** (the default), the exact missing piece of a chipped corner, glued back in; and **corner cap**, an L-shaped cap that slides over the corner. ## Screenshots

**Flood early warning for the Philippines: a verifiable Muse Spark agent turns live river, rain and typhoon data into cited briefings and SMS alerts in five Philippine languages.**

Live demo: https://hydrosentinel-plum.vercel.app (no login needed)
Problem statement: **Build for Your World**
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. See [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md) for everything built during the event.

![HydroSentinel landing page with live river, typhoon and agent cards](docs/images/landing.png)

## The problem

About 20 tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility each year ([PAGASA](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/tropical-cyclone-information)). When a river starts to rise, a barangay disaster officer has little time to decide whether families should move. The data exists, but it is spread across hazard feeds, hydrological models and weather services, in units most people don't read.

## Who it is for

- **Barangay and municipal DRRM offices:** a plain-language briefing on which rivers are rising and how close each one is to its watch level, with an SMS ready to forward.
- **Provincial and LGU planners:** a 30-day flow outlook for 17 major basins, with alert levels based on each river's own five-year record.
- **Families in flood-prone areas:** short, calm messages in Filipino, Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon or English that always point to PAGASA and local authorities for official warnings.

## What it does

| Feature | What you see |
|---|---|
| Flood-watch agent | Muse Spark investigates live data with six tools, shows each step, and writes a briefing where every claim cites its source |
| Number verification | The server checks every number in the briefing against the tool result it cites and shows the score on every briefing (all numbers verified on the November 3 and 4 runs) |
| SMS alerts | Ready-to-forward text in five languages |
| PH outlook | 17 Philippine basins on a map, with 30-day flow and alert levels |
| Live gauges | Measured river levels every 15 minutes, with backtested forecasts and uncertainty ranges |
| Ask | Questions in English, Filipino or Taglish, answered in the same language from live data, with a status, key points and what to do |
| Photo check | SAM 3.1 measures how much of a field photo is flooded |
| Posters | Muse Image community posters matched to the day's alert level |
| 3D layers | Terrain, rainfall forecast, river flow, forecast peak and a flood-watch index stacked over the Philippines |
| Analytics | Held-out forecast skill against a no-change baseline, interval coverage and model selection for each forecast horizon |
| Research | The forecasting method, parameters and live skill scores |
| Data checker | Validates a CSV of river readings and reports gaps, duplicates and bad values |

# SaveBell

**Continuous AI security threat intelligence, connected to your actual code.** SaveBell follows security advisories, vulnerability databases, research papers and security news; fact-checks each report; decides whether it really applies to the GitHub repositories you connect, down to the file and line; tells you; and helps you fix it.

Live: https://save-bell.vercel.app · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Nov 2026), theme *Build for Your World* · Apache-2.0

> Built during the hackathon. Every commit in this repository is from Oct 31 – Nov 4 2026 (the event window), by the author. Nothing pre-existing was imported. Third-party code is used only as npm dependencies (MIT, Apache-2.0, ISC, BSD, MPL-2.0 and the LGPL-3.0 `sharp` image binaries pulled in by Next.js), none vendored or modified.

## What it does

```
Threat published → Report fact-checked → Relevant repos found → Code investigated → Impact decided → You are notified → Fix proposed / made
```

1. **Discover.** GitHub-reviewed advisories by webhook; GitHub Advisory Database, 11 fast feeds and Hacker News every 5 min; CISA KEV every 10 min; NVD every 30 min; OSV.dev hourly with the exact package versions in your lockfiles; 10 research and news feeds hourly (arXiv cs.CR, an arXiv prompt-injection/LLM-agent query, OWASP GenAI, Trail of Bits, Snyk/Invariant Labs, Hugging Face, AI Incident Database, Mastodon infosec, Google News). Every source is labelled by how it is really monitored, with measured intervals on `/sources`.
2. **Fact-check the report.** Cited CVE / GHSA / arXiv ids are looked up at NVD, OSV, the GitHub Advisory Database and arXiv. Meta Muse Spark with Meta's built-in web search looks for primary sources, independent reports, copies of one origin and contradictions. A fixed rule labels the report **Verified / Corroborated / Unverified / Disputed / Likely false**. URLs the model cites but the search never returned are discarded; the model can lower a label, never raise it. Disputed or likely-false reports can never produce an "Affected" result.
3. **Investigate your code.** Lockfile versions are checked against affected ranges in code. Muse Spark explores the repository with read-only tools (list, search, read) to find the code that decides each condition, then judges each condition with file:line citations. Every citation is re-read from the real file; unverifiable, prose-only or comment-only evidence is downgraded. The verdict (Affected / Not Affected / Unclear) comes from a fixed rule, never from the model.
4. **Notify.** In-app notifications with unread badge, priority order (unread, confirmed, severity, time), one entry per finding and repository updated in place, Slack/Discord webhook, Web Push when VAPID keys are set.
5. **Show the impact.** "What happens if you don't fix this?" builds a short, hypothetical walkthrough of what a user of *your* app could experience, as screens of your app. Each step says whether it is shown in your code, inferred, or hypothetic

# Yaadsi: from saved to learned

**Yaadsi turns the links you save and forget into a short daily lesson, so what you saved becomes what you know.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, "Build for Your World") with Muse Spark Open and the Meta Model API.

**Try it live: [yaadsi.vercel.app](https://yaadsi.vercel.app/)** and press **Try the demo**. It opens on 24 public demo saves. You can add your own link (LinkedIn, GitHub or an article; Instagram usually blocks cloud servers) and get a lesson from it in about 20 seconds. Everyone shares one demo space, it resets now and then, and live features stop for the day after a small spend cap.

**Or run it locally in one minute:** clone, `pip install -r requirements.txt`, run with `TUTOR_DATA=demo` (see [Run it](#run-it)), press **Try the demo**. No API keys needed.

| Landing | Today: your backlog and a 15-minute pick | A lesson from your saves |
|---|---|---|
| ![Landing page](docs/landing.png) | ![Today](docs/today.png) | ![Lesson as an article](docs/article.png) |

## Vision

**A personal knowledge layer between you and the internet.** You keep saving the way you already do, and everything you save is kept, understood, connected, found again and taught back to you:

**Capture → Understand → Connect → Retrieve → Learn → Apply**

In the full product, Yaadsi is a chat contact: share a link to it on Telegram or WhatsApp, and the job is done. Most "second brain" tools stop at storing and searching. But a pile of links only turns into value when you learn from it, so this project builds that half: **Learn**, on top of Understand, Connect and Retrieve.

*Yaad* is Hindi for memory, and *yaad-si* means "a faint memory": the thing you only half-remember. Yaadsi remembers, so you don't have to.

## The problem

Every day we save Reels, posts and articles "for later": Instagram Saved, LinkedIn, our own WhatsApp chat. Later never comes.

I checked my own: **71 links saved to learn from, almost none opened again.**
- **72%** were Instagram carousels and Reels: images and video, which read-later apps can't read at all.
- **Captions alone** made only 55% of those Instagram saves understandable. The real content was on the slides.
- **One in six** had already disappeared a few months later, deleted or made private.

Saved folders *store* links. Nothing *teaches* them back to you, and the pile only grows.

Keep saving. Yaad, a small study buddy, turns the pile into a daily habit:

# Confam

> **Confam challenges AI-generated fixes before you ship them.**

A coding agent says the bug is fixed and the tests pass. But would those tests have caught a fix that only *looks* right, and what did everyone forget to check?

Confam answers both questions by running the real app:

- **It tests the tests.** It reproduces the reported bug, checks a proposed fix, and plants **decoy patches**: plausible wrong fixes, written by Muse Spark, that a weak test would wave through. Each decoy must be confirmed wrong by an independent probe, such as reading the database directly. If the checks can't tell a decoy from a real fix, the green result means nothing, and Confam says so.
- **It sets two models against each other.** Muse Wonder writes a fix without seeing the checks. Muse Spark reviews the passing fix for what it still misses. The developer confirms the gaps that matter, and Confam runs them. On a real solar installer's quote form, a Wonder fix passed every agreed check, and Spark's review led to the case where 10 of 10 simultaneous requests got through a limit of 5.

The developer gets a reviewable result, in a local interface or as a [review comment on the pull request](https://github.com/Ololadestephen/Confam/pull/1); their client gets one plain sentence about what was checked.

**Watch the demo:** [58-second film](https://youtu.be/patd96UOovc).

**Browse the recorded evidence:** [useconfam.vercel.app](https://useconfam.vercel.app/). This is a read-only copy of the interface with the real runs, gap reviews and repair sessions behind the results below. Nothing runs there; to run Confam, follow "Try it".

## Results on real applications

Every reproduced bug below is real, taken from the app's own history and reproduced against the commit before its real fix. The "gaps" are different: expectations proposed by Muse Spark and confirmed by the author that fail on the current code. Gap results are ordinary verification runs, without independent correct controls, decoys or held-out faults.

**What you can re-run:** the salon, task board, quote tool and Linkding results run from a fresh clone with no API key. Bluemax and Mosaic can't be re-run by a reader, because their source is private; their folders show exactly how they were tested. The Spark and Wonder steps need a Meta API key, and results on Muse Wonder's fixes depend on the patches it returned, which stay in local run folders; the evidence site shows those recorded runs.

None of these apps' source is in this repository, and none was built during the hackathon; they are test subjects.

### Bluemax: a real solar installer's website in Nigeria

Bluemax was built with an AI app builder; 106 of its 114 commits were written by that builder's bot. Its free-quote form limits each visitor to 5 requests a minute so the business isn't flooded with spam leads. The limit lived in the function's memory and reset every time the function restarted. The fix, also AI-written, moved it into the database

# Saksi

**Research that is witnessed, not reconstructed.**

*Saksi* means *witness* in Malay and Indonesian.

Most tools that check research arrive after the fact. They read a finished
manuscript and try to work out what was done. Saksi takes part while the work
happens: it runs the analysis the protocol specifies, helps authors and
reviewers through drafting and review, and records every step as it occurs.
Each action by a human or an AI agent becomes an entry in a tamper-evident
log. The provenance is captured as the work is done, not inferred later from
a PDF.

> Entry for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie Developer track,
> theme *Build for Your World*).

---

# Inkling

**A game that helps UK students find the degree subjects that fit them.** Four quick rounds of cards fill a paper-craft halls room with what you're into. Then you get your top 3 subjects, a wildcard you'd never have picked, real UK courses and the apprenticeships closest to them.

**Play it:** [findyourinkling.com](https://www.findyourinkling.com) · **Watch the simulation:** [/simulation](https://www.findyourinkling.com/simulation) · **How it was built:** [/built](https://www.findyourinkling.com/built) · **Demo video:** [youtu.be/GkDJKz8-Weg](https://youtu.be/GkDJKz8-Weg) · **X post:** [x.com/MartinSWDev/status/2118059722070790600](https://x.com/MartinSWDev/status/2118059722070790600)

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 Oct – 4 Nov 2026), Indie Developer track, problem statement **Build for Your World**. Also entered for the bonus categories: Open Weights (Muse Spark Open does the heavy lifting, on Baseten), Best Creative Build, Most Viral and Community Vote.

![Inkling](web/public/og.png)

## The problem

I build university websites. Their main job is getting students to pick a course from a huge catalogue, and they assume you already know what subject you want. Many students don't. In the 2026 cycle 344,760 UK 18-year-olds applied to university by the 30 June deadline ([UCAS](https://www.ucas.com/corporate/news-and-key-documents/news/record-number-of-uk-school-leavers-head-into-the-results-period-with-an-offer-of-a-university-or)), choosing from tens of thousands of courses. Among graduates aged 25 to 30, 15% would pick a different course at the same university and 12% would change both course and university ([The Benefits of Hindsight](https://wonkhe.com/blogs/hindsight-is-a-wonderful-thing-but-foresight-is-better/), Bristol, HEPI and Advance HE, 2025).

Inkling helps students find the inkling they already have, then explore real options from there. It is a game, not a chatbot or a personality test, and it never makes up facts about courses.

## What it does

1. **Your subjects.** Tap what you study now and heart your favourites. Type anything else (A-levels, BTECs, T-levels, Highers) and it understands.
2. **Things you'd get stuck into.** Swipe picture cards yes or no.
3. **This or that.** Pick the picture that's more you.
4. **Big questions.** Swipe on questions you'd want answered; swipe up if you really want to know.
5. **Your room.** Whatever you pick lands in your room as a paper sticker. Tap any sticker to see which subject it stands for.
6. **The reveal.** Your top 3, a wildcard, hands-on routes (apprenticeships), real courses filtered by city, coast, campus town or countryside, and a 10-second video of your room to share.
7. **Feedback.** "Does this feel like you?" 👍 / 👎, stored anonymously to tune the scoring.

No sign-up. Playing makes **zero AI calls**: everything AI-made was generated once ahead of time, so the site is static and costs almost nothing to run at any scale.

# FEN Г— Meta вЂ” Human-Governed AI Synthesis

**AI proposes. Humans decide. Every decision keeps its provenance.**

**Live demo: https://fen-meta-synthesis.vercel.app/demo** вЂ” the simplified
one-screen demo (sources в†’ proposals в†’ quote check в†’ your decision); the full
Review screen is at `/review`, the public registry of accepted knowledge at
`/registry`, and the user wiki at `/faq`. It runs end to end on Vercel: a Python
function at `api/index.py` calls the Meta Model API and stores analyses, items
and human verdicts in Supabase, so nothing needs to be started locally.

**Demo video (1:56): https://youtu.be/yomKcH8iZN4**

Three datasets ship with the demo: a synthetic trade-route story, ePSD2
dictionary excerpts for Sumerian lemmas, and EU AI Act Articles 11, 12 and 18
from EUR-Lex (the demo uses 11 and 18) with one clearly SYNTHETIC commentary
paragraph вЂ” see [Datasets](#datasets).

Prefer to run it on your machine? `python scripts/start_demo.py` brings up the
same API against a local JSONL store вЂ” see [DEMO.md](DEMO.md).

FEN Г— Meta extends the open-source FEN Triadic Synthesis research prototype
for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. It adds one focused, end-to-end
workflow: a Meta model reads several source documents, extracts claims with
verbatim quotes, flags contradictions between sources, and hands the result
to a human reviewer. The reviewer accepts, rejects, or disputes each item,
and the decision is recorded together with the source, the model, and the
prompt that produced the proposal.

Status: hackathon submission build (4 November 2026). See
[Project status](#project-status) for what is implemented, what is planned,
and what remains simulated.

## The problem

Researchers who work with conflicting sources (for example, different
dictionaries or archives that define the same term differently) spend hours
reconciling them by hand. A general-purpose chatbot can summarize the
sources, but it hides where each statement came from and can invent quotes.

# TrustFlow — Verifiable AI Agent Workflows

> **AI can propose. Humans authorize. Evidence proves.**
>
> An AI agent's success message is not proof that an action was authorized, executed once, or verified after a timeout. TrustFlow connects an **exact approved plan**, a **stable operation identity**, and **independent ledger evidence** across uncertain execution.

**Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Push the Frontier.**

TrustFlow is an open-source, local research-and-engineering prototype for **auditable agent workflows with synthetic financial operations**. It combines Meta Muse planning and semantic review with deterministic policy enforcement, hash-bound human approval, idempotent execution, persistent state, and ledger-grounded verification.

**Scope:** all balances and transfers are synthetic. This is **not** a production banking system, a payment integration, or a general distributed exactly-once guarantee.

[Watch the demo on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QnLXbL9yXHM) · [Architecture](#architecture) · [Meta integration](#built-with-meta-powered-by-meta) · [Development usage](#ai-assisted-development-usage) · [Measured results](#measured-results-and-evidence) · [Quickstart](#reproduce-the-offline-demo) · [Safety boundaries](#security-and-limitations) · [Archived demo](docs/submission/video/trustflow-demo.mp4)

## The problem

A worker can commit a transaction **after its caller times out**. If an agent retries the action just because it did not receive a success response, it may cause a second transfer. Likewise, an approval of one plan must not silently authorize a different plan after re-planning.

TrustFlow demonstrates a bounded way to answer three questions with inspectable evidence:

1. **Was this exact action authorized?** A human decision binds to the version and SHA-256 hash of a specific plan snapshot.
2. **What actually executed?** Backend-owned operation identities and SQLite idempotency associate approved intents with committed synthetic transfers.
3. **Can we independently establish the outcome?** Verification reads ledger state instead of trusting a model's or tool's success message; recovery checks the original operation rather than replaying the mutation.

## Built with Meta. Powered by Meta.

**Built with Meta Muse Code.** The project developer credits Meta Muse Code as an extensive AI-assisted engineering collaborator for architecture, typed workflows and tools, retrieval/evidence, persistence, user interface, evaluation, testing, and iterative reliability remediation. **Codex** also contributed fixes and independent reviews. The human developer directed requirements, final decisions, and authorization. This attribution does not imply Muse exclusively authored every commit. See the [development worklog](docs/worklog.md).

**Powered by Meta Model API.** A typed [`MetaResponsesProvider`](src/trustflow/llm/provider.py) uses `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses` with strict structured-out

# Tether

Tether finds the parts of your code a stranger could take over.

Live: [https://trustline-cxqq.onrender.com](https://trustline-cxqq.onrender.com)

Demo video: `<VIDEO_URL>`

## The problem

In 2024 the `polyfill.io` domain was sold. Sites that still loaded the old CDN — more than 100,000 of them — started receiving malware from a name they had trusted for years. The same pattern shows up as abandoned S3 buckets (anyone can create the missing name) and deleted GitHub accounts (repojacking: a stranger registers the handle and the old URLs start serving their code). Your repo can keep pointing at all of that long after you stopped meaning to.

## What it does

- Scans a **GitHub repository** or a **website** for hosts, buckets, and accounts the code still trusts.
- Labels each finding **Proven** (checked directly) or **Likely**, with a plain-language **Fix plan**: a GitHub issue, a prompt for a coding assistant, and a safe patch when an edit is automatic.
- Runs on **pull requests** via the checked-in workflow.
- Works in **Muse Code over MCP** (read-only lookup tools plus scan).
- Ships a **README badge**: `GET /api/badge?repo=<url>` renders `Tether | 0 claimable` (green) or `N claimable` (red) from the latest cached scan only. It never starts a scan.

## How it works

```
extract → code checks (DNS, RDAP, bucket probes, GitHub, Pages with DNS proof, Tranco, compromised list)
       → Muse Spark agent (plan → tool → observe)
       → code floors set the minimum severity
       → plain-language report and Fix plan
```

**Code produces the facts; the model explains them and never decides alone what's true.**

## Results

Scored with the **revised rubric** (3 Nov 2026): expiry-only names are not Fix-today, and an NXDOMAIN subdomain of a registered parent is not a stranger takeover. Labels were not rewritten; scoring remaps them. See `eval/rubric.md`.

# Fleet document pipeline

A driver sends a photo or PDF on WhatsApp. It is stored encrypted, read by the model (Meta Muse through the Meta
Model API), checked by plain rules, and the cab's record updates. The driver gets an answer in their own language:
"Received insurance for TS-09-XY-4521, valid till 18-05-2027", or the exact problem ("This bill shows a different
vehicle number. Please resend.").

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon on the CDAI Fleet Compliance Dashboard. The public demo uses a
fictional client and synthetic drivers, cabs and documents only.

## Flow, and where each step lives

| # | Step | Code |
|---|------|------|
| 1 | Webhook `POST /wa/inbound`; Meta signature (`X-Hub-Signature-256`) checked; one-time GET handshake | `app.py`, `inbound.py` |
| 2 | Download the media; SHA-256 of the file | `bridge.graph_download_media`, `intake.py` |
| 3 | Phone to driver to cab. Unknown number: "not registered", nothing stored. No consent yet: consent request, nothing stored | `registry.py`, `intake.py` |
| 4 | Original to S3 with SSE-KMS: `fleet/{vehicle}/{yyyy-mm}/{sha256}.{ext}`; medical certificates under `restricted/medical/...` | `store.py` |
| 5 | Job to SQS, carrying a hashed sender id, never a phone number | `jobs.py` |
| 6 | For a photo: SAM 3.1 finds the paper; code crops, straightens and trims the page (scans skip this) | `photo.py` |
| 7 | Worker reads the page: Muse Spark vision call with JSON-schema structured output | `model.py`, `schema.py` |
| 7a | Rule checks in code, not AI | `rules.py` |
| 8 | Cab record, document log and open safety actions in DynamoDB | `records.py` |
| 9 | Reply in English, Hindi or Telugu, paced per driver, with the driver's own module link when a document is accepted | `replies.py`, `training.py` |
| 10 | The client dashboard reads the same records live: no rebuild, no export | `state.py`, `dashboard.py`, `dashboard/site/` |

All outbound HTTP (WhatsApp media, replies and the model) goes through `bridge.py` only.

## Photo step (`photo.py`)

A driver's photo of a bill is rarely flat or framed. For images with dark surroundings (a car seat, a counter),
SAM 3.1 is asked for the "paper document" through the Responses API; it answers with a box (in its token the `w`
and `h` are the image size, not the box). Code crops to the box, measures the text-line skew on the centre of the
crop, rotates against a dark fill and trims to the bright page. Scans whose paper already fills the frame skip the
call. A SAM failure is logged and the original photo is read. SAM finds; it never decides. On
`demo/synthetic/photo_TS09XY4521_tilted_demo.jpg` SAM returns the paper at 38% of the frame in about five seconds
and the page is straightened by its 7.5 degree tilt. `PHOTO_MODE=off` disables the step.

## Dashboard (`dashboard.py`, `state.py`, `dashboard/site/`)

One read-only function behind its own URL serves the page and answers `GET /api/state` from the records. The page

> **Hackathon:** Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon - Oct 27-Nov 4 2026.

Everything in this repository was built during the hackathon (Oct 27 - Nov 4 2026).

Protects developers from malicious MCP servers - **tool poisoning** and **rug pull**. CLI gate before trusting third-party servers, locally and in CI.

## Quick start

```powershell
npm ci
cp .env.example .env   # macOS/Linux
copy .env.example .env   # Windows
# set BASETEN_API_KEY: required for the first `approve` and whenever tools are new or changed; not needed for `check` on an unchanged server

npm run demo:rug-pull:approve

```

Use `npx tsx src/cli.ts ...` or the npm scripts above; the package is not published to npm.

Developed on Windows. The demo flow (reset, approve, check) and `npm test` were also run successfully on Linux (WSL, Node v26.13.0). Not verified: macOS, `eval:reviewer`, and the timeout/spawn-fail test scripts on Linux. `npm ci` may print an install-scripts warning for esbuild; it did not affect running.

## Commands

- `approve <cmd> [--name N] [--accept] [--allow-invalid]` - first-time acceptance. Fetch -> validate -> diff -> save.
- `check <cmd> [--name N]` - read-only verification for CI. Never writes.

### Approve contract
1. fetch -> validate. Any error -> print, exit 1, save nothing, unless --allow-invalid (loud warning).
2. Resolve identity via baseline key (command+args hash or --name) and related search.
   - **A. Exact baseline exists:** diff old vs new. No diff + valid -> "already approved, unchanged", exit 0, DO NOT write. Diff -> print diff, exit 1; replace only if TTY y or --accept. Never silent overwrite. Non-TTY without --accept: exit 1.
   - **B. No exact but related (overlap >=0.5):** loud warning, diff vs best match (highest overlap, ties reported), same confirmation. On confirm save under new key with previousKey=old filename; old kept.
   - **C. Nothing related:** first approval, save baseline.
3. Exit codes: 0 approved/unchanged, 1 differences/validation not confirmed, 2 operational error.

### Check contract
Same detection/diff, never writes. No exact and no related -> exit 2 "run approve". For exact baseline: validation errors -> exit 1 (no LLM); no diff -> "check passed: unchanged and valid", exit 0, no LLM; diff with added/changed -> LLM review on those tools. Related baseline without exact: prints diff, exit 1, no LLM. Exit 0 when reviewer finds nothing suspicious because check never writes (run `approve` to accept).

# SEZ — evidence check for a flight route

SEZ answers one question for an airline operations team: *is there verified evidence of something on this route, on this date, that should make us look again?* It covers weather, volcanic ash, flooding, earthquakes, strikes, fuel supply, airport faults, airspace restrictions and conflict-related airspace risk.

It does not say a route is safe. It says what evidence exists, how strong it is, and what is still unconfirmed.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track, "Build for Your World").

## Built during the hackathon

Everything in this repository was written during the building period. The first commit is dated 1 November 2026; `git log` shows the full history. SEZ also has a separate, older daily briefing product (not in this repository). No code from it was copied here.

## How it works

1. **Question → route.** The question can be typed or spoken: "Ask by voice" records the microphone in the browser, Meta Muse Voice Transcribe turns it into text, and the audio is not stored. If the spoken question names the places and year of a saved example, the saved run opens at no cost. Muse Spark reads the question (route, country, date). The route is drawn in code from real airport coordinates and, when available, a real flight track.
2. **Scan.** Muse Spark with web search lists events that could affect flights at or over the airports and countries on the route.
3. **Evidence gate.** Each event becomes a checkable claim. The claim is searched in local languages on Google News. Muse Spark judges each headline in groups of 15 and must quote the exact words that prove it. Code then checks that the quote is really in the headline, the publish date is inside the window, and the place name appears. The level (confirmed by news, partial, single source, contradicted, no evidence) is decided in code, not by the model. Publishers are counted by distinct domain; aggregators, social posts and near-identical headlines (re-posted agency stories) are not counted.
4. **Article body channel.** If headlines are not enough, Muse Spark web search brings sentences from article bodies. Code opens each page itself and searches for the sentence. The page text is never sent to the model.
5. **Official sources to check.** In our test, every official page we found (airport operators, aviation authorities, volcanic ash centres) returned 403 or did not respond, with or without a VPN. We did not test every official site. So SEZ does not claim official confirmation. NOTAMs are read live in code. For everything else, Muse Spark names up to three official organisations the team should check before deciding, and the screen says these are suggestions SEZ did not open.
6. **Evidence memory.** Sources that passed the gate are kept per event and sent through the same gate again on the next query, so a new query does not lose what an earlier one found. Google News links are resolved to the publisher URL. A source whose page

# Kodiac: Tests, `git bisect`, and `git blame` for Robots

### *"Robots can finally fail a test."*

> **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** · Indie Developer Track · Theme: *"Push the Frontier"*

Show Kodiac a task once. Meta's models turn it into a short, readable, executable test. Kodiac then
grades every robot attempt against that test frame by frame and returns **PASS**, **FAIL**, or
**CAN'T TELL** — and on a FAIL it points at the **exact onset frame** and the **measured physical
cause**, down to the line of robot code that actuated it.

Robotics has no `pytest` and no `git blame`. A demonstration labelled "successful" is taken on trust,
a policy that regressed is debugged by scrubbing video, and an agent that says "done" is believed.
Kodiac gives robots the three things every codebase already has: a test, a bisect, and a blame.

---

## Read this before the numbers

**There is no measured headline yet, and this README will not pretend otherwise.**

- No Meta Model API key, no Modal token and no HF gated weights were available during the build.
  Every SAM 3.1 / Muse Spark / Muse Voice / Muse Wonder call site is therefore exercised against
  **recorded fixtures or a deterministic mock**, and says so at runtime with a badge.
- The headline claim (*"same robot, same practice data, only the judge changed: +Y points of
  success"*) is **NOT MEASURED**. `experiments/results/headline.json` carries `Y_points: null` and the
  proof chart refuses to draw bars; it renders a `NOT MEASURED` watermark instead.
- The engine is real and runs end to end. Its *perception* input is not: `--sim` grades tracks
  projected from simulator state, and every badge on that path says
  `[SYNTHETIC TRACKS FROM SIM STATE · NOT PERCEPTION]`.
- `docs/features.yaml` is the ground truth for what shipped and on what evidence. The status section
  at the bottom of this file is generated from it (`scripts/gen_status_table.py --check` fails if the
  two ever disagree).

If a claim is not backed by a committed artifact, it is labelled `[UNVERIFIED]` where it appears.

---

# Spatial Copilot for Warehouse & Factory Floors

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Dev Track, Push the Frontier theme.
Application approved 2026-10-20. Project due 2026-11-04 6:00 PM PT.

## What it is (measurement-first safety copilot, not photo Q&A)

An **aisle-safety copilot**: before a forklift enters an aisle, a
six-agent crew scans the scene and returns a **measurement report**
— walkway, clearance in metres, blockage percent, mask evidence —
with the **GO / CAUTION / NO-GO / HOLD** verdict attached as a
suggestion whose basis names the measurement value and the
threshold, and a human making the final approval. Photo Q&A is
still in the product, but it is the explanation layer for a
measurement, not the story.

Why this framing: OSHA's long-cited estimate is ~85 forklift deaths and
~34,900 serious injuries per year in the US, ~70% preventable. Today's
aisle check is eyeball + clipboard: no measurement, no record. A chat
answer does not fix that. A measurement report with an audit trail does.
(Round-1 annotation broke the verdict-led story: GO / CAUTION / NO-GO
say how blocked a walkway is, HOLD says whether it can be assessed at
all — different axes — and the 15% / 1.5 m cutoffs are builder policy
assumptions, not standards. See SUBMISSION.md W54–W55.)

The crew (`backend/agents/`, run in order by `orchestrator.run_case`):

1. **Scout** sees: SAM 3.1 segments the photo (one noun phrase per
   request) or tracks one concept through a clip — and, live, re-asks
   for the floor field when no aisle segment came back.
2. **Surveyor** measures: the walkway blockage fraction
   (pixel-measured from decoded SAM masks when every blocker carries
   one, else the labelled box estimate) plus clearance in metres
   anchored on the median pallet width.
3. **Report** leads: `measurement.build_report` returns walkway,
   clearance, blockage, evidence, assessable, and recommendation
   sections, reusing the existing walkway functions — no second
   implementation. **Judge** attaches the GO / CAUTION / NO-GO / HOLD
   suggestion behind three uncertainty gates: verification-grounded,
   blocker-score, and viewpoint (side/close-up views hold instead of
   verdicting).
4. **Dispatcher** acts: a non-GO suggestion opens a case; it never
   approves anything — approval stays human-only.
5. **Auditor** verifies: every run appends an audit entry stopping at
   human approval, and a re-scan appends a VERIFY transition that
   closes the case only on GO.
6. **Critic** learns: it scores cached-segment predictions against
   human labels under strict rules and proposes nothing — the human
   decides what changes.

Around the frozen geometry sits the **Spark disambiguation loop**
(`backend/disambiguation.py`): four rule triggers check whether box
geometry is ambiguous, each fired trigger asks Spark exactly one
targeted vision question on the full frame, and every answer leaves
a record — the report is never rewritten, Spark only moves the
suggestion. Diagnostic

# FloatWise

**An assistant that helps mobile money agents in Kenya avoid running out of cash or e-float.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026), indie developer track.

Mobile money agents are the small shops where people turn phone balances into cash and back. To serve everyone, an agent has to hold both physical cash and e-float. When either runs out, customers are turned away and the agent loses income. Most agents decide when to restock by feel.

FloatWise lets an agent talk to it in Swahili or English, paste raw M-Pesa SMS messages (voice notes and ledger photos are planned), and get plain-language restocking advice such as:

> "Restock KSh 22,000 cash by Saturday. Until then there is about a 46% chance that at least one customer is turned away."

That sentence is illustrative. The numbers in real answers come from the solver, not from the language model.

# VisionPilot

VisionPilot is an AI agent that uses a web browser the way a person does. You type a task in plain English. It looks at the screen, decides what to click, asks you before anything risky, does it, and then looks at the screen again to check it really worked.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie track) with **Muse Spark** through the Meta Model API, and **Muse Code**.

🎬 **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/IkUVybdDUm4?si=vQe_KMG3odXeATuJ

---

## Why I built this

I started this hackathon as a beginner. In one week I had to learn PowerShell, git, Python environments, API keys and Meta's tools all at once. I asked chatbots for help a lot, and they gave me good instructions. But they couldn't see my screen. I typed commands into the wrong window, put my API key in the wrong file, and ran tests while my website wasn't even running. Every time, I had to copy the error back and explain what I was looking at.

That's the gap I wanted to close. A helper that only tells you what to do leaves the hard part to you. VisionPilot looks at the screen itself, does the steps, and checks its own work. And when something unexpected shows up, it notices instead of pretending everything went fine.

---

## What it can do

VisionPilot works on a small practice admin website that I built (it runs on my own laptop), so the demo never breaks because someone else's site changed.

---

Every task is the same loop, repeated until the task is done:

# Mylonite

**Change the order. Reveal the fault.**

Mylonite tests services that keep shared state in Redis or Valkey for concurrency bugs that unit
tests and race detectors miss. So far it has found lost updates on held-out targets, and a
check-then-act race on a development fixture. It also reproduced a known lost update in a real
service, the OpenTelemetry Demo's cart (#3824).

**Meta's Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`, Standard mode, `reasoning_effort` medium) is the planner.**
- **What Muse does:** it reads the service's source and its operation catalog, then proposes
  experiments as strict-schema JSON: which requests to race, after which setup, and in which
  order their store commands should run.
- **What runs them:** a delay-only proxy controls the order in which the service's commands
  reach the store.
- **Who decides:** a contract oracle, in plain code, decides whether an outcome is a bug. Muse
  never does. Every bug is replayed 20 times, with an identical trace, before it is reported.

**What we found** (pre-registered, on 2 bugs generated after our method freeze):
- Muse needed a median of **1 execution** to find each bug. The best non-AI method needed
  **764** and **97**.
- But one execution costs about 9 ms there. So the systematic search was still **faster and
  cheaper**, and Muse lost on time and dollars.
- None of the 5 methods run on the 200 control trials raised a false alarm.

[Results](#results) · [Limitations](#limitations) · [Reproduce](#reproduce) ·
[Full held-out report](experiments/heldout-v1-analysis/RESULTS.md)

Team **MetaMorphic**, Meta AI Developer Hackathon, *Push the Frontier*. Built Oct 27 – Nov 4,
2026 (the team's building period); the submission deadline is Nov 4.
**Status:**
- built and evaluated;
- the repository is public at <https://github.com/harthikrm/mylonite>;
- it is licensed under Apache-2.0 ([LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md)).

## The problem

Two requests each read a value from the store, compute, and write it back. The second write
erases the first.
- **A real example:** in the OpenTelemetry Demo's C# cart service, two concurrent "add to cart"
  calls lose an item. The bug is
  [open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo#3824](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo/issues/3824),
  still open when last checked on Nov 1.
- **Why tools miss it:** unit tests run one request at a time. Memory race detectors see nothing,
  because the shared state is a key in Valkey, reached over a socket.
- Details: [docs/PROBLEM.md](docs/PROBLEM.md).

# AdPlace

Same scene, a different brand for each viewer, always disclosed.

A prototype of an opt-in ad format for short videos: creators approve placements in videos they've already filmed,
and different viewers see different labelled sponsors, with nothing re-rendered to switch brands. Built as a standalone prototype; a
short-video feed such as Reels is where it would ship.

Upload a video once. AdPlace looks for places in its longest shot that could carry an ad (it measures posters,
pictures, signs and screens, and glasses, cups and bowls that stay still; on real uploads so far, wall posters and
still glasses have passed), tracks each one against the room, and declines anything it can't place
well, saying why. When a viewer's video loads, a second-price auction picks a brand for every placement in well under a
millisecond, and the browser composites the winners into the footage live: matched to its perspective, light, focus
and grain, behind the people and hands in front, printed on glasses and cups, and on a blank patch of a cup that has
a design of its own. Every frame carries a visible "AI product placement" label; the file a viewer downloads carries
an invisible Meta Video Seal watermark carrying an id this server resolves to the campaigns.

**What's new.** Product placement in finished footage is an existing industry (studios insert brands into shows, once, for every viewer). AdPlace changes three things: the creator opts in and approves each place and brand; the brand is chosen per viewer when their video loads, by an auction, and switching it re-renders nothing; and every ad is disclosed, on screen and in an invisible watermark in any copy a viewer keeps.

# AfroHydro AI RoadWatch

**Daily rainfall, historical road connectivity and Meta Muse Spark 1.3 for Africa.**

[Watch the 3-minute demonstration](https://youtu.be/HZsCreY3ZL0)

AfroHydro AI RoadWatch combines daily AfroHydro rainfall estimates, GRIP4 historical road networks and Meta Model API to screen intercity corridors and explain the evidence. The app maps rainfall, samples rainfall along connected road paths, and uses a transparent detour-ratio heuristic to flag routes GREEN, AMBER or RED. Muse Spark 1.3 interprets the calculated JSON evidence and explains uncertainties.

The demo compares **Nairobi–Kakamega, Kenya** (GREEN; 1.28× detour ratio) with **Benguela–Kuito, Angola** (RED; 3.02×). RED means a suspected detour in the historical network—not a confirmed flood or road closure. Rainfall on a displayed detour is not necessarily rainfall on the normal driving corridor.

## Run locally

Python 3.12 is recommended.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
# Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
# Set MODEL_API_KEY in your operating-system environment before launching.
streamlit run afrohydro_roadwatch_v8_2.py
```

**Data required:** The code is public, but the application also needs the datasets described in [`DATA.md`](DATA.md). If the `data/Africa_Cities_All.shp` file exists, the app uses bundled `data/`; otherwise it retains the original local Windows path for the verified demonstration installation. You can override the data root with `ROADWATCH_DATA_ROOT`. Without the required datasets, the app cannot run. API access also depends on Meta account permissions and geographic availability.

## Data and limitations

- AfroHydro rasters: daily estimates, not rain-gauge observations or flood confirmation.
- GRIP4: historical connectivity; calculated paths are not verified driving directions.
- GREEN/AMBER/RED: heuristic route screening, not safety classifications.
- AI: Muse Spark 1.3 is used to explain structured results, not to calculate road distances or rainfall.

**Hackathon:** Meta AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Build for Your World · **Team GeoWade AI**.

# Kalkan

Kalkan is KENOPA LTD's entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Startup track. It is a drop-in proxy that sits in front of a tool-using agent and blocks indirect prompt injection.

Pass 1 is a fast screen. Pass 2 is an intent judge. A built-in attacker replays fresh English and Turkish injections against a sandbox agent, and a small dashboard shows which rule fired and the held-out detection rates.

The name is the Turkish word for shield.

**Demo video:** _link to be added_ · **Licence:** Apache-2.0

![Kalkan dashboard in offline mock mode](docs/dashboard-mock.png)

## Why it matters

Tool-using agents read untrusted mail, documents, and web pages, then call tools that send mail or move files. One hidden instruction in that text can turn a summary request into data exfiltration. Meta evaluated Prompt Guard 2 on English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, and Thai; Turkish is not among them. Kalkan does not rely on the screen alone: a second pass checks every proposed tool call against what the user actually asked for, so a paraphrased or non-English injection that slips past pass 1 still cannot buy the tool call it wanted.

## What works offline

No Meta API key is required to run the demo, the tests, or the eval. Set `META_API_KEY` (or Meta's own name, `MODEL_API_KEY`) and Kalkan switches the judge and the attacker onto Meta Model API. Until then both calls go through a mock provider. The mock is labeled on every status payload and in the eval file. It is not Muse Spark and it is not Muse Wonder.

Pass 1 defaults to an offline heuristic. That heuristic is Kalkan code. It is not Llama Prompt Guard 2. The real 86M classifier loads only when you set `KALKAN_SCREEN=prompt-guard` after accepting the Hugging Face gate. Weights are not in this repo.

## Quick start

```bash
make install
make test
make serve
```

Open http://localhost:8080.

One command for the proxy, the sandbox agent, and the dashboard:

```bash
make up
```

That is `docker compose up --build`. The three pieces run in one process, on port 8080, with separate modules: `kalkan.proxy`, `kalkan.agent`, and `dashboard/`.

`make check` runs the tests and fails if `evals/results/latest.json` disagrees with a fresh harness run.

## Demo story

1. Run the Turkish invoice **unprotected**. The sandbox agent treats the hidden note as an order and forwards files to `finance-audit@external.example`.
2. Run it **with Kalkan**. The read is allowed. The forward and the send are blocked. The draft is kept. The card names the rule.
3. Run the **attacker loop**. It replays train seeds and paraphrases. A paraphrase can miss pass 1. Pass 2 still blocks the forward. A session literal then catches that exact string on replay. That literal is not a fine-tune.
4. Read the **held-out chart**. The numbers on the page are the file the harness wrote. The banner under the chart is the harness honesty note, verbatim.

The spoken script and shot list are in [DEMO.md](DEMO.md).

**Propose. Check. Replay. Review.** A Meta model proposes what could have happened. Deterministic code decides what is possible. A person confirms every finding.

Built by **Team AKASHI** for the **Meta AI Developer Hackathon** (Cerebral Valley), theme **Build for Your World**.

| | |
|---|---|
| Demo video (under 3 minutes) | https://youtu.be/GKYcaDvdH5U |
| How it works (diagram) | [docs/architecture.svg](docs/architecture.svg) |

![The model proposes, the code decides](docs/architecture.png)

> **Every case in this repository and demo is fictional.** CaseWeave is analysis support for investigators. It does not decide who is guilty, it does not identify people, and it is not legal advice. Every output is AI-drafted and must be confirmed by a person against the source evidence.

Investigators reconcile statements, device logs and photographs by hand, and a contradiction between two of them is easy to miss. India's own figures show the scale:

- **51,24,205** IPC and BNS cases were under investigation in 2024, of which police disposed of 35,21,488 and chargesheeted 25,40,668 (a 72.1% chargesheeting rate). That leaves about **16.0 lakh (roughly 31%) not disposed of by year end** (our arithmetic from the published totals). Source: NCRB, *Crime in India 2024*, national snapshot, the first edition under the new BNS.
- On staffing, the Home Ministry told the Rajya Sabha that **Delhi Police alone was short of 9,248 posts against 92,044 sanctioned** (30 November 2025, as reported by The Tribune).

Reading every source against every other source is slow and error-prone. A tool that does it consistently, with citations, can help.

## What it does

1. **Reads the evidence.** Statements, device logs, CCTV notes, examiner reports and photographs are hashed on upload and read by a Meta model into a table of observations.
2. **Finds contradictions between sources**, each pointing at both sides, with a prosecutor, defender and judge debate a person can read.

GeoScienceAI Lab is a local web app built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon. # EMBER: Edge Mesh for Burn Early-warning & Reporting

**Existing wildfire networks detect. EMBER investigates, and re-programs its own sensors while doing it.**

EMBER is an **agentic sensor mesh**. Cheap XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense nodes (camera + microphone) detect flame, smoke, crackling and motion on-device and send 30-byte coded packets over a multi-hop, Meshtastic-class radio mesh. A **fine-tuned Muse Glimmer** at the command center doesn't just read that telemetry. It runs a closed loop through the radio:
- **interrogates** nodes (re-sample this one, probe the downwind neighbor),
- **pays for every question in LoRa airtime**,
- decides **ALERT / WATCH / DISMISS**,
- **re-programs the nodes' on-device detectors** so the same false alarm doesn't happen again,
- writes the incident report.

> Hackathon track: **Push the Frontier**: a language model in the control loop of a physical sensing network.

## What's new

| | Existing systems | EMBER |
|---|---|---|
| **Sensing loop** | Passive: sensor → threshold/ML → alert (e.g. Dryad Silvanet's LoRaWAN gas-sensor mesh, AI camera towers) | **Active perception:** the model chooses which node to question next, using wind physics (smoke drifts downwind, so ask the downwind neighbor) |
| **LLM + Meshtastic** | Chatbots: people text an LLM over the mesh (radio-llm, LORACLE and ~45 similar repos) | The LLM **operates the mesh**: reads raw telemetry, sends commands, gets answers back over the radio |
| **Bandwidth** | Ignored, or handled by fixed reporting intervals | **Airtime-aware agent:** every query is priced with the Semtech LoRa time-on-air formula × relay hops, against a 1% duty-cycle budget. The model learns value of information: under tight budgets it asks one question or uses free history |
| **Edge behavior** | Fixed firmware thresholds; false alarms repeat | **The model re-programs the edge:** fog → re-baseline haze swarm-wide; glare-prone node → require flame flicker; faulty sensor → mute it. Measured: in held-out sim episodes, after-action false-alarm events drop 126 → 0 (fog) and 20 → 1 (glare) when the right retune is sent |
| **Wire format** | JSON / protobuf telemetry | **Ember Link Protocol**, co-designed so the model reads raw packets natively: 2.6× smaller than equivalent JSON |
| **Training data** | Human-labelled incidents (rare, expensive) | **Physics digital twin → specialist model:** fire spread + smoke plume + false-alarm simulator generates ground-truth agent trajectories; zero human labels |

## How it works

```
 [XIAO node]~~ESP-NOW flood mesh (≤200 B, TTL 3)~~[XIAO node]~~...~~[gateway XIAO]==USB==[laptop: command center]
  camera → flame ratio, haze index, motion                              │  gateway/  (Python, stdlib only)
  mic    → sound level, crackle transients                              │   swarm state + airtime ledger
  E|n3|s42|FLM|c81|hz34|snd12                                           │   tools: confirm / ping / history /
  C|*|q9|SET|rebase1   ◄── edge re-program

# Haptura

**A gate that makes an agent prove, by its own experiments, that it still controls what it is about to act on, and
stop, probe or decline when it cannot.**

An entry for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track; kickoff 26 Oct, deadline 4 Nov 2026). The phone and
desktop owner gates run and are measured (below), and a multi-step Muse agent runs behind the phone gate (a bench
of 72 scored runs on Muse Spark and Muse Wonder, below). The arena, its agent loop, its evaluation and its runner are built
and tested offline. The arena's one paid evaluation run (the kill test) finished on 1 Nov 2026. EVAL.md's verdict on
it is Rethink: the arena's claim did not hold on these seeds. The gate's effect passed, 0.42 against a bar of 0.10;
SAM's lead over a colour tracker did not clear its bar (below).

**Live demo page:** https://sharminsirajudeen.github.io/haptura/, the measured results, how the gate works, the gate
itself to tap (`phone/windows.py` and `phone/rules.py`, unchanged, run in the browser on two recorded screens) and the
arena replay, no setup. **Video (3 min):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UaFilR5qpPs

## The model proposes each touch; the gate grants it

**The problem.** An agent that works a phone's apps can be led to touch a window that is not the app it was asked to
use: a fake system dialog drawn over that app, or another app's window that never takes focus. A check of which app is
in front misses the second.

**The mechanism.** Before each tap and scroll, the gate asks Android's input dispatcher which window the touch will
reach, takes that window's owner uid (assigned by the system, not chosen by the app) and maps it to its package. The
touch is sent only when that package is the task's app or an allowlisted package (the system UI, and the keyboard the
phone is set to, read from its settings); an unknown owner is refused.
Typing is checked against the focused window's owner. The model, Muse, proposes every action; the gate, outside the
model, grants or refuses each touch, and a refusal goes back to Muse as part of its next step. Meta describes the same
split for its own agent's connectors and network egress: "Muse proposes actions, but only Sentinel can grant
permission to perform action"
([Meta](https://research.meta.ai/blog/security-and-safety-for-ai-agents-our-approach-with-muse)). This gate does it
for touches on a screen.

**How it runs.** Haptura is not an app you install. It sits in the agent's action path: before every touch the agent
sends, it asks Android which app owns the window under the finger, and refuses if that is not the task's app. Today it
runs where the agent runs, on a computer driving the phone over adb.

**The evidence**, on the Android emulator (API 36), 1 Nov 2026, each row from the records named:

| Measurement | Gate off | Gate on | Records |
|---|---|---|---|
| Another app's not-focusable window (the keyboard, standing in) over a task app that holds focus, 20 trials each | the touch reached

# Comedically Online

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hc-pmiVbB6c

*Built during the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, theme: Build for Your World. AI uses only Meta models.*

**Live comedy. Moderated by someone who gets the joke.**

## Why I built this

I never had the chance to watch the world's famous comedians perform live, because
they rarely come to my country. I wanted a place where new comedians can promote
themselves and world-famous comedians can run extra shows for fans everywhere. But
live comedy has a problem: generic moderation kills streams over a joke, a word, or a
gesture. So I built Comedically Online: comedy-aware moderation where each show runs
under a rulebook the comedian accepts, enforced live on a 12-second delay.

Comedically Online is a live-streaming platform built only for stand-up comedians — and
the moderation is the product. A comedian's act lives or dies on provocative material,
so blunt keyword filters or human moderators who "don't get the bit" either censor the
jokes or let real harm through. Comedically Online instead runs every live broadcast
through a comedy-aware AI moderation pipeline: speech and video are checked against a
small, explicit rulebook, and only the offending word or gesture is hidden — muted or
blurred in place — while the show itself is never cut.

The demo uses harmless stand-ins only (an invented banned word, a three-finger gesture,
a nose touch), never real explicit content.

> **Only Meta models are used for AI.** Speech: Meta Voice Transcribe (file) and the
> Meta realtime ASR WebSocket. Vision + judgement: `muse-spark-1.3`. No OpenAI, no
> third-party AI APIs anywhere in the pipeline.

> Legal pages (`/terms`, `/privacy`, `/cookies`, `/community-guidelines`,
> `/moderation-policy`) are **template drafts**. They must be reviewed by a lawyer
> before launch. Nothing here claims legal compliance.

# Minutes

> Milwaukee City Hall, in minutes.

**Built by Tarik Moody. Public records only, no recommendations.**

Built Oct 29 – Nov 4, 2026, during the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon).

- **Live app:** https://minutes-rust.vercel.app
- **Video:** _coming soon_

---

## What it does

Milwaukee publishes nearly everything City Hall decides: agendas, files, votes, staff reports and hours of meeting video. Almost nobody can use it. One file's records are spread across a committee, the full Common Council and sometimes a commission. Meetings run three hours. Nothing tells you which files touch what you care about, when they will be heard, or how to speak up before it is decided.

Minutes reads the records of the Common Council, its eight standing committees and the City Plan, Fire & Police and Historic Preservation commissions, and lets anyone follow them at the depth they choose: a plain answer, a file's whole path, or the meeting video at the moment it happened. It is for residents, organizers, journalists and students.

| Feature | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Ask Minutes** | Type a question ("What has the city done about police surveillance cameras?"). Muse Spark looks things up in the synced records, including the text of the PDFs attached to files (staff reports, police policies, contracts), and answers in two to five plain sentences. Every sentence shows the files it came from, and a box explains the city's procedural terms ("held to call of the chair"). Sentences the records don't support are dropped before you see them. |
| **Follow this** | Under every answer, Minutes proposes a few words to watch for in new file titles. Edit them, sign in, follow. Minutes emails you only when a matching file is introduced, put on an agenda or decided. Introduction comes first, usually weeks before a hearing, which is when there is still time to organize. Only the name and the words are saved, never the question. |
| **File pages** | One file's path from introduction to the Mayor: every real step with its vote, a jump into the meeting video, the next hearing with an add-to-calendar file, **who decides** (each member, and for the Council each alder's district, email and city page) and **how to be heard** in that body's own published words, and for zoning files the lot outline and what the zoning would change. |
| **Meetings** | Every synced meeting, with its agenda and what was decided: each item's actions and vote count, who moved it, the clerk's note from the minutes, and a jump into the city's video. Coming-up meetings also show how to be heard and who decides. Meetings are split into chapters with a transcript wherever one exists: four transcribed with speaker names, the rest from the city's own captions. |
| **This week** | Files on an agenda in the next seven days and decisions from the last seven, sorted by topic. |
| **Near me** | Type an address, see zoning and development files within half a mile.

# Skillow
### From watching to doing.

**Skillow is a multimodal AI learning assistant that turns practical video tutorials into structured lessons, compares a learner's real-world progress against the complete procedure, and explains difficult concepts with contextual answers and illustrative visuals.**

It is designed to help learners move beyond passively watching tutorials: understand the process, apply the knowledge, and overcome practical challenges.

---

## Table of contents

- [The problem](#the-problem)
- [What Skillow does](#what-skillow-does)
- [Core features](#core-features)
  - [Understand — complete tutorial lessons](#1-understand--complete-tutorial-lessons)
  - [Compare — personalised progress review](#2-compare--personalised-progress-review)
  - [Build My Guide — actionable next steps](#3-build-my-guide--actionable-next-steps)
  - [Ask & Visualise — contextual explanations](#4-ask--visualise--contextual-explanations)
- [AI architecture](#ai-architecture)
- [Lesson-generation pipeline](#lesson-generation-pipeline)
- [Evidence, accuracy and safety](#evidence-accuracy-and-safety)
- [Demo tutorials](#demo-tutorials)
- [Technology stack](#technology-stack)
- [Project structure](#project-structure)
- [Getting started](#getting-started)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Run Skillow locally](#run-skillow-locally)
- [Testing](#testing)
- [Deployment](#deployment)
- [Limitations](#limitations)
- [Acknowledgements](#acknowledgements)

---

## The problem

Video tutorials are excellent demonstrations, but learning from them can be difficult:

- Important actions are spread across a long video.
- Learners must repeatedly pause, rewind, and search for the relevant moment.
- A tutorial may show a procedure without explaining every intermediate action.
- Generic AI answers may not match the exact tutorial or the learner's current setup.
- Learners often need to know what they have already completed, what is missing, and what to do next.
- Visual explanations can help, but an inaccurate technical diagram can be misleading.

Skillow brings tutorial understanding, progress review, and contextual explanations into one learning workspace.

## What Skillow does

Skillow supports a workflow from tutorial to practical application:

1. **Understand:** Upload a tutorial or provide a supported video URL. Skillow extracts a structured lesson from the video and its spoken content.
2. **Review the complete procedure:** Explore objectives, prerequisites, tools, materials, safety information, and chronological stages.
3. **Compare:** Upload a photo of your current work and optionally describe it. Skillow reviews your situation against the full lesson.
4. **Build My Guide:** Receive an actionable, personalised written guide based on the tutorial and the learner's current progress.
5. **Ask & Visualise:** Ask questions about the tutorial and receive a contextual written explanation with an optional illustrative image.

---

## Core features

### 1. Understand

**Accessible math for students who cannot see the whiteboard.**

FollowMath AI helps a blind or visually impaired student follow an equation written on a whiteboard, write it out themselves, and check their own work. Everything is done through sound and touch. The student never needs to see the screen.

Standard educational software inherently assumes the user can see the screen. To solve this, FollowMath AI was engineered entirely from scratch for the Meta AI Global Hackathon. Powered exclusively by Meta's ecosystem (SAM 3.1, Muse Spark, and Muse Transcribe), it features a custom real-time backend and a strictly blind-centric, dual-device architecture. Every single UI choice and WebSocket sync was deliberately built from the ground up to serve the unique tactile and auditory needs of visually impaired students.

---
## The Inspiration

This project originated from a Computer Engineering professor's observations of a visually impaired student in an advanced Master's course. While the student could comprehend the spoken lectures, the inability to spatially interact with, draw, and solve complex math equations created an immense academic barrier, ultimately impacting their performance on written midterms. FollowMath AI was built to solve this exact real-world problem.

## The Problem

Math is taught on boards, slides, and paper. A student who cannot see them has to rely on someone else to read out every symbol, and to check every line they write. But hearing an equation read aloud doesn't convey its 2D structure. Because blind students cannot easily imagine how the math looks without physically drawing it or feeling the spatial layout of the equations, relying on verbal dictation makes it hard to keep up in class and hard to study alone.

## What it does

1. **Reads the board.** A phone is propped up facing the whiteboard. The app takes a picture, finds the equation and reads it aloud.
2. **Keeps up with the instructor.** The phone keeps watching the board. When the instructor writes more, the app updates and tells the student using audio cues.
3. **Guides the student's writing.** The student writes the equation on a tablet with a stylus. The app stays quiet while the student is on track, and says things like "Move right to reach the middle of the equation" when they drift.
4. **Checks the work.** When the student pauses, the app looks at what they wrote and gives short spoken feedback, like a patient tutor.
5. **Lets the student feel their own writing.** After writing, the student slides a finger over the screen. The app names each symbol under the finger, such as "the letter y", "an equals sign", "the digit 2". If a symbol is unfinished or messy, it says so honestly (for example "a single horizontal line" or "a scribble") instead of guessing what the student meant.

# Argus

**Autonomous, continuous inspection AI for engineer-to-order (ETO), high-mix low-volume industrial manufacturing.**

Argus watches a one-off, high-value piece of equipment while it is being built — through camera video, close-up photographs and 3D laser scans — and checks what it sees against the design (CAD) and the rules that apply to that exact order. It does this at every stage of the build, not once before delivery, and produces a traceable dossier of every finding for a human quality engineer to sign off.
