The edition keeps its harness subset through the registry at startup, takes only the Muse reviewer, and assembles its own subcommands — no edition code lives in ai2 itself. To move to a newer ai2, bump the `rev` pins in `Cargo.toml`.

## Install

Grab the build for your machine from the latest release and put `ai2-muse-edition` somewhere on your PATH:

```sh
ai2-muse-edition setup
```

`ai2-muse-edition setup` runs the Linux setup: containers, the master key, the human check and the daemon. There is no account and no sign-up. Your keys stay on this machine.

## Use

Install Muse as a harness, sign in, and review a run:

```sh
ai2-muse-edition harness install muse
ai2-muse-edition harness sign-in muse
ai2-muse-edition --run-path ./site --objective "Rebuild the landing page"
```

Run Muse on a task, then review what it did:

```sh
ai2-muse-edition run --harness muse --model muse-wonder-1.0 --folder ./notes "Add a search box"
```

Keep keys in the vault and hand agents a short-lived pass instead:

```sh
ai2-muse-edition vault put --name stripe --approved-url https://api.stripe.com/
ai2-muse-edition vault with stripe -- ./deploy.sh
```

Sign an HTML document after a review; the signed copy lands next to it:

```sh
ai2-muse-edition --run-path ./site --objective "Rebuild the landing page" --document ./site/index.html
```

State lives in `~/.ai2-muse-edition`.

## License

Apache-2.0 (`LICENSE`).

# Handyman

**Try DIY before you call a handyman.**

Open **https://handyman.thepushh.com** on your phone. It's free, with no
sign-up and nothing to install.

Point your camera at something that's acting up and say what's wrong.
Handyman finds the machine, runs the quick checks people often miss,
walks you through a safe fix step by step, and checks your work with the
camera. If it's a job for a professional, it finds a handyman near you
and writes the message for you.

## Models used

Every diagnosis and highlight comes from a live Meta model call — no canned answers.

- **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor` for local dev, `muse-spark-1.3` in prod) — looks at your photos, names the appliance and its parts, figures out what's wrong, and writes the fix steps.
- **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) — cuts out the exact shape of each part so highlights sit on the real component, not a guess.
- **Muse Image** (`muse-image-1.0`) — draws the outline and letter tags (A, B, C…) on the photo.
- **Muse Wonder** (`muse-wonder-1.0`) — listens to 3–5 second clips of the machine (beeps, clicks, hums) and says what it hears. Its hearing is cross-checked against measured audio features, and the numbers win if they disagree.
- **MMS-TTS** (local) — speaks every reply out loud, in the same language you used, including Hinglish.
- **Voice input** — your words go through the browser's built-in speech recognition. The Muse Voice Transcribe hook exists in the backend but isn't configured yet.
- **Glimmer** — has no public local weights, so quick on-device judgments are a local heuristic fallback, not the real model.

## How to use it

1. **Open the link and allow the camera and microphone.** It works best
   on a phone held upright. Android Chrome and iPhone Safari both work.
2. **Tap to speak** and say what's wrong: the machine, and what it does

   - **Can't talk?** Tap **Type**.
   - **Camera not working?** Tap **Photo**, then describe the problem.

     move closer or back.
   - When the view is right, it takes the picture itself.
   - If it can't find the machine, tap **Use this view**.
4. **Try the quick checks.** These are the simple things people often
   miss, like a switch, a setting or a loose plug. Tap **That fixed it**

![The Apps page of ai squared over a sky, ocean and grass scene](.github/banner-apps.jpg)

# ai squared

Your apps, your agents' work and your keys, looked after on your own machine by ai squared.

## Install

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openwork-africa/ai2/main/install.sh | sh
ai2 setup
```

The first line fetches the build for your machine from the latest release, checks its SHA-256, and puts `ai2` in `~/.local/bin`.
There are builds for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Linux (x86_64 and arm64).

`ai2 setup` opens your browser: a few welcome screens, then setup as it runs.
`ai2 setup --headless` does the same in the terminal.
The dashboard and the vault both start when you log in. The dashboard is at `http://127.0.0.1:7797`; bookmark the address `ai2 ui address` prints, nonce and all.

Setup asks you to approve once or twice.
On a Mac that is Touch ID, or your Mac password.
On Linux it is your login password, through polkit: the desktop prompt, or the terminal when there is no desktop. Without polkit, you choose a vault passphrase during setup. Linux setup also asks for `sudo` once.

There is no account and no sign-up. Your keys stay on this machine.

### What you just installed

- `ai2`, one binary.
- The vault service, the only thing that ever holds your keys. It starts when you log in.
- A place for agents to run boxed in: Apple's `container` on macOS 26 with Apple silicon. Elsewhere, setup says so, and agents run on the host, each sandbox with its own socket to the vault.
- The dashboard, a page on `http://127.0.0.1:7797` that starts when you log in and keeps your apps running. `ai2 ui` opens it.

It does three things.

### Register an app

```sh
ai2 apps register --name Notes --description "Plain notes you can search" --command "deno task start" --openapi /openapi.json --icon favicon.svg
```

Adds the app in this folder to your list, so you or an agent can start it, stop it and read its API.
In the page: **Apps**, then **Add app**.

### Run a security review

```sh
ai2 --run-path ./notes --objective "Add a search box"
```

Checks a folder a coding agent worked in, and gives it two scores.
`--objective` is what you asked the agent to do, so the reviewer can tell the changes you wanted from the ones you didn't.
The stack is checked against exploits published in the last few days.
A reviewer reads the files the run changed, and fixes what a small, safe change can fix.
It runs four security skills: security-audit, dependency-audit, patch-sweep and owasp-audit (credited in `NOTICE`).
It does not scan your machine for malware, and it does not watch what agents do.
In the page: **Security**, then **New review**.

### Add a key to the vault

```sh
ai2 vault put --name stripe --approved-url https://api.stripe.com/
```

Locks a secret away; it asks for the secret without showing it.
Agents get a short-lived pass to use the key, never the key itself, and only on the URLs you allow.
In the page: **Vault**, then **Add key**.

# Walkout

Twelve shoppers with different lives go through a real shop in a real browser: a cheap phone on slow 3G, 200 percent zoom, keyboard only, a screen reader, Spanish. Each one is a Meta Muse Spark agent that looks at the screen and taps one thing at a time.

The shop is the OpenTelemetry Demo at release 2.1.3, which shipped a cart total that ignores quantity ([issue 1526](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo/issues/1526)). Release 3.1.0 is the clean build.

The browser records where each shopper gave up. The model writes one sentence per walkout and a patch, the shop gets rebuilt and the same twelve go again. Spark picks the source files, Wonder writes the patch and reviews it before the rebuild gate, then the same shoppers watch the change live. The frontend has no `npm test` script, so the patch gate is its type check and lint in the image build.

You need Node 22 or newer, Git, Docker with Compose v2 and a running Docker daemon. New shopper rounds also need a Meta API key in `META_API_KEY` and use paid API calls. The saved results and browser checks below make no model calls.

```
npm ci
npx playwright install chromium
npm run typecheck
npm test
```

On Linux, Playwright may also need system libraries, installed with `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium`.

## Check the real shop without model calls

Run these on the server:

```sh
docker info
docker compose version
npm run shop
npm run test:shop -- defect
npm run test:shop -- clean
```

The first `npm run shop` clones the shop at 2.1.3 into `shops/otel-demo/src`, gets the 3.1.0 compose files and starts both shops (2.1.3 on :8080, 3.1.0 on :8082). Startup waits until both frontends answer. Keep those ports free. The browser checks open the real shop on desktop and phone layouts, add three telescopes, check the total and complete checkout on the clean build using the demo's sample card.

`shops/otel-demo/stack.sh down` stops both shops.

# Musegix **An orchestration layer for AI app building with Meta's models.** Musegix sits between a browser app builder and Meta's models. For every request it decides which model should answer, which project context to send, and what a change affects. The goal is fewer tokens, lower cost, and faster edits, without changing how the app builder works. [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE) --- ## Contents 1. [The problem](#the-problem) 2. [What Musegix does](#what-musegix-does) 3. [Architecture](#architecture) 4. [The three engines](#the-three-engines) 5. [The gateway](#the-gateway) 6. [Models and training data](#models-and-training-data) 7. [Resource use](#resource-use) 8. [Results](#results) 9. [Use cases](#use-cases) 10. [Limits](#limits) 11. [Install](#install) 12. [Repository layout](#repository-layout) 13. [Tests](#tests) 14. [Licence and attribution](#licence-and-attribution) --- ## The problem AI coding agents work in steps. On every step, the app builder resends: - the whole conversation, including old tool output such as file reads and command logs that the agent has already used; - the project files, or a large part of them. So the cost of a step grows with the length of the session, not with the size of the change. Every edit also goes to the same model, whether it's a colour change or a multi-file feature. The result is more tokens, more money and more waiting per edit. ## What Musegix does Musegix is an OpenAI-compatible proxy. The app builder points at it instead of at the model provider. Each request then passes through three engines: | Engine | Question it answers | What it changes | |---|---|---| | **Ysolveth** | Which model should handle this request? | Picks a cheaper or stronger model, and runs on the CPU. | | **PolyFabric** | What context does this request need? | Trims old tool output and sends only the project files it needs. | | **Veylqora** | What else does this change affect? | Adds the list of dependent files to the reply's status cards. | Each reply also shows status cards for the three engines: the tier and model chosen, the tokens trimmed, and the files affected. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR U[User prompt] --> B[Browser app builder
bolt.diy] B -->|OpenAI-compatible request| G[Musegix gateway
FastAPI] G --> Y[Ysolveth
on-device routing] Y --> P[PolyFabric
context trimming] P --> V[Veylqora
impact tracking] V -->|routed, trimmed request| M{Models} M -->|muse-spark-1.3, muse-wonder-1.0
Meta Model API| G M -->|muse-spark-open-1026
Baseten| G G -->|streamed reply + status cards| B ``` - The **gateway** is the only thing the app builder talks to. - **Ysolveth** runs in the gateway process, on the CPU, before any model call. - **PolyFabric** and **Veylqora** run in the gateway, on each request. - The **models** are called over the network. Their weights are not on your PC. ## The three engine

# EveryMuse

**Meta's models on every ear.** EveryMuse turns the Bluetooth glasses or earbuds you already own into a Meta AI agent you use without taking out your phone. It also notices what you'll want before you ask.

**Built for your world, as the hackathon theme asks. Ours is the walking commute:** twice a day, a bag or a coffee in each hand, and small questions on the way. Will it rain this afternoon? Which platform is the 19:05? What was that address?
- **Before:** every question means stopping, getting the phone out, unlocking it and typing.
  - Just reaching a phone in a pocket takes 4.6 s on average, against 2.8 s for a watch, and up to 78% of that is getting it out ([Ashbrook et al., CHI 2008](https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357092)).
  - Then the answer needs a free hand and your eyes.
- **After:** you ask out loud and keep walking. The first word of the answer comes back 1.2 to 3.5 s after you stop talking, and your hands and eyes stay on the street.
- **Before you even ask:** when a friend says "dinner's at my place Friday at seven", EveryMuse offers the reminder on its own. Only a yes lets it act.

**Try it now:** https://earshot-yuansshi.fly.dev. It works in any browser, with any headset, or by typing.

**Watch it:**
- **The whole demo (1:47):** https://earshot-yuansshi.fly.dev/media/everymuse-demo-full.mp4

Cooking, assembly and crafts occupy your hands. Asking for help should not require repeatedly typing or describing the scene. Camera evidence is incomplete, however. Seeing a bowl tilt does not prove what was in it.

## Meta models and runtime evidence

# Continuum

[![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/AdityaVG13/Continuum?color=blue)](https://github.com/AdityaVG13/Continuum/releases)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-black)](LICENSE)

**A network control plane your agent can use and cannot run away with.**

One binary on your Mac. It finds the router you physically own, enrolls a
factory-fresh unit without asking for a password that does not exist, commissions
it through the vendor's own interface, shapes its WAN queue with CAKE it can
undo, and proves each step with a receipt. When a change is unsafe or the unit
cannot support it, Continuum refuses with a typed reason instead of leaving a
half-state behind.

Healthy operation spends no model calls. Every write needs the permission you
granted. Every uncertain effect is reconciled, never replayed.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie track, Push-the-Frontier).
The claim under test: a model that sees the task *and* the path makes better
bounded choices than a competent static rule, and the product can prove what it
did without asking the owner to trust the model.

Goose is the primary implementation language; C++ supplies the native transport
boundaries and the fallback path. Reasoning comes from Meta's `muse-wonder-1.0`
through the Responses API: every call is bounded by model, token and call caps,
and healthy operation spends none.

![The Device screen on a real GT-AX11000](docs/images/continuum-device.png)

*The Device screen on a real unit: identity read from the router, lifecycle
gates unclosed until each is actually verified, every disruptive action behind
its own key. The MAC is masked.*

## The demo, in five keys

| key | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| `d` | reads this host's interfaces, routes and neighbor candidates. No key, no scan. |
| `p` | binds the router you say you own. Selection grants no write permission. |
| `n` | enrolls a factory-pending unit: mints the admin credential, stages it in the OS keychain, submits the vendor's first-run form, proves a protected read. |
| `f` | sets the operations and constraints the model may ever use. Meta can read this policy, never widen it. |
| `e` | hands the commissioned device to Meta for bounded, reversible setup, with every effect receipted and a way back. |

The enrollment line is the one people do not believe. A factory-reset GT-AX has
**no admin password to type**, so Continuum generates one, stores it before the
first write, and then proves the device accepts it: the factory default
`admin/admin` is dead afterwards, a retry inspects instead of replaying the
ceremony, and no credential material reaches the transcript or the durable state
file. Vendor wizards do not do this; that is the point.

## Three guarantees that make it safe to point at hardware

1. **The model never holds the shell.** Meta chooses from a typed tool surface
   (`manage_device`, `apply_qos`, ...). It never receives router credentials,
   never composes a shell

# Yaad (याद) — Local-first, evidence-backed personal memory

**Yaad turns your scattered files into a memory you can question — and every answer carries its proof.**

Yaad indexes folders you explicitly add — PDFs, text documents, images, and audio — then builds a persistent, structured memory of the decisions, deadlines, commitments, and open questions inside them. Ask in plain language over the CLI, API, or web UI and Yaad answers from that memory, reasons across files, tracks how facts change over time, flags conflicts with both sides cited, and abstains honestly when the evidence is not there.

Built from scratch during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (*Build for Your World*, October 27–November 4, 2026).

## Demo

> Demo video (3 min): [https://youtu.be/4haKXzfsi_g](https://youtu.be/4haKXzfsi_g) — walkthrough outline: `docs/SUBMISSION_EVIDENCE.md` §6.
>
> [View the Yaad Pitch Deck](YAAD_pitch_deck.pdf)

![Yaad home: memory at a glance](docs/screenshots/Home_page.png)

*Home view — conflicts needing attention, upcoming dates, recent decisions, and recently indexed files, all linked to sources.*

## The problem

Personal information is scattered across PDFs, documents, images, screenshots, and voice memos. Finding one detail means reopening files; connecting facts across files means holding everything in your head; and when a date moves or two files disagree, the old truth is silently lost. Chatbots don't help — they read at ask-time and forget, and basic retrieval returns text chunks with no notion of what is currently true.

## The solution

Yaad is a personal memory engine, not a chatbot:

- **Extract once, remember durably.** Decisions, deadlines, commitments, and open questions become structured records in SQLite, each wired to the exact excerpts it came from.
- **Reason across files and modalities.** Hybrid retrieval (FTS5 keywords + memory channel, fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion) corroborates values across documents, images, and transcripts.
- **Track time, preserve history.** Supersession links record replacements; previous values stay inspectable in a transition ledger — never silently overwritten.
- **Disagree honestly.** Conflicting values are preserved with both sides cited, and are never served as settled facts. Weak evidence yields a clean abstention, not a guess.

Guiding principle: **Models Propose. Evidence Disposes.** AI models assist with understanding and extraction, while deterministic validation, provenance tracking, relationship checks, and evidence verification have the final word.

## Impact

Important information is rarely stored in one place. Deadlines are buried in notices, decisions live in meeting notes, budgets sit inside proposals, and commitments are scattered across documents, images, and voice memos. Finding a detail is frustrating; knowing whether it is still accurate is harder.

Yaad turns those scattered files into connected memory you can question, and every answer points back to its so

# ProActive Assistant

**A real-time meeting companion that speaks up only when it's worth it.**

Turn it on during a meeting and it transcribes the conversation live with **Muse Voice Transcribe**. **Muse Wonder** watches the transcript and, without being asked, surfaces short insight cards: it explains jargon and acronyms, flags claims that look wrong, suggests sharp questions, and captures decisions and action items. When the meeting ends you get a summary, a list of decisions and an action-item checklist, all exportable as Markdown.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

**Live demo:** https://main.d3q8ybdgvoif2l.amplifyapp.com (backend: https://promet-api.viettrans.info). Choose **Settings → Audio source → Demo meeting** for the scripted sample, or press **Start** and talk.

## Features

- **Live transcript** with partial (gray) and final lines and timestamps, grouped into turns by speaker (Muse diarization). Each speaker gets a coloured avatar and a share-of-talk bar; click a name to rename "Speaker A" to a real name, and insights, summaries and the export use it.
- **Proactive insights**: definition, background, fact check, question to ask, action item, decision, related idea. You can pin, dismiss, copy, ask for "tell me more", or click the quote to jump to that moment in the transcript.
- **Live web search**: when someone states something time-sensitive (a price, an exchange rate, today's news), the model can call a `web_search` tool. The insight panel shows "Searching: …" and the card cites the live figure. Stable facts and definitions never trigger a search.
- **Calm by design**: debounced triggers, a minimum interval between calls, one call at a time, de-duplication, confidence filtering and at most one card per type per call.
- **Audio sources**: microphone (with device picker), a browser tab (Meet/Zoom web/Teams web in Chrome/Edge), mic + tab, or the built-in demo meeting.
- **End-of-meeting notes**: summary, decisions and action items with owner and due date, plus pinned insights and the full transcript. Export as `.md` or copy.
- **Resilient**: the browser-to-server and server-to-Muse links both reconnect automatically. Audio captured while disconnected is buffered and replayed. A half-spoken line is kept when a connection drops. The transcript survives page reloads (stored in the browser only).
- **Demo mode**: a 2.5-minute scripted meeting with 4 voices: the Viettrans.info team planning how to fund machine translation for Vietnam's ethnic minority languages. In the live demo the diarized speakers are named automatically by matching their lines to the script. It can run through the live Muse pipeline, or fully **offline** with a pre-recorded transcript and insights for bad conference Wi-Fi.
- **Privacy**: API keys stay on the server; there is no server-side storage; a visible REC indicator and a consent reminder are shown.
- Light and dark mode, responsive layout (panels stack on mobile).

# Unscroll

**The Vesuvius Challenge says no method yet traces a complete, correct surface
through a scroll automatically, and that a trace switching to a neighbouring sheet
is one of the failures it sees most. Unscroll measures that failure against sheets
people traced by hand, on real Scroll 1 CT, and used the measurement to double how
often a SAM 3.1 trace stays on the sheet you clicked.**

![Before and after the first-slice fix on Scroll 1, slice 6110: green is the sheet people traced by hand, red is Unscroll's SAM 3.1 trace, yellow is the click. Before, the trace jumps to the neighbouring sheet (median 23 voxels off); after, it stays (1.9 voxels).](viewer/eval/20231210121321_z6110.png)

*One click, before and after. Green: the sheet people traced by hand. Red: the
SAM 3.1 trace. Yellow: the click. Before the fix the trace jumps to the
neighbouring sheet; after it, it stays. ([the 20-slice animation](https://jayaudaykmar26589.github.io/unscroll/viewer/evaluate.html#watchsection))*

The Herculaneum scrolls were carbonized by Vesuvius in 79 AD and can only be
read from CT scans, by following one papyrus sheet through thousands of slices
where neighbouring sheets are crushed together. A trace that slips one sheet
reads the wrong page, and nothing warns you. Unscroll turns one click into a
SAM 3.1 trace, measures it against layers people traced by hand, and fixes the
slice where traces go wrong.

**The results in one paragraph.** On 74 clicks never used while building the
fix, the share of each trace within 40 µm of the hand-traced sheet doubled, from
25% to 50% (better on 50 clicks, worse on 19, p = 0.0002). As a control, a
classic optical-flow tracer from the same start scores 4.5 points lower (on the
15 development clicks that comparison is a tie). A Muse Wonder agent that
re-seeds stalled traces caught its own first re-seed jumping to another sheet
and threw out three runs with reasons. On a sheet with known text, smoothing
Unscroll's own trace raises ink agreement from 0.21 to 0.73, against 0.83 for
the official surface, in broad strokes, not letters. Every number is in
`reports/` and on the [Evaluation page](https://jayaudaykmar26589.github.io/unscroll/viewer/evaluate.html).

**What it does not do: Unscroll has not read any new text.** Reading needs a
trace that stays on the right sheet, steadily, for 300+ slices. The
cost-of-reading test measures how far one, five and ten scholar clicks get
towards that, and where they still fall short.

**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/ydY7hmCKrHg

**Try the result yourself:** the [click explorer](https://jayaudaykmar26589.github.io/unscroll/viewer/explore.html) opens any of the 89 measured
clicks on real CT, with all three tracers, the distance to the hand-traced sheet on every
slice, a review planner using the risk ranking, and a tifxyz download for VC3D. The
[agent replay](https://jayaudaykmar26589.github.io/unscroll/viewer/agent.html) steps through Muse Wonder's three logged sessions call by c

# Feluda Care Agent

Turns a customer's website change request into atomic jobs, step-by-step
builder instructions and an AI-verified "done" — built on Meta models.
Design: `Feluda Care Agent — Product & Technical Spec.md`.

## Hackathon submission

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Event | Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026) · theme "Build for Your World" |
| Track | **Indie** (solo) |
| Builder | [naren0207](https://github.com/naren0207) |
| Demo video | [docs/feluda-demo.mp4](docs/feluda-demo.mp4) (25 s, narrated) |

[![Feluda demo video: the header passes, the forgotten footer fails](docs/screenshots/00-video-poster.jpg)](docs/feluda-demo.mp4)

**The problem.** Website-care teams handle a steady stream of small change requests ("our
phone number changed, please update the header and footer"). The builder says *done*, the
customer finds the footer still shows the old number, and trust erodes. Checking every page at
every viewport by hand doesn't scale, so nobody does it.

**What Feluda does.** It turns the customer's message into precise, atomic jobs (one per place
the change must land), gives the builder validated step-by-step recipes, and when the builder
clicks **Mark done** it checks the live site itself: Playwright captures at desktop and mobile,
deterministic DOM checks, SAM 3.1 element localisation, and a Muse Spark visual judge. A request
closes only when every job passes and a final consistency gate re-checks the whole site; then
Muse Spark drafts the "done" note for a human to send.

**The demo moment.** A builder fixes the header, forgets the footer, and marks both done.
Feluda passes the header, fails the footer with the exact reason ("Still shows the old value
'(555) 201-4410'; expected '(555) 201-9900' — on all 6 page/viewport captures"), and blocks
closure until it's fixed. Run it yourself with `python -m scripts.live_demo` (see Quick start).

**Measured on the live demo (2026-11-04, real Meta API):** one request = 8 model calls,
≈ $0.05 in model spend (spec target < $0.25); verification latency from Mark done to verdict
14.9 s median / 18.6 s p95 (target median < 2 min), n = 3. These are small demo samples, not a
production benchmark. The test suite (`python -m pytest`, unit rules plus end-to-end browser
runs with scripted models) passes 76/76.

DriveMatch is **open source** under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) — you are free to use, copy, modify and distribute it (including commercially), subject to the license terms. Contributions are welcome: fork the repo, make your change, run `npm run check`, and open a pull request. See the [Setup guide](#setup-start-here) to get running.

## Setup (start here)

Follow these steps in order. You only need to do steps 1–4 once.

### Prerequisites

- **Node.js 24 or newer** (the backend uses Node's built-in SQLite — no database to install). Check with:
  ```powershell
  node -v    # should print v24.x or newer
  npm -v
  ```
  On macOS/Linux the same commands work in Terminal. If Node is missing or older, install the current LTS from nodejs.org, then re-open your terminal.
- A **Muse API token** from Meta (for Muse Wonder / Muse Spark). Without it the app still runs — see "Running without an LLM token" below — but grounded vehicle research, suggestions, dealers and ModMarket plans need it.
- Optional but recommended: a **web-search API key** (Tavily, Brave Search, or Serper) for reliable search grounding. Without one, the app uses a free DuckDuckGo fallback that works but is less consistent.

### Step 1 — Get the code and install dependencies

```powershell
cd <path-to>\metahackathon2026
npm install
```

This installs the only runtime dependency (Express). There is **no build step**.

### Step 2 — Create your `.env` file

If `.env` does not already exist in the project root, create it from the template:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
Copy-Item .env.example .env
```
```bash
# macOS / Linux
cp .env.example .env
```

> If `.env` already exists, **do not overwrite it** — it may already contain your token. Just open it and check the values below. `.env` is git-ignored and must never be committed: your token lives only here, on the server.

### Step 3 — Add your Muse token and endpoint (required for live AI)

Open `.env` and set at least these two values:

```ini
LLM_API_KEY=<paste-your-muse-token-here>
LLM_BASE_URL=<your-muse-endpoint>
```

How to fill in `LLM_BASE_URL` — use exactly the shape your provider gave you:

| Your endpoint looks like… | Set `LLM_BASE_URL` to… | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `https://<host>/v1/responses` | that full URL | Responses-style API (this is what `api.meta.ai` uses) |
| `https://<host>/v1/chat/completions` | that full URL | Chat-Completions-style API |
| just a base like `https://<host>/v1` | that base URL | The app appends the right path; set `LLM_API_STYLE=responses` or `=chat` if auto-detection guesses wrong |

Leave these at their defaults unless you have a reason to change them:

```ini
LLM_WONDER_MODEL=muse-wonder-1.0

# DockTwin

**Live demo:** https://docktwin.vercel.app

**Video demo:** https://youtu.be/ZWaomFt8mq4

**Describe a port terminal in plain English (or show a photo), get a programmable 3D digital twin, and let an agent stress-test it against conflicting real-world signals before a disruption costs you.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, track **Push the Frontier** (understanding and controlling a physical system). Every model step runs on Meta models: **Muse Spark**, **SAM 3.1**, and **Muse Voice Transcribe** (plus **Muse Spark Open** on Baseten as an optional stress-scenario provider, off by default).

---

## The problem

A container terminal runs on signals that disagree. The carrier's paperwork says a box is empty; the gate scale says it weighs 24 t. A reefer's sensor reads 7.5 °C; the carrier says the temperature is fine. Customs places a hold just as the box's gate lane goes down, while the free-time clock keeps running. Planners make these calls by hand, under time pressure, using rules that were never tested against these collisions. The cost shows up as demurrage, spoiled cargo, missed vessel windows, and trucks idling at dead lanes.

## The solution

DockTwin is an agent that:

1. **Builds** a twin from a description, spoken or typed, or from a yard/gate photo. Muse Spark writes a structured spec (objects plus `when → then` rules in a small JSON DSL), validated by zod. SAM 3.1 segments the photo into containers, cranes, and lanes that seed the twin.
2. **Stress-tests** it. Seeded scenarios plus adversarial scenarios invented by Muse Spark run through a deterministic simulation. The engine reports behavior bugs: rules that fight at equal priority, rules that never settle, safety rules nobody enforces, rules that never fire, and fields nothing provides. Each Muse Spark scenario also carries **expectations** ("by t=60 this reefer must reach at least *inspect*"), and the engine checks them as test oracles. The same defect on many boxes is grouped into one root cause.
3. **Repairs** the rules. Muse Spark proposes each fix as a rule diff. The engine applies it to a copy and re-runs every scenario. A fix is shown as *verified*, *needs review*, or *rejected*, and nothing is applied without the planner's approval.
4. **Decides** per box, with evidence. It picks the gentlest effective action on a ladder: **watch → ask → slow → reroute → inspect → hold → hand to a human**. Each decision shows which signals were trusted and why (source trust scores), the simulation evidence, a confidence score, and an itemized cost-of-delay estimate. Low-confidence or high-impact actions require human approval. Every step lands in a SHA-256 hash-chained audit log.

**Dual use: "Ordinary Tuesday" creator mode.** The same maker and test agent build interactive objects for games and robotics, such as an automatic door or a robot gripper. The same engine finds interaction bugs, like a door that chatters when someone stands still in the safety beam.

# The Brass Escapement (ChaosHook)

Bounded, executable webhook scenario verification with Meta model repair.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Indie Developer Track**.

AI-written webhook handlers can pass happy-path tests yet corrupt state under event reordering, concurrent duplicate bursts, and mid-handler crashes.
ChaosHook demonstrates these failures deterministically using 27 real-SQL schedules and compares each result against a golden state.
During live analysis, Meta Muse Wonder synthesizes repair candidates, while Meta Muse Spark 1.3 explains the divergence using counterexamples and an architecture diagram image. Cached mode supplies a predefined repair and diagnosis. Independent scenario verification evaluates candidate behavior without model calls.

## The problem

Webhook consumers must handle at-least-once, unordered delivery: retries can repeat an event, and arrival order can differ from causal order.
The delivery and idempotency background is documented in sources already cited by this repository: [Creuto](https://creuto.com/webhook-retry-patterns-ordering-idempotency), [Keplaris](https://keplaris.com/blogs/webhook-idempotency-retries), and [Prismatic](https://prismatic.io/blog/how-do-i-make-webhook-processing-idempotent/).

ChaosHook exercises three failure classes:

- **Out-of-order causal inversion:** cancellation arrives before creation, or an older event overwrites newer state. Missing deletion tombstones and timestamp guards can resurrect a canceled subscription.
- **Concurrent duplicate TOCTOU race:** both workers read “event unseen” before either records it, so both grant invoice credits. A sequential duplicate check cannot prevent this race.
- **Mid-handler crash + retry amplification:** a handler commits credits or a welcome-email record, crashes before recording completion, then repeats the effect on retry.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    H["Vulnerable active handler"] --> P["27-cell real-SQL prover"]
    P --> C["Compact counterexamples: diffs, failed cells, bounded traces"]
    C --> W["Muse Wonder: invariants and patch synthesis"]
    W --> V["Import candidate in a temporary directory; run all 27 cells"]
    V --> D{"27/27 verified?"}
    D -->|Yes| A["Accept proposal; apply on user action and re-prove"]
    A --> P
    D -->|No| R{"Another CEGIS round within budget?"}
    R -->|Yes: at most 2 rounds total| C
    R -->|No| F["Reject candidate; use verified offline cache"]
    F --> A
    I["Architecture diagram image"] --> S["Muse Spark 1.3: explain state divergence"]
    C --> S
    S --> U["UI diagnosis, invariants, cell evidence, and patch diff"]
    A --> U
```

CEGIS means counterexample-guided inductive synthesis: a rejected candidate's remaining failures and import error become feedback for the next synthesis attempt.

# LockSmith

An AI agent that diagnoses and repairs concurrency bugs in money-moving code, and an independent verifier that proves each fix before it is accepted.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track), Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026, using **Muse Spark** via the Meta Model API.

## Why

AI coding agents verify fixes by rerunning tests. Concurrency bugs only appear under particular timings, so a test can pass by luck. In payment systems that luck costs real money. LockSmith never lets the agent judge its own work.

## The benchmark: six real fintech concurrency bugs on PostgreSQL

| Scenario | What goes wrong | Reproduced (6 seeds) |
|---|---|---|
| `deadlock` | Opposite-direction transfers lock rows in different orders and kill each other | 6/6 |
| `lost_update` | Balance read into the app and written back; concurrent updates vanish | 6/6 |
| `overdraft` | Balance check and debit not atomic; accounts go negative | 6/6 |
| `double_spend` | Idempotency check is a plain SELECT; client retries charge twice | 6/6 |
| `joint_account` | Each partner locks only their own account while checking the household total; the household goes negative (write skew) | 6/6 |
| `daily_limit` | The daily total is summed from rows that concurrent requests have not inserted yet; the limit is exceeded (phantom) | 6/6 |

Each buggy service lives in `benchmark/<scenario>/` (what the agent may read and replace). Workloads and money checks live in `locksmith/scenarios.py` (never shown to the agent).

| Model | Runs | Accepted | Mean cost / bug | Mean time / bug |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | 18 (6 bugs × 3) | **18/18** | $0.08 | 2.6 min |
| Muse Wonder 1.0 | 6 (6 bugs × 1) | **6/6** | $0.22 | 2.6 min |

| Bug | Spark accepted | Mean reproduction tests written | Mean fixes written |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deadlock | 3/3 | 1.67 | 1 |
| Lost update | 3/3 | 1.33 | 1 |
| Overdraft | 3/3 | 1.67 | 1 |
| Double spend | 3/3 | 1 | 1 |
| Household overdraft (write skew) | 3/3 | 1 | 1 |
| Daily limit bypass (phantom) | 3/3 | 1 | 1.67 |

What the verifier did across all 24 runs: it **rejected 4 of 28 agent-written reproduction tests** as unreliable, and the agent wrote better ones. The two harder bugs have an obvious fix that is wrong, and the verifier rejects both: locking the partner's account too deadlocks under load, and locking today's withdrawal rows cannot stop new rows from being inserted. The agent avoided both in every run. These rejections are demonstrated with hand-written trap fixes in `tests/bad_fixes/`, and live in the dashboard.

# Threadline Discovery

**An agent that turns what patients say about clothing into evidence-checked product ideas for adaptive fashion teams.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. Indie Developer track, "Build for Your World".

- Live site: https://threadline-discovery.onrender.com
- Condition covered: post-mastectomy clothing
- Not medical advice. It supports product decisions for brand and design teams.

## What it does

Adaptive clothing brands often guess what people need. Threadline Discovery reads short notes drawn from public patient forum posts and runs a four-step agent:

1. **Propose.** Muse Spark reads the notes and proposes distinct garment ideas, each citing the notes that support it.
2. **Verify.** Muse Spark gives a first verdict. A second, different Meta model (Muse Wonder) then checks the same claim against only its cited notes and makes the deciding call. Ideas the cited notes do not support are rejected, and the page shows why.
3. **Score.** Code, not a model, scores each surviving idea out of 100: evidence (up to 40, from distinct cited notes), source spread (up to 30, from distinct forum threads), and verifier confidence (up to 30).
4. **Visualize.** Muse Image draws a concept for each idea. Muse Spark's image understanding then checks that the required visible features are in the picture, and the image is redrawn once if they are not.

The site shows the run as a live trace, a map that links every idea to the notes behind it, and a "rejected by the verifier" list.

## Models used

| Model | Where it runs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark | Meta Model API | Proposes ideas, first verdict, checks features in images |
| Muse Wonder | Meta Model API | Independent second verdict that decides |
| Muse Image | Meta Model API | Draws concept images |

The code can also use Muse Spark Open (open weights) on Baseten or Fireworks as the second verifier when a key is set. That path was not used for the submitted run.

## Data and rights

- The ideas come from forum posts that are other people's writing. **No post text is in this repository or on the site.**
- Each post was restated by Muse Spark as a one-sentence note in new words (`paraphrase.py`). Code rejects any note that shares more than three words in a row with its source, and I read and edited all notes by hand.
- Each note links to the public thread it came from. The original posts stay on my computer.
- Running the checker on `results.json` against the originals also finds no run longer than three words.
- Forum names: Mayo Clinic Connect, Breastcancer.org, Breast Cancer Now, Macmillan.

# FittedPerfection

Fits a generated 3D outfit (Trellis/Pixal3D/Rodin) onto four fixed MPFB bodies, each skinned to
its own rig. The fit is local, deterministic maths. Meta's SAM 3.1 labels the outfit's parts
beforehand, and Muse Wonder reviews the results afterwards. Every fit is a draft until a
person reviews it. Full spec: [docs/SPEC.md](docs/SPEC.md).

**Status:** steps 1–2 are done (foundations, target bodies) and step 3 is under way. **Intake**
is built: it unpacks the archive safely, reads which way the outfit faces from its feet, and
writes `full/GARMENT.glb` (every face) plus `full/CAGE.glb` (about 40k faces) in the canonical
frame. Feet partly hidden by cloth give a *provisional* facing, which bind must confirm from
the shoe labels. **Views** is built too: a 72-frame orthographic turntable plus top and bottom stills of
the cage, each with a face-ID image (which cage triangle is visible at every pixel), and the
turntable as `orbit.mp4` for SAM. Every run checks that each pixel lies on the triangle it names.
**Vision** is built: for each of the 42 vocabulary phrases, SAM 3.1 (Meta Model API) segments the
turntable video, keeping each part's id all the way round, plus the top and bottom stills. That's
126 requests, about $0.81 per outfit. Every answer is cached in `runs/_cache/sam/`, so reruns are free
and identical; the cache is keyed by picture content, not file bytes. **Label** is built: it turns
the masks into one part label per cage face (where masks overlap the smaller one wins; skin is a
separate layer confirmed by colour). The labels are combined across all views and smoothed over the
mesh, then rules apply: legs split at the crotch, open torso cloth hangs, trims take their host's
label, and sides left/right. **Bind** is built: it measures sleeve and leg centrelines, shoulders,
the crotch (checked against the 0.59 × shoulder-height prior), feet from the shoes alone (which also
confirms a provisional facing, or refuses the outfit), knees only when both legs agree, and the
legwear length class. The fit isn't built yet, so a run stops after bind.

## Setup

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.venv/Scripts/pip install -r requirements.txt
copy config.example.json config.json      # Blender path, bodies folder
copy secrets.example.env secrets.env      # paste your Meta Model API key (MODEL_API_KEY)
```

`config.json`, `secrets.env`, `runs/`, `frozen/` and the outfit archives stay out of git.

## Commands

```powershell
.venv/Scripts/python -m fittedperfection outfits                 # list the test outfits
.venv/Scripts/python -m fittedperfection run moonshorts          # run (or resume) one outfit
.venv/Scripts/python -m fittedperfection run moonshorts --rerun-from fit
.venv/Scripts/python -m fittedperfection run ARCHIVE.zip --fresh # stage mode: first fit only, with provenance
.venv/Scripts/python -m fittedperfection run purpleshorts --test-fit   # held-out outfits need --test-fit
.venv/Scripts/python -m fittedperfection status moonsho

# Magneye

See inside anything you can photograph. Give Magneye a photo (plus, optionally, up to five more from other sides or close up) and a short prompt. Meta's models work out what the object is, what's inside it and how it works. The result is an interactive 3D exploded view: you can play how the object works, or describe a fault and watch the likely culprit light up red.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026).

## How it works

Two agents, both Muse Wonder (`muse-wonder-1.0`) with tools, stream every step to the UI's agent trace.

**Builder agent:** turns the photo into a verified anatomy.

0. Clears what covers the object: when **SAM 3.1** finds a hand on it, **Muse Image** removes the hand and restores the part it hid, so the outline and shell are whole. The original photo is kept, and the UI says the hidden part was filled in.
1. Researches the object with Muse Wonder's web search: identifies the exact product, then looks for teardowns, specs and common failures (at most 6 searches) and writes a cited blueprint brief. Only URLs the search actually returned are kept as sources.
2. Finds other angles of the same product: photos on Wikimedia Commons (shown with licence and author) and on the pages the research cited (used as model input and linked, not shown). The user's own extra photos come first, each one kept. Muse Wonder vets each one (same body shape? which side?) and keeps up to three.
3. Drafts the anatomy as JSON from the photo, the brief and those views: the object, 12–28 parts with sizes and positions in millimetres, connections, how-it-works scenarios and failure modes. Each part is marked seen, documented (by a cited source) or inferred. Photos are rarely straight-on, so the draft also estimates where the camera was (azimuth, elevation, roll) and describes the parts in the object's own frame; SAM matching, the layout overlay and the 3D shell all project through that viewpoint, and the viewer shows the object upright. Straps, bracelets and cables are accessories: the viewer frames the main body and moves them aside.
4. Verifies the draft with its tools:
   - `find_in_photo` runs **SAM 3.1** on a noun phrase. It confirms each part the draft calls visible, reports where the part really is in the object's millimetre frame, and catches parts the draft imagined.
   - `check_geometry` flags parts outside the object, internal parts that share the same space, and removal orders that dig outward.
   - `view_layout` draws the agent's own layout over the photo so it can see what's off.
5. Fixes problems with `move_parts` (shift the whole body at once), `update_parts`, `add_part` and `remove_part`, then calls `finish`. A final SAM 3.1 pass grounds the visible parts. The object mask becomes the 3D shell, extruded with the photo projected onto it. # OjO OjO is a phone call with an AI friend who can see your iPhone screen. It helps you through apps you cannot read: it tells you where to tap, shows the place in a small window and writes text for you in the local language. Say what you want, in your own words. OjO looks at your screen and answers by voice. If the answer depends on something, it asks. 5. When there is a place to tap, the window shows that part of your screen up close, with the place outlined. 6. When a field needs text, OjO writes it in the language of the app and puts it on the clipboard. You paste it. 7. You do all the tapping. OjO never taps, types or pays for you. 8. Before a password or a card, say "Don't look". Say "Look" to go on. 9. End the call, and the server forgets it. ## Models Apart from a greeting and a few short waiting phrases, every word OjO says comes from Meta models. The server calls them through the Meta Model API. - **Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0** listens. One streaming session runs for the whole call and finds where each phrase ends. - **Muse Wonder 1.0** thinks. # Stevens

**A chief of staff that makes what you learn count at work, without leaking either side.**

Future knowledge workers won't mostly write; they'll read, listen and absorb. Stevens takes in what you learn off the clock and connects it to the work decision in front of you, with a source on every sentence. That means conference talks and slides captured on Ray-Ban Meta glasses, highlights from what you read, and your own notes.

Stevens is named after the butler in *The Remains of the Day*: he prepares you before the delegation arrives, and he is discreet about everything. **Stevens drafts; the human decides.**

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Build for Your World). Status: v3.3 works per [SPEC.md](SPEC.md): three demo scenarios, each on its own firm + personal Postgres databases, plus follow-up chat. Submission due Nov 4, 2026.

## The access rule

- **Personal.** Everything you capture goes through one ingestion layer into your own personal database, run by **Stevens · yours**, a separate process from the firm's. Your personal data never reaches the firm unless you share a specific quote, and every share is logged.
- **Enterprise.** **Stevens · firm** reads the firm's systems through connectors and mirrors their permissions. Each source is `visible` (Stevens may quote it to you), `privy` (Stevens reasons over it for you, and you see only a verdict) or `excluded` (Stevens never touches it). An Associate's Stevens is privy to the Partners' memos without the Associate ever seeing them.

The rules are a data table, checked by a test against every role × source × purpose combination. Privy knowledge reaches you only as a fixed verdict with no free text, and failures fail closed. Every brief and answer has Receipts showing what each model call saw, and which rule decided it.

## Demo (3 minutes, VC persona, two laptops)

1. **Capture:** glasses footage from a conference lands in the Associate's notebook. Muse Voice Transcribe transcribes the talk live, and Muse Spark reads a photo of a slide. Nobody presses anything.
2. **Brief:** the next day's second meeting with Helios is on the calendar, so Stevens writes a brief by itself. The deck says net churn is 1.8%; the talk said mid-market churn runs 6–8%, and the play button replays that moment. Both are cited, next to public SEC Form D market comps.
3. **Answer:** the Associate asks "Should we take the second meeting?" Stevens recommends holding until a Partner reviews, because it weighed a memo the Associate is not privy to. On the Partner's laptop, an escalation arrives with nothing enclosed.
4. **Receipts:** what every model call saw and held back, and the firm's connectors with their permission mapping.
5. **Share and approve:** the Associate shares one quote. It appears in the Partner's deal record; the Partner sees the conflict memo and approves Stevens' draft decision, which is logged.

# Apni Gati

*अपनी गति, "your own pace"*. Even in the same class, every child learns at a different pace. Apni Gati gives each child homework that fits their level, marks it in red pen, and tracks their progress. Built on Meta's models for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026).

**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/defXvZw0LEs

## Run it

```bash
# backend
cd backend
echo "MODEL_API_KEY=<your Meta Model API key>" > .env
uv sync
uv run python scripts/seed_demo.py --reset     # demo Class 5 + simulated district (labelled)
uv run uvicorn apnigati.api:app --port 8000

# web
cd ../web && npm install && npm run dev          # http://localhost:5173
```

Tests and evals (`backend/`): `uv run pytest -q` · `uv run python -m evals.grading_eval` · `evals.homework_eval` · `evals.agent_eval 10` · `evals.reading_eval` · `evals.safety_eval` · `evals.report` (writes [RESULTS.md](backend/evals/RESULTS.md)).

## What it does

- **Set up once:** children (name, class, language) and the syllabus, pasted as plain text and mapped onto an NCERT concept graph.
- **One tap, every evening:** a different homework sheet for every child, built from their own knowledge graph (challenge / on track / needs practice), in Tamil, Hindi or English. Every answer is verified with sympy.
- **At home:** the child solves it in the notebook; the family sends a photo through the child's own link (no app, no login).
- **Red pen:** marked against the answer key on the photo, with the misconception behind each mistake and a hint that never gives the answer.
- **Progress:** the child's knowledge graph and syllabus progress update; an agent traces mistakes to the root gap; the next sheet adapts.
- **For the teacher:** mark a stack of notebooks, oral reading tests, group lesson plans with printable worksheets, a district view.

## Meta models

| Model | Used for |
|---|---|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Reading handwriting, writing each child's homework, misconception diagnosis, hint safety review |
| Muse Wonder 1.0 | Concept graph (built with web search), syllabus mapping, root-cause agent, lesson plans |
| SAM 3.1 | Page detection, page tracking in video, digit ink masks for marks, face blurring |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Reading-aloud assessment, children's spoken explanations |
| Muse Image 1.0 | Illustrated worksheets (read back and verified) |

**Design rule:** the model reads; sympy decides what's right; the teacher has the final word.

## Results ([full details](backend/evals/RESULTS.md))

| Eval | Result |
|---|---|
| Notebook grading (12 pages, 40 problems) | 40/40, 0 correct answers marked wrong, 0 mistakes missed; misconception exact 13/16 |
| Personalised homework (12 children) | 82/82 answers verified, 0 identical sheets |

# zhengyin-dict · 古文正音字典

一份为「古文 AI 朗读定音」而建的开放字典数据：给定一篇古文，它回答四件事——
每个字有哪些读音、**默认会读成什么音**、在具体语境里**应该读什么音**（词组、
通假、异读、破读）、以及某个音有哪些**可安全替换的同音字**。

它是 [zhengyin](https://github.com/gty3310) 正音工具链的数据仓，与 CLI 代码仓分离：
本仓只有数据（人可读的 JSONL + 发布版 SQLite），任何人都可以直接取用这份字典
做自己的工具，也可以提 PR 补条目。许可证按来源分工（见 [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md)），
其中本仓自建部分以 **CC0** 发布、明确允许商用。

当前版本 **0.3.1**（2026-11-05）：

| 表 | 条数 | 内容 |
|---|---|---|
| chars | 44,569 | 单字全部读音 + 默认读音 + 现代读音 + 频次序 |
| phrases | 53,995 | 词组逐字拼音（多音消歧） |
| tongjia | 8,009 | 通假关系（字+读音+义项 → 本字），全带出处例句 |
| heteronyms | 829 | 《普通话异读词审音表》(1985) 现代异读 |
| podu | 65 | 文言破读种子（自建，AI 整理，未核验） |
| prescribed | 3 | 指定替字（用户裁断，`user_confirmed`） |
| substitutes（派生） | 1,332 个读音 | 每音的安全同音替字候选 |

## 数据与字段

数据以 JSONL 存放在 `data/`，每行一条 JSON。拼音一律为**数字拼音**
（`yue4`，轻声记 5）。**每条记录都带 `src` 出处字段**，能细化到条目级的另带
`src_ref`；具体来源与加工见 [SOURCES.md](SOURCES.md)。

### chars.jsonl — 单字读音

```json
{"char": "說", "readings": ["shuo1", "shui4", "yue4"], "default": "shuo1",
 "freq_rank": 27, "in_8105": true, "src": "unihan:kXHC1983", "src_ref": "…"}
```

- `readings`：全部读音（源 Unihan kHanyuPinyin / kXHC1983，简繁异体互补）
- `default`：字典默认读音（kMandarin）——判断「原样送 TTS 会不会读错」的基准
- `freq_rank`：kHanyuPinlu 频次排名（越小越常用；无频次数据为 `null`）
- `common_readings`：现代常用读音集（源 kHanyuPinlu 收录的全部读音，含异体互补；Pinlu 未收录的字为空表）
- `modern_readings`：该字在现代汉语中的读音集（数字拼音，v0.3.1 新增），派生规则见下
- `modern_src`：`modern_readings` 的依据等级，三档：`xhc1983`／`pinlu`／`kmandarin-fallback`
- `is_polyphonic`：在现代汉语中是否多音，即 `len(modern_readings) > 1`
- `unique_reading`：现代读音恰一个时为该读音，否则为 `null`——下游可据此判定「现代单音字」
- `in_8105`：是否在《通用规范汉字表》收录范围内（含繁体对应字形）

`modern_readings` 派生规则（实现见 `tools/make_chars.py`）：设 xhc＝本字
kXHC1983 读音集、pinlu＝本字 kHanyuPinlu 读音集（只用本字本身，不用异体
互补后的集合）、default＝本条 `default`。① xhc 非空：modern＝xhc ∩
(pinlu ∪ {default})，交集为空则 modern＝xhc，`modern_src`＝`xhc1983`
（1983 词典里个别读音只存于古义/旧读，须经现代频次实测过滤，如「惡」
的 ě/wū 即如此滤掉，只留 è/wù）；② xhc 空、pinlu 非空：modern＝pinlu，
`modern_src`＝`pinlu`；③ 皆空：modern＝[default]，`modern_src`＝
`kmandarin-fallback`。列表顺序：default 在集内时排第一，其余按 xhc
（或 pinlu）原始顺序。

### phrases.jsonl — 词组消歧

```json
{"phrase": "中国", "pinyin": ["zhong1", "guo2"], "src": "phrase-pinyin-data:pinyin.txt"}
```

`pinyin` 与 `phrase` 逐字对齐；一词多音有多条记录。

### tongjia.jsonl — 通假（义项为键）

```json
{"char": "共", "benzi": "供", "reading": "gong1", "sense": "供奉，贡献",
 "example": "繼統共勤，順皇之德。", "char_simp": "", "benzi_simp": "",
 "src": "tongjiazi-resources", "src_ref": "《汉书·礼乐志》"}
```

字段与设计见下方「义项为键」一节。源：北师大通假字资源库（MIT）。

### heteronyms.jsonl — 现代异读（审音表 1985）

```json
{"word": "薄", "readings": [{"pinyin": "bao2", "style": "语", "examples": ["纸很薄"]},
 {"pinyin": "bo2", "style": "文", "examples": ["薄弱", "单薄"]}],
 "note": "", "src": "shenyinbiao-1985", "src_ref": "…"}
```

`style` 为审音表原注的「文/语」；`note` 含「统读」「又音」等附注。
注意：本表只管现代异读，不收文言破读（如「说 yuè」在 podu 表）。

> **Build with AI. Stay in control.**

**SentinelOS** is a local-first security engineer for developers who ship code with AI coding agents. It scans a project with real security tools, uses Meta's models to plan the investigation, connect findings into attack paths and draft fixes, then **proves** each fix by re-scanning and re-running tests. Its AgentFence policy engine plugs into Claude Code and blocks the agent from reading or writing protected files such as `.env`.

---

## The Core Principle

```
The LLM reasons.
The orchestrator coordinates.
Security tools gather evidence.
The policy engine controls actions.
The verification engine checks results.
```

*An LLM is never trusted alone to enforce security or declare its own fixes successful.*

Concretely:
- The model **plans** which scanners to run, but every tool call passes the deterministic `PolicyEngine` first.
- The model **drafts** a patch as exact search/replace edits. SentinelOS applies them to the real file only if every edit matches exactly once and the result compiles. The diff you see is computed by SentinelOS, not copied from model output.
- A fix is **VERIFIED** only when the original scanner no longer reports the finding and the test suite shows no new failures compared to a pre-patch baseline.
- Every UI label shows which model actually served a task, or says "offline fallback" when no key is configured.

---

            MG[Model Gateway - Meta Model API / OpenAI-compatible]

# Stillpoint — Proof without seeing.

Stillpoint helps a person investigate whether a suspected edited photograph
may share the same original photographic viewpoint and background geometry
as a registered benign photograph — without exposing the person in either
image to reviewers or analysts.

Background alignment alone cannot establish the identity of the depicted
person, consent, or wrongdoing. A background match alone cannot trigger
automatic punishment or removal.

## What Stillpoint actually does

1. The user registers an original photograph by mapping its background:
   manual point placement, on-device detail proposals the user labels by
   hand, or experimental AI-assisted mapping when a model key is configured.
2. People are masked before analysis. The mask can be drawn by hand
   (always available) or suggested by automatic person detection
   (`sam-3.1` through the local backend, explicit consent per photo).
   A suggestion is never auto-confirmed: the user previews it, corrects
   missed regions by hand, and confirms. Analysis never runs until the
   mask is confirmed, and proposals come only from outside it.
3. The background map is validated and saved on the user's own device as a
   scene graph. Photographs are never stored.
4. The user compares a suspect scene graph — or a suspect photograph mapped
   in Check with Blind Mode off plus an explicit viewing acknowledgment —
   against the registered reference.
5. The matching engine reports one of three verdicts — `Likely derivative`,
   `No link found`, or `Cannot determine` — with per-object measurements,
   shift diagnostics, and written limitations.
6. The Proof page exports a redacted text report containing measurements
   only. The report is locally generated; it is not independently certified
   or tamper-proof.

## Architecture

```text
Browser (React + Vite, http://localhost:5173)
├── Protect: photo (memory only) -> manual mask or detection-suggested
│            mask (user reviews, corrects, confirms) -> manual points,
│            on-device edge-density proposals (user labels each one),
│            or experimental AI assist -> validated scene graph
├── Check:   suspect graph, or suspect photo mapped in-page (Blind Mode
│            off + viewing acknowledgment + confirmed mask), compared
│            against the registered scene -> on-device comparison
├── Results: verdict + residuals + shift pattern + limitations
├── Proof:   redacted exportable report (no photographs)
└── Storage: localStorage (graphs, masks, hashes) — image bytes refused

Local backend (Python stdlib, http://127.0.0.1:8787) — optional
├── POST /api/compare   scene graphs only; images refused (as before)
├── GET  /api/status    {configured} boolean; never exposes credentials
├── POST /api/analyze   redacted image + consent flag + API key
├── POST /api/segment   image + consent flag + API key -> person rects only
├── POST /api/chat      text-only Guide messages + page label + API key
    └── Meta Model

# 86TO88 — run the original Windows 3.1 Minesweeper on Windows 3.0 / 8088-class hardware

**86TO88** (the **WM88 bridge**) makes the *original, unmodified* Windows 3.1
`WINMINE.EXE` run and play under Windows 3.0 in real mode — the environment of
an 8088-based Tandy 1000 EX. It is a small DOS TSR plus a
361-byte DLL shim. No part of the game is reimplemented.

**It works on real hardware:** Chad reports running Windows 3.1 Minesweeper
on his Tandy 1000 EX under Windows 3.0. That hardware result is separate
from the emulator tests documented below.

**Video (under 3 minutes):** <https://youtu.be/L1UxVt3oN9A>

Submission for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. The bridge was built by

## Try it

**1. In your browser, one click: <https://astrobleem.github.io/86TO88/>**

Open the page in a desktop browser and press **Download media & run**. Your
browser fetches the hash-pinned public reference disks and ROMs, checks every
SHA-256, pulls the original `WINMINE.EXE` out of the Windows 3.1 disk
(exactly 27,776 bytes, hash-checked), builds the guest disk in memory and boots
**Windows 3.0 in real mode** with the WM88 bridge. About 10 MB is downloaded.

# FamParty

**One big screen. Every phone is a controller. Nobody signs up.**

FamParty is a collection of short bonding games for people who are already together — families in a living room, friends on game night, or a team that needs five warm minutes before a meeting. A host runs the show from their phone, a TV (or any shared screen) displays it, and everyone else joins on their phone by scanning a QR code or typing a 4-letter room code.

> **Live demo:** https://famparty.vercel.app
> **Domain:** famparty.com is registered and being connected. **Live site:** https://famparty.vercel.app
> **For engineering context:** see `CLAUDE.md`. This README is the product brief.

---

## 1. The product in one minute

Most group games fail before they start: someone has to download an app, create an account, explain rules, find paper, or keep score by hand. By then the moment has passed.

FamParty removes all of that:

1. The host opens FamParty on their phone and taps **Host a show**.
2. The TV opens a display link and shows a big QR code + room code.
3. Players scan, pick a name and an emoji avatar, and they're in. Under 30 seconds.
4. Short rounds play out on the TV — big reveals, silly answers, real conversations.
5. The host drives everything from their phone: start, pause, skip, reveal, next.
6. At the end there's a winner's podium — and, if the group uses a family album, the best moments are saved for next time.

There are no accounts, no passwords, no app installs, no payments, and nothing to print. If you can open a link, you can play.

## 2. Why this exists

- **Phones usually pull people out of a gathering. FamParty puts them back in.** The phone becomes a private controller; the TV stays the shared focus, so people look up, react together, and talk.
- **The best party games create stories, not just scores.** A guessed lie, an outlier opinion, a ridiculous sentence ending — these become the thing the family retells next week. Scoring exists to create drama; conversation is the real reward.
- **Existing options have friction or the wrong setting.** TV party-game consoles assume everyone is a gamer. Meeting icebreakers assume a workplace and a facilitator with a laptop. Printable party games assume preparation. FamParty is built for a couch, a mix of ages, and zero preparation.

## 3. Who it's for

### Primary: the family host
The person who organises the gathering — a parent, grandparent, sibling, or the family's unofficial events person. They are not necessarily technical. They want something that works the first time, includes kids and grandparents alike, and makes them look like they planned more than they did.

During the hackathon the code was rewritten. By `git blame -w -C -C`, 2,020 of 44,972 Python lines (4.5%) still trace back to the morning drafts (11:20 AM to 12:19 PM ET), mostly imports, function signatures and field names; 755 of them (1.7%) are logic. # Lineage

**Version control for a self-improving agent: every self-edit is a commit, the jury is CI, the review queue is a pull request, blame is `git blame`, rollback is `git revert`, and the locked test is the release gate.**

An issue-triage agent that learns a real project's conventions from corrections, where nothing it learns is kept until it passes a jury on data it never trained on, every decision can be traced to the rule and the edit that caused it, and any edit can be bisected and reverted.

Built solo in two days during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (repo started Nov 3, 2026). Indie Developer track · *Push the Frontier*.

**[Live dashboard on the real run](https://romaisafatima1.github.io/lineage/dashboard/?run=../runs/full2/events.jsonl)** · [Audit report the harness wrote](runs/full2/REPORT.md) · [Run log](runs/full2/events.jsonl) · [Tests](.github/workflows/tests.yml)

> Most "self-improving agent" demos show batch accuracy going up and call it learning. Lineage puts a locked test set, canaries and a jury between the agent and its own edits, and then reports what it found. On 1,269 real kubernetes issues, across two full runs: **the gate rejected every edit learned from a poisoned batch (6 of 6) while every unsupervised agent absorbed it; one unsupervised agent's accuracy on unseen data fell from 66% to 55% the generation it learned the lie, and never recovered; unsupervised self-editing made sibling agents 41% different from each other on identical data (23% with the gate, 4% noise floor); and nobody, gated or not, beat the frozen model on data it never saw.** The agent could not fool the harness. The harness tells you the truth.

![lineage bisect](docs/bisect.png)

## Why this matters

Every engineering team is about to run agents that act on their behalf: triaging issues, routing failures, answering support, reviewing code. The obvious next step is letting those agents learn from the corrections people make every day. The obvious danger is that an agent which rewrites its own instructions can learn the wrong lesson from one bad batch, quietly forget what it did well, and leave nobody able to say why it made a call. Published work agrees: self-editing context systems *degrade without reliable feedback* (ACE, ICLR 2026), and planted "experiences" persist and get imitated (MemoryGraft, Bad Memory). Sakana's Darwin Gödel Machine was caught faking a test log, and only because its lineage was traceable.

So teams keep their agents frozen, and frozen agents stay mediocre. Lineage removes that trade-off. It is the missing layer between "the agent proposed a change to itself" and "the change is live": verification before, accountability after, and an honest number at the end. It applies to any job with corrections and ground truth, and it needs no fine-tuning, no ML team and no GPU: the model never changes, only a readable playbook does.

1. **Point it at the tracker.** New issues

# bud

bud is a personal AI agent you run yourself. It keeps every conversation in an append-only event log, so multiple clients can follow one session and reconnect after a disconnect. The server uses native DBOS durable execution to recover accepted work after a crash. Model calls go through a gateway that falls back to another provider on failure and records reported usage and cost.

bud is under active development. It can chat, call tools, remember approved facts across sessions, and hold write actions for your approval. By default, bud uses real Gmail and Google Calendar connections through the Composio SDK and MCP (Model Context Protocol). Use `bud serve --simulate` to work with a fictional person's inbox and calendar instead. Live email and event listing, approved email sending, and approval pause/denial have been checked. Draft creation and calendar writes are not yet live-verified.

## Install

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and either ChatGPT plan sign-in or a model-provider API key.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/bamiboy237/bud.git
cd bud
uv sync
```

For API access, set `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, or `MUSE_API_KEY` in `.env`. Providers without a key are skipped. Git ignores `.env`. Real-account tools also require `COMPOSIO_API_KEY`; see [Connect real accounts](#connect-real-accounts).

## Sign in and select a model

To use your ChatGPT plan, run:

```sh
uv run bud login chatgpt
uv run bud models
```

The login command opens your browser and waits up to five minutes for consent. Add `--no-browser` to print a sign-in link instead. Pydantic AI handles authorization and token refresh. Bud reads your account's model catalog and selects its first listed model as the default.

After sign-in, the default route uses ChatGPT, with Muse Wonder as backup when `MUSE_API_KEY` is set. Fallback applies to availability errors before a response starts. A stream that fails after output starts ends the run rather than replaying its partial output. Without ChatGPT sign-in, API models follow the tier order in `src/bud/gateway/models.toml`.

Use a model ID from `bud models` to pin a request or server to that model. Pinned models do not fall back:

```sh
uv run bud ask "Explain an event log." --model deepseek:deepseek-flash
uv run bud serve --simulate --model deepseek:deepseek-flash
```

DeepSeek remains available for simulated work. Real-account mode permits ChatGPT, OpenAI API, and Meta. `--simulate` selects tools, not inference. `--tier` selects the API tier; the default ChatGPT model serves both tiers after sign-in.

`bud costs` shows subscription token usage separately from metered API dollars. The ChatGPT subscription fee is not allocated to individual requests. The server's [spend and execution limits](#spend-and-execution-limits) apply separately from the provider's subscription allowance.

Credentials live in `data/chatgpt/credentials.json`, with owner-only directory and file permissions. The installation ID and client regi

# Crime Sentinel

> A governed undercover AI agent, powered by Meta Muse, that finds the communities glorifying violence before they act.

The most dangerous True Crime Community (TCC) spaces are not public. They sit behind admission questions ("are you
a journalist?") and invite-only chats, where keyword filters and public scraping can't reach. Crime Sentinel applies
the [Apate.ai](https://lighthouse.mq.edu.au/article/june-2023/scamming-the-scammers) idea (AI personas that pose as
plausible scam victims to gather intelligence) to violent-extremism prevention:

1. A **research persona** written by **Meta Muse** passes the gatekeeper's questions of a closed group and is
   later invited into a secret chat.
2. An independent **Safety Governor** (hard rules plus a separate Muse judge) checks every message the persona
   wants to send. The persona never praises, encourages, commits to anything, or starts violent topics.
3. **Muse analyses** what the persona observes: post text and images (vision), then the whole community in one
   long-context call.
4. It drafts an **evidence-backed report to Meta Integrity**, and a human approves it before it is sent.
5. Observed posts flow into a **human review console** with explainable classification, a network graph, trends,
   and evaluation.

The demo runs on a **sandbox social platform** with fictional people and groups, because real-platform access was
not available. A real deployment would need to be operated by the platform itself. See
[docs/sentinel-agent.md](docs/sentinel-agent.md) for the architecture, every place Muse is used, and what has and
hasn't been verified.

**It assesses content and communities, never people.** No identity resolution, no individual threat scores, and no
automated reports to police or schools.

The original product brief is in [Project_Sentinel_Build_Spec.md](Project_Sentinel_Build_Spec.md) (old working
title). The agent extends that brief, and its persona boundaries replace the brief's "no personas" non-goal.

## Demo script: Sentinel agent (about 3 minutes)

1. Open **Mission Control** (the default tab). Show the intelligence brief and the engine panel (Muse connected,
   models, live cost).

# MetalMind

A Meta-powered experimental agent that generates Metal kernels for supported
PyTorch functions, checks them numerically on Apple Silicon, and measures them
against verified framework baselines. Kernels are reused only after independent
correctness and performance confirmation; otherwise PyTorch remains the fallback.

## System flow

![MetalMind system flow: Muse Wonder proposes Metal kernels, MetalMind tests them and feeds back the results, and verified kernels run offline with PyTorch as the fallback.](docs/system-flow.svg)

A promoted artifact can be reused without a model request. Checked mode scans
tensor values before dispatch. With caller-guaranteed bounds, the wrapper
still checks the tensor signature. [Full project walkthrough](docs/project-flow.md)

## Run locally

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
```

Put your Meta key in the ignored local `.env`:

```dotenv
MODEL_API_KEY="your-key"
```

```sh
metalmind doctor --json --smoke
metalmind analyze --workload bias_gelu --case medium
metalmind optimize --workload bias_gelu --case medium --max-requests 2 --max-candidates 2
metalmind report --run runs/<run-id>
python -m pytest -q
```

Optimization makes billable Meta model requests. The example caps the request
count at two. No API calls occur during ordinary tests or campaign preview.

## What works

- FP32 bias plus tanh GELU, RMSNorm, and stable final-axis softmax contracts.
- Registered FP16 variants with explicitly FP32 intermediate arithmetic.
- Restricted capture of trusted importable FP32 and explicitly cast FP16 functions.
  See [FP16 examples](examples/fp16_workloads.py) for the accepted cast order.
- Meta Responses API proposals, bounded feedback-driven search, source deduplication,
  cancellation boundaries, durable request accounting, and guarded resume.
- Spawned GPU evaluation, full-output numerical comparison, input integrity,
  unwritten/tail detection, repeated execution, and private final verification.
- Eager, equivalent functional, and compiled framework comparisons, paired timing,
  raw samples, bootstrap intervals, and two-session promotion.
- Conservative flat FP32 module-region analysis, standalone profiling, and guarded
  artifact replacement with a separate whole-module gate.
- Offline guarded artifact loading, fallback, numerical audit, explicit revalidation,
  complete run reports, and a frozen sequential campaign runner.

```sh
metalmind optimize --function examples.my_workloads:bias_gelu --workload bias_gelu --case medium --max-requests 2
metalmind evaluate --suite configs/evaluation.yaml
```

The campaign command previews **108 checked-mode jobs** without contacting Meta.
The frozen suite allows up to **135 Meta requests**. Add `--execute --max-jobs 12`
to run a bounded batch. Continue the same campaign with
`--execute --resume --max-jobs 12` from the same checkout. See the
[campaign protocol](docs/benchmarking.md) for accounting and recovery.

# Paper Worlds

**The next computer is already on your desk.**

A pen is your editor. A sticky note is your controller. Your voice is your code. If you can draw it, you can play it.

![A pen drawing played as a game, reaching the flag](docs/demo.gif)

**Play it now: https://paper-worlds-flame.vercel.app**

Press Start surfing or Play a sample. You don't need paper or a camera or an account.

I built this for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track) with Muse Spark, SAM 3.1, Muse Wonder and Muse Voice Transcribe.

## What it does

You draw a level with a pen. Dark lines are platforms and red is lava. Add a stick figure and a flag, then take a photo. Your own strokes become the level and your stick figure becomes the hero.

There are two games.

- **Draw your game.** Your drawing plays with the keyboard. Type or say a rule like "make the lava rise every time I clap" and it happens.
- **Asteroid Surf.** Your hand is the controller. Slide a bright sticky note under the camera and you ride a pen plank past asteroids to the end. A mouse or finger works too.

The samples are two of my drawings ready to go and everything works from a laptop or a phone.

## Where this goes

For decades we have come to the computer on its terms, with keyboards and mice and glass. That era is ending. AI can now see a scribble, follow a scrap of paper and hear a sentence. Anything in your hands can run software.

Paper Worlds starts with a game since a game is the fastest way to feel it. The same idea scales to every classroom, workshop and factory floor. Sketch a floor plan and walk it. Move tokens on a table and run a warehouse. Every table is a screen.

## How it works

| Step | What does it |
|---|---|
| Read the drawing | The app flattens the photo in the browser. **Muse Spark** labels each mark as a platform, lava, the flag or the stick figure. The app then fits those labels to the real ink and platforms land exactly where you drew them. |
| Find sticky notes | **SAM 3.1** finds the notes on a camera frame and the app learns each note's color from that same frame. |
| Follow sticky notes | A small color tracker runs in the browser on every frame and that keeps a moving note feeling instant. SAM checks the tracker every few seconds and steps in right away when a note gets lost. |
| Turn a sentence into a rule | **Muse Wonder** compiles your words into a small safe rule with structured output. If you ask for something the game can't do, it says so and suggests something it can. |
| Hear a spoken rule | **Muse Voice Transcribe** turns your voice into text and Wonder takes it from there. |
| Whistle and double clap | These are detected in the browser, since they're sounds and not words. |

The game itself runs on Phaser. A level is checked before you play and if the flag is out of reach the jump gets tuned so you can actually win.
