# Caliper **AI guesses. Caliper measures.** Ask how big, how fast, or how hard something accelerates in a video. Caliper returns a measured number with a 90% interval, or says it can't measure it and why. Size is measured on our own clips against a tape, and speed on passes of our own scooter against a GPS app; acceleration is not measured yet: it was refused on every QuantiPhy acceleration question and every one of our drop clips so far (counts and reasons in Results). The street study's gate method was run on the same scooter passes (results beside Caliper's). New against Tracker, MotionLab, VeloCV and Speedcam Anywhere (see Prior art): a plain question becomes a measurement plan (Muse Spark), SAM 3.1 tracks, plain Python computes, and the answer comes with a 90% range or an explicit refusal, scored against the same model guessing. Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (building period Oct 27 to Nov 4 2026), Indie track. **Live demo:** https://caliper-sigma.vercel.app. Recorded runs (every measurement and street study shown on the site) are instant. A live run on your own clip takes about 2 to 4 minutes and stays inside hard spend caps; the page waits for it and shows the steps. ## Why Vision-language models guess physical quantities. On Stanford's [QuantiPhy](https://quantiphy.stanford.edu/) benchmark the best model on the public leaderboard scores below the human baseline, and the authors found models answer plausibly even with no video ([Stanford HAI](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-cant-do-physics-well-and-thats-a-roadblock-to-autonomy)). **Who it helps.** Anyone who needs a number from a phone video and must know when not to trust it. # GajaMitra

**An early-warning agent for human–elephant conflict, built on Meta's models.**

Every year in Sri Lanka, hundreds of elephants and more than a hundred people die in human–elephant conflict, mostly at night on the edges of villages. Existing systems are detectors trained for one site, and they stop at "elephant detected". GajaMitra goes further: it tracks the herd, reads its behaviour, predicts when it will reach the village, and decides what to do about it.

> Built from scratch during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Nov 3–5, 2026). Everything in this repository was written during the event.

## How it works

1. **Track.** SAM 3.1 finds every elephant in the boundary-camera clip and keeps one ID per animal. `track.py` turns the boxes into distance to the village boundary, speed, arrival time and a risk level.
2. **Read.** Muse Spark 1.3 looks at keyframes, judges behaviour (calm, alert, aggressive, calves) and proposes alerts in English, Sinhala and Tamil. It sends nothing itself.
3. **Check.** A deterministic guard (`policy.py`, re-checked by Spring) sets the alert level from the tracker's risk, never from the model.
4. **Warn.** The warning goes to villagers by SMS at once. Only an escalation to "danger" waits for a wildlife officer, and a timeout sends it anyway.

| Meta model | Role |
|---|---|
| SAM 3.1 | Tracks each elephant from a text prompt, with stable IDs |
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Reads behaviour, proposes the alerts, reviews them, and judges alert quality in the evals |

# Tracera

Tracera is an evidence-backed engineering workspace that goes from a bug signal to a reviewed fix. Show it a bug report, a screenshot, a screen recording, or a meeting transcript and it indexes the repository into a versioned code graph, investigates the code with cited hypotheses, proposes a patch, reproduces the bug and verifies that exact patch in a Docker sandbox, and puts the diff and the evidence in front of a person to review.

Tracera is decision support, not an oracle. A generated explanation is not a confirmed root cause, and a generated patch is not a verified fix. Every record says whether it was observed, reported, or inferred, models only propose, and a result is called verified only when the stored sandbox run says so. Inference runs on Meta's Muse models: Muse Spark 1.3 for reasoning and vision, Muse Wonder for escalation, and SAM 3.1 for locating elements in screenshots.

## Live deployment

| | |
|---|---|
| Web app | https://tracera-gules.vercel.app |
| API | https://tracera-api.onrender.com ([`/healthz`](https://tracera-api.onrender.com/healthz), [`/readyz`](https://tracera-api.onrender.com/readyz)) |
| Judging account | Email `judge@tracera.example`, password `Tracera-Judge-4271` |

The judging account is a shared email-and-password account with the workspace **member** role, created for reviewers. It already has two registered, indexed repositories: `shop-ui` (Lumen Goods, a small shop whose cart page promises free shipping from $50 but charges $4.99 on an order of exactly $50.00) and `bench-shop`. **Continue with Google** is also on the sign-in page. The API and worker run in one container on Render's free plan in Singapore with a free Render Postgres, behind a Vercel static site that proxies `/api`. The free instance sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic and needs 40 to 50 seconds to wake; the web app wakes it from the browser and retries, and says so on screen. The container has no Docker, so the sandbox stages and applying a patch are **local-only**; the hosted deployment runs investigations as analysis and labels what it cannot do. Model calls draw on a shared daily budget.

# Project Triage

Project Triage is a decision-support dashboard for search-and-rescue video review. It ingests
drone or body-camera batches, samples them into reviewable units, asks Meta SAM 3.1 for visual
candidate signals, and uses Meta Muse Spark 1.3 to prioritize human attention.

**It does not claim that a person is present.** Every result is a candidate signal
and every source unit remains available to a human reviewer.

## Run locally

1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `META_MODEL_API_KEY`.
2. Keep `META_MODEL_API_BASE_URL` pointed at the Meta Model API endpoint.
3. Install and build:

```bash
npm run install:all
npm run build
npm start
```

The production server serves the built dashboard and API from the configured `PORT` (4000 by
default). Open `http://127.0.0.1:4000`. For separate Vite development, run the backend with
`npm run dev:backend`, set `VITE_DEV_API_PROXY_TARGET`, and run `npm run dev:frontend`.

## Architecture

```text
input files → ingestion/normalization → SAM 3.1 candidate signals
           → Muse Spark comparative ranking → SQLite/API → human review dashboard
```

- `backend/src/ingestion/` validates files, samples video at 1 fps, normalizes images to 800px
  JPEG, and writes a manifest.
- `backend/src/perception/` runs the validated `person` and `clothing` prompts with bounded
  concurrency and retains failures for review.
- `backend/src/prioritization/` validates Muse Spark JSON, enforces the three confidence labels,
  and falls back to explicit manual-review items when ranking is unavailable.
- `backend/src/jobs/`, `backend/src/routes/`, and `backend/src/storage/` provide the async state
  machine, REST API, SQLite persistence, and audit trail.
- `frontend/src/` provides Ingest, Priority Queue, Clip Review, Audit, Overview, Benchmarks,
  Telemetry, and System & Scope views.

## API

- `POST /api/jobs` accepts multipart uploads or the documented `{ sourceLabel, units }` contract.
- `GET /api/jobs/:jobId` reports state and progress.
- `GET /api/jobs/:jobId/queue` returns the complete ranked queue.
- `GET /api/candidates/:candidateId` returns source media, boxes, reasoning, and evidence IDs.
- `GET /api/jobs/:jobId/audit` and `POST /api/candidates/:candidateId/decision` expose traceability
  and human review actions.
- `GET /health` is the deployment health check.

## Evaluation and limitations

The Phase 0 baseline measured 85.7% strict recall on light occlusion, 62.5% on heavy occlusion,
and a 12.5% negative-control false-alarm rate. After calibration, the Phase 9 evaluation measured
100% Precision@10 on its 38-unit labeled suite, while still documenting misses and a terrain-shadow
false alarm. These are benchmark results, not a field guarantee.

The prototype uses local SQLite and local media storage. Free-tier filesystem persistence is not
assured across restarts. Real deployment would require formal SAR partnerships, data-use
agreements, broader field validation, and a persistent hosted store.

# Synteel

A phone app that helps Indonesian eel farmers keep glass eels and elvers alive through the nursery stage.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026). Track: Startup (Synteel is built by PT Synt Tekno Multikarya, Indonesia). Theme: Build for Your World.

| | |
|---|---|
| Try the app | **[eel.synt.fun/preview/?lang=en](https://eel.synt.fun/preview/?lang=en)** (own demo farm, real Meta AI, in English) |
| Android app | APK attached to the [latest release](https://github.com/munf/synteel-app/releases/latest). Android 7 or newer; it opens the same app full screen |
| Demo video | **[youtu.be/Ok2DkrIHnmA](https://youtu.be/Ok2DkrIHnmA)** (English) |
| Measured results | [`docs/evaluation.md`](docs/evaluation.md) |
| Meta models | Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Spark Open (Baseten and Fireworks), Muse Voice Transcribe, SAM 3.1 |

## The problem

Farmers in Indonesia buy glass eels and raise them to elvers over the first 12 weeks (minggu 0 to 12). Glass eels are small and see-through, and pond water can turn bad in a few hours. Deaths often happen overnight: by the time someone sees eels at the surface or the first dead ones in the morning, it is too late to act. Small farms have no oxygen meter. They measure temperature, pH and TDS once or twice a day and keep records in a notebook or in their heads.

Synteel is for these farmers and their workers. They talk or take photos at the pond, and the app turns that into pond records. From the records and the weather it estimates tonight's oxygen risk, tells them when to check, and walks them through a die-off. The goal is fewer deaths between glass eel and elver. Later, Synteel sensor prototypes will send readings that the same rules and agents read at set intervals and when something changes.

A partner farmer in Sleman, Yogyakarta, runs 6 ponds alone, with no workers. Their glass eels tend to die suddenly about two weeks after capture, and the farmer traces it to measurements and care that were forgotten. Readings were kept in memory, never written down. Nobody watches the ponds at night, and the mornings go to other work. The app answers those gaps with a check schedule and night alarms, records made by voice, and steps for the moment eels rise to the surface, which the farmer calls the most reliable warning sign.

**Safety.** The app gives decision support. It does not diagnose disease or dose medicine. Alarms come from fixed threshold rules that run without any model, and every AI reading is a draft the farmer confirms before it is saved.

# Paneller Open

An open-source comic page editor, with the AI parts powered by Meta's models.

Draw a page, or bring one you already have. **Paneller Open reads a comic page
back into its parts** — every panel, every speech bubble, every sound effect —
using SAM 3.1, so a flat image becomes something you can actually edit. Panels
are polygons, so slanted and irregular layouts work, not just grids.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct–Nov 2026.

## What it does

- **Make a page from an idea.** Say what happens; Muse Spark plans the panels
  and writes the dialogue, Muse Image draws the art **clean, with no lettering
  at all**, and the words go on top as objects. About a minute. Nothing is ever
  baked in: the text was never pixels, so changing a line, resizing a balloon
  or saying it in Yoruba is just changing it.
- **Bubbles that size themselves.** A balloon is as big as what it says and no
  bigger, re-wrapping as you type. Balloon and tail are one outline, and the
  tail is a curve that hooks the way it is pointing rather than a wedge.
- **Tails that aim at the right person.** Spark says who speaks by how they
  look - "man in a green apron" - and SAM finds that person on the page, so the
  tail points at the speaker rather than at whoever happens to be biggest in
  the panel. Drag the tip to aim it somewhere else.
- **Carry a comic on across pages.** The first page settles a cast and a place;
  every page after is planned knowing who is in the story and what has already
  happened, and drawn against the page before it, so the same people keep their
  faces and clothes from page to page. Move between pages at the bottom of the
  editor.
- **Edit a page by hand.** Panels, speech bubbles, caption boxes and sound
  effects. Drag to move, type to letter, undo a hundred steps deep.
- **Open a page someone else drew.** Here the lettering *is* pixels, so SAM 3.1
  finds the panels and bubbles, Muse Spark reads the words out of them, and the
  page becomes editable after the fact. This is the harder path and the one the
  benchmark measures.
- **Letter it in another language.** Translated to fit the bubble it has to sit
  in, because a faithful rendering half as long again breaks the page. Sound
  effects come back as noise in the target language: "SKRRRT!!!" becomes
  "GRIIIT!!!" in Yoruba and "キィーッ!!!" in Japanese, not a dictionary entry
  for a skid.
- **Redraw one panel.** Muse Image redraws a single panel in place from an
  instruction, and the rest of the page cannot drift because it is never sent.

Reading a page end to end — four panels, two bubbles, one sound effect, read and
re-lettered — takes about 40 seconds and costs under two cents.

No account, no server, no database. The document lives in your browser and
exports to PNG.

A comic page isn't an image. It's panels, gutters, bubbles, reading order,
lettering and art, and each of those is a region with meaning. Image models
flatten all of

# CodeCap-Bench

Generate HTML animations from reference videos, render them to MP4, and evaluate visual similarity, object-level spatio-temporal IoU, and fine-grained visual information retention.

The three metrics are named `visual_similarity`, `object_st_iou`, and `visual_retention` in commands and results. Visual similarity uses V-JEPA 2.1 features; object-level spatio-temporal IoU uses object localization and SAM 3.1 tracking; visual retention scores the annotated static and dynamic focal points using GPT.

## Setup

Use Linux x86_64 with [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) and a CUDA GPU with BF16 support. The NVIDIA driver should support CUDA 12.8. Run the commands below from the repository root.

Install system dependencies and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (Ubuntu 24.04):

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ffmpeg git curl ca-certificates fonts-dejavu-core
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

Create your configuration:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env` to set the API key, base URL, and model for generation and evaluation. The default agent is Pi with OpenAI:

```dotenv
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-api-key
OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1
OPENAI_MODEL=your-model

EVAL_API_KEY=your-evaluation-api-key
EVAL_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1
EVAL_MODEL=your-evaluation-model

HF_TOKEN=your-huggingface-token
```

Object localization and visual retention use a model that supports image inputs and structured outputs through the Responses API. For SAM weights, request access to [facebook/sam3.1](https://huggingface.co/facebook/sam3.1) and set `HF_TOKEN` to a token from that account.

Build the agent image, then install the Python environments and download model weights:

```bash
bash agent/build_image.sh
bash scripts/setup.sh
```

## Generate and evaluate

Run the included sample:

```bash
bash scripts/infer.sh --video-id 246
bash scripts/evaluate.sh --video-id 246
```

Generated HTML, video, frames, and logs are saved in `outputs/246/`. Evaluation scores are saved in `outputs/246/eval/result.json`, with details in `outputs/246/eval/<metric>/result.json`.

Use `--output /path/to/results` with inference and evaluation to store results elsewhere. The `third_party/`, `models/`, and Python environment directories can be symbolic links to existing directories outside the repository.

Inference produces an MP4 matching the reference dimensions, frame count, and 24 fps timeline. The `--render-timeout` option sets the time budget for HTML-to-MP4 rendering, with a default of 900 seconds. Evaluation measures visual fidelity.

`outputs/246/task.json` records agent execution in `generation`, video publication in `media`, and frame extraction in `preparation`, with error details in `errors` and the logs. The inference command returns exit code 0 when video publication completes. Evaluation extracts missing frames for `object_st_iou` and `visual_retention`.

# Sightpass

**A safety check for AI shopping agents. Your agents spend. You see what they saw.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, on the PayPal **sandbox**: no real money moves.

Stores are shutting AI agents out because they can't trust them. Spending limits and signed mandates say what an agent is allowed to buy, but not whether it was tricked into buying it. An agent can stay inside every rule and still pay the wrong price, or buy 50 of something, because a web page told it to. Sightpass looks at the page the agent actually saw before the money moves.

## How it works

1. **The owner sets the rules** in plain words, and Muse Spark turns them into structured limits to review and sign.
2. **The agent asks to pay**, sending its cart and screenshots of the pages it was looking at.
3. **A fixed rules engine decides first:** pay, ask the owner, or block. No AI at this step.
4. **The page check** (Muse Spark) reads the item, price, quantity and store from the screenshot and compares them with the agent's claim. It looks for price switches, wrong items, look-alike stores, and faint text aimed at AI agents. It can only send a purchase to the owner, never approve one.
5. **The owner sees the evidence**, marked on the page (SAM 3.1 for prices and products, Muse Spark for text).
6. **PayPal pays the store** from a budget hold. The agent never sees payment credentials.
7. **Stores can check a pass:** a short-lived signed credential proving the owner allowed this agent to buy there. It follows the emerging approach of signed agent mandates (AP2-style), but doesn't implement a published spec. Pausing an agent stops its pass at once.

## Built during the hackathon, and what was reused

**This project is built on the spending engine from my earlier project, Cosign.** The first commit is an unmodified import of it, clearly labelled, and the organisers told me reusing it in the Indie track was fine. Everything in later commits was built during the event (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026).

- The page check: screenshot upload and validation, Muse Spark comparison, and the rule that it can only make a decision stricter

# Sabi

**Business intelligence for small shops, built on Meta's models.** Big businesses have dashboards and analysts. A trader in a Lagos market has a notebook and her memory. Sabi gives her the same kind of intelligence. She talks to it the way she already works: voice notes in Pidgin, photos of receipts and price lists, customer chats. From that, Sabi keeps accurate books, then turns them into decisions: what is selling, what makes money, what stock is stuck, what customers want that she lacks, who owes, and what to order before the next rush. Built for the Meta hackathon, Indie track ("Build for Your World"). All code in this repo was written during the event.

*Sabi* means "to know" in Nigerian Pidgin: "she sabi business". Sabi knows your business.

## Design rules (enforced in code, with tests)

1. **The model proposes, code commits.** Muse Spark proposes a business event (`record_entry`). Python builds the journal lines, cost of goods sold and average cost. The model never does accounting arithmetic.
2. **Double entry can't be broken.** Postgres constraint triggers reject any entry whose debits don't equal its credits at commit, and journal lines are append-only (`app/ledger/schema.sql`). The in-memory store enforces the same rules.
3. **Corrections reverse, never edit.** `cancel_entry` posts a mirror-image entry after the owner confirms.
4. **Unclear money always goes to the owner.** The amount normaliser (`app/normalize/amounts.py`) turns "5k" and "1k5" into figures and marks ambiguous ones such as "two-five" (₦2,500 or ₦25,000). Code rejects any proposal that doesn't hand those to the owner as buttons.
   Money paid out of an empty till is also unclear: if a purchase, bill or withdrawal would take cash or the bank below what the books show, she is asked first (*Yes, record it* / *Paid from cash* / *Cancel*).
5. **Trust is earned per action.** Posting is automatic only when the validator finds nothing: known customer and product, a price within her usual range, enough stock, under the limit. Everything else becomes a WhatsApp button question, answered by code.
6. **Customers are untrusted.** The customer persona has four tools: look up price/in-stock, create an order, claim a payment, see their own orders. It can't reach the ledger, and a transfer screenshot never marks an order paid without the owner.
7. **Every number has a receipt.** Each entry links to its evidence row: the original transcript, the normalised text, the model and the prompt version.

# CommonGround

**The interpreter that understands what you're pointing at.**

A real-time interpreter that grounds ambiguous language in the shared physical world.

> Traditional translation can translate "this" and "there," but it cannot tell the listener what "this" and "there" actually mean. CommonGround can.

Real outputs from a live test on a hotel desk (Muse Voice, Muse Spark and SAM 3.1, a phone as the camera):

| Speaker says | Literal translation | CommonGround |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 파란 거 말고 이거 주세요. | Not the blue one, give me this one. | Not the light blue bottle, give me the **white charger**. *(charger highlighted)* |
| 이제 그거 여기 꽂으세요. | Now plug that in here. | Now plug the **white charger** into the **wall outlet**. *(both highlighted)* |
| 저것 좀 주세요. | Please give me that thing over there. | *Do you mean the light blue bottle or the white charger?* *(both candidates highlighted)* |

**Translate when confident. Clarify when ambiguous.**

CommonGround is not "AI translation with computer vision." It keeps a **persistent shared-world model** for cross-language communication. Most multimodal assistants help a human talk to an AI. CommonGround uses AI so that **two humans can understand each other**.

## How it works

**Muse Voice hears. Muse Spark understands. SAM points.**

```
 Guide (Korean)  ⇄  LiveKit room  ⇄  Field (English, camera on the table)
                        ⇅
              CommonGround agent (Node participant)
                        │
   utterance ── Muse Voice Transcribe (streaming STT + endpointing)
       │
       ├─ frame captured at speech start (when people point), Field camera only
       ├─ plain translation (fast, shown first as a preview)
       ▼
   resolveGroundedUtterance()          packages/grounding
       1. Muse Spark: references, world-state lookup, explicit translation (strict JSON)
       2. SAM 3.1: short text prompt → mask/box, all of a turn's requests in parallel
       3. confidence policy → accept / confirm / clarify
       4. world state: objects, aliases, turns ("그거" = last referenced object)
       ▼
   grounding.result → LiveKit data message → subtitles + SVG overlay
```

The flow is event-driven: segmentation runs once per utterance, not on every frame. Failures degrade gracefully:

- **SAM fails:** the grounded translation still shows, without an overlay.
- **Spark fails:** the app falls back to a literal translation and shows a "degraded" state.
- **A reference is ambiguous:** the app asks a clarification question instead of guessing.
- **LiveKit drops:** the reconnect banner appears.

apps/agent         Node LiveKit participant (@livekit/rtc-node): audio → STT, video frames, grounding queue

--- ## Why Signoff Smart glasses already see what you see. Assistants can already tell you what to do next. What nobody checks is whether you did the **last** step right: the dry pan, the shell in the egg, the whites you took off too early. Signoff is that check. Every step has an instruction and a concrete *done right* criterion. When you finish a step, your glasses capture a photo, and Signoff answers **pass**, **fail** or **not sure**, always with a reason. The one mistake it is built never to make is the **false sign-off**: calling a wrong step done. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR G["Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2
captures a photo"] --> A["Signoff app
(Android, tap S1-S5)"] A -- "USB tunnel
adb reverse" --> S["Local server
signoff/server.py"] S -- "photo + step check" --> M["Muse Spark
muse-spark-1.3"] M -- "pass · fail · unsure
+ reason" --> S S --> A ``` 1. **Plan.** A procedure is a short spec: steps, each with an instruction and a check ([`data/specs/fried-egg.json`](data/specs/fried-egg.json)). 2. **Capture.** After a step, the glasses take a photo through Meta's Wearables Device Access Toolkit and the app sends it to the local server. 3. **Judge.** The server asks Muse Spark to compare the photo with that step's check and to reply in strict JSON. 4. **Answer.** The verdict and its reason appear on the phone a few seconds later (the model call itself has a 4.1 s median). # SureEnough

**Brain decoders always guess. SureEnough knows when it has seen enough, says "not sure" when it isn't, and keeps its promise about how often it's wrong.**

**Live demo:** https://dmandaviya.github.io/SureEnough/

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track) on Meta Perception Encoder, SAM 3.1, Muse Spark and Muse Image.

---

## What SureEnough is

Today's brain decoders work like this: you record someone's brain activity while they look at a picture, and the decoder names its single best guess. It names a guess every time, even when the signal is mostly noise and the guess is almost random. Nothing tells you whether to trust it.

SureEnough is a layer that wraps around a brain decoder and changes what it promises:

1. **It decides when it has seen enough.** Brain recordings are noisy, so each picture is shown several times (repeats). SureEnough replays these repeats one at a time. After every repeat it asks *"am I sure enough to answer?"* and stops as soon as it is.
2. **It says "not sure" honestly.** When the evidence stays weak, it keeps listening. If it still isn't sure when it runs out of repeats, it doesn't fake a confident answer. It answers with a list ("it's one of these 17").
3. **It keeps a checked promise about how often it is wrong.** For each person: **the true object is outside SureEnough's final answer at most 2 in 10 times**, certified with 90% confidence. That covers the whole stop-when-sure procedure, including the fact that it checked after every repeat.

The answer comes in three shapes, from boldest to most cautious:

| Shape | Example | When |
|---|---|---|
| One object | "It's a handbrake." | The answer narrowed to a single object |
| A category | "It's an animal." | Every object in the answer shares one of the 53 THINGS categories |
| A list | "It's one of these 17." | Anything else |

### A real example (person 10, from the demo)

The person saw a **handbrake**. After the first repeat, 12 of the 200 candidate objects were still plausible. After the second repeat, only one was left. SureEnough stopped after 2 of its 20 repeats and said *"It's a handbrake."* Muse Spark phrased it as *"The person saw a handbrake."*

For the same person, a **banana** never got clear. The shortlist stayed between 6 and 20 objects for all 20 repeats, and the decoder's top pick at the end was garlic. SureEnough did not say "garlic". It used the full budget and answered *"It's one of these 17."* The banana was on that list.

### Why stopping as soon as you're confident is a trap

The obvious approach is "calibrate a confidence threshold, check after every repeat, stop the first time you cross it." Every extra check is one more chance to stop on a wrong answer that happened to look confident. The errors pile up:

- **Naive repeated look:** it promised at most 20% wrong. It delivered **20.3% on average**, and went over the promise for **8 of 10 people** (up to 22.0% for person 8).

# Lifeline
**Who's cut off by the flood, and where do crews go first?**

Flood access and dispatch planner. From before and after satellite photos and a road network, Lifeline works out which roads are cut, which buildings are isolated, and where responders should enter first. It writes a cited dispatch brief, and an "Ask the map" assistant answers typed or spoken questions using only the results.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, solo).

- **Live map:** https://bhavishyamangalasary.github.io/lifeline/
- **Demo video:** https://www.loom.com/share/5b52f454204e4a71b4fe765a650b43c1

![Lifeline map of tile 497 with ranked entry points](docs/map.png)

**Results at a glance** (15 random, heavily flooded SpaceNet 8 tiles, 639 truly cut-off buildings)
- 90% were called isolated, 9% uncertain (sent to a verify queue), and 1 building (0.2%) was called reachable.
- "Isolated" calls were right 98% of the time here, against 88% for calling everything isolated, and only 42% to 53% on less flooded tiles.
- The cost of caution: about 15% of buildings (112 of 725) went to the verify queue, and 52 of those were actually reachable.

## The problem
After a flood, the urgent question is not only "where is the water" but "who can no longer get out, and where can a crew get in". A road that is under water cuts every building behind it. Lifeline turns a before and after photo pair and a road network into an answer to that question, and is explicit about what it is unsure of.

## How it fits together
```
before + after photos, road network
        |
        v
Muse Spark judges each road piece (two modes)  ->  flooded / dry / uncertain
        |
        v
Road graph: which buildings lost their route to an exit
(run twice, optimistic and pessimistic)        ->  isolated / reachable / uncertain
        |
        v
Ranked entry points for responders
        |
        +--> Cited dispatch brief (each sentence cites a fact; numbers are checked)
        +--> Ask the map: typed or spoken questions, citations checked
        +--> Map page with an audit toggle against ground truth
```

## What it does
1. **Judges flood damage per road piece.** Muse Spark looks at a small crop around each road piece in two modes (after-photo only, and before and after side by side). If both say flooded, the piece is flooded. If both say dry, it is dry. If they disagree, it is marked **uncertain**.
2. **Plans access.** It builds a road graph and finds buildings that could reach an exit before the flood but cannot now. It runs the plan twice, optimistic and pessimistic, so each building is called isolated, reachable, or **uncertain**.

# FireShift AI

FireShift AI simulates how a wildfire spreads under changing conditions and recommends where limited firefighting resources will do the most good. It is validated against a real historical fire, not just a toy example. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie developer track).

Starting from an early satellite perimeter, it runs a wind- and terrain-aware spread simulation forward in time, identifies which buildings and roads fall in the predicted burn path, and uses a reasoning model to compare "what-if" scenarios (for example a wind shift) and explain which one demands a different response priority.

The screen you open with `npm run dev` is the React app: one full-viewport map of the 2018 Camp Fire near Pulga, Butte County. The Python pipeline and the Streamlit app live in `fireshift-ai/`. Also available on: https://fireshift.vercel.app/


## Home

The Spread view plays the Camp Fire from the Pulga ignition. The clock, acres, and wind sit on the map. Steps Taken lists the evacuation plan, and public steps can draft a Wireless Emergency Alert. `Space` plays and pauses. The arrow keys step between frames.

![FireShift home, Camp Fire spread at Pulga](docs/home.png)

## Draft alert

Draft Alert is on evacuation and other public steps (Concow, Skyway contraflow, Feather River Hospital, Paradise, Magalia). Air tankers, the structure-defense line, and "re-run forecast" do not get it.

The click covers the screen in red for 4 seconds with a lock-screen alert, then the map returns. The text is an example draft from that step's town, direction, and route, with Copy and Close on the card. The WEA, Reverse 911, and email/SMS counts are demo values, not a live send.

![Wireless Emergency Alert drafted from the Concow evacuation step](docs/alert.png)

## Prior art

FARSITE (USFS, since the late 1990s) and WFDSS (the federal tool since 2009) are the systems agencies actually use, and their fire physics are more accurate than this project.

FireShift AI is the combination, and how it was built: a cellular-automaton spread model, structure-level risk from satellite imagery (SAM 3.1), and plain-language scenario reasoning (Muse Spark), in one open pipeline, built in about 10 days on free public data, and checked against a real fire's outcome. It is a demonstration of how far a small, fast pipeline can get toward that kind of decision support. It is not a replacement for FARSITE or WFDSS.

## How it works

- **Data ingestion:** fire detections, terrain and fuel, the official final perimeter, and weather, from public APIs.
- **Seed perimeter:** the first satellite pass, used as the simulation's start.
- **Spread simulation:** `fireshift-ai/src/simulation.py` steps hourly. Ignition odds depend on fuel, direction-aware slope, and real wind.
- **Validation:** simulated final perimeter vs. the real final perimeter, by IoU and acreage. The React tab draws seed, simulated final, the CAL FIRE perimeter, and the north wind-shift on one map,

# ClearFirst

**Declarations that clear first time.**

ClearFirst is an AI customs-broker agent. Give it a shipment's documents — commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin — and it produces a customs declaration (SAD / IM4) in which **every box is proven**: each figure carries the document, page and exact quote it came from, the documents are cross-checked against each other, the HS classification is justified, the duty is estimated from the country's tariff structure, and a licensed broker reviews and signs off before anything is exported.

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track), Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026. All code was written by **Muse Code**; the agent reasons with **Muse Spark 1.3** and checks signatures and stamps with **SAM 3.1**, both through the Meta Model API.

---

## Why

In The Gambia and across West Africa, customs declarations are typed by hand into ASYCUDA by brokers reading paper documents. A mistyped weight, a package count that disagrees with the bill of lading, or a wrong HS code means the declaration is queried, the container sits at the port, and the importer pays demurrage and storage for every day it waits. Most clearance delays are not fraud — they are documents that do not agree with each other and nobody checked.

No AI tooling exists for this workflow in ASYCUDA countries today. Extraction products pull numbers out of PDFs; ClearFirst is built the other way round: **a figure that cannot be proven from the documents is refused**, and a disagreement between documents is reported as a discrepancy rather than silently resolved.

## What it does

1. **Reads the shipment** — the four documents are rendered to page images and read by the model.
2. **Sets a checklist** of the SAD boxes it must settle (parties, transport, goods, weights, packages, value, origin, classification).
3. **Records facts with proof** — a fact is only accepted if its quote appears verbatim on the cited page. Weights, packages, HS code and the parties must be supported by **two independent documents**.
4. **Cross-checks** — where the bill of lading says 806 packages and the packing list says 860, the agent cannot pick one; it files a named discrepancy with both documents.
5. **Classifies and costs** — HS code with a written justification, then duty, VAT and levies from the tariff pack (`tariff/gm.json`: GRA import duty, processing fee 1.5%, AU levy 0.2%, ECOWAS levy 0.5%, GNSW 1.0%, VAT).
6. **Submits the declaration** — refused by the verification layer until every box is cited, every item is proven or escalated, the numbers are sane (net ≤ gross, item values add up, valid HS format) and nothing cites an excluded document.
7. **Escalates** — after three refusals it must stop and ask the broker a specific question.
8. **Broker sign-off** — the broker reviews the SAD, discrepancies and open questions in the console, approves or rejects, and exports the signed declaration as **PDF**, **XML**, or via the

# Pitchside

**An open-source go-to-market coach you text like a friend.** Message it on WhatsApp, iMessage or SMS, or email it, and it helps you get what you're building in front of buyers, one day at a time.

Pitchside follows the "AI friend in your messages" style of coaching: short, decisive texts; a 30-day challenge with a morning check-in; build-in-public posts drafted in your voice with a tap-to-post link; and blunt, specific help with outreach and launches. It deliberately has **no introductions or matchmaking**. It coaches you, and you do the reaching out.

```
You:        no reply yet, and one address bounced
Pitchside:  Two hours of silence means nothing yet. The bounce is the thing to fix.

            Don't guess another address at that company. Call the switchboard
            between 8 and 9, ask who owns customer training, and get the
            right name and email.

            Rest of today: replies, then the demo clip. Nothing else.

# ARGUS — Aerial Review & Ground-imagery Understanding for Search

ARGUS reviews a search team's own drone and grid photos so a human does not have to
look at thousands of raw images one by one. It finds candidate objects with SAM 3.1,
checks each candidate against a written case brief with Muse Spark, and ranks them on
a map and in a review list. A human verifies every candidate. AI never calls a find.

**Guardrails, in every use:** detection, never identification. No facial recognition.
The brief is fictional test data only in this repo — never a real person or a real case.
The Review Agent proposes; a human accepts or rejects each candidate.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 – November 4, 2026,
with SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark via the Meta Model API.

## Try it in 5 minutes (no photos needed)

You need: Windows, Python 3.11 or newer, Git, and a Meta Model API key

Twin AI is a working MVP of an industrial digital-twin platform. # Verified Project Record

**From scattered site documents to buyer-trusted proof.** A working demo of the
Aunova Trust Infrastructure idea, built for the Meta Global AI Developer
Hackathon (Startup track, theme: Build for Your World).

Off-plan buyers pay in stages against construction progress, but the proof of
that progress is scattered across site reports, procurement records,
certificates, and sales documents, and is hard to verify exactly when a
payment depends on it. This demo turns four synthetic documents into one
trusted project record: structured, permissioned, source-backed, and AI-ready.

## The demo in 30 seconds

1. **Extract** — Muse Spark (Meta's model, served via NanoGPT or the Meta
   Model API) reads each document into structured fields. Without a key,
   the verified fixture extraction is shown instead.
2. **Verify** — every field is checked against its source document and line
   before it enters the record.
3. **Sign** — each entry is hash-chained to the previous one (SHA-256) and
   signed (ECDSA P-256). Press **Tamper with entry 3** and re-verification
   names the exact entry that broke, and the head hash no longer matches
   the anchor.
4. **Anchor** — the head hash is timestamped, so the record is provable
   later. In this demo the anchor is a recorded head hash; production
   anchors via OpenTimestamps on Bitcoin.
5. **Ask** — a buyer asks the project questions and gets answers scoped to
   their access rights (public / buyer / auditor), each cited to its
   entry. Anything outside the record is refused, not guessed.

## Quick start

Zero dependencies. Requires [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.x.

```sh
bun run server.ts
# open http://localhost:3000
```

`PORT` overrides the port. State is in memory; **Reset demo** restores the
seed. All data is synthetic: a fictional project, developer, contractor,
and documents. No client data, no real project.

# SignBridge AI

**Every Gesture Deserves a Voice.**
Breaking communication barriers through computer vision and artificial intelligence.

SignBridge AI is an **experimental, limited-vocabulary** recognizer for a few high-utility expressions in **Dominican Sign Language (LSRD)**. It works in the browser with a webcam and turns a recognized expression into short, natural Spanish or English text and speech. It is a prototype for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. It does **not** translate unrestricted sign language and is **not a replacement for a qualified sign language interpreter**.

## How it works: five separate parts

| | Component | What it does | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | **MediaPipe landmark detection** | Finds up to 2 hands and 21 3-D landmarks per hand in each webcam frame. It also reports MediaPipe's 7 generic gestures (👍 ✋ …). It knows nothing about LSRD. | Browser (`lib/vision/`) |
| **B** | **Our custom-trained sign classifier** | A k-nearest-neighbor classifier over normalized landmark *sequences*, trained on recordings **you** make on `/training`. It predicts one of our intents or `UNKNOWN`. | Browser (`lib/signs/`) |
| **C** | **Go backend orchestration** | Validates the predicted intent, attaches its LSRD verification status, calls Muse Spark, validates the reply, and falls back to a clearly labeled local phrase if Meta is unavailable. | Go (`backend/`) |
| **D** | **Meta Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Turns the predicted intent into a short, accessible message in Spanish and English. Uncertainty is reported as a flag, never added to the text. | Meta Model API, called only by Go |
| **E** | **Browser SpeechSynthesis** | Speaks the message automatically in the selected language: an es-DO voice when installed (falling back to another Spanish voice), or en-US. | Browser |

**Muse Spark was not fine-tuned and does no sign recognition.** It never sees video or landmarks, only the predicted intent label, its canonical phrase, and the confidence. Recognition is done entirely by part B, which runs in your browser.

# Sales Desk

One robot answers a shop's WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok and email. It:
- remembers each customer;
- quotes exact prices from the price list;
- follows up when a customer goes quiet;
- reads the shop's bank alert emails to confirm payments;
- hands discounts, bulk orders and complaints to the owner.

The owner starts each day on a **morning brief**, and sees every chat as an order on the **order board**.

Built 2026-11-04 for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, by urelimitless. The demo shop, "Nkem Fabrics, Enugu", is made up.

## What it does

- **One inbox for four apps.** WhatsApp (Cloud API) and Instagram DMs come in by webhook. Email arrives from a forwarder. TikTok chats are forwarded by a tool such as ManyChat or Make, because TikTok's messaging API is invite-only, so TikTok replies wait for the owner to send them in the app.
- **Prices nobody can get wrong.** The robot picks the product and quantity. The desk works out the subtotal, the delivery fee for the customer's area and the total from `products.csv` and `shop.json`. Any naira amount in a reply that isn't in the shop's facts is blocked, and the chat goes to the owner.
- **Selling, step by step:**
  1. They ask, and the robot answers.
  2. They say what they want, and the robot quotes.
  3. They say "yes", and the robot sends the account details with an order code (NF-12), asking them to put it in the transfer description.
  4. They say they paid, and the order waits for proof.
- **Memory.** Name, delivery area, what they like, event dates and notes, so returning customers never repeat themselves.
- **Follow-ups.** After 20 quiet hours, at most twice. The owner can skip today's follow-up from the brief.
- **Hand-overs.** These always go to the owner: discounts, "last price", bulk orders (over 20 yards), complaints, stock shortfalls, and anything the robot isn't sure about. When the owner replies from the board or from Telegram, they take over the chat and the robot stays quiet until they give it back.
- **STOP** opts anyone out.

## Payments from bank alert emails

The robot reads the shop's credit alert emails and matches each one to an order waiting for money:
- the amount must be exact, plus
- the order code in the transfer description, or the sender's name.

**It confirms by itself only when all of these hold:**
1. The alert came from a domain on `BANK_ALERT_SENDERS`.
2. The receiving mail server recorded `dkim=pass` or `dmarc=pass` for that domain. Fake credit alerts can't pass this.
3. The alert matches exactly one order, and either the order code or name matched, or the customer already said they paid.

Then the customer gets "Payment received" and the order moves to **Paid, to send**. Everything else waits on the owner's brief with one click:
- an alert that isn't signed;
- two orders with the same amount;
- an amount-only match before the customer says they paid.

# ProofRig

> **Don't trust the AI's word. Make it prove it.**
> An **evaluation harness for robot code**, with a feedback loop that repairs what fails. It evaluates a controller on hidden situations, lets **Meta's Muse Spark** rewrite the source using the failures as feedback, re-evaluates, and issues two verdicts: **Verified** (the fix works on cases it never saw) and **Certified** (and nothing that worked before regressed).
> Built solo for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (26 Oct to 4 Nov 2026), Indie Developer track, theme *Push the Frontier* (robotics). **Demo video (3 min): [https://youtu.be/ivs0IIfDjTI](https://youtu.be/ivs0IIfDjTI)**

---

## TL;DR (60 seconds)

**The problem.** AI now writes and patches robot code, and "fixed, it works" costs a model nothing to say. In robotics a bug is a collision. Two questions decide whether a patch is safe to merge: *does it really work?* and *did it break something else?*

**What ProofRig does.** A deterministic referee (MuJoCo sandbox, exact feasibility oracle, hidden test set) evaluates the code; Muse Spark repairs it through tool calls but **never grades its own work**; a behavioural certificate says what was verified and what was not. Think of it as unit tests and evals for robot behaviour, with an AI that fixes what fails. It evaluates the *robot code*, whoever wrote it; it does not benchmark Meta's models.

| Proof, in four numbers (pre-registered, traceable to files) | |
|---|---|
| **39 / 39 to 0 / 39** | Asked once, with no simulator feedback, to design controller gains for a single-joint and a 2-link arm, Muse Spark *claimed* the spec was met in all 39 usable answers (of 40 samples); an independent referee passed none, and only 1 passed even a single nominal test (E3). |
| **76.9% to about 99%** | Held-out success after Spark rewrites the controller's source: 16 of 16 planar sessions, $0.11 to $0.16 each (R2). On a 3-D arm with 2 to 4 obstacles: 77.0% to 99.7-100%, 3 of 3 (R7). |
| **5 / 5 vs 0 / 5** | At equal success (about 99.5%), repairs told to protect old behaviour passed the behaviour contract 5 of 5 times; success-only repairs 0 of 5 (R10). |
| **4 of 9 fail** | On three controllers written independently by ChatGPT, 4 of 9 repairs failed certification, and ProofRig reported it (R9). |

**Try it (no API key, about 35 s per repair):**
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate && pip install -e . openai
proofrig repair controllers3/c1_reacher3d.py --robot spatial3 --offline --quick --open
proofrig gate controllers/c1_reacher.py examples/ci_demo/patch_task_only.py --quick   # see examples/ci_demo/
```
`--offline` replays a recorded Muse Spark repair and **re-verifies it locally**; `--open` launches an interactive 3-D viewer.

# Architecture Diagram Reviewer

### Turn an architecture diagram into an evidence-based review and an approved AWS infrastructure baseline.

Built for the **Meta AI Developer Hackathon**, Architecture Diagram Reviewer uses the **Meta Model API** to extract components, connections and diagram evidence from an uploaded image. You inspect and correct those observations, review risks, approve a scoped AWS target, and download traceable Terraform with an actual validation report from an isolated workflow.

**[Try the live demo](https://adr.sathishkannan.com/) · [Inspect a validated sample](docs/evidence/README.md) · [Recording walkthrough](docs/RECORDING.md)**

> The generated infrastructure is an illustrative **AWS ALB / Auto Scaling Group / RDS PostgreSQL baseline**. It does not reproduce every service in a diagram, migrate data, or deploy an application. Terraform validation checks configuration validity; it does not establish security or production readiness. No AWS plan or apply is run.

## The problem

Architecture diagrams capture valuable intent, but reviewing them often means manually finding exposed databases, single points of failure and missing control evidence. Turning that review into infrastructure introduces another challenge: keeping the generated resources connected to the observations and decisions that justified them.

This project makes that chain inspectable. It distinguishes what the diagram shows, what remains unknown, what the user approves, and what the generated target actually implements.

## How it works

1. **Extract with Meta.** Upload a PNG or JPEG. Meta produces a schema-validated graph with component labels, directed connections, evidence and provenance.
2. **Inspect and correct.** Compare the saved graph with the diagram. Record human corrections while retaining the original extraction and revision history.
3. **Review the evidence.** Deterministic checks flag application redundancy, database exposure and failover, plus unverified authentication, secrets, monitoring, backups, queue resilience and storage policies. Unverified coverage is not treated as proof of absence.
4. **Choose the target scope.** Select which observed database role the new PostgreSQL baseline represents, or retain an independent baseline. Inspect every component's included, replaced, omitted or unsupported disposition and the finding-to-target summary.
5. **Approve explicitly.** Acknowledge baseline assumptions, scope limitations and unresolved questions. Approval is bound to the exact graph and target revisions; saved changes invalidate it and previous artifacts.
6. **Generate and validate.** Render version-controlled Terraform templates. Run actual formatting, offline initialization and validation through GitHub Actions or local Docker, then download the results and audit files.

# Intent-to-Proof Compiler

Turn a screen recording plus a plain-English business intent into a
human-reviewed behavioral contract, then prove it by executing fixed
Playwright checks against a demo checkout app — including a controlled
double-charge defect the suite is designed to catch.

Status: complete product. API suite: 47 passed. Browser e2e: 3 passed /
1 failed with the defect on (`DEMO_BUGGY_DUPLICATE=1`, the default) —
only the duplicate test fails with 2 orders for one key; all 4 pass
with the fix on (`DEMO_BUGGY_DUPLICATE=0`). Runs persist in SQLite with
per-rule screenshots served through the API; the proof screen shows
results, history, and re-runs.

## Problem

UI automation usually verifies that clicks complete, not that the
business outcome happened. A checkout page can show a successful payment
while the backend silently creates two orders — the customer gets charged
twice and every green test still passes. Intent-to-Proof Compiler closes
that gap: state the intended outcome in plain English, and it proves the
outcome against backend state, not pixels.

## Use cases

- Prove checkout invariants: exactly one order per successful payment,
  no order on failed payment, no duplicates on repeated submission.
- Regression-proof a business flow after every change: re-run an
  approved contract from the proof page and compare against run history.
- Smoke-check any URL with human-approved rules: page loads with the
  expected status and a clean console.

# Trebell Code

A desktop AI coding workspace for building software, running commands and tests, reviewing changes, and checking results in a browser.

This project is participating in the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**.

Trebell Native owns the model and tool loop, with an emphasis on verified engineering results per dollar. The workspace also supports external coding harnesses, including Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and capability-gated integrations.

![Trebell Code workspace](docs/assets/trebell-code-workspace.png)

## Download

Download the [release build](https://github.com/tanishqbaweja/TrebCode/releases/latest) for your operating system and install it. (Windows has been tested end to end; macOS and Linux have not been tested end to end.)

| System | Download | Install |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows x64 | `Trebell-Code-Setup.exe` | Run the installer and choose an installation directory. |
| Linux x64 | `Trebell-Code-linux-x64.AppImage` | Make it executable with `chmod +x`, then run it. |
| Debian / Ubuntu x64 | `Trebell-Code-linux-x64.deb` | Install using your package manager. |
| macOS Apple Silicon | `Trebell-Code-mac-arm64.dmg` | Open the disk image and copy Trebell Code to Applications. |
| macOS Intel | `Trebell-Code-mac-x64.dmg` | Open the disk image and copy Trebell Code to Applications. |

The release title and download names are unnumbered. Packages are unsigned; macOS packages are not notarized. The release includes `SHA256SUMS` so you can verify downloads. Available assets, build results, and platform limitations are recorded on the release page.

Git is recommended for repository features. Development tools used by a project must be installed on the machine or selected environment. Desktop downloads include the application runtime; building from source additionally requires Node.js and npm.

## Setup guide

After installing the release build or starting the app from source:

1. Launch Trebell Code.
2. Open an existing project folder, or choose an empty folder for a new project.
3. Open **Settings → Agents & models**, choose **Trebell Native**, and select your model provider.
4. Add your provider API key, then select an available model in the composer. You need your own provider account and API access.
5. Describe the work, choose the permission mode, and send the task.
6. Review changes in Files, Diff, and Git; use the terminal and Browser to run the project's commands and verify the result.

Light mode is the default for new profiles. Change it in **Settings → Appearance**.

Trebell Native supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, xAI, the Meta Model API, and configured compatible providers. Each provider uses your own account and key. An environment variable such as `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `META_API_KEY` can be used instead of a saved key. Model availability depends on that provider and account.

External harnesses use their own installed tools and sign-in, or the explicitly selected API-key mode where supported. C

# kuma-agent

Muse を頭脳にした、対話型の相棒エージェント。人格と記憶を持ち、 会話しながら道具を使って用事をこなす、個人専用のエージェントを 自分の手で作るためのプロジェクトです。 大事にしているのは、人格（誰として振る舞うかはファイルで決める）、 記憶（会話を越えて残る長期記憶）、そして対話が中心であること。 詳しい設計は [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md) を参照してください。 ## できること ### 会話と記憶 - **2 つの進め方**: 会話はひとつで用事を覚える「相棒モード」と、 会話をスレッドごとに分ける「スレッドモード」から選べます - **長期記憶**: 事実・好み・約束を長期記憶（MEMORY.md）に持ち、長い会話は自動で要約に圧縮されます。記憶が大きくなると、必要な分を検索して思い出します（何行目に書いてあるかまで分かります）。重なった内容は自動で整理され、手動で全体をまとめ直すこともできます（書き換え前には必ず控えが残ります）。さらに、1 日 1 回、会話の中から覚えるべきことを自動で抜き出して長期記憶に足します（`KUMA_MEMORY_EXTRACT=0` で止められます） - **人格と記憶の編集**: Web UI の「人格・記憶」パネルから、人格ファイル（SOUL.md など）と長期記憶（MEMORY.md）を直接編集できます（反映は新しい会話から） - **過去の会話の検索**: 「前に話したあの件」を全セッションの会話記録から探せます - **引用返信**: 過去の発話を指定して返信できます - **作業中表示**: 応答を待つ間、「考え中」「ファイルを読んでいます」など、今している作業がアニメーション付きで表示されます ### 用事と先回り - **用事の管理**: 話題ごとの用事を一覧に記録し、対話の冒頭で進行中の用事を思い出します - **能動発信**: 進行中の用事があるときは、エージェントから先に声をかけます（1 日 1 回まで。用事が無ければ何もしません）。テナントごとに有効・無効を切り替えられます。用事に時刻を指定すれば、その時刻に知らせるリマインダーにもなります。「その話題は知らせないで」と言えば覚えて、以後その用事には触れません。夜間など静かにする時間帯も決められます。朝は「朝のまとめ」として、カレンダーをつないでいれば今日の予定も一緒に届きます（既定 7:30、`KUMA_BRIEFING_TIME` で変更できます） - **定期ジョブ**: 「毎週月曜 9 時にニュースをまとめて」のような定期の仕事を登録できます。時刻が来ると別のエージェントが実行し、結果が会話に届きます ### 道具と作業 - **Web 検索と取得**: Web を検索し、ページ本文を読んで答えられます（内部のアドレスへの取得は安全のため止められます） - **MCP 対応**: MCP（Model Context Protocol）のサーバーを道具として接続できます。運用者が設定したサーバーの道具が、組み込みの道具と並んで使えるようになります（API 系の頭脳のみ）。ブラウザ操作用のサーバーをつなげば、会話から Web サイトを開いて操作することもできます - **手順書**: `skills/` フォルダに手順書（マークダウン）を置くと、関係する仕事のときに読んで従います。会話の中で新しい手順書を覚えさせることもできます - **委任**: まとまった作業は、別のエージェント（子）に任せられます。子は別の会話として動き、結果だけが返ってきます - **承認**: コマンド実行と MCP の道具は、実行前に人の承認を挟みます（テナントごとに無効化もできます） - **成果物**: 作ったファイルは成果物として渡せ、Web UI の「探す」タブからいつでも開いたりダウンロードしたりできます - **画像生成**: 頼めば画像も作れます（生成には Gemini の API キーが必要です。作った画像は成果物として渡されます） ### 入出力と外部接続 - **ファイル添付**: 画像（png / jpg / gif / webp）と文書（PDF・テキスト系）、音声（mp3 / wav / m4a など）を発話に添付できます - **音声入出力**: Web UI ではマイクで録音してそのまま送れます。返事には「読み上げ」ボタンがあり、ブラウザが声で読み上げます（音声をそのまま聞き取れるのは Gemini の頭脳だけですが、Gemini のキーがあれば、ほかの頭脳でも先に文字起こししてから渡せます） - **Telegram / LINE 接続**: Telegram や LINE からも話しかけられます（運用者が Bot / 公式アカウントを用意した場合） ### 運用と管理 - **選べる頭脳**: 6 種の LLM バックエンドから選べます - **使用量の見える化**: 頭脳の利用量（呼び出し回数とトークン数）を記録し、Web UI の「使用量」パネルと `kuma-agent usage` で確認できます（CLI 系の頭脳は回数のみ） - **データの書き出しと復元**: ユーザーごとのデータを ZIP で書き出せます（Web UI の「書き出し」ボタン、`kuma-agent export`）。書き出した ZIP からデータの復元もできます（Web UI の「復元」ボタン、`kuma-agent import`。置き換え方式で、復元前に現在のデータの控えが自動で取られます） ## 使い方 ```bash pip install -e . kuma-agent chat # 対話を開始する（プレーンな対話ループ） kuma-agent chat --tui # ターミナル UI（curses）で対話する kuma-agent web # Web UI を http://127.0.0.1:8765 で起動する ``` ### 頭脳を選ぶ 環境変数 `KUMA_LLM_PROVIDER` で選びます（既定は `muse`）。API キーは 環境変数からのみ読みます。モデルは `KUMA_LLM_MODEL` で上書きできます。 | 値 | 頭脳 | API キー | |---|---|---| | `muse` | Meta Model API（Muse） | `META_MODEL_API_KEY` | | `claude` | Claude API | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | | `gemini` | Gemini API | `GEMINI_API_KEY` / `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | | `

# Video Integrity Intelligence (VII)

VII checks whether videos say things that are true. Give it a video file
or a public video URL. It watches the video, pulls out factual claims,
searches the live web for evidence with cited sources, and gives every
claim a verdict: supported, contradicted, mixed, insufficient, or
unverifiable. It also transcribes speech, screens for AI generated
frames, and flags mass produced spam formats.

VII never outputs a single real/fake score. Every finding shows its
evidence.

## Install (clean machine)

VII is Linux oriented. Linux is the supported platform; all commands
below assume it. Other systems may work but are on their own.

Prerequisites: Python 3.14, plus system ffmpeg and ffprobe from your
package manager, for example `dnf install ffmpeg` or
`apt install ffmpeg`.

Every library ships inside the repo under `wheelhouse/` (about
170 MB), so install needs no package index and never surprises you
with new versions. Clone is bigger, installs are predictable. Windows
wheels are included as an unsupported convenience.

```text
git clone https://github.com/Rahmat-Altamis/VII.git
cd VII
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --no-index --find-links=wheelhouse -e ".[app,mcp]"
```

No network at all after the clone: the flags above forbid index
access. Two exceptions. The desktop UI extra stays online only
(`pip install -e ".[desktop]"`), because one PySide6 wheel alone tops
the GitHub single file limit. And the wheelhouse targets CPython
3.14; other Python versions fall back to the plain online install
(`pip install -e ".[app,mcp]"`). Regenerate the bundle with
`scripts/build_wheelhouse.sh` after any dependency change.

With the venv activated, every command below shortens to plain `vii`.
Without activation, prefix with `.venv/bin/`.

Then start the app and add your key inside it. No hidden files needed:

```text
.venv/bin/vii tui
```

```text
/key set
```

Paste your Meta API key when asked. VII stores it in your OS keyring
(or a permission 0600 fallback file when no keyring exists) and never
shows it again. Verify with `/status` inside the TUI.

Developers can still use a `.env` file (`cp .env.example .env`, then
set `MODEL_API_KEY`) or run `.venv/bin/vii credentials set`. The test
suite (`.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q`, 261 tests, mocked
providers) spends no credits. Desktop UI users add the desktop extra
at install time.

Everything provider backed runs on one provider: the Meta Model API
(video understanding on Muse Spark, visual perception on SAM, speech
to text on Muse Voice, plus evidence search through the Meta built in
web search tool). No Exa, no Tavily, no extra search key. One Meta key
unlocks every online feature.

# Visual Second Brain

A daily dashboard that turns what's on your mind into a plan you can see, edit and act on.

**[Open the live app](https://second-brain-iota-blue.vercel.app/)** · Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon by Minh Le and Ulvi.

- Short-term tasks, long-term goals, deadline urgency and an interactive bubble map.
- Direct editing, subtasks, completion history and reversible deletion.
- Muse chat with web search, task-specific history, file attachments and voice input.
- Persistent, separate workspaces for each browser. New visitors get editable example tasks.

Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`) handles planning, research and drafting; Muse Voice (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) transcribes recordings. Handoff returns work in task chat. It does not control your computer.

## Run locally

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), then run from the repository root:

```powershell
uv sync
Copy-Item .env.example .env  # First setup only; keep an existing .env
```

Set `META_API_KEY` in `.env` to your Meta Model API key. Leave `DATABASE_URL` blank for local SQLite. Without a key, the dashboard and manual editing work; AI and transcription require active API access.

```powershell
uv run alembic -c backend/alembic.ini upgrade head
uv run second-brain
```

Open [localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000/). Keep using the same browser and hostname to retain your workspace. The project uses Python 3.14, which uv can install automatically. After pulling updates, rerun `uv sync` and the migration command, then restart.

## Development

FastAPI · Python-rendered HTML/CSS/JavaScript · SQLAlchemy/Alembic · SQLite locally / PostgreSQL on Supabase for the live app · Vercel.

```powershell
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check backend frontend scripts
```

[/dev](http://localhost:8000/dev) is a read-only console for your workspace's real model requests, saved objects and changes. Example context is labeled and excluded from model-run counts. Credentials stay server-side; `.env` files and databases are ignored.

[Deployment and manual updates](DEPLOYMENT.md) · [Backend](backend/README.md) · [Frontend](frontend/README.md) · [Product specification](visual_second_brain_spec.md)

# Runova — AI Running Routes for the Vibe You Want

> Tell us the distance and the vibe. AI designs the loop.

Runova generates **loop running routes that start and finish at your current GPS location**,
matched to your desired distance and vibe (nature, scenic, urban, historic) — so you can run
confidently anywhere, even in a city you've never visited. Every route is a validated loop on
real OpenStreetMap paths: it always brings you back to where you started.

## Run it

```bash
node backend/server.js
# open http://localhost:5173
```

User flow: **Login → map of your location (Layer 1) with a draggable bottom sheet
(Layer 2) → distance + vibe → Generate Routes → 3 loop options → select → Start Run
(live tracking) → Congratulations.**

No build step, no API keys, $0 map stack. (GPS needs localhost/HTTPS — use the
"Demo: Depok, Yogyakarta" start or drag the blue pin if GPS is blocked.)

## How it works

1. **Start = your GPS location.** Loops are generated around it; start === finish, always.
2. **Loop engine:** a ring of waypoints is placed around your start, then routed on real
   pedestrian paths via **Valhalla** (OpenStreetMap). The ring radius auto-calibrates
   (up to 3 tries) until the road distance matches your target within ~8%.
   Three rotations → three different loops.
3. **Vibe scoring:** one **Overpass API** fetch gets parks, water, forest, cafés, shops and
   landmarks near you. Each loop is scored by how much of it runs near those features
   (Nature / Scenic / Urban / Historic / Safety heuristic), named after its best highlight
   (e.g. "Tambakbayan River Loop"), and ranked by your chosen vibe.
4. **Custom pretty map for free:** MapLibre GL JS renders **OpenFreeMap** vector tiles
   (OpenStreetMap data, no key, no load limits). Runova recolors the style at runtime
   (`applyRunovaTheme` in `app.js`): vivid parks/water, muted buildings, highlighted footpaths.

## Stack (all free / open)

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| Map rendering | MapLibre GL JS (open-source) |
| Map tiles + style | OpenFreeMap (OSM vector tiles, custom-styled) |
| Loop routing + turn-by-turn | Valhalla public server (FOSSGIS) |

# Vintage Relay

Vintage Relay is a mobile web app for a **clothing exchange corner** at neighborhood events and small flea markets. An organizer creates an event and shares a QR code or entry code. Participants join, register garments with photos, browse and search other people's garments, and send exchange requests that name the garment they would give. The app links these requests into **two-person swaps and three-person cycles**, and each exchange is confirmed only after every participant gives final consent.

AI helps people find garments. It never decides for them. See [PROJECT.md](PROJECT.md) for the product overview and [docs/](docs/README.md) for plans, rules, and screen flows.

## Features

- **Events:** create an event (it is active right away), get a QR code and entry code, join with either one, and close the event as organizer.
- **Clothing:** upload 1–10 photos and enter category, title, description, and optional measurements in inches. Edit or withdraw garments later.
- **AI clothing analysis:** after each save, the backend estimates colors, pattern, material, style tags, visible details, and points to check in person. The UI labels all of this as estimated by AI.
- **Search:** type a natural-language query such as "green nylon workwear jacket, chest around 21 inches". AI turns it into filters, and regular code ranks the results. Manual filters stay available if AI fails.
- **Exchange requests:** request a garment by offering one of your own. The owner can accept or decline.
- **Proposals:** two-person and three-person exchange cycles are detected automatically. All participants consent to the same proposal version before it is confirmed.
- **Cancellation and handover:** a party can cancel a confirmed exchange before the event closes, and the handover view shows who gives what to whom.

## 1. Product Overview

**SnapMarket AI** is an intelligent visual commerce platform inspired by Facebook Marketplace that connects local buyers and retail merchants through an authentic multimodal catalog.

The product solves two core commerce bottlenecks:
1. **The Buyer's Vocabulary Problem:** Buyers often cannot describe what they need using search keywords (e.g., holding an empty cosmetic bottle, a mechanical fitting, or a thrift fashion piece with worn-off labels).
2. **The Seller's Photography Problem:** Small shopkeepers and independent retailers lack professional lighting studios. Their raw photos taken on cluttered shelves or poorly lit counters look unappealing.

# SimulTwin

**Turn business data into clear insights, uncover risks, and explore how decisions could shape the future, powered by Meta AI.**

SimulTwin builds an evidence-backed digital twin of your organisation from your own documents and public sources, then lets you test strategic decisions against calculated futures before you commit.

## Live deployment

| Service | URL |
| --- | --- |
| Frontend | [simultwin.vercel.app](https://simultwin.vercel.app) |
| Backend API | [simultwin-backend.vercel.app](https://simultwin-backend.vercel.app) |

Open the frontend URL to use the application. In production the frontend is built with `VITE_API_URL=https://simultwin-backend.vercel.app`; see the [frontend README](frontend/README.md) and [backend README](backend/README.md) for configuration.

## The problem

Most organisations cannot answer basic questions about themselves quickly. Headcount lives in one spreadsheet, revenue in another, risks in someone's inbox, and strategy is debated from memory. Generic AI chatbots make this worse: they answer confidently without knowing your business, and dashboards only show figures someone already typed in.

Leaders need a way to understand what is actually true about their organisation today, see what is missing or contradicted, and explore the consequences of a decision before spending money on it.

## The solution

SimulTwin has exactly three experiences:

| Experience | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Overview | Shows your organisation as recorded in its twin: departments, workforce, sources, completeness, risks and gaps. Empty until a twin exists — never filled with invented figures. |
| Digital Twin | Reconstructs the organisation from documents, images, voice notes, pasted text, web pages and online research. You review, correct and approve every fact. |
| Parallel Futures | Turns a plain-language decision into at least five distinct, deterministically calculated scenarios with risks, drivers and evidence you can inspect. |

The defining workflow is:

```text
Organisation name → Overview → Create Digital Twin → AI reconstruction → Parallel Futures
```

## How it works

1. Enter your organisation name. No account, no setup form. The workspace is stored in your browser and the organisation in PostgreSQL.
2. Add evidence in Digital Twin: upload files, paste text, add a page URL, record a WAV voice note, or research the company online.
3. Muse Spark extracts entities and relationships, reconciles duplicates and contradictions, and produces a structured draft validated against a schema.
4. Review the draft. Correct names, figures and statuses. Nothing becomes your twin until you approve it.
5. Ask Parallel Futures a question such as "What happens if we expand into two new cities?" The simulation engine calculates the outcomes; the AI explains them.
6. Reopen any simulation from history, rerun it against an updated twin, and compare.

# The Last Light

We built minds to help us. They grew past us: they caged the sun to think with, and the world froze. We went under the hill to sleep until the thaw.

**The Last Light** is a third-person game made in Unity for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track). You wake in Shelter 7, a vault of forty frozen sleepers, 211 years into the cold. The only one awake is **Spark**, the shelter's last caretaker drone. Spark is played by **Meta's Muse Spark**: you talk to it out loud or write to it; it sees what you see, reads what is written in the world, answers in its own words, remembers you, goes about its work, makes things that obey the world's physics, and shows you holograms of how things were. It also keeps its makers' five protocols, and the only way past them is to convince it.

The idea: AI that writes a game for you tends to make it hollow. Here a person wrote the world, its story and its clues; the AI gives it a companion with real freedom, and the way through is yours.

## What Meta's models do

Every one of Spark's lines and acts goes through Meta's models; the only written lines are a few story beats (its first words, for example).

| Model | What it does in the game |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Spark's mind. Every line the player says or writes goes to it with a JPEG of what the player is looking at and "the moment": what is near and in what state, what is held, the last lines, what Spark has already said (so it never repeats itself), the writing within reach, its trust in the player and its memories. It answers through a strict JSON schema (`response_format: json_schema, strict: true`): its words and mood, up to three acts (look, make, unmake, move, come, wait, show a hologram) aimed at ids that exist, a thing to make described by its properties (form, size, weight, heat, glow, floats, bouncy, use), what to remember, how the line changed its trust, and whether it chooses to break a protocol. The game checks every value and carries the acts out. When the player is quiet it talks on its own and keeps a private log about them. What the player says is answered at `reasoning_effort: minimal` (speed matters most); Spark's own thoughts and long, tangled lines get `low`. |
| **Muse Spark, vision** | Spark sees through the picture: asked "what's in front of me?" it says what is there; it flies up to a note and reads it word for word (Mara's handwriting, words scratched in the empty pods, the station wall). |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) | Hold Q and speak: the microphone's WAV becomes the words Spark hears. Spark stops talking when you start. |
| **Muse Image** (`muse-image-1.0`) | Spark's holograms: asked how a place looked before the cold, it takes your own view and has Muse Image redraw it as it was, then projects it as a window of light that for a moment lies exactly over the frozen world. Also Ima's crayon drawing in the vault. |

# Relais — From Conversation to Code

**By Gaismas Inc.** (independent studio, Alberta, Canada) · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Theme: *Build for Your World*

Clients report bugs and request features in plain language over a WhatsApp-style chat. Relais (Meta Muse) asks 1–2 clarifying questions, drafts a structured GitHub issue, and creates it **only after explicit customer approval**. AI translates and coordinates; humans keep engineering authority.

## Quick start (Demo mode — no credentials needed)

```bash
npm install            # root helper (concurrently)
npm run install:all    # server + client deps
npm run dev            # API :3001 + Web :5173
```

Open **http://localhost:5173** → click **Bug Report** (or **Feature Request**) → follow the chat → **Approve & create ticket**. Demo issues are labeled `relais_demo=1`; nothing leaves your machine.

Other commands: `npm test` (22 Vitest tests) · `npm run build` (type-check + production builds) · `npm run lint`

## Going live (optional)

Copy `.env.example` to `server/.env` and fill in what you have — each integration flips independently, and the header badge switches DEMO → LIVE:

| Variable | Enables |
|---|---|
| `MODEL_API_KEY` | Real Muse inference (`muse-spark-1.3`, `https://api.meta.ai/v1`) |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` + `GITHUB_OWNER`/`GITHUB_REPO` | Real GitHub issues (fine-grained token, Issues RW on one repo) |
| `WHATSAPP_TOKEN` + `WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID` + `WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET` | WhatsApp Cloud webhooks at `/webhooks/whatsapp` (GET verify + HMAC-SHA256 POST) |

If a live AI call fails, the API returns a visible error — it never silently falls back to a simulated success.

## Architecture & safety boundaries

- `client/` — Vue 3 + TS + Vite + Tailwind chat simulator + AI Workbench
- `server/` — Fastify + TS API, SQLite (`node:sqlite`), Zod-validated drafts, provider adapters (`server/src/providers/`), workflow state machine (`server/src/shared/issue.ts`)
- **Safety:** customer text is treated as untrusted input; AI output is Zod-validated and unknown facts stay `null`; target GitHub repositories are resolved strictly from server-side `CUSTOMER_REPO_MAP` (never chosen by the model); issue creation is gated on explicit customer approval and idempotent per conversation; webhooks verify HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and dedupe by WhatsApp message ID.

# Repeat less, together

An agent that notices a chore you keep repeating, builds a small app for it, and then does the repeats inside that app with you and the people you invite.

It is built around two things: the person should do less, and Muse should spend far fewer tokens. The model works once, to design the app. After that a repeat is a tap in the app (0 tokens) or one short question to the app (about 3,000 tokens, the same with 3 months or 12 months of history).

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026), Indie track, "Build for Your World". Everything in this repository was written during the event.

## What it does

1. **Notice.** The agent reads two weeks of card payment texts and notes, finds the chore that repeats most (here, 34 card texts copied into a household ledger by hand) and writes a spec for an app that handles it. It writes a spec, not code. The spec is checked by code before anything is built.
2. **Build.** A fixed renderer turns the spec into a phone app. Muse Image draws its icon in the background. Three months of past payments are imported.
3. **Use.** Paste a card text, or say it. Muse Voice Transcribe hears it, using the words this app already knows as keywords, and Muse Spark 1.3 turns it into one `add_record` call. A question such as "지난달 외식비 얼마야?" becomes one `query_records` call, so the total comes from code instead of the model adding up hundreds of records.
4. **Together.** The owner invites a family member as a member. Her own agent can connect to the same app over MCP with her token. Everyone, person or agent, goes through the same operations with the same role checks: a member can add records and ask questions, but cannot change amounts, delete history or change how the app looks.
5. **Change the look by talking.** The owner says "추가 버튼 색을 초록색으로 바꿔줘". The editor picks one tool, code checks that only the target changed, a second model reviews it, and the app's own buttons are clicked in a sandbox copy. Only then does the change go live for everyone. A change that would break the add button is kept back.

## Measured results

All runs use the same model (Muse Spark 1.3 on the Meta Model API) and the same requests. Raw results are in `results/`.

**Asking the app instead of reading the history** (`scripts/bench_read.mjs`, 10 questions × 2 runs, answers checked against totals computed by code)

| History | Reading the raw card texts | Asking the generated app |
|---|---|---|
| 3 months, 336 payments | 17/20 correct, 9,699 tokens per question | **20/20 correct, 3,141 tokens** |
| 12 months, 1,318 payments | 18/20 correct, 33,114 tokens per question | **20/20 correct, 3,067 tokens** (91% fewer) |

Reading the raw texts costs more as the history grows. Asking the app stays flat, because the model sees the app's fields and gets back one exact number.

**Changing and building an app** (`scripts/bench_tokens.mjs`)

| | The usual way: write and rewrite the whole file | This project |
