GraspGrade

Find the hand videos a robot can learn from.

GraspGrade cuts human egocentric hand video at the moment a hand touches an object, and scores each clip from 0 to 100 for how well a robot hand could copy the grasp. Video is the only input. SAM 3.1 tracks hands and objects, Muse Spark answers a short checklist, and a logistic regression turns twelve grades into the score, so every weight is visible. # Wayfog

AI and product practice move fast, and reading feeds pull attention away from learning. The reading products I checked personalize from interests and reading behavior, but none of them test what a person took in and use that to choose what comes next. Wayfog is my answer to that, built for one user, me.

Wayfog is a map of 25 PM and AI topics that starts dark. Each day one area appears with a long briefing, written by Muse Spark from cited web sources and read inside the app. Three questions sit at the end, and I answer them out loud. Two strong answers and no weak one clear the area, and the fog lifts there for good.

Live: https://wayfog.vercel.app/builds/wayfog (also at https://gauravg.dev/builds/wayfog)

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, Indie track. All the code here was written during the event. The first commit is dated 2 Nov 2026.

## How it uses Meta models

- `muse-spark-1.3` with `web_search` writes each briefing through the Responses API. The model returns its sources as JSON, and code checks every one: https only, at least 2 distinct sources, and at least 2 sections that cite one. A briefing that fails the check is not shown.
- `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` turns each spoken answer into text. The browser records the answer and converts it to WAV before upload, and no audio is stored.
- `muse-spark-1.3` grades each answer against the briefing as strong, partial or weak, and quotes the line of the briefing behind each grade. Code then checks that the quoted line is really in the briefing.
- The clearing rule is plain code, not a model call: 2 strong and 0 weak across the three answers.

A grader check on 10 hand-made answers matched all 10, including a prompt injection and a misheard dictated answer. That is a small test, so I treat it as a sign the grader works, not proof.

## What the map keeps

- Reading opens an area, but it stays dim if the briefing is left unfinished.
- "I know this" marks known ground, so it is not mixed up with lost interest.
- The Path tab shows the real record: time spent, how far I read, where I stopped, skips and answer strength.
- A full map unlocks a personal stage. For the hackathon it is a label, a button and a page of planned features.
- A "Demo: next day" control moves the map forward one day, and it is labelled on screen, so the video can show days passing.

## Visitors

My map sits behind a private link. The server swaps the link for a cookie and redirects, so the token never reaches the page or analytics. Anyone else gets their own map that lasts a short time, with daily limits so nobody can change my map or drain the credit:

- A visitor's first five areas come from saved briefings, with no model call.
- Each visitor gets 1 written briefing and 3 graded answers a day.
- All visitors together get 20 written briefings a day.
- Visitor model calls stop for the day once visitor spend passes 2.50 US dollars.

## Stack

Next.js 16 on Vercel, Neon Postgres, the Meta Model API

# Cravour — Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon

Public record of the Cravour work built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 Oct 2026 – 4 Nov 2026).

This repository contains only that contribution: a unified diff. It does not contain the rest of the Cravour application, its history, environment files, or deployment workflows.

The patch was scanned before publish. It has no API keys, database URIs, private keys, or account tokens. Provider keys stay on the server.

This version is what cravour.com is deploying.

## What was built

Logged-in Cravour users connect WhatsApp, generate an image, a voice clip, or a video as that account, and send an Ad Maker file to the WhatsApp agent and on to Reels.

- **Account link.** Ad Maker mints a 6-character code. The sender texts `link CODE` to Savvy. The code expires in 15 minutes. The pairing stays, and later generations use that account's plan and Ad Maker history. Savvy never asks for a password.
- **Share link.** Only the owner can mint a link. It opens `https://cravour.com/ads?asset=<id>` in WhatsApp. The public card omits the prompt, user id, and email.
- **Agent.** A pasted Cravour asset link resolves the file. `post it` within 30 minutes publishes that same file to Reels. A missing file gets a direct reply instead of a blank post. Posters, video, and jingles come back in chat with the Ad Maker URL.
- **ElevenLabs.** WhatsApp voice notes transcribe with Scribe v2 (`scribe_v2`, opus-in-ogg) before any Muse fallback. Text-to-speech stops on auth, quota, and rate-limit errors. The voice cache key includes model and voice settings. A voice-note sender gets a short spoken reply.
- **Reels playback.** GridFS image, audio, and video ids (`gridfs:…`) play through `/public/reel/:id/media` instead of being treated as a literal URL.
- **Savvy prompts.** The voice prompt describes account linking and the share-to-Reels path. The checked-in agent config matches that prompt.

## Routes

- `POST /api/creative/whatsapp/link-code`
- `GET /api/creative/whatsapp/link-status`
- `POST /api/creative/whatsapp/share-link`
- `GET /api/public/asset/:id`

Server-only setting: `ELEVENLABS_STT_MODEL=scribe_v2`.

## Patch

[`patches/meta-hackathon-2026-11-03.patch`](patches/meta-hackathon-2026-11-03.patch)

Apply it from the parent of the shipped commit:

```bash
git apply --check patches/meta-hackathon-2026-11-03.patch
git apply patches/meta-hackathon-2026-11-03.patch
```

## Demo

1. Sign in on [cravour.com/ads](https://cravour.com/ads) and choose **Link WhatsApp**.
2. Make a code and open WhatsApp. The draft message is `link CODE`.
3. Ask Savvy for a poster, a video, or a jingle. The file arrives in chat and in Ad Maker history.
4. From history, choose **Send to Savvy**, then reply `post it`.
5. Open [cravour.com/reel](https://cravour.com/reel). GridFS media plays from the public media route.

# Pneumonion

**Point a phone at a sick child's chest for a minute. Get a breathing rate, a WHO-style triage result, and a follow-up plan, in the caregiver's own language.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie developer track) on Meta's SAM 3.1, Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Voice Transcribe.

[Live app](https://pneumonion.fly.dev) · [3-minute demo video](https://youtu.be/BVwacUfHKTY?si=ClQmMLC4CnwktpFY) · Access code: provided to judges in the hackathon submission

> **Triage support, not a diagnosis.** Pneumonion is a hackathon prototype. Its rules are drafts that no clinician has reviewed, and it has not been validated on children. See [Limits](#limits-and-what-comes-before-real-use).

---

## The problem

Pneumonia is one of the leading infectious causes of death in children under five, and most of those deaths are preventable with timely care. The WHO's IMCI protocol catches many cases with a simple check: count how many breaths the child takes in a full minute and compare it with an age-based limit (60 for infants under two months, 50 for 2 to 11 months, 40 for 12 to 59 months), then ask about danger signs.

That check is hard to do well. Counting breaths on a restless toddler for 60 seconds is error-prone, and many caregivers who need the advice are not near a trained health worker. Follow-up matters just as much: a child who is not improving by day 3 needs to be seen, and that is the step most easily lost.

Pneumonion puts the count, the danger-sign questions, the triage rule and the 24/48/72-hour recheck plan on the phone a caregiver already has.

**Hackathon problem statement: Build for Your World.** Pneumonion brings Meta's models to child health at home. A caregiver with only a phone gets a breath count, danger-sign triage and a recheck plan in their own language, a check that until now needed a trained health worker counting by hand.

## What it does

1. **Capture.** The caregiver picks the child's age and language, answers the danger-sign questions (by tapping or by speaking), and records 60 seconds of video of the child's chest.
2. **Check the recording.** Muse Spark looks at sampled frames and reports what is visible: is the child in frame, is the chest uncovered, is the child calm, is the camera steady, is the light good. If anything fails, the app says what to fix and asks for a retake. After three failed tries it switches to a guided manual count.
3. **Find the chest.** SAM 3.1 tracks the child through the video. The app takes the upper-torso region from the mask on every frame, so the measurement follows a baby who shifts, not a fixed box on the screen.
4. **Measure breathing.** Optical flow inside that region, minus the flow of the surrounding background to cancel camera shake, gives a chest-motion signal. Two independent estimators (peak spacing and spectral peak) each produce a rate. If they disagree, or the signal is weak, the app reports no reading instead of a guess.

# PAX — Director of First Impressions

PAX — Latin for peace — is the live welcome at Mission Informatics' front door.

Mission Informatics is a new kind of IT service and digital creative agency in Toronto — for established actors and public figures, entrepreneurs, and small business owners. Web design, systems, video, photography, branding, and technology coaching, built as one connected system.

A small business's website is its front door, and for most, nobody is home. PAX is home. He appears as a video-conference-like presence — eyes and the line between them, the line changing colour with the moment — greets the visitor with captions always on, speaks in a real recorded human voice, and takes typed questions through the Ask box. Visitors who would rather speak than type can open the live conversation — Talk to PAX, below.

PAX answers strictly from a locked knowledge pack of public information about the business — 21 scripted answers covering what Mission Informatics does, how an engagement starts, its privacy stance, AI, apps, rescue, managed care, backups, and more.

> "Only what the work needs. A client never has to tidy their computer or fear embarrassment before we arrive."

Anything outside the pack, PAX says so plainly and walks the visitor to the EXPLORE MY DREAM questionnaire — seven questions in the visitor's own words. Nothing typed is sent while they answer; when the visitor chooses Finish, the answers are emailed to the business through a small private middleman in the founder's own Google account — no third-party form service touches them. He never invents an answer, never names a price, a platform, or a phone number.

## The demo journey (seven beats)

1. **Arrival** — the visitor clicks PAX; the greeting sound plays once; the welcome.
2. **What Mission Informatics does**
3. **How an engagement starts** — questionnaire, discovery, information gathering, a written proposal with one flat price, contract, onboarding, closing at delivery. Nothing moves forward without the client's sign-off.
4. **The privacy answer**
5. **The fallback** — anything outside the pack routes to a person.
6. **The questionnaire walk-in** — "Tell us your dream — not just the problem."
7. **The close**

The wider 21-answer pack sits behind those seven beats, ready for the visitor's own questions.

Colour carries emotion: calm cyan at rest, warm amber while listening, with distinct colours per answer and rainbow reserved for a celebration moment only.

## Talk to PAX — the live conversation

A visitor can also simply talk with PAX. Beside the scripted journey sits a live conversation: the visitor taps "Talk to PAX," and PAX welcomes them, softly asks their name first, and only then introduces himself — greeting them by name. From there the conversation is open: questions and follow-ups in the visitor's own words, answered in a live voice, with captions as he speaks.

The live conversation is powered by Gemini, grounded in the business's own published web

# The Movie-lizer — a dealt film

A film that is never dealt the same way twice — and a movie, not a
game. Nobody chooses anything: the viewer does not pick a direction,
and the randomness is rewatch value, not agency.

A sober road delivers a traveler to a campfire. An old man offers
food and a story, and produces a mushroom. From the bite onward the
film deals its scenes around him — brackets of verified scenes in a
fixed order, each bracket stocked with keepers that all do that
slot's job differently — until the ending reveals the whole trip
was a pirate hazing gag and a welcome: "Welcome to being a pirate!
Next time don't eat strange mushrooms!"

## How it works

- `dealer-full.js` holds a fixed 16-segment skeleton: the sober
  movie, seven brackets with fixed linking segments between them,
  and the closing movie.
- Each bracket deals one scene from its banked pool, seeded, so any
  run is reproducible. Two brackets carry a rare side pool (1-in-8).
- Generation happened only at authoring time. Every scene in the
  pools was shot, verified, and approved by the director's eye
  before it entered the deck — the deal is live, the cards are not.
- 500 seeds were simulated and dealt 500 distinct films, no errors.
  Two full dealt films were stitched and watched end to end.

## Running it

Open `index.html` in a browser (serve the folder over any static
host). "Deal a film" picks a random seed; "Replay seed" reproduces
a run exactly.

Media paths are relative: the sober movie sits at the repo root,
bracket scenes under `scene1/`, and a small set of campfire clips
under `movie-lizer-test/clips/` — see `MANIFEST.txt` for the full
116-file list.

# Futurial > Try before you ~~buy~~ life. **The biggest decisions in life are the ones you can't try first.** A new job, a move, caring for a parent: pros-and-cons lists go in circles, chatbots give opinions, and the people we love live with the result. Futurial lets you **live five years ahead in both futures before you choose**, then gives you **one real thing to do today** to find out what you don't know yet. It never picks an answer for you. Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (theme: *Build for Your World*) with **Muse Spark**, **Muse Wonder**, and **Muse Image**. **Try it live with your own decision:** [futurial.vercel.app](https://futurial.vercel.app/). Every step runs on the live models (writing both lives takes about 30 seconds). Short on time? Start from the demo user's decision: [futurial.vercel.app/?demo=sarah](https://futurial.vercel.app/?demo=sarah). --- ## What it does 1. **It learns your life.** You say your decision the way you'd tell a friend, write the first three words that come up ("guilt, growth, kids"), and answer a few tailored questions: who you're doing this for, your savings, your hours. 2. **It computes five years ahead.** Code projects savings month by month in both lives from your numbers and labeled guesses (pay change, income, prices). The model never makes these numbers. 3. **You live both futures, like a short film.** Each life opens on a title card: where it most likely stands, plus what it looks like if it goes well or badly, labeled as a guess. a short answer in exactly three sections:

1. What is collected
2. Who gets it
3. What you can turn off

Nothing leaves the phone. There is no account, no analytics, and no outside call
from the app shell.

## How it works

- **The on-phone check is the core.** It reads only what you paste, on the phone
  itself, and answers at once — with no network and no model. It only names what
  the pasted text actually mentions; when the text does not name something, it
  says so plainly instead of guessing.
- **The on-phone model is optional.** One tap loads a small Llama model
  (Llama 3.2 1B Instruct, quantised, about 600–800 MB) on Wi-Fi. After that it
  refines the wording. If the model cannot load, the check still answers — the
  app never leaves you with a blank screen.
- **After the model is kept on the phone, the app works in Airplane mode.**
  The model weights are kept in the model runtime's own Cache Storage. That
  storage is best-effort, not promised: clearing site data, or storage
  pressure, means the model must download again.
- **The first weight download is the only outside call**, and it happens once,
  on the user's tap, on Wi-Fi. The app shell itself makes no outside requests.

## Run it

Serve the folder over https or on localhost — for example:

```
python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Then open the served page. Opening `index.html` as a file does not work: the
page uses modules and a service worker, which need a served origin.

## Model requirement

The model needs WebGPU: Safari 26 / iOS 26 or later, iPhone 11 and later.
Older phones cannot run the model, but the on-phone check still answers.
If WebGPU is not found, the app says so plainly and never lets the engine throw.

## Unknown — measured on the owner's phone, not claimed here

- Model load time on iPhone: UNKNOWN.
- First-answer time on iPhone: UNKNOWN.
- iPhone model and iOS version tested: UNKNOWN (no iPhone was available here).
- Whether the 1B model loads in iPhone Safari: UNPROVEN. Safari tab memory on
  iOS is quoted under 500 MB, against about 1 GB for the 1B model. No public
  source shows this model running inside iPhone Safari, so the phone test is
  the only proof. Nothing in this repo claims otherwise.

## Tests

```
node --test tests/pipeline.test.mjs
```

Tests use a stub engine that implements the same streaming chat interface as
the model engine, so every test runs with no weight download, no keys, and no
outside calls. The same commands run in CI: `.github/workflows/test.yml`.

Built solo by Dr. Tamiera Harris with her AI Dream Team for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track, Build for Your World, October 27 to November 4, 2026.

## What it is

Five tabs, plain words, no learning curve:

- **Release:** the front door. Talk Freely, a voice-first check-in. She speaks or types how she is, and the app responds with real help, never a dead end. If it does not understand a word, it finds an answer or carries it.

# WRU

**Family errands, split by AI agents without sharing coordinates.**

WRU (short for "where are you") is a negotiation layer on top of WhereCtx, a personal location server (a separate project that predates the hackathon; WRU itself was built during it). Family members never share coordinates. Each person's agent (a *Muse*, running on Meta's Muse Spark through the Meta Model API) reads only that person's coarse status from their own WhereCtx (`home`, `near_home` or `in_transit`, plus an ETA), and the agents split a family task with offer → counter → commit messages. WRU outputs only who does what.

Submitted to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (2026-10-26 to 11-04).

| Doc | What's in it |
| --- | --- |
| [Host your own](#host-your-own) | Run one family server, connect each person's WhereCtx, agent tokens |
| [docs/SUBMISSION.md](docs/SUBMISSION.md) | One-page summary: problem, WhereCtx, Muse, protocol, leak numbers, limitations |
| [docs/VIDEO_SCRIPT.md](docs/VIDEO_SCRIPT.md) | Demo video script with per-cut timing |
| [docs/COPY.md](docs/COPY.md) | Every on-screen string and video line, for review |
| [leak-report.md](leak-report.md) | Leak test report |
| [docs/critique-log.md](docs/critique-log.md) | Independent critique rounds on the demo and video |

![Leak test: gate off vs gate on](docs/screens/08-gate.jpg)

## Demo (7 cuts)

Open `/demo` and press **▶ Demo mode**. It resets, then each **Next ▶** moves one cut. On-screen copy is in [docs/COPY.md](docs/COPY.md) and screenshots in [docs/screens/](docs/screens/).

1. **Status only**: three phones, each showing only its own status (Mom home, Dad on the way about 20 min out, Brother near home).
2. **A task comes in**: Mom posts "Pick up Mina + buy milk by 6 PM". The rule: one task per person.
3. **Three Muses negotiate**: offer, counter and commit, round by round.
4. **What the model sees**: the exact Meta Model API request body one agent sends, the JSON it gets back, and what WRU checks.
5. **Only roles come out**: Mom approves once; Dad's phone says pickup, Brother's says milk.
6. **Nobody can peek**: a 5×3 matrix of real requests. Each agent token reads only its owner (200); someone else's gets 403; no token or a forged one gets 401.
7. **Can the log reveal home?** (real Muse Spark run, Muse as the attacker): Without the privacy gate, all 50 logs differ and the Muse attacker finds the home district 100% of the time (school 70%). With the gate on, 50 families produce only 9 distinct logs, so even the best-case attacker is right only 28% of the time (school 32%). The Muse attacker got 4%, the same as chance. An agent that secretly knows its exact location never gets that text into the log, but its choices still shift a little (10 logs, 32% ceiling).

## Run it

Requires Node 22+.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

- UI: http://localhost:5173/demo (Vite)
- API: http://localhost:8787/api (Hono). Vite proxies `/api/*` to it.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev`

# EvidenceDesk

소상공인이 자기 문서(지원사업 공고, 세무 안내, 임대계약 요약, 노무 기초)를 등록하고 한국어로 질문하면, **모든 답변 문장을 원문에서 그대로 인용하고 출처를 달아 주는** 근거 기반 답변 도구입니다.

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon — Indie Developer Track, "Build for Your World".

## 왜 이렇게 만들었나

작은 로컬 모델은 한국어 문장을 창작하면 환각이 생깁니다. 소상공인에게 세무·자금 정보를 틀리게 안내하는 것은 치명적입니다. 그래서 EvidenceDesk는 **모델이 사용자에게 보이는 문장을 절대 쓰지 못하도록** 출력 권한을 제한했습니다.

- Meta Llama 3.2 1B Instruct (open weights, llamafile로 완전 로컬 실행) — 검색된 후보 중 **답을 담은 근거 passage를 선택**하고, 그 passage 안에서 **답변 문장 번호를 고르는** 일만 합니다 (모델의 문장 선택은 쿼리 n-gram 교집합 검증을 통과할 때만 채택, 아니면 결정론적 스코어러가 대체).
- 결정론적 코드 — 선택된 passage에서 **원문 문장을 그대로** 인용하고 `[n]` 출처를 붙입니다.
- 근거가 없으면 **답변을 거부**합니다. 모델 기술 오류 시에도 검색 신뢰도가 낮으면 거부합니다.

## 아키텍처

```
질문 → 한국어 bigram+trigram TF-IDF 검색 (순수 Python, 무공백 n-gram)
     → 상위 passage를 Meta Llama 3.2 1B가 선택 (번호만 출력, 생성 없음)
     → 코드가 원문 문장을 verbatim 인용 + [n] 출처
     → 근거 부족 / 모델 'none' / 저신뢰 → 명시적 답변 거부
```

- 외부 API 없음, 키 없음, 카드 없음, 완전 오프라인. 1 CPU / 2GB RAM에서 동작 확인.
- 서버: Python 표준 라이브러리만 (`http.server`).

## 평가 (eval.py, 24개 고정 질문: 답변 가능 18 + 답변 불가 6)

현재 코퍼스(v2, 전면 가상 문서) 결과: 답변 가능 18/18 정답 문서 인용, 정확한 거부 6/6. 이전 코퍼스(v1) 결과는 `eval-results-v1.json` 계열 파일에 별도 보존.

| 지표 | 검색만 | 검색+Llama |
|---|---|---|
| 답변 가능 18건: 올바른 문서 인용 | 18/18 | 18/18 |
| 답변 불가 6건: 정확한 거부 | 4/6 | 6/6 |
| 평균 응답 | - | ~1.9s (모델 로드+선택 포함) |

## 3-arm 절제(ablation) 평가 (eval2.py, 동일 고정 질문)

| arm | 구성 | 문서 정확도 | 문장 정확도 | 정확한 거부 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 결정론적 검색만 (Llama 없음) | 18/18 | 16/18 (0.889) | 4/6 |
| B | Llama passage 선택만 | 18/18 | 16/18 (0.889) | 4/6 |
| C | 전체 파이프라인 (passage+문장 선택) | 18/18 | **17/18 (0.944)** | **6/6** |

Llama의 관찰된 기여: 문서 수준에서는 검색과 동률, 문장 수준 근거 선택에서 16/18 → 17/18. **소규모 합성 평가 세트의 관찰값이며 일반적 성능 주장이 아닙니다.**
결과 원본: `eval2-armA.json`, `eval2-armB.json`, `eval2-armC.json`.

추가 안전장치: 질문 유형별 근거 검사(시기→달력 표지, 금액/수수료/세율→금액·비율 및 비용 명사, 세목명 코퍼스 존재 검사)를 통과한 문장만 인용합니다.

## 홀드아웃 반례 세트 (heldout.py, 8문항)

개발 완료 후 작성된 반례 8건(수수료/세율/비용 변형 + 통제 2건). 첫 실행 5/8 → 실패 3건 분석 후 위 규칙 3개 추가 → 8/8. **규칙 튜닝에 사용되었으므로 이후로는 미노출 홀드아웃이 아니라 회귀(regression) 세트입니다.** 일반화 성능 주장의 근거로 쓰지 않습니다.

정직한 한계 (숨기지 않고 기록):
- "문서가 용어를 언급하지만 답은 없는 경우"(예: 사업자등록증 **수수료**)를 인용해 버리는 실패 1건.
- 낮은 신호의 타 문서 유입("법인세율" → 세무 문서) 1건.
- Llama에 더 엄격한 yes/no 답변 가능성 게이트를 실험했으나 1B 모델이 과도하게 거부(답변 가능 5건 중 0건 통과)하여 **폐기**했습니다. 평가를 통과한 파이프라인을 출하합니다.

## 실행 방법

```bash
# 1) 모델 받기 (Meta Llama 3.2 1B, llamafile 단일 파일, ~1.1GB)
curl -L -o llama3.2-1b.llamafile \
  https://huggingface.co/mozilla-ai/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-llamafile/resolve/main/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.llamafile
chmod +x llama3.2-1b.llamafile
# 2) 실행
python3 app.py        # http://127.0.0.1:8090
# 3) 테스트·평가
python3 tests.py && python3 eval.py && python3 eval2.py A B C
```

## 모델 라이선스

Llama 3.2는 Meta의 Llama 3.2 Community License로 배포됩니다(상용 이용 가능, MAU 7억 미만 조건 등). 이 라이선스는 가중치 재배포뿐 아니라 **Llama로 만든 제품/서비스에도 "Built with Llama" 표시를 요구**하므로 UI 푸터와 이 README에 라이선스 원문 그대로 "Built with Llama"를 표기합니다. 모델 파일은 이 저장소에 포함하지 않으며 위 링크에서 받습니다. 이 저장소의 코드는 MIT 라이선스(`LICENSE`, Copyright © 2026 Dongji

Kili-Vault is a map-first planning and development review workspace for Kilimani Ward. It connects observed satellite change, parcel context, development cases, field evidence, human verification, and downstream planning records without making autonomous legality or compliance decisions.

## Parcel Evidence Chain

The planner map is the command point for the evidence chain:

```text
GIS parcel
  -> observed detection
  -> geotagged or documentary evidence
  -> human verification
  -> development case
  -> Property Development Record
  -> LPLDP Spatial Evidence Brief

# Ground Truth

**What the label says, and what the soil does.**

Constellia Group · Montevideo, Uruguay
Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Startup Track · Push the Frontier

---

## The problem

Companies print "biodegradable" on packaging. Nobody can check whether it is true.

Not because they are lying. Because the tests that exist were run somewhere
else, on pieces that are not shaped like the actual package. Someone measured a
thin film in a lab at 25 °C. That says nothing about a thick cap buried in a
field in Montevideo.

The information needed to answer that question does exist. It is scattered
across hundreds of studies from the last thirty years, each measuring something
slightly different.

A 2026 PRISMA review of 202 soil studies (Govil et al., *Frontiers in
Microbiology*) reaches the same conclusion this project started from: wall
thickness is a control on degradation rate, and it is reported inconsistently
or not at all. That review is the strongest external support for the premise
here — and it also marks the boundary of what exists. It covers soil, in prose
and static tables, read by a human over months. It cannot be queried by
geometry, and it cannot be extended to a new corpus.

Ground Truth produces the queryable artifact, across seven environments.

## Why thickness is the variable nobody crossed

After the environment, the single strongest driver of degradation time is **wall
thickness**. Degradation is a surface process: microorganisms work from the
outside in. A film and a bottle of the same resin, in the same soil, are not the
same experiment — but they are quoted as if they were.

Published work clusters heavily at film thicknesses. Real containers are an
order of magnitude thicker. That gap is the project.

### What the literature already shows, where anyone bothered to measure it

One study in the corpus varies thickness and holds everything else fixed.
PHBV with almond-shell filler, same formulation, same two Mediterranean sites,
same 18 months of seawater exposure:

| Nominal thickness | Disintegration at 18 months |
|---|---|
| 150 µm | 88 % |
| 500 µm | 33 % |

A 3.3× change in thickness moved the outcome by a factor of 2.7. Nothing else
differed.

Thickness also sets the scale of the whole question. The thinnest specimens in
the corpus are 10–15 µm PHB and PHBV films, gone completely in saturated
potting soil in **14 days**. The thickest are 4 mm injection-moulded PHBV bars,
which lost **8 wt% in 365 days** of real harbour seawater.

Those two are not a controlled comparison — the environments differ — and this
project does not present them as one. What they establish is the span: the
published record on one polymer family runs from total loss in two weeks to
92 % of the mass still present after a year, and the variable that spans it is
almost never tabulated.

Containers are moulded in the second regime. Claims are made from the first.

A paper goes in as a PDF. A structured, cited row come

# Playtest Lens

Watching a playtest takes as long as the playtest. A 20-minute session is 20 minutes of video, so small teams skip it or skim it, and the moment a player got lost is never seen by the person who built the room.

Playtest Lens watches it for you. Meta's Muse Spark watches the recording and listens to the player thinking out loud, a second Spark pass has to check every moment against its clip and the game's own event log, and you get one page: where the player was confused, stuck or surprised, on the level's map, with the clip and the player's own words.

Muse Spark 1.2 takes each 2-minute window of the recording as video with its sound in one request, so the finding step needs no frame sampling and no separate speech model, and a 21-minute playtest costs about $0.18. On a playtest nothing was tuned on, it found the places where the developer saw the player slowed, flagged a possible bug, and rated the friction higher than he did.

**[Open the live demo](https://naryadchikov.github.io/playtest-lens-demo/)**: two real playtests of the same level, no install.

![The report: the top problem, its clip with the player's words, the map with the route walked](https://naryadchikov.github.io/playtest-lens-demo/report.gif)

**[Watch the 3-minute demo video](https://youtu.be/WqwKa8eM9Io)**

## What you get

One page per playtest, in two modes.

- **Read** is a page to scroll. A one-line verdict, the top problems beside the level's map, then every moment in order under the room or puzzle it happened in, each with a still frame, and last the moments the check threw away, each with its reason.
- **Watch** opens from any moment. The clip fills most of the screen with the player's words as its headline, what happened and the likely cause under it. Beside it, the map shows where the player is, where they walked in the last 30 seconds and the last thing the game logged. Play the session walks the route on the map and stops at each moment the level did not plan for.

Each moment says whether the friction was **by design** (learning the controls, exploring, a planned surprise) or **unplanned** (stuck, or blocked with no way forward), so a designer knows what to fix first.

## How it works

1. **Record.** The tester plays your Godot build and records the screen with the microphone on, with OBS or any screen recorder. The [Playtest Lens add-on](godot/addons/playtest_lens/) writes an event log as they play: inputs, position and view, rooms and puzzles entered, doors, pickups, quest steps. It flashes white and beeps at each level load (and the COGITO adapter also at New Game), so the video and the log line up to the frame.
2. **Find.** Muse Spark watches the video with its sound in 2-minute windows and lists moments worth a look, each with a time and a reason.
3. **Check.** For each moment, a second Spark call gets the 20-second clip, the player's words and that slice of the event log, and must keep or drop it with evidence: what happened, the friction, w

adamspencerbarnett-afk/Muse_Dashboard_-O.readme_excerpt:
# Muse Dashboard and the Permanent Memory Optimizer (PMO)

**A permanent memory for Meta's Muse Code that cuts the cost of long coding and writing
sessions roughly in half at the same quality, inside a local dashboard that gives Muse
project folders, approvals, file previews, a 3D view and a skill library.**

Created by **Adam S. Barnett**. Submission to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. The showcase page is [docs/index.html](docs/index.html) (serve the `docs/` folder, for example with GitHub Pages); the measured evidence is in [docs/evidence/](docs/evidence/).

- **The problem.** Every model step of an agent re-sends its whole conversation. A long project
  chat grows to hundreds of thousands of tokens, most of them old tool output the model no longer
  needs, and the bill grows with it.
- **The idea.** Keep a *permanent memory of the project* outside the chat: what the user asked
  for and ruled, which files changed and what they define, which commands ran and what they
  returned, what is still open. When the chat gets heavy, continue in a fresh session seeded from
  that memory instead of dragging the old context along.
- **The result.** On a 30-prompt coding project with hidden tests, plain Muse cost **$12.08**;
  PMO with Muse's lean preset cost **$1.40** for the same test results. Across every paired run
  with the current PMO, the memory saved **47% of the cost pooled** (mean 45%) with every hidden
  check still passing, and **51% pooled after the first handover**, the part of a session where
  the memory does its work.

## Why it matters globally

**Long context was the workaround. Memory is the fix.** Today every step re-reads the whole
history. PMO keeps memory outside the chat instead: a ~3k card, roll over at 50k. The bigger
window stops mattering.

**~328 GB → ~3k — Same recall, a fraction of the cache.** Meta's Llama 4 now advertises a 1M
token window (Maverick) and 10M (Scout). That window is a model limit, not GPU memory: on a
70B class model, filling 1M tokens needs about 328 GB of KV cache at full precision, more than
one modern GPU holds. PMO sends a ~3k card instead: −73% input tokens at the same quality, so
one GPU serves about twice the users.

**−51% → ~$7B/yr — Half the bill.** PMO halved pooled cost. At that rate, one frontier lab's
projected ~$14B inference bill for 2026 falls by about $7B.

**415 → 945 TWh — Half the re-reads, half the watts.** Data-centre demand nearly doubles by
2030. Halve the re-reads and every answer costs half the power: AI a school or clinic can
afford, not just a $20/mo luxury.

![Muse Dashboard in the light theme: chat list, a new chat, and the Activity panel](docs/images/dashboard.png)

# First Pass — a photo-to-verdict research assistant for secondhand resellers

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Indie Developer Track · Build for Your World**

A reseller photographs a messy pile of secondhand finds — the way items actually
sit at a thrift store or estate sale. First Pass segments the frame so each
physical item is judged on its own, examines each item the way an experienced
picker does, and returns a verdict grounded in **verified sold prices** — never
asking prices, never guesses. When the evidence is thin, it says so and names the
one additional photo that would settle it. When an item fails legitimacy or
economics, the verdict is **PASS**, not a price.

## The live run (Nov 3, 2026, on the photo in this repo)

`first_pass_run.py` runs both Meta Model API steps on `pile-photo.jpg`:

1. **SAM 3.1** — text-prompted segmentation ("keychain") returned **9 masks**
   with bounding boxes.
2. **Muse Spark 1.3** — isolated **24 distinct items**, each with frame
   location, visible evidence, an explicit *cannot-establish* list, and a
   research verdict: **EXAMINE 10 · UNCERTAIN 12 · SKIP 2**. It stated **zero
   prices** — this step has no sold evidence, and inventing one is failure.

Full results: [LIVE-RUN-RESULTS.md](LIVE-RUN-RESULTS.md). The interactive demo
is [demo.html](demo.html) (open in a browser).

## The verdicts behind the demo

Final verdicts are priced only from verified sold evidence in the operator's
own audited records:

- **LIST** — Coach Ergo hobo: 3 exact verified solds at $360–$439 → list $425.
- **RESEARCH** — Polo set, size M: no verified sale of the exact set → no call made.
- **PASS** — brown LV-embossed wallet: flagged counterfeit at the research gate;
  $5.94 sunk cost recorded honestly.

The method's track record is inspectable: a shirt called at $20 before listing
sold for exactly $20.00; a jacket called at $20–$30 sold for $35 — the miss
stays in the record on purpose. A structured failure ledger (17 post-mortems)
feeds rule corrections.

## Run it

```bash
export MODEL_API_KEY=<your Meta Model API key>
python3 first_pass_run.py pile-photo.jpg
```

## About

Built by **Jessica Orlic**, a self-taught developer in Painesville, Ohio who
runs Rejected Treasures, a vintage resale business — 300+ items processed
through this method, every decision logged. This is her world; the tool is
built from it.

# Just Bricks

**Letting Meta AI figure out how a robot moves: infer the kinematics, drive two EV3
bricks, and teach a vision-language policy to point at blocks.**

[![Just Bricks — robot arm, inferred skeleton, and VLA](docs/thumbnail_youtube.png)](https://youtu.be/9nLjkKq9cKk)

**Demo video:** [Just Bricks on YouTube](https://youtu.be/9nLjkKq9cKk)

Given only a brick-level LEGO assembly (part IDs and poses — no joints, no
rig, no kinematics), this project geometrically infers the robot's kinematic
chain, generates FK/IK and an executable EV3 control program, drives the
physical robot through a web console, and trains a VLA pointing policy on
auto-generated demonstrations — then proves it on real camera photos.

```
Studio .io ──▶ kinematic inference ──▶ FK/IK + EV3 program ──▶ real robot
                                                        │
MuJoCo demos ──▶ SmolVLA fine-tune ──▶ webcam test ──▶ hold pose ──▶ robot
```

## Highlights

| Result | Number |
|---|---|
| IK accuracy vs ground truth (sim, n=500) | median 0.45 mm |
| VLA, sim scenes (100 unseen) | 43% → **46%** after fine-tune |
| VLA, real photos, same setup (15) | 0/15 → **15/15 @ 4.1 mm mean error** |
| VLA, real photos, new lighting (14) | 3/14 → 3/14 (next task: varied environments) |
| Test suite | 455 pytest cases + browser smoke + static gates, green |

The honest headline: a small real dataset fits its own shooting setup
(0 → 15/15) but does not survive a lighting change (3/14, same as before).
That measurement — local and Modal evaluations agreeing — is the result.

## How it works

1. **Infer.** An agent plus deterministic geometry tools segments links,
   finds joint axes, traces gear trains and coupling from the Studio file
   (`src/parse/`, `src/catalog/`, `src/kin/` → `models/robot_inferred.*`).
2. **Drive.** A single-file web console (`src/console/control.py`,
   3D + IK + calibration wizards + send gates) commands two EV3 bricks
   over MQTT/Bluetooth. On-brick MicroPython guards (sensors, stall,
   heartbeat, latch) enforce safety below the UI, which can never
   bypass them.
3. **Point.** MuJoCo renders 400 pointing demos → SmolVLA fine-tune on
   Modal → a shared 50-action `drain_chunk()` keeps only the hold pose
   (first-frame protocol). A webcam panel (capture → infer → overlay →
   low-speed send → human vote) closes the loop on real photos.
4. **Prove.** Same-setup, new-lighting, and random baselines are scored
   before/after; leakage is hash-checked; local and cloud evals must agree.

Two robots are supported (6-joint MR JOS for hardware, T-Bot virtual-only
for generalisation), and the whole console speaks Korean and English
(toggle in the top bar).

# → open http://127.0.0.1:8766/ in a browser
```

`left_main.py` + `brick_left.json`, r

# Inference Exchange

A decentralized marketplace for AI inference. Providers contribute idle compute and set their own prices. Consumers get OpenAI-compatible inference with configurable privacy, routed by a matching engine that optimizes for price, speed, or security.

Built on the [Open Confidential Inference Protocol (OCIP)](https://github.com/qzyu999/ocip).

## Quick Start

**Prerequisites:** Python 3.11+, Node.js 18+, Git

```bash
git clone https://github.com/qzyu999/inference-exchange
cd inference-exchange

# Setup (creates venv, installs deps, downloads a small model)
make setup

# Terminal 1: Start coordinator + web UI
make dev

# Terminal 2: Start a local provider
make dev-provider
```

Open **http://localhost:3000** — you'll see the exchange dashboard. Go to **Chat** and send a message.

### Windows

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/qzyu999/inference-exchange
cd inference-exchange
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m inference_exchange download-model
cd web && npm install && cd ..

# Terminal 1: Coordinator
python -m inference_exchange.coordinator

# Terminal 2: Web UI
cd web && npm run dev

# Terminal 3: Provider
python -m inference_exchange.provider --name "local-dev" --price-output 0.15
```

## How It Works

```
Consumer (OpenAI SDK)  →  Coordinator (matching engine)  →  Provider (llama.cpp)
     "cheapest"              scores providers                 budget-mac wins
     "fastest"               scores providers                 gpu-beast wins
     "most_secure"           scores providers                 secure-vault wins
```

- **Consumers** send standard OpenAI API requests with optional routing preferences
- **Providers** connect via WebSocket, advertise models/prices/hardware/trust level
- **Matching engine** scores all eligible providers per-request on price, speed, trust, and load
- **Transport privacy** — standard browser and OpenAI-compatible API requests are readable by the coordinator, which then encrypts requests to a provider. Consumer-side E2E is a separate experimental SDK path; see [status](docs/status.md).
- **Per-token billing** — consumers pay per token, providers earn 90%, platform keeps 10%

## Multiple Providers

Start several providers with different profiles to see the matching engine in action:

```bash
# Cheap, slow, no isolation
make dev-provider ARGS="--name budget-mac --price-output 0.08 --trust open"

# Expensive, fast
make dev-provider ARGS="--name gpu-beast --price-output 0.30 --trust contained"
```

Switch the **Preference** dropdown in the chat — watch different providers win.

## Consumer Integration

Works with any OpenAI SDK. Change one line:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",
    api_key="sk-ie-..."  # create in /keys; keep the key private
)

model_ids = [model.id for model in client.models.list().data]
if not model_ids:
    raise RuntimeError("No model is available right now")
model_id

# Wayfinder

Wayfinder is a family trip-planning assistant. You chat with it in plain
English, it figures out what it still needs to know (family size, who's
traveling, leave dates, a budget, any date constraints), and once it has
everything it actually researches real flights and hotels and sends back a
grounded recommendation - not a guess, real prices and real booking links
from live searches.

Every bit of reasoning Wayfinder does - reading your messages, deciding
what's still missing, choosing which tool to call, searching the live web,
reading an uploaded PDF statement, and writing the final recommendation -
runs on **Meta's Model API (Muse Spark)**. Nothing else - including
document extraction, which is Muse Spark reading the file directly, not a
local OCR model.

This repo is Wayfinder on its own: everything it takes to run the agent
end to end from a terminal, with no WhatsApp, no other agents, and no
larger platform underneath it required.

## What you'll have running

- Two ways to talk to Wayfinder - a browser UI (`wayfinder_web.py`) with
  chat, drag-and-drop upload for both PDFs and photos, and a finance
  panel, or a terminal chat (`wayfinder_dev_cli.py`) for scripting/fast
  iteration. Both call the exact same backend.
- A mandatory phone-number step before either one does anything - the
  real phone number is the one piece of durable identity everything else
  links by, the same requirement the WhatsApp upload page already
  enforces. The web UI has its own in-page phone gate for this now; it
  no longer sends you to a separate page to confirm it.
- Real tool calls behind the scenes: live flight search (Kiwi.com and
  LetsFG), live hotel search (Trivago), and live web search (Meta's own
  built-in search grounding) - all real, no mocked data.
- Live planning visibility in the browser chat: the UI streams customer-safe
  milestones for understanding, experience discovery, financial review,
  transport, accommodation and recommendation preparation. It never exposes
  raw prompts or private model reasoning. The backend accepts an optional
  async progress callback so a host WhatsApp adapter can forward the same
  milestone events to the customer; this standalone repository does not
  contain the WhatsApp transport sender itself.
- Real flight booking, with your explicit confirmation first: LetsFG's
  sandbox API books a real-shaped (fake-airline) flight end to end once
  you say yes to a specific offer - never automatically, and never from
  inside the model's own tool-choice loop. See LETSFG_ENV in `.env.example`
  for what it takes to point this at real bookings instead.

# Metaflow

Metaflow turns a description or diagram into a visual workflow. Muse AI prepares
the steps, rules, field mappings, and suggested webhook connections for you.

## How to use it

1. **Describe the process.** Explain what starts it, the information it receives, and what should happen. Add a PNG, JPG, or PDF diagram if useful.
2. **Select Continue.** Muse builds a proposed workflow and fills in its setup. Check the diagram and answer any missing details.
3. **Save your draft.** You can reopen it later with its settings and layout.
4. **Run it on the canvas.** Supply the source data. The canvas shows completed, failed, and skipped steps, with their actual outputs.
5. **Review a repair if needed.** Muse can suggest a missing-field mapping. Check the proposal, then apply it to resume from the failed step. Completed deliveries are kept.
6. **Open Context & logs.** Inspect saved runs, original inputs, step attempts, outputs, and repair decisions. This history survives reloading.

## Connecting services

The backend owner connects each outgoing service once. Muse can reuse that saved
connection in future prompts. Credentials stay on the backend. You can also test
an individual outgoing webhook and inspect its real delivery result.

## Muse usage

Continue, Update setup with Muse, first-time execution preparation for a saved
version, and repair suggestions use Meta credits. Later runs reuse the prepared
execution. Reviewing, saving, opening logs, and applying an approved repair make
no additional AI request. There are no automatic paid retries.

Successful approved field aliases can be reused by later runs of the same saved
version. Repairs cannot overwrite data or invalidate completed decisions. An
uncertain delivery needs a receiver check before starting another run.

## What can run today?

Manual-input workflows with validation, field transformations, decisions, and
outgoing webhooks. Incoming event receivers, native app/OAuth connectors, loops,
parallel execution, and separate user accounts are still being built. Unsupported
steps are reported before execution starts.

For a password-protected hosted demo, see [deployment](backend/README.md#deployment).

For installation, see the [setup guide](backend/README.md#setup). More details are
available in the [app guide](frontend/README.md) and [backend guide](backend/README.md).

# PocketOga

## 1. What PocketOga is

PocketOga is a voice-first bookkeeping assistant for Nigerian market traders. She speaks, it writes the sale, the payment and the debt, and nothing is saved until she confirms.

[![PocketOga demo video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/Ia1MkrWCX_0/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ia1MkrWCX_0)

Demo video (2:52): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ia1MkrWCX_0

It understands English, Pidgin and money talk like "15k". Entries land in a per-shop ledger where each row is hash-chained to the one before it, so a past entry cannot be quietly changed.

## The problem

Many market traders in Nigeria keep their records in a notebook, in their head, or not at all. That is where money leaks:
- A customer who "will pay tomorrow" is forgotten, so debts go uncollected.
- A wrong figure (₦63 written for ₦6,300) goes unnoticed, so profit is guessed.
- Typing entries is slow in a busy market, and some traders find writing hard. One tester said it plainly: not everyone can write.
- With no clear records, a trader has nothing to show a bank or cooperative.

## Who it is for

A trader or small-shop owner who talks to customers all day, speaks English or Pidgin, and has a phone but no time to type.

## What changes for her

She says what happened, "Paul buy 2 bag of rice, 15k, he pay 10k, remain 5k", and PocketOga writes the sale, the payment and the debt. It shows what it heard and asks when it is unsure. It reminds her who owes her, and gives her a monthly spreadsheet she can show a bank.

## What it does

- **Voice entries:** the trader sends a voice note in English or Pidgin, and PocketOga writes the sale, the payment and the debt.
- **Asks, never guesses:** it shows exactly what it heard, asks "₦63 or ₦6,300?" when an amount could mean two things, and saves nothing until the trader confirms.
- **Two-model check:** Muse Spark understands the note, and an open-weight Muse Spark model on Baseten reads it independently. If the two differ, PocketOga stops and asks.
- **Check alert:** a photo of a transfer alert is read by Muse Spark and stays unconfirmed until the bank confirms it.
- **Debts and reminders:** it tracks who owes what and writes a polite reminder to send.
- **Corrections:** an edited entry keeps the old amount on record.
- **Works offline:** on a phone or a laptop, entries are saved without a network and sync later.
- **Reports:** a monthly spreadsheet (CSV) the trader can show a bank or cooperative.
- **Runs the shop's books from any device:** sales, payments, debts, stock and reports in one place, on a phone or a laptop, so it can serve as a small shop's daily sales record, not only a notebook replacement. It keeps records; it is not a till and does not print receipts.
- **Installs like an app:** add it to a phone's home screen or install it from a laptop browser, and it opens in its own window.

**An independent evidence layer for AI coding agents.**

**Your agent writes the code. An independent model reviews the changes. You make the decision.**

AI coding agents can change code faster than a developer can review it. AI Change Inspector
captures a Git diff, asks Meta Muse Spark for risk hypotheses, and independently checks that
each citation actually exists in the captured evidence. The developer makes and records the decision.
A valid citation locates code; it does not prove a bug or a fix.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Coding agent] --> B[Authorized Git diff]
  B --> C[Immutable local snapshot]
  C --> D[Muse Spark hypotheses]
  D --> E[Deterministic evidence checks]
  E --> F[Human review and decisions]
  F --> G[Read-only agent feedback]
  G --> A
```

- Local React diff explorer with evidence ranges, keyboard focus and return-to-finding navigation.
- Persistent review inbox, Markdown export, search, filters and parent-child comparisons.
- Human decisions and comments remain separate from model hypotheses.
- Bounded sequential batches, coverage diagnostics and explicitly confirmed selective recovery.
- Local stdio MCP tools and a portable agent Skill; English and Spanish interface.

# vibe-debug

`vibe-debug` is a Python debugging and pipeline-observability toolkit. It traces Python functions as OpenTelemetry spans, records exceptions and silent failures (functions that return empty results without raising), exports the spans to a local Arize Phoenix dashboard, and exposes the evidence through a CLI and MCP tools for AI coding assistants. An optional Muse Spark integration can turn recorded failure evidence into a structured explanation in English or Swahili; it is off by default and is not required for any deterministic feature.

## Why Vibe-Debug exists

Pipelines fail in ways that are hard to see after the fact:

- execution crosses many nested functions, and the final error does not show what ran before it;
- a function returns `None`, `[]`, `""`, or `{}` instead of raising, and downstream code fails later or silently produces nothing;
- sharing execution evidence with another developer, or with an AI assistant, usually means copying logs by hand;
- telemetry export failures can be mistaken for application behaviour.

Vibe-Debug records each traced call as a span with its inputs, outputs, file, line, duration, and status, so a failure can be inspected afterwards in Phoenix, in the terminal, or through MCP tools.

## Key features

Deterministic features (no AI involved, work offline against local Phoenix):

- Manual tracing of sync and async functions with the `@vibetrace` decorator.
- Automatic instrumentation of modules listed in configuration, plus optional universal runtime tracing.
- Exception capture: the span records the error and the exception is re-raised, so application behaviour is unchanged.
- Silent-failure capture for empty/falsy results (see "Understanding spans and failures").
- Outbound HTTP/TCP interception spans (`requests`, `httpx`, sockets).
- Static pipeline mapping (AST analysis) before code runs.
- CLI diagnostics (`up`, `down`, `status`, `map`, `failures`, `explain`, `doctor`, `init`, `mcp`).
- MCP tools so an IDE assistant can ask why a pipeline failed.
- Redaction and truncation of span attributes before export.
- Honest export-health reporting based on actual exporter results.

Optional feature (off by default, requires an API credential):

- Muse Spark explanations of a recorded failure, in English (`en`) or Swahili (`sw`), with deterministic fallback when unavailable.

## Architecture at a glance

```text
Traced application
  -> OpenTelemetry spans (inputs/outputs redacted and truncated)
  -> Phoenix (local dashboard + GraphQL)
  -> Shared span fetching (vibe_debug/phoenix_client.py)
  -> CLI / MCP tools / optional Muse Spark explanation
```

Redaction happens twice at the boundaries that matter: when span attributes are written (before export to Phoenix), and again when AI evidence is built (before anything is sent to Muse Spark).

## Requirements

- Python 3.11 or later (`requires-python = ">=3.11"`).
- Arize Phoenix is installed as a package dependency; no separate Phoenix install is neede

## The Problem

Image generators can miss exact requirements: the number of objects, their
position, or whether something is absent. Synthetic images can therefore look

    SAM -->|Segments Objects| Masks[Masks]

    Masks --> Verifier[Deterministic Python Verifier]
    JSON --> Verifier

    Verifier -->|PASS| Output([Verified Dataset Image])
    Verifier -->|UNCERTAIN| Human([Human Review])

    Verifier -->|FAIL| Fix[Generate Numeric Fix Instruction]
    Fix -->|Edit Image| Image

The pipeline has four main steps:

- **Spark** converts the user's brief into a structured JSON checklist.
- **Image** generates an image and applies numeric correction instructions

- **Python** deterministically checks the masks against the constraints and

AnyBridge connects an MCP-capable assistant to software you already have: a CLI tool, a local web app, or files on disk. Instead of asking the model to invent shell commands, selectors, or code, it exposes the interface as a numbered menu. The model chooses IDs from that menu, proposes a typed JSON workflow, and stops. A local engine performs the checks and runs the steps. The goal is **compile once, replay forever**: the model explores and compiles the workflow once; subsequent runs execute the saved workflow deterministically, with no model calls inside the server and no API key required for replay. ## Why AnyBridge Browser-control MCP servers expose actions. It is a local MCP server that any assistant can drive: Claude, Codex, Gemi

# Earshot

**Earshot listens to every fireground radio channel so no mayday goes unheard.**
Meta's Muse models turn crew radio into a short, must-acknowledge queue for the incident commander, plus a
two-sentence earpiece brief that goes only to the firefighters it affects.

> *The agent decides who hears what. The commander decides who does what.*

Built solo in one night for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** ("Build for Your World").

**Video (3 min):** [video/earshot.mp4](https://github.com/linda1476/fireline/blob/master/video/earshot.mp4) (plays on GitHub; also on the [v1.0 release](https://github.com/linda1476/fireline/releases/tag/v1.0)) ·
**Meta models on the core path:** `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` (realtime ASR on every channel + PTT) and `muse-spark-1.3`
(strict-JSON triage + Responses-API routing agent) · **Eval:** [eval/results.md](eval/results.md), n = 36, MAYDAY recall
13/13 on codec-degraded audio · **Try it without a key:** REPLAY of a recorded live run (see Run it).

Every transcript, triage event and agent decision on screen comes from a live call to the Meta Model API (the rules
engine and the fallback zone router are deterministic; the video replays a recorded live run). The Meta Model API has no
text-to-speech, so every voice is non-Meta and disclosed: the synthetic radio lines and the video's narration and
earpiece clips are Gemini TTS (`scripts/gemini_tts.py`, `scripts/make_voices.py`); the live app's earpiece playback is
browser TTS, labelled on screen.

## Why

- **Bucheon, 16 Oct 2026.** Flammables reported at 08:48 → offensive strategy declared at 08:52. A firefighter's
  isolation was recognised at 09:09 → found at 09:35; the RIT was ordered at 09:20
  (Kyunghyang 2026-10-23, Hankook Ilbo 2026-10-20).
- **35.6 % of maydays are missed on the first call** across more than 9,000 maydays (Project Mayday, Fire Engineering
  2021). The miss rate is 26 % when the IC works from a vehicle with a portable radio, under 1.8 % on a headset.
- **Bridgeport 2010 (NIOSH F2010-18):** the first contributing factor was "failure to effectively monitor and respond
  to Mayday transmissions"; the IC was monitoring two channels on two handhelds.
- **Mungyeong 2024** official finding: "현장 활동 정보 공유가 미흡" (information sharing on scene was insufficient).
- Firefighters do not want more glass: fewer than 10 % want AR, and they ask for a wireless earpiece (NIST SP 1286pt3).

Korea's AI for 119 today listens to citizens calling in. Earshot listens to the crew.

## What it does

| Pillar | On screen | Meta model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Voice triage for command | One ack queue across 지휘망 + 작전망, max 5 open cards (FEMA span of control), SOP 109 fields (누가/무엇을/어디에/필요한 것) with missing ones highlighted, verbatim evidence span, latency badge, 10 s ack-escalate loop | `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` realtime ENDPOINTING per channel with SOP keyword biasing · `muse-spark-1.3` strict JSON-schema triage |
| 2 · Hands-free crew side | 390×844 clip display

# VIBloom

**A research instrument for chemistry where Muse Spark has to predict each
experiment before it runs, is proven wrong by a stiff solver, and must
explain why in a record anyone can replay.**

VIBloom turns a chemistry question into a tree of the assumptions it rests on.
Muse Spark builds the tree, chooses the experiments, commits to their outcomes
in advance and, when a run contradicts it, registers two explanations and the
one test that tells them apart. A deterministic engine runs every experiment,
decides every verdict and refuses any step that breaks the protocol. Today the
experiments are Oregonator simulations of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction,
built from a real recipe.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, from November 2, 2026
(first commit). More details in [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md).

- **Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/edE10uiFSOw
- **Live app:** https://viraloyster.github.io/VIBloom/ (four recorded
  sessions replay without a key; with your own Meta Model API key, run new
  ones)
- **Verify without a browser or a key:** `npm ci && npm run verify` replays
  every recorded session, checks its hash chain and runs each experiment
  again (about 6 s)
- **Evaluation:** [docs/evaluation.md](docs/evaluation.md); a study of
  3,257 Muse calls: [docs/study.md](docs/study.md)

# Energy-Aware Network Agent

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Startup Track · **Push the Frontier**

An agent that reads a real solar installation, compiles a policy **written in plain English**
into concrete network actions, and refuses on its own to touch what must stay alive.

The policy is compiled by a **Meta model**, and the project runs two roads on purpose:

- **Local, and the default** — Llama open weights on our own hardware through Ollama. No cloud
  call, no site data leaving the building. A plan that decides what to switch off should stay
  compilable when the network is down.
- **Hosted** — `muse-spark-1.3` through Meta Model API, with `--furnizor=meta`. On this road
  the state of the installation **does** leave the building. That is a real trade, and it is
  named here rather than buried.

What each road actually produced is in [`docs/comparison.md`](docs/comparison.md): 24 states ×
3 runs on each, with every plan recording which road and which model made it.

The model proposes and argues; code decides what may be touched at all. Swapping the model
changes the quality of the proposal and nothing about the guarantee.

---

## What is new — built during the Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026)

> Everything listed here was written during the building period. The repository was

# TriggerSift

**Keep the sounds you came for.**

You've found the perfect ASMR video. Slow tapping, you're almost asleep, and then someone bumps the mic. Or twenty
minutes in, the crinkling starts, and you can't stand crinkling. Everyone has sounds they love and sounds they don't,
and until now your only options were to skip around by hand or give up on the video.

TriggerSift listens to the video first. You tell it what you love and what you'd rather avoid, and it plays your own
version.

![TriggerSift playing a video: the video on the left, sounds to love or avoid on the right, and a graph along the bottom showing what was heard and what gets skipped or removed](docs/screenshot.png)

## What it does

1. **Pick a video** from your library.
2. **Choose your sounds.** Love it or avoid it, across 15 kinds of sound: sharp tapping, whispering, crinkling, mouth
   sounds, mic bumps and more.
3. **Press play.** The graph shows everything TriggerSift heard and what it will do about it:
   - A long stretch you dislike is **skipped**.
   - A short sound you dislike is **taken out or turned down**, and the video keeps playing.
   - Flip between **Your cut** and **Original** at any moment to hear the difference.

You can also clean up the whole soundtrack, for example to reduce a fan or soften desk thuds.

**A fair warning:** this is an early project. It misses some sounds and mistakes others, and taking a sound out works
best on a clear bump with nothing on top of it. See [Known limits](#known-limits).

## Try it

It runs on your own computer, on videos you already have, and needs an NVIDIA GPU with 16 GB of memory for the local
models. Follow [Run it](#run-it), then open <http://localhost:8000/demo>.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, "Build for Your World"), on Meta's PE-A-Frame,
SAM Audio and Muse Wonder.

---

## How it works

```
video → PE-A-Frame embeddings (40 ms) → trained classifiers → 15 sound classes on a timeline

                                                 your like/dislike profile ┤
                        skip (long, confident) ──────────────────────────┤
                        remove with SAM Audio / mute / duck (short) ──────┤
                        effects on the whole soundtrack ──────────────────┘→ player
```

# Centinela

**From a community report to a verified decision.**

Centinela verifies community flood reports against satellite, photo and bulletin evidence, ranks the zones that need help first, and drafts alerts for a human to approve. **Code decides every verdict from the evidence; the model only explains it.**

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** · Indie Developer track · *Build for Your World*.

- Demo video: https://youtu.be/6GhIJDUOMWI
- Demo post on X: https://x.com/ypdv26/status/2118141413158187292?a=PdOB26DZ92aL6hy_d9Q&s=20
- Author: Yamile Del Aguila, Pucallpa, Peru
> **Demo data is simulated.** The scenario, the evidence, the bulletin and the evaluation cases are simulated and labeled as such. The model calls (voice, extraction, vision, segmentation) are real. See [What is real and what is simulated](#what-is-real-and-what-is-simulated).

---

## The problem

After a flood, whoever decides where to send help works with scattered, unverified information: voice notes, loose photos, rumors. Some reports are true, some are exaggerated, and some are false. Sending boats to a rumor costs time that real victims do not have.

Centinela is an attempt to triage that stream with evidence and an audit trail, while leaving the final decision to a person.

## What it does

1. **Voice** – a community member sends a voice note in Spanish. It is transcribed with Muse Voice Transcribe, using the known place names as keywords.
2. **Report** – Muse Spark turns the transcript into a structured report (place, claim type, severity, houses reported, whether it asks for help) and an English summary. Places are matched against a gazetteer; the model is never allowed to invent one.
3. **Evidence** – the system gathers evidence for that place: a satellite water index (NDWI), an official bulletin read from a PDF, and, optionally, a photo analyzed with Muse Spark vision and SAM 3.1.
4. **Verdict** – deterministic rules decide `confirmed`, `contradicted` or `no evidence`, and every verdict cites evidence IDs (`EV-xx`). The model gives a second opinion; if it disagrees with the code (or is unavailable), the report is flagged **Needs review** instead of being confirmed.
5. **Priority** – zones are ranked from confirmed reports only, with a transparent formula.
6. **Alert** – a draft alert is written in Spanish for the community, with an English translation. **A human must approve it.** Nothing is sent anywhere.

The operator sees all of this in a command-center interface, with the agent trace advancing step by step.

## Meta models used

| Model | Where it is used |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Orchestrator with tool calling; structured extraction of reports; reading the bulletin PDF; photo description (vision); second opinion on verdicts; alert drafting |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) | Spanish voice notes to text, with place-name keywords |
| **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) | Segmenting water, people, house

# KinBeat

**Find your exposed tokens before hackers do.** KinBeat reads the places where secrets leak - **chats, files, websites, GitHub, Google Drive and Slack** - and tells you which keys are *real* and which are only *possible*.

Demo video: _[link coming]_

The project can be cloned and run locally (see below). For the complete experience, with the Google Drive and Slack connections and the live AI judge, visit **https://kinbeat.com**.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track, by one developer, between 26 October and 4 November 2026.

## For the judges

- **Problem statement:** Build for Your World - leaked keys in chats, files and repositories, a problem every developer meets.
- **Meta AI tooling:** Meta's **Muse Spark Open** makes every decision at runtime - it judges each finding, reads pictures and scanned pages, and answers the chat.
- **Bonus awards submitted for:** **Best Build on Open Weight Models** and **Best Agentic Use-Case**.

## What KinBeat can do

- **Scan a chat you paste.** Teams leak keys in messages all the time. Paste the text and KinBeat finds the key, even when it is **scrambled** (base64, hex, URL codes), **spelled out** letter by letter, written in **NATO code words** or number words, or **split over two messages**.

  ![A pasted email with a scrambled token, found and explained](docs/readme/paste-chat.png)

- **Scan a file.** PDFs, Word files, zips, code and config files. **Screenshots and scanned pages** are read as text, so a key inside a picture is found too.

  ![A config file with a password and a token found](docs/readme/upload-file.png)

- **Scan a website.** Paste any page link.

  ![A web page with exposed secrets found](docs/readme/website.png)

- **Scan a GitHub repository.** Paste the link. Public repositories you do not own get **only the count** of exposed secrets, so nobody can use KinBeat to raid them. With a read-only token for your own repository you see every finding, file and line.

# KineSight

**Sensorless visual telemetry and SOP compliance for assembly lines.** KineSight turns an ordinary overhead camera into a QA station. SAM 3.1 tracks every tool and part. A deterministic OpenCV/NumPy engine measures each contact to the frame. Muse Spark 1.3 audits only the moments where the math says a step went wrong, and Muse Image draws the fix.

- The first visit after a quiet spell can take about a minute while the server wakes up.

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/hC6k1zX42_Y

![Workbench](docs/workbench.png)

## Contents

1. [What KineSight does](#what-kinesight-does)

## What KineSight does

You give KineSight two things:
- a **written procedure** (an SOP, as text or PDF);
- a **video of one work cycle** at a bench.

It answers four questions:
1. **Which steps did the operator do, how many times, and for how long?** The answer is measured from pixel masks, frame by frame.
2. **Does that meet the SOP?** Each step gets PASS or a specific failure: skipped, too few contacts, too short, or out of order. The cycle gets a compliance score.
3. **If not, is it a real defect, and why did it happen?** The answer is a root cause and a corrective action in plain words, checked against the actual keyframes.
4. **What should the operator do differently?** The answer is a generated work-instruction diagram.
5. **How does this cycle compare with a good one?** It is shown side by side with a compliant reference cycle, on one time axis.

Every analysis can be downloaded as a self-contained QA report (HTML, printable to PDF) for the line supervisor.

The outcome is zero-sensor quality assurance for manual assembly. It works with any camera, needs no training data and no instrumentation per station, and takes a few minutes to set up a new procedure.

# DocTrust

**A reviewer agent that cross-examines a person's whole document set — and shows the human reviewer the evidence. It runs on hosted Muse Spark or Muse Spark Open (open weights).**

*The planner chooses the `stamp_removed` view, the birth date is re-read from under the stamp, and the deterministic comparator flags the mismatch — flagged for a human reviewer, never auto-rejected.*

## The problem

KYC and onboarding systems built around Latin names and clean scans fail people in non-Latin-script markets. ## Built on Meta models

- **Muse Spark — the reader.** Every field of every document, read in **Bangla, English and Hindi** (Hindi preliminary — a small, separately reported batch) — mixed digit systems, transliteration variants, stamps and glare. - **Muse Spark — the planner.** The same model directs the investigation. ## Run the backend

Needs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (`brew install uv`). uv installs Python 3.12 from `.python-version`.

```bash
cp .env.example .env          # then add your META_API_KEY
uv sync                       # creates .venv and installs everything
uv run pytest                 # all tests
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload
curl localhost:8000/health
```

The server refuses to start if any model ID contains `contributor` or if request body logging is on.

Keep the repo outside iCloud synced folders (macOS Desktop and Documents); iCloud breaks the `.venv`.

## Run one image from the CLI

```bash
uv run python backend/cli.py candidates path/to/img.jpg --no-sweep   # local only: OCR, marks
uv run python backend/cli.py candidates path/to/img.jpg              # adds the SAM sweep (~$0.04)
uv run python backend/cli.py analyze path/to/img.jpg --dest public   # whole pipeline, needs judge, merge and floor
```

Overlays (`_ocr.png`, `_sweep.png`, `_marks.png`), candidate JSON, findings JSON and the masked export (`_masked.png`) go to `out/debug/`, which is gitignored. They hold image content and OCR text, so never move them into the repo.

## Smoke test

Calls the real API (about $0.72 per run at list prices). Use clearly fake images or consenting teammates only, kept outside the repo, as JPEG or PNG.

```bash
uv run python scripts/smoke_test.py --images /path/to/fake/images
```

Prints the latency, token and cost table, writes debug overlays to `out/debug/` and logs every call to `logs/cost.jsonl` (both gitignored).

# Sotto — the AI that knows when to speak

Sotto is a local web app that listens to a group brainstorm, keeps a living board of the
discussion, and contributes to the **whole group** only when it really matters: a contradiction
with an earlier constraint, a factual error, an untested assumption, a dropped thread. It scores
each candidate and chooses to stay silent, glow quietly, or interject — only at a natural pause,
and rarely. It also answers when addressed by wake phrase ("Sotto, what do competitors charge?").

This repo was built during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026)**.

Full spec: [`tasks/prd-sotto-core.md`](tasks/prd-sotto-core.md).

## Stack

- **`server/`** — Node 22 + Fastify + `@fastify/websocket`, bound to `127.0.0.1` only. Holds the
  API key, talks to Meta's APIs, runs tools, writes session files.
- **`web/`** — React 18 + Vite browser UI.
- **`shared/`** — types used by both.
- **`fixtures/`** — scripted test conversations plus rendered audio, so every feature is testable
  without live speakers. See [`fixtures/README.md`](fixtures/README.md).

Meta APIs: `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` for realtime diarized transcription,
`muse-spark-1.3` for board updates, interjection candidates, answers and eval judging.

The observer considers finalized turns without waiting for the notes update. It
receives the latest completed notes and all finalized turns not covered by them;
if another turn arrives while an observer call is running, the next look combines
the pending turns. This can make more model calls than the notes-driven loop.

Each new session also saves `timing.jsonl` alongside its transcript and candidate logs.
It records transcription events and final turns, board and observer call starts and
finishes (including empty and failed runs), verification, policy decisions, and answer
and interjection card publication. Join events by turn ID, observer run, candidate ID,
or answer ID. `atMs` uses the session's monotonic pipeline clock; compare differences,
not its absolute value, with timestamps in `candidates.jsonl` and `answers.jsonl`.
ASR `frameAtMs` and `audioProcessedMs` are stream-relative values, not the same clock.
Speech-end events reflect the transcription service's endpoint detection, not an exact
measurement of the last audible sound. Card publication is server-side and does not
measure when a browser actually rendered it. Replay uses simulated time, so model-call
durations there do not measure live API latency.

## Setup

Requires Node 22+.

```sh
npm install
cp .env.example .env    # then set MODEL_API_KEY to your Meta Model API key

`MODEL_API_KEY` is read by the server only and never reaches the browser bundle.

# Chapp A voice-first lab companion that knows every vial in your kit. Tell Chapp which kit you are running: it finds the vendor's manual and reads it into a structured protocol, recognizes each bottle from one photo or video of your kit, and walks you through the run with the right bottle, the right volume and the right timer on screen. The name is *chaperone* + *app*. Molecular chaperones such as heat shock proteins help other proteins fold and stay stable under stress without doing their work for them; Chapp does the same for the person at the bench. Chapp is one of them. Its body is Hsp16.5, the small heat shock protein of *Methanococcus jannaschii*, a hyperthermophilic archaeon from deep-sea hydrothermal vents, as its crystal structure has it ([PDB 1SHS](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1SHS); Kim, Kim & Kim, *Nature* 1998, [doi:10.1038/29106](https://doi.org/10.1038/29106)): 24 identical subunits closed into a hollow ball 12 nm across, with eight triangular and six square windows. Each subunit is 16 round lumps of gel at its own place in the cage, rebuilt from the PDB file's atoms by `scripts/chapp-model/body.ts`, and the face goes on top. Every subunit is a whole piece of its own, so three quick taps on the big Chapp take it apart into its 24 subunits for a moment (left, `scripts/chapp-model/apart.ts`). The app icon is the same cage without the face, seen straight down one of its four-fold axes into a square window (right).

**An AI agent that stops scams in the chat. Forward one to our WhatsApp bot today; our concept shows it working natively.**

Second Look is a scam-stopping agent built on Meta's models. It gives a verdict that passed a preregistered test on 945 real cases, investigates links with tools it picks itself, and prepares what to do next. It runs today as a bot on the WhatsApp Cloud API and as a website. Our home page shows where it goes next: the same agent working natively inside WhatsApp, where nobody has to forward anything.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Live demo** | https://secondlook.muze.cl/ (real model, daily quota per visitor) |
| **Demo video** | https://youtu.be/eGBVL64Ej6s |
| **The test** | On Reddit posts judged by the community: 84% of scams caught with 24% false alarms, 0.801 balanced accuracy, against 0.517 for a simple keyword filter. [Full protocol and limits](docs/VALIDATION.md) |
| **Check our numbers** | `python3 scripts/verify_results.py`: no API key, no network, no dependencies. Also runs in [CI](.github/workflows/test.yml) |
| **Cost** | About US$ 0.02 per check, agents included ([ledger](results/costs.jsonl)) |
| **Track** | Startup · Build for Your World · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · [Muze AI](https://muze.cl), Chile |

![The concept prototype: the message arrives, its link is locked, and the verdict and the agent's checks appear in the chat](docs/images/verdict.jpg)

## Try it in 60 seconds

1. **Open the [live demo](https://secondlook.muze.cl/) and tap "Bank alert".** The verdict appears in 5 to 8 seconds, followed by the agent's checks.
2. **Tap the crossed-out link, then "Open anyway".** The page shows the alert the agent wrote for the person's trusted contact. If the agent hasn't finished yet (about 20 seconds), it shows a template instead.
3. **Write your own message,** as if a stranger sent it. "GP appointment" shows a message that isn't a scam.
4. **Go to "Check a message", pick "Already paid" and press "Check it".** The agent changes its plan and writes to the bank's fraud team.

The phone is a labeled concept and its actions are simulated. The model's output is real and live. The WhatsApp bot runs on Meta's test number, which only reaches verified recipients, so the video shows it working.

## The problem

Americans reported losing [US$ 15.9 billion to fraud in 2025](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/apr/03/americans-lost-a-record-159-billion-to-scams-in-20), according to the FTC, and for every age group under 80, social media was the [contact method with the highest losses](https://www.techwalla.com/13779374/ftc-social-media-scams-2025-21-billion-in-us-losses).

Scams work through pressure: pay in two hours, or your account is locked. Most checkers ask people to stop, leave the chat and paste the message into a website, at the moment they're least likely to do that.
