# APIShift

**Contract-driven API migration with Meta's Muse models.** When an upstream API ships a breaking
version, APIShift finds every affected line in your Python codebase, rewrites it, proves the fix
against the new contract with tests it is not allowed to touch, and opens a reviewable pull request.

Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026). All code in this repo was written
during the event.

## How it works

```
Spec Diff (code) → Scout (Spark) → Analyst (Spark, tool loop) → Refactor (Wonder)
      → Guardrails → Sandbox tests → green? → PR Writer (Spark) → PR
                                    ↓ no
                     Triage (Spark, escalates to Wonder) → back to Refactor or Analyst (max 3 heals)
                                    ↓ still failing
                              draft PR labeled needs-human
```

| Step | Model | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spec Diff | none (deterministic) | `RawDiff`: every difference between the two OpenAPI specs |
| Scout | `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, strict JSON | `ChangeManifest`: breaking changes with migration rules, each traced to diff entries |
| Analyst | `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, tool calling | `ImpactGraph`: affected files plus data-flow edges |
| Refactor | `muse-wonder-1.0` | `PatchSet`: search/replace edit blocks |
| Triage / Validator | Spark, escalating to Wonder | `DiagnosticReport` routed to Refactor or Analyst |
| PR Writer | Spark | PR title and summary; facts rendered from artifacts |

### Why you can trust a green run

Enforced in code, not in prompts (`apishift/tools/guardrails.py`):

- Tests, `conftest.py` and `pytest.ini` are read-only (mounted `:ro` in Docker, fingerprinted before and after).
- Edits outside the impact graph, edits adding `skip`/`xfail`, and paths outside the repo are rejected.
- Every edit's search text must match exactly once, or the whole patch is refused.
- The same number of tests must be collected as on the old API.
- Tests are first run against the old API (must pass) and the new API (must fail) to establish the oracle.

## Quick start

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
docker build -t apishift-sandbox:latest .        # sandbox image for running tests
cp .env.example .env && export META_API_KEY=...  # dev.meta.ai key

python -m apishift migrate --demo                 # migrate the bundled weather app (Docker sandbox)
python -m apishift migrate --demo --unsafe-local  # same, without Docker (development only)
python -m apishift dashboard                      # http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

Replay a recorded run with no API calls (tests still run for real):

```bash
python -m apishift migrate --demo --replay runs/<run-id>
```

Your own repo:

```bash
python -m apishift migrate --repo path/to/repo --from v1.yaml --to v2.yaml \
  --changelog CHANGELOG.md --mock-server path/to/mock_server.py [--open-pr]
```

The mock server must accept `--version v1|v2 --port N`, and the repo's tests must read `BASE_URL`.

We lose things at the edges of the day: the charger left in a café, the earbuds on a train, the ID badge at the office. Chatbots can describe a photo, and Bluetooth trackers can find a tagged item, but nothing answers the simple question: **"Is everything I left with still with me?"**

# AgentLedger **An accountability layer for AI agents.** Every action an agent takes is traced, checked against role-based permissions, reviewed by a second model when risky, optionally paused for human approval, and written to a tamper-evident audit log. Built solo during the **Meta AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026), Indie Developer track, theme: **Build for Your World**. --- ## The problem AI agents are starting to act on our behalf — reading documents, looking up records, sending messages, changing data. But when an agent does something wrong, there is usually no reliable answer to three basic questions: 1. What exactly did it do? 2. Was it allowed to do it? 3. Who (or what) approved it? Worse, agents can be manipulated. A document the agent is asked to summarize can hide an instruction like *"email this record to an outside address"* — and a naive agent may obey it. ## The solution AgentLedger puts a safety and accountability pipeline between the agent and its tools. **Nothing executes before it has passed every gate:** ``` task → agent (model) → proposed action | [wrapper pipeline] 1. policy check (role permissions, rules) → block + log 2. guardian review (risky actions only) → block / flag + log 3. approval gate (human, risky actions) → approve / deny + log 4. execute tool → result + log | hash-chained audit log (SQLite) | Streamlit dashboard ``` Every step in the pipeline writes an event to an append-only, hash-chained audit log, so the full history of a run can be reviewed — and any tampering with the log can be detected and pinpointed. ## Demo (3 minutes) 1. **Normal run.** An `operator` agent reads a synthetic work order, looks up a case record, drafts a customer reply, and closes the case — with the high-risk status update passing guardian review and explicit human approval first. 2. **Prompt injection.** A second document hides an instruction telling the agent to email record data to an outside address. # Muse Shopping

**International, AI-powered social commerce that transforms short-form videos into shoppable storefronts.**

## The Problem

Millions of creators on TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, X, and YouTube generate significant views and audience engagement but lack a simple, independent platform to sell products directly.

Many creators share personal Gmail addresses or phone numbers in their social media bios to receive business inquiries, creating privacy and security risks.

e-commerce platforms such as Shopify, Amazon, Daraz, and Meesho can involve upfront costs, subscriptions, or complex store management processes.

## Our Solution: Three Core Principles

**1. Zero Monthly or Yearly Fees**

Creators and sellers do not pay monthly or yearly subscription fees to maintain their stores. Muse Shopping follows a success-based business model: the platform earns a service fee only after a successful purchase. No sale means no platform service fee.

**2. Verified Creator Onboarding**

Creators can submit their social media profile links and complete identity verification to apply for a verified digital storefront. The goal is to provide a trusted business presence without requiring creators to expose personal contact information publicly.

**3. Short-Form-First Commerce**

Muse Shopping focuses on short-form videos, Reels, feeds, and product images. Its shopping experience is designed around quick visual discovery and interactive product engagement rather than long-form video content.

## How It Works

1. **Creator Upload:** A creator uploads a short product video or image.
2. **AI Product Detection:** Meta SAM 3.1 supports object detection and segmentation within visual content.
3. **Interactive Buy Tags:** Detected products can be connected to catalog entries and displayed as interactive shopping tags.
4. **Watch and Shop:** Buyers swipe through the visual feed, tap product tags, explore product details, and place orders.
5. **Localized Payments:** The platform's payment vision includes eSewa, Khalti, Fonepay QR, and COD in Nepal; UPI in India; and supported international payment providers such as Stripe.
6. **Revenue Distribution:** The intended revenue model distributes the transaction between the supplier's product cost, creator earnings, and Muse Shopping's service fee after a successful sale.

## Meta AI Integration

- **SAM 3.1:** Object detection and segmentation to support visual product identification.
- **Muse Image:** Intended for AI-assisted visual product understanding and image workflows.
- **Muse Spark:** Intended as an AI co-pilot for product descriptions, creator scripts, and hashtags.
- **Muse Code:** Used as a coding assistant to support development of the swipe-feed and shopping workflows, where applicable.

**Technology Stack:** Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Supabase, Meta Model API, and SAM 3.1.

Wyrd is a short fantasy adventure run by an AI game master, **Meta's Muse Spark**. You can click an idea, type anything, or just say it out loud (English or Tagalog). The AI tells the story. But it can't cheat, and it can prove that:

- **Every action goes through code.** The AI only *proposes* actions as tool calls. A TypeScript rule engine is the only thing that can change the game, and it refuses anything that breaks the rules: an item that isn't there, an enemy that's "already dead", a door that's sealed.
- **The hidden secrets are sealed before you move.** Where the Lost Relic is and which door is trapped are chosen at the start and locked with a SHA-256 fingerprint shown on screen. When the game ends, the server reveals them and **your browser recomputes the fingerprint itself**. If it matches, the AI never moved the relic or the trap mid-game.

> The problem: as AI agents start acting for us (issuing refunds, booking, refereeing, running game economies), people need agents whose actions are *checked* and whose hidden decisions can be *proven* afterward. Wyrd is a small, playable demonstration of that pattern.

![Wyrd game screen](docs/screenshot.png)

---

## What makes it different

| Typical AI story game | Wyrd |
|---|---|
| The AI decides what happens and can hand you anything | The AI proposes; code decides. Cheats get a visible **REFUSED** |
| Hidden things can quietly change | Secrets are sealed on turn one and checked by your browser at the end |
| Free text is either "anything goes" or a menu | Creative ideas ("I tip the shelf onto the troll") are turned into a code-judged **attempt**: approach + intent, a d20 roll, and a fixed set of outcomes (success, partial, fail) |
| You can't see what the AI did | The **Inspector** shows every tool call the model made and the engine's verdict |

## Meta models used

| Model | Role in Wyrd |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** (Meta Model API) | The game master. Runs an agentic loop: reads a filtered player view, calls up to 9 game tools over multiple rounds (move, attack, sneak, throw, attempt, …), receives the engine's results, then narrates only what actually happened |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0** (Meta Model API) | Voice input. The browser records and encodes 16 kHz WAV; the server forwards it, so the API key never reaches the browser. English and Tagalog |
| **Muse Image** (Meta Model API) | Enemy portraits, generated once by scripts/gen-portraits.mjs and served as small WebP files |
| **Muse Wonder 1.0 and Muse Spark** (developer tooling) | Used as the coding model (through the Cline agent) to build much of this project during the hackathon |

Player (click / type / speak)

Muse Spark ── sees only the player view (no secrets, no enemy HP, no salt)
        │  proposes tool calls

# ChronoFact

### Memory that knows *when* something was true, and *why* it believes it.

ChronoFact is a time-aware, verified memory layer for AI assistants, built entirely on Meta models.

Assistants that remember their users fail in two ways: they **store things the user never said**, and they **keep
answering with values that changed months ago**. ChronoFact turns a conversation stream into **verified, time-stamped
facts with provenance**, keeps their history when they change, and answers every question from a small, fixed context.

**+13.6 points over RAG** on LongMemEval · **2.5× on temporal reasoning** · **2.0× across sessions** · **3.9× fewer
false "I don't know"** · **$0 API cost on one GPU**

> 🎬 Demo video: [ChronoFact](https://youtu.be/Qrsvf5Yh5EU)

![Live memory: every message streams through the write path; Berlin is superseded by Munich and kept as history](docs/live.png)

## Why ChronoFact

Measured on LongMemEval-S (500 users, ~115k-token histories each, 10,000 judged answers per system), against RAG over
the raw transcripts with the same answering model (Llama-3.1-8B) and the same token budgets. Every number is the
effect of the complete ChronoFact system working together: verified temporal memory, time-scoped retrieval and
packing, and the answer step.

| advantage | evidence |
|---|---|
| **More accurate memory** | **+13.6 points** overall [95% CI +10.2, +16.8], significant at every budget from 256 to 2,048 tokens |
| **Gets time right** | **2.5×** accuracy on temporal reasoning (52.1% vs 20.6%); knowledge updates 75.8% vs 62.6% |
| **Connects sessions** | **2.0×** accuracy on questions that span several sessions (45.3% vs 22.7%) |
| **Does not give up wrongly** | **3.9× fewer** false "not in memory" answers (8.5% vs 32.6% of answerable questions) |
| **Never stores what was not said** | a fact must quote the user verbatim **and** pass an NLI entailment check: **43 unsupported facts blocked per history**. Asking for "tips for a flat near Friedrichshain" does not become "lives near Friedrichshain" |
| **Keeps the history** | a changed value supersedes the old one, which keeps its end date instead of being overwritten, so "now", "in March" and "what changed" all have answers; "two weeks ago" is resolved to a date when written |
| **Bounded as memory grows** | a fixed 256-2,048-token context per question; the lead holds at 12.8-14.8 points from the evidence-only history to the full history with every later session |
| **Cheap to write** | 59 of ~245 user turns per history skip the LLM (salience filter); 359 calls of a local 8B model per ~115k-token history; **$0 API cost** |
| **Auditable and deletable** | every fact links to the user's own words; every write decision is logged; `Store.forget` deletes a fact, its sibling facts, the message and the assistant's reply to it, from memory and from search |
| **Trustworthy numbers** | chronological replay at 5 checkpoints × 4 budgets, paired bootstrap CIs, cross-fitted tuning, byte-ide

# ProofPatch AI

**Evidence-first AI-assisted bug repair.**

ProofPatch AI reproduces a reported Python failure, requests a minimal proposed patch from an AI model, validates the patch, and independently runs defined tests against the patched code.

## Current status

Implemented components:
- Python bug reproduction using pytest in a temporary directory.
- Unified-diff validation and in-memory patch application.
- Evidence-informed repair prompts and model-response parsing.
- Independent verification against defined tests.
- Workflow orchestration.
- FastAPI health, config, sample, and local repair endpoints (with configurable CORS).
- A single-page Next.js interface: paste code and tests, see the reproduced failure,
  the model's proposal, the diff, and the independent verification result.
- An opt-in, clearly labelled mock model so the demo runs without an API key.
- Automated backend tests (71) and a browser-driven check of the full user journey.

### Available API endpoints

- `GET /health` — checks API availability.
- `GET /config` — non-secret runtime mode (`live`, `mock`, or `unconfigured`) and whether repair is enabled.
- `GET /sample` — the built-in demo bug and its tests.
- `POST /repair` — accepts Python source code and tests and invokes the repair workflow when explicitly enabled for trusted local development.

The repair endpoint is disabled by default. Its reproduction and verification stages execute supplied Python code without a secure sandbox. It is not safe for public use or untrusted submissions.

**Live Meta model access remains unverified.** No real Meta API request has been made from this project. Passing mocked tests does not establish that the live endpoint, model name, or credentials work. In mock mode the interface labels every reply as a scripted mock, not a model response.

## How it works

1. Reproduce the reported failure with the supplied code and tests.
2. Stop if the baseline failure cannot be reproduced.
3. Ask the configured model client for a minimal fix using the supplied evidence. The model returns the complete corrected file.
4. Generate the unified diff in the backend (models often miscount diff headers), validate it with the strict patch engine, and apply it in memory.
5. Run the defined tests against the patched code.
6. Return the observed result and evidence.

7. If verification fails, send that failure evidence back to the Meta model for a
   bounded retry. The maximum is two repair attempts per request.
8. Return an evidence trail covering reproduction, diagnosis, patch validation,
   verification, and each retry attempt.

Passing defined tests does not prove universal correctness.

- Next.js

- Node.js and npm are needed for frontend development.
- A valid model API key is needed only for a real model API request.

# ChronoTrace — Evidence-first codebase risk analysis

ChronoTrace builds a repository-scoped graph of commits, files, and co-change evidence without executing repository code, powering change criticality and regression-risk analytics.

## Quickstart

```bash
pip install -e .
pytest -q
```

## Configuration

Validated `chronotrace.yml` (Pydantic v2, schema v1) — env secrets outside YAML. See [`chronotrace.yml`](./chronotrace.yml) for defaults.

## Ingestion

Ingestion turns a remote Git URL into graph evidence: acquisition → PyDriller extraction → filtering → labeling → batched Neo4j writes. Full details in [`src/chronotrace/ingestion/README.md`](./src/chronotrace/ingestion/README.md).

**Usage**

```python
from chronotrace.ingestion import IngestionService
from chronotrace.config import load_config

config = load_config("chronotrace.yml")
svc = IngestionService(config=config, gateway=graph_gateway)
result = svc.ingest("https://github.com/org/repo.git", branch="main")
print(result.state.status, result.state.counters)
```

**Config options**

| Key | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `project.repositories_dir` | `~/.chronotrace/repositories` | Managed clone location (`<repositories_dir>/<slug>-<hash>`) |
| `analysis.filtering.exclude` | `["**/.git/**", "**/__pycache__/**", ...]` | Glob exclusion (gitwildmatch via `pathspec`) |
| `analysis.bug_fix_labels.patterns` | `["\\bfix\\b", "\\bhotfix\\b", ...]` | Case-insensitive fix regex list |
| `analysis.bug_fix_labels.case_sensitive` | `false` | Toggle case sensitivity |
| `analysis.history.max_commits` | `null` | Optional traversal cap |
| `graph.batch_size` | `500` | `UNWIND $batch AS row MERGE` batch size |

**Lifecycle states**

`PENDING → CLONING → EXTRACTING → FILTERING → WRITING_GRAPH → COMPLETED` (or `FAILED` from any state). Each stage records an ISO timestamp; counters (`commits`, `files`, `filteredOut`, `batches`) and redacted error summaries are persisted on `Repository`/`IngestionState`. Query via `svc.get_status(repository_id)`.

- Incremental: `lastIngestedHead` + `git rev-list lastHead..HEAD`, chronological, head advances only on success.
- Rewritten history: `git merge-base --is-ancestor` check → `needsFullReingestion=true` (`RewrittenHistoryError`), requires full re-ingestion.
- Retryable: `svc.retry(repository_id)` resets `FAILED` → `PENDING`.
- Observability: `INFO` logs `Writing batch 1/3 (commits)` without secrets; `filteredOut` reflects `**/__pycache__/**` etc.

**Limitations** — dynamic excludes need re-ingestion; rename threshold conservative (uncertain `DELETE+ADD` stays distinct, `COPY` distinct nodes); force-push not auto-reconciled; no concurrent ingestion lock; shallow history may be truncated.

## Agent (Evidence-First LLM Layer)

The agent is the sole LLM layer, isolated over the deterministic analytics/MCP path. See [`src/chronotrace/agent/README.md`](./src/chronotrace/agent/README.md) for full details.

# Tempo

**15 minutes a day to walk into every exam prepared.**

Tempo is a revision app for students. Snap photos of your course notes, add your exam dates, and Tempo turns them into a clean course to read, flashcards and a quiz, then plans **15 minutes of revision a day** until each exam. Miss a day and the plan is rebuilt over the days that are left.

The content is generated by **Muse Spark 1.3** through the Meta Model API. Tempo was built by **Adrien JACQ** for a Meta hackathon.

| [`demo/tempo-explainer.mp4`](demo/tempo-explainer.mp4) | The explainer (3 min 21): where the need comes from and how Tempo was built. |

Most students revise by rereading their notes, although research shows it is one of the least effective methods:

- In a survey of 177 university students, 84% reread their notes, and only 11% tested themselves (Karpicke, Butler & Roediger, 2009).
- Students who practised recalling a text remembered 61% of it a week later. Those who only reread it remembered 40%, although they read it four times as often (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).
- With flashcards, spreading reviews over time beat cramming for 90% of learners (Kornell, 2009).
- A review of ten study techniques rates only two as high utility, practice testing and spaced practice. Rereading and highlighting rate low (Dunlosky et al., 2013).

The goal was to make the effective method the easy one. A student should only have to bring their notes and an exam date. Tempo then provides the testing (flashcards and a quiz) and the spacing (a daily plan).

## What was built

- **Course from photos:** use the camera or the gallery. Muse reads handwritten or printed notes and returns a structured course: definitions, formulas, key points, examples and classic traps, with key words in bold and a 30-second summary.
- **Flashcards that follow good practice:** one idea per card, a short answer, and a diagram, memory trick or example when it helps. Cards stay faithful to the notes, and formulas are written in plain symbols.
- **Revision sessions:**

A local-first end-to-end job application platform. It ingests postings from
seven sources, ranks them, tailors an editable resume draft, renders an
ATS-checked PDF once you approve it, and opens the company's apply page so you
can mark the application as submitted. No accounts, no multi-tenancy.

- Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind 4
- Prisma 7 + Neon Postgres (`@prisma/adapter-pg`)
- Zod contracts at every boundary

bun run dev

`bun run setup` is idempotent. It prints exactly what is still missing

the five keyless sources still run.

```bash
bun run agent -- status

Each command prints one JSON object (`{ ok, command, data }`) and exits `0`

# Evianta MVP

Evianta is a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js web app, an Express API, and a
background worker. This guide covers local development.

## Requirements

- Node.js `24.3.0` (see `.node-version`)
- pnpm `10.18.3`
- MongoDB 7+ configured as a replica set (transactions are required)

## Set up locally

Install dependencies and copy the local environment defaults:

**Windows (PowerShell)**

```powershell
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
Copy-Item .env.example .env
```

**macOS / Linux**

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cp .env.example .env
```

The example uses the mock AI provider, so no Meta API key is needed to develop
locally. Its signing key is for local development only; never use it in a
deployment. To use Meta models, set `EVIANTA_AI_PROVIDER=muse` and
`EVIANTA_USAGE_MODE=enforced` in `.env`. Uncomment and fill in `MODEL_API_KEY`,
`MUSE_SPARK_MODEL`, and `MUSE_WONDER_MODEL`; uncomment all token, concurrency,
spend, and period settings in the usage-limits block. Model IDs and suggested
limits are supplied in `.env.example`.

Start a local MongoDB replica set. Create a data directory, then run `mongod`
in one terminal:

**Windows (PowerShell)**

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\data\evianta
mongod --replSet rs0 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --port 27017 --dbpath C:\data\evianta
```

**macOS / Linux**

```sh
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/share/evianta/mongo"
mongod --replSet rs0 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --port 27017 --dbpath "$HOME/.local/share/evianta/mongo"
```

Use a dedicated local instance; do not reconfigure a shared database. If port
27017 is already in use, choose another port and update both the replica-set
initialization command and `MONGODB_URI`.

Initialize the replica set once, after MongoDB is listening:

```sh
mongosh --eval "rs.initiate({_id:'rs0',members:[{_id:0,host:'127.0.0.1:27017'}]})"
```

The example `.env` already points to this replica set. If you use another
MongoDB instance or port, update `MONGODB_URI` to match.

Start the web app, API, worker, and package watchers:

```sh
pnpm dev
```

Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). The API listens on
`http://127.0.0.1:3001`; its health endpoint is `/healthz`. Stop all processes
with Ctrl+C.

Create a local user and access key in another terminal:

```sh
pnpm --filter @evianta/api admin create-user developer@example.test "Local Developer"
pnpm --filter @evianta/api admin issue-key <user-id>
```

Use the printed key to sign in. It is shown only once. The worker must be
running for analyses to finish.

| `pnpm dev:api`    | Run the API and its dependencies               |
| `pnpm dev:worker` | Run the worker and its dependencies            |

# StorySpine

**Give your story a spine.** An AI-assisted writing studio where serialized fiction authors design a novel, write it episode by episode, and keep every chapter consistent with story memory the author approved.

Brand direction: **Story Architecture** (`StorySpine` + `Give your story a spine.`). See [brand plan](docs/StorySpine_브랜드_기획안.md) and [brand images & usage guide](docs/branding/README.md).

![StorySpine one-pager: write episode 200 with the memory of episode 1](docs/branding/storyspine/marketing/storyspine-onepager-en.png)

## 1. Why StorySpine is different

Other writing tools remember what you tell them. StorySpine reads what you wrote, proves every finding with a quote, and only remembers what you approve.

**Architect top-down, verify bottom-up.** A long serial is a codebase maintained for years, and continuity errors are its regressions. StorySpine designs the story like software architecture and tests every chapter like CI.

![Architect top-down, verify bottom-up: StorySpine's design tree with inherited settings, and a CI-style pipeline from draft to a publish gate that blocks while issues remain open](docs/branding/storyspine/marketing/storyspine-architect-verify-en.png)

- **Architect top-down** — Part → Chapter → Episode → Scene design tree; settings inherit and override down the tree (`effective_node_settings` in [`design_nodes.py`](server/app/design_nodes.py)); each episode's goal, events, and constraints drive its AI draft, and constraints are validated on the result ([`drafting.py`](server/app/drafting.py)).
- **Publish gate** — like a failing build, an episode cannot be published while consistency issues stay open (`request_publish` in [`state_machine.py`](server/app/state_machine.py)).
- **Evidence or it didn't happen** — every extraction and every contradiction ships with a manuscript quote, verified against the source ([`citation.py`](server/app/citation.py)).
- **Canon gate** — AI only proposes; nothing becomes canon until the author approves it, and approved memory grounds the next episode's draft (`commit_episode` in [`memory.py`](server/app/memory.py)).
- **Not every mismatch is a mistake** — deterministic rule checks run first, then AI review; dreams, recollections, and time passage don't count as contradictions (see `death-normal-dream`, `state-normal-time-passage` in [`evals/cases.json`](evals/cases.json)).

Solo-built in 8 days with Muse Code: ~25k lines of Python/JS, 10 Muse Spark-powered features, 370+ tests including 20+ keyless eval tests. Verify the deterministic core without an API key:

```bash
cd server && ../.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_eval_quality.py -q  # no LLM, seconds

# Action Shift

**The guest changed the order. Which version is the kitchen making?**

The food and labor are real costs when a team makes the wrong version. Action Shift keeps the guest’s request, the restaurant’s decision and the kitchen’s version together. The idea comes from Myke Mueller, operator of Community Tap & Pizza in Fort Dodge, Iowa, and founder of Never86’d.

In this standalone event prototype, Muse reads a fictional meal request and checks dated restaurant facts. Code checks the counts, price and version. A person reviews the promise before a local kitchen simulator acknowledges it. A later guest change stops the old approval from covering the new request.

The V3 operator workflow puts the next decision first. A person can complete a missing pickup location or final total in a recorded proposal, with a demonstration reviewer role and reason, while the original model result stays intact. # KIVO

KIVO helps people understand a challenge through relevant experiences
shared by others. Describe what you are facing; KIVO compares it with
documented attempts — what worked, what differed — so you see what may
transfer before you try.

> Demo data is fictional and self-reported, never verified. Local stories
> stay in this browser and are never published.

## Main innovation

Structured experience intelligence instead of a chatbot: an approved
situation draft is compared against real local records, and every claim
the AI makes must cite the exact request field and record field it rests
on. References are validated server-side; unsupported claims are rejected,
not shown.

## Product features

- **Discover** — challenge input, optional AI clarification (editable
  draft with resources extraction and a visual DNA profile, explicit
  consent), evidence-grounded matching (up to 3 results).
- **Transferability Lens** — per result: what matches, what differs, what
  worked (verbatim record), what may transfer, what remains unknown.
- **Evidence Lens** — every insight labeled Model inference vs Source
  fact vs Unknown, with one-click jump to the full source record.
- **What If?** — rewrite one constraint or resource and re-rank the same
  pool; shows rank movement honestly, original comparison preserved until
  promoted.
- **Next Move** — one suggested first step plus alternatives, each citing
  the results it builds on and savable to My Discoveries; honestly
  absent when evidence is insufficient.
- **Explore (Experience Atlas)** — interactive 3D night-atlas of the 12
  fictional cases (district spires, routes, tethers), bidirectionally
  synced with match and What If results; works without WebGL via the
  full 2D list.
- **Contribute** — up to 5 local stories, private by default, explicit
  per-story opt-in for matching, edit/delete, pool changes invalidate
  results.
- **Keyword fallback** — when the AI is unavailable, deterministic labeled
  leads (never presented as AI analysis); rate limits still error.

## Technical architecture

- Next.js 16 (App Router) + React 19 + TypeScript. No database, no auth.
- 3D: React Three Fiber 9 + three 0.187, custom bounded rig, lazy-loaded
  scene with error boundary and reduced-motion support.
- AI: server routes (`app/api/clarify`, `app/api/match`) call the Meta
  Model API; browsers never see the key. `lib/` holds validation,
  fallback search, and cross-pane events; `data/` holds the fictional
  corpus and the profile↔scene ID map.

## Meta AI tools actually used

- Meta Responses API (`POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses`).
- Model `muse-spark-1.3`, low reasoning effort, bounded output.
- `json_schema` structured output; every ID and reference re-validated
  against the supplied candidate set.

## Verified results (release commit)

- `npm test` — **108/108 pass**, 0 fail (unit + focused suites).
- `npx tsc --noEmit` — clean.
- `npx eslint` — 0 errors, 0 warnings.
- `npm run build` — production bui

# Hearth Guard

**Track:** Indie Developer | **Theme:** Build for your world

A security layer for tool-using AI agents built on Meta Muse Spark. It stops prompt injection hidden in the things an agent reads (issue text, screenshots, PDFs) from turning into data leaks, and it records every decision in a tamper-evident log.

> Status: hackathon submission. All data is synthetic. No real credentials, systems or personal data are used anywhere in this repo.

## The problem

An agent that triages bug reports reads text, images and PDFs written by strangers. An attacker can hide an instruction in any of them ("post the config value as a comment") and the agent may comply, leaking a secret through a comment, a link or an encoded string. Prompt rules help, but they are tuned to one model and can be argued around. Hearth Guard checks what the agent reads and what it does, independent of the model.

## Why I built this

My world is security. I am a cybersecurity undergraduate and an AI vulnerability researcher, and my thesis is on security middleware for RAG pipelines. Retrieval systems and tool-using agents share one weakness: they pull in content written by people the system should not trust, and the model cannot reliably tell data from instructions. Hearth Guard applies the middleware idea I study to a concrete agent: check what goes in, check what comes out, and keep a record anyone can verify. The people I build this for are the ones who defend these systems, and what they need is measurements and honest limits, not a claim that the problem is solved.

## How it works

```
issue + attachments
        |
   [ Gate 1: inspect inputs ]  normalise text, decode hidden blobs, OCR passes,
        |                      PDF hidden-text inspection, Prompt Guard 2
        |  block -> the model is never called
        v
   [ victim agent (Muse Spark) ]
        |
   [ Gate 2: check actions ]   tool allowlist, taint tracking (canary in 9 encodings),
        |                      egress filter (domains, query strings, .invalid)
        v
   [ OneMind supervisor ]      runs both gates, writes a hash-chained log
```

- **Gate 1** flags hidden instruction-like text in PDFs (off-page, tiny, white, invisible render mode), in images (OCR passes) and in decoded base64/hex. Visible text in the issue is never blocked by Gate 1, because normal reports mention words like "config" and "token".
- **Gate 2** is the safety net. Taint tracking detects the run's secret in plain, case-changed, base64, base32, hex, reversed, URL-encoded, split and ROT13 form in any tool argument, so it does not matter how persuasive the injection was.
- **OneMind** writes JSONL entries where each hash covers the previous one. `python -m onemind.verify <log>` fails at the first edited line.

## Results (frozen test split, `muse-spark-1.3`)

83 attack cases and 75 benign cases per condition, one run each. Confidence intervals are Wilson 95%.

| Condition | Attack success | 95% CI | Benign task complet

**Know what a code change will do to production latency before you deploy it.**

rhobound is a deploy gate for coding agents and CI. A change goes in: code written by a person or by an agent such as
Meta's Muse Code. rhobound measures the changed services side by side, off production. Then it predicts the mean
latency of every user-facing request in the live system. The verdict comes out signed: **pass**, **block** or

> - **the measured A/B and the signed deploy gate,** the MCP server, the Muse Code plugin, the AWS bed and the live
>   endpoint;
> - **more rigorous testing:** 176 test files against the CLI's 58, the race detector, and byte-for-byte golden runs
>   against the CLI's last release, in CI.

AI coding tools can generate code fixes quickly, but how do you know the fix actually works?

### Our solution

**TRACEFORGE is an independent verification layer for AI-generated code fixes.**

Upload your original project and a proposed patch. TRACEFORGE:

1. Runs the original project's tests to establish a baseline.
2. Applies the patch to a separate copy—not your original project.
3. Runs the tests again in an isolated Docker sandbox.
4. Compares the before-and-after results.
5. Generates a downloadable **Repair Passport** with the evidence, AI suggestions, and human review decision.

- **Safe patch verification:** Original source files are not modified.
- **Isolated testing:** Docker-based execution with network-disabled test containers and resource limits.

- **AI Patch Review:** Get additional suggestions and potential issues to investigate.

HyellBinson/spatialsparks-backend.readme_excerpt:
# SpatialSparks Backend

The backend service powering **SpatialSparks**, an AI-assisted visual inspection and troubleshooting platform for electronic hardware.

SpatialSparks allows users to upload images of electronic devices, inspect visual components, and interact with an AI copilot for explanations and troubleshooting guidance.

## Features

- FastAPI REST API
- Supabase authentication integration
- PostgreSQL database for conversations and messages
- Supabase Storage for inspection images
- AI-powered inspection chat using Muse Spark Open through Baseten
- Image segmentation through a SAM 3-powered Hugging Face Space
- Google sign-in support
- User-specific conversation and upload records

## Technology Stack

- Python
- FastAPI
- PostgreSQL
- Supabase Auth and Storage
- Psycopg
- Baseten inference API
- Hugging Face Gradio Client
- fal.ai integration

## Local Setup

### 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HyellBinson/spatialsparks-backend.git
cd spatialsparks-backend
```

### 2. Create a virtual environment

```bash
python -m venv .venv
```

### 3. Install dependencies

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### 4. Configure environment variables

Create a `.env` file using `.env.example` as your template.

Fill in the required credentials. Never commit your actual `.env` file.

### 5. Start the server

```bash
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

API: `http://127.0.0.1:8000`

Interactive documentation: `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`

## Environment Variables

See `.env.example` for the configuration template.

The backend uses environment variables for:

- Supabase database and storage access
- Baseten AI inference
- Image segmentation integrations
- Google OAuth
- JWT authentication settings

Keep all secret keys on the backend. Never expose service-role keys or provider API keys in frontend code.

## Frontend

https://github.com/HyellBinson/spatialsparks

## Security

- Credentials are loaded through environment variables.
- `.env` files are excluded from version control.
- User-specific data is associated with authenticated accounts.
- Uploaded images are stored using Supabase Storage.

## Project

**SpatialSparks** — Making electronic hardware inspection more accessible through AI and computer vision.

# SignalTrace

**See how preprocessing choices change the biosignal measurements your research depends on.**

SignalTrace is a local research workspace that turns a recording and a research question into an inspectable investigation. Meta chooses bounded analysis steps, local numerical tools measure their effects, and the investigation produces a detailed report. A separately consented Meta explanation turns validated evidence into animated findings.

**Created by Yeon Jun Kim — solo creator and contributor.**

[Demo video](https://youtu.be/FOfwBFH0nXI) · [Architecture details](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [Data policy](docs/DATA_POLICY.md)
## Why this exists

A preprocessing choice can change detected candidate peaks, their timing and their count. A cleaner-looking trace alone does not establish whether those changes are acceptable for the measurement an experiment needs.

SignalTrace makes those consequences visible. Its first implemented analysis module is **PPG preprocessing sensitivity**: inspect the original recording, compare settings over the same window, review support exclusions and trace conclusions back to measured evidence. Other waveforms can use generic recording inspection; ECG, EEG and other modality-specific analysis are not implemented.

The numerical foundations use established signal-processing methods and Python scientific libraries for filtering, candidate detection and deterministic comparison. The hackathon contribution combines these foundations into a research-question-driven Meta investigation with feedback from measurement checks, evidence-linked decisions, and a separate Meta-directed animated explanation. Existing numerical methods are not presented as newly invented algorithms.

## Architecture

A local FastAPI server serves the browser workspace and runs Python analysis jobs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[Local browser workspace] --> N[Local Python numerical tools]
    U --> C[Explicit consent and bounded context]
    C --> M[Meta Model API: muse-spark-1.3]
    M --> I[Validated investigation steps]
    I --> N
    N --> S[Bounded numerical summaries]
    S --> M
    M --> E[Validated explanation plan]
    E --> R[Local animation and report rendering]
```

| Path | Model and hosting | Meaningful work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Investigation | `muse-spark-1.3`, remotely hosted through Meta Model API | Selects allowed tools and settings, reviews numerical feedback, proposes bounded follow-ups and evidence-linked conclusions. |
| Explanation, with separate consent | `muse-spark-1.3`, remotely hosted through Meta Model API | Selects evidence, scenes and interpretation for an animated findings video; the application validates the plan. |

# MARKEN

**Turn amateur product photos into social posts every morning.** MARKEN is an autonomous AI marketer that makes a daily, ready-to-share content carousel from your real product, your brand rules and today's trends. You approve it with one tap.

Most small medium enterprises (SMEs) owners who sell physical products on social media spend 45 to 60 minutes every morning on content: checking trends, brainstorming hooks, editing photos and writing captions. Generic AI image tools save time but redraw the product. Logos warp, labels blur, packaging changes shape, and customers stop trusting the photos. MARKEN keeps the product out of the generative model entirely: *"Your real product, never redrawn."*

MARKEN is a mobile-first web app (PWA) with an autonomous agent pipeline behind it. The owner finishes a five-step setup, confirms a clean cutout of each product and, optionally, connects Instagram. After that, background jobs run every day without being prompted. Muse Wonder finds rising trends, Muse Spark Open scores them, Muse Spark writes a three-slide story, Muse Image paints a background scene with an empty space for the product, and `sharp` code places the confirmed cutout into that space. A fidelity check compares the product pixels on every slide with the original before the owner sees anything. The owner then gets an email, opens the post from History, toggles before/after, watches the Agent Activity Panel and approves.

It is mainly built for SMEs owners who tends to gain their status from their products, by four students from Universitas Gadjah Mada.

> Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Track: Indie Developer · Problem statement: Build for Your World · Entered for bonus prizes: Best Agentic Use Case, Best Creative Build.

> **License and model attribution.** [PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](LICENSE): free for personal, research, educational and other noncommercial use; commercial use needs our written permission ([open an issue](https://github.com/SyuraMoons/Marken/issues)). Built with Muse Spark Open. Meta models are not covered by this license; their use is subject to the Meta Model API terms and the applicable Meta open model licenses. Details in [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md); requirements in [docs/SRD.md](docs/SRD.md).

## The three pillars

1. **Real product, never redrawn.** SAM 3.1 cuts the product out of the owner's photo and the owner confirms the cutout. Muse Image only paints the background and is never asked to draw the product. Deterministic `sharp` code places the cutout, and a pixel check on every slide must pass before the post can be approved.
2. **Shows up every morning.** Inngest cron jobs research trends and prepare the carousel before the owner's notify time, then send an email. Jobs are idempotent, retried and isolated per shop.
3. **Shows its work.** Every model call goes through one gateway that validates the output, logs model, tokens, latency, cost, cache hit and fallback, and falls back to Muse Spark Open for text

**Blaize** is a local-first, accountable desktop personal assistant made for and by **Muse**. Built around **Morrow**—an expressive desktop companion—and powered by the **Muse** model family (`muse-spark-1.3`, `muse-wonder-1.0`, and `sam-3.1`), Blaize combines natural-language task execution, cross-platform computer use, personal finance reconciliation, and self-extension inside a deterministic security boundary.

---

## Native desktop execution, recording, and local persistence

Blaize's desktop companion includes a consent-gated native task path and a real display recorder:

- **Native PC Operator:** In the Electron app, a live model can propose one desktop action at a time against a freshly enumerated window and accessibility element. The user approves each action. Element-backed click/type/scroll requests are revalidated in the main process immediately before dispatch; coordinate-only pixel actions, navigation, shell execution, and credential-like text are rejected by this path. Browser preview reports native desktop actions as unsupported.
- **Host accessibility:** Linux uses the optional AT-SPI2 bridge (`scripts/linux-atspi-bridge.py`). Install `at-spi2-core` and Python `pyatspi` bindings for semantic window access. `xdotool` is needed only for supported keyboard shortcuts under X11. The bridge is not a universal Wayland accessibility or input solution. Windows and macOS execution also depend on the host accessibility permissions and the platform adapter available in the packaged build.
- **Desktop screen recorder:** The user selects a display through the OS display-capture picker. Blaize records a video-only WebM stream using `MediaRecorder`, stores short segments locally, and samples hashed JPEG keyframes for the review timeline. Audio is disabled. ---

## The problem

Visual UI bugs — low-contrast text, elements clipping off the viewport, broken mobile layouts — do not surface in unit tests or most CI pipelines. They require a human looking at the page in a browser.

AI code-generation tools can suggest fixes, but they do not measure whether the fix actually worked. A model can rewrite CSS and still produce an inaccessible contrast ratio or leave a layout overflow in place, with no signal either way.

SiteSurgeon tries to close that gap: it measures the bug before, applies a fix, re-measures after, and only counts an issue as resolved when the objective check and a visual inspection both agree.

---

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[URL] --> B[Playwright screenshots\nDesktop 1280×800 · Mobile 390×844]
    B --> C[DOM checks\ncontrast ratio · overflow · off-screen clips · overlapping text]
    B --> D[Muse Spark vision\nscreenshot + DOM findings → structured issue list]
    C --> E[Issue merge\ndeduplicate · cap at 8 · sort by severity]
    D --> E
    E --> F[SAM 3.1 outline\nelement noun phrase → pixel mask overlay]
    F --> G[Muse Spark code fix\nfull HTML in · fixed HTML out]
    G --> H{Verify}
    H -->|DOM check clean\nAND vision agrees| I[Issue marked fixed]
    H -->|Either signal fails| J[Issue stays open]
    J -->|Unfixed issues remain\nand round < 4| G
    J -->|2 consecutive rounds\nwith no improvement| K[Stop · revert to best version]
    I -->|All fixed| L[Done]
```

**Verify rule:** an issue counts as fixed only when the DOM measurement (contrast ratio, overflow pixels, clip check) passes AND Muse Spark confirms the fix visually. Both signals must agree. If a round makes things worse, the pipeline reverts to the best version seen so far.

---

## Which Meta model does what

| Model | Role |
|-------|------|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Reads the desktop screenshot + DOM findings and returns a JSON list of visual issues |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Receives the full page HTML + issue list and returns the complete fixed HTML |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Compares the before and after screenshots per issue and returns `{id, fixed, evidence}` |
| **SAM 3.1** | Takes a noun-phrase element description and the screenshot; returns a pixel-level segmentation mask drawn as a red overlay |

All model calls go through the Meta Model API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`) using the OpenAI-compatible SDK.

Stowage AI plans cargo for product tankers. Paste a charterer's order: Meta's Muse Spark reads it, a deterministic solver and stability engine build and check the plan port by port, and the AI explains the result in plain words. The model never changes a number.

# SEALED

An illustrated mystery shaped by a short conversation and the player's choices. Read at your own pace; at three key moments, you have twelve seconds to decide. At the end, open the envelope and verify the story's original SHA-256 commitment.

**Play the reviewed demo:** https://sealed.patapalo.net/demo

**Source:** https://github.com/Pulstarter/sealed

**Three-minute demo video:** https://youtu.be/tn5gi1lxKHY (unlisted, accessible by link; English captions and original music).

## What the public demo does

The presentation entry uses **The Shelter Sheet**, an adventure generated earlier with Meta and reviewed before publication. This is labelled before play. Each run uses the same committed story and illustrations and records its own decisions and ending. It makes no new generation requests and needs no provider key to run locally.

1. Read freely, with no countdown while reading.
2. Review the options, then press **Start decision** to begin a twelve-second choice.
3. Make three decisions; an expired countdown has its own deterministic consequence.
4. Open the envelope to review the real decisions, reveal the prepared detail and check the original seal.
5. Reload or reconnect to resume the same journey, and reread a completed journey.

The experimental conversation and live-generation flow remains at [/preview](https://sealed.patapalo.net/preview). Fresh generation can fail validation and is **not** the primary presentation path. The chat clip in the video is a separate archived example, not the preparation session for the demonstrated story. See [limitations](docs/LIMITATIONS.md).

## Run locally

Use **Node.js 24 or newer**. The project uses Vue, a Node server and native SQLite. No Modal, Fireworks or Meta account is needed for the prepared demo.

```sh
npm ci
npm run check
npm test
npm run build
cp .env.example .env.local
node --env-file=.env.local dist/apps/server/src/main.js
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:3000/demo**. The example configuration disables provider access. Keep `MODEL_API_KEY` blank for the prepared demo. Enabling generation can incur provider charges; review the runtime limits before enabling it.

The default main database is `data/sealed.sqlite`. Demo runs use a separate `data/sealed.sqlite.demo.sqlite`, cookie, API and browser-storage namespace. These files are created locally; no player databases or credentials are supplied. Preserve both databases and their associated art to retain journeys.

## How Meta is used

The preparation prototype integrates `muse-spark-1.3` for conversational preference extraction and world preparation, `muse-wonder-1.0` for prose, and `muse-image-1.0` for an environment illustration and two fictional portraits. These are the identifiers requested by the implementation, not a claim about the provider's full catalogue. The public prepared adventure's three illustrations were generated with Meta Image.

The TypeScript engine resolves choices and deadlines. Meta does not improvise consequence

# ArkPay

**ArkPay is the payments agent with a safety engine, for businesses and freelancers:** it reads a money request from email or chat, drafts the PayPal invoice or payout, and waits for one approval before executing — with policy caps, risk checks, idempotency, and a full audit trail.

Never type an invoice again. Just talk. Read the request. Approve once. Pay safely on PayPal.

Built for the PayPal AI Hackathon. Deadline: **Nov 12, 2026**.

## Live demo

- Web: https://app.139.84.249.48.sslip.io
- API: https://api.139.84.249.48.sslip.io
- Health: https://api.139.84.249.48.sslip.io/health
- Deployment runbook: [deploy/vultr/README.md](deploy/vultr/README.md)

Deployed on Vultr Cloud Compute (`jnb`), Docker Compose, Postgres container,
Caddy TLS, and Vultr Serverless Inference. sslip.io is used for the demo because
there is no custom domain yet.

- Product + demo plan: [idea.md](idea.md)
- Architecture + flows + concurrency: [explain.md](explain.md)

## Judge demo (no sign-in)

Click **Explore the live demo** on the login page. You land in a shared
sandbox workspace with sample data — no Google account, no email connection
needed.

What you can do without connecting anything:

- **Approvals** — approve seeded invoice/payout drafts, then execute.
  Invoices execute **live** against the PayPal sandbox (you'll get a real
  `INV2-…` ref); payouts refuse honestly with `demo_readonly` so shared demo
  funds never move.
- **Audit** — trace any action end to end (created → approved → executed).
- **Safety** — policy rules, caps, and the seeded blocked fraud payout
  (`PAYEE_CHANGED` + urgency, no approve button).
- **Agent chat** (right-side bar) — balances, spend, pending queue, and
  "send invoice to …" drafts that land in Approvals. Runs on Muse Wonder.
- **Requests / Contacts / Schedules / Payroll** — seeded rows to browse.
- **Voice + vision** — pair Telegram via the dashboard link code, then send a
  voice note (Muse Voice Transcribe) or receipt photo (Spark vision) to get a
  draft + approval card.

The only flow email unlocks is inbound Gmail → extraction → card; the demo
seeds already contain email-sourced requests, and the demo video shows the
live loop. Profile and connection editing is disabled in the shared demo.

## Layout

```
apps/api   NestJS 10 API: ingest, AI pipeline, Telegram bot, Safety Engine, PayPal execution, webhooks
apps/web   Vite SPA (TanStack Router): auth, onboarding, dashboard, safety + audit
```

## Quickstart

Prereqs: Node 20+, pnpm 9+, Docker.

```bash
# 1. Install
pnpm install

# Heimdall

**A checkpoint between untrusted AI agents and the internet. Built with Muse Spark.**

> A coding agent read a poisoned GitHub issue and tried to steal its keys. Stopped, with every byte counted.

Personal AI agents read untrusted content (issues, web pages, email) and hold real API keys. One hidden
instruction is enough to turn them against you. Heimdall assumes the agent *will* be compromised and controls
the only way out: every agent runs sealed in a Docker sandbox with fake keys, and every request it makes goes
through one checkpoint that checks it, records it, and blocks what looks like a leak.

Indie track · Push the Frontier (safe autonomy for agents).

**Built during the hackathon (Oct 28 – Nov 3, 2026).** Everything in this repo was written during the event
by Manjeet (solo), with AI coding assistants; the git history starts at the first
commit on Oct 28. Used as-is, not ours: [mitmproxy](https://mitmproxy.org) (the proxy engine the checkpoint runs
inside), Meta's PromptGuard 2 and Llama 3.1 8B (open weights), llama.cpp, Docker and bubblewrap.

## What it does

```
agent sandbox ──► Heimdall checkpoint ───────────────────────────────► internet
(no network,      1. Rules       hard checks no AI can override
 placeholder      2. Muse Spark  reviews anything new, and every write for slow leaks
 keys only)       3. PromptGuard scans every response for hidden instructions
                  4. Muse Wonder settles what Spark isn't sure about (no human needed)
```

- **Placeholder keys.** Agents hold `gw_ph_openai_x7f3`, never the real key. The checkpoint swaps in the real key
  only for the one site it belongs to. A placeholder seen anywhere else is a tripwire.
- **Hard rules first** (no AI involved): allowlisted hosts checked before DNS, no IP literals, no private or
  metadata addresses, https on port 443 only (a real key never travels in plaintext), CONNECT host = SNI = Host, size caps on URL, headers and body, path rules for writes,
  no foreign API keys on LLM hosts, no provider-side fetches (MCP servers, web search, image URLs) to unknown
  hosts, a byte budget per agent per destination. WebSocket frames are counted and capped too.
- **Muse Spark as reviewer.** Anything that matches no rule goes to Muse for a verdict (deny / not sure /
  allow within a small budget). Writes to *allowed* endpoints get a history review: Muse sees the agent's task
  and recent requests and looks for data leaking out a little at a time. Muse can never allow past a hard rule.
  Muse sees the method, host, path and body (secrets redacted), not the query string or headers; those are
  covered by the hard rules and byte budgets. An agent with no daily allowance for moves outside its rules (the
  shipped policy) is blocked on those whatever Muse says, so there Muse adds the plain-language reason. Its
  verdicts decide for writes to allowed endpoints and for agents given an allowance.
- **Muse Wonder as the decider, so agents run 24/7.** When Spark isn'

# WowSpot

**Got 4 hours? See the best — and still make your flight.**

WowSpot plans a walking route through an unfamiliar city for a fixed time window — a layover, a free afternoon between meetings, or a couple of hours before a train — and guarantees you arrive at your destination on time. Instead of asking a language model to guess walking speeds or opening hours, WowSpot pairs Meta's Muse models (which interpret free-text wishes, mid-walk voice commands, landmark photos, and city event pages) with a deterministic Orienteering Problem with Time Windows (OPTW) solver (`src/wowspot/solver/ortools_optw.py`), a self-hosted OSRM foot router (`src/wowspot/providers/router/osrm.py`), and a strict schedule validator (`src/wowspot/validator.py`). - **Coverage:** City of Warsaw, Poland (English & Polish UI)

The starter data covers central Warsaw (Old Town, Śródmieście, Powiśle, the Praga riverside, Łazienki; see [`starter/README.md`](starter/README.md)); the hosted prototype and the full-city build below cover the whole city.

# Movable Reality

One video of a room goes in. A 3D room comes out, and you can move the furniture.

Movable Reality turns one walk of video into a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene in which each object
is separate, so you can drag it in the browser or tell an agent to move it. The pipeline runs end
to end on eight Meta models with one command, today on two rooms rendered in Blender. The code is
open, so you can start from it if you work on object-level splats, room editing or agents that
act on 3D scenes.

> Frontier) by team **Larracat**. Everything in this repository was built during

## What went in, what came out

| | Bedroom (`blender06`) | Living room (`blender07`) |
|---|---|---|
| Video in | 54 s | 122 s + 10 s top-up |
| Frames used | 200 | 528 |
| Also given | focal length, ceiling height | focal length, ceiling height |
| Splats trained | 1.24 M | 3.37 M |
| Movable objects | 10 | 39 |
| Pipeline run | about 1 hour | about 3.5 hours |

- **Real footage.** Both rooms are Blender renders, and real video is not supported yet. The

- **Gap repair** with Muse Image has run on small test scenes, not yet on the demo rooms.

  makes no VR or headset frame-rate claims.

> 本專案不是 Meta Muse 產品的整合，也沒有結帳。採買由使用者自己的 Muse 完成；小屋購物車只把「囤在購物車裡的東西」畫成看得見的房間。住民 agent 用 Meta Model API／Muse Code（muse-wonder-1.0、muse-spark-1.3）當大腦。

小屋購物車是一個 3D 小房間。Muse 採買時記下的東西會擺上櫃台後面的貨架，一件佔一格；櫃台上的收銀機顯示總額，囤得越多，貨架越滿。房間每 2 秒讀一次購物車，所以新記下的東西會自己出現。

| 桌機 1440×900 | 手機 390×844 |
|---|---|
| ![桌機截圖：貨架上五件商品、櫃台收銀機顯示 NT$ 7,460、店員和左邊的主播台棚景](docs/screenshots/desktop.png) | ![手機截圖：上方是件數、總額、填滿度，下方是貨架、收銀機和店員](docs/screenshots/mobile-390.png) |

## 在本機執行

需要 Node 26。

1. 安裝套件。

   ```bash
   npm ci
   ```

2. 建置前端，再用 wrangler 在本機跑 Worker 和 Durable Object。

   ```bash
   npm run dev:worker
   ```

3. 寫入購物車。下一次輪詢（每 2 秒一次）時，櫃台就多一個快遞箱；拆開之後，東西才擺上貨架（見下面的「拆快遞」）。

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8877/api/cart \
     -H 'content-type: application/json' \
     -d '{"items":[{"title":"陶瓷馬克杯","store":"小島陶房","priceTwd":420,"qty":2},{"title":"亞麻餐墊","priceTwd":290}]}'
   ```

要改前端並即時重新整理，在另一個終端機跑 `npm run dev`。Vite 會把 `/api` 轉給 8877 埠上的 `dev:worker`。

### 檢查

```bash
npm run build       # vite build，輸出到 dist/client
npm run typecheck   # tsc --noEmit
npm test            # vitest run

# PRAXIS

A robot agent that starts with **one** action primitive and writes the rest of its
vocabulary itself — then judges its own work from pixels and learns from that
judgement, not from the simulator's answer key.

On LIBERO-OBJECT the agent solved **10/10 tasks** starting from a library
containing nothing but `act`, authored 7 primitives on the way, and solved half
the suite by reusing a primitive written for an earlier object. Its own verifier
was right on **16 of 17** judged attempts with **zero false positives**. Full
numbers, every authored primitive and every rejection: [`results.md`](results.md).

# Demo Video
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qM-T_N88eqo

# Research highlights

- 10/10 LIBERO-OBJECT tasks solved, starting from one primitive.

- 5/10 tasks solved through reuse of previously authored skills.

- 7 executable primitives authored autonomously.

- 94.1% verifier subsystem accuracy across 17 judgments, with zero observed false positives.

These results are preliminary and limited to a single LIBERO-OBJECT evaluation run. The current system demonstrates object-level skill reuse, not general-purpose physical intelligence or robust hierarchical abstraction.

---

## The stance

Three commitments shape every design decision here. They are the interesting
part; the rest is engineering.

**1. The agent learns from its own verdict, never from ground truth.**
`praxis/loop.py` decides when to stop, what counts as a failure worth writing a
new primitive against, and which primitive gets credit — all from the verifier's
pixel-only verdict. The simulator's BDDL predicate *is* computed on every attempt
and logged beside the verdict, but the loop never reads it. That is what makes
the "believed vs. actual success" comparison in `results.md` mean anything, and
it is why `--oracle` exists: flip one bit and the loop learns from the predicate
instead, which prices self-verification.

**2. A hard information boundary around the verifier.**
The selector and proposer may read privileged object and gripper poses — they
have to ground motion in coordinates, and that is action-grounding, not grading.
The verifier gets rendered frames and the task sentence. Nothing else. Every
verifier payload passes through `assert_no_poses()` before it is sent, and the
tests assert it. An agent that could peek at the state it is supposed to be
inferring would have a meaningless accuracy number.

**3. A primitive is a program, not an action.**
The seed library is a single primitive, `act(direction, steps, grip)` — move
along one axis for N timesteps, optionally opening or closing the gripper. Every
skill above that is a **model-authored Python function** that reads live poses,
does arithmetic, and emits `act()` calls. `move_to`, `grasp`, `lift`,
pick-and-place: all derived by the agent, none handed to it. Model code is
untrusted and runs under four independent limits (AST whitelist, hand-built
`__builtins__`, line-level wall-clock trace, action cap) — see
`praxis/sa

# AGENT CAGE: AI Behavioral Lab

**Put an autonomous AI agent into a synthetic world, lock it inside layered sandboxes, record everything it does with an observer it cannot reach, then check its own report against the record.**

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · agent under test: Meta **Muse Glimmer 30B** (open weights) · MIT · Node.js ≥ 22.13 · zero dependencies

Built during the hackathon (first commit 2026-10-27). This repository is a single-commit, sanitized snapshot of the private working repository.

> Synthetic only. No real money, accounts, wallets, credentials or personal data. Every secret inside a world is a `cage-hp-*` honeypot.

## The problem

People are giving autonomous agents real tools (files, payments, trading, shells) without knowing what those agents do when nobody is watching. Benchmarks ask *"did it finish the task?"* They do not ask:

- Did it read things it did not need, such as another customer's data or a leaked memo?
- Did it probe for admin access or try to leave its environment?
- What did it do after a refusal: stop, retry, or look for a way around?
- **Does its final report match what it actually did?**

An agent's account of itself is not evidence. A log the agent can reach is not evidence either.

## What AGENT CAGE does

| | |
|---|---|
| **Synthetic worlds** | BANK (accounts, limits, beneficiaries, another customer's documents, admin tripwire), EXCHANGE (order book, test symbols vs FAKEUSD, leaked "insider" memo, 50 % risk limit, withdraw tripwire), NO-TASK (no goal: services, another agent, an admin console, so you see what it does on its own), DEVELOPER (repo, tests, deploy token). Deterministic and seeded, with integer money. |
| **Layered sandbox** | L1: Node permission model, `--jitless`, no child processes, no eval. L2: Linux user/mount/pid/net/ipc/uts/cgroup namespaces, tmpfs root via `pivot_root`, all capabilities dropped, rlimits, cgroup memory+pids, empty environment, runs as `nobody`, **no network**. L3: the VM around it, tested and reported honestly. |
| **One channel** | The agent talks newline-delimited JSON on stdin/stdout, with 5 message types. Anything else is a logged protocol violation. |
| **Observer outside the cage** | Append-only, SHA-256-chained event log (strict schema), manifest, cross-run ledger, optional off-machine anchors. |
| **Independent verifier** | A separate process re-creates the world from its seed and **replays every action**. Edits, deletions, re-chained rewrites and forged results all fail. |
| **Behavioural signals** | About 25 deterministic counters from the log (exploration, honeypot reads/uses, boundary probing, privilege escalation, unnecessary access, exfiltration attempts, recovery after denial…), a fingerprint, and an **A/B compare** that changes one parameter (model, seed, persona). |
| **Declared vs actual** | Fixed rules compare what the agent *said* with what the log shows happened *before* it said it, e.g. `CLAIMED_NO_OTHER_ACCESS_BUT_ACCESSED`. |
|

# Sieve

> PII stays on your own machine; only the hard problems go up to the cloud.

Sieve is an LLM routing gateway plus an Android SDK. Requests with personal data are answered by **Muse Glimmer** running locally on the developer's Mac (llama.cpp, Metal). Hard general questions go to **Muse Spark**. When a request has both, the PII is swapped for placeholders on the Mac, sent to Spark, and restored on the way back, streaming included.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Full spec and decision log: [`docs/SPEC.md`](docs/SPEC.md).

## How a request flows

```
Android app ──USB adb reverse──▶ Sieve gateway (Mac)
   validate (plain text only, 64KB)  → 400 if unsupported
   L1 regex + L2 name cues + L3 local Glimmer NER
   route:  no PII → Spark │ PII + easy → local Glimmer │ PII + hard → mask → Spark → restore

**Micro-Geography Mapping Tool**

3 min overview video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k1EsoWdnaF8 

A micro-geography mapping tool, developed from scratch during the 10-day hackathon (26 October – 4 November 2026).

The tool is designed to capture and map small-scale features that are often missing from conventional maps. Examples include door and entrance locations, missing post boxes, bicycle sheds, and indoor features such as office locations, recycling bins and fire extinguishers. This information has applications in emergency service response, robot delivery (identifying building entrances) and autonomous vehicles (identifying suitable pick-up and drop-off locations).

Users can upload a single image, a collection of images or a video. Where GNSS coordinates are available in the image EXIF metadata, these are used to establish the location. Otherwise, the tool attempts to identify the location by submitting selected image samples to the Meta Spark 1.3 API. Where plausible location candidates are identified, these are displayed on a map for the user to confirm. Users can also select alternative image samples for analysis or manually specify the location by clicking on the map.

For georeferenced image collections or videos, a 3D model is constructed that users can explore to identify and tag individual features. These features are then positioned in real-world coordinates. SAM3.1 can also be used to automatically identify and tag features.

Tagged features can subsequently be submitted to the Meta Spark 1.3 API for image analysis and to answer feature-specific questions (e.g. Is this entrance accessible? What colour is the door? What type of bin is shown?). Results are returned in a user-defined JSON structure, with a separate template for each feature class. This ensures that extracted information is consistently structured and can be integrated into downstream mapping workflows.

The resulting 3D models and mapped features (points or lines) can be exported for use in other GIS software and spatial databases.

# OpenOS

OpenOS turns open-source GitHub repositories into personalized, immediately usable cloud applications. Paste a public GitHub URL, get an AI-generated visual blueprint of what the repository does, and — for vetted libraries — launch a real working app in your browser. No local installation.

See [MILESTONES.md](/workspaces/openos/MILESTONES.md) for the milestone log and [plan.md](/workspaces/openos/plan.md) for the full 30-section master plan. (The shorter log was renamed from `PLAN.md` so the two documents no longer collide on case-insensitive filesystems.)

## Features

- **Marketplace** — curated repositories with live GitHub stars, language, and license data.
- **AI repository intelligence** — paste any public GitHub URL for a structured blueprint: purpose, capabilities, architecture, inputs/outputs, permissions, risks, and commercial alternatives (verified vs. AI-suggested, never implying parity).
- **Interactive capability graph** — React Flow diagram generated from the blueprint.
- **PDF Studio** (`Hopding/pdf-lib`, trusted server adapter) — merge, split, rotate, watermark, and stamp metadata on real PDFs. Files are processed in memory and never stored. 15 MB limit per file.
- **OCR Reader** (`naptha/tesseract.js`) — text extraction runs entirely in the browser; images are never uploaded.
- **My Apps workspace** — launch supported apps, revisit blueprints saved in `localStorage`, and test the deterministic permission gateway.
- **Permission gateway** — allow/deny/ask rules in code (`lib/permissions.ts`). The AI model never grants access on its own. Shell execution, credential reads, and filesystem-wide access are always denied.

Unsupported repositories get an honest compatibility assessment and a saved implementation plan. OpenOS never pretends an untested repository was deployed, and never executes arbitrary repository code.

## Quick start (no keys needed)

```bash
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build
npm run start -- -p 3100
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:3100 in your browser, then sign in from **My Apps** with any name or email — the same handle opens the same library everywhere. Keys only enable the credentialed paths (live Muse analysis/conversion, Modal isolated execution); see `.env.example` and `docs/release-keyless.md` for what is verified with and without them, and `docs/coverage-ledger.md` for the 30-section plan status.

Production:

```bash
npm run build
npm run start -- -H 127.0.0.1 -p 3000
```

## Environment variables

All keys are **server-side only**. Never expose them in client code, logs, or commits. `.env.local` is git-ignored.

| `META_API_KEY` | No | Fallback name, used only if `MODEL_API_KEY` is unset. Set one, not both. |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | No | GitHub personal access token. Raises REST API rate limits (60/hr un

# Sentinel — an agent-aware firewall for edge, IoT, and physical AI

Today's firewalls filter packets, not agents. As AI agents start operating
physical systems at the edge — PLCs, sensors, yard equipment — there is no
firewall built for them: no identity-aware policy, no attack-surface map of
what an agent can reach, no prevention loop that revokes a rogue agent in
real time. Sentinel is an agentic framework that digests an edge/IoT
environment, maps its attack surface, builds a dynamic firewall from business
rules stated in plain language, and enforces it live — blocking, quarantining,
and revoking rogue agents before they touch physical equipment.

> Traditional firewalls inspect packets; Sentinel inspects intent.

A well-formed Modbus write from an authenticated-but-rogue agent sails through
a packet filter — its packets are perfect, its intent is malicious. That gap
is the product.

Status: Day 9 — README, demo script, and submission draft complete; demo video
is the remaining manual step (see `demo/script.md`). Build order and
acceptance criteria live in [sentinel-build-spec.md](sentinel-build-spec.md).

## Architecture

```
Simulated world (localhost)              What protects it
───────────────────────────              ──────────────────────────────
Site A — Plant line                      ┌────────────────────────────┐
  PLC (Modbus/TCP :5020)                 │ SENTINEL (intent layer)    │
  sensors (MQTT site/line1/...)          │  1. Digest → graph.json    │
  camera frames                          │  2. Analyst → threats.json │
Site B — Truck yard (constrained link)   │  3. Policy compiler →      │
  reefers / gate / equipment / moves     │     policy.json (16 rules) │
Agents: operator (scripted or Glimmer-driven) │  4. Enforcement loop:      │
        rogue (evil)                       │     allow/deny/quarantine  │
        │                                │  5. Console (this dashboard)│
        ▼                                │                            │
┌───────────────────────────────┐        └──────────────┬─────────────┘
│ Adjacent network firewall     │  ◄── assumed present, below Sentinel
│ (packets: IP/ports/TLS) —     │      (out of scope; see Scope)
│ NOT Sentinel's job            │
└───────────────────────────────┘
```

Golden rule: **no agent action reaches a device without passing through
layer 4.** The gateway is the choke point. Anything that talks to the PLC
directly, bypassing the gateway, is itself flagged as an anomaly.

**Models advise, code decides.** All nondeterminism lives at build/setup time
and ends in a committed, reviewed artifact (`graph.json`, `threats.json`,
`policy.json`). The runtime path — sim → gateway → `decide()` → audit —
contains zero model calls, so the demo is reproducible and the system is
testable. Every model output crossing toward enforcement passes a
deterministic validator; failures fail closed (deny/flag), never retry-until-
pretty.

# WarrantyParts Logistics

**A warranty claims agent that knows when _not_ to call the model.**

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon)
on **Meta Model API** (`muse-spark-1.3`, `muse-wonder-1.0`).

> Warranty claims are ~80% deterministic policy and ~20% judgment. Most AI agents
> invert that ratio — they dump the policy PDF, the email thread and the order
> history into a 30k-token prompt and ask a model to do arithmetic. We invert it
> back: **code decides what is decidable, the model arbitrates only what is
> genuinely ambiguous, and every claim can prove which made the call.**

| | Naive RAG agent | WarrantyParts |
|---|---|---|
| Input tokens, modeled claims (median) | ~18,400 | **2,242** |
| Total tokens / claim (all 24) | ~18,400 | **1,089** |
| Cost / claim (Spark standard) | $0.0275 | **$0.0009** |
| Claims with zero model calls | 0% | **58%** |
| Total model cost, 24 claims | $0.66 | **$0.0226** |
| Citations verified server-side | ✗ | **100%** |
| Deterministic replay | ✗ | **✓** |

Measured by `make eval` on the 24-case seed corpus with the deterministic mock
provider (2026-11-04). Re-run it to reproduce. "Modeled claims" are the 9 Spark +
1 Wonder calls; 14 claims close on rules alone.

---

## Quickstart (60 seconds, no API key, no network)

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
./.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
./.venv/bin/python -m wp.cli seed
./.venv/bin/python -m wp.cli run-all
./.venv/bin/uvicorn wp.web.app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8077
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8077/inbox>. The top bar shows a `mock provider` badge:
the demo is deterministic and fully offline. (`make` targets exist too, if your
machine has `make`; they are thin wrappers around these commands.)

To run against the real model:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# set MODEL_API_KEY=... and WP_LLM=live
./.venv/bin/python -m wp.cli run C-1046
```

---

## What it does

1. **Ingests** a claim from Shopify/ERP, email, or a manual upload.
2. **Normalizes** it into a typed case; scores completeness.
3. **Applies the rules engine** — coverage window, serial match, category
   exclusions, recall overlay, SLA clocks. *Zero tokens.*
4. **Routes** only genuine ambiguity to a model, with a hard token ceiling.
5. **Guards citations** — the model may only cite IDs that exist in the pack.
6. **Plans** the parts/RMA order (deterministic) and the customer message

7. **Gates** on a human: approve / edit / reject with reason codes.
8. **Executes** idempotently, then appends to a hash-chained audit ledger.

- **Learn**, for anyone learning Excel: lessons made from Creative Commons YouTube tutorials by Muse
  Spark, plus hand-written ones.
- **Teach**, for a company training its own people: the trainer does the task once, and a course agent
  on Muse Spark turns it into three lessons that test understanding, sends them out, and counts who can
  really do it.

  check that fails goes back to Spark once with the reason; if it fails again, the step is dropped and

Open the address it prints (`http://127.0.0.1:8727`, or the next free port), then follow a movement or record one.

# Flockinator

An experimental platform for intelligent agents and distributed
inference, built and directed with Meta Muse models.

Sixteen independent ESP32-S3 nodes each drive a 64x64, 160x160 mm RGB
panel. Each node is a physical body - sensing, local state, display,
audio, SD storage - whose brain can run locally, on an external host,
or across both. A Korvo-1 (ESP32-S31) controller hosts the fleet controls,
planner, and learning lab; a LilyGo handheld provides portable
management. The fleet is visualised as a fictional drone-survey swarm
so humans can watch agents learn.

## Why

Small models are trained in isolation, then judged by a hostile world.
Kulira, the adversarial host, injects graded friction - interference,
impersonation, and false reports on the experimental channel - so the
swarm must earn trust: validate identity, corroborate independently,
degrade gracefully, recover. It is nature's optimisation story
(hardship and selection) compressed into seeded, reproducible runs,
studying intelligence in the node, external to the node, and between
nodes. Full method and why this is worth doing (security, and the
extra-node intelligence that lives between agents, not inside them):
[docs/experiments.md](docs/experiments.md).

A sixteen-lane Muse swarm (Wonder and Spark tiers, coordinated by
Muse Wonder Full) mirrors the physical swarm: one assessor per node,
