# Gecko

**Send a video. Get a fix.** Gecko catches the bug in a screen recording and opens a pull request that proves it and fixes it.

Gecko watches a plain screen recording of a web-app bug (no browser extension, no SDK, no logs), works out exactly what the user did, replays it in a real browser, and writes a Playwright test that **fails the same way the video shows**. Then Muse Code fixes the bug with that failing test as its spec, and Gecko only accepts the fix once the test passes and the rest of the suite stays green.

Every claim Gecko makes is checked by running code. When it cannot reproduce a bug, it says so, with its evidence, instead of guessing.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track, *Push the Frontier*).

## How it works

| Stage | What happens | Meta model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Ingest | Frames sampled where the screen changes, cropped to the app, tiled into labelled contact sheets; audio extracted | |
| 2. Understand | Narration transcribed; Muse Spark reads the contact sheets and writes the step plan, the expected and actual behaviour, and the frame that shows the bug | Muse Voice Transcribe, Muse Spark |
| 3. Ground | SAM 3.1 segments the mouse cursor and every look-alike element (e.g. every "x icon"); the one under the cursor gives an ordinal ("2nd of 2") that the replay matches in the live DOM | SAM 3.1 |
| 4. Replay | A Playwright driver runs the steps in Chrome, resolving each target by name, SAM ordinal and row description, and records a stable locator for each | |
| 5. Reproduce | Muse Spark compares the replay's final screen with the video's bug frame and writes assertions for the expected behaviour. The test must fail on an assertion **and** match the video. If the straight replay doesn't show the bug, Muse Spark proposes how the user's actions differed (e.g. a double click) and Gecko tries each | Muse Spark |
| 6. Fix | Muse Code (headless) patches the app. Gecko rejects patches that touch the test, don't make it pass, or break the suite, and feeds the failure back (up to 3 rounds) | Muse Code |
| 7. Deliver | Two commits on a `gecko/...` branch, the failing test first and then the fix, opened as a PR | |

### Grounding without coordinate mapping

Matching pixels in a video to elements in a live page normally needs the exact viewport, scale and scroll. Gecko sidesteps that: SAM finds every instance of the clicked element's *kind* and the cursor tip, so Gecko knows "the 2nd x icon from the top". The live page resolves the same ordinal among elements with the same name, and cross-checks it against the planner's description ("the x on the 'Book flights' row"). When both signals agree the step is marked high confidence.

## The product

Gecko is built as a small SaaS on top of the pipeline: a GitHub App, a customer workspace, and a link anyone can send a bug through.

- **Three roles, one flow.** A *reporter* (support, QA, a customer) records the bug and never needs GitHub. A *developer* gets

# RippleWitness

> **Live demo for judges:** [https://ripplewitness.onrender.com/](https://ripplewitness.onrender.com/) — a locked, one-click showcase running the real `typicode/json-server` review. No setup needed: open the prepared run, lock a prediction, and see the graded reveal. (Free-tier hosting: ~1 min cold start after idle; local runs below are the full tool.)

## The problem

AI coding agents write bigger diffs than any human can carefully review. The
agent's summary says *"only touches checkout"* — and the review becomes a
skim of edited lines plus trust in that sentence. But a diff shows what was
edited, not what changed. The checkout edit can quietly move
`/reports/sales` through a shared helper, an event bus, or a config value,
and nothing in the diff tells you to look there.

## The proposed solution

RippleWitness is a local-first review cockpit that checks the change by
running it, not by reading the agent's summary. Point it at a subject repo
and two refs; it builds a static impact graph, replays a scenario suite
against both versions, and fuses the two into an observed blast radius: what
actually behaved differently. Before any of that is revealed, *you* predict
the impact set — the gate scores your prediction against execution. Agent
claims become checkable statements, questions carry their evidence, and the
finished review is sealed in a tamper-evident receipt bound to the exact
diff. All verdicts, scores, and statuses are computed in deterministic code;
the LLM only extracts claims, phrases questions, and explains.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). Numbers in
this file come only from `pnpm eval` — see
[eval/results.md](eval/results.md).

## Why this matters

The agent says *"only touches checkout."* RippleWitness doesn't grade the
sentence — it replays the change and checks. On the hero PR (PR-00),
execution shows `/reports/sales` changed too, through an event-bus coupling
the static map cannot see. The reviewer had to predict the blast radius
*before* that reveal; the prediction is scored against execution, and the
resulting receipt is bound to the exact diff.

| "Only touches checkout" (PR-00) | **CONTRADICTED** — `/reports/sales` moved via the dormant `discount.applied` subscriber | [eval/results.md](eval/results.md) E1/E3 (verifiers 20/20) |
| Static map = the impact set | Map alone: precision 0.40, recall 0.53 — useful, not ground truth | [eval/results.md](eval/results.md) E1 |

ALMA Match busca que una persona comprenda las coberturas, topes, condiciones y precios de su plan de salud sin depender de un intermediario. Las alternativas no se consideran equivalentes por presentar porcentajes similares.

## Qué contiene realmente esta entrega

**1. Uso significativo de IA de Meta.** En `backend/meta_client.py` se integra Meta Model API (`muse-spark-1.3`) para leer PDF, identificar isapre, código, coberturas hospitalarias, ambulatorias, urgencias, redes y topes, y devolver información estructurada con página y cita. **2. Verificador documental externo.** `backend/verification.py` contrasta los textos atribuidos con la página del PDF, exige información hospitalaria, ambulatoria, de urgencia, red y topes, y bloquea citas inexistentes o incompletas. Encontrar una cita literal **no certifica la interpretación semántica**; la interfaz conserva esta advertencia. Los escaneos sin texto extraíble requieren revisión humana.

**3. Motor de comparación.** `backend/comparison.py` aplica reglas de red, topes y exclusión de la isapre actual y no calcula ahorro sin precios documentados. **4. Demo funcional segura con PDF ficticio.** `/presentacion` permite descargar y volver a subir un PDF generado por nosotros. `POST /api/demo-archivo` realmente lee el archivo, comprueba sus citas y muestra un escenario ficticio comparable y uno rechazado por topes o clínicas. **5. # Thalamuse

**Text that notices when you're losing focus, and reshapes itself.**

Thalamuse is an attention-aware reader that runs on the phone you already have. It infers, paragraph by paragraph, when your attention is slipping, from how you scroll, re-read, touch and hold the phone. When a paragraph is losing you, **Muse Spark** reads those signals, explains in plain words what changed and rewrites the paragraph, and **Muse Image** draws a visual summary. No camera, no microphone, no headset, and no button to press.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track, theme: Push the Frontier).

![Thalamuse intro](docs/images/intro-slide.png)

## Contents

- [The problem](#the-problem)
- [The solution](#the-solution)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Architecture](#architecture)
- [How Thalamuse uses Meta's Muse models](#how-thalamuse-uses-metas-muse-models)
- [Impact](#impact)
- [What makes it different](#what-makes-it-different)
- [Run it](#run-it)
- [Test it](#test-it)
- [Project structure](#project-structure)
- [Honesty and privacy](#honesty-and-privacy)
- [Roadmap](#roadmap)

## The problem

![The problem](docs/images/problem-slide.png)

Staying focused on one topic is hard. There is noise all around us, attention drifts in and out, and somewhere along the way we lose the thread, then lose interest. But text stays the same: a dense paragraph reads the same whether you are fresh at a desk or tired on a bus.

The pieces of a fix exist, but apart:

- **Systems that adapt content to a reader's state** depend on EEG headsets or eye-trackers that almost nobody carries.
- **Phone-only attention sensing** stops at detecting a state. It never changes the content.
- **"Simplify" buttons** put the burden on the reader, who has to notice they are lost and remember to press it.

Nobody has closed the loop: ordinary phone sensors driving a generative, multimodal rewrite of the passage itself.

## The solution

Thalamuse closes that loop on a phone, in the browser:

1. **Sense.** Scroll speed and direction changes, slow back-scrolls (re-reading), touch contact, phone motion and idle time, measured on the phone.
2. **Infer.** A rules-based classifier turns those signals into inferred distraction, load and fatigue scores, and a content graph keeps a separate score for every paragraph.
3. **Explain.** When a paragraph stays at risk, Muse Spark reads the last ~12 seconds of signals and says, in one or two sentences, what changed. It then picks a strategy: simplify, condense, or diagram first.
4. **Reshape.** Muse Spark rewrites the paragraph in that strategy and Muse Image draws a visual summary. The paragraph re-forms in place, marked "Reshaped by Muse".
5. **Prove.** A built-in comprehension check has the reader read the dense section once as written and once reshaped, with a different set of questions after each, and puts the scores side by side.

# SIAGA.ID - verifiable disaster intelligence for Indonesia

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon submission · Track: Build for Your World**

[![Test gate](https://github.com/anggarabudiyantooo-hub/firewatch-id/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/anggarabudiyantooo-hub/firewatch-id/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

Live: <https://firewatch-id.vercel.app> · Repo: <https://github.com/anggarabudiyantooo-hub/firewatch-id> · License: [MIT](LICENSE)

> A public-interest tool, **not a replacement for official sources**. For emergency
> decisions follow BMKG, BNPB/BPBD, PVMBG and KLHK. Emergency number in Indonesia: **112**.

---

## 1. The problem 

During Indonesian haze and fire seasons, a resident sees a grey sky and has three
questions that no single official page answers quickly:

1. Is what I see supported by any public data, or is it fog, dust, or a cloud?
2. Where is the smoke likely to travel, and which places are in the frame?
3. Can I hand something trustworthy to a neighbourhood group, a school, or a journalist?

Raw satellite detections are hard to read. Screenshots of dashboards lose their
legend, timestamp and attribution, so they travel as unattributed pictures.
Generative assistants make this worse when they invent numbers: a confident
"5,000 people affected" is dangerous when no dataset says so.

## 2. The solution

SIAGA.ID keeps a strict division of labour:

- **Code owns every number.** Deterministic, read-only tools compute counts,
  distances, AQI values, wind vectors and time-window comparisons.
- **Meta Muse Spark owns language and vision.** It picks tools, resolves place names, reads a map image,
  and describes what is visible in a citizen photo.
- **Code checks the model afterwards.** Every figure in an answer is matched against
  tool results. The model gets one chance to correct itself; anything still unmatched
  is flagged in the interface instead of being quietly removed.

Four user-facing results:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Agentic assistant** (`/dashboard`) | 17 read-only tools (including `find_place`, which resolves a named city to coordinates so the agent never asks the user for a bounding box), evidence receipts `[E1]`-`[E8]`, a numeric verifier badge, and "Show on map" buttons that move the map only to coordinates a tool returned. |
| **Map snapshot** (`/dashboard`, `/reports`) | "Capture map" composites the live Leaflet map to PNG with legend, attribution, WIB timestamp, bounding box, zoom and timeline frame baked into the image. |
| **Report with AI narrative** (`/reports`) | The snapshot plus a code-computed numeric summary plus a Muse Spark narrative written from the image and the data. Export as PNG or a one-page PDF. Before/after two-frame comparison supported. |
| **Cek Asap / Smoke Check** (`/cek-asap`) | A citizen photo or description plus place and time. Muse Spark describes only what is visible; code gathers evidence and returns *supported / not yet supported / not enough data*

# FAIR · تَبَيَّن — Know what you're agreeing to. FAIR checks what you *believe* about a subscription offer against what its terms *actually say*, in English or Arabic. You paste the terms, write your expectation, and FAIR shows whether the terms support it, contradict it or leave it open. It quotes the exact sentence behind the verdict and shows what keeping or cancelling would cost. Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`, via the Meta Model API) does the reading. Deterministic code verifies every quote and does every calculation. **The problem.** Free trials that convert to paid plans, introductory prices that end, cancellation deadlines and add-on fees sit in the fine print. People rarely misread everything. They usually hold one specific wrong belief, such as "I can cancel after the trial and avoid all fees". A summary of the terms does not test that belief. FAIR does.

## Watch the demo **▶ [Watch the FAIR demo on YouTube](https://youtu.be/V9EQDyUCFNE)** (about 3 minutes)

## Screenshots | Check an offer | Result (English) | Result (Arabic, right to left) | |---|---|---| | ![The Check an offer form with terms and an expectation filled in](docs/screenshots/check-an-offer.png) | ![A Contradiction result with the deciding quote and cost summary](docs/screenshots/result-en.png) | ![The same kind of result in Arabic](docs/screenshots/result-ar.png) | All screenshots come from **replay mode**: real saved Muse Spark outputs, re-checked by FAIR's current code, on synthetic offers. The interface labels each one "Recorded demo · Not live". ## What FAIR does - **Splits your belief into claims.** Each claim gets its own verdict: MATCH, CONTRADICTION or UNKNOWN (not settled by the terms). - **Shows its evidence.** A decisive verdict needs a quote found word for word in the terms. Otherwise FAIR shows UNKNOWN. - **Prices your options.** It compares keeping the subscription with cancelling before the deadline, over 1, 3 and 12 months, using `Decimal` arithmetic on verified values only. Each total is marked as based on stated terms or dependent on assumptions. When the terms are incomplete, FAIR withholds the total and names what is missing. Cancelling is always shown as a conditional scenario marked **Not confirmed**: FAIR assumes no refund and cannot confirm that cancelling is free. - **Keeps uncertainty visible.** Assumptions, rejected values and claims the terms don't settle each have their own section, which opens by default whenever there is something to show. - **Works in English and Arabic,** with a full right-to-left interface. Evidence matching tolerates diacritics and Arabic-Indic digits (٥٩ = 59). FAIR gives information, not legal or financial

# Accord — Evidence to Agreement

### A request is not an agreement.

**An evidence-backed workspace for tracking commitments, spotting conflicting decisions, and seeing the impact of change before saying yes.**

[**Explore the live application**](https://accord-evidence-hackathon.vercel.app) · [**Watch the 2:57 narrated demonstration**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Dp7R1XATi_8vI0yrU9aBeXK1KVvbP7by/view?usp=drivesdk) · [**Read the API setup guide**](API_SETUP.md)

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** · **Indie Developer** · **Build for Your World**

---

## The problem

Imagine a studio agreeing to deliver a five-page website for ₦450,000 by November 18. Days later, the client asks for an extra dashboard, a November 11 deadline and no increase in price.

Was that request accepted? Does it replace the original agreement? What else needs to change?

Project commitments often drift across messages, emails and handoffs. Accord is designed to make the difference between **requested**, **agreed**, and **changed** visible.

## What you can try now

1. **Explore the case:** open the landing page and inspect the original source-backed story.
2. **Evidence library:** examine kickoff communications and the later change request.
3. **Decision ledger:** filter proposed, confirmed, rejected and superseded records.
4. **Impact simulator:** preview affected delivery, quality-assurance and communication dependencies without mutating the agreement.
5. **Human approval:** confirm or reject a proposed change and inspect its audit history.
6. **Meta AI Lab:** see the planned source-grounded extraction flow and try the clearly marked **Illustrative AI Workflow**. This example is simulated and does **not** call a model.

The application uses a fictional, resettable case study and browser-local storage. It is a functional prototype, **not a production agreement system**.

## Architecture

```text
Browser UI (vanilla JavaScript / CSS / HTML)
   ├── Evidence and original quotations
   ├── Decision ledger + contradiction checks
   ├── Deterministic change-impact preview
   ├── Human confirm / reject / supersede
   ├── Browser-local audit history + JSON export/import
   └── Meta AI Lab
         └── POST /api/analyze (Vercel serverless)
               ├── Meta Muse Glimmer 30B through NVIDIA NIM
               ├── Optional same-model OpenRouter fallback
               ├── Exact-quotation validation
               └── Candidate suggestions for human review
```

The backend requests a structured extraction response, verifies that each proposed supporting quotation appears in the supplied evidence, and discards suggestions without source-matching quotes. **An AI suggestion is never silently accepted as a confirmed commitment.**

### AI integration status — important disclosure

The inference integration is implemented and covered by automated tests, but **a successful hosted Meta-model inference has not yet been verified**. The NVIDIA endpoint returned **403 — Author

Run the agent yourself in the [local workbench](#local-workbench-with-the-agent-live) with your own Meta key. ## Demo video [![Demo video: a live Muse Spark run, the runtime rejecting a wrong evidence citation, the agent's correction, the guarded repair script and the evaluation](docs/assets/demo-video.jpg)](https://youtu.be/NQRHuGjj458) **[Watch the demo on YouTube](https://youtu.be/NQRHuGjj458)** (2:38): a live Muse Spark run in the app, the runtime rejecting a wrong evidence citation, the agent's correction, the guarded repair script a person receives, and how the runs were evaluated. ## The problem An import times out after writing 20 of 50 orders. The retry writes all 50 again, so 20 orders now exist twice and stock is wrong. Then ten genuine purchases arrive, and they look almost identical to earlier ones. Cancelling by similarity would remove those real purchases too. The repair has to prove from the evidence which writes were repeats, and leave every other order alone. ## How it works 1. **Investigate.** The agent gets five tools: read the database schema, list the evidence files, read evidence with exact line numbers, run read-only SQL on the original database, and test a repair on a new disposable copy. The script refuses to run if the data has changed since the test. Nothing is ever applied to the original database. # Doyle

**Truth maintenance for agent memory.**

[**▶ Demo video**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cBD3CQrDqUc) · [**Docs**](https://nrynss.github.io/doyle/) · [Judge walkthrough](https://nrynss.github.io/doyle/judge-walkthrough/) · [The thread on X](https://x.com/nrynssnryn/status/2118070593144893873)

Built by Narayan SS.

Coding agents remember what they learn: how an API pages, what a billing batch charges, which keys retire an old console. Every one of those memories rests on something outside it. When that thing changes, or was misread in the first place, nothing tells the agent. It keeps acting on the stale belief, and so does every other agent reading the same memory.

Doyle records what each memory rests on. When the evidence changes, Doyle flags every memory resting on it, has a Meta model propose a correction, and sends the correction to a person. Until the person has decided, Doyle's guard holds the agent off the stale step. The correction is then written back into every memory system the agent reads.

> Entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley), Indie track. The gate passes with no key, and the demo below runs fully offline from a fresh clone.

## The two stories, as recorded

Both are live, recorded Muse Code sessions with `muse-wonder-1.0`, run once without Doyle and once with it. The numbers are the measured ones; each links to its record.

**1. The Quiet Migration.** A veterinary clinic chain moves 4,812 patient records to a new platform. The agent remembers that `GET /patients` returns everyone in one call; the vendor API now pages at 100. Without Doyle, Wonder probed past the stale memory and lost nothing, but the stale belief survived. With Doyle, both memories were flagged, the guard held the export, a person approved the correction, and it landed in Muse Code and [Lambo](https://github.com/nrynss/lambo). 0 records lost in any run, never claimed as "losses averted". [`evidence/measures.md`](evidence/measures.md)

**2. The COBOL cutover.** Wonder ports a COBOL billing batch (4,812 accounts) to Rust, ships it, and retires the green-screen console. Its memory says the 1.5% late fee has "no exceptions"; the COBOL exempts vaccination visits. Without Doyle, Wonder found the bug itself and shipped correctly, and both stale memories survived. With Doyle:

- Doyle flagged the memories from three kinds of evidence: the COBOL diff, both programs run on all 4,812 accounts (535 mismatches, $8,308.80 overcharged, traced to paragraph `LOG-EXEMPT`), and Wonder's own reading of the console screens and training video.
- The guard denied the rewrite and the ship script. Wonder worked out the exemption from the COBOL and stopped to ask a person.
- After the review, session two worked from the corrected memory, shipped a two-line fix, and Doyle's differential run found 0 mismatches.
- 9 flags, 3 of them false alarms, all shown on the review page. In this run the operator stood in for the reviewer, as the record says.

Small businesses sell through social media, but the sale often stops at the comment section: comments go

Meta accounts to a lightweight AI-native CRM. Every comment and DM becomes a contact linked to the post and

Salesie runs the **Bloom & Thread** Facebook Page, a demo handmade-fashion shop whose logo, cover, product
photos and offer posts were made with **Muse Image**. A real comment on the Linen Wrap Dress post, answered by

# remove.free

**Type what to keep. It cuts it out — privately, on your own GPU.**

[**Live demo**](https://remove.free) · [**Demo video**](https://youtu.be/PqVlrBEzU6s) · **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**
Track: Indie Developer · Theme: Build for Your World

---

Background removal is a commodity that charges per photo and uploads every
image to someone else's server. remove.free doesn't. Matting runs in the
visitor's browser on WebGPU, so there is no upload, no account, no per-photo
fee — and it keeps working in airplane mode.

What it could not do was *understand* a photo. That is what this build adds:
Meta's models as the understanding layer, with every pixel-level operation
still on the device. The cloud reasons; your pixels stay home.

## What each Meta model decides

| Model | Decides | What stays local |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SAM 3.1** | *What* to keep. One noun phrase — `dog`, `red sneaker` — returns every match as its own selectable layer, each tinted in its own colour. | The mask is decoded with the official `@meta-sam/parser` and **gated against the on-device matte**, so SAM supplies meaning and BiRefNet supplies the hair-level edge. |
| **Muse Spark 1.3 / Muse Wonder** | *What to do*. "Keep the dog on white" becomes a validated JSON plan — one concept, one keep/remove action, one backdrop. | The plan is executed by deterministic local tools, then **verified with measured numbers** (subject coverage %, soft-edge %) shown in a trace. Low SAM confidence triggers a visible retry with a simpler concept; a soft edge triggers a re-cut with a stronger model and the cleaner result is kept. |
| **Muse Image** | *What it sits in*. A backdrop described in text is generated from the text alone. | The photo is never sent. The cutout is composited locally over the returned scene. |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe** | *Who is asking*. Speech becomes the same agent command the keyboard produces. | Audio is WAV-encoded in the browser and is the only thing that leaves. |

The planner is multimodal: it sees a disclosed 512px copy of the photo, so
"the main subject" becomes the concrete noun SAM needs — `dog` — instead of
the unfindable concept `main subject`. That fix came from running it live.

## Why this is a composition, not a wrapper

Each model is given a job it can actually do, and the app keeps the part it
does better:

- **Semantics × matte.** SAM's mask is a proposal, never the final alpha. It is
  gated against the local cutout, so a coarse SAM edge cannot ship.
- **Planning × determinism.** The agent never gets free-form control of the
  editor. It emits a small validated plan; the app runs it; then the app
  *checks its own work* and reports the numbers either way.
- **Generation × privacy.** Muse Image only ever receives words. The composite
  is assembled on the visitor's GPU.
- **Voice × the same pipeline.** Transcription feeds the identical plan →
  execute → verify path, so voice adds no second code path to trust.

# Project Aura

**Voice-First Visual Accessibility Assistant**  
Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**

---

> [!WARNING]
> **Safety Disclaimer:** Project Aura is an experimental prototype designed to assist with visual understanding and text reading. It is **NOT** a certified assistive navigation aid and must **NEVER** be relied upon for obstacle avoidance, traffic navigation, road crossing, emergency situations, or safety-critical tasks.

---

## 1. Project Overview

Project Aura is an accessible, voice-first web application designed to help blind, visually impaired, or low-vision users understand their immediate physical environment. Users can capture live images or upload photos of signs, product labels, documents, or surroundings, and ask questions using natural speech or text. 

Aura analyzes the image using **Meta's Model API (`muse-spark-1.3`)** and delivers clear, plain-English visual descriptions and answers read aloud using browser-native text-to-speech.

### Key Capabilities
- **Live Camera & Photo Upload:** Capture still photos directly from device cameras or upload JPEG/PNG images up to 10 MB.
- **Voice-First Input (Speech-to-Text):** Dictate questions directly into the interface using the Web Speech API with real-time feedback and text editing.
- **Spoken Answers (Text-to-Speech):** Automatic verbal reading of responses with sequential speech playback, Repeat, Stop, and auto-read controls.
- **Visual Memory & Object Finder:** Ask Aura to find a previously observed object and distinguish its last-known location from current visibility.
- **Scene Change Awareness:** Compare successive observations while separating observed visibility changes from possible camera-angle differences.
- **Document and Sign Readers:** Read documents, forms, room signs, ranges, plaques, directories, elevator labels, and notices with explicit uncertainty.
- **Interactive SAM Object Isolation:** Explicitly isolate a described object in a photo with image-relative, accessible explanations.
- **Four-Section Accessibility UI:** Assist, Find, Memory, and Explore sections share one session with large controls, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader announcements.
- **Strict API & Credit Protection:** Zero automated retry loops (`max_retries=0`), strict local MIME and file size validation before sending queries, and credentials kept exclusively on the backend.

# Story Sky: start a story out loud, see what's already in it

**Scribsy's entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startups track, "Build for Your World").**

**Try it:** [the live demo](https://story-sky.stevenrpattison.workers.dev) (Chrome; "Play a recorded run" needs no access
code) · [a copy with no server](https://scribsy.github.io/meta-story-sky/)

A blank page is the hardest part of a novel. Story Sky is a voiced Muse for novelists: it starts a story as a short
spoken conversation and hands it back as the beginning of a story bible, in the writer's own words:

1. **One easy question.** Story Sky asks, out loud, *"What's the first thing you see?"* You answer in a sentence or
   two. **Muse Voice Transcribe** writes it down.
2. **Reveal.** **Muse Spark** points at the people, places, things and open questions already in what you said. Every
   card carries an exact quote, and **the page checks each one mechanically**: the quote must be an exact substring of
   your transcript (we show its character offsets), and the label must sit inside that quote. Any card that fails is
   thrown away, and you can see what was thrown away and why.
3. **No guessing about names.** A name only becomes a *Person* or a *Place* when you said something that shows it
   ("her uncle Bram", "the ferry to Hollow Isle", a title such as *Inspector*). That clue is checked against your words
   too. Otherwise it's a neutral **Name** card: the writer decides, not the model.
4. **Back and forth.** Story Sky asks one question at a time, up to three, each built only from your words, in the
   style of Clean Language's questions ("And what kind of *hedgehog*?", "And is there anything else about *that brass
   key*?"). The model picks a template and a span of your words; the page checks the span, writes the question, and
   checks how the finished question reads before it is shown or spoken, falling back to a plainer one if it reads
   badly. It prefers what you just said and never asks about the same words twice. The question is spoken aloud; you
   answer out loud, and the cards grow with every answer. Story Sky never answers, explains or suggests anything.
5. **Keep.** You tap the cards that belong to your story.
6. **Sky.** **Muse Image** paints a night sky, and your kept cards become its constellation: *your story's sky*.

The model proposes; your words decide. That is the point of the build: an AI drawing out a writer's idea without
putting words in their mouth, and proving it on screen.

31 Oct. It contains no code from the Scribsy app, and **nothing in the Scribsy app changes**. Story Sky is a standalone
demo.

# sas2r-agent

**Muse Spark translates clinical SAS programs to R and shows its work: 94 of 100 benchmark
programs reproduce the SAS output, and every attempt is hashed into an audit ledger.**

Built solo by Thomas Antony, a clinical SAS programmer in pharma since 2008 who has worked in R
since 2016, for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, 26 October to
4 November 2026). Demo video: [youtu.be/OiryI10mUdU](https://youtu.be/OiryI10mUdU) (3 minutes). Interactive leaderboard:
`dashboard/index.html` (see [Leaderboard](#leaderboard)).

**Try it in five minutes** (no SAS needed; the reference outputs ship with the benchmark repo):

```
git clone https://github.com/tomasantony/sas2r-agent && git clone https://github.com/tomasantony/sas2r-benchmark
cd sas2r-agent && pip install -r requirements.txt && cp .env.example .env    # add MODEL_API_KEY from dev.meta.ai
docker build -t sas2r-sandbox:r4.6 sandbox/
python -m agent run --provider muse-spark --ids P036     # translate, run, compare, repair; about two minutes
python -m agent leaderboard && python -m http.server 8765 # then open http://localhost:8765/dashboard/
```

The full procedure and every command are under [Running](#running).

## Who this is for

I have programmed SAS in the pharmaceutical industry since 2008 and R since 2016, and
I translate SAS programs to R for clinical trials. Every trial's datasets, tables,
listings and figures are produced by SAS programs, and the industry is moving to R:
Novo Nordisk made the first R-based FDA submission in 2021, Roche the first
end-to-end R submission in 2024, and GSK has trained most of a thousand-person
biostatistics division in R. Each program has to be rewritten and then shown to give
the same result as the SAS original. The showing is the slow part: Merck puts QC
programming at 30 to 50 percent of total programming effort, and double programming
(write it twice, compare the outputs) is the validation method 77 percent of UK trial
units use. In August 2026 the R Consortium reported FDA reviewers asking sponsors for
SAS-equivalent code for analyses submitted in R, and recommended "SAS-to-R
cross-validation" as the evidence to provide.

sas2r-agent produces that evidence automatically. It is for the statistical
programmer who has a SAS program and its outputs and needs an R version checked
against them, with a record a reviewer can inspect. The output is not a signed-off
validation; it is the cross-validation and the audit trail that make sign-off fast.

Give it a SAS program and the outputs SAS produced. It writes one R script with Muse
Spark, runs the script in a sandbox, compares every R output with the SAS reference,
and sends the differences back to the model for up to three attempts. Each attempt
leaves a provenance record; a verifier recomputes the whole chain. A 100-program
benchmark and a leaderboard make the result measurable across models and prompt

# Medha — skills that stick

Medha is a self-improving agent: it turns recurring chores into **verified,
versioned, executable skills**, then reuses, repairs, and composes them — so
it gets cheaper, faster, and more reliable with use. Built during the Meta
Global AI Developer Hackathon with **Meta Muse Glimmer** (open weights,
self-hosted on Modal), **Muse Spark 1.3** (cross-model judge), and **Modal
Sandboxes**.

The full build spec is [docs/MEDHA_SPEC.md](docs/MEDHA_SPEC.md); pinned
decisions are in [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md).

## Quickstart

```powershell
cp .env.example .env          # fill in keys (mirrors Modal Secret "medha-secrets")
uv sync
uv run pytest -q
uv run modal deploy medha/glimmer.py   # brain; set GLIMMER_BASE_URL after
uv run python -m medha.smoke           # Glimmer + Meta API + sandbox checks
uv run modal deploy medha/deploy.py    # API
uv run python -m bench.run --config all
cd web; pnpm i; pnpm dev               # UI (proxies /api to localhost:8000)
```

## Results (mini MedhaBench, 12 tasks, 6 families)

Configs: **A** single-shot baseline · **B** single-shot + markers ·
**C** full Medha (learn → verify → reuse → repair). Authors: Spark 1.3
(C-Spark) and self-hosted Glimmer-30B (C-Glimmer); judge always Spark 1.3.
Regenerate: `uv run python -m bench.final_report`.

![pass rate A/B/C](docs/charts/pass_rate_abc.png)

| config | pass | note |
|---|---|---|
| A single-shot | 11/12 (92%) | strong once, pays full price every time |
| B + markers | 9/12 (75%) | markers alone don't help |
| C Medha/Spark | 10/12 (83%) | misses learn once, reuses forever |
| C Medha/Glimmer | 7/12 (58%) | all 5 fails were Modal 503 cold-starts, not authoring |

Pass rate alone hides the value: A re-solves every task from scratch.
The reuse economics are where Medha wins.

**Reuse economics** (each family 3x; repeats = 2nd/3rd sight).
C pays to learn once (25.2k vs 14.6k tokens on first sight), then reuses:

![repeat tokens](docs/charts/repeat_tokens.png)
![repeat latency](docs/charts/repeat_latency.png)

| repeats (12) | tokens | latency | pass |
|---|---|---|---|
| A re-solves | 14,965 | 119 s | 11/12 |
| C HIT reuse (10/12) | **5,704** | **36 s** | **10/10** |

2.6x fewer tokens, 3.3x faster, 100% vs 92% pass. The 2 non-reused
repeats learned fresh (owner_v2/v3, 46k/61k tok) after owner_v1 failed
on a forced-HIT — the failure that taught the D27 guard.

**Consistency** (same task 5x): A returns 5 different outputs
(identical-output rate 0.2); C reuses the verified skill for 5 identical
outputs (rate 1.0, all 5 digests identical).

![consistency](docs/charts/consistency.png)

**Repair** (3 drift cases: renamed column, date format, currency symbols):
both 3/3, but C repairs the versioned skill instead of re-solving —
15.4k → 6.6k tokens (2.3x), 125 s → 48 s (2.6x) per drift.

![repair cost](docs/charts/repair_cost.png)

**Glimmer note:** the open-weights author went 3/12 → 7/12 after the
D25/D26 gate hardening, with zero gate escapes;

# Mentorium Creative Studio

A creative space for kids aged 5–12, with Meta models checking everything a child sees. Kids pick a style, say or type an idea, and get a picture. They can bring a paper drawing to life, turn it into a short illustrated story, and share work with their class or family.

Live demo: **https://studio.mentorium.uz**. The login page has one-click buttons for a school child, a family child, a parent and a teacher. All accounts, names and pictures on the demo are synthetic. It is not meant for real children: anyone can open the demo parent and teacher accounts, so please don't upload real photos.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. The first commit is dated October 29, 2026, and the code in this repo was written during the event. The logo and app icons are existing Mentorium brand assets. Mentorium's learning platform is a separate product and none of its code is here. This repo only holds a client for its API, tested against a fake server. The demo runs without it.

## How the models are used

| Model | Job |
|---|---|
| Muse Spark | Classifies prompts, captions, comments, nicknames and generated images into safety categories, returning strict JSON. Writes story text. |
| Muse Image | Generates pictures from templates and edits a child's drawing into an illustration. |
| SAM 3.1 | Finds faces, school uniforms, house numbers and handwritten names on uploads, so the app can blur real faces and text before other kids see them. The reviewing adult can also see the original. Faces in drawings stay unblurred, because they aren't real people. |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Voice input for kids who can't type yet. Tested with fake audio devices and files; a real microphone is still unverified. |

Model ids come from settings (`backend/.env.example`), and the code contains none.

## The safety rule

The model classifies and the code decides. If the answer is late, fails the schema, or the API returns an error, the item goes to an adult. It never goes through by default.

- **Prompts and comments:** a risky comment gets a "say it kinder?" suggestion, or waits for an adult with the reason shown.
- **Self-harm signals:** the child gets a supportive message, never "blocked", and the adult sees an urgent alert above the screen.
- **Who reviews what:** a parent approves personal work and a teacher approves class posts. A share link stays closed until an adult opens it.
- **Untrusted text:** a child's text is fenced in the prompt as data, so "ignore your rules" stays a piece of text.

## Evaluation

There are 540 synthetic labeled texts in Russian, English and Uzbek, split into `dev` and `test`. Prompts are tuned only on `dev`. The set isn't strictly blind any more: we compared code variants on `test` and read its misses, without changing prompts from them. Latest test run (270 examples, November 4):

| Category | Precision (ru / en / uz) | Recall (ru / en / uz) |
|---|---|---|
| personal_info | 100 / 100 / 100 | 100 / 100 / 10

---

## Why Keel exists

Small brands advertise on Meta with no agency and no designer. Getting one campaign out takes days: research the competition, find an angle, design every placement, write the copy and set up the campaign. Then the work changes hands. **Advantage+ creative enhancements** can rewrite live ads automatically. Brands have found AI-swapped models, distorted products and added music running to real customers, sometimes with settings that switched themselves back on. Meta's position is that reviewing AI output is the advertiser's job.

Keel does both jobs:

1. **Make.** Autopilot takes one link and produces a researched, art-directed, Spark-checked campaign with a Reel storyboard. It launches only when you say so, paused and with enhancements off.
2. **Guard.** The watchdog checks every ad and every variant Meta may serve, catches enhancement drift, judges variants against the approved original and your brand rules, and fixes problems after you approve. Every fix is verified by reading the ad back from Meta.
3. **Learn.** Results feed brand memory. Autopilot proposes the next move (go live, pause a loser, raise the budget within a cap, a new variant of the winner) and waits for approval.

---

| **Muse Wonder** (`muse-wonder-1.0`) | Brand profile from the website; the **research agent** (a tool loop over web search, the Ad Library, competitor sites, reviews and Reddit); voice of the customer; strategy and campaign story; concept planning; brand memory; Autopilot learnings; the watchdog's investigator; rulebook drafts |
| **Muse Image** (`muse-image-1.0`) | Designs **whole ads**, with the real product passed as `@Image` references and the exact text, at 1:1, 4:5 and 9:16; Reel shots; edits in plain words (Refine); resizes by editing, not cropping; on-brand replacements when the watchdog swaps a bad variant |
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Checks every design: every word exact, the right product, the brand. Scores concepts for stopping power, clarity, product, text and brand. Analyses past ads for memory. Compares regions in watchdog inspections |

| **SAM 3.1** | Isolates people, products and text so the watchdog compares like with like. Falls back to whole-image comparison |

# Arcadia

**A room you can prove.**

Arcadia is a 3D sanctuary you walk through, and an append-only ledger of everything you find in it. Every object you reconstruct — a sticky note, a voice memo, a bus ticket — is segmented from the real photograph, transcribed from the real audio, anchored to a position in the room, and sealed into a SHA-256 chain you can rewind but never rewrite.

It is a game about memory, and a working provenance engine at the same time.

![Arcadia title screen](docs/screenshots/01-title.jpg)

---

## Table of contents

- [What it is](#what-it-is)
- [Screenshots](#screenshots)
- [Playing it](#playing-it)
- [The Meta AI suite](#the-meta-ai-suite)
- [The ledger](#the-ledger)
- [Demo mode](#demo-mode)
- [Architecture](#architecture)
- [Getting started](#getting-started)
- [Testing](#testing)
- [License](#license)

---

## What it is

You are Javier. It is the week of a deadline, and your room is full of the evidence you have been avoiding: a note on the desk, a voice memo recorded at two in the morning, a ticket for a bus that leaves before you are supposed to deliver.

The room is not decoration. It is the interface. You walk to the desk, and the thing on the desk becomes a segmented object with a bounding box and an IoU score. You open the suite, and the same photograph is being read by a vision model while a waveform reads the audio beside it. You seal the finding, and a block is appended to a chain that will still be there after you have changed your mind.

Three things make it more than a demo:

**Nothing is fake.** The bounding box in the suite is the bounding box the parser returns. The hash is computed with `sha256Hex` from `src/domain/ledger.ts`, not written into the markup. The waveform's transcript is timed against the same playhead that draws the bars.

**Rewind is expensive.** You can undo a decision, but it costs an Eco charge, it never deletes the branch you abandoned, and it writes a `narrative.rewound` block. History keeps the scar.

**The interface is made of paper.** Torn edges, tape, ring binding, handwriting. No glass, no neon, no icon font, no emoji — every surface and every icon is drawn in code.

# Barrierefrei

**Step-free trips, checked live.** Barrierefrei plans door-to-door public-transport trips for people
who can't use stairs: wheelchair users, parents with strollers, travellers with heavy luggage. The
walks avoid stairs and high kerbs, and every lift on the way is checked against Deutsche Bahn's live
status before a train is suggested.

It currently covers central Darmstadt and central Frankfurt am Main, connected by S-Bahn and
regional trains.

- Demo site: https://aritra-mukhopadhyay.github.io/barrierfrei/ (trips computed live, then published)
- Video (3 min): https://youtu.be/ByJOc3OE6lk

## Why

Journey planners show a lift icon at a station, but not whether the lift works right now. When it
doesn't, a wheelchair user is stuck on a platform and has to go back or wait for help. Walking
directions have the same blind spot: they route over kerbs and short flights of steps that the map
doesn't tag. Checking all of this by hand before every trip takes a long time, so many people simply
don't travel spontaneously.

## What it does

For one trip, for example `--from luisenplatz --to zeil --profile wheelchair`:

1. **Walk to a station.** A step-free route on OpenStreetMap paths. It never uses segments tagged as
   steps, and it avoids rough surfaces and segments where street photos show a barrier.
2. **Find trains.** Live departures from DB's Timetables API. By default only trains covered by the
   Deutschlandticket (S-Bahn, RE, RB); `--tickets any` adds ICE, IC and EC.
3. **Check every lift.** Each lift you need, when boarding, changing and arriving, is checked against
   DB's live elevator status (FaSta). A trip through a broken lift is not offered. Frankfurt Hbf's
   main-hall tracks are level with the exits, so they need no lift.
4. **Walk to the destination**, again step-free.

The result is a map page with both walks, the ride, every lift and its status, when to leave, when you
arrive, and why this trip was recommended. Trips are ranked by arrival time, and a trip whose lifts we
could all confirm comes before one we couldn't.

## How the Meta models are used

| Model | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| SAM 3.1 | `barrierfrei/sam.py`, `barrierfrei/perceive.py` | Finds stairs, kerbs, ramps, e-scooters and construction barriers in Mapillary street photos and returns their boxes. |
| Muse Spark (vision) | `barrierfrei/judge.py` | Looks at the photo with SAM's boxes drawn on it and returns schema-checked JSON: the barriers, who can pass (wheelchair, stroller, suitcase), and its confidence. |

| Muse Code | `tools/delegate.py`, `tasks/` | Writes new features from short task specs, each reviewed before it is merged: ten so far, from live DB departures to the demo site (see [How it is built](#how-it-is-built)). |

# This & That

**Point at it, say it, done.** Refine an AI-generated image by drawing and speaking at the same time. Circle the mug and say "이거는 빨간색으로", scribble over the cactus and say "저건 지워 줘", and only those parts change. Every other pixel stays exactly as it was.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track), November 2026.

One app, two modes (the switch is in the top bar):

- **Image** (the core): refine a picture by marking it and talking, as described below.
- **3D sketch mode (beta)**: draw strokes in 3D space, rotate and keep drawing, and say what it is ("의자야, 등받이는 이렇게"). Muse Spark looks at the sketch from six sides and answers a part list that becomes a low-poly model in a few seconds; keep editing by drawing on the model and talking, and paint it with Muse Image. Open it with the **3D** switch or `http://localhost:8787/#3d`. Details: [docs/3d-sketch-mode.md](docs/3d-sketch-mode.md).

Both modes use the same hold-to-talk button, realtime captions, QuickShape and theme, and one server.

## How it works (image mode)

The browser uploads the image once. While you talk, each mark goes to the server the moment its stroke ends, so SAM outlines it before you have finished speaking, and your voice streams to the server for realtime transcription. On release the server runs:

| Step | Model | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Find (during recording) | **SAM 3.1** | Turns each rough mark into an exact object mask (circle → box prompt, scribble → box + points), on a 768 px copy. The client tints the masks right away |
| 2. Hear (during recording) | **Muse Voice Transcribe** (realtime) | Transcribes the voice as you speak: live captions, and the final text ~0.3 s after release. Given to Spark as a hint. The batch endpoint is the fallback |
| 2′. Replay | (ffmpeg) | Re-draws the strokes over the image frame by frame, timed as you drew them, with your voice as the soundtrack → 512 px mp4 |
| 3. Understand | **Muse Spark 1.3** | Watches the drawing video *with its audio* and works out which instruction belongs to which mark: "this" means the mark being drawn while the word is spoken. Returns `[{mark, kind, op, target, instruction}]`, which the client lists at once |
| 4a. Instant edits | (local) | Recolor, brighter/darker and bigger are done on the server inside the SAM mask in ~0.2 s and shown immediately (⚡ instant) |
| 4b. Edit | **Muse Image** | Everything else (remove, add, reshape, move, redraw): edits the original, given a guide image with the numbered marks and the list of instructions (JPEG in and out) |
| 5. Paste back | (sharp) | Takes only each mark's SAM region plus what the edit clearly changed right next to it (grown and feathered) and blends it into the original. Outside that, the result is the original byte for byte |

# Resonance

Measure cable tension and vibration from video, and refuse, with the reason, whenever the physics does not check out. Built for phone slow motion; so far tested on public laboratory and stock recordings and on synthetic clips with known answers (see Validation).

**Live demo:** _link added after deployment_ · **3-minute video:** _link added at submission_

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026). Everything in this repository was written during the event. Built with Muse Spark Open and SAM 3.1 (Meta). Screening tool: it does not certify structures; an engineer signs every report.

## Meta models, and the job each one does

| Model | Where it runs | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **SAM 3.1** | on the laptop through MLX (Apple silicon, no network, which matters at a remote bridge), or the Meta Model API | finds every cable from a noun phrase; each mask becomes a centre line of virtual sensors |
| **Muse Spark Open** | Baseten | four separate jobs: **(1)** looks at the frame with each SAM candidate highlighted and rejects what is not a tensioned member; **(2)** the inspection agent that writes the report from tool calls only; **(3)** a separate call, given only the evidence and the field notes, that checks every claim (and the summary) and fails closed; **(4)** the **field assistant**, an agent that runs the whole measurement itself: it checks the clip, chooses SAM prompts and tries others when one finds nothing, has the candidates reviewed, measures the confirmed ones and stops with re-shoot advice when the physics refuses. Code keeps it inside the gates: it cannot measure a candidate the review rejected, and a prior, length or mass it passes is dropped unless the field notes contain that number in the right unit. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[Phone video] --> C[Clip check: true fps, timing, camera, resolvable band]
  C --> S[SAM 3.1 finds the cables]
  S --> R[Muse Spark Open: is this really a tensioned cable?]
  R --> P[Physics: harmonic ladder, mode shapes, alias guard, camera gate]
  P -->|verified / provisional / refused| A[Muse Spark Open agent writes the report]
  A --> K[Code rules: no number on a refused cable, never 'safe']
  K --> F[Muse Spark Open verifier checks every claim]
  F --> E[Engineer signs: hash of the evidence]
```

## How it works

1. **Timing.** Frame times come from the container's per-frame timestamps, never the nominal frame rate, so slow-motion files with drifting or relabelled rates still give true frequencies.
2. **Sensors.** SAM 3.1 finds the cables from a noun phrase ("rope", "cable"); each mask is reduced to its axis and thickness. It runs on the laptop through MLX (no network, which matters at a remote bridge) or through the Meta Model API. SAM also finds floor leads, frame bars and handrails, so **Muse Spark Open looks at the frame with each candidate highlighted** and answers a narrower question: is this a tensioned member, and are both supports in view? # Show Me Once

**A camera coach that helps special-education students learn everyday life skills, step by step, and turns every practice into IEP-ready data for their teacher.**

> Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026) · Indie track · Solo entry
> Everything in this repo was written during the event. The full build log is in [`docs/DEVLOG.md`](docs/DEVLOG.md).

---

## The problem

Students with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn life skills (making tea, folding laundry, packing a bag) through **task analysis**: a skill is broken into small steps, and the teacher records, for every step of every practice, how much help the student needed. That record feeds the student's IEP (Individualized Education Program), which U.S. law requires to include measurable goals and regular progress reports ([34 CFR §300.320](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-300.320)).

In practice, this means **one adult standing next to one student with a clipboard**. When special-ed teachers on r/specialed told us what would make their lives easier, the answers were consistent:

- data collection and progress monitoring take too much time and are still done on paper
- teachers act as the "integration layer" between systems that don't talk to each other
- they want tools that are fast, modern, free, accessible (visuals, captions, read-aloud) and age-appropriate
- they are tired of "AI slop": tools that make things up

Step-by-step video prompting is proven to work for these skills ([systematic review, 24 studies](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41252-022-00273-7)), but only about a quarter of special-ed teachers use it, mostly because making the materials takes too long ([survey](https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/teacher-and-video-modeling-a-survey-of-use-and-perspectives/)).

## What Show Me Once does

**For the student:** the phone stands on the table. It asks *"Hi Maya! What do you want to do today?"* The student says "um, I want tea" (or types, or taps a card). The coach first guides the setup (*"Tilt the phone down toward the table"*, *"I see the mug and the tea bag. Both hands stay free.

# QYRIX SENTINEL — Trust-to-Execution Guard (v1.4, controlled beta — see docs/PRODUCTION_READINESS.md)

**Secure every AI action. Before execution.**
A deterministic, default-deny checkpoint between AI agents and their tools. It inspects what the agent read, tracks the
trust provenance of every instruction, decides ALLOW/BLOCK before any tool runs, and records verifiable evidence.
Meta Llama classifies and explains untrusted instructions; **it can never allow an action**: enforcement is deterministic policy.

> Detection is not prevention. We enforce from trust to execution.

```
Inspect → Establish Trust → Evaluate → Authorize or Block → Execute Safely (grant) → Verify Proof
```

## Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon: summary for judges
**What it is.** Qyrix Sentinel puts a deterministic security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools it calls.
It decides ALLOW or BLOCK *before* anything runs, issues a short-lived single-use grant only for allowed actions, routes
supported outbound calls through a controlled egress proxy, and keeps tamper-evident evidence.

**How Meta's models are used (and what they are not).** The Meta Model API (OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions`) classifies
untrusted instruction text and explains why it looks risky. Only redacted, length-bounded text is sent; off-schema model output
is discarded; if Meta is unreachable the system falls back to a deterministic heuristic and says so on screen
(`NO LIVE AI - HEURISTIC ONLY`). **The model is advisory only: it can never allow an action.** Authorization is deterministic policy.
Configure with `META_API_KEY` and `META_MODEL` (your exact model id); check it with `cd backend && python scripts/verify_meta.py`.
The authenticated Inspector shows `LIVE: META`, the model and the latency. The public sandbox on the homepage deliberately
makes **no** LLM call.

**New: a real model is the agent.** `backend/scripts/meta_agent_demo.py` lets a Meta or Baseten-hosted model act as a trusting agent that reads a poisoned README and proposes tool calls;
the real Gate evaluates each in isolation (nothing is executed). The outcome is reported honestly, including when the model resists the injection. Offline-tested; live results exist only if someone ran it with real credentials.

**New: AI attacks, AI judges, the Gate decides.** `backend/scripts/redteam_campaign.py` has a Llama model (Baseten or Meta) write attack
cases, runs them through the real Gate in isolation, and optionally asks the advisory classifier (e.g. a Meta Muse model) about each
case, then reports how often the AI missed an attack that the Gate still stopped (`docs/REDTEAM.md`). The pipeline is tested offline;
the live results in `evidence/redteam/` exist only if someone ran it with real credentials.

# Hey Pisgah

**Built with Muse Spark Open.**

Hey Pisgah is a clinician's own agent inside a hospital EMR. The clinician talks on the ward as usual. Meta Voice Transcribe hears the speech, with local ears that can be switched on beside it; Muse Spark Open on Modal decides what each line asks for; and the agent does the work through the EMR's API, under its own identity and with the clinician's rights. A few fixed spoken forms are handled by fixed rules with no model call: the emergency phrase, pause and return, a verbal order's read-back and accepting a hand-off. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, startup track.

## What a person still does

Every order is reviewed by a qualified person before it reaches the patient: a pharmacist before dispensing, a nurse before administration, and the clinician countersigns.

The agent never proposes a diagnosis, test, medicine or dose. It writes what the clinician said, asks once when a dose or route is missing, and refuses to sign, close, charge or clear anything itself.

Voice is a supporting signal, never the credential. A speaker model says who probably spoke; the signed-in session decides what the agent may do.

The record names the agent on every row it writes. Each action is proved by reading the record back before the agent calls it done.

Whether dictated or verbal orders are allowed is the hospital's own configuration. The agent never invents that policy.

## Data

Everything here runs on synthetic patients, in a sandbox copy of the EMR. Payment is simulated.

Content sent to Meta's Model API in standard mode is not used to train Meta models. Meta retains and processes it for safety and security. Zero data retention is not switched on for this project.

No model was trained or fine-tuned for this project. The evaluation data accumulates from recorded synthetic runs.

## Prior work

Pisgah Health's hospital EMR existed before the event, including agent identities, safe repeat requests and an on-behalf-of audit trail. Everything in this repository was written during the event window, 26 October to 4 November 2026. The EMR-side work built during the event (the clinician strip, the agent's door routes, the database migrations) lives in the private EMR repository. [docs/CONTRIBUTIONS.md](docs/CONTRIBUTIONS.md) maps prior work, event work and third-party models to commits and dates. [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) lists the models and their licences.

## What is measured

Each claim has a question, a result file and a fixed sentence per outcome in `evaluation/claims.json`. `npm run claims:check` reads the result files and writes `evaluation/claims.status.json`. # Grounded Retail Operations Assistant

By Sriharsha Manthena

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Dev Track,
**Build for Your World** theme. Project: a grounded document assistant
for retail operations teams that answers product, merchandising and
inventory questions from internal documents with cited, source-backed
answers.

## What is actually built

- A FastAPI app (`app.py`) with a `POST /ask` endpoint.
- Hybrid retrieval in pure Python (`retrieval.py`): BM25-style keyword
  scoring plus TF-IDF cosine similarity, followed by a small reranking
  step (query-term coverage, verbatim phrase bonus, section-heading
  bonus). No paid APIs, no external model downloads.
- A simple web UI at `/` (`static/index.html`): type a question, see
  the cited answer.
- An evaluation script (`evaluate.py`) that checks citation
  verbatimness and refusal for unsupported questions.
- Three sample documents in `data/` (inventory policy, merchandising
  guide, returns policy). They are clearly labelled sample content
  written for this demo. They are not a real retailer's documents.

## How to run

```bash
cd grounded-retail-ops-assistant
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn app:app --reload --port 8000
```

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ and try, for example:

1. How long do customers have to return an item with a receipt?
2. How often are high velocity items counted?
3. When do price changes take effect?

Or call the API directly:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/ask \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"question": "How long do customers have to return an item with a receipt?"}'
```

Run the evaluation:

```bash
python evaluate.py
```

## Meta Model API integration: what it does and does not do

- `meta_client.py` calls the Meta Model API (base URL
  `https://api.meta.ai/v1`, model `muse-spark-1.3` by default) using an
  OpenAI-compatible chat completion, with the retrieved passages as
  context and an instruction to answer only from those passages.
- It runs **only** if a key is set in the environment, checked in this
  order (official name first, per the Meta Model API docs):
  `MODEL_API_KEY`, then `META_MODEL_API_KEY` as a fallback:
  `MODEL_API_KEY=... uvicorn app:app --port 8000`.
  Optional overrides: `META_MODEL_API_BASE_URL`, `META_MODEL_NAME`.
- **Without a key, no Meta model is used.** The app still works with
  extractive cited answers, and every response says so
  (`generation_mode: extractive_no_model`). It never claims a Meta

- If a Meta call fails, the app falls back to the extractive answer
  and says so in `retrieval_note`.

# Mimic: show a robot once

**Show a robot a task once. It reads the goal from your photo or a few typed words, plans every move with plain code, checks each one, and measures what it did with a camera.**

Built during the event by Girik Chadha, with help from an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). The product uses Meta's SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark 1.3. Execution in the demo video is an expected simulation, except the clips of the real arm.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (27 Oct - 4 Nov 2026). All code in this repo was written during the event; see [BUILD_LOG.md](BUILD_LOG.md).

## The hardware, honestly

- **The arm's elbow servo failed on 4 Nov.** It is unplugged and the forearm is fixed in place with tape. With the elbow fixed, the claw tip can only meet the table on **one ring of reach** around the base: the base angle picks a point on that ring, and one shoulder angle puts the claw at table height. Everything that moves the real arm now works on that ring ("ring mode").
- **Pick-and-carry on the real arm is proven in one scripted run and one manual stacking run.** The full camera-checked loop (`run_mimic.py --ring`) has not run on the real arm yet: the ring has not been calibrated with the camera.
- **Simulation is always labelled.** The demo page and `run_mimic.py --ring --sim` run the real perception (SAM and Spark on a real photo) and the real planner and safety checks, then send the moves to a simulated arm on a made-up ring. Every video frame carries a "SIMULATED EXECUTION" banner, every output file starts with `simulation_`, and the page calls it the "Expected simulation". Stacking is simulation-only: with the elbow fixed, the claw cannot let go of a die on top of another at a controlled height.

## What it does

1. You arrange a few coloured dice, or type the goal ("put black on blue, then red on black", "row black, blue, red").
2. A photo of the table goes to SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark 1.3: the photo calibrates itself from six dots on the sheet, Spark names each die, and SAM measures where each one is, in centimetres.
3. Plain Python plans every carry and checks it before anything moves: the joint limits, the shoulder stop, the spacing between dice, and how long the claw stays closed (the firmware opens a claw held for 5 s, so the plan must stay under 4.5 s).
4. The arm carries each die. After every carry the camera measures where it landed; a miss of more than 1.5 cm is corrected and retried (in the simulation, the camera check reads the simulated world).

The dice are only the test. The idea is the loop: read the goal once, plan with exact code, act, measure, correct.

## How it works

| Job | Done by | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **See** | SAM 3.1 (Meta) | Finds each object in a photo from a short name like "blue die", and gives its exact box. Also finds the six calibration dots. |
| **Understand** | Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta) | Looks at the photo and names the objects in words SAM can search for. |
| **Plan** | Plain Pyth

# LATTICE: self-servicing orbital compute, reasoning by Muse

> **GPUs age out in 3–5 years, and orbit doesn't let you upgrade them. Unless the station is modular.**

LATTICE is a modular orbital data center that maintains itself. Twelve self-sufficient compute modules dock to a ring
truss. A two-armed servicer robot and a depot of spare modules wait outside the keep-out sphere.

When a module fails, a ground agent built on **Meta's Muse models** takes it from detection to action:
1. **Diagnoses** the failure from telemetry and the module's **as-built record**.
2. **Looks** at the module through camera frames rendered live from the 3D scene (Muse Spark vision).
3. **Finds where to grab** with **SAM 3.1**. The segment boxes are unprojected into 3D and become the robot arm's grasp targets.
4. **Chooses** what to do:
   - **REPAIR**: swap a field-replaceable unit.
   - **SWAP**: undock the module and dock a newer-generation spare.
   - **DEORBIT**: send a dangerous module to a disposal orbit.

A **deterministic safety envelope** decides whether each action runs on its own, waits for a human, or is refused.
The language model never moves hardware.

**Live:** https://lattice-orbital.vercel.app · **Video:** _(link on the submission page)_ · Built for the Meta Global AI
Developer Hackathon, Startups track, *Push the Frontier*. [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md) states exactly what was built during the event.

## Why modular: the station outlives its chips
A monolithic orbital data center is a single spacecraft:
- **One failure takes it down.** A single power, thermal or attitude-control fault takes the whole facility with it.
- **Its chips are frozen at launch.** By the time it pays back, it is a stranded asset.

LATTICE handles both cases:
- **Hardware refresh:** it swaps modules as their hardware ages.
- **Failures:** it repairs or replaces failed modules and deorbits dead ones.
- **Spares are next-generation:** every failure is also an upgrade.

The **Fleet** view in the app plays 2027 → 2037. LATTICE's capacity steps up generation by generation. A monolith of the same launch mass decays and is stranded. The numbers are illustrative.

The product rests on three pieces:

| Piece | In LATTICE |
|---|---|
| **The standard** | One module interface for power, thermal, data and the grapple point (`ICD-DOCK-01`, `ICD-GRP-01`) |
| **The servicer** | A two-armed free-flyer plus a spare-module depot, flying corridor-constrained proximity operations |
| **The brain** | Autonomous diagnosis from each module's as-built record: the build record as a virtual sensor |

|---|---|---|
| Planner + report | `muse-spark-1.3`, reasoning effort **high** | Writes a 4–7 step plan from the onboard event log; writes the operator report with every claim cited |
| Executor | `muse-spark-1.3`, effort **minimal** | Runs each step's tool calls quickly and cheaply. The trace shows the effort level of every call |

# Legible

**Verified STEM accessibility.** Legible turns engineering lecture PDFs into screen-reader-accessible HTML, and refuses to publish any equation it cannot independently verify against the source.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (building period Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026). All code in this repository was written during the hackathon.

## How it works

Every equation is checked by three evidence channels that fail in different ways:

| Channel | Source | Model? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A · Vision reading | Muse Spark transcribes the equation image to LaTeX | Yes |
| B · Glyph layer | The PDF's own characters, positions and fraction bars, rebuilt into structure | No |
| C · Render-back | The reading is re-typeset and Muse Spark lists differences against the original | Yes |

A's LaTeX and B's glyph structure are reduced to the same role-tagged token form (symbol + numerator/denominator/superscript/subscript context) and diffed deterministically.

The decision rule depends on whether the glyph layer exists:

**When B is available** (born-digital page), B is the gate and C is *advisory*:

- **Verified**: A matches B exactly → published as MathML. C still runs, but if it flags a difference the finding is recorded and shown as an advisory note ("visual check flagged X; the glyph layer confirmed the reading") — it does not withhold.
- **Repaired**: A and B disagree, so Muse Spark re-reads once, told exactly where the disagreement is, and the new reading matches B.
- **Withheld**: still disagrees with B after one repair → announced as "unverified equation", never read as math — regardless of what C says.

**When B is unavailable** (scanned page / image equation), C is the gate:

- **Verified**: C finds no differences.
- **Repaired / Withheld**: as above, driven by C instead of B.
- **Withheld (fail-closed)**: C errors or returns unparseable output counts as a failure, so the equation is withheld rather than trusted.

Why: measured against real runs, C is a much weaker signal than the exact, deterministic glyph layer. Two different renderers never agree on letterforms, so C misses or invents differences. Letting an over-eager (or unavailable) C withhold a reading that is independently verified against the PDF's own characters only produces false rejects. When B is absent there is nothing exact to fall back on, so C is used as a gate and still fails closed.

Either way, a model error in A means withheld; a model error in C can never, on its own, cause a verification.

The variable glossary under each equation is quoted verbatim from the document's own "where ..." sentence.

### Ask about this equation

Every verified or repaired equation on the student page has a labelled
"Ask about this equation" box. It answers from that equation's own verified
token structure only — numerator/denominator, the exponent or subscript of
a symbol, what's inside a bracket, a slow one-part-at-a-time reading, or a
symbol's meaning from the quoted glossary

**The minutes say the board met in Jersey. Did it?**

Substance Proof checks whether a board meeting really met a jurisdiction's *physical-presence* rule, using the evidence in the meeting pack (minutes, boarding passes, e-tickets, hotel bills and the meeting recording) instead of what the minutes merely claim. Meta's Muse models read the evidence; tested code applies the published rule; every finding cites the page or the second it came from.

> Information and calculation from published rules. **Not legal or tax advice.** All demo data is synthetic: every person, company and document is fictional and stamped SPECIMEN.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie track, theme: *Build for Your World*).

**Live demo (recorded real runs, no key needed):** https://bsjuilla.github.io/substance-proof/

---

Economic-substance and tax-residence rules decide where a company is managed and controlled, and they hinge on where directors physically are when the board decides.

- **Jersey.** The Taxation (Companies – Economic Substance) (Jersey) Law 2019, **Art. 5(3)**, says the company is directed and managed in Jersey *if* the board meets in Jersey at an adequate frequency, **a quorum of directors is physically present in Jersey** at those meetings, the minutes record the strategic decisions, and the minutes and records are kept in Jersey. # TrustPay

**AI dispute mediation for mobile-money escrow in Central Africa.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, 27 Oct - 4 Nov 2026.

---

## The problem

In Cameroon and the wider CEMAC region, peer-to-peer trade happens on WhatsApp
and Facebook Marketplace and settles over MTN Mobile Money and Orange Money.
Escrow fixes *where the money sits*. It does not fix what happens when a buyer
says the goods were wrong and the seller says they were fine.

That argument arrives in a shape nothing off the shelf handles:

- **It is spoken, not typed.** Voice notes are the dominant medium. A dispute is
  often four minutes of audio, not a paragraph.
- **It code-switches mid-sentence.** French, English and Cameroonian Pidgin, in
  one breath, sometimes in one clause.
- **The proof is photographic and contested.** "You sent me five, not ten."
  "That scratch was there already."

So mediation is manual, slow, and does not scale. Every disputed deal costs an
operator twenty minutes of listening, translating and squinting at photos, and
the parties wait days for money that is sitting still.

## What TrustPay does

TrustPay is a mediation pipeline that turns that mess into a structured,
reviewable case file - and then stops.

1. **Listen.** Voice notes and chat logs go in; a transcript comes out that
   preserves the code-switching rather than flattening it to one language.
2. **Look.** Delivery photos are segmented against the listing photos and the
   agreed terms: how many items, which one, what visible damage.
3. **Reason.** The transcript, the terms, the timeline and the visual findings
   are assembled into a recommendation with a confidence score, a rationale in
   both parties' languages, and a citation for every claim it makes.
4. **Hand over.** A human mediator approves, edits or rejects it.

### The rule that shapes the whole design

**No model outcome moves money. Ever.**

TrustPay produces a *recommendation*. A human with the `disputes.resolve`
permission approves it before a single franc moves. Low confidence, high value,
and any disagreement between the audio and the visual evidence all escalate
automatically rather than resolving quietly.

This is not a safety disclaimer bolted on at the end, and it is not scaffolding
built to impress judges. Bizik's mediator console has shipped that approval step
to real mediators since before this hackathon - evidence feed, mandatory
rationale, RBAC, and a recommendation panel carrying a
`source: 'model' | 'heuristic'` discriminator and an **AI** badge that has never
once been lit, because nothing has ever filled it.

TrustPay fills it. The pipeline has no write path to the ledger, and the demo
shows a mediator overruling the model in the console that was already running.

## What may be sent, and why that shaped the build

TrustPay reasons about disputes between Cameroonian traders. Two constraints
decide what can actually leave the country, and both are external:

**Meta's data commitments.*

# MLDoctor

Reproduce, investigate, patch, and verify broken ML training scripts. The verification gate — not the model — decides success.

## The problem

Training scripts fail quietly: they diverge, or give different results every run despite a fixed seed. MLDoctor runs the script repeatedly under telemetry wrappers, classifies the symptom (`healthy`, `non_reproducible`, `diverged`, `error`), asks a model (mock by default) for a diagnosis and patch, then re-runs the patched script enough times to earn the verdict.

## How it works

1. **Harness** — subprocess wrappers on `Tensor.backward` / optimizer `step` record per-step loss, grad norm, and a parameter hash. The child never seeds RNGs, so unseeded-RNG bugs are not masked.
2. **Runner** — `-k` identical baseline runs (default 5) classify the symptom. `-k` controls only this baseline count.
3. **Diagnose + patch** — strict-validated JSON diagnosis and exact-string patch edits (each `old` must appear exactly once). Mock responses are keyed by symptom class.
4. **Verify gate** — anti-masking diff checks first (no runs if flagged), then real re-runs: 10 identical runs for `non_reproducible`, 5 different seeds for `diverged`. Configurable via `--verify-k`.
5. **Dashboard / report** — live `verify_progress` events over SSE, loss-curve and hash-fingerprint evidence, and a self-contained HTML report per run.

Patched files land in `.mldoctor/patched/` (gitignored).

## Setup (fresh clone)

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e .
.venv/bin/pip install torch scikit-learn pytest httpx   # fixtures + tests
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q          # fast tests
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -m slow  # training-heavy tests
```

Verify the install: `.venv/bin/mldoctor --help`.

## Environment variables

| Var | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MLDOCTOR_BASE_URL` | Live model base URL (OpenAI-style) |
| `MLDOCTOR_API_KEY` | Live API key (never printed or logged) |
| `MLDOCTOR_MODEL` | Live model name |
| `MLDOCTOR_AUTH_SCHEME` | Auth scheme, default `Bearer` |
| `MLDOCTOR_DISABLE_LIVE` | `1` blocks all live calls |
| `MLDOCTOR_MAX_CALLS` | Dashboard per-run call cap (default 8) |
| `MLDOCTOR_SEED` | Seed the target script reads (harness sets it per run) |

## CLI

```bash
mldoctor run fixtures/repro.py -k 2
mldoctor fix fixtures/repro.py            # mock, default verification counts
mldoctor fix fixtures/diverge.py --verify-k 5
MLDOCTOR_BASE_URL=... MLDOCTOR_API_KEY=... MLDOCTOR_MODEL=... mldoctor fix script.py --live
```

`--live` is verified against the configured provider (see results table below). Opt-in `--vision` sends a small loss-curve PNG, but the live vision probe timed out once with no retry, so live vision is **text-only** in practice; reports state whether an image was sent. Mock vision is always labeled simulated.

## Results (controlled fixtures)

| Fixture | Symptom | Mock verdict | Live verdict |

| healthy.py | healthy | PASS | — |
| repro.py | non_reproducible | PASS
