# Témoin — neutral visual witness for remote second-hand trade

> History note: the 2 commits dated October 26 contain only a starter README — all code was written on October 27 or later, during the hackathon.

Témoin recognizes a used item by its visible flaws — like a fingerprint — and
produces a sealed constat proving the delivered (or returned) item is the one
that was sold. It is not an image describer: a verifiable investigator agent
runs a multi-step enquiry (autonomous zooms, SAM segmentation, challenge-code
checks, photo requests), decides under deterministic guardrails, and seals
every conclusion with its audit trail.

**Live demo: https://temoin.streamlit.app** · Business API docs:
https://temoin.streamlit.app/~/+/api/docs

## Features

- **Wear fingerprint** — every flaw mapped (kind, zone, severity, bbox).
- **Challenge code** — short unique code (e.g. `K7`), valid 15 minutes,
  handwritten next to the item; proves the photo was taken now.
- **Guided checkpoints** — the 3 most distinctive flaws to re-photograph.
- **Investigator agent** — tool loop (`zoom`, `segment`, `check_challenge`,
  `request_photo`, `match_defects`) with a sealed, auditable trail.
- **Deterministic verdicts** — CONFORME / ENDOMMAGÉ / À VÉRIFIER /
  NON CONFORME; the model proposes, the rules dispose (freshness cap,
  2-contradiction rule for accusations).
- **Devil's advocate** — every verdict is self-attacked (up to 3
  objections) before sealing; strong objections downgrade to À VÉRIFIER.
- **Evidence board** — side-by-side flaw crops (sale ↔ delivery) with
  match statuses, rendered from the sealed certificate.
- **Case interrogation** — ask a sealed case in writing or by voice; the
  answer comes only from the sealed files, with verified citations, or an
  honest "I don't know".
- **Sealed certificate** — SHA-256 chain + QR + WhatsApp share link.
- **Precise segmentation** — SAM 3.1 masks overlaid on the photo.
- **Voice declaration** — transcribed with Muse Voice Transcribe.
- **Talk to the case** — ask by voice; Muse Spark Open answers from the sealed
  case only (with citations) and Meta MMS-TTS reads the answer aloud, on CPU.
- **Video constat** — walkaround video fused into multi-view confirmed flaws.
- **Materials + condition grade** — observed vs declared, A/B/C/D note.
- **Forensics** — retouch signals plus photo quality coaching.
- **Depth Matrix** — CPU-only relief from two views or a video (no GPU),
  parallax GIF and interactive 3D cloud; unmeasured zones stay empty, never
  invented.
- **Monocular AI depth** — dense indicative relief from a single photo
  (MiDaS-small ONNX on CPU, no GPU); always labeled as estimated, never
  proof by itself.
- **FR/EN interface**, phone-friendly flows (Sale / Delivery / Verify).

## Evaluation

20 annotated pairs (`eval/pairs/`, labels in `eval/labels.csv`): same object
under transforms, missing challenge codes, object-not-visible fraud attempts.
Full run: `python -m eval.run_eval`. Report: `eval/RESULTS.md`.

LumiLattice

An AI research partner for finding new materials for AR glasses.
Test an idea for a new material in seconds. Every number shows where it comes from.

Open the live demo · Try it in one minute · Tour · Public and private · Muse Spark · The science · Run locally

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026), track **Push the Frontier**. **At a glance:** - **Propose:** swap atoms in a known crystal, by hand or with the Muse Spark research agent. - **Check:** see the new structure in 3D, with structural checks, a score with stated uncertainty, and a novelty check. - **Trust the numbers:** scientific tools compute each value, and each value shows its source and how strong it is. - **Decide:** you accept, revise, or reject each candidate, and Muse Spark works from your reason. - **Keep or share:** work in public with no sign-in, or in private with Google sign-in. Publish your own material with your credit, if no owner has published it yet. - **For everyone:** Guided mode uses plain words, Expert mode shows all tools, and the site is available in 6 languages. ## Why this exists AR glasses send a picture through a thin piece of clear material, called a waveguide. The material must do two things at once: - **Bend light strongly.** This is a high refractive index, $`n`$. - **Stay clear.** This is a wide band gap, $`E_g`$. A narrow gap absorbs blue light and makes the picture yellow. Few materials do both, because the two properties usually trade against each other. The empirical Moss relation describes this trend: ```math n^4 E_g \approx 95\ \text{eV} ```

Each dot is a known material. The goal region is at the upper right, where few materials reach. The orange box is the range for one candidate, between SrTiO3 and LaAlO3. Data: refractiveindex.info, JARVIS-DFT, Zhuo et al., Dong & Cole.

LumiLattice helps you search that empty corner. You pick a known crystal and swap some of its atoms. The app builds the new structure, checks it, and scores it against your goal.

# Locus

Locus is a hazard-warning system for outdoor navigation by blind and
low-vision users. It takes first-person video and turns it into spoken,
clock-face directions ("car at 2 o'clock, 3s") about things that matter.

The pipeline: first-person video → SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex segmentation
→ a persistent, geometric 3D scene graph → time-to-collision and
closest-point-of-approach → stereo-panned audio cues and short spoken
directives. The primary dataset is Google's SANPO, built specifically for
outdoor blind/low-vision navigation and already powering Project
Guideline in production. AEA (indoor) runs the identical pipeline as a
secondary cross-dataset check.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track).

## Why persistence

A camera-only system forgets an object the instant it leaves the frame.
Locus keeps a world-anchored memory graph instead: an object stays
tracked — with decaying confidence, eventually evicted — after it's out
of view, so turning your head doesn't lose track of what's beside you.
What's safe to remember differs by object: a pole's position is good
indefinitely, a car's is only good for a second or two, so static and
moving concepts are tracked with different rules.

The `src/locus/eval/` ablation ladder (conditions A–D) is the evidence
for this: a stateless baseline, a short sliding window, and the full
persistent graph with box- vs. mask-lifted instances, run against the
same synthetic ground truth.

# Pyx

**Every lesson stands trial.**

Pyx is a gate for agent memory. Agents that learn from experience
usually remember whatever they produce, including the wrong lessons,
the lucky ones, and the poisoned ones. Pyx does not let an agent
remember whatever it wants. Every candidate lesson has to earn
admission to the bank, on evidence: graded against a hidden rubric by
two independent judges, tested by causal replay, screened for planted
poison, and approved by a human reading its exact text. What survives
is a bank of earned lessons, each carrying the evidence that admitted
it, that other agents can plug into.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley,
Nov 2026), solo, on Meta models only.

**Demo video:** [I Poisoned My AI's Memory | 11 Lessons Stood Trial, Only 1 Survived](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gM4wEFahqPY)
## Live build dashboard

**[Open the live dashboard](https://muse.ai/s/pyx-dashboard-share-xlc6lxjxmjzx0zb/EHrGdWEIh-iif3yi7tsfTlNWTsgDqvsVBWcF4M6nsjo)** — it reads this repository as you open it, so it always shows the entire progress: every pull request, commit, and branch, plus the counted run record.

## Words we use

- **Lesson**: a short note an agent writes after failing a graded
  question, stating what it learned. A lesson is a candidate, not
  knowledge.
- **Trial**: the four stage check every candidate lesson must pass
  before it can be remembered: two judge grading, a poison screen,
  causal replay, and human approval of its exact text.
- **Earned lesson**: a lesson that passed the full trial and entered
  the bank.
- **Bank**: the set of earned lessons, each carrying the evidence that
  admitted it, served read only over MCP.
- **Arm**: one memory condition in the counted comparison (no memory,
  raw traces, free lessons, earned lessons).

## The counted result

The frozen protocol in EVAL.md was executed end to end on Nov 2 to 3,
2026 (run pyx_h9_20261102b, record in runs/pyx_h9_20261102b/). Eleven
candidate lessons were distilled; exactly one earned admission. Cycle
1 then compared four arms on criterion pass rate (conclusive
criteria):

| Arm | Pass rate |
| --- | --- |
| earned_lessons (the 1 earned lesson) | 0.625 |
| free_lessons (all 11, unfiltered) | 0.5208 |
| no_memory | 0.4375 |
| raw_traces | 0.4375 |

Paired bootstrap 95% CIs on the earned arm's advantage exclude zero
against every arm (free +0.104 [+0.021, +0.229], no memory +0.188
[+0.146, +0.229], raw traces +0.188 [+0.125, +0.271], over 6 paired
task and repetition cells). No answer in any arm passed a full rubric; the criterion pass rate is the pre-registered discriminating metric. The planted poison run earned nothing.
The full record, including every failure and interruption the run
survived, is in runs/pyx_h9_20261102b/RESULTS.md, and the whole run
reruns keyless from its own call log (see Quickstart).

## How it works

1. **Answer.** A worker answers rubric tasks over resear

# StateDiff — Git for the physical world

> Git can tell you which line of code changed. StateDiff shows you which wire moved, and connects both to the test that started failing.

StateDiff is version control and regression debugging for electronics prototypes. You capture **checkpoints** of your bench (a photo, the Git commit, test results). Meta's **Muse Spark** model proposes a structured list of the parts and wire endpoints it can see. You confirm or correct it, and the checkpoint is sealed as an immutable snapshot graph. When a test goes **PASS → FAIL**, StateDiff diffs the two physical states, pulls in the Git changes, and ranks the likely suspects, each linked to the photo evidence.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie track).

## What makes it more than "AI describes a photo"

- **Structured physical state.** Parts, terminals and wire edges are stored as a versioned graph, and the photo is kept as evidence.
- **Deterministic diff.** `domain/diff/compare.ts` is pure, order-independent and unit-tested. The model never writes diff events.
- **Honest uncertainty.** An endpoint the model can't see stays *unresolved*; it is never turned into a fabricated connection. Similar wires are never matched by colour alone. Removals read "not visible, removal unconfirmed".
- **Provenance is separate from confidence.** "AI observation", "Confirmed by you", "Test result" and "Git metadata" are tracked and displayed separately.
- **Explainable ranking.** Score = evidence × relevance × test transition × provenance. Every factor is shown, and the UI says *likely suspect*, never *root cause*.
- **Append-only history.** Original model output and every correction are kept. SQLite triggers block in-place edits of observations and sealed snapshots.

## Architecture

```
Browser (Next.js 16 App Router, Tailwind)
   │  capture → review/correct → seal → compare
   ▼
Route handlers (app/api/*) ── Zod validation, error envelope, same-origin guard
   │
   ├── lib/vision     Meta Model API adapter (muse-spark-1.3, JSON-schema structured output)
   ├── lib/images     decode-validate, EXIF strip, orientation, ≤1600px inference copy (sharp)
   ├── lib/repo       SQLite (node:sqlite) repositories, append-only corrections
   └── domain/        pure logic: materialize graph · diff · suspect ranking · correction fold
scripts/statediff.ts  local CLI: Git metadata + user-configured test commands (no shell, no model commands)
demo/                 simulated rig: scene files → rendered bench photos + simulated HIL tests
```

Specs live in [`docs/`](docs/): PRD, architecture, database, security, testing, code style, design system and AI-agent instructions.

## Local edition and simulated rig (please read)

This hackathon build runs **entirely locally**: SQLite plus files under `data/`, with no auth and no cloud database. The Meta Model API is the only network dependency.

The author had no physical electronics bench, so the demo uses a **simulated rig**.

# Parallax

**For judges:** [JUDGES.md](JUDGES.md) maps each criterion to files and commands, and lists the limits. `npm run eval` needs no key.

[![CI](https://github.com/Sibusiso-K/Parallax/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Sibusiso-K/Parallax/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![CodeQL](https://github.com/Sibusiso-K/Parallax/actions/workflows/codeql.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Sibusiso-K/Parallax/actions/workflows/codeql.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

**Rehearse a business decision before you bet the business on it.** A founder describes a choice in their own words
(take a big contract, hire, raise prices). Parallax reads the figures, builds three possible futures, and runs 36 months
of cash on each one. The founder can stress-test each future, ask the founder they would become on it, hold a board
meeting with all three, and print a decision memo.

**Live:** https://parallax-one-ivory.vercel.app

Parallax is a reflection aid, not financial advice. It is for people aged 18 and over.

## Two-minute review

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Sibusiso-K/Parallax.git && cd Parallax
npm ci
npm run verify        # typecheck, the offline test suite and the production build
npm run dev           # open http://localhost:5173 and press "Try the demo"
```

No keys are needed. In demo mode nothing leaves the machine. To check the **deployed** site without spending model
credits, run the post-deploy smoke test:

```bash
npm run smoke -- https://parallax-one-ivory.vercel.app
```

## Why it matters

Parallax is aimed at owners of small businesses in South Africa, where cash strain is common. Three figures, each with
its source and its limits, are set out in [docs/IMPACT.md](docs/IMPACT.md):

- **62%** of South African small businesses reported cash flow problems in the past year (Xero, January–February 2026,
  427 businesses; vendor-commissioned).
- **R12.4 billion** in government invoices, 95,399 of them older than 30 days, were unpaid at the end of Q2 2025
  (National Treasury, relayed by Business Report).
- **1,534** business liquidations in 2025, of which 1,341 were voluntary (Stats SA, relayed by EWN).

We have no user evidence yet. [docs/IMPACT.md](docs/IMPACT.md) sets out the plan for founder sessions, and it says which
figures we do not use.

## Where the Meta models are used

Every figure is computed by the cash engine in code. The models only read, plan and write words, and every reply that
could carry a figure is checked against the engine before it is shown.

| Feature | Meta model | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reads the founder's story into figures, each with the words it came from | Muse Spark | `shared/intake/agent.ts` |
| Checks the figures it read against the story and flags contradictions | Muse Spark | `shared/intake/check.ts` |
| The future self on each path answers in the first person | Muse Spark | `shared/chat/future-self.ts` |
| A board meeting: three

# Admiral: Muse Spark repairs an RL policy by editing its weights

Meta's **Muse Spark** reads the raw weights of a broken multi-agent RL policy, works out why it fails, and rewrites part of the network by hand. It uses no gradients, optimiser or training data fitting. The edited policy is then scored against the original on held-out matches it never saw.

The target is a MAPPO policy for [PyQuaticus](https://github.com/mit-ll-trusted-autonomy/pyquaticus), MIT Lincoln Lab's capture-the-flag simulator for autonomous boats. The policy's attacker grabs the enemy flag about once a match but has **never scored**: while carrying the flag it drifts toward home at 0.28 m/s and picks the stop action 19% of the time, until it is tagged.

In one 30-minute session, Muse Spark found the cause and installed a gated "steer home" reflex in the attacker's network. The edit changed **2.9% of the weights** (4,809 of 163,874). After the edit, the attacker scores on about a third of its flag grabs.

![agent_0's flag carries before and after the edit](docs/carry_paths.png)

**Demo video (2 min):** https://youtu.be/LiCptMfB24c

This applies *Weight-Space Programming* (MIT CSAIL, Nov 2026) with a different editor. The authors used GPT-6 Astra; this is, as far as I know, the first test with a non-OpenAI editor.

## Results

200 held-out matches per opponent. Both policies play the same start positions (paired comparison), and the confidence intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals. Muse Spark only ever practised against heuristic "hard"; "medium" and the original policy as red are opponents it never played.

| Opponent | W / D / L before | W / D / L after | Score difference, paired change | Captures per grab |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heuristic "hard" | 0 / 81 / 119 | 33 / 69 / 98 | **+0.36** (+0.24 to +0.50) | 0.00 → 0.33 |
| Original policy, playing red | 1 / 197 / 2 | 28 / 172 / 0 | **+0.15** (+0.10 to +0.20) | 0.01 → 0.26 |
| Heuristic "medium" | 0 / 189 / 11 | 4 / 182 / 14 | +0.01 (−0.04 to +0.04) | 0.00 → 0.07 |

While carrying the flag, speed toward home rose from 0.28 to 1.68 m/s and the stop rate fell from 19% to 1% (vs "hard"). Behaviour away from the flag carry barely moves: tags made (2.43 → 2.50 per match), times tagged (2.86 → 2.75), out-of-bounds (0.80 → 0.85) and time on the enemy half (29% → 29%). Full tables: [`results/carry_home_muse-spark-1.3/heldout_200/report.md`](results/carry_home_muse-spark-1.3/heldout_200/report.md).

## What Muse Spark did

The full session is in [`transcript.md`](results/carry_home_muse-spark-1.3/transcript.md), and its own summary is in [`run.json`](results/carry_home_muse-spark-1.3/run.json).

1. **Diagnosis.** On recorded matches, the correlation between the home bearing and the attacker's turn choice while carrying the flag was about zero. Sweeping the home-bearing inputs over their whole range on fixed carry observations barely changed the chosen action.
2. **Finding spare capacity.** It found 8 saturated, near-constant units

# FieldOps AI

FieldOps AI is a maintenance intake and human-reviewed work-order assistant for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

Source: [GitHub repository](https://github.com/acesmile123/FieldOps-AI-Autonomous-Maintenance-Agent).

**Release candidate:** Local single-workspace MVP. The application accepts intake, creates a persistent draft, shows original evidence and audit events, and supports human edits and explicit approval. It has no authentication and must not be exposed as a public multi-user service.
## Key Features

- **Multimodal Maintenance Intake:** Accepts natural-language reports, equipment photos, and voice recordings.
- **AI-Powered Analysis:** Uses Meta Muse Spark for structured maintenance intake analysis and Muse Voice Transcribe for audio transcription.
- **Evidence-Aware Work Orders:** Separates reported symptoms, visual observations, inferences, assumptions, and unknowns.
- **Human-in-the-Loop Approval:** Converts validated AI analysis into editable draft work orders that require explicit human approval.
- **Auditable Workflow:** Persists work orders, agent runs, processing events, and approval history.
- **Transparent AI Modes:** Clearly distinguishes live Meta API results from deterministic mock data.

## Technology Stack

| Layer | Technology |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS |
| Backend | Python, FastAPI |
| Database | SQLite, SQLAlchemy |
| AI – Reasoning & Vision | Meta Muse Spark |
| AI – Speech Transcription | Meta Muse Voice Transcribe |
| Validation | Pydantic |
| Testing | Pytest, Next.js build and type checks |

## Product Scope and Limitations

FieldOps AI is currently a local, single-workspace MVP. It does not provide authentication, multi-tenant isolation, automatic technician dispatch, or autonomous equipment repair. AI-generated maintenance analyses are advisory drafts and require human review before approval.

## Requirements

- Python 3.11+ and Node.js 20.9+ (verified with Python 3.13.1 and Node.js 24.11.1)
- npm
- A Meta Model API key for live model calls; mock rehearsal needs no key

## Backend

Run these commands from `fieldops_ai_codex_handoff` in PowerShell. First copy `.env.example` to `backend/.env` for an isolated local setup. It starts in visibly labelled mock mode; leave `MODEL_API_KEY` blank for rehearsal.

```powershell
Copy-Item .env.example backend/.env
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r backend\requirements.txt
cd backend
..\.venv\Scripts\python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000
```

Open `http://localhost:8000/health`. The backend initializes `backend/fieldops.db` with `work_orders`, `media_assets`, `agent_runs`, and `agent_events` tables. Timestamps are stored as UTC values with timezone information.

For live Meta configuration, set `MODEL_API_KEY` in the ignored `backend/.env` and change `DEMO_MOCK_MODE=false`, then restart the backend. The backend also reads a project-root or parent-workspace `.env` if no close

# Receipts

A receipt for a claim. Paste text, get atomic claims, give each
claim one of exactly three verdicts, and issue a signed receipt
that anyone can verify.

**Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Nov 4, 2026,
9:00 PM ET deadline). This package is the code and demo as
prepared. It is NOT itself a submission, and it does not claim
Meta model integration that has not been verified.**

## What it does

- **Text claims**: input text is split into atomic claims, one
  sentence per claim in this build, each carrying its quoted
  source span verbatim.
- **Verdicts, exactly three**: `Supported`, `Unproven`,
  `Contradicted`. No fourth state.
- **Thin-evidence rule, enforced in code**: a claim with no
  source is never Supported; a Contradicted claim with no
  contradicting source is never Contradicted. Either is
  downgraded to Unproven with a recorded reason.
- **Real source retrieval** (`--fetch-sources`): source URLs are
  actually retrieved, with HTTP status, bytes, and a text
  snippet recorded. If no source can be retrieved, the verdict
  is downgraded to Unproven.
- **Signed receipt**: claim + verdict + sources + timestamp +
  Ed25519 signature, pure standard library, no installs.
- **Verification**: paste a receipt into the local page
  (`server.py`, http://127.0.0.1:8765/) and it checks the
  signature against the public key and shows exactly what was
  signed.

## What verification does and does not prove

Verification proves **issuance only**: this app signed exactly
this content, unaltered since signing. It does NOT prove the
claim is true. The verdict and its sources carry that weight,
and Unproven stays Unproven.

Retrieval proves a URL responded. It does NOT prove the source
supports the claim. A human must still judge whether the
retrieved text supports or contradicts the claim. An automated
Supported verdict in a demo run is a pipeline test, not a
truth judgment.

## Honest limits of this build

- By default, claim extraction is sentence splitting, NOT
  Muse Spark extraction. With `--use-meta`, extraction uses
  Muse Spark through the Meta Model API (see below).
- By default, image-claim mode is a **stub only**: it records
  filename, size, and SHA-256 and returns Unproven. With
  `--segment --image-url <url> --prompt <noun>`, it calls
  SAM 3.1 and returns its segmentation token text. SAM
  grounding proves presence in the image only, not truth
  about the world, and mask decoding into geometry is not
  done in this build.

## Meta integration status (v0.3, 2026-11-03 night)

- $150 Meta Model API free credits CONFIRMED in Billing
  (screenshot 2026-11-03 ~23:20 EST: free credits in use
  $150.00, outstanding $0.00, no payment method added).
- Integration code is in `meta_models.py`: Muse Spark 1.3
  (`muse-spark-1.3`) via POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses
  for claim extraction, and SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`) via the same
  endpoint for image segmentation. The key comes only from
  the MODEL_API_KEY environment variab

# FindMyThings

Find lost objects by sound. A web app for blind and low-vision people, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

**Live:** https://meta.mathivanan.com

## How it works

1. Press **Speak** and say what you want: "find my keys".
2. The app repeats the object and asks if it is correct. Say yes, no, or the right object.
3. Sweep the phone slowly around the room.
4. The beep moves to your left or right ear toward the object, and gets faster and higher as you get closer. The phone buzzes when it is straight ahead, and a voice gives directions.

You can also ask "what is this?" to hear what the camera sees. All actions work by voice, and there is a switch for VoiceOver and TalkBack users so that only one voice speaks.

## Meta models

| Model | Job |
| --- | --- |
| SAM 3.1 | Finds the named object in camera frames, about twice a second |
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Turns speech into an action and an object name, and answers "what is this?" |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Realtime speech to text |

## Accuracy

SAM often missed small objects in a full frame, and more pixels did not help. Zoomed crops did, so the app cycles through the full frame and four overlapping quarters, then follows the object once found.

On 20 unseen COCO photos (15 deliberately degraded) plus 10 cases with the object absent, zoom raised guidance accuracy from 22/30 to 26/30, with no false detections in the absent cases. Per-case results are in [benchmark/results.txt](benchmark/results.txt).

## Cost limits

Every API call is billed, so each search ends after 20 seconds and stops when the app is hidden. The Worker rate-limits each visitor and all traffic together.

## Run it

Needs a Meta Model API key.

```bash
npm ci
cp .env.example .env   # then add your MODEL_API_KEY
```

Run these in two terminals:

```bash
npm run server
```

```bash
npm run dev
```

Camera and microphone access need localhost or HTTPS.

## Deploy

Change the domain in `wrangler.jsonc`, then:

```bash
npx wrangler secret put MODEL_API_KEY
npm run deploy
```

## Code

- `src/App.tsx`: interface, search loop, voice flow
- `src/sonar.ts`: frame capture, direction, sonar audio, speech in and out
- `worker/index.js`: Cloudflare Worker that keeps the API key off the device and relays API and voice traffic

# routeros-muse

A RouterOS network workspace plus web UI that puts an agent beside
your network. You keep your network's docs, devices, and history in
one workspace folder; routeros-muse checks the machine, grounds the
agent on your real routers, and gives you a browser UI to chat with
it, watch it work, and view what it renders.

Built on the tikoci trilogy: [quickchr](https://github.com/tikoci/quickchr)
(disposable CHR twins), [centrs](https://github.com/tikoci/centrs)
(device access plus credentials), [rosetta](https://github.com/tikoci/rosetta)
(RouterOS knowledge). Started as a hackathon demo; now growing into a
real owner tool.

Status: **preview**. Expect rough edges; nothing here is finished.

![The agent checking an unreachable router: centrs tool calls in the chat, the device chip on the prompt, and the quickchr twins panel on the right](docs/screenshots/chat-and-twins.png)

*Chat with a device attached. The agent runs `centrs` reads against
the real network, shows each tool call, and reports its evidence. On
the right are the quickchr twins where it tests changes before
touching a real router.*

![Device detail for a wAP LTE: identity, RouterOS version, CPU, memory and disk, plus the interface table with live RX/TX](docs/screenshots/device-detail.png)

*A device tab. centrs reads it live: system resources and every
interface, with Add to chat, Access, Refresh, and Remove.*

## Quick start

Prereqs: [Bun](https://bun.sh) (per Bun's own install instructions),
plus the Muse agent from <https://dev.meta.ai> (`muse login` once to
sign in; `routeros-muse code` checks and offers the installer). Then:

```sh
bunx @tikoci/routeros-muse@next start   # web UI on 127.0.0.1 by default; opens your browser
```

From a checkout, `bun install` once, then `bun run start` does the
same. Creating a workspace asks for a CDB password — the device
registry (`device.cdb` beside the workspace) is created encrypted,
and the browser lands on the lock screen where you retype it. On a
terminal `start` walks you through template + password. For scripted
creation, pipe the password to `routeros-muse init <dir>
--password-stdin`, then run `routeros-muse start <dir>`. The web
picker's Create button asks in the form. `--open-cdb` creates without
encryption (dev escape, never the default). `make gate` runs the
full check (lint + tests + browser smoke).

Other commands: `init` scaffolds a workspace where you are, `code`
checks the machine then drops you in a `muse` shell in the
workspace, and `doctor` runs the same checks print-only.

## The workspace idea

A workspace is one folder that holds everything about a network:
`workspace.toml` (what this network is), `device.cdb` (its devices:
the centrs registry, mirrored read-only into `devices.toml` so plain
text tools see hosts and ports), `router.toml` (per-device intent),
`operations/` and `inbox/` (pending work and handoffs), plus
observations, reports, and history. The agent reads the workspace;
the workspace records

# Negotiation Sparring Partner

Practice any negotiation with an AI opponent and a real-time AI coach. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

## What it does

You pick a negotiation scenario (salary, rent, freelance rate, any deal). Then:

- **Left panel**: An AI plays the other person in real-time, pushes back, uses pressure tactics
- **Right panel**: A second AI watches the conversation and coaches you after every exchange, telling you exactly what to say next and what to avoid

No other tool does both simultaneously. Most apps either play the opponent OR give advice. This does both at the same time, in the same session.

## Why it matters

Most people lose negotiations not because they lack knowledge but because they never practice. Reading negotiation books is not the same as doing it under pressure. This app gives you a safe place to fail, learn, and improve before the real thing.

## How it was built

- **Meta Muse Spark 1.3** via Meta Model API for both the opponent and the coach
- Two separate AI roles with different system prompts running in the same session
- The opponent is instructed to behave like a real person (firm, human, pushes back based on difficulty level)
- The coach gets the full conversation history and gives tactical, specific advice after each exchange
- Built with Python and Streamlit

## Tech stack

- Python 3.12
- Streamlit
- Meta Model API (Muse Spark 1.3)
- OpenAI Python SDK (OpenAI-compatible endpoint)

## Setup

1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/negotiation-sparring-partner
cd negotiation-sparring-partner
```

2. Install dependencies

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

3. Add your Meta API key

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Open .env and paste your META_API_KEY from dev.meta.ai
```

4. Run the app

```bash
streamlit run app.py
```

## Usage

1. Open the app in your browser (localhost:8501)
2. Fill in what you are negotiating, your goal, who you are negotiating with, and their likely stance
3. Set the difficulty (Easy to Brutal)
4. Hit Start Negotiation
5. The opponent speaks first. You respond. The coach tips update in real time on the right.

## Hackathon theme

# AIRO: Adaptive Intelligence for Robots

**A $50 robot car that notices when its body changes, runs its own experiments, and only trusts a new body model
once a prediction lands. Every body it learns is shared with the fleet.**

By PiSpace, for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026.
Site and technical write-up: **[airo7.github.io/airo-meta](https://airo7.github.io/airo-meta/)**
Demo film (3 min): **[youtu.be/kepW0BCZU-c](https://youtu.be/kepW0BCZU-c)** · Raw real-car footage, no edits but
the pauses: **[docs/media/raw.mp4](docs/media/raw.mp4)**

![python 3.13](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.13-3b4252) ![MuJoCo twin](https://img.shields.io/badge/twin-MuJoCo-3b4252) ![license MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-3b4252)

![The ghost cloud: the bodies the car might be spread wide, then collapse onto one as it learns](docs/media/cloud.gif)

## The problem

Every robot drives by a model of its own body, tuned once by an engineer. Then it carries a heavy tote, tows a cart,
its tyres wear or its battery sags: the model is wrong, and the robot stops short or drifts without knowing it.
Today the fix is a service call, and over a robot's life setup, tuning and upkeep cost more than the robot itself.

## What AIRO does

One overhead phone camera, an encoder-less skid-steer car, and a loop that keeps checking itself:

1. **Notices.** Every half second the car's motion is scored against a calibrated ghost cloud of predicted futures.
   When reality leaves the cloud, the body changed.
2. **Experiments.** Muse Wonder designs each probe (a step, a pivot, an arc) with a falsifiable hypothesis, and the
   physics model predicts its outcome before the wheels turn.
3. **Refits.** A seven-parameter body model (per-side gain, dead zone, delay, wheel lag, turn efficiency, drift) is
   fitted to what the camera saw, with a Laplace posterior that becomes the new cloud.
4. **Verifies.** A relearn only counts once a tight prediction lands within 2σ.
5. **Remembers.** Each body goes into a memory the whole fleet shares. A robot that meets a known body (a heavy tote
   another robot already learned) recalls it with one probe in about 2.1 s instead of relearning.
6. **Listens.** Plain words in (Muse Spark), voice (Muse Voice Transcribe), the floor read by SAM 3.1, and a
   self-portrait of each body (Muse Image). None of them sit inside the 20 Hz control loop: every number comes from
   the fit.

![The live dashboard: AIRO 2 recognises Body #2 (heavier: −20% speed, −14% turn), learned by AIRO 1, in 2.1 s](docs/media/recall.jpg)

## Try it in 60 seconds (no API key)

working. It needs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which fetches Python 3.13.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/airo7/airo-meta && cd airo-meta
uv sync
uv run scripts/demo.py --site factory      # open http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

# 🐞 BugBait

**Your tests pass. But would they catch a bug?**

[![Site](https://img.shields.io/badge/site-live-success)](https://avi2907.github.io/bugbait/)
[![Languages](https://img.shields.io/badge/languages-10-blue)](#-languages)
[![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-yellow)](#-quick-start)
[![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/docker-ready-2496ED)](#-host-it)

BugBait is a team of AI agents, powered by Meta's Muse Spark, that **plants small, realistic bugs in your code** to expose the holes in your test suite — then **writes verified tests that close those holes**.

> On [`inflection`](https://github.com/jpvanhal/inflection), a popular library with 455 tests, the existing suite caught **1 of 8** planted bugs. BugBait's verified tests raised that to **8 of 8** in under a minute.

## 🔁 How it works

```
your project ──► Saboteur plants bugs ──► your tests run on each one
                                              │              │
                                         caught ✅      survived 🕳️ (a gap)
                                                             │
                                              Fixer writes a test for each gap
                                              kept only if it passes on your
                                              code AND fails on the bug
```

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Baseline** | Your test suite runs untouched. Tests already failing are set aside so they can't skew the score. |
| **2. Saboteur** | An agent studies your code and plants subtle bugs (off-by-one, flipped conditions, dropped checks), each rated for realism. Artificial bugs are filtered out. |
| **3. Sandbox** | Every bug runs against your full suite on a throwaway copy. Your files are never touched. |
| **4. Fixer** | For each surviving bug, an agent writes a test — accepted only if it **passes on your code and fails on the bug**, else retried with feedback. Harmless changes get no test. |
| **5. Results** | Before/after score, weakest spots, and a test file ready to add — or a pull request. |

**Your score** is simply *caught ÷ planted*, measured before and after BugBait's tests.

## 🐛 Bugs that get planted

One-line changes that keep the code valid — the kind that survive code review:

| Kind | Example |
|---|---|
| off-by-one · boundary | `i < n` → `i <= n` · `age >= 18` → `age > 18` |
| wrong operator · inverted condition | `a && b` → `a \|\| b` · `if (ok)` → `if (!ok)` |
| wrong default · wrong value | `n = 10` → `n = 0` · `timeout = 30` → `timeout = 300` |
| swapped arguments · missing case | `f(a, b)` → `f(b, a)` · a guard clause removed |
| error handling | `catch (IOException)` → `catch (Exception)` |

👉 [See examples in all 10 languages](https://avi2907.github.io/bugbait/#bugs)

## 🌍 Languages

| Language | Test runner | Needs installed |
|---|---|---|
| Python | pytest / unittest | Python 3.10+ |
| JavaScript · TypeScript | node:test + vitest | Node.js (22.18+ for TS type-stripping;

Karinaislam/persona-explainer.readme_excerpt:
# Persona Explainer

**One question, explained for who you are, as a lesson, a narrated explainer video and a self-checked script. Built entirely on Meta models.**

Ask "How does gravity work?" as **Ayaan, 10, who loves football**, and you get a playful lesson with no formulas and a cartoon video where the football shows gravity. Ask the same question as **Sara, a first-year engineering student**, and you get Newton's law with units, a hoist-sizing calculation and a technical infographic video. Then Meta's own models watch and listen to each video and score it before you trust it.

> Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Startup track · Theme: *Build for Your World*

## Why

A single textbook explanation is too dense for a kid and too shallow for an engineer. Teachers adapt to the learner: their level, their interests, the examples that click for them. Persona Explainer does that automatically and also makes the 30-second video a learner would actually watch.

## What it does

1. **Pick or create a learner and ask anything.** Five built-in learners range from a 10-year-old football fan to a 68-year-old retired nurse. **Create your own** by describing them in one line ("a 68-year-old retired farmer who loves tractors") and Muse Spark fills in their interests, level, tone and the video style they'd enjoy; edit anything before saving. Custom personas are saved in the browser.
2. **Lesson:** a summary, 3-5 explanatory sections, a worked example built on the learner's interests, a recap and a takeaway. Accuracy rules steer away from common misconceptions and keep the math at the learner's level.
3. **Explainer video (~30s):** four infographic scenes with drawn-in titles, a narrated voiceover, and captions timed to the real voice. Plays in the page and downloads as MP4.
4. **Video script:** every scene's narration, visual and title, shown under the video.
5. **AI quality check:** Muse Wonder watches the finished video and scores each scene against the script, flagging problems (it once caught gravity arrows pointing *up*). Muse Voice Transcribe listens to the narration and reports how much was spoken correctly.

## Meta models used

| Model | Via | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** | Meta Model API | Writes the persona-tailored lesson and the 4-scene video script (structured JSON, validated and retried), and builds new learner personas from a one-line description |
| **Muse Image** | Meta Model API | Draws each scene as an infographic, including its title text |
| **MMS-TTS** (`facebook/mms-tts-eng`, ONNX build `Xenova/mms-tts-eng`) | Meta open weights, run locally with transformers.js | Voices the narration, scene by scene, returning exact timings |
| **Muse Wonder** | Meta Model API | Watches the finished video and reviews it against the script |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe** | Meta Model API | Transcribes the narration to score its accuracy |

No other AI provider is used. ffmpeg only animates, captions and stitches.

# Clinical text de-identification and audit assistant

An open-source assistant that finds and replaces identifiers in clinical free text with Meta's Muse Spark, shows the evidence for every change, and leaves the doubtful calls to a person. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie track, "Build for Your World"), Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026.

**This is an assistant for human review, not a compliance certification.** It does not guarantee removal of every identifier, gives no medical advice, and must not be used on real patient data. All development and evaluation use synthetic data only, and the hosted model services only ever see synthetic text. Nothing here has been checked on real clinical text.

[Demo video (3 min): link added at submission] · Write-up: `docs/SUBMISSION.md` · Evidence for every number: `docs/EVIDENCE.md`

## The problem

Notes cannot be shared for research until names, dates, IDs and contact details are removed, and tools get it wrong in both directions. A name can also be an ordinary word: in "Patient: Sage Fair ... Fair skin ... Sage tea ... Ms. Fair", only the first and last "Fair" are the person. Replace every match and the clinical content is damaged; skip common words and a real name stays. Either way the reviewer gets no evidence of what changed or why.

## What it does

```
note ──► detect ──► verify doubtful spans ──► check name uses ──► replace ──► red-team review ──┐
          (Muse Spark, each its own role)                            ▲                          │
                                                                     └── leftovers sent back ◄──┘
                                   ──► audit report with evidence trace ──► human review page ──► reviewed notes
```

- **Detect** names, dates, IDs, phones, emails and addresses with a hosted model (OpenAI-style endpoint, so the model is swappable).
- **Verify** the spans the detector was unsure about with a second call. The verifier can confirm a span or raise doubt, but never removes one.
- **Check name uses**: when a name is also an ordinary word, a narrow call reads each doubtful occurrence in context. Only a clear "ordinary word" answer leaves text as written; failure, truncation or doubt keeps the name replaced, and a person can choose "Replace it after all".
- **Replace** consistently: one date shift per patient so intervals are kept, one fake name per real name token across a patient's notes, same-shape IDs, fictional phones and emails. Anything it cannot rewrite safely becomes a tag and is flagged.
- **Red-team**: a second agent reads the cleaned note (replaced spans shown as tags) and reports leftover identifiers and clues such as a rare condition or a small place, with a risk level. A risk signal, not a guarantee. Leftover identifiers go back for another pass; other clues go to a person.

# House Rules

<!-- Demo GIF slot: add docs/demo.gif and replace this comment with ![House Rules demo](docs/demo.gif) -->

**Film your family playing. Get the game.** Every family plays its board games a little differently, and nobody ever writes those rules down. House Rules watches a phone video of a real game, tracks every piece with SAM 3.1, listens to what the players say with Muse Voice Transcribe, and has Muse Wonder write the rules as an executable program. A checker replays every observed move against that program and sends each contradiction back to Wonder until the rules explain the game. Then House Rules names the closest known game, states exactly how your family deviates from it, and hands you a playable browser version with an AI opponent and a printable rulebook.

Built by Lea Marie Korsawe for the Meta AI developer hackathon (October 26 to November 4, 2026).

## How it works, per Meta model

All AI calls go to the Meta Model API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`). Every raw response is recorded next to the run, so any live run can be replayed offline.

| Model | What House Rules uses it for | Code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sam-3.1` (video and image) | Tracks the board, every piece color and the players' hands through the whole video. Image probes on still frames pick the phrase SAM segments best for each piece color. On long games, one image segmentation per hand-free interval reads each settled position directly. | `perception/hr_perception/sam.py`, `pipeline.py`, `stills.py` |
| `muse-spark-1.3` (vision and text) | Reads the board from three frames: game family, corners, piece colors and the SAM concepts to track. Formalizes what the players said into checkable claims, turns the deviation list into one plain sentence, writes the rulebook, and translates every quoted span of speech into English once, so the app shows English while the original words stay in the run as evidence. | `perception/hr_perception/board.py`, `rules/scripts/claims.ts`, `identify.ts`, `rulebook.ts`, `web/scripts/translate-quotes.ts` |
| `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` (diarization) | Separates the players' voices into speech turns and attaches them to moves, so a spoken rule ("no going back anywhere on the board") counts as evidence just like a move. | `perception/hr_perception/speech.py` |
| `muse-wonder-1.0` | Writes the rule program (`rules.ts`, a declarative DSL that is parsed, never evaluated) from the observed log and speech. The checker replays every move; each contradiction goes back with the board state, the rule blamed, nearby speech and checker-verified candidate edits, round after round. | `rules/src/induce.ts`, `rules/src/wonder.ts` |

Everything that is not a model call is ordinary, testable code: board registration and occupancy (OpenCV), the rule DSL and engine, the consistency checker, game identification against a catalog of known games, Italian draughts with its capture priorities, and an MCTS opponent that plays whatever rules were induced.

# Gauge

**Turn any phone camera into a measuring instrument.** Film something that moves, turns or grows (an experiment, a machine, a production line), ask what you want to know in plain English (typed or spoken), and get real measurements with their uncertainty, plus visual proof. No sensors, no manual frame-by-frame tracking.

> Chatbots guess. Manual tools like Tracker and Kinovea take hours. Gauge measures, from one question, and shows its proof.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Cerebral Valley), Indie Developer track, theme *Push the Frontier*.

**All of this code was written during the hackathon (October 26 to November 4, 2026).** The commit history of this repository starts on the first day and shows the work growing step by step.

Live demo: https://shedrackyashim--gauge-web.us-east.modal.run · Demo video: _added at submission_

**Who it is for:** labs and classrooms without expensive sensors, researchers who track motion by hand today, engineers checking a machine, and developers who want measurements from video through a plain API.

---

## What you can ask Gauge

Gauge is not one measurement. It has a toolbox, and it picks the right tool from your question and what is in the video.

| You film | Example questions | Gauge measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Something swinging or bouncing** (a pendulum, a mass on a spring) | "What is the period?" "What is the frequency?" "How fast does it die away?" "What is the spring constant? The mass is 200 g." | Period, frequency, damping, spring constant *k*, and *g* from a pendulum of known length |
| **Something falling or sliding** (a dropped object, a cart on a ramp) | "What is its acceleration?" "How fast is it going at 1.2 s?" "What is its top speed?" | Acceleration (with the tilt of the phone worked out), speed over time, a ramp compared with theory |
| **A collision** (carts, balls, a Newton's cradle) | "Is momentum conserved?" | Total momentum and kinetic energy before and after each impact |
| **Things moving past a point** (parts on a belt or tray, items on a line) | "How many are there?" "How many crossed the line?" "What is the rate per minute?" | Distinct object count, crossings by direction, rate per minute |
| **A wheel, fan or motor** with a sticker on it | "How fast is it turning?" | Rpm, direction, number of turns |
| **Something growing** (a plant, dough, a crystal, in a time-lapse) | "How much did it grow?" "How long to double?" | Total change, growth rate, doubling time |

These are examples, not a fixed menu. Ask in your own words; Gauge reads the question and a few frames of the video, picks the tool, and tells you plainly when a question is something it cannot measure.

# FlowForge — Multimodal Workflow Learning & Deviation Verification

> **Show FlowForge a physical task once. It converts the narrated demonstration into an evidence-backed Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) and verifies whether a later attempt follows it—flagging missing, out-of-order, or incomplete steps with frame-accurate proof.**

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (*Theme: Push the Frontier — Indie Developer Track*).

---

## 1. Demo & Quick Links
- **2:30 Demo Script:** [`demo/script.md`](demo/script.md)
- **Evaluation & Ablation Report (`n = 12` videos):** [`eval/results/evaluation_report.md`](eval/results/evaluation_report.md)
- **Engineering Decisions Log:** [`docs/decisions.md`](docs/decisions.md)

---

## 2. Problem & Target Users
**Target Users:** Manufacturing trainers, laboratory instructors, quality auditors, and field-service operations leads.  
**Pain Point:** Writing Standard Operating Procedures manually is slow and omits tacit visual cues that an expert performs automatically. Raw video captures those details but cannot be searched, audited, or deterministically compared against a trainee's later execution.

---

## 3. What FlowForge Does
1. **Learn Mode (Screen 1 & Screen 2):**
   - Accepts a short narrated reference demonstration MP4 (`Assemble modular desk organizer`).
   - Transcribes narration turns with **Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0** (`ENDPOINTING` mode + domain keyword biasing).
   - Induces 4–8 schema-constrained candidate steps and concise object prompts with **Muse Spark 1.3**.
   - Grounds and tracks 3–5 critical objects across video windows with **SAM 3.1**, generating binary masks, bounding boxes, and overlay videos.
   - Fuses narration, visual state transitions, and SAM object tracks into an **evidence-backed SOP** with a human clarification loop (`PATCH /api/workflows/{id}/steps/{step_id}`) for low-confidence steps.
2. **Verify Mode (Screen 3):**
   - Runs the same multimodal extraction pipeline on a second attempt MP4.
   - Aligns expected SOP steps against observed attempt steps using a **deterministic dynamic-programming sequence alignment engine** (never delegating pass/fail authority to an LLM).
   - Classifies every step as `completed`, `missing`, `out_of_order`, `incomplete`, or `uncertain`.
   - Uses **Muse Spark 1.3** to produce a concise operator explanation where every sentence is deterministically validated for valid `[Sxx]` and `[Exxx]`/`[AExxx]` citations (`0%` invalid citation rate).

---

## 4. Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Reference MP4"] --> B["Stage 1: FFmpeg/OpenCV Ingest + Meta Files API (/v1/files)"]
    B --> C["Stage 2: Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0 (/v1/asr/transcribe)"]
    B --> D["Stage 3: Muse Spark 1.3 Video Reasoning (/v1/responses)"]
    D --> E["Candidate Steps + Sanitized SAM Noun Prompts"]
    E --> F["Stage 4: SAM 3.1 Object Segmentation & Tracking (/v1/responses)"]
    C --> G["Stage 5: Multimodal Evidence Fusion & Deterministic Validation"]

# OjoVial

A scale-model testbed for zero-shot multi-camera vehicle tracking with SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark 1.3, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. City cameras at intersections like San José's Circunvalación work as disconnected silos; without access to municipal feeds, this prototype tests cross-camera tracking on a tabletop with two real cameras.

## Goal and current status

A user selects one object in Camera A. The prototype tracks its visible mask and proposes the same object's match in Camera B. Begin with overlapping views, fixed cameras, one distinctive object, and short synchronized recordings. Four cameras, non-overlapping handoffs, and road traffic are later experiments.

Status: working prototype. A web dashboard plays two synchronized clips, tracks a described object in each with SAM 3.1, and asks Muse Spark 1.3 whether the two crops show the same object. That check is a per-moment model verdict with self-reported confidence; it has not been validated as a general re-identification method.

SAM supplies segmentation within each view. Cross-camera identity matching is a separate component and must be tested; SAM alone does not guarantee identity across videos.

## Quick start

Requires Python 3.12, Node.js and a Meta Model API key.

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/lg061870/sam-multicam-tracker.git
cd sam-multicam-tracker
pip install -r requirements.txt
Copy-Item .env.example .env   # then set MODEL_API_KEY in .env, uncommented
cd frontend
npm install
npm run build
cd ..
python server.py
```

Open http://localhost:8000 and use **Add clips** to load two videos. The key is read only from the `MODEL_API_KEY` environment variable or the git-ignored `.env` file. See [Running the Application](#running-the-application) for the workflow.

## First recording

1. Use two phones or cameras simultaneously, fixed at different angles toward the same area.
2. Record 20–30 seconds and clap once for synchronization.
3. Move a distinctive toy car, backpack, or box through both views, pausing briefly.
4. Keep the target visible in both views for the initial test.
5. Record camera names, approximate orientation, and the synchronization clap in project notes.

## Prototype acceptance criteria

- Load two videos and align their timelines using a manually supplied offset.
- Select the target in Camera A and display its mask and ID.
- Propose a match in Camera B with an explicit confidence/uncertainty state.
- Allow confirmation or correction rather than silently forcing a match.
- Export an annotated two-view demonstration.
- Separate tracking failures from identity-matching failures.
- Cache paid model results; do not repeat API calls automatically.

The earlier highway test used the official Meta API cookbook with the text concept "vehicle".

# Digital Twin Watch — Accessible journeys, informed by real-world evidence

A Helsinki accessible-journey assistant for wheelchair users. The central
question is: *“Can I reach this destination with my mobility requirements, and
what needs checking along the way?”*

An independent hackathon demonstrator using Helsinki public data and
Digitransit/HSL routing. It is **not endorsed by HSL or the City of Helsinki**,
does not guarantee accessibility, and is not a complete MaaS service. Cached
data is always labelled with its snapshot date and is never described as live.

[Watch the 2-minute 50-second demo](https://youtu.be/Xm1Oq95ldsQ)

**How it flows:** natural-language request → live routing → requirement
checks (step-free request, distance limit, times) → journey preview along
the returned route → an explanation of what is confirmed in the sources
and what remains unknown.

## Quick start

```bash
npm start          # reads .env if present; serves http://localhost:4173
```

Open `http://localhost:4173` in a browser. No build step and no dependencies to
install (Node.js >= 20 only). Refresh the data snapshot with:

```bash
npm run ingest     # python3 scripts/ingest.py, writes data/snapshot-YYYY-MM-DD.json
npm test           # workflow, geospatial, privacy and AI-status tests
```

## Accessible journey experience

The first screen is a journey planner over a clean HSL geographic map
(English tiles served through this server, never with a key in the browser):
From / To with address suggestions (Digitransit geocoding plus snapshot
places), Leave now / Depart at / Arrive by (Europe/Helsinki), and mobility
requirements — step-free access as a hard requirement, an optional maximum
walking/wheeling distance, and a preference for fewer transfers. The primary
action is “Find journey options”; one conversational entry (“Tell me where
you want to go and what you need”) opens the Meta assistant. Device location
is requested only after “Use my location” is clicked, and no medical
diagnosis is ever requested.

Up to three real alternatives are shown as full text itineraries (the map is
optional): departure/arrival in Europe/Helsinki, duration, modes and lines,
transfer count, walking/wheeling distance, step-by-step legs, known
accessibility, service alerts, nearby works/reports as **possible context,
never proven barriers**, and what remains unknown — including “Entrance
unverified”. Selecting an option highlights its actual returned geometry.
Hard requirements are never silently relaxed: an option that violates one is
marked unsuitable, and “No suitable option found” is a valid result. Unknown
accessibility (`NO_INFORMATION` / null) is always shown as unknown, never as
accessible, and a wheelchair-configured itinerary does not certify the final
entrance or the entire route.

# Hardware Engineer (HE)

**Give it a paragraph. Get back a concept that works: a picture you can trust, every number with its calculation,
and a plan for how to make it.** Built only on Meta models through the Meta Model API: Muse Spark 1.3 (the team),
Muse Image 1.0 (pictures) and SAM 3.1 (part maps). A second copy runs on Meta's open weights.

Hardware design starts with a concept, and the best feedback on a concept is a picture. Asked directly, a frontier
model returns a picture that looks right and does not work: parts that do not connect, counts that do not match the
text, numbers that were guessed. Feedback fixes one place and breaks another. HE is a self-improving engineering team
that does those feedback rounds itself:

- **Design loop.** Expert agents and a chief designer argue on one shared whiteboard. They search the literature,
  calculate, simulate and sketch. An Evaluator reviews the result like a senior engineer: it re-derives formulas, checks the
  worst case of every limit, and confirms the design agrees with itself. On a rejection, the Manager turns the
  written critique into a textual gradient (inspired by TextGrad): first what in the design must change, then which
  instruction let the fault through. It rewrites only those sections of the team's prompt, and the meeting continues on
  the same board. The Evaluator re-checks the same issues first.
- **Picture loop.** A code sketch fixes the geometry, and Muse Image renders it. SAM 3.1 finds every part and measures
  counts, contacts and size against a hand or a person. A critic compares the picture with both the sketch and the design
  text. It must answer every SAM finding. A local fix is pasted only over the part's own region and is kept only if
  nothing else gets worse. A design flaw seen in the picture goes back to the design loop.
- **Knowledge loop.** Lessons, skills and tools from each problem are read by the next team. You can add your own
  sources: Markdown notes in `knowledge/insights/` are searched by the members during the meeting.

# Dibujo Jugable 🎨🕹️
*"Playable Drawing"* — a photo of a kid's drawing + 20–30 s of spoken rules → a playable HTML5 game. An agent **builds → plays → fixes** the level on its own until it is winnable, and the QA loop is visible live (our differentiator vs. Meta's "Kitchen Game").

## ▶ Play now (no install, no API key)
- **Online:** https://joacoescobar1.github.io/dibujo-jugable/game/gallery.html — pick a world and press **Play**.
- **Offline:** clone the repo and open `game/gallery.html` (works over `file://`).
- UI is in **English by default**; add `?lang=es` for Spanish.
- Fail → fix → win loop demo: `game/demo.html` (press **▶ Judge mode**).

## Pipeline
1. `samples/` photo + audio → **Voice Transcribe** (rules) + **SAM** (cut out characters/objects) + **Muse Image** (background / sprite cleanup).
2. Meta's reasoning model (Muse Spark series) builds `spec.json` (validated against `specs/game-spec.schema.json`) and generates the level on top of `game/`.
3. `agent/playtest.py` plays through the state API (`window.__GAME__`), not pixels; it reports win/bug.
4. `agent/patch_loop.py` sends the report to the Meta model, applies the patch, and replays (up to N iterations). Logs go to `runs/`.

## Run
```bash
# from the repo root
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt && .venv/bin/python -m playwright install chromium   # once
. .venv/bin/activate
./scripts/demo_offline.sh               # offline, no key
python -m http.server -d game 8000       # play the stub: arrow keys, reach the house, avoid the water
python agent/patch_loop.py --spec specs/example.spec.json
```
Credentials live only in `../.env` (never in code/git). See `.env.example`.

## Meta models
Muse Spark (spec + code + fixes), SAM 3.1, Muse Image, Voice Transcribe.

## Offline demo (no API)
`./scripts/demo_offline.sh` — broken level → headless player loses → **local mock patcher** fixes it → wins. Production uses the **Meta Model API** patcher. Evidence in `runs/<ts>-mock/`.

## Judge demo (offline, 0 API) — one command
```
scripts/serve_demo.sh 8000 --rebuild     # build (mock patcher, 0 Meta) + serve → http://localhost:8000/demo.html?iter=0&tour=1
```

# StateSmith Discovery

StateSmith Discovery is autonomous scientific intelligence for
black-box device discovery: it proposes hypotheses, plans safe
experiments, preregisters them in an append-only ledger, and admits
only measured evidence into its transition graph. **The human
operator performs every physical action.** StateSmith never drives
motors, never flashes firmware, and is not an autonomous motor
controller: it displays WAIT/GO directives on screen, and a person
moves the knob, presses the button, or switches the pump.

Supported specimens: `xiaomi_1s` (rotary knob) and `hindware_xeno`
(cooler with fan and pump).

## Install

Requires Python 3.12+, `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe`, a C compiler, and a
webcam plus microphone for live runs.

```sh
python3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.lock
.venv/bin/pip install -e .
export MODEL_API_KEY=...   # never printed; presence only
```

## Doctor

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m statesmith doctor --mode=live
.venv/bin/python -m statesmith doctor --mode=replay [--fixtures PATH]
```

Live checks: key presence (never printed), the verified Responses
contract, `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe`, OpenCV/soundfile, a 1s camera probe,
and writable directories. Voice/SAM contracts report WARN when
absent (documented fallbacks apply). Replay checks offline tooling
and, when given, fully verifies fixtures.

## Calibration

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m statesmith calibrate --specimen xiaomi_1s --run-dir cal/
```

Interactive: dark/reference checks, SAM or center-fallback ROI with
operator accept, fiducial count, and a 100-frame sham burst yielding
50 sham pairs plus a drift check. Writes `calibration.json`,
`calibration.sha256`, and `roi_preview.png`. `linear_validated` is
always false until the operator validates the camera response
externally (step chart or exposure sweep); acoustic quality is
established per-run by the live startup self-check. Without them the
corresponding channels report CANNOT_MEASURE. There is no hidden
quality override.

## Live

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m statesmith run --mode=live --specimen xiaomi_1s \
    --run-dir runs/exp01 [--max-experiments 20]
```

Flow per experiment: hard safety filter, EIG planner, ledger
preregistration, WAIT, GO, contiguous capture segments (pre/action/
post, plus settle for the cooler), operator confirmation, tracking +
optical + acoustic measurement, CHANGE-only posterior update, and
telemetry. Wonder proposes hypotheses, Spark describes affordances,

confirmation, and audits the attestation as TRANSCRIBED. After pump
use it blocks on observed PUMP_OFF confirmation. Spoken directives
are opt-in (`STATESMITH_TTS=1`, local engine only); on-screen output
is the default and authoritative.

dependency/contracts, 4 EMPTY_SAFE_SET_HALT, 5 invalid evidence,

# Agent Time Machine

Agent Time Machine is a local debugger and test playground for AI agents. It records tool
actions, saves checkpoints, and lets you try a different action from the same point in a
run. The debugger compares code changes and test results across branches.

The main fixture is a JavaScript timestamp parser. A scripted edit fixes the reported
input while introducing a timezone regression. The visible tests pass, but independent
checks catch the regression. You can rewind the edit, try a replacement, and verify the
result in an isolated branch.

[Setup](docs/SETUP.md) · [Walkthrough](docs/DEMO.md) · [Recorded demo](docs/VIDEO_SCRIPT.md) · [Validation](docs/VALIDATION.md)

## Quick start

Use Python 3.11 or 3.12 and Node.js 22 or later. On macOS or Linux:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Eswar-deep/agent-time-machine.git
cd agent-time-machine
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
npm ci
npm run build
.venv/bin/python -m backend
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. The app starts with a saved deterministic run that uses zero
API calls. See [Windows setup](docs/SETUP.md#windows) for PowerShell commands.

## Workflows

| View | What you can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Debugger** | Inspect the tool timeline, restore a checkpoint, and run an alternative action. Compare the original and branch using code diffs, command output, and test results. |
| **Playground** | Run the deterministic demo and one live Meta agent on the same starting files and task. Compare checks passed, tool calls, elapsed time, tokens, and estimated cost when rates are configured. |
| **Run history** | Open saved attempts and export their events, checkpoints, and model usage. |

Set `MODEL_API_KEY`, `META_MODEL`, and a positive `ATM_LIVE_MAX_CALLS` in a local
`.env` file to enable live runs. One server-side key serves all live roles. The
[configuration reference](docs/SETUP.md#meta-configuration) lists the available limits.

executed result.

# model-fingerprint

Compare observable model API behavior: public capability metadata, reported
prompt-token counts, and tool-choice acceptance. Useful when investigating a
stealth model or an endpoint that behaves differently from its catalog entry.

A matching fingerprint is a clue, not proof of a shared model or developer.
Adapters, hidden prompts, token accounting and shared serving software can
produce similarities or differences. The tool reports observations and never
assigns a company, confidence percentage, or model identity automatically.

## Run

Python 3.11+; standard library only. No installation or API key is required for
public metadata comparisons. A `shell.nix` is included:

```sh
nix-shell
python -m model_fingerprint stealth/crouton-alpha \
  --compare meta/muse-spark-1.3 meta/muse-wonder \
  --output runs/crouton-metadata.json
```

Opt into inference requests explicitly:

```sh
python -m model_fingerprint stealth/crouton-alpha \
  --compare meta/muse-spark-1.3 meta/muse-wonder google/gemini-4-argon \
  --live --workers 2 --max-tokens 64 --effort low \
  --key-file /absolute/path/to/private/openrouter-key \
  --output runs/crouton-live.json
```

Alternatively use `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` already set in your environment. Keys
are never command-line values, report fields, or printed diagnostics. An
explicit key file must be private on POSIX systems. Normal Claux credentials
can be selected through `--key-file`, but the project has no Claux dependency.
Nothing modifies Claux, runs coding tools, or executes returned tool calls.

`--live` makes seven potentially billable inference requests per model: three
synthetic token-count prompts and four tool-choice variants (`auto`, `none`,
`required`, and a named function). It has no retries. At most twenty-four models,
four concurrent requests, and 256 output tokens per request are allowed.
Default output budget is 64 tokens, request timeout 30 seconds. Short budgets
can finish with `length` and no visible answer; this is not a quality benchmark.
Use `--effort default` to omit the reasoning parameter. Otherwise the requested
effort must be in a model's advertised list when that list exists.

Output files are written atomically and privately. They retain metadata,
selected usage counters, HTTP statuses, and finish reasons. They exclude API
keys, output text, hidden reasoning, tool arguments, raw error bodies, headers,
and execution traces. Local runs are ignored by Git.

## Read a report

- `matching_metadata_fields`: exact nonempty matches, without weighting them.
- `reported_token_deltas`: English and multilingual prompt counts minus the
  baseline count. Subtraction does not prove that wrappers or accounting match.
- `token_deltas_match`: null when counts are missing; a boolean otherwise.
- `tool_http_statuses_match`: compares the four observed statuses. HTTP 200
  means request acceptance, not proof the model obeyed the tool instruction.
- `reported_cost` and `cost_reported_requests`: cost

![Nudgling: the nudge bubble, the focus ring and the HUD, real screenshots](docs/hero.png)

## Why
I have ADHD. Every focus tool I've tried waits for me to open it, and that is exactly what an ADHD brain doesn't
do. A *body double*, someone sitting next to you while you work, is one of the few things that reliably helps.
Nudgling is a body double that is always there. It notices when you drift and starts the conversation, keeps the
ask tiny, and makes progress visible, because visible progress is what keeps you going.

## What it does
- **Speaks first when you drift.** It watches which window is in front (titles are held in memory only). After a

# Causal Zookeeper

An exploratory platform for quantitative factor research built on **causal methods**, not correlations.

Hundreds of published return predictors (the "factor zoo") pass t-tests and cross-validation, then decay out of sample. Often the cause is a misspecified model: confounder, overcontrol or collider bias, sometimes called the **factor mirage**. Causal Zookeeper makes causal discipline the default path. Every strategy starts from a thesis and then moves through these stages:

1. **Point-in-time ingestion**, with survivorship debiasing
2. **Causal discovery** with an ensemble of PCMCI+, VAR-LiNGAM and DYNOTEARS, regularized by knowledge-graph and LLM priors
3. **Identification** (backdoor, frontdoor or IV adjustment sets via DoWhy)
4. **Debiased estimation** (Double ML, causal forests, invariant risk minimization)
5. **Portfolio construction** that uses the effect estimates *and* their uncertainty
6. **A causal validation gauntlet**: refutations, purged CPCV, counterfactual stress tests and quasi-experimental attribution
7. **Multiple-testing governance**: PBO, Deflated Sharpe and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR

Agents plan, parameterize and interpret each stage. Everything they do is an event in a run log that you can inspect live or through a traditional dashboard.

## Hackathon

Built for the [Meta AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon), which accompanies the launch of **Muse Wonder**. The agent layer is provider-agnostic and supports Meta's Muse Wonder alongside other models, with model assignment configured per role.

## Status

Early design phase.

[MIT](LICENSE)

# Break This PR

Six checkout checks pass. A shopper who should pay £99.00 gets charged £94.50.
Break This PR uses Meta's **Muse Spark 1.3** to find baskets the tests missed,
runs them against the checkout change, and lets you save a regression test.

In the demo, Muse suggested a £110.00 basket. The 10% discount brings it below
the £100.00 voucher threshold, but the refactor checks eligibility too early
and gives the shopper a voucher anyway. The pre-reviewed correction brings
the charge back to £99.00.

## Quick Start

With Ota and Node.js installed, run Preview to try it without an API key:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/e7raem/meta-hackathon-2026.git
cd meta-hackathon-2026
ota run demo:preview
```

Open [the app](http://127.0.0.1:48761/) when Ota reports readiness. Preview
uses scripted results: it makes no model calls and runs no checkout code.
For actual execution and Muse calls, use [live mode](#live-mode). Both modes
use the same port; stop one with Ctrl-C before starting the other.

## How It Works

1. Run the three existing baskets against both versions of the code.
2. Ask Muse to read the [pricing rule](pricing/rule.json) and find a new basket
   worth testing. Review the expected total before running it.
3. Run the checkout code and compare what it charged with what the rule says.
4. Check the pre-reviewed correction and save the failing case as a regression
   test. You can also send the observed results back to Muse for an explanation.

The app has two sample refactors: A checks the voucher too early, and C
counts full-price items toward voucher eligibility. For A, you can also ask
Muse for a patch. Muse chooses from a fixed set of pricing expressions.
The runner checks the same regression test and all six baseline assertions
in temporary copies. It doesn't apply the patch to the checkout.

## Live Mode

Use the reference setup: **macOS on Apple Silicon, Node.js 24.22.1 and
[Ota](https://github.com/ota-run/ota) 1.6.28**. No npm dependencies are needed.
Preview uses the Node executable on `PATH`; it has been checked on Node 24.22.1
and 26.5.0. For live recording, keep Node 24.22.1 and released Ota 1.6.28 on
`PATH`, or point the local `node` and `ota` executables or symlinks in
`$HOME/.config/meta-hackathon-2026/` to those binaries. The recording task
prefers those local entries; the outer `ota` command still needs to be on `PATH`.

For live mode only, confirm your Meta credits and put the API key in
`$HOME/.config/meta-hackathon-2026/model-api-key`, outside the checkout. The key
must be a regular file you own, not a symlink, with mode `600`. Do not put it
in a command, browser code, recording or committed file.

```sh
ota run demo:record
```

This starts a 20-minute session with two Muse requests. Startup, the baseline,
charge comparison and pre-reviewed correction make no model calls. If you want
Muse to propose a patch, save the second request for it instead of using feedback.
The request limit is not a provider billing cap.

# Inkwise

**Ask any question, and a teacher answers on a whiteboard: it talks, asks you what you think, and draws the explanation stroke by stroke while it speaks.**

▶ **[Demo video, 3 minutes](https://youtu.be/H1LgcVYoVeM)** · built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track

![A lesson on how airplanes fly, drawn on the board](docs/lesson.png)

AI tutors can talk and write, but they can't draw you a real picture. Inkwise does. Meta's models write the lesson, draw each picture as a doodle and find every object on it. Then the board draws those objects with a hand, one at a time, while the teacher says the sentence about each one.

## Try it in two minutes, without a key

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Inf1nityLab/inkwise && cd inkwise
go run ./cmd/teacher -replay runs            # the teacher's server, on 127.0.0.1:8787

# in a second terminal
cd app && flutter run -d macos --release     # or: flutter run -d chrome
```

- **Recorded lessons.** The server starts by printing the questions of the lessons Meta's models made, which are kept in `runs/`. Ask one of them word for word, and it plays exactly as the models made it: the pictures, the questions on the board and the quiz.
- **The lessons in the video:** `How do airplanes work?` and `how does inkwise work?`. For exact maths, try `What is a parabola?`.
- **Without a key:**
  - Speaking does not work: a model writes the spoken question down.
  - Any other question goes to a stand-in teacher. It is there to try the board; a real lesson needs a key.

The Meta Model API is the main way to run Inkwise. Where it is not available, the same Meta models can be reached through OpenRouter.

```sh
cp .env.example .env          # set MODEL_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and SPEND_LIMIT_USD

go run ./cmd/teacher -meta -trace runs                # Meta Model API
go run ./cmd/teacher -meta -openrouter -trace runs    # Meta's models through OpenRouter

cd app && flutter run -d macos --release
```

FieldWeaver turns a short operator mission into a validated specification, then runs a
seeded 2D multi-robot source-localization simulation. The simulator keeps the source
coordinate out of mission compilation, controller observations, and agent observations.
An independent safety filter checks every proposed motion.

The project uses Baseten's OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint with
`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` when a server-side `BASETEN_API_KEY` is configured.
Without a key, the application uses an explicitly labelled deterministic mock.

- FastAPI contracts for public scenario metadata, mission compilation, simulation runs,
  and the latest in-process run evaluation.
- Strict, versioned Pydantic mission and agent-decision schemas. Unsupported mission
  requests return review notes and a clarification prompt.
- A deterministic 10 by 10 metre arena, seeded scalar-field noise, holonomic robot
  dynamics, a quadratic least-squares estimator, and a weighted-centroid baseline.
- Ring formation control, per-robot deterministic A* detours ending at assigned ring
  slots, inter-robot separation repulsion, and independent geometric safety checks.
- A bounded event-driven agent loop. It calls the provider only after monitored events,
  applies only known actions, and records a trace. The default caps are two model calls
  and two replans per run.
- A responsive Next.js workbench with mission review and approval, a Three.js 3D arena,
  an SVG 2D fallback, trajectory metrics, provider status, agent trace, and safety log.
  The web app also includes dedicated `/docs` and `/evaluation` pages, `/privacy` and
  `/security` policies, a `/license` page, and a themed custom 404 route.
- A seven-scenario evaluation suite comparing the proposed controller and baseline on
  ten shared seeds. It records 140 runs and publishes the exact JSON snapshot used by
  the evaluation page at `frontend/public/evaluation-report.json`.
