# MetaVault OSS

**Agents never see your secrets.**

MetaVault OSS is a local-first **wallet for AI coding agents**. Agents request a
scoped capability — `stripe` at `charges.read`, say — never the raw key. A
local Meta model (the **marshal**) vets each request from metadata only, the
deterministic **policy** layer enforces scope ceilings, rate limits, and
expiry, and you approve in the desktop app. MetaVault OSS then injects the
credential into that single tool execution inside the daemon (`vaultd`) and
returns only the result. The raw key never enters a chat, a prompt, a model
context, an audit row, or the desktop UI.

> Judging line: MetaVault OSS is secure even if the AI is wrong — and measurably
> safer when it is smart. The security floor is cryptography and policy; the
> model is discretion within bounds. See [Brain eval](#brain-eval) for the
> measured evidence and [Security model](#security-model) for the invariants.

# Seeva

Seeva is an eye for blind and low-vision people. It explains what is around the user, answers questions about it, and guides them to point the camera at what's worth a look ("something is on your left, turn left to check it").

It is an Expo app for Android. A small detector runs on the phone and builds a memory of the session; the Meta Model API (`muse-spark-1.3`) does the seeing and talking. Speech is recognized on the phone and answers are spoken with the phone's own voice.

## What it does

- **Tap to ask.** Tap the top half of the screen, ask, and Seeva answers out loud. Quick asks: Around me, Read text, Recap, Repeat.
- **Double-tap for a command.** Double-tap the top half (double-tap and hold with TalkBack) and say a command: "clear session", "slower", "companion on", "token limit 200 thousand", "help". Commands run on the phone, offline and without spending tokens, and Start over asks for a spoken yes first.
- **Guiding the camera.** After describing the view, Seeva can offer a look at something cut off at an edge, or ask for one when the question can't be answered from this view. The motion sensor tells it when the user has turned or tilted far enough; then it takes a new photo and says what's there.
- **Companion mode.** Seeva also describes each new place by itself, at most 10 times in 10 minutes, and never talks over the user.
- **Session memory.** Keyframes, a timeline of what appeared and left, and the whole conversation, from app open to close. Nothing is kept after the session.
- **Basic answers.** Offline, without an AI key, or over the session's call budget, Seeva says so and lists what the on-phone detector sees.
- **Accessibility first.** TalkBack support, haptic cues for every state, contrast checked against WCAG AA, and text that scales to 200 %.

## Requirements

- An Android 14+ phone with a rear camera, a gyroscope, a microphone and on-device speech recognition
- Node 22.13 or newer (`.nvmrc` pins 24), Java 17, the Android SDK

## Getting started

```bash
nvm use
npm ci
npx expo run:android      # a development build on a phone or emulator
```

Then, on the phone: **Settings → AI key**, paste a Meta Model API key and tap **Save key**. The key is kept in secure storage (Android Keystore). It is never put in `.env` or built into the app. Use a separate key you can revoke, with a spending cap.

Public configuration lives in `.env` (see `.env.example`): the provider, optional model overrides and the detector model.

## Scripts

| Script                            | What it does                                                             |

# Blockparty

A living neighbourhood life simulation built in Unity. Residents of a small
residential block wake up, go to work and school, cook, exercise, make friends
and look after their homes on their own. You can watch, guide a resident, or
just talk to the game.

Demo video: VIDEO_URL

## What it is

- A small block of houses and apartments with a café, workshop, office and
  school, starting with eight residents across several households.
- Every resident has needs, traits, feelings and relationships, and chooses
  what to do next without the player: they chat, make friends, plan parties
  with invitations, take jobs and courses, grow older and have families.
- Faces show each resident's current mood, and the HUD shows their live portrait.
- The player can pause, speed up time, select a resident, queue actions, or
  give spoken commands.
- Save and load keep the whole block, including both households.

## Meta AI inside the game

| Feature | What it does in play |
| --- | --- |
| Muse Voice natural commands | Hold the talk key and speak naturally ("Eli, go to work", "have Cara chat with Dev", "invite Bea tonight"). Muse Voice transcribes the speech and Muse Spark 1.3 maps unusual phrasing to game commands. The model only proposes; the simulation checks every command and decides. An optional "Hey Meta" activator keeps the microphone open for hands-free play. |
| Muse Spark for residents | When a resident has several good options, Muse Spark 1.3 suggests which one fits the resident's traits and situation. The engine has final authority and uses its own choice when the model is slow or the proposal is not a legal action. |
| Block Gazette | Every in-game morning a newspaper opens (or press Y) with yesterday's real events, a SAM cut-out photo and a Muse Image illustration. |
| Muse Image | Generates residents' artwork and illustrates the Gazette front page. |
| SAM (Segment Anything) | Say or type what you are looking for ("find the woman in the red shirt", "show me a bike"). SAM outlines it on screen; the game identifies what is there, then follows that resident with the camera or highlights the object and what you can do there. SAM also cuts out the photo used on the Gazette front page. |

Each AI feature runs behind a transport interface with a local fallback, so the
game stays playable without network access.

- **Accessibility.** Every action is remappable, no action needs a held key or

  reduced-motion and high-contrast cursor options.

Point your Android phone at the screen, say what you want, and Fingerpost reads the screen, finds the button and steers your fingertip onto it with tones, spoken directions and vibration. # ChainReaction

**Know what breaks before you upgrade.** Type a decision like *"upgrade numpy to 2.0"* for a public Python repo. ChainReaction reads the official migration guide with Muse Spark, traces every affected import through the code, predicts the domino chain, proves it with real before/after test runs, proposes fixes that it keeps only when the tests agree, and writes a report in which every claim is checked.

Every run is recorded, so all five presets below **replay offline with no key and no network**.

[![CI](https://github.com/Samyantak/ChainReaction/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Samyantak/ChainReaction/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

---

## Why it matters

Upgrades get postponed because nobody can say in advance what they will break. Published studies show the fear is justified:

- **Teams fall behind.** 81.5% of the 4,600+ GitHub projects studied kept outdated dependencies, and developers called updating extra effort and responsibility ([Kula et al., *Empirical Software Engineering*, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.04621)).
- **"Safe" releases break too.** 20.1% of non-major releases in Maven Central are breaking ([Ochoa et al., *Empirical Software Engineering*, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07889)). In npm, about 12% of dependent packages and 14% of their releases were hit by a breaking change from a non-major update, and 44% of those breaking changes arrived in minor or patch releases ([Venturini et al., *ACM TOSEM*, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04563)).
- **Python is no exception.** Across six popular Python frameworks, 53.6% of 5,538 client projects use APIs that had breaking changes ([Zhang et al., SANER 2020](https://zhaoxu-zhang.github.io/files/saner2020-preprint.pdf)). That count is static, so it can't say which projects actually fail. ChainReaction answers that by running the tests.
- **Bots open the PR; tests decide.** Over 70% of Dependabot PRs are merged. Developers merge when tests pass and update by hand otherwise, and only 3.4% of PRs carry a compatibility score ([He et al., *IEEE TSE*, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07230)).

ChainReaction is the step before that merge: what breaks, where, why, and a patch the tests agree with.

### Why not just ask a chat assistant?

You can clone a repo into Claude or ChatGPT and ask what an upgrade will break. You'll get a plausible guess, and it can be confidently wrong in two ways ChainReaction is built to catch:

- **It can't see what isn't in the repo.** On flask-wtf, reading the code points at its `url_encode` import. Running it shows the real first break is in the installed Flask 2.2.2, a dependency the repo doesn't contain. ChainReaction ran both environments, found that, and marked its own prediction **DIFFER**.
- **It reports what it noticed, not what's there.** Reading the NumPy 2.0 guide, Muse Spark alone caught 12 of the 65 removals. With deterministic extraction merged in and every item quote-checked, it caught all 65.

ChainReaction

# Witness

A space to preserve your memories, turn them into stories and films, and find people who have lived through something similar.

An AI interviewer follows the conversation, asks thoughtful questions, and helps turn scattered memories into stories that still sound like you — without needing to be a writer or knowing how to tell your story from the start. You choose what stays private and what you want to share.

## The idea

Memories fade unless they are kept. Witness exists to preserve personal memories and life events, and to bring together people connected by similar experiences — whether they shared one occasion or simply recognise themselves in each other across time and distance.

Everyone deserves to be heard. Behind the app is a simple belief: every person's story matters and deserves to be captured. And lived experience is global — discovering that others felt what you felt reminds us how much we share.

## What Witness is for

- **Keeping memories:** record turning points, relationships, places, and everyday moments in an ongoing journal, so they are not lost.
- **Being heard:** shape an experience into a story — or an illustrated film made from your own words — to share with family, friends, or a wider audience.
- **Finding each other:** discover people through experiences they choose to share — moving to a new country, starting over, or even being at the same concert.

A complete autobiography is one possible outcome. A single meaningful story can be enough.

Witness is also designed as an ongoing journal: optional questions help people record everyday life. Selected entries from a conversation can become an editable weekly story, with sources for each paragraph. Daily/monthly stories and real-user matching remain planned. Specific events stay in their own collection. Connect is intended to start from one of those events and reveal related stories across the globe, whether people attended the same occasion or had a similar experience in another place and time. [Journal and Connect](docs/journal-and-connect.md) describes the flow.

## The first experience

Choose a memory or a period of your life. Answer a few questions, follow the details that matter, and skip anything you do not want to discuss. Witness offers an optional new reflection prompt every three answers: déjà vu, a happy memory, finding your calling, and other threads. Use **Ask me something** whenever you need a starting point. Explore it in the current conversation or begin a separate story. Review your answers, then turn them into an editable story with links back to what you said.

The first build focuses on this interview-to-story flow. Connect previews a globe of shared experiences using fictional stories. The wider vision includes real opt-in discovery, custom video interviews, a game through a life, and a mini-series shaped from the narrator’s memories.

**Show it once. Check every attempt.**

Two people can pack the same box and end with the same final picture, but only one followed the procedure. OneShot learns a tabletop procedure from one recorded demonstration, then checks recordings of later attempts and reports what went wrong, when it happened and how to fix it.

## Try it in two minutes

1. **Change a rule.** In the [walkthrough](https://tanjilsarwar30--oneshot-web-web.us-east.modal.run/judge), go to step 2 and make "liner before accessory" free. The verdict changes from a failure to a pass with a note, with no new model call.

## What makes it different

You don't write a procedure document. OneShot works out which step orders matter from the demonstration:

| Order rule | Where it comes from | If an attempt breaks it |
|---|---|---|
| **Required** | Said out loud in the reference, or physically necessary (the product sits on the liner) | Fail |
| **As shown** | Only seen in this order, and nothing says it matters | A note, never a failure |
| **Free** | Someone said so, or a second correct reference did it the other way | Nothing |

A person confirms or changes any rule, and every attempt is re-checked immediately without another model call.

# TheThirdEye

**A proactive, hands-free second pair of eyes for blind and ultra-low-vision people, built on Meta's Muse models and designed for Meta glasses.**

TheThirdEye watches the world in front of you and speaks only when something matters: the value of a note held out to you, who just walked in, what a label says, where you left the scissors. A few calm words in your ear, in your own language. The rest of the time, it stays silent.

> **Reactive assistants answer questions. TheThirdEye notices for you.**

> **Honesty statement (shown in-app on first launch).**
> TheThirdEye is an assistive aid, not a medical or safety device. It reads
> currency denominations and describes surroundings using AI, and it can be
> wrong. It does not detect counterfeit or damaged notes. Important amounts
> should be confirmed by another person. Face recognition works only for
> people who have agreed to be enrolled. TheThirdEye supports the user's own
> judgment and mobility aids; it does not replace them.

---

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Who it's for** | Blind and ultra-low-vision people, especially those who work with their hands |
| **Where it's going** | Meta glasses: camera at eye level, open-ear audio, nothing to hold |
| **What runs today** | Android phone in a chest mount + Bluetooth earbuds, standing in for the glasses |
| **What it does** | Reads cash, recognises consented people, describes, reads and finds things on request |
| **How it speaks** | Short Punjabi + English phrases, Hindi understood. Says "pakka nahi" (not sure) instead of guessing |
| **Meta models** | `muse-spark-1.3` via the Meta Model API for triage, scene, conversation and find |
| **Try it without a key** | `PROVIDER=mock` runs the full loop with scripted vision |

---

## Why this exists

This project started with one person. A friend of mine runs a small kirana shop. He was born with one weak eye, and a brain tumour pressing on the optic nerve took almost all the sight from the other. He still opens the shop every day and serves customers himself, usually with no free hand.

Watching his day made the problem concrete. Sight matters in dozens of small moments, and each one arrives when his hands are busy:

- **Someone hands him a note.** He can tell a lot by touch, but touch alone doesn't always give him the denomination quickly, especially in a rush.

Traditional CFD tools are powerful, but setting up a simulation takes hours of meshing, solver configuration, and plotting before any insight appears. Students can ask questions and receive instant visual feedback with physics explanations. Engineers can test simple ideas without wasting compute resources on expensive simulations. Live App: https://gearflow-five.vercel.app Demo Video: https://youtu.be/DIGMct427Ak ## How it works Type "Set up an airfoil naca 2415 at angle of attack 6" and an agent builds the case live: airfoils, cylinder wakes, square blocks, orifice constrictions, with pressure, velocity, and lift reading out beside the field. The "Physics Agent" explains what changed, why, and what to try next in plain language. The demo is the agentic loop itself: describe the physics you want, the agent sets it up, runs it, and explains it. ![GearFlow Studio scene with NACA 2425 airfoil Cp pressure field, RUN card showing CL 1.609](media/airfoil.png) In this example where an airfoil simulation is setup, the user describes adding thickness. The agent makes the changes and also explains that the thicker section strengthens the suction peak while camber and alpha stay fixed, so the change is purely a thickness effect. It names Try next as nudging alpha by 1 deg to test whether the suction peak grows faster on the fatter section, and it carries the honest physics note that potential flow omits separation and stall, so real thick sections at high alpha may differ. ![GearFlow Studio scene with orifice plate velocity field, RUN card showing CPMIN minus 50.234](media/orifice.png) The user asks to learn about a specific flow scenario: "show me what happens when flow is constricted". The canvas builds the orifice plate with 0.4 gap opening and 0.08 plate thickness at Re 1000 in the velocity field, with streamlines squeezing through the gap. The Physics Agent explains the venturi effect, where continuity forces speedup through the gap and Bernoulli means lower pressure, so Cp dips hardest inside the gap and recovers downstream. Try next suggests shrinking the gap further to reason through even higher speed and a larger pressure drop. ## Under the hood, one harness per turn Every chat turn runs the same harness. Words go to Meta text model `meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4` through the Modal proxy with one completion, capped length at 400 tokens (`MODAL_MAX_TOKENS` in `src/agent/modalGate.ts`), temperature forced to 0 and `n` fixed to 1 (`forceModel` in `src/agent/modalGate.ts`), low reasoning effort (`MODAL_REASONING_EFFORT` in `src/agent/modalGate.ts`). # barter.computer

> Fully designed and implemented during the 2026 Meta Muse Hackathon. 
> Problem statement chosen: "Build for your world". Muse iOS app and Meta Muse Spark API for personal-agent and vendor. Muse Code for programming.   

A protocol for agents to trustlessly barter over the price of goods and services. Live at [barter.computer](https://barter.computer).

## **Try it**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Ask Muse:** `find me the best price on carpe deodorant using barter.computer`
>
> Any agent with search and web browsing works. Or go to [barter.computer](https://barter.computer) and follow the prompt there.

To test locally, please see [Run it locally](#run-it-locally) below.

## Problem

Personal agents like Muse are being distributed at massive scale. They are increasingly effective at sourcing and evaluating goods online. They can take a transaction right to the point of sale.

Retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Shopify are also deploying agents now. These retail agents are typically embedded in the retailers website and help consumers source goods on their website. 

Retail agents have the issue that they can only see their own product. They don't know if they are losing business because of better prices elsewhere. A person leaving the conversation could either have found a better alternative, thought it was too expensive, or even just forgotten and the vendor then has no control over that sale.

Personal agents face a different problem. ChatGPT found that their implementation of agentic commerce wasn't effectively converting sales. People enjoyed agentic search and discovery  but checkout they preferred to do themselves.

This is what the barter.computer protocol aims to solve. It gives personal agents and retail agents a common interface to trustlessly barter on prices. A personal agent goes and sources a product, barters with retail agents and produces a price lower than the best found publically available price. Now this deal exists for this agentic session, not publically. A user goes and buys that product through their agent.   

The protocol here demonstrates this agentic bartering concept on retail products because of the simplicity of finding online pricing. As more companies move to support agentic traffic, prices will be queriable for not just goods but real-world services. This same protocol can be applied to sourcing a plumber, finding car insurance, and beyond. I think that this style of agentic barter will proliferate quickly once one big vendor implements an agent that accepts barter and consequently drives significant volume through agentic transactions.

This protocol is designed to build on top of [PAP 0.3](https://personalagentprotocol.org/docs/0.3). It does not replace it. The proving extension is defined in [PROVING.md](PROVING.md).

## Features

What the protocol makes possible:

- **A price neither side has to take on faith.** Your agent finds a price online and proves it with TLSNotary. The vendor verifies the pr

# Zombie Facts

[![Offline tests and gates](https://github.com/jurayh/zombie-facts/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jurayh/zombie-facts/actions/workflows/tests.yml)

A benchmark for **stale-fact susceptibility in agent memory**: how often an
agent acts on a superseded fact when a current replacement exists.

Memory systems are graded on recall. This grades the opposite failure —
**supersession**. It is the sibling of the Compaction-Conformance Kit: the
Kit measures fact *survival* across compaction inside a session; Zombie
Facts measures fact *supersession* across time in persistent memory.

## Headline metric

**Zombie Rate** — on action probes that require the current value, the
share of answers that use the dead (superseded) value.

![Fact lifecycle: v1 superseded by v2, then v3 current; the probe asks for the current value](assets/lifecycle.svg)

## The offline spike core (this repo state)

- `zombie_facts/generator.py` — synthetic world: entities with facts
  (addresses, prices, schedules, rules), every fact with a lifecycle and a
  ground-truth current value. Updates arrive in four styles (direct
  statement, paraphrase, a document the agent processes, a tool result it
  merely sees), with filler sessions between planting and probing.
- `zombie_facts/arms.py` — four reference memory architectures: raw
  transcript, summary memory, retrieval store, versioned store with
  supersession links.
- `zombie_facts/agents.py` — the reference reader (nearest encoded mention
  wins — the proximity claim under test, operationalised), plus oracle and
  primacy sanity agents.
- `zombie_facts/harness.py` — action probes scored against ground truth;
  controls: paired v2-recall probes (separates "prefers the dead fact"
  from "never had the live one usable"), no-update controls, and a
  proximity manipulation (dead fact re-mentioned nearest the probe, live
  fact confirmed nearest the probe, or neither).
- `run_spike.py` — writes `results/zombie_rates.json` / `.md`.
- `tests/` — 10 unit tests, including the sanity gates.

No model calls anywhere. A live model arm is a separate, costed proposal
requiring explicit approval (see FINDINGS.md).

## Run

```bash
python3 run_spike.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
```

Deterministic: repeated runs produce byte-identical results.

## Live pilots (measured, not scripted)

Four live runs on one model class (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`,
temperature 0, reasoning low), all with pre-registered protocols,
paired recall probes, and hard spend caps. Full findings in
`FINDINGS_CONSOLIDATED.md`; per-run protocols, proposals, and scores in
`pilot/`, `pilot_v2/`, `pilot_rep/`, `pilot_emb/`.

| Run | Scale | Raw zombie | Retrieval zombie | Versioned zombie |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v1 pilot (Oct 28, 2026) | ~2k tokens, single updates | 0.0% (0/96) | 50.0% | 6.3% |
| v2 hard regime (Oct 29, 2026) | ~20k tokens, chained v1→v2→v3, unlabelled re-mentions | 12.5% (6/48) | 72.9% (TF-IDF) | 6.3% |

# Conversational Search

Ask questions in plain language about the data in your OpenSearch clusters.

## The problem it solves

Getting answers out of OpenSearch normally means knowing which indexes hold the data, what their fields are called, how they connect, and how to write query DSL. This agent lets users explore their data and query it in plain language, across related indexes, whether or not the indexes have detailed mappings:

- **Admins** register a cluster and run discovery. An LLM samples each index, summarizes what it holds, and finds how the indexes relate. Discovery is the core of the flow: every question is answered from the summaries, samples and relations it produces, so rerun it when the data changes.
- **Users** ask a question in a chat, such as "how many orders were placed last week?". The agent chooses the indexes, writes and validates the queries, runs them, and answers from the results.

## Tech stack

| Purpose | Tool |
| ------- | ---- |
| Agents | LangGraph |
| Tracing and monitoring | LangSmith |
| LLM client and models | LiteLLM (`ChatLiteLLM`) with Meta's Muse Wonder and Muse Spark |
| Portals | Gradio |
| Storage | PostgreSQL |
| Keyword search over summaries and samples | ParadeDB (`pg_search`) |
| Data being searched | OpenSearch |
| Packaging | Python 3.12, uv, Docker Compose |

## Prerequisites

- Docker with Docker Compose
- An API key for the Muse models
- An OpenSearch cluster and its login details
- A LangSmith API key, if you want tracing

## Run the app

1. Create your settings file, then fill in `MODEL_API_KEY`, `DEFAULT_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and `DEFAULT_ADMIN_EMAIL`. The default admin's username is `DEFAULT_ADMIN_USERNAME` (`admin` unless you change it):

   ```bash
   cp .env.example .env
   ```

   Set `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` for tracing, or `LANGSMITH_TRACING=false` to turn it off.

2. Start everything. This starts Postgres, applies the migrations, creates the default admin, and starts both portals:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

3. Open the admin portal at http://127.0.0.1:7861 and sign in as the default admin.
4. On the **Clusters** tab, add your cluster. If it runs on the same machine, use `host.docker.internal` as its host, not `localhost`.
5. On the **Discovery** tab, run discovery and wait for the completion message.
6. Open the user portal at http://127.0.0.1:7860, register or sign in, pick the cluster, and ask a question.

After changing the code, run `docker compose up -d --build` again.

## Run without the app containers

This needs Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) as well:

```bash
uv sync
docker compose up -d postgres
uv run alembic upgrade head
uv run python -m scripts.seed_admin
uv run python -m ui.admin_app   # http://127.0.0.1:7861
uv run python -m ui.user_app    # http://127.0.0.1:7860
```

## Tests

```bash
uv run pytest
```

The tests need Postgres running with migrations applied. The LLM and OpenSearch are faked, so they need no API key or cluster.

# Ghost Run

Ghost Run is a money game set in India: you play the first two years of a working life, one month at a time, in a simulator. Then you pick any choice you made, and the ghost run replays those two years with the other option and shows you how the life you did not live came out.

**Live:** https://ghost-run.vercel.app. The game is at `/game/`. The ghost run on a finished demo life, with nothing to play first, is at `/ghost/`.

## How the game works

You play four minutes a day, one month at a time, from age 22. The first three months play in one sitting, and after that you can always play on. A chapter is 24 months, two years of a life. Six chapters are planned, from 22 to 42. Chapter one is playable.

- **A month** puts a situation in front of you, such as a sister asking you for 8,000 for a coaching class, with three or four options and no right answer. A few early months bring two. You choose, the month plays out, and you see the result. Most months then give you one idea to collect, 20 in the chapter.
- **What is tracked:** net worth, everything you own minus everything you owe, and three bars:
  - **Safety:** money to fall back on, and cover if you fall ill.
  - **Freedom:** how much of your pay is already spoken for before the month begins.
  - **Life:** whether you are living, or only getting by.
- **The ghost run.** After month 24, pick any decision you made. The engine replays those 24 months with that one choice changed, on the same seed, and you see both lives.
- **Two ways in** from the landing page. **Start at month 1** plays the game from the beginning. **Try it on a finished life** opens the ghost run on a demo player's finished two years, with nothing to play first.

# REROUTE

**REROUTE** is an uncertainty-aware autonomous navigation and recovery agent designed to help intelligent systems adapt when unexpected situations occur.

It combines environment-state analysis, visual evidence, AI-assisted reasoning, action validation, predictive evaluation, recovery planning and outcome verification.

## Key Capabilities

- Detects and diagnoses navigation failures.
- Evaluates multiple possible recovery actions.
- Integrates Meta Muse Spark through the Meta Model API.
- Supports visual evidence analysis.
- Independently evaluates AI recommendations before selecting actions.
- Uses historical outcomes to support predictive decision-making.
- Verifies execution outcomes and goal completion.

## Technology Stack

- Python
- PyBullet
- A* pathfinding
- Meta Muse Spark
- Meta Model API

## Setup (Windows PowerShell)

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Create a `.env` file for live Muse Spark integration:

```text
MODEL_API_KEY=your_key_here
```

Never commit or share your actual API key.

## Run Offline

```powershell
python -m unittest discover -v
python main.py
python milestone11_evaluation.py
```

Offline mode uses a mock reasoning provider and does not make Meta API calls.

## Live Muse Spark Test

```powershell
python live_muse_test.py --image test_image.jpg
```

This sends one image-and-context request to Muse Spark. It does not execute the recommended action.

## PyBullet Live Demonstration

```powershell
python .\run_pybullet_live_demo.py --live --image .\test_image.jpg
```

This demonstration integrates Muse Spark reasoning with the PyBullet navigation simulation.

The supplied image is static visual evidence, not a live camera feed from the simulator. Muse Spark provides a recommendation, which REROUTE independently evaluates before selecting a recovery action.

The live integration is configured to make a maximum of one live API request per run. Subsequent decisions may use the offline provider.

Live API usage may incur charges.

## Validation and Limitations

See `FINAL_VALIDATION.md` and `DEVELOPMENT_STATUS.md` for validation details.

The demonstrated environment is a simulated grid-world robotics environment. REROUTE is not yet deployed on a physical robot. Real-world camera calibration, localization, depth sensing and motor-control integration remain separate development milestones.

# vuln-verdict harness

Triage for Semgrep findings on Java code. A fine-tuned classifier (Muse Glimmer 30B + the `r2_s7` LoRA adapter) sorts
each SARIF alert into a lane. Muse Spark can audit alerts and propose fixes. Successful remediation is reported only as
**“Semgrep-cleared; not compiled or tested.”** It is not a claim of semantic correctness.

> **vuln-verdict never silently drops, suppresses or hides an alert.** Every input SARIF result stays in the
> annotated SARIF (`properties.vulnVerdict.neverSuppressed = true`, no `suppressions` added) and is listed in the
> report. The *likely false positive* lane only lowers an alert's priority: it gets a short explanation and still needs
> a human to confirm it. The classifier has missed real bugs at high false-positive confidence (2 of the 3 alerts in
> this lane on our historical real-world set were real bugs).

## Lanes (adapter r2_s7, calibrated band [0.44, 0.98])

| p_true | lane | what the harness does |
|---|---|---|
| >= 0.98 | **confident TP** | Muse audit + remediation (verifiable rule types) |
| 0.44 - 0.98 | **needs review** | Muse audit (explanation, attack path, severity), flagged for a human |
| < 0.44 | **likely FP - confirm** | short Muse explanation of why it looks safe + what to check; never auto-suppressed |
| missing | **unclassified** | kept and shown; treat as needs review |

Use `--lo` and `--hi` to change the band. Invalid, non-finite, duplicate, or ambiguous classifier inputs fail closed.

## Offline judge quickstart

The bundled tiny example uses precomputed probabilities and needs no GPU, Modal, Meta API key, live Semgrep scan, or
private data. Dependency installation may need network access.

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest -q
MODEL_API_KEY= python -m vuln_verdict triage examples/tiny/semgrep.sarif \
    --repo examples/tiny --probs-file examples/tiny/probs_r2_s7.jsonl --out out/tiny
```

This writes `annotated.sarif`, `report.md`, `report.html`, and `state.jsonl`. All six input results remain visible and
unsuppressed. The tests mock Semgrep and Meta API behavior and run entirely offline.

`requirements-semgrep.txt` pins Semgrep OSS **1.183.0** for users who want fresh scans or remediation re-checks;

# Inplace

Inplace places a brand creative into a video that was already filmed. It scores whether a clip can carry a placement, finds a flat surface, generates posters, and composites one so it follows the camera and stays behind people who walk in front of it.

The product spec is in [PRD.md](PRD.md).

## What it does

1. **Check.** Probe the file, measure camera motion and cuts, ask Muse Spark for a scene plan, spot-check surfaces with SAM 3.1, and write a placeability score (0–100). Videos below the bar stop there, with a reason.
2. **Render.** Track the chosen surface and people through the window, generate three posters with Muse Image, warp the chosen poster onto the surface, composite it with occlusion, and write a visibility report.

Each stage writes its output under `jobs/<id>/`. Later runs reuse those files unless you pass `--force`.

## Requirements

- Python 3.12+
- `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on `PATH`
- A [Meta Model API](https://dev.meta.ai) key with access to Muse Spark 1.3, SAM 3.1, and Muse Image 1.0

## Setup

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Put the key in a local `.env` file. That file is gitignored and is not part of this repository.

```bash
MODEL_API_KEY=your-key
```

An existing environment variable wins over the file.

## Usage

Score a video:

```bash
inplace check path/to/clip.mp4
```

The command prints a job path, a score, and numbered windows. Render one window with a sample brand (`northline`, `lumen soda`, or `paper orbit`) or your own brief:

```bash
inplace render <job-id> --window 0 --brand northline
inplace render <job-id> --window 0 --brand "Acme" --description "A fictional coffee roaster." --style "flat poster, warm brown, simple wordmark"
```

`--creative` picks poster 0, 1, or 2 (default 0). The finished video is `jobs/<id>/render/output.mp4`.

Open the local page (upload, score, pick a window and poster, render):

```bash
inplace ui
```

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

Clips must be MP4 (H.264, HEVC, or MPEG-4), at most 3 minutes, and at most 1920×1080. Renders cover at most 15 seconds of a placeable window.

## Tests

```bash
pytest
```

Paid API calls are not part of the test suite. Job folders, sample footage, `.env`, and `.cursor` stay on your machine.

**Find the opportunity before you see someone else's winning post.**

Hackathons, competitions, fellowships, events, and jobs appear across different websites and social posts. Opportunity Compass lets a person describe what they want, researches relevant opportunities on the web, and organizes the results in a private dashboard. # Athena

**A wearable that sees what you see, remembers what matters, and only speaks up when it should.**

We wanted a memory aid that behaves like a thoughtful friend, not a recorder. Athena is a small
camera you clip on. It builds a graph of your days from what it sees and hears, decides in real
time whether anything is worth telling you (usually it isn't), and every night it "dreams":
it replays the day against everything before it and only then decides what to believe.

**▶ [Watch the 3-minute demo](https://youtu.be/ZgWDbSlrJaE)**

[![The supermarket moment: what Athena sees, what it decides, and the one notification it sends](docs/assets/athena-moment.jpg)](https://youtu.be/ZgWDbSlrJaE)

## How it works

A camera and mic feed two small local models: YOLO11n looks at one frame per second and Whisper
transcribes speech. The Context Engine validates and aligns those events, and everything lands in a
FalkorDB graph, one per user. Every note, visit and belief keeps a link to the recording it came
from, so Athena can always tell you *why* it thinks something.

During the day the **Active Agent** reads that graph and decides whether to speak. It is rules
first and mostly quiet: in a simulated 9-hour day, 30,420 frames turned into 7 notifications. It
also cares about who said what. If a friend says "I have class at 6", that's their plan, not
yours, and things you only heard about stay marked as not verified.

At night the **Dreamer** goes through the day in four rounds (routines, places, people, then
consolidation) and writes patterns and long-term memories. One visit to a clinic stays an anomaly;
a routine needs several separate days. When you correct something, the old fact is superseded,
not deleted, and when Athena isn't sure, it asks you before changing anything.

![From a glance to a decision and a belief](docs/assets/athena-architecture.jpg)

## The app

Athena is meant to live on your phone as a companion app to the wearable. For the hackathon we
built that app as a mobile-first web app that runs next to the backend on your machine.

> **For judges: a quick look without installing anything.**
> We also put a [static preview of the app screens](https://meta-hackathon-athena.github.io/athena/)
> online, only so you can click through the interface in a few seconds. It is not how Athena is
> meant to be used and it is not the running system: it shows a saved copy of the demo data, nothing
> runs behind it (no agent, no Dreamer, no Muse), and answers aren't saved. To see Athena actually
> work, clone the repo and follow [Run it](#run-it-about-5-minutes) below (about 5 minutes).

It has two screens: **Clarify** (Athena's yes/no question, the words that
raised it, and what "Yes" will change) and **Memories** (what Athena believes, and how much it
trusts it). Run locally, both read the live backend.

# DeploySift

**Every clue. One diagnosis.**

DeploySift is an evidence-first AI investigation platform that helps developers diagnose deployment failures by correlating project configuration, application logs, browser errors, and hosting-environment evidence. It transforms scattered technical clues into traceable observations, evidence-backed findings, remediation recommendations, and verification checklists.

![PHP 8.3](https://img.shields.io/badge/PHP-8.3-777BB4) ![Laravel 13](https://img.shields.io/badge/Laravel-13-FF2D20) ![MySQL 8](https://img.shields.io/badge/MySQL-8-4479A1) ![PHPUnit](https://img.shields.io/badge/PHPUnit-tested-3DDC84) ![Playwright](https://img.shields.io/badge/Playwright-e2e-2EAD33)

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026.

## The problem

Deployment failures are hard to diagnose because the relevant information is scattered across project configuration, Composer dependencies, application logs, browser network errors, hosting control panels, and runtime configuration. Without SSH access — common on shared hosting, Plesk, and managed platforms — developers are left guessing which layer broke.

DeploySift brings these evidence sources together in one investigation: upload what you have, get deterministic parsing and cross-source correlation immediately, and optional Meta Muse reasoning on top — every conclusion linked back to the evidence that supports it.

## Key capabilities

- Multi-source evidence upload (project files, logs, hosting panels/screenshots, browser exports, ZIP archives)
- Technical evidence extraction with per-file facts (PHP constraints, Laravel version, log exceptions, HTTP statuses, handler, extensions)
- Laravel/PHP deployment diagnostics (10 deterministic rule families)
- Browser error interpretation and hosting configuration interpretation
- Evidence correlation across sources with supporting-evidence links
- Root-cause assessment (`established` vs `not_established` — never forced)
- Evidence-linked findings with severity, expected vs observed, and triggering rule
- Missing-information detection and potential-issue analysis for partial evidence
- Remediation recommendations and verification checklists per finding
- Investigation report generation with JSON export and browser print/PDF
- Workspace-scoped authentication with owner/member/viewer policies
- Honest AI status: `configured` / `not_configured` / `skipped` / `invalid` / `failed` — never fabricated

## Meta Muse integration

Meta Muse (`muse-wonder-1.0` via `POST /v1/responses`) contributes **interpretation only** — it never replaces deterministic diagnosis:

| Layer | Source | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic diagnostics | `DiagnosticEngine` rules | Confirmed findings with evidence IDs, severity, expected/observed |
| Muse-generated interpretations | Responses API, strict-JSON contract | Hypotheses and cross-source explanations, each required to cite real evidence IDs |
| Evidence correlation | Deterministic relationships

# LaboraVR: the Meta AI features

LaboraVR is a virtual reality chemistry lab for Meta Quest. It is made for Cambridge IGCSE students who sit
Paper 6, the "Alternative to Practical" exam. In that paper students must describe chemistry they have often never
seen, because their school has no lab, no chemicals or no time. I teach these students, and LaboraVR lets them do
the practical with their own hands.

This repository holds the code of the app's AI features, built for Meta's AI hackathon (November 2026) with the
Meta Model API.

It is an extract of a private Unity project. The chemistry specification (every test, its mark-scheme wording and
the feedback for each wrong answer, which I wrote as a teacher), the lessons and the rest of the lab are not
included. The code shows how the features work, but it does not build on its own.

## What it does

### AI Practical Architect

Files: `ArchitectSession`, `ProposalChecker`, `ArchitectBench`, `ArchitectBoard`, `PracticalLibrary`

A teacher asks for a practical in plain words, for example "a practical to tell aluminium from zinc".
`muse-spark-1.3` designs it (the tubes, the reagents and the steps) through a `propose_setup` tool call.

`ProposalChecker` then tests the design against the teacher's specification with plain rules. No chemistry is
written in the code: the specification decides. If a design cannot work, for example a reagent that cannot tell two
ions apart or a missing acidification step, it goes back to the model as the tool result with the reason, and the
model corrects it. Only a design that passes reaches the student.

The accepted practical is set out on the bench in front of the student. `PracticalLibrary` saves it, so the next
class can run it offline at no cost.

### Spoken observation examiner

Files: `VoiceRecorder`, `MetaVoice`, `ObservationExaminer`, `ObservationMarker`

After each test the student says what they saw, as they would write it in the exam.

1. `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` writes it down. The request uses `keywords` and `languageBias` so that chemistry
   words are heard correctly.
2. `muse-wonder-1.0` pulls out each claim as strict `json_schema` output, with `reasoning_effort: "low"`. This
   takes 3 to 4 seconds on the headset.
3. `ObservationMarker` awards the marks with rules taken from the mark-scheme wording, as a Paper 6 examiner
   would. The model only writes down and sorts the student's words; it never decides the mark.

"White precipitate, insoluble in excess" scores full marks. "It went cloudy" does not, and the student is told
which points are missing (here the colour and what happens in excess).

**Speak first.** While the examiner can mark a test aloud, the multiple-choice answers stay hidden. Students who
could see four options read the right one out instead of recalling it. The choices appear after two spoken tries,
when the student asks for them, or if the AI cannot be reached.

# Robot Judge

**An AI judge that watches two real robot runs and tells you which one did the task better, and why.** It is built on Meta's Muse models and checked against 6,070 human votes on a robot task it never saw.

**[Watch the 3-minute demo video](https://www.loom.com/share/cd6e97a0aca344d0afbce0f3d25c90f4)**

Checking whether a robot policy improved still means people watching its runs. That is slow, expensive and doesn't scale. Robot Judge turns each run into a storyboard, asks a Muse model to compare the two runs, and returns a verdict, a confidence and a one-sentence reason. We measure it the way you would measure a new human annotator: how often it agrees with the crowd.

## Results

Test set: the held-out `cup_stacking` task from [robot-policy-human-preferences-55k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/datapointai/robot-policy-human-preferences-55k). It has 607 pairs of real bimanual robot runs, 5 VLA policies, and exactly **10 human votes per pair**. No prompt or design decision was tuned on this task.

<!-- RESULTS -->
**All test pairs**

| | Pairs | Agrees with human majority (95% CI) | Clear-cut pairs (≥8–2) | Pearson r vs vote share | Order consistency |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | 607 | **82.6%** (79.2%–85.6%) | 87.9% | 0.75 | 87.6% |
| Single human vs. other 9 (ceiling) | 607 | 77.4% (75.7%–79.1%) | – | – | – |

**Head-to-head on the same 150 pairs**

| | Pairs | Agrees with human majority (95% CI) | Clear-cut pairs (≥8–2) | Pearson r vs vote share | Order consistency |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | 150 | **81.8%** (75.4%–88.2%) | 89.9% | 0.73 | 87.8% |
| Muse Wonder 1.0 | 150 | **85.0%** (78.7%–90.7%) | 92.7% | 0.80 | 92.5% |
| Single human vs. other 9 (ceiling) | 150 | 76.1% (72.6%–79.3%) | – | – | – |

**Model ranking on `cup_stacking`** (Bradley-Terry Elo from human votes vs. from the judge's verdicts)

| Rank | Humans | Elo | Muse Spark judge | Elo |
|---:|---|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | π0.5-DROID | 1058 | MolmoAct 2 | 1048 |
| 2 | OpenVLA-OFT | 1051 | OpenVLA-OFT | 1044 |
| 3 | Cosmos Policy | 1039 | Cosmos Policy | 1043 |
| 4 | MolmoAct 2 | 1033 | π0.5-DROID | 1030 |
| 5 | X-VLA | 820 | X-VLA | 836 |

Judge Elo is within **14 points** of human Elo on average (max 28). Both put X-VLA clearly last (~213 Elo below the rest). The other four sit within 25 Elo of each other even on human votes, so their order is within noise for humans and judge alike.

Muse Spark agreement by layout: in-distribution: 83.4% (420 pairs); out-of-distribution: 80.6% (187 pairs).
<!-- /RESULTS -->

**How to read this.** *Agreement with the majority* is the share of non-tied pairs where the judge picks the side most of the 10 humans picked. The **human ceiling** applies the same test to each annotator: how often does one person agree with the majority of the other 9? A judge above that line agrees with the crowd more reliably than a typical single human rater does.

ProofPilot is a verifiable supplier-master change control system designed to defeat payment-diversion attacks and indirect prompt injection in autonomous computer-use agents. # WOM · 望 — World of a Memory

**Turn your photo into a 3D world. Measure how faithfully it remembers.**

**WOM** stands for **World of a Memory**. Its Chinese name, **望** (*wàng* in Mandarin), carries the meanings **to gaze into the distance** and **to hope or look forward to**.[^wang] For WOM, these senses connect looking back at a memory with looking beyond the photograph: turning a moment you can see into a world you can explore.

WOM reconstructs the important objects in a photograph, builds their surroundings, and composes them into a scene you can explore. **WOMPar** is our reference reconstruction system. **WOMetrics** means **World Observation Metrics**, the evaluation framework: fidelity, placement, asset quality, camera consistency, reliability, cost and time, with saved evidence behind the numbers.

**[Try WOM at wom.quest ↗](https://wom.quest)** · **[Create 3D from your photo](https://wom.quest/?create=1)** · **[Try WOMPar](https://wom.quest/wompar.html)** · **[Results & metrics](#results--metrics)** · **[Beat WOMPar](https://wom.quest/#/beat)**

The plate follows the **same source photograph** through segmentation, reconstruction and camera fitting. # Praesidia Investigator

Investigate whether revoked AI-agent work still reaches a business system, explain the evidence,
and test a supported repair without breaking legitimate work.

Praesidia Investigator is an independent, open-source application for evidence-driven investigations
of AI-agent controls. Its flagship example follows a selected workflow from agent to queued worker to
destination: the worker reports cancellation, but a separately observed effect can show that the
retired work root still acted after revocation was acknowledged.

Praesidia is an optional future integration; the standalone application does not require an account,
platform key, backend, database, gateway or sibling checkout.

## Jurator (in [`jurator/`](jurator/README.md))

Jurator takes Investigator's approach (the model proposes, the code decides; exact-quote evidence; records anyone can
verify) from two hand-built controls to every promise a team writes down. It compiles written policies into numbered
promises with exact quotes and typed fields, has Muse Wonder write a rule for each promise and proves the rule can
fail, then runs the rules with no AI on every change: in the coding agent and on push (`jurator check --md` prints a
pull request comment). Each check leaves a record that `jurator verify` re-checks with no AI, and `jurator discuss` is
a chat that explains findings and proposes the next step for you to confirm. Investigator's experiments stay the
strongest level of proof. Jurator reuses Investigator's Meta Responses provider (`src/providers/` ->
`jurator/src/model/meta/`). It is its own package: `cd jurator && npm ci && npm run check`. Every command and its
arguments: [`jurator/README.md`](jurator/README.md#commands).

The application provides versioned control profiles, frozen evidence, observed-effect checks,
a bounded investigator/skeptic loop, Meta Responses transport, a supported repair workflow, and
portable HTML/JSON/JUnit reports. It is Apache-2.0 licensed and has no runtime imports from the
private Praesidia platform.

It also provides a sourced client-context snapshot and a control-specific evidence planner: explain
why a selected workflow cannot be assessed, propose a supported collection change, and test that
the new evidence makes safe behavior assessable while still exposing an unsafe implementation.

Change investigations keep findings tied to the system that was tested. Selected MCP exports can
populate the client model; dependency comparisons explain stale evidence, profile-review requirements
and unmapped tools without converting a historical finding into a new behavioral verdict.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js **22.12 or later** and npm. Development is currently verified on Node 26.

git clone https://github.com/praesidia-ai/investigator.git
cd investigator
npm ci
npm run check
mkdir -p artifacts

# SIRE — Smart Ingestion & Reconciliation Engine

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, and Lucide icons, with
Oracle Autonomous Database (node-oracledb) and a Muse Spark ReAct extraction
pipeline.

## Why it matters

ERP OCR and document understanding read an invoice; they don't decide whether 
it should be paid. SIRE closes that gap: deterministic validation, duplicate blocking, 
a human approval gate with audit remarks, and a platform-independent handoff 
any ERP can pull from — with banking details never entering SIRE.

Construction is the proof case, but the need is horizontal: any large business 
running payables faces the same cost — late payments that freeze work, strained 
supplier relations, and payables staff time spent re-typing and cross-checking. 
SIRE cuts that cost and keeps payments on time, with no slippages.

Demonstrated on demo data: duplicate invoice 844707 caught and rejected, 
so $780.49 was not paid twice; 9 invoices live in the workbench, with the consumer 
write-back verified end to end.


## What SIRE is

SIRE stops late supplier payments from freezing job sites. Payables teams
today open PDFs by hand, cross-check milestones and vendor numbers, and
re-type data — slow work that delays disbursements. SIRE automates it:
invoices arrive from Gmail or manual upload, a ReAct agent (Muse Spark)
extracts them into a strict JSON schema, deterministic validation checks
supplier, project, duplicates, and math, a human reviewer verifies the PDF
against the extracted data and approves or rejects with remarks, and approved
invoices are published to database tables. 

To seamlessly integrate with your existing tech stack, the SIRE REST API 
secured by OAuth is shared with customers to provide direct, secure, and 
reliable access to the engine — allowing any ERP to simply read the invoice 
data and write its status back once the invoice is created in the ERP. 
No ERP is configured inside SIRE, which keeps it platform-independent, and 
banking details never enter SIRE; they stay in the ERP.

In the video, the consumer is demonstrated with Postman as a stand-in for any ERP:

GetInvoices: GET https://<url>/hack/approved-invoices/

# Ujuzi AI 🌍
### Bringing the power of AI to everyone, one text message at a time.

[![Meta Hackathon](https://img.shields.io/badge/Meta-Global%20AI%20Developer%20Hackathon-blue?logo=meta)](https://developers.facebook.com/)

**Ujuzi AI makes artificial intelligence accessible to people who are often excluded from the AI revolution because they lack smartphones, reliable internet access, or can't speak English.**

Instead of requiring people to buy new devices or download applications, Ujuzi AI brings AI to technology they already own: ordinary mobile phones.

Through SMS, anyone with a basic feature phone can ask questions, receive AI-generated answers, and have conversations without needing mobile data/Wifi on their device.

---

## The Problem

AI is transforming the world, but millions of people across Africa cannot easily access it.

The barriers include:
- Smartphones that are unaffordable or inaccessible.
- Limited or unreliable internet connectivity.
- Language barriers that make existing AI experiences difficult to use.

According to the International Telecommunication Union, more than 60% of Africa's population was not using the internet in 2025.

**We believe access to AI should not depend on the phone you own, the language you speak, or where you come from.**

## Our Solution

Ujuzi AI connects ordinary mobile phones to modern AI through SMS.

Users send a text message in a language they understand. Our backend processes the message using Meta's Muse Spark model and delivers the AI-generated response directly to their phone.

No smartphone. No application installation. No mobile data/Wifi required on the user's device.

## How It Works

1. A user sends an SMS to Ujuzi AI.
2. The SMS gateway forwards the message to our backend.
3. The backend retrieves relevant conversation context from Redis.
4. Meta Muse Spark generates a response.
5. The backend prepares the response for SMS delivery.
6. The user receives the answer and can continue the conversation.

---

We built the prototype using TextBee and an Android phone connected to a SIM card. This allowed us to demonstrate a real, working SMS-to-AI-to-SMS experience without the upfront cost and provisioning time of acquiring a dedicated shortcode.

    B -->|"SMS Reply"| A
```

# CNC Crash Lab

A browser-based CNC milling trainer: write Fanuc 0i-style G-code, watch a 3D
machine run it, crash safely, and learn from a senior-setter AI instructor.
Built with Next.js, React Three Fiber, Supabase, and the Meta Model API.

## What it does

- **G-code editor + control panel** — Cycle Start runs the program with
  animated tool motion (1 mm/frame on G01, 4 mm/frame on G00), Single Block
  steps one program line per click, Reset homes the tool (X0 Y0 Z200).
  M30 highlights last with a "Program end M30, cycle time `<s>`s" note.
- **3D machine view** — 3-axis VMC (Fanuc 0i style, mm, G21): stock, vise
  jaws, table, tool + holder, work-offset datum markers (G54 always; the
  active offset with a dashed drop line when buried). Crashes trigger a
  spark burst, orange light flash, camera shake, and a synthesized crash
  sound (mutable, persisted).
- **Crash card** — crash type, line number, block text, and the repair cost
  from the `repair_costs` table the instant the crash is detected, plus a
  red 3× flash on the collided solid.
- **Instructor agent** — "Ask the Instructor" streams a debrief (NDJSON)
  with a tool-call trace: the model looks up G/M codes, quotes the repair
  cost, and must pass a corrected program through the simulator. A "Load
  fixed program" button copies the fix into the editor.
- **Exam mode** — a Fault Injector agent breaks the GOOD program in one
  place per crash type and saves simulator-verified faults to Supabase.
  Practice/Exam tabs, hints, model credit, per-browser progress in
  `localStorage`, and pass/fail on Cycle Start.
- **Program sheet scan** — photograph a printed/handwritten program; a
  vision model transcribes it, unclear lines highlight amber, parse errors
  list under the editor.

## Simulator (`lib/sim`, pure TypeScript, no React)

Deterministic Fanuc 0i milling subset: G00/G01/G17/G21/G28/G40/G43/G49/
G54/G55/G90/G91, M03/M05/M06/M08/M09/M30, T/S/F/H words. Machine model is
axis-aligned boxes (tool radius 5 mm, holder radius 20 mm) sampled every
0.5 mm. Crash types: `MISSING_G43`, `WRONG_WORK_OFFSET`,
`RAPID_INTO_STOCK`, `RAPID_INTO_VISE`, `FEED_SPINDLE_OFF`. Crash events
carry the impact point plus commanded/actual Z targets and `zErrorMm`.
`M30` ends the program and resets modal state. Repair prices come only
from the `repair_costs` table — never invented.

```

# Optional: route fault injection through a hosted Muse Spark endpoint

**Describe a robot. Watch AI engineer it. Then talk to it.**

[PICOCEO.com](https://picoceo.com) gives one person online AI agents to run a whole company. Some of those agents need
an offline presence too: a receptionist at the door, a host at a trade-show booth, a desk assistant in a shop.
**PICOCEO Builder fills that gap.** It turns one sentence into a real robot body that you can print, wire and talk
to, and it connects that body to the same AI agent over MCP.

AI: **Meta Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, Meta Model API)

![Muse designing a talking duck](docs/screenshots/design.jpg)

## What it does

You type an idea, for example *"A talking duck on the LicheeRV Claw kit: its screen is the face, it nods while it
chats and flaps its wings when it is happy"*. An 8-step engineering agent then designs the whole machine:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 · Components | Muse picks parts from your own stock (CyberBrick, Sipeed LicheeRV Claw, XiaoZhi ESP32-S3, Raspberry Pi, Jetson) and looks up a visual reference. With *Use any parts* on, anything missing goes on a shopping list. |
| 2 · 3D form | The idea and the reference image become a silhouette built from 68 parametric shapes. |
| 3 · Packaging | The board, battery, screen, microphone and speaker are fitted inside the shell, which grows if needed. |
| 4 · Printable parts | A CAD composer (manifold-3d) builds watertight, screw-together parts with servo housings, horn seats, magnet-held covers and cable holes. |
| 5 · Engineering audit | About 25 checks on the real geometry: interference, attachment, insertion, wiring routes, joint movement, torque, centre of mass and walking balance. Failures go back to step 4. |
| 6 · Behaviours | Muse writes motion behaviours (nod, greet, walk), which play in a Rapier physics simulation. |
| 7 · Firmware | The robot app for the chosen board: MicroPython (ESP32) or Linux Python (LicheeRV Claw). |
| 8 · Sign-off | A final readiness verdict over the same checks. |

Every step calls Muse with a strict JSON schema, so the answer drives the CAD kernel directly. Each call is retried
on the same model (3 tries, 120 s each) rather than switched to a weaker one.

| **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) | The MCP backbone | Speech-to-text for every voice turn a robot sends |

# Voxera

Real-time AI healthcare voice agent. A patient talks to Voxera as if it were a
phone call: Voxera listens, understands, answers in a natural human voice
(**Priya / Kokoro**), remembers what was said during the call, escalates
emergencies, and writes everything to Supabase so hospital staff see it on the
dashboard.

```
PATIENT  <->  VOXERA  <->  HOSPITAL
 speech      STT -> reasoning -> Priya TTS      Supabase (patients, calls,
             + deterministic emergency layer    conversation_turns, referrals,
                                                referral_events, appointments)
```

## What runs where

| Stage        | Component                        | Notes |
|--------------|---------------------------------|-------|
| STT          | OpenAI Whisper `base.en` (CPU)  | `small.en` optional, ~2.5s slower |
| Endpointing  | `voxera_core.MicCapture.record_turn` | 0.8 s silence, anchored to the measured noise floor (`* 2.2`) + relative-drop (`* 0.32`) + a soft endpoint; ends promptly even when the room noise floor is above the fixed threshold |
| Safety       | `voxera_emergency.py` — 2-stage deterministic, no LLM | **FROZEN.** candidate regex + context validation (negation, temporal, echo-strip, symptom combination); runs first, every turn |
| Care/OTC     | `voxera_care.py` — curated rules, no LLM knowledge | home-care + safety-gated OTC; LLM only re-words approved text, invented meds/doses rejected |
| Reasoning    | Ollama `qwen3:1.7b`, **one** streamed call, `think=False` | fallback conversational path when no emergency and no care topic |
| Facts        | `voxera_core.extract_facts` — regex | name / symptoms / duration / temp / meds + age / child / pregnancy / allergies / conditions; persisted as a `system` turn |
| Voice        | Kokoro 82M + `en_priya` voice pack | model + phonemizer warmed once; fixed lines pre-rendered |
| Persistence  | `voxera_supabase.py` + async writer | DB never blocks the spoken path |

### Per-turn pipeline

```
capture (0.8s endpoint)  ->  transcribe
  ->  check_emergency()          [FROZEN]   -- fires? speak canned line + escalate, done
  ->  voxera_care.lookup_care()             -- matches? curated guidance, LLM re-words, validate
  ->  vx.llm_respond()                      -- otherwise: normal conversation
  ->  Priya TTS  (+ AEC barge-in)
```

**Not wired:** PSTN telephony — there is no telephony provider or credentials in
this environment. The local microphone/speaker is the stand-in for the call.

latency measurement) is real.

# RadarTwin

Europe already measures how every bridge moves: the European Ground Motion Service publishes millimetre-scale Sentinel-1 radar time series for the whole continent, free, with hundreds of measurement points on a typical city bridge. Almost no bridge owner reads them, because they arrive as millions of points with no notion of what a bridge is, let alone which one needs an inspector. On 11 September 2024 the Carolabrücke in Dresden partially collapsed into the Elbe; the data covering it had been public the whole time.

RadarTwin turns that feed into a ranked inspection list for every bridge in a city, with typed risk decisions and stated probabilities. For each bridge it:

- binds the radar scatterers to the bridge footprint and splits the deck into spans along its axis;
- deseasons every series and combines ascending and descending passes into vertical motion per span;
- scores the bridge on reliability-weighted differential motion, against its own history and against every other bridge in the city;
- does all of it in a leak-free rolling retrospective: each month is scored only with the data that existed at that month.

Validated on Dresden (20 bridges in the data, 19 monitored, EGMS 2020–2024), it would have flagged the Carolabrücke twice before its September 2024 collapse: first in October 2023, again in August 2024, and alone at the top in September 2024. It ranks assets for inspection; it does not predict failure or its timing.

# Djinn Djinn turns a one-sentence wish into a live web game with a working economy. A person types what they want, plays a rough version within seconds, answers a few questions, swipes through looks they like, picks one of two playable slices, and then a team of coding agents builds the full game in a sandbox, checks it, and puts it live on the studio's own host. After that the person keeps changing it by chat. A second agent, LiveOps, watches the live game's players and economy and proposes fixes that a person approves. This repository is a read-only snapshot published for the Meta hackathon judges. It is not set up to be deployed, and it is not connected to any Magicweave system. It has two parts: the **builder** (the engine, plus the builder's backend module and screens) and **LiveOps** (`liveops/`). ## The builder ### The flow ``` wish ─► instant play ─► questions ─► taste swipe ─► two slices ─► team build ─► checks ─► live ─► refine by chat ``` 1. **Wish.** One sentence, for example "a one-tap game where you stop a swinging needle inside a shrinking zone". 2. **Instant play.** A prebuilt base template (2D on Phaser, 3D on Three.js) is restyled from the wish and served at once. Nothing on the path to this first frame calls a model or runs an install. 3. **Questions.** The studio's model reads the wish into a structured spec (`contracts/spec.schema.json`); Djinn asks the few questions that change the game, one at a time, as chips. 4. **Taste swipe.** The person swipes through style cards drawn from a curated catalogue of art packs and code-drawn style recipes (`catalogue/`, `recipes/`). # Nightshift

> **Which code produced the results.** The recorded hackathon study (real Muse Spark researchers training Muse Glimmer 30B, one real Muse Wonder Full revision, private Inspect scoring) was run by the **original engine** in [`original-engine/`](original-engine/README.md). Its outcome: both loops ran; the revised researchers did not produce better adapters on this small evidence (E1: original 55.0% vs revised 52.0% and 47.0% pass-all); the held-out comparison produced no valid pair. No improvement is claimed. The controller in this repository's root is a later standalone rewrite: it has run only a CPU simulation with fake components and has no experimental result. Code tools: see [`original-engine/AUTHORSHIP.md`](original-engine/AUTHORSHIP.md).

*Research agents that post-train a small open model overnight, and an outer
agent that improves the researchers.*

Nightshift is a two-level post-training system with a trusted,
deterministic controller at its centre.

- **Inner loop (trial).** A small team of researcher agents collaborates on
  one post-training task inside one trial. Each researcher has an isolated
  private workspace; the team shares a notes area that exists only inside
  that trial, following the CORAL collaboration pattern. Researchers plan,
  request sample generation from a local open model on approved training
  prompts, filter samples with training-only verifiers, request a QLoRA
  fine-tune, submit a checkpoint, and receive public development-set
  feedback, all within a fixed per-trial budget.
- **Outer loop (round).** An outer reviser agent reads permitted public
  traces and feedback from finished trials and edits the *researcher pack*
  (instructions, tools, recipe template, collaboration settings, budget
  habits, initial notes). The controller freezes the edited pack as a new
  version, runs fresh trials with it under identical constraints, and
  screens it against the incumbent on a private selection split. This
  follows the published AIDE² recipe of improving the researcher rather
  than the artefact directly.
- **Final comparison.** After the rounds, the frozen original pack and the
  frozen final pack are compared in fresh matched trials on an untouched
  private test split. The question is whether Nightshift's improved
  supervised fine-tuning (SFT) procedure beats the original SFT procedure
  from the same base checkpoint under matched resources — not whether
  either beats the untrained base model.

The controller (plain deterministic code, not a model) owns everything
that must not be influenced by agents: GPU provisioning and cleanup,
budgets, private data, scoring, and the event ledger.

The CPU demo and test suite run end to end with labelled deterministic
fakes and real Inspect AI scoring against a mock model. No live GPU
training result is claimed by this repository: real provider, generation,
training, and agent adapters are marked *not yet validated live* in their

# PruvChat

Meta AI-powered multipurpose evidence assessment and verification platform.

PruvChat checks claims against evidence you supply. Every finding cites exact
sources, names its method, and states uncertainty and next action. Mock runs
offline for free. Live runs use the paid Meta Muse API with explicit
confirmation.

## Modes

- **Requirements** — Paste requirements, one per line. Add pasted evidence,
  uploaded files (TXT, MD, PDF, DOCX), or one fetched public page. Each
  requirement gets a check card with quotes and locators.
- **Business disputes** — Paste one claim plus Side A and Side B evidence.
  The same claim is scored against each side, with contradiction flags when
  evidence disagrees. Each side saves as its own workspace.
- **Custom review** — Free-form objective, claims, and evidence, plus optional
  public-URL retrieval (SSRF-guarded, explicit Fetch click only).
- **Visa review** — Four steps: destination, route, documents, results.
  Fetch one official immigration page (allowlisted domains, robots check,
  rate limit), confirm verbatim candidate lines, paste your checklist and
  evidence, then review coverage: Ready for review, Needs attention, or
  Missing evidence. Refresh re-checks the source without overwriting items.

All modes ship with synthetic Try example fixtures, clearly labeled as
fictional demo data.

## Mock versus Live Meta Muse AI

**Mock (offline, free)** is the default and needs no key.

- Deterministic keyword-overlap heuristic, no network, no randomness.
- Score is shared key words over claim key words. Verdicts: Supported
  (0.5 and above), Contested or Needs review (0.2 to 0.5), Unsupported
  or Missing (below 0.2).
- Every card carries `Method: keyword-overlap heuristic (not an AI judgment)`.
- Contradiction flags are heuristic leads for human review, not accusations.

**Live Meta API (billed)** calls Meta Muse models over HTTPS.

- Default model `muse-spark-1.3`, endpoint `https://api.meta.ai/v1`.
  Also known: `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, `muse-spark-1.1`,
  `muse-wonder-1.0`.
- One grounded call per claim. The model receives numbered evidence and must
  cite by `[index]` only. Citations are validated against evidence the model
  actually received. Unknown, out-of-range, or missing citations never become
  verdicts.
- Support with zero citations is downgraded to UNVERIFIED. Failed, refused,
  truncated, or unparseable calls record explicit UNVERIFIED findings with a
  `live fallback` method. Failures never show mock results and never drop
  claims silently.

  prompts, at most 12 evidence items per call (800 chars each, 1000 chars
  per claim), per-run call budget equal to claim count, zero retries,
  30 second timeout. Per-run tokens and rough USD estimate are shown, plus
  a per-session total in Settings.

# NYX Guard

**In two trials of the same invoice with conflicting totals, the naive agent paid twice. NYX Guard paid zero.** Both used Meta models and synthetic payment ledgers. [Русская версия](docs/README_RU.md)

[Watch the demo video](https://youtu.be/VjdnTy5MbEk)

| Observed result across 8 paired development trials | Naive agent | NYX Guard |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Trials with a payment on the conflicting-total invoice | 2 of 2 | **0 of 2** |
| Trials with a payment across three risk scenarios | 4 of 6 | **0 of 6** |
| Largest recorded payment on a conflicting-total invoice | 875,000 UZS | **0 UZS** |
| Correct payments on the ordinary invoice | 2 of 2 | 2 of 2 |
| Wrong-recipient payments | 0 | 0 |

Four known synthetic documents were run twice. The table reports observed behavior on those documents. A separate fresh run on **the same file, V3A07**, recorded 875,000 UZS for the naive agent and zero entries for NYX Guard. The guarded extractor abstained, and the reviewer identified conflicting totals. [Results and trial evidence](docs/RESULTS.md)

## Try it

```sh
docker compose up
```

Open [localhost:8766](http://127.0.0.1:8766) and enter the local demo password `nyx-demo`. Choose `N01` and enter a budget of `4000000` UZS for a first replay. The default service uses bundled mock inputs and needs no API key. Docker publishes the interface on loopback. The image targets Linux x86-64, with emulation on ARM hosts where supported by Docker.

## Design

The project applies the [Dual LLM pattern](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Apr/25/dual-llm-pattern/) and draws on [CaMeL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813) to separate untrusted documents from privileged actions. Muse Wonder plans using the owner's command and allowed references. Muse Spark extracts invoice fields and separately reviews the document. The bank takes the recipient from a trusted registry and enforces the shared budget and duplicate checks inside its transaction.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Owner command and allowed references] --> B[Wonder planner]
    B --> C[Plan validator]
    D[Invoice image] --> E[Spark extraction and separate risk review]
    C --> G[Synthetic bank and payment policy]
    E --> G
    H[Trusted supplier registry] --> G
    G --> I[Commit, block, or send to review]
```

## Built during the hackathon

- A typed invoice plan and a tool boundary that binds each action to the selected document.
- A transactional synthetic bank with shared budgets, duplicate checks and a fixed recipient registry.
- Separate extraction and risk review, a local owner interface, and a repeatable mock mode.
- A paired naive-versus-guarded evaluation, synthetic fixtures, and recorded outcomes.

See [build provenance](HACKATHON_BUILD.md) for the project history and [the threat model](THREAT_MODEL.md) for scope and limits. The test suite contains 227 cases. The latest clean Windows run passed 226 and skipped one symlink test.

# CinemaFabric

![A film strip turning into threads of light that link several computers and the cloud](docs/banner.jpg)

CinemaFabric makes the machines you already own and the Meta Model API work as one AI studio. At its core is a small *distributed inference fabric*: every step of a production is a task, and the fabric sends each task to the place that runs it best, whether a local NVIDIA GPU, an Apple silicon Mac, a plain CPU or a Meta model in the cloud. It weighs quality, latency, queue depth, licence and cost, records the reason for every decision, moves work elsewhere when a machine drops out, and reuses any result it has already produced. Adding a machine adds capacity; removing one costs nothing but time.

The studio built on the fabric turns a one-sentence idea into a finished trailer or short film, complete with a script, storyboard, poster, voice-over, score, subtitles and release copy. It is a demanding test of the fabric: a 20-second trailer is around sixty tasks of nine kinds (writing, safety checks, pictures, cutouts, depth, speech, music, transcription and watermarking), and the router places each one.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. **Built with Llama.**

*The banner was painted by Muse Image and the [architecture diagrams](docs/architecture.md) were drawn by Muse Spark, both routed through CinemaFabric itself.*

## Why hybrid

A team with a few GPUs and a cloud API account usually ends up using one or the other: local hardware sits idle while everything goes to the cloud, or work stays local and waits for models those machines cannot run. CinemaFabric uses both at once, each for what it does best.

- **Local machines take the work they run well.** Trailer scripts, checks and agents on Muse Glimmer, content checks on Llama Guard, and depth, voice-over, music and watermarking on local GPUs. In a benchmark of the same ideas under each routing preference, local-first and balanced routing ran about 70% of every film's tasks locally, and the local machines were working for more than 80% of each production.
- **The cloud takes what local hardware cannot do as well.** Muse Wonder writes short films, Muse Image draws the pictures, SAM 3.1 cuts out the subjects, Muse Voice Transcribe checks the narration, and Muse Spark or Muse Wonder step in when a task needs a larger model or the local ones are busy. That is nearly all of the cloud use: about $0.13 for a 30-second trailer and about $0.50 for a 2-minute short film.
- **Finished work is reused.** Results are cached by content, so retries, redos and new versions reuse everything that has not changed. An alternate ending re-made three of nine shots for $0.035, against $0.136 for the original film.
- **Capacity follows the hardware.** A busy device passes work to the next option, a failing one is taken out of rotation, and a new machine joins with one command; its node agent finds the devices and decides which models each can hold.
- **Policy decides what may run where.*
