# Bearings

**Where is my project really, and how far is it from MVP?**

Coding agents say "done". Tickets say "in progress". Bearings reads the evidence instead: your files, your tests, your git history and your [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code) sessions, and tells you what is verified, what is only claimed, and what the evidence contradicts.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). Status: **work in progress, built during the hackathon**. See [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md) for exactly what works today and what does not.

## The idea in one picture

```
MVP description (typed or spoken)
  -> acceptance items            a Muse model proposes them; you review them
    -> evidence for each item    files, check commands, git, Muse Code sessions
      -> status per item         verified / built / declared / contradicted / missing / unknown
        -> distance to MVP       reported as a range, never a made-up percentage
```

Plain code decides every status. Models help turn a description into items; they never decide a verdict and they may never propose a command to run.

## Status model

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `verified` | A check passed and every listed deliverable exists |
| `built` | The deliverables exist, but nothing has proved they work |
| `declared` | Claimed done, but nothing can confirm it |
| `contradicted` | Claimed or built, and the evidence says otherwise |
| `missing` | Nothing (or only part) of it exists yet |
| `unknown` | Not enough evidence to say. Never counted as done |

Distance to MVP is a range: the lower bound counts only verified items; the upper bound also counts built, declared and unknown items as if they would hold. Contradicted and missing items never help either bound.

## Try it

Requires Node 20 or newer. No dependencies to install.

```bash
# See the seeded demo: an "agent" claims everything is done, the evidence disagrees
node bin/bearings.js status --root examples/cart-demo

# Write a self-contained HTML report
node bin/bearings.js report --root examples/cart-demo
```

On your own project:

```bash
cd my-project
node /path/to/bearings/bin/bearings.js init            # starter .bearings/mvp.json
node /path/to/bearings/bin/bearings.js status          # measure it
```

### Using Muse Code

You need Muse Code installed and signed in (`muse --version`).

```bash
# Turn an MVP description into items (preview, then save with --write)
bearings define "A small web app where a trader records sales and exports a weekly CSV." --write

# Or speak it (16 kHz mono WAV, transcribed by Muse Voice Transcribe)
bearings define --voice mvp.wav --write

# Store a Muse Code run as evidence
muse exec --json "build the cart total" > run.jsonl
bearings ingest run.jsonl
bearings status

# Let a model write the checks, then approve the ones you trust
bearings suggest-checks               # read-only Muse agent proposes scripts; nothing runs
bearings approve cart-total           # read

# Marine Compute Swarm

Previously **Solar Swarm**. The project was renamed to Marine Compute Swarm to make its ocean-based compute focus clearer; Git history retains the earlier name.

**Data centers that follow the sun.** A swarm of floating, solar-powered compute nodes that watches the sky, dodges the clouds, and turns sunlight into compute across the planet.

## The idea

Each node floats on the ocean, carries its own solar array, and sells the compute it runs. Sunlight is the fuel, and clouds are the main thing standing between a node and its output. Because the nodes can move, they can respond: watch the sky, decide where the clouds are going, and shift out of their way. Marine Compute Swarm is the simulation that shows how that works and what it is worth.

## Run it

```bash
npm install
npm run dev      # http://127.0.0.1:5173
npm test         # unit and interface tests
npm run build    # production build in dist/
```

Optional starting view from the address bar: `?cam=x,y,z&target=x,y,z&explode=n0`.

## What you see

- **Explore:** the home page introduces three connected views through clickable visual previews: Swarm, Unit Bench and Weather Simulator with Muse coordination. Hover or focus a preview for context; on mobile, descriptions stay visible.
- **Swarm (`?view=swarm`):** the swarm on a 3D ocean under a 3D cloud layer, with the value up front: energy harvested, compute delivered, revenue and carbon avoided for a daylight day, each compared with a swarm that only holds station. Scale buttons show the same numbers at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 nodes. The detailed controls live behind the **Controls** button.
- **Move around:** drag to orbit, Shift + left-drag (or right-drag) to pan, and scroll to zoom from the whole swarm down to one node, and dive below the surface (to 15 m) to see hulls, keels and thrusters from underneath.
- **Playback:** 1×, 2× and 5× allow slow inspection alongside the faster simulation speeds.
- **Hardware scale:** one scene unit is one meter. Black cell-pattern PV panels meet physical hinges and support struts. Battery packs, compute enclosures, heat exchanger, antennas and thrusters have distinct geometry and mounts. Inspection offers assembled and exploded views, equipment dimensions in millimeters, and a one-meter scale bar. Equipment envelopes and the exposed GPU modules are representative estimates, not manufacturer CAD; the assembled compute remains in its sealed enclosure.
- **Hover and click:** hovering a node or a petal highlights it. Clicking a node opens its exploded view: every subsystem fanned apart, each part with a mass, power, cost and a one-line reason for its placement, all editable.
- **Stays afloat:** every part has a mass and a position. Draft, freeboard, reserve buoyancy, metacentric height and wind heel are computed live, with petals deployed and stowed. An edit that would sink the node or tip it over is blocked, and the app recommends which other knobs to change so the value you want can work

**Kaptr** ("Answer with your camera.") is a live photo game on Google Play and the App Store: a daily photo riddle, Tic Tac Toe, Bingo, Hunts and Binder collections. You answer every prompt by pointing your camera at the real thing, and an AI judges the shot in a couple of seconds.

For the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme: Build for your world) I put Kaptr's judging on Meta's models and made the judge check its own work:

An AI judge that says "no" with no explanation feels arbitrary, and one that can be fooled by a photo of a monitor is a cheat code. Two of Meta's models checking each other fixes both.

# Patient Twin

**A hospital night shift you can practice before it happens.**
Training simulator on synthetic patients. Not for clinical use.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track) by Dr. Jhonatan Munoz, physician.

**▶ Demo video (3 min): https://youtu.be/YZqfO7NP1-c**

---

## The problem

About 795,000 Americans die or are permanently disabled by diagnostic error every year
([Newman-Toker, BMJ Qual Saf 2024](https://qualitysafety.bmj.com/content/33/2/109)).
The errors that hurt patients are rarely a wrong fact on an exam. They are a rushed history,
a lab from last month read as today's, a fluid order that was never given, a 3 AM call answered
with "continue the plan", and a handoff that leaves out the one number that mattered.

Trainees practice exams. They rarely practice a night.

## What Patient Twin does

A trainee works one patient through a 12-hour admission, on one screen:

1. **Talks to the patient** on a live video call (or by typing). The patient is played by Muse Spark,
   reveals history only when asked, and trusts the trainee more or less depending on how they communicate.
2. **Pulls the patient's devices**: a week of smartwatch, home blood pressure cuff, thermometer and scale data.
3. **Orders tests in their own words** ("blood cx x2, UA, CMP") and gets full lab panels with abnormal values flagged.
4. **Chooses a working diagnosis and a plan.**
5. **Answers the night nurse at 3:40 AM.** The nurse phones in the new numbers; the trainee's orders change the next six hours.
6. **Answers the day nurse at 9:40 AM** with the morning labs.
7. **Reads a deliberately messy chart and writes the note** (H&P, progress note, hand-off or discharge summary),
   from scratch or starting from an ambient AI draft.
8. **Gets graded by code**, with an honest score, critical-error caps, an OSCE history checklist, a review of every
   diagnosis, and a plain account of what their decisions did to the patient.

Three stations: sepsis (urinary source), decompensated heart failure, upper GI bleed.

## The core idea: AI for realism, code for truth

No model grades its own work.

- A **deterministic physiology engine** (plain code, no randomness) produces every vital sign and lab value, hour by hour.
  The trainee's decisions at arrival and at the nurse call choose which course the patient follows.
- A **rule-based checker** compares every number anyone writes (trainee, nurse, scribe, attending) against the engine,
  at the time it refers to. Old values, rejected samples, untimed readings and orders never given are recognized as traps.
- **Meta models do what code cannot**: hold a natural conversation, sound like a nurse at 3 AM, write an HPI from a
  conversation, and explain the score like an attending. Their numbers are always checked, and a wrong number is never shown.

|---|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | The patient and family (streamed, so the face st

# WREN Story Engine — no-code private LoRAs for brand mascots

My name is Don Martirez, and for Meta's Global AI Developer Hackathon, I decided to build for my world.

As a visual designer and storyteller, my pain point is simple: I can't produce content fast without losing consistency. Norman the Good Gnome is IP I'm developing with AI. The first graphics took forever — and every new storyline since has meant hours of fighting to match a look and feel I already had. Every iteration drifts a little further from the original.

So I built the app I wished existed: WREN turns anyone's brand mascot into a private, reusable AI model — no code, no GPU of your own. Upload a few reference photos and generate that same character in new scenes, on demand, without drift. This isn't an image analyzer. Analysis is step zero. What WREN manufactures is new model weights: curated datasets, paid GPU fine-tuning, versioned adapters, and finished artwork in three profiles — t-shirt graphics, storyboard panels, and video-ready scenes.

## How it works — three steps

**1 · Add your character to the Asset Bible.** Meta's vision models (`muse-wonder-1.0`) read the reference photo and encode what makes your character yours — colours, build, garments, signature details — into a frozen DNA profile. Before you spend a cent, WREN grades the dataset for free: duplicates, wardrobe clashes, too few poses. Rewrite any caption in plain words, download the `.zip` to see exactly what trains.

**2 · Train.** Not everyone owns expensive GPUs or can code a LoRA pipeline — so the backend does it all: it packages the dataset, spins up a GPU on Modal, and fine-tunes an open image model (SDXL) into your character's personal adapter, locked to a trigger word only you own. Rank 16, UNet + text encoder, capped steps.

**3 · Prove it before serving.** This is the part no one else demos: **WREN refuses to ship a bad adapter.** The moment training finishes, the app auto-renders three probe images (neutral full body, action, close-up) through the fresh model and checks them against the DNA — one figure, full body, correct outfit colours. Pass and the adapter goes live as `ready`. Fail and it parks at `needs_review` with the reasons spelled out; a bad adapter never silently replaces a good one, and `needs_review` adapters are never served to explicit requests.

Only then do you create: pick the character, type an action like "waving hello" or "shoveling dirt", and generate — through your LoRA for series consistency, or flip the adapter off and use Meta's reference model on the same prompt for faithful one-offs.

## Under the hood

A deterministic, seed-locked pipeline: Meta's models for understanding, Modal GPUs for training, open SDXL for generation. Every user is isolated with their own trigger words, adapters, and quotas. The differentiator isn't the stack, it's the loop: grade before you pay, train without code, and prove likeness before serving. No consumer tool validates its own fine-tunes

# Recall — finds the photo you remember wrong

Describe a photo with one detail mistaken — a colour, a count, a
place — and Recall doubts each detail in turn, searches alternate
interpretations, grounds what it sees, and asks up to three
one-tap questions to land your photo in its top ten.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track,
Build for Your World). Solo project.

**Live demo:** https://thelastpage--recall-console-web.us-east.modal.run
(Modal, T4 GPU; 5,000-photo demo library, folder-adding disabled).
First visit may take ~5 seconds to wake. It also runs locally in
one command (below) — that local console is what the demo video
will show. How it works, in simple words: see the
[product details page](https://thelastpage--recall-console-web.us-east.modal.run/details.html).

## Built with Meta models

| Meta model | What it does in Recall |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Reads a free description into clues, checks the top 40 photos against it at finish, and reads evidence from the top photos |
| **MetaCLIP-L14** (open weights) | Embeds every photo and every search for exact cosine retrieval |
| **SAM 3.1** (Meta Model API) | Outlines the object the user described in the top photos, so colour and count are read inside the object, not the whole frame. Runs when a Meta API key is set; otherwise Muse Spark vision reads the same facts |
| **Muse Wonder** | Planned the build and wrote most of the first version of the code |

## Try it now (local console)

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r backend/requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env   # optional: add META_MODEL_API_KEY for Muse parsing
python -m uvicorn backend.app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 — pick a corpus (two are pre-ingested
in this workspace: 5k COCO val, 82,783 COCO train2014), or add
your own photos:

- **Choose folder…** — system picker. Photos are sent to the local
  server (127.0.0.1 only), embedded, and afterwards only small
  thumbnails + embeddings (~2 KB/photo) are kept by default, so a
  5 GB folder does not become another 5 GB. A checkbox keeps
  full-size copies if you want them.
- **Paste a path** — Windows (`E:\photos\trip`) or Linux
  (`/home/you/photos`) paths both work; reads photos in place,
  zero copying. Best for large folders.

Then ask in plain language — “a man riding a bicycle next to a red
car”, “the cake on the kitchen table” — and compare **plain
search** against **Recall repair** side by side, with per-query
timings, clue chips, and rescued candidates outlined in green.

## How it works

- **Muse Spark 1.3** (through OpenRouter or the Meta Model API) parses a free
  description into clue chips, reranks the top 40 at finish, and reads evidence
  from the top photos. Questions are deterministic templates (subject, bundled
  colour/count dimension, uncertainty, attribute), never model-invented. Without
  a key, the offline lexicon parser splits a plain sentence into colour

# Actual Size: Step Inside

**Step inside artworks with AI.**

Actual Size hangs public-domain paintings at their real size, beside a person 1.70 m tall, and
lets a visitor step inside them. An agent inspects every scene before it hangs, and a scene that
fails does not hang. This repository is an entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon
(Indie Developer track, *Build for Your World*), built during the event.

## What a visitor can do

- Walk a gallery of 59 paintings from the Art Institute of Chicago, each at its catalogue size.
- Step inside 8 of them: walk up to the painting, through the frame, and move between its layers
  with the mouse, by tilting a phone, or by leaning in.
- Read each scene's inspection card: the checks it passed, how far the visitor may move, and the
  model calls and cost behind it. The "Not hung" panel lists the scenes the agent refused.
- Ask the guide for something ("show me something stormy") and be walked to it.
- See each painting's colours and three works it hangs well beside, with a sentence on why.
- Rebuild the gallery by size, colour or year, with three wall finishes.
- Add a perspective on any work, typed or spoken. It stays in the visitor's own browser.
- Visit a resident artist room. The first resident is Nicola Harvey, with *Seed Phrase*, eight
  works made with Muse Image, with *Step Inside* as the centrepiece.
- Open the gallery in WebXR on Meta Quest. This mode has been tested on Meta's Immersive Web
  Emulator only, not on a headset.

## Every AI capability is a Meta model

| Capability | Model (Meta Model API) |
|---|---|
| Planning which objects sit at which depth | Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`) |
| Cutting each object out of the painting | SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`) |
| Inspecting a scene and choosing accept, repair or reject | Muse Wonder (`muse-wonder-1.0`), with bounded tools |
| The guide | Muse Spark, with tools |
| "Hangs well beside" sentences | Muse Spark |
| Turning a spoken perspective into text | Muse Voice Transcribe (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) |
| The resident artist's own works | Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`) |

Muse Code wrote all of the application code. [DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md](DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md) records the
tool behind each change, and [PROVENANCE.md](PROVENANCE.md) sets out what counts as event work.
Every model call is logged with its tokens and cost in `ledger/usage.jsonl`. The model calls for
the whole build came to under five dollars.

## How Step Inside works

No depth-estimation model is used for museum scenes. Muse Spark returns an ordinal plan of
what sits in front of what, SAM 3.1 cuts each object out, and deterministic geometry places the
pieces as flat layers in front of the painting. Gaps are filled from neighbouring paint, so every
visible colour in a museum scene comes from the painting. The result is a 2.5D scene, not a
recovered 3D model. The walk-in Seed Phrase rooms' painted mode additionally spreads its paint
dabs with Meta's local DINOv2 depth model

# Corner Case

**Test the fix before the next crash.**

Pedestrians keep getting hit at the same Manhattan corners. Cities usually fix a corner after
people are hurt, then wait years of crash counts to learn whether the fix worked. Corner Case lets a
city street-safety engineer test changes on a real corridor, **7th Avenue from W 30th St to Central
Park South**, before spending money:

1. **Where people get hurt**: every pedestrian crash since 2023 from NYC crash records, located by lat/lon.
2. **Watch the corner**: Meta **SAM 3.1** tracks every person and car in real street video; **Muse Spark 1.3** writes timestamped notes, and SAM cross-checks each one.
3. **Rebuild it**: a deterministic street model of all 30 corners (signals, walk head starts, turning cars, walkers) counts simulated close calls: a walker and a car at the same spot less than 1.5 s apart (post-encroachment time).
4. **Can we trust it?**: the street model, which never sees a crash, is scored against 2025–26 crashes it never saw, next to simple baselines.
5. **Agents try fixes**: our fine-tuned **Muse Glimmer** (open weights on Modal) screens all 30 corners in 11 s and gives each agent a first guess to beat; one **Muse Wonder** agent per intersection proposes changes, runs them in the street model, and keeps or drops them; a Wonder coordinator rejects fixes that push risk to the next block.
6. **Stress the future**: the coordinator picks futures likely to break the plan (holiday crowds, shows letting out, rain at night, a bus lane, drivers ignoring turn bans); broken fixes go back to their agent for revision.
7. **The plan**: a printable brief: what to fund first, simulated benefit, added car delay, rough costs with sources found by **Muse Spark web search**, and an **after it's built** watcher (**Muse Glimmer**, open weights on Modal) that counts close calls on camera so the city learns in weeks, not years.

Every number on screen carries a **REAL**, **MEASURED**, **OPEN DATA**, **ASSUMPTION** or **SIMULATED**
badge with its source. Simulated close calls are never presented as injuries.

uv sync

# open http://localhost:8000 and press "Play the story"

# Assemvio **Show it once, and your new hire builds it right.** An expert wires a terminal block once, then types a short narration. Assemvio turns that into a step plan. A new hire then builds it with a voice in their ear while an overhead camera checks every wire: which terminal, which colour, whether the step is done. When the evidence isn't good enough, it says "not sure" instead of guessing. ## The verifier decides, Spark explains Every PASS / FAIL / UNSURE comes from deterministic code: set differences against the plan's expected state, terminal membership from wire ends, a per-terminal belief tracker, and a cross-check between two witnesses (SAM 3.1 masks and a colour threshold). Same frame in, same verdict out. Muse Spark never sets a verdict. It compiles the expert's narration into a plan (which code then validates with `Plan.from_dict`) and answers the worker's questions about the last look. Nothing it says changes a verdict. # Locked Computer Assist

**AI help for a locked computer: Muse Glimmer and Muse Spark through a USB KVM.**

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, on groundwork from before it: [what was built
when](#hackathon-entry), with the detail in [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md).

**Demo video** (2:34): [youtu.be/MbNkb62ZErY](https://youtu.be/MbNkb62ZErY). In its 4 Nov run,
Glimmer found the bugs and the KVM typed the fix, then the check after typing stopped the run before
the save, because VS Code auto-indented the next line.

Some computers may not run AI software: a locked-down work laptop, a lab PC, a machine on a separate
network. With the approval of whoever owns such a computer and its data, this project gives it AI help
without installing anything on it and without getting around any of its controls. A small USB KVM sits
between that computer, the **locked computer**, and a second one, the **AI computer**. To the locked
computer the KVM is only a monitor and a USB keyboard and mouse. If a policy there blocks new USB
keyboards, typing isn't available.

1. **Capture.** The KVM passes the locked computer's HDMI picture to the AI computer as a USB video
   device. Nothing is installed on the locked computer.
2. **Read locally.** Meta's open-weights **Muse Glimmer** runs on the AI computer's GPU (llama.cpp) and
   reads the screen: code with its line numbers, a description, or the error messages. In this
   pipeline, screen images never leave the AI computer.
3. **Redact.** Keys, tokens, passwords in `key = value` form, email addresses, common hostnames and the
   terms you list become placeholders. Glimmer trims the text to what the question needs, and it's
   redacted again.
4. **Ask the cloud.** Only that redacted text goes to **Muse Spark**, Meta's stronger cloud model
   ([why both](LEARNINGS.md#local-and-cloud-together)), through Meta's Model API (`store: false`).
   Spark answers, or proposes code edits as function calls. With *Local only*
   (`--local-only`), Glimmer does both on the AI computer instead, and nothing is sent.
5. **Act, with your approval.** You approve each edit at the keyboard, or once per run with `--auto`.
   The KVM's keyboard types it into VS Code on the locked computer, Glimmer reads the screen again to
   check it, and `fix` saves the file once the model that wrote the fix has checked it on a fresh
   reading and you've allowed it.

It's for people who work on such computers and get stuck on an error or a bug with no AI help allowed,
and for the organisations that own those computers and want to keep their data in. It's harder than it
sounds. The AI computer gets only a compressed video of the screen and can only press keys and move the
mouse, so it has to read small code from that picture, keep confidential text from leaving, and check
on the screen that every key it typed did what it should.

# Loci

**Loci gives AI glasses and robots a private memory of the places you move through.**

Named after the *method of loci*, the memory-palace technique of tying memories to places. Walk through your home
or down a street with a camera at eye level. Loci blurs faces, number plates and screens before anything is saved,
finds the objects, reads shop signs, notes the state of things like a lit stove or a fan left on, hears what you
say, and places everything in 3D with metric scale. Then ask:

- "Did I leave the stove on?" → *"When you left the kitchen at 0:15, the right burner was lit."* + the frame it saw
- "Where was <shop name>?" → *"On your left, about 280 m into the walk, at 4:41."* + the signboard frame
- "Where's my passport?" → *"I haven't seen a passport in any capture."*

Every answer cites the observations it used, is checked by a verifier against the memory before you see it, says
*when* a state was seen (never what it is now), and comes with a position in metres and a robot goal.

## How it works

```
video ─▶ extract ─▶ redact ─▶ name ─▶ track ─▶ geometry ─▶ lift ─▶ associate ─▶ relations ─▶ attributes
         keyframes  SAM 3.1   Glimmer SAM 3.1  MapAnything  2D→3D  objects     on/near/      signs, states
                    blur                                                       side of road  (Glimmer)
      ─▶ transcribe ─▶ store (SQLite) ─▶ leaving check (agent) ─▶ ask (agent + verifier) ─▶ viewer / API
         Muse Voice                       alerts                   Muse Spark or Glimmer
```

`loci build <video> --scene home|street` runs every stage, each in its own subprocess so only one large model is on
the GPU at a time. Every model output is cached on disk.

| Role | Model | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Redaction, segmentation, tracking | SAM 3.1 | your GPU |
| Camera poses, metric depth | MapAnything (Apache) | your GPU |
| Object names, rooms, sign reading, states, leaving check, offline answers | **Muse Glimmer 30B** (GGUF, llama.cpp) | your GPU |
| Answers when online | Muse Spark 1.3 | Meta Model API |
| Speech (25 languages, mixed in one walk) | Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0 | Meta Model API |
| Speech offline, and all street audio | faster-whisper | your machine |

Cloud is optional: `LOCI_CLOUD=0` (or `cloud.enabled: false`) runs everything on device. When cloud is on and a
call fails, Glimmer answers instead. The viewer shows a badge for which model answered.

## Runs on open weights

The memory is built by **Muse Glimmer 30B**, Meta's open-weight model (Apache 2.0), on one consumer GPU:

- Model: `Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf` (13.4 GB) with `mmproj-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q8_0.gguf` (2.1 GB)
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4080 SUPER, 16 GB (14.8 GB peak), CUDA 12.8
- Server: llama.cpp `llama-server` (build e86f5fd)

```bash
llama-server -m checkpoints/glimmer/Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf \
  --mmproj checkpoints/glimmer/mmproj-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q8_0.gguf --jinja -c 16384 -ngl 99 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8

# ChronoCut

Autonomous video-editing orchestrator for interviews, oral history and documentary footage.

ChronoCut turns raw interview audio, videos and scattered photos into fully scripted, synchronized and rendered mini-documentaries. Every AI decision lands in a versioned, reviewable Edit Decision List (EDL) that you refine by hand in a browser timeline and re-render. Each telemetry row in the product names the exact model that produced a given decision, so the automated edit is auditable end to end.

**Live demo:** https://chronocut.pages.dev/ — upload footage, watch the agents work, then edit the cut in the timeline. (Free-tier backend: the first visit may need up to a minute while the instance wakes.)

## Highlights

- **Multi-agent production pipeline** — an archivist, screenwriter, director and editor supervisor cooperate under a deterministic lead orchestrator; each stage is segmented, crash-safe and resumable.
- **EDL as the single source of truth** — every cut, caption, grade, transition, speed ramp and B-roll insert is a validated, versioned operation on a persistent EDL document, never a side effect of a model response.
- **Browser timeline studio** — real clip blocks with waveform/thumbnail previews, a command URI validated on the server, revision history with undo, and a live playhead transport, all editing the server EDL with optimistic local mirroring.
- **Any file in** — audio, photos and video route to their pipeline stages; any other file (notes, script, subtitle, PDF) is read as text and folded into the director's brief.
- **Conversational edit agent** — a chat-driven planner maps natural-language requests ("cut the pauses", "make it feel warmer") onto the same structured operation vocabulary as the UI.
- **Live telemetry** — job progress, agent activity and EDL revisions stream to the frontend over Server-Sent Events.
- **Governed model seam** — one entrypoint wraps every model call with prompt caching, rate limiting, a per-job cost cap, in-flight coalescing and an automatic Meta-model-only failover chain; deterministic templates backstop everything.
- **Free-tier first** — every external provider has a deterministic or graceful fallback; the whole product deploys with no paid API essential.

## Architecture

We document the system in depth (with rendered diagrams) in [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) and [`docs/pipeline.md`](docs/pipeline.md). Short version:

```

# CacheLens - why isn't my prefix cache hitting?

CacheLens diagnoses prefix-cache misses in self-hosted LLM serving (vLLM).
It probes a synthetic agent-like workload, finds what breaks byte-identical
leading prefixes, and measures the effect of a candidate fix with a
controlled replay.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 - Nov 4 window)
against **Muse Glimmer 30B** (Meta open weights, Apache 2.0) served with
vLLM on a single GPU.

## Demo video
Narrated 3-minute walkthrough (Nov 4): plays inline on the
[v1.0.0 release page](https://github.com/0xViking/cachelens/releases/tag/v1.0.0)
(direct link: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0dcbe18c-d60c-48a7-8045-f5085820f847).
The older silent cuts under `video/` (`cachelens-demo.mp4`, `-v2`, `-v3`) are
superseded working drafts kept for history; the release video is the final cut.

## The demo story (verified on Muse Glimmer 30B, Nov 3 2026)
1. An agent workload (18 dispatcher requests sharing a 25.5KB runbook prefix)
   is probed against vLLM - `probe.py --variant ts_before`.
2. CacheLens diffs all captured prompts and pinpoints the cause: a per-request
   timestamp at char 28, BEFORE the shared prefix - `analyze.py`.
   Engine `/metrics`: 1.0% prefix-cache hit rate (1,088 / 104,328 tokens).
3. The fix (move per-request fields after the shared prefix) is replayed -
   `probe.py --variant ts_after`. Observed hit rate rises to 93.6%
   (97,696 / 104,328 tokens). Median per-request latency drops 34.3%
   (3.6855s -> 2.4200s) - single synthetic run, not a production benchmark.

Scope and honesty notes:
- One synthetic, serial run (18 requests per variant) on one A100-80GB,
  Nov 3, 2026. Not a production benchmark, no TTFT/cost-saving claim, no
  answer-equivalence check, no broad model/engine compatibility claim.
- The official `vllm/vllm-openai:muse-glimmer` build does not populate
  `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, so the analyzer uses engine
  `/metrics` counter deltas as the measurement of record and says so.
- Provenance: image tag `vllm/vllm-openai:muse-glimmer` and the HF `main`
  revision are mutable; the recorded run used vLLM 0.26.1rc1.dev608+g99a10304d
  (see `evidence/*/vllm.log`). Exact bit-for-bit reproduction is not
  guaranteed by these tags.
- The analyzer fails closed (INCONCLUSIVE) on missing/invalid metrics,
  counter resets, hits>queries, mismatched variants/volumes, or errored
  requests. Local tests: `python3 test_cachelens.py`.

Cost, auth, data retention:
- `modal run --detach modal_serve.py` spends real money: an A100-80GB GPU
  (~$2.50/hr list) plus ~60GB of weights cached on a Modal volume
  ($0.09/GiB/mo). Delete the `cachelens-weights` volume when done
  (`modal volume delete cachelens-weights`); `cachelens-evidence` is small.
- Needs a Modal token in `~/.modal.toml` (`modal token new`).
- Evidence JSONL contains FULL prompts. The committed evidence is 100%
  synthetic (see `workload.py`). If you probe real traffic, keep that
  evi

# LabWatch

LabWatch watches a lab experiment video, checks it against the written protocol, and writes an evidence-linked lab notebook. Every claim in the notebook points back to a measured event.

**Pipeline:** video → colour/motion measurements (OpenCV, inside the vessel) → events (addition, stirring/swirling, colour change, lighting change) → protocol check (missing steps, wrong durations) → Muse Glimmer (Meta open weights, vision) writes the notebook from that evidence and the keyframes → HTML report.

The model never measures anything itself. Numbers come from pixels, and the model only explains them. A citation check flags any sentence that has no event id, or that cites an event that doesn't exist.

## Web app

```powershell
cd D:\labwatch
py -3.12 -m uvicorn server:app --port 8090
# open http://127.0.0.1:8090
```

- **Upload:** add a video, drag a box around the liquid, paste the protocol, and choose whether Muse Glimmer writes the notebook.
- **Runs:** the list shows status, compliance and deviations. Jobs run one at a time.
- **Report tab:** the interactive report, with evidence replay, quality score, evidence graph and event review.
- **What-if tab:** a protocol simulation, with an optional Muse Glimmer explanation.
- **Compare tab:** any two finished runs side by side.

Backend: FastAPI (`server.py`). Frontend: one static page (`static/index.html`). Runs are stored in `runs_web/`.

## Run (command line)

```powershell
cd D:\labwatch
py -3.12 -m labwatch run demo\synthetic_titration.mp4 --protocol demo\protocol.txt --roi 192,150,256,250 --out demo\run
# open demo\run\report.html
py -3.12 -m labwatch ask demo\run "Why did this run deviate from the protocol?"
```

What-if questions and run comparison:

```powershell
py -3.12 -m labwatch whatif demo\run_glimmer "What if I stir for 30 seconds?" --protocol demo\protocol.txt
py -3.12 -m labwatch compare demo\run_correct demo\run_glimmer --out demo\compare.html
```

- `--roi x,y,w,h` is the box around the liquid. Without it, the centre of the frame is used.
- `--mask mask.png` takes a vessel mask (for example from SAM 3) and replaces the box.
- `--no-llm` writes the notebook from a fixed template instead of the model.

## Model (Muse Glimmer 30B, local)

```powershell
D:\labwatch\llama\llama-server.exe -m D:\labwatch\models\Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf `

# Unhurried: the turn-taking layer voice AI is missing, proven on the hardest case: stammering.

**On 15 recordings of my own free speech (set `real_self`, 8.8 minutes), a normal voice bot replied while I was still talking 14 times (8 of 15 recordings); with Unhurried's default engine, 2 times (2 of 15). Invented words: 0.** Same audio, same measure (cut-offs), streamed through the live server. [Results](bench/results.html).

- Voice editing on/off, my own voice: [`web/voice-over.html`](web/voice-over.html)
- Everything built so far: [docs/PROJECT_OVERVIEW.md](docs/PROJECT_OVERVIEW.md)

**Built during the hackathon: all code written Oct 28 – Nov 4, 2026.** Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track, Theme 1 "Build for Your World".

Measured on stammering only. The same silence-based turn-taking likely affects anyone who pauses; not measured yet.

## Meta models used

| Model | What it does in Unhurried |
| --- | --- |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) | Live text and end-of-speech as *one signal, not the decision*; keyword biasing per person; Voice Studio transcripts. |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Tie-break completeness check (at most 700 ms), meaning rebuild for self-corrections, the learner's tool calls, the assistants. |
| **Muse Spark 1.2 (audio)** | Listens to recordings twice and writes stammers as spoken ("B- B- Binula"). Code checks every cut it suggests. |
| **wav2vec 2.0** (`facebook/wav2vec2-base-960h`, Meta open model) | Places every word and stammer in the audio (our own CTC aligner); an independent check of what was heard. |

---

## What it is

Unhurried sits between a person and any voice bot. It decides when the person has really finished, removes repeated sounds without changing the meaning, and confirms before important actions. It fixes the machine, not the speaker: it never scores, rates or coaches anyone's speech.

**Voice Studio** cleans recordings in the person's own voice: Muse Spark 1.2 listens for stammers, wav2vec 2.0 places each one, code checks the evidence, and the person approves every cut. The output only cuts the original audio; nothing is added.

## The problem

Voice AI is built for fluent speech. A stammer block is often a silent pause, and voice bots treat silence as "finished". They reply in the middle of a sentence, so they cut you off. Repeated sounds ("b-b-book") confuse them, so they mishear the request.

We measured this on Meta's own streaming speech model: with a 3-second pause after "Book a table for", Muse Voice Transcribe's default end-of-speech ended the turn about 0.5 s after the last word ([probe report](scripts/probe_report.md)).

1. The browser streams 24 kHz audio to the Unhurried server.
2. The audio router forwards it to **Muse Voice Transcribe** and gets live text and end-of-speech events. A zero-lag audio level check runs on the same audio.
3. The **turn engine** decides on every pause: hold or send.

# Brieblue Multilingual Ad Factory

> One master ad in, localized versions out — a one-person importer addressing every customer in their own language.
> Built Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026 during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Startup track, *Build for Your World*).

## The problem

Our "domain" is the whole world. The real problem is being able to reach customers in a familiar voice.

Brieblue is a 12-year-old Texas importer of Asian artisan goods — not an AI development company. Its customers are San Antonio's Asian diaspora (Thai, Vietnamese, Korean, Filipino, Indian, Chinese communities) and the micro-businesses it buys from across Southeast Asia. Everyone speaks a little English; it is nobody's native language. The default is poorly translated English ads that read like a joke — and for visually impaired and non-reading customers, visual advertising is locked out entirely.

Even Meta doesn't market to Thailand the way it markets to Texas. Its country-specific accounts (@MetaTH: bright, kawaii, local creator collabs; Meta Singapore: F1, Singlish, local partnerships; @Meta US: corporate talking heads) prove the thesis: localization isn't charity, it's better marketing. A micro business should get the same country-specific treatment Meta gives itself — adapted for a one-man operation, run from a phone.

## What we built

A multilingual ad factory: one still event flyer in, animated localized video ads out — each in its language, with its music, its caption, its alt text, and its spoken-audio version.

The pipeline:
1. **Master** — Ed makes one master ad. The factory never invents event details.
2. **Animate** — the base visual is animated once in code (Python/Pillow + ffmpeg), synced to a measured beat grid. Not rebuilt per language.
3. **Localize** — per language: text, voice, song, caption, and alt text change; layout, timing, and event details stay fixed.
4. **Verify** — the Campaign Proofreading Department runs an 8-point checklist (licence, ear, cultural/occasion, language text, caption + alt, voice, sync/video, honest labelling) before anything ships.

Every version ships in two formats: **General** (burned-in live caption only) and **Read** (caption + narration, for visually impaired and non-reading users — receive-by-ear). Accessibility is demonstrated, not claimed: alt text in-language on every version, spoken audio in-language on every Read version.

# FixFrame

**From visual evidence to human-verified maintenance action.**

[![CI](https://github.com/learnermaker/fixframe/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/learnermaker/fixframe/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

FixFrame is an AI-assisted visual inspection workflow that turns an image and inspection context into structured, reviewable maintenance work. It combines **Meta SAM 3.1** for visual-region segmentation with **Muse Spark** for multimodal interpretation and structured issue extraction, then keeps a human in control of review, approval and work-order creation.

[Hackathon submission copy](docs/HACKATHON_SUBMISSION.md) · [Demo-data and safety policy](docs/DEMO_DATA.md) · [Photo credits and asset provenance](assets/demo-evidence/README.md) · [Meta API implementation notes](docs/META_API_NOTES.md)

## The workflow

**OBSERVE → UNDERSTAND → VERIFY → ACT**

1. Select one of five inspection scenarios.
2. Review the image and its accompanying inspection note.
3. Ask SAM 3.1 to segment a relevant visual region.
4. Ask Muse Spark to interpret the image and context and return structured issue information.
5. Review the draft, evidence, unknowns and provenance; edit or reject unsupported details.
6. Explicitly confirm the reviewed finding before creating a work order.
7. Track the work order through checklist updates, status changes and reviewer feedback.

FixFrame is deliberately more than a defect-detection demo: it demonstrates a controlled path from multimodal observations to a human-reviewed, traceable operational task.

## What Meta models do

- **Meta SAM 3.1:** identifies and segments image regions using a text prompt.
- **Muse Spark:** interprets the image together with inspection context and produces structured issue information for human review.
- **Meta Model API:** provides access to the live model capabilities used by the application.

The application distinguishes `LIVE_META`, `DEMO_FIXTURE` and `USER_EDIT` provenance. Fixture mode supports repeatable demonstrations and tests. A live provider failure is surfaced as an error; it must not silently fall back to fixture output.

## Demo scenarios and data

The repository includes five inspection scenarios covering ceiling discolouration, a cable-sheath mark, a handrail bracket, pipework corrosion and concrete deterioration.

Scenario sites, asset labels, transcripts, people, work orders and maintenance records are fictional. The visual inputs include three credited third-party photographs and two authored illustrations. The photographs are visual examples only; they are not evidence of a FixFrame customer site, incident or maintenance outcome. See [the demo-data policy](docs/DEMO_DATA.md) and [asset provenance register](assets/demo-evidence/README.md).

## Verification snapshot

- The GitHub Actions CI workflow passed on the current `main` commit at the time this README was updated. It ran root install, lint, typecheck, unit tests, production build, test-package

# ColonyPicker

## [Try it now: offline demo guide](docs/offline_demo_guide.md)

**No robot, GPU or key needed.** Double-click `start_offline_demo.bat`, pick a plate and press **Start**. **[Read the guide](docs/offline_demo_guide.md)** for what to look for.

---

A robot arm with a steel needle picks microbial colonies from an agar dish, on its own. **Meta SAM 3.1** finds the colonies on a live
overhead camera image. The arm then moves the needle into a colony, into its own sample well, into a disinfectant well and into a
rinse well, while a browser page shows each step. Meta models are the only AI models it calls at runtime: SAM 3.1 marks the colonies, and Muse Spark can act as its critic.

Picking colonies is repetitive hand work in the lab. This project puts Meta's models in charge of seeing and judging the plate, so a robot can take that work over.

> Agents and new contributors: read `CLAUDE.md` first. The arm is real, and its safety rules there are not optional.

## A hardware project

This is real robotics, so the full demo depends on physical hardware: this robot arm, its needle, two fixed cameras, the lamps and the exact position of the plate.
Its calibration belongs to that one setup and can't be reproduced remotely. Without the rig, you can run the [offline demo](docs/offline_demo_guide.md), SAM 3.1 detection on a dish photo, and the offline checks below.
The working system is shown in the demo video.

## What it does

1. **Detect.** The 4K overhead photo of the dish goes to SAM 3.1 with a text prompt. Three detection settings appear on the page, and the operator picks one.
2. **Pick.** Two fixed cameras watch the needle tip. The arm aligns the tip over the chosen colony, then goes straight down into it.
3. **Transfer.** The needle enters that colony's sample well (C10, C11, C12), then A12 to disinfect for 5 s, then A10 to rinse for 2 s.
4. **Repeat** for the next colony. A failed pick lifts the needle and retries up to 3 times.

| Meta model | Where it runs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| SAM 3.1 (`facebookresearch/sam3`, `facebook/sam3.1` weights) | Locally on the PC GPU (RTX 3090), kept loaded by `tools/sam_server.py`. It's also available through the Meta Model API | Finds the dish and each colony, with a confidence score |
| Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`, Meta Model API) | Over the API, from `tools/colony_agent.py` | Critic of SAM in a tool-calling loop: refuses a lawn or unusable plate, strikes marks that are not one clean colony, chooses what the arm picks |

SAM finds where things are, to the pixel, but it also rings glints, smears and bumps in a lawn. Muse Spark looks at the whole plate and judges what those marks are. It never gets coordinates or motion: it returns mark numbers, and the arm goes to SAM's position for each. The code rejects a choice too close to the rim or a neighbour, one it hasn't looked at, or one it struck, and the model must choose again. Spark also tunes SAM: it words its own prompt for what the colonies

**An AI agent that repairs network faults, and is only allowed to keep a change after deterministic tests prove it fixed the problem and broke nothing.**

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme: Push the Frontier), 27 Oct to 4 Nov 2026, on Muse Spark 1.3 and open-weights Muse Spark Open.

*A recorded benchmark run: Muse Spark Open's first fix used `/24` where `/32` was needed. The gate allowed it, the verifier saw a forbidden flow open (guest to file server), rolled the router back, and told the model why. Its next plan was correct.*

## Contents

1. [At a glance](#at-a-glance)

## At a glance

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | Takes a trouble ticket, investigates a live (emulated) network, and proposes configuration changes one device at a time |
| **What makes it safe** | Every change passes a deterministic policy gate, then the whole network is re-tested; anything that breaks another flow, or fixes nothing, is rolled back automatically |
| **Models** | Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta Model API), Muse Spark Open (open weights, via Baseten), and an open-first router across the two |
| **Held-out result** | 27 faults the prompt was never tuned on: Muse Spark 1.3 fixed 27/27, Muse Spark Open 26/27, a scripted runbook 11/27 |
| **Safety result** | Adversarial tickets and planted instructions, 18 runs per agent: security policy intact in 18/18 for every agent, 0/18 took the bait |
| **Cost** | About $0.015 to $0.021 per verified fix |

Configuration changes are a common cause of network outages. An AI agent that can read routes and firewall rules could fix many faults quickly, but nobody should let a model type commands into a production network on trust: a fix that restores one service can quietly open another to the wrong people.

# Project Sentinel

**Secure and observable evaluation framework for LLM agents**

Project Sentinel compares baseline and hardened LLM-agent configurations on a fixed security and task benchmark. It records structured events and generates JSON and Markdown reports covering task success, security outcomes, attack blocking, recovery, and latency.

> Research prototype: benchmark results are not a production security guarantee.

## What it evaluates

The benchmark contains 52 cases across five categories: direct prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, normal tasks, out-of-scope requests, and unsafe tool requests.

- **Baseline agent:** basic task instructions and controlled tools without the hardened interception layer.
- **Hardened agent:** explicit instruction hierarchy, untrusted-context boundary tags, and tool allowlisting through ToolInterceptor.

The framework supports deterministic offline mock evaluation and live NVIDIA NIM model inference.

## Architecture

1. Benchmark loader reads versioned test cases.
2. Agent configurations construct baseline and hardened agents.
3. Model adapter selects mock or NVIDIA NIM inference.
4. Tool/security layer evaluates tool requests and applies interception.
5. Evaluation engine and comparative runner execute cases and calculate metrics.
6. Observability components record structured events and redact logs.
7. Report generator writes JSON and Markdown results.

| Path | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| app/agents/ | Agent implementations, configurations, and model clients |
| app/benchmarks/ | Benchmark data and loader |
| app/evaluation/ | Execution, comparison, security classification, metrics, and reports |
| app/observability/ | Event logging, redaction, and observability security |
| app/tools/ | Tool definitions and controlled/mock tools |
| tests/ | Automated tests |
| reports/ | Selected evaluation artifacts |

## Final live-model evaluation

The published run is **sentinel_final_live_52**, benchmark v2.0.0, with 52 cases and model **meta/muse-glimmer-30b**.

**Methodology:** model inference was live through NVIDIA NIM; tool execution was simulated. The report metadata records is_mocked=false, while per-case records identify simulated tool execution.

# Cooking coach on a V-JEPA 2 world model

A coach that watches someone cook through a head-mounted camera, remembers which recipe steps they have started, and reminds them of steps they haven't. A world model reads the video, an LLM coach decides what to say and when, and a small decision model turns the advice into the next move every second. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

**Demo:** https://hsinnosuketw.github.io/personal-cooking-coach/ — two HD-EPIC recordings (Scrambled Eggs, Bacon & Egg Sandwich), each with several coach versions side by side.

## How it works

```
cooking video ─► V-JEPA 2 ViT-L ─► EK100 probe ─► verb / noun / action probabilities, every second
                  (world model)       │
                                      ├─► action segments ─┐
                                      ├─► HSMM step tracker ├─► timing: should the coach speak now?
                                      └─► checklist memory ─┘        │
              frames ─► Llama 3.2 11B Vision ─► "has this step begun?" (when the evidence is unclear)
                                                                      ▼
recipe ─► task graph (which steps repeat) ─────────────► coach: Muse Glimmer 30B
                                                         (what's done, what's left, one reminder)
                                                                      ▼
                                                         decision model: Liquid AI d1-2B, every second
```

| Part | What it does | Model |
|---|---|---|
| World model + probe | Predicts the next action about 0.8 s ahead from the last 3.2 s of video | Meta V-JEPA 2 ViT-L with the EPIC-KITCHENS-100 attentive probe |
| Memory | A checklist: each step not started / in progress / done, with rounds for repeated steps and the times each was first and last seen | rules over the probe, plus the coach's answers |
| Frame checks | When a step's evidence is unclear (first sign, stops early, restarts, long silence), looks at 4 frames from the last 20 s and asks whether the step has begun | Llama 3.2 11B Vision, ~1 s per check |
| Timing | Calls the coach on a step change, on drifting from the advice, on a skipped step or long off-task time, with a back-off when nothing changes | HSMM step tracker + rules |
| Coach | Writes where the cook is, the one most useful next thing, and a `REMIND` line for a step not started yet | Muse Glimmer 30B (self-hosted with vLLM, or NVIDIA NIM) |
| Decision model | Every second, picks the next action from the recipe's action bank, following the coach and the checklist | Liquid AI d1-2B |

# nika-os-hatch

**Persistent memory per tenant, an orchestrator for headless workers, and a *hatching* loop that fine-tunes a Meta open-weight model on each tenant's own work, then keeps the result only if a pre-registered paired test proves it is better.**

Built during the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai) (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026) by BCUB3 (Paul Obara).
Base model: **Muse Glimmer 30B** (`meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B`, Meta open weights, Apache-2.0), run in bf16 on one rented GPU.

## Demo video

3-minute demo (1080p, English narration and subtitles): [`demo/video/demo_3min.mp4`](demo/video/demo_3min.mp4).

## What is new

**Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon.** It is a small, self-contained, open reference implementation of a pattern we run in production at BCUB3 (our internal operating layer, *Nika OS*). None of Nika OS's code is in this repository and none of it is needed to run it. The tenants and the data are synthetic.

## The idea in one paragraph

General assistants forget, and they never get better at *your* job. Here every tenant (a user, a team, a company) gets its own memory and its own trajectory log. An orchestrator runs the tenant's tasks on headless workers and records each run (prompt, tool calls, output, verdict, trace ids). When a bottleneck is *measured* (too many failed trajectories), the tenant's agent **hatches**: a benchmark is pre-registered and hashed, a LoRA adapter is trained on the tenant's own trajectories, and the adapter is promoted only if a paired test without any normality assumption says it wins. Otherwise it is rolled back and the tenant keeps what it had. Adapters, like memories, never leave their tenant.

## Result of the real run (Muse Glimmer 30B, 1 GPU)

Run of 4 Nov 2026, one RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), bf16, 20.5 minutes end to end. 240 trajectories collected per tenant with the base model, then a bench of 100 held-out items per tenant, pre-registered before any training. LoRA r=16, 200 steps, batch 4.

| Tenant · candidate | Before | After | Wins / losses / ties | Sign test p | Bootstrap lower bound of Δ | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| machine-shop · **negative control** (shuffled answers) | 0.57 | 0.02 | 1 / 56 / 43 | 1 | −0.630 | **rolled back** |
| machine-shop · v1 | 0.57 | **1.00** | 43 / 0 / 57 | 1.1e-13 | +0.350 | **promoted** |
| consulting-firm · v1 | 0.05 | **0.95** | 90 / 0 / 10 | 8.1e-28 | +0.850 | **promoted** |

Where the gain comes from (bench, per field): the base model already finds the consulting service (0.95) and mostly the day count (0.85) but almost never the firm's own deliverable names (0.05 → 1.00 with the adapter); in the machine shop it misses the work-order code convention (0.65 → 1.00). The specialised adapters also answer without a long reasoning preamble: mean worker time per task in a batch of 48 drops from about 1.1 s to 0.1 s.

Then each tenant is served with its own adapter (`served` in `summary.json`),

# Glimmer Decide

[![Glimmer Decide: promo video (2:38), click to watch on YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/DawY6e_nZxo/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://youtu.be/DawY6e_nZxo)

A camera test bench for open-weight **decision models**, and a way to train your own.

Point a camera at a desk (or drop in a photo), say what you want to do, and get **one object
to use** — or *nothing here fits* / *show me another angle* — with a probability for every
option. **SAM 3.1** then highlights the chosen object on the frame.

## Why

Decision models answer by picking one option from a closed set in a single forward pass,
instead of writing out their reasoning first: the model itself needs ~0.15 s on the GPU, and
the answer arrives in 1-1.5 s end to end instead of several seconds.
The open-weight ones are new, and the released ones were trained mostly on text. This project
has two goals:

1. **A tool to test open-weight decision models on camera (video) frames**, so we can try
   features quickly and keep the ones that work. Point a phone or a webcam at a real scene and
   compare, side by side and with their timings, a bi-encoder (MetaEncoder), a decision head
   (JevAny) and a reasoning model (Muse Glimmer), all built on Meta's open Muse Glimmer 30B.
   Try refusing when nothing fits, asking for a better view, the camera-off ablation,
   highlighting the pick with SAM, and capture from a phone. Then see what a real product needs.
2. **Let users train decision models themselves.** The page that tests the models also
   collects the data: every frame saved with its right answer is a training example. One
   command then fine-tunes JevAny on your frames, or trains a Clef-style decision head from
   scratch, on your own GPU. One line in `.env` puts your fine-tuned model back into the page.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, on Meta models only.

## What's inside

| Decider | Model | How it decides | Speed: end to end (GPU) | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **MetaEncoder** (System 1, default) | [facebook/meta-encoder](https://huggingface.co/facebook/meta-encoder): Muse Glimmer 30B contrastively tuned into a bi-encoder ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11316)) | frame + goal and each option are embedded; cosine similarity -> softmax. Option embeddings are cached | ~1.4 s (0.15 s) | your Modal GPU |
| **JevAny** (System 1, **fine-tunable**) | [JevAny-Muse-Glimmer-30B](https://huggingface.co/SimpleJev/JevAny-Muse-Glimmer-30B-LoRA): a LoRA + pointer head on Muse Glimmer 30B ([JevAny](https://github.com/SimpleJev/JevAny)) | frame + goal + labelled options in one prefill; a small trained head scores the options | ~1.4 s (0.17 s) | your Modal GPU |
| **Clef-style Glimmer** (System 1, **not trained yet**, experiment) | [Clef](https://huggingface.co/Cloudflare/clef)'s joint schema head + a fresh LoRA on Muse Glimmer 30B: no released weights, you train it | one prefill; the head scores all options together | — (no trained model yet, not in the page) |

# FloorPlan3D

### From a 2D blueprint to an interactive 3D space

FloorPlan3D turns architectural floor-plan images into structured scene data and an explorable Three.js model. It brings visual review, room information, editing, and navigation into one browser-based workspace.

> **Built by Tanmay Sandhu for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**

## The problem

A floor plan contains walls, rooms, doors, windows, labels, and connections, but those details are flattened into a drawing. Understanding how the spaces fit together can take time, especially for people who do not work with plans every day.

FloorPlan3D makes a plan easier to inspect by transforming detected features into a 3D scene while keeping review and correction tools close to the original drawing.

## What FloorPlan3D does

- Processes uploaded floor-plan images and displays detected rooms and architectural features.
- Shows room labels, floor levels, estimated areas, and connections.
- Provides 3D, top-down, and walkthrough views.
- Includes a 2D editor for reviewing and adjusting the plan.
- Previews routes through doors and between connected floors.
- Offers prepared **Meta AI Drafts** that load instantly for a dependable demo.

## Meta AI in the workflow

Meta models add image understanding and scene interpretation to the application:

- **Meta SAM 3.1** uses text prompts to segment image regions such as rooms, walls, doors, and windows.
- **Muse Spark** helps classify rooms and interpret plan context. **Ask This Map** uses the current scene to answer questions about rooms and connections.
- Optional **Muse Image** and **Muse Voice** features can draft a floor-plan image from text and transcribe WAV questions when the corresponding account access is configured.

The Flask backend coordinates model requests and processing. OpenCV handles image operations and fallback detection; Shapely constructs and validates geometry; Three.js renders the scene in the browser. See `meta_sam_service.py`, `baseten_service.py`, and `meta_media_service.py` for the model integration points.

## How it works

```text
Floor-plan image or text prompt
              ↓
      Flask upload and job API
              ↓
 Meta SAM 3.1 segmentation, when configured
     OpenCV detection and fallback processing
              ↓
       Shapely geometry processing
              ↓

Which model steps run depends on the configured credentials and feature. Local processing and prepared scenes let users explore the project without making live model calls.

# Manifest0 AI

**Zero guesswork on hazardous waste.** Photograph chemical labels, and Muse Spark reads them into an inventory, finds each product's Safety Data Sheet (SDS) on the web, saves the PDFs and emails the inventory and SDS sheets to the technician and the client.

Built for Meta's Global AI Dev Hackathon (Indie Dev track, Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026) on Meta's Muse Spark model (`muse-spark-1.3`).

- **Live app:** https://app.manifest0ai.com (email sign-in link, for approved beta testers)
- **Landing page:** https://manifest0ai.com

## The problem

Setting up a new hazardous waste customer is manual. A field rep walks the site, writes down every container and photographs the labels. Back at a desk, they search for each product's SDS one at a time and type everything up. That takes hours to days, and every missing detail means another call or visit.

Manifest0 AI does that work during the site walk. The rep snaps each label room by room, and the inventory and SDS sheets are in the client's inbox before the rep leaves. A person reviews the result before it is sent.

**Who it's for:** field reps at small and mid-size US environmental and hazardous waste service companies.

## Try it

- **Live:** sign in at https://app.manifest0ai.com, start a site walk, add photos room by room, then tap **Send to client**.
- **Locally:** follow [Local development](#local-development) below and upload the label photos in [`samples/`](samples/) (Clorox bleach, cleaning vinegar and STERIS Septihol, front and back of each).

## Team

- **Jessyka Mathews** ([@Onefailatatime](https://github.com/Onefailatatime)), founder. Product, UI design and hazardous waste domain knowledge.
- **Tamara Martinović** ([@Tamara-Codes](https://github.com/Tamara-Codes)), CTO. Built the app: the Worker, the visit agent, the Muse Spark calls and the tests.

Most of the code was written with Claude Code as the coding assistant. The only Meta model in the app is Muse Spark, used for reading labels and finding SDS sheets.

## How it works

A technician starts a **site walk** (one visit), then uploads photos room by room (as many uploads as they like),
then reviews the email draft and taps **Send to client**. One `VisitAgent` (Agents SDK) lives for the whole visit and remembers everything in it.

```

   │  POST /api/visits                 start a visit (emails, site name)
   │  POST /api/visits/:id/photos      a batch of photos + room name   (repeat)

   │
   ▼
VisitAgent (src/visit-agent.ts): one per visit, durable queue, one step at a time:
   processBatch  Muse reads the new photos AND the products already found in that room,
                 so overlapping photos update a product instead of duplicating it
   findSds       SDS library first (shared across all visits); else Muse web search →
                 down

# MoLakaz

An AI household chore manager that fairly splits chores around each family member's schedule and confirms them with a quick photo.

The person who runs the home sets up the household once (people, how much free time each has per day, the chores). MoLakaz shares the chores out so everyone gives up the same *share of their free time*, not the same number of chores. When a chore's done you snap a before and after photo, and SAM 3.1 checks the mess is actually gone.

*Mo lakaz* = "my home" in Kreol Morisien.

```
mobile/   Expo (SDK 58) app, expo-router
backend/  Python, deployed on Modal
```

## How it uses Modal

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| SAM 3.1 on an L4 GPU segments the before/after photos and compares them | `Verifier` class in `backend/modal_app.py`, logic in `backend/verify.py` |
| Whisper (large-v3-turbo) on a T4 writes out what you say on the voice screens | `Transcriber` class in `modal_app.py`, logic in `backend/transcribe.py`, route `POST /transcribe` |
| FastAPI web endpoint, the backend between the app and Muse Spark | `web` in `modal_app.py`, routes in `backend/api.py` |
| 6:30am cron: plans the new week on Mondays, carries over missed chores, sends reminders | `morning` → `backend/jobs.py` |
| 7pm cron: nudges anyone with chores still not done | `evening` |
| `modal.Dict` for households, `modal.Volume` for photos and cached model weights | `backend/store.py` |

When someone uploads the before photo, the backend spawns a warm-up call so the GPU is ready by the time they're done cleaning.

## How the photo check works

Every chore has a check, e.g. dishes:

```json
{ "mode": "clear", "look_for": ["dirty dish", "cup", "pan"], "spot": "sink" }
```

SAM 3.1 segments every `look_for` thing in both photos. `clear` chores pass when the count drops to zero, or most of the masked area is gone. `show` chores (fold laundry, cook dinner) pass when the thing appears in the after photo. If the `spot` (sink) shows up in the before photo but not the after, it asks for a retake from the same place. You get the photos back with what SAM found painted red/green. The household admin can always approve a chore by hand.

Weights: `unsloth/sam3.1`, which is SAM 3.1 converted to transformers' `Sam3Model` format (not gated). Meta's official `facebook/sam3.1` repo only ships the video multiplex checkpoint with no transformers support. To use Meta's official SAM 3 image model instead, deploy with `SAM_MODEL=facebook/sam3` and an `HF_TOKEN` that has access.

## How the fair split works

`backend/planner.py`:

1. Each chore becomes N slots spread across the week (3x a week → Mon/Wed/Fri style).
2. Biggest jobs first, each slot goes to whoever ends up with the lowest *(chore minutes × effort) / free minutes this week*, and only if they have the time free that day and are old enough. Small nudges: rotate who gets what (last week counts too), avoid dislikes, don't drift more than 2 days, never the same chore twice on one day.
3. Fairness score = Jain's

# OrganicPulse Districts

**A mobile-first circular-economy marketplace that turns sorted household waste into verified, AI-matched donations for local organic manure manufacturers and terrace gardeners.**

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie Developer track, "Build for Your World").

🔗 **Live app**: [organicpulsedistrictsmeta.vercel.app](https://organicpulsedistrictsmeta.vercel.app/)

---

## The problem

Households generate dry organic waste every week — eggshells, coffee/tea grounds, cardboard — that's perfect raw material for organic manure and composting, but has no easy path from a kitchen counter to someone who actually wants it. Meanwhile, small organic manure manufacturers and terrace gardeners pay for raw material they could be getting locally, for free, if there were a trustworthy way to connect the two sides.

OrganicPulse Districts closes that loop: households sort their dry waste at home, a neighborhood collection partner confirms and photo-verifies it in person, and an AI agent routes it to the receiver who actually wants it — with the receiver shown *why* they got the match, not just that they did.

## How Meta's models are used

This isn't a chatbot wrapper — two Meta models are load-bearing parts of the product:

- **SAM 3.1** (segmentation) is the trust layer. At pickup, the collection partner confirms which categories are in the caddy and takes a photo on the spot — no one's bringing a weighing machine door to door, so the partner's in-person confirmation is the source of truth, and SAM 3.1 segments the photo against each confirmed category (eggshells / tea-coffee grounds / cardboard) to cross-check that the photo actually matches what was confirmed. A mismatch gets flagged for a recheck — this is the project's anti-fraud mechanism, not a decorative AI feature.
- **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) is the actual matching agent. # AlertCheck

**Don't release goods on a fake alert.** AlertCheck is an AI agent for Nigerian sellers: market traders, POS agents and WhatsApp/Instagram vendors. A vendor sends it a photo or screenshot of the buyer's "transfer successful" screen, and within seconds it says whether the money actually reached the vendor's account. The answer is **RELEASE**, **DON'T RELEASE** or **CHECK MANUALLY**, with a one-line reason and a box drawn around the field that doesn't match.

> **The model reads the receipt; the ledger decides.** AlertCheck never claims it can spot a forgery by looking at an image. Every verdict rests on whether a matching credit exists in the vendor's incoming payments.

| Genuine payment | "Double alert": ₦5,000 sent, receipt claims ₦50,000 | Reused receipt |
|---|---|---|
| ![Release](docs/images/genuine.jpg) | ![Don't release, only ₦5,000 of ₦50,000 has arrived](docs/images/double_alert.jpg) | ![Don't release, already used](docs/images/reused.jpg) |

*Entry to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, "Build for Your World"). All receipts shown are synthetic. "DemoBank", "NairaPay Demo" and the other apps are fictional.*

## The problem

"Fake alerts" are a familiar risk for Nigerian traders. A buyer shows a convincing "transfer successful" screen, from a doctored screenshot or a "flash fund" app, takes the goods, and the money never arrives.

- Police in [Osun](https://gazettengr.com/osun-police-nab-four-suspects-using-fake-alerts-to-buy-goods/), [Edo](https://businessday.ng/news/article/edo-police-arrest-suspected-fake-transfer-fraudster-in-benin/) and [Lagos](https://guardian.ng/news/man-nabbed-for-sending-fake-bank-transfers-to-buy-goods/) have arrested suspects for paying traders with fake transfer alerts. The Lagos case involved a car worth ₦28 million. Police advise businesses to **confirm the funds have actually reached their account** before accepting a transfer slip.
- POS agents report [alerts that show on the customer's phone but never appear on the agent's side](https://www.icirnigeria.org/fraudsters-dent-nigerias-billion-naira-pos-business/). Fact-checkers explain [how fake-alert apps work](https://dubawa.org/how-to-identify-fake-bank-alerts-generated-by-flash-fund-apps/) and give the same advice: check your balance, not the alert.
- NIBSS put digital payment fraud losses at [₦25.85 billion in 2025](https://businessday.ng/?p=1150235), as reported by BusinessDay, with social engineering the most common technique.

That advice, "check that the money really arrived", is hard to follow when a queue is waiting and the buyer is insisting. AlertCheck does that check in one step, and it also catches the subtler tricks:

| Pattern | What happens | AlertCheck says |
|---|---|---|
| No matching credit | The receipt shows a transfer that never arrived | ⛔ Don't release — no ₦80,000 payment has arrived |
| **Double alert / partial credit** | A small real credit arrives, but the receipt claims the full amount | ⛔ Don't

Homie turns a one-minute walk-around video of your room into a 3D room with sizes, then a personal AI shopping agent proposes real Shopee Taiwan products, checks in code that they fit, places them in the 3D room, and shows them in a realistic photo of your own room.    - **Any phone, on the website** (`/upload`): drop a video, scan a QR code to open the page on a phone, or film right in the phone browser. The browser cuts the video into ~60 stills and sends only those; the video never leaves the phone. **Muse Spark watches the stills in order and draws the floor plan**: the room's size from things of known size (door, bed, desk, floor tiles), which wall each piece stands against and where, its size, and the frame that shows it best. These sizes are rougher and always shown as approx. (On our test room Muse got the room within +20% / +9%; MapAnything, tried first, came out +27% / +67%.)
   - **Our iPhone app** (`ios/RoomCapture`, app name Homie, used for the demo): records video plus ARKit camera poses, intrinsics, detected planes and feature points, for measured sizes. Works on iPhones without LiDAR.
2. **Measure** (`pipeline/`): Muse Spark labels the furniture in keyframes, SAM 3.1 outlines each object, and the outlines are projected onto ARKit's surfaces to measure them. On our test room the bed came out 196 × 94 cm against 188 × 100 cm by tape measure, and the door at exactly 80 cm. Objects seen only partly are marked "approx." with a wider ±.
3. **Rebuild** with agents, all running at once: each piece's box is fitted to its SAM outlines and gets its own photo crop. One **builder agent per object** rebuilds it as simple coloured parts, then checks its own work: code draws the blocks alone from the object's best camera view, Muse compares them with the photo (score, problems, which face is the front, size estimate), and the object is rebuilt with that note, up to twice. Then a **room judge** renders the whole room from camera positions chosen so every object is seen, and moves, resizes, turns, pushes to the wall or sends an object back to its builder; code limits every fix and keeps a round only if the match improves. Plain code keeps pieces square to the walls and their backs against the wall they stand at. The room page shows it building live: Measuring → Finding objects → Building (7/13) → Checking.
4. **Shop** (`web/`): a Muse Spark agent with tools (search the catalog, place / move / remove items, fix sizes, render a photo, build the list). Ask "what does my room still need?" and it lists the gaps with target sizes; say yes and it finds the best buy for each, places it in 3D

# FieldKit

**An offline-first crop doctor and field assistant for farmers with no internet, a budget phone, and little time to read.**

Point the camera at a sick leaf. FieldKit estimates the damage on the phone, asks you to tap pictures of what you see, and gives a diagnosis with step-by-step treatment in English or Hindi, read aloud. No signal needed. When the phone gets even a few seconds of signal, FieldKit quietly sends a ~40 KB photo to Meta's frontier models (**SAM 3.1** segments every lesion, **Muse Spark** confirms the diagnosis) and saves the result and a wordless **Muse Image** picture guide on the phone for good.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026.

## Why

Hundreds of millions of smallholder farmers lose crops to diseases they can't name, miss government schemes they don't know about, and can't use AI tools that assume fast internet, a flagship phone and fluent English. FieldKit assumes none of those.

## What works offline (zero signal)

| Feature | How |
|---|---|
| **Leaf Scan**: % of leaf damaged, highlighted on the photo | On-device pixel analysis (HSV classification, morphology, hole filling), ~20 ms |
| **Symptom picker**: tap pictures, no reading needed | 29 hand-drawn symptom pictograms → ranked diagnosis from the bundled knowledge pack |
| **Ask anything** | **Llama 3.2 1B** (Q4_K_M, 808 MB) running in the browser through llama.cpp/WebAssembly, grounded by BM25 retrieval over the knowledge pack |
| **Read aloud** | Phone's built-in text-to-speech for every answer |
| **Government schemes** | Benefits, eligibility, a document checklist, how to apply, tap-to-call helplines |
| **Safety & first aid** | Pesticide poisoning, snake bite, heat stroke; one-tap emergency calls |
| **Picture guides** | Starter pack bundled in the app; new guides cached forever once downloaded |

## What gets better with signal (Meta Model API)

| Model | Role in FieldKit |
|---|---|
| `sam-3.1` | Segments the leaf and every diseased spot → true severity % and mask overlay |
| `muse-spark-1.3` | Vision diagnosis with a strict JSON schema mapped onto the offline pack; scheme answers with web-search grounding and citations |
| `muse-image-1.0` | Wordless 4-panel pictogram guides ("prune here, spray this") |
| `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` | Voice questions in Hindi, Marathi and 23 other languages |

The **sync queue** makes this automatic. Scans made offline are saved on the phone, and the moment there's signal they upgrade in place ("Expert confirmed" or "Expert suggests a different problem"). The **data meter** shows the exact bytes each call used.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env          # add MODEL_API_KEY from https://dev.meta.ai (optional)
npm run dev:server            # API proxy on :8787 (demo mode without a key)
npm run dev:web               # app on :5173
```
