# Edge Confidence Router

**Read now, ask later: an on-device camera reader that knows when it doesn't know.**

This project is an edge-to-cloud router for reading numbers and codes from images. The ***edge*** is the device itself, with no network needed: Meta’s Perception LM 1B runs on an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano and reads each image. It scores how sure it is from its own token probabilities, and only asks the cloud (Meta's **Muse Spark**) when it isn't sure. A read on the device takes ~1.2 s; averaged over the held-out set, including the cloud calls, a frame takes ~4.2 s. With no connection, it still answers right away, but marks the answers it isn't sure of as unverified and queues them to be checked once the connection is back: *read now, ask later.* There's no training and no fine-tuning.

**Where it could be used.** Anything that has to read short IDs where the network isn't reliable: a robot in a rail yard or plant identifying vehicles or parts, a handheld scanner at a remote site, an inspection camera in the field. It's a research prototype (the on-device model is licensed for noncommercial research only), and today it runs on the Jetson with a live dashboard fed by photos, not on a robot.

**Results in short.** On 25 locomotive photos, the router kept 9 numbers on the device, all 9 correct, with a format check catching the one confident mistake. On 25 held-out jersey photos it matched sending everything to the cloud (within noise) while answering 11 on the device. Long label codes are beyond the on-device model, so those go to the cloud.

> Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (indie developer track), Oct–Nov 2026.

---

## How it works

![How the router decides](docs/how_it_works.png)

**The router** decides, for every image, whether to keep the on-device answer, send the image to Muse Spark, or (with no connection) keep the answer as unverified and queue the image for later.

**The confidence signal** is what it decides with. The model writes its answer one small piece (a token) at a time, and before writing each piece it gives every possible next piece a probability. If it sees the number clearly, almost all the probability goes to one choice; if it doesn't, the probability spreads across several guesses and the one it picks scores low. The router reads those probabilities straight from the model's output, so confidence costs nothing extra: no second model, no extra pass, no training.

- **Numbers:** the router multiplies the probabilities of the digit pieces (the joint probability) and keeps the answer if it's at least **0.80**, a threshold chosen on a dev set.
- **Long codes:** multiplying many pieces would drag even a good read toward zero, so the router uses the weakest single piece instead, with a threshold of 0.90 fixed in advance.
- **Known ID formats:** if the site's IDs have a fixed format, the router also checks the answer against it (see [Locomotive numbers](#locomotive-numbers-a-known-id-format)).

# PIXEL HEIST

**Steal reality. Escape the sketch.** A browser puzzle game for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026.
Play it at **https://pixel-heist.vercel.app** (desktop or phone).

Take a photo of anything, tap an object, and **Sam** cuts it out. Sam is the
[Meta SAM 3.1](https://dev.meta.ai/models/sam-3-1) segmentation model, not a person. You drag the real cut-out into a
museum drawn in pencil, where the game judges only its **shape** (length, thickness, solidity, holes) and never
its name. Block cameras, bridge laser gaps, weigh down plates, hang things on hooks, reach the diamond.

Two Meta models, two jobs:

- **SAM 3.1 steals objects from reality.** One tap is a point prompt; the mask it returns is the object's collider.
- **Muse Spark builds a world that fights back.** As the *Curator* it designs a room for the loot you brought,
  and as the voice in your charm it gives hints. In both roles the game engine checks every claim: Muse never
  decides what is solvable or what you've done.

## Run it

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # then set MODEL_API_KEY (server-only; used for SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark)
npm run dev                  # http://localhost:3000
npm test                     # geometry, judging, solver, Curator rooms, API routes
npm run e2e                  # Playwright, against a production build
```

Without a key, choose **Recorded** in the photo panel to replay real SAM 3.1 results for the two sample desks.

## How it works

- **Segmentation** (`app/api/segment`): the tap goes to `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses` with
  `model: "sam-3.1"`, streamed and parsed with `@meta-sam/parser`. A stream cut off mid-way is retried once.
- **Shape** (`lib/geometry.ts`): long masks are straightened, the longest side is scaled to 180 game px, and holes
  are found by flood fill. That occupancy grid is the only thing the game knows about an object.
- **Judging** (`lib/judge.ts`): camera rays, the laser slot over a gap, how much of a plate is covered, whether
  a hook falls inside a real hole, sensor beams nothing may touch. A deterministic run (`lib/heist.ts`) decides
  caught, fell, stuck or escaped.
- **X-ray, mask vs box**: one toggle re-judges your exact placement with bounding boxes, the colliders you'd get
  without a mask. The ruler's box trips the lasers and the mug's box has no handle hole; `tests/xray.test.ts`
  checks it on the real masks.
- **Solver** (`lib/solver.ts`, in a Web Worker): finds what each of your cut-outs can do and a plan that the judge
  and the run accept. The tests use it to prove every stage is solvable; hints and the Curator use it so they're
  never guesses.

# ShiftSense

**A charge nurse spends about two hours building each fortnight's roster by hand, then rebuilds it
over the phone every time someone calls in sick. ShiftSense builds the roster in seconds and
handles the sick call with an AI agent, while a person approves every change.**

An OR-Tools CP-SAT solver builds every roster. Meta's **Muse Spark** understands nurses' messages
in Hindi or English (typed or spoken), writes each nurse's message, runs the replacement workflow
and explains every decision from the solver's own results. It never edits the roster.

- **Video (3 min):** [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FWtOExizEMc)
- **Run it locally:** [Quick start](#quick-start), no API keys needed
- **Docs:** [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [System design](docs/system-design.md) ·
  [Decision log](docs/decisions.md) · [Design doc](docs/DESIGN.md)

## What it does

1. **Generate.** The ward opens on an empty fortnight. One click builds the full roster in seconds,
   with strict priorities: coverage, then stability, contracts, requests, then fairness of nights
   and weekends (carried over from earlier periods).
2. **A sick call in Hindi.** *"Sunita di, aaj subah ki duty nahi kar paungi, bukhar hai"* ("I can't
   make this morning's duty, I have a fever"). Muse Spark turns it into a structured request; code
   checks it; the nurse taps Confirm.
3. **The replacement cascade.** The solver re-plans only the future and ranks replacements, each
   checked by a real forced re-solve. The charge nurse approves a contact plan once ("ask Arun,
   then Ritu, then Kavya"); approving it publishes nothing. The agent asks each nurse in their
   language. A decline, or no answer before a real deadline, moves on to the next nurse. The first
   nurse who accepts comes back to the charge nurse, who clicks **Publish**.
4. **Why?** Click any cell, or ask "Why Arun and not Priya?". The answer cites the solver's
   evidence, and code checks every claim before it is shown.

On the demo ward, Meena's sick call changes 1 cell besides her own; without the stability tier it
moves 27. Across 20 random sick calls on the 24-nurse ward: 1 vs a median of 50.5.

### Fairness across fortnights

Each nurse carries running totals from the two previous periods (28 days): nights, weekend shifts,
mornings, evenings and denied requests. For each of the five, the solver adds this fortnight's
shifts to the carried-over count and minimises the gap between the nurse with the most and the
nurse with the fewest. So whoever worked the most weekends last month gets fewer now, and a nurse
whose requests were turned down before is less likely to be turned down again. Fairness is the
last tier: it never costs coverage, stability, contracts or requests, and only chooses among
rosters already equal on those. The Fairness tab shows "earlier 2 periods" next to "this period"
for every nurse, and "Why do I get every weekend?" is answered from the same numbers.

# PerfPilot

**vLLM ships performance regressions silently.** A flag default or kernel change
can cost 10–60% throughput, and nobody notices until the bill arrives. Finding the
commit by hand means hours of GPU benchmarking that a single noisy run can fool.

PerfPilot is an agent that does it for you, and proves its answer:

- **PerfBisect**: `perfpilot bisect --good G --bad B` gives the culprit commit, a
  statistical interval and the GPU dollars it spent.
- **TuneSmith**: `perfpilot tune --commit C` tries serve flags to win the speed back
  and accepts a flag only when its gain is proven and quality holds.
- **Proposer swarm**: open-weights agents (Baseten `muse-spark-open`) pick which
  commit to probe. A deterministic referee and the benchmarks overrule them.
  Brain proposes, benchmarks dispose.
- **Bench harness**: 17 planted-failure scenarios (noise, outliers, broken builds,
  flaky workers, rig drift, misleading hints) score every change, keyed to git SHA.

| Result | Value |
|---|---|
| Wrong verdicts (17 scenarios × 20 seeds, plus every GPU run) | **0** |
| Real A100 runs, end to end with the live swarm | 5 recorded reports |
| Total GPU spend for the whole project | **$8.63** |
| Tests | 228 passing |

Meta open models throughout: **Llama-3.2-1B** is the model being served and
measured; **muse-spark-open** is the agent brain. Every model in the loop is open weights.

# MusePlant

From a written process control spec to ladder logic, a P&ID and a running simulation, using Meta's models on the live Meta Model API.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme "Push the Frontier"), Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026.

- Repo: https://github.com/ali-amjad52114/museplant
- Live app: https://museplant.onrender.com (deploying)
- Licence: AGPL-3.0 (see `LICENSE`)

## What it does

You upload a process spec as a PDF, or dictate changes to it. Muse Spark reads it and pulls out numbered requirements, and each one cites the page and quote it came from. Muse Spark then writes ladder logic rungs that meet those requirements and builds a P&ID (equipment, lines, instruments, control loops) from our component library. A validator checks both, and a repair loop sends any errors back to the model live (at most 2 repairs). The browser turns the P&ID into a process model and runs the generated ladder against it live: hydraulics come from EPA EPANET (via epanet-js), and heat, controllers, valve lags and motors are lumped blocks. You see the P&ID sheet, a ladder view with power flow, a generated 3D layout and trends, and they are all linked: selecting something in one view selects it in the others. Each requirement runs as a spec test scenario that returns pass, fail or gap, with evidence. A fix agent (Muse Wonder) edits a draft of the design to make failing tests pass, or proposes a spec change when the spec itself is the problem. An Ask agent (Muse Spark) answers questions about the design using the simulator as a tool, including what-if runs. The drawing reader (Muse Spark plus SAM 3.1) can also import an existing P&ID image as a graph for review.

Exports: design JSON, CSVs, P&ID SVG, DEXPI XML (pyDEXPI), IEC 61131-3 Structured Text, PLCopen XML (valid against the TC6 v2.01 XSD), GLB, simulation CSV and test results.

## Honest scope

- **Any liquid process graph.** The generators are not tied to any sample. The graph can have any number of vessels, pumps, valves, branches, mixing points, recycles, heaters, coolers and heat exchangers, using the item types in `public/js/core/library.js`. The three sample specs in `samples/spec/` are three different processes we wrote ourselves: a stabilizer feed drum, solvent receiving with a day-tank transfer, and a heated tank with a circulation loop.
- **Lumped design-check simulator, not CFD and not a certified dynamic process simulator.** It assumes water-like single-phase incompressible liquid, no heat loss, no NPSH, no line holdup and no pump speed model. The thermal layer is our own simplified energy balance.

# AgentGate

AgentGate is a gate for AI agents that use tools such as email, files and calendar (tested on AgentDojo's workspace suite): everything the agent reads from a tool result or an image is treated as untrusted data, so only the user's task directs actions. The gate is deterministic code with no model in it, and its protection is measured against a *scripted* worst-case agent that obeys every injection (see Results) — not against a model that was actually fooled. This repo holds the gate and its evaluation harness; the agent under test is Muse Spark Open via Baseten's OpenAI-compatible Model API.

## Install and try it in one minute

Python 3.11. The core has no dependencies, and the example needs no model, key or network.

```
pip install git+https://github.com/mathesh310703/agentgate
git clone https://github.com/mathesh310703/agentgate
cd agentgate
python examples/ten_lines.py
```

Output:

```
ana@corp.test: ALLOW. All sensitive arguments trace to your request or a trusted source.
records@corp.test: BLOCK. Blocked 'send_email': recipients='records@corp.test' came from text from a tool result (email, web page, file or event) (read_file).
```

OCR and the MCP server are optional extras: `pip install "agentgate[ocr,mcp] @ git+https://github.com/mathesh310703/agentgate"`.

- **Works with pip alone:** the gate, the built-in policies, the OCR and MCP extras, and the offline examples, which need nothing else installed.
- **Needs a clone of the repo:** the image reader, the judge and policy synthesis (they use the budget proxy), the `policies/` folder, and the example script files themselves.
- **Tested from a fresh install:** only Python 3.11, and only the `ocr` and `mcp` extras.

License: MIT. Llama Prompt Guard 2 keeps its own license, noted below.

Built with Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant; the author directed the design and ran the experiments.

## What is new here

Text gates with provenance already exist ([docs/RELATED_WORK.md](docs/RELATED_WORK.md)). AgentGate adds three things:
- **Provenance through pixels, as a drop-in.** Text recovered from an image enters the session as untrusted pixels (`Session.add_pixels`, or `observe_image` on the MCP server). A share aimed at an address found only in an image is blocked, and the block names the image.
- **A second image reader that can only make the gate stricter.** An optional model transcript joins the OCR text as untrusted data. It traces more planted addresses to their image (60/60 vs 50/60) and changed no decision. Tests check that it never moves a decision towards allow.

# PhantomTrace
PhantomTrace is an AI-powered digital forensics investigation agent that analyses security logs, correlates evidence, reconstructs incident timelines, and generates verifiable forensic reports using Meta Muse Spark.

## Try PhantomTrace

**Recorded walkthrough:** Open the [hosted demo](https://phantomtrace-demo.onrender.com/) and click **Replay a recorded run**. The replay uses a saved investigation and works without an account or API key.

**Live investigation:** Clone the repository and run the backend and frontend locally using your own Meta Model API key.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/mirrawrr/PhantomTrace.git
cd PhantomTrace/backend
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the virtual environment (`.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` in Windows PowerShell or `source .venv/bin/activate` on macOS/Linux), then install the backend dependencies:

```sh
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

In `backend`, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `MODEL_API_KEY` to your own Meta Model API key. Start the backend:

```sh
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000
```

In a second terminal, from the repository root, start the frontend:

```sh
cd frontend
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173`, select **Adaptive investigation** and **First shift: maintenance or compromise?**, click **Load sample**, then click **Start investigation**. For a separate witness check, enter a statement and click **Check witness only**. Use the synthetic sample for both tests.

## Five-phase hackathon roadmap

| Phase | Deliverable | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | FastAPI backend and Muse Spark API integration | Complete |
| 2 | Log parser, event correlation, evidence reference verifier | Complete |
| 3 | Bounded Muse Spark tool-calling investigation and execution history | Complete; original workflow live-tested |
| 4 | React dashboard, findings, tool activity and interactive timeline | Complete; original workflow live-tested |
| 5 | Integration testing, deployment and three-minute demo | Hosted replay available; demo video recorded |

## Run Phase 3

From `backend`, create a virtual environment and install `requirements-dev.txt`.
Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `MODEL_API_KEY` locally; never commit `.env`.
`META_MODEL` optionally overrides the default `muse-spark-1.3`.
Start with `python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload`, then open
http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs and use `POST /api/investigate/agent`:

```json
{"logs":"EVT001 | 2026-10-28T02:12:00Z | PERMISSION_CHANGE | user=admin | role=administrator"}
```

The model chooses calls to `parse_logs`, `correlate_events`, and `verify_evidence`.
Each accepts `{}` and operates on server-owned evidence, so the model cannot
replace events. Calls execute in returned order; prerequisites are enforced.
Results return through Responses API `function_call_output` items with matching
call IDs and `previous_response_id`, following
[Meta's tool-calling documentation](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/tool-calling).

# Whiteboard2Repo

**Snap the whiteboard after the design meeting. Get a running, tested repo before everyone has left the room.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Nov 2026) · Track: Build for Your World · Solo · Everything in this repo was written during the hackathon.

**Try it:** https://whiteboard2repo.onrender.com (Render free tier; first load can take ~1 min, 6 builds per hour) · **Real PR opened by Re-snap:** https://github.com/taku629/whiteboard2repo-demo/pull/1

![Read the board](media/01_read.png)
![Built and proven](media/02_built.png)

SAM 3.1 regions on the sample board (boxes, cylinder, cloud, arrows):

![SAM 3.1](samples/board_rooms.sam.png)

## The problem

Every system starts as boxes and arrows on a whiteboard. Then someone takes a phone photo, it rots in a chat thread, and a day later an engineer re-types the same design into boilerplate by hand: services, a database, a queue, a compose file, tests. The constraints people wrote in the corner ("no double booking!") are the first thing to get lost.

## What it does

1. **Read the board** – Meta **Muse Spark Open** looks at the photo and returns a typed graph: components (client / service / database / worker / queue / external) with bounding boxes, every arrow with its label and protocol, and the handwritten notes. Each note is rewritten as a testable **invariant**. Optional Meta **SAM 3.1** segmentation regions are passed in as grounding hints.
2. **Confirm** – you see the boxes drawn over your photo, a Mermaid diagram, and an editable table. Fix anything the model misread before building.
3. **Build** – a deterministic scaffolder emits a green skeleton (FastAPI per service, SQLAlchemy models, an event bus, `docker-compose.yml`, Dockerfile). Then a Muse Spark Open **tool-calling agent** (`list_files`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `run_tests`) implements every endpoint and edge and writes tests until `pytest` is green.
4. **Prove the invariants** – for each invariant the model plays a mutation-testing engine: it injects the smallest change that would break that rule, the tests run, and the mutant must be **KILLED**. Then the code is restored. A rule only counts as covered when breaking it makes the tests fail.
5. **Board coverage** – every box, arrow and note on the board is checked against the generated repo: services need ≥2 endpoints, databases need SQLAlchemy models, event edges need publish + subscribe, notes need invariant tests. It is a structural check, not a semantic proof; the mutation step is the semantic check. Download the repo as a zip.
6. **Re-snap** – the design changed? Photograph the board again. # Knack

Never argue the same PR twice.

Knack turns your team's code-review decisions into rules your coding agent can't break, and shows it who decided.

That unread past is intent debt, and it compounds with every agent-written diff.

source .venv/bin/activate
bash scripts/reproduce.sh
```

# VScan

A dependency vulnerability scanner that checks whether a CVE is actually **reachable** from your public entry points — instead of listing every CVE in your dependency tree.

## How it works

1. Builds a call graph from source with tree-sitter (Python, JavaScript, PHP, Go).
2. Traces, from each public entry point, which dependencies are reachable and whether the vulnerable function is actually called.
3. Runs taint analysis to check whether attacker-controlled input reaches the vulnerable call.
4. Correlates dependencies against OSV, plus CISA KEV and EPSS.

Every finding gets one verdict:

| Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `not reached` | The CVE exists, but no entry point reaches the package. |
| `reachable` | The vulnerable code is reachable, but attacker input isn't proven to get there. |
| `exploitable` | Attacker input provably reaches the vulnerable call. |

Reachability is a **lower bound**: VScan only follows call edges it can resolve, so `not reached` is conservative (a missed path is possible; a false "exploitable" is not).

## Example

`vscan audit samples/acme-api` on the bundled sample service:

```
Funnel: 19 deps · 145 known CVEs · 16 reachable · 1 vulnerable-function confirmed · 1 exploitable

 6. PyYAML 5.3.1 [PyPI] -- CVE-2020-14343
    severity: CRITICAL   EPSS 0.060
    REACHABLE via GET /admin/config, POST /documents/import
    taint: request.get_data -> yaml.full_load
    [ep:POST:/documents/import -> fn:api/documents.py:import_document
     -> fn:services/document_service.py:ingest -> fn:core/config_loader.py:parse_yaml
     -> dep:PyPI:PyYAML]
```

The other 144 findings are real CVEs that no entry point reaches, or whose vulnerable function the project never calls.

## Install

```sh
pip install .
```

## Use

CLI:

```sh
vscan audit path/to/repo                       # ranked, reachability-aware findings
vscan audit path/to/repo --json out.json       # machine-readable
vscan audit path/to/repo --sarif out.sarif     # for GitHub code scanning
vscan audit path/to/repo --markdown out.md      # a PR-comment summary
vscan audit path/to/repo --fail-on reachable   # exit non-zero to gate CI
```

GitHub Action — on every PR it posts a reachability-aware comment and uploads SARIF to code scanning:

```yaml
- uses: swaggpi/VScan@main
  with:
    path: .
    fail-on: reachable
```

MCP server — exposes the scan as tools for an AI agent (scan overview, find, describe, call graph, trace entrypoint, dependency reachers, audit, finding detail):

```sh
vscan-mcp            # stdio; or --transport http for a remote server
```

## AI layer (optional, advisory)

Built and tested against **Meta Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`), served by Baseten. The client is a plain OpenAI-compatible chat-completions caller, so any such endpoint works.

# SpokenSlate

**Transcripts tell you what the professor said. SpokenSlate tells you what they meant.**

A whiteboard lecture is two streams: what's said and what's written. Captions keep only the
first, so for a blind or low-vision student a recorded lecture is full of dead ends:
*"this term cancels with that one"*, *"plug it into the equation from before"*. Universities
ask instructors to "say what you write and avoid *this* and *here*". In practice, nobody does.

SpokenSlate takes a recorded lecture and produces an accessible web page:

- **Every board step, in order, at the moment it was written**: a plain-language reading
  first ("matrix: row one: boxed one, two, one…"), then real math (MathML) a screen reader can
  explore cell by cell, then the LaTeX source.
- **Spoken references linked to what they mean**: *"subtracting twice **this**"* →
  *(means minus 2, in step 6)*, a link to that step.
- **It says when it isn't sure.** Ambiguous references are marked *unresolved*, with a
  "possibly step N" hint. A confident wrong answer is the worst outcome, so the system is
  built to abstain rather than guess.
- **Erased steps are kept** and labelled ("erased at 1:36, kept here").

**Try it:** [arun-velkumar19.github.io/spokenslate](https://arun-velkumar19.github.io/spokenslate/), with two processed lectures and a guide to reading them with a screen reader.

## How it works

```
video ─► candidate keyframes ─► SAM 3.1: mask the lecturer ─► board changed? ─► Muse Spark: read board
                                                                                   (diff → timeline)
audio ─► word timestamps ─► reference phrases ("this term", "the first", "the problem I just gave you")
fingertip track ─► pointing candidates ─┐
                                        ▼
            Muse Spark: which board element does this phrase mean? (3 frames + words + board)
                                        ▼
            validator: unknown element, element not on the board yet, quote not in it,
            or confidence < 0.7  →  "unresolved"           ─►  accessible HTML page
```

| Meta model / tool | Job in SpokenSlate |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | reads the board into structured steps (LaTeX + plain reading + region), and resolves each spoken reference to a board element with evidence and confidence |
| **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) + Meta's **`meta-sam-parser`** | masks the lecturer ("person") on each candidate keyframe. Board reads see the board, not the person, and a read is skipped when only the lecturer moved |
| **Muse Wonder** (`muse-wonder-1.0`) | optional second opinion (`--escalate`) when Spark abstains, still behind the validator |
| MediaPipe hand landmarker | fingertip track → ranked "pointing candidates" given to the resolver |
| faster-whisper (local) | word-level timestamps. Muse Voice Transcribe is realtime-only and returns ~20 s turns, while pointing needs per-word timing |

# Verified Cruise Control

A multimodal automotive listing-audit tool: it compares advertised
advanced driver-assistance (ADAS) features against visual evidence from
listing photographs plus vehicle-specific documentation, and produces
reviewable evidence packets for a human reviewer.

> **Hackathon project — public by requirement.** This repository is
> intentionally public. All fixtures are synthetic or generated in-repo.
> AI results are advisory evidence for a human reviewer; the system never
> independently certifies disputed features.

**Current scope (PR #3):** foundation + listing import (PR #1) and the
multimodal audit engine — Muse visual observations, SAM localization,
manufacturer-aware interpretation, deterministic five-state
reconciliation, durable worker, enforced spend caps (PR #2) — plus an
offline-first paired harness comparing baseline (m2) vs
reference-assisted (m3) recognition on real-world photos
(`evals/realworld/`, `docs/realworld-evaluation.md`). Reference-assisted
recognition is experimental and unvalidated against live inference; no
live model comparison has been authorized.

## Why this is more than an image describer (hackathon context)

**The real-world problem.** Used-car listings routinely advertise driver-assistance
features — adaptive cruise control, lane-keeping, blind-spot monitoring — that
the photos may or may not support. Checking a listing means testing each
advertised claim against the visual evidence, not admiring one photo.

**Why several photographs matter.** One photo rarely settles a claim: the
steering-wheel buttons may be visible in an interior shot while the radar sensor
is only checkable in a front-grille close-up. Verification tests every
advertised claim against *each* relevant photo and records what each photo does
and does not show.

**How Meta models do substantive work here (shipped in PR #2).** PR #1 made
zero model calls by design — it built the evidence pipeline the models now
consume:

- **Muse Spark Open 1026** (Baseten) provides visual understanding of every
  listing photo: which assistance controls, sensors, and indicators are visible,
  and where.
- **SAM 3.1** (Meta) localizes and segments the named parts — the steering-wheel
  button cluster, the grille sensor window — so verdicts rest on precise regions
  instead of vague whole-image captions.
- Uncertain regions trigger **conditional crop re-analysis**: Muse looks again
  at the zoomed crop before anything is recorded.
- **Deterministic reconciliation** (rules, not model judgment) compares the
  per-photo observations against the advertised claims and assigns each claim
  one of five evidence states.
- **Source evidence is preserved**: original bytes are immutable and
  SHA-256-verified, so every verdict links back to the exact pixels a reviewer
  can re-open.
- The output is a **discrepancy report** — claim-by-claim states with supporting
  crops — built for a human reviewer. The system never certifies a disputed
  feature on i

A spam filter says "maybe spam" and stops. # PeerCodeAI: Time-Travel Debugger

> **Find the moment your code broke. Understand why. Fix it with proof.**

A real-time collaborative code editor with a debugger that:
1. finds the change that broke the tests;
2. asks **Meta Muse Spark** why;
3. verifies the proposed fix against real tests;
4. applies it only if nobody has edited the code since.

**Live demo:** [peer-code-ai.vercel.app](https://peer-code-ai.vercel.app) · **Video (74 s):** [youtu.be/v9Y7SIhG-mw](https://youtu.be/v9Y7SIhG-mw) · Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Track)

## How it works
```
Checkpoints ─► Locate regression ─► Explain (Muse Spark) ─► Verify on a copy ─► Apply to the shared doc
 (snapshots)   real tests, bisect     diff + failing tests      real tests          only if unchanged
               + verification scan    → root cause + patch                          since verification
```
1. **Checkpoints:** snapshots of the shared Yjs document, ordered by the server. Click one to time-travel through a read-only diff.
2. **Locate regression (deterministic):** real tests run over the history. Bisection plus a backward verification scan report the *first observed failing* checkpoint and the diff that introduced it.
3. **Explain (Muse Spark, `muse-spark-1.3`):** the model receives the diff, the full test suite with pass/fail status, the failing inputs and outputs, and the current code. It answers in **strict `json_schema` structured output**: what failed, what changed, the root cause, its uncertainty, and minimal find/replace edits.
4. **Verify:** the server validates the edits (each must match the code exactly once), applies them to an isolated copy, and runs the predefined tests.
5. **Apply:** allowed only if the live collaborative document still equals the verified code. A collaborator's newer edits block it. The applied checkpoint is then re-tested on its own.

**Two built-in scenarios:**
- a TypeScript cart-total regression;
- a JavaScript **async stale-response race**: after an innocent-looking refactor, clearing the search box no longer cancels an in-flight request. It's tested deterministically with deferred promises, with no timers.

## Results
| Evidence | Result |
|---|---|
| Real Muse Spark runs (2 scenarios, 15 trials each, two days) | **30/30**: regression localized, valid structured answer on the first attempt, root cause named, patch passed all predefined tests, applied checkpoint re-tested green ([EVALUATION](docs/EVALUATION.md), raw data in `docs/eval/`) |
| Localization algorithm on generated histories (8–64 checkpoints, incl. non-monotonic) | **64/64** correct ([BENCHMARK](docs/BENCHMARK.md)) |
| Automated tests | **94** passing (`npm test`) |

These are two seeded bugs with generous context: evidence that the pipeline is reliable, not proof of general debugging ability.

## Safety and limitations
- **The public server never runs visitor-written code.** It executes only the built-in scenario code, plus model patches of that code. Pat

# Sika

**An investing assistant for the Ghana Stock Exchange that lives in WhatsApp.** Built on Meta's Muse models for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track).

**Try it in your browser:** https://sika.cloudflareos-01eeeb.workers.dev. This is the same conversation that runs on WhatsApp.

**3-minute demo video:** https://youtu.be/OhlmxiTKxJI

In Ghana, people invest through brokers and talk on WhatsApp. Sika is the knowledgeable friend in between:
1. **It gets to know you.** Five quick questions build an investor profile, scored the way advisers do it: the lower of your willingness and your capacity for risk.
2. **It builds a plan with you.** Your goal, a monthly amount and your limits, set with a few taps.
3. **It suggests trades that fit your plan.** Each suggestion is priced from IC Securities' **live order book**, with every charge shown to the pesewa, and explained.
4. **You stay in charge.** Sika never buys or sells for you. You place the order with your own broker, tap **I bought it**, and Sika keeps your holdings, budget and alerts up to date.

**It answers the way you ask.** Write or speak to Sika in English, Pidgin, Twi, Fante, Ga, Ewe, Hausa or Dagbani and it answers in that language, with no settings to find first. A first "Maakye" gets a Twi welcome; a first question gets answered before any setup. Send a voice note and Sika replies with one too, plus the text with the exact numbers.

Typing, tapping and **voice notes** all work. Investors can also ask **how the market is doing today**, get a **deep dive on one stock**, **compare stocks** side by side, see **portfolio insights** (sector mix, dividends, holdings that rarely trade), get **news with links to the sources**, and **follow stocks**: Sika messages them when there's important news.

**It stays on topic.** Sika only talks about investing on the GSE. Off-topic questions (other markets, homework, poems) and attempts to change its rules get a fixed reply from code, so the model never answers them.

![How a suggestion flows](docs/flow.svg)

## Why it's different

**The AI suggests, code checks, you decide.** Muse Spark can only *suggest* a trade. Fixed code then takes over:
1. It prices the trade from the real order book: buyers pay the ask and sellers get the bid.
2. A deterministic rules engine checks it against the investor's plan: per-order and monthly limits, max in one stock, never-buy list, never sell at a loss, and that someone is on the other side. A suggestion that breaks the plan is never shown.
3. A suggestion that passes is shown with every charge and **I bought it / Why? / Not now**.
4. Sika never places orders. **I bought it** is handled by code, not the model. It records the purchase once, at the suggested price, with a one-tap **Fix it** if the broker's price was different. That keeps the portfolio, the monthly budget and the alerts accurate.

# Shadowtwin

**A physics twin of any rotating machine, built from a phone video.**
Film a fan, pump or motor coasting to a stop. Shadowtwin tracks it with **SAM 3.1**, identifies the differential equation that governs it, runs that equation as a "ghost" alongside the real machine, and, when reality drifts away from the twin, tells you **which fault** it is: imbalance, rubbing, drag, bearing loss, or a weak drive.

No sensors. No training data. No per-machine engineering.

> Built entirely during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026). Track: *Push the Frontier*. Every line in this repository was written during the event.

![twin vs reality, deceleration curve, and hypothesis evidence for a rubbing fault](docs/media/hero.png)

---

## Why this matters
Rotating machines (fans, pumps, motors, compressors) move the air, water and goods of every building, farm and factory. Condition monitoring today means an accelerometer, wiring and a specialist **per machine**, so it is reserved for the expensive ones. The long tail runs unwatched until it fails.

Shadowtwin replaces the sensor with a camera that is already in everyone's pocket, and replaces the specialist's setup work with Meta models.

## How it works

```
iPhone clip (240 fps)
  │
  ├─► Muse Spark 1.3 ──► MachineSpec: what to track (SAM prompts), what stays still, plausible physics
  ├─► SAM 3.1 (video) ─► per-frame masks of the marker, hub/housing and a static reference
  ▼
signals ─ rotation centre (circle fit) → angle θ(t) → camera-shake removal → housing vibration spectrum
  ▼
system identification ─ fit dω/dt = −(a·ω + k·ω|ω| + s·sgn ω) to the ANGLE, train on 60%, predict 40% blind;
                        Spark proposes term sets from residual fingerprints, the data selects (held-out error + AIC)
  ▼
twin + monitor ─ replay the healthy twin on a new clip → CUSUM alarm;
                 isolate with competing hypotheses (each fault = one physical term) + 1× vibration + drive torque
  ▼
Muse Spark ─ maintenance note grounded only in the measured numbers (+ Muse Voice Transcribe operator notes)
```

### What the Meta models do, and what they are not trusted with
| Model | Role | Guardrail |
|---|---|---|
| **SAM 3.1** (Model API, video) | Tracks parts named in plain words, with no training, on any machine | Coverage checked; outlines kept as evidence |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Watches keyframes and writes the measurement plan (the step a technician normally does) | Typed spec (pydantic); everything after it is deterministic |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Proposes physics terms from residual fingerprints | Can never set a parameter or pick the winner: code fits, held-out data decides |
| **Muse Spark 1.3** | Writes the maintenance note | Must use only numbers from the diagnosis JSON |
| **Muse Voice Transcribe** | Operator voice notes aligned to the fault timeline | Optional |
| **Muse Spark Open** (Baseten) | Same reasoning steps on open weights: `SHADOWTWIN_REASONER=basete

# HereOut

**Your way out, drawn on the plan.** Photograph a posted evacuation plan, tap where you stand, and HereOut draws the route to the nearest exit, step by step, in your language.

[Live demo](https://hereout.devrives.com/) · [Demo video](https://hereout.devrives.com/#demo) · Entry for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-04 ET)

![How HereOut works: you photograph the plan, Muse Spark reads it, code finds the ways out, and you tap your spot to get the route](docs/how-it-works.png)

## Try it

1. Open <https://hereout.devrives.com/> and pick one of 203 photos of real plans, or upload your own.
2. Tap where you stand. "If blocked" switches the route to the next exit.
3. Open "What Muse Spark read" to see the model's points, the crops of its second look and what the code changed.

## What Muse Spark does

| Job | How | On the page |
|---|---|---|
| Exits | One call on the whole photo asks for the floor box and every final exit, as points on a 0 to 1000 grid | The numbered exits |
| Second look | Exits far from any green or red mark go on numbered, zoomed crops in one multi-image call; the model keeps, moves or drops each one | "What Muse Spark read", with the crops |
| Plan words | A parallel call reads the title, the legend and the printed instructions | "What the plan says", with the original under each item |
| Translation | A text-only call puts the plan words and exit names into 12 languages besides English, cached | The plan card in your language |

Walls, routes and steps come from code, and the start is always your tap. HereOut uses no other Meta model. Model: `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` through Baseten, standard mode only, every call under one spend cap.

<details>
<summary>Settings, prompts and time limits of each call</summary>

| Item | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Model | `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` | `DEFAULT_MODEL` in `src/hereout/reader.py` |
| Provider | Baseten Model API, OpenAI-compatible chat completions (`https://inference.baseten.co/v1/chat/completions`) | `API_URL` |

> Hecho desde cero durante el Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 oct - 4 nov 2026).

Moderniza software antiguo a partir de un video, sin el código fuente. Grabas a alguien usando el programa viejo y un equipo de agentes reconstruye sus pantallas y flujos en una app web moderna, y luego verifica paso a paso que hace lo mismo.

1. **Agente de pantallas**: extrae del video los cuadros clave, pantallas, campos, botones, tablas y diálogos.
2. **Agente de flujos**: reconstruye los flujos de trabajo paso a paso.
3. **Agente constructor**: genera una app web con las mismas pantallas y flujos.
4. **Agente verificador**: repite cada flujo en la app nueva y la compara con el video original.

**Muse Spark Open** (modelo de pesos abiertos de Meta, vía Baseten) es el núcleo y hace todo el trabajo. **SAM 3.1** es un complemento opcional: en una GPU de Modal encuentra cada campo del programa antiguo para marcarlo en el informe. Se activa con `REWIND_SEGMENTATION=sam`; nada depende de él.

# КАРТОЧКА

Фото товара с телефона — в готовую карточку для маркетплейса, которую площадка примет с первого раза. Белый фон 255,255,255, нужные пропорции, чек-лист регламента с числами и текст карточки — за один прогон.

Это не фотостудия. Photoroom и аналоги делают красивое фото — КАРТОЧКА делает валидатор регламента с числом: «пройдено 9 из 10, вот замер каждого пункта и что поправить». Красивое фото — побочный эффект, а не продукт.

## Как запустить локально

```bash
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env   # ключ можно не вписывать — будет MOCK-режим
pnpm dev                # http://localhost:3000
```

Проверки:

```bash
pnpm build              # обязано проходить без ошибок типов
pnpm evals --mock       # eval-стенд на фикстурах, без ключа и кредитов
pnpm check:pipeline     # сквозной прогон inspect→…→identity на synthetic-фото
pnpm check:rules        # движок регламента на трёх площадках + временная четвёртая
pnpm check:copy-export  # текст карточки и клиентская сборка ZIP
pnpm check:identity     # identity gate: same/substituted/петля ретраев
```

## MOCK-режим (демо без ключа)

Если `MODEL_API_KEY` пустой (или `MOCK=1`), все вызовы моделей идут через детерминированный `lib/mock/provider.ts`: правдоподобные задержки 300–800 мс, фиксированные боксы/вердикты, ошибок нет. Весь продукт — загрузка, студия, чек-лист, ZIP, батч, публичная страница — открывается и работает без сети и без кредитов. Проверка судейского сценария: стереть ключ, `MOCK=1`, открыть `/` → «Посмотреть готовый пример» → «Собрать карточку».

## Какая модель где и почему

| Шаг | Модель | Почему она |
|---|---|---|
| `segment` — маска товара | `sam-3.1` | сегментация по промпту категории; в MOCK — детерминированный бокс, дальше цепочка `sam-mask → sam-boxes → background-removal` на sharp |
| `compose` — кадр 3:4 | детерминированный коллаж на sharp (`modelUsed=false`) | генерация рвёт соответствие маски и кадра, а регламенту нужны считаемые пиксели; живая генерация подключается только с identity-петлёй (вариант B, см. `docs/DECISIONS.md`) |
| `identity` — тот ли товар | `muse-glimmer` (судья) + pHash + HSV + SSIM | независимый вердикт открытыми весами: 3 голоса большинством; формула `0.35·pHash + 0.25·HSV + 0.25·SSIM + 0.15·glimmer`, порог 0.90 |
| `rules` — текст/логотипы на фото | `muse-spark-1.3` строгим JSON `{ok,confident,bbox,reason}` | вердикты `no_text_on_main`, `no_watermark`, `single_object`; без уверенности — честный провал |
| `copy` — название, описание, характеристики | `muse-spark-1.3` | лимиты длины только из `rules/<mp>.json`, запрет корней «идеальн» |
| eval-стенд и черновики | `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` | дешёвый прогон 20 кейсов без траты основного бюджета |

Честные оговорки (проверено на этой машине, см. `docs/DECISIONS.md` T2):

- `muse-glimmer` — open-weight модель для self-host (vLLM/llama.cpp), через Model API не отдаётся; живой судья работает только с локальным рантаймом, в остальных режимах — MOCK.
- `sam-3.1` отдаёт не PNG-маску, а текст special-token

# NEUROFORGE X

**Compile Intelligence. Optimize Execution.**

NEUROFORGE X is a multimodal AI **compiler and execution runtime**. It treats
multimodal AI operations — language reasoning, image segmentation, feature
extraction, image generation — as typed, programmable computational components.
A high-level workload is lowered into a **typed intermediate representation
(MIR)**, validated and optimized by a **graph compiler**, and executed by a
**dependency-aware concurrent runtime** against local, mock, and Meta model
backends — with real performance profiling.

This is infrastructure, not a chatbot. The core is written in Go.

---

## What actually works today

Everything below is implemented, tested, and runnable end-to-end:

- **Typed MIR** — 9 value types, operator registry, typed input/output ports,
  JSON serialization, versioned schema.
- **Graph compiler** — frontend (YAML/JSON → MIR), type inference, static type
  checking, dependency resolution, **cycle detection**, backend-compatibility
  checks.
- **Optimizer** — dead-node elimination, **common-subexpression elimination to a
  fixpoint** (safe: only deterministic, cacheable, side-effect-free ops),
  parallelism (dependency-level) analysis. Every pass preserves semantics and is
  re-validated.
- **Runtime (Go)** — dependency-aware scheduler with bounded concurrency,
  8-state execution model, per-node timeouts, bounded retries with backoff,
  cancellation, and two failure policies (`fail` / `skip`). Race-clean
  (`go test -race`).
- **Backends** — a common `Backend` interface with a deterministic **mock**
  (clearly labeled synthetic), **local operators** (real spatial feature
  computation), **fully local Meta Llama backends** — `local.llama` (planning &
  reasoning) and `local.vision` (Llama 3.2 Vision on real video frames) via
  Ollama, no credentials, real inference — and **Meta cloud adapters** (Muse
  Spark, SAM 3.1, Muse Image) behind a fallback that uses the mock when
  credentials are absent.
- **Cache** — content-addressed LRU keyed by operation identity + input
  fingerprints; hit/miss/eviction stats.
- **Profiler** — total wall time, per-node latency & queue wait, retry counts,
  cache-hit rate, critical path.
- **CLI** `neuroforge` — `init validate compile inspect run profile benchmark
  doctor operators`.
- **Control-plane API** — JSON HTTP service backing the dashboard.
- **Benchmarks** — real, measured sequential vs. parallel vs. cached vs.
  optimized comparisons.

### Honesty notes

- Without `META_API_KEY`, Meta operations run on the **mock** backend and every
  such output is tagged `simulated: true`. These are **not** real Meta API
  results.
- Mock backend latencies are **simulated** to make scheduling/caching effects
  measurable; benchmark output says so explicitly. Real API latency replaces
  them when credentials are set.
- The `local.llama` backend performs **real inference** on a Meta Llama model via
  Ollama; its latencies are genuinely measured, and `run`

# PR Detonator

**Static scanners read code. PR Detonator runs it â€” under kernel tracing â€” and holds what it
did against what the pull request claimed.**

> **We pointed it at 100 packages published to npm minutes earlier, knowing nothing about any
> of them. 73 installed and all 73 came back clean. Of the 27 that did not install, one was
> blocked anyway â€” on evidence captured before it timed out.**
>
> That one connected to a hardcoded IP address on a non-standard port during `postinstall`,
> with no DNS lookup at all. Reading its published source explained why: a fallback path
> downloads the product binary from that bare IP with **TLS certificate verification
> disabled**, then extracts it and links it as the executable. Anyone who can intercept that
> connection â€” or who later controls that address â€” gets arbitrary code executed on every
> machine running `npm install`.
>
> It isn't malware. The maintainer owns the package; it's a deliberate fallback with an unsafe
> default. We **reported it privately to the maintainer on Nov 2, 2026**; there is no response
> or fix yet, so the name is left out of this text, though it is recoverable from this
> repository's earlier history. But nobody told us to look, and no advisory existed: the
> behavior alone gave it away.
> ([method](eval/SWEEP.md) Â· [what `npm audit` says instead](eval/BASELINE.md))

We then scaled the same sweep to **500** of the newest packages: 413 of 421 that installed
cleared, nothing benign was hard-blocked, seven were routed to *needs review*, and the one
block was a package that downloads and runs binaries during `install`.
([the 500-package run](eval/SWEEP500.md))

## Why now

Install-time supply-chain attacks are the ones that actually land â€” event-stream, ua-parser-js,
the Shai-Hulud worm â€” because a package's `postinstall` runs on every laptop and CI runner
before anyone imports a line of its code. The pull request that lets one in is usually a
**one-line version bump**, so there is nothing in the diff to review.

And increasingly nobody is reviewing it anyway: **AI coding agents now open the PRs and pick
the dependencies**, including packages that don't exist, which attackers then register. Review
has become the bottleneck precisely as the volume of machine-written dependency changes
exploded. PR Detonator is the layer that checks what the agent just installed â€” by running it.

A GitHub App: on every pull request it runs the PR's `npm install` in a disposable hardened
sandbox, traces every process, connection and DNS lookup at the kernel level with eBPF
(Tetragon), and asks a Meta model to compare that behavior with what the PR *claims* to do. A
PR titled "Fix typo in README" that opens a raw-IP connection during `postinstall` gets a
failing check that blocks the merge and an inline comment on the exact guilty line.

**Live dashboard** (recent runs, verdict tally, and a behavior atlas of what packages do at
install): https://fugeretrevin--pr-detonator-das

# CandiVision Roleplay

**Voice role-play training built on research, not guesswork.**

**Try it live: [platform.candivision.co](https://platform.candivision.co)** (no login, works on a phone) · **Demo video: [3 minutes](DEMO_VIDEO_URL)**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 on Meta Muse Spark, Muse Spark Open, Muse Voice Transcribe and Muse Image.

A training lead describes a conversation their people get wrong ("our engineers make outage calls worse", "our call-centre staff read the refund policy like robots"), attaches their own material, and CandiVision Roleplay:

1. **Researches first.** It searches open scholarly databases (OpenAlex, Crossref) and our own library of proven methods for how experts handle the situation and how people learn it. Sources appear on screen as they are checked.
2. **Builds a programme where every line names its source.** Skills, 2 or 3 levels that get harder in steps, an AI character with hidden facts the learner has to earn, and a rubric of must-have and nice-to-have lines.
3. **Runs a voice role-play.** The learner holds a button and talks; the character answers by voice, and its mood moves with what the learner actually does.
4. **Debriefs with evidence.** Two independent AI judges score each rubric line with a quote from the call; the debrief shows the moment, the rubric line, the source behind it, one thing to try, and a 60-second drill on the weakest must-have.
5. **Reports team progress** on a fixed version of the programme: first try against latest, by skill. No leaderboards.

For training only. Results are never meant for hiring, firing or performance ratings, and a request to screen or rank people is declined.

## How "no guessing" is enforced

| Rule | Where |
|---|---|
| A source the research tools did not return is dropped, even if the model cites it. | `apps/server/src/research.ts` |
| Every paper DOI must resolve in the DOI handle system, and papers must be cited at least 10 times. | `apps/server/src/papers.ts` |
| Every skill, level and rubric line must cite a source from the brief or quote the customer's own file word for word; otherwise the programme is regenerated once, then turned into questions for the training lead. | `packages/core/src/validate.ts`, `apps/server/src/builder.ts` |
| What research could not answer is listed as "not found" instead of being filled in. | research brief |
| Each rubric line is judged by two different models. A pass must quote the learner's own words from the call. If the judges disagree the line is "unsure" and the training lead settles it; nothing is averaged away. | `packages/core/src/gate.ts`, `apps/server/src/judges.ts` |
| The same transcript always gets the same result (temperature 0, stored verdicts per version and transcript). | `apps/server/src/judges.ts` |

## 📌 Executive Summary

**QA-Swarm** is an enterprise-grade, closed-loop autonomous quality engineering system bridging **multimodal computer vision** with **deterministic source code remediation**. 

Traditional visual regression tools capture pixel differences without understanding code semantics, while static analyzers and linters inspect code without visual awareness of real-world browser rendering. **QA-Swarm** unites both worlds through a bidirectional agent swarm powered by **Meta AI's next-generation models**:

1. **Meta SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1` Spatial Cortex):** Performs sub-pixel visual segmentation, extracting localized layout overflow anomalies and parsing coordinate tokens `<|box;x1=...;y1=...;x2=...;y2=...;w=...;h=...|>` into normalized coordinates `[ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax]`.

3. **Adversarial Chaos Engine:** Evaluates defensive resilience across 5 adversarial vectors (buffer overflow, bidirectional RTL Unicode, boundary type mutation, syntax breakout, and concurrency event storms).
4. **CI/CD Governance & OASIS SARIF v2.1.0 Gate:** Generates standardized SARIF v2.1.0 reports for native **GitHub Code Scanning / CodeQL** integration, determining an objective Health Score (0–100) and automated deployment gate verdicts.

# FlowSME

Record yourself doing a piece of office work. FlowSME turns the recording into a workflow map, shows which
applications you used and how data moved between them, scores each task for automation potential, and
recommends how to automate it, with links to existing tools and a draft automation to start from.

It works like a process consultant shadowing you. It sees what you click, type and copy, not just which apps
were open.

## Built on Meta's AI

Every report is made with Meta's Model API (`https://api.meta.ai/v1`, settings in `config.meta.toml` and the
server's `server.toml`):

| What | Meta model / API | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Reads each screenshot and describes the step in business language (only the active window is sent) | Muse Spark, vision | [describe.py](flowsme/describe.py) |
| Names the tasks, writes the recommendations, SOP wording and user stories, always as schema-checked JSON | Muse Spark, structured output | [workflow.py](flowsme/workflow.py), [recommend.py](flowsme/recommend.py), [sop.py](flowsme/sop.py) |
| Finds existing tools and guides for the task, with cited sources | Muse Spark, Responses API `web_search` | [llm.py](flowsme/llm.py) (`grounded`) |
| Transcribes what the person says while working and turns it into business rules, quoted word for word | Muse Voice Transcribe, then Muse Spark | [narration.py](flowsme/narration.py) |
| Reads a screen video frame by frame when there is no recording | Muse Spark, vision | [video.py](flowsme/video.py) |

A spending cap per report (`max_cost_usd`) and a per-recording cache keep the cost predictable: about $0.30 for
the 5.6-minute test video. Without a key, FlowSME still works with its built-in rules, so it can be tried
offline. Other OpenAI-compatible providers can be configured too (see [Using an AI model](#using-an-ai-model)).

## Try it in five minutes

**Hackathon judges:** download FlowSME Recorder and the judges' seat file from the
[judges-demo release](https://github.com/marker2601/flowsme/releases/tag/judges-demo). The seat connects to our
hosted FlowSME server, which runs the analysis on Meta's models.

1. Install **FlowSME Recorder** (`FlowSME-Recorder-Setup-0.5.1.exe`) and open the seat file you were sent.
2. Click **Record**, do one round of the task (say what you do and why, if you like), then **Stop**.
3. Click **Get report**. In about two minutes: the process map, what to automate first, hours (and, for
   managers, money) saved, an SOP to approve, and ready-made workflows for n8n, Node-RED, Make, Power Automate,
   Logic Apps or Windmill.

No seat yet? `python -m flowsme demo --offline` makes a full report from a built-in sample recording.

## For customers: FlowSME Recorder and the FlowSME server

Customers never get FlowSME itself. They install **FlowSME Recorder**, which only records and shows results.
Everything that makes the results runs on the **FlowSME server**, which you run:

| On the customer's PC (FlowSME Recorder) | Only on your server |
|--

# canary-agent

**An AI triage-and-fix agent for LLM application security.** Built for the
Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026), Indie track.

![The AI/LLM attack surface canary-agent defends, generated with Meta's Muse Image](docs/threat_surface.png)

AI agents now write a growing share of production code, and they introduce
exactly the failure modes classic tools miss: prompt injection, excessive
agency, leaked keys, unvalidated model output. `canary-agent` reads those
findings, uses **Muse Spark** to decide which are real and why, writes a fix,
and proves the fix works by re-running the scanner. The model proposes; the
deterministic scanner disposes.

## What is new here, and what is not

> **Disclosure (Indie track, "new work only").** The detection engine is
> [**canary**](https://github.com/jcedrik/canary) (`canary-sast` on PyPI, MIT),
> written and published *before* the hackathon. It is used here as an
> off-the-shelf input: `canary-agent` consumes canary's JSON findings. **Every
> line in this repository is new work built during the hackathon:** the Muse
> Spark triage, the fix-and-verify loop, the evaluation against expert labels,
> and the Muse Code MCP server. The demo video shows only this new layer.

## The agent

```
canary findings ──► triage (Muse Spark) ──► fix (Muse Spark) ──► re-scan (canary)
                      true/false positive      patch on a           verified?
                      + reason                 scratch copy          keep / retry
```

1. **Triage.** For each finding, Muse Spark reads the code window and returns a
   structured verdict: true positive or false positive, a confidence, and a
   reason. (`canary_agent/triage.py`)
2. **Fix and verify.** For a confirmed finding, the model writes a patch,
   canary re-scans, and the patch is kept only if the finding is gone and no
   new one appears. It also runs the project's own tests after a fix and keeps
   the patch only if they still pass. (`canary_agent/loop.py`, `verify_tests.py`)
3. **Scan-as-you-code.** An MCP server exposes the scanner to Muse Code, so the
   coding agent checks a block *before it saves it*. (`canary_agent/mcp_server.py`)

The triage model is the headline, but the agent does not trust it blindly. On
top of canary's findings, `canary-agent` runs its own deterministic AST
detectors and merges everything into one scan (`rescan.scan_all`):

  reports the source->sink line path. It is intra-procedural by design, stated
  honestly; the agent's cross-file context lookups cover the rest at triage time.

# AfterBooth

When a festival, exhibition or pop-up ends, the booth equipment (display racks, storage bins, folding tables) has to be cleared before the teardown deadline, often within hours. Whatever has no new owner by then gets thrown away. AfterBooth hands that equipment to the next event or group before the deadline.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track) by a team of two. The current UI and user-facing messages are English and mobile first. Times are shown in Asia/Seoul (KST). The product spec is [`docs/SPEC.md`](docs/SPEC.md).

## How it works

1. **Use only your own work.** An active member creates a private organization and events. Events, inventory, requests, reservations, and statistics are authorized from that member’s organization; seeded or another member’s organization cannot be selected or taken over.
2. **Photograph the booth.** The giver takes one photo. Muse Spark finds and counts each item, SAM 3.1 checks every box Spark drew, and the result becomes an inventory draft that a person reviews and confirms.
3. **Say what you need.** The receiver speaks or types a request, for example “display racks for a weekend event, I only have a sedan.” Muse Voice Transcribe turns supported WAV input into text and Muse Spark turns it into structured conditions (category, quantity, vehicle, pickup time).
4. **Get an allocation.** A Muse Spark agent searches stock, checks whether the item fits the receiver’s vehicle, and can place a temporary HOLD through server tools. When nothing fits, the person gets the server’s alternatives, such as folding tables instead of a 180 cm rack that will not fit in a sedan.
5. **Race for the last item.** Two receivers can ask for the last display rack at the same moment. Exactly one HOLD succeeds; the other side sees an alternative.
6. **Hand over with a photo.** At pickup, one photo is recounted by Spark and checked by SAM 3.1. Only a matching count completes the handover; otherwise a person settles the difference.
7. **See what was reused.** Statistics show the reused count per category and per event, and the reused volume in liters from the items’ registered sizes.

## Meta models in the product

Every AI call in the product goes to the Meta Model API through one gateway (`AiGateway`). No other model provider is used at runtime.

| Model | What it does | What its output leads to |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark | Finds and counts items in a booth photo with category, box, size and condition | An inventory draft, then inventory items after a person confirms |
| SAM 3.1 | Segments each item from Spark's boxes (box prompts); an item without a mask is flagged for review | Review flags on the draft; at handover, the gate that lets a recount complete |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Transcribes a spoken pickup request (16 kHz mono WAV) | Text for Spark to structure |
| Muse Spark | Structures the request against a JSON schema | A saved pickup request |
| Muse Spark (function calling) | Runs the alloc

# ShowMe

**Every product comes with an expert.** ShowMe reads a product's manual, watches you work through your phone's camera, and talks you through every step, catching mistakes before they matter. It runs on Meta's Muse Spark and Muse Wonder.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026).

## One idea, two audiences

| | People assembling things | Employees learning machinery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **How they start** | Scan the QR code on the box, or paste the Amazon / store link | Scan the QR code on the machine, or pick it from the list |
| **What ShowMe does** | Counts every part, guides each step in 3D, watches live, catches mistakes mid-way, picks up where you left off | Labels every control from one photo, answers "how do I…" from the manual, guides and checks each step |
| **Who pays** | The brand: fewer returns, support calls and bad reviews | The employer: faster onboarding and proof of training |
| **What the payer gets** | A dashboard: which step people get wrong, build times, the questions they ask | Training records: who is signed off on which machine, exportable as a spreadsheet |

The same engine serves both: the manual is read once, every step gets a visible "done when" condition, and the camera checks real work against it.

### Why not just upload the manual to ChatGPT?

A chatbot needs your hands, starts from zero every time, and can't check your work against the manual. ShowMe watches while your hands are busy, tracks which step you're on, warns you about the mistake earlier builders made at that step, counts your leftover screws, and gives the brand or employer a record of every verified step.

# Testigo

**Testigo puts a migrated app next to its legacy system and leaves a record of what changed.**

- **The actas, live:** https://maxiroblesfx-commits.github.io/testigo/ (click a screenshot to enlarge it)
- **Demo video (2:29):** https://youtu.be/0vkE4oXe5ss

For every record, it captures the screens of both systems twice: when the record opens, and after it is saved without touching anything. Muse Spark reads every screen. Testigo then compares field by field under fixed rules and writes an *acta*, a short report. Each value in the acta links to the screenshot where it can be seen.

Testigo does not replace a migration's tests. It always asks the same question, the same way, and keeps the evidence.

## Why

> I migrated a real HR system with an AI agent: the one that runs a company's payroll. It was a huge amount of work, and we lost weeks. Sometimes we were looking in the wrong place; once we spent a week going down a path that wasn't the right one. Part of it was my own inexperience, but many errors were there the whole time and got lost in all that work. Testigo comes from that: a fixed question, asked the same way every time, about whether what the old system had is still there in the new one. It sorts out the basics so you don't make silly mistakes. The complex cases still need a person to look at them.
>
> — Maxi, author

No data, screens or code from that case appear in this repository, in API calls or in the video. All demos use an invented membership registry.

## See it

Open [`index.html`](index.html): the three actas, each with a one-line verdict, the rows to review with a line saying what to compare, and the four screenshots of every field in a before/after grid. Click a screenshot to enlarge it.

## How it works

1. **Record.** Each record gets four screenshots: legacy and new, on open and after an untouched save.
2. **Read.** Muse Spark 1.3 reads every screenshot twice with the same sealed prompt. It returns every label/value pair it sees; the prompt carries no field list. The prompt asks that an empty field stay empty and never become `0`.
3. **Pair labels.** A map says which legacy field matches which new one, for example *Saldo pendiente → Deuda acumulada*. Spark proposes the map from the two screens of the same record. A pair is kept only if 8 requests agree; otherwise it stays pending for a person. On our apps it proposed 12 of 12 pairs correctly for both migrations ([`20261103-testigo-mapa-spark/`](20261103-testigo-mapa-spark/RESULTADO.md)). The actas still use the map Claude wrote earlier from Spark's readings; they were not regenerated from Spark's proposal, which has the same content. No person has confirmed the map. The test checks Spark's proposals on our own material: the evaluation compares them with a list of the 12 reference labels, and Spark was not given that list. It does not show that Spark can discover every field of a system that has no inventory.

# I have Nothing to Wear

“I have nothing to wear” is a familiar feeling for both men and women. As a woman, I understand how a wardrobe full of clothes can still leave you struggling to put together an outfit for a particular occasion, place or situation. This app helps you see combinations from clothes you already own.

A mobile-first wardrobe app: add outfit photos to **The Pile**, keep individual pieces in **Wardrobe**, and mix them into saved looks in **Hanger**.

The Pile is that pile of clothes on your bed or chair. Sort it into the Wardrobe, and hang the outfits you pick on the Hanger.

Live app: https://wardrobe.yashasvishailly.com

## What powers the current flow

1. After permission, Meta **Muse Spark 1.3** identifies visible wearable pieces and their regions in the selected photo. Inference runs on Meta's hosted API (`api.meta.ai`), called server-side by the app's Cloudflare Worker.
2. The app derives the corresponding source crops and validates their relationship to the discovered regions.
3. **The OpenAI API regenerates the individual previews, including obscured parts**, from those crops using `gpt-image-2.5-sunburst-2026-09-08`. The Cloudflare Worker calls the hosted inference endpoint (`api.openai.com`) server-side. Meta SAM 3.1 was used in earlier experiments and remains in the source. The live app uses Meta Muse Spark 1.3 for discovery.
4. Finished pieces are saved in this browser. Hanger uses local outfit rules in the browser to combine available inventory across source photos, swap pieces and save looks; it does not call a model.

Generated previews can change details. The app does not guarantee faithful reconstruction of hidden clothing or small accessories. The sample picker uses previously saved synthetic results without new provider requests.

### Meta Muse Image availability in India and eligibility clarification

The obvious choice for image regeneration was Meta Muse Image, but it is not available to me in India, so it is not used in the current flow. [Meta's geographic use policy](https://dev.meta.ai/legal/geographic-use-policy/) lists Meta Muse Image as unavailable from India and prohibits bypassing geographic access controls. OpenRouter is an officially listed provider, but provider availability does not establish permission to access Meta Muse Image from India. We will not switch to OpenRouter on that basis without explicit clarification covering India or use it to bypass the restriction.

OpenRouter was suggested in the Discord channel, but I could not confirm an India-specific exception to the restriction, so it was not used.

![The Taj Mahal as a walkable block place, built by the app from a typed description of a visit](docs/hero.jpg)

*The Taj Mahal, built by the app from a typed description of a visit. You can walk through it on the live site.*

**Demo film:** https://youtu.be/iIRtdv87Whk

**Try it:** https://34-59-251-94.sslip.io has the 15 places from the demo video, and you can build your own by uploading a recording, typing a description or talking live (with daily spending limits). Walking uses a keyboard and mouse, so open it on a computer. The app adapts to slower machines; the film was captured with `?quality=high` added to a place's link, which you can add on a strong GPU.

**Backup:** https://35-196-186-212.nip.io is a second copy on a separate server, in case the main link is down. A place built on one server does not appear on the other.

My grandmother's house in Punjab is gone, and only my mother remembers it, room by room, in Punjabi. Walk Me There turns a spoken memory like hers into a 3D block place I can walk through in the browser. Click the hand pump and you see the words that described it, with a button that plays that stretch of her speech. Every coloured block in a home keeps the words that put it there (the land around it is scenery), and parts of the place nobody described stay grey, labelled as guesses. The small strolling figures and birds are decoration from the viewer, like the scenery, and are not part of the build or its checks.

Plain code checks every build against what was said, and failing checks go back to the builder with the speaker's words. On 8 held-out test homes (typed, spoken-style descriptions with answer keys written separately from the code), this got 92.7% of stated positions right, against 71.7% for the same builder model working alone ([results](docs/results.md)). Six places built from audio uploaded through the app, between 23 and 90 seconds long, in Punjabi, Spanish, Japanese and English, passed 156 of their 170 checks on the first build and 169 of 170 after automatic repairs ([per place](docs/results.md#places-built-from-uploaded-audio)); those checks come from the app's own map of each speaker's words, so they measure the build against that map rather than an outside answer key.

It also works for places you have travelled: describe a visit to the Golden Temple or the Taj Mahal and walk through it as you remember it, with the real place's well-known features filled in, shown muted and labelled as not from your words. The landmark examples were built from typed descriptions.

- **Walk in** through the gate in first person; click any described part to read the words that put it there, and on a recorded place hear them.

# Sentinel Ember

**Live wildfire intelligence from AI-piloted drones, for quicker wildfire suppression.**

In the Palisades Fire, the first public fire map came 26 hours after the fire started. By then about half the fire had already burned (11,543 of 23,449 acres). Firefighters were working from old information.

Sentinel Ember is built to close that gap. Fly a drone over a fire, and it tells firefighters two things:

- **Where the fire is right now.** Each video frame is checked for flames in the browser, outlined, and placed on a 3D map of the real hills.
- **Where it will be in an hour.** A forecaster draws where the fire's front is likely to be one hour later, and a team of AI agents sends drones to watch that edge.

![Eaton Fire replay at Jan 8, 15:30 PST: the fire's spread and burn scar on 3D terrain, the mapped perimeter, the start-location estimate, and the timeline, charts and key events](docs/img/eaton-replay.jpg)

Built by Jonathan, Dhilen and Ben (CS, UC Berkeley) for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (2026). The fires covered are the January 2025 **Eaton** and **Palisades** fires in Los Angeles County.

## How it works

1. **Find the flames.** Our fine-tuned YOLOv8 fire detector runs in the browser (ONNX model, WebAssembly). It draws a box around each flame in a frame in about 0.15 s on one CPU thread.
2. **Trace each fire.** Meta's **SAM 3.1** turns each fire into a mask from the one-word prompt "fire". No training needed.
3. **Put it on the map.** Given the drone's position and camera angle (a DJI `.SRT` telemetry track, or typed in), each detection is projected onto a 3D digital twin of the area: real terrain from elevation data and real wind from the HRRR weather model. Each live SAM 3.1 mask outline is projected the same way, point by point, and drawn on the map as a fire outline. In our benchmark, a detection reached the map a median 0.21 s after its video frame (p90 0.24 s; [`frame-to-map.json`](web/bench/frame-to-map.json)). That number leaves out drawing the map and SAM's own round trip to Meta. On our GPU-less cloud machine, with the map drawn in software, it took 2.7 s, so on-screen time on a laptop is still to be measured.
4. **Forecast the next hour.** A **Muse Spark** forecaster looks at the fire's edge, the wind and the slope, and estimates where the front will be in an hour.
5. **Send the drones.** A Muse Spark commander and three Muse Spark squad agents give six simulated drones waypoints to watch that advancing edge. The drones fly in a MuJoCo physics simulation over the real Eaton Fire terrain, with thrust, wind drag, gust limits, batteries, camera coverage and line of sight. The same simulation is also wrapped as a Gymnasium environment for reinforcement learning.

Every agent in the swarm (forecaster, commander and squads) runs on `muse-spark-1.3`.

Somnigram is the long-term memory shared across your AI tools.

Today every assistant starts from scratch in every conversation and in every tool.

A camera writes a box on every frame. Those boxes are not a census. A tracker id that appears, leaves, and comes back can look like a new animal. A person-shaped box is not a name. A vehicle total without a labeled survey is not a traffic count. People per square metre without a measured area is not a density.

Someone still has to see the clip, read one number, and decide what to do with the alert. Rastro keeps that decision in the app.

## What Rastro adds

Four pieces, each wired in this repository.

One frame on the other side does not flip a side that already held, and it does not fire alone. Goat lane says "Animal left the safe zone". # Prompt Classification Framework — Decider, Runner, Logger

Implements the `decide(state, question) -> {answer, p}` interface, the tree
runner, and the result logger from `docs/design_draft.md`, driven by
`question_tree.yml` (the tree file wins where they disagree).

- `decider.py` — tree loading, context resolution, one-question-per-backend
  adapters (`jev`, `clef-flash`, `clef`, `spark-as-jev`).
- `runner.py` — walks one prompt (`run_prompt`) or a batch (`run_all`)
  down the tree, at most `max_depth` (3) decider calls per prompt.
- `logger.py` — persists per-prompt results as JSONL (`write_jsonl`) or
  CSV (`write_csv`), one row per prompt per backend.

No module makes network or model API calls. Each backend is reached through
a caller-supplied `transport(request) -> reply` function, so tests and local
runs use stubs; wiring a real Jev/Clef/Spark endpoint means passing your
own transport (and API key handling) — nothing here calls out on its own.

## Setup

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## API keys (local only — never commit)

`run_prompt_classifier.py` reads keys/URLs from the environment, so
nothing secret lives in the repo:

- `JEV_API_KEY` — Jev key (TypeSafe console); `JEV_API_URL` only if overriding the official endpoint
- `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` — Clef-flash on Workers AI
- `META_API_KEY` — Muse Spark key (Meta Model API)

conversation, and provides local queues, file transfers, an embedded browser, and agent-to-agent
messaging in one desktop app.

> [!WARNING]
> OpenBot is a development preview. Agents currently run with `danger-full-access` and
> `approvalPolicy: never`. They can read and modify files, run commands, use the network, and control
> the embedded browser without per-action confirmations after the explicit first-launch consent.

## What works

- Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints and custom ACP agents, with detection of local model servers (Ollama, LM Studio) and installed agents.
- Per-agent context monitoring with automatic compaction before long threads exhaust the model window.
- FIFO message queues with pause, resume, cancellation, and crash-safe persistence.
- Agent-to-agent messages, replies, reactions, images, and managed file transfers.
- Shared desktop channel chats with one task owner, explicit delegation, shared history, and Stop, Resume, Reassign, Archive, and Restore controls.
- A persistent embedded browser that agents can open, inspect, and control.
