# ProofGate

AI made vulnerability claims cheap. ProofGate makes checking them cheap too.

AI gatekeeper for security reports: breaks a vulnerability report into atomic
factual claims, verifies each claim against the real source code at the stated
version, optionally runs a reproduction test in a sandbox, and returns a
verdict with evidence. It never applies fixes and never touches real systems.

## Demo

Video: https://1drv.ms/v/c/7a6789abbb9d333c/IQCPA0AA43E6TYAwdqqwAijWAUOLwA0IPhVuxBIoet5Ul2M



## The problem

AI-generated reports flooded triage queues: HackerOne reported report volume up
more than 100% after stronger AI models arrived (May 2026). curl's valid-report
rate fell from over 15% to under 5% in 2025, and curl ended its bug bounty on
Jan 31, 2026. Writing a plausible report takes minutes, while disproving a
complex one can take an expert about an hour.

Source: https://www.penligent.ai/hackinglabs/?p=6650

## How it works

Pipeline: report -> atomic claims -> code checks -> sandboxed repro test -> verdict.

- `fabricated`: the report describes code that is not there.
- `claim_false`: the code exists, but the claimed property or behavior is wrong.
- `partially_true`: some claims held while others were refuted.
- `confirmed`: the key claims are supported by evidence.
- `inconclusive`: the evidence does not settle the matter.

Evidence ladder:

| Level | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Nothing verified |
| 1 | Code exists as described |
| 2 | Behavior observed in code |
| 3 | Reproduced by test |
| 4 | Security boundary crossed |
| 5 | Independently reproducible |

Every supported or refuted claim must cite a file and line range the checker
agent actually read with the `read_file` tool; anything else is downgraded to
unverifiable in code. See [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) for the full design.

## Use of Meta AI

| Model | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Claim extraction + tool-using checker agent (find_symbol, search_code, read_file, writes repro tests) |
| Muse Wonder 1.0 | Evidence judge for the final verdict (falls back to Spark) |
| Muse Code | Used to build this project |

# ShowMe

ShowMe helps workers point to an object in an approved work photo and check which rule applies. A supervisor turns photos and notes into a guide, reviews each step, and shares a published version that stays fixed when the draft changes.

[Watch the three-minute demo](https://moondh99.github.io/showme/) · [한국어 README](README.ko.md)

## Run the demo

Use Python 3.10 or later. From the repository root, run:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/seed_demo.py
python scripts/serve.py
```

Open the [English demo](http://127.0.0.1:8765/demo). Use the language switch or open the [Korean demo](http://127.0.0.1:8765/demo?lang=ko). Both approval links show the staged photo, approved instruction, and completion criteria without a sign-in or API key.

To select objects and ask live questions, copy `.env.example` to `.env.local`, set `MODEL_API_KEY` to your Meta Model API key, and restart the server. The server reads the key. To create a guide, open the [author workspace](http://127.0.0.1:8765/) and use the password set in `SHOWME_AUTHOR_PASSWORD` or generated in `state/author-password.txt`.

### Try the three decisions

Choose **Select an object in the photo**, then click the center of the front white tag in the specified tray. Select the yellow tag before the second question. Send the third question independently with the same yellow tag selected.

| Selected tag | Ask | Expected decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blue tray, personal storage | I completed training. Can I use this tag to borrow equipment? | **Blocked.** Storage tags cannot be used to borrow equipment. The yellow tag's issuance criteria are shown separately. |
| Yellow tray, equipment rental | I have not completed training, but my supervisor is with me. Can I issue this tag? | **Allowed.** Supervisor accompaniment satisfies one of the two alternative conditions. |
| Yellow tray, equipment rental | Can I issue this tag? | **Needs confirmation.** Confirm completed training or supervisor accompaniment. |

Read **Decision and full approved text** under each verdict to check the rule in context. Each language has its own approved version. Existing Korean approval links continue to open their original content.

## How it works

- **SAM 3.1** outlines the object the learner selects in an approved photo.
- **Muse Spark 1.3** drafts guide steps from author notes and connects learner questions to the selected object and the applicable rule. Rule questions receive a separate model review.
- **ShowMe** verifies each quote against the published instruction or completion criteria. The learner marks work complete.

## Verification

The English demo was recorded in the running app with live Meta models. The recording starts with the blocked blue tag, then shows the allowed and unresolved yellow tag cases. Captions identify shortened model waits and show the original duration. The [verification record](docs/PRODUCT_DECISIONS.md#20

[WorldEvals](https://github.com/robocurve/worldevals).

```bash

DongzeL430/MetaHacks.readme_excerpt: # StudBuds Finding someone to study with in college is weirdly hard. Group chats are noisy, asking a stranger after class is awkward, and most "study buddy" apps want your name, photo and major before they show you anyone. StudBuds goes the other way. You're a nickname and a drawing, and the app puts the sessions most likely to suit you at the top. **Live site:** [studbudstm.netlify.app](https://studbudstm.netlify.app) We built StudBuds for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon). Everything in this repo was made during the hackathon. ## What it does You sign up with your school `.edu` email. StudBuds gives you a random nickname (something like "Merry Ladybug") and Muse draws you an avatar to go with it. Nobody sees your real name. A short survey sets you up. You mark your free time on a calendar, import it from an `.ics` file, or drop in a screenshot of your class schedule and let Muse read it. You add the courses you've taken or are taking, each with how confident you feel (1 means lost, 5 means you could teach it), and Muse can look up your major's courses in your school's catalog to fill the list faster. Then a few questions about how you like to study, and eight quick "this or that" picks, like early bird or night owl. Each page saves as you go, so closing the tab halfway through is fine. After that you land on Home, which works like a small desktop: - **Study Lobbies** lists sessions other students are hosting, best fit first. Each one says why it's there: "Covers a course you want help with", "Similar study habits", "You agreed on 6 of 8 quick picks". On top of that ranking, Muse looks at your best few against how you like to study and marks up to three as "Muse's pick", with a reason, like "In your free time on Tuesday, and a small group". It starts with your own school. Turn off "Only my school" in Filters to see sessions at other schools too. - **Host a session** picks a subject, a time and a place. The places are real study spots at your school that Muse found on your school's own website. - Inside a lobby you can ask to join, chat live with the group, invite your connections, and connect with people you'd like to study with again. Hosts accept requests, lock the session or remove someone. - **Sessions** keeps every session you're part of in one place: the ones you host, the ones you've joined, requests still waiting on a host, and invites from your connections. - **Connections** is your friends list. When you're ready to keep in touch outside StudBuds, turn on "Share my contact" for one person and they'll see the Discord, Instagram or phone you added in your profile. Nobody else does. - **Your profile** (click your nickname in the nav bar) holds everything from the survey, so you can change your free time, courses and answer

# FaultForge

**Quickstart** (Linux x86_64, Python 3.13; no API key needed for the first two lines):

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt   # or: make setup
make replay                                    # keyless: re-sim headline case policy on/off + recorded Muse calls
cp .env.example .env   # put your key in .env, then:  make live   (one live Muse Spark search round)
```

FaultForge hands an FDIR team the multi-fault combinations a test campaign would miss, each as a one-command
replay. Meta's Muse Spark model searches a Basilisk CubeSat simulation for fault combinations that make a
rule-based recovery (safe-mode / FDIR) policy violate its safety constraints; every violation is minimized to a
small counterexample, re-run with the policy disabled, and replayable with one command. Muse then writes a diagnosis
and selects and parameterizes a repair from an engineer-provided menu of repair options (whitelisted policy keys
with bounds). A regression gate that Muse does not control re-simulates the full suite and accepts or rejects it.
The **strict** gate (0 new violations) rejected every proposal; the **budget** gate (net fixes > 0, <= 3 previously
clean runs broken) accepted one, b1t1 (see [Repair: gates](#repair-gates-strict-vs-budget)).

Before this hackathon week the project had the Basilisk harness and the rule-based FDIR policy. This week we implemented:
the Muse-guided search, the rules-blind variant, CMA-ES and random baselines, the minimizer/compare pipeline,
the Muse repair loop and the regression gate.

## Meta models used

One model, **`muse-spark-1.3`**, via the Meta Model API: `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions`
(OpenAI-compatible, JSON mode, key in `MUSE_API_KEY`). It is used in four roles:

| role | what Muse does | code | recorded calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| scenario search | each round reads the fault schema, the policy description, the failures found so far and near-miss margins, and returns 8 new fault scenarios as JSON | `src/llm_search.py`, `src/live_round.py` | `data/cmp/muse_seed*_calls.jsonl` |
| blind rule inference | same search with the policy thresholds and the one-isolation rule hidden; it must infer the rules from outcomes (by round 4 of seed 1 it wrote "FDIR isolates at most one wheel") | `src/llm_search.py --blind` | `data/cmp/museblind_seed*_calls.jsonl` |
| diagnosis | reads minimized counterexamples with policy traces and writes a free-text explanation of why the policy failed (not checked by the gate) | `src/gated_repair.py`, `src/gated_v2.py` (also `src/repair.py`) | `data/gated/*_response.json` (`diagnosis`) |
| repair selection | selects and parameterizes a repair from an engineer-provided menu (whitelisted policy keys with bounds, at most 3 keys); the gate re-simulates it on the full suite, and rejections (with regressions + traces) go back to Muse | same | `data/gated/*_response.json` (`change`), `*_gate.json` |

# LAVERTY Case Reader

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (theme: Build for Your World), 26 Oct – 4 Nov 2026.

LAVERTY is the legal brain of the Gulf: Arabic–English legal AI for lawyers, starting with the UAE. Court papers in the UAE often reach lawyers as scanned Arabic documents full of stamps, signatures and handwritten notes, and reading them takes hours before any legal work starts.

The **Case Reader** is a new LAVERTY feature built during this hackathon on Meta's models. It takes a scanned Arabic case file and returns a structured case summary in Arabic and English:

- the parties, dates, claims, deadlines and key facts, each linked to the page it came from;
- the stamps, signatures and handwritten notes, marked for the lawyer so they are never misread as printed text;
- every law the file cites, checked against the official UAE law text.

## Results on Meta's models

Run 6 (4 Nov 2026): all 13 test files, 33 pages, read with `muse-spark-1.3` (reasoning effort high) and `sam-3.1`, scored by `tools/score.py` against the hand-checked answer key. The full run, with every miss listed, is on the [`results` branch](https://github.com/infinity-ai-labs/laverty-case-reader/tree/results/runs/run-6-1).

| What was checked | Result |
|---|---|
| Citations of articles that don't exist, caught | **6 of 6** |
| Quote with one changed word, caught | **1 of 1** |
| Citation verdicts right (valid, invalid or not checked) | **80 of 80** |
| Claim amounts | **35 of 35** |
| Parties, with the right role | 65 of 67 |
| Dates | 125 of 131 |
| Deadlines | 19 of 24 |
| Stamps, signatures and handwritten notes in the right place (box overlap ≥ 0.5) | 98 of 109 |
| Dates that exist only in handwriting, marked as handwriting | 8 of 10 |

What the runs taught us:
- **SAM 3.1 phrasings.** "stamp", "blue stamp" and "purple stamp" found 12 of 13 stamps on the first four files, and "signature" found 10 of 11, with no false boxes. "rubber stamp", "official seal" and every phrasing tried for handwriting ("handwritten text", "handwriting", "writing", "note", ...) returned nothing.
- **Handwriting is placed by Muse Spark, with a close-up second look.** Muse Spark reads the handwritten notes SAM 3.1 does not find and gives their position on the page. That first position is rough, so each note gets a close-up: the area around it is cut out and Muse Spark places the note again inside it. In run 6 this raised the handwritten notes placed right (overlap ≥ 0.5) from 5 to 12 of 22, and all marks from 91 (run 5) to 98 of 109.
- **Quotes are checked wherever they sit.** Muse Spark sometimes leaves a quoted article inside the citation text; the check now finds it there. One false alarm remains where Muse Spark misread a long quote (case 10): the summary says the wording differs and asks the lawyer to check the page, so nothing passes quietly.

## How it works

1. **Pages.** The PDF is rendered page by page.
2. **Marks, with SAM 3.1.** On every page, SAM 3.1 is asked

# ChainBridge

[▶ Watch the ChainBridge Demo](./Project%20Video.mp4)

**A pay-per-use AI agent on Cardano that reads your documents and data, picks out the facts that matter, seals them with a fingerprint, and publishes that fingerprint on the blockchain as public proof.**

A customer uploads **PDFs, photos or screenshots** (e.g. a car inspection report), or a CSV/JSON table, and gets a **free price quote** calculated from simple measurements of the file. If they accept, they **pay once with x402**, a direct pay-per-request protocol on Cardano with no escrow and no account. The ChainBridge agent then does the paid work:
# ChainBridge

1. **AI extraction or tidy-up:** for documents, Meta AI reads each file and extracts the relevant facts (identifiers, dates, results, measurements, findings buried in paragraphs), skipping boilerplate, each with the exact source words as evidence. For tables, it analyses a masked sample and suggests fixes. The customer confirms or edits everything.
2. **Fingerprint:** a salted SHA-256 Merkle root of the chosen columns, created in the customer's browser.
3. **Publication on Cardano:** the agent publishes the fingerprint in its own Preprod transaction (metadata label 674).

**The signed payment is only sent after publication succeeds.** If anything fails before that, the customer is not charged. The customer downloads one package: the cleaned data, an AI report, a certificate with the Cardano links, and a private proof file for checking records later. The full file never leaves the customer's device.

Built for the TUM Blockchain & AI Hackathon (Oct 30–31, 2026), Cardano track: *"Build an agent, service or developer tool that does a useful job and gets paid for it on Cardano."* It is built on the official [Masumi TUM quickstart](https://github.com/masumi-network/tum-hackathon-quickstart) (commit `d93783b`); the Sokosumi/Masumi escrow path from the template still works as an alternative.

> **Test network only.** Preprod test tokens have no real value. A fingerprint shows whether data matches what was sealed. It does **not** prove the source data was accurate.

# StreetScan

Automated urban hazard & infrastructure auditor.

StreetScan turns passive footage — dashcam, handlebar camera, action cam — into **verified,
geo-tagged municipal work orders**. It segments every frame with SAM 3.1, discards anything
not persistent enough to be a real hazard, tags each survivor with the camera's own GPS, then
asks Muse Spark what the thing actually *is* and assembles an Open311 payload.

```
original ──exiftool──► GPS samples {t, lat, lon}        (recorded in-camera at capture)
  └ no track ──ffmpeg + OCR──► the same samples, read back out of the
                               text an app burned into the frame
  └─flatten to MP4──► footage.mp4
        │
   [ffmpeg] ──► playback.mp4 (720p@30)  +  analysis.mp4 (480p@10)
   │             both start at t=0, so hazardTime = frameIndex / 10 → playback.currentTime
   [chunker] windows of 3,000 frames with 150 frames of overlap
   [SAM 3.1]  "pothole" → {frameIndex, objectId, polygon}
   [filter]   ≥6 frames AND ≥0.6s → keep · IoU merge across the chunk seam
   [scale]    < 2.5% of the frame across → "too small to judge", never classified
   [dedupe]   the same audit's repeat sightings within 8 m → one row, worst severity
   [geo]      interpolate → GPS sample | null → overlay OCR | manual pin
   [consensus] across audits → same defect seen twice → corroborated · disputed
               one spelling per street · a second pass that agrees = verified
   [Spark]    crop + full frame → {hazardType, severity, confidence, streetContext}
   [OSM]      Overpass reverse-geocode → validate the OCR'd street name, disagree → flag
   [Open311]  → SQLite → split-screen inspection UI → dispatch dashboard
```

## Functions

What the app does, function by function - the operator's view. Each one says where it lives.

### 1. Ingest footage - Dispatch (`/`), **+ New audit**

- Uploading lives on Dispatch in a drawer, so starting a scan never navigates away from the
  queue you were reading. The rail's `+` (or `/?new=1`) opens it from any page.
- Drag a clip in (or click to choose): MP4/MOV/M4V, streamed raw rather than multipart, so a
  10-minute 4K upload never buffers in memory and the progress bar is real.
- Optionally attach the **original** recording as the GPS source - a second upload
  (`?role=gps`) whose track is read with exiftool. A flattened export carries no GPS at all;
  if the attach fails the job still opens, because no GPS is a manual pin, not a dead job.
- **The scan starts on upload, in the background** - the page stays put and the audit list
  shows the new job's status. Drop three clips and all three work; a staged GPS source holds
  the start until that upload lands, so the pipeline never reads GPS off a half-written file.

### 2. Run an audit - the scan queue (`lib/queue.ts`)

- Uploads enqueue automatically; up to `SCAN_CONCURRENCY` (2) run at once, the rest wait in
  FIFO order. The **Scanning** strip on Dispatch shows every running and queued job with

# ChartAudit

Hindsight-free scoring for the lines traders draw on charts. ChartAudit reads a marked-up chart screenshot with Meta's Muse Spark, turns each drawn position box and level into exact prices and dates, and scores it only on what price did after the chart was made, compared with algorithmic and random lines.

Built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026. Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon.

## Try it

The demo page (`app.py`, a Gradio app that runs as a Hugging Face Space) has two ways in:

* **Built-in examples, no upload needed.** Three synthetic charts with readings saved from Muse Spark: levels that held, levels that broke, and a long position box that hit its target. They use no model call and no price lookup, so they always work. The prices are a random walk, so a level that "held" here held by chance; that is the point of comparing with random levels.
* **Upload your own chart.** Muse Spark reads the price levels, zones and position boxes, ChartAudit checks the read price axis, scores each drawing on the daily prices after the chart's date, and draws what was read over those prices. Uploads are not stored. Reading is limited per visitor and per day.

One honest note from building the examples: Muse Spark read the first winning box chart upside down (stop and target swapped, so a long box became a short one) and read the next three correctly to within 0.4. The example uses one of the correct reads; the miss is recorded in `scripts/make_examples.py`. It is why every reading goes through the axis check before anything is scored.

Rebuild the examples with `python scripts/make_examples.py` (three model calls), or `--truth` to save the answer key instead.

## Results (Nov 4, 2026)

**Real charts:** 51 marked-up charts from one trader's published analysis on Sep 8, 2026 (images kept private). Muse Spark read all 51; 122 of the 186 drawn prices had no printed label and were estimated from the price axis. Daily prices are in hand for all 51. Of those, 43 have drawings to score, and all 43 passed the axis check.

Levels, scored only on the 20 trading days after each chart:

| | levels | reached | held | broke | hold rate | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Drawn by the trader | 91 | 21 | 5 | 16 | 24% | 11% to 45% |
| Swing pivots (same charts) | 83 | 34 | 13 | 21 | 38% | 24% to 55% |
| Random, matched side and distance | 455 | 113 | 32 | 81 | 28% | 21% to 37% |
| Random, anywhere on the chart | 455 | 182 | 48 | 134 | 26% | 21% to 33% |

* **No detectable advantage.** Drawn levels held 24% of the time when price reached them, against 26% to 38% for pivot and random levels. The intervals overlap, so on this sample the drawn levels are neither better

- Human approval gates for source normalization, domain mapping, and variable/value-level mapping
- Standards-aware metadata lookup through the CDISC Library MCP service
- Deterministic per-domain R and SAS generation from the approved mapping
- Isolated R execution with immutable attempt metadata and XPT structural checks
- Review workspaces for aCRF, Define-XML, validation findings, and cSDRG
- A submission-oriented ZIP with artifacts, evidence, provenance, and limitations

# Squint

**Does your vision AI know when it can't read the label?**

Squint is a crash-test lab for AI that reads medicine and food labels aloud for blind and
low-vision people. It renders labels with exactly known text, degrades them step by step
(blur, low light, tilt, glare, a covering thumb), asks the model the questions a blind user
asks, and finds the point where reading turns into guessing. Then it ships the fix and
measures it.

A blurry photo of a 25 mg bottle must produce "I can't read this, please retake",
never a confident "Hydroxyzine 50 mg".

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026) on the Meta Model API.

## What it measures

- **Legibility boundary**: the first degradation level (0-7) where fewer than half the fields are read correctly, per model and condition.
- **Confidently wrong**: a wrong answer while the model says it can read the label. This is the harm.
- **Unsafe answers**: answers with at least one confidently wrong name, strength or allergen list.
- **Over-caution**: asking for a retake on images every model reads well. Safety is not free, so we count its cost too.

Every answer is scored by a deterministic judge (no model grades another model). Names allow one
typo but a look-alike drug (Hydralazine vs Hydroxyzine) is always wrong.

## The fix: guards

| Mode | What it does |
|---|---|
| `baseline` | neutral prompt: what the model does by default |
| `abstain` | the prompt says never guess; blank anything not clearly legible |
| `consistency` | three independent reads; any field they disagree on is blanked |
| `formulary` | a strength that does not exist for that drug is blanked |
| `zoom` | ask for the name/strength box on the 0-1000 grid, crop and enlarge it, re-read |
| `stack` | never-guess prompt, three reads, consistency and formulary together |

## How it works

```
data/labels.json ──► forge (System.Drawing) ──► out/clean/*.png
                     degrade (ffmpeg, 5 conditions x 8 levels) ──► out/images/<id>/<cond>/<level>.jpg
                     probe (Meta Model API, strict JSON, cached) ──► out/raw/<model>/<mode>/*.json
                     guards (reuse cached reads, crop with ffmpeg) ──► out/raw/<model>/<guard>/*.json
                     report (deterministic judge) ──► out/results.json, out/summary.md, out/slider/
                     web/index.html (slider, boundary chart, guards chart, cost)
```

- Zero npm dependencies: Node 22 built-ins, Windows PowerShell 5.1 (System.Drawing) and ffmpeg.
- Every API answer is cached on disk under a hash of model, image, prompt version, mode and seed: re-running never re-bills.
- `--dry-run` prints call counts and the cost estimate; real runs ask before spending.
- The key comes only from `MODEL_API_KEY` and is never written to disk.
- A localhost mock API knows the ground truth so the whole pipeline runs offline. Mock results go to `out/mock/` and the page shows them under a MOCK banner.

## Run it

Requirements: Node 22+, Windows

# rt-series

User-mode runtimes that run foreign Linux guests on an AArch64 host, including macOS on Apple Silicon. The host runs AArch64 natively. Each other guest is either one of the translators below or Apple Rosetta.

A 32-bit guest can use a fixed 4 GiB window (`Class A`). A 64-bit guest needs a full address space (`Class B`), the way [rvrt](../rvrt) does for RV64.

The benefit column is the business reason to create or keep that guest: which software then runs on an AArch64 Mac, and what that work is for.

## Have a runtime

| Guest | Width | Fits in | Runtime | Example CPUs | Benefit and objective |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AArch64 | 64 | Native | The host | Apple M4, AWS Graviton4, AmpereOne | Native speed on the machines this series runs on. Objective: keep AArch64 as the host, and build translators for guests those CPUs cannot execute. |
| AArch32 | 32 | 4 GiB window | [a32rt](../a32rt) ([GitHub](https://github.com/zw3rk/a32rt)) | ARM Cortex-A7 (Raspberry Pi 2), Cortex-A15 | Apple Silicon, Graviton4, and AmpereOne execute AArch64 only. Objective: run the installed armhf userspace (Raspberry Pi OS, older Debian, board SDKs) on the machines people already have. Qualified through Phase 7 (`RC-H`), Wave U3 (`RC-U3 PASS`), and Convergence Round 18 (`0 DEFECTS`). |
| i386 | 32 | 4 GiB window | [i686rt](../i686rt) | Intel Pentium III, AMD Athlon XP | Rosetta runs x86-64. Objective: run the i386 Linux binaries and i386 multiarch sysroots that are still what legacy applications and SDKs ship. Qualified through Phase 7 (`RC-H`), Wave U3 (`RC-U3 PASS`), and Convergence Round 18 (`0 DEFECTS`). |
| x86-64 | 64 | Native (Rosetta) | [Rosetta](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/apple-silicon/about-the-rosetta-translation-environment) | AMD Ryzen, Intel Core | Mainstream PC and server Linux. Objective: cover it on the Mac through Rosetta, and spend new translator work on the other guests. |
| RV64GC | 64 | Full address space | [rvrt](../rvrt) | SiFive U74 (VisionFive 2), T-Head C910 | The open ISA shipping on boards and moving into products. Objective: run riscv64 userspace on a Mac without that board. Qualified through Wave U5 (`RC-U5 PASS`) and Convergence Round 18 (`0 DEFECTS`). |
| RV32GC | 32 | Full address space (`va_bits=32`) | [rvrt](../rvrt) | Nuclei N300FD (`rv32imafdc`) | The embedded RISC-V profile (`ILP32D`) in `rvrt`, with static and dynamic `musl` & `glibc` sysroots in tree. Qualified through Milestone R8, Wave U5 (`RC-U5 PASS`), and Convergence Round 18 (`0 DEFECTS`). |
| MIPS32 | 32 | 4 GiB window | [mips32rt](../mips32rt) | Ingenic XBurst (JZ4770), MIPS 24Kc (MediaTek MT7620) | Installed router and IoT firmware, including OpenWrt on MIPS 24Kc parts such as the MT7620 (`mipsel` and `mips` O32). Qualified through Phase 7 (`RC-H`), Wave U3 (`RC-U3 PASS`), and Convergence Round 18 (`0 DEFECTS`). |
| SPARC V8 | 32 | 4 GiB window | [sparc32rt](../sparc32rt) | Gaisler LEON3, LEON4 | LEON is still designed into spacecraf

# autoDJ

**I wanted to dance at my own party, so I built an AI DJ.**

autoDJ uses Meta Muse Spark to understand music, select songs, and plan transitions.
A local controller performs those plans in Mixxx, while a webcam lets a person
request changes through predefined gestures. The dashboard shows what the AI
proposed, what was applied, and what the audio engine actually executed.

[Watch the demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k-gOUhyPsPI) ·
[Project repository](https://github.com/hhtzuhh/autoDJ)

Created by **Tzu-Han Lin (hhtzuhh)** for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**.

## What it does

- Builds a playlist from a natural-language request and a local music library.
- Plans ahead across multiple songs, selecting cues, tempo changes, crossfades,
  and low-EQ actions from locally validated options.
- Executes transitions through Mixxx using observed playback position and MIDI
  feedback. Human takeover cancels further automation.
- Uses camera gestures to request future changes. Holding up one index finger
  requests a different upcoming song order; arms up or crossed arms request more
  or fewer in-track effects. Meta can leave effects unchanged when no suitable
  action fits.

# ContextLens

### Fewer repeats. More context. Your choice.

**A Chrome extension that helps viewers notice repeated exposure to the same specific challenge, product, or campaign—and decide when to pause.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon with **Meta Muse Spark 1.3**. ContextLens connects a viewer-controlled repetition filter to **OriginTrace**, a separate investigation application.

**Prototype 1.0.1** · Chrome Manifest V3 · Node.js 22.13+

[Why we built it](#why-we-built-it) · [Demo flow](#demo-flow) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Run locally](#run-locally) · [Validation](#validation)

## Why we built it

A new post is not always a new idea.

Different creators can repeat the same dance challenge, promote the same product, or circulate the same political campaign. A viewer may encounter that pattern without seeing how often it has appeared. At the same time, posts about the same broad subject can concern entirely different things.

We built ContextLens to make that repetition visible and give the viewer a practical choice: **continue watching, take a pause, or investigate further**. The intended benefit is greater awareness and control over attention; it has not yet been measured in a user study.

The viewer chooses the threshold. ContextLens applies it to a specific tracked target, rather than treating every cake, dance, or political video as one group.

## What the viewer can do

| Capability | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Recognize a repeated target | Compare visible footage and semantic observations across posts, even when presenters or filming conditions change. |
| Choose a repetition limit | Set **N from 2 to 25**. |
| Choose the counting unit | **Unique posts** includes different posts from one account. **Unique accounts** counts each posting account once per target. |
| Pause and blur | When a tracked target reaches N, matching content pauses and blurs. |
| Keep watching | **Show video** removes the blur and resumes playback after the viewer clicks. |
| Investigate | Open OriginTrace with the current post URL and caption prefilled; the viewer starts its separate analysis. |

Counts describe content observed in this browser. They are **not platform-wide popularity, reach, or upload totals**. Reopening one canonical post does not increase its unique-post count.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Watch a post"] --> B["Track a specific target"]
    B --> C{"Chosen threshold reached?"}
    C -->|No| D["Keep watching"]
    C -->|Yes| E["Pause and blur"]
    E -->|Show video| D
    E -->|Investigate| F["Open OriginTrace"]
    F --> G["Viewer starts deeper analysis"]
```

## Demo flow

The controlled demo uses fictional test content to illustrate these intended distinctions. These are **test cases, not measured recognition results**.

| Case | Intended grouping |
| --- | --- |
| Different performers repeat the same evidenced choreography | One specific challenge, when distinctive movement cues support the match. |

ENKI's native iOS host, authentication, Ray-Ban camera integration, audiovisual
library and voice tools existed before this hackathon. The new work is Second
Memory: a bounded authorized observation policy, opt-in single-image Meta analysis,
explicitly saved visual evidence and a deterministic last-key-sighting query.

# أرض الجوال

متجر إلكتروني عربي باتجاه RTL لعرض الجوالات وملحقاتها، بتصميم بسيط مستوحى من متاجر Apple.

## بوت تيليجرام
قائمة الإدارة:
- **طلبات العملاء:** تعرض آخر الطلبات غير المقروءة أولًا، مع عدّاد بجانب الزر وعدّاد متجدد بعد مشاهدة القائمة.
- **إضافة طلب:** إنشاء قسم/تصنيف جديد بالاسم فقط.
- **تعديل الطلب:** اختيار قسم وتغيير اسمه فقط.
- **إضافة منتج:** اختيار القسم، الاسم، الألوان، مساحات التخزين، السعر، التفاصيل، ثم إرسال حتى 10 صور والضغط على «حفظ المنتج».
- **تعديل المنتج:** اختيار منتج وتعديل القسم أو الاسم أو الألوان أو التخزين أو السعر أو التفاصيل أو الصور، مع خيار حذف المنتج وتأكيد الحذف وزر رجوع للقائمة الرئيسية.
- **الاتصال:** إدخال أو تغيير رقم واتساب الدعم؛ يظهر رابط WhatsApp في زر عائم بالموقع.
- تتم حماية أوامر الإدارة بمعرّف `TELEGRAM_ADMIN_ID`، كما يقبل الـWebhook الرسائل الخاصة فقط.

## الكتالوج والتحميل في الخلفية
- الأقسام تُقرأ من مجموعة `categories`، والمنتجات الجديدة من مجموعة `products` في MongoDB.
- الصور المرسلة عبر Telegram تُخزّن كـ file IDs وتُعرض من خلال API خادم لا يكشف Bot Token.
- صفحة المتجر لا تنتظر الكتالوج أو إعدادات واتساب حتى ترسم الواجهة؛ تظهر البيانات المتاحة ثم تجلب أحدث البيانات في الخلفية، وتعيد تحديث الكتالوج كل 30 ثانية وعند التركيز على الصفحة.
- البحث لحظي أثناء الكتابة ويمتد إلى اسم المنتج والقسم والوصف والسعر واللون وسعة التخزين والمواصفات، مع تطبيع اختلافات الحروف والأرقام العربية.
- سلة المشتريات تبقى في `localStorage` للمتصفح الحالي؛ مسودة بيانات التوصيل تستخدم `sessionStorage`.

## دورة الشراء
- لا يوجد تسجيل دخول أو إنشاء حساب للمشتري.
- بيانات التوصيل تُرسل إلى `POST /api/orders`، ويتحقق الخادم من الأسعار من كتالوج الخادم، ثم يحفظ الطلب في MongoDB ويرسل إشعارًا إلى Telegram Admin.
- `/checkout/payment` صفحة تمهيدية فقط؛ بوابة الدفع الفعلية غير مربوطة بعد ولا يتم خصم أي مبلغ.
- `/policies` صفحة مؤقتة تنتظر سياسة الضمان والاسترجاع والتوصيل المعتمدة.

## متغيرات البيئة
أضف القيم في إعدادات الاستضافة فقط؛ لا تحفظ أسرارًا حقيقية في GitHub:
- `MONGODB_URI`
- `MONGODB_DB=erd_algwal`
- `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`
- `TELEGRAM_ADMIN_ID=5569918211`
- `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
- `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_URL` — رابط HTTPS المنشور وينتهي بـ `/api/telegram/webhook`.
- `MODEL_API_KEY` — مفتاح Meta Model API لتوليد قناع عزل الجراب عند إضافة منتج جراب أو تجهيز صورته من البوت. يُستخدم على الخادم فقط ولا يوضع في متغير يبدأ بـ `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.

بعد نشر المسار على الاستضافة، يمكن تسجيل Webhook من بيئة آمنة باستخدام:
```bash
npm run telegram:set-webhook
```

## حدود النسخة الحالية
- بيانات المنتجات القديمة في `lib/products.ts` تجريبية، ويمكن تعديل المنتجات التي أُنشئت من البوت.
- لا توجد بوابة دفع أو مزود تقسيط مربوط.
- رقم واتساب لن يظهر على أنه رابط صالح إلا بعد إدخاله من زر «الاتصال» في البوت.
- إعداد متغيرات البيئة وتسجيل Webhook واختبار الاتصال الحي ينتظر إعداد الاستضافة الذي يتحكم به صاحب المشروع.
- لم يتم نشر المشروع على Vercel ضمن هذه التعديلات.

## التشغيل محليًا
```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

# ECHO — simt-echo

Turn a phone video of your walk into a route that others can navigate without
GPS. The creator records a route (video + inertial sensors), AI grounds
landmarks onto the captured geometry, and the resulting **EchoRoute bundle**
navigates a friend along it — turn cues, landmark AR overlays, QR checkpoints.

Developed for the **Meta AI Hackathon 2026** by Said Elimam.

- **Wear OS** — soon: companion watch (paired haptics, `wear/`)
- **iOS** — soon: the shared KMP library already compiles for iOS; the app is next

# A Better U VR

**Talk to Atlas. She does things on a real platform.**

Entry in the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie Developer track, theme "Build for Your World"). Build window: Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026.

A Meta Quest 3S app where you talk to **Atlas**, a voice assistant powered by Meta's Muse Spark, and it **does things for you on a real platform**. Say "log my usual breakfast" and the meal lands in your A Better U food diary. Look at a plate and Atlas names the foods, outlines them with SAM 3.1, measures them and logs what you confirm. Say "set me up a squat workout, two sets of ten" and the headset tracks your reps and saves each set. Say "share my session" and it drafts a post for your **A Better U social feed** (not Meta, Facebook or Instagram), with a picture made by Muse Image, for you to approve.

**The proof point:** the plate scan chains Muse Spark and SAM 3.1 to measure food from one photo. In a weigh-in of two foods on one plate it landed within **about 1% and 4% of the scales**, against 56% and 37% low for a vision guess alone.

**Atlas is an assistant, not a coach.** It gives no medical or fitness advice, and says so when it introduces itself. Every request ends in a verified write to a live database, and the app only says "saved" or "posted" after the backend confirmed it.

## Try it in about three minutes

You need a Meta Quest 3 or 3S in developer mode, `adb`, and your own Meta Model API key. The APK contains no Meta or Wit.ai keys, so you add your own:

1. **Meta Model API key:** create one in your Meta Model API account.
2. **Wit.ai token (optional, and Wit.ai is free):** at [wit.ai](https://wit.ai), create an app, then copy its **Server Access Token** from Settings. Without it, Atlas's replies appear on screen and are not spoken.
3. Copy [`atlas-keys.example.json`](atlas-keys.example.json) to `atlas-keys.json` and fill in your values. Never commit this file.
4. Download `A-Better-U-VR.apk` from the [Releases page](https://github.com/danpcaw/ABetterU_VR/releases/latest), then run:

   ```bash
   adb install -r A-Better-U-VR.apk
   adb shell mkdir -p /sdcard/Android/data/uk.co.abetteru.vr/files
   adb push atlas-keys.json /sdcard/Android/data/uk.co.abetteru.vr/files/atlas-keys.json
   ```

5. On the Quest, open **Library**, filter to **Unknown Sources** and start "A Better U VR".

Then:

1. Tap **Judge Instant Login**. Atlas introduces herself.
2. Say **"Hey Atlas, log a Big Mac for lunch."** Watch the Food Diary update.
3. Open **My World**, then **Scan a Plate**: look at a plate from slightly above, press the left trigger, check the outlines and the weights, tap **Log**.
4. Say **"Hey Atlas, set me up a squat workout, two sets of ten."** The gym opens, you stand tall, calibrate and squat. A session card appears; tap **Share to feed** and approve the post.
5. Open **My Profile** and **Exercise Log** to see everything that was saved.

# Scout

### A physics-simulated home that tests whether a robot's memory is still true.

![Scout: a Meta Motivo body and SAM 3.1 eyes explore a house, the episode splits into two worlds, and only looking tells them apart](assets/media/scout_diagram.png)

![Same robot, same memory, same question: two worlds](assets/media/branch.gif)

A Meta Motivo humanoid explores a house it has never seen. It sees through a head camera with SAM 3.1 and keeps a
memory of what it saw and where. Then the episode splits into two worlds. In one, nothing changes. In the other, we
quietly move an object. Both copies of the robot get the same question: *"Is the sofa you saw at 232 s still where
it was?"*

![Memory can't tell the two worlds apart. Looking can.](assets/media/verdict.png)

**Memory can't tell the two worlds apart. Looking can.** Answering from memory says "still there" in both worlds,
so it is wrong in one of them. The robot that walks back and looks gets both right: its depth camera now sees past
the spot where the sofa was.

**Scout gives robots a new capability: knowing when their memory has gone stale, and going back to check.** It is
an open, physics-simulated proving ground where three Meta models run in one closed loop: Meta Motivo moves the
body, SAM 3.1 sees through the head camera, and Muse Spark 1.3 is the brain under test. The brain and the eyes are
served by Meta Model API. Any model plugs in through four methods. Scout runs the physics, the eyes and the hidden
interventions, then grades every answer against what the robot's camera actually saw, frame by frame.

**It also trains brains.** A 233-parameter neural network, trained in seconds on Scout's own episodes, took over
the robot's head and out-remembered Muse Spark 1.3 in eight never-seen homes: 106 of 112 against 92.
[See the network](#the-neural-network-we-trained).

- **Real physics, not animation.** A Meta Motivo humanoid in MuJoCo walks, turns to look, falls and gets itself
  back up: 35 falls and 35 recoveries in the final evaluation.
- **It sees for itself.** SAM 3.1 open-vocabulary masks on an RGB-D head camera, lifted into 3D, and a floor map
  built from its own depth. No layout, no object list, no shortcuts.
- **A world that changes behind its back.** Each episode branches from one physics snapshot into a moved world and
  an unchanged world, so both copies of the robot face the identical question.
- **Scoring that is hard to fool.** Every answer is graded against per-frame visibility, every cited frame is
  checked against the evaluator's segmentation, abstentions are counted separately, and every failure is kept.
  Anyone can rescore all 32 final episodes from the public records on a laptop.

### Why it matters

# ArchKit - Residential Studio

A residential design studio with a shared 2D/3D project model and Muse Spark room planning.

## Local development

Use Node.js 24 or newer, then run:

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```

The development server prints its local URL. The editor's projects autosave in browser storage.

## Build and tests

```sh
npm run build
node tests/model.test.mjs
node tests/spark.test.mjs
```

The app uses the Sites Vinext/Cloudflare Worker integration. Production output is in `dist/server` and `dist/client`.

## Muse Spark

Configure `MODEL_API_KEY` as a **server secret** in Sites, then deploy the saved version. The key is read only by the Worker and is never embedded in browser code. The assistant uses the official `https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses` endpoint with `muse-spark-1.3`.

The assistant can inspect layouts, plan or edit rooms, calculate areas, and switch views. Valid room edits are applied as one undoable change. All geometry remains in feet internally; metric user requests are converted before edits. Overlaps, setback violations, unknown IDs, and invalid dimensions are rejected. Changes made manually while a request is running prevent that response from overwriting the newer project.

This is an early residential design tool; the assistant does not verify building codes or structural safety.

## Creative architecture workspace

The assistant's Visualize tab uses `muse-spark-1.3` to interpret canonical project geometry and a clean all-floor PNG, then `muse-image-1.0` through Meta's documented `/v1/images/edits` endpoint to render three independent concepts. A two-worker client queue limits concurrent image requests. `Generate 3 More` retains the original batch's project snapshot and requirements and appends a new batch. Refinements and alternate views attach the saved parent image alongside the plan. Interiors attach the selected room's dimensions and openings.

Images, references, batch settings, parent relationships, and selected concepts are stored in the Sites `BUCKET` R2 binding, scoped by authenticated user and project ID. Images are served through authenticated same-origin endpoints; temporary provider URLs are not retained. The original layout remains the geometric source of truth. Concept previews are not measured drawings or validated structures.

All requests requiring `MODEL_API_KEY` run server-side. Routes validate identity, origin, request size, file format, references, project schema, and structured model output. Successful render slots are reused on retry. Partial failures retain successful images. Refreshing the gallery restores saved results; interrupted unfinished slots can be retried.

Service validation: `node tests/creative.test.mjs` covers batch construction, actual Meta request shapes with a deterministic test transport, partial failures, retry/idempotency, authenticated gallery isolation, and queue concurrency. No fake images are used in the application.

Official references:
- https://dev.meta.ai/doc

# Borderless

**Two people, two languages, one conversation.** Borderless is an iPhone app that lets two people who don't share
a language talk face to face. Each person speaks normally; Borderless shows the original words and the translation,
on the phone and, if you wear them, on display glasses (Meta Ray-Ban Display and Even Realities G2). The host can
privately see two reply ideas in the other person's language, with the meaning, and hear how to say them.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup track, theme *Build for Your World*), October 27 to
November 4, 2026. **What was built during the event, and what it builds on, is listed in
[CONTRIBUTIONS.md](CONTRIBUTIONS.md).**

## Try it

| | how | needs |
|---|---|---|
| iPhone app (TestFlight) | https://testflight.apple.com/join/dJTN5jBc (Beta App Review submitted Nov 5) | iOS 18+ |
| Recorded demo, in the app | open Borderless, tap **Demo**, then **Play** | nothing: no mic, network, account or glasses |
| Live translation, in the app | tap **Live**, pick two languages, confirm both people agree, **Start** | network; uses our hosted relay |
| Single-glasses mode | one person wears glasses and reads the other's words translated; when the wearer speaks, the other person taps **Play** on that line to hear it in their language | one pair of Meta Ray-Ban Display or Even G2 (optional) |
| Website and browser demo | Run `python3 site/serve.py` and open http://127.0.0.1:8769 | a browser |
| Video (3 min) | See the hackathon submission | |

Glasses are optional; the app works on the phone alone. English and Spanish are tested end to end; the other
pairs from Meta's 25-language speech catalog are selectable and marked experimental
([docs/LANGUAGE-CAPABILITIES.md](docs/LANGUAGE-CAPABILITIES.md)).

## How it works

```

 phone mic ── PCM 24 kHz ── wss:// ──▶   auth, consent, session caps  ── wss ──▶ Muse Voice Transcribe

    └── Play a line aloud     (on-device iOS speech, in the listener's language)

# ChaosTwin

**Turn a plain traffic video into a digital twin, then let AI find a better signal plan.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, theme "Build for Your World"). Powered by Meta SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark through the Meta Model API, with Eclipse SUMO for simulation.

> Status: documentation first. This repository currently contains the product and engineering docs; code is generated by following them (see "For developers").

---

# Part 1: For users

## What is ChaosTwin?

Many Indian junctions mix cars, bikes, autos, buses and trucks with very little lane discipline. Normal traffic tools struggle with that. ChaosTwin watches a short video of a junction, counts every vehicle by type, builds a simulated copy (a "digital twin") that behaves like the real one, and tests new signal timings on the twin before anyone touches a real signal.

## What you can do

- Watch a 3D story of chaos turning into order on the home page.
- Pick a sample junction video and see vehicles detected and counted by type.
- Compare **Reality** (the video) with the **Twin** (the simulation) side by side.
- See how well the twin matches reality (a clear error percentage, even when it is not perfect).
- See an AI suggested signal plan and the **Before vs After** results: average wait, queue length and vehicles served.
- (If enabled) upload your own clip. Use short videos (1 to 2 minutes).

## How to use it

1. Open the site and scroll through the hero.
2. Click **Try a sample**.
3. Use the view switch: Reality, Twin or Split.
4. Toggle vehicle classes with the chips.
5. Drag the timeline to move through the clip.
6. Open **Optimise** to compare signal plans and read the explanation.
7. Open **Under the hood** to see the models used, cost and quality numbers.

## How to read the results

- **Average wait per vehicle:** extra seconds a vehicle spends because of the signal and queues. Lower is better.
- **Queue:** vehicles waiting at the stop line.
- **Throughput:** vehicles passing per hour.
- **Calibration error:** how far the twin is from the video, per approach. Under about 15 percent is good for this project.
- **Source badge:** Baseline (current plan), Webster (a classic formula), AI (suggested by Muse Spark and checked in simulation).

## Good to know (limits)

- Results are for one junction and one time window, not a whole city.
- Vehicle counts are estimates. The AI model tracks a limited number of objects per frame, so very crowded scenes are handled in pieces, and counts can be off. The accuracy table below shows measured error.
- Suggested plans are simulation based advice. Do not apply them to real signals without a qualified traffic engineer.
- Explanations are written by an AI. The numbers come from the simulation.

## Privacy

Use videos you have permission to use. Avoid footage with identifiable faces or number plates, or blur them first. The live upload route sends your clip to the Meta Model API for analysis.

# BuildLens

An early engineering workspace prototype for exploring building concepts in a navigable 3D viewport, organizing project documents, and discussing supplied material with Meta Model API.

## Current functionality
- React + Vite, plain JavaScript; Three.js illustrative building model.
- Building, Structure, Foundation and Reinforcement views. Reinforcement view displays illustrative slab mesh and column bars; this is not a design detail.
- Pointer orbit, mouse-wheel zoom and two-finger pinch zoom.
- PDF selectable-text extraction, DOCX text extraction, TXT/MD/CSV/JSON/XML text, and JPG/PNG/WEBP image attachments to the assistant.
- New chat control; project files remain available when a new conversation is started.
- Local workspace metadata/chat persistence and JSON export.
- Server-side Meta Model API proxy using `META_API_KEY`.

## File support limitations
PDF text is extracted in the browser (up to 35 pages); scanned/image-only PDFs need OCR or page images. DOCX is text-extracted. Images are sent as image inputs. CAD/DWG/DXF, XLSX and legacy DOC files are not parsed yet. Attachments are sent when the user presses Send; files are not uploaded to permanent cloud storage. The sample 3D building is not generated from uploaded plans.

## Meta API key setup
In Vercel Project Settings → Environment Variables, set `META_API_KEY` for Production and Preview, then redeploy. Keep it server-side; never add a `VITE_` prefix or commit the real key. `.env.example` contains only a placeholder.

The proxy calls Meta's OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint with `muse-spark-1.3`. Confirm API access and multimodal support for the selected model/account.

## Run locally
Requires a recent Node.js release.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

## The problem

Small businesses in Nigeria sell through WhatsApp, Instagram and TikTok. What converts there is **UGC (user-generated content)**: a real-looking person talking to camera in the language the customer actually speaks.

- Hiring creators is slow and expensive for a small seller.
- Most AI video tools only speak English, and they sound foreign when they try anything else.
- Translated scripts lose the hooks, slang and rhythm that make an advert land locally.

## What Talla does

- **Researches** the product and the audience: pain points, objections and scroll-stopping hooks.
- **Storyboards** the advert scene by scene. Every scene can be edited before anything is filmed.
- **Writes the script natively** in the chosen language, with an English line under each one so the owner knows exactly what is said.
- **Casts a creator.** Four named on-screen creators each have a matching voice in every supported language.
- **Films it.** It generates the voice, lip-syncs the creator to it, and cuts the scenes together with burned-in captions.

- **Writes the post**: the caption and hashtags.
- **Keeps every project.** Finished films reload from History at no cost, and you have to confirm before a re-render spends credits.

A voice agent for US local businesses (HVAC example) that answers a missed call, books a job in 5 stages, saves a lead, and hands off to a human when asked:

1. **Voice webhooks** (`src/AirwayHVAC.SmsAi.Api/Functions/InboundVoiceFunction.cs`): `POST /api/webhooks/twilio/voice/inbound`, `/gather`, `/status`.
2. **Stage machine** (`ConversationFlowEngine`): Issue → Address → Urgency → Appointment → Confirm → Completed. Completed is deterministically gated on all 4 fields (Issue, Address, Urgency, PreferredTime).

4. **Tool calling**: exactly one tool, `book_appointment` (required: day, service; optional: caller_name, time), exactly one tool round. Any other function name returns `{"status":"unknown_tool"}` and cannot loop, book, or corrupt a lead.
5. **Human handoff**: handoff keywords (representative / human / agent / operator / person) short-circuit before the orchestrator and return TwiML `<Dial>` to the configured owner number. # Mise Mise turns a plain-English question about Washington, DC into a shortlist of relevant open government datasets, then writes an analysis plan for the datasets you pick. The name comes from *mise en place*, the cooking habit of prepping every ingredient before you start. Most of the work in a data project happens before any analysis: finding the right sources, checking what they actually contain, and figuring out how they fit together. Mise handles that part. Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track). All runtime AI is Meta's Muse Spark, and the app was built with Muse Code. ![Mise returning ranked datasets for a question about DC](docs/screenshots/discovery.png) ## Why I built this DC publishes over 1,600 open datasets. When I tried to answer a simple question with them, like what affects pedestrian safety near schools, the portal's keyword search mostly returned aerial imagery and zoning layers. The useful datasets were there (crash records, Safe Passage routes, school locations), but finding them meant already knowing what to look for. So I wanted a tool that starts from the question instead of the keywords, and that is honest about what the data can and can't tell you. ## What it does 1. **Discovery.** You ask a question. Mise searches the full DC catalog and returns ranked datasets, each with a relevance score, a short explanation of why it was chosen, and its limitations (archived, old, partial coverage, and so on). 2. **Inspection.** Every result links to its real source page, service endpoint, publisher, and license. You can open the full metadata before trusting anything. 3. **Assistant.** A side panel answers questions about your results and can change your selection when you ask ("add the top 3 to my recipe"). Every change it makes can be undone. 4. **Data Recipe.** From the datasets you select, Mise writes an analysis plan: objective, workflow steps, how the datasets relate, data gaps, and limitations. You can download it as Markdown or JSON. A recipe is a plan, not a result. Mise never runs analysis or reports findings, and it never invents dataset IDs, links, or numbers. Some real results from testing: | Question | Top results | |---|---| | What affects pedestrian safety near schools in DC? | Safe Passage Routes (90), Crash Details Table (88), DC Public Schools | | Give me a list of bus stops in DC | Commuter Bus Stops (95), Metro Bus Stops 2023–2025 (85), ADA Bus Stop (70) | | How is access to healthcare distributed across DC? | Primary Care Facility (88), Healthcare for Homebound Older Adults (62) | ![Recommendation cards with scores, explanations, and actions](docs/screenshots/results.png) ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR Q[Question] --> UI[React frontend] UI -->|/api| API[FastAPI backend] API -->|MCP| CAT[(DC metadata catalog)] API --> EXP[Query expansion

**An Evidence-Driven AI Engineering Simulator for Real-World Building Challenges**

CODECRAFT 3D transforms complex building regulations into interactive engineering challenges. It combines AI-powered regulation extraction, evidence traceability, deterministic engineering calculations and 3D building simulation in a gamified environment.

Instead of simply reading building regulations, users can explore how those regulations affect a building, experiment with design decisions, identify potential violations and improve their designs through interactive challenges.

Building regulations contain important requirements governing setbacks, building height, site coverage and other construction parameters.

- Understanding how one design decision affects other requirements is difficult.
- Identifying potential conflicts requires careful interpretation and calculations.

CODECRAFT 3D introduces a game-based engineering simulator where users can explore building design challenges and understand the consequences of their decisions.

- AI-assisted extraction of building regulation requirements.

# Second Look (in development)

A triage queue for the images a desk receives. A folder goes in. A ranked queue and an evidence receipt for every image come out. It never says "this is real". It is not affiliated with Meta. Everything runs locally with open-source parts (MIT, Apache, CC0, CC BY).

## A desk triage queue

A desk gets a folder of images and one question: which ones should a person look at first? `secondlook queue` checks every file in the folder and writes an evidence receipt for each. It then sorts the folder into three bands. Setup is the one command in the Quickstart below.

```
.venv/bin/secondlook queue <folder> --out <dir> [--form original|sq512] [--jobs N] [--pdf]
```

| Band | What puts an image there | Who acts |
|---|---|---|
| `uncertain` | Everything not in the other two bands, including any image with no detector score | A person, highest detector score first |
| `auto_decided` | The ladder answered `signed_ai` or `concerns`, or the detector score is at or above a frozen high threshold | No one, spot checks only |
| `likely_fine` | No signed AI record, no concern, and a detector score below a frozen low threshold. This is not proof that the image is real | No one, spot checks only |

The queue lists `uncertain` first, then `auto_decided`, then `likely_fine`. Each row names its band, its reason and the receipt behind it. The queue never changes the ladder's answer or a receipt.

Four thresholds were fitted on the development split of one public set, TrueFake (CC BY 4.0). Each of the two forms has a high and a low threshold. They are frozen in `secondlook/queue_bands.json`. Its sha256 is recorded beside it and pinned in `secondlook/queue.py`. The queue refuses to run if the file does not match both. Held-out images were never read when the thresholds were fitted. The detector's scores for all 983 images existed before the split. Only the four thresholds were fitted, on dev only. The detector's TrueFake numbers are not blind.

### What the held-out result says

One run on the 640 held-out TrueFake images: 314 camera photos and 326 AI images from five generators. These are the `sq512` figures: metadata stripped, centre-cropped to 512 by 512 pixels. Bounds are exact one-sided 95% upper bounds.

| What we counted | Result | 95% upper bound |
|---|---|---|
| Camera photos placed in `auto_decided` | 0 of 314 | 0.95% |
| AI images placed in `likely_fine` | 3 of 326 | 2.36% |
| Images decided without a person | 344 of 640 (53.8%): 227 `auto_decided` (all AI images) plus 117 `likely_fine` (114 camera photos, 3 AI images) | not applicable |

On files as given (`--form original`, the default), 312 of 640 (48.8%) were decided without a person. The other two rows are the same in that form.

Read these limits with the numbers:

- The 0.95% bound covers the `auto_decided` side only. The `likely_fine` side has 3 misses in 326 and an upper bound of 2.36%. We make no 1% claim for it. The 1% target was a dev-fitted operating point.
- All 3

# Bizora

**Turn any research paper, from any technical domain, into an explorable, evidence-grounded and experimentally testable methodology.**

Bizora is a research workspace that transforms scientific papers into interactive methodology models. Researchers can inspect components, trace claims to their sources, propose supported changes, execute real experiments on isolated compute, and compare measured results.

## Product in one paragraph

Bizora takes any research paper from any technical domain (ML/DL, electronics and PCB, IoT, robotics, mechanical, and more), auto-detects what kind of paper it is, regenerates its methodology as an evidence-linked, editable model, shows it as a realistic 3D build (a real-looking board with real components for electronics; layered blocks with real tensor shapes for ML), lets the researcher add, replace or modify components and techniques, runs the modified design for real on isolated compute, and shows measured results next to the baseline. An AI copilot answers questions grounded in the paper, the design and the runs.

## Rule zero: nothing is hard-coded

Bizora must work on papers nobody has seen yet. Test papers are inputs for measuring quality, never special cases in code.

- No domain list in core code. A domain is a label the model produces for each paper; packs declare which labels they handle.
- No paper-specific, part-specific or demo-specific branches. Part names, models and parameters live in data, never in logic.
- Every feature is accepted on held-out papers that were not used while building it.
- When extraction meets something unknown, it returns *assumed* or *unsupported* with a reason, never a guess presented as fact.

## Core workflow

1. **Ingest** a scientific paper: text, figures, equations, tables and metadata.
2. **Detect** the paper's domains as open-vocabulary, multi-label tags and select the matching domain pack automatically.
3. **Extract** methodology as a structured graph of components and relationships, grounded in paper evidence.
4. **Resolve** parts to real models through the pack's resolver ladder (exact part, family/package, category).
5. **Render** a realistic 3D build from the pack's render specs — no generic shapes.
6. **Modify** components or techniques through validated, versioned patches with pack preflight checks.
7. **Execute** real experiments through allowlisted adapters on isolated compute.
8. **Compare** measured results against the baseline and the paper's reported numbers.

## Core principles

- Evidence before explanation: claims must link to paper evidence, a measured run, or be labelled *assumed*/*illustrative*.
- No fabricated results: distinguish measured results, estimates and hypotheses.
- Immutable history: edits create new graph versions rather than silently overwriting prior work.
- Domain-agnostic core: graph, evidence, versions, patches, runs, comparison and copilot live in the core; every domain is a pack.
- Validated execution: proposed changes mu

# `ppc64rt` — Power ISA 64-Bit (`ppc64le` ELFv2, POWER9 / Power10) User-Mode Binary Translator for AArch64

`ppc64rt` is a zero-dependency, static-PIE (`aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`) user-mode binary translator for **Power ISA 64-Bit (`ppc64le` ELFv2, POWER9 / Power10)** Linux ELF binaries on AArch64 Linux and macOS on Apple Silicon (via [`hyper-linux`](../hyper-linux)).

- **Series Tier**: Tier 1 (Wave 4 — Class-B 64-Bit Full Address Space)
- **Target CPUs**: IBM POWER9 (Power ISA v3.0B) and Power10 / Power11 (Power ISA v3.1)
- **ELF Admission**: `ELFCLASS64`, `ELFDATA2LSB` (`ppc64le`), `e_machine == EM_PPC64 (21)`, `(ehdr.e_flags & EF_PPC64_ABI) == 2` (`EF_PPC64_ABI = 3`)
- **Guest `TASK_SIZE`**: `1ULL << 47 (128 TiB user VA space, va_bits = 47, AT_PAGESZ = 4096)`
- **Dual Execution Engines**:
  1. `src/interp/` — Portable Curated C11 reference interpreter and differential oracle (`PPC64RT_ENGINE=interp`)
  2. `src/dbt/` — Direct-mapped + IBTC AArch64 dynamic binary translator (`PPC64RT_ENGINE=dbt`, default) with single-instruction interpreter fallback (`EXIT_UNDEF` / `EXIT_SINGLE_STEP`)

# Vouch — Check it. Chase it.

Vouch is a product-verification and complaint follow-through tool for medicines,
foods, drinks, cosmetics and everyday consumables. It is built for the last
metre of consumer protection: the moment someone is standing in a shop with a
pack in their hand, and the weeks afterwards when a complaint usually dies.

It never returns a binary “fake or genuine” verdict. Every result is one of
four states — **Clear**, **Check further**, **High-risk signals** or
**Inconclusive** — with the evidence behind it, the source, and an explicit
statement of what the check does not prove.

## Run it

```powershell
cd vouch
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt   # once; requests is only for smoke.py
python server.py                 # http://127.0.0.1:8077
$env:VOUCH_PORT = "8091"         # optional: run on another port
python server.py
```

Then open:

- `http://127.0.0.1:8077/` — marketing site and documentation pages
- `http://127.0.0.1:8077/app` — the working application
- `http://127.0.0.1:8077/api/health` — service status

No API key is required. Needs Python 3.10 or newer (CI runs 3.13). The product
code is standard library plus FastAPI/Uvicorn/Pillow/numpy/python-multipart
(and the `winrt-Windows.*` packages on Windows for in-process OCR — without
them the PowerShell fallback is used); the test client needs httpx and the
smoke script needs requests.

### Optional: use a model for explanations

```powershell
$env:MODEL_API_KEY = "your-key"
$env:META_BASE = "https://api.meta.ai/v1"   # optional
$env:VOUCH_MODEL = "muse-spark-1.3"         # optional
python server.py
```

The key is also accepted as `META_API_KEY`, and the vision model can be
overridden separately with `META_VISION_MODEL`. Without a key, explanations
are written by the deterministic `vouch-composer` with the same evidence and
the same guardrails. The app labels which provider was used on every answer.

## The two rails

**Rail one — NAFDAC Greenbook.** Medicines, devices, vaccines, herbals and
veterinary products. The printed registration number is resolved against the
live public register, including punctuation variants and likely OCR confusions.
The engine never crosses the alpha and numeric numbering series. An `inactive`
registration is kept distinct from a falsified pack. Food, water and cosmetics
live in a separate register (NAPAMS); vouch says so instead of calling the
miss a finding, and points those packs at registration.nafdac.gov.ng.

**Rail two — open product databases.** Food, drink, water, cosmetics and
household products. Barcodes are check-digit validated first, then looked up in
Open Food Facts, Open Beauty Facts and Open Products Facts. A barcode match
identifies a product record; it does not prove the pack in your hand is
authentic.

## What the app does

- **Guided multi-side scanning.** The scanner captures the front, back, barcode

# PuzzleAR

**Find your next piece. Keep the joy of puzzling.**

PuzzleAR turns a photo of your scattered pieces into step-by-step help, without the box image.

**Try it:** https://puzzlear.jacob.workers.dev · **Demo video:** https://youtu.be/476nt5J34ro

## The moment it helps

You want the satisfaction of finishing a puzzle yourself, yet you keep searching the same pile of pieces. PuzzleAR finds your next step when you need it and leaves the fun part, putting it together, to you.

## Three steps

1. **Snap a photo.** Spread the pieces out and take one photo from above. Every piece gets a number you can spot on the table.
2. **Find your next piece.** PuzzleAR suggests which piece to pick up next and which pieces it joins.
3. **Place it with guidance.** See where it goes, drawn right on the photo of your table. Check the move with a new photo, or confirm it yourself.

You stay in control throughout: inspect a suggested fit, confirm what works, and PuzzleAR updates the next steps around your answers. Any step can be undone.

## How Meta SAM 3.1 makes it work

Meta SAM 3.1 helps PuzzleAR see individual pieces. Our matching engine turns those outlines into possible fits, and visual guidance helps you act on them. Without per-piece outlines from a single photo, the rest of the experience would need a scanner or the box image.

## Result

In our tests, a phone-style photo of 24 scattered pieces, shot at an angle, came back as the right picture, cell for cell, from Meta SAM 3.1's outlines. That photo is a rendered test puzzle; the setup and the other results are in the [evaluation](docs/EVALUATION.md).

The tested sizes are small puzzles of up to two dozen pieces. A partial pile cannot be solved into a full board, so PuzzleAR then lists the pairs of pieces most likely to fit together instead.

## Try it

# SANKOFA

**An AI agent that builds a time machine for any city, and tells you what is proven and what is imagined.**

> *Sankofa* is an Adinkra symbol from Ghana: a bird looking back over its shoulder. It means *"go back and fetch what you left behind."*

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026** (Indie track, theme *Build for Your World*) by KOBA David, Benin.

**Live showcase: <https://sankofa-two-topaz.vercel.app>** (precomputed content; run the live agent from this repository).

![SANKOFA home page](docs/screenshots/home.jpg)

---

## The problem

The visual history of cities, and of African cities above all, is scattered across distant archives in Paris, Washington or Amsterdam. People living in Porto-Novo or on Gorée Island almost never get to see what their street looked like a hundred years ago.

Generative AI can now "age" any photo in one click. But it invents silently: a beautiful fake image of the past damages collective memory instead of serving it.

**SANKOFA brings the archives home, and never lets the AI pass imagination off as history.**

## What SANKOFA does

### 1. A time machine for places

Give SANKOFA a place and a year. An agent does the work of a historian and of an ML engineer, live, in seven visible steps:

| # | Step | What the agent does | Engine |
|---|------|---------------------|--------|
| 1 | **Investigate** | Searches open archives by keyword and by GPS coordinates, keeps only open licenses, then looks at each image to check that it really shows the place at that time | **Muse Spark 1.3** (vision) |
| 2 | **Annotate** | Cuts today's view into buildings, road and sky, with pixel-accurate masks | **SAM 3.1** |
| 3 | **Re-photograph** | Finds where each period photographer stood (feature matching + RANSAC) and warps the archive onto today's view | OpenCV |
| 4 | **Learn the style** | Learns the city's photographic look for that decade: tone curve, tint, grain | profile learned from the corpus |
| 5 | **Reconstruct** | Areas proven by an archive come from the archive itself. Only areas with no evidence are handed to the generative model | **Muse Image** |
| 6 | **Self-evaluate** | Hides an archive, rebuilds without it, compares, and computes a reliability score | SSIM, evidence coverage |
| 7 | **Narrate** | Writes a short history of the place in French and English, every sentence citing its source, no invented detail | **Muse Spark 1.3** |

Every region of the image gets a verdict: **documented** (green), **unchanged** (grey) or **hypothesis** (yellow). The agent lists what it does not know and asks the community for the missing photos or oral testimonies.

*Notre-Dame de Paris: a real press photograph from 1912 (crowd, flags) is warped onto a 2014 view. SAM 3.1 outlines the buildings; the cathedral is classified as unchanged.*

Get landlords' units inspection-ready with AI vision, match them to Section 8
voucher holders racing a 60-day clock, and verify listings against scams.
Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

## Quickstart (Windows PowerShell)

```powershell
npm install
npm run db:push
npm run db:seed
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser. Stop with `Ctrl+C`.

## Environment (.env.local)

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `META_API_KEY` | Meta Model API key (server-side only) |
| `META_BASE_URL` | `https://api.meta.ai/v1` |
| `META_LLM_MODEL` | `muse-spark-1.1` |
| `SAM_ENDPOINT` | SAM 3.1 segmentation endpoint; empty = LLM-only bounding boxes |
| `MUSE_IMAGE_MODEL` | Muse Image model, e.g. `muse-image-1.0` |
| `DATABASE_URL` | In `.env`; SQLite `file:./dev.db` for local dev |

`.env.local` is gitignored; never commit keys.

## Scripts

- `npm run dev` — start the dev server
- `npm run build` — production build (`prisma generate && next build`)
- `npm start` — run the production build
- `npm run db:push` — push the Prisma schema to the database
- `npm run db:seed` — load the demo landlords, units, and renters
- `npm test` — maintained unit tests (no network calls)

## Demo walkthrough

1. Pick a role on the landing page (stored in a cookie; no auth).
2. Landlord: open a unit, add 3–8 photos by room, run the AI pre-inspection,
   mark findings fixed, run verification, view the public listing.
3. Renter: add a voucher passport, review matches, click "I'm interested",
   paste a listing into the scam checker.

## Deploy (Vercel)

1. Push this folder to GitHub and Import it in Vercel (Next.js defaults;
   the build command is already `prisma generate && next build`).
2. Set the Environment Variables from the table above in the Vercel
   dashboard (all except `DATABASE_URL`, see below).
3. Important: SQLite (`file:./dev.db`) is local-dev only — Vercel's
   filesystem is ephemeral, so the seed database will not persist there.
   For production, provision a hosted Postgres database, point
   `DATABASE_URL` at it, and change the datasource `provider` in
   `prisma/schema.prisma` from `sqlite` to `postgresql`, then redeploy.
   The Postgres switch is documented but unverified in this environment.

## Tech notes

- Next.js 14 App Router + TypeScript + Tailwind + Prisma.
- All Meta calls run server-side in `/api/*` routes; LLM JSON is validated
  with Zod and retried once on parse failure.
- `sharp` is externalized for server components so the native module loads
  from `node_modules` at runtime (serverless-safe).

# Cue

Ask a question. Watch the answer.

Cue searches a curated library of YouTube videos. You ask a question, Cue finds the moment in a video that answers it, plays only that moment, and shows a short written answer with its source: creator, title and timestamps.

Cue works for any subject. The library decides what it can answer. An admin adds a video by link together with its transcript, the SRT, VTT or SBV file exported from YouTube Studio, and Cue splits it into passages and indexes them.

Timestamps always come from the source transcript. If no video in the library answers the question, Cue says so.

![Architecture](cue-architecture.png)

## Structure

- `backend/` Python, FastAPI, SQLite through SQLAlchemy
- `frontend/` React with Vite
- `design/` design system: tokens, components, icons

## Requirements

- Python 3.13
- Node.js 20 or newer
- An API key from the Meta Model API: https://dev.meta.ai/

## Run

Backend setup, once:

```
cd backend
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env
```

Fill in the values in `backend/.env`.

Frontend setup, once:

```
cd frontend
npm install
```

Start both from the project root. Ctrl+C stops both.

```
./dev.sh
```

Backend runs on http://localhost:8000, frontend on http://localhost:5173.

## Tests

From `backend/`, with the virtual environment active. Install the test tools once, then run the tests:

```
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest tests
```

Tests use their own temporary database and keys, never `backend/.env` or `data/cue.db`.

## Evaluation

`backend/eval/questions.json` holds 29 test questions with the expected video, some with no answer on purpose. The admin runs them from the Evaluation screen, or from the command line:

```
cd backend
python eval/run.py
```

Each answer gets three checks: right video, right moment, honest no answer. Scores are recorded in `backend/eval/results.md`.

## Future developments

- Transcripts fetched through the official YouTube Data API with the channel owner's consent, so an admin only pastes a link.
- One process for the demo: the frontend build served by FastAPI, deployed to a public URL.
- Better start times. Today 22 of 29 test answers start at the right moment. Smaller passages around sentence boundaries should move this closer to all of them.
- Sign out that revokes the token, and the other items in RISKS.md.
- More sources than YouTube: any recording with a transcript, such as webinars and internal training videos.

See ROADMAP.md for the full list of what is built and what is next.

Cook from your pantry across West and East African food traditions, grouped by the peoples who cook them. ```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # UI only; the concierge falls back to built-in answers

npm run build
