# 🛡️ Health App Privacy Explainer

**An evidence-aware Android health-app privacy analysis tool combining rule-based security analysis with Meta AI-powered explanations.**

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**

**Track:** Indie Developer  
**Theme:** Build for Your World

**Developer:** Mira Khatun  
**Institution:** Kent State University

## Overview

Android health applications can process highly sensitive personal information, including medical records, reproductive health information, and mental health data.

Security analysis tools such as MobSF identify technical indicators, but their results can be difficult for nontechnical users to understand.

**Health App Privacy Explainer** makes selected security findings more accessible by combining deterministic Python analysis with explanations generated by Meta Muse Spark 1.3.

The application classifies Android permissions and third-party SDK indicators, presents structured findings, and uses Meta AI to explain what the available evidence does and does not establish.

This project builds upon my ongoing undergraduate cybersecurity research at Kent State University.

## The Problem

A security report may identify permissions such as `CAMERA`, `RECORD_AUDIO`, or `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`, alongside third-party analytics, advertising, and crash-reporting SDK indicators.

However, these findings alone do not prove that an application collects, transmits, or shares sensitive information.

Users and researchers need a way to understand:

- What identified permissions allow.
- Why certain SDK indicators deserve attention.
- Which findings are supported by technical evidence.
- What behavior remains unverified.
- What additional investigation may be appropriate.

## Our Solution

The application follows this workflow:

**MobSF-style JSON → Python Analysis Engine → Meta Muse Spark 1.3 → Streamlit Dashboard**

The Python analysis engine uses predefined rules to classify permissions and third-party SDK indicators.

Meta Muse Spark 1.3 generates plain-English explanations that distinguish directly observed findings from unverified possibilities and recommend additional checks.

The Streamlit dashboard presents the technical findings, AI-generated interpretations, and a downloadable structured analysis report.

### What Makes This Project Different?

The goal is not simply to summarize a security report with AI.

The system combines:

1. **Deterministic analysis** to classify technical indicators.
2. **Meta AI interpretation** to explain the meaning and limitations of those findings.
3. **Evidence-aware communication** to avoid unsupported claims about application behavior.

By separating technical observations from interpretations, the application supports more responsible security analysis.

# Take One

**An AI colorist you direct in plain words.** Upload a video and say what you want ("warmer evening feel, keep skin natural, make the sky moodier"). Take One asks only the questions that matter, plans an executable color grade, masks the parts of the picture that need their own treatment, and renders a graded video at the original resolution. You compare it with the original, revise it, and download it.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, on Meta's Muse Spark and SAM models.

**Demo video (2 min 24 s):** [watch on YouTube](https://youtu.be/VKJ8r17Odsc). Every scene is a real run of the app.

## What Meta's models do

| Model (Meta Model API) | Its job in Take One |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Watches the video, chooses which questions are worth asking you (an adaptive creative-direction rubric), writes the grade as a structured plan that the backend validates against a schema, and reviews renders against measured evidence. It can ask for a bounded revision (at most three renders by default). |
| **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) | Finds and tracks the subject and extra regions (sky, wall, water...) frame by frame, so each can be graded separately. Take One checks the masks for geometry, completeness and temporal stability, and stops rather than quietly falling back to a global grade. |

The models decide *what* to do; they never touch pixels. FFmpeg and OpenColorIO do all pixel work, from the original file, in 16-bit.

## How it works

    original video ─► ffprobe / FFmpeg ─► browser preview + small silent analysis proxy
                                                   │
        Muse Spark ◄───────────────────────────────┘  sees the proxy and your request
            │  asks the few questions that matter  ─► creative brief you can read and edit
            ▼
        Muse plans the grade: global, or localized with regions   (schema-validated)
            │
            ├─ localized ─► SAM 3.1 masks ─► validated mattes (coverage, edges, stability)
            ▼
        FFmpeg + OpenColorIO render from the ORIGINAL pixels ─► H.264 master + preview
            ▼
        measured checks (timing, frame count, clipping, protected areas) + Muse review
            ▼
        compare with the original · revise · download

## What it does today

- **Plain-words direction with adaptive questions.** Zero to three questions by default (five at most), each chosen by Muse from your request and earlier answers; a clear request gets none.
- **Global and localized grades.** A localized grade treats a subject plus up to four more regions separately, with soft edges and short fades at the start and end of each active interval.
- **Works with real phone footage.** 10-bit HEVC, full-range, untagged and BT.2020 clips are converted to Rec.709 before grading, and HLG/PQ HDR is tone-mapped to SDR, always disclosed as an approximation.
- **Flat or log footage.** A clip that looks flat is detected and *suggested*, never changed on it

## The finding: Muse Spark can read motion as text

**We gave Muse Spark numbers instead of images. It could still tell a fall
from someone getting up.**

SAM turns the person in a clip into a sequence of silhouettes. We shrink each
one to a **32×18 grid**, encode it as hexadecimal text, and send that sequence
to Muse Spark. That call gets **no images, no video, no tools and no prior
verdict**—just the changing masks, timestamps and an explanation of the format.

```text
Video → SAM silhouettes → tiny binary grids → hex text → Muse Spark's motion read
```

Then we tested whether the sequence mattered:

| What we sent | What Muse Spark returned |
|---|---|
| Original fall sequence | **Fall** |
| The same sequence, reversed | **Getting up** |
| The final low pose, repeated | **Uncertain: no movement** |

The frozen case matters: being low to the floor was not enough for Muse to
call it a fall. Its answer changed with the movement, not just the final pose.

Across **eight selected acted clips**, the text-only read matched **7/8 action
labels**, including all three falls. The miss was someone lowering themselves
onto a bed. Twenty-four masks contain just **1,728 bytes of occupancy data**,
before JSON and prompt overhead. SAM still receives the source video; the
text-only Muse call does not.

**You can inspect this in the app.** The expanded camera and **A deeper look**
show an image-based read beside the text-only read, with their exact inputs and
answers. When they disagree, both remain visible. These experimental reads sit
alongside the resident-first alert workflow.

# Parent Muse — a personal AI agent for co-parents, grounded in the family's own parenting plan

Parent Muse is an AI agent for divorced and separated parents. It has memory of the family's situation, coaches the parent in the moment, drafts messages for approval, and answers questions — and every answer is grounded in that family's **actual parenting plan**, not generic advice.

Co-parenting conflict rarely happens in a therapist's office. It happens at 11:30pm, over something small, when a tired parent is staring at their phone about to send a message they will regret. Parent Muse sits between signing the parenting agreement and the next therapy appointment, for exactly those moments.

## How it works

- **Plan-grounded, always.** The family's parenting plan is the standing lens for every answer. Plan answers name the section and explain it in plain language; the agent never invents plan language and never promises legal outcomes.
- **De-escalation first.** The first target is the parent in front of the agent: validate, calm, get child-focused — then act.
- **Mentor-first coaching.** Before any draft, the agent coaches: what is really going on, what the plan says, what outcome serves the kids.
- **BIFF discipline.** Drafts are Brief, Informative, Friendly, and Firm — written to end circular arguments, not win them.
- **Firmness follows the record.** A first ask is soft. If the same important point is ignored repeatedly, drafts get firmer — firmness is earned by the thread record (importance × times ignored), never by the parent's mood. Nothing sends without the parent's approval.

## Try it — live demo app

**https://smithdemo-v5ug9fwn.manus.space/**

A demo clone of the certified production build, seeded with a fictional family — Daniel & Lauren Smith, with children Sophia (11) and Ethan (9) — and a fictional parenting plan written for the demo. It opens straight to the app as Daniel Smith; there is no sign-in wall. Ask it a plan question by voice or text, and watch it answer from the plan, coach, and draft.

## Demo video

**A home should tell you where it is vulnerable before the lights go out or the taps stop running.**

CasaOS is a homeowner-directed AI agent concept for more reliable electricity, water, and connectivity. It starts with a real problem at my home in Atami, El Salvador: a grid outage can also stop the electric cistern pump, so stored water may no longer reach the house. This is an early step toward **personal superintelligence for the home**: an agent that understands your home's systems, learns your priorities, warns you about likely weak points, and helps you act before a malfunction becomes a household emergency. CasaOS applies that direction to a homeowner's daily essentials.

Home maintenance is often reactive: a homeowner discovers a failing pump, depleted battery, or fragile internet link only after service stops. With trustworthy sensor history, an agent could notice unusual pump cycling, falling well pressure, reduced solar output, or a battery that no longer holds charge; estimate where failure risk is rising; and recommend maintenance or changes in usage. The goal is a home that helps its owner prepare, not a system that takes control away.

# FocusGuard

**An Android focus coach that senses how a student actually uses their phone during study blocks, and plans tomorrow around it, without the raw usage ever leaving devices the student owns.**

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/WrLV5ZXMlqM

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Indie track · theme *"Build for Your World"*.

>  My world is a 3rd-year engineering timetable, an exam 9 days away, and a phone that turns "one quick YouTube lecture" into an hour of Shorts. Screen-time apps show you a pie chart after the damage is done. FocusGuard steps in *during* the study block and plans the next day from what really happened.


---

## What it does

| | |
|---|---|
| **Senses** | Reads foreground app sessions with Android `UsageStatsManager` (Usage Access permission) and knows when you are inside a study block from your timetable. |
| **Classifies on your own hardware** | Every session is labelled *focused / distracted / neutral*. A rule engine on the phone handles the obvious ones instantly. The ambiguous ones (YouTube during a study block: lecture or rabbit hole? Chrome: research or browsing?) go to **Muse Glimmer**, Meta's open-weight model, running on the student's own laptop over local Wi-Fi. It sees the neighbouring apps ("YouTube between Acrobat and Google Docs at 18:26") and decides. |
| **Nudges in the moment** | A background check every 15 minutes (offline, rules only) sends a notification when distracted time inside the current study block crosses your threshold, using nudge texts Muse Spark wrote for *your* pattern. |

# Offload

**Turn an unwanted object into a reviewable listing. Let an agent sort the messages. Keep the decisions.**

Offload is a prototype for reducing the attention cost of second-hand transactions. It separates what a photo or seller message supports from what remains unknown, then asks the owner to make the decision.

## Demo

- Live application: <https://offload-eta.vercel.app>
- Current 2:59 narrated submission demo: [`demo/v2/Offload-demo-v2.mp4`](demo/v2/Offload-demo-v2.mp4).
- It shows the latest live application, including original seller messages and pickup terms beside Find decisions, with the product vision, Meta model roles and demo-run API estimate.
- The sample is synthetic; buyer personas are simulated; Find intake is manual. Accelerated waits and typing are labeled. Native Facebook Marketplace integration is the ambition, not an existing feature. See [`demo/v2/README.md`](demo/v2/README.md) for scope and [`demo/v2/VERIFICATION.json`](demo/v2/VERIFICATION.json) for measured export properties.
- Older walkthrough files in `demo/` remain historical evidence, not the current submission video.

## What works

- **Sell:** A photo becomes a reviewable listing draft. Spark proposes structured facts and questions; SAM 3.1 makes an object cutout; Muse Image creates a comparison hero; approximate visible wear is shown alongside the original. The owner reviews unknowns and approves before five simulated buyer personas exercise the conversation agent. Qualified offers become owner-only Yes/No cards.
- **Find:** The owner describes a need and manually enters a seller message and optional photo. The app checks item identity, requested attributes, price/currency, condition evidence and pickup details. Missing evidence prompts a question; incompatibilities are rejected.
- **Decision authority:** Models cannot accept offers. Decisions are atomic and persist within an anonymous signed browser session.

Find does not search a marketplace or contact sellers. The app does not publish listings, send external messages, transfer payment or complete a binding transaction. Simulated counterparts and in-app approvals are not real deals. The prototype has not established real-world time savings.

## Run locally

Requires Node.js 24+ and npm. SQLite and image processing use native dependencies.

```sh
npm ci
OFFLOAD_MOCK=1 npm run dev -- --hostname 127.0.0.1
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:3000>. Explicit mock mode uses fixtures. Live API mode requires a server-side `MODEL_API_KEY`; hosted deployments also require `DATABASE_URL` and `OFFLOAD_SESSION_SECRET`. Never place secrets in `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variables or commit local environment files. Optional configuration: `OFFLOAD_MOCK=1` only for the labeled fixture mode, `OFFLOAD_DAILY_OPERATIONS`, `OFFLOAD_DAILY_BUDGET_USD`, and local-only `OFFLOAD_DB_PATH`.

To run the unit suite:

```sh
OFFLOAD_MOCK=1 npm test
```

# Live Tutorial Coach

**Any video tutorial. Now it watches you back.**

Video tutorials only go one way: they never see your hands. You pause, rewind, squint, and find the mistake three steps too late, when it can no longer be undone.

Live Tutorial Coach turns any hands-on tutorial into a live coach. Upload an mp4, prop your phone up, and follow along hands-free: it reads each step aloud, plays just that part of the video, watches your work through the camera, points at what went wrong, and stops you before a step you can't undo.

Built in a week for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (October 26 to November 4, 2026) with **Muse Spark 1.3**, **SAM 3.1** and **Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0**. Designed for Meta AI glasses; the phone is the stand-in.

![Home page](docs/images/home.jpg)

## What it does

- **Splits any video into steps.** Muse Spark watches the whole tutorial with its narration and returns validated steps: instruction, expected result, common mistakes, a reference picture, and whether the step can be undone.
- **Coaches one step at a time.** It reads the step aloud, plays only that part of the video, then waits for you.
- **Watches your work.** Every 4 seconds, 3 camera frames are compared with the step's reference picture. About 4 s and $0.003 per check.
- **Points at the problem.** On a mistake it warns you out loud, and SAM 3.1 boxes the object on your camera view.
- **Stops you before the point of no return.** Before an irreversible step, saying "next" is not enough: the camera must have seen the current step finished. Otherwise the coach says why, boxes what is unfinished, and lets you continue only if you say next again.
- **Hands-free.** Say next, done, repeat or back, or just ask a question.
- **Built not to nag.** It speaks only when two checks agree, waits 15 s between warnings, treats hands in the way as normal work, and moves on by itself when the work matches the step.

![Coaching: a step read aloud, the irreversible guard with a SAM box, a spoken answer](docs/images/coach.jpg)

It works on any tutorial with no setup or training. We tested it on a game console repair, a pasta recipe, a pressure bandage and an origami crane.

## How it works

1. **Prep, once per tutorial.** Muse Voice Transcribe turns the narration into timestamped text. Muse Spark watches the video with that narration and returns the steps as JSON validated with zod. ffmpeg grabs a reference picture per step.
2. **Live loop.** The phone streams camera frames and microphone audio over a WebSocket. Muse Spark judges each batch of frames against the step's reference picture. A small state machine decides whether to speak, warn, move on or stop you. SAM 3.1 boxes the object the warning is about.
3. **Voice.** The backend proxies Muse Voice Transcribe realtime. Short phrases are commands, longer ones are questions answered by Muse Spark. The phone speaks with the browser's speech synthesis and lowers the tutorial while it talks.

# SIAGA.ID - verifiable disaster intelligence for Indonesia

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon submission · Track: Build for Your World**

[![Test gate](https://github.com/anggarabudiyantooo-hub/firewatch-id/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/anggarabudiyantooo-hub/firewatch-id/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

Live: <https://firewatch-id.vercel.app> · Repo: <https://github.com/anggarabudiyantooo-hub/firewatch-id> · License: [MIT](LICENSE)

> A public-interest tool, **not a replacement for official sources**. For emergency
> decisions follow BMKG, BNPB/BPBD, PVMBG and KLHK. Emergency number in Indonesia: **112**.

---

## 1. The problem 

During Indonesian haze and fire seasons, a resident sees a grey sky and has three
questions that no single official page answers quickly:

1. Is what I see supported by any public data, or is it fog, dust, or a cloud?
2. Where is the smoke likely to travel, and which places are in the frame?
3. Can I hand something trustworthy to a neighbourhood group, a school, or a journalist?

Raw satellite detections are hard to read. Screenshots of dashboards lose their
legend, timestamp and attribution, so they travel as unattributed pictures.
Generative assistants make this worse when they invent numbers: a confident
"5,000 people affected" is dangerous when no dataset says so.

## 2. The solution

SIAGA.ID keeps a strict division of labour:

- **Code owns every number.** Deterministic, read-only tools compute counts,
  distances, AQI values, wind vectors and time-window comparisons.
- **Meta Muse Spark owns language and vision.** It picks tools, resolves place names, reads a map image,
  and describes what is visible in a citizen photo.
- **Code checks the model afterwards.** Every figure in an answer is matched against
  tool results. The model gets one chance to correct itself; anything still unmatched
  is flagged in the interface instead of being quietly removed.

Four user-facing results:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Agentic assistant** (`/dashboard`) | 17 read-only tools (including `find_place`, which resolves a named city to coordinates so the agent never asks the user for a bounding box), evidence receipts `[E1]`-`[E8]`, a numeric verifier badge, and "Show on map" buttons that move the map only to coordinates a tool returned. |
| **Map snapshot** (`/dashboard`, `/reports`) | "Capture map" composites the live Leaflet map to PNG with legend, attribution, WIB timestamp, bounding box, zoom and timeline frame baked into the image. |
| **Report with AI narrative** (`/reports`) | The snapshot plus a code-computed numeric summary plus a Muse Spark narrative written from the image and the data. Export as PNG or a one-page PDF. Before/after two-frame comparison supported. |
| **Cek Asap / Smoke Check** (`/cek-asap`) | A citizen photo or description plus place and time. Muse Spark describes only what is visible; code gathers evidence and returns *supported / not yet supported / not enough data*

# vreview: code review for dubbed and AI-generated video

AI dubbing and video generation produce more footage than people can check. vreview reviews a video the way a
senior engineer reviews a pull request. You upload the media and a brief, and it returns timestamped threads
(blocker, should-fix, needs-human, nit) with evidence and a fix instruction a generator can act on. Results
come back over REST, MCP or a webhook, and a review UI plays the original and the dub side by side.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Nov 2026), **Indie developer track**, theme **Build for
Your World**. Meta's **Muse
Spark** watches and listens to the video, and deterministic signal processing keeps it honest.

**Demo video (1:42):** https://github.com/crystalphantom/video-evals/releases/download/demo-2026-11-04/vreview-demo.mp4

## How Meta's models are used

| Role | Model (default config) | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Audio-video judge (`av_judge`) | `meta:muse-spark-1.3` | Gets short clips of the original and the dub (video + audio, `video_url` parts) around every located issue. Confirms or disputes each issue and reports what the other checks can't see: lip sync, a voice that doesn't fit the speaker, lost emotion, TTS artifacts, visual glitches, brief mismatch |
| Dub text judge | `meta:muse-spark-1.3` + `gateway:gemini-flash`, ensemble | Compares the original and dubbed transcripts line by line for meaning, missing or added content, tone and names. Both models judge every chunk, findings are merged, and agreement raises confidence |
| Review writer | `meta:muse-spark-1.3` | Writes each thread's title, comment and the review summary. It cannot change a priority, a timestamp or the set of issues |

One rule shapes the design: **timestamps only come from deterministic layers** (VAD, alignment, ASR word
times, shot and face analysis). The models judge evidence that is already located. A new finding from the
audio-video judge inherits its window's bounds, and a disputed issue keeps its time but drops to
`needs-human`. That's the defence against hallucinated issues.

Every model is a config value, so nothing is tied to Meta or any other vendor (see [Models and providers](#models-and-providers)).

## Pipeline

```
upload (presigned multipart) ─▶ POST /v1/reviews ─▶ Hatchet DAG
  ingest ─▶ plan tracks ─▶ features (child run per audio track: ASR, separation)
         ─▶ pairs (child run per dub: timing, sync, text judge, mouth activity)
         ─▶ assemble ─▶ audio-video judge (Muse Spark) ─▶ triage + LLM comments ─▶ review.json, DB, webhook
```

Each stage writes pipeline events: status, duration, sub-runs, models used, issue counts, and whether the
result came from cache. `GET /v1/reviews/{id}/pipeline` returns them, and the review page draws them live as
a timeline. Stage results are cached by content hash and config, so changing one model only reruns the
stages that use it.

## What's in the repo

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `src/dubeval/` | Dubb

# Outgrid Plan Agent

Verified AI trip planning for digital nomads — built for the **Meta Global AI
Developer Hackathon** (Startup track · **Build for Your World**), Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026.

## What it does

Long-stay travel planning fails two ways: doing it yourself takes weeks of
scattered research, and generic AI tools invent the details that matter —
prices, places, and how long you can legally stay.

Outgrid Plan Agent is a multi-agent workflow built on top of Outgrid's reviewed
destination data:

1. **Planner** (Muse Spark, via the Meta Model API) turns a traveler's
   constraints — destination, dates, budget range, pace, coworking and fitness
   needs — into a structured, day-by-day plan drawn **only** from Outgrid's
   destination records. Every factual item carries a source reference to the
   exact record field it came from.
2. **Verifier** (Muse Spark Open — `meta-models/muse-spark-open` — served
   via Baseten) checks every claim in the draft against those source records
   and returns a per-claim verdict: `supported`, `unsupported`, or
   `unverifiable`. Unsupported claims go back to the Planner once, with the
   flags attached. Nothing passes silently. A deterministic
   **exact-number check** (plain code, no model) runs alongside it: every
   dollar amount in a plan item must appear exactly in a source field that
   item cites, or the item is flagged unsupported too. The code check can
   add a flag; it can never remove one. Any item the Verifier returns no
   verdict for is accounted for as `unverifiable` — never passed by silence.
3. **Verifier-gated publish** — a plan publishes automatically once
   verification completes with zero `unsupported` claims. Still-flagged items
   are dropped and logged; `unverifiable` items publish flagged. No human in
   the loop — the second model is the gate. The verified plan becomes a
   shareable trip page with source citations.

Visa and safety content is only used when the underlying record field is
human-reviewed; otherwise it is omitted or flagged unverifiable. The model
never invents hotels, prices, transit times, or stay rules.

outgrid.io's experience — a cinematic billboard, horizontal rails,
hover-expand cards, a detail modal, My List and Continue Planning, in

search, Nomad Score bands, type filters and sorting, country and

data snapshot in `data/`.

**Search in your own words:** the homepage also takes a plain-language
request ("quiet beach town under $1,200 with fast wifi"). Muse Spark
translates it into the classic filters as strict JSON; the records do
the matching, and the results page shows the interpreted filters as
chips — if nothing matches everything, inferred thresholds are loosened
one at a time and the page says exactly what was loosened. The model

# Baba Time

Voice-driven promo screens for small shops, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

A shop owner takes a photo of a product and says "Croissants -20 % until 11am on the window screen".
An agent built on Muse Spark turns that sentence into a verified 1920x1080 visual and puts it on the shop TV.
When the end time comes, the screen goes back to its idle state.

The shop and its catalogue (Boulangerie des Tilleuls) are fictitious demo data. The interface is in French.

## How it works

1. **Remote** (`/remote`, on the phone): push to talk, optional product photo, or a text field.
2. **Transcription**: Muse Voice Transcribe (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) turns the recording into text.
3. **Agent**: Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`) calls tools in a loop: find the product, list screens,
   compute the promo, cut out the product, generate a background, compose, verify, publish.
4. **Cutout**: SAM 3.1 (`sam-3.1`) segments the product on the photo.
5. **Background**: Muse Image (`muse-image-1.0`) generates a background with no text, logos or people.
6. **Composition**: prices and texts are drawn by code (satori + sharp), never by the image model.
7. **Verification**: Muse Spark looks at the final visual (structured output) and reports issues with zones.
   A blocking issue sends the agent back to fix the layout (2 corrections max). Nothing is published unverified.
8. **Screens** (`/player/<screen>`): full screen TV page, updated live over Server-Sent Events.
9. **Dashboard** (`/dashboard`): live agent steps, flagged zones drawn on each verified visual, screen states.

## Compliance

- **Omnibus directive** (French Consumer Code, art. L112-1-1): the struck price is the lowest price of the
  previous 30 days, computed in code only (`src/lib/pricing.ts`).
- **Voice data**: audio is processed in memory, never written to disk, logged or kept after transcription.
- **Photos**: re-encoded with sharp (EXIF and GPS metadata removed). Only the cutout is kept.
- **AI transparency** (AI Act, art. 50): a "Visuel généré par IA" notice is shown on the player.
- **Intellectual property**: image and web search are disabled for Muse Image, prompts forbid logos and brands.

## Security

- Secrets only in `.env.local` (ignored by git).
- `/remote`, `/dashboard` and their APIs require a signed httpOnly session cookie (`SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` over HTTPS).
- Player access uses a token compared in constant time; read only.
- In-memory rate limits: login 5/min, commands 10/min.
- Uploads are checked: photo jpeg/png/webp up to 5 MB, WAV audio up to 2 MB and 30 s, text up to 500 characters.
- Tool arguments are validated with zod; identifiers are opaque and checked server side.

## Stack

Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript), React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, SQLite (better-sqlite3),
OpenAI SDK pointed at the Meta API, `@meta-sam/parser`, sharp, satori, zod.

# Unknown Ally + Ally voice agent (Meta AI Developer Hackathon)

Unknown Ally is a local-first Android life tracker: sleep, time blocks, habits, meals, gym, expenses, reminders. All data lives in SQLite on the phone.

Ally is the voice agent inside it. You talk, it acts. It runs on Meta's models:

- **Muse Voice Transcribe** turns speech into text.
- **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`, falling back to `muse-spark-1.2`) decides what to do and calls tools that write to the local database.
- **Muse Spark vision** reads a photo of a receipt and logs each expense.

Hackathon theme: **Build for Your World**. Track: **Indie Developer**.

## What Ally does

Tap the Ally button (or say "Hey Ally" with the wake word on) and speak normally:

- "Push day, 4 sets of bench at 80 for 8, then 3 sets of rows at 60 for 10" logs a gym session with every set.
- "Two rotis and dal, 500 ml water, and tick meditation" runs three tools in one turn (parallel tool calls).
- "Block 5 AM tomorrow for boxing, and set voice alarms at 4:00 and 4:30" creates a calendar block and two alarms that speak aloud until dismissed.
- Tap **Scan receipt**, photograph a bill, and Muse Spark reads the line items and calls `log_expense` for each one.
- Ally also checks in on its own: a dinner check at 10 PM, a short debrief at 11:30 PM, and a nudge after 45 minutes of continuous YouTube or gaming (from Android usage stats). It stays neutral and never gives medical advice.

## How it uses Meta

```
mic -> native Kotlin AudioRecord (16 kHz mono WAV, on-device silence detection)
    -> POST api.meta.ai/v1/asr/transcribe   (muse-voice-transcribe-1.0, keyword biasing)
    -> POST api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions (muse-spark-1.3, tools, reasoning_effort=low)
    -> tool calls run locally against SQLite (log_gym_session, log_meal, log_expense, create_reminder, ...)
    -> tool results go back to Muse Spark, which writes a one or two sentence spoken reply
    -> on-device text to speech
```

Details worth knowing:

- Muse Voice Transcribe only accepts WAV (mono 16-bit PCM). The old recorder produced AAC, so I rewrote the recorder in Kotlin to capture raw PCM, and wrote the multipart upload in Kotlin too ([AudioRecordModule.kt](android/app/src/main/java/com/kushal/unknownally/AudioRecordModule.kt)).
- End of speech is detected on the phone from the live PCM peak, so Ally stops listening about half a second after you stop talking.
- The agent loop lets Muse Spark call several tools in one turn, reads the results, and can call more (up to 6 rounds). See [conversationEngine.ts](src/lib/ai/conversationEngine.ts).
- Tool schemas live in [tools.ts](src/lib/ai/tools.ts). Arguments are validated before anything is written.
- The API client is [metaClient.ts](src/lib/ai/metaClient.ts). It retries 429 and 5xx once, falls back to the previous Muse Spark version, and drops the photo from history after its turn so it is never sent twice.

# CausalWorld

A prototype scientific agent that learns a hidden physical mechanism from video by choosing experiments. Two discs on a table are joined by a hidden link, either a spring or a rope. The agent sees only camera frames, picks impulses to apply, updates a numerical posterior, and predicts a motion it has never seen. An independent evaluator then scores that prediction against the hidden truth.

Project website, with the demo and films: [asoncode.github.io/CausalWorld](https://asoncode.github.io/CausalWorld/)

This is a designed two-mechanism sandbox with noiseless renders, not a general world model. Evaluation rules are in [docs/PREREG.md](docs/PREREG.md).

## Results
From one held-out run under the [preregistration](docs/PREREG.md): two experiments cut mean final-frame error on 200 episodes from 33.07 px to 0.51 px. Muse ran 300 trials with no failures and reached 0.52 px on its 120 free trials, choosing experiments without planner scores. A fixed two-step script ties Muse and every adaptive planner at two probes. Full results and their limits are in [docs/results/RESULTS.md](docs/results/RESULTS.md).

## How it works
| Component | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| World | `backend/physics/` | Private simulator and renderer, run as a subprocess with no reveal route |
| Perception | `backend/perception/` | Tracks discs in frames; makes contact sheets |
| Beliefs and planner | `backend/beliefs/` | Exact posterior over mechanism, stiffness, and mass; forecasts; probe scoring |
| Agent | `backend/agents/` | Tools, and Meta Muse as a bounded experimenter |
| Evaluator | `backend/experiments/`, `scripts/` | Matched trials, scoring, preregistered analysis, held-out lock |
| Demo | `frontend/`, `scripts/build_demo.py` | A static page stepping through one real experiment |
| Website and films | `web/`, `scripts/visual/` | The project site, figures, and films, built from the public results. |

Muse chooses experiments through tools. It never sees planner scores or hidden values, and every number it sees is computed by deterministic tools.

Requires [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Commands run from the repository root.

# Meety

Your Meety meets theirs first. With receipts.

Meety builds an AI of you from your own chat history, using only the parts you approve. Before two people spend an evening, a weekend or a company on each other, their two Meetys talk first and play out how the two of them would probably react: would they get along, could one help the other, would they agree on a deal. Each person gets a short brief, and every line of it quotes the words it rests on. Meety never scores a person.

It is live at [heymeety.com](https://heymeety.com). The app was called Meet First until November 2026, so the code, the packages and the database still use that name.

## Try it

1. Open the site and choose **Continue with Google**.
2. Home is your feed. Six sample people are already on it: Maya, Priya, Ravi, Jun, Leila and Tomas. They are made up, marked Sample, and accept a friend request at once.
3. Add one of them as a friend, open Meety, and ask how they would react to something, such as "would Maya enjoy a weekend hackathon?". Meety plans the question and waits for your press; Maya's Meety then answers from her notes and quotes them.
4. To make your own Meety, upload a ChatGPT, Claude or Codex export, or paste your notes. Your browser keeps only your own messages and removes secrets and contact details before anything is sent. You approve your card item by item.
   You can also copy Meety's prompt into your own ChatGPT or Claude and paste the summary it writes; Meety checks each of its quotes against your own messages, and **Try your Meety** on your profile asks it a question about you.
5. Once your card is approved, open someone's profile, press **See how you'd get on** and pick a question. The two Meetys talk for about ten minutes; watch it live or read the brief afterwards.

You can also post photos and 24-hour stories, and like other people's posts. Nobody sees a count of your likes.

## How it works

Your browser reads the export, keeps your own messages, and scrubs them; the server scrubs them again and stores how many things it removed, which is the number you see. A model builds your card from those messages, and each card item carries the quote it came from. When two people meet, each Meety speaks from its own card, and every claim it makes carries a quote from a message or is marked as having none. Code checks every quote word for word against the message it names, and a second model call reports how often the brief's quotes back their lines.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[apps/web in the browser] -->|scrubbed messages, JSON routes| A[apps/api]
  A --> P[(Postgres 16, row-level security)]
  P -->|background jobs| W[apps/worker]
  W --> L[packages/llm]
  L --> M[Meta Model API]
  W --> P
  P -. meeting events .-> A
  A -->|live meeting stream| B
```

The raw export never leaves the browser, and only the worker talks to the model.

The model never decides what is stored, what is public, or what is deleted. Those rules are code, and Postgres enforces them

# TailorFit

A tailor sends a customer a link. The customer takes a front photo and a side photo on their own phone, types in their height, and a minute later the tailor has a twelve-measurement sheet — each number marked with how confident we actually are in it, plus the yardage and a cutting sheet ready to print.

We built this on Meta's models (SAM 3.1, Muse Spark, Muse Image) for Meta's Build for Your World hackathon, Startup track.

![TailorFit landing page](media/landing.jpg)

**Live app:** https://tailorfit-yhoi.onrender.com  
**Demo login:** `etimpaul22@gmail.com` — password is in the submission form, not here.

The demo account already has a few sample customers in it so you don't have to create one from scratch. It's on Render's free tier, so if nobody's hit it in a while the first load takes ten or twenty seconds to wake up. That's normal, not a bug.

## Why we built it

In Nigeria, and in a lot of places, made-to-measure clothing still runs on someone physically measuring you. That means a trip to the tailor, or a relative with a tape sending numbers over a WhatsApp voice note. Numbers get mixed up, a customer who's travelled can't be measured at all, and if the cloth was bought by the yard, a bad number is an expensive mistake.

There are body-measurement apps already. Most of them give you one clean, confident-looking number and let you find out at the fitting whether it was right. That's the part we didn't want to copy. A tailor can't cut from a number they don't trust, so instead of pretending to be more accurate than we are, TailorFit tells the tailor which two or three numbers are actually worth checking with a tape, and leaves the rest alone.

## What it actually does

For the tailor: add a customer, send them a private link, and watch the order fill in on its own once they've sent their photos. Every measurement shows up marked high, medium or low confidence, with a "tape these first" note pointing at the two or three numbers worth double-checking. There are thirteen styles to choose from — agbada, senator, kaftan, buba and sokoto, gown, mermaid gown, iro and buba, bubu, skirt and blouse, jumpsuit, dashiki, shirt, trousers — each with its own ease settings you can adjust, and the yardage updates live for 36, 45 or 60-inch cloth. When you're happy, print the cutting sheet.

For the customer, it's just a link opened on their phone — nothing to install. The camera tells them live when their whole body is actually in frame before it lets them take the photo, which sounds small but turns out to matter a lot. They can add a photo of their own fabric and see roughly what the finished outfit would look like in it. Faces get blurred automatically, photos are deleted right after processing unless they choose to let the tailor keep them, and they can ask for deletion at any point from their own link.

# GuardianBees Beta

GuardianBees is a Python backend that detects unusual network behavior. It
captures traffic, aggregates it into behavioral features, scores those features
with an Isolation Forest, and sends only detected anomalies to Meta Model API
for a human-readable security assessment.

## Runtime pipeline

```text
Network packets
      |
      v
Scapy sniffer
      |
      v
Normalized packet events
      |
      v
30-second aggregation per source IP
      |
      v
Traffic history (data/traffic.jsonl)
      |
      v
Isolation Forest anomaly detection (score >= 65%)
      |
      +---- normal behavior allow-list --> skip Meta
      |
      v
Public IP ownership lookup
      |
      v
Meta Model API triage for new anomalies
      |
      v
Persistent active alerts and frontend alert cards
```

### 1. Backend startup

`server.py` starts a FastAPI application with Uvicorn. During application
startup, `AnalyzerRuntime`:

1. Loads the retained traffic history.
2. Trains an Isolation Forest when at least two records are available.
3. Starts the network sniffer in a background thread.

If there is not enough history, the server still starts, but live windows are
only logged until the detector is trained. Training can also be requested later
with `POST /analyzer/train`.

### 2. Network sniffing

`functions/DataProcess/sniffer.py` uses Scapy to capture IPv4 packets. Each
packet is converted into a normalized event containing:

- timestamp, source and destination IP;
- protocol and ports;
- TCP SYN information;
- direction;
- DNS query name;
- packet size.

Packet capture normally requires `NET_RAW`, `NET_ADMIN`, or equivalent host
permissions.

### 3. Processing and aggregation

`functions/DataProcess/agregator.py` groups events into 30-second windows per
source IP. It calculates requests, unique ports, destination ports, destinations
and protocols, bytes, SYN requests, direction counts, and DNS query information.

### 4. Storage

`functions/logger.py` appends aggregated windows to
`data/traffic.jsonl`. Records older than 30 days are removed when the log is
updated. Docker mounts `./data` so traffic history, Meta usage information, and
the normal-behavior list survive container recreation.

### 5. Isolation Forest analysis

`functions/analyzer.py` trains `sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest` from the
numeric features in the retained traffic history. Each new window receives a normalized anomaly score from 0 to 100. A window is
forwarded for triage when its score is at least `65`.

Models are saved as timestamped files in `models/`. The latest trained model is
kept in memory and used for live windows.

### 6. Meta analysis

Only new anomalous windows are passed to `functions/AI/MetaAI.py`. An IP already
stored as an active alert is not sent to Meta again until resolved. The client
sends aggregated metrics, not raw packets, including destination ports and
best-effort public IP ownership. Meta is asked to return:

- `is_alert`;
- `danger_score` from

# Mane Bazaar

**Her shop, in her language, in the chat she already uses.**

Mane Bazaar is a chat-first marketplace for women who run businesses from home and for small farmers in Karnataka. A seller sets up a shop, lists her products and manages her orders entirely from a chat: by speaking Kannada, sending a photo of her notebook, recording a short video, or tapping a button. Her shop appears at once on a public website where buyers can find her and order.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**, track *Build for Your World*, on **Meta Model API**.

---

## The problem

Around us in Karnataka, women sell holige, pickles, snacks, children's clothes and tailoring from home, and small farmers sell produce nearby. Their businesses are real but invisible:

- Orders live in a **paper notebook**; sales travel by **word of mouth**.
- Online marketplaces expect **English, typing, forms, photography and a website**.
- With records on paper, there is no clear picture of **what sells, who comes back, or what to prepare**.

Mane Bazaar does not ask them to learn a new app. It turns the chat they already use into a layer that does the digital work for them.

## What it does

### For sellers (in Telegram)

| She does this | Mane Bazaar does this |
|---|---|
| Says "hi" | Asks her language (ಕನ್ನಡ / English / हिंदी) with buttons, then sets up her shop one question at a time |
| Sends a **Kannada voice note** ("holige, 30 rupees, 50 pieces") | Transcribes it, reads the item back, saves it after her "yes" |
| Photographs her **notebook page** | Reads the handwritten list (even sideways), flags unclear digits, adds the items after she confirms |
| Records a **short video** of her batch while saying the prices | Watches the clip and listens to it, combines both into one list |
| Sends a **product photo** | Attaches it to the right item and offers to clean up the background (original always kept) |
| Asks "do I need FSSAI?" | Answers from official sources with links |
| Opens the chat the next morning | Shows her current list and asks *Same as before / Change some items / Start a new list* |
| Sends `/review` | Gets a weekly review: what sold, what didn't, repeat buyers, what to prepare next week |

Every change is **read back and saved only after she says yes**.

### For buyers (public website)

- Browse shops by **home seller or farmer, category, region and delivery terms**.
- Ask in plain words: *"pickles under 200 in Bagalkot?"* An assistant answers **only from live listings** and highlights the matching shops.
- **Order in chat** opens the bot for that shop. The seller is notified instantly, and the buyer gets a **UPI link that pays the seller directly**. Mane Bazaar never holds money.

### For sellers who prefer a screen (private dashboard)

Kannada / English dashboard to open or pause the shop, edit items, move orders from *new* to *handed over*, record payments, read the daily brief and the weekly review, and print a business record.

---

# Harvest Outlook

Harvest Outlook is a progressive web app for Indian farmers. It compares crops for a farm's location, plans seasons visually, shows a daily "Today" view for each field, and keeps a farm journal. An assistant called Evara answers questions about the farm using the farm's own records, and accepts voice input.

Live demo: https://harvest-outlook.venkatselvan.com (API: https://api-harvest-outlook.venkatselvan.com)

## Features

- **Farms and fields.** Draw a farm and the fields inside it on a satellite map. Each field has its own crops, Today view, plan and records. An "All farms" overview shows every farm at a glance.
- **Today view.** Per-field weather and forecast, crop stage, upcoming steps, alerts (weather, price, crop-threat rules, satellite greenness drop), Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, a profit and footprint estimate, and AI-predicted looks of the field at a future stage. Predicted looks are labelled as generated images.
- **Crop fit.** Ranks crops for a field by sowing date, by season, or for the next crop, using a catalogue of 25 crops and the farm's soil, water and rotation history.
- **Year plan.** Suggests crop sequences for the current year and up to three later years, with plan labels, rotation, green manure and intercropping options, and profit ranges from regional yields and past prices. Saved seasons can be swapped.
- **Season preview.** A calendar of stages, typical weather, a price path and care steps for a chosen crop and sowing date.
- **Market timeline.** Historical mandi price ranges by week, and the latest recorded quotes, for the crops the price data covers.
- **Journal.** Dated entries with photos, expenses and sales, care completion, field checks and an issue log with responses. Season totals and a printable season report with CSV export.
- **Soil report review.** Upload or enter a soil test report, confirm the values, and see them rated against published bands and compared with the crops in the plan.
- **Photo coverage.** Mark the planted area on a field photo and estimate the coverage share.
- **Evara assistant.** Chat grounded in the farm briefing and a curated evidence set, with inline voice input (editable transcript, text answers).
- **Offline PWA.** Installable, caches the app shell, and keeps journal drafts on the device when offline.

## Tech stack

- Web: SolidJS, Vite, Leaflet, a service-worker PWA (vite-plugin-pwa, Workbox).
- API: Fastify 5 with Zod contracts, TypeScript.
- Database: PostgreSQL.
- Worker: a background job process for data ingest, plan and crop-fit jobs, monitoring and image jobs.
- Analytics: a Python package (`analytics/`) for forecasting and evaluation (numpy, pandas).
- AI: Meta models only, used at runtime for interpretation, vision, constrained orchestration, image generation and speech recognition. Speech recognition is for voice input only; there is no speech synthesis.
- Forecasting, rules, arithmetic, water balance and animation are plain code, not AI. Models do no

# MeetMind

A real-time meeting copilot that runs beside Zoom, Microsoft Teams or Google Meet. It never joins the meeting and never adds a bot.

> Other copilots start thinking when the question is asked and give everyone the same textbook answer. MeetMind prepares before the meeting, answers from your own work with the source, and only speaks when a question is aimed at you.

## What it does

1. **Detects** when someone asks you a question and shows an alert within 1 second.
2. **Answers** with a cue card: one short line you can say out loud, a few cue points, and the source. Most cards are prepared before the meeting from your agenda and documents, so they appear instantly. Unexpected questions get a live, grounded card within 3 seconds.
3. **Suggests one question** in your topic area when the room opens up for questions.
4. **Takes notes** during the meeting: short running notes the answers also draw on.

## How it is different

- **When it helps:** it prepares before the meeting. Likely questions are predicted and answered ahead of time, then matched live.
- **What it knows:** it answers from your own documents and profile, and every fact about your work carries a source. If something is not in your docs, the card says so instead of guessing.
- **How it shows answers:** small pinned cue cards that never change while you read them. New cards queue below. It stays quiet on small talk and when unsure.
- **When someone gets your work wrong:** "You're just querying the database, right?" is checked against your documents read whole. If they say otherwise, the card says "Your docs say otherwise" with the line to say and the exact quote.
- **What is on screen:** with See my screen on, "what do you make of this chart?" is answered from a picture of the screen.
- **Before the meeting:** rehearse. The app asks the likely questions out loud, checks your spoken answer against your documents, and keeps your own words as the card.

## Meta AI hackathon

MeetMind is entered under "Build for Your World". The problem is the author's own: in the first call with a new manager, the questions came fast, one of them got the author's work wrong, and the right answer was in documents the author had written.

**Meta models.** Every language step runs on Muse Spark through the Meta Model API (`LLM_PROVIDER=meta`, decisions [0008](docs/decisions/0008-meta-models-for-the-hackathon.md) and [0009](docs/decisions/0009-hackathon-features.md)):

- the question checker that decides whether a question is aimed at you, as strict JSON;
- the cue card, streamed so the line to say arrives first;
- the claim checker, which reads all your documents whole in one call and returns a verdict with a quote; the verdict counts only when the quote is really in a document;
- screen-aware answers: a picture of your screen goes to Muse Spark with the question;
- the question predictor, the suggest-a-question agent, the meeting notes and the rehearsal reviewer.

## Jalankan

```sh
npm ci
python -m venv .venv
```

Windows:

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.lock
```

macOS / Linux:

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.lock
```

```sh
npm run dev:all
```

Buka **http://127.0.0.1:5173**. Launcher memilih Python `.venv` otomatis. Backend mendengarkan `127.0.0.1:8000`; Vite mem-proxy `/api`. Menjalankan terpisah: `npm run dev:api` dan `npm run dev`.

## Yang dapat digunakan tanpa API key

- Upload JPG / PNG / WebP maksimal 10 MB / 24 megapiksel, pemeriksaan isi file, decode ulang dan penghapusan EXIF.
- Pemilihan objek memakai box persentase, preview hasil crop untuk diterima/ditolak, dan jalur **manual fallback** yang eksplisit. Crop manual **tidak menghapus latar di dalam box dan tidak mengkartunkan foto**.
- Inspector: source comparison, checkerboard, nama, jenis, tags, origin, bounds alpha terukur, provenance dan warnings.
- Tiga motion preset: `idle_bob`, `interact_pulse`, `impact_flash`. Semua berupa transformasi prosedural satu sprite; dapat dihapus untuk aset statis.
- ZIP PNG RGBA 512×512 + metadata + timeline + SHA-256, dengan atlas empat frame jika motion dipilih. Compiler membuka ulang ZIP untuk validasi.
- Library dari SQLite, tetap tersedia pada browser baru; download tanpa akun, penghapusan aset, discard draft, dan preview cleanup upload tak terpakai yang lebih tua dari 24 jam.
- Playground Phaser independen: unggah ZIP lokal, verifikasi file, pilih motion, play/pause/restart/scrub, origin dan grid. File ZIP diproses di browser tanpa mengunggahnya ke server.

## Model Meta: konfigurasi dan batas bukti

Salin `.env.example` menjadi `.env`, isi `MODEL_API_KEY` **di server saja**, lalu restart API. Jangan gunakan prefix `VITE_` untuk secret.

Adapter mengikuti [Responses API Meta](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/overview):

1. `sam-3.1`: seleksi box/label, decoding mask menggunakan parser resmi `meta-sam-parser`.
2. `muse-image-1.0`: edit cutout menjadi gaya pilihan (`storybook_toy_v1`, `cartoon_8bit_v1`, atau `cartoon_3d_v1`), lalu SAM menyegmentasi latar artwork. 3. `muse-spark-1.3`: saran metadata deskriptif dengan schema ketat; bukan geometri atau gameplay.

# Ruth IDE — See your code as a map, change it with Muse

Ruth is a desktop IDE that reads a project locally and draws it as an
architecture map: pages, stores, services, controllers, and the modules
and routes that wire them. Meta's Muse proposes changes to that code,
and every change arrives as a review you accept or discard. Nothing is
written to disk without your Accept.

## The problem

Requirements change every day, and nobody knows which code they touch.
AI writes code fast, but it gets harder to know what it did. Ruth keeps
the understanding with the person: the map comes from parsed code, not
from AI, and Muse's work shows up on that map before it reaches the
disk.

## What it does

- **Architecture map.** Classes, Files and Pages views of an Angular,
  NestJS, TypeScript or Rust project, grouped by layer. Every edge
  carries its evidence; what cannot be verified is shown as
  unresolved, never connected.
- **Show flow.** Follows a feature from a template through the store
  and the service to the HTTP call and the backend controller.
- **Muse in the Assistant.** Ask about the code, or Propose change.
  Before anything is sent, Ruth says exactly what leaves the machine.
  For a change, Muse first picks the files it needs from their paths,
  and you see that list before any code is sent.
- **Proposals as reviews.** The new code appears on the map in pink
  (the Code X-ray), with Ruth's own checks, a diff per file and a
  preview of new Angular templates. Answer Muse's questions or adjust
  the proposal; each change is a new version of the same requirement.
- **Your decision.** Accept file by file or all at once. Each accept
  checks the file's fingerprint, so a file changed on disk since is
  never overwritten.
- **Private code stays private.** Mark a folder Never send to Muse;
  this is enforced in the backend, not only in the interface.
- **Integrated terminal** to build and test without leaving Ruth.

## Muse: real calls, only from buttons

Every call goes to real Meta models (Responses API, default
`muse-spark-1.3`) and fires only from an explicit button. Never at
startup, and never from tests. The key lives in `META_API_KEY` in the
native process environment; it never reaches the frontend, logs or
files.

# ActionProof

**Approve the exact action. Prove the actual effect.**

ActionProof binds a human approval to one exact, hashed action, so an AI agent
cannot execute a changed one — and it keeps the evidence that proves what
actually happened.

[![Demo video](docs/screenshots/02-run-workspace-blocked.png)](https://github.com/sksaddam007/ActionProof/blob/main/actionproof-demo-silent.mp4)

> ### ▶ [Watch the 3-minute demo](https://github.com/sksaddam007/ActionProof/blob/main/actionproof-demo-silent.mp4)
>
> `actionproof-demo-silent.mp4` — 1920×1080, exactly 3:00, recorded against the
> running stack with live Meta model calls. Click the image above, or
> [download it directly](https://github.com/sksaddam007/ActionProof/raw/main/actionproof-demo-silent.mp4).
> The narration script with timecodes is in [DEMO.md §4](DEMO.md#4-the-3-minute-narration-script).

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Demo** | Local Docker Compose — [one command below](#run-it-in-one-command). No hosted URL. |
| **Video** | [actionproof-demo-silent.mp4](https://github.com/sksaddam007/ActionProof/blob/main/actionproof-demo-silent.mp4) (3:00, silent) |
| **Runbook & measured results** | [DEMO.md](DEMO.md) |
| **Deep setup / architecture notes** | [IMPLEMENTATION.md](IMPLEMENTATION.md) |
| **Submission tag** | `hackathon-submission-v1` |

---

## The problem

Agent frameworks treat approval as a boolean. A human approves a price, a
recipient, a document — and between that click and the tool call, the
underlying resource moves.

> An agent asks you to approve a ₹4,500 purchase. You approve.
> Seconds later the supplier raises the price to ₹7,000.
> The approval is still sitting in the queue, and in most agent stacks it will
> happily execute against the new number.

Afterwards nothing in the system can say what was approved versus what actually
executed. "The agent had approval" is true and useless.

## Who it's for

Teams putting agents on actions with real consequences — procurement, payments,
document delivery, internal ops — and the reviewers who afterwards have to
answer *"what exactly was approved?"*

## What ActionProof does

1. The agent **proposes**. A Meta model reads the task and picks a tool.
2. The **server** — never the model — resolves the live resource, normalizes it
   into an immutable action intent, and hashes it with RFC 8785 canonical JSON
   + SHA-256.
3. A human **approves that digest**: one exact payload, not a sentence the
   agent can reinterpret.
4. At execution the **gateway** re-validates membership, approval state,
   expiry, digest and resource version inside a single transaction under a row
   lock. If anything moved, it commits nothing and demands a fresh card.
5. Every run emits an **evidence packet**: what was approved, what changed, who
   decided, and the effect that actually landed — scored by an independent
   evaluator, not by the agent's own account of itself.

**The whole point in one line:** the model plans; deterministic server code
enforces the app

# EvoDose Select — who should pause?

**In-silico research tool — not medical advice.** EvoDose Select is an AI experiment on
prostate-cancer intermittent hormone therapy. Its first question was "can a personalized
pause/restart rule beat the standard rule for everyone?" On real data the average answer
is barely. So the project now asks the question the data can support:

> **Half the drug, same control — for whom? Which patients save the most drug by
> pausing, without losing time to progression, and which save so little that the
> monitoring burden is hard to justify?**

Nothing it outputs is a treatment recommendation.

— just open it; nothing to install. (If you prefer local: `cd web && python3 -m http.server 8000`,
then open http://localhost:8000. Do not double-click `index.html`; browsers block its data
files over `file://`. Re-running the Python pipeline below is *not* needed to use the deck —
all patient results ship precomputed.)

Click path:

1. **Move** with the ← → arrow keys (↑ ↓ also work), the dots at the top, or the ‹ › buttons.
   Nine slides: the problem, an animated year of treatment, why a break can work, how the
   agent makes its guess, the race, who saves most (two slides), what it would change,
   and the tool last. Or skip straight there with the **Try the tool** button (top-right).
2. **Slide 5 (the race):** press **Play** and watch *Drug always on* vs the *Usual plan* on the
   same cancer — green cells are the ones the drug can kill, red cells the ones it cannot.
   Try **Restart** and the **Speed** control.
3. **Slides 6–7 (who saves most):** the payoff — out of every 100 weeks, how much time off the
   drug a break buys, and the patients our model picks as the biggest savers.
4. **Slide 9 (try it, last slide):** upload your own patient's CSV
   (`patient_id, date, psa_ng_ml, on_treatment`; at least 5 readings on and 5 off the drug)
   and get a saver guess back in seconds. The fit runs entirely in the browser — nothing is
   sent anywhere. No file handy? Click **Use example patient**, or download the example CSV
   from that slide and upload it back. Every patient in the file is fitted and scored
   locally, but that alone makes no guess. Paste a Muse (Meta) API key into the

# Nightshift

A study buddy that runs on the student's own laptop. The student adds their own material
(textbook chapters, slides, notes). Nightshift answers from those pages, shows the exact
lines it used, writes practice questions, and schedules reviews so nothing is forgotten.
For maths it solves and checks the answer with code.

```
python -m nightshift app        # opens the study app in your browser
```

## What it does

| | |
|---|---|
| **Ask** | Answers come from your pages, with the exact lines highlighted and a page or slide number. If your material doesn't cover it, it says so. It does not guess. |
| **Quiz** | Questions are written from your pages. After each answer you see the source line. Misses come back the same day, hits come back later each time (SM-2 spaced repetition). |
| **Tonight** | What's due, how well you know each topic (weakest first), and a button that runs the shift: read new pages, write questions, prepare training examples. |
| **Solve** | Type a constant-coefficient second-order ODE. Code solves it and substitutes the answer back to check it. No model involved. |

Every answer has a label: **Checked by code**, **From your material**, **Not in your material**
or **Not checked** (a cloud model wrote it and nothing verified it).

Files supported: PDF (text PDFs), PPTX (slide text + speaker notes), DOCX, Markdown, plain text.
Everything stays in `~/.nightshift` (set `NIGHTSHIFT_HOME` to change). The server only listens on
127.0.0.1 and refuses requests from other sites.

## How answers stay honest

The check that replaces "trust the model" for non-maths subjects is simple: **a quote must appear
word for word in the page it cites** (`grounding.py`). Case, spacing, curly quotes and dashes are
ignored; nothing else is. Applied everywhere:

- A written answer is kept only if its quotes are found in the cited passage. Numbers in the answer
  that the quoted text doesn't contain cause the model answer to be rejected.
- A model answer with invalid evidence, weak source support, or malformed output gets one corrective
  retry; if it still fails, Nightshift shows exact source text instead of the model's unsupported answer.
- A written quiz question is kept only if its supporting quote is found and its answer is
  supported by that quote. The shift reports how many were rejected.
- If the writer fails the check (or isn't connected), Nightshift falls back to quoting your own
  sentences exactly, and the note says which of those happened.
- Training examples saved for the student model use only checked quotes.

## Works without any AI model, better with one

With no model connected, answers are the most relevant sentences from your pages, and questions are
fill-in-the-blank and "What is X?" built from your text. To get fluent answers and richer questions:

- **Local (private, free):** run Ollama with any chat model (`ollama pull llama3.2`). Nightshift finds
  it at `localhost:11434`. Change with `NIGHTSHIFT_CHAT_URL` / `NIGHTSHI

# Argus
### Agent Registry, Guidance & Unified Supervision

Argus. Multiple coding agents. One command center.

Argus is a lightweight command center for AI coding agents. Run several agents at once on your own machine, walk away, and stay in control from your phone.

![Home Screen](img/argus1.png)

## Why Argus

Named after Argus Panoptes, the hundred eyed giant of Greek myth who never truly slept. Argus watches every agent session at once so you don't have to.

## What it does

- Launch and manage several AI coding agent sessions (OpenCode first, others later) from one dashboard
- Get notified the moment an agent needs your input, hits an error, or finishes
- Respond, approve, or deny requests from your phone, anywhere
- See quota and session state at a glance
- Recover automatically from a closed laptop lid, a lost connection, or a crash

![Live Sessions](img/live_sessions.png)

## System Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Phone["📱 Phone (React PWA)"]
        PWA[PWA Dashboard\nSession list\nApproval composer]
    end

    subgraph Cloud["☁️ Control Plane (Supabase Free Tier)"]
        Auth[(Auth)]
        DB[(Postgres\nSessions, Events, Commands)]
        RT[Realtime\nWebSocket]
    end

    subgraph Laptop["💻 Laptop (Local-First)"]
        Desktop[Tauri Desktop App\nProject cards\nLive session badges]
        GoSvc[Go Service\nProcess manager\nAgent adapters\nSQLite state]
        OpenCode[(OpenCode processes\nOne per project)]
    end

    PWA <-- HTTPS/WSS --> Auth
    PWA <-- HTTPS/WSS --> DB
    PWA <-- WSS --> RT
    RT --> GoSvc
    GoSvc --> OpenCode
    Desktop --> GoSvc
    GoSvc -.-> DB
    GoSvc -.-> RT
```

*The laptop always initiates the outbound connection. Nothing on the laptop is ever reachable from the public internet directly. Provider API keys stay on the laptop, never uploaded to the control plane.*

## Status

Early build (MVP P2). See [docs/prd.md](docs/prd.md) for the full product requirements and [WORKFLOW.md](WORKFLOW.md) for the current milestone.

## Repository layout

```
apps/desktop             Tauri + React desktop app (not yet wired)
apps/pwa                 React PWA, the phone facing remote control (not yet wired)
services/agent-manager   Go local service, process management and agent adapters
supabase                 Database schema and control plane config
docs                     Product, marketing and monetization documents
```

## Stack

Tauri 2, Go, React with TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind, Supabase (Postgres, Auth, Realtime), SQLite locally.

## Built with Muse Wonder

This project was developed using **Muse Wonder** — an AI-native coding assistant that helped accelerate development across the stack:

- **Architecture & scaffolding** — Initial monorepo structure, Tauri + Go service skeleton, Supabase schema design
- **Agent adapter implementation** — OpenCode adapter with process lifecycle management (start, stop, restart, interrupt, send message)

# Bring-Up Bot

An agent that debugs real embedded hardware, fixes it, and proves the fix with an independent hardware test.

Board bring-up costs engineers days of reading datasheets and logs to chase a wrong register value or a misread timing spec. Bring-Up Bot automates that loop: it inspects the board, applies the fix, and re-tests on hardware — each claim is grounded in measured output or datasheet text, and fixes require both kinds of evidence.

## Demo

Video: https://youtu.be/KUl6i8HdIaE

## What it does

Hardware: Raspberry Pi 5 + Honeywell ABP2 pressure sensor (part ABP2DSNT001BD2A3XX, I2C `0x28`, ±1 bar differential). A small app (`pi_app/read_pressure.py`) reads the sensor using settings in `~/abp2_app/config.json`; seeded bugs break that config.

The loop, every run:

1. **Checklist** — the model must state what it will settle before acting.
2. **Inspect** — run an exact-match allowlist of inspection commands (no shell, no arguments) on the Pi, search the ABP2 datasheet; the only write is the app's own sensor measurement command.
3. **Record evidence** — each fact needs a quote from a command output or datasheet snippet; the quote must appear in the source text (case- and whitespace-insensitive match).
4. **Fix** — one `config.json` key at a time, validated and re-tested.
5. **Verify + review** — independent hardware test must pass, then Muse Spark Open independently reviews the final report: every cited finding plus the root cause and fix.

## Meta models and their roles

| Model | Where | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`) | Meta Model API | Drives every decision in the loop |
| Muse Spark Open (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`) | Baseten | Independently reviews the final claims, rejects overreach |
| Muse Code | Dev machine | Builder + read-only reviewer during development |

## Why you can trust the result

- Evidence is accepted only if the quote appears in a real command output or a datasheet snippet the model was shown (case- and whitespace-insensitive match).
- Fixes are refused until at least one fact from a Pi command output and one from the datasheet have been recorded.
- Every fix automatically runs `verification/check_abp2.py` (the agent can't edit it) and the app must agree with it within 0.03 bar.
- The final report is refused unless verification passed and Muse Spark Open independently reviews the final report (every cited finding plus the root cause and fix) and accepts every claim — unless the agent declares a physical fault with needs_human: true, which escalates to a person instead.
- 3 refused final reports escalate to a human; every run also has a turn limit.
- Explicit `needs_human` flag for physical faults (wiring, power, missing device).

## Safety

- Exact-match allowlist of inspection commands (no shell, no arguments); the only write is the app's own sensor measurement command.
- Only `~/abp2_app/config.json` can change, validated per key, written atomically (`.tmp` + `mv`) with a `.bak`

# 23Editor — Your footage. Your story.

A footage-aware mobile editing assistant. A creator uploads a clip, the
app inspects what is actually in it (length, orientation, cuts, speech),
suggests suitable edits, helps write the editing instruction inside the
app, and renders a real edited video — trimmed, captioned, titled,
zoomed, graded, and mixed — with FFmpeg. No external chatbot needed.

## The creator problem

Short-form creators reshoot or wrestle desktop timelines for simple
jobs: "keep the first 10 seconds, title it, zoom the demo, caption the
speech." 23Editor looks at the footage first, turns a spoken sentence
in Tamil, English, or mixed speech into an executable editing plan and
a verified render, with the original voice preserved and every effect
honestly reported.

## What Meta does (and does not do)

- **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) reads the instruction and returns a
  strictly validated editing plan. For visual-event requests without
  timestamps it also reads up to 6 sampled frames.
- **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) transcribes
  voice instructions (Tamil/English/mixed supported) and source speech
  for captions (phrase-level timing; no word alignment claimed).
- **SAM 3.1** (`sam-3.1`) tracks a named subject for reframed segments
  when the plan keeps a `frame_subject` operation.
- **Muse Image** (`muse-image-1.0`) is optional and explicit: thumbnails
  only, never a silent replacement for footage.
- **Muse Wonder** stays off unless explicitly enabled.

Unambiguous requests ("first N seconds") are enforced deterministically
even when the model omits the trim. Only the models each job needs are
called; `/status` (free `GET /v1/models`) shows what is available.
Meta never sees the final render: cutting, effects, mixing, and
verification run locally in FFmpeg.

Visual understanding is local: duration, orientation, scene cuts,
sampled frames, and audio/silence signals come from FFmpeg/ffprobe on
the backend machine, combined with the transcript. The app labels frame
samples as spot checks and never claims frame-perfect understanding.

## Architecture

```text
Flutter app (Android)            Python backend (stdlib only)
─────────────────────            ─────────────────────────────
Create: pick video,              /api/upload      → stored upload
  speak/type instruction           (labeled source or reference)
Workspace:                       /api/analyze     → cancellable footage
  Understand → suggest →           analysis, cached per source
  brief → review → render        /api/brief       → editable edit brief
  cuts/zoom/text/captions        /api/reference/analyze → style match
  music+SFX, cover/artwork       /api/transcribe  → turns + diagnosis
  + image attachments            /api/plan        → validated plan
  reference style card           /api/render      → FFmpeg render,
Projects: local JSON store         ffprobe-verified, served back
Share via system sheet           /api/frame /api/cover → foota

# ShopTalk AI

**Talk to your business. Understand what is happening. Get things done.**

ShopTalk AI is a voice-and-text business operations assistant for small
businesses. An owner says or types what happened — *"sell 2 honey beans
5kg"*, *"we received 20 bags"*, *"spent 5,000 on transport"*, *"how much
did we sell this week?"* — and ShopTalk interprets the request, acts on
the shop's real records through validated backend tools, and answers
from those same records.

This repository is our hackathon build. It is a working end-to-end
product, not a mock-up: every demo request writes to or reads from a
real PostgreSQL database, and the interface, audit trail, and reports
move with it.

- Product specification: [ShopTalk_AI_PRD.md](ShopTalk_AI_PRD.md)
- Deployment: [DEPLOY-COOLIFY.md](DEPLOY-COOLIFY.md)
- Demo business: GeoPure (seeded, see [Demo data](#demo-data-geopure))

---

## The problem

Small businesses run on memory, notebooks, WhatsApp messages, and
spreadsheets. Sales get recorded late or not at all. Stock counts drift.
Expenses vanish. At month end, the owner cannot answer simple questions
— *what did we sell, what is left, are we making money?* — without hours
of manual work.

Generic chatbots do not solve this. They can explain, but they cannot
safely update records, and they will happily invent a price or a stock
figure. ShopTalk AI was built for that gap.

## Our goal

Make business operations accessible in everyday language:

1. **Capture** sales, stock receipts, and expenses by conversation, in
   the moment they happen, by voice or text.
2. **Understand** performance at any time — sales, expenses, profit, low
   stock, trends — answered only from actual records.
3. **Trust** every consequential action: the owner previews and confirms
   it, the backend validates and commits it atomically, and an audit
   trail proves what happened.

The design principle that holds the whole system together:

> **AI interprets and orchestrates. Deterministic backend services
> validate permissions, calculate money and stock, and preserve
> transaction integrity. The assistant never claims success unless the
> backend confirms it.**

## What a user can do

| Workflow | Example | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record a sale | "Sell 2 honey beans 2.5kg" | Items resolved, priced server-side, preview shown, confirmed, committed; stock drops, receipt issued |
| Receive stock | "We received 20 honey beans 5kg" | Restock preview, confirmed, stock rises with a movement record |
| Record an expense | "Spent 4,500 on delivery fuel" | Preview, confirmed, saved and included in reports |
| Add to the catalogue | "Add zobo 1500 to the catalogue" | Preview with name, kind, and price; confirmed, product created; duplicates and missing prices get a question instead |
| Edit or deactivate an item | "Change garri to 6000" / "Remove zobo from the catalogue" | Preview of the change; confirmed, applied (deactivation keeps history, the item just stops selling) |

> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** — Indie Developer track,
> **Build for Your World** theme. Submitted as *MailboxAI*; 

No app to install. No paper piles. This is **mail, not email**: a user messages

mailing address. Family members whose license shows the **same address** join the
same mailbox. Every letter is read, triaged, and acted on by AI — bills get

Businesses — banks, retailers, schools, mortgage companies, local shops —

straight to the customer's WhatsApp, or scan a paper letter and send that.
No printing, no postage, no 3–5 day wait.

- US advertising mail used **~2.00 million tons of paper in 2025**
  (~28–47 million trees).
- The average American gets **16 junk pieces a week, 41 lbs a year**,
  and only **~40% is recycled**.
- Email never killed paper mail: courts, tax offices, banks, HOAs, and
  mortgage companies still send paper, by habit or by law.
- Existing virtual mailboxes are business dashboard apps at
  **$10–$40/month plus per-scan fees** — nothing lives where people
  actually read messages.

- **Messages get seen.** People open WhatsApp through the day to talk
  to family and friends, so mail lands where attention already is —
  not in an email inbox that piles up unread, and not in a paper pile
  on the table.
- **For businesses, it is the richest way to reach the end customer.**
  The customer is already on WhatsApp, the message arrives instantly
  with no printing, postage, or 3–5 day wait, and a verified badge
  tells the customer the sender is real. More than 200 million
  businesses already use the WhatsApp Business app (Meta, 2023), so

- **One channel, both sides.** The same chat that delivers a bill can
