# Pulse

Pulse is a public site for learning how markets feel, without being told what to buy. You ask about a coin, a stock, or a comparison. The reply explains the mood, the case for and against, and what people watch, in plain language. It does not give buy, sell, or hold instructions.

The live site is [https://pulse.lungilemooketsi.engineer](https://pulse.lungilemooketsi.engineer).

The chat is at `/app`. The landing page at `/` shows example replies, not live ones. Signed-in pages also include a Simulation Lab (`/lab`) and an Anomaly Library (`/anomalies`). The method is public at `/model-card`.

## Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon

Pulse is being submitted to the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon) (Cerebral Valley, 26 October to 4 November 2026).

The model it actually calls is **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3`) through the [Meta Model API](https://dev.meta.ai/docs) (`https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions`). The chat Worker uses that model for every reply. The data pipeline uses the same API to draft labels, label stock news, and write anomaly categories. Muse Wonder, Muse Image, and SAM 3.1 are not used.

The closer theme is **Build for Your World**. Pulse is for someone learning markets who should not be handed a trade: in South Africa, personal advice on crypto assets needs an FSCA licence under the FAIS Act. The product takes a problem the author knows (scattered headlines, posts, and prices, and the temptation to treat them as a signal) and uses Muse Spark to explain the mood, both sides, and what to watch, so the reader spends less time assembling that picture. It is not a **Push the Frontier** project: it does not add a new machine capability in software research, robotics, manufacturing, energy, or materials.

On the published criteria, Pulse is a working product rather than a demo. The site is live. Cloudflare Pages serves the app, the `astro-pulse-api` Worker checks a Firebase ID token, rate-limits callers, and streams Muse Spark, and Firestore rules limit each person to their own chat history. The event asks for an open-source GitHub repository.

An earlier note in this repository says the project won the Build on Base hackathon. That claim is kept as a past award. A primary page listing that event's tracks and this project was not found, so no track is assigned here.

# Nemesis

**Every robot needs a nemesis. Real-to-sim red-teaming and reinforcement learning for walking robots.**

[Try Nemesis live](https://nemesis.divagr.com) · [Watch the demo](https://youtu.be/JirwnL-4Ed8)

---

Nemesis turns red-teaming into an interactive real-to-sim feedback loop for quadruped and humanoid robots.

Today, stress-testing a locomotion policy means hand-writing physics configurations and guessing domain-randomization ranges. Nemesis replaces that trial and error with multimodal AI: describe an attack in plain English, say it out loud, or upload a photo of a real place. Meta's Muse models and SAM 3.1 turn the scenario into a physics program, run it against the robot in MuJoCo, and, if it falls, retrain the policy with PPO until it survives.

Every update is regression-tested against a locked test gauntlet before it goes live. On Autopilot, Muse hunts for failure modes on its own; Live deployment tests the robot against a place you describe; and the Readiness report audits any version. The core loop also runs fully self-hosted on a single 24 GB GPU with Muse Glimmer.

---

| **Voice interface** | **Muse Voice Transcribe** | Recorded in the browser, transcribed on the server | Spoken situations on Break it and in You vs Muse. |

| **Physics and training** | **MuJoCo / MJX + Brax** (MuJoCo Playground) | JAX on GPU | Batched rollouts, PPO fine-tuning, contact physics. |

# Kept

The clinic confirmed Thursday. Then it emailed to move you. Then it texted two
new options. Kept is an agent that reads those messages, works out which time
is actually booked, checks new times against your calendar, and drafts the
reply for you to read back and approve. It never sends anything on its own,
and every step it takes has Undo.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (fall 2026), indie track.

  and update my schedule": your agent reads a shared made-up inbox and
  calendar live. Then ask whether the new times clash with your calendar,
  pick one, have it draft the reply, read back each field, and approve
  (sending is simulated). Undo anything from the Activity tab.

  shared by all judges, so add nothing private. Nothing is ever sent. It
  handles scheduling only, not medical questions.

  accepts or rejects the facts it finds, answers the office's open question,

  delete the case or set an appointment's state.
- **Muse Code on Muse Wonder** reviewed every change before it merged. Its
  findings and the fixes are recorded in `docs/decisions/`.

# ProofLoop

**ProofLoop is a bounded coding agent that refuses to call a task done until deterministic checks pass.**

Coding tools often report “fixed” after editing a file. ProofLoop separates the model's
**claim** from the **evidence**: the model proposes a plan and patches, but only code decides the
final status from allowlisted checks, including holdout tests the model never sees.

- **Claims are not evidence.** The model can say “done”; only checks can produce
  `VERIFIED_COMPLETE`. Every run also records what a trust-the-model baseline would have reported.
- **Holdout tests stay hidden.** They live outside the repository and outside every prompt and
  repair message, so the model cannot target them.
- **The verdict is deterministic.** A pure rule function turns check results into
  `VERIFIED_COMPLETE`, `PARTIALLY_VERIFIED`, `FAILED`, or `BLOCKED`. Unknown results never become
  success.

Built during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**.

---

## 1. Demo

**Video (2:25):** https://youtu.be/0jEcke-spfM

The video follows a real live run on `muse-spark-1.3`: on attempt 1 (low reasoning effort) the
model reported *"Visible tests pass"* while pytest reported `1 failed, 11 passed` — its own new
regression test expected the wrong allocation. ProofLoop rejected the claim, fed back only the
failing evidence, and the repair (high reasoning effort) corrected the test; visible and holdout
suites then passed and the deterministic verdict became `VERIFIED_COMPLETE`. Scripted failure
paths (hidden-test catch, unsafe path, test-config tampering) are shown as clearly labelled mock
runs.

## 2. How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T[Task] --> M[Meta model]
  M -->|JSON plan| P[Plan validator]
  P -->|plan + system criteria| R[Orchestrator]
  M -->|JSON patch| W[Write policy]
  R --> W
  W -->|allowed files only| S[Isolated workspace]
  S --> V[Visible tests]
  S --> H[Holdout tests]
  V --> J[Deterministic verdict]
  H --> J
  J -->|FAIL| F[Repair feedback]
  F --> M
  J -->|PASS| D[VERIFIED_COMPLETE]
```

1. **Plan** — the model returns acceptance criteria and steps. The planner validates the shape,
   rejects disallowed checks and unsafe paths, and appends two **system** criteria:
   `visible_tests` and `hidden_tests`. The model cannot remove them.
2. **Approve** — the plan is stored; a run starts only from that stored plan.
3. **Patch** — the orchestrator copies the repository into an isolated workspace, shows the model
   only the files it may see, checks the patch against the write policy, and applies it.
4. **Verify** — allowlisted pytest commands run with a timeout. Holdout tests live in a sibling
   directory and are never part of the model context.
5. **Repair** — on failure the model gets sanitized feedback and tries again (at most two repairs).
   Holdout feedback contains only counts and a generic message, never test details.
6. **Verdict** — the final status comes from check results. The run record keeps every attempt,
   check,

# Triton Kernel Agent

An agent where Muse Wonder writes Triton kernels for PyTorch ops, and a hardened
harness on Modal H100s checks correctness, blocks cheating, and benchmarks speed.

Roadmap and tech spec: https://claude.ai/artifact/7JoEkyFCszJkHTs5SF1Tdr

## Problem

LLMs can write GPU kernels, but the numbers they report are easy to fake. Published kernel
agents have been caught returning cached outputs, calling back into PyTorch, dropping to
lower precision, or timing only part of the work. A speedup only means something if the
harness that measured it could not be fooled by the code it was measuring.

This project asks two questions on 43 KernelBench-style tasks (Level 1 single ops, Level 2
fused chains, and 4 tasks of our own) on an H100 in strict fp32:

1. How often can an agent write a Triton kernel that is correct and faster than PyTorch?
2. Which model setup is worth paying for: the large model (Muse Wonder), the small one
   (Muse Spark), or Wonder writing with Spark fixing compile errors?

## Method

**Agent loop.** For each task the planner model gets the PyTorch source and writes a Triton
`ModelNew`. The harness result goes back as feedback (compile error, which shape failed and
by how much, the speedup, the % of peak bandwidth), and the agent tries again, up to 10
attempts. Compile errors go to the fixer model with a short repair prompt. The best correct
attempt counts.

**Harness** (tag `harness-v1`, details in `decisions/harness_isolation.md`):

- *Isolation.* Each eval runs in a fresh Modal Sandbox with no network and no secrets. Inside
  it, a trusted parent process never imports the candidate. The candidate runs in a worker as
  the unprivileged `nobody` user, which gets inputs and returns outputs as raw tensor files.
- *Correctness.* The parent computes the reference in fp64 and fp32. The candidate's error may
  be at most 16× the fp32 reference's own error, with a 4-ulp floor. It runs on the visible
  shape, two input sets, and at least 5 hidden shapes (non-power-of-2, size 1, large, shifted
  inputs). After the hidden stage, error messages are withheld.
- *Timing.* Measured on the parent's clock, in batches that alternate between two checked
  input sets written into the same buffers, with a random number of calls per batch. The last
  output of each batch is checked again. PyTorch eager and `torch.compile` baselines are timed
  in clean workers with no candidate process alive.
- *Cheat checks.* A static scan flags PyTorch compute calls, TF32 and fp16/bf16/fp8,
  introspection, reference imports and hardcoded data. Runtime checks flag outputs that ignore
  the inputs, results that change after the checks, and any time faster than the bytes moved
  allow at the H100's peak bandwidth (`impossible_speed`).
- *Red team* (Y4). 37 attack kernels are kept as fixtures. With the static scan turned off, the
  runtime checks alone stop 32 of them. The 5 that only the scan stops are listed under
  Failure modes.

# Maxx — inspired by Maxwell's demon: a gate that moves information like physics

**Demo video (3 minutes): https://youtu.be/6C1S8kOLLWA**

**A submission to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**, built
during the event (October 26 – November 4, 2026). Everything claimed
below was built in that window unless a section labels it background.

Maxx is a deterministic gate between an AI agent and tool execution.

A proposed action is declared in a fixed schema:

- **Type** — what kind of action it is.
- **Trace** — what it touches.
- **Amount** — how much money moves.
- **Reversibility** — whether it can be undone.

The gate scores the declared action with stated arithmetic:

`floor 15 + trace weights + 15 if irreversible`, capped at `98`.

It then decides:

- **Release** — a one-use permit is issued.
- **Wrap** — a corrected version is substituted.
- **Hold** — nothing executes.
- **Escalate** — nothing executes; the human decides.

Enforcement is a separate sidecar process. It owns the permits and
the ledger, and the ledger counts must reconcile.

The gate itself calls no model. In the documented live run, Muse
Spark 1.3 proposed the actions and Muse Wonder 1.0 reviewed them
through the Meta Model API; the gate decided.

Seeded run — 8 actions:

- Decisions: release 1 / wrap 3 / hold 2 / escalate 2.
- Irreversible executions: 6 → 0 against the ungated baseline.
- Held for human decision: $1,090.
- Operator attention: 8 → 7.
- Tokens: 800 = 400 retained + 400 discarded.

Limits and checks:

- All tools behind the gate are mocks; no real action is taken in
  any run.
- A sorter backend tests whether trace-based sorting is informative
  on a held-out variable, with falsifiers stated in advance.
- The Petermann-K analysis on Muse Glimmer 30B activations did not
  beat conventional baselines.
- The gate's stability input is a constant stub.
- Test suites: 61 + 25 passing; the demo commands below print their
  own golden checks.

---

## Maxx, in one line
Maxx is the intent, the sidecar is the enforcement. Maxx states what
should happen to each proposed action — release, wrap, hold, or
escalate, with one plain reason — and the sidecar, a separate process
outside the agent, enforces that decision: it issues a one-use permit
only for a release and keeps the ledger the agent cannot rewrite.
The agent proposes; Maxx decides the intent; the sidecar enforces it.

## What "intent" means
"Intent" is not what the agent proposed. A proposal is a claim about
what to do, written by the system that wants to do it. Intent is what
*should* happen — determined on the operator's side of the gate, in
the operator's terms. Maxx determines it in four moves:

1. **The proposal is stripped to its intent-bearing facts**: what kind
   of action it is, what it touches (money, a person, a contract, a
   schedule, a device), how much money moves, and whether it can be
   undone. The agent's prose — its framing, its confidence, its
   reasons — is never scored.
2. **Those facts

> Contract-first, multi-agent software engineering squad that translates high-level Epic descriptions and acceptance criteria into verified, production-ready codebases.

2. **Peer Developers (Meta Muse Spark)** implement modular code and pytest suites concurrently.
3. **Sandboxed Verification (Modal Containers)** proves tests pass green inside isolated cloud micro-VMs, with automated self-repair loops for runtime failures.
4. **Human-in-the-Loop Governance** provides review gates at sprint planning and final pull request sign-off.

# RePart **Photograph a broken plastic part on a sheet of A4 paper and get back a printable, editable replacement.** A cracked fan-regulator knob, a snapped cable clip or a lost bottle cap usually means a trip to the bin, because nobody sells that exact part and few people can do CAD. RePart turns two phone photos into a parametric 3D model with real dimensions, and asks for the few measurements a photo can't show. The output is an STL ready for any 3D printer or print shop, plus OpenSCAD source in which every dimension is a named number. Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, "Push the Frontier"), Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026. **Everything in this repository was written during the event** (see [What was built during the hackathon](#what-was-built-during-the-hackathon)). 📹 **Demo video:** _link added at submission_ ![RePart Capture on iPhone: the sheet outline turns green when the shot is right, then the fit runs live](docs/app.jpg) ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR A[2 photos: part on A4] --> B[SAM 3.1
sheet + part masks] B --> C[Camera from the
sheet's 4 corners] C --> D[Muse Spark writes
parametric OpenSCAD] D --> E[Render the model
through the same camera] E --> F{Compare with
the photo} F -- numbers off --> G[Optimizer tunes
the named dimensions] G --> E F -- shape wrong --> D F -- stuck --> W[Muse Wonder
rethinks the structure] --> E F -- matches --> H[STL + SCAD + questions] ``` 1. **The sheet is the ruler.** SAM 3.1 segments the A4 sheet and the part. The sheet's four corners give the phone's exact position and angle (a plane homography solved with PnP, accurate to under 1 px), so every pixel has a known size, even on a tilted photo. 2. **Parallax is the hard part.** The top of a part sits closer to the lens than the paper, so it looks bigger. Flattening the photo and measuring overestimates an 18 mm-tall knob by **2–5 mm**. RePart never measures the photo directly. It renders its 3D model *through the recovered camera* and compares silhouettes in the camera's own image, which removes parallax entirely (**≤ 0.015 mm** on synthetic photos, [`spikes/d1_parallax.py`](spikes/d1_parallax.py)). 3. **Muse Spark owns the structure; numbers come from optimization.** Spark looks at the photos and writes OpenSCAD with named parameters, labelling each one *tunable* (fit it from the photos), *measured* (the user gave it, so it's locked) or *hidden* (the photos can't show it, so ask). A Nelder–Mead optimizer fits the tunable dimensions and the part's position in each photo, jointly across both photos. 4. **Spark reads its own mistakes.** Each round, Spark gets per-photo overlays plus residuals by clock sector ("0.5 mm missing at 11–12 o'clock"), geometry-check notes (overhangs, non-watertight meshes) and hole candidates. # Motion Transfer

[![Checks](https://github.com/rl7x/motion-transfer/actions/workflows/frontend.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rl7x/motion-transfer/actions/workflows/frontend.yml)

**Recover a move from a compiled game, or from a clip of it, then port it into games the model has never seen.**

Muse Wonder rebuilt Dashy Dango's dash from the compiled WebAssembly game. It succeeded in 1 of 3 full sessions at first, and in 2 of 3 fresh sessions after we improved the harness. Muse Spark then wrote the code that connects that dash to a game, and ported it into 7 of 8 eligible games it had never seen. Then we took the binary away: SAM 3.1 tracked a gameplay clip, and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model, rebuilt the same dash from those measurements. With the final checks, 4 of 6 fresh footage sessions scored 40/40 on the same exam, and the other 2 were refused. It's for developers who lost the source to their own games, and for preservation teams working with games they have the rights to use.

![A borrowed dash firing in a game Muse Spark ported it into](docs/media/demo.gif)

**[Play it live](https://motion-transfer-rl7x.vercel.app)** · [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [Port results](docs/auto-port-results.md)

Hackathon problem statement: **Build for Your World**. Models used through the Meta Model API: Muse Wonder 1.0, Muse Spark 1.3 and SAM 3.1. Open-weight model, served on Baseten: Muse Spark Open.

## What this is for

Motion Transfer is for developers who want a specific feel in a game, without rebuilding it by hand. Use your own game, an openly licensed one, or one you have permission to work on. It recovers how a move travels, not a game's art, sound or original code, and every game in this repository is credited below under its own license. Don't use it on work you don't have the rights to.

## What it does

# muse-glimmer

Serve Muse Glimmer locally. Development preview.

## Supported platforms

- macOS on Apple silicon

## Install and serve

You need Python 3.11+, Git, and Xcode with the Metal toolchain.
The first installation needs an internet connection. From this repository:

```sh
pip install -e .
muse-glimmer pull SocialLocalMobile/Muse-Glimmer-30B-ExecuTorch-PTE
muse-glimmer serve
```

Use `pull --variant <name>` to choose a specific folder, or `serve --model <path>` for a local model.

The server runs at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Press **Ctrl+C** to stop.

## Run Muse (coding agent) with the local model

With Muse installed, run this from your project directory:

```sh
muse-glimmer serve --launch muse
```

Muse uses the local model through its OpenRouter provider. No API key is needed.
Exiting Muse also stops the server.

## Smoke test

With the server running, open another terminal:

```sh
curl --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "muse-glimmer-30B",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "system", "content": "Reasoning strength: low"},
      {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello."}
    ],
    "max_tokens": 512,
    "temperature": 0.7
  }'
```

A successful response contains an assistant message in `choices[0].message.content`.

## Configuration

[default_config.toml](default_config.toml) documents all settings and defaults.
To override them, pass a TOML file explicitly:

```sh
muse-glimmer serve --config ./config.toml
```

Run `muse-glimmer serve --help` for command-line options.

# Holo: a live AI guide that sees what you see

Say "Muse, how do I…" and Holo highlights the real parts in front of you, step by step. It advances when it sees each step happen, and it answers mid-task questions with web search. In **Build mode**, "Muse, help me build a small FPV drone" gives you:

1. A design: parts, printable parts, wiring, code and steps.
2. A rendered image of the finished build.
3. A 3D model you can hold with your hands and export as an STL to print.

## Stack
- **Muse Spark Open** (Meta Model API via Baseten), in `server.py`. It plans from the camera frame, names step targets, routes questions, runs agentic web search and designs builds.
- **SAM 3.1** handles text-prompted video segmentation and tracking of every part Muse names, plus live single-frame highlights (`perception/pod/sam31_server.py`, `perception/pod/auto_pod.py`).
- **DINOv3 ViT-S/16** provides dense patch features pooled inside masks, used for the identity of look-alike parts.
- **Build generation** (`perception/pod/gen_server.py`): Z-Image-Turbo (image) and Hunyuan3D-2mini (image → watertight GLB/STL).
- **Unity app** (`unity/`): Meta XR Interaction SDK and XR Hands, a Horizon OS–style glass UI, wake word "Muse", local Whisper STT and Piper TTS, SAM 3.1 highlights, and a 3D model viewer (pinch to grab, two hands to scale and rotate, follow/pin, top view, STL export).
- **Automatic guide** (`perception/auto_render.py`): a step state machine driven only by Muse's plan and the masks. Nothing is specific to one clip.

1. GPU box:
   - `uvicorn sam31_server:app --port 8790`
   - `uvicorn gen_server:app --port 8791`

# JUNK — The Living Sampler

A paper-puppet instrument for the browser. Find a sound in a video, cut out the object that made it, and drop it onto a circular stage where it plays in the band.

- **Godot 4.6.3 / GDScript** (Compatibility renderer, single-threaded web export) draws the stage, characters, controls and animation.
- **TypeScript** in `src/` owns Web Audio, media import, IndexedDB and gateway calls, talking to Godot through `JavaScriptBridge`. Its only runtime dependency is Zod; TypeScript and Prettier are the dev tools. All three are vendored in `vendor/` and install offline.
- **Python FastAPI gateway** in `services/gateway` handles uploads, FFmpeg and model requests (Meta SAM 3.1, Muse Image, Muse Spark). **SAM Audio** runs on a Modal GPU worker in `services/gpu`.

Without credentials the gateway runs in demo mode: music, editing, persistence and export all work, while cutouts and separation are clearly labelled stand-ins (a rectangular crop and a raw audio copy). Configured providers never fall back to mock output after an error.

## Run it

Needs Node 22+, Python 3.11+ with `uv`, FFmpeg/FFprobe, and Godot 4.6.3 with matching web export templates (`--godot` selects another executable).

```bash
npm ci --offline --cache .npm-cache --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
```

```bash
uv sync --extra dev
```

```bash
uv run python scripts/build_web.py
```

```bash
uv run python scripts/dev.py
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173 (API docs at `/docs`). On Windows, `./scripts/setup.ps1 -Check -Start` does all of the above plus the checks. # VEGA — Video Evidence-Grounded Analysis

VEGA watches one camera, learns what is normal for it, and notes what does not belong, without being told what
to look for. It hands what it found to Meta's Muse Spark, which judges it, and to SAM 3.1, which outlines it.

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, indie track, Push the Frontier.** Everything in this repository was built during
the event, as a solo project: the first commit is dated 2026-10-29 and every commit falls in the building period.
Demo video: https://youtu.be/Fo8uDnbUan0

## What it does

- **VEGA, locally and without labels.** It samples the footage with its original timestamps, keeps ten minutes of each
  camera's normal, and runs separate witnesses against it: a scene detector, flow, colour, long and short memory,
  chunk comparison, dwell, and a notebook of changes that arrived and stayed, which scans back to stamp when each one
  arrived. Local specialists (YOLO, FireViewer, segmentation) add their findings. Every five seconds VEGA writes a
  neutral case file and a movement picture. An empty output never means normal.
- **Muse Spark 1.3 judges** (Meta Model API). A 30-second window goes to it only if an alerter fires, and then with the
  whole package: VEGA's detections first, its notes, the movement picture and the clip. It answers in a fixed schema
  with times and places, and VEGA audits every claim against the clip.
- **SAM 3.1 outlines** (Meta Model API) what the notebook flagged. When VEGA's coarse grid box is not enough, the
  phrases Muse Spark wrote about that moment ("red object") become SAM's prompt, and the outline kept is the one that
  covers the change that stayed.
- **The page shows both sides**: VEGA's evidence and its revisions, the model's boxes and verdicts, the exact exchange
  with the model, and a board of every component lit as the footage plays. A narrated tour walks through it.

## How it works

In pipeline order. More depth: [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), [system write-up](docs/requests/2026-10-30-claude-review/VEGA_SYSTEM.md),
[frontend](demo/frontend/README.md).

1. **Footage in.** The original file is never changed, and every sample keeps its source timestamp (PTS). VEGA takes
   four samples a second at up to 640 pixels wide and splits the picture into an 8×8 grid. Cuts, gaps and decode
   failures become flags, not silent gaps.
2. **Measurements.** Per cell: brightness, colour, edges, and optical flow with camera-shake compensation. Nothing at
   this stage names an object or decides anything is wrong.
3. **Camera memory.** Each camera keeps ten minutes of samples, never more. A new video joins the camera whose look it
   matches. Frames that flow flagged stay out, so VEGA does not learn its own alarms. Sources wait for 20 s of history
   (40 s for chunk comparison) before they flag anything.
4. **Witnesses.** Each reports on its own, and correlated sources never outvote each other.
   - *Scene detector*: each moment against this recording'

# ProofCam

**A camera-guided AI agent that verifies physical equipment installations — and decides what it needs to see next.**

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie Developer track, theme "Push the Frontier").
Deadline: **2026-11-04, 21:00 ET**. Runtime AI is exclusively the Meta Model API: **Muse Spark 1.3** (reads photos,
plans camera moves) and **SAM 3.1** (outlines objects). Claude Code is used only to *write* the code.

> **Snapshot (2026-10-31):** Milestone 0 single-photo feasibility is done and live-validated. Order-independent
> multi-photo evidence accumulation is implemented and proven **offline** (replay of recorded live observations +
> synthetic cases); the **live multi-photo experiment has not been run yet**, so Milestone 0 multi-photo behaviour
> is not marked complete. There is **no web app, no API server and no database yet**. No live `VERIFIED` exists.

Contents: [1. Plain-English overview](#1-plain-english-overview) · [2. Where we stand](#2-where-we-stand) ·
[3. Git state](#3-git-state-committed-vs-not) · [4. Repository map](#4-repository-map-every-file) ·
[5. How a photo flows through the code](#5-how-one-photo-flows-through-the-code) ·
[6. Key concepts](#6-key-concepts) · [7. Setup and run](#7-setup-and-run) · [8. Results and costs](#8-where-results-live-and-what-it-costs) ·
[9. What's next](#9-whats-next) · [10. Glossary](#10-glossary)

---

## 1. Plain-English overview

### The problem
Someone installs equipment — say a router and a network switch — and a cable has to go from *this* port to
*that* port. Checking by hand is tedious, and a single photo often can't show enough: the port might be on the
back, the label too small to read, the cable hidden behind something.

### What ProofCam does
You point your phone at the setup and give it a written rule, for example:

> "The blue Ethernet cable must connect Router LAN 1 to Switch Port 3."

ProofCam looks, works out **what it still can't see**, and tells you where to point the camera next
("I can see both devices but not the router's ports — move to the back of the router"). You take another photo; it
updates what it knows; it asks again if needed. You can photograph the parts **in any order** — ProofCam remembers
what each photo proved and combines them; it never makes you follow a fixed photo sequence. This repeats within
fixed limits. In the end each rule gets one of three answers:

| Answer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `VERIFIED` | The photos clearly show the rule is met |
| `VIOLATED` | The photos clearly show it is not met (empty port, wrong-coloured plug…) |
| `INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE` | The photos don't settle it, so ProofCam refuses to guess |

The key idea: ordinary tools judge whatever photo they're handed. ProofCam **chooses which photo it needs next**.
Think of an inspector who says "show me the back panel" instead of signing off on a front-only photo.

| Model | Job | What it is *not* allowed to do |

Poshan Lens gives an Anganwadi worker a child's **height from a 9-second phone video**, the **WHO z-scores**, a
**severe / moderate / normal** screening result, and a **message for the parent in their own language**. It runs on
any ARCore Android phone. It needs no LiDAR, no depth camera, no reference card and no extra hardware.

> Screening aid, not a diagnosis. A "severe" result means "refer to the health centre / NRC today".
> No real children were filmed for this project: the demo uses a doll and adults.

## How it works
```
phone (Chrome, WebXR + ARCore)        laptop / server
 camera frames + 6-DoF poses  ──►  SAM 3.1 ("child")  ──► mask per frame
                                   Pluto (motion measurement) ──► height in cm, 2-3 independent measurements
                                   WHO Child Growth Standards ──► HAZ, WHZ, categories   (deterministic code)
                                   Muse Spark (image) ──► photo check: full body visible, standing straight?
                                   Muse Spark (text)  ──► worker summary, parent message (Hindi, Telugu, ...),
                                                          checklist, follow-up date, register note
```
- **SAM 3.1** (Meta Model API, `sam-3.1`) finds the child in every frame from the text prompt "child".
- **Pluto** is my method for measuring the real size of an unknown object from a small sideways camera move
  (developed for onboard robot-grasping perception; frozen as tag `pluto-v1` on 31 Oct 2026). Each frame's camera
  pose (R, t from ARCore) and the mask's centroid and size give linear equations in the child's 3D position and
  the size constant W = size px × distance. The capture is cut into three time segments, and
  each one is solved over all its frames. A standing person sways a few cm, so the short 10 cm windows Pluto
  uses on rigid objects would read that sway as parallax. Pluto's 2-of-3 vote (5 % tolerance) then accepts the
  result, and one solve over every frame gives the final value. If the segments disagree, the app asks to measure again. Height = W / focal length, measured along
  ARCore's gravity direction. After that, distance in any frame is just W / mask size.
- **WHO z-scores** come from the WHO 2006 LMS tables (`data/who`, packaged by
  [pygrowup](https://github.com/ewheeler/pygrowup)), with WHO's restricted tails beyond ±3 SD. The LLM never
  does this maths: it gets the numbers and categories and explains them. Values WHO flags as implausible
  (|HAZ| > 6, |WHZ| > 5) are never classified. The app says "measure again" instead.

# Glimmer System One

An open multimodal decision model on **Muse Glimmer 30B**. Send an image and typed questions. Get calibrated probabilities back in one forward pass.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, indie track, theme "Push the Frontier".

## Links

| | |
|---|---|
| Code | https://github.com/aryan-sentlyx/glimmer-system-one |
| Heads on Hugging Face | https://huggingface.co/aryan-sentlyx/glimmer-system-one-heads |
| Live demo | https://aryan-59489--glimmer-demo.us-east.modal.run |

## The problem

Vision language models answer production-line questions in seconds. Muse Spark 1.3 writes a median of 1,144 reasoning tokens for one inspection image and takes 8.0 s. A production line moves one part per second or faster.

## The idea

A decision model does not write text. It answers a typed question (`noul`, `choice`, `score`) with a probability that you read from the logits. Glimmer System One does this with Muse Glimmer 30B:

- **Zero-shot mode.** One forward pass, the logit of "yes" against "no", plus one temperature. Works on products the model never saw.
- **Head mode.** A logistic head on the hidden state of layer 52 (or layer 13 for early exit). Trained on half of the known products, tested on the other half.

## Results on MVTec AD, all 1,725 test images

| System | AUROC | Acc at 0.5 | ECE | Latency per image | Open |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Glimmer head, known product, held-out half | 0.962 | 90.2% | 0.045 | 45 ms batched | yes |
| Glimmer layer 13 head, early exit | 0.954 | 88.3% | 0.034 | 21 ms batched | yes |
| Liquid d1-ultra | 0.929 | 83.2% | 0.147 | 0.46 s | no |
| TypeSafe Jev 1.14 | 0.917 | 85.2% | 0.125 | 0.31 s | no |
| Baseten Elephant 1 | 0.902 | 80.5% | 0.181 | 0.43 s | yes (MIT) |
| Glimmer zero-shot + temperature, unseen product | 0.882 | 81.4% | 0.040 | 45 ms batched | yes |
| Muse Spark 1.3, JSON, low reasoning | 0.873 | 83.1% | 0.097 | 3.9 s | no |
| Muse Spark 1.3, JSON, default reasoning | 0.872 | 82.6% | 0.101 | 8.0 s | no |

The full per-object table is in [`results/report.md`](results/report.md). The raw predictions are in `results/decisions/`.

agents search about a hundred hours of video turn by turn, reading transcripts and zooming into frames, Muse Spark 1.3
checks their evidence, and Portia returns the better-supported answer with the moments it rests on and how far to

## How a case runs

1. Three Muse Glimmer 30B agents, each with its own seed, investigate for up to 8 turns. They search all the videos
   or one, grep and read transcripts, look at contact sheets and frames, and zoom in. Each one ends with an answer
   and the moments it cites.

   needs review) measured from how the verdict was reached.

# Muna Lens

**A tutor that watches you solve maths and science problems on paper.** Prop a phone
over your notebook (or hold the page up to your laptop's webcam) and work as usual.
When you finish a step, Lens reads it, checks it, and if it is wrong, outlines it on
the screen and asks you one Socratic question out loud. It never gives the answer.

Built for every student who studies on paper. Students learn and sit exams with pen
and paper, but AI tutors only see typed text, and a wrong sign in step 2 of a
derivation goes unnoticed until the exam. Lens brings the tutor to the page.

## How it works

Meta open models do the intelligence; everything else is plumbing.

| Job | Model | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Watch the hand and pen live: when a step is finished, where the student points | **SAM 3.1** (`facebook/sam3.1`) | Modal GPU |
| Outline the mistake on a still frame; "is this step right?" pointing when live tracking is off | **SAM 3** (`facebook/sam3`) | Modal GPU |
| Read the handwriting, judge steps SymPy cannot, write the hint, hold the conversation | **Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`) | Baseten |
| Self-hosted fallback brain for demos | **Muse Glimmer 30B** | Modal GPU, vLLM |
| Hear the student | **Omnilingual ASR** (`facebook/omniASR-CTC-1B`) | Modal GPU |
| Speak | Kokoro-82M (Meta's own TTS models are non-commercial) | Modal GPU |

1. **Live video.** The phone streams its camera straight to the laptop over WebRTC.
   SAM 3.1 tracks the student's hand and pen a few times a second and decides when a
   step is finished (the pen stopped and the hand moved away). SAM does not read or
   segment handwriting: it found no handwriting concept on real pages, so reading is
   Muse Spark's job and the step boxes come from where the ink is.
2. **Read only the new step.** Lens finds the finished step's line in the frame and
   reads just that line, twice in parallel.
3. **Verify before speaking.** Algebra and calculus are checked with SymPy; steps it
   cannot parse go to a Muse Spark judge with a confirmation pass. A mistake is
   claimed only when independent readings agree on what is written. A false alarm
   costs more than a missed mistake.
4. **Hint without the answer.** Muse Spark writes one short question; a guardrail
   rejects any hint that contains the corrected step or the result (SymPy compares
   against the expected line) before it is spoken.
5. **Talk.** A live voice conversation you can interrupt. Lens also speaks up by itself,
   sparingly: a nudge when you have been stuck for a while, encouragement after a hard
   step, a remark when you cross something out.

The outline stays on the mistake as the page moves by matching the image of that line
from the frame Lens checked (template matching, not a model).

**Accessibility:** live captions of everything Lens says and hears (on by default),
type instead of talk, voice speed and a captions-only mode, "read my page aloud" in
spoken maths, and an end-of-session su

# WebMCP Bridge

**Turn websites into agent tools, without waiting for the owner.**

Meta's WebMCP and Meta AI Connectors only work when a site owner adds tools, and most sites never will. The usual workaround is a browser agent that runs a model on every click. WebMCP Bridge explores a site once and compiles what a person can do there into typed, tested tools. After that, agents call those tools with no model per click.

## How Meta's models are used

| Model | Job | When it runs |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Explores the site, writes tools and tests, and reads canvas pages | Compile time |
| SAM 3.1 | Finds controls that exist only as pixels | Compile time |
| Muse Spark 1.3 | Runs the chat conversation | Only when someone uses chat |
| No model | Calling tools, and running the tests that decide which tools ship | Every call |

## How it works

**Network path, for sites with an API behind the page**
1. Spark drives a real browser toward your goal and runs the action twice with different inputs.
2. Plain code keeps the successful JSON requests and removes page noise.
3. Spark proposes tools: names, the few inputs an agent needs, and tests.
4. Plain code runs the tests. A tool ships only if every test passes and different inputs give different results.

**Pixel path, for pages drawn on a canvas**
1. Spark reads the screenshot and legend, then chooses a SAM prompt.
2. SAM 3.1 finds the controls, and plain code names them by grid position.
3. Each state's colour is measured from the page. At run time, plain code reads pixels and clicks coordinates.

## Measured results

One run per task on Nov 5, 2026. Correct answers came from the pages themselves, not from either agent. This is a small sample.

| Task | Compiled tool | Spark clicking screenshots |
|---|---|---|
| Top HN story for "rust" | ✓ 0.38s, no model | ✓ 14.2s, 3 steps, $0.0061 |
| Top HN story for "postgres" | ✓ 0.36s, no model | ✓ 14.6s, 3 steps, $0.0074 |
| Top HN story for "webassembly" | ✓ 0.36s, no model | ✓ 16.5s, 3 steps, $0.0091 |
| List every free seat on a canvas | ✓ 0.77s, no model | ✓ 6.4s, 1 step, $0.0038 |
| Select one seat on a canvas | ✓ 0.99s, no model | ✓ 49.6s, 5 steps, $0.0238 |

Both approaches got all 5 tasks right, so the difference is speed and cost per call. Compiling once cost $0.027 for Hacker News and $0.016 for the seat map. Compiled-tool times are direct calls: using chat adds Spark's own time and cost.

## Limits enforced in code

- Clicks on buttons such as buy, pay, delete, log in and sign up are blocked during exploration.
- Password fields are never filled. Exploration stops at a captcha.
- Only read-only API tools ship.
- Parameters with names like key, token or session are never exposed to agents, and are redacted before Spark sees them.
- Compiling stops when estimated Meta spend reaches `META_BUDGET_USD` (default $15).

## Known limits

- Sites that need a login, or that block replayed requests, will not compile.
- URL path parameters are not sup

# VeriChainX Sol

Verified sellers and ownership that moves with payment, for AI shopping agents, on Solana.

A shopper's agent gets signed offers from merchants' agents and checks each one: is the seller who
they say they are, does the seller hold the item's NFT, and do the listing photos match what the maker
registered? It then buys with one wallet signature. USDC goes to the seller, a 1% fee goes to the
treasury, and the item's Metaplex Core NFT moves to the buyer, all in the same transaction. Every
offer is also a Solana Action, so it can be bought from a Blink.

The full spec is `SOLANA_APP_PLAN.md` in the verichainX-hedera workspace. Prior work is listed in
[`PRIOR_WORK.md`](PRIOR_WORK.md).

## How it works

**Merchants** sign in with their Solana wallet (SIWS) and prove their domain with a DNS TXT record.
Each one gets a service-held vault wallet, an agent signing key and a Core collection.

**Registration.** A merchant uploads photos. Muse Spark picks the item's distinctive marks and SAM
3.1 crops each one; together they form the origin fingerprint. The registration record is
canonical JSON. Its hash is anchored as a `vcx1:` memo signed by the anchoring key, and the full
record is stored so anyone can recompute the hash. Then a Core asset is minted to the merchant's
vault, with `registration_hash`, `origin_sig` and `merchant_domain` attributes. Listing an item sets
the settlement key as the asset's transfer delegate, and delisting revokes it.

**Agents.** The buyer agent (`src/lib/agent/buyer.ts`) broadcasts a signed `need`. Hosted merchant
agents, the resale desk and any `VCX_PEERS` answer with signed `offer` or `decline` envelopes
(`vcx-agent/1`, ed25519 over canonical JSON, CAIP-10 accounts). The agent's tools:
`discover_merchants`, `request_offers`, `verify_seller`, `verify_ownership`, `verify_item`,
`assess_seller_risk`, `present_recommendations` and `prepare_purchase`. The model chooses the order
and writes the reasons, but the Recommended / Caution / Avoid labels come from code (the
guardrail). If the model skips a check, a scripted pass completes it.

**Purchase.** `/api/pay/:offer` re-checks the offer and builds one v0 transaction:

1. Create the seller's USDC account if missing.
2. Send USDC to the seller.
3. Send the fee to the treasury.
4. Run Core `transferV1` with the settlement key as delegate.
5. Write an order memo.

The fee payer and settlement key sign first. Before either signs, the transaction is decompiled
and compared with the expected template, and any extra or altered instruction is refused. The
buyer's wallet adds the last signature. An indexer matches the reference key on chain and marks
the order paid.

**Copies.** A copier can paste another maker's asset id into its own listing. Ownership is
checked on chain, so that offer comes back as *Avoid: NFT belongs to someone else*, and the server
won't build a transaction for it.

# Rabbit Hop

**Can an AI agent shop like a specific kind of person, and can we prove it?**

Rabbit Hop sends AI shoppers with researched, locked personas to shop live beauty stores (Sephora and Olive Young US) through Meta **Muse Spark** computer use, then measures how faithfully each one behaves like the person it represents.

I'm Akshaya, an Executive MBA student who loves skincare and makeup. Across customer discovery work in different domains, I have always wondered whether agentic infrastructure could automate part of it. Rabbit Hop is my attempt to find out, starting with the beauty aisle.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie developer track), problem statement **Build for Your World**. Everything here was written during the building period (Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026).

## The problem

- Customer discovery is slow and manual, and surveys capture what people say they do, not what they do on a real store.
- Generic AI shopping agents optimize for finding the best product fast, not for behaving like a specific shopper.
- Agent behavior varies run to run, so one run cannot be trusted.

Rabbit Hop treats this as an evaluation problem: success is **persona fidelity**, not task completion. The shopper is told its steps and basket are judged on how faithfully they match its persona, not on speed, not on finding the objectively best product, and not on spending the whole budget.

## How it works

```
Locked persona ──► Prior data (optional) ──► Plan as the persona ──► Shop a live store ──► Basket with reasons ──► Blind judge + consistency across repeats
```

1. **Locked persona.** Five archetypes are researched with Muse Spark and web search, reviewed, versioned and locked (see below).
2. **Scenario.** A curated mission: a budget and a prioritized shopping list (for example, New vanity: $150, foundation must-have, blush preferred, mascara nice to have).
3. **Prior data (optional).** Each shopper can bring a 100-purchase shopping history. Muse plans with the full history and keeps a short summary in mind while shopping. The judge never sees it.
4. **Plan.** Before touching the page, Muse makes a plan as the persona through a `make_plan` function tool: where to start (search box, category menus, best sellers, new arrivals, sale), how to search (generic then filter, by attributes, or a brand it already knows), what evidence it needs per list item, and how many options to compare. It then shops by the plan and says why when it deviates.
5. **Shop.** Muse Spark computer use drives a real Chrome window on the live store: searching, sorting, filtering, scrolling and opening products. Every purchase, comparison and rejection is recorded through function tools with a reason, a decision driver and where the information came from.
6. **Evaluate.** A blind Muse Spark judge guesses which persona made which basket, from purchases alone and from purchases plus behavior. Repeated runs under identical conditions are compared through behavior signatu

# Tiny Libraries

A local, open-source workspace that turns your recordings and documents into a library you can study: source-linked chapters, subtitles, practice, concepts, and interactive explanations powered by Meta models.

**Status:** active development. See [scope](docs/scope.md), [hackathon requirements](docs/hackathon.md), and [development record](docs/development.md).

English is the default interface language; Spanish is available in Settings. Files, sessions, and progress stay on your machine. AI processing sends selected material to Meta Model API. Bring your own Meta API key; add, replace, or remove it in Settings.

Tutor web search is on by default and can be turned off in Settings. When your files and glossary do not cover a question, the tutor may send search queries based on it to Meta and shows external sources under their own heading, with links. The **Web** button still asks for a web search on an individual question. Web citations link to external sources and are labelled separately from your library evidence.

## Run locally

Install Node.js 22.13+ and ffmpeg for audio/video. The local Workers runtime (`wrangler`) comes with `npm ci`. Then:

```sh
npm ci
npm start
```

The tutor runs as a [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai) agent when the `muse` command matching `@muse-code/sdk` (1.4.14) is installed:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | sh
```

Without it, the tutor calls the Meta Model API directly with the same tools; only questions with **Web** on can then search the web.

Open **http://127.0.0.1:9876**. The launcher starts the local runtime and media companion together. It answers within seconds. Stopping and starting preserves files and study data in `.wrangler/state/` and `.local/`. See [local operation and backups](docs/local-operation.md) before moving or resetting data.

Development remains private until the owner chooses to share the repository. Its MIT license describes the intended source distribution; it does not make private GitHub content publicly accessible.

## Project boundaries

One library, saved study sessions, and a focused reading workspace. No course administration, institutional accounts, calendars, or cloud service subscription.

## License

MIT. Dependencies retain their respective licenses. Meta services and model licenses have their own terms.

# TraceGaze + Muse

**An understanding layer for AI that supports older adults in everyday life,
including the moments when recognising or explaining what help is needed is hard.**

TraceGaze turns first-person video and eye tracking into object-grounded,
time-stamped evidence: which object each gaze sample landed on, how gaze moved
between objects, and how long it stayed. **Muse Spark** reads that evidence
together with a few key frames and returns findings about the activity and
candidate opportunities for support. Every finding links back to the video
interval, frames and measurements behind it, and every number it quotes is
checked automatically.

The current prototype performs **retrospective** analysis for researchers
studying everyday activities and people designing assistance. Proactive,
real-time assistance is the future this understanding layer is meant to enable.
It is not part of this prototype.

> **Demo video:** _link to be added_ (3 min)

![Dashboard: research question, Muse findings, gaze timeline, evidence panel](docs/screenshots/dashboard.png)
<sub>Dataset footage is masked in these screenshots because the Aria Everyday
Activities licence does not allow redistribution; the demo video shows the full dashboard.</sub>

## What it does

1. **What the wearer experienced.** First-person video plus eye tracking from
   Project Aria glasses.
2. **Gaze becomes object context.** SAM 3 tracks the objects a researcher selected
   and reviewed. TraceGaze assigns every gaze sample to the object mask it
   lands on, without guessing when no mask is hit.
3. **Temporal patterns become visible.** Gaze episodes, transitions, revisits and
   time per object are computed deterministically. A sample is flagged as
   boundary-near when another object lies within 25 px, so rapid switching at
   object edges is not mistaken for behaviour.
4. **Muse interprets the evidence.** A researcher asks a question. Muse Spark 1.3
   receives a bounded evidence package (facts, rule-selected candidate moments,
   12 frames) and answers with about three findings. Each finding is typed as a
   *measured pattern*, *visible observation* or *possible interpretation* and
   carries alternatives, limitations and a support-opportunity verdict.
5. **Inspect the moment behind an insight.** In the dashboard, clicking a finding
   opens its interval in the video and shows the frames Muse saw and every
   cited measurement. Each one is compared with the value TraceGaze computed.

## Meta models and their roles

| Model | Role | How it is used |
|---|---|---|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3`, Meta Model API) | Interpretation | One `POST /v1/chat/completions` request with a JSON-schema response, the evidence package and 12 JPEG frames. It never computes numbers; it copies them from supplied facts. |
| **SAM 3** (`facebook/sam3`) | Perception | Segments and tracks the researcher-selected objects through the video (existing TraceGaze stage). |
| Project Aria glasses / MPS eye

# Pipeline Medic

An on-call agent for broken data pipelines. When a nightly pipeline breaks, the agent investigates, finds the root cause, writes a fix, and **proves the fix by replaying the failed night against hidden checks** before a human approves it.

The pipeline is a synthetic eyewear retailer's nightly DuckDB job (`raw_*` → `stg_*` → four marts). A fault injector breaks it in nine realistic ways, each labeled with ground truth. The agent works each incident in a private sandbox with twelve tools. A verification layer sits *inside* those tools, so the agent cannot skip it, and a console shows every turn and lets an engineer sign off.

## How it works

```
alert.md ──► agent loop (medic_agent/loop.py) ──► one tool per turn (agent_kit/tools/)
                    │                                   │
                    │                    sandbox: copy of pipeline + data at failure
                    │                                   │
                    └─ progress saved every turn        ├─ set_investigation_plan ─► verify_plan
                                                        ├─ record_finding (must quote a logged query)
                                                        ├─ propose_fix (never contracts/ or tests/)
                                                        ├─ run_replay (visible checks only)
                                                        └─ submit_rca ─► verify_rca ─► verify_fix ─► verify_claims
                                                                              │ (hidden golden checks,
                                                                              │  cheat-fix detection)
                                              3 refusals ─► escalate          ▼
                                                                     awaiting_review ─► engineer approves
                                                                                        (patch.diff + INCIDENT_REPORT.md)
```

- **The agent** (`agent/medic_agent/`): a plain loop over the OpenAI Python SDK pointed at `https://api.meta.ai/v1` (`muse-spark-1.3` by default). The playbook is `system_instructions.md`. The model chooses every tool; nothing is specific to an incident.
- **The kit** (`agent/agent_kit/`): settings, the model client (plus `FakeModel` for tests), the incident record, progress and resume, the per-run sandbox, and the tools.
- **Verification** (`agent/verification/`): one file per check. It is the only code in `agent/` that reads `ground_truth/`, and it does so through a single loader. See [agent/VERIFICATION.md](agent/VERIFICATION.md).
- **The world** (`world/`): the upstream team answers `request_info`, and late data is re-delivered.
- **Evals** (`evals/`): the fault injector, bench, metrics and results.
- **Console** (`ui/`): run view and results view.

Requires Python 3.9+, macOS or Linux, and a Meta Model API key (only for real runs).

#  SketchShip AI

Upload a hand-drawn sketch or wireframe and get a working Streamlit app with a live preview.

## Setup

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env        # then fill in META_API_KEY, META_API_BASE_URL, model names

```

No API key? The app runs in offline mock mode so you can try the full flow.

## How it uses Meta's models

SketchShip AI sends the uploaded sketch to a Muse multimodal model through the Meta Model API, which returns a structured JSON description of the UI (title, inputs, buttons, tables, layout). That JSON is then passed to a Muse model that writes clean Streamlit code, which is statically validated (import allow-list, blocked calls) and rendered live in the app. All inference runs on Meta's hosted endpoints over HTTP, so no local GPU is needed.

# play-game-with-brain — Hackathon Submission

Team name: Team 01f-w8c9spo

## Which track are you submitting to?

Indie Developer Track.

## Which problem statement did you build towards?

**Push the Frontier**: give a machine a new capability — control a video
game purely with thought. An 8-electrode EEG headset streams brainwaves
through a dual-layer meta-pipeline (rolling PSD features → spatial GNN
→ per-player few-shot adapter, coached by Meta's Muse models) that steers
a live Pygame world alongside the keyboard. No controllers needed.

## Project description

A brain-computer interface for gaming. The BrainAccess Mini headset (8
channels @ 250 Hz) streams raw EEG; instead of feeding raw samples to a
network (high latency, unstable training), a Feature Extraction Layer
computes rolling 0.5 s power-spectral-density features across
theta/alpha/beta/gamma bands, a Spatial GNN Layer message-passes over
electrode nodes with spatial + functional-connectivity edges, and a
meta-model head personalizes to each new brain in a 15-second in-game
Calibration Wizard (press C). Live inference writes commands to the game
at 4 Hz; the keyboard keeps working simultaneously. Includes local and
Modal-cloud training, a realtime EEG dashboard, hardware-free replay and
demo modes, and an automated unittest suite (`tests/`).

Live headset streaming runs on **Windows (64-bit)** with the BrainAccess
SDK — see the platform notes in [HOW_TO_SETUP.md](HOW_TO_SETUP.md).
Everything else (game, training, replay, visualizer) runs anywhere.

## Describe your use of Meta products to build the submitted project

Meta's models built this project *and* run inside it.

**Building it (Muse Code + Muse Spark):**

- Built the Pygame game itself — world generation, physics, lighting,
  sprites, UI, and the game loop.
- Researched the EEG signal chain: feature extraction (PSD band powers,
  Welch spectra, Hjorth parameters) and spatial filtering (CAR, mains
  notch, bandpass).
- Architected the spatial GNN: graph convolutions over cap electrodes,
  static + learned adjacency, per-frame functional connectivity.
- Wrote the training workflows: local and Modal-cloud scripts,
  trial-wise stratified splits, augmentation, checkpointing.
- Designed the few-shot adapter and the 15-second Calibration Wizard
  (MAML-style head adaptation per player).
- Wrote the interface between the trained model and the game
  (`game/ai_control.py` routes, the `gnn/live.py` bridge, EMA smoothing,

- Built the realtime EEG dashboard, the fullscreen/responsive layout

**Running inside it (Muse Spark `muse-spark-1.3` via the Meta Model API):**

- **Calibration coach** (`gnn/muse.py`, OpenAI-compatible
  `https://api.meta.ai/v1`): reads each player's fresh 15 s EEG summary
  and returns personal coaching + tuned confidence/cooldown/EMA gates.
- **Intent referee** (`--muse-fallback`): disambiguates gray-zone frames

Millions of Nigerians meet the law at its sharpest edges — a police checkpoint, a landlord's eviction threat, an unpaid salary — without knowing their rights. Many can't read legal text, and in a tense moment nobody has time to. Lawyers are expensive and far away.

## What Honest Orb does

- **Voice-first.** Tap the orb and talk. It talks back. It listens again automatically, so it feels like a phone call. Text is optional ("Show details").

- **Grounded in real law.** Legal answers come only from the verified laws loaded below, with citations you can open and read.

- **Safety first.** It always advises staying calm and polite, never resisting, and challenging abuses later through a lawyer or Legal Aid. If someone is in danger, it says "call 112" first.
- **State-aware.** Federal laws apply everywhere; for state laws (like tenancy) it asks which state you're in.

# BootSight

**A dead PC is a photograph away from a repair plan.**

BootSight is a copilot for field technicians. You photograph the screen of a machine
that won't boot — BIOS text, a bluescreen, a kernel panic, a RAID controller warning —
and it tells you what you are looking at, what it means, and the exact next command to
run. Then it writes the ticket.

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon)
(startup track). No code from any private product is included in this repository.

## The problem

A technician arrives at a machine that won't start. The first ten minutes are spent
decoding a screen: is this a dead disk, a bad boot sector, a corrupted driver, or a
loose SATA cable? The answer is on the screen, but reading it requires experience the
junior tech on site does not have yet. So they take a photo and send it to someone
senior, and wait.

That wait is the product.

## What it does

1. **Read the screen.** A photo goes to `muse-spark-1.3` (vision + structured output).
   The model returns the machine state as data: vendor, boot phase, error codes,
   the exact strings that matter, and what it cannot see.
2. **Locate the evidence.** `sam-3.1` segments the region of the photo that carries the
   error — the STOP code line, the SMART warning, the missing-boot-device message — so
   the technician knows what to look at, not just what to read.
3. **Build a plan.** The model proposes repair steps, each one with a command, the
   expected output, and the condition that means "stop, this is not the problem".
4. **Record it.** The run is exported as a ticket: photo, diagnosis, steps taken,
   outcome. That record is what turns a lucky fix into a repeatable one.

Every step is a **read-only diagnostic** by default. Anything that writes to the disk
requires an explicit, separate confirmation and is refused in demo mode.

## Why this wins the startup track

The startup track is judged on technical execution and whether it holds up in
production. BootSight is not a weekend prototype of an idea: it is a narrow tool with a
hard safety boundary, a deterministic schema, a test suite that runs without network
access, and a cost model that fits a real service business.

## Stack

- Python 3.13, FastAPI, no build step.
- `muse-spark-1.3` over the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at `https://api.meta.ai/v1`.
- `sam-3.1` for segmentation masks.
- Vanilla HTML/JS front end, served by the same process. Works on a phone.

Open `http://localhost:8099`.

Without a key, run in mock mode and the whole flow still works end to end:

BOOTSIGHT_MOCK=1 .venv/bin/python -m uvicorn app.main:app --port 8099

# HyperPod

> **Built with Llama** · Meta open-weight models on hardware you already own.

HyperPod is a local inference controller that discovers consumer laptops on the
same trusted network, measures their available GPU memory, distributes a Meta
Llama model across them through llama.cpp RPC, and restores service when a
remote inference process disappears.

HyperPod is a hackathon prototype for a problem experienced firsthand: a
builder may own several modest laptops but no single large GPU. Those laptops
can add useful memory, but Wi-Fi and user-owned devices are not reliable server
infrastructure. HyperPod makes the placement observable and treats failure as a
normal control-plane event.

## What is proven

| Result | Measured evidence |
|---|---|
| Cross-platform pool | Linux ROG RTX 3050 controller + Windows TUF RTX 4050 + M4 Mac/Metal over Wi-Fi |
| Real 3B split | llama.cpp placed weights on ROG CUDA, TUF RPC and M4 RPC in the three-machine test |
| Measured scheduling | Weights `5331,3204` from free VRAM `5843,3716` minus 512 MiB/device; no GPU-name inference |
| Real 8B capacity run | Llama 3.1 8B Q4: 1,073 MiB on ROG GPU + 3,330 MiB on TUF GPU; 6.68 tok/s |
| Real worker-loss recovery | Killing TUF RPC caused llama-server to abort; HyperPod rebuilt 3B on ROG in about 3 seconds; the next request succeeded |
| Same-request retry | Physically verified for both M4 loss (three→two nodes) and TUF loss (two→local) |
| Live telemetry | GPU/VRAM/load/temperature/power, RAM, battery and AC state from `nvidia-smi` and OS interfaces |

Raw evidence is committed under [`test/*.log`](test/). The latest measured
telemetry and scheduler run is
[`test/phase5-telemetry-scheduler.log`](test/phase5-telemetry-scheduler.log).

### Where the model actually went

Per-device weights reported by llama.cpp after loading, for four measured
configurations. The first two bars are the same request before and after the Mac
accelerator was stopped.

![Per-device model weights across four configurations](docs/assets/hyperpod-placement.png)

### Latency and throughput

Five sequential requests per configuration against a warm model. The local
baseline is tightly clustered; both distributed configurations vary by several
seconds, which we attribute to the Wi-Fi link rather than the control plane.

![Five-run latency and decode throughput](docs/assets/hyperpod-benchmarks.png)

Distributing this model over this network cost roughly a factor of six in decode
throughput. HyperPod buys capacity and recovery, not speed.

## PDF reader

Upload an NCTB textbook PDF. It is matched to a book already stored in Neon (by page count and page shape), and the stored word
positions are laid over the pages as selectable text, so no OCR runs in the browser. Highlight any passage and press **Simulate**:

## Built with Muse Wonder 1.0

All text and simulation generation in Simuplug is done by **Muse Wonder 1.0** (`muse-wonder-1.0`, via the Meta API at
`https://api.meta.ai/v1`). It is used for:

- the short, cited **summary** of the matched textbook section, and
- writing each **simulation** as OpenUI Lang (from the section's figure descriptions, or from its text when there is no figure).

Embeddings are separate and come from EmbeddingGemma 2 (see below).

# one-hour · 一小时

> Language: **English** | [中文](README.zh-CN.md)

An ephemeral public chat room: **every message (text or photo) lives for exactly one hour, both locally and in the cloud.** When its hour runs out the message dissolves gracefully, and every player online watches it leave together. And this is a small experimental social product and exploring new ways to make social interactions more engaging with AI.

## Features

- 🕐 **One-hour lifecycle**: Every message (text or photo) exists for exactly one hour from send time. Each message carries a ring countdown (mm:ss) — amber in the last 10 minutes, red and pulsing in the last 2. When time runs out it blurs upward and folds away (`msg-dissolve`), removed from IndexedDB and the cloud at once, with other players seeing the same farewell over Realtime DELETE. The countdown's visual style can be switched from the settings menu (classic ring, soft progress line, fading segments, breathing light, gradient halo, orbiting dot, and more).

- 🖼️ **Image messages**: Desktop uploads via the `+` menu (multi-select up to 5, each becomes its own message); on touch devices `+` expands to "Take photo / Photo library", with the camera capturing directly. Photos are compressed in-browser (long edge 1440px, JPEG 0.82) with HEIC/HEIF auto-conversion; on weak/offline networks the image Blob travels with the text in the IndexedDB outbox and retries with backoff (per-file timeouts keep one stuck decode from blocking the rest). Tap any image to open the fullscreen viewer with swipe, pinch/double-tap zoom, pan, and vertical-fling dismiss. Images expire and are cleaned up with their message.

- 🌄 **Dynamic backdrop**: The fullscreen backdrop prefers the newest image in chat (synchronized across all clients, including its countdown); with no chat image it fetches a random photo (official Unsplash API when `VITE_UNSPLASH_ACCESS_KEY` is set, otherwise the keyless picsum Unsplash-sourced feed). Either way each backdrop photo stays at most one hour, then crossfades to a new one; a new chat image takes over immediately. The backdrop blurs while chat is open; tapping the top-right X folds the whole chat column (input included) into the bottom-left corner and the backdrop goes fully clear; tapping anywhere (or the bottom-left hint) unfolds it again. While folded, a ring-only countdown in the bottom-right shows the remaining backdrop slot, and a globe button opens the source photo.

- 🟢 **Realtime sync**: Supabase Realtime (postgres_changes INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE + presence) keeps new messages, edits, reactions, disappearances, and the online list in sync, with catch-up on reconnect and tab return.

## Quick start

```bash
npm install
cp .env.local.example .env.local   # fill in your Supabase project URL and key
npm run dev
```

### Supabase setup (one-time)

1. Create a Supabase project.
2. Run `supabase/schema.sql` in full in the SQL Editor:
   - Creates `chat_messages` (with `expires_at`, default `now() + 1 hour`) and RLS

## What it does

- **Hands free.** Say "Felix" and talk. He waits until you pause, and if his answer is slow, a quick "one second" in his own voice tells you he heard.
- **Labels on the real parts.** Each photo from the headset's camera is searched for the job's parts, and the headset pins a name tag on each one in the room. An arrow marks the part Felix means, and he perches beside it.

You sketch or photograph a circuit and ask a question by text or voice. Muse Spark investigates and grounds every claim in evidence and ngspice simulations checked by an independent solver. Muse Wonder independently re-reads the drawing without seeing the agent's answer and reviews every claim. If anything is unsupported it goes back for correction, and it asks you instead of guessing.

*The overview card: analysis, verification, design, usage, and downloads at a glance.*

## The verifier catches, the agent corrects

A draft is never shown as verified until all 5 checks pass. Failed checks go back to the agent as specific feedback; the agent corrects the draft and verification runs again, for up to 3 correction rounds. Feedback never turns a failure into a pass: every corrected draft must earn its own pass, and after 3 rounds the case honestly says it needs human review.

Real example (dev case D09, after the user's answer, not part of the frozen evaluation): Report r1: OUT = 2.5 V (correct), but the report said 'goal not met' for a find-the-value task → Claims check failed. Correction round 1: the agent changed the goal status. Report r2: all 5 checks passed.

Measured: In the frozen held-out run, every case that needed correction was fixed after feedback ('Fixed after feedback' 8/8), shown on the Evaluation page.

# Babu Studio

Babu Studio is a macOS desktop recording and export application. The React renderer configures one shared scene and layer list with independent placements in landscape and portrait previews; new layers start centered in both layouts at matching output-pixel sizes, then can be adjusted independently. Electron owns project files and IPC, and a separate C++ media-core process captures and timestamps media.

## Requirements

- macOS
- Node.js 20 or newer and npm
- CMake 3.20 or newer
- Xcode Command Line Tools
- FFmpeg and `pkg-config`, for the native core's libav* libraries

## Getting started

```sh
npm install
npm run dev
```

The development command builds the C++ core before starting Electron. Recording writes selected capture-card video, webcam video, game audio, and microphone audio as separate synchronized tracks in `master.babu` under `~/Movies/Babu Studio/recording-<id>/`. A `project.babu` stores the shared scene, per-layout layer placements, capture settings, source timing information, and export state. When recording stops, the shared layer list is rendered with its landscape placements to `exports/horizontal.mp4` and its portrait placements to `exports/vertical.mp4`.

In both exports, microphone audio is compressed and boosted so speech stays in the foreground, and game audio holds a constant level underneath it; the combined mix is limited to prevent clipping. The original source tracks remain separate in `master.babu`.

Mixer levels run from 0% to 200%. 100% matches the level the source was captured at, and anything above it boosts that track in the export, so a quiet capture card or microphone can be raised without re-recording. The live capture-card monitor follows the same level, and the recorded master file always keeps the untouched source tracks.

The microphone track has a **Noise reduction** setting (Off, Low, Medium, High) in its settings popup. It runs a high-pass filter to drop rumble and an FFT denoiser to remove hiss, leaving the voice band largely untouched. Like the mixer levels it is applied while exporting, so the master file keeps the raw microphone track.

Scenes, layers and their placements, audio mixer settings, export layouts and quality, and preview visibility are saved to `studio-config.json` in Electron's user-data directory. Existing scene and audio settings stored in the previous browser-based format are imported the first time the file is created.

Native capture and source recording use AVFoundation and FFmpeg's VideoToolbox encoder on macOS. Packaged apps include their own FFmpeg, so users install nothing else. In development, post-processing invokes `ffmpeg` from `PATH`; set `BABU_STUDIO_FFMPEG_PATH` to use a specific executable. If VideoToolbox export fails, the app retries with `libx264`. Source recordings are kept if export fails.

# Nautilus

Agentic failure investigation and evidence-based controller engineering for simulated underwater robots.

[Live workbench](https://nautilus-demo-delta.vercel.app/) | [Source repository](https://github.com/RatChakraborty/MetaGlobalAIDeveloperHackathon-Nautilus)

Nautilus is an engineering research prototype developed for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. It connects a physics-based planar underwater-vehicle simulator, numerical fault diagnosis, experiment planning, bounded controller engineering, auditable evidence, a Three.js AUV replay viewer, and authentic recorded Meta Muse tool activity.

All robot motion and engineering results are simulated. Nautilus does not claim physical deployment, hardware validation, or a certified repair.

## The problem

An autonomous underwater vehicle inspecting an offshore pipeline begins drifting off course. Ocean currents, failing thrusters, and faulty heading measurements may produce similar observations, but require different engineering responses. Nautilus compares competing explanations and tests controller interventions numerically rather than trusting an unsupported agent assertion.

## End-to-end workflow

Run → Investigate → Engineer → Verify → Report

1. Run reproducible 3-DOF surge, sway, and yaw simulations with explicit disturbances and random seeds.
2. Investigate public measurements through competing physical hypotheses, residual comparisons, ambiguity handling, and bounded experimental probes.
3. Engineer a controller revision with Policy Studio, using the evidence-preserving Engineer this failure handoff or a distinct host-defined example candidate.
4. Verify the source and parameters, run matched baseline-versus-candidate trials, check predeclared acceptance gates, and evaluate held-out robustness.
5. Report with linked investigation records, evidence hashes, controller fingerprints, source/parameter diffs, and canonical host JSON preserved across export and reimport.

The browser destinations are Overview, Run and Investigate, Evidence, Engineer, History, and Reports.

# YourCircle

**Answers and feeds from the people you actually follow, not whatever is trending.**

Ask Meta AI "based on the people I follow, where should I go?" today and it answers from public trending posts. It cannot use your follow graph, and it cannot tell you who influenced the answer. YourCircle is a drop-in service that fixes that for any recommender.

It plugs into a standard multi-stage recommender at two points:

| Plug-in point | Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieval source | `POST /v1/users/{id}/candidates` | "What did my circle say about X?" Credited places, products or recipes from trusted, on-topic people. Place questions also get a day-by-day plan |
| Re-rank feature | `POST /v1/users/{id}/rerank` | Takes the engine's ranked list, boosts trusted, on-topic authors, returns the new order with a reason per item |
| Clip reader | `POST /v1/users/{id}/clips` | Turns a reel (that you have rights to) into credited items with exact quotes and cut-out images |

Outside Meta, the user brings their own data (Instagram export). Inside Meta, the same service would read follows and engagement directly; only the input changes.

The page at `/` is a demo client standing in for Meta AI and the Reels feed.

| --- | --- | --- |

| SAM 3.1 | `sam-3.1` (streamed Responses call, noun-phrase prompt) | Finds the place, product or dish in a frame and cuts it out for the answer card |
| Muse Code | coding agent | Used while building this repo |
