### Visual Intelligence for Rural Water Infrastructure

**Don't just report the repair. Show what changed.**

MajiProof is a multimodal AI platform designed to transform field photographs into structured infrastructure inspections and evidence-based repair comparisons.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026**, MajiProof explores how frontier AI and computer vision can improve the transparency and accountability of rural water infrastructure maintenance.

---

## 💧 The Problem

Rural water infrastructure is essential to community resilience, public health and sustainable development.

However, maintenance workflows often depend on fragmented photographs, technician reports and manual inspections. This makes it difficult for NGOs, water-service organizations and infrastructure supervisors to establish:

- What went wrong?
- Which infrastructure components were affected?
- What maintenance was performed?
- What visibly changed after the repair?
- What evidence is still missing?
- Does the infrastructure require further inspection?

Reporting a repair is not the same as demonstrating what changed.

## 🚀 Our Solution

**MajiProof turns field observations into visual intelligence and accountable inspection evidence.**

Using multimodal AI and computer vision, the platform helps field workers and infrastructure supervisors:

1. Capture before-repair evidence.
2. Analyse visual conditions using AI.
3. Identify and segment relevant infrastructure components.
4. Capture after-repair evidence.
5. Compare observable changes.
6. Generate structured inspection reports.
7. Submit findings for human review and approval.

Our goal is to make infrastructure maintenance more transparent, interpretable and evidence-driven.

---

The visual reasoning layer.

Styld is a wardrobe app. You film your clothes rail or photograph your pieces, and Styld turns each garment into a
clean, shop-style picture you can browse, combine into looks and pin to boards. It runs at https://styld.app in
English and Slovenian.

Try it at https://styld.app: sign in with Google or an email code, and every account starts with 3 free credits.

This repository is Styld v2, written during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 October to 4 November 2026).
[Built during the hackathon](#built-during-the-hackathon) says what is new and what came from v1.

## What it does

- **Scan your clothes.** Film a rail or a pile for up to fifteen minutes, or take photos. The phone cuts a long video
  into parts. Meta SAM 3.1 finds every garment and tracks it through the video, and Styld cuts each one out of the
  sharpest, fullest frame it appears in. A garment seen in several parts becomes one card. A photo costs 1 credit and
  half a minute of video 5.
- **Pressed pictures.** Meta Muse Image 1.0 redraws the cut-out as a pressed, shop-style picture, for free. The real
  photo is kept and is one swipe away. A back is drawn only from a real photo of the back. A redraw, with an optional

- **Turn a piece.** For 5 credits, Muse Image draws a strict side view from the front picture and Veo 3.1 Lite
  animates the piece turning on a hanger.
- **Wardrobe, looks and boards.** Browse by group, type and filter, build looks, and pin pieces, looks and pictures to
  boards with a collage. Muse Image paints a board's stickers from words (1 credit). The house boards
  (`@styld.women`, `@styld.men`) use garments generated with Muse Image, always labelled Generated.
- **Try on.** In the Lab, a person picks one of their own Gallery photos and up to nine

**Precheck a personal fall arrest system (PFAS) plan before it goes to the general contractor.** A subcontractor's safety coordinator pastes or uploads a fall protection plan. # Expertium: a verifiable industrial knowledge engine

Expertium turns a manufacturing nonconformity into a traceable quality record: answers grounded in cited procedures, a proposed corrective action, human approval, and a tamper-evident audit log.

Built solo by Luis Herrera (Peru) for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track.

## Live demo
* https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WzPiYtQtylw

## The problem
When a quality deviation occurs on a factory floor, floor operators and quality managers struggle to manually locate the exact regulatory procedure across massive internal documentation. Deciding on immediate corrective actions without immediate compliance context delays production and risks failing external regulatory audits due to a lack of verifiable, tamper-evident evidence.

## How it works
Four agents share one model, **Muse Spark 1.3** on **Meta Model API**, enforcing strict structured outputs:

*   **Knowledge:** Finds the applicable technical procedure and extracts precise cited source sections.
*   **Quality:** Evaluates the current operational nonconformity against the retrieved compliance criteria.
*   **CAPA:** Automatically generates corrective and preventive actions with assigned owners and due dates, then pauses the process to wait for mandatory human approval.
*   **Audit:** Seamlessly records all agent outputs, cited documentation, and final human approvals into a hash-chained, tamper-evident quality log.

### Example case
A line operator reports a *"pressure deviation in line 2"* during a production batch. The **Knowledge Agent** instantly retrieves the specific pressure threshold protocol, the **Quality Agent** flags the critical deviation, the **CAPA Agent** generates an emergency pressure valve inspection task assigned to maintenance, and once approved by the supervisor, the entire process is permanently sealed into the audit log.

## Measured results
Averages over demo cases:

| Metric | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| Cost per case | **$0.008** |
| Latency per agent step | **10.2 s** |
| Backend tests | passing (`cd backend && pytest`) |

**Conclusion:** It demonstrates high operational efficiency and economic viability, processing complex cases at an ultra-low cost of \$0.008 USD per process. Furthermore, the average latency of 10.2 seconds per agent validates the speed of the automated multi-agent workflow compared to traditional manual auditing.

**Adaptive Bayesian calibration and guarded quantum circuit placement, explained with Meta Muse Spark.**

Built for the **[Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon — Indie Developer Track](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon)**.

Q-Bridge helps researchers answer two connected questions: **What should we measure with a limited calibration budget? And does the resulting evidence justify changing a circuit’s placement across quantum processors?**

The Python engine directs calibration toward measurements with the highest expected placement benefit. The dashboard makes its decisions and uncertainty inspectable. Meta’s hosted Muse Spark model turns recorded evidence into research explanations through genuine function calling.

# CodeMesh 3D

Turn an ordinary phone video of an object into a textured, game-ready 3D asset (GLB).

Upload a walk-around video (or a set of photos), type what the object is, and CodeMesh finds it in every frame with **SAM 3.1**, recovers the cameras and depth with **MapAnything** (Meta, Apache-2.0 weights), builds a clean mesh, projects the original 4K photography onto it, bakes a normal map, and checks its own work by re-rendering the model from the real camera positions and comparing against your footage.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley, Nov 2026).

## Try it live (no install)

**https://fjziemski--codemesh-web.us-east.modal.run**

1. Open the link in any desktop or phone browser. The first visit after it has been idle takes a few seconds to wake up ("Connecting to the backend…").
2. Drop in a short walk-around video of an object (or 2-300 photos), tick the data-use notice, and press **Upload and start**.
3. Type what the object is (for example "electric kettle"), press **Find object**, check the masks, then **Build 3D model**.
4. In a few minutes you get the 3D viewer, the accuracy score, the quality grade and Muse's modeling decisions. **Download GLB** to open it in Blender, Unity or Unreal.

Tips: walk one slow circle (30-45 s) with the whole object in frame, then add a short look from above. Don't upload people, faces or private spaces: inputs go to Meta's Muse Spark Contributor tier. Finished jobs are listed under Recent jobs on the home page.

## The idea

Making a 3D asset of a real object still means a scanning rig, or photogrammetry followed by hours of cleanup: scans come out as lumpy, holey, million-triangle meshes that no game engine wants. CodeMesh 3D treats a phone video as **evidence** rather than as the model. Meta's models extract what is in the footage (which pixels are the object, where every camera was, how far away each surface is), and **Muse Spark acts like a 3D artist**: it looks at the photos, decides what the object is made of (a lathe-turned body, a box, a handle), builds a clean, simple mesh with modeling tools, and checks every change against the real footage. The goal is a model that looks made, not scanned: one watertight piece, sensible topology, UVs, a texture and a normal map.

## How it works

| Step | What happens | Tech |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest | Picks the sharpest, non-redundant frames from the video at full resolution (handles iPhone HDR/HEVC and rotation) | PyAV, OpenCV |
| Segment | One text prompt or click → the object is tracked through every frame (one video request, not per image) | **SAM 3.1** (Meta Model API) |
| Geometry | Camera poses, intrinsics, depth and confidence from all views at once | **MapAnything** (Meta) on Modal L4 GPU, AMD Radeon 780M via ROCm, or CPU |
| Fuse + mesh | Visual hull carved from the full-resolution SAM silhouettes, refined with depth (free-space carving opens cavities such as a mug's inside), repaired to one watertight piece, decimat

# Second Look — Know what changed in Dad's room, with proof

**Live demo:** https://harshitaggarwal01.github.io/splatdiff/ — static on GitHub Pages. *Try it now* replays a real recorded check; your own videos, voice notes, the family agent and the glasses view ask for **your own Meta API key**, kept in that browser tab only and sent only to api.meta.ai. The full server version runs with `python server.py`.

**Status:** submitted to the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, Push the Frontier) on Nov 4, 2026 — built in one day. See *How this was built* and *How the demo video was made*.


Second Look compares two short phone walkthroughs of the same room — a BEFORE and an AFTER — and reports which objects were **added**, **removed**, or **moved**. Every kept finding is backed by SAM 3.1 detections (boxes, frame ids, confidences). Any claim the reasoning model makes that SAM evidence does not support is **dropped and shown as dropped**, struck through with the reason, in a section called "Struck from the report".

SplatDiff is the engine codename from the author's earlier 3D-scene research; this product uses no Gaussian splats.

The lead story: Dad is 82 and lives alone. After a hospital discharge or a near-miss, his daughter films the OT-approved safe setup as a baseline — walker next to the bed, lamp within reach, path to the bathroom clear. On her next visit she films again. Second Look shows her what changed in between: is the walker still within reach, has clutter appeared on the floor, was the lamp moved away from the bed?

**The grounded room-change check is the working product.** The glasses view described below is "Dad's point of view" — a working simulation, not a Meta product integration.

## Why

The CDC reports that about 1 in 4 adults aged 65+ falls each year, and home hazards are a modifiable risk factor. Families often visit periodically, and small changes between visits go unnoticed: a walker pushed out of reach, clutter building up on the floor. Those changes can create hazards. Second Look does not claim to reduce falls — it detects changes to the objects in a room, which is one factor among many (strength and balance, medications, vision and blood pressure all matter too, which is why an OT assessment remains the gold standard).

A false alarm wastes trust; a miss can matter far more. So Second Look follows one rule — **grounded or dropped**: a finding is kept only if SAM 3.1 evidence supports it, and everything else is shown struck, with the reason, rather than hidden. And because a missed "walker moved" is the catastrophic error here, we say plainly: **false negatives matter more than false positives.** Our grounding story is about killing false claims; it says nothing yet about recall in a real, cluttered room, which is barely tested — one real pair so far (see *Real footage*).

You do not need two walkthroughs on day one. Value starts at visit #2. Film today's safe room as the baseline; next visit, we show you what

# WeSolve: a swarm of Meta AI agents that makes vLLM faster on a Mac

**Author:** Onur Sürücü · [o.surucu97@gmail.com](mailto:o.surucu97@gmail.com) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/onur-surucu/)

[![WeSolve: AI Agents Rewrote vLLM’s GPU Code and Made It 21% Faster (watch on YouTube)](https://img.youtube.com/vi/nS6i200dKHg/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nS6i200dKHg)

▶ **[Watch the video on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nS6i200dKHg)**

**Working demo** (27 s, [demo/wesolve-swarm-live.mp4](demo/wesolve-swarm-live.mp4)): the swarm at work in round 3. On the left, the lead in Muse Code; on the right, every agent's commands, thoughts and messages as they happen, read from Muse Code's session logs.

> WeSolve, an agent swarm, sped up a mixture-of-experts LLM (Meta's MobileMoE-S) on a local Apple Silicon Mac (M1 Pro, vLLM) by up to 21% end to end, prompt reading and generation together (430 → 519 tokens/s), with bit-identical output. Generation alone got up to 27% faster, and prompt reading took up to 11% less time.

<sub>32 concurrent requests, 256 new tokens each, medians of 5 runs against vLLM as shipped: 1,024-token prompts 430 → 519 tokens/s (+21%), 128-token prompts 911 → 1,097 (+20%). In the 1,024-token run unchanged vLLM was slower than in earlier runs; against MLX's compiled code, timed alongside, that gain is 11% (see *Limits*).</sub>

An indie-track project for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026).

**What we did.** We built **WeSolve**, a swarm of AI agents running Meta's own models (Muse Spark and Muse Wonder) in Meta's coding agent, Muse Code. We pointed it at vLLM serving Meta's on-device model MobileMoE-S on an Apple M1 Pro. The swarm read the code and our measurements, found where the time goes, and wrote new GPU kernels for the model's mixture-of-experts layers. With its best kernels, **a whole request, reading the prompt and generating the answer, finishes up to 21% faster with 32 concurrent requests**. Generation alone is up to 27% faster, prompt reading takes up to 11% less time, and every answer stays the same, token for token.

**How WeSolve works, in plain words.** One agent can look at one thing at a time; a team can look at everything at once. WeSolve splits the problem among many agents: explorers each study a different part of the code, a verifier checks what they claim, several builders compete to write the fix, and a lead coordinates. They all write in shared notebooks, so each one sees what the others found and changes course when someone else's finding points to a better path. Nothing counts until a referee has measured it: the new code must give exactly the same answers and be faster in the real engine. Each round starts from what the last one learned.

## Results

**What we measure: the whole request.** A request has two phases:
- **prompt reading** (prefill): the model processes the prompt;
- **generation** (decode): it produces 256 new tokens, one decode

# Shotprint

**The video template marketplace for AI agents.**

A stock video template is a project file a person has to edit. A Shotprint template is written for an agent
to run: every shot's timing, framing, camera, light, text and sound, with a storyboard per shot and
swappable cast, product and places. Download one with its fill recipe and any agent can make the spot.

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/CJ13Z9KZNR4 · **Live demo:** https://shotprint.dev · technical details at https://shotprint.dev/technical (judges: the passcode for Live mode is in the
submission notes)

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Startups track

## How it works

1. **Marketplace**: browse templates by goal, industry, tone and cast, and download one. The package
   holds the template and its fill recipe (`sandbox/kit/.claude/skills/template-fill`), so any agent can
   run it with the image and video models it already uses. Each template is benchmarked: the original is
   remade from the template alone and shown side by side.
2. **Studio**: one agent, no forms. Attach a video that works and Muse Code turns it into a template
   (measured, written, benchmarked; kept private or listed). Pick a template and it makes your spot. Every
   project runs in its own microVM, every file on a live canvas you can steer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UI[Studio] --> W[Worker · D1]
  W --> VM
  subgraph VM[one microVM per project]
    S[session server] --> MC[Muse Code] --> KIT[kit tools]
  end
  MC --> META[Meta Model API]
```

## Technical details

How the agent turns a video into a template, each step a tool in `sandbox/kit`:

| Step | Tool | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Its own microVM | one VM per project | Its own kernel, filesystem, CPU, memory and spend caps |
| Measure | `bin/dissect` | Cuts, shot times, loudness, lines and shot boards in about 30 s, no model calls |
| Read the craft | `tools/motion.py` | Camera moves from optical flow; Muse Code reads framing, lens, light and text |
| Write the template | `make-template` skill | `TEMPLATE.md`, `template.json`, a storyboard per shot, a swappable asset set |
| Benchmark | `bin/template check` | Remakes the reference from the template alone, side by side with the original |
| Keep or list | `catalog.json` | Private to the workspace, or listed on the marketplace |

## Meta models

| Model | Role |
|---|---|
| Muse Code | The agent that makes the film or the template |
| Muse Spark · Muse Wonder | Its reasoning (Demo · Live) |
| Muse Image | Plates, cast and product sheets, storyboards |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | Measures the spoken lines of a reference |

Video clips: MiniMax-H3 (open weights) on our own GPU, off in the live demo.

## Run

```bash

cp .env.example .env      # META_API_KEY
npm run sandbox:image     # Docker, or sandbox:image:vm for Apple's container
npm run dev               # http://localhost:5180
```

Deploy to Cloudflare (Workers, D1, R2, Containers):

# Catch Up

Missed something? Press once.

Catch Up keeps the last 2 minutes of sound in memory, and nothing leaves your device until you press. One key or tap turns the last 30, 60 or 120 seconds of a meeting, a class, a conversation in person or a video into a short card in English, Japanese or Simplified Chinese.

Built with Muse Voice Transcribe and Muse Spark on Meta Model API.

[Open Catch Up](https://catch-up-lyart.vercel.app) · [Public source repository](https://github.com/sese0318/catch-up)

## What the card holds

1. Whether you were just asked something.
2. One line you can say out loud that restates or confirms what you heard. It never answers for you, and it carries an AI-suggested tag. It stays in the language the speaker used, with a gloss in your card language when the two differ.
3. A summary of 1 or 2 sentences.
4. Up to 5 facts (names, dates, numbers, places, terms and tasks), each marked when the model is unsure.
5. The key quote, word for word.
6. A receipt that names what was sent, the route, the model and the time. Every receipt ends with Catch Up saved nothing.

The card language starts from your browser language (Japanese, Chinese, or English for everything else). You can change it, and the choice stays on this device.

## Who it is for

Anyone who loses a few seconds of a conversation and wants back in without asking the room to repeat. People whose attention drifts for a moment, people who find speech hard to follow in noise, and people listening in a second language.

Catch Up is an accessibility and language tool, not a medical device. It never reads emotions or identifies anyone by voice.

## How it works

1. **Pick a source.** People in the room through the microphone, a tab in this browser, or apps on this computer. Tick People here know I'm using Catch Up. Show heads-up opens a line to say or paste into the chat, and it names the most a press can send, up to the last 2 minutes. The page keeps the last 2 minutes in an AudioWorklet ring buffer in memory.
2. **Press.** Click Catch up, press Ctrl+Alt+C (Ctrl+Shift+Space and Ctrl+Alt+Space also work), or tap the button on a phone. The page slices the window you chose and checks that someone spoke. If no one did, nothing is sent. Otherwise one 16 kHz mono WAV goes to the server.
3. **Read the card.** The server hands the clip to a Meta model and streams the card back. While it is written, the panel shows a short line you can say to buy a moment.

On a computer, Float on top keeps the panel in a small window above your call, in browsers that support it.

## Meta Model API first

| Route | Models | How it hears the clip | When it runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Submission route, Meta Model API | Muse Voice Transcribe `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` in PUSH_TO_TALK mode, then `muse-spark-1.3` | Voice Transcribe writes a transcript, and Muse Spark turns it into the card with a JSON schema | Every live press in the Meta-only setup |
| Optional adapter, open weights | Muse Spa

# SortPilot — From Vision to Robot Action

> **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon Submission**  
> *Track: Robotics / Autonomous Agents*

SortPilot is an uncertainty-aware robotic action-planning system that transforms cluttered waste scenes into explainable, constraint-aware, and executable robotic sorting plans.

It is **not merely an image classifier or object detector**—it bridges multimodal scene perception with deterministic robotic planning, dynamic operator constraints, human-review quarantining, and 2D simulation.

---

## 1. System Architecture

```
[ Uploaded Waste Scene Image ]
              │
              ▼
   [ Multimodal Perception Layer ]
   ├── Fixture Provider (Default: Offline Zero-Cost Demo)
   └── Baseten Provider (Live Meta Muse Spark Open 1026)
              │
              ▼ Structured Scene Inventory
   [ Object Schemas: ID, Label, Material, BBox, Uncertainty, Review Flag ]
              │
              ▼
   [ Deterministic Policy & Action Planner ]
   ◄── Operator Constraints:
       • 🔋 Hold batteries/hazardous for human inspection
       • ⚠️ Require review of uncertain items
       • ⚡ Prioritize hazardous items first
       • 🍃 Hold organics for contamination inspection
              │
              ▼ Explainable Action Sequence & Replanning
   [ 2D Robotic Workcell Simulator ]
   ├── Sorting Conveyor / Table
   ├── Articulated Robot Arm & 2-Finger Gripper
   └── 5 Physical Destination Bins:
       ♻️ Recycling | 🍂 Compost | ⚡ Hazardous | 🗑️ Landfill | 🔍 Inspection Station
              │
              ▼
   [ Telemetry, Movement Cost, & Safety Audit Stream ]
```

---

## 2. Key Capabilities

1. **Real Meta Muse Spark Open Multimodal Perception**:
   - Analyzes raw scene imagery using Meta's `muse-spark-open-1026` via Baseten.
   - Extracts object identities, materials (PET, aluminum, organic, lithium), categories, and bounding boxes.
   - Captures uncertainty and occlusion indicators.
2. **Deterministic, Explainable Action Planner**:
   - Prevents unconstrained LLM hallucinations from driving physical actuators.
   - Formulates ordered pick-and-place trajectories with explicit reasoning strings.
3. **Operator Constraints & Zero-Cost Replanning**:
   - Allows recycling operators to toggle policies (e.g., holding batteries or quarantining ambiguous items).
   - Instant deterministic replanning (`POST /replan`) generates diffs and re-orders actions **without requiring additional API calls**.
4. **Human Review & Inspection Quarantine**:
   - Unsafe or uncertain objects are routed to a dedicated physical inspection holding station instead of automated recycling streams.
5. **2D Animated Robotic Workcell Simulator**:
   - Visualizes arm transit, pick operations, gripper states, and deposits into 5 bins.
   - Calculates simulated travel distance and movement costs.
6. **Built-in Benchmark Evaluation**:
   - Measures safety violations, validity rate, and travel cost against a naive unconstrained baseline (`GET /evaluate`).

# barqlo Sales Brain

One Arabic-native AI brain that runs a company's entire customer operation.
Not a bot per workflow, not a workflow per company: one central brain — one memory,
one judgment — that every channel and every sector plugs into.

Built by Mahmoud Hazaa (Banha, Qalyubia, Egypt) for the Meta Global AI Developer
Hackathon 2026, Startup track. Live site: https://barqlo.pages.dev

## The problem

Small and mid-size businesses across the Middle East drown in customer messages
they cannot answer fast enough — in Arabic, across WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram,
Messenger and web chat. The usual fix is a pile of disconnected bots: one per
workflow, one per company, each with its own memory, each free to invent an
answer. Leads get lost to spelling variants (انا / أنا / إنا treated as different
words), prices get hallucinated, and the owner finds out too late.

## The solution

One brain, two agents, and a database that decides:

1. **One brain.** Every message from every channel enters one unified message
   contract. Identity comes from the channel's database row — never from what
   the sender claims. Tenant data never mixes: each company's data, history and
   customers stay isolated.
2. **Two agents.** A Preparation agent drafts every reply. A Verification agent
   checks the draft against the business's real data and policies with
   deterministic rules — real prices only, real unit/project numbers, no denial
   without a real search, counts that match database totals, no "all" claimed
   from a sample, gaps stated honestly. One correction attempt with specific
   feedback, then re-verification. A reply that still fails goes to an honest
   fallback, an owner alert, and an audit record — it is never sent as-is.
3. **The database decides.** The AI proposes; the database decides. The model is
   forbidden from inventing units, prices or availability.
4. **Arabic-native.** A normalization layer runs before any Arabic matching:
   hamza/alef variants are one letter, ة/ه are one, ى/ي are one — plus Egyptian
   and Gulf dialect understanding, intent detection, and extraction of name,
   phone, budget, city and interest from free conversation.
5. **Owner and customer, strictly separated.** A separate owner path understands
   natural-phrasing commands ("send me today's summary") and owner alerts go
   only to the owner. The same sentence is interpreted differently by role:
   a digest request from the owner returns an operational summary; from a
   customer it never returns owner data.

The same brain runs every sector. Sector knowledge lives in data and config
rows, not in sector-specific code: real estate, clinics, restaurants and more
load their knowledge into the same brain.

The brain's core is rebuilt on Meta's Muse Spark models through the Meta Model
API. In production, one HTTP node calls:

- Endpoint: `https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions`
- Model: `muse-spark-1.3` (temperature 0.3)
- Auth: a single Header Auth cre

# Troupe

**Eleven agents. Eight in the room. One brief. No consensus.**

Troupe is a controlled experiment: a cast of AI coding agents, each with a different temperament, independently generates a self-contained HTML motion graphic from the same brief. The outputs are rendered side by side, validated, measured, and scored blind.

> Built during the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon**, November 3–4, 2026.

![Troupe studio](docs/screenshot-hybrid.png)

## The problem

Motion design has a first-hour problem. Before any craft happens, a designer has to explore directions — and that exploration converges: everyone starts from the same references, so the first round looks the same. A client sees two or three options, not eight, because each option costs hours.

Troupe is for solo designers, small agencies, and brand teams who need several directions before the first client call. One brief goes in; eight renderable 8-second loops come out in about 90 seconds, for about a cent.

The blind vote is the decision mechanism: identities, order, colors, and preview links are hidden until reveal, so the team scores the motion, not the person. It produces starting points, not production work.

## The experiment

**Question:** does persona conditioning change the style, reliability, or originality of coding-agent output?

**Hypotheses:**

| # | Hypothesis | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | Personas increase stylistic diversity | Pairwise visual + palette distance |
| H2 | The anxious perfectionist is more reliable | Console errors, render failures |
| H3 | The chaotic experimentalist is more original but less reliable | Render errors + blind vote |
| H4 | Best-of-eight personas beats a neutral baseline | Blind vote + rubric |
| H5 | A critique round improves the outputs | Before/after scores |
| H9 | A shared 3D library increases visual ambition | Blind vote + visual review |
| H10 | 3D reduces reliability and increases cost | Render errors, tokens, latency |
| H11 | 3D reduces stylistic diversity | Visual/palette similarity |
| H12 | A shared layout/camera grammar improves composition | Visual review + blind vote |
| H13 | Persona camera biases increase 3D differentiation | Visual similarity below 0.78 |
| H14 | Too much camera movement hurts legibility | Brand legibility at 1s/4s |
| H18 | Hybrid improves legibility over pure 3D | Wordmark legibility |
| H19 | Hybrid keeps 3D ambition | Blind vote + visual review |
| H20 | Hybrid reduces diversity | Visual/palette similarity |
| H23 | A Big Five record increases persona adherence | Kernel visible in output |
| H24 | Explicit style kernels reduce visual diversity | Visual similarity |

The honest result may be: *personality changes style more than quality; the benefit is diversity*. That is still a useful finding.

# 🔭 Issue Scout

**Live demo:** https://issuescout.arca.computer (Cloudflare Worker)


> **Everything in this repository was built during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon on Nov 4, 2026.**

**Problem statement:** *Build for Your World.* Open-source maintainers and first-time contributors both lose hours to issue triage: which of 300 open issues is actually doable for a newcomer, and where do I even start? Issue Scout is the tool I wished I had when making my first contribution.

## What it does
Enter a GitHub repo (`owner/name`). An agent powered by Meta's **Muse Spark** model:
1. Fetches open issues via the GitHub REST API.
2. **Scores each issue (0–10) for newcomer-friendliness**, with a one-line reason.
3. **Picks the top 3.**
4. For each pick, runs a **tool-calling loop**: the model decides to call `get_repo_tree`, `get_readme`, and `read_file` (GitHub API) to ground itself in the real repo, then writes a concrete fix plan: files likely involved, step-by-step approach, and tests.

The UI streams an agent progress log (including every tool call) and renders ranked issues and plans.

## Meta models / APIs used
- **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`) via **Meta Model API** — `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/chat/completions` (OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, `Authorization: Bearer $META_API_KEY`).
- Used for (a) structured JSON scoring/ranking of issues and (b) multi-step **function/tool calling** for the plan-writing agent. Small `max_tokens` and low reasoning effort keep cost low.

# OINC Farm Twin

A manager's simulation of OINC's Sibu mushroom factory, built in Godot 4.7 on 5 Nov 2026.
Bags (bongkah) flow through the bag line, incubation and fruiting, under weather, using
electricity, water and raw materials. An AI steward (Muse Spark 1.3) runs the farm through
tools, and asks before it changes anything.

the game shows the source of every one under **Numbers**.

```sh
godot --path .                       # play
godot --headless --path . -- --selftest          # 120 simulated days, 14 checks
godot --headless --path . -- --ask "raise the target to 450"   # one order to the steward
godot --path . -- --shot out.png --hour 21 --sky rain --inspect C3   # save a picture

# LEGION-100

**Verified multi-agent execution infrastructure for consequential tasks**

> Intelligence is abundant. Control over consequence is scarce.

**Release status:** publicly published functional development snapshot (WO057). Licensing policy is confirmed; file-level provenance review and public clean-room reproduction remain open. LEGION-100 is a source-available Veraxis research implementation. The repository documents 100 registered agents operating across 13 bounded, executable state-machine worlds. Seven world structures were developed from GAIA2 scenario categories and six from OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop operational patterns. This is not a claim that any synthetic world reproduces all conditions of a production enterprise system.

LEGION's central question is not whether 100 agents can exchange messages. It is whether a collective can satisfy **causal obligations**, admit consequential actions under verifiable authority, produce actual state changes, preserve receipts and readbacks, and earn completion from an **independent Judge**.

## Technical scope

The core execution boundary is:

`mission → executable world → 100 registered agents / assigned active roles → causal controller → ZTL evidence/admissibility → CAGE and VEIP governance → native world tools → consequential state effects → receipts + independent readbacks → independent Judge`.

The agents *propose* actions. The control and governance layers determine whether actions may be executed. The world adapter enacts eligible operations and produces evidence. The Judge decides whether the resulting collective mission satisfied all specified obligations. The consequential-action boundary and upstream CAGE attribution are described below.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[Mission + world state machine] --> A[100 registered agents]
  A --> C[Causal controller + obligation DAG]
  C --> Z[ZTL eligibility]
  Z --> G[CAGE governance / VEIP warrants]
  G -->|allowed| T[Native world tools]
  G -->|refused or deferred| L[Refusal and causal log]
  T --> E[Effects + receipts]
  E --> B[Independent readbacks]
  B --> J[Independent Judge]
  J --> V[VCC@1]
```

### Why 100 does not mean 100 NIM calls

Each world registers 100 workers. Role assignment determines which workers actually pursue obligations. The public index shows between **2 and 12 actively assigned roles per world**. The system must report active agent contributions separately from registration counts; worker registration, model calls, coordination events and native effects are distinct measurements.

## Where LEGION lives

The repository root retains the inherited Google CAGE project layout. The LEGION-specific research implementation is concentrated in:

- [`worlds/`](worlds/) — published world assets.
- [`tests/legion_struct/`](tests/legion_struct/) — causal runtime, structural worlds, controller, adapters and tests.
- [`tests/legion_scale/`](tests/legion_scale/) — coordination and scaling experiments.

# Talk to Your Editor

An editor that learns how you cut, from your own before and after.

You talk to it like texting a person. It cuts your next video your way, and every finished video teaches it more of your judgment, so the longer you use it, the less you have to fix. Nothing is final until you say so.

## The loop

1. **Teach it.** Give it a before and an after, your raw video and your finished edit, by file or by link. A finished video can teach it too.
2. **It tells you what it noticed.** In plain words: you cut the retakes, you kept the last take, you trim long pauses. Not a list of every cut. It asks before it saves anything.
3. **It edits your next video your way.** Retakes out, long gaps trimmed, joins placed on the room sound, never mid-word. Likely retakes are cut and shown as spots you can bring back with one tap; genuine judgment calls wait as spots for your review.
4. **Finish where you want.** Finish inside the app, or export the edit as a timeline file to the program you already use.

## Muse proposes, code decides

Muse Spark proposes the changes. Muse Wonder reviews the risky calls: restores, take swaps, long cuts, anything near the opening or closing. Deterministic checks decide what is safe to apply. Anything that fails is flagged for you with the reason, never applied quietly.

The model may only speak five operations:

| Operation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `cut_words` | Remove an exact span of kept words. |
| `restore_words` | Restore an exact span of currently cut words. |
| `set_join_pause` | Set the pause at one numbered join, between 0.08 and 0.50 seconds, bounded by the neighboring speech. |
| `replace_take` | Atomically swap one take for another: restore one span, cut another, both or neither. |
| `flag_for_review` | Make no change; a person decides. |

## Run it

```bash
python3 -m pip install -e .
tye serve
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765; Studio opens on the conversation. Set MODEL_API_KEY for live Muse direction; without a key, the app runs offline with a deterministic mock and the same checks. The optional `.[speech]` extra adds local transcription (Whisper, running on your computer).

## The proof it learns

The demo is one real video: a 10-minute raw talking-head recording, and the creator's own finished edit of it at 165.4 seconds.

- The app's edit runs 175.6 seconds before review.
- Transcribe both edits and diff them: 667 of his 692 words match his finished edit, 96.4 percent.
- Said plainly: the style pack's calibration examples all come from this same video, so that score is measured on the video the app learned from. It is not a general accuracy number. On a new video there is no score; it is tested by watching the edit.
- The held-out test is a second video, Day 48, which the app never learned from: on a video it never learned from, it kept about 90% of my words, with no dead air, in about 3:15 against my 2:42.

# Data Alchemist

**A flight recorder for AI data analysts.** It records every statistical test an agent runs, writes the report itself, and only keeps findings that survive confirmation on data the agent never saw.

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon) (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026).

## The problem

Ask an AI agent "what drives our sales?" and it will run dozens of tests, then show you the few that look impressive. You never see how many were run. At alpha = 0.05, 14 hidden tests give a 51% chance of at least one false positive; 45 give 90% (1 − 0.95^m).

We measured it on Muse Spark. On 5 synthetic datasets with **no real effect**, it made 56 claims: 39 correct denials and **17 asserting a link that does not exist** (0 to 7 per dataset). Nothing in its answer says which. After our engine's check, **0 of the 17 were kept**.

These are early numbers: 5 datasets, one prompt, synthetic data. See [Limits](#limits).

## How it works

```
Agent  ──►  Test API (registry)  ──►  Engine report  ──►  Confirmation on held-out half
              logs every test         written by the        run once, after the number of
              (variables, subsample,  engine, never by      promoted hypotheses is frozen
              code)                   the agent
```

- **Registry** (`core/registry.py`): the agent gets p-values only through our test API (correlation, chi-square, ANOVA, Mann-Whitney, regression with adjustment, nonlinear and interaction tests). Every call is logged, so the number of tests *m* is known. Unregistered or altered extractions are refused.
- **Engine-written report** (`core/report.py`): shows *m*, raw discoveries, and each rejected claim with its reason, plus a selection check comparing registry p-values with reported ones. The agent never writes conclusions.
- **Explore / confirm split** (`core/split.py`, after Cox 1975): the agent explores one half freely. The number of hypotheses to promote is fixed before the untouched half is opened, and it can be opened only once.
- **Claims** (`core/claims.py`): every claim must reference registered tests. A claim with no test behind it is rejected. Effects are reported as associations or "robust to adjustment", never as proven causes.
- **Multiplicity control** (`core/multiplicity.py`): Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg, Benjamini-Yekutieli and e-BH, each with its assumptions stated.
- **Model adapter** (`core/agent_adapter.py`): Muse Spark, through the Meta Model API, is the first model audited. It explores only through the instrumented API and returns structured claims tied to registry ids. The engine itself is model-agnostic.

## Pre-registered protocol

`docs/PROTOCOL.md` fixes hypotheses, metrics and decision rules before the benchmark runs. The main rule:

> We say **p-hacking** only if the registry's p-values are uniform while the reported ones concentrate below 0.05. Otherwise the honest conclusion is **over-claiming**.

The harness is the rocket. The model is the pilot.

Rocket is a model-agnostic harness that turns an app idea into a verified, store-ready Flutter app and can ship it to TestFlight under the user's own developer account. Product goal: [docs/VISION.md](docs/VISION.md).

Building the app is no longer the hard part. The repeated plumbing around it is: auth, onboarding, paywall, privacy and terms, account deletion, store metadata, signing, upload. # Roomind — shared AI rooms where teams and agents work live

> Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TtOO0cJjn_s

*Start solo like any AI chat. Hit Share, and the same chat becomes a live room: teammates and agents, one memory, a referee that speaks only with evidence, and a receipt for every decision — all priced on screen.*

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Cerebral Valley), Indie track — **Build for Your World** (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026).

## The Problem

Shared AI chats are read-only: you can send someone your Claude or ChatGPT thread, but they can't continue it with you. Teams paste screenshots, lose context, and re-ask the same questions — while group chats agree fast on thin ideas with nobody checking.

## Our Solution: Roomind

Open a solo chat. The moment you need people, Share mints invites and the *same* chat becomes a room: every member chats and asks, the agent answers everyone, one memory serves the team, a dissent referee cards thin agreements, stamped decisions land in a ledger, side rooms split off and report back — and a meter prices every model call.

## Features

**Rooms & chat**
- Solo-first: start alone with the agent, Share when you need people.
- Single + team invite links with live joined/left counts and +5 seat top-up.
- Unique nicknames per seat; per-member model choice (your pick, your meter).
- Live chat plus ask/answer slots — each answer lands under its own question.
- Streaming answers with Sources and checkable reasons (Tavily search, full-page reads, Open-Meteo weather).

**Memory**
- Remember/recall via chat; forget with one × per fact; one-click briefs.

**Referee (dissent)**
- Evidence-only cards on rushed or rule-breaking agreement, with quoted receipts.
- Manual "Challenge us", mute with a room-wide badge, expert hats per card.

**Decisions & work**
- Editable proposal cards; stamped decision ledger (overlaps replace, never pile).
- Tasks (assignee + due + Done), versioned docs (draft → propose → approve), live polls, daily reminders with popups (ledger deadlines mirror automatically).

**Side rooms**
- Split off a picked subgroup (one level); member-only roster; one-click share-back lands in main chat and as one ledger row.

**Teammates & red-team**
- @Researcher/@Planner/@Critic answer when mentioned; add/rename/remove your own.
- Away tasks run in the background and land in chat plus under the done task.
- Red-team attacks with ranked flaws, severity, Holds line, and cooldown.

**Running & publishing**
- Owner/operator/member roles, kick, room lock, step out, leave, ownership transfer, close forever.

- Sidebar meter: per-model spend plus room cap; header shows live approval from thumbs.

# NDC Scout: which NDC actually reimburses best?

> Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Developer track, theme "Build for Your World".
> Built on Meta Model API (Muse Spark) with tool calling and a deterministic verifier.

> ⚠️ `sample_data/` is **synthetic**: fictitious labelers, invented prices,
> illustrative payer formulas. See [docs/END-TO-END.md](docs/END-TO-END.md) to
> load real FDA and CMS data.

## The problem

A generic drug is sold as many NDCs: different labelers and package sizes, all
the same medicine. Pharmacies are paid per claim by formulas that treat those
NDCs differently.

- **Medicaid (NADAC + fee) and PBM MAC payers** pay the same whichever NDC you
  dispense, so the winner is the NDC you **buy** cheapest.
- **AWP-based payers** price each NDC separately, so a high-AWP NDC can pay
  far more.

So the best NDC changes from payer to payer. A pharmacy with a mixed book
needs the one with the best **expected** margin, and nobody has time to work
that out for hundreds of drugs. NDC Scout does: it ranks a drug's NDCs by
margin per fill for one payer or a payer mix, and flags anything a human
should check.

## What it does

```
$ ndc-scout ask --drug "atorvastatin 40" --payer partd-awp --qty 30
  [turn 1] model -> search_drugs, list_payers
  [turn 2] model -> rank_ndcs(atorvastatin-40mg-tab, partd-awp, 30)
  [turn 3] model -> final answer
  [turn 3] verifier: PASS
RECOMMEND 99102-0441-90  ($7.90 per fill)
  ! 99104-0022-10: Wholesaler price is 80 days old
```

- **The agent** (Muse Spark through Meta Model API) understands the request,
  picks tools, and explains the result in plain language.
- **The engine** (`ndc_scout/engine.py`) does every dollar of the math.
- **The verifier** recomputes every number the model reports. If anything is
  wrong, the model gets one repair turn with the exact discrepancies, and a
  wrong answer is never shown as verified.
- **Flags:**
  - blocking: missing NADAC, unit mismatch, not in your catalog
  - warning: stale price, discontinuing
  - info: slow mover, MAC-capped

  Every warning or blocking flag is surfaced under "needs a human".
- **Spend guards:** a per-run budget, a local monthly cap that **refuses**
  calls once reached (Meta has no hard cap), and a token and cost log.
- **Compare AWP vs MAC:** a chart ranking every NDC's margin under a MAC-based
  payer against an AWP-discount payer side by side — the two formulas often
  disagree on which NDC is best.
- **Rate audit:** cross-checks one payer's MAC rates against every other
  MAC-based payer for the same drug, and against the public NADAC floor, to
  flag a contract that looks stingier than it should — a possible sign of a
  payer underpaying relative to its peers. Deterministic, same as every other
  number here; no model involved.

## Run it

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m pytest -q                       # 46 tests, no API calls
ndc-scout serve                           # http://127.0.0.1:8000  (mock mode if no key)

# Temp Check

Live copilot for founder calls. Listens to the call, keeps a deal card updated as the founder talks, flags when a number contradicts an earlier one (with both quotes), suggests the next question, and writes the temp-check memo when you hang up.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 on two Meta Model API models:

- **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`) for speech to text, 10-second chunks over `POST /v1/asr/transcribe`
- **Muse Spark 1.3** (`muse-spark-1.3`) for structured extraction and the memo, over the OpenAI-compatible `POST /v1/chat/completions` with a JSON schema

No framework, no database, no build step. One HTML file and one dependency-free Python file.

## Why

I run three to four founder calls a day for an AI accelerator. About one in a hundred reaches investment committee. On the call the job is to listen; after the call the job is to write a memo with every number the founder said. Those two jobs fight. If I type, I miss the tell. If I listen, I lose the numbers. The worst case is quiet: $1.2M ARR at minute two becomes $900K at minute nine, and nobody notices until a partner compares notes a week later.

Temp Check makes the record while the founder is still on the line, so the follow-up question gets asked on the call instead of in an email.

## How it works

```
mic ──(AudioWorklet, 24 kHz PCM, 10 s)──► browser packs WAV
      │
      ▼
POST /api/chunk  ──► Muse Voice Transcribe  ──► chunk transcript
      │
      ▼
Muse Spark 1.3 (json_schema) ◄── thesis + current deal card + transcript so far + new chunk
      │
      ▼
updated deal card: fields · claim ledger (verbatim quotes) · flags · next questions · fit notes
      │
      ▼  (on demand)
Muse Spark 1.3 ──► one-page temp-check memo (markdown)
```

Details that matter:

- **Claim ledger.** Every material claim (ARR, MRR, growth, customers, margin, burn, runway, raise, cap, committed, lead, team, sales motion) is stored with the founder's verbatim quote and the chunk index. The server merges each new card with the previous one so a claim or flag is never lost, even if the model forgets to echo it.
- **Contradiction flags.** A later claim that conflicts with an earlier claim on the same field raises a flag with both quotes. Red for revenue, raise, valuation, customers, committed. Yellow for softer drift ("all inbound" → "we hired two SDRs") and for ambiguous definitions ("ARR" that is really pipeline).
- **Thesis fit.** `THESIS` in `server.py` is a plain-text block (stage bar, standard terms, known pass reasons). Edit it for your fund. It rides along on every extraction call.
- **Graceful degradation.** If the API rejects `json_schema` the server retries with `json_object`, then plain text plus a JSON extractor. A typed-input box bypasses transcription if the mic misbehaves. `MOCK=1` runs the UI with canned responses and no credits.

# deed-ledger

An AI agent that takes orders for small stores. Nothing it tells a customer counts as true until the store's own
records say so: every claim is read back from the database before the message goes out.

Customers order through WhatsApp with typed text, a photo of a handwritten list, or a voice note. Meta's models read
what they sent and plan the next step. Code checks every proposal, the customer confirms a readback of every line
and the total, and staff prepare the order from a console on their phone. Each message, decision and tap is saved
exactly once. WhatsApp is the first channel, not the product: it sits behind one interface (`MessagingChannel`).

Built for the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon), Indie track,
October 26 to November 4, 2026.

## Qué es Deed

**Deed is an architectural pattern: a double-entry ledger for an agent's effects.** The agent's claim is one leg of
the entry; the world writes the other. A fact exists only when the two balance, and facts govern what the agent is
allowed to do next.

Deed is the product that implements three levels. They are not the same thing:

| Level | What it is | Analogue |
|---|---|---|
| **Pattern** | The design rule: who may write what, and when something counts as a fact | Saga, Outbox, Event Sourcing |
| **Protocol** | The shape of the entry: who · what · witness · verdict · dependencies | A bank statement; TCP's segment |
| **Measurement** | The arithmetic on top: balance, liveness, and reliability under dependence | Statistical process control; an audit |

The pattern's name is **Double-Entry Effect Ledger**; "Agentic ledger" is the short name.

### What it is NOT

- **Not an audit log.** A log records what the actor says it did, written by the actor. Deed records what an
  independent party can corroborate.
- **Not LLM-as-judge.** No model issues a verdict, ever.
- **Not output verification.** The question is not "is the answer good" but "did the effect happen in the world".
- **Not a hallucination detector.** A claim with no trace in any system is marked unverifiable, not refuted.
- **Not a signed-receipt library.** Those exist (about twenty projects, and three IETF SCITT drafts as of October
  2026). A receipt records one party's observation. Deed is the bookkeeping on top of receipts.

### The eleven conformance criteria

Each one is testable. Fail one of the four load-bearing ones (★) and it isn't Deed; it's an audit log with good
branding. The other seven can be partial and it is still recognisably Deed.

| # | Criterion | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **C1** ★ | **A claim is not a fact.** The actor writes only the claim leg and a pointer to where its counter-leg must appear. Separation of write permissions, enforced structurally. | ✅ built and tested |
| **C2** ★ | **Every fact carries evidence from a source the actor does not control.** No evidence, no fact. | ✅ built and tested. The order's Libro view (`/console/deed/:pedido/li

# Tygart-OS on Meta Muse: The Fact-Gated Fleet

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon · Startup Track**
Tygart Media — Will Tygart, with Glint (his AI chief of staff)

Publishing at machine speed breaks facts quietly: a single AI editing pass invents plausible, confident, wrong "fixes" — and no human can hand-check thousands of live pages. Tygart-OS runs its real production fleet (six sites, 4,415 live pages) on Meta's Muse models with a separation-of-duties design: a **Trio** — Scout (low effort) flags, Fixer (medium) drafts, Adjudicator (max) strikes anything it cannot ground verbatim in the source, so the proposer never approves its own work — plus the **Hopper**, one dumb intake box with per-destination translator routers that confirm every routing by read-back.

On the hackathon's credits it produced 2,769 monetization candidates, 2,062 adjudicated fixes, 36 staged work orders, and a mined corpus of 174 session recordings — **$102.50 counted of the $153.31 envelope**, every run receipted. (Counted = every Meta Model API leg that returned usage, summed in the run ledger; legs that returned no usage are recorded as unmetered, not estimated.)

## Vocabulary (the four words everything else uses)

- **Paste** — material that has been ingested and checked: every claim in it grounded in a verbatim quote from its source, anything ungroundable struck. *Not* copy-paste: paste is what checked information is called while it is still unshaped, before any destination has had a say. The Trio makes the paste.
- **Hopper** — the one intake box the paste collects in. Nothing leaves the hopper until the operator taps Assemble.
- **Tip** — one destination's accepted shape, named for a cake-decorating tip: paste leaves the hopper only through a tip, so it can only come out in a form that destination already accepts — an import file, a portal form, a UI drive.
- **Trio** — the three-pass check itself: Scout (low effort) flags, Fixer (medium) drafts, Adjudicator (max) strikes. The proposer never approves its own work.

## The Trio — paste-making

The Trio is ingestion plus consistency check — paste-making — run on Muse Spark 1.3 at three reasoning-effort tiers:

- **Scout (low)** listens and drafts in the field — fast, cheap, honest about what it cannot identify.

# RealityTest

**Unit tests for the physical world.**

RealityTest is an open-source app that evaluates observable physical tasks from short videos.
The first use case is robotic pick-and-place. You upload a clip, name the object
(e.g. `red cube`), and draw the target region (e.g. the blue tray). **Meta SAM 3.1** tracks the
object across frames, and a **deterministic geometry engine** returns:

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PASS` | ≥ 3 of the last 5 usable observations have the object's mask centroid inside the target polygon, the object was seen outside earlier, coverage is sufficient, and there is one unambiguous object |
| `FAIL` | Coverage is sufficient and the object stays **visible** outside the target in ≥ 3 of the last 5 usable observations |
| `INCONCLUSIVE` | No detection, ambiguous objects, low coverage, object lost or occluded at the end, unsuitable video, or an API/stream failure |

Every verdict comes with visual evidence: the real SAM 3.1 masks and boxes over the video, the
movement trail, the target zone, a per-frame timeline, the decisive frames with their original
frame indices and object IDs, tracking coverage, and explicit limitations.

> RealityTest checks **2D image-plane geometry**. It does **not** prove 3D containment or contact,
> and it is **not** a safety certification.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. MIT licensed.

---

## How it works

```
video ──► Meta Model API (sam-3.1, /v1/responses, stream) ──► @meta-sam/parser
                                                                   │  boxes + masks per frame,
                                                                   ▼  stable object IDs
           user-confirmed polygon ──► geometry engine (centroid ∈ polygon) ──► PASS / FAIL / INCONCLUSIVE
```

1. The video is uploaded to `POST /v1/files` (`purpose: user_data`). A Responses API request is
   sent with an `input_text` concept prompt and an `input_video` part, using `stream: true`.
2. The stream is consumed until `response.completed`. It is decoded **only** with the official
   [`@meta-sam/parser`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@meta-sam/parser) (`parseVideoStream`,
   `decodeMaskToRaster`, `decodeMaskToSVGPath`), never with regexes. Frame indices come from the
   `<Nf>` markers, so sparse or out-of-order frames are handled. Object IDs are kept verbatim.
3. For each frame, the mask raster is decoded and its centroid is computed in source pixels. The
   engine checks the centroid against the polygon you drew. Display coordinates are converted to
   source pixels with letterbox-aware math (`src/lib/evaluation/geometry.ts`).
4. Verdict rules are in `src/lib/evaluation/evaluator.ts`. The coverage threshold defaults to 60%
   (`EVAL_COVERAGE_THRESHOLD`). AI errors are **never** turned into a PASS or FAIL.

### Provenance labels

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Live Meta SAM 3.1** | Real API call made for this evaluation |
| **Recorded API fixture** | A saved response from a previous

**Teach an indoor route once. Verify its landmarks on the way back.**

Waymark turns operator-recorded indoor observations into an evidence-linked topological graph. Meta Muse Spark Open reads static visual landmarks and signage, then compares a new observation against learned reference images. A deterministic verifier holds the location unless the expected landmark has sufficient visual support, all learned signage, and two distinct image observations.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie Developer / Build for Your World, November 4, 2026. Intended direction: indoor spaces without reliable GPS, such as offices, event venues and airport interiors. No airport deployment or navigation accuracy is claimed.

Python 3.10+; no Python packages required for the app.

```sh

# Atria Lens

Atria Lens helps deaf and hard-of-hearing people catch the moments that matter, without staring at captions all day.
Glasses listen; when something is meant for the user (their name, a question to them, their order, their train,
a safety warning) Atria shows a short line on the glasses and taps their wrist with a distinct vibration rhythm.
Everything else (someone else's order, background chatter) stays quiet.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** with Meta models only:
- **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`): real-time speech to text, live captions
- **Muse Spark Open** (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`): decides what matters and for whom, auto tasks,
  Deaf-mode simplification, daily summaries, "Ask Atria"

**Demo build:** iOS app [v2.4 release](../../releases/tag/v2.4) (unsigned IPA, install with Sideloadly / AltStore).

## How it works

```text
Glasses (ESP32-S3: mic + OLED HUD)
   │  LC3 audio, 16 kHz, BLE (20 ms frames)
   ▼
iPhone app (Expo / React Native) ── no own server, the phone talks to Meta directly
   ├─ Muse Voice Transcribe 1.0 ── live text ──► captions on the glasses
   ├─ instant rules (name, order number, "excuse me", safety) ── fast alerts
   └─ Muse Spark Open 1026 ── is it for me? real or not yet? which kind? ── confirm / cancel
   │
   ├─► Glasses HUD: short alert line
   └─► Band (ESP32-C3: vibration motor + OLED mascot): rhythm per meaning
```

### Vibration language on the band

| Meaning | Rhythm |
|---|---|
| Your name | • • • |
| A question to you | • — |
| Someone wants your attention | • • |
| Your order / number is ready | — |
| Announcement (train, gate, stop) | — — |
| Safety warning | keeps buzzing until you press the button |

### Features
- **Auto tasks:** say "One latte, please" and Atria starts waiting for your order by itself.

# Trace & Tell

> An evidence-aware family archive that helps people discover questions worth asking before memories lose their context.

**Status:** In progress; not deployed. The public `/demo` now walks through synthetic originals, recorded Meta observations and comparison, a human-authored question, invented testimony and an evidence-linked gallery. Four historical Meta inferences succeeded (one standalone and three app runs); the comparison returned no questions. Human-authored questioning and the single-user hosted save/reopen journey passed. Real A/B security acceptance and general model quality remain open. See the [submission packet and release gates](docs/submission-readiness.md), [dated implementation evidence](docs/m1b-m2-implementation.md) and [M1a audit](docs/m1a-implementation.md).

**Project name:** Trace & Tell is a working product name; it has not been verified as the final name entered on the hackathon application.

## Motivation

Old photographs, notes and letters can survive after the people who remember their context are no longer able to explain them. Trace & Tell aims to help a family record keeper examine such material, recognise potentially useful clues, ask a person a meaningful question and preserve the answer with its source.

The product does **not** infer people's identities, kinship or medical conditions from photographs. It does not promise to restore memories, diagnose conditions or establish family history automatically.

## Intended Experience

1. Create a private collection and add photographs, handwritten notes or typed notes.
2. Review **observations** suggested from visible content, correcting or rejecting uncertain readings.
3. Examine evidence-backed **connection hypotheses**, including contrary or missing evidence.
4. Select and edit questions to ask a relative or another knowledgeable person.
5. Record **testimony** as text; audio capture and transcription are a subsequent milestone.
6. Compose a small private exhibition with explicit source links and unresolved questions.
7. Reopen the collection and revise it without erasing the provenance of earlier decisions.

An accepted hypothesis remains a hypothesis. A person's testimony is attributed to its speaker and recorder; neither becomes independently verified fact merely because it appears in an exhibition.

npm install

Meet Mita turns study material students already have into an anime-style interactive presentation guided by Mita, an expressive 3D learning companion.

Upload a PDF or one to five ordered photos of notes. Meet Mita uses that material to shape a lesson with dialogue, contextual picture cards, recall checkpoints, and questions the learner can ask while the lesson is open. The experience gives a chapter a clear route through its ideas, with Mita guiding the learner along the way.

## Why this format

Students often receive course material as static files. Meet Mita tests a focused design idea: a familiar, character-led presentation may make those materials easier to begin and easier to stay with. Audience research helps shape who the experience is for; the effect on study behavior remains a question for learner testing.

These figures describe the intended audience's digital and media context; they do not measure Meet Mita's impact.

## How Mita supports a learner

Mita is designed to be a warm, curious guide who explains unfamiliar terms in everyday language before using the formal vocabulary. Her playful side serves the explanation, and she treats a mistake as something to work through. When a correction matters, her guidance stays direct and respectful.

# Trailhead

> Your footsteps become the trail.

A learning companion that never hands you a curriculum. It follows your
curiosity, draws the map afterwards from where you actually went, checks what you
really remember, and when a prerequisite is missing, fills in only that piece.

**Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. Problem statement: Build for Your World.**

## The problem

This solves a learning problem I live with as someone with ADHD.

A curriculum gets abandoned, because following a plan to the end is the very thing
that doesn't happen. "Review your notes later" fails for the same reason: later
never comes. And a mind map that gets generated and handed over is a nice artifact
that nobody opens again.

What actually happens is that you wander, and you ask the same question again. So
Trailhead doesn't ask you to change. It works from what you already do.

Trailhead is a tool that helps with learning. It doesn't diagnose, treat or
measure anything about ADHD or attention.

## What it does

- **No curriculum up front.** Say "I want to learn AI" and it asks what brought you
  to it, once. A broad interest is enough: ask for the big picture or say
  "I don't know" and it starts explaining that interest with a concrete example,
  without another preference question. Structure is the result of your questions,
  not the input to them. Once you've asked a few things, or when you ask what's next,
  it offers a short path built from them, as buttons you can ignore.
- **Throw anything at it.** Drop or paste a screenshot, photo or diagram. Muse Spark
  works out what it is and places it on the map. It never asks where to file it.
- **The trail draws itself.** Every question and every image grows the map. Wandering
  isn't a flaw to correct: it's recorded as ground you covered.
- **Seeing isn't knowing.** The map tracks what you remember, not what you visited.
- **Fills only the hole.** When a concept depends on something you haven't seen, it
  says so, explains just that one piece, and goes straight back to your question.
- **Tests memory inside the conversation.** When you come back to something related,
  it asks what you remember before saying anything. Fail, and the concept is marked
  fuzzy and re-taught. There are no notifications and no "come back later".

| On the map | Meaning                                                    |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Remembered | Answered a recall check correctly                          |
| Seen       | Looked at, memory not tested yet                           |
| Fuzzy      | Failed a recall check, or untouched for 30 days            |
| Hole       | Needed by another concept, but never looked at             |

Agentic quantum circuit optimizer for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.
A **Muse Spark 1.3** planner (Meta Responses API) picks strategies, a **Muse Code** swarm of

Calling the venv's Python by path (`.venv/bin/python3`) makes every command use the venv,

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python3 -m pip install -e ".[test]"   # installs the package + all deps + pytest

.venv/bin/python3 -m quantum_optimizer.orchestrator --provider none   # deterministic swarm, no API key
```

Type each command on its own line; pasting several at once can add hidden characters.

.venv/bin/python3 -m quantum_optimizer.orchestrator --only grover3 --viewer --angle 40 --director-backend off --no-nemotron-review

# HearingHistoryLab
# Part 1 — Taking the test

## What this is

A hearing self-test for adults roughly 20 to 80 that tracks hearing
over time: a short session once a month, or after a loud concert. Each
session produces one honest measurement per pitch and ear that you
compare with your own past measurements, on your own equipment.

Everything is relative to your own history. The app never claims
absolute or clinical values.

Live test at this URL https://alanbork.github.io/HearingHistoryLab/hearing_history_lab.html

## Why history is the whole point

A single session is a snapshot; only repeat sessions show whether your
hearing is *changing*. Because every session starts from your past
thresholds instead of from scratch, check-ups get faster the longer
your history grows — and the snapshot chart can overlay your past
results with your usual range, so drift stands out at a glance instead
of hiding in a table.

## How to run it

Double-click `hearing_history_lab.html`. It opens in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox via
`file://` with no install, no build step, no libraries, and no network
requests of any kind. Your data never leaves your browser.

**Headphones — the single most important part.** Use a good pair of
wired over-ear or in-ear headphones that seal comfortably and stay put.
Wired matters: Bluetooth headphones apply their own processing and
volume quirks that drift between sessions, and every session needs to
sound identical. Never use speakers — your room changes the sound more
than your ears do.

**The same setup, every time.** Reuse the same headphones, the same
device, and the same fit each session. If anything does change, later
sessions open with a quick check that flags it honestly.

**Volume to maximum, enhancements off.** Set the device volume to max,
and switch off any equalizer, bass boost, spatial audio, or loudness
normalization. Those features quietly move levels around behind our
back.

**A quiet room.** Background noise buries the quietest beeps, which are
exactly the ones that pin down your thresholds. A closed door and a
paused TV are enough.

## What a session feels like

First time only, a warm-up: a beep repeats while you raise a slider
from silent until you just hear it, at each pitch in each ear. Then you
pick which pitches to measure on a rough preview chart.

Then the real measurement, one of two ways (your choice, remembered):

- **Ascending tone (recommended).** Beeps rise automatically and you
  tap the side you hear the moment you hear anything — one tap per
  run. Runs flow into each other silently; when the session is done a
  voice says "Session complete", so it works with your eyes closed.
- **Staircase.** Each trial plays two quick beeps or a single longer
  tone in one ear, and you answer both *which ear* and *which
  pattern* on a two-by-two grid.

Everything starts silent and climbs only with your input; nothing ever
starts loud. Set aside about 20–30 undisturbed minutes the first time.
If your ears tire, paus

# Baton

**Meta splits it. Three AIs build it at once.**

Baton is a Mac menu bar app. You type one idea. Meta's **Muse Spark** (through the Meta Model API) splits the work at
the start and hands each part to the AI that is best at it:

| AI | Gets the work it's best at |
|---|---|
| **Claude** | the main code: app structure, UI, careful multi-file features |
| **Codex** | terminal work: setup, packages, scripts, tests, running and fixing |
| **Gemini** | live web research, facts, docs and written content |

Then all three **run at the same time** in one project folder, each on the person's **own subscription**, with no paid API
keys for Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini. If an AI's tool isn't installed or its plan runs out, its card still holds a
ready-made prompt: **drag it** into the Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini app, or press **Copy & open**.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (theme: *Build for Your World*).

**Two ways to run Meta's model:** Muse Spark on the Meta Model API (default), or Meta's open-weights **Llama 3.2**
fully offline on your Mac through Ollama (Settings → "Use local Llama"). The demo video uses the local Llama path:
my Meta Model API account lists the models but can't make requests until a card hold succeeds.

## The problem

People who build with AI hit the same wall: one AI's usage limit ends halfway through the job. Switching to another AI
loses the plan, and the second AI breaks what the first one made. Meanwhile, each AI is clearly better at some kinds of
work than others, and most of a premium plan gets spent on work another AI does just as well.

## How Meta's model is used

Muse Spark is the brain. It does three real jobs:

1. **Writes the contract first.** The stack, the exact folder layout, every shared name (files, ids, functions, data
   shapes) and style rules. That is what lets three AIs work at the same time without seeing each other's work.
2. **Splits the work and assigns owners.** Each AI gets its own files and folders. No two AIs own the same path, which
   Baton also checks in code. Meta writes each AI a complete, ready-to-paste prompt and says why that AI got the job.
3. **Checks the work.** "Check the work" sends Muse Spark the contract, each AI's report (`.baton/<ai>.md`) and the
   file list. It answers with what's done, what doesn't fit together, and the single best next prompt.

Baton wraps every prompt with rules it adds itself (owned paths, hands off others' files, write a report), so they
can't be left out.

An interactive scientific demonstration that simulates simplified downhill lava-flow pathways across a synthetic volcanic terrain, then uses a **Meta model** (via the Meta Model API) to interpret the computed results.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track).

> **Not a hazard forecast.** The terrain is synthetic and the flow model is purely geometric. Nothing here estimates real-world risk, probability, or timing.

## Project status

| Component | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Terrain generation, flow-path simulation, 2D/3D visualization | **Working**; covered by unit tests |
| Meta Model API analysis | **Implemented but not yet verified with a real response.** API credentials had not arrived by the submission deadline. |

1. **Generates a deterministic volcanic elevation grid** (100 × 100 cells). It includes a stratovolcano cone, a summit crater breached to the south-south-east, five radial erosion valleys, a parasitic cone, a closed basin, and a regional tilt.

The flow path is computed entirely by deterministic code. The LLM only interprets results; it never computes them.

# OpenWeeder

**A low-cost precision weeding robot for small farms, taught by Meta AI.**
A small car drives along a row. A camera looks straight down. **SAM 3.1** outlines every plant, **Muse Spark** judges
which are weeds, and a servo **wiper arm** swings a nozzle across the row to spray **only the weeds**. A farmer teaches a
new crop with about ten photos. The big cloud models then teach a small offline detector, so the robot can work without
internet.

`Meta SAM 3.1` · `Muse Spark 1.3` · `Muse Image 1.0` · `YOLO11n` · `Raspberry Pi 4` · `Python 3.11` · `Flask`

> **Status in one paragraph.** The whole pipeline works end to end and is tested: teach a crop, generate and label a
> dataset, train YOLO, plan the spray geometry, and drive the real hardware stop-and-go on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a safety
> watchdog. **The offline YOLO model is not accurate enough yet** (it finds 7-12% of weeds); **SAM + Muse is**
> (45-61% of weeds found on real photos, 0-1 crop hits), but it is slow (about 35 s per picture). We report both, with the
> measurements, in [Results](#results-honest-numbers). The pump is a dummy GPIO output for now (switched by a push button
> outside the Pi), so the robot logs exactly where it would spray.

## Contents

| Judging criterion | Where to look |
|---|---|
| **Impact** | [The problem](#the-problem) · [Results](#results-honest-numbers) (liquid saved) |
| **Use of Meta AI tooling** | [How we use Meta AI](#how-we-use-meta-ai) · [AI teaches AI](#the-core-idea-big-ai-teaches-a-small-model) |

---

## The problem

Smallholder farms weed by hand or spray whole fields. Broadcast spraying wastes herbicide, harms the crop and soil, and
costs money. Weeding by hand is slow and hard on the back. A robot that sprays only the weeds needs to know **which plant is
a weed on THIS farm**, and every farm grows something different. Training a custom detector for each crop normally needs
a lot of labeled photos.

OpenWeeder's answer: **the farmer labels about three photos, and Meta's models do the rest.**

In our simulator (placeholder robot numbers) spraying only the detected weeds used about **7 ml instead of 101 ml**, 93%
