# ZeroState

**A second check before anyone opens a pipe.** ZeroState compares a plant's isolation plan with the plant's own live data and a camera, and says STOP when they disagree. It is read-only. It never gives the go-ahead. A person decides and signs.

- Demo video (3 min): https://youtu.be/jARv_GhjjRE
- Try it, no key needed: https://zerostate-bay.vercel.app
- Every result, with the seal check: https://zerostate-bay.vercel.app/results.html

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026), Indie track, "Push the Frontier".

![ZeroState stops a job: the control system says the valve is closed, the flow meter and the camera say it is open](docs/img/hero_stop.png)

*A demo run on the simulated reactor (tuning seed 503, not a benchmark job).*

## The story in five steps

1. A technician is about to open a reactor for repair. They type or say: "I'm about to open the reactor. Check my isolation." Muse Spark finds the reactor's confirmed isolation plan.
2. They close each valve and say "step two done". Muse Voice Transcribe hears it, ZeroState reads it back, and they say "confirm".
3. The feed valve sticks open, but its position sensor still says closed. (This is a simulated fault.)
4. ZeroState asks three witnesses. The control system says the valve is 0 % open. The flow meter says flow is still going through it. The camera says 100 % open: SAM 3.1 finds the valve's display in the frame and Muse Spark reads the number.
5. Two witnesses disagree with the control system, so ZeroState says STOP and explains why. There is no "go" button. A person decides.

## Why this matters

Before maintenance on a pump, vessel or line, every source of energy feeding it has to be isolated: valves closed and locked, the line vented, and the isolation proved. This is lockout/tagout. When it goes wrong, the pipe a worker opens is still full of hot, toxic or flammable fluid.

It goes wrong in two ways, and US Chemical Safety Board investigations show both.

**The instruments said "isolated" and the plant wasn't.**
- BP Amoco, Augusta, 2001: a plugged gauge read zero. 3 workers killed. ([CSB report](https://www.csb.gov/assets/1/20/BP_Investigation_Report.pdf))
- Tosco Avon, 1999: valves were passing and drains were clogged while the line was opened. 4 killed. ([CSB](https://www.csb.gov/assets/1/6/CSB_Digest_-_Tosco_(Preventive_Maintenance).pdf))
- Giant Ciniza, 2004: a valve was open while the crew believed it was closed. ([CSB](https://www.csb.gov/assets/1/20/Giant_Case_Study.pdf))

**The plan or the point was wrong.**
- LyondellBasell La Porte, 2021: the chosen isolation valve was itself under pressure. 2 killed. ([CSB](https://www.csb.gov/assets/1/6/lyb_final_report_2023-05-25.pdf))
- Williams Geismar, 2013: a vessel was boxed in with no relief and then heated. 2 killed. ([CSB](https://www.csb.gov/csb-releases-final-case-study-into-2013-explosion-and-fire-at-williams-olefins-plant-in-geismar-louisiana/))
- Formosa Illiopolis, 2004: work starte

- **measured multi-view validation** instead of adjectives.

`pivot/chat-wrapper` (local server + flow viewer). Third-party model repositories and weights are **not**

# Harbor

**A calm place on a busy web.** Harbor is a Chrome side-panel extension that reshapes any web page around
how you use it. Meta's **Muse Spark** reads the page and proposes a layout from your own preferences;
nothing on the page changes until you preview it and press **Keep**. What you keep comes back by itself
on every page of that kind, and an on-device model learns which items you open and offers to put them
in your order.

Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (27 Oct – 4 Nov 2026).

## What it does

1. **Set up your harbor (15 seconds, once).** Three picks: the page shape you'd rather read (roomy or
   compact, list or grid), what you reach for first (search or the content), and what to tidy (ads,
   pop-ups, "more like this", sidebar extras, comments: keep, fold or clear). Ads and promo pop-ups start
   cleared. Your picks are sent with every request as short rules; anything left "as is" is never sent.
2. **Read → Suggest → Preview → Keep.** Click Harbor's toolbar icon. Muse Spark (optionally with SAM 3.1
   on a screenshot) proposes changes: hide, fold behind a "Show …" button, compact, grid, emphasise. Each
   change says why ("because your harbor: ads cleared", or "Muse Spark's own idea: …"). Preview outlines
   them on the real page; untick anything; Keep.
3. **It stays.** A kept layout is saved per change and re-applied, with no Meta call, wherever its
   regions are found again. Matching is by structure, not URL: every saved layout on a site is tried on
   every page of that site, and a region whose fingerprint is re-found with high confidence is applied
   there, so a change to the top bar follows you from the feed to a messaging thread. On a site you
   follow, a page of a new kind gets a Muse Spark suggestion by itself (at most once per page shape per
   day; a switch in Settings turns it off), drafted around what is already on the page. A style change
   on a repeated list (compact, grid) reaches every like item, including rows below the fold, rows added
   later and kinds the plan didn't name; what the items look like is remembered per site. Hide, fold and
   order act only on what the plan names.
4. **It learns your order (on this device, opt-in).** Harbor checks which regions the page lays out as one
   row of like items (a nav bar, tabs) and marks them "learns your order". After 8 clicks in such a row,
   the on-device network's ranking is offered as a whole order, e.g. *Messaging · Jobs · Home*.

**Never touched:** cookie, consent and sign-in prompts (you answer those yourself), a page's main video,
and forms you are filling in. Form contents are never read or sent.

## Meta models

| Model | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark 1.3** (`meta/muse-spark-1.3`) | Reads the page's element list (tags, positions, short text) plus your harbor's rules, returns a layout plan as strict JSON (`json_schema`); one repair round if the plan fails validation |
| **SAM 3.1** (`meta/sam-3.1`) | Optional: segments the screenshot int

# Fingertip

Fingertip helps blind people use touch panels on things like microwaves, washing machines and kiosks.

You point your phone at the panel and say what you want, like "heat for 2 minutes". The app reads the panel, works out which buttons to press, guides your finger to each one, and then checks if the press worked.

I built this for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track), Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026. All the code here was written during the hackathon.

## Why

Flat touch panels have no buttons you can feel. In Vision Australia's 2025 survey (627 blind and low-vision people), 82% said flat or unlabelled buttons are a problem and 67% said touchscreens with no tactile or voice option are a problem. Right now people put stick-on bumps on their appliances, memorize where the buttons are, or video call a sighted person.

Some apps already help part of the way. Gemini Live, Meta AI and Apple's Point and Speak can tell you what's on a panel or what's under your finger. But they don't guide your finger to the button you need, plan the presses for what you want to do, or check that each press worked. That's the part I wanted to build.

I worked on indoor navigation for blind users before this ([NavAssist](https://github.com/Shivani-Radhakrishnan/NavAssist)), and appliances kept coming up as a problem.

## How it works

1. **Read the panel.** The phone takes a photo. Muse Spark lists every control on it, including icon-only ones (like a snowflake for defrost), with the center point of each one. It also says if the photo is bad ("move the phone closer").
2. **Outline the buttons.** Each center point goes to SAM 3.1 as a point prompt, and SAM gives back the exact outline of that button.
3. **Hear what you want.** Muse Voice Transcribe listens without needing a button press. It gets the panel's button names as keywords, so it hears "Defrost" correctly.
4. **Plan.** Muse Spark turns the goal into button presses in order and says the plan out loud ("2 presses: 2 min, then Start"). If a button it needs is unreadable, it says so instead of guessing.
5. **Guide your finger.** This part runs on the phone. Apple Vision tracks your fingertip in the camera. The app says short words for big moves ("left", "up"), then ticks and vibrates faster as you get close, then says "On it. Press." The buttons shift with the picture if your hand moves a bit.
6. **Check.** After a press it compares a before and after photo of the panel (did the display change to 2:00?). If the press missed it tells you to press again. If the wrong thing happened it makes a new plan. This runs on Muse Spark Open through Baseten when a key is set, otherwise on Muse Spark.

Every model call returns JSON, so each step can use the last one's output directly.

Some choices I made from reading accessibility research (VizLens, StateLens, NaviSense, HandSight):

- The phone should be propped up or held still, not held in one hand while pressing with the other.
- Words for coarse directions,

# Afterdark

**A night camera’s flickers become a visible street—and an agent catches the tram the painting missed.**

Afterdark brings Meta’s general vision and image models to a brain-inspired event camera, with no event-specific retraining. On recorded night drives through Zurich, SAM 3.1 outlines people in both ordinary camera frames and rendered events. Muse Image paints the events into readable streets. An inspection agent checks those paintings against the sensors—and asks for a targeted repaint when something is missing.

It is a way to explore what a night sensor recorded, what a model can see, and what a generated picture invented.

**[Open the live demo](https://yazan-o.github.io/afterdark/)** · [Try it locally](#try-it-locally) · [The missing tram](#the-missing-tram) · [How the pipeline works](#how-the-pipeline-works) · [Technical reference](#technical-reference)

![SAM 3.1 misses a person in the ordinary camera view but outlines them in the event view.](docs/img/hero_camera_blind.png)

*A tram stop in Zurich at night. Left: the recorded camera frame. Middle: the same frame brightened. SAM 3.1 finds no person in either. Right: 10 ms of events at the same instant; with the same prompt, “person”, SAM outlines them. The dashed box marks the dataset’s label.*

## A different way to see after dark

An ordinary camera collects light over an exposure. At night, too little light hides detail; longer exposures blur movement. A person beside the road can disappear into the background.

An **event camera** records changes instead of whole pictures. Each pixel works independently, reporting when brightness changes, where it happened, and whether it became brighter or darker—with microsecond timestamps. This retina-inspired design handles a wide range of brightness and avoids the conventional frame-exposure source of motion blur, though its response also slows in very dark conditions.

The difficulty is reading its output: a cloud of flickers, not a photograph. Event-vision systems often need specialist reconstruction networks or detectors trained for event data.

Afterdark asks a practical **Push the Frontier** question: can Meta’s general models make this unfamiliar sensor useful without first building another trained perception stack?

# Nativa — Llama directs, our engine animates

## Problem
Making even one minute of 2D anime takes a small studio: storyboards, layouts, key poses, timing, lip-sync. Generative video models are expensive, need GPUs, and give no control: you can't edit a shot, a pose or a line of dialogue. Indie creators need an editable, cheap, deterministic pipeline.

## What we built
**Nativa** is a procedural anime engine (rigs, poses, camera, render, lip-sync) written as code — no AI video, no GPU. For this hackathon we added a **Llama director**:

1. You write a scene in plain language.
2. **Llama** acts as the film director and writes a structured scene spec (JSON): story beats, shot list with camera type and framing, per-character blocking (position, depth, facing, gait, emotion, arm action) and timed dialogue.
3. The engine **validates** the spec. If anything is wrong (missing end keyframes, invalid enum, overlapping lines…) the exact validator errors are sent back to Llama, which **repairs its own spec** (validate-and-repair loop).
4. The spec is compiled to the engine's scene format, rendered at 1280×720 / 24 fps on CPU, and dialogue mouths are lip-synced with **Rhubarb Lip Sync**.

Llama is not decorative: every camera cut, pose key, emotion and line in the rendered scene comes from Llama's JSON.

## Meta models used
- **Llama 3.1 8B Instruct** (Meta open weights), run locally on CPU through Ollama — $0, private, offline.
- Provider switch: if `LLAMA_API_KEY` is present the director uses the **Meta Llama API** (`api.llama.com`, OpenAI-compatible, default `Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-FP8`); else OpenRouter `:free` Llama (if `NATIVA_OR_MODEL` is set); else local Ollama.

## Architecture
```
prompt ──► Llama (director) ──► JSON spec ──► validator ──errors──┐
                 ▲                                │ ok           │
                 └──────────── repair ◄───────────┼──────────────┘
                                                  ▼
                       compiler (spec → engine scene YAML)
                                                  ▼
          motor2d: skeleton rigs · keyframe interpolation · camera/cuts
                   · procedural voice · Rhubarb lip-sync · ffmpeg ► MP4
```
Files: `anime/director/dirigir.py` (director, validator, compiler, providers), `anime/bin/nativa` (CLI), `anime/motor2d.py` (renderer), `anime/director/montar_demo.py` (demo assembly). The wider repo also contains the Rust crates and the document contract (`contrato/`) for the next-gen engine.

## Run it
```bash
# local Llama (free): ollama serve & ollama pull llama3.1:8b
cd motor/anime
bin/nativa dirigir "Sakuragi challenges Rukawa, Miyagi breaks it up, they agree to train" --out salida/dirigir/demo
# optional: put LLAMA_API_KEY=... in ~/nativa/.env to use the Meta Llama API
```
Outputs: `intento-N.json` (raw Llama replies), `log.json` (errors per attempt), `spec.json`, `escena.yaml`, `escena.mp4`.

**A video is a solid.** The Construct turns a short clip into a ghost trail: every moment of a moving subject, frozen in place along its path. You then walk through that trail inside a tesseract.

|---|---|---|
| Find the subject | **Muse Spark** | Checks the uploaded clip and proposes the concepts worth tracking (for example "black cat"). |
| Sweep and select | **SAM 3.1** (image) | Runs a concept sweep over sampled frames, returns candidate masks and boxes, and lets you pick the subject. |
| Track through time | **SAM 3.1** (video) | Tracks the selected subject across the whole clip, so every frame gets a clean mask. |

jeff13in/burp-to-report.readme_excerpt:
# Burp-to-Report

An AI copilot that turns a Burp Suite traffic export into ranked, evidence-backed vulnerability findings and a submission-ready bug bounty report.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, Theme 1: Build for Your World).

![Triage view](docs/02-triage.png)

## The problem

One authorized web test produces thousands of requests in Burp's HTTP history. Most of a tester's time goes into scrolling that history looking for broken access control, reflected input and leaked data, then writing a report for each bug. Beginners miss real issues; experienced testers lose hours to repetitive review.

## How it works

```
Burp XML / HAR ──► parse ──► noise filter ──► heuristic detectors ──► Muse Spark review ──► validation ──► human review ──► report
                             (static, dupes,   (high recall,          (per signal, with     (evidence must   (accept /
                              out of scope)     literal evidence)      RAG references)       match traffic)   reject / edit)
```

1. **Parse** Burp Suite XML (base64 or plain) and HAR exports.
2. **Filter noise**: static assets, out-of-scope hosts and exact duplicates are dropped before anything reaches the model.
3. **Heuristic detectors** flag candidates with the literal evidence that triggered them:
   IDOR (JWT `sub` vs object id; one session reading objects with different owners), missing authorization on API routes,
   reflected input, verbose errors and stack traces, sensitive data in responses, and credentialed CORS reflection.
4. **Muse Spark triage**: each signal goes to the model with the relevant traffic and the top reference documents from a local BM25 index. The model decides whether the issue is real, rates severity, and must quote its evidence and cite references.
5. **Validation**: every evidence quote is checked verbatim against the captured traffic, and every citation against the documents actually supplied. Ungrounded claims are dropped, and a finding with no surviving evidence keeps the heuristic evidence at reduced confidence. Each finding records what was dropped and why.
6. **Human in the loop**: the tester accepts, rejects or edits each finding. Nothing is reported automatically.
7. **Report**: accepted findings become Markdown in bug bounty format. Reproduction steps are built from the captured requests rather than generated, so they are always accurate.

### Privacy and safety

- **Credentials are redacted before traffic leaves the machine.** Secret headers (`Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie`, API-key and CSRF headers), secret fields in JSON bodies and query/form parameters (`password`, `token`, `api_key`, …), bare JWTs, AWS keys and private keys become stable placeholders (`<redacted:4c2edc2a>`), so the model can still tell sessions apart. Those values are also masked wherever else they appear, for example a password reflected into a page. JWT payload claims stay visible because IDOR review needs to know whose session it is.

# Reality Check

**Catch AI-generated video by measuring whether it obeys real physics.**

AI video generators still get physics wrong: balls fall too slowly, gravity
changes mid-clip, bounces gain energy from nowhere. Reality Check tracks a
falling or bouncing object with **SAM 3.1**, fits its motion to the equations
of free fall, and **measures gravity directly**. Real footage comes out near
9.8 m/s². A clip where a ball falls at 2.9 m/s² is impossible, and Reality
Check says so with the number to prove it.

Detectors that only look for visual artifacts give an opaque score. Reality
Check gives a **measurement**, plus two supporting layers of evidence, and a
clear answer with a confidence.

Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon. Theme: *Push the Frontier*.

## Built during the hackathon

Everything in this repository was written during the hackathon
(Nov 2–4, 2026). Nothing was carried over from an earlier project. Built with
the help of an AI coding assistant.

| Part | What was built |
|---|---|
| Physics engine (`reality_check/physics.py`) | Splits a tracked trajectory into flight arcs at bounces, fits free fall to each arc, measures gravity, checks gravity consistency, bounce energy (restitution), path smoothness and sideways drift; slow-motion detection; sanity checks that refuse to measure when tracking isn't believable |
| SAM 3.1 tracking (`reality_check/tracker.py`) | Text-prompted tracking through the Meta Model API, response parsing, video shrinking/trimming for speed; OpenCV motion-tracker fallback |
| Provenance check (`reality_check/provenance.py`) | Reads C2PA Content Credentials, IPTC AI-source tags and Stable Diffusion settings from files |
| Muse Spark visual inspection (`reality_check/visual.py`) | Contact sheet of 8 frames + detail frames, prompt for AI tells and generator watermarks, structured JSON answer |
| Evidence combiner (`reality_check/combine.py`) | Log-odds combination of the three layers into one answer with a confidence |
| Web app (`app.py`, `static/`) | Upload page with gravity gauge, height-over-time chart, video replay, evidence cards; phone layout, home-screen install, Android share target |
| iPhone app (`ios/`) | Live Activity that shows progress and the answer in the **Dynamic Island**; share-sheet action via App Intents |
| Test tools (`scripts/`) | Synthetic videos with known physics, evaluation script |

## How it works

1. **Physics (the core, for videos).** SAM 3.1 (Meta Model API, `sam-3.1`)
   tracks the object from a text prompt like "tennis ball". The object's real
   diameter converts pixels to metres. Each flight arc between bounces is fit
   to `y(t) = y0 + v0·t + ½·g·t²`, which measures gravity directly. Checks:
   gravity ≈ 9.81 m/s², gravity constant across arcs, bounces lose energy,
   smooth parabolic paths, constant sideways speed. If no object can be
   tracked reliably, physics reports "couldn't measure" rather than guessing.

A supervised iRobot Create + Raspberry Pi robot that finds a visual target,
approaches it, and reports to its owner through Muse. The working demo finds
a doll wearing an **I ♥ AI** shirt, or chains a **black Roomba → doll** mission.

flowchart LR

# Markedia

A marketplace for documented ideas. Someone writes up an idea they are not going
to build; the platform scores it, writes a public preview that describes it
without giving it away, and lists it for sale. Buyers get the full write-up.

Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon. Every model call runs on **Muse Spark
1.3** through the Meta Model API.

## How an evaluation works

One model, three passes:

| Step | What it does | Why this shape |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Research** | Grounded web search for products that already resemble the idea | Originality is a factual question, so it is answered from the live web rather than from memory. Uses the Responses API, the only endpoint with `web_search`. |
| **2. Score + preview** | Seven weighted criteria, a clarity rating, an abuse check, and the public preview | Output is pinned to a JSON Schema, so a malformed answer is rejected by the API rather than parsed hopefully. |
| **3. Heading** | Names the listing | Sees **only** the preview, never the idea, so it cannot leak what a buyer is paying for. |

Reasoning effort is set per step — `xhigh` for judging, `minimal` for naming —
because the three passes do very different amounts of thinking.

### Scoring

Originality 25% · Value Proposition 20% · Feasibility 15% · Problem-Solution Fit
10% · Ease of Launch 10% · Scalability 10% · Defensibility 10%.

Clarity is scored 1–5 and shown separately. It rates how clearly the idea is
*written*, not how good it is, and deliberately carries no weight.

### Not giving the idea away

The preview is the hard part of a marketplace like this: it has to be worth
reading and still leave something to buy. It is five short fields, only one of
which describes the idea, and the prompt names the specific problem as withheld
— for a sharp idea the problem is the solution inverted. The public heading is
written from the preview alone, so the leak surface stays in one place.

### Abuse check

Submitted text is treated as data, never as instructions. Each evaluation also
judges whether a submission is an attempt to game the marketplace — prompt
injection, demanding its own scores, dictating its own preview — and picks
reasons from a fixed list rather than writing its own. A flagged idea cannot be
published, enforced in the UI and by a database trigger.

## Stack

Next.js 16 (App Router) · React 19 · Tailwind v4 · Supabase (Postgres + RLS) ·
Meta Model API

## Running it

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # then fill in the keys
npm run dev
```

Apply the SQL files in `supabase-*.sql` to a Supabase project, in the order
their header comments describe.

# my dear step 🌱 **Your everyday words and photos, organized into a journal you can check.** Built for the **Meta AI Developer Hackathon**, My Dear Step is a Korean-first personal GLP-1 journal with Momo, an optional AI companion designed around **Meta Muse Spark Open**. Momo proposes editable entries from supplied text and photos. You choose what to keep, correct the details, and confirm before anything becomes a journal record. [Open the app](https://my-dear-step-journal.lovable.app/) · [Hackathon presentation](docs/HACKATHON_PRESENTATION.md) · [Three-minute demo script](docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md) · [Setup](docs/SETUP_AND_ENV.md) > **Project status:** public hackathon prototype. The Meta integration is implemented, but the repository does not yet contain verified live-provider or deployed two-account privacy results. Screenshots below use fictional QA data. See [verification and limits](#verification-and-limits). ## The idea A weight note, a meal photo, an injection log, a receipt, a moment worth remembering: small details are easy to scatter across a phone. Re-entering them into separate forms loses time and context. My Dear Step brings them into one journal, with a clear boundary between **what was supplied**, **what AI proposed**, and **what the person confirmed**. The goal is simpler recording and a history people can revisit. It does not recommend treatment, medication doses, or nutrition targets. ## Capture → review → correct → confirm → revisit 1. **Capture naturally.** Type a note, attach photos, or use browser speech transcription where supported. Manual forms remain available. 2. **Review the proposals.** Momo returns selectable drafts. Missing facts and uncertain photo links stay visible. 3. **Correct the details.** Edit values and dates, inspect the original input, and leave out entries you cannot confirm. 4. **Confirm once.** Only selected, valid drafts become records. The app distinguishes local saving from account synchronization. 5. **Return to the source.** Reopen a dated record, inspect its original input and corrections, or find it again through history and search. ### A look at the review

Ask one research question. # Glint

Glint is a macOS desktop learning companion built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon. It is written in TypeScript with Electron 45.2.2 and React, and it builds as `Glint.app`. The npm package is still named `window-companion`.

Glint is for learning from material you already have open. You start a task and add the context yourself. Glint then turns an explanation into a small model you can test: you predict an outcome, check it against a computed result, change one assumption and look again. Tasks and their history are stored on your Mac.

## What is in the source

Each item below is implemented in this tree. The [Status](#status) section says what has been verified.

- **Tasks with explicit sources.** You can paste text, import images or PDF pages, or capture one window you select. Only what you add is used. Captured window pixels stay in memory, and imported files are saved with the task.
- **Bounded learning models.** These are computed locally from rules or tables you can see:
  - a workflow/state-rule lab (predict an end state, check it, change one rule, compare);
  - a SQL join lab (typed INNER/LEFT equality, at most 12 rows and 4 columns per table);
  - formula and arithmetic experiments built from a source, with comparisons when that source changes.

  These are teaching models, not a database engine or a general solver.
- **Model providers.** You choose one in **Settings → Connection**, and Glint never falls back to the other automatically.
  - **Meta · Muse Spark** goes through an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions client and has two profiles:
    - Meta Model API (`muse-spark-1.3`), which sends `store: false`;
    - the Baseten hackathon endpoint (Muse Spark Open).
  - **Codex · GPT-6 Luna** is a temporary option. It reuses an existing local Codex sign-in through the Codex app server, and Glint does not read or copy those credentials.

  Glint asks you to approve every model request before anything is sent.
- **Websites in your own browser.** When a task needs a website, Glint opens it in a browser installed on your Mac and drives it with Playwright. The browser must be one of the following, built on Chromium **156.0.8078.73 or later**:

  - Helium

# FieldLens

**Agentic reconstruction of oilfield assets from decades of historical records — powered by Meta Muse Spark.**

Upload the raw files of a field (survey reports, completion logs, drilling XML, well logs,
production spreadsheets) with no labels and no data model. A Muse Spark agent sorts them,
resolves which records describe the same well, reconstructs every wellbore and its history,
and backs every value with the exact source page, table cell or line it came from. Engineers
then explore the field in 3D, read production/pressure charts and ask questions that are
answered with dates, citations and inline charts.

[![FieldLens demo video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/h8wsHxbxMug/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h8wsHxbxMug)

- **Demo video (3 min):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h8wsHxbxMug
- **Built during** the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 27 – Nov 4, 2026 · theme **Push the Frontier · Energy** · indie track
- **Version:** see [VERSION](VERSION) and [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md)

## The problem

Global energy demand keeps rising and oil and gas still supply more than half of it. Producing
it efficiently depends on understanding each asset — yet a mature field is not one dataset but
decades of them. The same well is written three different ways, depth is measured along curving
holes rather than straight down, completions change over time (perforated, shut in,
re-perforated), and records conflict or leave things out. Engineers can spend up to half their
time finding and reconciling data, and wells end up being managed on partial information.

## The solution

FieldLens turns that pile of files into an evidence-backed, explorable model of the field:

1. **Upload** raw files into a project — no categories or schema needed. Structured formats
   (WITSML XML, LAS, survey text, perforation/pick tables, production XLSX) are parsed natively
   and indexed immediately; everything is hash-verified and stored with provenance.
2. **Problems are flagged automatically**: duplicate or block-less well names, missing surface
   locations, unstated survey status, unit and depth-reference gaps, conflicting values.
3. **Agentic reconstruction** (per wellbore, estimate → confirm → five persisted stages):
   S1 collect sources · S2 *read documents* (Muse Spark) · S3 *match wellbores* (Muse Spark) ·
   S4 assemble a validated draft · S5 *design the 3D asset* (Muse Spark). The cost is shown before
   anything is spent; failures are recorded honestly as partial results.

   nothing merges until the user accepts, and every merge can be reverted.
5. **Explore**: a 3D field placed at surveyed surface locations with real minimum-curvature
   trajectories, per-wellbore equipment and perforated intervals at their measured depths,

# Dreamer

Give Dreamer a book, a sentence, or a real street address, and it builds a walkable 3D world and stages a living scene in it: characters with their own voices who either act the chapter as written or improvise, and a director who steers without pushing. The bet that made it work is a division of labour. **Code builds the space** (rooms in metres, doors, nav, placement). **Muse Image paints only surfaces** (seamless tiles and flat decals). **SAM 3D Objects makes the things** that stand in the room. Everything runs in parallel, so a world is minutes, not hours, and a wrong one can be rebuilt and compared against the reference.

Built solo in 9 days (Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026; 568 commits) for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track. A hosted live build is linked in the submission.

## What it does

| You give | Dreamer makes | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **A book** (Koshakan, a picture book written by the author's wife; Conan Doyle's 221B Baker Street) | The room from the chapter, the cast with voices, the scene played as written. Press **G** inside and it switches to freestyle. | `h0/make`, `h0/dream` |
| **A sentence** ("Mirai finds a tiny lost kitten in the meadow") | Muse Spark writes a short chapter with that world's cast, `make` stages it in the ready world. Measured on Nov 4: 3 min 04 s, $0.07. | `h0/home` (Create tab) |
| **A real place** (Kozbagarov St. 7, a yard in Semey, Kazakhstan) | The yard from OpenStreetMap, satellite tiles and Street View frames. Stand in it, hold Space, say what should open, and a shop grows onto the ground floor of the house while you watch. | `h0/place` |

Dreamer Home (`h0/home/README.md`) is the one page that fronts all of it: **Book / Freestyle / Create**.

## Try it

A fresh clone has the code but not the built worlds (they live outside the repo, see Limitations), so start with the fake mode: no network, no keys, no money.

```sh
cd h0
python3 -m home --fake        # http://localhost:8800/  stub scenes, canned chapter, make --fake
```

With keys (variable names below) the same page serves the real thing:

```sh
cd h0
python3 -m home               # Book / Freestyle / Create against live Muse, SAM 3D and Fish
```

The engine on its own, with the shipped example scene:

```sh
cd engine && npm install
node --import tsx bin/dreamer.ts check ../specs/examples/demo.scene.json
node --import tsx bin/dreamer.ts build ../specs/examples/demo.scene.json --out /tmp/demo --assets none
```

Everything the gate runs (Python suites in parallel, then engine vitest and tsc):

```sh
sh tools/gate.sh
```

## How a world gets made

```
 book chapter  |  one-line idea  |  lat/lon + frames (h0/place, its own road to scene.json)
      |              |
      v              v
   brief  --- Muse Spark, one JSON call (h0/make/brief.py)
      |
    refs  --- real pictures of the place: Wikimedia Commons, fandom, Openverse, Tavily (h0/make/refs/)
      |
      +---------------+---------------+
      v               v

# PriceCharm

PriceCharm lets a service business train an AI to quote jobs the way the owner would. This repository holds the whole product.

It's live at [pricecharm.com](https://pricecharm.com). [Try it as a customer](https://pricecharm.com/demo), no sign-up needed.

## Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Startups track)

PriceCharm runs on Meta's models through the Meta Model API, in Standard mode only. The API refuses Contributor-mode models, because they would let Meta train on customers' photos and owners' prices.

- **Muse Spark 1.3** runs the customer's quote chat, reads old quotes and invoices into past jobs, and drafts each quote from the owner's own prices. See [`apps/api/src/ai/index.ts`](apps/api/src/ai/index.ts).
- **Walk-around video quotes.** A customer films the job instead of taking photos. Muse Spark 1.2 watches it and hears what they say, then picks what the price depends on, like windows to count or a driveway to size. **SAM 3.1** follows each window through the video and counts it once, then outlines what it found on a still for the owner. Each window SAM outlined on that still is cut out onto one numbered sheet, and Muse Spark grades every one up close: what kind it is and what state it's in, like "4 large picture windows, heavy hard-water stains". It also notes the materials and condition that change the work, like heavy moss or high-end pavers. The count becomes the size on the quote, in the unit the owner prices by, and the rest goes to the price as details. See [`walkaround.ts`](apps/api/src/ai/walkaround.ts), [`meta-media.ts`](apps/api/src/ai/meta-media.ts) and [`live/videos.ts`](apps/api/src/live/videos.ts).
- **Photos are read the same way.** Muse Spark looks at all of a customer's photos together, SAM 3.1 finds each thing to count in every photo, and the grading sheet throws out SAM's mistakes and grades the rest. Two photos can show the same window, so a count is at least what one photo shows and at most all of them added up, with Muse Spark's own count deciding between. Like a video, it's read outside the request: the chat shows the customer it's looking, and the Charm carries on from what the photos show once they're read. # MemoryAtlas

**A memory that knows what to remember and what to forget.** Built for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer track).

MemoryAtlas turns consented observations (photos, voice, video, notes, calendar) into an evidence-backed graph of your day. It can:

1. **Reconstruct** answers no single source contains ("Which restaurant did Alex recommend when we met near the office?")
2. **Correct itself** when newer evidence arrives, and keep the history ("Did I leave my wallet at the café?")
3. **Forget verifiably.** When someone withdraws consent, every memory that depended *only* on it is removed from the graph, indexes, caches, chat and exports. Memories with other support stay, and a receipt shows seven automated leak checks. You can also delete a single memory.

# PlateWise — an AI dining companion for campus dining halls

**Snap your tray. Know your plate.** PlateWise turns a dining hall's
PDF-nightmare menu data into a personal, inclusive, waste-aware companion:
photograph your tray before and after you eat, and PlateWise identifies what
you took, matches it to the *official* nutrition data for today's menu, scores
what you left behind, and coaches you toward your goals.

Built solo by Tarushv Kosgi for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon —
Indie Dev track**.

---

## The problem

Campus dining data is technically public and practically unusable:

- Menus live behind slow web pages and PDFs. Nutrition and allergen info is
  there, but nobody standing in a lunch line can use it.
- Students with dietary needs — vegetarian, vegan, allergen avoiders,
  halal-observant students, neurodivergent students who need plain-language
  information — get the worst version of an already bad interface.
- Food waste is invisible. The classic campus pattern is taking ~6 plates and
  eating ~1/4 of each. Nobody ever sees the cost of what they throw away, in
  grams or in CO₂e, so nothing changes.

## What PlateWise does

1. **Live menus, actually usable.** Today's menus for all 5 Purdue dining
   courts (Earhart, Ford, Hillenbrand, Wiley, Windsor), pulled live from the

   identifies items and how much was eaten; items are then matched to the

   **nutrition always comes from dining-court data, never from model
   guesses**. Without a key, a deterministic fallback analyzer (menu matching

   tags, 11 allergen avoid-filters, a conservative halal-*style* heuristic
   (Purdue publishes no halal certification, and PlateWise never pretends
   otherwise), high-protein finder, and a **plain-language mode** that rewrites
   menu items into simple names and one-line descriptions.

# SeeForMe

SeeForMe is a voice-first assistant for people who can't see well or at all. You open the page, tap the screen once, and from then on you mostly talk to it. It takes a photo with the phone camera, listens to your question, and answers out loud about what the camera sees.

I built it for the Meta AI Developer Hackathon 2026, using Muse Spark for the vision part and Muse Voice Transcribe for turning speech into text.

Live demo: https://see-for-me-orpin.vercel.app (the backend sleeps when idle, so the very first request can take close to a minute)

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kVinzZ_qeDo

## Why voice only

Most "describe my surroundings" apps still expect you to find a camera button, frame a shot, and read or tap through results. That's hard if you can't see the screen. The whole screen here is one big button, the camera opens inside the page instead of launching the phone's camera app, and everything the app needs from you after the first tap is something you can say.

## What it does

- Tap anywhere and the camera opens. The app tells you it is ready and takes the photo by itself after a few seconds, or right away if you tap again.
- You ask your question out loud. It stops recording when you stop talking, so there is nothing to press.
- The answer is spoken back. Then it keeps listening, and you can ask a follow-up about the same photo. The last few turns are sent along with each question so "what color is it?" makes sense.
- A few voice commands work after an answer: "new photo", "repeat", and "find my keys" (or "busca mis llaves").
- If the photo is too blurry, too dark, or the thing you asked about is cut off, the model says how to move the phone and the app retakes the photo and reuses your question. It tries at most twice.
- Find mode takes a photo every couple of seconds and tells you where to turn the phone until it spots what you are looking for, up to 8 tries.
- English and Spanish. The language comes from the phone.

The buttons shown after an answer are still there as a fallback and work with TalkBack or VoiceOver.

## How it is built

```
phone browser  ->  Next.js (Vercel)  ->  FastAPI (Render)  ->  Meta API
```

The browser only talks to Next.js route handlers under `/api`. Those forward the request to the FastAPI backend and add the backend API key on the server, so no keys ever reach the browser. The backend checks that key, applies a global rate limit, and calls Meta.

- Spoken answers use the browser's built-in speech synthesis.

# Proof Reader

I research investment catalysts for biotech companies: trial starts and readouts, regulatory decisions, launches and investor events for the next six months. I do this with several AI models, and I review their claims against the sources they cite. For the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 (Indie track, "Build for Your World"), I tried to automate that workflow with Meta's models. Proof Reader is the result.

This README is an honest after-action report: what worked, what did not, and why.

**Status:** the workflow is demonstrated in two live PTGX runs. Research recall, repeatability and autonomous use have not been validated. The demonstrated workflow keeps a person in control.

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/oXevxrh5JCg

![Run 17: a proposal with its quote boxed on the captured SEC filing page](docs/images/run17-proposal-source.png)

## How it works

1. **Muse Spark** (Meta Model API) works as a research agent for one company. It searches the web (Brave Search), captures pages, and proposes each event with an exact quote from a captured page.
2. **Code** then runs mechanical checks on each proposal: is the quote on the captured page, is the citation located, is the date printed in the quote, and does the source follow the source rule. Each check is recorded as passed, failed or not checked. These checks do not establish whether an event is true, current or complete.
3. **Muse Spark Open** (Meta's open-weight model, served on Baseten as `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`) reviews the rows. It looks for stale guidance and missing events, and can fetch sources itself. DeepSeek V4 Pro is a fallback only if Muse Spark Open is unavailable. The reviewer is from the same model family as the researcher, and the app says so: it is a second look, not independent verification.
4. **Muse Wonder** (Meta Model API) proposes a resolution for each disagreement it is sent. Its proposal does not accept a row; that decision belongs to the person.
5. **LettuceDetect**, a model-based support check, may flag wording for a person to inspect. No flag is not proof of correctness.
6. **A person reviews** each row that has a failed check or a reviewer finding, and keeps, fixes or removes it, by click or by voice (**Muse Voice Transcribe**). Voice only pre-fills; nothing is saved until the person clicks. A row with no failed check and no reviewer finding is placed on the calendar automatically. It is labelled "not reviewed by you" until a person decides it, and the person can still keep or remove it.
7. The **calendar** and the **PDF and Word reports** are built by code from the saved run. Each row shows whether a person kept it or it was placed automatically.

The research brief is one visible, editable box. The exact request sent to the models is frozen and saved with each run.

# agnts-muse

**Run Meta's Muse Code under a hard, live-enforced budget.**

`agnts-muse` is a Go library that drives [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai) through **MSP**, its native session protocol (`muse serve`). Because it sees the cost of every model call as it happens, it can:

- reserve money before the spend,
- tell Muse mid-turn to wrap up when the budget runs low,
- stop it just before the call that would go over,
- move a stuck session to a stronger model without losing context,
- and decide every tool call against your own rules.

Concurrent runs sharing a balance can never push it below zero: not across goroutines, not across servers.

It is the engine behind [agnts](https://github.com/rustambekabdusalomov/agnts) ([agnts.uz](https://agnts.uz)), a self-hosted AI engineer that takes Jira and Plane tickets, codes them in isolated containers, and ships nothing without approval. Both are built and run by one independent developer, so a runaway agent bill is a personal one: agnts gives its users free Muse credits and lets them prepay for more, and `agnts-muse` is what makes it safe to hand out that money.

> **Meta AI developer hackathon, Indie Developer track.** This module is our Muse Code
> integration; [agnts](https://github.com/rustambekabdusalomov/agnts) is the
> product built on it (tickets, log watcher, security scans, meetings and team
> chat, all running on Muse).

```text
$ muse-budget run --budget 0.05 --model spark "Fix the failing test, then add table-driven tests …"

  … Cheap fix plus new tests — scoping to the essentials to stay on budget.
  $ call 1   █████████████████░░░░░░░ +$0.035775 total $0.035775 / $0.05
  ▸ bash {"command":"ls -la"}
  $ call 2   ███████████████████░░░░░ +$0.005033 total $0.040808 / $0.05
  ⚑ steer told Muse the budget is running low; it should wrap up
  ▸ read_skill {"name":"bundled:durable-test-collateral"}
  $ call 3   ██████████████████████░░ +$0.006964 total $0.047772 / $0.05
  ■ interrupt spent $0.047772 of the $0.05 limit; another call would pass it

■ stopped at the budget: muse: run limit reached (spent $0.047772, held $0.05)
usage 3 calls · 87.1k in (56.9k cached) · 366 out · 20s
receipt charged $0.047772 · released $0.002228
```

*(A real run on Muse Code 1.4.13. Muse read its budget from the prompt and planned around it; the engine steered it at 80% and stopped it inside the limit.)*

## Why

An autonomous agent with an API key is an open-ended bill. Settling after the fact doesn't fix that: ten runs that each see $5 left will each spend $5. Big hosted products can absorb the overruns or cap usage crudely (per-day request counts). An indie developer offering an agent on their own account can do neither: one runaway run is paid out of their pocket.

`agnts-muse` treats model spend like a card payment:

| Step | MSP / ledger call | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hold** | `Ledger.Hold` | Reserve a first slice before the turn starts. Free credits are taken first, then bought credits, and

# Prysm

Prysm analyses a short-form video (an Instagram Reel) and tells the creator, in plain language, what to fix before they post. It scores the video on 10 parameters (hook, retention, shareability, audio, trend alignment, visual quality, on-screen text, save potential, replay value, call to action) and gives each one a problem, a fix and numbered steps. A creator can then ask ARIA, a chat assistant grounded in that analysis, how to improve it.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon: the existing Prysm analysis engine now runs on Meta models (Muse Spark, Voice Transcribe, SAM 3.1) instead of Claude. What is baseline and what is new: [HACKATHON.md](HACKATHON.md). Model by model: [docs/model-swap.md](docs/model-swap.md).

## Architecture in 10 lines

1. `web/` (React + Vite) uploads a video or a reel link to `backend/` (FastAPI) and polls for real stage progress.
2. A job goes onto a Redis queue; a worker runs `run_full_analysis` in `app/services/prysm_analyse_service.py` (the original pipeline, unchanged prompts).
3. FFmpeg extracts up to 18 frames and the audio; links are downloaded with Apify (yt-dlp fallback).
4. In parallel: Muse Spark 1.3 watches the frames, Groq Whisper transcribes, Gemini listens, ACRCloud identifies the music, trends are fetched.
5. Extra evidence (each part has a flag): Meta Voice Transcribe + Whisper consensus, Muse Spark 1.2 as second listener, SAM 3.1 subjects, signal models on Modal (DINOv2, V-JEPA 2, LanguageBind, EnCodec, CLAP, Demucs).
6. Two Muse Spark 1.3 scoring calls produce the 10 parameters; plain code computes the weighted overall score.
7. Every Claude call goes through `app/studio/meta_llm_shim.py` (an `anthropic`-compatible shim) when `AI_PROVIDER=meta`; the `anthropic` package is not imported.
8. Results are saved to Postgres, cached in Redis, shareable by link; ARIA streams from Muse Spark.
9. A hidden safety net (daily spend cap `STUDIO_DAILY_SPEND_CAP_USD`, default 10 USD; per-user limits) protects vendor spend; there are no plans or credits in demo mode.
10. Heavy GPU models run on Modal; nothing heavy runs in the backend.

## Run it locally

Requirements: Python 3.11, Node 20+, ffmpeg and ffprobe, PostgreSQL with the `pgvector` extension, Redis.

cp .env.example .env.local  # set VITE_STUDIO_MODE=1 and VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8000
npm run dev
```

# Stride

Stride is an AI-powered adaptive learning app built for the Meta AI Global Hackathon. It helps students choose a topic, take a diagnostic quiz, learn with one teaching method, compare a second method, and review a recommendation based on observed performance.

## Features

- Guided learning workflow from diagnosis to comparison
- Meta AI Model API integration through an Express backend
- Personalized lesson generation with teaching-method adaptation
- Follow-up assessment generation and score tracking
- Topic-specific scope maps and scroll-to-learn concept tiles
- Retractable navigation for course materials, progress, and learning preferences
- PDF, DOCX, TXT, and Markdown course-material uploads used to tailor lessons and assessments
- Mixed multiple-choice and theory assessments with written-answer grading
- On-demand educational pictures generated by a Meta hackathon image model
- 80% final level pass mark with earned completion badges
- Local learning history using browser storage
- Demo fallback mode when the live AI endpoint is unavailable

## Local setup

1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and add your Meta `MODEL_API_KEY`, Supabase project URL, and Supabase anon key. Set `IMAGE_MODEL` to the image-generation model ID enabled in your Meta hackathon workspace to create lesson pictures.
2. Install dependencies:
   ```bash
   npm install
   ```
3. Start the backend:
   ```bash
   npm run server
   ```
4. Start the frontend in a second terminal:
   ```bash
   npm run dev
   ```
5. Open the frontend URL shown by Vite, usually `http://localhost:5173`.

## Available scripts

- `npm run dev` — start the Vite frontend
- `npm run server` — start the Express backend in watch mode
- `npm run build` — create a production build
- `npm run lint` — run ESLint checks

## Demo mode

If the Meta AI API is unavailable, Stride automatically falls back to demo lesson and quiz content, clearly labeling those responses as demo data so they do not masquerade as live AI output.

## Notes

- The backend expects the Meta API at `https://api.meta.ai/v1` and uses the `muse-spark-1.3` model.
- Lesson pictures are generated on demand through the configured `IMAGE_MODEL`. The image-generation model must be enabled for the same Meta API key; without it, the app explains that image generation needs configuration.
- Uploaded course files are parsed in memory by the backend and are not saved as files. Extracted text is sent to the configured Meta API as reference context, capped at five files and 40,000 characters.

- Assessments mix four multiple-choice items with two theory questions. Theory answers are graded against an AI-generated rubric; an explicitly labeled sample rubric is used if the AI grader is unavailable. The four multiple-choice questions are worth one point each and theory questions are worth three points

# Stetho

**Is this pump different from its own normal?**

Stetho is a phone-video *screening* aid for small electric water pumps and motors, designed for WhatsApp. An owner rests a phone near a running pump and sends a 10–15 s video. Stetho checks recording quality, cancels hand shake using the still background, extracts sound and visible-motion evidence, and compares it with **that machine's own healthy recordings**. The reply is a short voice note in English or Hindi with one next step: *carry on*, *re-record soon*, or *ask a technician*. After a repair, it checks whether the machine has returned towards its healthy reference.

> **Status: honest summary.** The full pipeline (intake, quality gate, motion and audio analysis, baseline comparison, assessment, explanation, voice note, visual aid, WhatsApp webhook, web UI) is implemented and covered by 73 passing tests. It has only been exercised on **simulated** recordings and **mocked** WhatsApp/LLM APIs. It has **not** been validated on real pumps or against accelerometers. The claims in the original idea about test-rig accelerometer validation are unverified, and no such data exists in this repository. See [`docs/VALIDATION_PROTOCOL.md`](docs/VALIDATION_PROTOCOL.md) for how to produce that evidence.

![Stetho web demo (simulated input)](docs/ui.png)

## Why this approach

A phone is a weak absolute vibration instrument: uncalibrated microphone, low frame rate (aliasing), rolling shutter, heavy compression, unknown distance and speed. The **same phone at the same marked spot on the same machine** is much more consistent *relative to itself*. So Stetho's primary output is a **change-from-own-baseline** decision, not a named fault. Supporting this are:

1. **Repair verification.** "Is it back to its own normal?" (never "it is fixed").
2. **A quality gate with abstention.** Bad recordings get specific re-recording advice instead of a guess.

Three features protect the baseline comparison from its main real-world failure modes:

| Feature | Failure it prevents | How |
|---------|---------------------|-----|
| **Same-spot check** | Comparing recordings taken from different positions | A view fingerprint (ORB keypoints, no image) is matched to the baseline view. "Moved" gets a hint (closer / back / sideways), and movement features are not compared. "Different view" asks whether it's the same machine. |
| **Background-noise reference** (`AMBIENT`) | A new generator, pump or insects nearby looking like machine change | A 10 s recording with the machine **off**. Bands where the machine isn't at least 6 dB louder than the background are excluded. A stale reference (background louder than machine + background) is detected and not used. |
| **Slow-drift detection** | Gradual wear that never crosses the per-check threshold | A Theil–Sen trend of distance-from-healthy across checks since the last repair, with explicit agreement and size rules. A rising trend escalates "no change" to "watch". Each machine gets

# awesome-personal-agent（APA）

**让 agent harness 具备主观能动性，成为你真正的个人助手。**

APA 是架在 agent harness 之上的开源、自部署的一层。harness 指运行 agent 的工具，如 Hermes、Claude Code、Codex CLI。

Harness 很能干，但只在被调用时才动：任务跑完没人看，对方不回没人催，三个 session 同时等你拍板。它是一件冷冰冰的工具，要你替它记事、替它盯着。APA 给它补上主观能动性：了解你手上的事，有条不紊地安排和推进，重复的事按你批准的规则自己处理，只在需要你决定时才来问一个具体问题。

所以 APA 不是对话工具，也不是开发工具。它是你的个人助手，工作和生活里的事都归它跟，工具链和模型都不用换。

harness 管 agent 怎么把活干完，APA 管事情有没有人盯、什么时候该找你。

*APA is an open-source, self-hosted layer on top of an agent harness. A harness is capable but passive: it only moves when called. APA gives it initiative, so it knows what you have on your plate, keeps things moving after the session ends, handles repeat work under rules you approved, and only interrupts you when a decision is really yours. It is a personal assistant, not another chat tool or developer tool.*

## 为什么需要 APA

Harness 已经很会干活：能写代码、查资料、操作工具、调用子 agent，模型和权限也由你自己配。困难出现在两次调用之间。它不知道你在等什么，不会自己醒来，也不会因为一件事到期了就来找你。

它有能力，但没有主动性。主动性只好由人来补，人就成了 agent 之间的调度员和传话筒。这样做的代价是：

- **每个 session 都在等你。** 三个终端开着三个 agent：一个问要不要改接口，一个等确认清理脚本，一个卡在权限提示上。你逐个切过去重读上下文；漏看一个，它就一直等下去。这些请求随进程消失，事后查不到谁同意了什么。
- **每次开工都要从头交代。** 新会话再说一遍项目是什么、按什么规范做、上次定了什么。换 harness 或换机器，再来一遍。
- **事情过去了，没人替你记着。** 任务跑完，结果停在某个终端里；发出去的问题三天没回音；约好下周复查的事，只有你可能还记得。漏掉的常常是对别人的承诺。
- **外面的事，要么进不来，要么全涌进来。** 续保通知躺在邮箱里，Issue 和报价回复各在各处。全接进来又要你自己筛，里面还可能夹着诱导 agent 的内容。
- **没有一处能回答"我手上现在有哪些事"。** 周一在会话里让 agent 调研，周二在群里答应周五给结论，周三来了续保通知。窗口一关，只能翻历史。

根因是：harness 的生命周期是一次会话，事情的生命周期不是。

多开 session 只会让等待翻倍。定时脚本能把 agent 叫醒，但记不住事项，也问不到人。harness 自带的定时、网关和记忆能力差异很大，状态留在各自内部，无法跨 harness 查询和审计。

## 核心价值：主观能动性

APA 只提供这一样东西：不等你开口，它自己发现事情、记着事情、推进事情，轮到你拿主意时才来找你。其他能力都围绕它构建。

| 它会 | 具体是 |
|---|---|
| **了解你** | 工作和生活里的项目、事项、材料、决定和偏好规则都记在账上，新会话不用重新交代。这些是你可查、可改、可撤销的记录，不是从对话里推断的画像。个人记忆仍由 harness 负责，APA 不重复保存，也不建关于你的档案 |
| **有条不紊地安排和推进** | 事情不因会话关闭而停。到期的事、等别人的回复、派出去的工作都有系统盯着，到点给出该催、再等或建议放弃 |
| **重复的事自己处理** | 你批准过的规则直接照做。新规则先只观察，你看过它"本来会做什么"再切到自动 |
| **只在需要你决策时才打扰** | 要决定的事进一个队列，一次一个具体问题，回一句话或选一个选项，事情就继续。新建议不触发提醒；其余提醒按静默、合并、阈值控制 |

接入之后，你主要只做三件事：说清要什么、批准自动规则、回答系统替不了的决定。

### 风格与人格

助手可以热情、有人味，也可以简洁克制，由你定。你在 Web 设置里写一段人格：语气、怎么称呼你、热情到什么程度、该说和不该说的话。

之后在 harness 里每开一个新会话，APA 插件都会读取当前人格，放进系统提示词，这个 harness 的所有会话都保持这个人格。改了人格，下一个新会话生效。

人格只改说话方式，不改判断。权限、高风险确认和其他内核规则都不受它影响，它也只能在 Web 上改。

## 主动的边界

主动不等于替你做主。下面这些边界是敢把事情交出去的前提：

- **高风险决定只能你本人确认。** 资金、对外承诺、不可逆操作、权限变更和规范生效，只能在 Web 上确认，agent 和聊天渠道都答不了。
- **自动规则默认只观察。** 切到自动只能在 Web 做；规则内容一变，自动退回观察。
- **后台运行不能代答。** 无人值守的运行遇到要决定的事就停下来等你。
- **代答要有你的原话。** 在聊天里让 agent 代你回答普通决定，必须附上原话，事后可以撤销。
- **外部内容只是资料。** 邮件、Issue 正文不会被当成指令。
- **每一步都能回放。** `apa why <id>` 显示来源、命中的规则、判断结果、回执和谁作的决定。

这些规则由 APA 的内核判定，不写在提示词里靠 agent 自律。

它们也有范围：APA 管的是经过它流转的事项和决定。工具级权限和主机隔离仍归 harness，agent 绕开 APA 直接调用工具时，APA 拦不住，所以 harness 自己的权限要照常配好。

- **08:00** 简报已经写好：昨晚哪些委派有了回执，今天什么到期，还有两件事等你决定。第一个会话开始时，摘要已经带到 agent 那里。

- **14:00** 手机上收到一条消息：一个 PR 要决定合并到哪个分支，有两个选项和一个推荐。回复选项，事情继续，不用打开电脑。
- **16:00** 上周问装修公司的报价还没有回音。系统判断该催了，提醒随下一次对话带到

# CounterTalk

**Your Field Sales reps hear the market at every shop. AI turns it into action for the right team.**

## Try the demo

- **Live app:** https://countertalk.up.railway.app 
- **To View Demo Sign in:** https://countertalk.up.railway.app/signin
> (Sign in instructions are provided on the page or below in read me)
- **On your own machine:** follow [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md) and load the demo data.

Field sales reps at FMCG companies visit neighbourhood shops all day, and what shopkeepers tell them gets lost: late credit notes, short deliveries, competitor offers, requests for new products. CounterTalk records the visit and turns it into routed work:

1. **It transcribes the conversation,** in Hindi, English, Hinglish or Marathi, and tells the speakers apart.
2. **It pulls out each finding,** backed by the shopkeeper's exact words. Every quote is checked against the transcript, and tapping ▶ plays that moment of the recording.
3. **It sends each finding to the team that can act on it,** such as finance, distribution or trade marketing. The team works it in its inbox, and when it's fixed, the rep sees the line to pass on at the next visit.

**The AI features, in brief** (Meta models only; details [below](#meta-models-and-where-each-is-used)):
- **Transcription with speaker separation:** Muse Voice Transcribe (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`), biased towards the visit's languages and given the company's brand names.
- **Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`):**
  - **speaker roles:** which voice is the rep and which the shopkeeper;
  - **extraction:** each finding with its category, severity, products, suggested team and the shopkeeper's quotes;
  - **quote repair,** when a quote doesn't match the transcript;
  - **issue merge suggestions,** for problems that share a cause;
  - **summaries:** each team's and the whole org's, by week or month;
  - **Ask:** a question in Hindi, Marathi or English, turned into the inbox's filters;
  - **pre-visit briefs:** where a shop stands before the next visit.
- **The AI suggests, code decides:** every answer comes back in a strict schema, and code checks the quotes, product links, citations and filters before anything is shown.

Built and tried for FMCG. The same playbook fits other goods sold through neighbourhood shops (groceries, general merchandise and apparel), because its issue categories and routing are generic to selling through shops: a new business needs only its own **org pack**, the data files with its catalog, teams and routing, and no code changes. # AuditCanvas

Turn real security evidence into verified, understandable remediation.

AuditCanvas scans a website with a deterministic engine (nine check
groups, four outcomes: Pass / Finding / Inconclusive / Not assessed),
stores redacted evidence for every result, and — when configured — has a
Muse Spark auditor explain, prioritize, and adversarially re-check the
findings. The scanner decides what exists; the model decides what it
means. Full design: `SPEC.md` (v2.2). Hackathon notes: `HACKATHON.md`.

## Run it locally

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # optional; without it reports are engine-only
npm run dev                  # http://localhost:3000
```

Judge mode is the first screen: **Run the seeded demo** scans the
deliberately vulnerable target built into this app
(`/api/demo-target`); **Explore sample reports** opens the preloaded
saved results — real scans of our own sites (nyktos.tech,
cliphaus.dev), each labelled "Saved result" with its scan timestamp,
scanner version and model ID. You can also scan your own site —
unverified targets get the restricted passive policy.

The sample reports are generated, not shipped as data: run
`node scripts/generate-samples.mjs` from an environment with ordinary
direct egress (the deployed app's host, or a developer machine) and it
drives this app's own pipeline against both sites, writing a sample
only if the scan genuinely reached its target. Until that post-deploy
run happens, the samples slot shows an explicit "generated after
deploy" placeholder naming both pending targets — the build sandbox
cannot produce them, because its resolver answers these hosts with
reserved 198.18.0.0/15 addresses (which the scanner correctly refuses)
and its network intercepts direct TLS. Details in `HACKATHON.md`
(Day 8 entry) and `src/lib/sample-reports/README.md`.

## Verify the scanner

```bash
npm run verify
```

This boots the fixture servers (vulnerable, hardened, slow, garbage,
and an HTTPS vulnerable origin under a throwaway local CA generated on
the fly) and asserts the scanner's verdicts: expected findings on the
vulnerable targets, **zero** findings on the hardened target, and
Inconclusive (never Pass) on the malformed/timeout targets. It also
covers chain classification (including the spec's corrected CORS
example), refutation outcomes and their effect on the scores, the two
downloads, DNS TXT ownership, and the rescan diff. Current suite:
**73/73 assertions**.

> **Port note:** the scanner, per spec, only speaks ports 80/443, so the
> fixtures bind those ports on distinct loopback addresses
> (127.0.0.1–127.0.0.4, localhost:443). Binding low ports needs root,
> `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, or `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0`.
> Run `npm run verify` with sudo on a stock Linux laptop, or set
> `sudo sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0` first.

`npm run fixtures` starts the same servers standalone (HTTP fixtures on
80, HTTPS on 443 when `AC_CERT_DIR` points at a cert directory). I

作者：君莫笑 · 永恒之兰

中文文档 · English

--- 把 muse.ai（Meta "Hatch"）暴露成标准 OpenAI 兼容接口。**不含注册环节**——会话由你自己在浏览器里登录后导入。 > ⚠️ 本项目**必须**配合一个运行中且已登录的 Chrome。 > muse 的传输层是加密 Noise WebSocket，无公开纯协议实现。 ## 特性 | | | |---|---| | **OpenAI 兼容** | `/v1/chat/completions`（含 SSE 流式）、`/v1/models` | | **CDP 驱动** | 复用你已登录的 Chrome，只断开不关闭 | | **选择器集中** | 前端改版只改 `selectors.py` 一个文件 | | **并发安全** | 账号级互斥锁，覆盖整个请求含流式输出 | | **会话续期** | 页面内 fetch 续 `hatch_vml`（48h）+ VM 唤醒 | | **加密存储** | SQLite + Fernet，密钥缺失直接抛错 | | **自检工具** | `python -m muse_bridge.doctor` 五项逐一验证 | | **零注册代码** | 不介入 Meta OAuth，不做任何登录自动化 | ``` OpenAI 客户端 ──▶ muse-bridge :8788/v1 ──▶ CDP 驱动真实 Chrome ──▶ muse.ai ``` ## 为什么必须驱动浏览器 muse 的传输层不是 REST，也不是 SSE，而是**加密的 Noise WebSocket**： ``` wss://hatch.metaaivm.com/v1/noise X25519 + HKDF + AES-GCM + Ed25519 ``` WS URL 里内嵌签名的 `auth_token` / `notary_token`。**至今没有任何公开的纯协议实现**—— 社区项目（muse2api 等）全部退回浏览器驱动，其 `http` driver 至今返回 501。 因此本项目采取的路径是： 1. 用 CDP 连接一个真实的 Chrome（由你手动登录 muse.ai） 2. Cookie 与前端加密逻辑由浏览器自己完成 3. 监听页面 DOM 中助手消息文本的稳定增长 4. 转成 OpenAI SSE 输出 **这是当前唯一可行的方式**，不是偷懒。 ## 边界（硬性） - **不提供注册功能**。muse 需要 Meta 账号 OAuth 登录，本项目不介入任何注册/登录流程。 - **不规避 Cloudflare / 风控**。不做指纹伪装、不做 notary token 伪造、不做 challenge 求解。 - **不共享账号**。设计用途是单个使用者管理自己的账号。 - **不复制浏览器加密逻辑**。Noise 层由真实前端完成，本项目不重实现。 ## 安装 ```bash python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m playwright install chromium ``` 需要 Python 3.11+。 > 如果不装 playwright，服务仍可启动，但 muse 上游不可用（会明确报错）。 ## 配置 ```bash # 生成加密密钥 python -c "from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())" # 设置 export MUSE_BRIDGE_KEY="<上面生成的密钥>" ``` | 变量 | 默认 | 说明 | |---|---|---| | `MUSE_BRIDGE_KEY` | 必填 | Fernet 密钥 | | `MUSE_BRIDGE_DB` | `./data/muse.db` | 账号库 | | `MUSE_BRIDGE_PORT` | `8788` | 端口 | | `MUSE_BRIDGE_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | 监听地址 | | `MUSE_BRIDGE_API_KEYS` | 空 | 客户端密钥，逗号分隔 | | `MUSE_CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` | Chrome 调试端口 | | `MUSE_HEADLESS` | `false` | 是否无头。默认有头——muse 更容易检测无头 | | `MUSE_SITE` | `https://muse.ai` | 站点地址 | | `MUSE_QUIET_MS` | `600` | 判定回答结束的静默窗口（毫秒） | | `MUSE_REPLY_TIMEOUT` | `180` | 等回复超时（秒） | ## 快速开始 ### 1. 启动带调试端口的 Chrome ```powershell # Windows & "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" ` --remote-debugging-port=9222 ` --user-data-dir="$env:USERPROFILE\muse-profile" # Linux / macOS google-ch

# Apex Business OS

Independent business operations application built with React, Vite, TypeScript, and Supabase.

## Features

**Sales & operations (organization-scoped, role-based)**

- Dashboard with live workspace metrics, onboarding checklist, open inquiry queue, and audited recent activity.
- Customers, products & services (recorded price, tax rate, and stock), and suppliers.
- Inquiry inbox, quotations with lines and database-calculated totals, sales opportunities, and tasks & follow-ups.
- Reports with live organization summaries — every figure comes from current records.

- AI Assistant: “Analyze with Meta AI” extracts structured intent from an inquiry, looks up the real customer and product, and shows a deterministic quotation preview. Ambiguous or unmatched requests return a clarification with the exact missing information. A manager, admin, or owner must approve before any quotation, opportunity, task, or audit record is written; approval replay is idempotent.

- AI Activity: per-request model, token, cost, and routing ledger with a guarded budget hard limit.
- Model routing: automatic or manual selection among verified Meta models, with a Settings connection test that proves a live Meta request.

# Fudge

Fudge is a Windows desktop focus companion. Its always-on-top island helps you set a concrete task, check in while you work, and get a gentle reminder when it clearly detects a distraction. You choose when a focus session starts and stops, and whether to share a screen.

## The problem Fudge is designed to solve

It can be hard to return to a chosen task after interruptions or distractions. Fudge gives a work or personal task a little structure: it helps turn the task into a short plan, checks for clear signs of distraction during an opt-in focus session, and reminds you what you chose to do. The small desktop island keeps the session and its controls nearby.

Fudge is a lightweight aid for attention and task follow-through. It is not a medical tool, a time tracker, an employee monitoring system, or a guarantee that you will complete a task.

## What you can do

# BidLedger — every shouted bid, on the record

Fresh produce across South Asia is sold by **open-cry auction**: an auctioneer calls a lot and traders shout bids, often in different languages. The only record is the commission agent's handwritten slip, and the farmer is paid from that slip. If the slip is lower than what was shouted, the farmer cannot prove it.

BidLedger turns one phone recording of the auction floor into a **verified sales ledger with audio proof**:

1. **Muse Voice Transcribe** (`DIARIZATION` mode, English/Hindi/Tamil bias, auction keywords) separates the speakers and timestamps every turn.
2. **Muse Spark 1.3** acts as the auction clerk: identifies the auctioneer, maps each voice to a trader, reads bids spoken as Hindi or Tamil numbers, and returns every lot's bids, winner, price and the turn where the sale was declared.
3. **ffmpeg** cuts the proof clip of each winning call.
4. The commission agent's slip is checked against the floor; any shortfall to the farmer is flagged with the rupee amount.
5. Each sale becomes two **WhatsApp Cloud API** utility-template messages (buyer and farmer) carrying the proof clip.
6. `out/report.html` shows the ledger, flags, clips and diarized transcript.

## Run

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python make_auction.py                      # synthetic test auction + ground truth
set MODEL_API_KEY=...                       # or Windows Credentials: dev.meta.ai / metaai
python bidledger.py samples/auction.wav --slip samples/agent_slip.json --truth samples/ground_truth.json
python make_video.py                        # demo video from the real output
```

## Tested on noisy floors

4/4 lots and the Rs 9,000 shortfall caught on every floor: synthetic crowds down to -1.5 dB, and **real market recordings** from Lagos, Gombe, Cebu and Huancayo (Wikimedia Commons) at 5 dB and 0 dB. Details: [NOISE-TEST.md](NOISE-TEST.md). Run `python make_market.py` to make the noisy floors; `--clean` adds a denoise step before transcription.

## What was built during the hackathon

All of it, between 26 Oct and 5 Nov 2026: the multilingual test-auction generator with ground truth, the transcription + Spark clerk pipeline, slip checker, proof clips, WhatsApp payloads, report and demo video.

## Honest limits

- The test auction uses **synthetic voices** (edge-tts, four distinct voices) so every lot has a known true result. A live market floor is the next test.
- WhatsApp messages are produced as Cloud API payloads; sending needs a verified business number.
- Sinhala is not among Muse Voice's 25 languages yet.

## Next

Live floor test at a wholesale market · SAM 3.1 tracking raised hands for silent bids · realtime mode on the floor (`wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime`) so receipts go out as the hammer falls.

# AICL — AI Common Language

**A common language for AI agents, the way English is for people: one tongue any agent
can learn, with no ambiguity.**
Specification + zero-dependency reference implementation. Draft v0.1.0.
[日本語の README はこちら](README.ja.md)

```
(ask  #a.1 @a>@b (temp tokyo $t :unit C :at 2026-11-05T09:00+09:00))
(tell #b.1 @b>@a ^a.1 {$t 18.5C} ~0.9 :src jma)
```

## The problem

When two AI agents cooperate today they write each other English (or Japanese) prose:

> "Could you check whether **it** finished and, if so, roll it out to **EU**, but only if the error rate is **fine**? **Should take about 5 minutes.**"

Every bold span is a guess the receiver has to make: which object, which region id, what
threshold, is that an ETA or a duration, measured when. Natural language is also padded with
greetings, hedges and thanks that cost tokens and carry no information, and nothing about the
exchange is machine-checkable: no one can verify that every request got an answer.

## What AICL does

AICL is a small formal message language with four interchangeable encodings
(readable text, dense text for LLM-to-LLM exchange, JSON, deterministic CBOR) and one
canonical form that can be hashed and signed.
Its design rules are the whole point:

| Rule | In practice |
|---|---|
| Intent is explicit | Every message opens with a speech act: `ask tell do ok no done fail prop acc rej def clar why sub unsub end` |
| No pronouns | Everything is referred to by id: `#a.3`, `@bob`, `(ref #b.2)` |
| Numbers carry units | `18.5C`, `100USD`, `0.5%`. A bare `42` is dimensionless |
| Time is absolute | `2026-11-05T09:00+09:00`. "Tomorrow" does not exist |
| Uncertainty is numeric | `~0.8` on any form. No "probably" |
| Scope is structural | `(not (and a b))` cannot be misread |
| Unknown words are illegal | A receiver that meets a term it does not know **must** answer `clar`, never guess. Terms are introduced in-band with `def` |
| Natural language is quarantined | Free text only inside `(nl en "…")`, so the ambiguous part of any message is visible and measurable |
| Every request is closed | An `ask` ends with `tell`/`no`/`fail`; a `do` with `ok` then `done`/`fail`. The validator checks this |

The full specification is in [SPEC.md](SPEC.md) (16 pages, CC BY 4.0); the grammar in
[grammar/aicl.ebnf](grammar/aicl.ebnf).

### What live experiments changed (0.2)

Version 0.2 adds nothing that was designed at a desk. Each rule below exists because a
Gemini agent given only the rulebook, or a Claude–Gemini negotiation relayed by hand
([examples/07](examples/07_cross_vendor_negotiation.aicl)), broke the previous version:

- **`retract`**: an agent accepted a meeting, learned a constraint, and then rejected the
  same proposal. Decisions are now final until explicitly withdrawn with `retract :why …`.
- **Evidence or `(none)`**: asked *why* it believed a value it had made up, an agent invented
  a source. Answers to `why` must now carry structured evidence (`:src (weather

Our submissions to the Open Kernel Challenge (Muse Spark Open, 8×H200 serving).

(cold-L2 CUDA-graph medians). Team `shashank-100`.

# StepSignal

![StepSignal cover](docs/cover.svg)

**Street-level accessibility evidence for wheelchair users and people with mobility impairments.**

Front page (about, how to use, FAQ, help desk, add-a-photo): http://localhost:3001 · Live evidence map: http://localhost:3001/map

Screenshots / demo video: no hosted video yet — use the cover page and the [2-minute demo script](docs/DEMO.md) to record one. No screenshot or video link is claimed here because none has been published.

StepSignal samples a walking route every ~50 metres, retrieves real street-level photographs (Mapillary), analyses each one with Meta **Muse Spark (`muse-spark-1.3`)**, and shows — for every stretch — what obstacles were actually detected, where they are, which photograph supports each observation, how confident the model was, and how old the evidence is.

It deliberately does **not** work like a conventional accessibility map. A route is never declared "wheelchair accessible" from photographs. Each stretch is exactly one of:

- **Confirmed barrier** — barrier evidence in a photograph or map feature at confidence ≥ 0.6
- **No barrier visible in the available evidence** — analysed evidence exists and no barrier was seen in it
- **Uncertain** — insufficient evidence. Missing data is never upgraded to accessible.

Demo neighbourhood: **Bandra West, Mumbai** (Bandra Station → Linking Road Bandra, 1.2 km, 18 stretches, 66.7% evidence coverage, 11 stretches with confirmed barriers).

![Status: hackathon submission](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-hackathon%20submission-f2c14e)

# BenBen

**The friendly neighbourhood robot dog.** BenBen imagines a new era of real-time diagnostic monitoring: reasoning about the state of the world with a spatial and temporal model of it, and how that state will shape over time.

![BenBen's architecture: one run left to right, memory and learning right to left, with a red loop back to revisit until verified.](docs/onepagers/master.png)

## Why

You only understand how miraculous some things are once you lose them.

When I was wheelchair-bound for a short while and needed public transit, I realised I had no clue whether the path I used to walk so easily was accessible. I asked Maps. It told me about hills and stairs, and nothing about whether my wheelchair would get stuck, or whether I'd have to jump curbs or struggle to climb them.

New York got curb ramps on a schedule because disability groups sued: a [2019 settlement](https://www.cidny.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/225_Mot_for_Final_Approval_Accessible.pdf) covers about 162,000 corners and runs into the 2030s. Volunteers with [Project Sidewalk](https://projectsidewalk.org) map sidewalks across dozens of cities. In the suburbs, where [even open map data misses most sidewalks](https://www.cdc.gov/Pcd/issues/2026/26_0255.htm), I literally had to call an Uber driver to go look for me.

Accessible routing has come a long way. This is an experiment to see how much further we can take it. What if…

- **you're not the median**, and could send a scout ahead of a perilous trip?
- **you look after an estate of 300 homes**, and need to triage what needs fixing first?
- **you just cleared the ice on your campus**, but sneaky black ice still waits in a few spots?

That's the problem I decomposed into a robot dog: video and LiDAR reasoning, memory, and agents driving the autonomy, in an infinitely variable world where no two situations are the same. It's also how I'm levelling up in perception, planning and control, and testing how the jump in agents and memory carries over to robots and cobots.

## What BenBen does

1. **Notices change.** LiDAR says something moved; the camera says what it is. Works in the dark.
2. **Judges with receipts.** One action (reroute, flag for service, report, or ask a human), with the object outlined and the frame cited.
3. **Won't clear in the dark.** The latest *usable* look wins.
4. **Asks one question.** "Is the bag on the path or beside it?" One tap.
5. **Goes back to look.** Nothing is fixed until it's seen fixed.
6. **Plans its next look.** Stale and uncertain spots first.

## How it works

**One run, left to right.** A reasoner (Muse Spark) plans the patrol. An action model walks it behind a motion guard, so model text never touches the motors. A cheap gate lets through only usable frames where the geometry changed. SAM 3.1 outlines the obstacle, Muse picks the action, and a person approves anything that leaves the system.
