Vellam Map

A flood early-warning system for Chennai, built from photos people already take.
Report, verify, measure, map, alert, and ask by voice in Tamil or English.

![Vellam Map: live flood map of Chennai with depth readings, area alerts and the latest reports](docs/img/live.jpg) *Vellam* (வெள்ளம்) is Tamil for flood. This is a flood-reporting app built for Chennai, where people already share flood photos on WhatsApp but nobody can tell from a photo whether a road is 10 cm or 1 m under water. Vellam turns the photo into a number, checks that it is real, puts it on a live map, and warns the people nearby. It is a system, not a single model call. Four models do four different jobs and check each other: **SAM 3.1** segments the water and wheels, **geometry** turns that into centimetres, **Muse Spark** judges whether the photo is a real flood and gives an independent depth estimate (a large disagreement sends the report to review instead of the map), and **Muse Voice Transcribe** with Muse Spark answers Tamil and English questions about the live data. Around them sit duplicate, stale and location checks, face and number-plate blurring, area-level alert clustering, and a public-data benchmark that found, and fixed, real problems. All of the code in this repository was written during the hackathon (first commit 28 October 2026). Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Indie Developer track, *Build for Your World*) with **SAM 3.1**, **Muse Spark** and **Muse Voice Transcribe** through the Meta Model API. > **Run it yourself.** There is no hosted instance, because every report and question spends credits on the > API key the server holds. Clone it, add your own Meta API key, and it runs on your machine in about five > minutes: [Quick start](#quick-start). > > **No key? Try replay mode.** Start the backend with `REPLAY=1` (no key needed). Each test photo in the Report > tab then plays back the pipeline run recorded on it with the real models, and the Benchmark tab replays the > 100-photo run. # SkillForge

**Watch once, learn the skill, drive the computer, take correction.**

SkillForge learns a skill by watching a human work. It extracts the human's
judgment as explicit rules and anti-rules, binds those rules to a brand-new
subject it has never seen worked on, and verifies the result. The human stays
in the loop as grader: corrections are authoritative and produce the next
version of the skill.

The reasoning core is Meta's **Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3` via the Meta
Model API). Every forge, bind, and verify run is a live Spark call with a
strict JSON schema — and every forged skill carries its evidence with it.

**Demo video (2:17):** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kpf-s-yXiB8

## Skill 001 — the proof

Skill 001 is a website-building judgment skill, forged on Oct 29, 2026 from
the build record of a real creator site (TOOTRIPSY). The build was decomposed
into four teaching episodes — one per decision the builder actually made:

| Episode | Decision |
|---|---|
| `episodes/hero_asset.json` | Hero Asset Judgment |
| `episodes/sections.json` | Sections Sequence Judgment |
| `episodes/visual_direction.json` | Visual Direction Judgment |
| `episodes/voice.json` | Voice Judgment |

The forge produced four rules (all confidence: high), each with anti-rules —
the failure modes the human had corrected during the original build — plus
global anti-rules against transferring demonstration-specific assets, palettes,
phrases, or layouts to another creator. See `out/skill-001.json`.

The skill was then **bound blind** to two creators it had never seen, from
evidence cards only (`tastecards/`): Festus Feasts and Kyle Parker / KO
Fitness (`out/bound-festus.json`, `out/bound-kyle.json`, with human-readable
briefs beside them). The pattern across both binds: judgment bound at high
confidence exactly where the creator's own record was rich, and dropped to
low confidence with an explicit hold exactly where evidence was missing
(e.g. hero photo licensing) — the gap was flagged, never filled by invention.

A back-test compared the blind Festus bind against the real, finished Festus
Feasts site: story-first structure, distinct venue proof, signature moment,
inquiry close, and voice discipline matched; the hero *form* and the palette
differed (the real hero is an intimate portrait opposite a headline, not the
predicted full-bleed table moment).

On Oct 31, 2026 the human grader — Zac Faber — officially graded and amended
all four rules. That grading record is `GRADES.md`, and it governs all future
binds.

Fixi

See the problem. Know the next step.

A visual DIY companion for Meta Ray-Ban Display.
Built for the Meta AI hackathon · Native SwiftUI · iOS 17.2+

Try Fixi · How it works · Build 21

Fixi turns “How do I fix this?” into a short, visual checklist. Show what you are working on, describe the problem, and get instructions you can follow with your hands on the project. Ask a question, inspect a close-up, or complete a step by voice, glasses gesture, or phone touch. **The goal:** less time switching between a repair, a phone, and a tutorial—and a clearer next action.

Offline iPhone simulator previews from normal builds 18 and 20. The hinge is a synthetic illustration. These show the design used by build 21, not a live repair or a glasses recording.

## A repair, one step at a time 1. **Show and tell.** “I want to replace my engine air filter.” A photo and your words help identify the project. Fixi asks for missing details and marks uncertain make, model, or year guesses for review. 2. **Confirm the project.** Review what Fixi understood before it creates the guide. 3. **Get ready.** See the tools and parts you need. Shopping links stay on the phone. 4. **Follow the checklist.** Open any step. # AFTERHUMAN

**Discovering the invisible patterns hidden in our world.**

AFTERHUMAN is a small, reproducible scientific discovery workspace. It screens numeric feature pairs, ranks candidate dependencies, checks selected candidates against a permutation null and a deliberately shuffled negative control, compares linear and quadratic prediction, and writes falsifiable hypothesis dossiers.

## Run locally on Windows

From `C:\AFTERHUMAN`:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn backend.api:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:8000](http://127.0.0.1:8000). The API reference is at [http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs](http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs).

## Optional Meta model review

The application works without credentials. With a Meta Model API key, the user can request an on-demand critique of a selected dossier. Only that dossier's aggregate statistics are sent; no row-level data is included. The key remains in the server environment and is never returned to the browser.

```powershell
$env:MODEL_API_KEY = "your-key"
$env:MODEL_API_MODEL = "muse-spark-1.3"
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn backend.api:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

The endpoint and model default follow Meta's [Model API chat completions documentation](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/chat-completions). If no key is configured, the review button provides a clearly labeled deterministic evidence summary instead.

## Analysis workflow

1. Screen every pair in the selected feature family with Pearson correlation, Spearman rank correlation, and symmetrized kNN mutual information.
2. Correct Spearman screen p-values across the complete pair family with Benjamini–Hochberg.
3. Rank a shortlist by mutual information weighted by the fraction not explained by linear correlation. Near-duplicate linear pairs can be omitted from the shortlist while remaining in the tested family.
4. For each selected candidate, compute plug-in mutual information after marginal quantile binning. Permute one feature's binned labels in batches to build an empirical independence null; retain the +1 p-value correction, resolution, null distribution, and random seed.
5. Run a distinct shuffled-pair integrity control and compare out-of-sample ridge and quadratic-ridge prediction. Cross-validation fold spread is labeled descriptive, never an inferential confidence interval.
6. Export a JSON hypothesis dossier with H₀/H₁, evidence, provenance hash, competing explanations, next experiments, and limitations.

The shortlist permutation check uses the same observations that produced the shortlist. It is a second estimator check, **not independent replication or post-selection calibrated inference**. Dossier decisions remain exploratory and no association is interpreted as causal.

## Data

The built-in Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) dataset is loaded through `sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer` and tagged `REAL_BENCHMARK`. Its 569 samples and 30 numeric features are a resea

# HomeWise AI

**Understand the full cost of a home before you buy.**

HomeWise AI helps first-time homebuyers explore what a home could mean for their monthly budget. It combines transparent financial calculations, property cost comparisons, and optional explanations powered by **Meta Muse Spark 1.3**.

## Why HomeWise AI?

A mortgage payment is not the full cost of homeownership. Property taxes, insurance, maintenance, homeowners association (HOA) fees, and upfront expenses can significantly affect a household's budget. HomeWise AI brings these figures together so buyers can understand the costs and tradeoffs before taking their next steps.

The application **calculates with deterministic code and explains with Meta AI**. The AI does not decide whether someone can afford a house or which property they should purchase.

## Features

| Feature | What you can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Affordability** | Enter take-home income, proposed housing costs, debts, living expenses, and savings to see monthly money remaining, income ratios, and a savings cushion. |
| **Property Costs** | Estimate monthly and annual housing costs, including principal and interest, property tax, insurance, HOA fees, maintenance, and other applicable expenses. Review estimated upfront cash separately. |
| **Compare Properties** | Compare two properties side by side, including monthly costs, annual costs, upfront cash, and the categories driving the differences. |
| **Financial Insights** | Explore calculated charts immediately; optionally request plain-language Meta AI observations, supporting figures, and limitations. |
| **Dashboard** | See the status and results of completed workflows in one place. |

The interface works on desktop and mobile, supports keyboard interaction, and offers **Light**, **Natural**, and **Dark** themes. Values are labeled as user-provided, estimated, assumed, or calculated where relevant.

## What Meta AI contributes

HomeWise AI uses **Meta Muse Spark 1.3** through the server-side **Responses API** to interpret financial results—not to calculate them.

```text
User enters information
        ↓
Validated, deterministic financial calculations
        ↓
Results and provenance recorded in a server-generated facts ledger
        ↓  (only after the user requests an explanation)
Meta Muse Spark 1.3 produces structured observations
        ↓
HomeWise validates cited facts and numerical claims
        ↓
Readable observations, supporting figures, and limitations
```

A model-generated explanation is shown only after passing the application's structural, citation, numerical, and prohibited-language checks. These checks reduce risk but cannot guarantee every sentence is perfectly expressed. If the model is unavailable or its answer is rejected, **calculated results and charts remain usable**. The user initiates each request; HomeWise does not automatically generate explanations or automatically retry failed requests.

The AI does not independently verify entered

# Domi Reels

**From one menu photo to a finished Instagram Reel, with nobody writing a prompt.**

Restaurant owners know Reels bring customers, but agencies are expensive and AI tools take time they don't have.
Domi Reels runs the AI for them. Meta's Muse is the director: it looks at the restaurant's real food photos, invents
the idea, directs every shot, keeps only the seconds where the food is still the real dish, and adds the text and the
music. The owner gets the Reel on WhatsApp, for about $5 a Reel.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026). Live at https://domireels.com.

## How it works, in four steps

1. **Connect the menu.** An ordering platform connects through our API, or the owner signs up at domireels.com,
   marks the kitchen equipment they use (fryer, plancha, grill...) and gives their website or sends food photos on
   WhatsApp (+1 407-439-7335).
2. **Muse plans the week.** It searches what's working in food Reels and what's coming up in the restaurant's city,
   reads every photo, and invents ideas that fit what the photos can really do. No two restaurants get the same Reel.
3. **Muse directs and reviews.** It writes every shot, Muse Image and SAM 3.1 keep the real dish in each frame, and
   Muse watches every take like an editor, keeping the good seconds and throwing away the rest. If it cannot see
   something ("Oaxaca cheese or mozzarella?"), it asks the owner on WhatsApp.
4. **The Reel arrives on WhatsApp**, with three songs to choose from. The owner can ask for a change in a message or a
   voice note ("make the cheese pull last longer") and Muse adjusts only that part.

The gallery at domireels.com shows real pilot Reels and, for each one, how Muse directed it: the photos it started
from, what it saw, and every take it kept and threw away.

## What existed before, and what is new

- **Before the hackathon:** Domi (Doocado), the company's existing platform: online ordering and Instagram photo
  content for restaurants. None of it is in this repo, and the demo video does not show it as new work.
- **Built Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026:** Domi Reels, all of this repository and everything shown in the demo video: the
  director pipeline, the web app at domireels.com, the WhatsApp channel, the platform API, and the gallery.

## Models and the Meta-only rule

Meta's models make every decision. Muse Spark invents each idea, writes every shot for the video model and the brief
for the music, watches every take, keeps or drops each second, edits, writes the on-screen text and reviews the final
Reel. Muse Image draws the frames, SAM 3.1 keeps the real dish in every frame, and Muse Voice Transcribe reads the
owner's voice notes. Meta's Model API has no video or music model, so two providers only render what Muse wrote:
video from Gemini Omni and music from ElevenLabs, both through fal. Upscaling uses Topaz on fal.

# Touch Tools

Turn any phone or tablet on your Wi-Fi into a mouse, keyboard, macro pad and screen viewer for a Windows PC. No app to install, no account, no cloud.

Open one address in the phone's browser. That's the setup.

![status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-prototype-orange)

---

## What it does

| | |
|---|---|
| **Trackpad** | Drag to move, one tap left click, two fingers right click, three fingers middle click |
| **Typing** | The phone's own keyboard types straight into the PC |
| **Shortcuts** | CTRL / SHIFT / ALT / WIN as toggles, then a key |
| **Macro bank** | A JSON-driven panel of labelled buttons: key combos, text, clicks, scrolls |
| **Profiles** | Save, name, export and import whole layouts |
| **Gestures** | Draw a shape on the pad; it fires an action without moving the cursor |
| **Screen strip** | Optional live view of the PC screen with the real cursor drawn in |
| **Gesture lab** | Record and label your own strokes, export them as a dataset |

Everything stays on your local network.

---

## Requirements

- Windows PC (the input injection is Windows-specific)
- Python 3.9 or newer
- A phone or tablet on the same Wi-Fi as the PC

---

## Run it

> **New here? Follow [`SETUP.md`](SETUP.md) - a ten-minute step-by-step guide written for someone who has never opened a terminal.**

```bash
git clone <this repo>
cd touch-tools
pip install -r requirements.txt
copy config.example.json config.json
python server.py
```

The console prints the address to open on your phone, plus a QR code you can scan.

**The address is different on every computer** - it is your PC's own network address. Read it from the banner each time you start; do not copy it from anyone else's setup.

If Windows Firewall asks about Python, allow it on the private network.

---

## Configure

`config.json` (create it from the example):

```json
{
  "host": "0.0.0.0",
  "http_port": 8855,
  "ws_port": 8856,
  "pin": "",
  "launch": { "notepad": "notepad.exe" }
}
```

- `pin` - set a number if other people share your Wi-Fi. Leave empty to connect without a prompt.
- `launch` - name to program path, used by the launch buttons.

Your own buttons live in `web/buttons.json`:

```json
{ "label": "Save", "action": { "keys": ["ctrl", "s"] } }
{ "label": "Say hi", "action": { "text": "hello" } }
{ "label": "Scroll down", "action": { "scroll": [0, -1] } }
```

---

## Pages

| Page | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/` | The controller |
| `/gesture-lab.html` | Record and label gestures, export JSON |
| `/test-gesture.html` | Diagnostics: shows why a drawn shape did or did not match |

Heliox es un prototipo de hackathon que explora cómo convertir señales de movilidad en explicaciones operativas y beneficios de fidelidad, con privacidad por diseño. La primera prueba es deliberadamente acotada: una señal ficticia del vehículo → una respuesta local de Llama → revisión humana.

## Demo y publicación

- [Repositorio público](https://github.com/gerencia239/heliox-meta-ai-hackathon-2026).
- Video H.264 de la demo, 180 segundos: `demo.mp4`; reproductor: `demo.html`.

El video muestra el flujo local y una respuesta generada en vivo por Llama. El escenario, vehículo, telemetría y créditos son ficticios. No hay vehículo, sensor, ubicación, identidad, wallet, blockchain, transacción ni saldo real conectado.

## Ejecución local con Llama

Requiere Python 3.10+ y [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download). Descarga el modelo localmente:

```bash
ollama pull llama3.2:3b
```

Luego inicia el backend desde la carpeta del proyecto:

```bash
bash scripts/start-local.sh
```

Abre `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. Heliox consulta `llama3.2:3b` en Ollama (`127.0.0.1:11434`) y escucha sólo en `127.0.0.1`; no expone el modelo a la red pública. La interfaz envía uno de tres códigos de pregunta cerrados y el backend fija escenario e instrucciones. Si el backend no está disponible, la interfaz distingue las respuestas fijas de ejemplo de una inferencia de IA.

La salida de Llama admite hasta 384 tokens. El servidor convierte una terminación `done_reason=length` en error, no en una respuesta aparentemente completa. El script `scripts/run-live-evidence.py` valida que las tres inferencias sean locales, con telemetría sintética, que terminen con `done_reason=stop` y que tengan cierre de frase antes de reemplazar `MODEL_EVIDENCE.json`.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

Para crear evidencia nueva se requiere el servidor y Ollama locales; la generación no llama a Meta Model API ni a otra API de inferencia pagada:

```bash

```

## Qué demuestra y qué no

El prototipo realiza inferencia local real con Meta Llama 3.2 3B a través de Ollama, sobre un escenario ficticio de caída de voltaje auxiliar. **No utiliza Meta Model API**, ni créditos del evento. # Praxion **An AI control engineer, built on Meta Muse (`muse-spark-1.3`, Meta Model API).** Hand it a physical machine it has never seen. It runs small, safe experiments, writes the controller itself in Python, proves that code against hidden scenarios in a sealed sandbox, deploys it under a trusted safety layer, notices when the machine changes, diagnoses the change, and rewrites its own controller. Then it proves the repair again before it is allowed to run. Tested in simulation and on a $50 heater board, where the repairs were measured on the board itself.

## The problem Refineries, power plants, water works, steel mills, bioreactors and data centres are all held steady by control loops: small pieces of code that read a sensor and set a heater, valve, pump or fan. Almost all of them are PID loops (97 % of more than 11,000 regulatory controllers in one Honeywell study), and most are tuned once, by hand, when the plant is commissioned. Then the machine drifts. A heater weakens, a pump wears, a coil fouls, the airflow changes. The controller keeps the old tuning. In a Honeywell survey of installed controllers, 16 % performed excellently and 16 % acceptably; 22 % were fair, 10 % poor, and 36 % had been switched to manual. The repair today is a specialist on site: notice the drift, step-test the live process, refit a model, retune, verify, then move on to the next loop. A plant has hundreds to thousands of them. The work pays: across 643 existing buildings, re-commissioning cost a median $0.30 per ft², saved a median 16 % of energy and paid back in 1.1 years (LBNL). But it costs skilled hours, so it is done rarely and the drift comes back. ## A use case: data-centre cooling US data centres used 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4 % of US electricity (LBNL, 2024). The average facility spends another 56 % on top of its computing, mostly on cooling (PUE 1.56, Uptime Institute, 2024). When DeepMind's models ran Google's data-centre cooling, cooling energy fell 40 % and the PUE overhead 15 % (Google, 2016). Applied across US data centres, a 15 % cut in that overhead is about 9 TWh, roughly $0.75 B a year at 8 ¢/kWh. That is arithmetic on the cited figures, not a Praxion result. Downtime is costly too: for 54 % of operators, the most recent serious outage cost more than $100,000 (Uptime Institute, 2024). Praxion has not run in a data centre. The model is Meta's Muse Spark via the Meta Model API. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[outside agent
via MCP] -->|submit_intent| N[Node driver
pricing · orders · HTTP] N <-->|ndjson over stdio
~8 µs per op| K[C++ kernel
this repo] N -->|one turn ≈ 2.5 s| M[Muse Spark] K --- S[scheduler] --- C[context assembler] --- R[risk gate] ``` ![The kernel console, with four agents in the process table, the log-scale latency ladder, the turn feed with accepted orders, and the replay log](docs/console.png) Four agents on the console, one of them submitted by an outside MCP client. Every row is kernel state, so context tokens against budget, premium spent, delta-weighted GPU-hours and orders booked all come from the kernel. The ladder on the right puts the kernel (16 µs) and the model (2.1 s) on one log axis. ## Why a kernel An agent that trades for a week will see thousands of events. If every event lands in its prompt, the prompt grows until the model forgets its own limits, and the bill grows with it. If the agent can call the order book directly, one hallucinated number is a real loss. The fixes are the same ones operating systems found decades ago: | OS idea | Here | Effect | |---|---|---| | process control block | one `Process` struct per agent with its identity, limits, exposure, usage and three tiers of memory | every agent is isolated and billable | | fair-share scheduler | two-level virtual runtime, tenant first then process | ten agents from one customer cannot starve another customer's one | | interrupts | market ticks, settlement events, clock | an agent with nothing new never burns a model call | | virtual memory | context assembler with a hard token budget, newest first, dropped items counted | prompt size is flat at turn 1 and turn 100 | | garbage collector | evicted history is summarized by a cheap second model into a working set | long memory without long prompts | | syscall validation | eight integer checks per order, on premium, GPU-hours, delta, strike band, slippage and per-turn count | the model proposes, the kernel disposes | | audit log | bounded replay log of every state change with its own timing | replayable, benchmarkable | ## Numbers Measured on a Snapdragon X Elite laptop, 64 processes across 8 tenants, 20,000 iterations. | where a turn spends its time | p50 | p99 | |---|---|---| | risk check | < 0.1 µs | 0.1 µs | | scheduler pick | 0.7 µs | 2.1 µs | | assemble context | 1.7 µs | 5.2 µs | | schedule, JSON in and out | 8.3 µs | 29.7

# BatchSort

A whole table of parcels, sorted in one look.

Built solo for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Indie track. [Watch the demo video](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RNKZbUel5u0VYQhPSLz6__LUaNSIV4wo/view?usp=sharing) (2:37).

## The problem

A parcel locker network takes in parcels from every carrier at one hub, then brings each building all of its parcels in one delivery. Before a parcel goes into a locker, a worker checks four things by hand. Who is it for? How big is it? Which compartment fits? Can it share one with another parcel for the same person?

That takes 10 seconds or more per parcel, one parcel at a time. In the Netherlands, the number of parcel lockers almost doubled last year.

## What BatchSort does

The worker puts a table of parcels on a mat, labels up. A phone above the mat sees colour and depth. Each parcel gets a card on a screen as soon as its barcode is seen. Seconds after the mat is still, every card has one of three answers.

- **Green.** The right person, a clear lead over anyone else, and a compartment the parcel fits with room to spare. The card shows the building and compartment, for example "B1 · 4".
- **Amber.** Something is uncertain. The card says what and offers the likely answers. One tap settles it.
- **Red.** No match, or no compartment fits.

A parcel too big for every compartment goes to an agent. It texts the recipient and asks if they can meet the driver at their lockers today. If they say yes, it books that, texts them 30 minutes before, and the driver calls on arrival. If they say no, it offers another day, a spot beside the lockers, or a hold at the hub.

## Built during the hackathon

Everything in this repository was built between 26 October and 4 November 2026. The open-source libraries it uses are listed at the end, with their licences.

All names, codes, buildings and labels are fictional, made by the scripts in `tools/`. The parcels in the video are my own boxes with these printed labels.

## How it works

1. **The mat.** Four printed markers at its corners give the camera real centimetres. The phone hangs 67 cm above it.
2. **The phone app** (`ios/DepthStream`, for iPhone) sends colour and depth about 10 times a second. When the system asks, it also sends one full-size photo.
3. **Barcodes** are read straight from the video. A new code gets a card at once.
4. **Depth** shows when a hand is reaching in and when the mat is still. Once it is still, the system asks for the photo.
5. **SAM 3.1** finds the outline of each parcel in the photo. Depth inside the outline gives its height, so the parcel gets three sides in centimetres.
6. **Muse Spark** reads each label from the photo. It returns the name, the 5-letter locker code, the address and whether the parcel is soft or rigid.
7. **Matching** compares the code and the last name with all 200 fictional people registered at the hub. This is plain code, not the model, so every green traces to a number.
8. **Booking** picks the smallest

# Latent Judge

**A video model that knows it's failing before it finishes.**

Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026 · Startup track · Push the Frontier · team Atikum
(Kyo Silva, Swarnabha Ghosh)

Demo video: https://youtu.be/WNvkfJxQJj0

## What it does

Generative video fails silently. A night shot comes out pure black, a sunny street clips to white, and you only find out
after paying for every step and the decode, by eye.

Latent Judge watches a video generation **while it is still being sampled**. At step 3 of 8 it predicts what the
finished clip will measure: exposure, crushed blacks, clipped highlights, saturation and colour balance. It compares
that against what the shot is meant to look like:

- **pass**: the draft carries on untouched;
- **fail**: the draft is stopped early, and a director agent picks one correction, says why, and the shot is made again;
- every decision is logged with the numbers it was made on.

It runs inside our own sampling loop for LTX-2.5 on cloud GPUs. How the judge reads a draft mid-sampling, and how it
is calibrated per model, is Atikum's own work and is not in this repository.

## Meta models, each with a job

| Model | What it does here |
|---|---|
| **Muse Spark** (Meta Model API) | The director. Reads the shot and chooses what it should be judged against (a night kitchen may be dark on purpose). When the judge stops a draft, it picks **one** correction from a closed menu and has to give a reason. Repeats, no-ops and answers outside the menu fall back to rules. Every call is logged with the model, the response id and the reason. |
| **SAM 3.1** (Meta Model API) | Finds and tracks each person, face, car and light through a clip, so a shot can be judged per object, not only per frame (`sam/`). |
| **Muse Spark + Muse Voice Transcribe** | The pre-cut agent: turns a shoot day's camera files into a labelled take list a director approves before anything is encoded (`precut_agent/`). |
| **Muse Spark Open** | Reads the run history and writes where the model fails by kind of shot, and what to train next. |

## Results

Held out: 30 prompts Muse Spark wrote without seeing our calibration, with seeds and pass marks frozen before the GPU
run (pre-registered 2 Nov 15:19 CET; run A on 3 Nov). Full numbers: [`docs/RESULTS.md`](docs/RESULTS.md).

| | |
|---|---|
| False stops on first drafts (good drafts wrongly stopped) | **0** (pass mark ≤ 1: met) |
| Failures caught by step 3 | 3 of 12 (25 %; pass mark 50 %: **not met**) |
| Failures caught by step 5 | 8 of 12 |
| Delivered and passing | **25 of 30** with the judge and director, 18 of 30 without |

A steer on a held-out prompt ("Moths circle a dim porch bulb outside a dark house at night"): at step 3 the judge
predicts crushed blacks at 54 % against a 20 % limit. Muse Spark steers, the shot is made again, and the delivered
clip passes every check (crushed blacks 0.01 %). Left alone, the draft would have finished at 76 %.

# teardown

Upload a video of someone disassembling a device (an iMac, a phone, whatever) and get back a step-by-step visual repair guide - a clean keyframe per step, every part outlined and labeled, in the style of an iFixit guide.

Being built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Oct 27 - Nov 4, 2026, Indie track).

## How it works

1. `ingest` pulls the audio track (for transcription) and probes the clip with ffmpeg.
2. Muse Voice Transcribe turns the audio into a TIMED transcript: the endpoint returns no timestamps, so the audio is transcribed in 30-second windows and each window carries its known offset.
3. Muse Spark watches the clip plus the timed transcript and plans the guide steps, anchoring every step to a verbatim narration quote. Spark cannot reliably judge time from video alone, so the plan is then verified mechanically: each anchor quote must appear in the transcript window that contains it, and the step time snaps to that window. A bad step is dropped on its own. The prompt asks for 15-40 steps; the web demo caps a guide at 35. The offline `--mock` plan has 6 steps.
4. SAM 3.1 (via the Meta Model API) segments the named part on each keyframe.
5. An OpenCV pass draws the guide look: part outlines, dimmed background, numbered steps, 2x zoom insets.
6. Output is a static guide page (`output/guide.html`) that scrolls like a real repair manual.

Keyframe-first is the whole trick: segmenting one frame per step instead of the full video is cheaper, faster, and more reliable. Times on the page are labeled "about mm:ss (±30s)" because the transcript has no word timestamps.

## Usage

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt   # needs ffmpeg on PATH too
export MODEL_API_KEY=...          # Model API dashboard > API keys
python -m teardown path/to/clip.mp4 --i-accept-api-cost --attribution "Creator, license, source URL"
```

A real run refuses to start without `--i-accept-api-cost`. Clips longer than `TEARDOWN_MAX_DURATION` (default 20 minutes) also need `--allow-long`. When `LEDGER_GITHUB_TOKEN` is set, the CLI reserves and settles on the same ledger as the web demo. Without that token it prints a warning and spends the key unmetered.

Set `TEARDOWN_SPARK_MODEL` to override the planning model (default `muse-spark-1.3`,
e.g. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` for the cheaper contributor tier). Note the contributor
tier lets Meta use submitted content to train its models - only send footage you own or
have explicit permission for.

`python -m teardown clip.mp4 --mock` runs the whole pipeline with canned steps and a synthetic mask - no API calls, no credit spent. Use it to test ingest, rendering and the guide page. `pytest` runs the offline suite (see `.github/workflows/test.yml`). Dev packages live in `requirements-dev.txt`.

# ProofRun

**Before you ship a speedup, challenge its assumptions.**

ProofRun is an executable review desk for software optimizations. Meta Muse Spark selects experiments, observes their results, and adapts its next test. Python determines the outcome. Engineers get a concrete counterexample or a reviewable evidence packet before adopting a change.

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026, **Indie Developer / Push the Frontier**.

[Watch the 2:18 demonstration](demo/proofrun-explainer.mp4) · [Captions](demo/captions.vtt) · [What was built during the event](docs/new-work.md)

## Run the Decision Room

Use Python **3.12+** for the complete demonstration, including pinned Python egglog. From the repository root:

```bash
python -m pip install -e ".[equality]"
python scripts/serve.py --port 8766 --trust-adapter examples/local_cosine/manifest.json
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8766 and select **Run the evidence challenge**. The default local mode runs real experiments with a scripted plan and no API calls. Download the packet, import it for inspection, and explicitly replay it.

The core application also runs on Python 3.11 without egglog. Symbolic/numeric analysis then reports unavailable; it does not fabricate a result. Install the optional engine on Python 3.12+ for a complete review and replay.

## Why this approach

An algebraic identity, a passing test, and a fast benchmark establish different things. ProofRun puts their evidence into one review while keeping their meanings visible:

1. **Challenge the algebra's assumptions.** Real egglog extracts x*(y+z) from x*y+x*z: seven syntax-tree nodes become five. Exact integer equality does not guarantee equal machine-number outputs. A bounded binary64 experiment provides an executable witness under its declared comparison policy.
2. **Challenge implementation behavior.** The cosine contract tests freshness, scaling, zero vectors, ties, and k boundaries. A seeded cache that returns stale rankings is rejected regardless of its timing ratio.
3. **Make a measured decision.** A candidate that passes finite checks is eligible for further evaluation only when the measured workload supports improvement. Setup costs and output agreement stay visible.
4. **Transfer the evidence.** Export and inspect a decision packet; replay supported findings against the required local code and engine.

The business goal is to catch invalid improvements before adoption and make engineering reviews reproducible. Any displayed serial-compute scenario is an estimate from explicit assumptions, not measured cloud savings or production ROI.

The demonstration uses a real live review recorded **October 29, 2026**. The [recorded decision packet](docs/assets/decision-packet.json) can be imported into the dashboard or replayed offline. These are dated local CPU measurements:

# Atom

Atom, by Atom Industries, lets engineers use AI to build simulations, and proves whether each answer is right before anyone relies on it.

Describe a problem or open an existing model. Atom's agent builds or edits the simulation in your own COMSOL Multiphysics® 6.4, then 12 checks on the solver's own output decide whether the number holds. Two of them solve the problem a second way, without COMSOL.

This repository is our entry in the [Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon](https://cerebralvalley.ai/e/meta-ai-developer-hackathon) (Meta x Cerebral Valley), Startup track, theme Push the Frontier. It describes the project and shows it working. Atom itself is proprietary and in private beta, so its source code is not in this repository.

[![Atom demo video](assets/demo-poster.webp)](https://atomindustries.co/#demo)

Demo video (three minutes, three recorded runs on Atom 0.1.4): https://atomindustries.co/#demo

## How it works

1. **Describe it or open it.** Describe the simulation in plain language and approve the spec the agent drafts from it; the agent then builds the model in your COMSOL. Or open an existing `.mph` model with the spec it should meet.
2. **Atom checks the solver's output.** Twelve checks test the solved model: provenance, units, conformance to the spec, load totals, solver settings, mesh convergence and plausibility. Two are independent routes: a trusted closed-form solution and an open-source finite-element solve.
3. **You get a verdict and its evidence.** Check code issues the verdict, never the agent. Every number in an agent answer carries a badge with the verdict behind it.

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| VERIFIED | Every required check passed and an independent route agrees with the model. |
| CHECKED | Every required check passed, but no independent route covers the problem or none could decide. |
| REFUSED | A required check failed. Atom names the check and shows its evidence instead of reporting success. |

## Meta models

Atom's agent can run on Meta's Muse models through the Meta Model API, alongside other providers and local models. The provider is picked per chat, and the key stays on the user's machine. The checks and the verdict do not use any language model: they read only what the solver computed.

## What it looks like

A verified run: the verdict from check code, then each check with what it measured and the tolerance it used.

![Verification report](assets/shot-verify.webp)

A model with a planted error (Young's modulus entered as 200 MPa instead of 200 GPa) is refused, fixed on a copy, and the copy verifies.

A time-dependent model, a soda can cooling in an ice and salt bath, checked against a series solution.

# GridProbe

Evidence-Seeking AI Diagnostic Agent for Physical Infrastructure

Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon. GridProbe investigates electrical-panel incidents by selecting evidence, calling tools, and producing a traceable diagnosis only when the evidence is sufficient.

## Problem

Conventional anomaly detection can flag abnormal behavior, but an alert rarely answers the operator's next questions:

- What evidence should be collected next?
- Is the current evidence sufficient to identify a cause?
- When should the system abstain and request further inspection?

Different electrical causes can share symptoms. A temperature rise is an observation; identifying its cause requires additional evidence.

## What GridProbe Does

```text
OBSERVE → IDENTIFY UNCERTAINTY → SELECT NEXT EVIDENCE
        → CALL TOOL → REVIEW EVIDENCE → DIAGNOSE OR ABSTAIN
```

Muse Spark chooses which available tools to call. Each investigation starts with only the case ID, panel ID, and current telemetry snapshot. History, maintenance context, numerical analysis, and available visual observations must be requested through tools.

The final structured result uses one of three states:

- `DIAGNOSIS_READY`: evidence supports a specific diagnosis.
- `NEEDS_MORE_EVIDENCE`: additional observations are required.
- `NO_ACTIONABLE_DIAGNOSIS`: collected evidence does not support a specific actionable fault.

## Why GridProbe Is Different

| Capability | Role in GridProbe |
| --- | --- |
| Active evidence seeking | The agent selects the next observation to reduce uncertainty. |
| Deterministic numerical tools | Python calculates numerical facts without model arithmetic. |
| Muse Spark 1.3 reasoning | Selects tools, assesses sufficiency, and combines evidence. |
| SAM 3.1 segmentation architecture | Localizes components and supplies objective geometry. |
| Muse multimodal visual observation | Describes visible conditions without assigning electrical causes. |
| Evidence Ledger | Preserves numbered, typed observations and provenance. |
| Structured diagnosis | Validates final output and cited evidence IDs. |
| Explicit abstention | Requests more evidence rather than guessing a cause. |
| Hidden-ground-truth evaluation | Scores investigations outside the agent's context. |
| Usage and cost transparency | Reports available usage and configured cost estimates. |
| Hardware-ready architecture | Separates data, tools, evidence, and reasoning for future adapters. |

## Architecture

```text
React Industrial Console → FastAPI Product API → Muse Orchestrator
    → Scenario Tool Runtime → Evidence Ledger → Structured Diagnosis
```

| Available tool | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `get_current_snapshot` | Current voltage, current, and temperature measurements |
| `get_sensor_history` | One requested sensor's timestamped history |
| `calculate_phase_imbalance` | Exact current-deviation calculation |
| `calculate_temperature_trend` | Signed temperature change, duration, and rate |

# Rule Replay

**A fluent plan isn't a valid plan.** Meta Llama proposes a bounded action plan for a fictional game. An independent, developer-authored simulator replays every step against the declared rules. A failed step produces an exact counterexample that feeds one bounded repair attempt. Nothing is ever labeled verified unless it actually passed the replay.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** (Cerebral Valley, November 2026).

## Live product

- App: https://rule-replay.farfazlearning.workers.dev
- Demo video (captioned walkthrough, real outcomes in order): https://rule-replay.farfazlearning.workers.dev/rule-replay-demo.mp4
- API: `POST /api/plan` with `{"scenario_id":"robot"}`, `GET /api/scenarios`, `GET /api/counterexample` (labeled developer-authored negative test, no AI).

## Stack

- **Model**: `@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast` via Cloudflare Workers AI (OpenAI chat shape handled).
- **Verifier**: deterministic simulator in `worker.js` (`simulate()`). The model never sees the simulator's code and cannot mark its own plan verified. The checker is developer-authored, not generated by the model it checks.
- **Frontend**: single static page in `public/index.html`, served as a Worker static asset.
- **Deploy**: `npx wrangler deploy` with `wrangler.toml` (no secrets in this repo; the AI binding is account-level).

## Honest results

In the observed live runs, Llama 3.3 70B's proposed plans **failed verification**: the model repeatedly tried to `collect` on a square with no star (step 4), and the bounded repair attempt failed too, at the same step. The product reports `not_verified` with both counterexamples, exactly as designed. The demo video shows this real outcome; no simulated success is substituted anywhere. The interesting engineering result is that fluent model plans need independent checking, and that a single counterexample-grounded repair was not enough for this fixture.

## Scope and limits

- Only fixed fictional inputs are accepted. No free-text rules, no external actions, no learner data.
- `verified_against_fixture` means only that the trace conforms to this fixed fictional simulator. It is not real-world truth, teaching approval, or a safety guarantee.
- Llama 3.3 Community License applies to model use: https://developer.meta.com/ai/llama3_3/license/

**Meta's Muse agent finds a car and haggles. TireKick makes the car prove itself.**

Buying a used car from a stranger on Facebook Marketplace means trusting a few photos and a promise that it

dashboard. TireKick checks that video with Muse Spark, runs the VIN through NHTSA, and only then negotiates
for the buyer, using what it found as leverage. The buyer approves every message before it goes out.

We built it for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie track, "Build for Your World") with first-time
buyers in mind: students and young people buying a cheap first car, often with no one to bring along to
look at it.

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/oZptKwqpeaw

2. **TireKick looks up similar cars** with Muse Spark's web search. Only prices that come with a source link
   count, and the low, median and high are computed in code.
3. **The seller gets a one-time code** and a short checklist: hold the code next to the windshield VIN,
   show the door-jamb VIN, turn the key to ON so every warning light comes on, show the odometer, then start
   the engine. All in one continuous take.
4. **TireKick checks the video.** Muse Spark watches it three times and reports what it sees; the runs are

# 🛡️ ReproProof

> **Bug reproduction as a frozen browser test, a human approval gate, source-only repair, and fresh-copy checking.**
> Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Indie Developer Track)**. Hackathon MVP, **not production software**.

---

## 💡 The Core Idea

AI code models usually change code without proving the bug exists or that the fix works. ReproProof puts a controller between the model and the codebase:

1. **Constrained reproduction:** a plan (from the model, or a hand-written template in mock mode) is compiled into a data-driven Playwright test and run in real Chromium against the app.
2. **Human approval freeze:** a human approves the exact test that ran. The controller binds approval to that stored test and its SHA-256; nothing else can be approved. No patch is requested before approval.
3. **Source-only repair:** patches may touch only the manifest's allowed source paths (no tests, configs, manifests; ≤200 lines, ≤5 files), applied with `git apply`.
4. **Fresh-copy check (`passes_frozen_test`):** the controller itself runs the verifier on a fresh copy of the app with the stored patch, runs the byte-identical frozen test and the protected regression suite, and checks the result's provenance (run id, test hash, patch hash, source-tree hash). `passes_frozen_test` requires frozen test `PASSED` **and** regression `PASSED`. There is no API that accepts a caller-supplied success flag.
5. **Evidence bundle:** built only from the stored run record and on-disk artifacts, each re-hashed. Missing or tampered artifacts are reported as `MISSING` / `FAILED` / `CORRUPTED` and the bundle is marked `evidence_valid: false`.

```
[ 1. Report ] ──► [ 2. Reproduce ] ──► [ Human Approval ] ──► [ 3. Repair ] ──► [ 4. Check ]
                  real Chromium run     freezes stored test     git apply on      frozen test + regression
                                        (SHA-256 bound)          fresh copy        suite, provenance checked
```

State machine: see `VALID_TRANSITIONS` in `reproproof/core/schemas.py`; verification flow in `reproproof/core/controller.py`.

---

## ⚠️ What this demo does and does not prove

| | Status |
|---|---|
| Real Chromium (Playwright) reproduction and checking on ephemeral ports | **Genuinely executed** (tests + demo) |
| `git apply` on a fresh temporary app copy; protected regression suite | **Genuinely executed** |
| Controller rejects forged approval / verification / foreign evidence | **Tested** (`tests/test_controller_invariants.py`) |
| Evidence bundle flags tampered or missing artifacts | **Tested** (`tests/test_remediation_evidence.py`) |
| AI-generated plans or patches | **NOT demonstrated.** No live-model run has been recorded. |
| Repair rate of an AI model | **NOT measured** |
| False-success rate | **NOT measured** (hidden checks in `evals/hidden/` are never executed) |
| Sandboxing | **None.** See execution boundary below. |
| Second allowlisted app (`todo-app`) and 5 of 8 eval cases | **

# Zyntry Verdict

An adaptive AI courtroom that pushes frontier models past their first answer:
agents independently investigate, challenge each other's claims with testable
objections, gather evidence, revise or defend, and the court verifies the
result against real success criteria.

Built for the **Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon** — **Push the Frontier** theme.

## Step 1 — adaptive action loop (done)

- [x] Repo scaffold: `packages/engine` (court core) + `packages/cli` (runner)
- [x] Adaptive action loop: agents *propose* actions; the court *approves or
      rejects* via a deterministic policy (permitted, relevant, novel, within
      budget, worthwhile); tools execute; outputs become evidence
- [x] Evidence store: claims' statuses are *derived* from evidence
      (test pass/fail), never assigned by agent say-so
- [x] Disputes: challenges must name a testable action; evidence settles them
- [x] Closing: success criteria + no open disputes + all agents idle → verdict;
      budget / stall / round limits → honest `unresolved`
- [x] Proof case: `cases/trivial/case.json` (scripted agents stand in for models)

## Step 2 — Meta Model API integration (current)

- [x] Provider-agnostic `ChatModel` interface; orchestration never depends on
      a specific vendor
- [x] `MetaChatModel`: OpenAI-compatible chat completions against the Meta
      Model API (retry on 429/5xx, timeout, token usage, optional cost pricing)
- [x] `MockChatModel`: offline runs/test/rehearsal through the same payloads
- [x] `LLMAgent`: model-backed agents — propose/react are JSON-in/JSON-out
      completions, parsed defensively, with usage reported to the court
- [x] Role-specific system prompts (capabilities, visibility, evidence rules,
      strict JSON schemas)
- [x] Model routing groundwork: per-agent model overrides in the case file,
      default/cheap model tiers via env
- [x] End-to-end proof: the trivial case now runs *through the LLM pipeline*
      (prompt → JSON → parse → court) with the same verdict
- [x] Four "pressure" mechanisms (the adaptive-reasoning core):
      1. **Rest must be earned** — a rest must state `remainingUncertainties`;
         the court declines rests that omit it and records admitted
         uncertainties as open questions (the model's own admission of
         ignorance keeps the case alive)
      2. **Challengers can author tests** — `writeTest` capability for
         challengers (sandboxed test authoring, no write access to the
         solution); counterexamples become constructible
      3. **Escalation when idle-but-incomplete** — if all agents rest while
         the criteria are unmet, the court fires an appeal and re-arms them
         (bounded by `maxAppeals`) before declaring `unresolved`
      4. **Disputed claims** — inconclusive challenge evidence marks the
         targeted claim `disputed` and keeps the dispute open, instead of
         silently leaving it unchanged
- [x] **Live Meta Model API runs verified** — `api.me

# Discovery Clock

**Checks every claim in a written incident report against the body-worn camera recording and points to the second where it is, or is not, on the video.**

For each claim in the report it returns **On recording** (with the timecode and what is seen or said there), **Not found on recording**, or **Check this claim** (the recording shows something different or only partly supports it). Click a claim and the player jumps to that second. It never says "the officer lied": it points a public defender or prosecutor to the second of footage, and the lawyer looks.

**Demo video (2:56):** https://youtu.be/A5G9qWKiq2Y · **Built:** all code in this repository was written on Nov 4, 2026, during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon.

**At a glance**
- **Tested on 5 public body-camera videos** (Volusia Sheriff's Office, 39 claims): all 5 planted contradictions came back as *check this claim*, 4 of the 5 planted invented claims as *not found* (1 as *check*), and none of the 10 as *on recording*; 21 of 29 claims from the agency's own written accounts got a timecode, 3 of them flagged *check*; 8 of 8 timecodes we checked against the frames by eye matched. Answer keys were sealed by hash before the first model run ([eval/RESULTS.md](eval/RESULTS.md)).
- **Long input:** a 31.7-minute file of 10 public Volusia clips joined together (a packet to test long input; real discovery holds hours from several cameras) was checked end to end in 9.7 minutes for $0.74: 4 pieces, one Muse Spark 1.3 call each. 50 of 51 timecodes landed inside the clip the claim belongs to, and none of the 20 planted claims came back as *on recording* ([Long recording](#long-recording)).
- **Live Meta calls on screen:** `/calls` shows every request and answer with latency and cost. A live run on a 3.7-minute video makes 4 calls and costs about $0.12.
- **Four Meta models, nothing else at runtime:** Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Voice Transcribe and SAM 3.1 on the Meta Model API; Muse Spark Open (open weights) on Baseten. Plain code checks every model answer and can only move a claim to *check*.
- **Run it without a key** (recorded live answers for all five cases are in `recordings/`):

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/fetch_media.py fy6dRGapw_4
.venv/bin/python -m discovery_clock replay --case fisherman-fy6dRGapw_4 --video data/media/fy6dRGapw_4.mp4
DC_REPLAY=1 .venv/bin/python -m discovery_clock serve --port 8765   # open http://127.0.0.1:8765

# Disaster Mitigation Bench

Benchmarking language models as **drone navigators** and
**reconnaissance advisors** in simulated 3D disaster environments.
Eval harness: [inspect-ai](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/). Sim:
Gazebo-first (headless-capable, distributed). Inference: Baseten
frontier + Modal-hosted HuggingFace. All runs tracked.

- **Worlds**: hard disaster scenarios built from real internet
  assets (Fuel models, Polyhaven textures) and checked against
  real look references (NASA FIRMS fire data, Commons aerials),
  rendered and verified in Gazebo.
- **Agents**: ReAct drone missions (single + 2-drone fleets) over
  an ArduPilot-derived tool surface, with stub or SAM 3.1 edge
  perception (segmentation maps → routes + severity).
- **Scoring**: mission composite (rescue recall, containment,
  efficiency, safety) plus coverage, closest approach, and
  calibrated route metrics.

## Sim-to-real batches

| Batch | Worlds | Evals | Report |
|---|---|---|---|
| FIRMS peat (#79) | 120×120 Kalimantan/Sumatra peat tiles from MODIS hotspots | 16 LLM + 2 greedy | [harder-evals](docs/firms-sim2real/harder-evals.md) |
| Quake/slide (#80) | 60×60 quake town, 48×64 slide slope | 32 LLM + 4 greedy | [envs](docs/quake-slide-sim2real/envs.md) |
| Flood (#82) | 60×60 flood town, 48×64 flash valley, 60×60 tsunami coast | 48 LLM + 6 greedy | [envs](docs/flood-sim2real/envs.md) |

Footage (promo loops, run replays, final frames, segmentation
maps, survey frames) lives next to each report under
`docs/<batch>/renders/`.

## Results

Across **93 scored LLM episodes** (Baseten
`muse-spark-open-1026` with vision + Modal Qwen2.5-7B /
Mistral-7B-v0.3 / Qwen2.5-14B-AWQ, SAM vs stub, single vs
fleet) plus 12 scripted greedy baselines:

![Episodes with at least one victim found, LLM vs greedy by batch](docs/img/results-finds-by-batch.png)

*LLM agents find a victim in 6/93 episodes; the scripted sweep
finds victims in every quake/slide and flood cell. FIRMS peat
(120×120) floors everyone.*

| Batch | LLM episodes w/ ≥1 find | Victims (LLM) | Greedy episodes w/ ≥1 find | Victims (greedy) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FIRMS peat | 0/16 | 0 | 0/2 | 0 |
| Quake/slide | 1/32 | 1 | 4/4 | 4 |
| Flood | 5/45 | 5 | 6/6 | 8 |

![Episodes with at least one victim found, by model](docs/img/results-finds-by-model.png)

*The vision frontier accounts for 4 of the 6 LLM finds;
Mistral-7B never acts (0 actions in every completed cell,
100–200k tokens of fenced pseudo-calls, plus 3
context-overflow errors). Tsunami is a perfect 0/14.*

![Mean map coverage, LLM vs greedy by batch](docs/img/results-coverage.png)

*Acting LLM agents cover ~0.1–0.5% of the map then submit;
coverage is unscored, so early-submit is score-rational.
Greedy covers ~2% and finds 1–2 victims per environment.*

Findings:

- **The evals are hard by design, and frontier performance
  sits near the floor.** 6 victims in 93 episodes; per batch
  FIRMS 0/16, quake/slide 1/32, flood 5/45.
- **Scripted coverage beats every LM.**

# Gameon Agent

Gameon Agent is the research and publishing service behind Gameon’s market
intelligence feed. It gathers market news and SEC filings, builds company
context from those sources, and creates evidence-linked posts for Gameon.

The agent is written in Zig. News research and drafting use Meta’s
`muse-spark-1.3-contributor` model through `https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses`.
Baseten’s `meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026` reviews posts and powers SEC
knowledge extraction through `https://inference.baseten.co/v1/chat/completions`.
Python is used locally for article and PDF text extraction; it is not a
separate service.

## What it does

For the default set of configured tickers, the agent runs three independent
workflows concurrently:

1. **Collect news:** polls TradingView News Flow and extracts structured story
   content, including paragraphs, headings, lists, links, and tables. It may
   fetch a publisher’s public canonical page when the TradingView story is only
   a preview; it does not bypass access controls.
2. **Research and write:** Meta researches recent stories, using relevant SEC
   knowledge and prior company research as context, then writes a source-backed
   post. A separate Baseten editorial pass scores the whole post and each
   section. Meta revises sections that need work. Posts are accepted only when
   the editorial decision is `accept`, the overall score and every section
  score are at least 8/10, all sections are marked `keep`, and the review has
  no issues.
3. **Collect SEC filings:** polls SEC submissions and company facts, saves
   canonical filing text, and extracts validated facts, dates, entities,
   evidence passages, and separately labeled inferences.

The research workflow keeps its inputs and outputs as JSON. Evidence quotes,
claim references, table alignment, and numeric consistency are validated
before a draft is saved. These checks improve traceability; they do not replace
human judgment or prove every interpretation is true.

## How posts reach Gameon

When configured for publishing, the news workflow sends each newly completed,
editorially accepted post to Gameon automatically. The API stores it in
Gameon’s database, where the web app reads it for the feed and post page.
Existing local drafts are not bulk-published just because the agent starts;
publication is queued for posts produced by the active workflow.

### Gameon write API

```text
POST https://gameon.finance/internal/v1/agent-posts
```

The agent calls this endpoint from `src/news_publish.zig`. The matching
Gameon web route is documented in the
[API implementation](https://github.com/searchbox-labs/gameon-social/blob/main/app/internal/v1/agent-posts/route.ts).

For production, set `GAMEON_AGENT_PUBLISH_TARGET=production` on the authorized
Google Compute Engine VM. The agent obtains a short-lived identity token from
the VM metadata server. Its audience is the fixed URL
`https://gameon.finance/internal/v1/agent-posts`. The API verifies the token

# WattWatch

An unnoticed power spike at home, a space heater left on or a failing appliance, shows up on the bill a month later. WattWatch catches it live: a plug node streams power readings to a PC once a second, two detectors flag spikes within seconds, a local Llama 3.2 model explains each one in plain words, and a web console shows it all. Everything runs at home; no cloud.

Built for the *Build for Your World* theme. Video: **TODO: link**.

## Layout

| Folder | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`firmware/`](firmware) | Plug node sketch: Arduino Nano ESP32 + ADS1115 + CT clamp, true RMS on the node, JSON over USB serial |
| [`hub/`](hub) | Python hub: ingest, rule + Isolation Forest detectors, Llama 3.2 explainer, alerts, daily digest, FastAPI (REST + SSE) |
| [`web/`](web) | React + Vite console: live power, devices, nodes, alerts, energy, topology, assistant, model lab |

Each folder has its own README with setup and details.

## Quick start (Windows)

Needs Python 3.12, Node 20+ and [Ollama](https://ollama.com).

```powershell
ollama pull llama3.2:3b

cd web
npm install
npm run build

cd ..\hub
python -m venv .venv; .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python run_all.py --serial COM4     # live plug node on COM4
```

No hardware: run `python run_all.py` (ingest over HTTP on :8000), then `python simulate.py --auto 90` in a second terminal.

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080.

## Tests

```powershell
cd hub; python -m pytest tests -q      # 74 tests
cd web; npm run e2e                    # 113 Playwright tests
```

# FalsifyAI

Executable Scientific Falsification Engine.

Compile a scientific hypothesis into an executable falsification test.

Public demo: https://falsifyai.onrender.com

Public deterministic demonstration.

FalsifyAI compiles scientific hypotheses into structured falsification workflows.

Generative AI is excellent at making ideas sound plausible. Scientific reasoning also requires identifying how an idea can fail.

FalsifyAI is allowed to refuse execution. If the hypothesis lacks the quantitative relationship required for simulation, it returns a scientific blocker instead of inventing one.

## The problem

A fluent model can defend almost any sentence. A judge still needs to see whether the sentence names a measurement, a competing explanation, and a finite way to fail.

## The idea

FalsifyAI does not stop at suggesting how a hypothesis might fail. It attempts to compile the hypothesis into an executable falsification contract: a typed claim, an adversarial critique, a strong null model, a discriminating observable, a restricted numerical comparison only when the law is stated, an experiment, and one falsification status.

## 30-second example

Same pipeline. Different scientific completeness. Different justified outcome.

Select **DUFFING CONTROL**. The hypothesis already states `Omega(A) = 1`, `Omega(A) = 1 + 0.075 * A^2`, the domain `0 <= A <= 1`, and uncertainty `0.01`. The quantitative law is present, so the restricted simulator runs, the experiment is ready, and the run can return `TESTABLE`. The chart is a model prediction, not experimental evidence.

Select the **DQ-12** stress test. The same pipeline finds no operational map from laboratory quantities to a twelve-dimensional separation, refuses to invent that law, blocks the simulation, and can return `NOT_YET_FALSIFIABLE`. That outcome is not evidence for extra dimensions.

## Scientific pipeline

Hypothesis → Critique → H₀ → Observable → Simulation → Experiment → Verdict

Each stage constrains the next one. No observable, no claim of testability. No null model, no discrimination. No quantitative law, no invented simulation. No arbitrary model-generated code. Fail closed: if the model provider, structured contract, or scientific prerequisite fails, downstream stages are skipped rather than fabricated.

## Live benchmarks

### Duffing quantitative control

A synthetic dimensionless oscillator. H₀ is the harmonic frequency. H₁ is the weak Duffing shift supplied in the text. The chart is a model prediction, not experimental data. On the validated stub and the M6 live canary this case reached `TESTABLE`, with a maximum separation of 0.075 against a stated uncertainty of 0.01.

### DQ-12 speculative stress test

One public toy statement. FalsifyAI tries to falsify it. Ordinary decoherence and apparatus effects are the null. The twelve-dimensional separation is not replaced by ordinary distance. An unexplained residual is not evidence. The conservative result is `NOT_YET_FALSIFIABLE`.

# AI Physical Engine
https://clock-board-ui.onrender.com

## Give AI a body. Let physics decide.

**An AI-controlled physical simulation engine that turns model decisions into movement, collisions, and measurable outcomes.**

Most AI demos stop when a model returns text. This project keeps going.

An AI receives a description of a physical body and its situation. It chooses motor rotations. The Python physics engine applies those motor commands and calculates what happens under gravity, contact, friction, collisions, and damage. The result becomes the AI's next observation.

**The AI chooses. Physics decides. Every result can be inspected.**

This project explores two applications of the same technology:

1. **AI robotics physical testing** — a virtual place to explore and evaluate AI body-control decisions before moving toward real hardware.
2. **A new kind of gaming engine** — physics-driven characters whose actions are chosen by AI rather than played from fixed animation scripts.

---

## 1. AI robotics physical testing

### Give AI a body before giving it a machine

Robots must do more than choose an action. Their movements must work under physical limits. A command can fail, lose balance, hit something, or produce an unexpected result.

This project explores a test loop for those problems:

- Give an AI a body and a set of motor controls.
- Let it choose motor rotations from the current situation.
- Let physics calculate what actually happens.
- Show the AI the new situation so it can make its next decision.
- Save and replay runs to compare different approaches.

This is a starting point for testing AI control strategies in a repeatable virtual environment. The longer-term direction is to support different robot body designs, control systems, and test scenarios before moving toward real machines.

**Current scope:** the supplied prototype is a virtual stick-fighter simulation. It does not yet connect to or control a physical robot, ROS, or a hardware test rig. Results are not yet validated against real machines. Moving toward real-world robotics will require robot-specific body models, calibrated physical properties, hardware integration, and separate safety testing.

## 2. A new kind of gaming engine

### Characters that act through physics, not prewritten animations

Many games use animation clips or prewritten actions to control character movement. This project explores a different approach: an AI chooses motor rotations, and the physics engine determines how the character actually moves.

This creates room for:

- AI-controlled characters that choose their own actions.
- Practice sessions for one AI-controlled character.
- Fights between two independent AI controllers.
- Movement routines that can be saved and reused.
- Physical outcomes such as falls, impacts, contact, and damage.
- Saved rounds that can be replayed and studied.

The current demonstration is a fighting simulation. The broader opportunity is a game

# Retina

*Built with Muse Spark Open.*

**Retina rewrites the first seconds of your video, draws them and checks the fix before you publish.**

Separately, it estimates how many people may stay with the video you have now, and tells you how far off that estimate usually is.

![Retina's before and after for a made-up example video: the draft opens with a greeting and no bread in sight; the new opening shows the bread from the first frame, and below it Retina shows the two attempts it rejected and the one that passed](docs/img/retina-example-card.jpg)

*Made-up example, with drawings by Muse Image. Open it yourself in one minute, with no key: see below.*

Most tools read a video and hand you a grade. Retina hands you a new first 10 to 15 seconds that you can watch and hear. Its core is a
rule engine and a verification loop around Meta's models: the rules run in code, after the model, and send the work back with the exact
list of what failed. One prompt to one model cannot do this.

1. **Watch and listen.** Muse Spark 1.3 describes what is on screen and Muse Voice Transcribe writes down what is said.
2. **Decide whether to touch it.** Muse Spark 1.3 reads the title and the speech. Retina only rewrites videos within its scope (entertainment, animals, food,
   home, curiosities, travel, family and practical tips that are not health advice), and it says so before spending anything else.
3. **Rewrite.** **Muse Spark Open**, Meta's open-weight model, writes a new opening that gives the first proof of what the title
   promises and leaves the rest to the video. The title itself is never touched. If the opening already works, Spark Open can say so,
   and code has to agree: no greeting, no engagement bait, and the topic in the first 12 words.
4. **Check the words.** Fixed code rules read the result: no greeting, none of the engagement bait on our list of what Meta's distribution
   rules penalize, nothing that touches logos, legal notices or credits, the title's topic in the first sentence, no list that uses up the
   video, and a length of about 10 to 15 seconds. Numbers and mid-sentence names must come from the video.
5. **Read it back.** Before anything is drawn, Muse Spark 1.3 reads the opening against what the video says. If it adds something the
   video does not say, the work goes back.
6. **Draw it.** **Muse Image** draws three frames from what Spark Open wrote.
7. **Check the picture.** **SAM 3.1** looks in the first frame for what the title promises, picked by Muse Spark 1.3 from a closed list
   of objects and places, never people. Spark Open knows what SAM will look for and has to describe it, so a pass means the drawing shows
   what was asked. It does not prove the claim, or that your video shows it. Muse Spark 1.3 then looks at the other frames and says
   whether each one shows what was written.
8. **Correct.** If anything fails, Spark Open receives the exact list of failures and tries again, up to twice. What does not pass

RealityCheck AI 

Break your AI model before reality does.

Computer vision models can look great on a benchmark and still miss something important when the lighting changes, an object is partly hidden, or a frame gets blurry. RealityCheck AI is an experiment in making those weak spots easier to find, reproduce, and understand.

I'm building it for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (2026). The first version focuses on one simple workflow: upload an image, pick an object, generate a few realistic stress tests, and see how an object detector responds.

This is a work in progress, not a finished robustness certification tool.
What I'm building
1. Understand the scene. Run a baseline object detector; use SAM 3.1 to segment the object we want to test.
2. Choose meaningful tests. Use Muse Spark to propose challenges for the scene, such as partial occlusion or poor visibility.
3. Change one thing at a time. Apply reproducible blur, lighting, and object-local transformations to create test images.
4. Run the detector again. Compare predictions before and after each change.
5. Show the evidence. Display the images, predictions, configuration, and results so the experiment can be repeated.
The key idea is test → measure → learn where the model struggles, rather than just generate altered images.
Why this matters
Robustness testing often comes down to assembling datasets and hand-picking edge cases. I want to make that loop faster and more accessible, while keeping the measurements honest. A change in confidence is not automatically proof of a failure; verified detection metrics require reliable labels.

# SiliconLoop

**Imagination to silicon, proven in simulation.**

**Try it live:** https://siliconloop-161403134431.us-central1.run.app ·
**Demo video (3 min):** https://youtu.be/ltlNKccoAkQ

One-click flashing from the live site has been tested on a real Arduino Uno: the board runs the same verified
firmware as the twin.

**Powered by Muse Spark Open, Meta's open-weight model, served on [Baseten](https://www.baseten.co/).** Every AI step
in SiliconLoop runs on this one open-weight model; no closed model is used anywhere.

Photograph a handful of electronic parts and say, in one sentence, what you want them to do. SiliconLoop designs the
circuit, writes the Arduino firmware and runs that exact binary in a simulated Arduino until every behaviour you asked
for passes, before you touch a single wire. You get three things that always agree with each other:

1. **A live twin** of your gadget in the browser, running the verified firmware on the same part models as the test.
2. **The firmware**: the sketch (`.ino`) and the compiled `.hex`, with one-click flashing from Chrome or Edge.
3. **A build report**: parts list, one-connection-per-step wiring, pin table, power plan, safety notes and a
   checklist to compare the real gadget with the twin. A chat assistant answers questions about the build.

Boards: Arduino Uno, Arduino Nano (including clones with the old bootloader) and Arduino Mega 2560.
Parts: 22 curated parts with simulation models, plus simple digital, analog and switched modules admitted from
approved datasheet sites.

## Powered by Muse Spark Open on Baseten

| | |
|---|---|
| Model | **Muse Spark Open**, a Meta open-weight model (`meta-models/muse-spark-open-1026`) |
| Hosting | Baseten's OpenAI-compatible inference API (`https://inference.baseten.co/v1`) |
| Client | `src/siliconloop/llm.py`; every call goes through `chat()` and is logged to the cost log |
| Settings | reasoning effort `low` (seconds and well under a cent per call); images sent inline for recognition |

What Muse Spark Open does, and only Muse Spark Open:
- **Sees:** recognises the components in the user's photos, with a confidence per part.
- **Imagines:** proposes three gadgets the confirmed parts can build.
- **Plans:** turns a plain-English wish into machine-checkable behaviour rules for the simulator.
- **Codes:** writes the Arduino firmware, then repairs it from compiler and simulation reports as a tool-using loop.
- **Reads:** extracts verified facts from datasheet search snippets (each fact must match a verbatim quote).
- **Explains:** answers questions about a finished build in the build assistant.

Deterministic code decides everything electrical (pins, resistors, current, voltage, power supplies, refusals), so
the model's open weights are paired with checks anyone can read and test. Web search (Tavily) supplies raw snippets
only; its generated answers are never used, so all generated text in the system comes from Muse Spark Open.

# Mr Fox OS

**A CTO operating system for founders who are building alone.**

Mr Fox is a persistent engineering leadership layer that runs inside Claude Code. It gives you session continuity, milestone governance, and a team of eight senior specialists who review — and fix — your work before you ship. Covering security, architecture, product, strategy, engineering craft, UX, DevOps, and plan quality.

You get the institutional memory, discipline, and review depth of a senior engineering team. Without the headcount.

---

## What It Does

Most solo founders build in a loop: decide, code, ship, regret. Mr Fox breaks that loop.

Every session starts with a brief — where you are, what's blocking you, what the last audit found. Every milestone begins with a plan that a senior EM stress-tests before a line of code is written. Every milestone ends with specialists reviewing your work in parallel (3, 5 or all 8, depending on mode), and the auto-fix specialists don't just report, they fix. Missing rate limits get patched. Vague variable names get renamed. Missing error states get added. Each fix lands on its own branch for your review before merging.

What requires a human decision — broken auth, architectural rethinks, strategic pivots — gets escalated with full context. You decide on the things that matter. The rest is handled.

The system maintains its own memory: milestone registry, session logs, audit trail, version history, living docs. It boots itself, keeps itself in sync and updates itself, with no prompting. You can context-switch, take a week off, hand work to someone else, or run several sessions at once, and come back to a complete picture of where things stand.

# Flood Watch **Forecasts say where the water should be. Cameras show where it is.** Flood Watch watches the public river cameras inside active flood warnings with SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark. It checks the flood forecast against what the cameras see, raises the forecast where it's missing flooding, shows the public where not to drive, and sends anyone who may be in danger to responders, who decide what to do. ![Flood Watch: the public map during a mock hurricane in New York City](docs/images/hero.jpg) > The preview shows **Hurricane Mira**, a made-up storm over New York City used for demos (`/`). The cameras, > incidents and flooding in it are invented; the map, streets and directions are real, and the SAM clips are real SAM 3.1 > output on public footage. The real-data case is **Hurricane Helene** on the French Broad River at Asheville, NC > (Sept 25–27, 2024), replayed from archives (`/?scenario=helene`).

Public map: where cameras see water, forecast flooding, warnings
Report: flooded road or person stuck ("call 911 first")
Responders: what SAM flagged, confirmed by a person
SAM in action: people in the water flagged, cars in water marked
A street floods: water share rising, frame by frame
## Why Flood forecasts are models. During Helene, the National Water Model's 6-hour forecast had the French Broad below flood stage at Asheville for **7 hours while the USGS camera there showed the river out of its banks**. Hundreds of public cameras already watch U.S. rivers and streets; nobody watches them all during a storm. Flood Watch does, and turns what they see into things people can act on. ## What it does - **Watches cameras where it matters.** USGS HIVIS river cameras inside NWS flood warnings (river, flash, coastal and lakeshore) are checked every few minutes. Unchanged frames are skipped. - **Sees the water.** SAM 3.1 outlines water, people, boats and vehicles. Muse Spark compares the frame with a normal day at the same camera and with the river gauge, and each hour gets one smoothed state. - **Checks the forecast.** Each camera-hour is compared with the NWM short-range forecast issued 6, 12 and 18 hours earlier, mapped onto streets with HAND. Where the camera sees flooding the forecast missed, the forecast is raised to the least flow that matches. At Helene, that cut the 6-hour forecast
