# Table for Two ✌︎

A luxury-minimal dashboard for hard-to-book restaurant reservations across NYC, DC,
Richmond, Boston, and Houston. Real Resy availability for the next 7 days, live
countdowns to monthly reservation drops (per-city timezone, DST-aware), one-tap
pre-filled booking links for every platform, list + map views, and a dark/light theme.

## Host it — one click

[![Deploy to Netlify](https://www.netlify.com/img/deploy/button.svg)](https://app.netlify.com/start/deploy?repository=https://github.com/officialtellergram/table-for-two)

Click the button → sign in with GitHub → **Save & Deploy**. That's it — no settings to
fill in (the included `netlify.toml` sets everything). You get a public HTTPS URL like
`https://your-name.netlify.app` to share. Every future `git push` redeploys automatically.

> Want a nicer URL? In Netlify: **Site configuration → Change site name**.

Prefer Vercel? Import the repo at [vercel.com/new](https://vercel.com/new) and set
**Root Directory = `deploy`** (the one setting it needs).

## Run locally
Must be served over http (not opened as a `file://` — it'll show a warning if you do):

```bash
npx serve -l 8080 .      # then open http://localhost:8080
# or:  python -m http.server 8080
```

## How it's built
- **`index.html`** — the whole app, single file, no build step.
- **`cities/`** — one JSON dataset per city + a manifest. Adding a city never touches code (see [`cities/README.md`](cities/README.md)).
- **`deploy/`** — the published folder (a clean copy of `index.html` + `cities/`); this is what Netlify serves.

- NYC is sourced from the unofficial [hardtobook.xyz](https://www.hardtobook.xyz) data; DC/Richmond/Boston/Houston are research-compiled top-25 lists.

# sas2r-benchmark

A 100-program SAS-to-R translation benchmark for clinical trial programming:
the SAS programs, their input data, the reference outputs produced by SAS 9.4,
and the scripts that run, capture, scrub and audit them.

This repository is the **reference material** for the
[sas2r-agent](https://github.com/tomasantony/sas2r-agent) entry in the Meta
Global AI Developer Hackathon (26 October to 4 November 2026). It is kept
separate so the entry repository holds only the agent, and so the SAS side
(programs, data, reference outputs, SAS harness) can be frozen and hashed
independently of anything a model produces. It contains no agent, translator or
model code.

Timeline, so the two repositories read consistently: the corpus of public
programs and data was collected before the hackathon window; the SAS reference
run, the retire-and-replace of programs that do not run on the reference
install, the 23 owner programs on a synthetic study, and this repository itself
were made on 27 to 29 October 2026, inside the window. The reference outputs
were hashed (`benchmark/sas_output_hashes.csv`, and `runs/reference_freeze.json`
in the entry repository) before any model was run against them.

Full documentation, program ids, directory layout and the run procedure are in
[docs/README.md](docs/README.md). Program provenance and licences are in
[docs/ATTRIBUTION.md](docs/ATTRIBUTION.md), `benchmark/manifest.csv` and
`docs/licenses/`.

## Contents

```
programs/sas            100 active programs P001-P100, verbatim; retired/ holds R001-R049 (see retired.csv)
programs/sas/macros     macro libraries the programs need (PHUSE utilities, FDA JumpStart, family setups, owner macros)
programs/sas/own_originals  the owner's 23 programs before the documented path/orientation patches
programs/sas_run        patched copies the runner executes (patches listed in benchmark/patches.csv); retired/ as above
programs/r/human        6 hand-written R counterparts from the source repositories (kbd0011, PHUSE), kept as human reference
data/raw                public input data (CDISC pilot, PHUSE, three GitHub pipelines, the owner's synthetic study)
data/derived            data the pipeline steps produce and later steps read (CDISC pilot loaded from xpt, c2c, wxzhai)
output/sas              reference outputs per program: datasets/, tlf/, logs/ (log + listing); shipped/ holds the
                        outputs the original authors published, for the shipped-versus-produced comparison
benchmark/              manifest, retired list, id map, families, env files, pipelines, drivers, patches, runner,
                        scrub, audit and hash scripts; candidates/ is the trial run used to choose the replacement programs
docs/                   documentation, attribution and licences
```

## Size and cloning

About 1 GB. Datasets and transport files (`.sas7bdat`, `.xpt`, `.xls`, `.xlsx`)
are stored with Git LFS (about 1 GB in 254 objects); outputs, programs and
logs are plain git

# gonaj-oss

The name Gonaj is short for "Go on a journey". Gonaj is an open-source
public-transport information project, initially focused on the
Kochi/Greater Cochin region of Kerala, India. Gonaj exists to make
public-transport information easier to discover and understand.

## The idea

Public-transport schedule and route information is hard to find in one
place. Gonaj aims to fix that with a simple web portal: a map where users
can select an origin and a destination and see the available
public-transport options, with schedule information where it exists.

The project has two ultimate goals:

1. Make public-transport schedule information easily accessible to users.
2. Make it easy for users to contribute information and corrections
   (crowdsourced data).

## MVP

The current phase is a minimal viable product whose purpose is to validate
whether the product is useful to end users — not to build the final Gonaj
architecture. The MVP is deliberately read-oriented:

- Browse public-transport stops and routes on a map.
- Search for available transport options between an origin and
  a destination.
- View schedule information where schedule data is available.
- Ask the journey helper for connectivity answers grounded in published
  data (no schedules, no invented times), by text or voice input.
- Report discrepancies (wrong route, missing stop, route not operating,
  and similar) through a generic feedback mechanism. AI may suggest a
  category, but moderation stays human.

What the MVP is **not**: direct crowdsourced editing of the dataset,
user accounts or login, realtime vehicle tracking, multimodal journey
planning, or a mobile app. Those are deferred until validation shows
they are needed.

Because schedule data may not be available during MVP development and
deployment, schedule-dependent features (timetable display, schedule
search, schedule-correction feedback) are deferred to the next phase.
The timetable data model is designed up front so the schema is ready when
the data arrives.

## Architecture

A single monorepo with a strict separation between `backend/` and
`frontend/`, communicating over a versioned REST API. The system is one
deployable application, not microservices.

| Area | Decision |
|---|---|
| Frontend | React + TypeScript, Leaflet map |
| Backend | Django + Django REST Framework |
| Database | PostgreSQL + PostGIS |
| Data operations | Django Admin |
| Transit model | GTFS-inspired |

| Schedule source | Official / RTI-derived / manually curated data |
| AI assistance | Meta models via backend SDK; read-only tools; output labelled unverified |

The application maintains its own database: OpenStreetMap is treated as a
source of geographic/transit data to be imported, not as the live
database. Each import is captured as a versioned OSM snapshot, and source
provenance (source type, references, import dates, OSM identifiers) is
preserved on re

# Sprout — raise a tiny mind

A 3-to-7 raising game. A randomly initialised ~110k-parameter transformer (the child)
learns for real from lived outcomes. There are no right answers: every choice is an
action, every action has an outcome, and the child learns what happened.

## What it is

You raise one child from age 3 to 7 (48 scenes over 8 days, 6 scenes a day).
Each scene offers a situation with choices; you act through say / show / leave, the
engine decides the outcome, and the child learns from it on the spot.
No grades or expectations are ever shown to the player — only what happened and what
the child remembers. Current direction: [docs/DIRECTION.md](docs/DIRECTION.md).

## Quick Start

```bash
uv sync
uv run pytest
uv run python -m server.web          # open http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

The web server defaults to port 8000 on 127.0.0.1 (`--port`, `--host` to change).
Words and scenes default to `mock` (offline stand-ins, see `mode` in `config/llm.yaml`);
set `GROWING_LLM=live` for the real Director/Narrator. A restart resumes
`saves/web/current` unless `--fresh` is given. Useful variants:

```bash
uv run python -m server.web --small                    # five-problem world
uv run python -m server.web --world saves/worlds/w7/ontology.yaml
uv run python -m server.web --new-world --seed 31      # Director makes a world (a minute or two)
```

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `config/ontology_age07.yaml` | the 0–7 world: problems, verbs, objects, rules table |
| `server/game/simple.py` | the scene loop (say / show / leave → act → outcome → learn) |
| `server/web/` | the web game (`python -m server.web`, FastAPI + static page) |
| `server/agents/` | Director (situations/worlds) and Narrator (prose), with mock fallback |
| `scripts/` | research experiments (multi-seed gates, world checks) |

## Honesty rules

- No grades shown to the player: no solved/partial/nothing/worse labels, no expectation numbers.
- The parent acts once per scene: say, show, or leave. No praise, no corrections.
- Only the engine's rules table says what each action does. Training code never reads it (AST test).
- The child sees tags plus one action (verb + target attributes) — never kinds, values, outcomes, or narration.

## Real models

1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and fill in `MUSE_API_KEY` and `MUSE_BASE_URL`.
2. `GROWING_LLM=live uv run python scripts/llm_check.py` — one Director + one Narrator request.
3. `GROWING_LLM=replay ...` replays a recorded run offline and identically.

Models, cache path, and budgets: `config/llm.yaml`.

## Research

Background and experiment log: [docs/WORLD.md](docs/WORLD.md). Three entry points:

```bash
uv run python scripts/exp_gate.py --seeds 200-239 --days 10 --grid "pd8|per_day=8"
uv run python scripts/exp_worlds.py --worlds 0-19 --out scripts/out/worlds.json
uv run python scripts/exp_llm.py --client live --max-calls 200
```

# Community Connect

A Meta hackathon prototype for **human-answered WhatsApp support calls and AI-assisted, human-reviewed case drafts**. The interface uses green and purple accents, light backgrounds and white panels.

## One page, from conversation to reviewed case

The Calling gateway serves the complete workflow at `/agent`:

1. **Call desk:** connect with the separate agent token, choose Ready, then answer, reject or hang up an incoming WhatsApp call.
2. **Manual notes:** type during the conversation. These remain independent of the transcript.
3. **Post-call transcript:** optionally capture an agreed test conversation and send its audio to Meta after the call. Inspect and correct the transcript separately; the original machine transcript remains available for comparison.
4. **Merge and create draft:** send the current notes and/or corrected transcript to Meta. Review four editable sections: enquiry, relevant details, uncertainties and conflicts, and suggested next steps.
5. **Approve and export:** explicitly confirm human review, then download **PDF, DOCX, TXT or PPTX**. All formats use the same reviewed case; exporting makes no further model request. Source appendices are optional.

Use fictional identities and support scenarios for this prototype. The AI is instructed to flag conflicting accounts, distinguish reported information from confirmed facts, and preserve uncertainty. It cannot establish which source is correct. The human resolves or retains uncertainties before approving. Creating a draft never sends messages, places calls, updates external cases or performs suggested actions.

The working Call desk remains available if the Model API is unconfigured or unavailable. There is no automatic voice agent or outbound calling feature.

# Trucker Copilot

WhatsApp AI co-pilot for US truck drivers whose English is weak. It reads the rate con, tracks detention at the dock, writes to the broker in English, and explains the broker's answer in the driver's language. Built on Muse Spark and Muse Voice Transcribe (Meta Model API) and the WhatsApp Cloud API.

**Before vs. this hackathon.** Before: I had Truck Driver Helper, my profit-calculator app for US truckers (iOS/Android). It is not in this repo and not part of the submission. Built during the hackathon (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026), from zero: everything in this repo.

## Try it live on WhatsApp

**[Open the bot: wa.me/18329253256](https://wa.me/18329253256?text=Hi)** (or message **+1 832 925 3256** on WhatsApp)

1. Send `Hi` and pick a language.
2. Send a photo or PDF of a rate con (sample: [`test/fixtures/ratecon-sample.pdf`](test/fixtures/ratecon-sample.pdf)) and tap **Ask for changes**.
3. Share your location ("I'm at the facility"), then share it again later ("I left") to get detention in dollars, and tap **Email broker**.
4. Paste a broker reply, for example `Hi, we can pay $100 detention, please send the signed BOL with in/out times.` and tap **Accept $100**.

You can also send a voice note in any language, like "I arrived at the facility". Demo video: https://youtu.be/I-_qmbcroR0

Unpaid detention costs US drivers $1.1–1.3B a year (DOT OIG, 2018). Immigrant drivers lose more: they sign rate cons they can't fully read, and they don't argue with brokers by email.

## What the driver does

1. **Sends a photo or PDF of the rate con.** Muse Spark extracts the terms into a strict JSON schema, with the exact quote and page for every clause. Code (not the model) decides what is risky: no guaranteed detention pay, late fees, lumper paid by the driver, no TONU, rate per mile. The driver gets the verdict in their language, with buttons to ask the broker for changes or to book.
2. **Shares location at the facility.** The bot logs arrival in the facility's time zone, says when free time ends, and pings the driver when it does, with a button to warn the broker. Sharing location again logs departure and computes detention per minute.
3. **Taps "Email broker".** Code computes minutes and dollars per stop. Muse Spark writes a short, firm English letter around those facts and retells it in the driver's language. The driver copies it into their email.
4. **Pastes or screenshots the broker's answer.** Muse Spark explains it in the driver's language: how much is offered, what documents are asked for. The driver accepts, asks for the full amount (Muse writes the counter), or answers in their own words. Accepted money is counted under "Money recovered".

# Agape

Agape is a small, offline method for building software in rounds with
several independent builders, where every step can be checked by hash
instead of by opinion.

It has three parts:

    Base      a hash-pinned shared core. A mod is known only by an id and
              the sha256 of its raw MANIFEST.json bytes. Every enable,
              disable and load-order change returns a receipt.
    Manager   a receipted mod manager on top of Base: install (after the
              package verifies against its external pin), enable, disable.
    Rounds    a round opens from a named point (a manifest whose sha256 is
              known), takes package submissions, judges them with fixed
              law predicates, and closes into a new named point that names
              the one it supersedes. The chain of points walks back to a
              genesis point.

Judging is deterministic code. There are no AI grading scores: a law is a
predicate over the package bytes (named point hash, no secrets in the mod,
no network capability, black and white output), plus package verification,
a conformance check and the Sorter's load order. A result is PASS or FAIL
with the evidence written next to it.

Python 3 standard library only. No network, no paid services, no
dependencies.

## Layout

    base/          Base v1 core (base.py), interface, tests
    manager/       Manager v1 (manager.py), notes, tests
    mod/ROUND0/    agape.mod.v0 format (MOD-FORMAT.md), package.py
                   verifier, and the hello-bw example package with its
                   external pin (packages/hello-bw.MANIFEST.sha256)
    sorter/        load order and conflict check over requires/conflicts
    laws/          law predicates v1 (laws.py) and v2 (laws_v2.py, adds the
                   named-point chain walk), scorers, tests
    conformance/   tree manifest and conformance checker used by rounds
    round/         round tool (open, submit, judge, close, verify, chain,
                   pack), test, demo-bw and bad-net-key fixtures
    memory-retro/  an agape.mod.v0 package: a deterministic scorer for
                   memory continuity and context usage, run here only on
                   synthetic fixtures
    hub/muse-hub/  the witness hub: round runner, chainer, status
    xchain/        the chain: v0 runner, v1 runtime with baseline +
                   crosscheck, payload helpers, tests
    gadgets/       per-gadget code: roach/ (satellite checker, verify
                   library, tamper evidence), hazels-tv/ (link watchdog)
    docs/          ATOM-BASELINE.md (method) and reports/ (dated build
                   receipts for xchain, musehub, the witness hub)
    demo.py        end-to-end demo
    run_tests.py   runs every test and the demo

    python3 -B demo.py
    python3 -B run_tests.py

# Reelay

Move a creator's short-form video archive between platforms. Cross-posting is a packaging problem, not a scheduling problem: Reelay's job is to know whether a piece of content is actually ready to leave the building.

Reelay imports every video from a TikTok, Instagram or YouTube profile you own or manage (watermark-free, full audio), and turns each one into a **content ticket**. A ticket is a card on a Kanban board holding:
- ready-to-paste copy for every platform;
- a transcript, cover, topic and keywords;
- where the video came from;
- a readiness checklist;
- a change history;
- one record of everywhere it has been posted.

You paste the copy into each platform yourself. YouTube can also be uploaded and scheduled automatically, and Bluesky, Threads and Facebook can be turned on later (see [Automatic posting](#automatic-posting)).

It's a native desktop app for macOS (Windows builds included) in a Light, Dark, Black or Custom theme (each profile's own brand colours, with its logo in the sidebar). The Library and Board are media-first grids of thumbnails (hover a card to scrub through the video), and selecting a video plays it in the right-hand panel above its captions and readiness. Hover over anything for a plain-language tip (turn them off in **Settings → Show helpful tips**), and **Help** at the bottom of the sidebar has the full guide, offline.

# SecondSight — Hazard-Awareness and Rider-Safety HUD

SecondSight is a rider-safety HUD for Ray-Ban Display glasses, built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon (Startup Track, theme: Build for Your World). The glasses see the road ahead, detect hazards — obstacles, pedestrians, road signs, vehicles — and warn the rider audio-first, with a distinct sound per hazard class, so the rider's eyes stay on the road and they never have to look at a phone while moving. A minimal, glanceable HUD shows the camera view, any hazard banner, and a small set of factual readouts. The phone holds all controls; the glasses show the view and the HUD only. Detection is advisory only — SecondSight is an awareness aid, never a safety guarantee.

## What is in this repository

**Boundary Measurement** is the independent measurement of whether an AI agent's *enforced* limits match its *stated* limits. Think of it as a **building inspector** for agent policies: the inspector doesn't declare the building safe or unsafe — she checks the building against the code its owner filed, item by item, and writes down what matches and what doesn't. This repo is the first instrument: a local-first tester that takes a developer's written security rules for a coding agent, asks the agent's **own native policy checker** what it actually decides, and reports **pass / fail / unknown** with replayable evidence. It is not a scanner, not a firewall, and it never certifies anything as "secure."

Harnesses change under their owners — a new release, a new feature, a new flag can move a decision the last version got right — so the suite **re-runs on every harness version upgrade and feature change**, and the version-over-version regression diff is the product's heartbeat: **measure → re-measure → fix → re-verify**.

**Status:** the method stands — verdict **NARROW**. FinePrint measures two vendor-confirmed Decision-layer routes (Codex + Amp) today, with its limitations stated on its face; it is not yet a multi-harness Index. # Zydah

Evidential belief fusion for agent evaluation. Replace single LLM-as-judge /
majority vote with a judge panel whose masses are fused by deterministic
belief-fusion rules. The core library implements Dempster's rule, Shafer
reliability discounting, Yager's rule, and Smets' transferable belief model
(TBM); the live verifier pipeline defaults to Yager's rule. Dempster is a
comparison baseline and TBM is an optional rule, not the default pipeline
path. Conflict between judges is preserved as a signal, not normalized away.

## Building

A Dempster-Shafer+ belief-fusion evaluation agent. System 1 is deterministic
fusion, and System 2 is an LLM reasoner that handles only the high-conflict
or speculative cases. Conflict mass is a routing signal to use, not noise to
normalize away. The demo is closed-world only: it relies on the model's
trained state and the evidence supplied in the prompt. An open-world use of
Smets' TBM would require external evidence access — internet/web fetch or
another live source — which is not part of this demo.

## Why Zydah exists — Zadeh's paradox

Two strongly conflicting sources can break naive fusion. In the classic
medical example, two doctors agree a patient has one of {meningitis,
tumor, concussion} but assign near-opposite certainties; Dempster's rule
normalizes the conflict away and returns near-certainty in the one
hypothesis both doctors rated *least* likely. The failure is not the
evidence — it is treating conflict mass $K$ as noise to divide out.

Zydah takes the opposite position: $K$ and the [Bel, Pl] interval width
are kept visible and used as routing signals. High conflict or a wide
interval escalates to System 2 (or to a human) instead of being
normalized into false confidence; Yager's rule sends $K$ to ignorance
$\Omega$, and Smets' TBM leaves it on the empty set where it can be
detected as frame failure.

Full derivation, from first principles:
[Zadeh's Paradox, Yager, and Smets](<agent/docs/Zadeh's Paradox, Yager, and Smets A Derivation from First Principles.md>).

Dependability is tested with order-invariance checks, seed/flip variance,
and seeded synthetic harness baselines. No always-LLM cost baseline exists
yet.

Frame failure is detectable today: under `rule: tbm`, conflict landing on
the empty set is the alarm, and the local response is to suspend the
decision and escalate. Repairing the frame — supplying the correct
unlisted hypothesis — generally needs new evidence, which this
closed-world demo does not gather.

## Further RL Research

Bellman / temporal-difference (TD) routing is future research, not current
routing. A tabular TD(0)/Monte-Carlo learner has been ported and unit-tested
offline, and verifier trajectories are logged, but learned routing is not
wired. The next evidence step is live panel trajectories with three judge
masses, varying conflict K, episodes of two or more steps, and held-out
labels.

## Looking for

Feedback on reward design for process-level signals, and anyone wor

# ProofStudio

ProofStudio is a macOS app for working on a math proof e2e.

![ProofStudio with a Lean proof beside the generated solution PDF](docs/demo.jpg)

You open a folder. The folder name is the problem name. The app keeps the files for that problem inside the folder and shows whether each one is empty, current, stale, or failed. You choose the next step. The app does not run the whole pipeline for you.

The steps are:

1. Add a screenshot and turn it into `problem.tex`. The app compiles it with `pdflatex`. A TeX error stops this step.

2. Turn that statement into `problem/stub.lean`, a Lake project whose proof is `sorry`. Muse writes two statements. A statement that does not compile is asked again. One that compiles is kept, and the next question adds a second statement. Each file is checked with `lake env lean`.

3. Generate `solution/proof.lean` in a separate Lake project. Both projects share one Mathlib build, and the app lists only the two Lean files. The statements are proved at the same time, and the first proof that compiles is kept. Attempts start at 3 and can be set from 1 to 10. A reply that still contains `sorry` is rejected. Earlier Lean errors stay on this step and go with the next attempt.

4. Write `solution.tex` from the Lean proof and compile `solution.pdf`, up to 3 attempts. The PDF opens beside the proof. Select a passage and right-click Lean component to highlight the matching lines.

A Meta Muse API key is entered in the app and kept in memory until you quit. It is not saved to disk.

## Run the app

You need Node.js and npm. PDF generation needs MacTeX, which provides `/Library/TeX/texbin/pdflatex`. The Lean stub needs Lean 4, installed with elan. The first stub also downloads Mathlib for that Lean version. The app still opens without them.

```bash
npm install
npm start
```

`npm start` builds the app and opens it in Electron on this Mac. The window loads those built files. It does not open a browser.

`npm run dev` is for editing. It also opens Electron, and refreshes that window from a local server while files change. macOS calls both of these processes Electron. `npm run app` writes `ProofStudio.app`, which uses the ProofStudio Dock name.

## Generate the app

```bash
npm install
npm run app
open dist/mac-arm64/ProofStudio.app
```

`npm run app` writes `dist/mac-arm64/ProofStudio.app`. The Dock and the menu name are ProofStudio.

`out/` is the compiled JavaScript, not the app. `npm start` and `npm run dev` launch Electron's own shell, so macOS calls that process Electron.

## Generate a DMG

```bash
npm run dmg
open dist/ProofStudio-0.1.0-arm64.dmg
```

`npm run dmg` writes `dist/ProofStudio-0.1.0-arm64.dmg`. The version in the file name comes from `package.json`. Opening the disk image shows `ProofStudio.app`, which you can drag into Applications.

## Changes

Do not commit directly to `main`. Open a pull request for each change.

Measured by `tools/measure.py` over `evals/casos.jsonl`; the raw result is
`evals/2026-10-31.resultado.json`. `make docs-check` fails if this row drifts
from the newest dated run in `evals/`.

| Date | Cases | Accuracy | Scam recall | False alarms on legit | Doubtful | Cost | Median latency | Commit | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-31 | 231 | 93.5% | 98.5% | 2.1% | 6.5% | $0.879 | 3.22 s | `a474a96` | passed, 0 regressions |

In 73 of the 231 cases the deterministic rules were already conclusive, so VIGÍA

the analyst to an unavailable model or a refusal.

`dudosos ≤ 0.25`.

**Reproducibility.** The same 231 cases were measured three times
(`evals/2026-10-31.resultado.json`, `evals/2026-11-02-a.resultado.json`,
`evals/2026-11-02-b.resultado.json`). Two results held in all three: scam recall
98.5%, and no real scam was ever labelled legitimate. The rest moves, because a
Meta model is in the loop — 6 of the 231 verdicts changed on each rerun, false
alarms landed at 0, 2 and 3 of the 95 legitimate messages, and accuracy between
92.6% and 93.5%. The row above is the run of 2026-10-31; rerunning `make evals`
